passages.text: The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, was the largest state the world had seen, reaching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus. Its kings ruled dozens of peoples through satraps, roads and a common administrative language, and mostly let them keep their gods and laws.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Royal Road ran about 2,700 kilometers from Susa to Sardis; Herodotus says a traveler took ninety days and a relay of royal couriers about a week.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Qanats, tunnels that carry groundwater out to the plains, spread across Iran under the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Darius I struck the gold daric and the silver siglos, the first coins used across the whole empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Darius began Persepolis, with its terrace, hundred-columned halls, bull capitals and staircases carved with tribute-bearers from every province.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text from Babylon, records Cyrus restoring temples and sending deported peoples home; the modern description of it as a charter of human rights is disputed by historians.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The kings invoked Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions; how far the court followed Zoroaster's teaching is debated.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Cyrus let the Judean exiles in Babylon return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, as the Hebrew Bible records.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Some twenty satrapies paid tribute in silver and kind, each under a governor watched by the king's inspectors.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads, coinage and a long peace tied the Mediterranean to Central Asia and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial Aramaic served as the language of administration from Egypt to Bactria.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Later Iranian dynasties, the Sasanians above all, looked back to the Achaemenids.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Alexander and the Seleucids kept the satrapies and much of the administration.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Persepolis was listed by UNESCO.
Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis in 330. Darius was killed by his own satrap the same year, and Alexander took the empire as its heir.

sectionTitles: Craft and exchange in the historical record

passages.text: The Achagua are an Indigenous people of Colombia’s Orinoco region, with continuing communities at Umapo and El Turpial. Their history connects riverine exchange, cassava cultivation, household cooperation and an Arawakan language maintained through everyday use and teaching.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Quiripa beads were made by shaping freshwater shells into small discs, perforating them and stringing them together. Achagua craftspeople were among several peoples producing them. The process turned local material into a portable means of payment and a visible marker of prestige.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Quiripa circulated beyond the plains into the Andes and Guiana. The historical synthesis warns that a uniform exchange value for a string has not been established. Calling it currency should therefore not imply one centrally regulated coinage or an unchanging price across the region.

passages.title: Craft and exchange in the historical record
passages.text: Trade also intersected with violence: accounts describe Achagua captives being exchanged for quiripa. Beads demonstrate neither peaceful commerce alone nor an isolated economy. Their history includes both skilled manufacture and the exploitation of people within expanding exchange networks.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: Bitter cassava is a major crop. Achagua households process it into casabe flatbread and toasted fariña, alongside growing maize. Fishing becomes particularly important in the dry season. Food production combines cultivation, processing skill and attention to changing river conditions.

passages.title: Food and household work
passages.text: ONIC describes households organised around an older couple, their younger children and married daughters’ families. Sons-in-law may build separate homes as the group grows. Residence, food production and consumption are connected through this family organisation rather than being isolated household choices.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: Children learn Achagua with parents, grandparents and other relatives while farming, fishing and making crafts. The Ministry of Culture’s study treats these activities as settings for education. Practical knowledge and language are transmitted together, rather than only through formal classroom lessons.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: The study describes leaders coordinating community activities in Achagua. When outside meetings use Spanish or Piapoco, interpretation helps elders participate. Multilingual communication is therefore an institutional skill, while the continued use of Achagua supports involvement by people who do not readily use those other languages.

passages.title: Language, learning and participation
passages.text: Indigenous teachers use Achagua at school alongside other language learning. Grammars, a bilingual dictionary and reading materials provide written resources, although the study identifies shortages. Maintaining a language involves new educational work as well as the continuity of speech at home.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Research at Umapo gathered accounts from knowledge holders and worked with families and Yaaliakeisy students. Its interviews and workshops provide direct evidence of how participants remembered and taught traditions. The small local study cannot measure the knowledge of every Achagua community.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Knowledge holders recounted Chumachumarri, a tree associated with the origin of foods, and described other narratives linking people and nature. The researchers recorded these as community traditions. They are evidence of ways of explaining the world, not independently dated accounts of prehistoric events.

passages.title: Recording and renewing community knowledge
passages.text: Students used modelling clay and posters to explore identity. Community participants also helped shape a learning room for sharing narratives at Yaaliakeisy. The project created a concrete educational space, while acknowledging disagreements and uneven interest in transmitting older traditions.

Achagua history continues through living communities, language and educational work. Changes in belief and livelihood do not amount to the disappearance of the people. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint records the end of a snapshot interval, not an Achagua extinction or conquest.

sectionTitles: Historical records and the return of ancestors

passages.text: The Aché are Indigenous communities of eastern Paraguay whose histories include forest hunting and gathering, violent dispossession, settlement and continuing cultural work. Research on Northern Aché families documents practical knowledge, cooperation and changing livelihoods; it should not be treated as a description of every Aché community.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: A child’s bow from Arroyo Bandera, now in the Museo de América, was made before 1997. Its slightly curved wooden body carries a twisted plant-fibre string secured around both ends. The object preserves the combination of carving, cord-making and binding needed to produce working equipment.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: The museum names the bow rapa and records separate Aché terms for its wood and cord fibre. Its account also describes using an unstrung bow to reach animals in burrows. Such versatility connects tool design with detailed knowledge of different hunting situations.

passages.title: Tools, materials and skilled manufacture
passages.text: An Aché arrow at the Spencer Museum combines bamboo, wood, plant fibre, resin and feathers tentatively identified as guan. Its maker is unrecorded, and its date spans the late nineteenth century to 1976. The catalogue supports a study of material selection, not an exact manufacturing year or excavated findspot.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: At Chupa Pou in 1981 to 1982, researchers observed maize, manioc, beans, peanuts and other crops. Groups cleared and planted large fields, while some men began smaller plots. Farming arrangements were changing within the settlement itself, rather than representing a timeless Aché agricultural system.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: The same fieldwork describes men and women moving a temporary brush barricade through a lagoon to concentrate fish. Springs supplied domestic water, while rivers and streams served washing and bathing. These observations connect collective fishing skill with the practical organisation of settlement life.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Forest foods in the Northern Aché studies included hunted mammals, honey, palm starch, fruit and larvae. Obtaining a meal required several kinds of work and knowledge. Researchers describe different contributions by men and women, with patterns tied to the studied trips and households rather than universal rules.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Food gathered on forest trips was distributed widely between families, particularly meat and honey. The authors compared those trips with life at Arroyo Bandera in 1998, where food was more often directed toward families who shared similar foods back. Cooperation changed with residence and production.

passages.title: Food, work and cooperation
passages.text: Settlement livelihoods also included paid work and occasional sales of palm-woven fans, mats, bows and arrows. Purchased foods and tools entered household economies alongside farming and forest resources. Cultural continuity could include participating in new markets, rather than preserving one fixed way of obtaining everything.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: Paraguay’s Indigenous-community census history describes captures and a massacre between 1959 and 1972, followed by international denunciations in 1974. The violent breakup of forest communities cannot be described simply as voluntary modernisation. The record identifies assaults on people, not the end of Aché existence.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: Archival research reconstructed the fate of an Aché girl called Damiana, abducted in 1897 and taken to Argentina. After her death, remains entered scientific collections associated with racial investigation. Letters and publications helped identify material later located in Berlin, exposing violence within the history of collecting.

passages.title: Historical records and the return of ancestors
passages.text: La Plata returned remains to the Aché community in 2010; Berlin returned further identified remains in 2012. The researchers explicitly recognised the community’s wish for burial. These events changed the relationship between institutions and the people whose ancestors they had held.

passages.title: Language and community authorship
passages.text: In August 2025, teachers and representatives from six Aché communities met at Cerro Morotĩ to review and correct a dictionary draft. Community members and LETRA Paraguay had developed the material together. This was active editorial and linguistic work, not merely outsiders recording passive informants.

passages.title: Language and community authorship
passages.text: The national language secretariat’s digital vocabulary page credits members of the Aché people as authors and LETRA Paraguay as compiler. Online and mobile resources extend language work into new media. Their availability documents a continuing language project without establishing how widely each resource is used.

Aché communities survived campaigns of capture and violence and continue to maintain language and collective institutions. Dispossession transformed residence and livelihoods, but it did not produce a historical extinction date. The imported map ends at 1500 because its snapshot interval ends there, not because Aché history stopped.

passages.text: The Maya Achi are living communities of Guatemala’s Baja Verapaz region. Rabinal is an important centre of their cultural life, where textile work and community teaching remain active. The history of the people is broader than any single archaeological town, dramatic character or political regime.

passages.title: Discovering settlements and working landscapes
passages.text: Surveyors mapped Saq’ijel, a Postclassic town only somewhat smaller than Cahyup, in the hills above Rabinal. Residential areas and ceremonial centres occupied a landscape with several substantial communities. This evidence challenges a picture in which all local life revolved around one isolated capital.

passages.title: Discovering settlements and working landscapes
passages.text: The researchers placed fields on the basin floor and settlements on higher slopes. They proposed irrigation from upland springs, but had not systematically surveyed the lowlands. Their reconstruction links land, water and settlement while preserving the difference between mapped remains and a plausible farming model.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: In Álvarez’s Rabinal field study, potters prepared clay brought from nearby hills and built vessel walls with coils, using a broken pot as a support. Larger vessels were worked by moving around them. Smaller ones could be rotated on the maker’s knees, showing how technique adapted to scale.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: Potters shaped and smoothed bases, added necks, and applied red clay mixed with water before firing. Finished pots and pitchers were sold by their makers in the plaza. These observations connect household technology with market livelihoods; they do not establish an unchanged method stretching back to prehistory.

passages.title: Making pottery and supplying households
passages.text: The study also records censers, candlesticks and small figures representing occupations such as carrying, milling and selling. Some objects served ceremonies while others depicted daily work. Families participated in production, and goods travelled to markets beyond Rabinal as well as being sold locally.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: An unfinished Rabinal huipil in the British Museum combines a dark cotton ground, narrow coloured warp stripes and brocaded zigzags and triangles. The decoration required complex weaving even where the design appears simple. The catalogue dates the cloth only to before 1973.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: The same garment uses a single wide panel. Brocading was omitted where its future owner would cut the neck opening, so the unfinished cloth preserves a decision made for later assembly and wear. This is a collected textile from Rabinal, not a fabric recovered from an ancient building.

passages.title: Textile design and teaching
passages.text: A Rabinal workshop in late 2025 brought children, young people and adults together with cultural practitioners from Pacux. Participants used winding and warping tools and counting techniques to make huipils and other textiles. An exhibition displayed the results, documenting a specific effort to pass skills between generations.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Rabinal Achí combines spoken narrative, masked dance and music. UNESCO traces its development to the fifteenth century. Its conflict between Rabinal Achí and K’iche’ Achí stages political authority and obligations, while its performance preserves an artistic tradition rather than proving every narrated incident occurred exactly as shown.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Since colonial times, performances have formed part of the January feast of Saint Paul. Cofradías, local religious brotherhoods, coordinate the festival. Sustaining the drama therefore requires institutions, preparation and community responsibilities as well as the knowledge of individual performers.

passages.title: Theatre, music and collective memory
passages.text: Masks represent ancestral beings, linking participants with the dead and with future generations. UNESCO also identifies poverty and the reduction of the drama to spectacle as threats. Preserving the performance involves its meanings and relationships, not only keeping costumes or repeating dance movements.

passages.title: Survival and community institutions
passages.text: The Rabinal memory museum grew from local organising and a temporary exhibition in 1999. Its founders describe remembrance of army and paramilitary violence as central to its purpose. Exhibitions and educational activities aim to dignify survivors and strengthen younger people’s understanding of their history.

The Maya Achi continue as living communities. Mass violence devastated their lives without erasing the people. Rabinal’s community museum explicitly joins remembrance of loss with cultural renewal. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only the end of imported coverage.

sectionTitles: What the written record can reveal

passages.text: The Achire were Indigenous coastal communities in what is now Sinaloa, Mexico. Accounts place them among the marshes and fisheries of the Pacific coast. Their history concerns mobile households and practical coastal knowledge, rather than a documented empire with a single capital.

passages.title: Plant fibres and coastal technology
passages.text: Ortega’s account describes Guasave and Achire people weaving straw and tule into baskets. Plant fibres became containers through skilled handling of local materials. The description is documentary evidence of a craft, not the identification of a basket excavated from a securely dated Achire site.

passages.title: Plant fibres and coastal technology
passages.text: The same account records small woven rafts used near the shore. Their scale and coastal use matter: this supports knowledge of local navigation, but does not establish ocean crossings or a fleet of large boats. Rafts and baskets represent distinct applications of plant-fibre technology.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: Historical descriptions place related people together in mobile groups and describe fishing, shellfish gathering, hunting and wild fruits as central to subsistence. Their movements connected several food sources across the marshes; mobility should not be mistaken for the absence of social organisation.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: Baena Reina’s reading of Mota y Escobar records fish and shellfish exchanged with settled neighbours for maize and beans. These exchanges linked coastal harvesting with farming communities. Access to cultivated foods therefore does not, by itself, prove that the Achire grew those crops.

passages.title: Food, movement and exchange
passages.text: The same study places Achire movements between the Guayabal area and the coast near the Mocorito River. Travelling with portable possessions suited this way of using the shoreline. The route is a description of movement, not a surveyed boundary of an exclusive territorial state.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: The municipal history identifies an Achire settlement in a report dated 1605, more than a century after the map’s imported endpoint. It supplies a concrete locality and date for examining colonial encounters, while leaving the settlement’s size and internal layout unspecified.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: The bishop’s language, reproduced in the later scholarship, disparaged the communities he described. His observations about trade and movement can be examined without adopting that ranking of peoples. The account conveys a colonial observer’s perspective; it is not an Achire account of their own lives.

passages.title: What the written record can reveal
passages.text: Villalobos Fernández distinguishes a short discussion of Guasave and Achire communities from a much wider survey of fishing implements. Illustrations from central Mexican manuscripts and descriptions of other fisheries do not automatically identify Achire equipment. The wider comparisons must remain separate from specifically attributed practices.

The sources checked here do not establish a dated end to Achire communities or a verified present-day successor identity. Their later history needs further documentary tracing. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint cannot represent their disappearance: the municipal history explicitly records Achire inhabitants in 1605.

passages.text: Acho Dene Koe is a living Dene First Nation centred at Fort Liard. Its traditional territory and waters extend across the Northwest Territories, British Columbia and Yukon, with relationships to François Lake as well. Modern jurisdictional boundaries do not encompass the whole of this homeland.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: The Liard River serves different forms of travel across the year. Community knowledge describes canoes and other boats on open water, and dog teams on the frozen river. The same corridor connects fishing places, camps and neighbouring communities as its surface changes with the season.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: Fish are eaten fresh, smoked or dried, and some catches feed working dogs. The seasonal account describes autumn storage in raised caches and winter net fishing through ice. Two survey participants also described distributing surplus fish to Elders, linking harvesting with responsibilities to other people.

passages.title: Water, food and seasonal knowledge
passages.text: The Nation’s 2021 study collected knowledge from five members through a survey adapted to pandemic restrictions. It recorded fishing practices and observations of environmental change to support future monitoring. These findings preserve named community knowledge without claiming to exhaust the Nation’s experience or establish every cause of change.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Fort Liard’s craft account describes selecting young, light-coloured spruce roots that bend without breaking easily. Long, straight roots reduce the number of joins needed in stitching. Their usefulness depends on choosing and preparing the material, not simply finding any root in the forest.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Makers split and peel the roots, soften them, and use flexible outer pieces for stitching. Prepared roots can be dried and moistened again when needed. This sequence turns a woodland material into a sewing element that can be stored and fitted to later work.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: Birchbark basket making begins with a cut pattern and a prepared surface. Floral designs are laid out before damp quills are inserted through small awl holes. Decoration therefore forms part of a planned construction sequence, rather than an addition that can be placed anywhere without regard to the basket’s shape.

passages.title: Making strong, decorated baskets
passages.text: An inner bark lining, a sewn bottom and a split willow rim help form the container. A matching lid can be joined with moosehide strips. The published method includes sandpaper, a planer and clothespins, showing a living craft that combines inherited knowledge with available tools.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The Fort Liard craft enterprise, founded in 1976, sells work made by producers in the community. Its range includes birchbark baskets, moccasins, mittens and mukluks. The business connects household skill with income and visitors, while its products combine older techniques with modern materials.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The surviving Fort Liard treaty adhesion names Chief Thomas E. Kinla and two headmen alongside Commissioner Thomas William Harris. Dated 17 July 1922, it is a specific documentary trace of the encounter. Its existence does not mean that later disputes about land or the treaty’s meaning were resolved.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The Nation’s wellness plan describes the lasting effects of infectious disease and residential or boarding schools. It also records continued harvesting and community action. These accounts place cultural survival alongside serious colonial losses, rather than presenting either disruption or continuity as the whole story.

passages.title: Work, institutions and historical change
passages.text: The 2024 plan proposes bringing Elders and young people together for sewing, hide tanning, tool making and community history. It also supports stories, language and land-based learning. These are stated priorities for passing knowledge on; the plan alone does not show that every proposed activity has already happened.

Acho Dene Koe continues as a First Nation with a living homeland and community institutions. Treaty and land negotiations concern rights and government, not the disappearance of the people. The map’s 1500 endpoint is imported coverage, not a historical fall date.

passages.text: The Achuar are Indigenous peoples of Amazonian Ecuador and Peru, related through language and exchange to other Jivaroan-speaking peoples. Their cultural knowledge is continually developed through household work, teaching and encounters with neighbours. Sharing knowledge does not make these distinct peoples interchangeable.

passages.title: Pottery and a named instrument
passages.text: Achuar women make mokawas, vessels used to serve chicha in ritual settings. The University of Seville’s collaborative project describes polished surfaces and geometric decoration as part of a visual language connecting people, land and spiritual relationships. These are living practices documented with potters, not designs assigned from an anonymous archaeological fragment.

passages.title: Pottery and a named instrument
passages.text: The project worked with the communities of Pumpuentsa, Patukmai and Kurintza and with Indigenous collaborators including Isabel Wisum, Carmela Akintua and Delia Sanchik. Its 2026 exhibition presented pottery as continuing creative work. Naming the participants helps preserve authorship that broad labels such as Amazonian art can conceal.

passages.title: Pottery and a named instrument
passages.text: A two-headed anaconda gong in the Spurlock Museum is attributed to Severo Vargas at Nuevo Mundo, Ecuador, in 1973. The catalogue identifies carved wood and an Achuar cultural affiliation. It is evidence of a named maker’s work, with a recorded place and year, rather than a prehistoric discovery.

passages.title: Pottery and a named instrument
passages.text: The gong entered the collection as a gift from Norman and Dorothea Whitten. Its catalogue supplies material and manufacturing information but no detailed account of its performance. The object can document wood carving and musical culture without inventing the sound, occasion or meaning of a particular ceremony.

passages.title: Gardens, houses and practical knowledge
passages.text: Peru’s ethnographic summary describes women managing gardens, planting, weeding and harvesting, while men commonly help clear the ground. Gardens supply cassava, plantains and other foods. Household layouts vary between dispersed dwellings and more closely grouped communities.

passages.title: Gardens, houses and practical knowledge
passages.text: A 2024 documentation project follows Jea house construction in Mashientz, Sharamentza and Pumpuentsa. It describes gathering palm wood and thatch, and its photographs identify builder Humberto Antuash weaving a roof with palm leaves. This is direct documentation of contemporary building skill, not an estimate of an ancient house’s age.

passages.title: Gardens, houses and practical knowledge
passages.text: The Jea project studies how household spaces organise activities and relationships, as well as the frame and roof. Planned interviews, drawings and voice journals aim to record builders’ explanations alongside physical construction. Recording the structure alone would leave much of the knowledge of using and maintaining a home undocumented.

passages.title: Learning, exchange and community decisions
passages.text: Giovannini’s Achuar plant study began in 2011 to inform a manual for local Indigenous health workers. Ginger, originally from Asia, was among the frequently used plants. Its presence shows that community plant knowledge can incorporate introduced species; a record of medicinal use is not itself a clinical test.

passages.title: Learning, exchange and community decisions
passages.text: Comparison with other Amazonian studies found many shared plant uses. Giovannini interprets this as evidence of knowledge exchange and adaptation to changing needs, rather than separate invention of every remedy. The interpretation concerns the studied knowledge and does not make all communities’ medical traditions identical.

passages.title: Learning, exchange and community decisions
passages.text: In Sharamentsa, a June 2024 planning collaboration used pre-dawn guayusada discussions to decide educational priorities. Elders and participants connected teaching with Achuar language, practical skills and forest life. The research describes one community’s decision process, not a universal rule for every Achuar gathering.

passages.title: Learning, exchange and community decisions
passages.text: Forest walks combined routes and ecological observations with stories and knowledge of important places. Participants used these materials to develop plans and models for an educational campus and an office building. These were collaborative proposals; the study does not establish that the proposed buildings had been completed.

Achuar communities and their language continue in Ecuador and Peru. Missionary incursions, commercial pressures, war and oil development altered community life without constituting a single fall or extinction. The map’s 1500 endpoint is a coverage limit.

passages.text: Achumawi names related communities of the Pit River region in northeastern California. It is also associated more narrowly with the Ajumawi band around Fall River. Local communities historically governed themselves and maintained relationships through language and marriage; the regional label should not erase their differences.

passages.title: Stone structures and managed fisheries
passages.text: At Ahjumawi Lava Springs, rock walls around cold-water springs direct Sacramento sucker fish into enclosures. Openings can be closed during the catch and reopened afterwards. Crystal Spring preserves a particularly elaborate arrangement of channels and chambers, linking the design to fish behaviour and flowing water.

passages.title: Stone structures and managed fisheries
passages.text: Inner walls expose gravel to spring water, where suckers deposit eggs. Foster interprets this layout, regular clearing and Indigenous explanations of maintenance as fishery management as well as capture. The interpretation rests on several kinds of evidence; the walls alone would not reveal all the builders’ intentions.

passages.title: Stone structures and managed fisheries
passages.text: Foster observed Floyd Buckskin’s fishing at Ja-She Creek. The account describes an Elder directing the catch and reopening the trap after sufficient fish were taken. Fish were dried or smoked, shared with relatives and sometimes exchanged for venison or acorns, carrying the harvest into later meals.

passages.title: Tools for working in water
passages.text: Tule blinders collected in 1902 protected fishers’ eyes from glare during night spearing. Barter describes a braided headband and woven panels, but notes their unworn condition: they may have been made for Hudson’s collection. They preserve manufacturing knowledge without proving that this particular pair was used.

passages.title: Tools for working in water
passages.text: A surviving fishing net uses fine, twisted Apocynum plant-fibre cord. Two differently coloured closing cords may have helped orient it in moving water. Barter distinguishes that proposed use from the net’s observable construction and also notes discrepancies between older equipment labels.

passages.title: Tools for working in water
passages.text: The collected fishhooks combine a bone barb, a wooden shank and fine binding, with each hook attached to its own line. Barter could inspect the parts but could not establish exactly how the stored set was arranged for fishing. The surviving object leaves that practical detail unresolved.

passages.title: Basketry, food and changing landscapes
passages.text: UC Davis holds an Achumawi seed beater, catalogued as CHM 22, in Merriam’s basketry collection. The implement broadens the material record beyond fishing to gathering plant foods. The collection includes used household objects and notes about their uses; its general collecting dates do not precisely date this particular piece.

passages.title: Basketry, food and changing landscapes
passages.text: The regional account describes partly underground winter homes and lighter summer shelters of brush or tule matting. Fish, waterfowl, acorns and other seasonal foods supported settlements near streams and wetlands. Household life depended on several linked habitats, rather than fishing alone.

passages.title: Basketry, food and changing landscapes
passages.text: Much of the Fall River homeland passed into power-company and ranch ownership. California State Parks acquired the present park land in 1975. Protecting a park landscape is therefore one recent chapter in a much longer Indigenous history, not the beginning of its cultural importance.

passages.title: Community continuity and stewardship
passages.text: In 1986 and 1987, the Pit River Tribal Council and California State Parks collaborated to protect the fish traps. The structures remained connected to people with practical knowledge and responsibilities, rather than being only abandoned features for outside researchers to interpret.

passages.title: Community continuity and stewardship
passages.text: The Tribe’s constitution identifies autonomous bands within a common political body and makes protection of land, resources, culture and descendants explicit purposes. Its 1964 adoption records a modern institution exercising community responsibilities; it is not a claim that Pit River peoples first existed in that year.

Achumawi communities continue within the wider Pit River Tribe. Colonial dispossession did not erase their identity, and the Tribe maintains institutions for land, culture and community welfare. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint is not an extinction or conquest date.

sectionTitles: Objects and evidence of everyday work

passages.text: Acjachemen communities belong to the landscape around San Juan Capistrano and surrounding parts of southern California. Juaneño is a mission-derived name. Their history connects independent villages, coastal and inland resources, colonial dispossession and continuing cultural life.

passages.title: Objects and evidence of everyday work
passages.text: An Acjachemen basket from San Juan Capistrano, now Autry object 811.G.770, combines juncus wrapping with a bundled deergrass foundation. Black-dyed juncus supplies the design; sumac forms the starting coils. Bound ends and a tapered rim show the maker’s attention to a secure finish. The museum acquired it in 1937, but the record does not date its manufacture.

passages.title: Objects and evidence of everyday work
passages.text: The mission museum identifies a grinding stone used to process acorns. It connects an everyday food to the work of breaking it down for preparation. The public description does not supply an excavation layer or manufacture date, so the stone cannot by itself establish when that practice began.

passages.title: Objects and evidence of everyday work
passages.text: At Puhú in Black Star Canyon, animal remains studied by Tomczyk and Acebo indicate continued hunting of local mountain fauna during the colonial period. Their analysis found little or no contribution from livestock, challenging the story that residents depended on stolen animals before the reported 1832 massacre. Food waste provides evidence distinct from settlers’ accusations.

passages.title: Objects and evidence of everyday work
passages.text: The Puhú researchers suggest that colonial ecological changes may have increased access to some native animals in this mountain setting. That is an interpretation, not proof that colonization benefited Indigenous people generally. Their work involved Tongva, Acjachemen and Payómkawichum collaborators; the village is not presented as exclusively one present-day community’s heritage.

passages.title: Villages, plants and shared responsibilities
passages.text: Permanent villages and seasonal camps formed a connected landscape. The community history describes locally independent clans linked through marriage, exchange and ceremony. Chiefs worked with councils of Elders, making political and ceremonial responsibilities part of community life.

passages.title: Villages, plants and shared responsibilities
passages.text: Culture bearer Heidi Harper Lucero describes growing basketry and food plants at home as urban development reduces gathering places. She also continues gathering juncus in ancestral locations. Her account links a finished basket to the longer work of tending plants and maintaining access to land.

passages.title: Villages, plants and shared responsibilities
passages.text: Lucero describes bringing gifts when she gathers, collecting extra for Elders and giving elderberry jelly to others. Food gathering is therefore connected to obligations and generosity in her account. These are her documented practices as an Acjachemen and Ohlone person, rather than a rule assigned to every household.

passages.title: Villages, plants and shared responsibilities
passages.text: Lucero also explains that permits and changing relationships with land managers can interrupt cultural work. Access renewed only for short periods fits poorly with activities requiring longer care. Her experience shows why preserving a technique involves relationships with places and institutions as well as teaching hand skills.

passages.title: Archives, teaching and cultural achievements
passages.text: In 1996, the language project acquired film and tape materials held by the Smithsonian with foundation support and community donations. Organizers began copying words and phrases into a database. This was painstaking recovery of existing knowledge, not the creation of a new language.

passages.title: Archives, teaching and cultural achievements
passages.text: Sonia Carmen worked through John Peabody Harrington’s field notes, prepared flash cards and shared recordings at language meetings. Archivist Lisa Woodward explains that the resulting collection includes pronunciation guidance and references back to source pages. Those references help learners trace an entry to its historical record.

passages.title: Archives, teaching and cultural achievements
passages.text: Elder Jacque Nunez describes using online language materials to teach grandchildren while living away from the homeland. Rebecca Robles connects language with stories and spiritual traditions. Their accounts show that preservation includes ordinary family use and teaching, alongside museum collections and scholarly study.

Acjachemen people continue to affirm their identity and teach their language and culture. Elder Rebecca Vallejo explicitly rejects the idea that colonization annihilated the people. The imported map’s 1500 endpoint is not a historical end date.

passages.text: Adal was a Muslim sultanate in the Horn of Africa, connected with the Gulf of Aden coast and the Harar plateau. Its principal centres included Dakar and later Harar. Cities and communities continued as political authority changed.

passages.title: An urban achievement
passages.text: Harar’s narrow lanes connect houses with a central concentration of religious and commercial buildings. Five historic gates corresponded to routes into the city and its neighbourhoods.

passages.title: An urban achievement
passages.text: Traditional Harari houses and their decorated interiors remain distinctive. Later Indian merchants introduced verandas, and builders combined the two traditions. Surviving houses therefore preserve several periods, not one Adal-era design.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Excavations at Harar recovered cattle, goat and sheep bones, along with other animals. Cattle were the most frequent domestic species among identified fragments. These deposits span several centuries, so the sample cannot define a single meal or an exclusively Adal-era diet.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Many cattle survived to adulthood, while goats at Harar were less often slaughtered young than those at the earlier town of Harlaa. Researchers interpret this as greater emphasis on maintaining herds. Bone ages reveal choices in animal management, rather than recipes.

passages.title: Food, animals and household work
passages.text: Harlaa’s excavated trade goods and imported marine fish should not simply be transferred to Harar’s story. Harar’s studied assemblages contained no fish bones and few luxury imports. Neighbouring towns had distinct histories and material economies.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Excavations at six mosques tested traditional foundation dates. The recovered radiocarbon evidence ranges from the late fifteenth to early twentieth centuries. It records different episodes of building and use, not six identical foundation dates.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: At Din Agobera, a burial near the prayer niche supplied an early date range, from the late fifteenth to mid-seventeenth century. The excavators infer that the mosque was already present. The burial fill does not directly date its construction.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Later repairs changed Harar’s mosques substantially. At Din Agobera, a lighter corrugated roof replaced the heavy roof formerly supported by pillars. Older-looking buildings may contain materials and layouts from repeated rebuilding.

passages.title: Discovering the city’s religious history
passages.text: Aw Meshad’s teaching residence accommodated pupils studying the Quran, law and Arabic. Excavated drainage and floors belong to its later history, with dates in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They cannot demonstrate an unchanged Adal-era school.

passages.title: Continuing knowledge and craft
passages.text: Harari weaving, basket making and bookbinding remain living crafts. Their continuity is part of the city’s heritage; it does not establish an Adal-era date for every surviving technique.

In the sixteenth century, military reverses, internal struggles and conflict accompanying Oromo movements weakened the sultanate. Its principal seat shifted toward Aussa, followed by separate Aussa and Harar polities. This political fragmentation did not end Harari urban life or the region’s Muslim communities.

sectionTitles: Earthworks and the limits of evidence

passages.text: Adena is an archaeological name for related material and ceremonial traditions in the Ohio River region. It is not the recorded self-name of one tribe or kingdom. Local histories differ, and the label should not erase the people and communities whose work created the surviving objects and earthworks.

passages.title: Carving, clothing and archaeological context
passages.text: Excavated from a Chillicothe burial in 1901, the Adena Pipe depicts a human figure carved in Ohio pipestone. Ear ornaments, a loincloth and a feather bustle make the hollow smoking implement a detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Carving, clothing and archaeological context
passages.text: The figure’s large ear ornaments helped archaeologists interpret similar objects found around other burials. Yet none of the people excavated from this mound had those ornaments. The image can illuminate ways of wearing objects without proving that the person buried with the pipe dressed exactly like its figure.

passages.title: Carving, clothing and archaeological context
passages.text: A surviving textile from the central grave has fine yarns worked in alternate-pair twining. Researchers considered the yarn likely to be plant bast fibre. This small fragment preserves evidence of skilled fibre preparation and weaving, while its identification remains more cautious than naming a particular plant species.

passages.title: Carving, clothing and archaeological context
passages.text: Tree bark preserved from the same grave was identified as black locust. Later radiocarbon work produced different ages for bark and textile. An older garment or shroud kept as an heirloom is one proposed explanation. The results date organic material and require interpretation; they do not give the stone pipe a direct laboratory date.

passages.title: Food, buildings and household skills
passages.text: At Cowan Creek Mound, excavators found charred goosefoot seeds and squash rind on the floor of a circular structure, associated with remnants of a woven container. The squash supported an inference of cultivation. The original botanist regarded the goosefoot seeds as wild, a useful reminder that collected and cultivated foods could occur together.

passages.title: Food, buildings and household skills
passages.text: Paired postmolds beneath Cowan Creek Mound reveal a circular timber structure. Initially called a dwelling, it was later interpreted as a place for mortuary ceremonies before mound construction. The physical post pattern is secure evidence of a building; choosing between household and ceremonial uses requires the wider context.

passages.title: Food, buildings and household skills
passages.text: The National Park Service describes communities living for extended periods near waterways while combining gardening with hunting and gathering. Nuts, berries and seed-bearing plants complemented cultivated foods. This mixed economy required familiarity with seasonal habitats as well as the practical work of growing, collecting and storing food.

passages.title: Food, buildings and household skills
passages.text: Pottery provided containers for gathered plants and other stored food. The same regional account describes increasingly durable and decorated vessels, alongside timber shelters covered with plant material and earth. Making containers and maintaining homes were important technical activities, even though monuments are more conspicuous in the surviving landscape.

passages.title: Earthworks and the limits of evidence
passages.text: Grave Creek Mound in present-day West Virginia grew through successive construction stages, approximately 250 to 150 BCE. Burials at different levels support the sequence. Repeated additions show a monument changing through use; the surviving mound does not represent one afternoon of construction or necessarily one ruler’s commission.

passages.title: Earthworks and the limits of evidence
passages.text: The 1838 investigation of Grave Creek used tunnels and a shaft rather than modern controlled excavation. An inscribed stone reportedly found there has never been authenticated and is disputed by specialists. It cannot securely establish an Adena writing system or contact with a distant civilization.

passages.title: Earthworks and the limits of evidence
passages.text: Greber explains that sites labelled Adena and Hopewell overlap in time. Combining objects from many regions into one checklist can conceal local differences. Studying individual valleys and site sequences gives a better basis for discussing changing ceremonies and craftsmanship than treating these labels as rival kingdoms with clean borders.

Adena and Hopewell categories overlap as local practices change. This is not a documented conquest or fall of a kingdom, and the ending of an archaeological classification is not evidence that its communities vanished.

sectionTitles: Architecture and the work of skilled makers

passages.text: The Aghlabids governed Ifriqiya, centred on Kairouan in present-day Tunisia, while acknowledging the Abbasid caliph. Their court, towns and Mediterranean connections supported distinctive architecture, craftsmanship and learning.

passages.title: Water engineering for daily needs
passages.text: Kairouan’s reservoirs receive runoff and water from tributaries of the Merguellil valley. Water first enters a settling basin, then passes through an outlet into a larger storage basin and covered cisterns. The sequence separates sediment removal from storage and drawing, showing how the builders organized a practical response to unreliable rainfall.

passages.title: Water engineering for daily needs
passages.text: Rubble masonry, thick plaster and buttresses helped the basins retain water and withstand its pressure. The heritage account explains their use for people facing shortages, including poorer residents, as well as caravans and livestock. Public storage supplemented household wells and cisterns rather than replacing every private supply.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The Great Mosque’s pillared prayer hall reuses Roman and Byzantine columns and capitals. New arrangements brought older building materials into an Islamic place of worship. A fluted dome and carved supports emphasize the area before the mihrab, showing that reuse and new design were combined rather than being separate architectural choices.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The mihrab combines carved marble, painted wood and lustre-glazed ceramic tiles. These different surfaces create a layered setting for prayer. The catalogue links the ninth-century tiles with Iraq; the building also contains later restorations, so not every surviving feature should be attributed to Aghlabid builders.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: Raqqada museum’s teak fragment BS 200 came from the Great Mosque’s minbar, the preacher’s pulpit. Its carved vine leaves and grape clusters belonged to the stair’s upper edge. Joining separately carved components produced an elaborate furnishing whose craftsmanship served the weekly act of public preaching.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The fragment is dated through historical accounts and comparison with other ninth-century decoration. Its workshop remains debated: references to Baghdad do not settle where it was carved. Removal during restoration around 1920 explains how this component entered the museum record; it was not excavated from Raqqada’s palaces.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: Bowl C 34, recovered at Raqqada, combines green, brown and yellow glaze with repeated kufic lettering for al-Mulk, or sovereignty. Its surface shows how calligraphy could become part of vessel decoration. The catalogue associates the colours with copper, manganese and antimony or iron compounds, connecting the appearance to material choices.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: The bowl is usually assigned to the late ninth-century Aghlabid repertoire, but its 1960s excavation lacked a detailed record. Similar forms and techniques continued under the Fatimids. Style therefore supports an approximate attribution, while the missing archaeological context prevents a securely dated manufacturing year.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: Gold dinar M 200 carries the date 192 AH, rendered by the museum as 808 CE. Its kufic inscriptions include the dynastic emblem ghalaba within a layout related to Abbasid coinage. Unlike a vessel dated mainly by style, this coin contains direct written evidence for its issue date.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: The museum attributes the dinar to Kairouan and describes Aghlabid gold coinage circulating in Mediterranean commerce. That connects a small object with government and exchange. The catalogue does not provide this specimen’s excavation findspot, so its present museum location cannot reconstruct a particular merchant’s route.

passages.title: Learning, livelihoods and political change
passages.text: Sahnun’s compilation of Maliki teachings in the Mudawwana became a major reference for North African law. Kairouan’s scholarship was an achievement alongside its buildings and objects.

passages.title: Learning, livelihoods and political change
passages.text: Farmers and artisans supplied grain, olive oil and textiles to exchange networks. Those networks also trafficked enslaved people across the Mediterranean and Sahara. Prosperity depended on unequal relationships as well as productive work.

The Fatimids conquered Aghlabid Ifriqiya in 909, ending the dynasty’s rule. Local building practices and infrastructure continued under the new rulers. The map has no Fatimid geometry at 909, so a successor link would give a misleading location for the event.

sectionTitles: Care for country and new enterprises

passages.text: Ewamian people are Traditional Owners around northern Queensland’s Gilbert and Einasleigh rivers. Their history connects river livelihoods, colonial resistance and continuing cultural responsibilities.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: Rivers and lagoons provided food and routes through country. Ewamian accounts describe fish, shellfish, water birds and water plants, with fishing spears, finely woven nets and stone traps. These methods combined knowledge of particular waters with skills in making tools and working fibres.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: At Talaroo Station, Ewamian heritage officers, rangers and an archaeologist recorded scars on Cooktown ironwood trees. Brickey and Buhrich’s 2014 report identifies these as sugarbag scars, made by cutting into heartwood with a stone axe to reach native bees’ honey and wax. The altered living trees preserve evidence of harvesting.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: The same Talaroo survey recorded grinding grooves beside the Einasleigh River, together with fishing places and story places. Their shared landscape links material traces with travel, food and cultural memory. The conference abstract does not date individual grooves or identify everything ground there, so those details remain unspecified.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Agwarmin is the imported map spelling. The State Library lists Agwamin, Wamin and other related names, while noting disagreement over whether they name a people, a language or dialects. Ewamian is the community’s own organizational spelling. A shared label should not erase these distinctions.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Language documentation survives in records associated with Tindale, Sutton and Roth, but the State Library describes the evidence as limited. Its 2020 account also identifies community revival with Pama Language Centre. Archival survival and renewed teaching are separate parts of the language’s history; an old speaker assessment is not a current census.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Ewamian rangers organize language workshops and camps on country with Elders and young people. This work places language learning beside the identification and protection of cultural sites. Knowledge is passed through relationships and activities as well as through written records.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: The community’s history records resistance to miners at Gilberton and later dispossession as more miners and pastoralists arrived. Elders were forced onto missions and reserves. Work as ringers, cooks and domestic workers could keep people on their cultural estate, but did not undo the loss of control over land.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: The 2013 determination recognized continuing native title rights. The community explains these through activities including access, camping, fishing, gathering, teaching and caring for important places. Different rights apply to different land interests; recognition should not be described as unrestricted ownership of every parcel in the region.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: Ewamian People Aboriginal Corporation represents native title holders, but decisions affecting rights require agreement by the holders at community meetings. This is a living institution for collective responsibility. Its role connects land negotiations with the authority of the wider community.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: At Talaroo Hot Springs, ranger work includes removing damaging infrastructure to restore natural water flows and controlling weeds. Elsewhere, prescribed burns protect ecological and cultural places, and surveys guide heritage management. These are specific applications of environmental knowledge, supported by monitoring and collaboration with park managers.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: Talaroo is managed as an Indigenous Protected Area and a nature refuge. The community combines protection of important habitats with compatible uses and economic aspirations. Different management zones permit different activities, allowing conservation responsibilities and community needs to be considered together.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: The CSIRO collaboration assessed natural and cultural resources against Ewamian enterprise aspirations. Its tasks included choosing development pathways, preparing investment prospectuses and producing guidance for other Indigenous groups. The achievement lies in linking technical assessment to community priorities; an assessment alone does not prove that every proposed business was established.

Ewamian people continue to care for country and exercise recognized rights through community institutions. Native title recognition and collective governance document this continuity. The map’s final snapshot in 1815 is not an extinction or conquest date.

sectionTitles: What records preserve and leave out

passages.text: The Ahantchuyuk, also called the Pudding River or French Prairie people, were a Kalapuya community in Oregon’s Willamette Valley. Champoeg connected their food gathering, travel and exchange with neighbouring peoples.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Families moved seasonally between food sources, including camas prairies and acorn-gathering areas. Yampah grew near Champoeg. David Lewis’s reconstruction also describes trade for preserved salmon and lamprey at the falls. Food knowledge included storage and exchange as well as knowing when and where to gather.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Alexander Henry’s January 1814 account describes local hunters wearing a deer’s head and imitating the animal’s movements to approach deer. Lewis places this observation in Ahantchuyuk country. It records skill in reading animal behaviour, but remains a visitor’s account of a particular encounter rather than a complete description of every hunt.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Grand Ronde Elder Greg Archuleta explains that Kalapuya cooks baked camas bulbs, mashed them into cakes and dried them for storage and trade. Prolonged cooking changes the bulbs’ inulin. This account connects food processing with portable provisions; it describes a broader Kalapuya practice rather than an excavated Ahantchuyuk household.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Archuleta’s account also connects plant management with basketry: flexible hazel supplied useful material, while seed fans and baskets helped harvest tarweed. Such technologies depended on selecting suitable plants and maintaining productive gathering places. The account concerns regional traditions and does not establish identical methods in every village.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The Grand Ronde Reservation log book, catalogued as Mss555_F3, includes a March 1856 census naming the French Prairie band. It lists household heads and family sizes alongside other communities. This is concrete evidence of people living after removal, not support for treating the map’s 1500 endpoint as their disappearance.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The same volume records supplies issued to arriving households and property left by earlier settlers. These accounts reveal the administrative organization of reservation life. Their scope is limited: a government distribution ledger cannot by itself describe all household food, possessions, work or continuing cultural practices.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The 1855 treaty text promises payments, clothing, provisions, tools and agricultural support, with a physician, teacher and blacksmith after removal. Reading its clauses shows what the United States undertook to provide. The promises should be distinguished from what families actually received and from their own existing skills.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The treaty also allowed land to be divided into household allotments and tied continued possession to residence and cultivation. These provisions sought to reorganize land use and work under federal supervision. They help explain why removal meant a transformation of institutions as well as a change of location.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: Grand Ronde families remained connected after termination. Tribal leaders organized, raised funds and testified before Congress to restore federal recognition, achieved in 1983. This was the work of the wider confederation, within which Ahantchuyuk history continues. The campaign restored legal recognition of an existing community.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: Yampah has been restored at Champoeg with Tribal input, according to Archuleta’s public account. Restoring an important food plant makes the site more than a monument to settler government. It connects a named place with continuing knowledge about the plants that supported its earlier community.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: The Lifeways program offers cultural classes that recognize the different tribes and bands within Grand Ronde. Reconnecting people with particular homelands and practices is an achievement in teaching and community life. The confederation’s shared institutions do not require every constituent history to be treated as identical.

Removal to Grand Ronde transformed Ahantchuyuk community life. Their history continues within the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde. Federal termination in 1954 ended recognition, not the people; recognition was restored in 1983. No historical disappearance in 1500 is established by the map.

sectionTitles: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity

passages.text: Ahé is the self-name of the Karipuna of Rondônia, a Tupi-Kawahib people associated with Brazil’s Jacy-Paraná and Mutum-Paraná rivers. They are distinct from the Karipuna of Amapá.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: In his 2022 oral-history interview, Adriano Karipuna recalls learning to make arrows and catching fish with them as a child. His mother roasted the catch and kept it in banana or babassu leaves for the next day. The recollection connects skilled fishing, household food preparation and avoiding waste.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: Adriano also remembers a palm-thatched house near the river. He describes the roof’s cool interior alongside its need for regular replacement as insects weakened the material and rain entered. This is a particular household’s experience of building and maintenance, rather than a claim that every Karipuna house was identical.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: Forest loss affects more than the availability of food. In the same interview, Adriano explains that clearing and burning destroyed places supplying material for bows and arrows. He still fished with surviving arrows, while making new ones had become difficult. Environmental damage therefore interrupted the practice of a learned craft.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: In his 2017 account, Adriano describes fishing, cassava flour, Brazil nuts and açaí as sources of subsistence and income. Produce was sold to buyers in town. The combination shows that forest and river livelihoods could support exchange with urban markets while remaining important to life in the village.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: Studying in town brought transport costs, living expenses and racist treatment from classmates, Adriano reports. He described education as a way to gain skills useful to his people. His account makes the journey between village and city part of community history, rather than treating urban residence as the loss of Indigenous identity.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: A 2023 field study at Panorama records garden plots and a flour-processing house, with flour used at home and sold in Porto Velho. These working spaces connect cultivation, processing and income. The report also identifies difficulties transporting and packaging produce for sale.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: The field study records an Indigenous teacher passing the language to children. Community concerns included aligning school activities with the Brazil-nut harvest. This joins classroom learning with seasonal work, rather than assuming that education happens only inside a school building.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Funai reports from the 1970s describe visits between the contact post and large communal houses on the Contra and Mutum-Paraná waterways. ISA’s historical account contrasts official descriptions of successful contact with the illnesses and deaths that followed. Administrative records need to be read alongside their consequences for families.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: The 2023 study combined interviews, field notes and questionnaires with community members and health workers. Its findings are a dated account of conditions and priorities, not a timeless description of Karipuna culture or a current census of everyone belonging to the people.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Greenpeace’s account of its work in 2019 describes combining aerial observations and satellite images with Karipuna reports of invasion. These different forms of evidence made forest clearing visible beyond the territory. They document particular monitoring efforts; a short-term change in clearing does not establish lasting protection.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Karipuna leaders also spoke in international forums and built solidarity with other Indigenous peoples. These public interventions carried community demands beyond Rondônia. Protecting land, communicating its significance and insisting on continued existence are achievements in political organization as well as responses to danger.

The Karipuna continue as a living people. Recent fieldwork documents food production, language teaching and collective demands, despite invasion and barriers to services. Their recognized territory and continuing community life cannot be reduced to the map’s 1492 to 1500 interval.

passages.text: Ahtna communities continue to care for their lands and waters in Alaska. Their history connects skilled fishing and copper working with living Tribal institutions, resource stewardship and the transmission of knowledge.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Excavations at Ringling near Gulkana recovered copper pieces, tools and hearths. The association suggested heating during metalworking; analysis of the metal’s crystal structure subsequently supported annealing. Heating made worked copper easier to shape again, showing a controlled manufacturing technique rather than simply the collection of attractive nuggets.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Ringling’s rolled copper cones have several possible explanations. A Gulkana resident described their use as detachable fishing-spear tips; comparable forms could also serve as rattles or unfinished tool components. The finds reveal skilled sheet-metal work, but their shape alone does not settle every object’s purpose.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Museum knife 2/2661 is attributed to Ahtna people of the Copper River. Its catalogue records hammered metal and hide, but does not identify the metal as copper. George Heye acquired it around 1909 from an unknown source. The acquisition date therefore cannot establish when it was made or an excavated context.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: A 1954 photograph identifies a dip net made by Grandma McKinley for Tenas Charley at Copper Center. Willow and spruce roots formed its frame and mesh. The record preserves a named maker and the practical transformation of plant materials into fishing equipment.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Ben Neeley’s childhood recollections describe summer salmon fishing on the Copper River followed by travel toward Tangle Lakes for large-game hunting. Winter trapping and spring fishing and trapping fitted into a seasonal round. Movement linked different food sources rather than indicating an absence of established homes and knowledge.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Miller’s winter-access study used interviews with experienced Copper River Basin residents, including Ahtna trappers. Most recalled more reliable river ice in earlier decades. Shorter periods of usable ice could reduce access to trapping grounds and other resources. This is a study of particular people’s observations, not a forecast of safe crossing conditions.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Interviewees described variable snow, wetter conditions and thicker brush affecting winter routes. Miller also records changes in employment and transport. These factors worked together: altered trapping patterns cannot be explained by temperature alone, and the experiences of selected residents should not be treated as a census of all Ahtna households.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Dry Creek families were forced out for an army airfield in the winter of 1942 to 1943. At Gulkana, road and bridge works divided the village and disrupted fishing. The ethnographic account uses residents’ recollections to recover losses that official construction histories could overlook.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: The Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission brings together Tribal governments and Native corporation landholders, which are distinct institutions. Its work combines ecological knowledge, research and advocacy for continued access to subsistence resources. Organization across communities makes knowledge useful in collective decisions about fish, wildlife and plants.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: At Tanada Creek, a seasonal weir guides salmon through a camera-equipped passage before they continue upstream. Staff record passage and maintain the structure through the run. Repeated observations help track abundance and timing, making everyday fieldwork part of long-term stewardship and Tribal participation in management.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: The Tanada project also collects ear stones, or otoliths, from sockeye carcasses at Tanada Lake. Their growth layers help researchers estimate fish ages. Combining age information with counts offers a fuller picture of the returning population than either measurement alone. This is a documented research method, not an ancient archaeological find.

Ahtna people and Tribal institutions continue. Contemporary resource stewardship expresses ongoing relationships with the land. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval does not establish an ending or a disappearance.

sectionTitles: Places, records and discoveries about language

passages.text: The Aikanã are a living people of Rondônia, Brazil. Their own name identifies both people and language. Older records use several other names, including Huari, which must not be confused with the distinct Wari people.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Vasconcelos describes an elder making bows and different arrows for particular targets, including animals of different sizes and fish. The account records design choices connected to use. It documents a living craft observed during fieldwork, not an excavated weapon or a securely dated practice in 1492.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: The Aikanã belong to a wider regional network associated with marico bags made from palm-leaf fibres. Transforming leaves into durable carrying equipment required selecting and preparing material as well as skilled construction. Shared technologies link neighbouring peoples without making their languages or identities interchangeable.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Regional food practices combine cultivated gardens, hunting and gathering. Chicha is prepared from cultivated or gathered ingredients through processing, fermentation and straining. The documentation project places these practices in a history of intercommunity contact; the regional pattern should not be read as an identical menu for every Aikanã family.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Craftwork also enters exchange with the surrounding society. Vasconcelos records ear ornaments, bracelets, necklaces, bags, rings and wooden objects being made for sale. Production for a market is part of the documented history of work and adaptation; it does not make the makers less Aikanã.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Cascata preserves pottery remains and rock paintings near an old village and burial area, according to Grund. Aikanã memories identify it as a place of residence and meeting. These traces matter alongside oral history, but the article does not date every object or establish that all were made by one people.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Aikanã and Kwaza are distinct languages with no demonstrated membership in a larger language family. Similar grammatical features can reflect long contact between speakers. Calling a language an isolate describes what has been established about linguistic relationships; it does not mean its speakers lived without neighbours or exchange.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Aikanã speakers can link a sequence of actions while marking whether the person doing the next action changes. Van der Voort illustrates this with recorded speech and discusses exceptions in narrative use. This detailed grammar is part of the community’s intellectual heritage, rather than evidence that one language is more advanced than another.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: The study prints a story told by Raimunda Dadü Kwã’ĩ at Barroso on May 6, 1996, with linguistic analysis and translation. Naming the narrator, place and recording date makes the evidence traceable. The recording date documents one performance of an older story; it does not date the story’s origin.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The DOBES project records everyday activities, personal histories, conversations and environmental knowledge, alongside word lists and grammatical work. Its multimedia record recognizes that a language lives in social use. Cooking, building and knowing plants belong in its documentation as much as isolated dictionary entries.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The 2018 teaching book Nós Kwazá Aikanã was created from cultural-mediator workshops for schools in Kwazá do Rio São Pedro. Named Aikanã and Kwazá authors and illustrators connect community knowledge with climate and territorial education. This is a concrete educational work produced with community participation.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The same book asks pupils to speak with elders, retell histories and explain pictures. Its authors describe a shared Kwazá Aikanã identity while recognizing different languages and family histories. These exercises make younger learners participants in transmission rather than passive recipients of an account written only by outsiders.

The Aikanã continue despite epidemic losses, forced labour and dispossession. Grund’s fieldwork records living narrators preserving the history of places transformed by colonization. The map’s 1500 endpoint is not a historical disappearance or the end of the people.
