sectionTitles: Treasure, craft and careful detective work

passages.text: Avar rulers and their followers established a powerful, diverse realm in the Carpathian Basin after arriving in 567-568. Its history includes settled villages, skilled metalworkers and extensive family networks as well as mounted armies. The map continues the label later than the independent khaganate.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: A study of four fully excavated Hungarian cemeteries reconstructed family trees extending as far as nine generations. Some 300 of the 424 sampled people had identifiable close relatives in the same cemetery: a family album assembled from ancient DNA.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: In those communities, male family lines tended to remain locally rooted while women arrived from other communities. Marriage helped connect settlements. This describes the studied cemeteries, not an inflexible rule for every Avar household.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Researchers found little evidence of unions between close biological relatives. They suggest that remembering ancestry mattered across generations. DNA can reveal biological connections; adoption, affection and other social bonds require different evidence.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Leobersdorf and Modling, two seventh- and eighth-century communities near Vienna, used similar material culture but had different ancestry and marriage networks. Matching clothes or ornaments do not automatically mean that two families shared the same origins.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Environmental and archaeological research indicates expanding settlement and farming into the mid-700s. The familiar image of an entire population permanently on horseback misses the people growing food and maintaining villages.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The Vrap treasure was discovered in Albania in 1901 inside a copper cauldron. Its vessels, gold belt fittings and pieces of precious metal were gathered together, but that does not tell us who buried them or why.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: Some Vrap belt fittings show griffins and curling vines. Casting such small, elaborate objects required careful metalworking. The museum interprets decorated belts as statements of rank, rather like formal clothing with an exceptionally expensive buckle.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The treasure includes drinking vessels, a pouring ewer and a bucket. They reveal an elite world of serving and displaying precious metal; they are not a picture of the tableware in every village home.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The Met now labels the ensemble Avar or Byzantine. Proposed explanations include a leader's wealth or a craftworker's materials, and scholars disagree over where some pieces were made. Those uncertainties are part of the discovery.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The eighth-century Ewer of Zenobius has five marks imitating Byzantine official stamps. Examination shows they were engraved, not struck. A convincing-looking quality mark is a clue to investigate, not automatic proof of origin.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: The Zenobius ewer carries a Greek inscription, possibly copied from a Byzantine model by an Avar craftworker. Greek letters on a valued object do not establish the language spoken in the owner's household.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: Other Avar-period objects have short runiform inscriptions. Their readings remain disputed, including the Szarvas example. A confidently translated sentence in an imagined Avar language would conceal how much is still unresolved.

Charlemagne's campaigns in the 790s and early 800s dismantled Avar political power. People and local traditions continued within neighbouring societies. The map's later Avar label is not evidence that an independent khaganate survived to 1000.

sectionTitles: An oasis with a complicated political past
Later family life in the lower Awash

passages.text: Awsa centred on the lower Awash valley, where a Muslim imamate was followed by an Afar sultanate. The imported 1650 to 1815 span crosses political phases; its broad outline should not imply uniform rule over every Afar community.

passages.title: An oasis with a complicated political past
passages.text: In 1577, Imam Muhammad Jasa moved his seat from Harar to Awsa, seeking greater security amid regional conflict. The desert surroundings helped make the oasis attractive as a refuge. Awsa’s political history therefore began before this record first appears on the map.

passages.title: An oasis with a complicated political past
passages.text: The ruling Aydahiso lineage belonged to the Mudaito grouping. Succession usually privileged the ruler’s family, but choosing a successor could still cause argument. Nineteenth-century traditions about Mohammed Hanfare’s preference for a nephew show that a royal family tree did not settle every political decision.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Awsa could mean the cultivated area beside the Awsa canal as well as the wider sultanate. Settled farmers lived along the canal, while neighbouring areas supported herding. Calling everyone a nomad would miss the farmers whose fields helped sustain this political centre.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Officials known as malokti coordinated irrigation and controlled flooding, managed access to pasture and organized responses to cattle disease, including isolating sick animals. Keeping herds healthy and arranging who could graze where were practical responsibilities of government, alongside taxation.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Farmers had practised irrigation here for centuries before large modern plantations arrived. River water supported a concentration of people and political authority in otherwise dry surroundings. In Awsa, understanding channels and seasonal water was part of the foundation of state power.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: Menelik’s forces defeated Awsa in 1895, but direct Ethiopian administration did not immediately follow. In the 1960s, the British company Mitchell Cotts still had to negotiate with the sultan over land for Tendaho cotton development. Military defeat and everyday control of territory were different things.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: Cotton brought income to some Afar landholders, while plantation expansion and water regulation reduced grazing access for pastoralists. These twentieth-century changes created winners and losers within the region. A project that increased crop output could also make it harder for a herding family to feed its animals.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: The sultanate established an education fund and sent twenty-five Afar students to Egypt via Yemen in 1964. Historian Maknun Ashami, who later studied in Cairo himself, describes the scheme. It connected local political resources with opportunities to attend schools and universities abroad.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: Research published in 2024 describes women bargaining with highland merchants at Asaita’s Tuesday market. Transactions included animals, grain, salt, flour, spices and detergents. The market linked household supplies with livestock income, and women’s commercial work mattered even where formal leadership remained dominated by men.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: The same study records women’s work in managing water sources and moving homes when families followed pasture. A move could mean loading household structures onto camels or donkeys, then rebuilding. Packing for a trip was substantial work when the house came along too.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: Interviewees also described relatives contributing to weddings and sharing resources during emergencies. Women helped organize these exchanges and household decisions. These are observations from recent Lower Awash communities, showing continuing family networks without treating modern arrangements as a complete picture of life in 1700.

passages.title: A small written sample
passages.text: “áh roóbu” means “This is rain” in Afar. Linguist Richard Hayward prints the phrase in his modern grammar chapter, using accents to mark high tone. This is an attested linguistic transcription from the 1998/2001 handbook, not a manuscript from the early sultanate. It gives a short example of the region’s living language.

The map’s 1815 endpoint is not Awsa’s fall. Sultan Ali Mirah fled during violent conflict with Ethiopia’s military government in 1975, a major rupture in the sultanate’s political power. Afar people, language and community institutions continued.

passages.text: Aymara-speaking communities built several powerful highland societies around Lake Titicaca and beyond. They were never one timeless kingdom. The linked map records span 1279 to 1500; their outlines simplify overlapping peoples and territories, especially the southern extension toward the Atacama. Aymara history continues today.

passages.title: Highland power and stone memorials
passages.text: Ayllus connected households into larger social groups. Some Aymara polities organized upper and lower divisions, with several levels of leadership. Calling them kingdoms is convenient, but it can hide authority shared among different leaders and communities.

passages.title: Highland power and stone memorials
passages.text: Families and leaders maintained links to farming settlements at different elevations. Highland herders could obtain valley crops through relatives and exchanges across these scattered territories. Political geography could resemble an archipelago on land, with long journeys between its islands.

passages.title: Highland power and stone memorials
passages.text: At Sillustani beside Lake Umayo, the official inventory records 91 funerary towers from different periods. Some use carefully fitted stone and others rough masonry. The site preserves a changing tradition of commemorating the dead across Colla and Inca rule.

passages.title: Highland power and stone memorials
passages.text: Sillustani’s best-known tower is named for a lizard carved on a stone block. It rises about 12 meters, with a base over seven meters across. A small carved animal and an enormous structure can belong to the same architectural project.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: Across the cold Andean highlands, farmers make chuño by letting potatoes freeze at night and dry during sunny days. Trampling removes moisture and skins. Properly dried potatoes can keep for years: winter weather becomes part of the pantry’s equipment.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: A museum’s evidence for that food need not be ancient. Michigan’s collection includes chuño bought in a Cusco grocery in 1966. Such specimens help document a living food technology alongside the much older accounts of Andean potato preservation.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: An Aymara tunic from Bolivia in the Metropolitan Museum dates to the late eighteenth century. It is woven from camelid hair and measures roughly 67 by 89 centimeters. A surviving garment makes the skilled handling of animal fibers tangible.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: A twentieth-century Aymara tupu in Chile’s pre-Columbian museum combines silver and glass. This large pin fastened or adorned women’s clothing at the chest. Everyday dress can carry metalworking skill and an enduring emblem of identity.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: María Choque told an interviewer in 2023 that she began making thread at six, taught by her grandmother. Socks and hats came before more demanding garments. Her account gives one family’s learning sequence, from watching an elder to mastering difficult work.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: The same reporting describes October shearing that leaves wool on the animals for warmth. During February festivities, families attach wool flowers and pompoms to camelids. Even the suppliers of the wool can end up wearing some of the decoration.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: A modern Chilean schoolbook prints “Kamisaraki jilata”, meaning “How are you, brother?” It appears in Estela Gamero’s bilingual greeting song. These Latin letters record living Aymara; the sample is from a present-day teaching resource, not an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: Spanish authorities forced Karanqas communities into concentrated towns and demanded labor for the Potosí mines. These policies separated people from land and strained households. Colonial rule transformed local institutions, but Aymara communities kept rebuilding relationships and practices across the region.

Inca conquest and Spanish colonization changed Aymara political autonomy and landholding. Neither ended the people or their language. The map’s 1492 and 1500 endpoints are display boundaries; modern communities in Bolivia, Chile and Peru continue teaching, weaving, farming and organizing their cultural life.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: A modern Chilean schoolbook prints “Kamisaraki jilata”, meaning “How are you, brother?” It appears in Estela Gamero’s bilingual greeting song. These Latin letters record living Aymara; the sample is from a present-day teaching resource, not an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: Spanish authorities forced Karanqas communities into concentrated towns and demanded labor for the Potosí mines. These policies separated people from land and strained households. Colonial rule transformed local institutions, but Aymara communities kept rebuilding relationships and practices across the region.

Inca conquest and Spanish colonization changed Aymara political autonomy and landholding. Neither ended the people or their language. The map’s 1492 and 1500 endpoints are display boundaries; modern communities in Bolivia, Chile and Peru continue teaching, weaving, farming and organizing their cultural life.

passages.text: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.
A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.

sectionTitles: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire

passages.text: The Azande formed several connected kingdoms in central Africa. This record’s 900 to 1000 dates and enormous outline are unreliable for those states: the histories discussed here concern the much later kingdoms and their communities. The evidence does not establish a medieval Azande empire.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Azande rulers belonged to the Avongara aristocracy. Kings appointed governors to smaller areas, and princes could fight over succession. Political connections did not make every Zande community part of a single centralized state.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: In the first half of the nineteenth century, Zande expansion crossed the Congo-Nile watershed from the Mbomu valley. Gbudwe established a kingdom around Yambio while confronting slave traders and neighboring powers.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: Colonial borders divided Zande lands among Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, French Equatorial Africa and the Belgian Congo. Communities and ruling families survived those partitions, but their political autonomy and connections were profoundly disrupted.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A photograph from Yambio, taken between 1927 and 1930, shows a large soro granary reached by a ladder. Grain was stored upstairs; woven reeds or grass enclosed additional storage below. This family’s pantry had its own upper floor.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: In another Yambio photograph from 1927 to 1930, women sit together beating finger millet with sticks. The grain supplied porridge and beer. Preparing food could be a shared task long before it reached a cooking pot.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A potter photographed between 1927 and 1930 stands beside coil-built earthenware vessels used in everyday life. Evans-Pritchard admitted that learning pottery from Zande men went badly for him. Expertise did not transfer just because the visitor owned a notebook.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A 1927 photograph records wives and children in Prince Rikita’s homestead, with crops beside the approach and houses behind them. This is a particular aristocratic family, showing how a royal lineage continued after Gbudwe’s defeat.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: The game abanga could use a carved board or holes in the earth. A photograph dated 1927 to 1930 shows the ground version tucked under a hut’s eaves, with a stool ready nearby. No game box was required.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: A kundi harp collected between 1927 and 1930 has five strings, wooden tuning pegs and a hide-covered soundbox. Plant materials form the strings and their attachments. Musicians and makers combined different natural materials to control tension and sound.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: Colonial schooling could mix instruction with coercion. At Wau’s technical school, established in 1905 to teach carpentry, reading and writing, Rikita’s son Rumba was among pupils held as guarantees of their families’ submission.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: A Zande written sample is “Rikita ni-fu-re na kporo.” The researchers translate it as “Rikita gave me a district to administer.” Published in their 2011 study, it comes from a historical narrative published in 1963, using a modern Latin-script transcription.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: When researchers shared these older recorded stories with Zande speakers in Bangassou, participants wanted copies to take home. Language research could also return accounts of ancestors and political life to people whose heritage the stories preserved.

Gbudwe was killed in 1905 and colonial rule replaced autonomous kingship. In 2022, a new Azande monarchy was established within South Sudan, combining four historical kingdoms as a modern institution. It was not a return of their former sovereign powers.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

sectionTitles: Building a state and a capital
A constitution in its own words
Light, water and the awkward business of toilets

passages.text: Baden grew from divided margraviates into a much larger grand duchy along the Upper Rhine. Karlsruhe became an important capital, while Mannheim and other towns developed manufacturing and new transport. The imported 1715 to 1878 outline is misleading at its early dates: it projects a later, enlarged territory backward over lands Baden acquired much later. The grand duchy itself continued until 1918.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: In 1771, Karl Friedrich of Baden-Durlach inherited Baden-Baden, joining Protestant and Catholic territories under one ruler. Further acquisitions between 1802 and 1810 included Heidelberg, Mannheim and lands farther south. The familiar long shape of Baden emerged through these changes, rather than existing unchanged in 1715.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: Karlsruhe’s founding offer in 1715 welcomed settlers of different Christian denominations. Such promises helped a new town attract inhabitants, but everyday equality remained contested: religious communities still argued over their treatment and public rights. A ruler’s invitation was the beginning of negotiations about living together.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: Baden’s expanded territory brought together places with different legal traditions. Johann Niklas Friedrich Brauer adapted the French civil code into a Baden law book. Announced in 1808, a uniform civil law finally took effect in 1810. Governing a bigger state required more than drawing a larger border.

passages.title: A constitution in its own words
passages.text: Writing sample: section 14 of the constitution of 22 August 1818 says, “Die Gerichte sind unabhängig innerhalb der Grenzen ihrer Competenz.” It means “The courts are independent within the limits of their jurisdiction.” This German wording, including the spelling Competenz, comes from a modern transcription of the historical document.

passages.title: A constitution in its own words
passages.text: The same constitution protected property and personal liberty and provided two parliamentary chambers. Its rights were unequal: eligibility for the second chamber required being Christian, at least thirty, and meeting financial qualifications. Reading both the promises and the exclusions helps explain why constitutional reform did not finish the struggle for political rights.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: Karlsruhe’s first public oil lamps appeared in 1759. They burned rapeseed oil and were lit only on moonless nights when the margrave was present. The moon had a surprisingly important job in the lighting budget, and a ruler’s absence could leave everyone relying on it.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: In 1764, a new Karlsruhe waterworks used horses to drive wooden pumping machinery. It lifted groundwater from about three metres below ground. Keeping water moving required animals, mechanisms and maintenance long before electric pumps could be switched on.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: After the map’s 1878 cutoff, but still during the grand duchy, Karlsruhe expanded its sewers from 1883. Toilets did not immediately join them: water closets were expensive for working families, and officials worried about fouling the river. Cesspits remained part of the system; in 1893 officials permitted sewer expansion for flushing away human waste. Underground pipes alone did not solve the toilet question.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: On 12 June 1817, Karl von Drais rode his running machine from Mannheim toward Schwetzingen and back, covering about fourteen kilometres in a little over an hour. Riders pushed against the ground with their feet. Pedals were still in the future: the engine was the person sitting on top.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: These early machines were largely wooden, with a few iron parts. Drais sold construction plans that craftsmen turned into vehicles. A wheelwright’s workshop, rather than a modern bicycle factory, supplied the skills behind this invention’s first examples.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: Food prices made 1817 much harder for families than the bicycle story suggests. After the disastrous harvest of 1816, a one-kreuzer bread roll in Mannheim shrank from seven Loth to two and a half Loth, roughly 112 grams to 40 grams. The price stayed the same while the portion became much smaller.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: Johann Peter Hebel turned calendar writing into memorable literature. His 1811 Schatzkästlein collected 127 short pieces from earlier issues of the Rheinländischer Hausfreund. He revised expressions for readers beyond the local dialect area. A calendar could offer stories and observations alongside its practical job of marking the year.

passages.title: Revolution reached ordinary streets
passages.text: When Prussian troops bombarded Rastatt in July 1849, civilians took shelter in cellars, the palace and fortifications. The revolutionary stronghold surrendered on 23 July. Captivity and disease followed for prisoners. The struggle over government reached homes and families as well as soldiers and political leaders.

Grand Duke Friedrich II definitively renounced the throne on 22 November 1918, after a provisional government had formed. Baden changed from a monarchy into a republic. Its people, towns and institutions continued; the imported map endpoint of 1878 does not mark the end of the state.

passages.text: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.
A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.

sectionTitles: A capital of earth and brick

passages.text: Bagirmi developed southeast of Lake Chad around Massenya in the sixteenth century. Its rulers negotiated, fought and sometimes paid tribute to Bornu and Wadai. Both Bagirmi labels on this map refer to phases of this kingdom, with imperfect imported borders.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: Bagirmi’s rulers used the title mbang. Conversion at court did not make the entire population religiously uniform. Bornu’s influence included scholars as well as armies, and periods of tribute alternated with renewed independence.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: In the eighteenth century Bagirmi raided southern and southeastern communities and profited from selling captives. Later invasions also carried Bagirmi’s own inhabitants into slavery. Royal prosperity and ordinary people’s security could move in opposite directions.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: Historian Viviana Pâques compared oral traditions and written evidence during research in 1966 and 1967. The sources did not always agree on reigns or dates. A royal list is historical evidence to investigate, rather than a ready-made calendar immune to disagreement.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Archaeologist Annie Lebeuf located the old capital, Boum Massenya, east of the Chari. By her 1967 report, its great earth enclosure survived as a low, uneven trace. An almost vanished wall can still reveal where a city once organized its defenses.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Fired-brick remains marked the palace, mosque and houses of prominent residents. Some old bricks had been reused for road fill. Archaeologists therefore had to read both surviving buildings and displaced materials, rather than expecting a complete abandoned city waiting untouched.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Lebeuf describes Massenya chiefly as a royal and administrative centre. A capital need not also be the kingdom’s busiest trading town. Its palace and officials gave it importance even when the most active buying and selling happened elsewhere.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: In 1898 Sultan Gaorang ordered the old capital burned and abandoned as Rabih threatened it. The later settlement called Massenya occupied a different location. Keeping those places separate helps explain why a modern town and an archaeological capital share a name.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: In 1852 Barth met Faki Sambo, a blind Fula scholar educated at al-Azhar in Cairo. They discussed books and distant places. The encounter connects a Bagirmi scholarly household with an intellectual network stretching well beyond the Lake Chad region.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Sambo served Barth a cold rice pudding with dates from Kanem; Barth offered coffee. Manuscripts and conversation shared the scene with refreshments. Even a meeting that later becomes historical evidence may have begun with something good to eat.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Barth described weavers and dyers, including Kanuri craftspeople producing dark cloth. His account also names officials responsible for pasture, woods and waters. Running a kingdom involved regulating useful resources as well as issuing commands at court.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Barth recorded the language name as “tar Bágrimma”. This is his nineteenth-century Roman transcription, not a surviving text written by a Bagirmi court scribe. It offers a small linguistic trace alongside the much richer spoken knowledge of the people he met.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: A modern Bagirmi book supplies an attested writing sample: “Kup an Duniya”, translated by its publisher as “The Beginning of Creation”. This illustrated Christian publication demonstrates continuing use of the language in print; it is not a text from the Muslim sultanate.

French protection in 1897 and further restrictions in 1903 ended Bagirmi’s independent position. Its rulers continued under colonial control, and Bagirmi communities remained part of the region’s history. Neither imported map cutoff marks their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
Making music, costumes and public memory

passages.text: The Bahamas became independent in 1973 after a much longer history of Lucayan communities, colonial settlement, slavery and struggles for political rights. Pottery, house yards and living craft traditions reveal how people worked, raised families and made things together across the islands.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: A pottery recipe began with a surprising ingredient: dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara. Researchers sampled red deposits on Long Island and experimented with Palmetto Ware, the Lucayan pottery containing burned, crushed conch shell. The shell helped difficult local material hold its shape. Experiments indicate relatively low firing temperatures, showing careful adaptation to the islands’ available resources.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Long Bay on San Salvador, impressions preserved in pottery reveal woven materials that have largely decayed. Hutcheson’s study compares these with other Late Lucayan sites; at Palmetto Grove, impressions even preserve evidence of woven spun thread. Clay kept a record of fibre work. Different patterns suggest variation in craft, but do not automatically identify a specific ethnic group.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Clifton on New Providence, excavators distinguished two Lucayan settlements using radiocarbon dates and objects, rather than assuming all nearby remains belonged to one village. Griddles, hollow vessels, shell beads and tools differed between the sites. Marine remains show the importance of conch and other seafood. The researchers favoured successive settlement over a long-lived pair of simultaneous villages.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: Laundry left clues at early nineteenth-century Clifton. Buttons, beads and fasteners clustered between houses and outdoor kitchens; the excavators interpreted them as losses during washing and drying. Food remains and cooking tools marked other activity areas. The yards supported sewing, childcare and conversation as well as chores, within the constrained lives of enslaved households.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge

sectionTitles: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
Making music, costumes and public memory

passages.text: The Bahamas became independent in 1973 after a much longer history of Lucayan communities, colonial settlement, slavery and struggles for political rights. Pottery, house yards and living craft traditions reveal how people worked, raised families and made things together across the islands.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: A pottery recipe began with a surprising ingredient: dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara. Researchers sampled red deposits on Long Island and experimented with Palmetto Ware, the Lucayan pottery containing burned, crushed conch shell. The shell helped difficult local material hold its shape. Experiments indicate relatively low firing temperatures, showing careful adaptation to the islands’ available resources.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Long Bay on San Salvador, impressions preserved in pottery reveal woven materials that have largely decayed. Hutcheson’s study compares these with other Late Lucayan sites; at Palmetto Grove, impressions even preserve evidence of woven spun thread. Clay kept a record of fibre work. Different patterns suggest variation in craft, but do not automatically identify a specific ethnic group.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Clifton on New Providence, excavators distinguished two Lucayan settlements using radiocarbon dates and objects, rather than assuming all nearby remains belonged to one village. Griddles, hollow vessels, shell beads and tools differed between the sites. Marine remains show the importance of conch and other seafood. The researchers favoured successive settlement over a long-lived pair of simultaneous villages.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: Laundry left clues at early nineteenth-century Clifton. Buttons, beads and fasteners clustered between houses and outdoor kitchens; the excavators interpreted them as losses during washing and drying. passages.text: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.
The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.

sectionTitles: Food and homes in the Congo basin
A later language sample and storytelling

passages.text: Bantu names a large family of languages and the many societies that speak them, not a single empire. The map’s early “Bantu” and later “Bantu peoples” labels are broad historical approximations. This shared account follows the wider history; its dated examples do not all belong to either displayed interval or polygon.

passages.title: Languages, movement and exchange
passages.text: Early Bantu-speaking communities expanded from western Africa over many generations, with movement into forest and savanna regions. They met and mixed with other populations. This long history produced hundreds of languages and diverse communities; it was not one army marching across an empty continent.

passages.title: Languages, movement and exchange
passages.text: Urewe pottery around the Great Lakes illustrates how ideas can travel between neighbors. Scholars caution that its makers need not all have spoken the same language, or have introduced farming and ironworking together. Pots preserve skilled choices about clay and design, but they do not come with a spoken-language label.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: At Iyonda in today’s DR Congo, charred millet grains survived in early Iron Age pits. The Imbonga phase is broadly dated around 400 to 200 BCE, although individual grain dates span wider ranges. Such tiny remains make real crops visible in a rainforest history once known mainly through pottery.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: Plant tissue from Iyonda, Mbandaka and Bolondo also points to tubers. Charring suggests that some were roasted in hot ash. Around 1350 at Mbandaka, grains showing germination may reflect malting for beer: a plausible interpretation, rather than a surviving recipe.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: At Bolondo, house platforms were repeatedly raised from the settlement’s beginnings around the mid-fourteenth century. Over time they joined into an artificial island. Building upward helped people live beside the Tshuapa River through changing water levels: floors could be part of a family’s flood strategy.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: Fish bones are abundant at Bolondo, and chemical traces in human remains show the importance of forest and freshwater foods. Millet was present, but researchers caution against imagining a diet dominated by cereal farming. Living by a river could mean a very different dinner from life on a dry plateau.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: At Kalundu in Zambia, excavators recovered finger millet and a sorghum grain dated between 1320 and 1415. Finger millet can supply porridge, malt and other foods, and stores well. Researchers therefore suggest that nearby Isamu Pati’s grain bins may have held millet, an important household reserve.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: Fourteenth-century Great Zimbabwe shows another regional achievement: carefully laid granite enclosure walls surrounding living spaces made with clay and granitic sand. UNESCO describes family areas with kitchens, living huts and courts. Behind the monumental stonework were people cooking, resting and sharing the work of a household.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: At the coastal Swahili town of Songo Mnara, House 44 had coral-and-lime walls, plaster floors in most rooms and shaped coral around its doorways. The house belonged to the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Even comparatively simple urban homes involved specialized building materials and careful finishing.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: House 44 also had a latrine in the back room’s southwest corner. Archaeologists found that it was filled in during a change when a fresh sand layer covered accumulated deposits. Toilets leave evidence too, which is fortunate for historians, if less glamorous than finding gold.

passages.title: A later language sample and storytelling
passages.text: Swahili provides one written example from the much later history of a Bantu language. In an 1870 collection of Zanzibari tales, a lion asks, “Nani ninyi?” The facing English text reads, “Who are you?” These are the book’s Latin letters, not a reconstruction of prehistoric Bantu speech.

passages.title: A later language sample and storytelling
passages.text: In that tale, a hare finds honey and invites companions to share it, then tries to escape when its owner, the lion, appears. The collector noted that narrators could add touches as they told stories. Such performances reveal creativity and humor; they are literature, not literal reports of talking animals.

Neither 1500 BCE nor 1530 CE marks the end of Bantu-speaking peoples. These are endpoints of imported map labels. Their languages and communities continued to change, form states, exchange ideas and develop new histories; there was never one Bantu empire with a single fall.

sectionTitles: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom

passages.text: Barbados’s island history long predates the plantation colony. Archaeology records shell tools, pottery and fishing, while Bridgetown’s buildings reveal the organization of colonial trade and slavery. Independence in 1966 and the republic established in 2021 are distinct political changes within a continuing society.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Heywoods, a conch-shell adze from archaeological Context 7 produced a calibrated date range of 2530 to 2200 BCE. The shaped shell is evidence of toolmaking before pottery became common on the island. The dating study also discusses contamination and marine-shell problems, so this evidence does not establish an exact arrival year for the first islanders.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: Excavators at Heywoods washed deposits through fine mesh to recover small fish bones. Elizabeth Wing identified an assemblage dominated by open-water fish, especially flying fish and tuna, alongside fewer reef fish. Shell remains also point to collecting around mangroves and the shore. These finds reveal varied coastal food gathering in the precolonial settlement landscape.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: The later Heywoods settlement produced footed bowls, animal and human pottery ornaments, and a spindle whorl. Shell adzes, beads and cut conch added evidence of manufacture. These finds connect food preparation, ornament and textile-related work; pottery classifications describe material traditions rather than proving a single ethnic identity.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The 1661 slave code tried to control movement through written passes and ordered overseers to search enslaved people’s houses twice weekly for fugitives. It also specified an annual clothing allowance. These provisions expose intrusion into domestic life and mobility; a written requirement does not demonstrate that clothing was actually supplied or that people complied.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The rebellion that began on 14 April 1816 was organized across estates. Participants included Bussa, an estate ranger, the carpenter King Wiltshire and Nanny Grigg, a literate domestic worker. Colonial forces defeated the uprising, but its organization shows enslaved people using occupational contacts and knowledge in their struggle for freedom.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: Much surviving documentation of the rebellion comes from officials who suppressed it. The National Archives presents governors’ letters and military reports for critical reading, alongside a sketch of an insurgent flag. These sources preserve evidence of resistance through the language and interests of colonial authorities; their viewpoint requires interpretation.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: For some Barbadian families, moving house meant moving the actual house. Wooden chattel houses stood on blocks and could be taken apart and relocated. Residents might own the building but rent plantation land beneath it, so portability helped preserve their home when a landowner required them to leave. A clever building method answered a very real insecurity.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Bridgetown’s winding streets, warehouses and dock facilities record a port built around commerce. Buildings adapted European forms to tropical conditions, including storage designed against storms and damage to goods. The same harbour infrastructure supported the traffic in enslaved people, so architectural achievement and the coercive economy that sustained it must be considered together.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Samuel Jackman Prescod entered the House of Assembly in 1843, after free men of colour meeting property requirements had gained voting rights. More than a century later, Edna Bourne became the first woman elected to the House in the 1951 adult-suffrage election. These changes broadened institutions whose early membership had been tied to property.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Crop Over developed from end-of-harvest celebrations and was revived as a national festival in 1974. The decorated cart parade recalled plantation transport and drew extensive local participation. Other early events attracted criticism for favouring visitors and wealthier audiences, making the festival’s development a debate about who could take part and whose culture it represented.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Kamau Brathwaite made Barbadian places central to works including Mother Poem, Sun Poem and Barabajan Poems. The editors of Poui describe his attention to beaches, villages, canefields and threatened landscapes, as well as experiments in rhythm and language. His writing gave these environments literary importance while questioning how they were being transformed.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, spoken-word artist Adrian Green emphasized differences among the speech of Barbadian parishes and neighbourhoods. His performances use the language he speaks in daily life. Rather than treating the island as having one uniform voice, he describes local variation as a resource for artistic expression and communication.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1966. Becoming a republic in 2021 changed the head of state of an already independent country. Barbados continues as a nation, and its separate map records represent coverage intervals rather than successive disappearances and refoundings.

The dating study also discusses contamination and marine-shell problems, so this evidence does not establish an exact arrival year for the first islanders.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: Excavators at Heywoods washed deposits through fine mesh to recover small fish bones. Elizabeth Wing identified an assemblage dominated by open-water fish, especially flying fish and tuna, alongside fewer reef fish. Shell remains also point to collecting around mangroves and the shore. These finds reveal varied coastal food gathering in the precolonial settlement landscape.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: The later Heywoods settlement produced footed bowls, animal and human pottery ornaments, and a spindle whorl. Shell adzes, beads and cut conch added evidence of manufacture. These finds connect food preparation, ornament and textile-related work; pottery classifications describe material traditions rather than proving a single ethnic identity.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The 1661 slave code tried to control movement through written passes and ordered overseers to search enslaved people’s houses twice weekly for fugitives. It also specified an annual clothing allowance. These provisions expose intrusion into domestic life and mobility; a written requirement does not demonstrate that clothing was actually supplied or that people complied.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The rebellion that began on 14 April 1816 was organized across estates. Participants included Bussa, an estate ranger, the carpenter King Wiltshire and Nanny Grigg, a literate domestic worker. Colonial forces defeated the uprising, but its organization shows enslaved people using occupational contacts and knowledge in their struggle for freedom.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: Much surviving documentation of the rebellion comes from officials who suppressed it. The National Archives presents governors’ letters and military reports for critical reading, alongside a sketch of an insurgent flag. These sources preserve evidence of resistance through the language and interests of colonial authorities; their viewpoint requires interpretation.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: For some Barbadian families, moving house meant moving the actual house. Wooden chattel houses stood on blocks and could be taken apart and relocated. Residents might own the building but rent plantation land beneath it, so portability helped preserve their home when a landowner required them to leave. A clever building method answered a very real insecurity.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Bridgetown’s winding streets, warehouses and dock facilities record a port built around commerce. Buildings adapted European forms to tropical conditions, including storage designed against storms and damage to goods. The same harbour infrastructure supported the traffic in enslaved people, so architectural achievement and the coercive economy that sustained it must be considered together.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Samuel Jackman Prescod entered the House of Assembly in 1843, after free men of colour meeting property requirements had gained voting rights. More than a century later, Edna Bourne became the first woman elected to the House in the 1951 adult-suffrage election. These changes broadened institutions whose early membership had been tied to property.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Crop Over developed from end-of-harvest celebrations and was revived as a national festival in 1974. The decorated cart parade recalled plantation transport and drew extensive local participation. Other early events attracted criticism for favouring visitors and wealthier audiences, making the festival’s development a debate about who could take part and whose culture it represented.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Kamau Brathwaite made Barbadian places central to works including Mother Poem, Sun Poem and Barabajan Poems. The editors of Poui describe his attention to beaches, villages, canefields and threatened landscapes, as well as experiments in rhythm and language. His writing gave these environments literary importance while questioning how they were being transformed.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, spoken-word artist Adrian Green emphasized differences among the speech of Barbadian parishes and neighbourhoods. His performances use the language he speaks in daily life. Rather than treating the island as having one uniform voice, he describes local variation as a resource for artistic expression and communication.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1966. Becoming a republic in 2021 changed the head of state of an already independent country. Barbados continues as a nation, and its separate map records represent coverage intervals rather than successive disappearances and refoundings.

sectionTitles: Living with a river that changes its address
A table with ducks and baskets with animals
A living language and later everyday life

passages.text: Barotse refers here to the Lozi kingdom and its many communities around the upper Zambezi floodplain in western Zambia. The imported 1878 to 1914 window covers a late phase of royal and colonial history. Its polygon lies mainly north of the floodplain heartland described below and should not be treated as a verified kingdom boundary.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: Families raised earth into settlement mounds above the surrounding plain. Seasonal flooding still required movement to higher ground. The Kuomboka journey carries the Litunga from Lealui toward Limulunga; other households also relocate. Moving season follows the river’s timetable.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: The Mwayowamo canal, dated 1887 to 1889 in Zambia’s heritage account, connected Lealui and Limulunga and supplied Lealui with water. Other channels drained fields or carried boats. These were useful engineering works with several jobs, rather than a decorative moat around a palace.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: Fishers built malelo weirs to retain water as floods receded. Opening a gap let water pass into a waiting basket and helped catch fish. Temporary maongo shelters of reeds, grass or branches served people at fishing camps and during seasonal moves.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: A wooden food bowl now in the British Museum has six swimming ducks carved on its lid. Dated about 1891 to 1901, it carried a collector’s label saying it was used by headmen. A remarkable serving dish, but not a census of everyone’s dinnerware.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Court objects drew on different communities’ skills. The museum identifies Kwangwa and Mbunda carvers among those meeting demand for wooden vessels at the Lozi court. The kingdom’s artistic achievements belonged to people with distinct identities, not to one ruler working alone.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Women made tightly coiled baskets for storing valuable goods. A surviving example from about 1900 to 1920 uses Makenge root fibre and pigment. Its orderly woven surface turns a flexible plant material into a carefully shaped, lidded container.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Overseas demand changed basket decoration during Lewanika’s reign. The Metropolitan Museum contrasts earlier geometric designs with animal figures made for European customers. On this basket, figures march around lid and body: a procession you could carry under your arm.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: The canal-building story also includes coercion. Historian Jack Hogan’s archival research identifies enslaved labour as central to major royal public works. Admiring the engineering should leave room for the workers whose effort was demanded rather than freely offered.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: Slavery was formally abolished in 1906, but Hogan follows its slow decline over the next two decades. A proclamation did not instantly free every person from a master’s control. The difference between a law and everyday freedom is part of the kingdom’s history.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: Barotse National School opened in March 1907 with seven pupils, according to the education history summarized by Peggy Mwanza. An agreement with Lewanika allocated a share of local tax revenue to education. The tiny opening class belonged to a much larger argument about who should fund schooling.

passages.title: A living language and later everyday life
passages.text: “Bà-shímànì bà-ká-sèh-à” means “The boys will laugh.” This Silozi example was published by linguists in 2025 from work with speaker Mubiana Liswaniso in 2022 to 2024. The Latin letters, tone marks and hyphens reproduce their notation. It is a modern language witness, not a royal document from 1878.

passages.title: A living language and later everyday life
passages.text: A 2015 canals report describes a continuing practical problem: sandy ground and scarce building stone made durable latrines difficult. It also records boreholes serving schools and health centres. These are dated modern observations, showing why water management includes safe drinking water and sanitation as well as boat routes.

Colonial agreements gradually reduced independent royal power; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. In 1964 a new agreement addressed Barotseland’s place within independent Zambia and replaced earlier British obligations. That political change did not end Lozi communities or royal traditions. The parliamentary explanation records the settlement’s intended framework, not a guarantee that every later dispute was resolved.

sectionTitles: Evidence close to the map’s century
Food and farming in the wider medieval period

passages.text: The Basques are a continuing people, not a kingdom that existed only from 500 to 600. This map’s outline spreads too far across northern Iberia to serve as a reliable linguistic or political border. The early medieval western Pyrenees were a region of movement, exchange and competing powers. Archaeology illuminates local communities, while their exact languages and identities cannot simply be read from their belongings.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: A drought in 1987 exposed human remains and objects on the shore of the Ullibarri-Gamboa reservoir. The discovery led to excavation of Aldaieta’s sixth- and seventh-century cemetery. Lower water had briefly opened a window into a much older landscape.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: At San Pelayo in Dulantzi, a sixth- or seventh-century burial preserved amber necklace beads. Their forms resemble those found at Aldaieta. Small personal ornaments help archaeologists compare communities across the region, even when the people themselves left no written biography.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: Another San Pelayo burial retained metal fittings from a wooden bowl, alongside rounded pottery vessels. The bowl fittings resemble examples from cemeteries around the Rhine and Loire. Wood often disappears underground, while its metal parts keep a clue to the missing object’s shape.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: A study of fifth- to ninth-century rural communities found that the sampled Basque-region diets relied heavily on plants, including substantial amounts of millet. Researchers investigated chemical signals in bones. These reveal broad food patterns rather than the recipe for a particular family’s supper.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: The same study found no simple rule that a grander burial meant a richer diet. Even people buried in silos or wells often ate the same broad kinds of food as other community members. A grave’s location and the meals of a lifetime tell different parts of a person’s story.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: At Zornoztegi and Aistra, researchers tested 50 samples of charred seeds spanning the fourth to fourteenth centuries. Wheat and barley generally grew with low or moderate water availability and little evidence of manure. The burnt seeds preserve traces of farming decisions long after the fields have changed.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: The seed study also suggests that farmers may have rotated crops with legumes to replenish soil. This remains an interpretation to test with more evidence. A field could need a change of crop, just as a household needed more than one kind of food.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: Medieval Zornoztegi appears as a farming village without obvious differences between family groups, while Aistra has evidence of local elites and may have collected dues. Comparing their crops helps researchers ask who grew food, who received it and how much work households invested.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: In 1545, Bernat Etxepare published the first printed Basque book in Bordeaux. Its fifteen poems include religious verse, love poetry and reflections on his imprisonment. The language comes from the Garazi area of Lower Navarre, giving a particular regional voice a place in print.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Writing sample: “Euskara, jalgi hadi mundura” means “Euskara, go forth into the world.” The Etxepare Institute prints this as its motto, echoing the poet’s invitation to his language. This attested modern spelling is used in the Institute’s publication; Etxepare’s sixteenth-century spellings differed.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Etxepare’s book used spellings such as “heuscara” for the language’s name and “beçala” for “like” or “similar to.” The sole known surviving copy is held in France’s national library. A whole literary milestone now depends on the survival of one small book.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: For the later Basque whaling ship San Juan, historian Selma Huxley followed documentary clues in Spanish archives before underwater archaeologists found the wreck at Red Bay in 1978. Written records and surviving ship timbers could then be studied together, connecting names on paper with the craft of shipbuilding.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Basque cultural life continues through writers, filmmakers, musicians and language learning. The Etxepare Institute supports this work internationally. The map’s sixth-century endpoint is therefore a limit of this particular imported record, not the end of Basque people or their language.
Basque communities and their language continue. Their histories passed through many political institutions and borders; the map’s 600 endpoint is not a collective conquest or extinction date.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: Who could shape the new state?
A written ideal and its limits

passages.text: The Batavian Republic replaced the old Dutch Republic in 1795 with French military support. It experimented with national representation and a centralized state before becoming the Kingdom of Holland in 1806. The atlas’s 1800 to 1815 label runs beyond the republic’s life and covers only its European outline.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: The National Assembly first met in 1796 after indirect elections in 126 districts. Voters chose electors, who chose representatives. Men had to meet age and other qualifications, including limits on recent poor relief and a political declaration. Revolutionary citizenship still had gates to pass through.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: The 1798 constitutional project replaced the old provincial confederation with a stronger national framework. The National Archives preserves a handsome parchment record of the referendum result. Its calligraphy and expensive material show how the new authorities made a vote into a public founding document.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: Jewish campaigners in the Felix Libertate club pressed for equal citizenship. On 2 September 1796 the National Assembly formally granted Jews the same civil rights as other citizens. Religious barriers were challenged, though eligibility for political participation remained restricted.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: Historian Myriam Everard traced a women’s newspaper launched in Amsterdam in 1796 through advertisements in another publication. No issues were known to her. Those notices reveal women as an audience in revolutionary political culture, even where the newspaper itself has disappeared.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: In January 1795 people danced around a liberty tree on Amsterdam’s Dam square, renamed the Square of the Revolution. A small twig survives in the Rijksmuseum. A branch saved as a souvenir can carry evidence of a political celebration just as a grand monument can.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: The 1801 school law made education a national concern. Municipal governments were to provide enough schools and adequately paid teachers so children could attend. This was an ambitious administrative program; a law’s promise did not mean every child instantly had an equal school experience.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: School inspectors served on departmental education boards appointed by the national executive. Teaching was becoming something that officials could inspect and organize across regions. The surviving inspection archive lets historians follow the machinery behind a classroom reform.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: A 1799 iron standard metre in the Rijksmuseum sits in a wooden case lined with red velvet. It has no little centimetre marks: the important thing was the exact length of the whole bar. This unusually pampered ruler helped define a shared unit of measurement.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: A colored drawing dated September 1799 records a coastal signal mast at Scheveningen. Its semaphore communicated through visible signals before electrical telegraphs. The drawing makes military communication equipment part of the republic’s surviving material record.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: French and Dutch troops camped near Kraantje Lek at Overveen and were also lodged with local people. Several hundred soldiers could change the rhythm of a quiet district even without a battle there. In 1803 troops from the camps were sent to nearby Zandvoort during a British bombardment.

passages.title: A written ideal and its limits
passages.text: A draft of the 1798 constitution begins “Alle menschen zijn, als menschen, aan elkander gelijk”: “All people, as people, are equal to one another.” This is Dutch from the surviving draft; the final printed constitution used different wording in Article 3. Even constitutional sentences have revision histories.

passages.title: A written ideal and its limits
passages.text: The liberty proclaimed in Europe did not automatically free enslaved people in Dutch colonies. On Curaçao in 1795, Tula drew on revolutionary ideas to demand freedom. The museum connects his resistance with the same slogans celebrated around Dutch liberty trees, exposing the unequal reach of those promises.

French pressure replaced the republic with the Kingdom of Holland under Louis Napoleon in 1806. National institutions and reform projects outlasted individual constitutions, while the inhabitants continued through another change of government. The 1815 map endpoint is not the republic’s fall date.
