sectionTitles: Skilled hands and time to play

passages.text: The imported name “Boihaenum” appears to refer to ancient Boiohaemum, associated with Maroboduus and the Marcomanni. Its outline lies mainly in eastern Moravia and Slovakia, poorly matching the commonly proposed Bohemian core. Neither these borders nor a continuous kingdom from 1 BCE to 300 CE are established. The examples below distinguish regional Germanic communities from Roman military installations.

passages.title: Homes and household work
passages.text: Roman-period settlements in Bohemia and Moravia often occupied low ground near streams and rivers. Excavations reveal houses, wells, storage pits and craft installations. These communities depended on farming and practical access to water, even when Roman writers preferred dramatic stories about warriors.

passages.title: Homes and household work
passages.text: Many local buildings had rectangular floors sunk partly below ground, with posts supporting the roof. Woven branches coated in clay probably formed their walls. Archaeologists can reconstruct the plan more confidently than the vanished roof, furniture or exact number of people sleeping inside.

passages.title: Homes and household work
passages.text: Food storage included underground silos and structures interpreted as raised granaries. Small farmstead groups combined homes, storage and work areas; the museum suggests that a family or small group could occupy one. A household had to keep future meals safe as well as cook today’s.

passages.title: Homes and household work
passages.text: Plant remains from regional settlements include barley, wheat, millet, peas and lentils. These crops make settled cultivation visible even where ancient outsiders described people mainly as hunters. Fields, harvests and grain storage occupied a large part of ordinary life.

passages.title: Homes and household work
passages.text: At Mlékojedy in Bohemia, a studied sample contained 3,568 animal bones from 122 excavated features. Only 3.2 percent belonged to wild species. Cattle, pigs and sheep or goats dominated, giving a very different picture from a diet supplied chiefly by heroic hunting expeditions.

passages.title: Skilled hands and time to play
passages.text: Local potters made vessels by hand and decorated some with a small toothed wheel rolled across the clay. Fine tableware could have a dark, almost metallic-looking surface. Practical containers offered scope for careful finish and recognizable patterns as well as holding food.

passages.title: Skilled hands and time to play
passages.text: A workshop at Hoštice in central Bohemia produced bone gaming dice during the Roman period. Bone and antler also supplied combs, clothing pins and sewing needles. The dice are a small reminder that life included games alongside the work needed to keep a household running.

passages.title: Neighbors across the Roman frontier
passages.text: Trade crossed the Danube frontier: Germanic visitors reached Roman markets and Roman traders travelled inland. War interrupted these relationships, especially in the Marcomannic conflicts of 166 to 180 CE. The frontier was a place of bargaining and diplomacy as well as armies.

passages.title: Neighbors across the Roman frontier
passages.text: At Mušov in southern Moravia, Roman military buildings had underfloor heating. Hot air from a furnace passed beneath floors supported on little brick pillars. The small bath complex probably served senior personnel privately; it does not show that nearby village families all enjoyed heated bathrooms.

passages.title: Neighbors across the Roman frontier
passages.text: Mušov also preserves foundation trenches of a building identified by its plan as a Roman military hospital, about 71 by 42 meters. Rooms surrounded a courtyard and communicating corridors. This evidence concerns care within an occupying army, not a documented public health service for the surrounding population.

passages.title: Neighbors across the Roman frontier
passages.text: An original Latin writing sample from Mušov is “LEGXGPF”, stamped on Roman bricks and tiles. It abbreviates Legio X Gemina Pia Fidelis, the Tenth Twin Legion, Pious and Faithful. The maker’s mark links construction materials to the legion’s brickworks at Vindobona, modern Vienna.

passages.title: Neighbors across the Roman frontier
passages.text: A corroded lump from a Roman ditch at Mušov turned out, under a CT scan, to contain two iron leg guards nested together. Both protected left legs and were different sizes. They were not a matching pair, an ancient equipment puzzle solved without pretending every lump of rust is obvious.

passages.title: A name outlasted one ruler
passages.text: The Roman historian Velleius Paterculus wrote “quam incolebat Maroboduus”, meaning “which Maroboduus inhabited”, when explaining the name Boiohaemum. These are Latin words preserved through literary manuscripts and a modern edition. They are an outsider’s description, not a sample of the inhabitants’ own spoken language.

passages.title: A name outlasted one ruler
passages.text: Rome prepared an expedition against Maroboduus in 6 CE, but the campaign was abandoned. He remained an important political figure until he was driven out in 19 CE and went into Roman exile. His alliances should not be stretched into the map’s entire three-century interval.

Maroboduus lost power in 19 CE. Much later, Roman forces withdrew toward the Danube in 180 CE after another period of war. Neither event ended regional community life, and 300 CE is an imported map cutoff rather than a documented fall of “Boihaenum.”

sectionTitles: A village fitted into a hillside
Belongings, offerings and a named woman

passages.text: This map record concerns the Boii of northern Italy, one of several ancient populations called Boii. Its 500 to 323 BCE interval begins earlier and ends earlier than the best documented Italian history. Monte Bibele supplies unusually vivid evidence for communities where Etruscan and Celtic traditions met; it does not represent every Boii household.

passages.title: A village fitted into a hillside
passages.text: At Monte Bibele, builders laid out houses on terraces cut into a steep hillside. Local sandstone formed the walls, with clay binding and timber supports. Paths between the buildings made an organized settlement possible on ground that was anything but conveniently flat.

passages.title: A village fitted into a hillside
passages.text: House interiors could hold one or two hearths, pottery, weaving weights and tools. Other spaces stored grain and pulses. Preparing food, making cloth and managing supplies were everyday work carried out within a compact village, rather than in separate modern shops and factories.

passages.title: A village fitted into a hillside
passages.text: The village included a large water cistern. Collecting and keeping water was part of the settlement’s design, alongside houses and paths. Its presence gives us firmer evidence about water provision than any guess about precisely where each family washed.

passages.title: What was in the pots?
passages.text: Thirteen samples from House 2 contained charred wheat, barley, flax and small broad beans. A destructive fire accidentally preserved this evidence by turning plant material into charcoal. Archaeology sometimes gets its clearest pantry inventory from a household disaster.

passages.title: What was in the pots?
passages.text: Some House 2 crops seem to have occupied separate storage vessels. Wheat and barley became mixed when the fire destroyed the room. A burnt heap can therefore combine food that the family originally kept carefully apart.

passages.title: What was in the pots?
passages.text: A separate study of three buildings recorded more than 10,000 charred plant remains, including lentils, peas, broad beans and grass peas. Some pots held a single crop. These are storage and food-processing clues, not a surviving cookbook telling us exactly how dinner tasted.

passages.title: What was in the pots?
passages.text: Fourth- and third-century BCE grinding stones at Monte Bibele used volcanic rock from around Orvieto, at least 300 kilometers away across the Apennines. Even an ordinary task like grinding grain could depend on distant materials and people moving heavy goods through difficult terrain.

passages.title: Belongings, offerings and a named woman
passages.text: An earlier sacred deposit at Monte Bibele contained small bronze human figures and miniature pots. The museum associates it with water and a cult active from the early fifth century BCE. This sacred landscape began before the later Celtic presence in the village.

passages.title: Belongings, offerings and a named woman
passages.text: Writing sample: a bowl from grave 40 bears the Etruscan words “mi titaias”, meaning “I am Titaia’s.” This is the scholarly Latin-letter transcription of an inscription originally written right to left in Etruscan letters. The grave dates to the late fourth or early third century BCE.

passages.title: Belongings, offerings and a named woman
passages.text: The same burial contained a distaff made with bone tubes, glass beads and five spindle whorls. Spinning equipment connects the grave with textile work, while the bowl preserves a woman’s name. Such personal possessions bring us closer to individuals than a broad tribal label can.

passages.title: Belongings, offerings and a named woman
passages.text: Another inscribed vessel was pieced together using both its decoration and a potter’s fingerprint that crossed two adjoining fragments. The fingerprint helped prove that the pieces belonged together. Someone’s small mark in wet clay became an unexpectedly useful clue more than two thousand years later.

passages.title: War and changing communities
passages.text: Rome’s victory in 191 BCE ended the political independence of the Italian Boii after prolonged conflict. That date concerns conquest, not the sudden disappearance of everyone associated with the name. Ancient writers’ labels and the identities people used themselves need not have matched neatly.
Roman conquest ended independent Boii power in northern Italy in 191 BCE. The map stops at 323 BCE, well before that event. Communities and their identities continued to change under Roman control.

passages.text: Bolivia declared independence in 1825, before this map interval. The modern state encompasses many Indigenous and other communities whose schools, crafts, healing knowledge and political struggles cannot be reduced to a single culture.

passages.title: Institutions and community education
passages.text: The Casa de la Libertad commemorates the deputies who signed the independence act on 6 August 1825. Its portraits include Casimiro Olañeta painted by Melchor María Mercado. Portraits preserve how political figures were represented, alongside the documentary record of their actions.

passages.title: Institutions and community education
passages.text: The 1952 revolution expanded suffrage to women and adults excluded by literacy requirements. This changed who could participate in national elections. Independence had not automatically brought equal political participation a century earlier.

passages.title: Institutions and community education
passages.text: Nationalization in 1952 transferred major tin-mining enterprises to state control. Agricultural reform followed in 1953. These measures changed ownership and rural relationships; they were political and economic transformations rather than the disappearance of Bolivian communities.

passages.title: Institutions and community education
passages.text: Avelino Siñani and Elizardo Pérez founded the Warisata school in 1931. Its school-ayllu model drew on community organization and collective work. Education here was an Indigenous-led effort to connect learning with the practical needs of local life.

passages.title: Institutions and community education
passages.text: Warisata included workshops whose production helped sustain the school, alongside a community parliament and student responsibilities. The model treated making, governing and learning as connected activities. A lesson could involve useful work beyond a desk.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: Kallawaya healers learn through apprenticeship and travel across different environments, building knowledge of plants and ritual practice. UNESCO records this specialized Andean tradition. Describing its cultural knowledge does not establish that every historical remedy was effective.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: The Kallawaya account also identifies women’s work in maternal and child care and in weaving textiles used in ritual settings. Healing knowledge belongs within a wider social world of relationships, images and ceremonies, rather than an isolated collection of ingredients.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: In 2017, eight Kallawaya communities helped produce a publication documenting their knowledge. Distribution was intended for the communities themselves to support younger generations. Preservation did not require turning every piece of knowledge into a public commodity.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: During Alasita in La Paz, people acquire miniature objects associated with hopes and wishes. They may seek Andean ritual consecration or Catholic blessings. The tiny objects express what participants value; the account records belief, not a promise that miniatures can fulfill wishes.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: People also exchange Alasita miniatures as symbolic payments of debts. This creates a social meaning beyond buying a souvenir. A very small object can stand for a much larger relationship between people.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: Children commonly learn Alasita practices while accompanying parents, and craft competitions encourage makers’ creativity. The tradition connects family learning with skilled miniature production. Its 2017 UNESCO recognition concerns living practice, not an abandoned ancient ritual.

passages.title: Care, crafts and family knowledge
passages.text: Article 8 of Bolivia’s 2009 constitution includes the Quechua words “ama qhilla, ama llulla, ama suwa”: “do not be lazy, do not lie, do not steal.” This is the spelling printed in that legal witness. A modern constitutional quotation is not an ancient manuscript or a statement that everyone speaks Quechua.

Bolivia continues as a state. Civilian government returned in 1982, and the 2009 constitutional framework recognized its plurinational character. Political institutions changed while its many peoples continued. The map’s 1878 starting point does not date their origins or the 1825 republic.

passages.text: Borgu was a region of related kingdoms and diverse communities, including centers such as Nikki, Bussa and Illo, in present-day Benin and Nigeria. Its political connections crossed languages and local identities. The imported 1878 to 1914 outline captures only a late period and should not imply a single centralized government.

passages.title: Kings, communities and the road
passages.text: Origin traditions link the ruling houses of Bussa, Nikki and Illo through Kisra and his descendants. Historians study how such stories changed with political circumstances. They express kinship and authority, but cannot simply be read as a dated travel diary from a distant homeland.

passages.title: Kings, communities and the road
passages.text: Borgu lay across busy commercial routes linking regions including Asante and Hausaland. In 2013, researchers followed an old route from Djougou through Bori and Ndali toward Nikki, interviewing residents and recording abandoned sites. Local knowledge helped turn a line on a map into identifiable places.

passages.title: Kings, communities and the road
passages.text: Not every prince protected travelers. Olayemi Akinwumi’s research examines royal participation in armed banditry, especially during the nineteenth century. Attacks could drive merchants onto other routes, undermining the very commerce that sustained towns and rulers.

passages.title: People who kept trade moving
passages.text: Women were central to the Nupe-Borgu region’s nineteenth-century economy. They traded locally and over long distances, carried goods, supplied food and arranged finance. Looking only at male chiefs or famous caravan leaders misses much of the work that made trade possible.

passages.title: People who kept trade moving
passages.text: Managing a household and doing business were often connected activities. Weise’s study brings women’s provisioning and brokerage into a history long dominated by male travelers’ accounts. These opportunities existed within an unequal economy that also included enslavement and forced movement.

passages.title: People who kept trade moving
passages.text: The 2013 survey recorded Nikki-Maro as a quarter associated with outside trading communities. Residents told a story of a Muslim newcomer who helped the king rebuild after war and hosted merchants nearby. This is a remembered explanation of how commerce and religious hospitality became connected.

passages.title: Ordinary materials, lasting skills
passages.text: At Temtoré, researchers found pottery fragments, metalworking slag and cowrie shells. Potters had decorated vessels with cords, combed waves and incised patterns. Broken household objects can preserve evidence of craft and exchange even when a ruler’s name is not attached to them.

passages.title: Ordinary materials, lasting skills
passages.text: Near Nikki, the team documented substantial rammed-earth walls at Gèsèwèrè Gààni. They identified a roughly rectangular enclosure, while leaving its precise history open for further work. Building with compacted earth could produce imposing structures without quarried stone.

passages.title: Ordinary materials, lasting skills
passages.text: A modern Baatonum dictionary gives this writing sample: “À n seko tɔbura, a màa bɔɔ wuro tɔbiri.” Its meaning is “If you greet the blacksmith, greet the bellows operator too.” This is the spelling in the version labeled September 2017, not a precolonial inscription.

passages.title: Ordinary materials, lasting skills
passages.text: That dictionary’s example makes a useful point about teamwork: the person shaping the metal is not doing everything alone. The same entry names the worker operating the forge’s bellows. Everyday vocabulary can preserve recognition of specialized labor that a royal chronicle might overlook.

passages.title: Partition and living connections
passages.text: Colonial partition in 1898 placed communities of Borgu under different European administrations. In Nigeria, Bussa and Kaiama were combined into a new Borgu Emirate in 1954. Later Kainji dam resettlement changed homes and livelihoods again; the region’s history continued well beyond the map’s 1914 cutoff.

passages.title: Partition and living connections
passages.text: At Nikki’s contemporary Gaani festival, the Sinaboko presides over ceremonies and receives horsemen and dignitaries. Decorated horses, riders’ clothing and practiced equestrian skills make political memory visible in a public gathering. This living celebration is documented by the festival organizers in 2026.

The 1898 colonial partition ended the region’s earlier independence through separate British and French administrations. The imported 1914 endpoint is not a common fall date for all Borgu states. Communities, royal traditions and cross-border relationships continued in Benin and Nigeria.

sectionTitles: Work that connected mountains and ports

passages.text: Late medieval Bosnia linked mountain settlements, mining districts and trading routes to the Adriatic. Kings shared power with influential noble families. Surviving coins, textiles and carved tombstones reveal skilled work and social differences; the atlas interval continues beyond the royal kingdom’s collapse in 1463.

passages.title: Work that connected mountains and ports
passages.text: Srebrenica’s silver deposits made it an important mining and trading centre. Extraction required miners, processing skills and supplies. The value of exported metal helped sustain towns as well as the households of rulers.

passages.title: Work that connected mountains and ports
passages.text: Ragusan merchants established communities in places including Fojnica, Visoko and Foča. Local merchants also participated. Business involved credit, workshops and markets, rather than only dramatic journeys by wealthy visitors.

passages.title: Work that connected mountains and ports
passages.text: Silver travelled through Ragusa and onward to Venice, while salt and cloth were important imports. Vlach carriers helped move goods. Every distant purchase depended on the less glamorous work of loading and transporting it.

passages.title: Work that connected mountains and ports
passages.text: At Boljuni, inscriptions name makers such as Grubač and scribes such as Semorad. Carving the stone and composing its message could involve different specialists. These names let some craftspeople step out from behind their finished work.

passages.title: Cloth, family connections and remembrance
passages.text: Excavators at Kopošići in 2015 uncovered an oak coffin and unusually well-preserved brocade in a grave dated to the fifteenth century. The cloth originally had a purple background with lions or griffins, worked in gilded-silver threads.

passages.title: Cloth, family connections and remembrance
passages.text: The museum identifies the burial as Mirko Radojević’s using written evidence and a reported paternal relationship to the neighbouring burial of Batić Mirković. The name is an evidence-based attribution; DNA alone does not provide a historical person’s name.

passages.title: Cloth, family connections and remembrance
passages.text: The brocade was probably imported and records an elite family’s access to expensive material. Its survival is extraordinary, but this ceremonial burial garment cannot tell us what most villagers wore while farming or cooking.

passages.title: Cloth, family connections and remembrance
passages.text: Stećci are large medieval grave markers, often carved from limestone. Slabs, chests and other forms could carry images or writing. Their varied shapes show that commissioning remembrance involved choices about expense, skill and appearance.

passages.title: Cloth, family connections and remembrance
passages.text: These tombstones were used by Catholic, Orthodox and Church of Bosnia communities. They are not the exclusive signature of one religious group. Most were made in the 1300s and 1400s, within a longer regional tradition.

passages.title: Authority in stone and silver
passages.text: Ključ’s fortifications used steep terrain together with built defences. Different sections spread across the ridge. The setting helps explain why a stronghold’s effectiveness depended on landscape as well as the thickness of its walls.

passages.title: Authority in stone and silver
passages.text: A groš of Tvrtko II in the History Museum’s catalogue measures about 21 millimetres and weighs about two grams. Its shield carries a crowned T, with helmet and elaborate crest above: a compact royal announcement in metal.

passages.title: Authority in stone and silver
passages.text: DnS TuARTCO - REX BOSnE means “Lord Tvrtko, king of Bosnia.” This Latin legend appears on the catalogued fifteenth-century groš of Tvrtko II. The lettering is preserved as transcribed by the museum; a coin title does not imply universal literacy.

Ottoman forces captured King Stjepan Tomašević in 1463, and Sultan Mehmed II ordered his execution. The royal kingdom ended, while Hungarian counterattacks and later campaigns produced changing frontiers. Towns, families and working communities continued under different rulers; 1492 is this map segment’s endpoint, not Bosnia’s extinction.

passages.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina emerged from Yugoslavia’s dissolution and joined the United Nations in 1992. The imported map begins in 1994, during a devastating war, and continues into peace and rebuilding. It shows the country’s outer outline, not the wartime lines of control or the separate layers of its later government.

passages.title: Carved furniture and family workshops
passages.text: Woodcarvers in Konjic make furniture, decorated interiors and smaller objects with recognisable hand-cut motifs. The work can turn a functional household piece into something passed down within a family. The craft remains both paid work and a hobby.

passages.title: Carved furniture and family workshops
passages.text: Young woodcarvers learn on the job in practising workshops and from older relatives. Family-run businesses help train apprentices and maintain the skills. Knowing which tool to use and how to guide it cannot be passed on by a finished chair alone.

passages.title: Carved furniture and family workshops
passages.text: Konjic woodcarving is practised by people from different ethnic and religious communities. The craft also connects diaspora households with the region. Its continuity depends on working makers and customers, as well as the preservation of beautiful older furniture.

passages.title: Blue thread and conversation
passages.text: Zmijanje embroidery decorates women’s clothing and household textiles with deep blue thread and geometric patterns. The technique is associated with villages near Banja Luka. A recognisable local style can travel on a sleeve, a wedding garment or a piece of bedding.

passages.title: Blue thread and conversation
passages.text: Women traditionally embroider together while singing and talking. Learning happens by watching and practising alongside experienced makers. The gathering combines careful handwork with social life: a sewing session can also be a place to exchange news.

passages.title: Rebuilding a bridge
passages.text: Mostar’s Old Bridge was rebuilt in 2004 after its destruction during the 1990s war. The project drew on detailed study of the earlier structure, materials and techniques. Restoring a crossing also restored a familiar part of the city’s daily routes.

passages.title: Rebuilding a bridge
passages.text: Surviving original bridge material is displayed in a museum, while the reconstruction remains identifiable as a reconstruction. Researchers used documentation and archaeological evidence to guide the work. Visitors can encounter both the rebuilt landmark and pieces that survived its destruction.

passages.title: Children’s belongings become evidence
passages.text: Mela’s white ballet shoes are preserved in the War Childhood Museum with her memory of ballet classes in 1994. Her teacher explained that they had been made in Sarajevo before wartime production stopped. The shoes record a child’s learning and a local manufacturing history.

passages.title: Children’s belongings become evidence
passages.text: Another contributor, Emir, donated his father’s razor. His father, a teacher, was killed in the Srebrenica genocide; the family kept the object after leaving. An ordinary possession can preserve a person’s memory when war has taken away much else.

passages.title: Children’s belongings become evidence
passages.text: The museum uses personal objects in workshops designed for different age groups. Books, letters, photographs, toys and recorded memories become starting points for learning. The evidence allows children’s experiences to enter history alongside treaties and military events.

passages.title: A currency with two scripts
passages.text: The first convertible-mark banknotes entered circulation on 22 June 1998, with coins following that December. The currency gradually replaced the mixture of money used during and after the war. New everyday cash was part of rebuilding a shared monetary system.

passages.title: A currency with two scripts
passages.text: A ten-mark specimen reproduced by the Central Bank reads “KONVERTIBILNIH MARAKA” and “КОНВЕРТИБИЛНИХ МАРАКА”, both meaning “convertible marks”. The same wording appears in Latin and Cyrillic scripts. This is lettering on a documented banknote, reproduced in a 2017 anniversary publication.

The 1995 peace agreement ended the war and reorganised the country without extinguishing its statehood. Bosnia and Herzegovina continued with the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska as its two entities, alongside shared state institutions.

sectionTitles: Homes, guests and a remarkable book

passages.text: This record concerns Bosnia and Herzegovina under Austro-Hungarian administration, rather than an independent kingdom. Occupation began in 1878 while the Ottoman sultan formally retained sovereignty; annexation followed in 1908. Railways, museums and new institutions developed amid unequal imperial power and diverse local communities.

passages.title: Imperial government and local voices
passages.text: The 1910 statute introduced a representative Council, but supreme administration remained with the Joint Ministry of Finance in Vienna. Having an assembly did not mean that residents controlled all the decisions affecting their lives.

passages.title: Imperial government and local voices
passages.text: Zemaljski ustav (statut) za Bosnu i Hercegovinu means “Provincial constitution (statute) for Bosnia and Herzegovina.” The Parliament’s monograph reproduces this 1910 document title. It is a contemporary South Slavic text in Latin letters, alongside a German version.

passages.title: Imperial government and local voices
passages.text: The Council’s work was interrupted during the First World War, and the emperor abolished it in 1915. This falls just beyond the atlas’s 1914 endpoint. The history of representation did not progress smoothly in one direction.

passages.title: Building connections and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Railway construction began soon after the 1878 occupation. The early narrow-gauge system used equipment transferred from an earlier construction project. Builders adapted what they could obtain rather than beginning with a perfectly standardized railway.

passages.title: Building connections and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Early passenger accommodation could be improvised from freight vehicles, with cloth roofs and curtains added. Travelling by train did not automatically mean a comfortable carriage. Transport history includes the experience of sitting through the journey as well as laying track.

passages.title: Building connections and keeping knowledge
passages.text: The museum library began operating in 1888. At first, curators managed it alongside their other duties; Franjo Topič later became its specialist librarian. Sorting and preserving information was a practical part of building a research institution.

passages.title: Building connections and keeping knowledge
passages.text: The library moved into new museum buildings in 1913. Its collections brought together archaeology, history, plants, animals and geology. Researchers could compare objects and written studies across subjects rather than treating the past as only a list of rulers.

passages.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book
passages.text: The Despić house belonged to a wealthy Orthodox merchant family. Its oldest part dates to the 1600s and later additions altered it. The building preserves a layered household history, not a house created all at once in 1878.

passages.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book
passages.text: The Despić brothers staged plays to entertain their guests. A domestic gathering could become a small theatre. This is an example from a prosperous urban household, not evidence that every family had a stage in the sitting room.

passages.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book
passages.text: Makso Despić served as a treasurer under Ottoman rule and later as a city councillor under Austria-Hungary. One person’s career crossed an imperial transition, showing how local experience could continue while the government above it changed.

passages.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book
passages.text: In 1894 the National Museum purchased the Sarajevo Haggadah from the local Sephardic Koen family. The manuscript was made much earlier outside Bosnia. Its acquisition records a specific Sarajevo family connection, rather than a medieval Bosnian place of manufacture.

passages.title: Homes, guests and a remarkable book
passages.text: A haggadah organizes the readings and rituals of the Passover Seder, a family meal with guests. This copy combines Hebrew writing, parchment leaves and painted scenes. Its purpose connects sophisticated bookmaking with people reading and listening around a table.

Austro-Hungarian rule ended in 1918 as the monarchy disintegrated. Authority passed through a local National Council and Bosnia and Herzegovina entered the new South Slav kingdom. The atlas’s 1914 endpoint therefore stops before the administrative period ended; its communities and institutions had further, changing histories.

sectionTitles: Words that came back from the sea

passages.text: The Bosporan kingdom joined Greek cities and neighbouring communities around the Kerch Strait, between Crimea and the Taman Peninsula. Its ports connected grain-growing country with the wider Greek world. The map shows only 323 to 1 BCE within a much longer history, and its broad northern outline should not be read as continuous royal control over every place inside it.

passages.title: A kingdom with several neighbours
passages.text: Bosporan rulers used different titles for different subjects: archon, or chief magistrate, of Greek cities such as Bosporus and Theodosia, but king of peoples including the Sindi. Panticapaeum and Phanagoria were important centres on opposite sides of the strait. One royal court dealt with communities that had different political traditions.

passages.title: A kingdom with several neighbours
passages.text: In 285/4 BCE Athens honoured King Spartokos III after his gift of 15,000 medimnoi of grain. A medimnos was a measure of dry produce. The decree turns a shipload-sized problem, feeding a city, into a surviving written record of international friendship.

passages.title: A kingdom with several neighbours
passages.text: The Athenians voted a gold crown and bronze statues for Spartokos. The surviving decree names an Agora location and a second, less securely reconstructed setting. Food supplies could win a ruler a very public thank-you, even far from his own kingdom.

passages.title: Houses, streets and exercise
passages.text: At Phanagoria, fourth-century BCE remains include paved streets, wells, water pipes and rectangular houses with tiled roofs. This neighbourhood evidence begins before the map window. Fetching water and keeping a roof over the family were part of city life alongside the impressive temples.

passages.title: Houses, streets and exercise
passages.text: Builders commonly put mudbrick walls on stone foundations during Phanagoria’s Greek and Roman periods. Later residents reused older building stone, which helps explain why archaeologists often recover only fragments of a house plan. An ancient wall could end up doing a second shift in somebody else’s building.

passages.title: Houses, streets and exercise
passages.text: A gymnasium is reported at Phanagoria from the third century BCE, adding a place for physical training to the city’s public buildings. The surviving foundations tell us about organised activity; they do not provide a class register showing which children could participate.

passages.title: Houses, streets and exercise
passages.text: Imported pottery reached Phanagoria from centres including Athens, Chios and Thasos, while local potters also made vessels inspired by Greek models. A household’s pots could therefore connect local craftwork with distant workshops and sea routes.

passages.title: Keeping a ship afloat
passages.text: A wooden vessel found underwater at Phanagoria in 2012 preserves a rare piece of working maritime technology. Radiocarbon analysis places its wood in the middle of the first century BCE; a bronze bow fitting bears symbols associated with Mithridates VI. Researchers connect the ship with his military fleet.

passages.title: Keeping a ship afloat
passages.text: Scientific examination found clay mixed with animal hair and feathers on the inside of the hull, over tarred fibres in the seams. Outside was a mixture containing wax, conifer resin and the mineral realgar. Researchers interpret these coatings as protection against water, fire and marine organisms. The ship had a surprisingly complicated coat.

passages.title: Words that came back from the sea
passages.text: A marble monument from Phanagoria addresses Hypsikrateia, companion of the first-century BCE king Mithridates VI, using the name Hypsikrates. Its last word, in a modern transcription of the ancient Greek, is χαῖρε, meaning “farewell” in this funerary setting. The inscription identifies her as the king’s wife; it does not establish exactly how she died.

passages.title: Words that came back from the sea
passages.text: The same inscription preserves a small human correction: the stonecutter first wrote one grammatical form of “woman” or “wife”, then changed it to the form needed when addressing her. Even a solemn stone monument could need proofreading.

passages.title: Words that came back from the sea
passages.text: Later harbour builders reused inscribed stones as construction material. Underwater excavation recovered royal dedications and civic records from that reused stonework. Recycling helped scramble their original settings, but also preserved messages that can now be studied.

passages.title: Beyond the map’s last year
passages.text: The kingdom continued into the Roman imperial period. A Phanagorian inscription honours Aspurgus, a king recognised by Rome in 14 CE. Another records a portico restored in 220 CE after war damage. These are later chapters of Bosporan history, not evidence that the kingdom stopped when this map record does.

The map’s 1 BCE endpoint is not the kingdom’s fall. Bosporan royal institutions persisted into late antiquity, and the end of royal coin production does not by itself date the end of government. During the early sixth century CE, imperial intervention brought Bosporus under Byzantine rule. Different cities experienced these changes on different schedules.

sectionTitles: Learning, with a little help from cattle
A new country, and a very big evening

passages.text: Botswana’s history includes many communities and languages. Colonial Bechuanaland became an independent republic in 1966. Family teaching, craft businesses, schools and community museums reveal histories that continue beyond changes of government.

passages.title: Family lessons in clay
passages.text: Among the Bakgatla ba Kgafela in Kgatleng, UNESCO’s 2012 account describes women shaping pots by hand. They build from the base toward the rim, smooth the clay with a wooden paddle and fire the finished vessels in a pit kiln. A useful pot begins well before dinner: preparing the earth, shaping it and firing it all take skill.

passages.title: Family lessons in clay
passages.text: The same account describes daughters and granddaughters learning by watching experienced potters and practising. Pots serve several household purposes, including storing water, cooking and fermenting sorghum beer. This is education through repeated, practical work. UNESCO also recorded difficulties passing on the craft as experienced makers became fewer and cheaper mass-produced containers competed with their pots.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: Basket maker Thitaku Kushanya recalls starting at home in Etsha 6 when she was five, learning from her mother. She says she sold her first basket at eight for one pula and fifty thebe. This is her own remembered childhood, not a rule about when all children learned. A carefully made basket could be both a family lesson and a first sale.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: Research published in 2017 describes women weaving together in courtyards while children played nearby. In interviews, makers explained how sales paid for food, schooling and healthcare. The basket on a shop shelf was therefore connected to conversation, patient work and household budgets. These accounts come from particular communities in Ngamiland, rather than a survey of every family in Botswana.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: The study photographs patterns called Ribs of the Giraffe and Flight of the Swallow in baskets from Gumare and Maun. Makers used narrow palm strips, coloured with roots and bark. One photograph shows a needle opening a hole for the next stitch. The animal belongs to the design: no giraffe is required in the sewing kit.

passages.title: Baskets, family and conversation
passages.text: The Kavora women’s basketry collective explains that its name comes from its home ward within the Etsha villages. Putting that name on a basket identifies the people and place behind it. The group connects sharing its craft with its ambition to provide a sustainable livelihood for daughters and granddaughters. A basket can carry a maker’s hopes for the future as well as a pattern.

passages.title: Learning, with a little help from cattle
passages.text: Botswana’s 1976 university appeal invited public support for a larger campus. The university later recorded donations of cattle, money, grain and eggs. Contributions took forms that different households could offer. The campaign is remembered in a statue outside the library. A university can begin with books and building plans, but in this case its fundraising history also includes a herd.

passages.title: Learning, with a little help from cattle
passages.text: At Swaneng Hill near Serowe, Patrick van Rensburg developed an approach linking secondary education with practical skills. An account written in 1999 explains that its associated brigades offered school-leavers work and training in construction trades. Lessons could involve making and building as well as reading. This was a particular educational experiment, not the curriculum of every Botswana school.

passages.title: A new country, and a very big evening
passages.text: For part of the colonial period, the Attorney General’s office serving Bechuanaland was in Mafikeng, across the border in South Africa. Its own institutional history records a move to Gaberones by 1965. Following an office’s address can reveal political change: administrative work was moving into the territory as independence approached. The older spelling Gaberones refers to today’s Gaborone.

passages.title: A new country, and a very big evening
passages.text: A contemporary Kutlwano announcement looked ahead to independence celebrations in September 1966. It promised hilltop bonfires as the new flag replaced the British flag at midnight leading into 30 September. Reading the announcement brings the anticipation into view: the political change was also being planned as a public occasion. It records what organizers intended, rather than proving every planned bonfire took place.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: A women’s club in the BORAVAST area, active from the late 1960s, brought together activities such as sewing, crochet and baking bread. Research completed in 2024 traces how this work developed into a community museum project, with fundraising and local partnerships. A museum’s story can begin with people making useful things together, rather than with a royal collection.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: The Tsodilo hills preserve thousands of rock paintings alongside a much longer archaeological record. UNESCO describes traces of human activity across at least 100,000 years, with gaps. That does not make all the paintings 100,000 years old. Their individual dates are often uncertain, and the painted record extends into much more recent centuries. Different kinds of evidence keep different clocks.

passages.title: Everyday work becomes history
passages.text: Tsodilo is also a sacred landscape for Hambukushu and San communities. UNESCO records continuing associations with ancestral spirits, hills and water holes. Archaeologists study physical traces, while communities maintain relationships with the place. These are distinct kinds of knowledge, and a heritage designation does not turn a living sacred place into merely an outdoor picture gallery.

British rule ended with independence on 30 September 1966. Botswana continues as a republic. The older map record’s endpoint in 1938 and the later record’s opening in 1960 are coverage dates, not the disappearance and rebirth of the country’s people.

sectionTitles: Medicine, water and the bathroom question

passages.text: Brazil became independent in 1822 as an empire on lands long inhabited by Indigenous peoples. Enslaved Africans and their descendants labored for centuries until legal abolition in 1888; a republic replaced the monarchy in 1889. Industry, health research and samba grew alongside social inequality and authoritarian rule. The 1988 constitution promised health, education and Indigenous rights. Family life and sanitation differed widely by region and era. Brazil continues, while the imported map starts in 1878, long after independence.

passages.title: Empire, freedom and republic
passages.text: Brazil declared independence in 1822 and became an empire. The 1878 start on this map is a surviving border snapshot, not its birthday. Indigenous peoples had histories and governments long before either date.

passages.title: Empire, freedom and republic
passages.text: The Golden Law of 13 May 1888 ended legal slavery in Brazil. Enslaved Africans and descendants had endured centuries of forced labor; their communities also fought for freedom. A two-article abolition law could end ownership on paper, but could not instantly provide homes, wages or political equality.

passages.title: Empire, freedom and republic
passages.text: On 15 November 1889 a decree proclaimed a federal republic, ending the monarchy. The state changed its form of government; people did not disappear and a new name on a map did not cure inequality.

passages.title: Empire, freedom and republic
passages.text: Quilombola communities, linked to histories of resistance to slavery, still exist. The 2022 census counted them as living communities, not a vanished chapter of the empire.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: The Estado Novo of 1937 to 1945 pushed industrialization and created the IBGE. The 1943 labor law compilation organized many workplace protections, yet the regime also censored and jailed opponents. A factory paycheck and political freedom did not arrive together for everyone.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: Twentieth-century urbanization moved many families into growing towns and cities. A child’s route to school, a parent’s trip to work and access to running water could look very different from rural life; this varied sharply by place and income.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: Brazil’s 1988 constitution called education a right of all and a duty of the state and family. It named free public teaching and access to schooling, including for people who missed it at the usual age. A legal promise and a child’s actual classroom can be different things.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: The same constitution recognizes family responsibilities and children’s rights to food, school, play and family and community life. It is a written civic goal, not a claim that every Brazilian household follows one pattern.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: In Rio, early twentieth-century samba grew in yards, neighborhood gatherings and the first samba schools. Partido alto could involve playful improvised verses: imagine a musical word game with a crowd that knows when a line lands. These Afro-Brazilian traditions were once marginalized.

passages.title: Work, school and time together
passages.text: Carnival has never been one identical party across Brazil. IPHAN recognizes distinct traditions including samba, frevo and maracatu. Friends and neighbors made costumes, songs and processions together; the local gathering matters as much as the big parade.

passages.title: Medicine, water and the bathroom question
passages.text: In 1904 Rio faced a deadly smallpox outbreak. Oswaldo Cruz backed mandatory vaccination, but coercive enforcement and mistrust helped ignite the Revolt of the Vaccine. Medicine worked best when people could trust how it was offered; the revolt was also about power and daily bodily privacy.

passages.title: Medicine, water and the bathroom question
passages.text: Oswaldo Cruz and colleagues built a Brazilian research institute that produced sera and investigated diseases including plague and yellow fever. Public health was laboratory work and street work: mosquitoes, rats, water and crowded housing all mattered.

passages.title: Medicine, water and the bathroom question
passages.text: The 1988 constitution says “A saúde é direito de todos e dever do Estado,” meaning “Health is everyone’s right and the state’s duty.” That short original Portuguese line became a guiding principle for the public health system, SUS.

passages.title: Medicine, water and the bathroom question
passages.text: Brazil’s national health council traces SUS to sanitary reform and the 1986 health conference as well as the 1988 constitution. It was built through public argument and institutions, not invented by a single doctor overnight.

passages.title: Medicine, water and the bathroom question
passages.text: Toilets tell a serious story. In the 2022 census, 97.8% of people lived in a home with a bathroom for that household, while 62.5% had sewer collection. So “has a toilet” and “waste is safely carried away” are different questions, even now.

passages.title: Rights, languages and continuity
passages.text: From 1964 to 1985 Brazil was governed by a military dictatorship. State censorship, arrest, torture and disappearances harmed families; archives preserve evidence of those abuses. Saying “the economy grew” cannot erase what happened to dissidents.

passages.title: Rights, languages and continuity
passages.text: The 1988 constitution recognized Indigenous peoples’ social organization, customs, languages and original rights to traditionally occupied lands. Those rights concern living peoples; a single national border cannot show their territories or experiences.

passages.title: Rights, languages and continuity
passages.text: Portuguese is the language of the constitutional sentence shown here, but it is not Brazil’s only language. The 2022 census documented hundreds of Indigenous languages and many children still hear and use languages at home that a national map does not label.

passages.title: Rights, languages and continuity
passages.text: Brazil continues as a republic. Its empire ended in 1889 and dictatorships ended, but Indigenous peoples, quilombola communities, regional cultures and the wider population carried their histories forward. Border polygons are a starting view, not a verdict on whose land it was.

Brazil continues as a republic. The empire ended in 1889, and later authoritarian regimes ended, but the country and its diverse peoples did not. The imported 1878 map start is later than independence and cannot validate every historic or Indigenous boundary.

sectionTitles: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
A port for journeys across the Atlantic
Households, school and a portrait before cameras

passages.text: Bremen was a free trading city on the Weser. The imported 1715 to 1878 interval is incomplete: French rule interrupted independence, and the city continued afterward. The small outline also omits its later port at Bremerhaven.

passages.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
passages.text: Bremen’s imperial recognition as a free city dated to 1646, before this entry begins. A settlement at Stade in 1741 resolved remaining disputes with neighboring Hanover over its status. Even a trading republic needed treaties: ships and merchants benefited when the city could defend its right to govern itself.

passages.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
passages.text: In 1810 the Hanseatic cities were annexed to Napoleon’s empire, and Bremen became the center of the Department of the Weser Mouths. Its restored government later joined the German Confederation in 1815. This interruption matters: a continuously colored map shape does not mean the same government remained in charge throughout.

passages.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
passages.text: The revolution of 1848 brought a parliamentary election in which male citizens aged twenty-five and over could, in principle, vote on equal terms. A new constitution followed in 1849, giving the elected assembly legislative powers alongside the Senate. This was an expansion of participation, but citizenship, age and sex still limited it.

passages.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
passages.text: The gains did not all last. Opponents within Bremen’s leadership sought support from the restored German Confederation, and in 1854 a revised constitution reversed equal voting rights among citizens and strengthened the Senate. The city’s own modern account treats this as a rollback, rather than a smooth march toward democracy.

passages.title: Rights, rulers and a city’s printed words
passages.text: Writing sample: “Sammlung der Verordnungen und Proclame” means “Collection of ordinances and proclamations.” These German words begin the title of the Senate’s printed legal series, including its 1849 volume preserved by Bremen’s State and University Library. The old spelling Proclame survives in the title; publication date and dates of individual orders must be checked separately.

passages.title: A port for journeys across the Atlantic
passages.text: The Weser’s silting made access for seagoing ships a persistent problem. In 1827 Bremen acquired land from Hanover near the river mouth and began building Bremerhaven. This separate port gave the city an outlet nearer the open sea, changing the geography of a state whose interests stretched well beyond its old streets.

passages.title: A port for journeys across the Atlantic
passages.text: Bremerhaven’s emigrants’ house opened in April 1850 for people waiting to sail overseas. It could lodge up to 2,000 people, while a steam-equipped kitchen could prepare 3,500 portions. Sailors and dockworkers also ate there. Those figures describe its capacity, but they convey the scale of feeding a temporary community.

passages.title: A port for journeys across the Atlantic
passages.text: The emigrants’ house had nine large dormitories arranged rather like a ship’s between-decks accommodation, with bunks intended for three or four people. Washing rooms stood before the dormitories, and medical rooms offered care. Travel involved waiting, sharing space and staying healthy before passengers had even crossed the ocean.

passages.title: Households, school and a portrait before cameras
passages.text: Bremen’s territory also contained rural households. The surviving Mittelsbüren farmhouse was built in 1586 or 1587 and remained part of village life for centuries. Its hall and open Flett hearth illustrate a setting where cooking and warmth centered on a fire; separate living, sleeping and kitchen areas were later additions.

passages.title: Households, school and a portrait before cameras
passages.text: When Bremen senator Johann Smidt visited Paris in 1811, he tried a fashionable mechanical portrait process. A device helped trace his profile, after which an engraver made reduced prints. Smidt complained that the result did not look like him and tried another artist in 1814. Disappointing portraits certainly existed before awkward photographs.

passages.title: Households, school and a portrait before cameras
passages.text: Bremen introduced state compulsory schooling in 1844. The School Museum studies that change through teaching equipment, schoolbooks, photographs and written records. These sources make it possible to investigate how rules about attendance became part of childhood, rather than assuming every child had always received the same education.

passages.title: Households, school and a portrait before cameras
passages.text: The water tower completed on the Stadtwerder in 1873 looks like a brick castle, but its corner turrets had practical jobs. Two served as steam-engine chimneys, one contained stairs, and another held the rising and falling water pipes. The 47-meter structure wrapped water-supply machinery in an unusually grand architectural coat.

Bremen joined the North German Confederation in 1867 and became a constituent state of the German Empire in 1871, surrendering its separate foreign-policy role. The city continued beyond 1878; the imported endpoint marks no destruction or disappearance of its people.

sectionTitles: The pots that fed a town
When the town paid for visitors
Cloth and connections across the sea

passages.text: Medieval Brittany grew through changing kingdoms and a duchy on the Atlantic edge of Europe. Its towns, farms and multilingual communities supported an ambitious ducal court. The imported outline omits Nantes and parts of the historical duchy. Its 800 to 1600 span includes independent rule and the period after union with France.

passages.title: A palace with practical engineering
passages.text: Jean IV’s castle of the Hermine at Vannes, begun around 1380, combined residence and fortification. Excavation recovered decorated floor tiles and substantial walls. Palace comfort depended on builders, carpenters and water engineers as much as impressive heraldry.

passages.title: A palace with practical engineering
passages.text: Castle latrines had passages separating them from living spaces. Waste conduits ran through the walls toward pits and the moat. A grand address did not remove the need to think about where the toilet went, or what happened afterwards.

passages.title: A palace with practical engineering
passages.text: Water diverted from the Marle powered a mill integrated into the castle. Wet deposits preserved wooden objects, while excavators also found tableware, rings, jew’s harps and a bone recorder fragment. The palace’s remains include work, meals and music.

passages.title: The pots that fed a town
passages.text: Potters at Chartres-de-Bretagne supplied Rennes from the late tenth century, expanding production strongly in the eleventh to thirteenth centuries. Local raw materials produced pale, hard pottery well suited to cooking. Everyday technical choices helped fill thousands of kitchens.

passages.title: The pots that fed a town
passages.text: A rounded cooking pot called an oule could prepare food over heat. Jugs carried and poured liquids, while bowls helped with food preparation and dairy products. The medieval pottery range was practical rather than a table setting with a special dish for every course.

passages.title: The pots that fed a town
passages.text: Excavators found masses of pottery spoiled during firing at the workshops. These rejected pieces reveal what the potters made and how they worked. A failed pot could be bad news for its maker but excellent evidence for an archaeologist.

passages.title: When the town paid for visitors
passages.text: Rennes’s fifteenth-century accounts record the practical cost of receiving ambassadors: lodging, transport, firewood, candles and even laundry. In 1475 some English visitors stayed with residents and others in inns. Diplomacy created plenty of work away from the negotiating table.

passages.title: When the town paid for visitors
passages.text: Official banquets might serve many kinds of meat, fish during fasting periods, sauces, pastries and seasonal fruit. These were expensive displays for important guests. They describe courtly hospitality rather than the daily dinner of a Breton farming family.

passages.title: When the town paid for visitors
passages.text: Bread could accompany the food or serve as an edible support in place of a plate. Musicians and entertainers appeared between courses. The accounts let us glimpse the occasion, though they do not preserve every seating plan or number of guests.

passages.title: Words in three languages
passages.text: A dictionary printed at Tréguier on 5 November 1499 describes itself as “en troys langaiges”, meaning “in three languages”. This historical French wording comes from the Catholicon’s title. Its three languages were Breton, French and Latin, a useful combination in a multilingual society.

passages.title: Words in three languages
passages.text: The Catholicon connects manuscript scholarship with early printing: Jehan Lagadec supplied the text and Jehan Calvez printed the 1499 edition. A dictionary made words easier to compare and study. It also reminds us that the language spoken at home need not match the language of a learned book.

passages.title: Cloth and connections across the sea
passages.text: By the fifteenth century, fine linen from the area around Quintin, Uzel and Loudéac travelled to Spain. Castilian merchants settled in Nantes and built family connections through marriage and godparenthood. Maritime trade involved households and relationships as well as cargo.

Union with France in 1532 turned the duchy into a province while preserving its territorial identity and particular institutions. Breton communities and languages continued. The imported endpoint 1600 is a map interval, not the disappearance of Brittany.

sectionTitles: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology

passages.text: British Guiana was formed in 1831 by joining British-controlled Demerara-Essequibo and Berbice, in present-day Guyana. Its earlier history involved Dutch colonies. The imported 1783 to 1914 dates are not the colony’s lifespan, and the associated outline chiefly covers neighbouring Suriname, so it is not an accurate map of this colony.

passages.title: Power, labour and freedom
passages.text: Britain kept the Dutch-origin Court of Policy after taking control. British Guiana’s political institutions therefore combined successive colonial inheritances. The 1831 union created one colony from administrations whose settlement and governing structures were already much older.

passages.title: Power, labour and freedom
passages.text: The 1834 abolition legislation did not immediately end compulsory work for everyone. Under “apprenticeship,” many people still owed unpaid labour to former enslavers for most of the working week. Full emancipation in the colony followed on 1 August 1838.

passages.title: Power, labour and freedom
passages.text: Resistance continued during that transition. In August 1834, Damon led an uprising on the Essequibo coast against the new labour arrangements. Colonial forces suppressed it and executed him. People subjected to plantation rule actively challenged what officials called a gradual path to freedom.

passages.title: Power, labour and freedom
passages.text: In 1839, eighty-three formerly enslaved people pooled money to buy Plantation Northbrook, later called Victoria. They paid 30,000 guilders. This collective purchase gave families a place to build a community beyond the plantation labour system, a concrete achievement after emancipation.

passages.title: Power, labour and freedom
passages.text: Indian indentured migration brought another major population to the colony. Guyana’s surviving registers cover arrivals from 1838 to 1917. Their personal details help descendants recover family histories from a labour system designed to supply cheap contracted workers.

passages.title: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology
passages.text: Georgetown’s layout still records its plantation origins. Canals once divided long plantation strips running away from the river, while a connecting raised street linked settlements and military grounds. Urban geography can preserve an older agricultural plan beneath later buildings.

passages.title: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology
passages.text: Former plantations became neighbourhoods through a grid of streets. Some canals survived, while those on Church Street and Hadfield Street were filled in during the early twentieth century to make more space. A growing city reshaped the waterways inherited from its past.

passages.title: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology
passages.text: An Akawaio cassava press collected near the Essequibo River in 1913 to 1916 survives in the Smithsonian. Its plaited plant-fibre tube illustrates a clever basketry principle: stretching the tube narrows it, squeezing the grated root inside. Skilled weaving created a working food-processing machine.

passages.title: Canals, neighbourhoods and Indigenous food technology
passages.text: A Guyanese cassava sieve dated around 1910 uses cane, wood, cordage and dye. Such tools separated coarse pieces from prepared meal. The museum attributes this example only tentatively to a Carib community; its careful weaving nevertheless preserves an individual maker’s practical skill.

passages.title: A tiny printed survivor
passages.text: When imported stamps ran short in 1856, Georgetown’s newspaper printers produced an emergency supply. One-cent stamps served newspaper postage and four-cent stamps domestic letters. Clerks initialled the locally printed stamps to discourage forgery: a handwritten safeguard on a mass-produced object.

passages.title: A tiny printed survivor
passages.text: In 1873, twelve-year-old Vernon Vaughan found an 1856 one-cent stamp among his uncle’s papers. That surviving scrap became famous among collectors. An ordinary postal object, spotted by a child, preserves evidence of the colony’s printers, currency and communications.

passages.title: A tiny printed survivor
passages.text: The stamp carries the Latin motto “Damus Petimus Que Vicissim.” Translation: “We give and we ask in return.” The Smithsonian’s infrared-image description records the wording, normally difficult to read against the dark magenta paper. It is an authentic printed colonial sample.

British Guiana became independent Guyana on 26 May 1966. The imported endpoint of 1914 does not mark the end of British rule. This card describes the historical colony named by the record; its mismatched map polygon must not be treated as an accurate boundary.

sectionTitles: A small word for the stars

passages.text: Early medieval Armorica became a meeting place of local communities and migrants from Britain. Broërec was a particular region around Vannes within this wider story, not another name for the whole peninsula. The imported Broërec outline is misplaced far to the northwest; it should not be used as a reliable border.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: Similarities among Breton, Welsh and Cornish place names and languages support migration from Britain in the late fifth and sixth centuries. Its scale is debated: newcomers could influence existing communities without every family arriving on a boat.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: The council of Tours in 567 distinguished Romans and Bretons living in Armorica. That is unusually clear evidence in a period with few written records. The peninsula contained interacting communities rather than a single population with one simple origin story.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Broërec belonged to the country around Vannes, between the Ellé and Vilaine rivers. The name is associated with Waroc. Geography mattered: this southeastern Breton region faced different neighbours and political pressures from communities at the peninsula’s western tip.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Under Carolingian rule, Vannes, Rennes and Nantes formed parts of a frontier march. Broërec later entered the larger Breton political world. The county’s territory eventually passed into the ducal domain, while its bishopric and regional identity continued.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: At Lenn Sec’h in Caudan, archaeologists uncovered a farm used during the sixth to ninth centuries. Its enclosure covered about 5,300 square metres, bounded by substantial ditches. These traces give us a household landscape beyond the better-known stories of rulers and saints.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: Pits at the Caudan farm were used to dry grain before it went into underground storage. A large, deep silo also survived. Getting the harvest safely through the year required planning after the cutting and gathering were finished.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: One medieval building at Caudan was constructed on ground-level timber sills. The surrounding ditches reached roughly two metres in width and depth. Most of the building itself has disappeared, but the excavated layout still reveals how the farm was organised.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: At Landévennec, excavation found a small early oratory surrounded by a cemetery. The monastery’s beginnings belong around the turn of the fifth and sixth centuries. The traditional story of Guénolé and eleven disciples is a founding legend, while the buildings provide physical evidence.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: By the ninth century, after the earlier map phases, Landévennec’s monks copied books and followed the Rule of Benedict. A religious community could also be a centre of learning and a substantial landholder. Copying a book meant sustained skilled work by hand.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: The excavated ninth-century monastery included a church, living buildings and a courtyard edged by a covered gallery. A Viking raid in 913 interrupted its flourishing life. Its long history helps connect the small early foundation with the more elaborate institutions that followed.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: In Pierre-Yves Lambert’s reading, the Old Breton word “nimer” means “constellation”. It appears above a Latin star-name in Angers manuscript 477, folio 14b. This is the scholarly transcription of an attested word in Latin letters; another scholar interpreted it as “number”.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: The relevant part of Angers 477 was written in 897 and contains many Breton notes beside Latin learning. Scholars identify Breton scribes but debate where they worked. The book therefore illustrates later Breton scholarship and its connections, rather than a securely located school in early Broërec.

Armorica and Broërec did not vanish when these map intervals ended. Local political structures became part of wider Breton kingdoms and the duchy. The Vannes region retained a recognisable identity through those changes.

sectionTitles: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
Railways and vegetables with longer journeys

passages.text: Brunswick, or Braunschweig, was a northern German duchy ruled by the Welf family, earlier commonly called Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. This record covers 1783 to 1878, including the interruption of ducal rule under Napoleon’s Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813. Its imported outline is seriously incomplete: it shows southern pieces while omitting the capital, Braunschweig, and the northern core. The narrative describes the historical duchy, whose monarchy survived until 1918.

passages.title: Rulers and a restless capital
passages.text: In 1830 angry townspeople drove Duke Karl II from Braunschweig and set his palace on fire. The replacement residence was a nineteenth-century building, not the same palace restored unchanged. The palace museum preserves a history in which relations between ruler and residents could become a crisis in the streets.

passages.title: Rulers and a restless capital
passages.text: The constitution issued on 12 October 1832 kept hereditary monarchy but established a representative chamber. The State Archives preserve a large file of drafts, additions and discussions from its preparation. A constitution emerged through argument and revision; the surviving paperwork lets historians examine that process instead of relying only on a duke’s portrait.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: In 1835 the Collegium Carolinum divided teaching into technical, commercial and humanistic departments. The commercial course prepared future merchants, while the humanistic section helped students prepare for university. A school serving a small state could connect literary education with the practical needs of business and engineering.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: The institution became a polytechnic school in 1862. Applicants had to be at least sixteen and demonstrate adequate knowledge before enrolling. Subjects included engineering, mechanical construction, chemical technology, pharmacy and forestry. Some specialized courses later closed when they proved uneconomic, so even an ambitious technical school had to balance its plans against its resources.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: The duke supported Carl Friedrich Gauss with a scholarship that continued after his return to Braunschweig in 1798. In 1801 Gauss’s calculations helped astronomers find Ceres again after observations of the small planet had been interrupted. His work joined abstract mathematics with the practical problem of knowing where to point a telescope.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: Writing sample: in a letter sent from Braunschweig to Wilhelm Olbers on 8 April 1803, Gauss hoped “einst das ganze Land mit einem Dreiecksnetz zu beziehen,” meaning “one day to cover the whole country with a network of triangles.” This German sentence, transcribed in the university library’s catalog, describes his plan to map the land through measured angles and connected survey points.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: A state railway linked Braunschweig and Wolfenbüttel in 1838. When agreement with neighboring states over joint planning proved difficult, the duchy built its own line. Railway workshops and manufacturers followed. Trains needed more than rails: repairs, machines and eventually signaling equipment helped create work around the new transport system.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: Sugar-beet cultivation expanded around 1850, supplying factories in the surrounding countryside. By the 1870s Braunschweig had a school for the sugar industry. Making sugar involved farming, machinery and technical learning as well as boiling something sweet. Local machine builders adapted their work to the needs of sugar processing.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: Asparagus was difficult to ship fresh over long distances. Around 1850, preserving it in tins helped growers sell it beyond its short harvest season, and local cultivation expanded. A vegetable that had to be eaten quickly could now wait on a shelf. Braunschweig’s fields and canning businesses grew together.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: An older water system brought spring water into Braunschweig through wooden pipes, following the slope of the ground. It supplied public fountains on market squares and remained in use into the nineteenth century, until the new central waterworks took over in 1865. Water infrastructure could be centuries old while still serving everyday needs.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: The new waterworks entered full operation on 1 January 1865. It treated Oker river water in settling and filter basins, then used steam pumps to send it into a cast-iron network. Industrial wastewater had helped make the old arrangements inadequate. Growing industry created jobs and also forced the city to rethink its water supply.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: The waterworks’ 54-metre tower, roughly 177 feet, resembled a Gothic church tower. Inside, it concealed a chimney and tall water pipes that helped balance pressure when pumping changed. The impressive exterior housed a very practical job: making the flow in the pipes steadier.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: A report from the second half of the nineteenth century describes severe crowding in the Klint neighborhood, a date range that may extend beyond this map’s 1878 cutoff. In some buildings twenty to thirty people shared one toilet, and cesspits stood near water outlets. These were documented conditions in a poor district, not the arrangements of every home in the duchy.

The revolution of 8 November 1918 ended ducal rule and Brunswick became a Free State. Some institutions continued: the regional court kept working under its new republican name without an immediate replacement of its staff. The imported cutoff at 1878 therefore predates the monarchy’s actual end by forty years.
