passages.text: Buganda grew around the Kabaka, chiefs and clans in the Lake Victoria region. Its history can also be read in barkcloth workshops, the wooden architecture of Kasubi and recordings of court musicians. Royal government changed under colonial rule and was later abolished; Baganda cultural life and a restored royal institution continue.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: Kasubi's palace became a royal burial ground in 1884. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, used a circular plan, a domed thatched roof and wooden supports. Monumental architecture here depended on skilled work with plant materials, rather than masonry.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: The documented interior combined palm-frond structural rings with long poles wrapped in barkcloth. A drum house and gatehouse faced the courtyard. These details connect construction, textile work and ceremonial movement within one royal compound.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: After the destructive 2010 fire, restoration drew on surviving building knowledge as well as documentation. Kasubi left UNESCO's danger list in 2023. Conservation work announced in 2026 addresses disaster preparation, site management and community participation.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Craftspeople harvest the Mutuba tree's inner bark in the wet season and beat it with wooden mallets. Working under an open shed keeps it from drying too quickly. Repeated skilled handling produces a soft sheet from bark, without weaving threads.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Barkcloth served as bedding, curtains, storage material and clothing as well as ceremonial dress. Its household uses place the craft within ordinary work and comfort, alongside the royal and funerary settings in which it remains especially visible.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: UNESCO identifies Ngonge clan craftspeople and a hereditary chief craftsman as custodians of this knowledge. Imported cotton reduced demand during the nineteenth century. Continued ceremonial use and later promotion helped sustain skills through a changing textile economy.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The 2021 album Buganda Royal Music Revival places archival sessions beside recordings made in 2017. Its credits name recordists and dates, allowing listeners to distinguish historical documentation from later performances rather than treating all tracks as one ancient sound.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The collection includes the endongo lyre, the large akadinda xylophone and an entenga ensemble of tuned drums. These are different approaches to melody, resonance and ensemble coordination, not interchangeable examples of drumming.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: Performers credited include lyre player Albert Bisaso Ssempeke and royal harpist Temutewo Mukasa. Naming musicians preserves individual artistic work within a court tradition too often described only through kings and ceremonies.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: The Lukiiko developed from advisory councils of chiefs and clan heads. Its organization changed during the nineteenth century and under the 1900 agreement. Its present cultural and consultative role should not be projected unchanged onto earlier royal government.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: Article 118 of Uganda's 1967 constitution explicitly abolished royal offices. For Buganda it made that provision effective from 24 May 1966. This distinction explains why histories mention both years when describing the suppression of the kingdom.

Buganda's royal political institutions were suppressed during the 1966 crisis and the constitutional changes of 1967. Their restoration in 1993 established a cultural role within Uganda. Baganda communities, crafts and music continued across that interruption; the map's final snapshot is not their disappearance.

They do not describe one unchanging population. Volga Bulgaria followed a separate history. Later Balkan art and books belong to the explicitly dated periods below.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: The early-eighth-century Madara Rider shows a horseman above a fallen lion on a high rock face. Its setting made a ruler's image part of the landscape. It is a royal monument, not evidence that villagers routinely went lion hunting.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Inscriptions beside the rider record events associated with rulers including Tervel and Omurtag. Text and image together provide evidence for early Bulgarian political memory; the cliff is more than a giant picture frame.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Boris I's adoption of Christianity in the 860s transformed official religious institutions. It did not instantly replace every household practice or erase the older histories of the people living in the state.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Early Bulgar cemeteries at Balchik, Novi Pazar, Kyulevcha and Topola contained ceramic jugs, bowls and other table vessels. Scholars compare their shapes with metal, glass and wooden examples from wider Eurasian traditions. Similar shape alone does not prove a pot was imported.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Four pottery kilns at the early medieval settlement of Topola demonstrate production, not just consumption. The study associates these vessel traditions especially with the first half and middle of the 700s. Someone had to make the dishes before anyone could argue about washing them.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Preslav excavations recovered agricultural and craft tools alongside pots, cups, bowls and amphoras. These ordinary objects connect the capital to food production and skilled work, rather than only to the activities of its rulers.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: The Preslav museum distinguishes locally produced pottery from vessels imported from Byzantium. A household could use objects with different production histories; an imported container does not by itself tell us who lived in the house.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Earrings, bracelets and rings at Preslav include copper, bronze and silver examples, with glass, amber and other materials also represented. Dressing up had a much wider material range than gold treasure alone suggests.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: A gold ring found at Pliska has a split and thinned ends that may reflect resizing. Its human portrait cannot be securely named. The wear and adjustments suggest an object with a history of use, not simply an untouched badge of a famous king.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: At Patleina near Preslav, excavations in 1909 found fragments of a tenth-century ceramic portrait of St Theodore. Its large face was assembled from square tiles about 12 centimetres across: a carefully planned image made from separate fired pieces.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Monastic workshops around Preslav made painted tiles for churches and palaces. The saint portrait uses dark outlines, coloured slips and glaze. Archaeological workshop discoveries support local production, rather than assuming that every impressive object came from Byzantium.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Early Bulgarian inscriptions describe elite gifts and feasting. A recent study interprets these occasions as ways to display rank and strengthen personal ties. Royal hospitality was political work; it is not a menu for the average family.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: In 1355-1356 the monk Simeon copied a lavish Gospel book for Tsar Ivan Alexander. Its parchment pages carry Slavonic text in Cyrillic. The manuscript's named scribe gives us a specific person behind the broad label “medieval learning.”

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: The same book uses gold for chapter titles in its margins and red for directions used in worship. Colour helped readers navigate the text. These are features of an expensive royal commission, not evidence that every household owned illustrated books.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: A royal family portrait opens the Gospel book, while a word puzzle on folio 273v encodes Ivan Alexander's name. A medieval book could combine sacred reading, family image-making and an elaborate puzzle.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: Κανα συβιγι Ωμουρταγ is the ruler's title and name, conventionally rendered “Kan sybigi Omurtag.” It begins a ninth-century Greek funerary inscription for Turdatzis on limestone. The sample follows the scholarly transcription, joining a line break. The title is Bulgar vocabulary written in Greek letters, not modern Bulgarian.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: The inscriptions studied by Matilde Casas Olea preserve forms of ninth-century everyday Greek rather than only polished literary language. They show how Bulgarian rulers used a neighbouring written language in their new Balkan setting.

Byzantine conquest ended the first Bulgarian kingdom in 1018. Renewed Bulgarian rule emerged in the 1180s, and Ottoman conquest ended the later medieval kingdoms in the late 1300s. Bulgarian communities, religious life and literary traditions continued. Neither the map's 1000 change of label nor its 1400 boundary is a disappearance of a people.

passages.text: This record covers modern Bulgaria from the state established in 1878 through monarchy, communist government and parliamentary democracy. It is distinct from the medieval Bulgar labels. Buildings, scientific work and living community traditions show how political change intersected with education, food and daily life.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: The Tarnovo Constitution of 1879 set the framework for Bulgaria's early parliamentary institutions. Its operation was interrupted during authoritarian periods, so the existence of a constitution did not mean uninterrupted democratic government.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: The National Assembly building, designed by Constantin Jovanovic and constructed in 1884-1886, made the new institutions physically visible in Sofia. Its neo-Renaissance design belongs to a wider European architectural conversation.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia united in 1885; Ferdinand declared independence in 1908. These were separate steps, which is why the map's 1878 beginning should not be read as the date when every question of sovereignty was settled.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: In March 1943, Bulgarian authorities deported more than 11,000 Jews from occupied Macedonia, Thrace and Pirot into German custody; almost all were murdered at Treblinka. This responsibility is part of the country's wartime history.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: Public and political protests helped stop deportations from Bulgaria's core provinces, but Jews there still endured discriminatory laws, forced labour, dispossession and internal expulsion. Survival and persecution must both be remembered.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: After the Second World War, the communist government nationalized businesses and forced farmland into cooperatives. Changes of ownership and work reached into family routines, rather than remaining only a story about leaders.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: Chitalishta are community cultural centres, first established in 1856, before modern statehood. Communities created places for learning and cultural activities; older members continue to pass knowledge and skills to younger participants.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: These centres organize performances, celebrations, exhibitions and local documentation. Their collaboration with schools joins formal lessons with skills learned by doing. Learning continues outside the classroom through community activities.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: For the beginning of March, people exchange and wear red-and-white thread ornaments associated with wishes for a safe spring. The tradition is shared across several neighbouring countries, not exclusively Bulgarian.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: A first blossom, swallow or stork can signal that it is time to remove the thread. Families, teachers and craftworkers pass on the making skills. Nature gets a say in the calendar: the stork does not need a smartphone reminder.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: Stamen Grigorov investigated the microbes in Bulgarian yogurt in 1905. The achievement was explaining fermentation already practiced by food makers, not inventing yogurt from nothing.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: The Serdica dairy in Sofia introduced mechanized pasteurization for industrial yogurt production in 1960. The producer's history describes earlier cauldrons, starter cultures and reusable containers, connecting laboratory knowledge with the practical work of feeding people.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: Sofia's Central Mineral Baths were built in 1906-1913, with colourful majolica decoration. Their architects treated a place for washing as an important civic building. The former bath now houses the regional history museum: the building itself is one of its historical objects.

passages.title: A small sample of Bulgarian
passages.text: България е република с парламентарно управление. This means “Bulgaria is a republic with a parliamentary form of government.” It is Article 1(1) of the 1991 Constitution, written in modern Bulgarian using Cyrillic, not a medieval inscription.

Bulgaria continues as a sovereign parliamentary republic. The monarchy's end in 1946 and the transition from communist rule beginning in 1989 were changes of government, not the disappearance of the country. It joined the European Union in 2007.

passages.text: Bunyoro in western Uganda connected royal institutions with farming, exchange and specialist production. At Kibiro, pottery and living salt-working practices reveal a history beyond royal genealogies. British conquest reshaped the kingdom; later abolition and cultural restoration of the monarchy are separate from the continuing lives of Banyoro communities.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Excavations at Kibiro on Lake Albert uncovered abundant pottery associated with a salt-producing settlement. In his 1991 report, Graham Connah placed the origins of this important economic center early in the second millennium CE. This is evidence about a settlement and livelihood, not a secure founding date for Bunyoro.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Many Kibiro pots carried patterns impressed with roulettes, including carved rollers. Connah interpreted these as connections toward the upper Nile or regions farther west. Similar decoration supports comparison and contact; it does not by itself identify the makers' language or ethnicity.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Uganda's heritage submission identifies pottery used in leaching and boiling salt. Broken vessels therefore preserve traces of an industrial process as well as decorative choices. Its broad dates are less precise than a dated excavation context and should be used cautiously.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: At Kibiro, workers spread and recycle earth over salt gardens so saline water rises into it. They collect the salty material, leach it and boil the resulting liquid to crystallize salt. The sequence combines knowledge of soil, water and heat.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Women carry out the salt work and inherit rights to garden plots through female relationships. These arrangements tie expertise to access to a productive place. Fishing complements salt production in the lakeshore economy.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Kibiro was proposed on Uganda's World Heritage Tentative List in 2025. That proposal documents a living workplace, not simply an abandoned ruin. Tentative status is distinct from inscription on the World Heritage List.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: Empaako is an additional name used among Banyoro and neighboring communities. Addressing someone by this name can express affection and respect or ease tension. It identifies a relationship between people rather than merely distinguishing one individual from another.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: In UNESCO's documented naming ceremony, paternal aunts consider the child's resemblance to relatives and the clan head announces the name. A meal of millet and smoked beef, gifts and a planted tree follow. Household ritual joins kinship with food and obligations of care.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: The tradition entered UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2013 because transmission and use of its associated language were weakening. Recognition concerns support for a living practice; it does not mean that the community or naming tradition had ended.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: The British-Buganda coalition defeated and deported Kabarega in 1899. Colonial incorporation and the transfer of territory changed the scale and authority of Bunyoro. These events concerned a political kingdom whose people and dynasty continued afterward.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: Historian G. N. Uzoigwe interprets Bunyoro's contraction through interacting causes: decisions by rulers, disease affecting people and animals, and violent British conquest. This is a historical argument about a long crisis, not evidence for one battle explaining every loss.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: In the 1964 referendum, voters in Buyaga and Bugangaizi chose a return to Bunyoro after their earlier transfer to Buganda under colonial rule. The vote shows that territorial change also involved local political choices, not only decisions made at royal courts.

Conquest in the late nineteenth century ended Bunyoro's independent political power. Uganda abolished kingship in 1967, and the monarchy returned with cultural functions in 1994. Banyoro communities and practices continued through those changes. Neither the salt village's age nor the map's last snapshot establishes a single lifetime for the kingdom.

passages.text: This map label fits the kingdom of Burgundy and Arles, linking the Rhône valley with lands around western Switzerland and Alpine passes. It is distinct from the duchy centred on Dijon. The imported outline is approximate and continues long after the independent royal dynasty ended.

passages.title: Ruling a country of routes
passages.text: Control of Alpine passes made Burgundy valuable to emperors travelling toward Italy. Royal estates lay among counties, while bishops received political powers. The kingdom was held together through relationships, land and strategic roads rather than one uniform administration.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: At Colletière beside Lake Paladru, early eleventh-century families lived inside a timber enclosure. Three wooden buildings, a workshop and livestock facilities survive archaeologically. Waterlogged conditions preserved wood, seeds and leather that would normally rot away, giving this small community an unusually clear material record.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: Cereal grains, sickles, hooks, net floats and fish scales reveal farming and fishing. Animal bones show different foods in the main house and smaller buildings. Researchers interpret those differences as signs of social rank within the settlement, rather than a single menu shared by everyone.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: Colletière also produced chess pieces and musical instruments, including a bowed instrument called a vielle. Its inhabitants had tools for weaving, carpentry and metalworking. Work filled much of life, but the surviving objects leave room for music and a board-game argument too.

passages.title: Small feet, skilled hands
passages.text: A tiny leather shoe from Colletière belonged to a child. A small maple shoemaker’s last helped shape footwear for very young children. These objects put families into a story otherwise easily crowded with kings, mounted warriors and abbots.

passages.title: Small feet, skilled hands
passages.text: Leather offcuts show that shoes were made locally. Oak cutting templates, metal awls and tools for threading laces reveal the stages of the craft. Different models and stitching methods suggest that medieval shoemakers cared about variety as well as keeping feet covered.

passages.title: Royal women and a growing monastery
passages.text: At Payerne, the Burgundian royal family supported a religious community before the year 1000. Adelaide, daughter of Queen Bertha and herself an empress, connected it with the monastery of Cluny. Women in the dynasty helped shape institutions as well as royal family relationships.

passages.title: Royal women and a growing monastery
passages.text: Builders began Payerne’s great Romanesque church in the eleventh century. Later priors altered and embellished it. The standing building is therefore a layered achievement of masonry and patronage, not a church completed in one royal building season.

passages.title: Help at a mountain crossing
passages.text: The Great Saint Bernard hospice is securely documented from 1125, with an earlier foundation traditionally placed around 1050. Its religious community assisted pilgrims crossing the Alps. Food, shelter and spiritual care belonged together at a route where reaching the other side was a serious undertaking.

passages.title: Help at a mountain crossing
passages.text: By 1177 the hospice’s wider network counted 78 hospices, houses, priories and churches. Gifts and properties supported the work. The famous rescue dogs belong to much later evidence, so a medieval traveller should not automatically be pictured meeting one.

passages.title: A royal gift in Latin
passages.text: A charter dated 24 April 1011 names Neuchâtel as “Novum castellum”, meaning “new castle”. This is a Latin phrase preserved in the published transcription of Rudolf III’s gift to Queen Ermengarde. The original parchment survives in the Isère archives, with a royal wax seal.

passages.title: A royal gift in Latin
passages.text: The gift transferred revenues from royal estates, including the work of unfree peasants attached to them. A later note records Ermengarde’s donation to the church of Saint-Maurice in Vienne. The document links affection, property, labour and religion in one royal household’s decisions.

Rudolf III died in 1032, ending the dynasty. Incorporation into the Empire unfolded through 1038. Burgundy retained a royal title, while regional lordships increasingly shaped everyday government. Its people and settlements continued beyond this political transition.

passages.text: Burgundian rulers first established a kingdom near the Rhine, then governed a new realm around the western Alps and Rhône after Roman authorities settled survivors in Sapaudia in 443. Their subjects included established Roman provincial communities. This is the fifth- and early sixth-century kingdom, centuries before the famous medieval duchy of Burgundy.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: A Roman-law collection compiled in the Burgundian kingdom borrowed from earlier Roman legislation rather than starting law from scratch. Modern scholarship places it in the early sixth century. Its subjects include inheritance, sales, contracts and guardianship: royal government reached into household affairs.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: Its guardianship rules gave a willing mother priority over other prospective guardians. This concerns legal management for children, especially their property. It recognizes a maternal role without establishing equal legal standing for all women.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: The collection required a seller to stand by a completed sale. Market exchanges could become courtroom arguments when someone wanted a bargain undone. These rules reveal lawmakers’ intentions, rather than how every village transaction worked.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: One provision required compensation when someone deliberately frightened a horse so badly that it died. Denying an offense and then being proved responsible increased the payment. Working animals mattered enough for a very particular dispute to enter a legal handbook.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: The courts’ calendar made room for harvesting and grape gathering as well as Christian festivals. Ordinary lawsuits were forbidden during these breaks, although fiscal business had an exception. Even legal paperwork had to reckon with the farming year.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: The cemetery at Sézegnin near Geneva contained more than 700 burials spanning the late fourth to eighth centuries. That long sequence crosses the Burgundian kingdom’s rise and conquest. It lets archaeologists investigate communities over generations rather than treating every grave as a separate incoming people.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Regional excavations distinguish earth graves, wooden burial containers and later stone constructions. Changes in materials and arrangement help date funerary practices. A stone-lined grave tells us about burial choices and labor; by itself it does not identify the language spoken by the person buried there.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: At Geneva’s Saint-Antoine cemetery, researchers examined people of different ages but found some of the youngest children underrepresented. A separate burial area is one possible explanation. Archaeologists cannot simply count the surviving graves and assume they represent every child born in the community.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Sigismund founded the monastery at Agaune, now Saint-Maurice, in 515. Royal support linked the dynasty to an important Christian shrine. The foundation also created an institution whose daily routines and surviving records outlasted the independent kingdom.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Agaune became known for continual praise, with groups of monks taking turns singing. Think of a choir relay: the aim was continuity of worship, not requiring one exhausted singer to carry on forever. It was a demanding organized routine within this monastery.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: The abbey stood on an important Rhône route toward Alpine crossings. Its 515 inauguration is associated with a sermon by Bishop Avitus. Travel, royal ceremony and religious learning met at a specific place, rather than belonging to separate worlds.

passages.title: A few words from their legal world
passages.text: The Latin heading “De tutelis minorum” means “On the guardianship of minors.” It appears as title 36 of the Roman-law collection transmitted from the kingdom. This is administrative Latin preserved through manuscript copying, not a reconstructed sentence in the poorly documented Burgundian vernacular.

Frankish armies defeated the kingdom in 532, and Frankish rulers divided it in 534. Communities, laws and religious institutions continued after royal independence ended. The map’s 600 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not the date of the conquest.

passages.text: The imported record starts in 1945, when this area was under French rule. Upper Volta had been dissolved as a separate colony in 1932 and was restored in 1947, so the 1945 outline is not evidence of an independent Burkina Faso. Independence followed in 1960; the present name dates to 1984.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: Upper Volta became independent on 5 August 1960. Its name referred to the river system; in 1984 it became Burkina Faso. The change belonged to Thomas Sankara’s revolutionary government, which had taken power the previous year.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: A dated French writing sample survives in the legislature’s report of 29 October 2024: “Unité-Progrès-Justice,” meaning “Unity-Progress-Justice.” The report quotes this as the former motto while approving its replacement. Words on official documents can change with politics, just as flags and country names do.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: Sankara was killed in the October 1987 coup that brought Blaise Compaoré to power. Much later, two coups in 2022 removed first the elected president Roch Kaboré, then the military leader Paul-Henri Damiba. These are changes of regime within a continuing country.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Francis Kéré’s first building, Gando Primary School, was completed in his home community in 2001. It tackled the practical problems of dark, overheated classrooms using locally available clay mixed with cement for stronger bricks, with an overhanging roof protecting the walls from rain.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: At Gando, the metal roof sits above a separate brick ceiling. Air enters through windows and warm air escapes through openings overhead. The building does some of the cooling work itself: a lesson in engineering before the teacher has even written on the board.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Community members helped build the school, combining familiar construction skills with the architect’s engineering. Kéré’s account emphasizes methods that could also simplify future maintenance. A school building needs people who can repair it, as well as people who can design it.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: At the living royal court of Tiébélé, Kasena house shapes have social meanings. Figure-of-eight mother houses accommodate elderly residents, widows, unmarried women and children; young married people occupy rectangular houses, and adolescent or unmarried men circular ones. UNESCO documented this arrangement when the site was inscribed in 2024.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Tiébélé’s buildings use earth, wood, straw and cow dung. Men construct the houses, while women preserve and teach the knowledge of symbolic wall decoration. Older motifs coexist with new ones, learned through observation and practice: these walls belong to an active community, not an abandoned stage set.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: Farmer Yacouba Sawadogo improved traditional zaï planting pits after the droughts around 1980. Compost goes into the pits before seeds; rows of stones slow rainwater running away. He also put water pots in trees for birds that could bring seeds. Small holes helped produce very large changes.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: From 1984, Sawadogo organized seed-sharing gatherings. Farmers brought crop samples after harvest; seeds were stored at his homestead, then selected before the rains. This was experimentation shared across villages, with the next season’s meals depending on the results.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, a festival of African cinema and television. Its 2021 edition ran in October after the pandemic forced a delay. Film selection and screenings made the capital a meeting place for storytellers across borders, adding a different kind of public gathering to markets and ceremonies.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: In Dori in 2024, teenager Djeneba Dicko described how a nearby water point reduced the exhausting search for water for her family. UNICEF reported eight solar-powered supply systems. Displaced resident Nafissa Sanou managed one at Petit Paris, cleaning the collection area and reminding users about hygiene.

Burkina Faso continues as a state despite repeated changes of government and armed conflict. The two coups of 2022 ended particular governments; they did not end the country’s communities, farms, schools or cultural institutions.

passages.text: This imported label spans a kingdom, colonial administration and the modern republic. The 1815 to 1878 map outline is displaced south of Burundi and should not be read as its historical frontier. Burundi regained independence as a kingdom in 1962; the monarchy ended in 1966, while the country continued.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The kingdom had its own political traditions before colonial rule. At Kiganda in June 1903, King Mwezi Gisabo retained his kingship but accepted German sovereignty under coercive terms. A surviving king therefore did not mean that the kingdom remained fully independent.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: On 1 July 1962, the UN trusteeship administered by Belgium ended and Burundi became an independent kingdom. Four years later, Michel Micombero’s coup abolished the monarchy. These are two different turning points: the end of external rule and the end of a royal institution.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The assassination of the first democratically elected president in 1993 was followed by widespread civil war and displacement. The Arusha agreement of August 2000 was a major peace effort, but it did not instantly stop every armed group. The UN was still condemning attacks on civilians in 2001.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The 2018 constitution’s cover reads “REPUBURIKA Y’UBURUNDI,” Kirundi for “Republic of Burundi.” The French equivalent appears beside it. This is a sample from a particular written state document, in the Latin alphabet, within a society where spoken traditions also remain important.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Burundi’s heritage submission associates the Gishora royal residence with King Ntare Rugamba in the early nineteenth century. It describes separate spaces for the drum sanctuary, royal dwelling, servants and royal granaries. The annual sorghum-sowing ceremony connected political authority with the farming year.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Gishora’s roof structure was woven like an upside-down basket, then raised and supported with poles. Papyrus bindings, timber and thatch turned skilled plant work into architecture. The 2026 heritage account describes these construction techniques; it does not establish that every piece of the surviving building is nineteenth-century material.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: The royal drum performance combines synchronized percussion with dance, poetry and song. Drums form a semicircle around a central drum; some maintain a continuous beat while others follow its changing rhythm. Two or three performers dance in turn. Coordination is part of the achievement, not merely volume.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Drum-making and performance skills pass on through practice and teaching. UNESCO describes many bearers as descendants of sanctuary keepers, with performances at public celebrations and for visitors. A tradition once connected with kings can remain meaningful after the monarchy itself has ended.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: In Ruyigi in 2022, trained community workers and “Light Mothers” weighed children, recorded their growth and visited households. Their equipment included scales, height gauges, arm-measuring tapes and registers. Those small tools allowed concerns to be noticed near home and referred to a health facility.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: The same programme paired measurement with practical food discussions. Parents learned how to combine available foods rather than receiving only a number on a chart. Health workers followed up with families, showing how local experience, record-keeping and professional care could work together.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: At Kagari School in 2025, thirteen-year-old Jeannette participated in a hygiene club. She told UNICEF that reusable sanitary pads and what she learned in the club helped her stop missing lessons during her period. Privacy and ordinary supplies can affect education as directly as a textbook.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: At Gashoho Health Center, the same report found new women’s and men’s latrine blocks under construction after older facilities became unusable. Staff had hygiene supplies including soap, chlorine, protective clothing and bins. A health centre needs a clean environment around treatment rooms as well as care inside them.

Burundi’s monarchy ended on 28 November 1966, but Burundi did not disappear. The republic continues, and royal drumming survives as a living cultural practice. Political institutions, community traditions and the lives of ordinary people follow different timelines.

sectionTitles: Visitors, candles and a shared meal

passages.text: Modern Belarus became independent as the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991. The map begins in 1994, the year of its new constitution and first presidential election, rather than the beginning of Belarusian history. This card follows the republic and its people, including living crafts, learning and the political constraints on public life.

passages.title: Turning stalks into useful things
passages.text: Belarusian straw weavers make baskets, boxes, hats, toys and decorations. A material left after harvesting grain becomes a container or an intricate ornament. Modern makers develop their own designs within inherited techniques, so the craft is still changing.

passages.title: Turning stalks into useful things
passages.text: Some makers create pawuks, elaborate diamond-shaped hanging structures. Traditionally these were believed to protect a household from evil and illness. Their protective meaning belongs to religious and folk belief, while the careful geometry is visible in the object itself.

passages.title: Turning stalks into useful things
passages.text: Skills pass from parents and grandparents to younger makers, and through studios, craft centres, festivals and online teaching. Some artisans earn money from their work; others weave as a hobby. A family tradition can now travel through a screen as well as across a kitchen table.

passages.title: Visitors, candles and a shared meal
passages.text: During the first weekend of July, pilgrims gather at Budslaŭ to honour an icon of Mary. Some arrive on foot. Masses, a candlelit night procession and a youth prayer vigil bring different generations together for a shared religious occasion.

passages.title: Visitors, candles and a shared meal
passages.text: Local residents welcome pilgrims into their homes and share meals. Families pass on knowledge of the ceremony alongside crafts, customs and cooking. The festival therefore depends on hospitality and household work as well as the gathering inside the church.

passages.title: Money people handled
passages.text: Belarus replaced older banknotes during a currency redenomination in 2016. The replacement notes belonged to the 2009 series, despite entering everyday use years later. The year printed on money and the year somebody first spent it can be different.

passages.title: Money people handled
passages.text: From January 2017, the 2009-series notes and coins were the country’s sole legal tender. Banks exchanged old money without charging commission, and the National Bank taught cashiers and the public about security features. Paying for groceries also required recognising the new cash.

passages.title: Making classrooms more inclusive
passages.text: In 2017, a national resource centre for inclusive education opened at the Belarusian State Pedagogical University with UNICEF support. It trained teachers and other specialists to support children with different learning needs. Better access required practical changes in teaching, not simply a promise on paper.

passages.title: Making classrooms more inclusive
passages.text: The centre helped develop teaching and learning materials and share professional experience. Training future teachers also included ways to welcome children with diverse abilities into regular education. These were documented improvement efforts, rather than proof that every child already received the support they needed.

passages.title: Written words and public life
passages.text: The Russian title of the constitution includes “Республики Беларусь”, meaning “of the Republic of Belarus”. This is an attested Cyrillic phrase in the legal text catalogued by WIPO, here in its 2022 consolidated version. Belarusian and Russian are both official languages.

passages.title: Written words and public life
passages.text: The first presidential election took place in two rounds in June and July 1994. Alexander Lukashenka won the second round. The vote followed the new constitution, which had introduced the presidency as a central institution of the independent state.

passages.title: Written words and public life
passages.text: After the disputed presidential election in 2020, largely peaceful protests met a violent response from the authorities. UN investigators documented the crackdown. This political history affected families, students and workers alongside the country’s creative and educational life.

Belarus continues as a state. Independence in 1991 and later constitutional changes altered its political institutions; they did not end its communities or cultural traditions. The map’s starting year is a coverage choice, not a founding date.

sectionTitles: Laws, letters and a seal in Greek
Children wore clothes and maybe played
Bread, meals and clues in bones

passages.text: The empire called “Byzantine” by modern historians was the eastern Roman Empire, centred on Constantinople. Its people called themselves Romans; Greek became its main official and literary language, but its territories included many languages and communities. Across more than a thousand years, the state’s reach changed dramatically. Buildings, books, clothing, food remains and everyday written objects help us see lives beyond the court.

passages.title: Romans in a Greek-speaking empire
passages.text: “Byzantine” is the historian’s name for this eastern Roman state. Medieval inhabitants called themselves Rhomaioi, or Romans. Greek later became the principal state and church language, but people in its territories included different languages and religious communities. No child in 395 woke up to discover that their family had suddenly become “Byzantine.”

passages.title: Romans in a Greek-speaking empire
passages.text: The empire’s map shifted repeatedly. Egypt and North Africa belonged to it for part of the early period but not after the seventh-century Arab conquests; after 1204 several Byzantine governments claimed a Roman inheritance. One polygon cannot represent one unchanging border or one uniform culture.

passages.title: A city built to endure
passages.text: Constantinople’s Theodosian land walls gained a second defensive line in the fifth century; UNESCO notes a major construction stage in 447. The surviving walls are evidence of masonry, planning and repair, not a promise that no attacker could ever enter.

passages.title: A city built to endure
passages.text: After an earlier church burned, Justinian sponsored Hagia Sophia’s reconstruction from 532 to 537. UNESCO names its designers, Anthemios of Tralles and Isidoros of Miletus. Its enormous dome and later influence are remarkable, but the present World Heritage area also includes many Ottoman buildings from centuries after this empire.

passages.title: A city built to endure
passages.text: Researchers have identified at least 33 Byzantine cisterns beneath the area later enclosed by the Ottoman Topkapı Palace. Storing water was as important to a great capital as decorating its churches. These cistern remains span different dates; the count is not a census of every Byzantine neighbourhood.

passages.title: Laws, letters and a seal in Greek
passages.text: Between 529 and 534, Justinian ordered a vast reworking of Roman law. Its Code gathered imperial enactments; the Digest arranged older jurists’ writings; the Institutes introduced students to legal study. That was scholarship with practical consequences for courts, not just an emperor’s name on a thick book.

passages.title: Laws, letters and a seal in Greek
passages.text: A tenth-century lead seal of Eustathius, a deacon and patriarchal notary, was found at Hagia Sophia in Thessaloniki. The museum transcribes part of its Greek inscription as ΒΟΗΘΕΙ ΤΩ ΣΩ ΔΟΥΛΩ, “help your servant.” The full appeal begins with an abbreviated word for “Lord”; this sample preserves the Greek letters without pretending the expanded word was carved in full.

passages.title: Laws, letters and a seal in Greek
passages.text: The other side of Eustathius’s seal gives his name and church offices. A lump of lead could identify the sender of a closed document; it is a tiny trace of administration and a person, not proof that every resident read Greek or owned such a seal.

passages.title: Children wore clothes and maybe played
passages.text: A small hooded tunic from Byzantine-period Egypt, dated about 430 to 620, survives in the Met’s collection. Its coloured woven decoration gives a rare physical glimpse of a child’s clothing. It cannot tell us the wearer’s name, whether it was worn every day, or what children wore throughout the empire.

passages.title: Children wore clothes and maybe played
passages.text: A carved bone figure from Egypt, dated to the seventh to ninth century, may have been a toy. The Met also notes another possibility: an amulet connected with protection or fertility. A possible toy is fun to imagine in a child’s hand, but its actual owner and use are unknown.

passages.title: Bread, meals and clues in bones
passages.text: A fired-clay Byzantine bread stamp dated 500 to 900 could press the words “Jesus Christ Victorious” into an unbaked loaf. The Met identifies this as bread prepared for Christian worship. It shows food, craft and faith meeting on a kitchen-sized object; it is not evidence that every loaf carried a stamp.

passages.title: Bread, meals and clues in bones
passages.text: Researchers studied chemical traces in the bones of 38 people from two western Anatolian communities. Results suggest a narrower spread of diets at the inland Barcın Höyük cemetery than at coastal Kadıkalesi Anaia, whose graves belong to the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Bones give clues over years of eating, but they do not hand us a recipe or a menu for all Byzantines.

passages.title: Where did the waste go?
passages.text: At Marea in Byzantine-period Egypt, excavators found waterfront latrines with platforms beside channels that drained into a lake. This is an actual local waste system, not a claim that every Byzantine house had plumbing. The site’s major planned buildings date largely to the later sixth century.

passages.title: Where did the waste go?
passages.text: Marea also yielded a potsherd with writing about repairs to a nosokomeion, or hospital, around the turn of the sixth and seventh centuries. Archaeology and a humble written scrap together reveal care infrastructure. A mention of a hospital does not tell us who could enter it or whether a treatment worked.

passages.title: Learning and religious life
passages.text: Higher education in the capital included poetry, rhetoric, mathematics, astronomy, law and medicine. Students read ancient Greek authors such as Homer and Euclid; teachers often charged fees and sought patrons. This describes educated circles, not a school timetable shared by every Byzantine child.

passages.title: Learning and religious life
passages.text: In the later medieval empire, the church calendar shaped many people’s weeks through fasts, feasts and services, and rites marked births, marriages and deaths. Communities and personal practice varied. These repeated gatherings are part of social history, alongside palaces and battles.

passages.title: Learning and religious life
passages.text: The disputes over religious images in the eighth and early ninth centuries damaged many icons. After 843 the use of icons returned, and artisans made manuscripts, enamels, carved ivories and domed churches. The surviving objects show choices by patrons and makers; their beauty should not hide the conflict around them.

passages.title: An empire interrupted, then ended
passages.text: In 1204 the Fourth Crusade captured Constantinople and installed Latin rulers. Byzantine courts continued elsewhere, especially at Nicaea, Epirus and Trebizond; the Nicaean rulers retook the capital in 1261. A “Byzantine Empire” label across those years hides competing states and a city under different rule.

passages.title: An empire interrupted, then ended
passages.text: Ottoman forces captured Constantinople in 1453, ending the eastern Roman imperial court there. Other Byzantine-ruled lands lasted briefly beyond the capital’s fall, and people, churches, art and learning continued. The end of a government was not the disappearance of a population.

Ottoman forces took Constantinople in 1453, ending the eastern Roman imperial government based there. The empire had already fragmented in 1204, been restored in 1261, and contracted further. Other Byzantine-ruled territories survived the capital briefly; the people and eastern Christian traditions did not vanish. The imported 1400 to 1492 polygon is a coarse map interval, not evidence that the court still ruled in 1492.

passages.text: Caddo peoples built distinct river-valley communities linked by language, kinship and exchange. House traces, a surviving canoe and pottery reveal skilled work alongside farming and ceremonial life. Colonial dispossession forced major movements, but Caddo people continued and today sustain the Caddo Nation and renewed artistic traditions.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: At the George C. Davis site in east Texas, excavators found overlapping post patterns left by wooden buildings. Radiocarbon evidence places the main community between the ninth and early fourteenth centuries. Buildings were repeatedly renewed as people lived around ceremonial mounds.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A magnetic survey detected structures invisible on the surface. Excavation in 2003 confirmed one large building with a central hearth and four internal roof supports. The pattern reveals engineering and interior space, although it does not identify every activity or occupant.

passages.title: Homes, hearths and travel
passages.text: A dugout canoe eroding from a Red River bluff in northwestern Louisiana was radiocarbon dated to about 1000 CE. The surviving wooden vessel gives direct evidence of water transport beyond later written descriptions.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Late-seventeenth-century accounts describe corn stored in raised granaries, seed kept for planting and dried beans, squash and fruit. Storage helped households bridge seasonal shortages. These accounts mainly concern Hasinai communities and cannot describe every Caddo settlement.

passages.title: Food and shared work
passages.text: Housebuilding, planting and harvest brought people together. Maternal kinship connected households, while chiefs consulted community elders. Such relationships organized practical work as well as public decisions.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Caddo potters built vessels by joining coils of prepared clay to a base, then thinning and smoothing the walls. Temper mixed into clay and controlled drying helped a vessel survive manufacture and firing. Cooking pots and decorated bottles required different choices of shape and finish.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Engraved designs cut across a vessel's surface, unlike incised lines pressed into damp clay. Researchers and potters debate whether some ancient engraving occurred before or after firing. Modern experiments illuminate the skill without proving one method was universal.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Jereldine Redcorn's 1998 bottle Taysha has hollow tripod feet containing clay balls that rattle. Its form joins visual pattern with sound. It is a documented modern artwork drawing on ancestral pottery, not an excavated ancient vessel.

passages.title: Pottery as technology and art
passages.text: Redcorn learned through study, experiment and conversations with archaeologists when there was no local group of elder potters to teach her. Her work shows renewal as active investigation and artistic choice, not simply copying old designs.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The 1835 cession forced Caddo groups from lands in present Louisiana and Arkansas. Families moved toward Texas and, in some cases, Mexico. The agreement did not give them a secure replacement home.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: In 1859, renewed pressure forced people from the Brazos reservation to Indian Territory. They left cultivated land and family graves behind. This was a rupture in community life, not the disappearance of Caddo people.

passages.title: Dispossession and a continuing Nation
passages.text: The Caddo Nation's education services include cultural learning and vocational support. These are contemporary institutions serving people with changing needs, alongside the continued importance of language, arts and family histories.

Caddo communities endured repeated dispossession, including the forced move of 1859. The Caddo Nation and Caddo cultural life continue. The end of an imported map interval is not an extinction date, and the many earlier communities should not be treated as a single kingdom with one fall.

sectionTitles: Colonial change and a continuing city

passages.text: Old Calabar was a cluster of Efik trading towns and powerful households on the Cross River waterways, including Duke Town, Creek Town and Old Town. Its history predates this map’s 1878 to 1914 interval, which spans growing British colonial control.

passages.title: Households, languages and trade
passages.text: A trading “house” meant more than one building. Extended families occupied compounds with buildings around yards; free relatives, wives and enslaved people lived within this unequal social order. Wattle-and-daub construction made the town a landscape of linked homes and family institutions.

passages.title: Households, languages and trade
passages.text: Merchants learned trade English through contact and correspondence with visiting sailors. This practical literacy included numbers, measurements and names for imported goods. Antera Duke’s first language was Efik; his written English was a tool he adapted to his own purposes.

passages.title: Households, languages and trade
passages.text: His diary opens “I be angiry with my Dear awaw ofion”: “I was angry with my dear [wife] Awaw Ofiong.” The 1785 to 1788 diary survives in transcription. This original trade-English sample reveals personal feelings as well as commerce.

passages.title: Households, languages and trade
passages.text: Anchoring a ship involved negotiations and fees called comey. In July 1785, Antera accompanied Duke Ephraim aboard a Liverpool slave ship to collect them. Such payments connected town leaders, merchants and ships; the port’s political institutions were intertwined with the destructive Atlantic slave trade.

passages.title: Households, languages and trade
passages.text: Food provisioning was a large business too. The Hannover’s 1720 records list 11,400 yams purchased at Old Calabar, alongside enslaved people. Farmers, carriers and traders supplied the food that kept voyages going. The account exposes both the scale of agricultural work and its connection to forced transport.

passages.title: Making, learning and healthcare
passages.text: A 1914 missionary account describes Hope Waddell Training Institution, founded in 1895, teaching carpentry, printing, bookbinding, engineering and tailoring. A school day could involve making a useful object or preparing printed pages, not only reading them. These were organized vocational courses within a mission institution.

passages.title: Making, learning and healthcare
passages.text: That account also records a change in girls’ education: an initially combined institution separated the girls’ section, with girls’ institutions established elsewhere nearby. This shows how training opportunities were organized by gender. The source describes the mission’s arrangements, not the schooling of every Calabar child.

passages.title: Making, learning and healthcare
passages.text: A covered gourd bowl collected at Calabar by 1911 has its lid secured with twisted fibre cord and its surface decorated by burning designs into it. The museum cautiously attributes it to Ibibio makers. Practical containers could also be carefully decorated objects; a tied lid was a sensible piece of design.

passages.title: Making, learning and healthcare
passages.text: The colonial report for 1906 counted 798 cases at St Margaret’s hospital in Calabar and 7,129 outpatients. Two Catholic sisters assisted with female patients. The report separately described a European hospital, making racial divisions in colonial healthcare visible alongside the work of nurses and patients seeking treatment.

passages.title: Colonial change and a continuing city
passages.text: The treaty of 10 September 1884 promised British protection and restricted the chiefs’ dealings with foreign powers. It did not draw a detailed territorial boundary. Its later interpretation became contentious, a reminder that the language of a treaty and the expansion of colonial power were different parts of the story.

passages.title: Colonial change and a continuing city
passages.text: The International Court of Justice’s 2002 judgment described British indirect administration and recorded Nigeria’s answer that it could not give a precise date when the chiefs ceased to exist as a distinct entity. A map label ending in 1914 therefore should not be read as a documented, one-day destruction of Old Calabar.

passages.title: Colonial change and a continuing city
passages.text: Calabar continued as a city long after these political changes. Its university became a separate institution in 1975 and began teaching in three faculties in October 1976. This later educational history belongs to the living city in Nigeria, rather than extending the old trading polity’s sovereignty into the present.

The towns’ autonomy was progressively absorbed into British colonial administration after the 1884 treaty. No exact single ending is established here; Calabar’s people, households and city continued beyond the imported 1914 cutoff.

sectionTitles: Power, money and a new capital
Working, eating and answering nature’s call
Learning, medicine and words that survive
A fragile dynasty and an archaeological afterlife

passages.text: The Caliphate of Córdoba was the Umayyad state of al-Andalus from 929 to 1031. Its rulers combined political leadership with a claim to supreme religious authority. The map’s 1000 to 1100 interval extends beyond the caliphate’s end. Its broad North African outline also exaggerates uniform control: authority there depended on contested ports and shifting local alliances. This card covers the caliphate, separately from the earlier emirate.

passages.title: Power, money and a new capital
passages.text: Claiming to be caliph put Córdoba into competition with the Abbasids and Fatimids, who also claimed leadership of the Muslim community. Money carried the argument into people’s hands: gold dinars reappeared around 929, and coins named the ruler, mint and year. Gold supplies from Africa could be irregular, while silver production was much larger.

passages.title: Power, money and a new capital
passages.text: Across the Strait of Gibraltar, Ceuta became a caliphal base in 931. Control of the wider Maghreb was repeatedly challenged. After a Fatimid offensive in 958, Umayyad holdings there contracted to Ceuta and Tangier. Fortified harbors, gifts to local leaders and military alliances mattered more than the map’s single uninterrupted patch of color suggests.

passages.title: Power, money and a new capital
passages.text: Madinat al-Zahra stood less than ten kilometers from Córdoba, with the palace high above the city on terraces. It brought government offices and ceremonial rooms together while Córdoba remained important. The city below included workshops, a mint, soldiers’ quarters and residents’ houses. A capital needed bakers and builders as well as people with impressive titles.

passages.title: Power, money and a new capital
passages.text: The Salón Rico, built between 953 and 957, was a stage for receiving diplomats and celebrating victories and religious festivals. Carved columns and carefully ordered places for guests made rank visible. The caliph’s surroundings were part of how government communicated its authority, even before anyone began a speech.

passages.title: Working, eating and answering nature’s call
passages.text: The eastern service quarters preserve a clay-built oven where staff prepared food for the nearby elite residences. Rooms at the back of the courtyard formed a separate home with its own latrine, perhaps for a senior kitchen official. Archaeologists can identify the workplace much more confidently than the job title of its supervisor.

passages.title: Working, eating and answering nature’s call
passages.text: That service building also had an unusual double latrine. Elsewhere, the Court of the Pillars had two latrines and a Roman sarcophagus reused as a water basin. The basin once belonged to a very different setting. Even a dazzling palace had to solve the practical problems of water, waste and people needing the toilet.

passages.title: Working, eating and answering nature’s call
passages.text: Excavated portable stoves from the second half of the tenth century supported cooking pots above a fire. An opening let the cook tend the fuel; smaller holes admitted air and allowed smoke to escape. Service and security workers could use these compact devices for cooking or keeping dishes warm. Think of a small ceramic cooking station.

passages.title: Working, eating and answering nature’s call
passages.text: Royal meals used deep, wide bowls decorated in green and manganese colors. Painted animals could appear as diners ate their way toward the bottom: dinner with a surprise stag! Other vessels displayed calligraphy about power. These finds describe prestigious dining; they do not tell us that every household ate from the caliph’s tableware.

passages.title: Working, eating and answering nature’s call
passages.text: Court comfort depended partly on people who had been enslaved. Ja’far, a powerful chamberlain described in texts as a eunuch, belonged to the world of enslaved and freed court servants. His impressive house lay beside the ruler’s residence. High office could follow enslavement, but the beauty of the buildings should not hide that coercive history.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and words that survive
passages.text: Learning helped Córdoba attract scholars and teachers. Al-Hakam II’s library employed people who collected and copied books, including ancient scholarship translated into Arabic. Bookshops served city markets, and caliphal support included free Qur’an teaching. These were different routes into learning, rather than one school system shared equally by every child.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and words that survive
passages.text: Tenth-century marble sundials found at Madinat al-Zahra marked hours and prayer times. One included a small circle recording the required height of its shadow-casting needle, handy if the needle needed replacing. Mathematics met an everyday problem: knowing when to pray without a wristwatch.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and words that survive
passages.text: The physician al-Zahrawi organized medical knowledge into thirty chapters, including dentistry, diet and surgery. His surgical writing illustrated instruments, making complicated tools easier to explain to another practitioner. Surviving later copies preserve this achievement; the manuscript displayed in the NYU exhibition was copied in 1464, centuries after the caliphate.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and words that survive
passages.text: A small Arabic sample survives on an ivory box made for Prince al-Mughira in 968: “بركة من الله”, meaning “blessing from God.” This is the Louvre’s transcription of part of the Kufic inscription around the lid, shown here in modern Arabic type. The longer inscription names the recipient and dates the object to the year 357 of the Islamic calendar.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and words that survive
passages.text: Al-Hakam II’s addition to Córdoba’s great mosque made the mihrab an octagonal chamber under a shell-shaped dome. Its horseshoe entrance received elaborate mosaics associated with craftspeople sent by the Byzantine emperor. The building preserves both local architectural ambition and exchange across political and religious boundaries.

passages.title: A fragile dynasty and an archaeological afterlife
passages.text: Hisham II inherited the throne as a child. Al-Mansur emerged as the effective ruler, while the caliph’s role became largely ceremonial. Al-Mansur built another political center east of Córdoba. Later succession struggles and civil war brought repeated sieges to Madinat al-Zahra and eventually destroyed its life as a functioning royal city.

passages.title: A fragile dynasty and an archaeological afterlife
passages.text: Ruins can preserve things that written histories overlook. At Medina Azahara, archaeologists have recovered roads, water infrastructure, decorated buildings and ordinary objects. The site’s long abandonment protected much of this evidence. Excavations begun in 1911 gradually brought a forgotten capital back into view, including the kitchens and toilets that royal chronicles rarely celebrate.

The caliphate ended in 1031 after prolonged struggles for power. Regional rulers had already broken away into the smaller states known as taifas. Its imported map label continuing to 1100 should not be read as another seven decades of caliphal government.

sectionTitles: A fish bone can change the story
Shells became tools for making more things
Wood, nets and a remarkable cat
People carried their histories across the sea
Why there is no invented Calusa sentence here

passages.text: The Calusa built a powerful maritime society in southwest Florida, with Mound Key as a political centre. Fishing, shellworking and engineered waterways supported large communities without a farming-based economy. The map’s 1492 to 1530 window catches only a short part of a much longer history, whose older traces survive in mounds and waterlogged deposits.

passages.title: Keeping dinner alive
passages.text: At Mound Key, researchers investigated large enclosed watercourts beside the main canal. Organic materials dated their construction to about 1300 to 1400. The team interprets them as places to hold live fish, requiring knowledge of water movement and fish behaviour. Dinner could keep swimming until it was needed.

passages.title: Keeping dinner alive
passages.text: Waterlogged deposits preserved palm-fibre cordage, wood, seeds, fish scales and bones. The bones include schooling fish such as mullet, pinfish and herring. These small remains let archaeologists test the fishing interpretation against actual contents, rather than guessing the purpose from the enclosure’s shape alone.

passages.title: Keeping dinner alive
passages.text: On the high shell mound, traces of a large building reveal several construction phases beginning around 1000. Spanish accounts later described the ruler’s house as holding 2,000 people. Excavation supports an exceptionally large building; the capacity remains a historical description rather than a count of excavated residents.

passages.title: A fish bone can change the story
passages.text: Mullet can gather in predictable schools and can be preserved by dry-smoking. Yet early archaeological samples did not make them look especially important. Karen Walker revisited stored bone collections to test whether a Spanish observer’s account of a major mullet fishery fitted the physical evidence.

passages.title: A fish bone can change the story
passages.text: The reanalysis found that fragile bones, sample sizes and identification shortcuts had hidden part of the picture. Later Mound Key samples showed a stronger mullet signal than Pineland samples. The result suggests a fishery that varied by place and period, rather than one unchanging menu across the whole region.

passages.title: Shells became tools for making more things
passages.text: At Useppa Island and Buck Key, unfinished tools, shell fragments, pounders and grinding implements identify workshop activity. Researchers linked these deposits to increased production after about 800. The piles preserve stages of manufacture: a broken or unfinished object can explain a craft better than a perfect museum piece.

passages.title: Shells became tools for making more things
passages.text: Shell axes and adzes helped workers shape wood. Dietler’s study compared 441 tools from 93 archaeological sites and found evidence of exchange with neighbouring communities. His proposal that leaders strengthened their power by encouraging these industries is an interpretation built from that production and distribution evidence.

passages.title: Wood, nets and a remarkable cat
passages.text: The 1896 excavation at Key Marco recovered netting, cordage, wooden bowls and boxes from wet deposits. Waterlogged preservation saved materials that often rot away. The collection makes daily life unusually tangible: coastal households needed containers, strong fibre and repaired fishing equipment as well as impressive buildings.

passages.title: Wood, nets and a remarkable cat
passages.text: The Key Marco collection includes net weights and net-mesh gauges, alongside bone pins and points. A gauge helped a maker keep openings consistent as a net took shape. Catching fish began with careful handwork on shore, long before anybody paddled out onto the water.

passages.title: Wood, nets and a remarkable cat
passages.text: The small wooden Key Marco Cat combines human and feline features. Its catalogue records differing published dates within the broad span 700 to 1500, and uncertainty over whether its maker was Calusa or a predecessor. Its survival shows extraordinary carving skill without allowing us to name the artist or translate its meaning.

passages.title: People carried their histories across the sea
passages.text: Eighteenth-century slave raids and violence drove people from South Florida. Archival research follows Calusa and other refugees to Cuba in 1711 and again in 1760. These were people seeking safety, not an archaeological culture simply fading out of existence; the surviving records follow only parts of their journeys.

passages.title: Why there is no invented Calusa sentence here
passages.text: The Randell Research Center reports that the Calusa left no written records of their own. Spanish accounts preserve outside descriptions, while carvings and other objects carry visual meaning that cannot be read as translated sentences. No securely readable original Calusa writing sample is known from the evidence used for this card.

The 1530 map cutoff is not the end of Calusa power. Later encounters and resistance continued, while eighteenth-century slave raids, disease and displacement broke apart the political society. Refugees reached Cuba in several movements, including 1760. This process has no single securely established fall year, and displacement should not be confused with every person dying.

sectionTitles: Making a state, keeping many histories
A community can question its king

passages.text: Modern Cameroon grew from territories administered by France and Britain. Independence and federation created a new state, while distinct community institutions, languages and artistic traditions continued.

passages.title: Making a state, keeping many histories
passages.text: French-administered Cameroon became independent on 1 January 1960. The map’s 1945 starting date therefore includes colonial administration, not fifteen extra years of independence. Political freedom also arrived amid bitter struggles over which movements and leaders would govern.

passages.title: Making a state, keeping many histories
passages.text: The British-administered Cameroons voted in two parts in 1961. The north joined Nigeria in June; the south joined Cameroon in October. A single modern outline can hide these different decisions, and a border on a map cannot explain how every community experienced them.

passages.title: Making a state, keeping many histories
passages.text: The presidential website prints the French motto “Paix- Travail-Patrie”: “Peace, Work, Fatherland”. This short attested writing sample uses Latin letters. French and English have equal official status under the constitution, alongside the country’s many other languages.

passages.title: A community can question its king
passages.text: Among the Bamoun, Nguon brings community concerns to the Mfon, or monarch. Every two years, ritual chiefs collect people’s opinions, then enter the palace for a private discussion. Listening comes before the public spectacle.

passages.title: A community can question its king
passages.text: The following day includes a public trial of the monarch’s governance. Chiefs present complaints, and sanctions can include fines or removal. It is an unusually vivid lesson in accountability: even someone with a throne may have to explain himself.

passages.title: A community can question its king
passages.text: Celebrations conclude with a Sunday parade and return to the palace. Families, associations, radio, schools and universities help transmit Nguon. A practice can remain rooted in community life while also traveling through microphones and classrooms.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: Cameroon’s written heritage includes maps made by King Njoya in the early twentieth century. The Library of Congress acquired one in 2021. Rivers surround the Bamum kingdom, and place names appear in Bamum writing: local people were mapmakers, not simply dots on someone else’s map.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: Njoya’s survey team numbered about sixty people. His earliest surviving map traced the route from his farm to the capital. Big geographic projects can begin with a familiar journey; later maps pictured the kingdom and the city of Foumban.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: In a 2025 report, ten-year-old Eyong Blessing described learning through videos on a tablet in Melong. Her family had fled the Northwest conflict. The local e-container brought digital lessons within reach of pupils who otherwise had little access to such equipment.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: The e-container model uses recycled materials and solar power, with online and offline lessons. Teachers also receive training. Demand in Melong sometimes required dividing a class into four groups, a reminder that a clever classroom still needs enough time for every child.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: At Alahlie, a solar-powered borehole serves a school, displaced families and their neighbors. Schoolgirl Anita recalled missing lessons to fetch water. A nearby reliable tap can return hours to a child’s day, as well as supplying water for washing.

passages.title: Maps, tablets and school taps
passages.text: A community water committee and local councils undertake the borehole’s maintenance. The machine needs people as well as sunshine. UNICEF’s 2025 account places this work within a region where conflict had damaged services and forced families from home.

Cameroon continues as a state. Conflict and displacement in its Northwest and Southwest have damaged daily life and schooling; the country’s communities and cultural institutions nevertheless continue their histories.
