sectionTitles: A French line and living communities

passages.text: Canada became a federation in 1867, while First Nations, Inuit and Métis societies had lived across the land long before it. The state grew by adding provinces and territories, treaties and railways, but Indigenous peoples were excluded from Confederation talks and later faced land loss and residential schools. Innovations such as insulin and public health insurance improved many lives, while migrants and minorities challenged discriminatory laws. A Prince Edward Island kitchen, a child’s school or an Arctic community tells a more varied story than a single map polygon. Canada continues; the imported map interval begins in 1815, before Confederation.

passages.title: Who formed the federation?
passages.text: In 1867 the colonies of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick joined Ontario and Quebec in a new Canadian federation. It was a constitutional beginning for the state, not the first arrival of people or government on these lands. The map’s 1815 start is earlier than Confederation.

passages.title: Who formed the federation?
passages.text: Indigenous peoples and women were excluded from formal Confederation negotiations. Some French Canadians and Nova Scotians opposed the plan for their own reasons. A founding agreement can be important without representing everyone it affected.

passages.title: Who formed the federation?
passages.text: Treaty 1 was negotiated in 1871 with First Nations; ten more numbered treaties followed by 1921. These remain relationships with promises and obligations, not proof that Indigenous communities vanished into Canada. Government treaty map boundaries are estimates, not verified cultural borders.

passages.title: Who formed the federation?
passages.text: Thousands of Chinese workers helped drive the Canadian Pacific Railway through British Columbia’s mountains in the 1880s. A federal head tax on Chinese immigrants began in 1885. A spectacular rail achievement came alongside a law that burdened the families of people who built it.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: At a Prince Edward Island farm house interpreted by Parks Canada, the kitchen woodstove heated water for cooking and chores. Sewing and mending took time. A home could be a workplace for the whole family, not just somewhere to sleep.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: The same house has a chamber pot: on a freezing night, carrying a pot was easier than walking to an outhouse. An upper-middle-class Ontario family around 1890 drew well water, heated bath water on the stove and used a backyard outhouse. Indoor plumbing arrived unevenly.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: At another historic Ontario house, Parks Canada points out why an outhouse and a drinking-water well were kept apart: waste from the pit could spoil the water. The joke is easy; the health risk was not. This is one household’s landscape, not all of Canada.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: School memories from the 1940s and 1950s include first kindergarten days, teachers pupils adored and teachers they feared, including the strap. These oral histories show one set of classrooms; schooling also varied across language, province and family income.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: Federally funded, church-run residential schools separated an estimated 150,000 Indigenous children from families and tried to suppress their languages and cultures. Survivors’ artwork and testimony preserve their experiences. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission called the system cultural genocide.

passages.title: Family, school and home
passages.text: Women’s war work included medicine, industry and household labor. A National Film Board documentary celebrated these roles, but it was also morale-building propaganda. A camera’s praise did not capture every worker’s wages, loss or discrimination.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: A Toronto team of Banting, Best, Collip and Macleod developed insulin treatment in 1921 and 1922. Collip’s purification and Macleod’s laboratory support mattered alongside Banting and Best’s experiments. For a child with diabetes, the achievement could turn a fatal diagnosis into a treatable one.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: Public health insurance did not appear overnight. Saskatchewan began universal hospital insurance in 1947; federal cost-sharing laws for hospitals and doctors followed in 1957 and 1966. The 1984 Canada Health Act set national funding conditions, with care organized by provinces and territories.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: Some women won a federal vote in 1918, while First Nations people did not gain the same federal voting access until 1960. A 1929 court ruling also allowed women to be appointed to the Senate, but did not end all discrimination. Political rights came in stages, not one universal gift.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: After Japan entered World War II, the Canadian government forced people of Japanese ancestry away from the West Coast. The policy harmed families and property despite their lives in Canada. It belongs in the home-front story beside military service and factory work.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: A 1967 immigration points system replaced formal country-of-origin criteria, and Canada’s population became more diverse. Government research also finds that official reform did not make bias vanish from decisions, jobs or housing. A new rule can open a door while people still face barriers beyond it.

passages.title: Health, inventions and rights
passages.text: The 1982 Charter became part of Canada’s constitution and protects many rights. Its language guarantees concern English and French federal institutions, while Indigenous languages and other community languages also matter in homes and public life.

passages.title: A French line and living communities
passages.text: A Canadian constitutional text says “Le français et l’anglais sont les langues officielles du Canada,” meaning “French and English are Canada’s official languages.” This short written French sample is from an official legal text; it does not describe every language spoken across the country.

passages.title: A French line and living communities
passages.text: Inuit leaders pressed for a territory shaped by a land claim and self-government; Nunavut was created in 1999. Its creation did not begin Inuit history. The Canadian state and Indigenous nations continue to change their relationships.

passages.title: A French line and living communities
passages.text: Canada continues. Its present map is not proof that every boundary in the imported 1815 onward polygons was historically accurate or agreed by Indigenous nations. The state’s legal formation and the longer histories of its peoples require separate timelines.

Canada continues as a federation. Its 1867 constitutional beginning did not begin the histories of First Nations, Inuit, Métis and other peoples who live there. The imported 1815 map start predates Confederation, and its polygons do not verify Indigenous territories or every later border change.

passages.text: Cantia is a Latin name used by Bede for Kent. This card serves both imported labels, but the map’s Cantia outline spreads far beyond the south-eastern kingdom and must not be treated as its verified territory. The Cantia interval of 600 to 800 and Kent interval of 800 to 1000 are map coverage, not the lives of two separate kingdoms. The named sites below are in historical Kent; several institutions continued after royal independence ended.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: An Old English sample from Aethelberht’s laws reads “Gif feaxfang geweorð ·L· sceatta to bote.” In Christopher Monk’s translation, grabbing someone by the hair calls for compensation of fifty sceattas. The wording survives in a twelfth-century copy of a much earlier code. Hair-pulling even had its own entry in the legal price list.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.

passages.text: Cao Wei was the most powerful of the Three Kingdoms, controlling the northern heartland of China. Founded by Cao Cao's son Cao Pi, it inherited the Han administrative system and produced significant literary and military achievements.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Cao and his sons Cao Pi and Cao Zhi wrote some of the finest poetry of the age, the Jian'an style named for the last Han reign period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cao Pi's Discourse on Literature, the first systematic essay of Chinese literary criticism, argues that writing outlasts rank and wealth.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ma Jun builds a south-pointing chariot, a cart whose figure keeps pointing south as it turns, through gearing whose design is reconstructed with differential gears.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The tuntian system of military-agricultural colonies, begun by Cao Cao in 196 under the last Han emperor, settled soldiers and refugees on frontier land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Administrative innovations passed to the Jin dynasty, among them the nine-rank system for grading officials, introduced in 220.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The fourteenth-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms later romanticized this era.
Sima Yan forced the last Wei emperor to abdicate and founded the Jin dynasty, in the last month of 265 by the Chinese calendar, February 266 by ours.

passages.text: The Cape Colony joined an Atlantic port to an expanding southern African frontier. Its communities included Khoikhoi, San, Xhosa, enslaved people and their descendants, and settlers. British rule, slavery, trade and wars made daily life profoundly unequal.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: A parliament did not mean everyone had equal power. The Cape obtained representative government in 1853 and responsible government in 1872, allowing local ministers more control within British imperial rule. These changes concerned colonial institutions in a society already divided by ownership and coercion.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: On the eastern frontier, successive wars between 1779 and 1878 brought conquest and dispossession. Xhosa and Khoikhoi communities lost land and livestock as colonial settlement advanced. The map’s expanding outline therefore represents upheaval in people’s homes and livelihoods.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: Cape slavery legally ended on 1 December 1834, but most formerly enslaved people had to serve another four years as unpaid apprentices. Full release from that compulsory system came in December 1838. A declaration of freedom and the ability to leave a master were different milestones.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: An inspection of Cape Town’s Slave Lodge in 1803 described dark, unhealthy rooms where even daytime inspection needed a lantern. In 1807 officials decided to sell its enslaved residents and reuse the building as government offices. A change of building use did not free those people.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: The Slave Lodge excavation found a well, cobbled floors and the edge of a latrine. Its preliminary animal-bone sample included sheep, cattle, fowl and pig, alongside fish and shellfish. These mixed historical deposits help researchers investigate food and water without supplying a complete household menu.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: Other Slave Lodge finds include scissors, pins, buttons, beads and stoneware marbles. Small things bring sewing, dress and play into view beside official records. A marble is a welcome reminder that history also happened near the floor.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: At Koopmans-de Wet House, a Cape buffet made around 1780 to 1800 has a zinc basin, folding shelves and fold-out leaves. Glasses and porcelain could be washed in the dining room. This sideboard had a much busier job than merely looking elegant.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: The house museum displays Chinese, Japanese and British ceramics in a reconstruction of a wealthy Cape home. Its dining service and other furnishings need their own collection histories: some were later donations. They show the goods reaching the Cape, rather than an untouched family dinner table.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: A pantry trapdoor once connected to the kitchen below; its ladder or stair was removed during restoration. Such a practical opening reveals how serving and cooking were organized. Behind an impressive dining room lay the work of carrying, preparing and clearing meals.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: A surviving newspaper title gives a short Xhosa writing sample: “Imvo zabantsundu”. Its English section was called “Native opinion”, the historical wording recorded in the library catalogue. John Tengo Jabavu published the paper at King William’s Town from November 1884, creating a printed forum for readers.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: The Royal Observatory was authorized in 1820 to improve knowledge of southern stars and navigation. Fearon Fallows initially worked from a prefabricated hut; his 1824 catalogue listed 273 southern stars. Careful measuring could begin before the impressive permanent building arrived.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: The observatory also helped ships keep time. Visible time balls gave captains a signal for checking their clocks; electrical connections later coordinated signals across several towns. Astronomy here was useful to sailors deciding where they were, not only to people admiring the night sky.

The Cape Colony ended as a separate colony when it joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910. Its peoples continued, but Black South Africans had been excluded from the negotiations establishing the Union. The imported map interval ending in 1914 runs beyond this constitutional change.

sectionTitles: Court life, including the awkward bits
What buildings, books and fields reveal

passages.text: Charlemagne’s imperial coronation in 800 gave a new Roman title to a large Frankish monarchy. Its rulers joined conquest with Christian government and support for learning. The realm divided among his grandsons in 843; later Carolingian kings and emperors did not continuously govern one united empire. The map’s label through 1000 combines different political phases.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Einhard, a writer close to Charlemagne’s court, says the ruler enjoyed the warm baths at Aachen and invited sons, nobles and attendants to join him. The royal bath could be a social occasion. This describes a privileged court, not bathing facilities in every village.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: According to Einhard, Charlemagne had his sons and daughters taught the liberal arts. Boys also practiced riding and hunting, while girls learned textile work. The account reveals a royal educational ideal with different expectations for boys and girls, rather than universal schooling.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Einhard says the aging ruler disliked doctors who urged him to exchange roasted meat for boiled meat. Even an emperor could be an uncooperative patient. The anecdote preserves a court writer’s portrait, not evidence that its dietary advice was effective medicine.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Charlemagne reportedly practiced writing on tablets kept beneath his pillow, but began late and made little progress. The same biography praises his interest in learned subjects. Being a powerful patron of books did not automatically make handwriting easy.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Aachen’s palace chapel organized worship around an eight-sided central space, with an upper gallery and a dome. Ancient columns were reused in the building. Its architecture connected the Carolingian court with prestigious Roman and Christian traditions through materials as well as ceremony.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The chapel’s surviving bronze gates belong to its early history, but the brilliant mosaic decorating today’s dome was installed in 1880 to 1881. A beautiful old building can contain several centuries at once. Archaeologists and architectural historians separate those layers before reconstructing Charlemagne’s surroundings.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Scholars such as Alcuin helped develop court learning and the copying of books. Carolingian minuscule used clearer, more regular letter forms that made manuscripts easier to read. This was a major scribal achievement, although producing a book still required skilled labor and expensive materials.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: A Gospel book made around 825 to 850, probably at Metz, survives on parchment with ink and painted decoration. Its arcaded canon tables cross-reference passages in the four Gospels. They are both attractive pages and practical finding aids: a manuscript could help readers navigate as well as impress them.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The famous plan sent from Reichenau to St Gall around 820 consists of five pieces of parchment sewn together. It was prepared for Abbot Gozbert as a framework for thinking about a monastery. It is evidence for planning and ideals, not a photograph proving every building existed exactly as drawn.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The plan’s Latin dedicatory letter invites its readers to “perscrutinare,” meaning “examine closely,” and “sollertiam exercere,” meaning “exercise ingenuity.” These short phrases are transcribed in the abbey library’s scholarly catalogue. The designers expected the recipient to think about the plan, not simply copy it without judgment.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: At Mérigest near modern Sénart, archaeologists identified a ninth-century rural unit with two timber-post buildings, a well and three successive cooking ovens. One building was probably a house. Successive ovens show replacement over time; they should not be imagined as three simultaneous kitchens in one family home.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Pits at the same site contained a millstone and iron objects including a cowbell, spur and key. Archaeologists suggest the metal may have been gathered for recycling. Grinding grain, managing animals and salvaging useful material become visible through objects whose owners’ names are lost.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Imperial expansion also involved coercion. A law issued during Charlemagne’s Saxon wars threatened death for refusing baptism. It shows rulers using severe penalties to impose Christianity. A legal threat is evidence of policy, however, not a record of how often a punishment was carried out.

The partition of 843 created distinct kingdoms, though imperial titles and Carolingian dynasties continued. Charles the Fat’s later reunion collapsed in 887 to 888. The atlas’s 1000 endpoint is therefore not the fall of a continuously united empire.

A small clue to caring for children
An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book

passages.text: Founded by Phoenician settlers on the Gulf of Tunis, Carthage became the centre of a powerful Punic network linking North Africa, western Mediterranean islands and Iberia. Ports, inscriptions and archaeological remains show a place of traders, craftspeople and families as well as generals. The map uses “Carthaginian Empire” and “Carthage” for successive slices of this same history; the later Roman city on the site was a different political phase.

passages.title: A port that connected worlds
passages.text: The archaeological site preserves Punic harbour remains. They anchor Carthage’s maritime story in physical infrastructure, although the surviving basins cannot by themselves tell us the cargo or crew of every voyage. Ships and ports connected communities around the western Mediterranean.

passages.title: A port that connected worlds
passages.text: A British Museum gallery describes silver coins that Carthage minted in Sicily between about 400 and 300 BCE to pay armies. Some carry short Punic inscriptions meaning “in the land,” “of the paymaster” or “in the camp.” Even an army needed accountants; these coins are evidence of organized payments, not of what every sailor or soldier earned.

passages.title: Who made decisions?
passages.text: Carthage was governed through elected chief officials often called suffetes or shofetim, councils and public assemblies. Our picture comes mainly from later Greek and Roman writing, checked against inscriptions, so the precise powers and who could participate are debated. It was a city with institutions, not simply Hannibal giving orders to everyone.

passages.title: Who made decisions?
passages.text: The Louvre’s Punic stelae and an Ohio State edition of a Carthaginian temple tariff also preserve names of dedicators and rules for offerings. They show people making vows and priests administering a sanctuary. Those records are narrow windows into religious life; they do not tell us what every family believed.

passages.title: A house with water close at hand
passages.text: At Kerkuane, a separate Punic town on Cape Bon, excavators found houses entered through corridors into courtyards. Some plans included wells, washbasins and baths, with rooms arranged around the open centre. That gives a concrete glimpse of domestic space in Carthage’s wider Punic world; it is not a floor plan of every Carthaginian home.

passages.title: A house with water close at hand
passages.text: Kerkuane also preserves streets, shops and workshops. Its visible ruins mostly belong to the late fourth and early third centuries BCE; the town was abandoned around the middle of the third century and not built over by a Roman city. That is why these ordinary workspaces survive more clearly than much of Punic Carthage.

passages.title: Yes, there were toilets
passages.text: Excavations at Bir Massouda in Carthage found two structures interpreted as household latrines and a third as a public latrine. Their construction dates to about the late fifth or early fourth century BCE. The evidence is unusually specific: archaeology can reveal where people dealt with the least glamorous part of city life.

passages.title: Yes, there were toilets
passages.text: Those three latrines help researchers study waste collection, but they do not prove every home had a toilet or that Carthage had modern plumbing. If you are wondering whether ancient history includes toilet questions: the archaeologists were wondering too.

passages.title: A small clue to caring for children
passages.text: A spouted Punic pottery vessel from Carthage, dated to the first half of the third century BCE, is catalogued as a feeding bottle. Its shape offers a rare object connected with caring for young children. The object does not reveal who held it, what was inside, or how common such vessels were.

passages.title: Punic words in stone
passages.text: A limestone stela catalogued by the Louvre as AO 5175 begins with the Punic words 𐤋𐤓𐤁𐤕 𐤋𐤕𐤍𐤕 (LRBT LTNT): “to the Lady, to Tanit.” This is a modern Unicode rendering of the attested consonant letters, not a photograph of the carving. Punic is the language; the Phoenician-derived alphabet is its script. The stone records a dedication, not the literacy of every Carthaginian.

passages.title: Punic words in stone
passages.text: The same stela names Baal Hammon and its dedicator, with his father and grandfather. The Louvre says its final words are not yet understood. A family name on a stone can outlast an empire, but historians must still leave unread words unread.

passages.title: An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book
passages.text: A surviving Carthaginian inscription, known as KAI 74, sets out what priests received from different offerings. One clause exempts a worshipper poor in livestock from a priestly share. It is a rule on a stone, not proof that every sanctuary followed it in every century.

passages.title: An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book
passages.text: Roman writers admired an agricultural work associated with the Carthaginian Mago. Later Greek and Latin versions carried its farming advice, including guidance on trees, into Roman literature. The Punic original does not survive intact, and modern scholars debate whether “Mago” was a single author or a name attached to collected knowledge.

passages.title: Defeat did not erase everyone
passages.text: Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE was a startling military feat, but it did not win the second war. Roman victory in 201 weakened Carthage; the city still existed for more than fifty years before the third war and the siege that ended in 146 BCE.

passages.title: Defeat did not erase everyone
passages.text: In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Punic capital and enslaved its surviving inhabitants. The Roman city built later on the site is part of Carthage’s long history, but its monuments are not evidence that Punic Carthage possessed Roman theatres or baths. People and Punic cultural practices elsewhere in North Africa continued through political change.

Rome captured and destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE, ending it as an independent capital. Survivors faced enslavement, while a Roman city later rose on the same ground. The political power ended; this was not the extinction of everyone with a Punic language or tradition. The map’s two imported labels and rounded years describe coverage, not two different Carthaginian civilizations or a historical end in 100 BCE.

passages.text: Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE was a startling military feat, but it did not win the second war. Roman victory in 201 weakened Carthage; the city still existed for more than fifty years before the third war and the siege that ended in 146 BCE.

passages.title: Defeat did not erase everyone
passages.text: In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Punic capital and enslaved its surviving inhabitants. The Roman city built later on the site is part of Carthage’s long history, but its monuments are not evidence that Punic Carthage possessed Roman theatres or baths. People and Punic cultural practices elsewhere in North Africa continued through political change.

Rome captured and destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE, ending it as an independent capital. Survivors faced enslavement, while a Roman city later rose on the same ground. The political power ended; this was not the extinction of everyone with a Punic language or tradition. The map’s two imported labels and rounded years describe coverage, not two different Carthaginian civilizations or a historical end in 100 BCE.

A crown’s expansion could therefore coincide with families losing their homes; cultural exchange should not be mistaken for continuous equality or safety.

sectionTitles: Agreements, money and a surviving word

passages.text: Celtiberians were communities of inland Iberia, with cities, distinct local identities and a Celtic language. This imported outline covers far too much of the peninsula, and its 1500 to 500 BCE interval precedes the best documented Celtiberian towns. The examples below are explicitly later Iron Age and Roman-period evidence, not a picture of a single Bronze Age kingdom.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: The archaeological reconstruction at Numantia presents a rectangular house with three rooms. The front room combines grain grinding and weaving, with a hatch down to a cellar. This is a model of later Celtiberian domestic space, not an intact ancient house with its original furniture.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: In the same reconstruction, the central hearth room was used for eating, sleeping and family gatherings. Storage occupied the back, and a side door led to an animal pen. Household space had to accommodate people, provisions, tools and livestock, sometimes very close together.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: A 2024 study examined four storage contexts from the Celtiberian town destroyed in 133 BCE: an attached storeroom, part of an underground cellar and two cupboards. These protected spaces preserve pottery used for storing, cooking and serving. Archaeologists can distinguish kitchen tasks without finding a written shopping list.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: The storage deposits also contained evidence of textile work and brooch manufacture. A room used to keep supplies could hold craft equipment too. These finds connect ordinary domestic storage with the production of clothing and the metal fasteners that kept it together.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: Researchers sampled six grinding tools and fourteen pottery vessels from Numantia, spanning the Late Iron Age and Roman occupations. Starch traces revealed cereals, oats, acorns and legumes. The tiny residues preserve food evidence that a spectacular weapon or jewel cannot provide.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: The plant study found evidence for both cultivation and seasonal gathering. Acorns linked households to nearby oak woodland; altered starch also indicated heating during preparation. The results show continuity across political changes, although they do not give us an exact ancient recipe or a complete menu.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: Numantia’s especially distinctive painted pottery series belongs to the first century BCE, after the famous siege. Potters painted black designs on red clay using iron oxide, and also made multicolored vessels. Their birds, fish and human figures show that artistic traditions continued after military defeat.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: A bronze hospitality token from La Caridad at Caminreal dates to the late second or early first century BCE. Such objects recorded agreements with reciprocal obligations between people, family groups or communities. A portable piece of metal could preserve a relationship extending beyond its owner’s household.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: The Museo de Zaragoza preserves a silver coin from Turiasu, modern Tarazona, dated 100 to 50 BCE. Local minting gave a city a recognizable presence in everyday exchange. This is later evidence for urban institutions, not proof that the map’s vast earlier territory shared one currency.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: A first-century BCE bronze text from Contrebia Belaisca records a dispute about land sold for an irrigation channel. Salduie wanted the canal; Alaun objected, and the judges ruled for Salduie. Getting water to crops required negotiation and legal decisions as well as digging.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: Writing sample: the Novallas bronze has “LITANOM” in line 3, interpreted by its editors as a form meaning “wide.” The Celtiberian text uses Latin capital letters and dates around the late Roman Republic or early Augustus. This short, qualified translation is possible even though the complete fragment remains incompletely understood.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: Scipio’s army surrounded Numantia with camps and barriers in 134 to 133 BCE, aiming to force surrender through hunger. The town fell in 133 BCE, and survivors were taken captive. This was a devastating local conquest; it must not be described as the instant disappearance of every Celtiberian community.

Roman conquest and administration gradually transformed Celtiberian communities. Numantia’s fall in 133 BCE was a major event, but later pottery and written Celtiberian demonstrate continuing local life. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is much too early to mark the end of these communities.

sectionTitles: Water, school messages and medical information

passages.text: The map begins this record in 1945, during French colonial rule, but the Central African Republic became independent in 1960. This card follows the modern state and examples from its diverse communities, rather than treating all Central Africa as one people.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: On 13 August 1960, the Central African Republic gained independence from France. A US recognition message addressed Prime Minister David Dacko that day. The 1945 map date belongs to the colonial period, not to the republic’s independence.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: Jean-Bédel Bokassa turned the republic into an empire in December 1976. In September 1979, a French-backed coup brought David Dacko back to power and ended the imperial regime. The country’s inhabitants did not begin again from scratch when the state’s title changed.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: The Séléka coalition seized Bangui in March 2013 after a rebellion begun in late 2012. Further violence, including attacks by anti-Balaka groups, devastated civilian communities. In 2014, the UN established MINUSCA with civilian protection at the centre of its mandate. These events describe a crisis within a continuing country.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: A short Sango writing sample is “zo kwe zo,” translated by linguist William Samarin as “everyone’s a human being.” His scholarly account identifies it as Barthélemy Boganda’s slogan and notes its appearance on an early national stamp. The spelling here follows that published transcription in the Latin alphabet.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Aka singers in the southwest developed music in which four voice parts intertwine. Individual singers can vary their contributions while the group continues: the result is intricate collective improvisation. UNESCO recognized this tradition in 2003 and placed it on its representative list in 2008.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Instruments include the enzeko drum, the harp-like geedale-bagongo and the single-string mbela bow. Clapping accompanies dancing, and particular instruments suit particular occasions. An orchestra does not need dozens of identical instruments to create a complex sound.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Children learn Aka music by participating in community occasions from an early age. Songs and dances accompany events such as new camps, hunting and funerals, transmitting knowledge and relationships through participation. This is a specific community’s practice, not a musical description of every Central African household.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: Irène Ndende returned to Bangui’s Castors neighbourhood after displacement. In a 2025 interview, she described the difference made by a home water connection installed in 2023: after working in distant fields, she no longer had another water-fetching journey waiting. Infrastructure can change the shape of an ordinary evening.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: At a public water point in Benz-Vi, nineteen-year-old Benisia Agdugebo sold porridge and fritters to neighbours arriving with containers. UNICEF’s reporter watched the place become a setting for greetings and conversation. The tap supplied water, but the gathering also supported a small breakfast business.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: EduTrac launched in Bangui in December 2015 to collect school information by text message. Headteachers could report attendance and security incidents without waiting for paper reports to travel. One described reports previously taking months to bring a response; faster information was the goal, not a guarantee that every problem was solved.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: The rollout needed patient teaching of its own. Some headteachers had to learn how to send SMS messages, and telephone companies had to connect the service number. French and Sango radio announcements helped explain the project. Even useful technology begins with people understanding how to use it.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: A 2016 trial in twenty-one Mambéré Kadéi health centres used the Argus app to send disease reports by SMS. Reporting became more complete and timely in the study. Where phones had no signal, the project paid for motorcycle taxis to a connected village: digital medicine sometimes still needed a road journey.

The imperial regime ended in 1979; the Central African Republic continued. Later rebellions and peacekeeping changed authority and everyday security without erasing the state or its communities. Families, teachers and cultural practitioners continued rebuilding connections through these disruptions.

sectionTitles: Modern discoveries of a much older past

passages.text: This record represents independent Chad from 1960, following French colonial rule. Its borders enclose many communities with distinct histories; the modern republic is not interchangeable with earlier Kanem, Wadai or other states.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: Chad’s independence was proclaimed on 11 August 1960. Diplomatic records also preserve an older capital name: the American embassy opened at Fort Lamy in 1961, in the city now called N’Djamena. Names on old letters can reveal political changes that a modern map conceals.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: Hissène Habré ruled from 1982 to 1990. In 2016, the Extraordinary African Chambers in Senegal convicted him of torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Survivors’ efforts to secure a trial are part of Chad’s history alongside the rulers whose actions they challenged.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: A small writing sample comes from the 2020 children’s comic title “Lafya,” which UNICEF translates from Ngambaye as “peace.” Its eight-year-old heroine learns about life during school closures. Versions in French, Arabic and Ngambaye show that public education can use several languages within one country.

passages.title: Modern discoveries of a much older past
passages.text: The Franco-Chadian research mission found a nearly complete skull, jaw material and teeth at Toros-Menalla site TM 266. Scientists assigned them to Sahelanthropus tchadensis, around seven million years old. Published work identifies them as evidence relevant to early human evolution, not the remains of a Chadian nation millions of years ago.

passages.title: Modern discoveries of a much older past
passages.text: Other fossils make the setting more surprising than today’s desert suggests. Fish, crocodiles and water-associated mammals occur alongside animals linked to woodland and savannah. In 2002, researchers used these remains and sediments to reconstruct a lakeside environment near sandy desert. Ancient landscapes can hide inside modern dry ground.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: Around Lake Chad, dihé is a food harvested from blue-green microorganisms in shallow waters. FAO’s account describes women straining it through palm baskets, letting water drain in sand basins, cutting the thickened material into pieces and drying them in the sun. Harvesting and processing require learned skill.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: In field notes from March 2002 near Boudou Andja, women’s leader Harita Cierom asked for sturdy clothing, gloves, boots and support for a producers’ association. Salty water made the work hard on skin and clothes. Her request puts the workers, rather than only the finished food, into the historical record.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: Massa communities live on both sides of the Logone River in Chad and Cameroon. In the annual Guruna retreat, boys and men take cattle to a camp away from home. Elders teach cattle care alongside community history, music, dance, handicrafts and wrestling: school can happen far from a classroom.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: UNESCO’s Guruna account describes girls helping prepare food and decorations without staying overnight. Older women transmit those skills, while fathers, elders and specialist masters guide other instruction. Public ceremonies and performances let participants demonstrate what they have learned; the learning involves the wider community.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: Between 2000 and 2005, researchers and health teams tested combined visits for nomadic families and their livestock. Physicians and veterinarians shared transport and equipment while providing their separate vaccinations. Bringing both services together reduced costs and reached more women and children per day than human-only rounds in the study.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: A later study in Danamadji found that pastoralists valued combined vaccination, but keeping the programme running required dependable funding and coordination. Even livestock enclosures mattered for safe, workable vaccination days. The useful invention here was organizing services around mobile families rather than expecting families to fit a distant clinic.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: During the pandemic, Chad used radio, television and phones for lessons. UNICEF’s May 2021 case study also reported handwashing kits, soap and bleach delivered to at least 1,083 primary schools. Reopening involved water and hygiene as well as books; a classroom timetable alone could not do the job.

Chad continued after Idriss Déby’s death in 2021 and the military takeover led by his son. The 2023 constitution again described a sovereign republic. These institutional changes do not mark an ending for Chad’s many peoples or their cross-border connections.

passages.text: Choctaw history connects southeastern homelands with communities that endured removal and built new institutions. The linked Oklahoma outline is wrongly displayed in 1492: it belongs to a much later removal history. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mississippi Band are distinct continuing governments.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya in Mississippi is central to Choctaw origin traditions. The earthen mound stands about 25 feet high and over 200 feet long. Its meaning reaches beyond its size: Choctaw accounts identify this place as a heart of their people’s history.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya returned to the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in 2008. That transfer brought a place lost during the removal era back into community care. An ancient monument can be part of a very present-day political and cultural relationship.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologist Ken Carlton describes pottery fragments as important clues to ancestral Choctaw history. Tempering materials, construction and decoration help compare sites, but he also emphasizes a difficult gap in seventeenth-century evidence. A recognizable pot is useful evidence, not a person’s identity card.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: The Nation’s Historic Preservation Department reconstructed a winter home from around three centuries ago with thick plastered walls and a curved entrance that reduced drafts. A central fire warmed the room; the drawing is a researched reconstruction rather than a photograph of an excavated house.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: In that reconstruction, cane platforms worked as couches by day and beds by night. Food could be stored underneath; cane containers held clothes and possessions. The space beneath the bed had a useful job long before anyone invented a plastic storage box.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: Choctaw food traditions include banaha bread and fruit dumplings. The Nation’s food history emphasizes that ingredients and recipes changed over time. Families can preserve a recognizable tradition while adapting what grows nearby and what is available in the kitchen.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Choctaw stickball uses two wooden sticks with cupped, laced ends to handle a small ball. Traditional scoring involved hitting a goal post. Shaping the sticks and weaving the ball are skills in their own right, alongside the speed and teamwork needed on the field.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The Choctaw Nation now uses stickball to teach children cooperation and family values, and offers workshops in making equipment. The game has survived changes in clothes, rules and organization. Learning a sport can also mean learning how to make the things needed to play.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: A short written sample on the Nation’s modern language page is “yakoke”, meaning “thank you”. The same page supplies recorded lessons and a dictionary. This is contemporary Choctaw written with Latin letters, not a claim that this spelling appeared on a 1492 artifact.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek preceded the largest waves of forced migration west. Poor supplies and planning contributed to devastating losses, particularly among elders and children. Choctaw accounts describe the journey through the institutions and relationships families struggled to preserve.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: In 1834, Choctaws adopted a new constitution in Indian Territory and organized three districts. Their council house was called Nanih Waiya, carrying the name of the Mother Mound into a new homeland. Rebuilding included laws and meeting places as well as houses and farms.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi despite pressure to leave, then faced dispossession and difficult working conditions. Their descendants organized the Mississippi Band’s 1945 constitution. Their history is related to Oklahoma Choctaw history, but their government is not simply a branch of it.

Removal changed Choctaw landholding and institutions; it did not end Choctaw history. Distinct Choctaw governments and communities continue in Oklahoma and Mississippi. Neither the 1650 map endpoint nor its anachronistic 1492 Oklahoma outline dates the beginning or disappearance of these nations.

passages.text: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.
The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.

passages.text: Chanka history centers on Andahuaylas in Peru’s south-central highlands. Archaeology reveals farming communities and hilltop settlements, while later accounts remember their conflict with the Incas. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is a late snapshot, after Inca incorporation, rather than the lifetime of an independent Chanka state.

passages.title: Settlements and food
passages.text: Many Chanka-period settlements occupied high ridges after about 1000 CE. Archaeologist Lucas Kellett argues that access to highland farming and herding, during environmental stress, helps explain this pattern alongside conflict. The hilltop location had economic consequences as well as defensive advantages.

passages.title: Settlements and food
passages.text: Excavations at Luisinayoc and Achanchi recovered plant remains including maize, potatoes, beans and quinoa. These foods grow best under different conditions. A varied farming economy helped households work with the mountains’ changing elevations rather than rely on one crop alone.

passages.title: Settlements and food
passages.text: Kellett’s survey documented complexes combining corrals and terraces around Chanka settlements. Some lay near Luisinayoc and across several elevation zones. Managing animals and crops involved connected workplaces outside the houses, with journeys between grazing areas, fields and home.

passages.title: Settlements and food
passages.text: Burned maize from Achanchi supplied radiocarbon samples for dating occupation. Several calibrated ranges fall in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. A damaged food remnant can therefore reveal both what people used and roughly when their settlement was active.

passages.title: Buildings and medical knowledge
passages.text: At Sondor, the eastern sector has circular buildings and Chanka pottery, with a radiocarbon date around 1100 CE. Buildings grouped around small patios provide evidence for life before Inca rule. Later occupation reused parts of this settlement.

passages.title: Buildings and medical knowledge
passages.text: The Incas reshaped Sondor’s Muyumuyu hill with six large terraces and a monumental staircase. Two rocks at the summit were enclosed by a low wall, suggesting ceremonial importance. The spectacular terraces belong to this later transformation of the site.

passages.title: Buildings and medical knowledge
passages.text: A study of people buried at five Andahuaylas sites dated around 1000 to 1250 identified 45 skull operations among 32 individuals. Researchers could compare techniques such as scraping and drilling. The evidence describes an early regional medical practice, not a treatment available equally to everyone.

passages.title: Buildings and medical knowledge
passages.text: Healed bone around some surgical openings demonstrates that patients survived. The researcher also reported shaved hair and traces interpreted as applied remedies. Such observations reveal attempts to care for injured people, while leaving many details of pain relief and recovery unknown.

passages.title: Conflict, words and continuing memory
passages.text: Later histories make a Chanka attack on Cusco a turning point in Inca expansion, conventionally dated 1438. The defeat is central to the story, but that precise date comes from reconstructed historical chronology. It is not a date inscribed by a witness on the battlefield.

passages.title: Conflict, words and continuing memory
passages.text: A present-day written sample is “Añay”, meaning “thank you”, identified as Quechua Chanka in a Peruvian language-justice book. This modern printed form illustrates a living regional language variety. It should not be presented as a recovered inscription from a medieval Chanka settlement.

passages.title: Conflict, words and continuing memory
passages.text: The modern Sondor Raymi dramatizes Chanka origin traditions and the march toward Cusco. Its performers include children and women, and the event uses both Lake Pacucha and the archaeological site. Community theater makes history public, while its scripted scenes remain modern interpretation.

passages.title: Conflict, words and continuing memory
passages.text: Researchers working in Andahuaylas encountered an election sign declaring Chanka identity and collaborated with the municipal museum. Their book’s preface describes radio interviews and local publications as well as excavation. The name still belongs to a living conversation about the region’s past.

Chanka political independence ended through incorporation into the Inca state during the fifteenth century. Chanka communities and regional identity did not disappear. Later colonial and national transformations belong to that continuing history; the imported 1500 endpoint does not mark an extinction.

sectionTitles: A place built for gathering and listening
Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple

passages.text: Chavín de Huántar was a powerful ceremonial center in Peru’s northern highlands, especially around 1100 to 400 BCE. Its temples, sounds and images drew connections across the Andes. Chavín also names a wider artistic and religious tradition; shared imagery does not establish one empire. The imported dates are map coverage, extending well beyond the center’s main flourishing.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: Stone-faced buildings and artificial terraces enclosed plazas, while galleries ran through the temple interiors. Vents and drains were integrated into this architecture. A visitor encountered an engineered sequence of open gathering spaces and much more restricted passageways.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: The Lanzón, Tello Obelisk and carved stone heads combine human and animal features in striking ways. The sculptures are surviving objects of Chavín’s ceremonial world. Their intricate imagery required viewers to look closely, and scholars still debate particular meanings.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: Excavators found marine-shell horns within Chavín’s ceremonial architecture. The shells were modified into instruments and some remain playable. Transporting a large sea shell to a highland temple joined distant environments through an object that people could hear as well as see.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: Acoustic experiments investigate how shell-horn tones move through galleries and ducts. The architecture emphasizes certain sounds, offering a plausible way ceremonies could affect listeners outside a player’s immediate view. The experiments recover acoustic possibilities, rather than a recording of one ancient performance.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: Wear on the shell horns provides evidence that they were used. No written Chavín texts are known, so there is no authenticated sentence to display with a translation. Carved figures and musical instruments preserve communication without supplying a deciphered script.

passages.title: A place built for gathering and listening
passages.text: A related North Coast Cupisnique bottle, dated 1200 to 800 BCE, resembles a cluster of lúcuma fruits. The Met suggests its bulging form evokes fruit inside a net bag. This object belongs to a connected artistic tradition, rather than a documented find from Chavín’s temple.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: Food production combined valley-bottom cultivation with resources from higher slopes. Crops included tubers, grains and lupines, while camelids, deer and guinea pigs supplied meat. Different elevations helped create a varied food landscape around the ceremonial center.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: Excavated houses include rectangular structures built from stone or adobe. The surviving evidence is fragmentary, but it brings ordinary dwellings into view beside the monumental architecture. Household life required shelter, storage and working space even when visitors came for ceremonies.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: Research at La Banda examined animal bones from domestic deposits and identified locally produced meat. This differs from earlier interpretations that emphasized imported dried camelid meat at other parts of Chavín. Different neighborhoods could participate in different food arrangements.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: La Banda also yielded evidence for manufacturing bone tools. An animal’s usefulness continued after its meat was consumed: bone could become equipment for other tasks. The study places such production within a domestic sector rather than treating every find as temple ritual.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: At Wacheqsa, modest domestic occupation became a more substantial settlement around 800 BCE. The excavator proposes that craftspeople there supplied objects for Chavín’s authorities. The change is documented archaeologically; exactly how those workers were organized remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Fields, kitchens and work beyond the temple
passages.text: A study of 56 potsherds from Canchas Uckro, about 25 kilometers away, identified mostly local ceramic traditions. Some vessels indicate exchange, but production was independent of Chavín. Shared religious connections did not require every neighboring potter to follow one temple’s recipe.

Recent research places Chavín’s main ceremonial and urban flourishing around 1100 to 400 BCE; broader definitions of the tradition extend later. These sources do not identify a single conqueror or firmly established cause for the center’s decline. Its changing influence was not the end of Andean communities, and the map’s 1 BCE endpoint is not a supported fall date.

sectionTitles: A writing system becomes a printed public voice

passages.text: Cherokee history includes distinct southeastern communities and continuing nations in Oklahoma and North Carolina. Writing, newspapers, basketry and food knowledge record achievements made by individuals and families as well as governments. Forced removal devastated communities, but Cherokee people rebuilt institutions and maintained connections to their homelands.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Sequoyah developed a syllabary for writing Cherokee. In 1825 the Nation commissioned English and Cherokee type for a press. Adapting a writing system to movable type connected linguistic invention with practical publishing equipment and organization.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: The first Cherokee Phoenix appeared at New Echota on 21 February 1828. Its Cherokee and English columns made the same newspaper accessible across languages. Surviving issues are material evidence of Cherokee authorship and political communication before removal.

passages.title: A writing system becomes a printed public voice
passages.text: Publication continued in a new setting with the Cherokee Advocate, established in Tahlequah in 1844. It printed both languages as the Nation rebuilt schools, homes, businesses and government buildings after removal.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: A rivercane basket from the Qualla Boundary, catalogued as 15/8659, was collected in 1927 or 1928. The museum records its twill-plaited construction but does not name its maker. The collection date should not be mistaken for the year it was woven.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Lottie Queen Stamper recalled her family making white-oak baskets after work in the fields. Preparing splints required carefully splitting wood into usable strips. Her recollection connects an admired finished object to seasonal farm work and demanding preparation.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: Stamper expanded into rivercane and plant dyes, then recorded patterns in notebooks and on graph paper for students. Teaching changed how designs circulated between families and materials while preserving close attention to technique.

passages.title: Baskets, materials and teaching
passages.text: In 1940, Stamper studied a photograph of an older double-weave basket held in Britain and worked out its pattern. Other Cherokee elders still knew this technique. Her achievement strengthened its teaching; describing her as the sole rediscoverer would erase those weavers.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Eastern Cherokee speaker Tommy Cabe describes gathering sochan greens with relatives in spring and later teaching his own children. His account includes care for the plant and gratitude before picking. It documents one living family tradition in its own voice.

passages.title: Food, language and family knowledge
passages.text: Cherokee Nation offers immersion education in Tahlequah, online teaching and a master-apprentice language program. Different ways of learning connect children and adults with speakers, continuing the language beyond what any historic printed page can preserve.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: In May 1838, federal troops and state militias began forcing Cherokee families into detention. People often had little time to collect possessions. Subsequent travel by roads and waterways brought further hardship, illness and death.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: The 1839 constitution was part of rebuilding, but it did not immediately resolve conflicts between earlier western migrants, removal supporters and those forced west. A new government should not be mistaken for an uncomplicated recovery from dispossession.

passages.title: Displacement, government and continuity
passages.text: Cherokee Nation and the United Keetoowah Band are based in Oklahoma; the Eastern Band is based in North Carolina. Each has its own government and citizenship system. The broad label Cherokee on this map includes histories that need these distinctions.

United States removal policies caused enormous loss of life, homes and land. They did not end Cherokee peoples or political life. Cherokee Nation, the United Keetoowah Band and the Eastern Band continue as distinct nations; the map's eighteenth-century endpoint describes only its available historical coverage.

sectionTitles: A history with farms as well as horses
A buffalo robe represented many days of work

passages.text: Cheyenne history connects earlier communities around Minnesota with later Plains villages, mobile hunting groups and powerful alliances. The broad western polygon shown in 1492 should not be treated as a verified Cheyenne border for that year: the documented westward migrations came later. Northern Cheyenne and Southern Cheyenne communities continue today; the imported 1783 cutoff is not their ending.

passages.title: A history with farms as well as horses
passages.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ historical account remembers Cheyenne cultivation of corn, beans and squash before the later hunting economy. Fields and settled homes therefore belong in this history too. The familiar image of a mounted buffalo hunter captures one important period, not every generation.

passages.title: A history with farms as well as horses
passages.text: At Biesterfeldt in eastern North Dakota, archaeologist W. Raymond Wood described a fortified village of roughly sixty earth lodges, dated about 1750 to 1790. A larger lodge faced a central plaza. The Cheyenne identification is plausible but circumstantial, so the ruins cannot simply be labelled with certainty.

passages.title: A history with farms as well as horses
passages.text: Biesterfeldt pottery resembles wares from Missouri River farming villages. This helps archaeologists compare how communities made and used everyday vessels, even where written records are sparse. Wood argued that migration happened in separate groups, with settled villages existing in more than one river region at once.

passages.title: A buffalo robe represented many days of work
passages.text: In 1846 to 1847, traveller Lewis Garrard watched Cheyenne women stretch hides on the ground with wooden pegs and thin them with scraping tools. The National Park Service’s study reconstructs this work from his account. A robe ready to trade had already required substantial processing.

passages.title: A buffalo robe represented many days of work
passages.text: Softening continued over several days before smoking the hide. Finished robes entered a market for warm clothing and carriage coverings far beyond the Plains. The work of women in camp helped keep distant customers warm; the commercial story starts well before the trader counted the goods.

passages.title: A buffalo robe represented many days of work
passages.text: A Northern Cheyenne scraper attributed to Lame Deer combines elk bone, hide ties and metal. The object entered a museum loan in 1921, although its earlier history is unknown. Its mixed materials show practical toolmaking that incorporated metal into a shaped animal-bone handle.

passages.title: Play and pictures
passages.text: A deer-bone cup-and-pin game was collected from Little White Man in Montana in 1924 or 1925. The museum records its pieces as strung together. This particular object preserves a trace of recreation alongside more frequently displayed weapons; its catalogue does not give enough information to recreate the rules.

passages.title: Play and pictures
passages.text: The Cheyenne Dog Soldier Ledgerbook contains 106 coloured-pencil drawings by fourteen artists. The ruled pages of an ordinary account book became a place to record people, clothing, horses and events. Artists adapted a new material to established practices of representing personal and collective history.

passages.title: Play and pictures
passages.text: The ledger’s scenes concern events between 1864 and 1869, and the book was recovered after the attack at Summit Springs. Cheyenne people and historians have identified particular artists and events through its detailed images. These are pictorial accounts, not sentences that can be translated word for word.

passages.title: Violence, return and survival
passages.text: On 29 November 1864, United States volunteers attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village at Sand Creek, killing children and adults. Calling this a massacre matters: it was not simply a meeting of two armies. Remembering the victims remains part of Cheyenne public history.

passages.title: Violence, return and survival
passages.text: Northern Cheyenne families resisted removal to Indian Territory and some fled north in 1878. After further suffering and conflict, families resettled in Montana, where a reservation was established in 1884. Their return explains why Northern and Southern Cheyenne histories need distinct geographical chapters.

passages.title: Words and learning today
passages.text: The Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes’ own webpage writes “Tsistsistas” and translates it as “Human Beings” or “The People.” This is an attested modern written self-name, using the spelling published by the community. It is separate from the pictorial storytelling of the nineteenth-century ledgerbook.

passages.title: Words and learning today
passages.text: The same tribal language programme offers community and online classes, supports language learning in Head Start and child care, and pairs adults with experienced speakers in a Master Apprentice programme. Language learning therefore includes small children, working adults and elders, rather than ending when school finishes.

The map stops in 1783, long before nineteenth-century massacres, warfare and forced reservation settlement. Cheyenne people continue in the Northern Cheyenne Tribe in Montana and in the Cheyenne and Arapaho Tribes in Oklahoma, as well as elsewhere. These contemporary communities should not be collapsed into one vanished Plains state.

The linked Oklahoma polygon is anachronistically shown in 1492: settlement there followed nineteenth-century removal. Chickasaw and Choctaw histories intersect, but these are distinct nations.

passages.title: Towns, shelter and storage
passages.text: Traditional Chickasaw towns included summer houses, winter houses, storage buildings, ball grounds and a council house. Elevated locations helped avoid floods and see approaching threats; some towns were defended by wooden palisades. Their planning brought food, politics and recreation close to home.

passages.title: Towns, shelter and storage
passages.text: Winter houses used heavy timbers and thick clay-based covering for insulation. A narrow, winding entrance helped keep cold wind out, and some floors were partly below ground. The Nation compares the plan to a snail shell: the turn in the doorway did useful work.

passages.title: Towns, shelter and storage
passages.text: Corn cribs stood on tall posts above the ground, with a removable ladder. The Nation’s account describes rubbing oil on the posts to discourage small animals. Keeping the harvest dry and harder to steal was a serious household engineering problem, especially when the thieves were rodents.

passages.title: Towns, shelter and storage
passages.text: Women cracked and ground dried corn using pounders made from hollowed tree trunks. Drying the crop turned a seasonal harvest into food available through the year. The pounding equipment belonged to a whole sequence of growing, storing and preparing food.

passages.title: A kitchen and a council house

The Nation’s history describes women working together to feed a village; the modern pork recipe should not be projected into the precontact past.

passages.title: A kitchen and a council house
passages.text: Long wooden pashofa paddles have broad, flat ends for stirring and scraping the pot. Durable hardwood paddles could pass through generations, their handles polished by use. A family heirloom does not have to sit on a shelf: sometimes its job is preventing scorched dinner.

passages.title: A kitchen and a council house
passages.text: At Good Spring, now Tishomingo, Chickasaw leaders met in a log council house to shape their government. A committee drafted the constitution ratified in 1856. The surviving structure gives a tangible setting for the political work of rebuilding after removal.

passages.title: A kitchen and a council house
passages.text: The original council house later served as a playhouse and smokehouse on a governor’s farm. It was returned to the capitol grounds in the 1930s and is protected inside a museum. The same logs have housed both national decisions and very different everyday activities.

passages.title: Resistance, words and continuity
passages.text: In 1736 Chickasaw defenders defeated a French attack at Ackia, near present-day Tupelo. Colonial rivalry shaped alliances, including Chickasaw connections with the British. The battle matters because European claims on a map did not automatically mean effective control of Chickasaw towns.

passages.title: Resistance, words and continuity
passages.text: The 1837 Treaty of Doaksville arranged Chickasaw settlement within Choctaw territory. Forced removal caused hardship and death despite leaders’ efforts to control timing and logistics. In 1855 a treaty established separation; the 1856 constitution then organized renewed Chickasaw government.

passages.title: Resistance, words and continuity
passages.text: A modern written Chickasaw sample is “Chikashsha saya.”, translated in the Nation’s phrasebook as “I am Chickasaw.” The phrasebook pairs words with everyday uses. This Latin-letter sample is a present-day teaching witness, not an invented transcription from a fifteenth-century object.

passages.title: Resistance, words and continuity
passages.text: Chickasaw citizens resumed elections in 1971 after decades of federal restrictions. A new constitution ratified in 1983 restored a three-department governmental system. Institutions changed, while families maintained a sense of nationhood across removal, statehood and renewed self-government.

Chickasaw sovereignty suffered forced removal and severe federal restrictions, but the nation continued. Its renewed constitutional government serves a living community. The 1650 endpoint and the 1492 date attached to an Oklahoma outline are map coverage problems, not the end or origin of Chickasaw history.
