passages.text: Chile declared independence in 1818, decades before this map record begins. Industrial towns, family work and public-health debates reveal a republic whose institutions were interrupted by dictatorship and restored in 1990.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: At Santa Laura, surviving saltpeter-processing equipment includes a leaching shed and a grinder. These are traces of the machinery that turned desert deposits into fertilizer traded overseas. Industrial achievement depended on workers and transport as well as mineral wealth.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Humberstone preserves living quarters and communal spaces around its square, while railway remains link it to Santa Laura. The two sites together show a workplace and a settlement. A factory did not stop affecting family life when a shift ended.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Workers from Chile, Peru and Bolivia built the shared Pampino culture of the nitrate towns. Former workers and descendants later returned for commemorations such as Saltpeter Week. The industry declined, but its communities retained memories and connections.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: In late nineteenth-century Santiago, overcrowded housing and inadequate drinking-water and sewer systems helped infections spread. Elegant mansions and new public works existed alongside these conditions. A growing city could look prosperous while many residents lacked basic services.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: A 1872 decree introduced hygiene teaching in schools, but training and implementation lagged. Physician Isaac Ugarte criticized its shortcomings in 1884. Declaring a subject compulsory did not instantly produce teachers equipped to teach it.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: In many urban working households during 1900 to 1950, mothers combined paid employment with domestic work. Older daughters could take over childcare and cleaning; sons often assisted fathers in their trades. Childhood responsibilities varied sharply with class and gender.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Long working hours, insecure wages and illness placed working families under strain. Social workers and public-health nurses increasingly entered this domestic world as the state expanded assistance. The evidence concerns a changing social policy, not a claim that every household received help.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: Quinchamalí and Santa Cruz de Cuca pottery uses black surfaces with white accents. Makers produce useful pots and dishes alongside decorative figures. These living traditions turn everyday materials into objects that can serve a meal or tell a local story.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: One recognizable figure is the guitarrera: a rural woman holding a guitar. It connects pottery with local people and music. The 2022 UNESCO safeguarding record identifies a particular regional tradition, not a pottery style shared by all Chileans.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: The Spanish sentence “Las personas nacen libres e iguales en dignidad y derechos” means “People are born free and equal in dignity and rights.” It opens Article 1 of the consolidated constitution consulted in its 2023 version. This is a legal principle, not proof that equality has always been achieved.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: After the 1973 coup, the military authorities dissolved Congress and assumed legislative functions. The interruption changed where laws were made and who could participate. It belongs in the same national history as factories, schools and artistic work.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: The 1988 plebiscite rejected extending Augusto Pinochet’s presidency. Congress resumed on 11 March 1990. Voting and the rebuilding of institutions were parts of a transition; the country and its communities did not begin from scratch that day.

Chile continues. Independence was declared in 1818; the 1973 dictatorship interrupted representative government, and Congress returned in 1990. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage date, not the birth of Chile or its diverse peoples.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

sectionTitles: Making a living beside the desert
Care for the dead and clues to life
What survives and what remains unknown

passages.text: Chinchorro identifies ancient fishing and gathering communities of the Atacama coast, famous for carefully prepared human mummies. The map’s linked 2000 to 400 BCE intervals capture only a late slice and extend beyond the chronology of the UNESCO sites, approximately 5450 to 890 BCE. These are archaeological labels, not a kingdom’s borders.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: The World Heritage sites include the slopes of Arica’s Morro, Colón 10 and the Camarones river mouth. Dense accumulations of discarded shells sit alongside settlement and burial evidence. Generations of meals helped leave an archaeological record of sustained coastal life.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Fishers shaped shell into hooks, using stone files to smooth the material. They also made hooks from plant spines. Cords and stone weights completed equipment assembled from several different parts of the landscape; a shell could help catch tomorrow’s dinner.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Sea-lion rib bones became tools for opening shellfish. Hunting equipment included detachable harpoon heads. These objects document specialized ways of obtaining food rather than a population simply picking up whatever washed onto the beach.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Plants such as rushes supplied material for mats and cords, while food came from coastal and inland environments. Permanent structures and cemeteries suggest communities could remain in favored places while people still traveled to use different resources.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Some bodies survived because the desert dried them naturally. Others show deliberate preparation, with internal supports, modeled surfaces and pigments. Distinguishing those processes matters: a preserved person is not automatically evidence that someone performed artificial mummification.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: The so-called black mummies used dark manganese-rich coatings, with wooden supports and plant-fiber ties beneath modeled surfaces. Red examples used red ochre and often dark faces. The colors identify materials and techniques; they are not names of separate peoples.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Elaborate preservation was applied to children as well as adults. UNESCO describes people across the social spectrum among the prepared bodies.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Researchers examined arsenic in hair from 45 ancient people from the Arica region, spanning several archaeological periods. Some Chinchorro individuals had high values. The findings help investigate environmental exposure and movement, but cannot diagnose every member of an ancient community.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: A 2012 study proposed that more reliable freshwater and abundant marine food supported population growth and cultural innovation. Its explanation for mummification combines archaeological dates, environmental evidence and a model of learning. It is a tested proposal about processes, not a recovered Chinchorro account.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: No deciphered Chinchorro writing is available in the evidence used here. Tools, pigments and burial arrangements convey choices and meanings, but cannot supply a reliable original-language quotation. We cannot translate the spoken words of these ancient communities.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: Conservators found that changes in humidity could encourage microbes to damage preserved skin. Harvard and Chilean researchers studied samples to understand the process. Caring for an ancient burial today therefore involves microbiology and careful storage as well as archaeology.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: In 2014, archaeologists brought specially prepared materials about Colón 10 to an Azapa school class. Children asked about food, habits and mummification before being invited to the site museum. Local heritage includes learning about how people lived, alongside respectful care for their remains.

Elaborate mummification changed and eventually ceased; its ending is not a dated military conquest. Researchers have proposed changing water supplies, marine resources and population patterns as contributing factors. The map’s 400 BCE endpoint should not be treated as a proven disappearance date for the people themselves.

passages.text: Chinook communities made the lower Columbia River and its Pacific coast a busy center of river life. Today the Chinook Indian Nation joins five constituent groups. The map’s 1492 to 1500 outline covers part of this region, not every Chinookan community or the full span of Chinook history.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: The present Chinook Indian Nation identifies Lower Chinook, Clatsop, Kathlamet, Wahkiakum and Willapa as its constituent groups. Their communities lie around the river mouth and neighboring shores. This modern political association should not be mistaken for a single ancient empire governing every Chinookan-speaking village upriver.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cedar plankhouses could shelter several related families, each with its own fire. In a 1902 account, Catherine George remembered houses at Gray’s Bay with several household fires. Seasonal movement could also involve lighter summer shelters. A village was therefore a community of households whose living arrangements changed with work and season.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Household society had inequalities. The community-reviewed history describes leading families toward the back of a plankhouse and commoners and enslaved people nearer the front. Large shared houses were places of kinship and cooperation, but also of unequal power and, for enslaved residents, a lack of freedom.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cathlapotle, farther upriver near modern Ridgefield, offers a regional Chinookan comparison outside this map outline. Excavators recorded house depressions, hearths and post traces. These buried features preserve the layout of wooden buildings even when their walls have disappeared; they do not establish a coastal Chinook capital.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cathlapotle’s fish remains include salmon, sturgeon and smelt, with smaller fish also represented. Some excavated deposits held dense concentrations of bones. Archaeologists can study discarded meals to learn about fishing and processing: yesterday’s kitchen rubbish becomes tomorrow’s research material.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Trade beads and pieces of Chinese porcelain at Cathlapotle connect a river town to the overseas fur-trade era. One porcelain fragment had been reshaped into a scraper. Imported objects were not simply stored as curiosities; someone could give a broken piece a new working life.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Canoes carried people and goods through networks linking the coast and the interior. Small gathering boats served short trips, while larger craft carried cargo and traveled coastal waters. A canoe could be everyday transport, a fishing platform and a connection to relatives in another settlement.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Carver Tony Johnson describes placing depth pegs in a canoe hull so that hollowing could stop at the intended thickness. Hot stones and water then produced steam to soften and spread the sides. A graceful wooden boat required careful measuring as well as strength and patience.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cedar supplied much more than boat hulls. The project’s account describes bark made into water-resistant clothing, roots used for baskets and shredded material used for baby diapers. The same tree could help a family travel, carry supplies and look after its smallest members.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: An epidemic in 1830 and 1831 killed many lower Columbia people, including the influential leader Comcomly. Survivors regrouped in communities along the river and Willapa Bay. The loss of relatives and neighbors altered settlement and family life; it did not erase Chinook people from their homeland.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: At Tansy Point in 1851, Native leaders resisted removal east of the Cascades. Treaties negotiated there promised provisions and continuing residence in their homeland, but were never ratified. Chinook scholar Rachel Cushman connects this failure with family memories of a hungry winter when promised food did not arrive.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: A modern Cathlapotle plankhouse opened in 2005 after more than a hundred volunteers worked on the reconstruction. Archaeology informed the building, which became a setting for education and tribal events. This is a new structure supporting living communities, not a surviving wooden house from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: In 2019 the Chinook Indian Nation completed the purchase of ten acres at Tansy Point. Cushman describes the fundraising and community effort that made it possible. Recovering land at the treaty site created a place for commemoration and future restoration work, turning historical memory into a practical commitment.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: Chinuk Wawa developed as a language of communication among different peoples, drawing on Chinookan languages and other sources. The nation recommends resources in it today. It must be distinguished from the older Chinookan languages and from the assumption that everyone in this coastal region spoke identically.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: A short written sample is “kakwa nsayka ulman-tilixam laska munk-kemteks nsayka”, translated “As Our Elders Teach Us to Speak It”. This is the parallel title of Grand Ronde’s 2012 Chinuk Wawa dictionary, in the spelling recorded by Smithsonian’s catalogue. It is a modern teaching witness, not a sentence dated to 1492.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: Federal acknowledgement granted in 2001 was reversed in 2002. The Bureau of Indian Affairs still describes the Chinook Indian Nation as non-federally recognized on its current historical-background page. That administrative status concerns the relationship with the United States; Chinook families and national cultural life continue.

There was no Chinook ending in 1500. Despite epidemic loss, land dispossession and the continuing recognition struggle, the nation maintains stories, language and community traditions. The imported date marks the end of this map record only.

passages.text: Choctaw history connects southeastern homelands with communities that endured removal and built new institutions. The linked Oklahoma outline is wrongly displayed in 1492: it belongs to a much later removal history. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mississippi Band are distinct continuing governments.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya in Mississippi is central to Choctaw origin traditions. The earthen mound stands about 25 feet high and over 200 feet long. Its meaning reaches beyond its size: Choctaw accounts identify this place as a heart of their people’s history.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya returned to the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in 2008. That transfer brought a place lost during the removal era back into community care. An ancient monument can be part of a very present-day political and cultural relationship.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologist Ken Carlton describes pottery fragments as important clues to ancestral Choctaw history. Tempering materials, construction and decoration help compare sites, but he also emphasizes a difficult gap in seventeenth-century evidence. A recognizable pot is useful evidence, not a person’s identity card.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: The Nation’s Historic Preservation Department reconstructed a winter home from around three centuries ago with thick plastered walls and a curved entrance that reduced drafts. A central fire warmed the room; the drawing is a researched reconstruction rather than a photograph of an excavated house.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: In that reconstruction, cane platforms worked as couches by day and beds by night. Food could be stored underneath; cane containers held clothes and possessions. The space beneath the bed had a useful job long before anyone invented a plastic storage box.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: Choctaw food traditions include banaha bread and fruit dumplings. The Nation’s food history emphasizes that ingredients and recipes changed over time. Families can preserve a recognizable tradition while adapting what grows nearby and what is available in the kitchen.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Choctaw stickball uses two wooden sticks with cupped, laced ends to handle a small ball. Traditional scoring involved hitting a goal post. Shaping the sticks and weaving the ball are skills in their own right, alongside the speed and teamwork needed on the field.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The Choctaw Nation now uses stickball to teach children cooperation and family values, and offers workshops in making equipment. The game has survived changes in clothes, rules and organization. Learning a sport can also mean learning how to make the things needed to play.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: A short written sample on the Nation’s modern language page is “yakoke”, meaning “thank you”. The same page supplies recorded lessons and a dictionary. This is contemporary Choctaw written with Latin letters, not a claim that this spelling appeared on a 1492 artifact.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek preceded the largest waves of forced migration west. Poor supplies and planning contributed to devastating losses, particularly among elders and children. Choctaw accounts describe the journey through the institutions and relationships families struggled to preserve.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: In 1834, Choctaws adopted a new constitution in Indian Territory and organized three districts. Their council house was called Nanih Waiya, carrying the name of the Mother Mound into a new homeland. Rebuilding included laws and meeting places as well as houses and farms.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi despite pressure to leave, then faced dispossession and difficult working conditions. Their descendants organized the Mississippi Band’s 1945 constitution. Their history is related to Oklahoma Choctaw history, but their government is not simply a branch of it.

Removal changed Choctaw landholding and institutions; it did not end Choctaw history. Distinct Choctaw governments and communities continue in Oklahoma and Mississippi. Neither the 1650 map endpoint nor its anachronistic 1492 Oklahoma outline dates the beginning or disappearance of these nations.

passages.text: The Cholas of the Kaveri delta, restored under Vijayalaya in 848, ruled the Tamil south for four centuries and sent fleets across the Bay of Bengal. Their bronze Natarajas, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and their village assemblies are the high point of Tamil civilization.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rajaraja I finished the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, its granite tower about 66 meters high.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze images of Shiva Nataraja, cast by the lost-wax method, reached their classic form in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rajendra I sent a fleet against Srivijaya in 1025 and sacked its ports along the Strait of Malacca.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Merchant guilds such as the Ayyavole Five Hundred traded across the Indian Ocean, and Chola embassies reached Song China in 1015 and 1077.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tanks, sluices and the Kaveri's old anicuts irrigated the delta's rice fields.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ocean-going ships carried armies to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Sumatra.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Village assemblies chose their committees by lot from eligible landholders, as the Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 920s record.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Great Living Chola Temples were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chola bronzes and temple styles were carried to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Pandyas of Madurai defeated the Cholas repeatedly from the 1210s and absorbed the last of the kingdom by 1279.

sectionTitles: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
Living knowledge and a language greeting

passages.text: Chumash communities lived along the California coast, in nearby inland valleys and on the northern Channel Islands. Their villages were connected through fishing, trade and kinship, rather than one empire with a single capital. The map’s 1492 to 1650 dates cover only a slice of their history. Chumash people and distinct communities continue today; modern Santa Ynez examples below belong to that particular community.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Builders bent willow poles into domes, tied smaller branches across them and covered the framework with overlapping reeds or cattails. A roof opening let air circulate and could be covered during rain. In good weather families cooked outdoors, keeping smoke out of the house.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Acorns needed patient preparation: shelling, grinding and rinsing to remove bitter tannins. Cooks then heated the meal and water in tightly woven baskets by adding hot stones. The cooking vessel could stay away from the flames while the stones supplied the heat.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: A tomol combined wooden planks, plant-fiber stitching and a sealant of pine pitch with natural asphalt. Builders smoothed the boat with sandstone and shark skin. Some seawater still seeped in, so a crew member had the essential job of bailing it out.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Historical sweathouses stood partly underground and were entered by a roof ladder. Heated stones kept the interior hot. The museum describes cleansing and purification uses, mostly among men, and larger buildings serving as meeting places. Social space could also be a very sweaty space.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: Shell beads carried considerable economic importance. Archaeologist Lynn Gamble argues that highly standardized saucer beads were already used as money about 2,000 years ago. Her evidence includes labor-intensive manufacture and wide distribution. Archaeologists test that interpretation by comparing likely currency with beads made chiefly for adornment.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: On Anacapa, shells, fish and marine-mammal bones, hooks and other tools reveal visits extending back thousands of years. Its limited fresh water helps explain the archaeological interpretation of seasonal camps. A good fishing place did not automatically provide everything needed for a permanent village.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: The Santa Ynez Band’s historical account describes a society containing skilled makers, laborers, chiefs and religious specialists. Women could hold leadership and religious offices. Village politics and expertise mattered alongside the fishing boats and finely worked baskets that visitors often notice first.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: In February 1824, a soldier’s beating of a Chumash person at Santa Inés sparked a revolt that spread to other missions. This happened after Mexican independence. Forced labor for the army and payment in promises rather than ready money had intensified resentment.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: In September 2004, Chumash paddlers crossed 21 miles to Santa Cruz Island in the tomol called ‘Elye’wun. The trip took over ten hours, with young people aged 14 to 22 joining the paddlers. Reviving a boat tradition meant sustained teamwork as well as skilled construction.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: The Santa Ynez Band began its language program in 2008 with six apprentices and expanded it in 2013. Language workers developed teaching materials and a speaking curriculum. These efforts help knowledge move from archival documentation into conversations between living people.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: The same community offers basket-making and cooking workshops, family archery and cultural activities for children. Basket students work with juncus and an awl, learning through their hands. Such programs bring relatives and different generations together while building practical skills.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: Writing sample: “haku tikaliʼ” means “Hello, how are you?” in the Santa Ynez Band’s Samala magazine of November to December 2022. This is a modern written greeting in Samala, a Chumash language. It is an attested community teaching example, not an invented ancient inscription.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: That magazine’s language class encouraged students to keep a lesson binder somewhere handy at home and teach their families what they learned. Introductions and short conversations gave learners something to use between lessons. The homework was a chance to talk together.

Mission colonization brought disease, forced labor and displacement; land loss continued after secularization in 1834. Chumash people survived these upheavals. The Santa Ynez Band maintains cultural and language programs, while other Chumash communities also preserve their identities. The map’s 1650 endpoint is not an extinction date.

Small carvings and the work of craftspeople
When new dating changes an old story

passages.text: Cimerians is the imported spelling of Cimmerians, people prominent in eighth- and seventh-century BCE accounts of the Black Sea, Caucasus and Anatolia. The map’s 1500 to 500 BCE span is not a documented lifetime: 1500 is far earlier than the historical evidence, and its broad outline is not a secure kingdom boundary. Archaeological objects can be difficult to separate from those of neighboring peoples.

passages.title: News carried on clay
passages.text: A clay tablet from Nineveh preserves a report sent by Sennacherib to his father, the Assyrian king Sargon II. It belongs to Sargon’s reign, 721 to 705 BCE. The letter passes on news that an Urartian army had suffered a major defeat against the Cimmerians. Information traveled through named messengers and correspondents.

passages.title: News carried on clay
passages.text: Writing sample: “a-na LUGAL be-lí-ia” means “To the king, my lord.” These are the opening words of that letter in the edition’s Latin-letter transliteration of Akkadian cuneiform; LUGAL represents a sign meaning king. It is an Assyrian written witness about Cimmerians, not a sample composed in the Cimmerians’ own language.

passages.title: News carried on clay
passages.text: Another Assyrian letter, from the age of Ashurbanipal, discusses Cimmerians while interpreting an eclipse and Jupiter’s position. Its scholar even presents a year of scant rain as a favorable sign for the king. The letter reveals how celestial observations and persuasive advice could become part of decisions about real opponents.

passages.title: News carried on clay
passages.text: The Cimmerians also affected diplomacy far to the west. Gyges, king of Lydia, sought assistance from the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal against them. Akkadian records preserve this connection. A threat near Sardis could therefore set messages moving between royal courts separated by a long journey across Anatolia and Mesopotamia.

passages.title: Horse equipment, age and a difficult identification
passages.text: Bronze horse bits and cheekpieces from Azerbaijani graves dated to the later eighth and seventh centuries BCE show the equipment behind mounted travel. Some cheekpieces have three holes; others were made from twisted bronze. Their archaeological connections involve both Cimmerian and Scythian traditions, so the hardware does not supply its rider’s name.

passages.title: Horse equipment, age and a difficult identification
passages.text: A burial discovered in Adygea in 2023 contained an older man, a horse, bronze bridle equipment, an axe-like scepter and a Colchian brooch. Researchers date it to the late eighth century BCE and identify the man as proto-Maeotian. Participation in Cimmerian campaigns is their proposal, not an established personal biography.

passages.title: Horse equipment, age and a difficult identification
passages.text: The Adygea man was estimated to be over fifty-five and had survived a head injury. Tests of the horse’s unusual skeleton did not support an initial suspicion that it was a mule or hinny. Chemical traces in both individuals’ teeth also complicated a simple local-origin story. One grave can require several kinds of detective work.

passages.title: Small carvings and the work of craftspeople
passages.text: At Sardis, a bone ornament from an occupation surface around 650 BCE shows a curled animal with carefully cut details. Only 4.3 centimeters across, it has been interpreted as the end fitting of a dagger or short-sword sheath. Scholars connect its style with steppe traditions and have proposed a Cimmerian association.

passages.title: Small carvings and the work of craftspeople
passages.text: Another Sardis bone inlay, tentatively dated around 625 to 580 BCE, fits two large-beaked birds’ heads into a disk just 2.5 centimeters across. A small projecting peg on its back helped attach it to something else. The catalogue leaves its cultural attribution as Scythian or Cimmerian, while the carver’s fine work remains visible.

passages.title: Small carvings and the work of craftspeople
passages.text: A related curled-animal roundel from the same Sardis district appears possibly unfinished on its back and inside. Excavators suggest that this could indicate local manufacture by an artist working in steppe traditions. Such a find raises the possibility of craftspeople working in the city, alongside the much better documented stories of raids.

passages.title: When new dating changes an old story
passages.text: Gordion’s great burned citadel was once dated around 700 BCE and blamed on a Cimmerian attack. Tree-ring research and radiocarbon dates from barley, lentils and flax moved the destruction back to about 800 BCE. Seeds left in pots helped overturn a famous historical explanation; the fire can no longer prove that later attack.

passages.title: When new dating changes an old story
passages.text: At Sardis, another destruction layer once carried a Cimmerian label. Reassessment of a Corinthian jug found broken across its floor showed that the pottery was older than first thought. Excavators now date this layer to the later eighth century BCE. A genuine ancient conflict does not identify the cause of every burned building.

Cimmerian military power weakened through defeats and changing alliances. Ancient accounts place a decisive defeat by the Lydian king Alyattes near the end of the seventh or beginning of the sixth century BCE. The sources then lose sight of a distinct Cimmerian political force; this is not evidence that every family disappeared, or that the map’s 500 BCE cutoff marks one final event.

passages.text: Coast Salish is a collective name for many independent Indigenous Nations around the Salish Sea, including coastal British Columbia and Washington. Their related languages, trade and family connections never made them one empire. The map’s broad outline and 1492 to 1500 interval are approximate coverage; each example below names its community, and the people continue today.

passages.title: Villages, food and careful engineering
passages.text: Suquamish winter villages stood along waterways, with cedar-plank houses shared by multiple families. During spring, summer and early fall, relatives traveled by canoe to fishing, hunting and gathering camps. A household’s year followed the places where food and useful materials became available.

passages.title: Villages, food and careful engineering
passages.text: Ancient salmon backbones can preserve clues invisible to the eye. A 2021 study used DNA to identify the sex of fish from four ancestral Coast Salish settlements in Burrard Inlet. Two sites, Tum-tumay-wheuton and DhRr 22, contained significantly more male chum salmon; the other two did not show that pattern.

passages.title: Villages, food and careful engineering
passages.text: The researchers interpret those remains as evidence of selective fishing before European colonization. Male chum are larger, and leaving more females can support future spawning. They also acknowledge that the fishers’ exact motives cannot be recovered from bones alone. Local choices mattered, even between neighboring settlements.

passages.title: Villages, food and careful engineering
passages.text: Hul’q’umi’num’ and WSÁNEĆ sea gardens use low stone walls to hold sediment and form terraces where shellfish thrive. Maintaining them includes turning the beach sediment and removing excess sea lettuce. This is gardening with tides: in winter, the lowest water can send the work crew out in the middle of the night.

passages.title: Villages, food and careful engineering
passages.text: Parks Canada’s report for 2018 to 2023 records more than 320 metres of sea-garden walls rebuilt and over 11,700 square metres of beach habitat maintained with Indigenous partners. Elders, community members and volunteers put inherited knowledge into practice while restoring a local food supply.

passages.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning
passages.text: Some Coast Salish families raised small woolly dogs for their thick hair, which could be spun into textiles. A tear in a blanket now at the Burke Museum exposed unusual yarn; testing confirmed dog hair. The blanket, catalogued 2.5E1965, preserves remarkable skill, although its maker’s name was not recorded.

passages.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning
passages.text: A spindle whorl is a disk fitted around a rod. Its weight helps a spinner control the twist and thickness of yarn; the carved face points toward the person spinning. In the Burke exhibition, wood, stone and bone versions show how a small, carefully balanced tool can do a large amount of work.

passages.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning
passages.text: The same exhibition describes cleaning wool with diatomaceous earth, a powder sprinkled into the fibers. Beating the wool over a cedar mat lets the powder fall through, carrying dirt and oil away. Long before a blanket could keep someone warm, its fibers needed a very thorough clean.

passages.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning
passages.text: A modern Tulalip Lushootseed lesson prints “haʔɬ dadatu təkʷtəkʷəlus”, translated “Good morning owl.” It is a real phrase from the community’s language department, written in its modern alphabet. Lushootseed is one of the region’s languages; this friendly owl greeting is not presented as a sentence shared by every Coast Salish Nation.

passages.title: Woolly dogs, skilled hands and family learning
passages.text: In 2019, Tulalip News reported two full Lushootseed classes at Marysville Pilchuck High School. Lessons used everyday subjects such as weather, feelings and daily routines, alongside archived recordings of elders. Students could hear community speakers directly while learning words to use beyond the classroom.

passages.title: Land, government and continuing community
passages.text: At the 1855 Treaty of Point Elliott, Suquamish leaders ceded extensive lands while reserving a homeland and fishing, hunting and gathering rights. The Tribe’s history describes difficult translation through Chinook Jargon into local languages. Those hurried negotiations had consequences that generations later still had to challenge in court.

passages.title: Land, government and continuing community
passages.text: The destruction of Old Man House in 1870 struck at Suquamish communal life. Families continued living around the site before being forced onto individual allotments in 1904. Requirements that children attend boarding schools further separated young people from family teaching and language.

passages.title: Land, government and continuing community
passages.text: On July 23, 1923, sixteen Squamish bands amalgamated into the modern Squamish Nation. They pooled property, interests and accounts held in trust to strengthen collective government. This was a deliberate response to colonial interference and unequal treatment, not the beginning of Squamish identity.

passages.title: Land, government and continuing community
passages.text: The 1974 Boldt decision affirmed treaty tribes’ right to half the harvestable salmon at their usual and accustomed fishing places and established them as co-managers with Washington State. The ruling followed a long struggle over promises made in nineteenth-century treaties.

passages.title: Land, government and continuing community
passages.text: Musqueam community member Jordan Wilson recalls keeping vigil at the ancient village of c̓əsnaʔəm in 2012. The vigil lasted over 200 days as people worked to protect the site. He also recalls learning respect, patience and care for family while fishing with his grandfather.

There was no single Coast Salish state to fall in 1500. Colonial land loss, coercive schooling and restrictions on community life caused profound harm, but the Nations survive as distinct peoples and governments. Language teaching, weaving, fisheries management and protection of ancestral places remain living responsibilities.

passages.text: This record follows modern Colombia, whose republican institutions developed before the map’s 1878 starting point. Coffee farms, domestic machines, music and constitutional change reveal a diverse society shaped by both creative work and armed conflict.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: In the Eje Cafetero, small coffee plots often operate as family farms on steep terrain. Generations adapted cultivation and settlements to the mountains. The landscape records work and accumulated knowledge, rather than a crop growing effortlessly on picturesque hills.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: Some coffee-region houses combine living space with productive activity. Traditional bahareque construction uses a framework and earthen materials, and the settlements incorporate cane or bamboo alongside clay roof tiles. A house can be both home and part of the farm’s working equipment.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: These small farms remain sensitive to international coffee prices. A distant market can affect a household that grows a familiar drink. UNESCO’s 2011 inscription recognized a working landscape, not a countryside frozen outside economic change.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: Colombia’s National Museum preserves a Singer sewing machine dated around 1890, made from wood and metal. Its catalog number is 4625, and it entered the collection as a 2001 gift. It is a surviving domestic technology, not an archaeological excavation.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: The museum connects sewing with expectations that women learn skills associated with marriage and household care. Such machines could support useful work while also reinforcing gendered ideas about education. One object can reveal opportunity and constraint at the same time.

passages.title: Coffee farms and household work
passages.text: In the 1970s, records by the Hermanitas Singer promoted buying sewing machines in installments. Household equipment, popular entertainment and consumer credit met in a memorable sales strategy. Even a practical machine could acquire a musical advertising career.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: During the War of the Thousand Days, paper-money issues used to finance fighting contributed to rapid price rises. For households, conflict could therefore mean that ordinary purchases became harder even away from a battlefield.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: The Banco de la República was established in 1923. Its institutional history places that creation against earlier monetary instability. Managing currency became part of the republic’s attempt to build more durable national institutions.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: Traditional Vallenato brings together an accordion, a small hand-played drum and a ribbed scraper. Its stories can be nostalgic, playful or humorous. The UNESCO account describes a northern Colombian tradition, not the only music of the country.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: At parrandas, friends and family gather around Vallenato performance. Music also passes through formal teaching. Learning can happen in an academy or among relatives listening closely enough to join the next song.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: “Colombia es un Estado social de derecho” means “Colombia is a social state governed by the rule of law.” This Spanish phrase opens Article 1 of the 1991 Constitution, published in its corrected edition in July. It expresses the constitution’s commitment, not a verdict that all its promises are fulfilled.

passages.title: Money, music and words
passages.text: The government and FARC-EP signed a revised peace agreement on 24 November 2016. The UN welcomed it while emphasizing implementation and continuing violence in affected areas. An agreement marked a major change without proving that every armed conflict had ended.

Colombia continues as a republic. The 1991 constitution replaced the 1886 charter; the 2016 agreement changed the conflict with FARC-EP. Constitutional and peace transitions did not end the state or its many communities. The map’s 1878 beginning is not a founding date.

sectionTitles: A horse needed more than a rider
Loss of freedom and continuing government

passages.text: Comanche communities built a powerful network across the southern Great Plains through mobility, diplomacy, trade and warfare. The map’s Texas outline at 1500 is anachronistic: documented Comanche movement into northeastern New Mexico belongs to the early 1700s. This card follows that later history and the continuing Comanche Nation, rather than treating the imported dates as its lifetime.

passages.title: Families and decisions
passages.text: Before reservation confinement, an extended family living in neighbouring tipis formed a central unit of work and consumption. Related families travelled together, while larger divisions joined around shared interests. Membership could shift: these were adaptable social relationships, not a permanent ladder of offices.

passages.title: Families and decisions
passages.text: Communal hunts, trade and peacemaking were discussed in informal gatherings and more formal councils. That meant a successful leader needed to work with other people’s opinions. A large territory did not require every decision to travel through a single king’s palace.

passages.title: A horse needed more than a rider
passages.text: During the eighteenth century, horses increased the reach of bison hunting and made distant communication easier. They also became valuable trade goods. Comanche power rested partly on coordinating people and animals across enormous distances, with routes extending into Mexico.

passages.title: A horse needed more than a rider
passages.text: Large herds ate large amounts of grass. Communities moved camps and sometimes divided into smaller groups to avoid exhausting grazing. Choosing where to stay involved water, forage and the needs of many animals; a campsite had to satisfy its four-legged residents too.

passages.title: A horse needed more than a rider
passages.text: Trade included hides, metal goods and weapons, but also enslaved captives. Raiding and commerce were intertwined, and both could harm neighbouring communities. Understanding this regional power means keeping the suffering behind some exchanges visible alongside the skill involved in long-distance trade.

passages.title: Useful objects with individual histories
passages.text: A Comanche cradleboard collected from Ta-ki-ti in Oklahoma in 1909 combines wood, wool cloth, brass fittings, glass beads and hide. Its beadwork and tied construction bring baby care and skilled making into the same object. The record names its former owner but does not identify its maker.

passages.title: Useful objects with individual histories
passages.text: A painted rawhide bag collected from Koma in 1909 preserves another part of domestic life. Called a parfleche in the museum catalogue, it is both a container and a decorated surface. Its documented Oklahoma ownership gives the object a firmer context than an anonymous label saying only “Plains.”

passages.title: Loss of freedom and continuing government
passages.text: The United States Army’s Red River War of 1874 to 1875 forced Comanche groups onto reservations. This was a violent restriction of land, movement and political independence. Quanah Parker was among the leaders of this period; his story belongs after this map record’s 1783 cutoff.

passages.title: Loss of freedom and continuing government
passages.text: Comanche voters adopted a constitution in 1966, with later amendments. This continuing national government is a different institution from the mobile political divisions of the earlier Plains period. The people’s history includes rebuilding institutions as well as losing territory.

passages.title: Learning still involves doing
passages.text: At a modern Comanche Nation youth camp, children learned colours through a game of Twister and studied animals, the flag and community history. Former campers also became coordinators. The lesson could involve balancing on a coloured circle as well as listening to an adult.

passages.title: Learning still involves doing
passages.text: A modern Nation fair report describes elders and children joining a buffalo-processing event. Children helped carry meat, while participants discussed making tools from bones. This documented gathering connects food, teaching and intergenerational company without assuming every family lives in the same way.

passages.title: An invitation in living Comanche
passages.text: The Nation’s language programme writes “Nahmaʔai tanʉ nʉmʉniwʉnʉ̠!”, translated there as “Let’s all speak Comanche together!” This is a modern community-published sample, including its distinctive letters and marks. It invites participation in language renewal; it is not a sentence recovered from the map’s sixteenth-century setting.

The 1783 map endpoint does not mark a Comanche disappearance. Military defeat and forced reservation settlement in 1874 to 1875 sharply curtailed independence, while the Comanche Nation continues with its own government, families and language programmes.

sectionTitles: Written words and a changing kingdom

passages.text: These map entries concern the kingdom centred on Mbanza Kongo in present-day northern Angola. Its court, churches, textiles and diplomatic connections developed over centuries. The entry beginning in 1900 belongs to its late colonial setting; it does not represent the Congo Free State.

passages.title: A capital and its connections
passages.text: Mbanza Kongo stands on a plateau about 570 metres high. Royal residences, a customary court, a sacred tree and royal burial places made the capital a political and spiritual centre, rather than simply a fortress on a hill.

passages.title: A capital and its connections
passages.text: After Portuguese contact in the late fifteenth century, builders combined local materials and knowledge with European stone-building techniques. Churches joined an older sacred landscape; adopting Christianity did not erase every earlier custom.

passages.title: A capital and its connections
passages.text: The civil wars after 1665 fractured royal power and displaced people. Restoring a king in 1709 did not automatically restore the earlier centralized kingdom: rival courts and provincial interests had changed the balance of power.

passages.title: A capital and its connections
passages.text: By the nineteenth century, ivory and rubber became increasingly important exports. SAHO describes smaller trading villages and people moving inland to obtain rubber, showing how changes in work could redraw the settlement landscape.

passages.title: Clothes, belief and practical skills
passages.text: Kongo weavers made luxurious cloth from raffia palm fibres. European collectors admired its softness and elaborate geometry, sometimes comparing it with velvet. A plant fibre could become a diplomatic gift and a display of extraordinary skill.

passages.title: Clothes, belief and practical skills
passages.text: A surviving Kongo textile was inventoried in the Danish royal collection in 1674. Its interlacing patterns belong to a visual world also found on carved ivory horns: different materials could carry related ideas about elegance.

passages.title: Clothes, belief and practical skills
passages.text: A brass crucifix dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century gives Christ African facial features and a wrapper resembling local raffia cloth. Kongo artists interpreted Christian imagery through familiar bodies, materials and patterns.

passages.title: Clothes, belief and practical skills
passages.text: In nineteenth-century Kongo communities, some ritual specialists used carved power figures in matters of healing, protection and justice. Mangaaka figures could help communities seal agreements and resolve disputes. These are documented regional practices, not proof that every household owned such a figure.

passages.title: Clothes, belief and practical skills
passages.text: Late royal politics also depended on everyday relationships. Historian Jelmer Vos describes chiefs connected through kinship, churches, school friendships and trading journeys. A king could be someone a chief knew personally, not a distant stranger.

passages.title: Written words and a changing kingdom
passages.text: A small written Kikongo sample is “zambiampungu”, meaning “God Almighty” in the Christian vocabulary of the 1624 catechism. This preserves the historical spelling quoted by scholar Mbelolo Ya Mpiko; the modern separated form is Nzambi a Mpungu. The book used Latin letters.

passages.title: Written words and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Translation itself changed ideas. The catechism gave some existing Kikongo terms new Christian meanings, including words connected with judgment and religious specialists. A bilingual book was therefore a negotiation over meaning, not merely Portuguese sentences wearing different letters.

passages.title: Written words and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Colonial officials pressured village leaders to recruit men for poorly paid plantation work in Cabinda. The 1913 revolt challenged both Portuguese coercion and King Manuel Kiditu’s cooperation with it: labour demands struck at what people thought legitimate leadership should provide.

Portuguese domination and colonial incorporation ended Kongo’s independent government through a long process, not a single disappearance in the map’s final year, 1914. Kongo communities and the sacred traditions of Mbanza Kongo continued.

passages.text: This is Congo-Brazzaville, the state west of the Congo River, distinct from the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The map begins in 1945, while the territory was still under French rule. Independence came in 1960; modern Congolese history also includes painting, music, schools and changing urban life.

passages.title: Statehood and inherited infrastructure
passages.text: In 1958 the old framework of French Equatorial Africa was dismantled as its territories became republics. Congo’s full independence followed in August 1960. The map’s 1945 starting date therefore should not be read as an independence date.

passages.title: Statehood and inherited infrastructure
passages.text: The Congo-Océan railway linked inland Brazzaville with the Atlantic port of Pointe-Noire. Built under French colonial rule in the 1920s and completed in 1934, it crossed difficult terrain in the Mayombe region and became an important transport inheritance for the later state.

passages.title: Statehood and inherited infrastructure
passages.text: That railway carried an appalling human cost. The historical study describes coercive labour recruitment and more than 17,000 African deaths. A line on a transport map can conceal the lives and families whose labour made it possible.

passages.title: Art, music and learning
passages.text: Brazzaville’s Poto-Poto painting school began in 1951. Artists including Marcel Gotène helped make it an internationally recognized centre, where masters and younger painters worked within a continuing artistic community.

passages.title: Art, music and learning
passages.text: In March 2023 an exhibition brought together different generations of Poto-Poto-trained artists. The school had received UNESCO’s Picasso medal in 2002: its story continued well beyond the first famous painters.

passages.title: Art, music and learning
passages.text: Congolese rumba belongs to both Congo-Brazzaville and the neighbouring DRC. It accompanies celebrations and mourning, at home, in public and in religious settings. It is a shared musical culture crossing a state boundary.

passages.title: Art, music and learning
passages.text: Young rumba musicians can learn in neighbourhood clubs, training schools and community groups. Apprenticeship includes making instruments as well as playing them. Women helped shape important romantic and religious styles.

passages.title: School days and written words
passages.text: At Pointe-Noire’s École primaire 28 juin 1968, children once brought drinking water from home or bought it outside. UNICEF’s August 2022 account describes a new school water point. A tap can change an ordinary school day more than a grand monument.

passages.title: School days and written words
passages.text: The same school project involved a management committee with teachers, parents and community members. Children ran their own hygiene clubs, giving pupils responsibility for practical improvements around them.

passages.title: School days and written words
passages.text: At Brazzaville’s Bernadette Bayonne school, mothers Panive, Nadia and Berlude prepared meals for pupils in a 2021 canteen programme. The report says all 967 enrolled pupils could receive a daily meal; this is one documented school, not a nationwide count.

passages.title: School days and written words
passages.text: The canteen project also supplied handwashing equipment. Feeding children and providing a place to wash their hands were treated as parts of the same school environment, showing how education depends on everyday care as well as lessons.

passages.title: School days and written words
passages.text: A short written French sample is “Unité-Travail-Progrès”: “Unity, Work, Progress”, the motto in article 4 of the 2015 constitution. That article names French as official and Lingala and Kituba as national vehicular languages. The official document represents only one part of a multilingual country.
The Republic of the Congo continues. Independence ended colonial government, while later political changes altered the state’s institutions. Its history has no final disappearance date.

sectionTitles: A person in the written record

passages.text: Medieval Corsica was a mountainous island of villages, local lords and ports connected to Italy. Pisa and Genoa competed for influence, while island communities and powerful families pursued their own interests. The map colours the whole island as one unit, but this is a regional history: no single independent Corsican state governed it continuously from 1000 to 1492.

passages.title: Ports, government and village politics
passages.text: In 1133, the pope divided jurisdiction over Corsica’s six bishoprics between Pisa and Genoa. Church appointments were part of the competition for influence. Genoese capture and settlement at Bonifacio in the late twelfth century also gave that maritime republic a strong coastal foothold.

passages.title: Ports, government and village politics
passages.text: Thirteenth-century Bonifacio connected southern Corsica, Sardinia and Liguria. Ships carried hides, cheese and salted foods toward the Ligurian coast, and brought back cloth and pottery. These connections put overseas goods within reach of island ports long before modern ferries.

passages.title: Ports, government and village politics
passages.text: Calvi exported wine and cereals from the Balagne district. Coastal trading towns did not automatically govern all the surrounding countryside: much of the island remained rural, and local opposition repeatedly limited Genoese control.

passages.title: Ports, government and village politics
passages.text: The agreement of 1453 with the Office of Saint George specified a tax of twenty Genoese soldi per hearth, a household taxation unit. The amount did not vary with wealth. A small-looking fixed bill could therefore weigh very differently on rich and poor households.

passages.title: Ports, government and village politics
passages.text: Under that agreement, much civil justice remained local, within a district called a pieve. Officials and judges came from the neighbourhood. Criminal cases and appeals were exceptions, so settling a dispute close to home did not mean complete independence from higher authorities.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: Excavations at Cotone near Bastia reveal a settlement abandoned around the middle of the fourteenth century. Several dozen houses occupied a rocky height above the plain, protected by walls and a small castle. The village’s position combined a wide view with a steep walk home.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: Cotone’s carefully built dry-stone houses mostly exceeded fifty square metres. The excavator thought they generally had an upper floor. Rooms often had separate outside entrances, while a small vaulted oven in one room probably served for heating or cooking. The evidence preserves a working home, not its recipe book.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: More than half the pottery fragments recovered at Cotone came from a group including green-and-brown decorated jugs, small amphoras and plain red pitchers attributed to Ligurian and Pisan workshops. Local cooking pots also appeared. Broken crockery lets archaeologists connect a mountain village’s tables and kitchens with Mediterranean trade.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: At Bonifacio, the municipality built a cistern beneath the porch of Sainte-Marie-Majeure in the thirteenth century. It collected rain from the church and neighbouring roofs and could hold about 650 cubic metres. Water was drawn through openings in the porch’s broad pillars: a church entrance also helped keep the town supplied.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: The Franciscans were established at Bonifacio by the late thirteenth century, outside the town walls. Their convent stood among vegetation including wild olives and junipers. Religious communities needed buildings and land for daily work as well as places for prayer.

passages.title: Houses, water and dinner preparations
passages.text: A well built in 1398 by the master mason Abrigho de Pistoïa supplied the Franciscan community and watered its vegetable and fruit garden. A surviving piece of water engineering brings us closer to the friars’ ordinary chores: drawing water, tending plants and keeping meals possible.

passages.title: A person in the written record
passages.text: The 1453 oath list preserves the Latinised name “Franciosus de Murato”, meaning “Franciosus from Murato”, as transcribed by linguist Jean Chiorboli. People were often identified by a personal name and home locality; some entries added a father’s name to avoid confusion. This is administrative Latin, not a recording of everyday Corsican speech.

passages.title: A person in the written record
passages.text: Ajaccio’s foundation in 1492 belonged to a wider Genoese effort to reorganise the island around coastal centres. This process could be harsh: it accompanied the destruction of lordly strongholds and the depopulation of some southern districts. Building a new port could transform the lives of people far beyond its walls.

The imported record stops in 1492, when Corsican society was being reorganised rather than disappearing. Genoese government continued beyond that date. In 1562 the Republic established a new Corsican magistracy after the Office of Saint George returned the island to direct republican administration.

sectionTitles: A military building becomes a museum

passages.text: Costa Rica’s independence dates to 1821, before the imported map interval. Coffee transport, public institutions and household technologies shaped the republic. Its 1948 to 1949 abolition of a permanent army became a major constitutional transformation, without making the country free of every conflict or inequality.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: From the mid-nineteenth century, ox teams hauled coffee from the Central Valley to Puntarenas. UNESCO describes journeys lasting ten to fifteen days. Moving a crop to a ship required patient work overland before international trade could begin.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: Early twentieth-century cart decoration developed recognizable regional designs, followed by flowers, faces and miniature landscapes. Wheels could announce where a driver came from even before a conversation started. The ornate modern cart developed from a more utilitarian vehicle.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: A metal ring striking the wheel hub gives each cart a characteristic sound. Craftspeople selected wood with its acoustic qualities in mind. Here the transport had its own soundtrack, long before anyone fitted a radio.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: Coffee growers adopted different varieties over time: tall Typica plants were followed by Bourbon and later shorter forms. Villa Sarchí and Villalobos arose through local mutations. Agricultural knowledge involved observing and selecting plants, not simply repeating one unchanged method.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: Large banana plantations developed on the Caribbean side under United Fruit. During the 1930s the industry shifted toward the central and southern Pacific coast. A crop’s changing geography affected where work, settlements and transport networks were concentrated.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: The National Museum displays coffee and commercial tokens alongside stamps and banknotes depicting prominent buildings. These surviving objects connect buying, wages and public imagery. They are collection evidence about economic life, not excavated remains of an ancient settlement.

passages.title: Coffee, carts and everyday technology
passages.text: Railways, trams, telegraphs and photography appeared during the late nineteenth century. Later, electricity, household appliances and telephones became more widespread. These changes reached society over time; their invention did not mean every household immediately owned them.

passages.title: A military building becomes a museum
passages.text: Bellavista Barracks preserves spaces used for ammunition storage, cells, a kitchen, showers and toilets during the 1920s to 1940s. Even a fortified building needed meals, washing and sanitation. The less glamorous rooms help explain how people actually lived within its walls.

passages.title: A military building becomes a museum
passages.text: Photographs in the museum trace the barracks’ transformation, while towers, corridors, courtyards and stairways retain evidence of its earlier use. The same structure can serve different institutions, so its surviving appearance does not identify one unchanging purpose.

passages.title: A military building becomes a museum
passages.text: On 1 December 1948, José Figueres struck a section of the Bellavista wall in a symbolic ceremony abolishing the army. The place later became the National Museum. A remembered political gesture is attached to a specific surviving site.

passages.title: A military building becomes a museum
passages.text: “Se proscribe el Ejército como institución permanente” means “The army is prohibited as a permanent institution.” This Spanish sentence is Article 12 of the 1949 Constitution. It is an attested legal text rather than a slogan reconstructed from memory.

passages.title: A military building becomes a museum
passages.text: The same constitutional article provides for police and permits military forces in specified defense or continental-agreement circumstances, always subordinate to civilian authority. The distinction matters: banning a permanent army is not the same as abolishing all public security forces.

Costa Rica continues as a republic. The 1948 abolition ceremony and 1949 constitutional provision changed its security institutions; they did not end the state. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage boundary, not the date independence or Costa Rican communities began.

passages.text: Cree peoples include many communities and regional language varieties across a vast area. The map’s single outline does not represent one empire or an exact boundary for every period. Plains examples and James Bay examples below are identified separately; their histories continue after 1715.

passages.title: Technologies for winter and travel
passages.text: Aanischaaukamikw, the Cree Cultural Institute, holds two nineteenth-century toboggans attributed to the Mistissini area. A sled distributed a heavy load over snow, helping hunters bring an animal back to camp. The surviving objects make a practical winter problem visible.

passages.title: Technologies for winter and travel
passages.text: The institute notes that ubagaan can also refer to a pickup truck. The material and engine changed; the useful idea of carrying a heavy load survived. Language can adapt an old, familiar tool name to a new machine.

passages.title: Technologies for winter and travel
passages.text: A pair of child-sized snowshoes made at Waskaganish travelled on museum loan to Zurich. The 2013 to 2014 report treats them as living technology, still made and used. Learning to move over deep snow was part of growing into the work and journeys of the bush.

passages.title: Technologies for winter and travel
passages.text: At Rocky Mountain House, Cree traders joined several other First Nations and Métis in exchanging furs and food for goods such as metal pots, axes and glass beads. Indigenous traders also carried goods between communities, making decisions and earning profits within their own networks.

passages.title: Learning through family and place
passages.text: In a 2014 account from Oujé-Bougoumou, a seamstress describes making Adelyna Sara Snow’s walking-out outfit. She measured the child with newspaper patterns and chose floral beadwork inspired by plants near Chisasibi. Family clothing could carry both careful handiwork and connections between places.

passages.title: Learning through family and place
passages.text: Adelyna shared the ceremony with three other children and walked from the lodge escorted by her parents. The account records smiles, relatives and demonstrations of gathering wood. It is a particular family celebration of a child’s first steps on the land, rather than a rule for every Cree community.

passages.title: Learning through family and place
passages.text: On the Plains, Wanuskewin preserves bison-jump areas, campsites and a medicine wheel within a much older gathering landscape. Several Indigenous nations have relationships with the place. These remains provide regional context for Plains Cree history without assigning every ancient builder a modern ethnic label.

passages.title: Learning through family and place
passages.text: Wanuskewin’s school lessons use the Plains Cree style of tipi to discuss values associated with its poles and the stages from childhood to older age. Building knowledge can be taught together with social responsibilities. This is the centre’s contemporary educational programme.

passages.title: Languages and living institutions
passages.text: Cree varieties differ across regions. The Algonquian Dictionaries Project locates Plains Cree in the western part of a much wider language continuum, while Woods, Swampy and Moose varieties have their own distributions. One spelling or pronunciation should not be presented as everybody’s only correct form.

passages.title: Languages and living institutions
passages.text: A written James Bay Cree sample is “ᐙᒋᔮᐦ”, presented with “Welcome” and Wachiya on Aanischaaukamikw’s bilingual website. These are Cree syllabics on a modern public page. The sample belongs to that regional witness, not to a supposed universal 1492 Cree inscription.

passages.title: Languages and living institutions
passages.text: The 1975 James Bay and Northern Quebec Agreement followed Cree and Inuit legal opposition to a huge hydroelectric project. It established important rights for the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee. That agreement is regional: it is not a treaty signed on behalf of every Cree nation across Canada.

passages.title: Languages and living institutions
passages.text: In 2023, Eeyou Istchee leaders linked local health committees with regional health and school authorities. Communities identified their own priorities, potentially including youth mental health or diabetes support. The arrangement treats families, education and health services as connected parts of everyday well-being.

Cree peoples and governments continue. Colonial pressures and industrial development altered land use and institutions, while communities maintained and renewed their languages and authority. The 1975 agreement is one Eeyou Istchee chapter in that continuing history; the map’s 1715 endpoint is not a disappearance.

sectionTitles: Written Greek, fresh water and a famous maze

passages.text: The Crete shown here around 300 to 200 BCE was an island of rival Greek city-states, including Knossos, Gortyn and Lyttos. Its single map colour hides shifting alliances and separate governments. This card concerns Hellenistic Crete, long after the Bronze Age palaces; the outline does not represent one unified Cretan kingdom.

passages.title: Cities with their own choices
passages.text: A decree from Itanos records a decision of its council and assembly to honour Patroklos, a Macedonian commander sent by King Ptolemy. They granted him citizenship and honours that also extended to his descendants. A powerful foreign friend could become part of a city’s political family.

passages.title: Cities with their own choices
passages.text: Itanos guarded sea routes as well as land. Archaeologists date one southwestern fortification tower between the middle fourth and middle third centuries BCE. They suggest, cautiously, that Ptolemaic troops may have built it. Its strong masonry is firmer evidence than the proposed identity of its builders.

passages.title: Cities with their own choices
passages.text: War could reach people who never carried a shield. In his account of the conflict around 220 BCE, Polybius says Knossian forces burned Lyttos while its army was away and carried its women and children to Knossos. Returning soldiers found refuge with their allies at Lappa.

passages.title: Streets, meetings and meals
passages.text: At Lato, the main street climbed from a fortified gate toward the agora, the central public space. Excavators identified shops and workshops on one side and homes on seven terraces on the other. Much of the visible town belongs to the fourth and third centuries BCE.

passages.title: Streets, meetings and meals
passages.text: A large underground reservoir near the centre of Lato is interpreted as the public cistern because of its size and position. Carrying and storing water mattered in a hill town. A useful public building could be mostly hidden beneath everyone’s feet.

passages.title: Streets, meetings and meals
passages.text: Lato’s prytaneion, a civic building, contained a hall with a central hearth and space reconstructed for about eight dining couches. The city’s magistrates, called kosmoi, ate there and received official guests. Hospitality could be part of government business, with dinner built into the architecture.

passages.title: Streets, meetings and meals
passages.text: The great stairway at Lato also served as a gathering place. Its straight rows of steps could seat an estimated eighty people watching ceremonies or public events in the agora. Narrower stairs divided the seating into sections, so getting to your place need not mean climbing over every neighbour.

passages.title: A home could change jobs
passages.text: House A at Nissi-Eleutherna began in the third century BCE and was used again in a later phase. Its plan includes a courtyard, sleeping spaces, a kitchen, storage and a work-and-living room with a cistern. The varied spaces show how several household needs fitted together within one building.

passages.title: A home could change jobs
passages.text: Later, in the late second or early first century BCE, that house also became a pottery workshop. Lead clamps and a repaired vessel reveal that people mended crockery as well as making it. Grinding equipment, loomweights and stored cereals belong to its domestic story too. These finds are later than this map’s displayed century.

passages.title: A home could change jobs
passages.text: Comparing houses at Lato and Trypetos, archaeologist Ruth Westgate found arrangements unlike the familiar courtyard houses of some other Greek cities. She suggests women may have moved less restrictively through these homes. It remains an interpretation of architecture; other Cretan towns had different layouts, and walls cannot tell us every household rule.

passages.title: Written Greek, fresh water and a famous maze
passages.text: Between 220 and 209 BCE, a garrison commander at Itanos named Lucius, son of Gaius, dedicated a reservoir and nymphaeum to King Ptolemy IV and Queen Arsinoe III. The inscription identifies him as Roman. People serving an Egyptian dynasty could come from well beyond Egypt or Crete.

passages.title: Written Greek, fresh water and a famous maze
passages.text: Its Greek words “τὸ ὕδρευμα καὶ τὸ νυμφαῖον” mean “the reservoir and the nymphaeum”. The latter was a water feature associated with nymphs. This sample follows the scholarly edition’s accents and spacing. A short carved dedication preserves both a practical water project and the royal names attached to it.

passages.title: Written Greek, fresh water and a famous maze
passages.text: A Knossian coin dated 300 to 200 BCE carries a labyrinth design. The Ashmolean Museum points out that its pattern has a single route to the centre, unlike a puzzle with many wrong turns. The city put its legendary maze onto something small enough to hold in your hand.

The map stops at 200 BCE, but Cretan cities continued through further alliances and wars. Roman conquest began in 69 BCE, more than a century later, and Gortyn became the provincial capital. Political independence changed; the island’s communities and urban life continued under Roman rule.
