sectionTitles: Rulers, towns and people at work

passages.text: This map label refers to medieval Croatia, including the later native kings and the kingdom’s association with Hungarian rulers from 1102. Coastal towns, monasteries and inland communities had different connections and institutions. It is a different historical entry from the modern Republic of Croatia.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Zvonimir’s royal authority was linked to the papacy, while his marriage connected him to Hungary’s ruling family. After his death, competing claims helped reshape the kingdom. Medieval succession could turn a family relationship into a question affecting towns, nobles and armies.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Two wooden boats found in Nin’s harbor are dated to the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The surviving remains measure roughly seven and eight meters long. Their ribs and planking give physical evidence for the small craft that moved along the Adriatic coast.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: The boat type known as a kondura combined rowing with square sails when winds were favorable. Oars offered another way to move when the breeze was unhelpful. Conserved remains and modern replicas help researchers explore these practical arrangements, though a replica is not the medieval boat itself.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Čika, a widow from a prominent Zadar family, founded the Benedictine convent of St Mary in 1066. Her daughters were connected with the community, and Vekenega later became abbess. Women could hold lasting responsibilities for a religious institution, its property and its records.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: The Zadar convent preserved a parchment cartulary containing records from 1066 to 1236. Its writing includes Beneventan, Carolingian and Gothic forms. Across generations, the book kept track of the community’s affairs while handwriting styles changed around it.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Béla IV’s Golden Bull of 1242 granted privileges to Gradec, now part of Zagreb. The charter addressed local government, courts, taxes, markets and boundaries. A royal document could shape ordinary questions such as who judged a dispute and how a town organized trade.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The Baška tablet came from St Lucy’s church at Jurandvor on the island of Krk. Carved around 1100, it formed part of a stone screen near the altar. Its thirteen lines of Glagolitic writing preserve a record of land given to the church by King Zvonimir.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The tablet’s account names witnesses and records that Abbot Dobrovit built the church with nine brothers. This is unusually personal information preserved in a heavy piece of limestone. The stone combines a record of property with the memory of a small religious community.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The main doorway of Trogir’s Cathedral of St Lawrence carries a date of 1240 and the name of its sculptor, Radovan. The inscription also names Bishop Treguan. A signed architectural sculpture can connect a surviving building with particular people and a specific year.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: Earrings with hollow metal beads survive from medieval sites including Biskupija near Knin. Gold and silver examples belong to forms used in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Jewelry records skilled metalworking and contacts with wider Mediterranean fashions, alongside the more familiar history of kings and churches.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: Zagreb’s twelfth-century cathedral had three aisles and Romanesque architecture. It suffered severe destruction during the Mongol invasion of 1242, followed by rebuilding in a Gothic style. The later building therefore carries a history of damage and reconstruction within its fabric.

passages.title: Two small samples of writing
passages.text: Latin on Radovan’s portal, 1240: “Per Raduanum”, meaning “by Radovan”. The phrase is quoted in art historian Vladimir Peter Goss’s discussion of the inscription. It preserves a medieval maker’s name in the Latin language and alphabet used for this public church inscription.

passages.title: Two small samples of writing
passages.text: The Baška tablet includes “Zvanimir kralj hrvatskij”, meaning “Zvonimir, the Croatian king”. These are medieval Croatian words shown in Branko Fučić’s scholarly Latin-alphabet transcription. The original stone uses Glagolitic letters; this excerpt is a transcription of that script, not a reproduction of its letter shapes.

The change of monarchy in 1102 joined Croatia and Hungary under a ruler, while Croatia retained a distinct kingdom and institutions. Medieval Croatian history continued beyond this map label’s 1279 endpoint. The later Pacta conventa text cannot be treated as a surviving original treaty from 1102.

passages.text: The modern Republic of Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991. War and territorial disputes marked its first years, with peaceful reintegration of the remaining eastern region completed in January 1998. It later joined the European Union and adopted the euro. This entry is distinct from the medieval Croatian kingdom.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Peaceful reintegration in eastern Croatia involved more than transferring offices. UN reporting discussed pensions, welfare payments, policing, returning residents and protection of rights. Restoring daily routines and trust was part of the work of bringing a war-affected region back under Croatian administration.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: The Pelješac Bridge opened in July 2022. Its approximately 2.4-kilometer crossing carries four lanes of road traffic, while its height allows ships to pass below. Roads and sea routes meet at the same structure, so engineers had to make room for both.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: The Zagreb earthquake of March 2020 damaged hundreds of education buildings. Schools were already closed because of the pandemic, so pupils were not in classrooms when it struck. The damage assessment estimated that thousands would need different teaching locations while buildings were repaired.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 and began using euro coins and banknotes in January 2023. Currency change affected ordinary shopping and household budgets as well as banks. A familiar price tag now had a different unit printed beside the number.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Primary schooling is compulsory and free, lasting at least eight years. Children can also attend separate music or dance programs alongside general school. A pupil’s week may therefore include both ordinary classroom subjects and time learning an instrument or practicing dance.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: A bronze statue of an ancient athlete was raised from the seabed near Lošinj in 1999. Croatian and Italian specialists spent six years conserving it. The statue belongs to antiquity, but recovering, studying and displaying it was a modern achievement in archaeological conservation.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Researchers found a rodent’s nest inside the hollow bronze, probably made by a field mouse, along with laurel leaves and fruit remains. These small traces became part of the statue’s story. For a while, an artwork that would eventually receive its own museum had also served as somebody’s very unusual mouse house.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Wooden toy makers in Hrvatsko Zagorje use local woods such as willow, lime, beech and maple. UNESCO’s account describes family production, with men traditionally carving and women painting. Each toy is handmade, so matching horses or whistles may have small differences.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: The toy repertoire has expanded to include cars, airplanes and other modern forms, alongside horses and miniature furniture. Some toys are tuned musical instruments used in children’s learning. A living craft can keep familiar techniques while changing what children get to play with.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Decorated gingerbread hearts from northern Croatia often carry a little mirror and a written message. They can be gifts expressing affection or respect. The decoration matters as much as the dough: this is a craft of making a keepsake for another person.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Gingerbread makers have passed their skills through family workshops, historically connected with candle making and honey drinks. Metal molds gradually replaced wooden ones, but individual decoration remained important. A shared outline could still become a distinctive gift in a maker’s hands.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Croatian, article 1 of the constitution: “Republika Hrvatska jedinstvena je i nedjeljiva demokratska i socijalna država.” Translation: “The Republic of Croatia is a unified and indivisible democratic and social state.” This is the Constitutional Court’s 2014 consolidated witness of the constitution first enacted in 1990.

The Republic of Croatia continues. The map’s 1994 starting point falls after independence and during the war, not at the state’s founding. Peaceful reintegration of the eastern region concluded on 15 January 1998, while rebuilding lives and institutions extended beyond that administrative milestone.

sectionTitles: Titles, records and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Medieval Croatian kingship developed among communities whose lives survive in inscriptions, church buildings, tools and human remains. Royal titles and land grants show relationships between rulers and religious institutions; archaeology adds evidence of riding, food and health. The accession of an Arpad ruler in 1102 changed the dynasty while Croatian kingship and local society continued.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Tomislav's royal title survives through copies of papal letters associated with the Split councils, preserved in a much later compilation. The source tradition matters: a copied title is evidence to assess, not a surviving contemporary coronation record.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The familiar coronation at Duvno in 925 arose from later historical reconstruction. The Croatian Encyclopedia explains why that location claim was rejected and why a precise ceremony cannot be confidently reconstructed from the surviving evidence.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The Baska Tablet is a limestone slab originally belonging to the church screen at St Lucy's near Jurandvor on Krk. Carved around 1100, it placed a written record within a building used by a religious community.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Its text records King Zvonimir's gift of land, witnesses and an abbot's account of church construction. The inscription links property, prayer and patronage; damage and difficult readings prevent every personal name and clause from being treated as certain.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The tablet uses Croatian Church Slavonic and Glagolitic letters between rounded and angular forms. Its later reuse in the church floor damaged the surface. Both its script and its wear are part of the evidence for how the stone was used.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: A bronze fitting from the cemetery near St George at Putalj was first catalogued as a Gothic buckle. Petrinec reidentified it as part of an early Carolingian spur set, dating to the late eighth or early ninth century.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The Putalj fitting has parallels in the Solin area and graves at Biskupija. It documents connections in riding equipment before the later royal-title evidence, but one imported style cannot establish every rider's birthplace or a whole community's identity.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: Bone-collagen analysis at sites including Glavice-Gluvine and Radasinovci-Vinogradine suggests millet contributed to early medieval diets. This is a chemical inference about food consumed, not a surviving meal or proof that everyone followed the same menu.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The later Sibenik-Sveti Lovre sample differs from the other early medieval groups in that study. Its chemistry suggests a different protein mix, possibly including freshwater fish. The researchers' uncertainty is more informative than a single supposed national diet.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: At the ninth- to eleventh-century Konjsko cemetery, researchers recorded dental and skeletal signs of stress and disease. Their comparisons help recover the lives of people absent from royal documents, while the small sample limits conclusions about the wider population.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: St Mary's cartulary at Zadar records Coloman's 1102 coronation at Biograd. An inscription at St Mary's also supports Zadar's recognition of his rule in 1105, connecting written accounts with a surviving architectural setting.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: Pacta conventa survives as a note appended to a manuscript from the 1380s. Most recent scholarship rejects it as an authentic contemporary treaty. A possible agreement with nobles should be distinguished from accepting this later text as its original record.

In 1102 Coloman became king of Croatia and Dalmatia, bringing Croatian kingship under an Arpad ruler. This marks dynastic change rather than the extinction of Croatian society or the royal title. The terms of any contemporary agreement with nobles cannot simply be read from the much later Pacta conventa.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure

passages.text: Cuba’s history lives in household objects as well as public events. Wooden tools, discarded dishes, readers at work and music shared between generations reveal different kinds of knowledge. The examples below distinguish particular communities and periods across the island’s changing political history.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: At Los Buchillones on Cuba’s north coast, archaeologists recovered palm thatch and wooden parts of collapsed buildings. A 2006 study placed occupation before 1220 CE through 1640 or later. One partly excavated structure appeared to stand on pilings over water. The surviving pieces let researchers investigate how homes were built; the precise arrangement of every building is still a matter of reconstruction.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: The Los Buchillones wood collection includes axe handles with holes prepared for stone heads, and two grooved fragments interpreted as knife handles. The grooves could hold stone blades. Woodworking supplied the part that fitted a tool to a human hand. The collection combines excavated finds and earlier collected objects, so individual pieces do not all have equally precise find records.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: Carved seats called dujos also survive from Los Buchillones. Some were made from a single piece of wood, with sculpted human or animal features and supporting legs. Researchers classify them as ceremonial seats. Their careful carving shows skilled work, but they should not be treated as a sample of every household’s everyday furniture.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: At Habana 958 in Old Havana, a latrine cut into bedrock held pottery, glass, bones and seeds from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Excavators distinguished waste left during use from later rubble used to fill it. An old toilet can preserve clues to meals and household possessions. Archaeology sometimes finds its best reading material in very unglamorous places.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: Excavations in 1999 and 2000 at El Padre, a nineteenth-century coffee plantation near Madruga, recovered two circular pieces cut from discarded crockery. The report interprets them as game counters. Such small objects offer glimpses of activities beyond imposed plantation work. They do not establish which game was played or who used each piece.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In a tradition traced to nineteenth-century Cuba, a lector read aloud to cigar workers as they worked. Reading brought literature and political information into the workshop. Historian Araceli Tinajero studied newspapers and interviewed readers to investigate the practice. It is a little like sharing an audiobook with the whole workplace, except the person doing the reading is actually there.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In 1881, Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that mosquitoes carried yellow fever between people. The Yellow Fever Board led by Walter Reed confirmed mosquito transmission in 1900. Finlay’s insight helped change how people investigated and prevented the disease. The distinction between proposing an explanation and testing it is part of the story of scientific discovery.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: A photograph taken by the Kaweiro Group in 2015 shows a mother and daughter joining other Native families in eastern Cuba for a workshop about local medicinal plants. The Smithsonian included it in its 2018 Taíno exhibition announcement. It records knowledge being discussed across generations and challenges the idea that Indigenous people vanished. The photograph does not establish whether a particular remedy works.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: Cassava bread connects Cuban households with a wider Caribbean tradition. UNESCO’s 2024 account describes variations in thickness, texture and flavour across Cuba and four other countries, with skills commonly passed on at home and within communities. Learning to make a familiar food can also mean learning from an older relative or neighbour. There is no single recipe that represents every family.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Rumba combines singing, movement and percussion, with roots in communities including Havana and Matanzas. Instruments can include household or workplace utensils, and the audience joins the exchange through clapping and response. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children and adults learning through imitation within families and neighbourhoods. A musical education can begin by watching someone nearby and joining in.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Punto brings poetry and melody together. Singers perform ten-line stanzas, sometimes learned in advance and sometimes made up as they sing. UNESCO’s 2017 account describes learning by imitation and workshops in Houses of Culture. Improvising a rhyme while keeping a tune takes practice. It gives thinking on your feet a very musical meaning.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: For Las Parrandas in central Cuba, competing neighbourhoods spend months preparing floats, costumes, lights and decorations. UNESCO’s 2018 account even mentions people trying to discover the other side’s surprise before the celebration. The preparations combine craft skills with friendly suspense: imagine keeping a spectacular float secret from the neighbours. Participation and practices vary between communities.

Spanish sovereignty ended after the 1898 war, followed by U.S. occupation and the republic in 1902. Batista’s government ended in the 1959 revolution. These political transitions did not end Cuban communities or culture, including Indigenous descendants and traditions shared across generations.

sectionTitles: An early center with a distinctive shape
Water, maize and the earth underfoot
Carved signs and an uncertain ending

passages.text: Cuicuilco was an important early center in the southern Basin of Mexico, now within Mexico City. Its monumental and residential remains belong principally to a much earlier history than this map’s imported 1492 to 1500 interval. The outline locates the archaeological site; it should not be read as an independent fifteenth-century kingdom. Its early urban development preceded Teotihuacan’s regional prominence.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: Cuicuilco occupied a strategic area where streams descended from the Tlalpan uplands. Nearby lakes and oak-pine woodland supplied different resources, while routes connected the basin with the Toluca Valley. Its surroundings help explain why people gathered here.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: The great circular platform grew through at least eight enlargements, according to INAH. Its builders packed an earthen core inside a covering of volcanic stone. A monument could be a long series of community building projects rather than one construction day.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: A ceremonial structure conventionally called the Kiva preserves red linear decoration made with hematite, an iron-oxide pigment. Andesite slabs and river stones formed its construction. The surviving red lines offer a glimpse of buildings as painted spaces, not simply bare ruins.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: Potters made tripod vessels with lids shaped like bird heads. INAH places the ceramic examples it describes within roughly 600 to 200 BCE. Practical containers could be carefully designed objects, with an animal form waiting on top of the lid.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: An E1 building burial included pottery, a necklace and two figurines representing a man and a woman. Such a particular set of offerings records choices made for one burial; it does not establish a standard funeral kit for every household.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: Investigators documented irrigation channels predating the lava. At Cuicuilco D, a reconstructed channel system incorporates smaller channels and a dam. Moving water was part of creating a productive settlement, not merely a concern for its ceremonial buildings.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: A 2026 soil study argues that builders selectively dug up, transported and reused older soils near the Estela monument. Microscopic observations, chemistry and conflicting soil ages support that interpretation. Old carbon in reused earth can be older than the building that contains it.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: Charred maize plants were found near the great platform and the Estela. Researchers relate the context to agricultural themes in ceremonial life. These traces show maize’s place in the settlement’s material world, although they do not give us a complete family menu.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: The Xitle eruption began with ash and later produced lava flows over Cuicuilco and nearby farmland. The damage affected the means of growing food as well as buildings. Geological layers preserve this environmental upheaval even where its exact timing remains debated.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: The Estela is an andesite column about 3.9 meters tall with carved circles and diamond shapes. Interpretations connect it with ritual or astronomical recording, but the checked research supplies no deciphered sentence. A translated greeting in its builders’ language would be invented.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: The date of the eruption remains a research problem. A 2016 archaeomagnetic study proposed roughly 90 BCE to 20 CE; a recent geochemical paper follows radiocarbon recalibrations placing the onset shortly after 380 to 400 CE. These estimates should not be blended into a falsely precise fall year.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: Ramírez and Pastrana describe evidence of later visits and some habitation after the eruption. Parts of the landscape that escaped the lava remained usable. The end of Cuicuilco’s greatest importance was therefore different from everyone vanishing permanently from the site.

Cuicuilco lost its earlier regional importance, and Xitle lava covered much of its built and agricultural landscape. The precise sequence of decline, eruption and migration remains debated. Later activity continued; neither a single unquestioned fall year nor the map’s 1500 endpoint explains the site’s history.

passages.text: The imported labels “Kushites” in 700 to 800 and “Cushites” in 900 to 1000 cover the Somali Horn. They are broad regional labels, not the Nile kingdom of Kush or a documented united empire. Cushitic is a family of related languages that includes Somali. This card follows regional communities through archaeology, with earlier and later examples clearly dated; it does not assign every ancient object to a modern people.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: At Xiis on the Gulf of Aden, excavators found imported pottery and glass in stone burial mounds. Goods came through connections reaching Roman territories, southern Arabia and Mesopotamia. The early centuries CE therefore reveal coastal people participating in far-reaching exchange, even without a large local city or imperial government.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: One Xiis child, estimated to have been about eight or nine years old, was buried with beads, an iron anklet and a glass flagon dated to the third century CE. The vessel probably came from Roman Syria or Cyprus. A small grave can preserve both personal care and a remarkably long journey.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: In the later medieval settlements surveyed around Borama, many houses used flat stones bound with mud. Typical examples had two or three rooms within about 20 to 40 square metres. At Fardowsa, two much larger six-room houses suggest that some households had considerably more space.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: The same survey found grinding stones and digging-stick weights near farming land. These are clues to daily work: preparing ground and turning grain into food. Some settlements had few imported luxuries, so their history cannot be told only through merchants and distant ships.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: Mosques were important gathering places in these later towns. At Abasa and Hasadinle, pillars helped support the roof. Their builders worked with the same stone-and-mud techniques used in houses, linking public religious spaces to skills also useful around the home.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A StateHorn account of historically documented pastoral life explains why movement mattered: rain could make a grazing area usable for a season, while dry months depleted wells. Along the Guban plain, shallow wells reached water beneath sandy ground. Knowing when and where to travel was a practical skill, not aimless wandering.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: At Siyaara near Berbera, archaeologists found thousands of local and imported pottery fragments dated from the tenth to sixteenth centuries. Seasonal fairs connected arriving ships with caravans and mobile herding communities. A place could become an important meeting ground without being a busy town every month of the year.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A milk pot collected in southern Somalia in 1934 to 1935 combines wood, woven plant fibre and a lid with a central knob. It is a much later example of household craftsmanship from within this broad region. The ordinary job of carrying and protecting milk required careful work with several materials.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: An Issa head-rest catalogued to about 1910 to 1912 is carved from wood, with a conical base and ornament. It stands just 14.5 centimetres high. This later Somali object offers a different answer to the bedtime equipment question: a pillow need not be a bag of feathers.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Here is a modern Somali writing sample: “𐒍𐒖𐒇 𐒈𐒝𐒑𐒛𐒐𐒘”, far Soomaali, meaning “Somali writing”. These are Osmanya letters, from a script devised in 1920 to 1922. The sample is printed in the Unicode Standard; it is not medieval writing from either map interval.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Getting Osmanya onto computers involved cooperation across generations. Michael Everson described how Osman Abdihalim Osman Yusuf Keenadiid and his family supplied a photocopied book that helped the encoding project. Their collaboration produced a revised proposal in 2001: preserving writing can involve family books as well as software.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: In 2015 to 2016, ten young adults from London’s Somali community worked with the British Museum’s Somali collections. They explored objects, contributed knowledge and developed new ways to tell their stories. Descendant communities are participants in explaining this heritage, not merely people described by old collection labels.

Neither 800 nor 1000 marks the disappearance of the Horn’s peoples. Later regional trade and settlement changed, including disruption around the end of the Adal sultanate in the sixteenth century. That was a transformation of particular political and commercial networks, not an ending for Cushitic-speaking communities.

passages.text: This eastern Libyan region combined Mediterranean towns, pastoral communities and the Sanusi religious network. The map’s 1715 to 1878 interval covers Ottoman and Karamanli rule; it does not represent one independent kingdom or the much earlier Greek city of Cyrene.

passages.title: Government and connected places
passages.text: Before permanent inland posts, Karamanli officials worked through tribal leaders responsible for order and taxation. Their authority followed communities more than a neatly bounded district with a government office in its center.

passages.title: Government and connected places
passages.text: Ottoman forts at Al-Marj and Al-Qayqab were built in 1851 to 1852 along the inland Benghazi-to-Derna road. Surviving structures and local testimony helped geographer Xavier de Planhol reconstruct this expanding administrative network.

passages.title: Government and connected places
passages.text: Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sanusi founded the Bayda lodge in 1843. His movement joined religious teaching to practical organization; lodges became places where worshippers, learners and traveling merchants could meet.

passages.title: Government and connected places
passages.text: By the mid-nineteenth century, lodges linked caravan routes, coastal inlets and older settlement sites. Religious communities provided education and work, while tolls, gifts and trade helped sustain the network.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday arrangements
passages.text: Visiting Benghazi in 1852, James Hamilton described courtyard houses roofed with juniper trunks, mats and plaster. Drinking water arrived in skins or barrels from outside wells; courtyard wells supplied brackish water.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday arrangements
passages.text: Hamilton also reported a Benghazi doctor supervising street cleaning and inspecting meat before sale. Public health involved markets and streets as well as sickbeds.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday arrangements
passages.text: In Derna, Hamilton saw streams divided into channels through the town, with water distributed to gardens at regular times. Palms, bananas and vines grew around houses: the watering schedule mattered to everybody downstream.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday arrangements
passages.text: Near Cyrene, Hamilton witnessed someone buying half a mare: shared ownership, rather than a spectacularly unwise veterinary operation. The buyer cared for her, and the owners shared her foals under an agreed arrangement.

passages.title: Learning, writing and wider connections
passages.text: The Sanusi founder’s first teacher was his aunt, Sayyida Fatima, in Algeria. Later, at Jaghbub, he assembled a library including law, literature, history and astronomy. His own education reminds us that learned women also shaped this intellectual world.

passages.title: Learning, writing and wider connections
passages.text: A small Arabic sample is “المسائل العشر”, meaning “The ten questions”, from the cataloged title of al-Sanusi’s religious work. The cited Cairo printing dates to 1353 AH, or 1934/35; the author died in 1859, so this is a later edition of nineteenth-century scholarship.

passages.title: Learning, writing and wider connections
passages.text: Cyrenaica’s trade reached far beyond its coast: barley went to England, cattle to Malta and Izmir, wool to Genoa and Marseilles, and butter to Istanbul. Everyday farm products tied households to Mediterranean markets.

passages.title: Learning, writing and wider connections
passages.text: Caravan commerce also carried ivory, skins, salt and ostrich feathers. It included enslaved people, and the trade persisted despite an Ottoman prohibition in 1857. Those routes brought both livelihoods and devastating coercion.

The map stopping in 1878 is not a historical collapse. Ottoman rule continued until the Italian invasion of 1911 and the 1912 settlement; local resistance continued beyond that transfer of imperial claims.

sectionTitles: Things made by hand, often together

passages.text: The Czech Republic, also called Czechia, became a separate country on 1 January 1993 after the peaceful division of Czechoslovakia. Its modern story includes international research, new infrastructure and the continued care of much older crafts. The map begins this label in 1994, one year after independence.

passages.title: Research, water and everyday services
passages.text: At ELI Beamlines near Prague, extremely intense laser pulses help scientists study matter under unusual conditions. The HAPLS laser grew from cooperation with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the United States and was integrated into the Czech facility in 2018.

passages.title: Research, water and everyday services
passages.text: A large research laser needs much more than a bright beam. ELI’s engineering includes pulse compression, measurement equipment and computerized control, while helium cooling helps manage heat in the amplifiers. Getting the experiment ready is a team effort involving optics, software and precise machinery.

passages.title: Research, water and everyday services
passages.text: Prague’s wastewater works were badly affected by the 2002 flood. The later New Water Line was designed with a watertight structure so floodwater could pass over it while protecting the equipment inside. The city planned for the river to rise again.

passages.title: Research, water and everyday services
passages.text: Parts of the rebuilt treatment-plant area became a public park with paths and river views. A roughly two-hundred-year-old oak influenced the site’s eastern boundary. Sewage treatment and a pleasant walk can share an address, provided the engineering is doing its job.

passages.title: Research, water and everyday services
passages.text: The government describes nine years of compulsory schooling. This common basic stage gives children a shared educational foundation before later choices of study. It belongs to the modern system; school arrangements changed considerably over the longer history of the Czech lands.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: Puppet theatre combines wood carving, costume making, writing and performance. Traveling puppeteer families helped establish traditions later adapted to local speech and comic characters. Today, practice and workshops keep those skills moving between generations in both Czechia and Slovakia.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: Traditional blueprinted cloth starts with a protective paste stamped onto fabric. Indigo dye colors the exposed cloth while the covered areas keep their pattern. Family workshops preserve carved printing blocks and recipe notebooks. The technique is shared with several neighboring countries.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: Glass-bead Christmas ornaments begin with a heated glass tube blown into a brass mold. Makers silver and color the resulting beads, then thread cut pieces onto wires. A delicate star can be assembled from many tiny glass parts rather than blown as one object.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: In northern Bohemia, ornament making has passed through families and home workshops. UNESCO’s account identifies the Kulhavý workshop as the one that survived a difficult period of economic change, working with domestic bead makers. Museums and classes now help teach the craft.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: Around Žatec, hop fields connect with drying buildings, warehouses and the town’s trading facilities. Tall supports and wires guide the climbing plants. This is an agricultural landscape whose work continues beyond harvest, through drying, sorting and storage.

passages.title: Things made by hand, often together
passages.text: Žatec’s industrial buildings preserve specialized equipment and spaces for drying, packing and certifying hops. Some continue their original work; others have new uses. The chimneys and warehouses record how a crop could shape a town’s streets and skyline.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Czech, article 1 of the constitution adopted in 1992: “Česká republika je svrchovaný, jednotný a demokratický právní stát”. Translation: “The Czech Republic is a sovereign, unified and democratic state governed by law.” This is an excerpt from the enacted text, which took effect on 1 January 1993.
Czechia continues as an independent republic. Its creation in 1993 was a constitutional separation from Slovakia, with shared cultural and family ties continuing across the new border.

passages.text: Czechoslovakia was created in 1918 from lands formerly within Austria-Hungary. It joined Czech lands, Slovakia and, in the interwar period, Carpathian Ruthenia. Its history included parliamentary democracy, wartime destruction, Communist rule and the peaceful separation into two republics at the end of 1992.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: Bratislava’s new Comenius University opened its medical faculty in 1919. Professors arriving from Prague helped establish clinics for surgery, children’s medicine, dentistry and other specialties. Teaching in Czech and Slovak helped build a new generation of doctors in Slovakia.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: Medical students needed physics as well as anatomy. In 1923/24, Bratislava began first-year teaching through a medical physics institute, initially housed in a grammar-school building. It moved into new university premises in 1926. A university could begin with borrowed rooms and grow laboratory by laboratory.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: Young people arriving to work and train at Baťa’s shoe enterprise in Zlín could be only fourteen. Dormitories housed both young men and young women. The company’s organized world stretched beyond the factory gate into study, accommodation and daily routines.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: Architect František Lydie Gahura used a repeating 6.15-meter concrete framework for the Zlín dormitories. Shared facilities occupied lower floors, with rooms above. The buildings belonged to a planned industrial town where even a bedroom followed an architectural system.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: In 1961, chemist Otto Wichterle developed a way to cast soft contact lenses. The National Technical Museum preserves an early machine and material connected with the first production. Carefully controlled spinning could shape something small enough to sit on an eye.

passages.title: Learning, work and useful inventions
passages.text: Wichterle’s Christmas 1961 experiments used pieces of a Merkur construction set. Its metal strips, bolts and nuts had been familiar toys for decades. This was an unusually productive answer to “What did you build with your toys?”

passages.title: Weekends, clothes and political choices
passages.text: The tramping movement grew around weekend escapes into the countryside, borrowing imagery from the American Wild West. Campers developed songs, nicknames and shared camps. You could leave the city for a small adventure without crossing the Atlantic.

passages.title: Weekends, clothes and political choices
passages.text: Handwritten camp journals, illustrated chronicles, a carved totem and flags survive in museum collections. Some flags had been confiscated by Communist police. These objects preserve both the fun of belonging to a group and the times when authorities viewed independent gatherings with suspicion.

passages.title: Weekends, clothes and political choices
passages.text: Prague’s House of Fashion opened in 1956. A checked cotton dress made by Módní závody Praha between 1956 and 1960 survives in the National Museum’s collection. Clothing history includes everyday fabrics and shop counters, as well as political speeches about how people should live.

passages.title: Weekends, clothes and political choices
passages.text: The 1920 constitution gave adult citizens voting rights without distinction of sex. It also specified Sunday elections. Women could participate in national political life, although the law’s age requirements and other electoral conditions still mattered.

passages.title: Weekends, clothes and political choices
passages.text: During the Prague Spring of 1968, Alexander Dubček’s leadership loosened controls and pursued reform. Soviet-led Warsaw Pact troops invaded in August. The effort to change Communism from within met military force, and the consequences reached classrooms, workplaces and public debate.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Czech, the 1920 constitution, section 1: “Lid je jediný zdroj veškeré státní moci v republice Československé.” Translation: “The people are the sole source of all state power in the Czechoslovak Republic.” Parliament preserves this historical wording, including the older form of the country’s name.

Czechoslovakia ceased to exist at the end of 1992. The Czech Republic and Slovakia became separate states on 1 January 1993 through a peaceful political settlement. The map’s 1994 boundary is a snapshot transition, not the actual date of dissolution.

sectionTitles: A mountain capital built in layers
Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later
A real inscription, with an unsettled meaning
After conquest: Roman baths and public water

passages.text: Dacian communities lived around the Carpathians and lower Danube. Powerful rulers built mountain fortresses and sanctuaries before Roman conquest. This shared card separates those communities and kingdoms from the later Roman province. The map’s Dacians and Dacia snapshots are broad approximations, not exact historical borders.

passages.title: A mountain capital built in layers
passages.text: Sarmizegetusa Regia combined a fortress, a sacred area and civilian settlement. Builders cut artificial terraces into the hillside. More than a hundred terraces belonged to the civilian area, although only some have been excavated. Living in this capital meant adapting a mountain to human needs.

passages.title: A mountain capital built in layers
passages.text: Paved paths and a monumental stairway connected parts of the sacred area. Round and rectangular shrines used stone and timber, while channels and cisterns helped manage water. The surviving foundations preserve impressive engineering, but do not tell us every detail of the ceremonies once held there.

passages.title: Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later
passages.text: A study of seven Dacian sites in Transylvania found charred remains of cereals, legumes and fruits. These traces bring ordinary meals into view alongside famous battles. The evidence comes from particular excavated places; it cannot tell us what every Dacian household ate.

passages.title: Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later
passages.text: Burned seeds can survive long after a meal, basket or wooden house has disappeared. Archaeobotanists use such remains to investigate farming and food. A kitchen accident can leave a clue for someone many centuries later, although the original cook probably would not have appreciated that consolation.

passages.title: Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later
passages.text: A later research abstract identifies wheat, barley, rye and millet, together with broad beans, peas and lentils, at Late Iron Age sites in Transylvania. Flax and camelina also appear; the researcher connects these oil and fibre plants with production beyond food alone, including textiles.

passages.title: Dinner, clothes and keeping food for later
passages.text: Silos, clusters of charred grain and large ceramic containers provide evidence for storing supplies. Researchers interpret these finds as planning for food beyond the next meal. Storage mattered to households and larger centres alike: a harvest had to last much longer than the day it was gathered.

passages.title: Busy workshops and distant connections
passages.text: Excavators working at Sarmizegetusa in 1954 reported eight furnaces on a workshop terrace, along with ironworking evidence. Other finds included iron tools, painted pottery and glass vessels. The capital was a place where people made and used things, as well as a seat of political power.

passages.title: Busy workshops and distant connections
passages.text: The DACIT research project places the fortresses within a wider world of Mediterranean exchange and expanding iron metallurgy. Its archaeologists and engineers document ordinary objects as well as monuments. A digital model of a tool can help preserve evidence of skilled work that a king’s portrait would leave out.

passages.title: A real inscription, with an unsettled meaning
passages.text: A large pottery vessel found in 1954 bears repeated stamps in Latin letters: “DECEBALVS PER SCORILO.” One proposed translation is “Decebalus made it through Scorilo.” Historian Dumitru Protase argued for this Latin reading; the extra idea of making is supplied in interpretation, not written as a separate word.

passages.title: A real inscription, with an unsettled meaning
passages.text: Other scholars interpreted the same stamps differently, including a reading that connected Decebalus and Scorilo as son and father. Protase disputed that explanation. This is an authentic ancient text, but its language and precise meaning remain debated. It is not a securely translated sample of everyday Dacian conversation.

passages.title: After conquest: Roman baths and public water
passages.text: At the Roman city of Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, excavators found a run of 22 joined ceramic pipe sections near the financial procurator’s palace. The researcher interprets it as a bath water supply dating to around 170 CE. This evidence belongs to the Roman period, not the earlier mountain kingdom.

passages.title: After conquest: Roman baths and public water
passages.text: A loose ceramic tube does not automatically prove that a house had a bathroom or a sewer. The same study explains that tubes could also be used in building vaults. Archaeologists need to know where an object was found and how it connected to its surroundings before announcing ancient plumbing.

passages.title: After conquest: Roman baths and public water
passages.text: Two public fountains stood beside the Roman city’s forum in the Severan period, around the late second and early third centuries. A benefactor dedicated them in honour of the imperial family. Useful water, public generosity and religious display could share the same space; fetching water was part of city life.

Roman conquest in 106 ended Decebalus’s kingdom. A Roman province followed in part of the region and lasted until the third century. These political changes did not mean that the population simply disappeared. The map’s Dacia endpoint of 200 is neither the conquest date nor the end of Roman rule.

passages.text: At Abomey, the royal palaces combined government, skilled craft production and the storage of royal treasures. Their architecture and imagery expressed Aja-Fon traditions and preserved memories of successive rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palace builders used earthen walls and traditional materials to organize enclosed compounds around courtyards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polychrome reliefs gave palace walls a visual language of royal history and symbolism.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Outer, inner and private courtyards structured access through each palace, making social distinctions part of the built environment.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Royal families continue ceremonies and care for sacred places, including royal tombs and structures associated with a king's spirit.

sectionTitles: A society connected across the Red Sea
What pots can tell us about dinner

passages.text: The imported name Damot, its northern Ethiopian and Eritrean location, and its BCE dates point toward ancient Dʿmt. However, the map’s 300 to 200 BCE interval is later than much of the best-known evidence. This card explains the earlier regional society around Yeha; it does not confirm a Dʿmt kingdom with those exact borders and dates.

passages.title: A society connected across the Red Sea
passages.text: South Arabian inscriptions and architecture appear alongside local traditions in the northern highlands. Archaeologist Rodolfo Fattovich emphasized a mosaic of different communities rather than one uniform culture. Connections across the Red Sea shaped this region, but they did not make every settlement identical.

passages.title: A society connected across the Red Sea
passages.text: Yeha’s Great Temple, built in the seventh century BCE, was dedicated to Almaqah. Its surviving walls rise about fourteen metres. The building later became a Christian sacred place, so the same imposing stonework has belonged to very different religious settings over its long life.

passages.title: Builders, stone carriers and water
passages.text: Grat Beʿal Gibri combined stone masonry with horizontal wooden beams. This system supported a building of several storeys. Engineers reported new structural modelling in September 2026, but its impressive theoretical load capacity does not tell us how many storeys the ancient palace actually had.

passages.title: Builders, stone carriers and water
passages.text: Builders used different stones for different jobs. Rubble could come from near Yeha, while the Great Temple’s fine limestone blocks travelled from the Wuqro region, roughly ninety kilometres away in a straight line. A beautiful wall also represents quarrying, transport, planning and many people’s hard work.

passages.title: Builders, stone carriers and water
passages.text: Researchers identified a basin cut into rock that stored water from a seasonal stream. They suggest small channels and cisterns could supply local fields without copying South Arabia’s giant dams. Managing a useful supply of water did not always require the biggest possible construction project.

passages.title: What pots can tell us about dinner
passages.text: Excavated pottery includes jars, bottles, bowls, cups and lids, with polished surfaces and incised decoration. Some vessels had geometric patterns around their shoulders or necks. These remains preserve choices about storage, serving and appearance even when the names of their makers and users have disappeared.

passages.title: What pots can tell us about dinner
passages.text: A 2024 study examined tiny organic traces absorbed into pottery and material surviving inside vessels from Yeha and Melazo. It detected both plant and animal fats. A pot can keep traces of its contents long after the meal is gone: useful evidence for archaeologists, though no complete ancient cookbook.

passages.title: What pots can tell us about dinner
passages.text: Some samples contained chemical markers associated with fruit fermentation. The researchers also found a slight predominance of plant-related residues in a group of small serving pots. These clues concern the tested vessels; they do not identify every ingredient or establish what every household ate.

passages.title: What pots can tell us about dinner
passages.text: One storage vessel from the palace may have held moringa seed oil. The identification remains tentative and needs further study of local raw materials. Even with that uncertainty, laboratory work can ask surprisingly specific questions about what people once kept on a storeroom shelf.

passages.title: Family memory and written names
passages.text: At Yeha, shafts cut down into rock opened into burial chambers. Several people were buried together, possibly in family groups, with objects placed beside them. These tombs connect the monumental city with relationships between the living and the dead, though archaeologists cannot reconstruct each household from the burials alone.

passages.title: Family memory and written names
passages.text: An altar inscription from Ṣ́ǝrḥan names a woman, Taʿattarat, who dedicated it to the goddess ḏāt Ḥamēn. It also names a ruler and his ancestry. Her appearance in this surviving text adds an individual woman to a record otherwise dominated by kings, buildings and scattered objects.

passages.title: Family memory and written names
passages.text: “𐩨𐩬 𐩨𐩬”, transliterated bn bn, means “son of the son”: a grandson. The phrase occurs in that early first-millennium BCE altar inscription. These are normalized Old South Arabian letters based on the published reading; the carving itself varies some letter directions. Family ancestry could be part of a ruler’s public identity.

No securely identified event makes 200 BCE the fall of this polity. A Yeha excavation found a break in occupation before later Aksumite settlement, but that local sequence cannot explain every community’s history. The earlier monumental society changed, while the region continued into new political and religious eras.

passages.text: These map labels span several phases: Bulgars on the Black Sea steppe, a Danube state formed among Slavic and other communities, and medieval Bulgarian kingdoms. They do not describe one unchanging population. Volga Bulgaria followed a separate history. Later Balkan art and books belong to the explicitly dated periods below.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: The early-eighth-century Madara Rider shows a horseman above a fallen lion on a high rock face. Its setting made a ruler's image part of the landscape. It is a royal monument, not evidence that villagers routinely went lion hunting.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Inscriptions beside the rider record events associated with rulers including Tervel and Omurtag. Text and image together provide evidence for early Bulgarian political memory; the cliff is more than a giant picture frame.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Boris I's adoption of Christianity in the 860s transformed official religious institutions. It did not instantly replace every household practice or erase the older histories of the people living in the state.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Early Bulgar cemeteries at Balchik, Novi Pazar, Kyulevcha and Topola contained ceramic jugs, bowls and other table vessels. Scholars compare their shapes with metal, glass and wooden examples from wider Eurasian traditions. Similar shape alone does not prove a pot was imported.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Four pottery kilns at the early medieval settlement of Topola demonstrate production, not just consumption. The study associates these vessel traditions especially with the first half and middle of the 700s. Someone had to make the dishes before anyone could argue about washing them.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Preslav excavations recovered agricultural and craft tools alongside pots, cups, bowls and amphoras. These ordinary objects connect the capital to food production and skilled work, rather than only to the activities of its rulers.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: The Preslav museum distinguishes locally produced pottery from vessels imported from Byzantium. A household could use objects with different production histories; an imported container does not by itself tell us who lived in the house.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Earrings, bracelets and rings at Preslav include copper, bronze and silver examples, with glass, amber and other materials also represented. Dressing up had a much wider material range than gold treasure alone suggests.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: A gold ring found at Pliska has a split and thinned ends that may reflect resizing. Its human portrait cannot be securely named. The wear and adjustments suggest an object with a history of use, not simply an untouched badge of a famous king.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: At Patleina near Preslav, excavations in 1909 found fragments of a tenth-century ceramic portrait of St Theodore. Its large face was assembled from square tiles about 12 centimetres across: a carefully planned image made from separate fired pieces.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Monastic workshops around Preslav made painted tiles for churches and palaces. The saint portrait uses dark outlines, coloured slips and glaze. Archaeological workshop discoveries support local production, rather than assuming that every impressive object came from Byzantium.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Early Bulgarian inscriptions describe elite gifts and feasting. A recent study interprets these occasions as ways to display rank and strengthen personal ties. Royal hospitality was political work; it is not a menu for the average family.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: In 1355-1356 the monk Simeon copied a lavish Gospel book for Tsar Ivan Alexander. Its parchment pages carry Slavonic text in Cyrillic. The manuscript's named scribe gives us a specific person behind the broad label “medieval learning.”

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: The same book uses gold for chapter titles in its margins and red for directions used in worship. Colour helped readers navigate the text. These are features of an expensive royal commission, not evidence that every household owned illustrated books.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: A royal family portrait opens the Gospel book, while a word puzzle on folio 273v encodes Ivan Alexander's name. A medieval book could combine sacred reading, family image-making and an elaborate puzzle.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: Κανα συβιγι Ωμουρταγ is the ruler's title and name, conventionally rendered “Kan sybigi Omurtag.” It begins a ninth-century Greek funerary inscription for Turdatzis on limestone. The sample follows the scholarly transcription, joining a line break. The title is Bulgar vocabulary written in Greek letters, not modern Bulgarian.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: The inscriptions studied by Matilde Casas Olea preserve forms of ninth-century everyday Greek rather than only polished literary language. They show how Bulgarian rulers used a neighbouring written language in their new Balkan setting.

Byzantine conquest ended the first Bulgarian kingdom in 1018. Renewed Bulgarian rule emerged in the 1180s, and Ottoman conquest ended the later medieval kingdoms in the late 1300s. Bulgarian communities, religious life and literary traditions continued. Neither the map's 1000 change of label nor its 1400 boundary is a disappearance of a people.

sectionTitles: A port with an unusual government
A working family and small traces of daily life

passages.text: This entry represents the Free City of Danzig, a Baltic port and surrounding territory created in 1920 under League of Nations protection, with special Polish rights. Most inhabitants were German-speaking; Polish and Jewish communities also shaped local life. Its actual history ran from 1920 to 1939, beyond the map’s shorter 1930 to 1938 display interval. This is today’s Gdańsk, but the card concerns that particular interwar political arrangement.

passages.title: A port with an unusual government
passages.text: The city had its own Senate and parliament, the Volkstag. Poland represented it abroad, while the territory belonged to Poland’s customs area and Poland had rights to use its port. A joint harbor board managed important port affairs. Everyday trade therefore depended on cooperation between institutions with different national loyalties.

passages.title: A port with an unusual government
passages.text: Writing sample: Article 3 of the constitution published in 1922 reads, “Die Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus.” It means, “State authority comes from the people.” This short German sentence is preserved in a modern transcription of the published constitution. Later repression makes the promise especially striking.

passages.title: A port with an unusual government
passages.text: The constitution gave male and female citizens over twenty the right to elect representatives, subject to stated legal exclusions, and declared equal civic rights for women and men. These were promises written into law. Reading them alongside the later persecution shows why a constitution’s words and a government’s behavior need separate examination.

passages.title: A port with an unusual government
passages.text: The Free City had separate postal services connected with its German and Polish institutions. The surviving equipment, papers and photographs in the Polish Post Office museum make this unusual arrangement tangible. Mailing a letter involved offices and routes that also carried political significance in a city with competing national claims.

passages.title: School lessons and playing fields
passages.text: The Polish Gymnasium began classes on 9 May 1922 in former barracks. In its first school year it had 199 pupils and ten teachers. Some children were not fluent in Polish, so language teaching received particular attention. A school could be a place to strengthen a family’s cultural ties as well as learn ordinary subjects.

passages.title: School lessons and playing fields
passages.text: School costs affected children’s choices. The Polish Gymnasium charged twenty Danzig gulden a month, and the city’s historical account explains that many pupils moved into Polish commercial schools instead of completing the gymnasium course. Academic schooling was not simply a matter of turning up with a notebook; a family had to afford the fees.

passages.title: School lessons and playing fields
passages.text: Gedania, founded in September 1922, organized several sports for women and men. Its prewar membership reached about 550, mainly Poles, but also included Jews and Germans until the mid-1930s. Rowing and yacht clubs also appeared in 1922. The waterfront offered people exercise and friendships as well as work.

passages.title: A working family and small traces of daily life
passages.text: Franciszek Szmelter leased the railway station’s round-the-clock restaurant in 1933. His wife Maria, who came from a Jewish family in Mostar, helped manage the business and kept its accounts. Museum collections preserve family photographs and restaurant cutlery marked with their surname, linking a large transport hub to one household’s work.

passages.title: A working family and small traces of daily life
passages.text: Maria also ran the Polish Station Mission, helping people find jobs and somewhere to live and offering overnight rooms at the station. Railway and school employees sometimes earned extra money in the restaurant after their regular work. The family’s business was therefore also part of a network of practical help and supplementary income.

passages.title: A working family and small traces of daily life
passages.text: Small printed papers reveal habits that official ceremonies miss. The Polish Academy of Sciences Library preserves interwar advertising labels, photographs and slips confirming confession, which allowed their holders to receive Easter communion. Such religious paperwork records one community’s practice; the Free City’s residents did not all share the same faith.

passages.title: When public promises were broken
passages.text: The Nazi Party won an absolute majority in the Volkstag election of 28 May 1933. Political power increasingly served Nazi aims.

passages.title: When public promises were broken
passages.text: The Great Synagogue, which had survived the violence of November 1938, was sold to the city under Nazi domination and demolished in May 1939. A major community landmark disappeared before the war began.

passages.title: When public promises were broken
passages.text: Photographs from 1935 show antisemitic markings on Jewish-owned businesses. A 1939 image records another Jewish shop forced to close. These are concrete traces of persecution in ordinary shopping streets: it changed where families could work and whether their neighbors were allowed to participate safely in city life.

On 1 September 1939, Nazi Germany attacked Polish installations and annexed the Free City. The political arrangement ended amid war and repression. After the war, the city became part of Poland; much of its German population fled or was expelled. Modern Gdańsk continued with a profoundly changed population.

sectionTitles: Meals, learning and a little humour
Writing and how to read it

passages.text: Darfur’s Keira sultanate developed around the seventeenth century in present-day western Sudan. It joined a Fur ruling dynasty with subjects of many languages and backgrounds. The map’s 1530 start predates the usual chronology, while its 1815 endpoint omits a long later history.

passages.title: Government and connections
passages.text: Arabic land charters record grants to chiefs, religious teachers, merchants and royal relatives. These documents help historians reconstruct actual relationships between the court and influential people, rather than relying only on lists of sultans.

passages.title: Government and connections
passages.text: Such grants concerned privileges and claims over the people living on estates as well as land. They should not be pictured as ordinary modern house deeds: taxes, labour and political authority were bound into the arrangement.

passages.title: Government and connections
passages.text: The traveler Muhammad al-Tunisi reached Darfur in 1803 at about fourteen, seeking the father who had left his family years earlier. He was reunited with him and eventually managed estates that the sultan had granted to his father.

passages.title: Government and connections
passages.text: His journey followed the Forty Days Road from Egypt. The story shows how a family could be spread across a long trading route, with a young person traveling far beyond home to renew a broken connection.

passages.title: Government and connections
passages.text: Al-Tunisi’s account describes a court working through seven interpreters. That detail makes multilingual government tangible: a royal order could need several people’s language skills before it reached everyone concerned.

passages.title: Meals, learning and a little humour
passages.text: One recorded food was weka made from dried okra, pounded and sieved before becoming a sauce for asida. This early nineteenth-century description preserves actual preparation steps, rather than merely saying that people ate grain and vegetables.

passages.title: Meals, learning and a little humour
passages.text: Another sauce used heglig fruit, from the Balanites aegyptiaca tree. The fruit was soaked, strained and cooked with meat. Different plants could therefore supply the sauce served alongside the same staple food.

passages.title: Meals, learning and a little humour
passages.text: Al-Tunisi disliked some of the food his hosts offered him. The museum’s discussion reminds readers that this was a visitor’s taste, not an objective verdict on everyone’s cooking. Even a useful historical witness can be a fussy dinner guest.

passages.title: Meals, learning and a little humour
passages.text: The account includes fifty-two drawings made by its author and covers clothing, illnesses, plants, dances and food. Illustrations and descriptions preserve details of daily life, while still reflecting what one educated visitor chose to notice.

passages.title: Meals, learning and a little humour
passages.text: Translator Humphrey Davies explains a court title rendered “the Sultan’s Buttocks”: its holder commanded the force at the rear of the army. The unusual name described a military position; it was not the traveler inventing a schoolyard insult.

passages.title: Writing and how to read it
passages.text: The opening words of al-Tunisi’s book title are “تشحيذ الأذهان”, literally “Sharpening minds”. This Arabic text describes his early nineteenth-century experiences but was composed later. It is a visitor’s written account, not a sample of the Fur language or a royal proclamation.

passages.title: Writing and how to read it
passages.text: The Arabic account also transcribes Fur words and songs. Its preparation involved al-Tunisi and the French scholar Nicolas Perron decades after the journey. Historians therefore consider translation, recollection and editing when using it as evidence.

Darfur was conquered by al-Zubayr’s forces in 1874. Ali Dinar restored the sultanate in 1898, before British conquest and incorporation into Anglo-Egyptian Sudan in 1916. The map’s 1815 endpoint marks neither of those endings; Darfur’s communities and languages continued.

passages.text: Lenape peoples belong to homelands around the Delaware River and neighboring Atlantic regions. They include distinct Unami and Munsee communities. The imported outline extends well beyond the core homeland; it is not a precise national boundary. Its 1500 to 1650 interval is map coverage, not the lifetime of living Lenape nations.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: Wolf, Turkey and Turtle clans organize important family connections. Delaware Nation explains that clan membership follows the mother’s line and that elders and matriarchs helped select community chiefs. Villages had their own leadership; a shared Lenape identity did not require one ruler over every settlement.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: A tribal teaching sheet reconstructs a house with a central fire, roof openings for smoke, and mats insulating the walls. Corn and herbs hang above the living area; food and belongings sit beneath sleeping platforms. Even the ends of the house have jobs, including dry firewood and winter storage.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: Food preservation helped gardens last beyond harvest. Corn could be hung up, squash sliced into rings and dried, and meat or fish smoked or dried. Later, water softened dried ingredients for cooking. The pantry therefore depended on sun, smoke and careful work rather than a refrigerator.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: One recorded cooking method enclosed a whole fish in clay before baking it in hot ashes. Breaking away the hardened coating also removed skin and scales. The tribal food guide describes a package that helped cook dinner and peel it afterward, an ingenious use of a familiar material.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: Spring shad runs drew people together along rivers. A teaching reconstruction shows stakes and weighted nets forming a fish weir, with the catch split and hung near a fire to dry. Fishing was a seasonal harvest requiring construction, timing and food-processing skills as well as catching fish.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: Making a dugout canoe meant hollowing a tree trunk without splitting it apart. The tribe’s canoe guide describes controlled burning followed by scraping with an adz; wet hide protected wood that should not burn. Fire helped shape the boat, but only where the builder wanted it.

passages.title: Families, food and river skills
passages.text: Language teacher Nora Thompson Dean described a lively football game in 1971. Men who caught the deerskin ball had to stop and kick it onward, while women could run, throw or kick. The ball was stuffed with deer hair. Players needed to know which rules applied to their team!

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: A museum shoulder bag dated 1740 to 1770 is attributed probably to a Lenape maker. Its deerskin carries porcupine-quill work, metal cones and deer hair. The careful attribution matters: a beautiful surviving object can reveal skilled techniques even when its early collecting history leaves questions.

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: A different bag, identified as Delaware and made in Oklahoma around 1850, combines glass beads, cloth, hide and ribbon. White outlines sharpen its bold geometric patterns. The museum places this work within artistic adaptation after removal; families carried design knowledge into new circumstances.

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: The 1737 Walking Purchase dispossessed Lenape communities in eastern Pennsylvania. Archival historians explain how an alleged land agreement was exploited through a prepared route and unusually fast walkers. A transaction presented as a measured walk became a means of taking far more land and pushing people west.

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: In September 1778, White Eyes, John Kill Buck and Captain Pipe negotiated a treaty with United States commissioners. Article III allowed troops to pass through Delaware country, promised payment for food and horses, and proposed a fort to protect families while warriors were away. Diplomacy concerned household safety as well as armies.

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: A small written sample in the community’s modern dictionary is “wanìshi”, meaning “Thank you!” The page provides audio and an example sentence. This is a present-day written teaching resource for Lenape, not a claim that this spelling appeared on an object from the map’s sixteenth-century interval.

passages.title: Objects, diplomacy and living language
passages.text: Lenape people today belong to several distinct nations, including Delaware Nation and Delaware Tribe of Indians in Oklahoma, Stockbridge-Munsee in Wisconsin, and Munsee and Delaware First Nations in Ontario. Forced removals help explain this geography. Shared history and family ties coexist with separate governments.

The map’s 1650 cutoff is not a disappearance. Later diplomacy, dispossession and removals reshaped Lenape life, while descendants maintain distinct nations, community institutions and language teaching.

passages.text: Five dynasties of Turkic and Afghan sultans ruled from Delhi from 1206 to 1526, at their height under the Khaljis and Tughluqs reaching the far south. They brought Persian letters, Islamic architecture and Sufi shrines to northern India, and their India shaped the Mughals.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Qutb Minar was begun under Qutb al-Din Aibak and finished by Iltutmish; at 72.5 meters it is the tallest brick minaret in the world.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The true arch and dome arrived with the sultanate; the Alai Darwaza of 1311 is the first building in India built entirely on those principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Amir Khusrau of Delhi wrote Persian verse and is credited with the beginnings of Hindustani music and poetry.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Chishti Sufis such as Nizamuddin Auliya drew Hindus and Muslims alike to their shrines and their music.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian was the language of court and chancery, and Indo-Persian history writing began with Minhaj-i Siraj and Barani.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Alauddin Khalji fixed market prices and had the land measured for revenue; paper and the spinning wheel spread through India in these centuries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Persian wheels lifted water for irrigation.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indo-Islamic culture and the Persian chancery passed to the Mughals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Qutb Minar and its monuments were listed by UNESCO.
Babur's guns and cavalry defeated Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in April 1526, and the Mughal Empire began.
