sectionTitles: A successor state and a wider region
Homes and food before the kingdom
How ordinary lives enter the record

passages.text: After Morocco’s invasion of Songhay in 1591, surviving rulers established an independent government downstream in Dendi. Their history belongs beside that of the diverse Niger River communities, rather than a single unchanging state. The imported 1878 to 1900 outline lies much too far north, in the Sahara; it does not locate historical Dendi reliably.

passages.title: A successor state and a wider region
passages.text: The Moroccan victory in 1591 ended the great Songhay Empire’s earlier supremacy. Some members of its ruling class moved down the Niger and continued an independent government. Dendi therefore belongs to the history of survival and political rebuilding after imperial defeat.

passages.title: A successor state and a wider region
passages.text: Late Dendi cannot safely be drawn as one permanent kingdom. Documents cited in Niger’s 2004 court submission include separate French treaties with Gaya in 1895 and Karimama in 1897. These records show several centers of authority; the submission itself was arguing a contested boundary case.

passages.title: Homes and food before the kingdom
passages.text: Birnin Lafiya reveals an older Dendi landscape, occupied approximately from the fourth to thirteenth centuries. Excavators found a compound with circular rooms, rammed-earth walls and a partially enclosed courtyard. This predates the post-1591 successor kingdom by centuries.

passages.title: Homes and food before the kingdom
passages.text: Some floors were paved with broken pottery; others used laterite. A potsherd-covered step led into one room. An old pot could become part of the floor beneath your feet: the excavated surfaces show how carefully ordinary spaces were constructed.

passages.title: Homes and food before the kingdom
passages.text: Plant and animal remains at Birnin Lafiya include pearl millet, African rice, cotton and many floodplain fish. Charcoal also points to useful fruit trees, including shea. The household food supply drew on both cultivated land and the river.

passages.title: Homes and food before the kingdom
passages.text: Reassembled vessels include large containers, probably for storage or liquids, and burnished bowls likely used for food and drink. Archaeologists also recovered glass, stone and shell beads. Kitchen equipment and small ornaments help populate a history otherwise dominated by rulers.

passages.title: Trading, language and remembered journeys
passages.text: Dendi-speaking commercial neighborhoods also developed farther south in Borgu towns such as Parakou, Djougou and Kandi. Farias argues that these trading communities may predate the migration after 1591. Speaking a related language did not mean belonging to one kingdom.

passages.title: Trading, language and remembered journeys
passages.text: In these commercial centers, Dendi also served people whose first languages were different. A shared trading language helped customers, travelers and hosts communicate. Its continued use is one of the region’s achievements that cannot be measured by the size of a royal army.

passages.title: Trading, language and remembered journeys
passages.text: A short written sample is “Dèndí cínè”, meaning “the Dendi language”, as printed in Farias’s 2013 study. This is modern scholarly Latin transcription, with tone marks. It represents the living language, rather than a claimed quotation from a seventeenth-century royal manuscript.

passages.title: Trading, language and remembered journeys
passages.text: Kompanti’s foundation traditions, recorded in 2013, describe families leaving Boyeri after warfare involving Kandi late in the nineteenth century. Researchers recorded Gulmanceba and Fulani neighborhoods, including people whose ancestors had escaped dependence elsewhere. Community history preserves refuge and rebuilding as well as battles.

passages.title: How ordinary lives enter the record
passages.text: The Kompanti interviews named cultivators Tchayenu Dagu and Sibo Hamani and former weaver Sido Alfari. Such witnesses link family memory with practical knowledge of land and work. Their accounts were collected in 2013, not treated as untouched recordings from the nineteenth century.

passages.title: How ordinary lives enter the record
passages.text: A small 2014 excavation at Kompanti recovered pottery fragments, a glass bead and a cowrie fragment. Its shallow deposits were consistent with a relatively recent settlement. Comparing material remains with oral histories lets researchers test a story instead of simply choosing whichever version sounds grandest.

French conquest and colonial administration curtailed the region’s independent authorities around the turn of the twentieth century. The map’s 1900 endpoint is not a securely established single fall date for every Dendi community. River settlements, trading connections and Dendi speech continued across the new administrative divisions.

sectionTitles: Law and a wider political world

passages.text: This record covers medieval Denmark in 1100-1400, a Christian kingdom of farms, towns, landowners and churches. Its rulers also held territories beyond modern Denmark. The later Kalmar Union did not erase Denmark, and the map's 1400 boundary is not the end of the kingdom.

passages.title: Behind a medieval town house
passages.text: Excavations at Thomas B. Thriges Gade in Odense uncovered part of a brick house from the early 1200s. Brick was still an expensive material, so the building suggests a wealthy household. It is not a model for every Danish home.

passages.title: Behind a medieval town house
passages.text: From the 1300s, some Odense backyards had barrel-shaped latrine installations. Archaeology reveals planned places for waste within increasingly crowded plots. A town needed maintenance and disposal systems as well as churches and markets.

passages.title: Behind a medieval town house
passages.text: One latrine preserved wooden bowls and two carefully shaped sticks. The excavator suggests a wiping arrangement using cloth or leather and water. This is an interpretation of particular finds, not proof that medieval Denmark had one standard toilet kit.

passages.title: Behind a medieval town house
passages.text: Odense's backyards also held animals and garden plots. Bone finds record meat consumption, while written sources mention cabbage and apple gardens. Town residents could combine craft or commerce with producing some food.

passages.title: Building and displaying belief
passages.text: Roskilde Cathedral was built in brick during the 1100s and 1200s. Its Gothic design helped spread brick church architecture through northern Europe. Turning clay into durable, repeated building units supported ambitious construction.

passages.title: Building and displaying belief
passages.text: The cathedral accumulated porches, chapels and alterations over later centuries. A visitor's view is therefore a sequence of building projects. Its later royal tombs should not all be imagined inside the earliest medieval church.

passages.title: Building and displaying belief
passages.text: The National Museum preserves imagery of the golden altar frontal from Lisbjerg Church, dated 1135. Mary and the child occupy its religious programme. A richly decorated altar focused attention during worship; it was not ordinary household furniture.

passages.title: Building and displaying belief
passages.text: Medieval Danish landowners, townspeople and church institutions used objects and images to express status. The museum distinguishes these settings. A costly surviving church object reveals a patron's priorities more readily than the daily possessions of a poor family.

passages.title: Law and a wider political world
passages.text: Valdemar II issued the Law of Jutland at Vordingborg in 1241 with the participation of leading royal and church figures. Writing law made rules easier to preserve and consult, although possessing a law book did not guarantee equal treatment in every dispute.

passages.title: Law and a wider political world
passages.text: Mæth logh skall land bygges means “With law shall the land be built.” This Danish opening survives in Lund manuscript 25 of the Law of Jutland. That particular copy dates to the 1400s-1500s, later than the 1241 law and this map segment; its spelling is not modern Danish.

passages.title: Law and a wider political world
passages.text: Danish rule included northern Estonian territory, explaining Baltic features in some atlas snapshots. The 1346 sale to the Teutonic Order changed sovereignty. A distant possession should not be treated as evidence that its inhabitants became culturally identical to people in Jutland.

passages.title: Law and a wider political world
passages.text: In 1397 Erik was crowned over Denmark, Norway and Sweden in the union associated with Queen Margrete. Sharing a monarch joined political interests without turning the three kingdoms into one uniform community.

Denmark continued beyond 1400 within the changing Kalmar Union. The union was a political arrangement among kingdoms, not the disappearance of Danish society. Later divisions and religious changes belong to subsequent phases; this medieval atlas segment has no single national fall date.

passages.text: Twentieth-century Copenhagen became a meeting place for physicists working on quantum theory. This focused chapter follows the institute, discussions and everyday arrangements that helped international collaboration take root.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Bohr's Institute for Theoretical Physics was dedicated in Copenhagen in March 1921, after fundraising and approval of the project.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: During the 1920s, visiting researchers exchanged ideas in Copenhagen. Discussions could happen in small groups and at dinners with the Bohr family.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: In 1927, Bohr presented complementarity: different experimental arrangements can require different, mutually exclusive descriptions of a quantum phenomenon. The proposal became a focus of debate.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the 1930s, a new mathematics institute was built beside the physics institute. Shared classrooms and a canteen were intended to support closer collaboration.

sectionTitles: Ships carried work as well as warriors

passages.text: The atlas assigns Denmark-Norway to 1000 to 1100, so this card explains early medieval Danish and Norwegian connections. It must not be read as the much later union’s founding date. Rule and alliances changed repeatedly, while ships, crafts and money linked communities across the sea.

passages.title: A kingdom depended on connections
passages.text: Cnut became king of Denmark in 1018 and gained Norway in 1028, while also ruling England. Managing several kingdoms involved representatives, diplomacy and gifts as well as force. His personal power did not create one uniform society.

passages.title: A kingdom depended on connections
passages.text: A Danish silver penny in the British Museum, dated 1019 to 1035, uses a portrait and cross closely related to an English design. Money can reveal imitation and adaptation across kingdoms, rather than a separate national invention in each place.

passages.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors
passages.text: Skuldelev 1 was a cargo vessel built in western Norway around 1030. Its heavy pine planks and broad form suited carrying substantial loads. A vessel’s practical design helps distinguish transporting goods from the demands of a fast warship.

passages.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors
passages.text: The same vessel was repaired using oak near the Oslofjord and eastern Denmark. Repair timber records a working life across different places. A ship could outlast its first crew’s plans and become a patchwork of skilled maintenance.

passages.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors
passages.text: Skuldelev 3, built from Danish oak around 1040, carried goods in coastal waters. Loose deck planks covered the ends, leaving an open central hold. Its layout made room for cargo while preserving space for handling the vessel.

passages.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors
passages.text: The museum suggests that Skuldelev 3 could have carried an owner with associates or family to markets or assemblies. This is a plausible interpretation of its capacity, not a passenger list recovered from the ship.

passages.title: Ships carried work as well as warriors
passages.text: Making Ottar’s modern experimental wool sail drew on textile researchers and the wool of about 200 small sheep. That figure belongs to the reconstruction project. It makes the large amount of textile work behind sailing visible without inventing an ancient production total.

passages.title: Grooming and skilled household work
passages.text: Viking-period combs, tweezers and ear picks survive in archaeological collections. Some combs had protective cases. These objects show attention to personal grooming, although they cannot prove that every person followed the same bathing schedule.

passages.title: Grooming and skilled household work
passages.text: Spinning, weaving and sewing required sustained work. The museum interprets complicated textile techniques as evidence that some women specialized in production. That is more specific than imagining all clothing as a quick extra task after the other household jobs.

passages.title: Grooming and skilled household work
passages.text: Keys are often presented as the universal badge of a Viking housewife. The museum cautions that they are actually rare among female grave goods. A memorable symbol should be checked against the whole archaeological sample.

passages.title: A short message on silver
passages.text: CNVT REX DANOR means “Cnut, king of the Danes.” This Latin title appears on a coin type from Lund dated 1082 to 1084, illustrated in the Royal Blood study. Its ruler is Cnut the Holy, a later king than Cnut the Great.

passages.title: A short message on silver
passages.text: The reverse of that coin type names a moneyer and mint. The study identifies many moneyers associated with its production. Coin legends could preserve the work of named specialists as well as the ruler whose authority they advertised.

Cnut’s Norwegian rule ended in the changes around 1035; Danish and Norwegian histories continued through other rulers and later unions. The atlas’s 1100 endpoint is not a single political collapse. Its imported name and very broad polygon require caution and do not verify sovereignty over every shaded place.

passages.text: This chapter follows sixteenth-century Denmark-Norway through astronomy, printing and royal architecture. Tycho Brahe's observatory shows how scientific work depended on buildings, instruments and supporting crafts.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Under Danish royal patronage, Tycho Brahe built Uraniborg on Hven between 1576 and 1580. The island is now Swedish but was then Danish.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Uraniborg included a printing office and a water mill for making paper. Publishing and material production supported the observatory's work.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Tycho established Stjerneborg in 1584. Sheltered instrument spaces reduced exposure to wind and helped stabilize observations.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederik II began rebuilding Kronborg as a Renaissance castle in 1574. Its courtyard, carved sandstone and decorated chapel formed a major royal setting.

passages.text: Diaguita names encompass distinct communities and archaeological traditions on both sides of the Andes. The Chilean ceramic tradition and the peoples of Argentina’s Calchaquí valleys are related topics, not one uniform empire. The broad imported outline and its 1492 to 1500 dates should not imply a single government or historical lifetime.

passages.title: Distinct communities and practical knowledge
passages.text: In northwestern Argentina, peoples including the Quilmes and Tolombones maintained their own settlements and leaders. Their shared Diaguita designation can obscure that political variety. Communities cooperated and competed within a landscape of valleys, mountain slopes and valuable resources.

passages.title: Distinct communities and practical knowledge
passages.text: Mountain farming required creating usable ground. Diaguita farmers built low stone retaining walls and filled behind them to form terraces. Water channels and reservoirs helped direct scarce water toward crops. A sloping hillside could become a series of workable growing surfaces.

passages.title: Distinct communities and practical knowledge
passages.text: In Chile’s Norte Chico, irrigation supported maize, beans, quinoa and squash, while coastal resources supplied fish and shellfish. The museum also describes seagoing rafts with inflated sea-lion-skin floats. Valleys and ocean contributed different things to household livelihoods.

passages.title: Distinct communities and practical knowledge
passages.text: Modern Huasco Alto families grow crops and fruit near valley homes, while goat herds use more distant seasonal pastures. These living practices have their own colonial and later history. The goats and orchards must not be casually placed in a scene from 1492.

passages.title: What excavations and pottery reveal
passages.text: El Olivar near La Serena preserves houses, burial areas and rubbish deposits from successive communities. Large excavations followed discoveries during road construction in 2014. Carefully recording discarded material and its location helps reconstruct everyday activity alongside more spectacular objects.

passages.title: What excavations and pottery reveal
passages.text: The site also exposes a scholarly disagreement. Francisco Cornely used pottery changes to build a chronological sequence; Mary Shepherd Slusser emphasized stylistic unity in material from 63 excavated graves. Recent investigations have renewed interest in her interpretation.

passages.title: What excavations and pottery reveal
passages.text: A double kero cup in La Serena’s collection came from El Olivar’s FUN 8 area during the 2016 rescue excavation. The catalogue identifies it as Diaguita-Inca. Its documented recovery connects an unusual vessel with a particular archaeological context.

passages.title: What excavations and pottery reveal
passages.text: Another El Olivar vessel is a shoe-shaped jar with human features, recorded as inventory 72 and excavated by Cornely in sector R. Its memorable shape shows how potters combined containers with representations of people. The nickname describes its form, not footwear.

passages.title: What excavations and pottery reveal
passages.text: A vessel found in the Mapocho valley combines an Inca maka form, Diaguita decoration and materials associated with Aconcagua pottery. Museum curators suggest local artisans made it within those overlapping connections. They interpret it as probably holding maize beer, rather than claiming its contents were directly preserved.

passages.title: Language, loss and living communities
passages.text: The early Kakán dictionary described by the museum is lost, so it cannot supply a trustworthy quoted sentence here. A documented modern voice is leader Dora Clarisa Suárez’s Spanish “acá estamos”, meaning “here we are”. Her words assert the presence of Fuerte Alto’s Diaguita-Calchaquí community.

passages.title: Language, loss and living communities
passages.text: After defeat in 1665, Kilmes families were forced to leave their Calchaquí homeland and travel over 1,000 kilometers to the Río de la Plata. A colonial settlement was established in 1666. This traumatic removal concerns a particular people, not a single ending for every Diaguita community.

passages.title: Language, loss and living communities
passages.text: During pandemic school closures, an Amaicha del Valle teacher worked with community authorities to teach through local radio. Broadcasts reached children in distant places. The community’s council and leadership helped adapt a familiar technology to keep education going.

Inca expansion and Spanish colonial campaigns altered sovereignty at different times across this region. Some communities faced forced relocation, while others followed different trajectories. Diaguita peoples continue in Chile and Argentina; the map’s 1500 endpoint does not date their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Family introductions, learning and a living language

passages.text: The Navajo, or Diné, are a living Indigenous people whose homeland spans the American Southwest. Navajo Nation sources call it Diné Bikéyah. This shared card covers the map’s Navajo, Navaho and Diné Bikéyah labels. Their different outlines and 1492 to 1650 date windows are imported coverage, not reliable borders or the beginning and ending of a single state.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: In northwestern New Mexico, Navajo builders made small masonry pueblitos during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Many stood on boulders or outcrops with wide views. They provided shelter and cooking space as well as refuge during conflict, so a defensible position also had to work as a home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Pueblito remains include roofs, hooded fireplaces, nearby hogan foundations and small openings used to check a doorway. A family could cook, keep out weather and watch an entrance in the same compact building. These practical architectural details survive alongside the story of warfare.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Diné weavers adopted wool from introduced churra sheep and incorporated it into their textile traditions. The upright loom let makers build a cloth through the patient crossing of threads. Behind a finished blanket stood an entire chain of work, beginning with keeping the animals alive.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: At Hubbell Trading Post, established in Ganado in 1878, Navajo customers exchanged blankets, wool, sheep and pelts for goods such as flour, coffee, tools and cloth. The post also supplied news and jobs. A shopping trip could therefore carry both household supplies and neighborhood information home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: The predominantly red geometric style called Ganado Red became associated with the trading post. Hubbell promoted particular designs for outside buyers, while Navajo weavers supplied the artistry and labor. Rugs linked skilled household production to a market whose tastes could influence what makers were asked to weave.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: A 2016 Hubbell workshop offered hands-on dyeing, spinning and weaving, together with learning about Churro sheep. The program had begun in 2000 to share fiber skills and animal husbandry. Before anyone could weave a beautiful design, the wool still had to become usable yarn.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: In 1864, United States forces drove Navajo people from their homeland to Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico. In a 2018 anniversary message, Navajo leadership remembered four years of imprisonment and suffering there. The Long Walk was forced displacement, not a voluntary migration to find better farmland.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The treaty concluded at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868 allowed a return home. Its text also promised the purchase of 15,000 sheep and goats and support for the journey. Reading the document makes rebuilding tangible: families needed animals, food and transport as well as permission to leave.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first modern Navajo council was created in 1923, and reforms in 1989 reorganized national government through separated branches. These are changes in the institutions of a continuing people. They should not be mistaken for the invention of Navajo community life or its first traditions of leadership.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first group of 29 Navajo Marine recruits arrived for training in May 1942. They helped develop a military code with an initial vocabulary of 211 terms and a system for spelling English letters. The achievement combined language expertise, memorization and radio training; it was more than ordinary conversation overheard on a battlefield.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Navajo scholar Shelly C. Lowe explains that her clan comes through her mother and passes to her children. Introducing clan relationships and home community helps people place one another within a network of relatives. An introduction can be a miniature family map rather than just a name.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Remembering school in Ganado, Lowe describes designing rugs on craft paper, beadwork and other cultural arts in class. She also heard Navajo from school cooks and aides as well as relatives. Language and skills traveled through ordinary encounters, from the classroom to the people preparing lunch.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Written language sample: yá’át’ééh, translated by Lowe as “It is good,” is a Navajo greeting printed in her 2022 interview. This is an attested modern spelling of a living language. It is not presented as an inscription surviving from the map’s sixteenth-century window.

The Diné endured forced removal and returned after the 1868 treaty. Their nation, families and language continue, with government institutions changing over time. None of the imported map endpoints should be read as the extinction of the Navajo people.

passages.text: Djibouti became independent from France on 27 June 1977. The atlas record starts in 1945, so its early outline represents a French territory rather than an independent republic. This Red Sea gateway connects ports, inland towns and pastoral communities; their histories extend beyond the borders and institutions of the modern state.

passages.title: Changing government and older heritage
passages.text: In 1967 the French territory received the name Territory of the Afars and Issas. A contemporary administrative account lists a high commissioner, government council and territorial chamber, alongside towns including Tadjourah, Obock, Dikhil and Ali Sabieh. These were colonial institutions; the new name did not itself establish independence.

passages.title: Changing government and older heritage
passages.text: The change to sovereignty came on 27 June 1977. Hassan Gouled Aptidon was president at recognition. One small but revealing diplomatic change occurred that day: the American consulate in the French territory became an embassy to the new republic. The same place now participated in a different international relationship.

passages.title: Changing government and older heritage
passages.text: Far older history survives at Abourma, on the Makarassou massif in the Tadjoura region. UNESCO’s conservation mission describes prehistoric engravings extending across nearly three kilometres. Their varied scenes preserve traces of past pastoral lives. Work to protect them belongs to modern Djibouti; making the engravings did not.

passages.title: Changing government and older heritage
passages.text: The constitution’s French motto reads “Unité-Egalité-Paix”: “Unity, Equality, Peace.” Article 1 prints those words and names Arabic and French as official languages. This is a short sample of modern state writing, not a claim that people used French throughout the region’s earlier history.

passages.title: Family knowledge and celebrations
passages.text: Somali-Issa communities in Djibouti, Ethiopia and Somalia share Xeer Ciise customary law. UNESCO’s 2024 account describes reconciliation and compensation, with rules taught through tales, proverbs, games and poetry as well as formal education. Remembering and discussing law can be a social practice, not only a matter of reading statutes.

passages.title: Family knowledge and celebrations
passages.text: Xeedho celebrates the first week of a daughter’s marriage. Her mother prepares dried dromedary meat, fries it in butter and preserves it in ghee inside a carved wooden container. Basketry, leather, shells and cloth turn the food into an elaborate gift. A family recipe can require craft skills as well as cooking.

passages.title: Family knowledge and celebrations
passages.text: The gift also presents a puzzle. UNESCO’s earlier account of the Somali wedding practice describes the groom and his friends searching for hidden rope ends and untying knots to reach the container. Mothers, daughters and nieces pass on the skills. Someone has worked very hard to make dinner difficult to unwrap.

passages.title: Water, transport and medicine
passages.text: Beyadeh’s solar-powered water system changed an everyday journey. UNICEF’s 2019 report pictures Fatouma collecting water only five metres from her home and describes water supporting a family nutrition garden. Pumping and storing water close to houses reduced the work of carrying it across a hot, dry landscape.

passages.title: Water, transport and medicine
passages.text: Water affected school attendance too. In that report, Halima explained that her children had missed school when she needed help collecting water after childbirth. A Beyadeh teacher described cleaner school toilets after the project. A reliable tap could therefore help with lessons, hygiene and family care at the same time.

passages.title: Water, transport and medicine
passages.text: The modern Djibouti to Addis Ababa railway began commercial operations in January 2018. The port authority describes direct links between container and cargo terminals and the railway to Ethiopia. Moving a container from ship to train links dockworkers, railway crews and inland businesses in one chain of practical tasks.

passages.title: Water, transport and medicine
passages.text: A port also needs to repair ships. In March 2026 the port authority described a repair yard 217 metres long and 36 metres across, with a 20,000-ton lifting capacity. The visit included its repair and refuelling services: maritime trade depends on workshops and maintenance as well as the vessels people see arriving.

passages.title: Water, transport and medicine
passages.text: Mosquito control requires checking whether old methods still work. WHO’s 2024 country account describes a malaria treatment-effectiveness study that informed a revised national policy, and changes to insecticides used inside buildings in response to resistance. Local health workers’ training and surveillance were part of that response.
French rule ended with independence in 1977. Djibouti continues as a sovereign republic, while cross-border family, commercial and cultural connections remain part of its history.

sectionTitles: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence

passages.text: Dominica’s history includes Indigenous pottery, plantation slavery, resistance and an independent republic established in 1978. Its earlier archaeological sites and continuing craft traditions reveal more than changes of government. Creole music, dance and language research show communities making and teaching knowledge across generations.

passages.title: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence
passages.text: At Woodford Hill, Andre Samuel found two nearly complete Cayo pottery jars in an eroding headland in 2004. A later survey recovered pottery, stone flakes, charcoal, fish bones and shells behind an old warehouse. These finds illuminate manufacture and food use, but older material was mixed with modern glass, metal and ceramics.

passages.title: Discoveries and the limits of the evidence
passages.text: At the Eden River mouth, pottery includes incised and modelled decoration, possible griddle fragments and pieces assigned to different ceramic traditions. The mixed deposit records repeated use of the locality. It cannot be treated as one household assemblage or used to prove that a change in pottery meant one people replaced another.

passages.title: Slavery, resistance and freedom
passages.text: Jacko escaped from enslavement at Castle Comfort Estate and established a refuge in the mountainous interior near Belles, at the place now called Jacko Flats. His community sheltered people escaping coastal plantations. He was killed by colonial Rangers in July 1814 during the suppression of Maroon resistance.

passages.title: Slavery, resistance and freedom
passages.text: Dominica’s emancipation observances remember both legal abolition in 1834 and the end of apprenticeship in 1838. Lectures, exhibitions, drumming and bèlè performances connect public history with artistic practice. Remembering the two dates separately helps explain why the first legal change did not immediately end coerced work.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: Sandra Thomas made a wicker-plaited larouma-fibre basket in Dominica in 2002. The Smithsonian records both the artist and the material; its staff member Susan Secakuku bought the basket directly from Thomas the following year. This is documented contemporary craft, with an identified maker, rather than an anonymous archaeological object.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: Kalinago Barana Aute presents craft, cassava-bread making and canoe-building demonstrations led by community practitioners. Its model cultural village includes a covered communal meeting place. These activities make skills available for teaching and paid cultural work; the buildings are a modern interpretation of heritage, not surviving ancient houses.

passages.title: Kalinago work and community
passages.text: The Kalinago account of their territory describes colonial land sales and dispossession, followed by retreat toward the east coast. Recognition of communal land in 1903 did not begin their history. Even when colonial authorities suspended the chief’s office, community members continued to recognize elders as leaders.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Pearle Christian’s description of traditional instruments explains how a tambou bèlè uses rope and pegs to tension its skin: greater tension raises the pitch. Drum bodies can be made from kegs, metal cans or hollowed trunks. The instrument joins practical knowledge of materials with the demands of dance and collective performance.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: The bamboo flute has a blowing hole and six finger holes, allowing the player to change pitch. In jing ping music, the accordion supplies a reed-driven melody. These instruments show different routes to a local sound: shaping plant material into an instrument and adapting an imported instrument to Dominican performance.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Daryl Phillip’s 1994 account describes quadrilles as coordinated sequences for four couples. Musicians must understand the steps and change rhythm to suit them. Sequence names vary with place and language: Woodford Hill uses Kokoy terms alongside the Creole names found elsewhere. The dances preserve local differences within a shared form.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Mabel Cissie Caudeiron composed Creole songs, founded the Kairi Artistic Troupe and researched music, dress and dance. She also helped organize the 1965 National Day celebrations. Her work brought practices associated with ordinary Dominican life onto public stages and into written accounts, years before political independence.

passages.title: Music, dance and language
passages.text: Established in 1981, Kommité pou Etid Kwéyòl organized literacy classes and the first Jounen Kwéyòl celebration that October. Its publications include proverbs, riddles called timtim, and a Kwéyòl-English dictionary. This work treats a spoken community language as a medium for reading, teaching and research.

Colonial association with Britain ended in 1978, when Dominica became an independent republic. Kalinago community life and Creole cultural institutions continue. The end of a map interval is not the end of these communities or of the country.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
Community learning and looking after one another
Music at gatherings, knowledge at home

passages.text: Craft, care, learning and music illuminate the Dominican Republic’s everyday history. Archaeological finds and living traditions reveal different communities and periods.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: Divers at La Aleta, a flooded cavern in the southeast, recovered a woven basket fragment with a published date range of about 1275 to 1435 CE. It unravelled after recovery. The team left other baskets underwater until suitable conservation could be arranged. Keeping fragile finds intact is part of archaeology.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: La Aleta also yielded a carved tree-gourd container, dated in the report to roughly 1020 to 1180 CE. Its cut designs resemble patterns on pottery. It shows how a plant could become both a useful vessel and decorated work. Researchers interpret the cavern finds as possible offerings, so a container found there is not automatically kitchen rubbish.

passages.title: Discoveries: baskets, containers and colonial buildings
passages.text: At La Isabela on the north coast, the remains of a warehouse include traces of its outer walls and inner posts. The 1490s settlement combined substantial buildings with palm-thatched housing. Columbus’s residence used rammed earth and cut limestone. These differences show how a colonial town combined several building techniques. They do not mean all residents had the same space, comfort or authority.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: The ruins of San Nicolás de Bari in Santo Domingo preserve the site of a hospital begun in 1503 and enlarged during the early sixteenth century. A government heritage guide describes rebuilding with earth, stone and brick, and later service as a royal and military hospital. Buildings can document organised care even when they cannot tell us how a particular patient felt or whether a treatment succeeded.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: Casa de Tostado is a sixteenth-century stone house now used to display the furnishings of a wealthy nineteenth-century Dominican family. That is two different historical layers: the age of the building and the period represented by its collection. A handsome museum room can reveal household tastes and resources, but it is not a typical home for every family.

passages.title: Care, homes and family records
passages.text: Birth, marriage and death registers help researchers connect generations of Dominican families. The Library of Congress guide points to digitised records and warns that not everything has been indexed for name searches. Sometimes an original register must be browsed page by page. A family-history search can therefore resemble detective work, with handwriting instead of fingerprints.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: English-speaking Caribbean migrants and their descendants built Cocolo communities in the Dominican Republic. Alongside work in the sugar economy, they established churches, schools, benevolent societies and mutual assistance lodges. These institutions supported learning and community ties. Their history shows that migration involves creating places to gather and help one another, as well as moving from one island to another.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: Cocolo dance drama brings together African musical and dance traditions with stories from biblical and European literature. UNESCO describes performances including David and Goliath, presented at celebrations such as Christmas and carnival. Music, costumes and acting turn a familiar story into a shared community event. Passing on the performances requires opportunities for younger people to learn.

passages.title: Community learning and looking after one another
passages.text: In Villa Mella, members of the Brotherhood of the Holy Spirit play hand-drums called congos. UNESCO describes music, prayer and dancing at festivals and in ceremonies of mourning. Here music helps people celebrate together and remember those who have died. These are practices of a particular community and brotherhood, rather than funeral customs shared by every Dominican household.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Merengue is danced in pairs to music that can include accordion, drum and saxophone. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children learning by observing, joining in and imitating others. Social gatherings can become informal classrooms, with the lesson carried in movement and rhythm. It is one kind of homework for which sitting perfectly still would miss the point.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Bachata groups combine lead guitars with instruments such as bongos, maracas, a güiro and bass. Songs often explore affection, longing and memories. UNESCO’s 2019 description places this music at celebrations and social gatherings, with learning both informally and in schools. A song can give a roomful of people a shared feeling, even though their own stories are different.

passages.title: Music at gatherings, knowledge at home
passages.text: Cassava bread is a round bread made from the cassava root. UNESCO’s 2024 account links Dominican practice with traditions in four other countries, while emphasising differences in texture and flavour. Skills pass through households and communities. A familiar food can carry family knowledge across generations.

The Dominican Republic emerged from Haitian rule in 1844, underwent Spanish annexation in 1861, and regained independence in 1865. Political institutions have changed while communities continue to create, learn and share traditions. The map’s 1878 starting point is not the country’s founding date.

passages.text: Newfoundland’s dominion-era history included fishing households, financial crisis and expanding public services. An appointed commission replaced responsible government in 1934. The map’s 1938 to 1945 slice falls inside that commission period; it is not the full lifespan of the dominion, which joined Canada in 1949.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: In the inshore fishery, families divided the work between boats and shore. Women and younger sons helped split and salt the catch; women spread fish on wooden racks called flakes. They brought it in at night or when rain threatened. Weather forecasts mattered to supper and income.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: Women’s work also included gardens, preserved foods and clothing. In 1921, nearly 25,000 women were recorded working in the fishery, around 38 percent of its workforce. A story told only through boat crews would leave out much of the labor that made the trade possible.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: Cottage hospitals brought small medical teams closer to coastal communities. Typical facilities had one or two doctors, nurses and between ten and thirty beds. Staff also offered public-health instruction and midwifery training, extending their work beyond the patients already in the wards.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: From 1935, the medical ship MV Lady Anderson carried a doctor and nurse to isolated south-coast settlements. Local medical workers could request assistance by telegram. For these communities, a visiting hospital could arrive by sea.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: NONIA connected craftwork with health care: proceeds from knitted and woven goods helped pay nurses. Its nursing work transferred to government in 1934, while craft production continued. The new district nurses handled maternity, school health, nutrition and child welfare, often with little nearby medical backup.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: Teacher training at Memorial College reopened in 1935 after a funding-related closure. A five-week summer program trained additional recruits, but it could not provide the same preparation as the year-long course. Getting more teachers into classrooms did not automatically make their training equal.

passages.title: Fish, families and public services
passages.text: The 1936 curriculum added health, social education and industrial training. Some land-settlement schools taught carpentry, gardening and natural history. Yet by 1949 more than half of schools had only one room, and many lacked running water or electricity. Improvements reached communities unevenly.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: The commission sworn in on 16 February 1934 had a governor as chair and six commissioners appointed by Britain. Newfoundland retained the dominion name, but elections and legislative sessions ceased. Major decisions still needed London’s approval.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: Second World War military spending and stronger export prices transformed public finances. Newfoundland moved from dependence on British grants to financial self-sufficiency and even lent money to Britain. The economic recovery also sharpened questions about what should replace commission rule after the war.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: “Quaerite Prime Regnum Dei” means “Seek ye first the kingdom of God.” This Latin motto accompanies the arms officially readopted in 1928, reviving a seventeenth-century grant. The spelling follows the provincial government’s published motto; this is heraldic language, not everyday speech.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: Voters faced three choices in June 1948: responsible government, Confederation with Canada or continued commission government. None won a majority. A July runoff removed the commission option, and Confederation won 52.3 percent. The close result records a real division over the country’s future.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: Terms of union were negotiated after the vote, and Newfoundland joined Canada on 31 March 1949. This changed its constitutional place and restored an elected provincial government. Communities, family connections and local traditions continued across the political boundary in time.

passages.title: Government, writing and union
passages.text: The Mi’kmaq of Newfoundland continued their community life through these political changes. At Confederation in 1949, they were not recognized as status Indians under the federal system and did not receive the associated benefits. Joining Canada did not mean equal recognition for every community.

Commission rule ended with union with Canada on 31 March 1949. Newfoundland became a province, while its peoples and cultures continued. The imported 1945 endpoint marks the end of this map slice, not the end of the dominion’s separate constitutional history.

sectionTitles: A changing government, a continuing city

passages.text: Benevento was a Lombard duchy and later a principality, but this imported record runs from 1000 to 1279, across the end of its ruling dynasty in 1077 and into papal government. Its later outline wrongly includes Sicily and greatly exaggerates Benevento’s territory. This card follows the city’s final Lombard rulers and its medieval life afterward; it does not describe a Beneventan state ruling that entire polygon.

passages.title: A changing government, a continuing city
passages.text: Benevento’s inhabitants accepted papal authority in 1051 after expelling their princes. The rulers returned in 1055, but their authority was increasingly subordinate to the pope. This uneven transition explains why 1077, the death of the last Lombard prince Landulf VI, is a dynastic endpoint rather than the first moment anyone considered papal government.

passages.title: A changing government, a continuing city
passages.text: Under the popes, Benevento developed local institutions as well as papal administration. The oldest surviving version of its city statutes dates to 1202. Consuls exercised local jurisdiction, although their powers changed and were contested. Medieval government could involve argument among citizens, officeholders and distant rulers, rather than one person making every decision.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Some houses connected across streets by raised passages called pontili. Permission from the ruler was required, and the street underneath had to remain public. A family might gain a convenient route between properties while everybody else still needed room to pass below.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: A will dated December 1092 records a house with a fireplace. Other homes had upper floors reached by outside masonry stairs. These details distinguish particular buildings from a fantasy of identical medieval cottages. Comfort and construction varied from household to household.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Benevento’s documented crafts included pottery, shoemaking, tailoring, carpentry, stoneworking and metalwork. Mills operated along the rivers, especially a channel diverted from the Sabato. These activities connected the city to farms and waterpower: a prince’s court needed a much larger working community around it.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: At Sant’Ilario a Port’Aurea, archaeologists studied a rubbish deposit in a chamber probably first used as an ossuary. Its pottery dates from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, after Lombard rule and partly after this map interval. Bowls, jugs, cooking pots and large storage vessels preserve the equipment of meals and provisions.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Laboratory analysis of glazed pottery from two medieval sites in Benevento identified a group likely made locally. Some dark fragments may have been overfired rejects. The thirteenth- to fifteenth-century pottery tradition therefore preserves mistakes as well as attractive dishes. A pot that went wrong in the kiln can tell researchers how its successful neighbors were made.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: The cathedral expanded during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, removing an older burial area in front of the church. Excavations beneath today’s floor distinguish those medieval changes from earlier churches and from modern rebuilding. A familiar place could be repeatedly reorganized as the community’s needs and ambitions changed.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: Funerary inscriptions for ninth-century Lombard princes were reused in the cathedral’s later facade. Their words outlived the tomb arrangement for which they had been carved. The stones are now museum evidence of both the earlier dynasty and the practical medieval habit of reusing valuable building material.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: A 2024 study brought scattered cathedral sculpture fragments back into conversation with one another. Its author proposed an earlier twelfth-century date for parts of the rebuilding and bronze door than some previous accounts had used. Reassembling fragments can change a building’s history; dates printed in older guides are not automatically the last word.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: Santa Sofia’s twelfth-century cloister includes carvings of seasonal agricultural work, with months from June to December surviving. Other capitals display fantastic creatures. The sculptors placed familiar labor beside imaginative beasts, giving a person walking around the courtyard much more to look at than a row of plain supports.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: An inscription in Santa Sofia’s cloister honors Abbot John IV, who governed from 1142 to 1176. Its Latin words “stat Quarti fama Iohannis” mean “the fame of John the Fourth endures.” This modern transcription comes from a carved capital and belongs to papal-era Benevento, after the Lombard dynasty had ended.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: Beneventan was also the name of a distinctive handwriting style used across southern Italy. A regional example is the Montecassino Exultet roll of about 1075 to 1080, now British Library Add. 30337. It contains Latin for an Easter ceremony, with red musical signs above the words. Script, language and tune did different jobs on the same parchment.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: On an Exultet roll, pictures faced the opposite direction from the words. As the reader let the scroll descend from the reading platform, listeners could see the images the right way up. This southern Italian format considered two audiences at once: the person singing the text and the people watching below.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: The battle near Benevento on 26 February 1266 ended with Charles of Anjou defeating Manfred, king of Sicily. It belongs to the city’s later medieval setting, nearly two centuries after the Lombard dynasty ended. The battle’s famous name should not be mistaken for the fall of an independent Lombard duchy in 1266.

Landulf VI’s death in 1077 ended the Lombard dynasty. Benevento continued as a papal city, with later occupations and local institutions. The imported 1279 endpoint is not the principality’s historical fall date.

sectionTitles: A household on a windy headland
Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
A window ledge with homework potential

passages.text: Dumnonia was an early medieval British kingdom in the south-western peninsula, associated with Devon and Cornwall. Its rulers probably used several centres, including Tintagel. This card follows the map’s 600 to 800 window but also uses earlier evidence from Tintagel’s prosperous fifth to seventh centuries. Those finds illuminate an exceptional coastal settlement, not every household across the kingdom.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Tintagel offered steep cliffs, a narrow approach and broad sea views, but it also had fresh water. Some small rectangular buildings contained hearths. The settlement combined an unusually defensible position with the everyday necessities of warmth, cooking and drinking.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Excavators uncovered stone walls, paving and steps on the southern terraces. A thick wall farther east could have supported a building or held back a terrace. Finding a wall is straightforward; deciding exactly what its builders needed it to do takes more work.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Surveys identified roughly a hundred buildings across the headland. Their uses are not all settled: homes, stores and workshops remain possibilities. An impressive settlement plan cannot by itself tell us which room held somebody’s bed or where children spent their days.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: Fifth- or sixth-century amphora fragments from Tintagel came from Greece. These vessels carried wine and olive oil. Broken jars therefore record journeys across seas as well as the food and drink that wealthy occupants could obtain.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: Local slate discs probably closed reused amphorae with the help of beeswax. An imported container could begin another useful life after its original contents were gone. Keeping a good jar was sensible long before anyone had a kitchen cupboard full of them.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: A rotary quern from the northern ruins probably belongs to the post-Roman settlement. It ground grain into flour. Fragments of bowls, a stemmed glass and a flask, probably from southern France, reveal a very different part of meals: rare vessels that displayed the occupants’ status.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: The 2016 excavation recovered barley, wheat and some oats from post-Roman rubbish deposits. The grains survived because they were charred. Rubbish can be an excellent historical archive, although most people making dinner were probably not thinking about future archaeologists.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: Few weed seeds and little chaff accompanied those cereals. Researchers suggested that grain arrived already threshed and cleaned, probably from the surrounding countryside. Preparing food linked the coastal settlement to work on nearby farms.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: Some barley had sprouted. That might represent preparation for beer, but the researchers also considered spoiled grain burned for disposal. The same tiny find can fit two different kitchen stories; it cannot settle the menu on its own.

passages.title: A window ledge with homework potential
passages.text: A seventh-century slate reused as a window ledge carries the Latin words “viri duo”, meaning “two men”, in English Heritage’s transcription. It also has names, Greek letters and Christian symbols. This is a surviving piece of local writing, not a reconstructed sentence invented for the map.

passages.title: A window ledge with homework potential
passages.text: The lettering combines styles associated with ordinary documents and decorated Gospel books. Specialists interpret it as possible writing practice by someone with scribal training. It supports literacy in a privileged Christian setting, not the claim that every child attended school.

passages.title: Letters, beliefs and later stories
passages.text: Aldhelm wrote to King Geraint and Dumnonia’s bishops about disagreements over calculating Easter and other church practices. The letter, probably from around the opening of the eighth century, shows a kingdom participating in literate religious debate. A calendar disagreement could reach the king’s desk.

passages.title: Letters, beliefs and later stories
passages.text: Tintagel’s famous connection with Arthur first appears in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s twelfth-century account, centuries after the early settlement. Archaeological evidence for wealthy occupants does not establish that the legendary king lived there. The real jars, buildings and writing are interesting without a royal autograph.

Dumnonia lost territory through West Saxon expansion rather than one securely dated final event. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records war with Geraint in 710 but does not give its outcome; a later writer adds that he fled. Devon became part of Wessex, while a British kingdom continued in Cornwall. The imported 800 cutoff is map coverage, not the disappearance of the region’s people.

passages.text: Dutch Brazil was a West India Company colony in northeastern Brazil, established by conquest in 1630 and lost in 1654. Sugar production, slavery, religious communities and ambitious scientific collecting shaped its short history. The imported map’s 1650 to 1715 range must not be mistaken for the colony’s actual lifespan.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Johan Maurits provided loans for Portuguese operators to reopen abandoned sugar mills. Dutch officials depended on people already familiar with the industry. Taking control of a colony did not instantly supply the practical knowledge needed to run its machinery and plantations.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Plantation labor was coerced. Enslaved African men, women and children were transported to Dutch Brazil, and the governor personally owned and traded enslaved people. His support for painting and science cannot be separated from the violence that supported colonial wealth.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Drawings associated with Zacharias Wagener record a Recife slave market and a woman branded with Johan Maurits’s initials. These are rare visual witnesses to an experience that polished colonial landscapes often concealed. They depict real systems of ownership and dehumanization.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Two religious schools, Talmud Torah and Etz Hayim, operated beside the Kahal Zur Israel synagogue. Rabbi Isaac Aboab da Fonseca arrived in Recife in 1642 at the community’s invitation. Worship, study and migration linked this neighborhood to Jewish communities across the Atlantic.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Excavation at the synagogue site revealed eight floor levels, fragments of Dutch pipes, glazed pottery and a ceramic piece with a menorah. These finds show how a building accumulated changes and everyday objects. The furniture now displayed there was reconstructed through research, not found intact.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: The site also preserves a mikveh, a bath for religious purification. This gives a concrete glimpse of ritual life involving water. It should not be treated as evidence that every Recife household had the same bathing arrangements.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Frans Post’s Brazilian Landscape with a House under Construction presents European, Indigenous and African figures in an apparently harmonious setting. The museum cautions that this idealized scene hides slavery’s harsh realities. A painting can preserve useful details while also giving a misleading impression of society.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Post made the painting after returning to the Netherlands. His Brazilian scenes therefore combine remembered experience with later artistic choices. They are valuable historical evidence, but not snapshots taken while the events unfolded.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Collectors did not work alone: Indigenous Brazilians, enslaved Africans and Portuguese residents brought specimens to naturalists. Research tracing the surviving botanical images emphasizes these often uncredited contributions. The knowledge printed under European authors’ names depended on many other people.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: A surviving plant specimen, an oil painting and a printed woodcut can be compared for Spigelia anthelmia, recorded as a remedy for intestinal worms. That chain shows how plant knowledge entered books. It documents historical medicine, not a recommendation to use the plant today.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: The same research follows Cleome gynandra, an African leafy vegetable eaten by enslaved Africans in Brazil. Editor Johannes de Laet grew seeds in the Netherlands in 1646, but the plant died as the weather turned cold. Food plants traveled with people, even across climates where they struggled.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: “Historia naturalis Brasiliae” means “Natural history of Brazil.” This Latin title appears on the 1648 book preserved in the John Carter Brown Library. It is an authentic printed sample of scholarly writing connected with the colony, rather than a reconstruction of ordinary conversation.

Dutch forces surrendered in January 1654, returning the occupied region to Portuguese rule. This ended the colonial government, not the lives or histories of its diverse inhabitants. The imported 1715 endpoint is incorrect for Dutch Brazil and remains a map-data issue to correct.

Food tools with stories to tell
Homes, clothes and travelling by river

passages.text: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: The Surinaams Museum preserves a mahogany four-poster bed made in 1829 by the furniture maker Podekowitz on Paramaribo’s Wagenwegstraat. It belongs to a collection rich in furniture associated with the colonial elite. This was substantial, carefully made furniture, rather than a picture of how everyone slept. A single grand bed cannot represent all the country’s bedrooms.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Needlework samplers in the same museum record how young European women practised embroidery and mending in the late nineteenth century. Surviving stitches make learning visible: someone had to repeat a movement, control the thread and improve. The collection also preserves early-twentieth-century baby clothes. These are particular surviving objects, rather than evidence that every family dressed or taught its children alike.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Gerrit Schouten’s 1817 miniature scene shows a riverboat with six enslaved rowers, a steersman and a covered passenger compartment. The shelter has windows with shutters propped open by sticks. The model records both ingenuity and inequality: passengers could travel out of the sun and rain while others did the rowing. It is an artist’s carefully constructed view, not a photograph of a named journey.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Afáka Atumisi developed a writing system for Ndyuka. Its signs represent syllables. A 2012 study explains that the sign for tu, meaning two, uses two strokes, while fo, meaning four, uses four. A little counting can help a reading lesson. The system is a distinctive achievement in making spoken language visible, though some signs can represent more than one sound.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Immigration registers for indentured workers arriving from British India between 1873 and 1916 can record parents, siblings and other relatives. Officials later added marriages, children and sometimes grandchildren born in Suriname. These documents help descendants reconnect family stories across oceans. Some registers were lost or badly damaged, and spelling varies, so an unsuccessful name search does not show that a person never existed.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In September 2024, nineteen volunteers aged 12 to 70 joined a supervised archaeology project at Jodensavanne. Four young participants came from neighbouring Redi Doti, an Indigenous village. The work included excavation, maintenance and conservation; a caption records young volunteers sifting earth for artifacts. Learning about the past can involve patient observation and teamwork as well as books.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Jodensavanne’s heritage is cared for through cooperation with Redi Doti. UNESCO describes the Indigenous village and the Jodensavanne Foundation sharing responsibility for preservation and agreeing together on changes to the management plan. This recognises living communities as participants in caring for history. A historic site is also part of someone’s present-day neighbourhood.

Suriname gained internal autonomy in 1954 and became an independent republic in 1975. These changes ended colonial government, not the histories of its communities. Crafts, languages and family knowledge continue through living people, with traditions changing as they are shared.

sectionTitles: An unusual republic with a wide reach

passages.text: The Dutch Republic was a seven-province confederation formed in 1588 during revolt against Spain. Provinces kept substantial independence while the States General handled war, diplomacy and shared costs. Seventeenth-century shipping, art and print helped some households prosper, but the VOC and WIC also used violence, conquest and slavery overseas. A look inside homes finds working women, schoolchildren, board games, laundry, potty chairs and tiny surprises in archaeological cesspits. Spain recognized the republic in 1648; French troops and Dutch Patriots ended its old political order in 1795. The imported map’s 1600 to 1783 dates are only snapshots.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: After renouncing Philip II in 1581, the northern provinces eventually chose to govern without a new monarch. From 1588 seven provinces formed a confederation; the States General handled shared defense and diplomacy, but local provinces kept much authority.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: The States General founded the VOC in 1602 and let it make treaties, build forts, hire soldiers and wage war in Asian waters. Calling it only a spice shop hides the company’s armed and political power.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: The WIC carried enslaved Africans to the Americas and fought for colonial footholds. The VOC used violence and slave labor around the Indian Ocean too. Dutch prosperity was connected to harms borne by people far beyond the republic’s European outline.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: Spain recognized the republic as independent in the 1648 Peace of Münster. The treaty also addressed overseas possessions and religious practice, reminding us that freedom for a state did not mean equal freedom for everyone under its influence.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: French troops and Dutch Patriots ended the old republic in January 1795 and proclaimed a Batavian Republic. Dutch families, towns and languages continued even though the seven-province political system changed.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: Rembrandt, Vermeer, Frans Hals and Jan Steen made work during a remarkable Dutch painting market. Their art is a major achievement, but a painted rich interior is not a census of every kitchen.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: A Rijksmuseum schoolroom painting shows a master, girl and boy pupils, writing papers and an hourglass on the desk. It is a glimpse of teaching tools, not proof that all children could attend school for the same length of time.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: Printed maps and newspapers let readers follow battles such as the 1629 siege of Den Bosch. Families who could access news had a way to talk about distant war over a table at home.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: An engraved glass dated 1600 bears “Concordia res parvae crescunt,” Latin for “Through unity small things grow.” That short written motto spoke to the provinces’ union; Latin appeared on an object used in Dutch life, alongside Dutch as the common language.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Rijksmuseum objects suggest many seventeenth-century homes had open doors, with children or neighbors dropping in. Privacy worked differently, and household life depended heavily on women’s organization and labor.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Many women earned money as well as running kitchens and caring for children. Remember that when a painting seems to show a woman merely standing inside: a household was also a workplace.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: A “kakstoel” was a small child’s chair with a hole and a pot underneath: a potty with furniture ambitions. A physician warned against leaving children on it too long. This is a museum object, not evidence that every child used one.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Petronella Oortman’s splendid dolls’ house had two kitchens, a laundry room and even running water in the miniature show kitchen. It displayed adult wealth, not a typical home or a children’s toy.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: The contents of two Jordaan cesspits reveal everyday cooking and drinking vessels in modest Amsterdam households, with an occasional piece of Chinese porcelain. Archaeology can tell us about dinner and waste when written diaries cannot.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: People did not always wash their bodies often with water; clean linen could signal cleanliness instead. Pregnant women faced real danger in childbirth, and friends visited mothers in lying-in rooms afterward. These customs varied by class and household.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Board games like Goose Game could involve money rather than being only children’s play. The same household might hear neighborhood chatter, handle laundry and discuss war news while children learned their letters.

The old Dutch Republic ended in 1795 when a French-backed revolution created the Batavian Republic. Dutch people, communities and language continued. The imported 1783 endpoint is a map-data limit, not the republic’s historical end.
