passages.text: German South West Africa was a colony imposed on existing African societies in the territory now called Namibia. German rule lasted from 1884 to 1915. Settler expansion, African resistance, genocide and forced labour shaped this period; the map’s 1914 to 1920 interval captures only its late aftermath.

passages.title: An imposed colony
passages.text: Nama, Oorlam and Herero communities already had their own political relationships before German rule. Herero cattle wealth and expanding trade were central to nineteenth-century changes. Colonial “protection” treaties entered this existing world; they did not create a society on empty land.

passages.title: An imposed colony
passages.text: Windhoek became the seat of German colonial administration in 1891. Colonial authorities divided the town into white and Black residential areas. Where a family could live became part of racial government, as consequential in daily life as decisions made in official offices.

passages.title: An imposed colony
passages.text: A metal pass marker from Swakopmund, dated 1907, survives in a German museum exhibition. It bears a crown, place-name and identifying number. The portable metal object made colonial classification tangible, reducing an individual to an official number.

passages.title: An imposed colony
passages.text: In the war beginning in 1904, German troops forced Herero survivors into the waterless Omaheke after the battle at Waterberg. Nama communities also resisted. Mass killing, deadly confinement and deprivation formed a genocide whose consequences continue in families and communities today.

passages.title: Letters, families and material traces
passages.text: Hendrik Witbooi’s letter journals preserve an African leader reasoning about colonial power and trying to build cooperation against it. UNESCO recognizes these documents for their political and literary importance. His community’s ideas survive in its own correspondence, alongside the records made by colonizers.

passages.title: Letters, families and material traces
passages.text: In a letter dated 13 October 1885, Witbooi told Maharero that he was short of supplies, including coffee and tobacco, and asked for them along his route. Diplomatic journeys required provisions. Even a political letter could include what amounted to a shopping request.

passages.title: Letters, families and material traces
passages.text: The same letter ends “Ik ben Uwen Vriend”, meaning “I am your friend”. This is a short example of Witbooi’s historical Dutch correspondence, preserved here through a 1929 printed transcription. Dutch writing was one medium for communication between African leaders in this multilingual region.

passages.title: Letters, families and material traces
passages.text: An incoming 1892 letter from Samuel Maharero discusses where people should settle near rivers and fears that outsiders would take the land. It closes with greetings to Witbooi’s wife and children. Diplomacy, family relationships and the practical question of where to live belonged in the same correspondence.

passages.title: Letters, families and material traces
passages.text: Nakambale Museum’s photographic exhibition includes images made by Finnish missionaries, the oldest from 1893. One shows King Kambonde, his wife and a missionary’s wife. Such photographs preserve clothing and encounters, while their framing reflects the people who operated the camera.

passages.title: Railways, labour and survival
passages.text: Railways changed the movement of goods across the colony, but tracks did not build themselves. A Namibian museum review draws attention to African labourers, including prisoners forced to work during the 1904 to 1908 war, whom older displays centered on German engineers largely omitted.

passages.title: Railways, labour and survival
passages.text: During the 1915 South African campaign, Black workers repaired damaged tracks, extended railway connections and unloaded supplies. Surviving photographs show these tasks. Moving water, food and ammunition made military movement possible, although the workers often receive less attention than commanders.

passages.title: Railways, labour and survival
passages.text: The German surrender document was signed on 9 July 1915 and reproduced in a contemporary campaign account. It records a military and governmental defeat. It did not restore independent government to the African communities whose land had been colonized.

German colonial rule ended with surrender to South African forces in July 1915. South African administration followed, rather than immediate Namibian independence. Herero, Nama and other communities survived dispossession and genocide, maintaining families, political claims and remembrance beyond the colonial regime.

sectionTitles: Three regimes under one map label
The Nazi years and their aftermath

passages.text: This imported “Germany” label covers 1878 to 1945 but spans three very different governments: the German Empire, Weimar democracy and Nazi dictatorship. Industry, social insurance and city water changed family life; war and hyperinflation brought hardship. Weimar cinemas were lively, while Nazi laws expelled Jewish children from schools and led to genocide and world war. The Nazi state collapsed in 1945, and Germany was occupied and later divided. The people and their histories did not vanish. A separate German Empire card and postwar records tell parts of the same longer story.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: The imported map calls 1878-1945 “Germany,” but that label crosses the 1871-1918 Empire, 1918-1933 Weimar Republic and 1933-1945 Nazi dictatorship. These governments were not interchangeable, even when a map uses the same word.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: By the turn of the twentieth century, industrial work, social insurance, gas and electricity changed life for some families. Women often took paid work because food costs rose faster than household income. Birth and class still strongly shaped opportunity.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: Germ theory turned water and cleanliness into public health questions. New water connections and hygiene campaigns could reduce danger, but a tap or indoor toilet did not arrive in every workers’ room at once.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: After World War I the monarchy fell and a republic was founded. The 1919 Weimar constitution said political authority came from the people. This democratic promise had to survive postwar hunger and political conflict.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: Hyperinflation in 1923 could make wages and savings lose value at frightening speed. Some people found ingenious ways to manage, but many households lost the security they had worked for.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: A family in a city could see a new film at a cinema, while a rural family still worked long days in the fields. Weimar films, including Metropolis, were striking creative achievements; they did not describe every person’s daily life.

passages.title: Three regimes under one map label
passages.text: A short German sentence from the Weimar civic tradition is “Die Staatsgewalt geht vom Volke aus,” meaning “State authority comes from the people.” It marks the republic’s democratic ideal, not a promise the next regime honored.

passages.title: The Nazi years and their aftermath
passages.text: The Nazis took power in 1933 and stripped Jewish neighbors of rights. The 1935 Nuremberg Laws classified people by ancestry. Laws then pushed Jewish children and teachers out of ordinary schools and doctors out of work.

passages.title: The Nazi years and their aftermath
passages.text: Nazi Germany’s invasion of Poland began European war in 1939. It and its allies and collaborators murdered six million Jewish people in the Holocaust and millions of others. A child’s school lesson about this era should name the victims and the perpetrators, not call it only “a hard time.”

passages.title: The Nazi years and their aftermath
passages.text: Families lived very different wars: persecution, forced flight, military service, bombardment and resistance were not the same experience. The state’s crimes and the varied choices of people within it must be kept distinct.

passages.title: The Nazi years and their aftermath
passages.text: After Nazi defeat in May 1945, the United States, Britain, France and Soviet Union held power in separate occupation zones. The regime ended, but German people remained; two German states formed in 1949.

This 1878-1945 map label ends with Nazi defeat and Allied occupation, not the disappearance of German people. The German Empire and Weimar Republic had already ended as regimes, and separate East and West states formed in 1949. A reunified federal republic began in 1990.

passages.text: Germany reunited on 3 October 1990 when the German Democratic Republic joined the Federal Republic. The 1949 Basic Law’s promise to protect human dignity continued, but unification involved real changes to jobs, schools, medicine and daily routines. People from the former East and West did not all have the same experiences. Earlier worker migration and later family histories also made Germany multilingual. The imported map begins in 1994, four years after the political event. Germany continues as a federal republic.

passages.title: Reunification and rights
passages.text: On 3 October 1990, East Germany joined the Federal Republic under the Unification Treaty. The map’s 1994 start is four years later, so the card follows the legal date, not the first available polygon.

passages.title: Reunification and rights
passages.text: East Germans held a free parliamentary election in March 1990 after peaceful protests and the Berlin Wall’s opening. Their choices mattered in how unity happened; it was more than politicians redrawing a border.

passages.title: Reunification and rights
passages.text: The Basic Law begins, “Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar,” meaning “Human dignity is inviolable.” This short written German line became a constitutional guide for the reunited country. It is a promise the state must keep working to honor.

passages.title: Reunification and rights
passages.text: Reunification did not erase differences in wages, public services or family memories. The Federal Archives describes the difficult state of some eastern health facilities around 1989-94 and emergency support that kept care going.

passages.title: School, family and the home
passages.text: The unification treaty recognized school and professional qualifications earned in the GDR. Imagine finishing school just as the state on your diploma disappears: the rule helped graduates continue their studies or work. State education systems still had to adapt.

passages.title: School, family and the home
passages.text: Before 1990, West Germany recruited workers from Italy, Turkey, Spain and other countries. Some stayed, reunited with family and raised children in Germany. Reunification inherited this history; German family life never had only one language or one origin.

passages.title: School, family and the home
passages.text: The 2022 German housing census still records a home’s WC and bath as separate features. That may sound fussy until you ask whether a family has a private place to wash as well as a toilet. Housing quality remains a real-life question beneath an orderly country outline.

passages.title: School, family and the home
passages.text: A household might carry memories of a crowded postwar room, a GDR prefab apartment or a West German worker dormitory into the same reunited country. These are different family stories, and no one example should stand for all Germans.

passages.title: Continuing state
passages.text: Germany remains a federal republic. The former GDR ended as a separate state in 1990 when it joined the Federal Republic; people from both sides continued. The 1878-1945 “Germany” record is a separate map-era label, not today’s founding date.

passages.title: Continuing state
passages.text: The Basic Law, schools, and civic life continue to change. Remembering the Holocaust and the divided years helps explain why human dignity, democratic choice and family stories are central to this card.

Germany continues as a federal republic after the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The imported 1994 map start is later than reunification. East and West Germans, migrant families and other communities carried different histories into the continuing state.

passages.text: British rule joined the coastal Gold Coast colony and several differently administered territories under a changing constitutional framework. The history of the communities living there is much broader than colonial government. Farmers, fishers, potters, traders, teachers and writers shaped the society that became independent Ghana.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Coastal forts such as Ussher and James in Accra and Christiansborg in Osu predate the formal British colony. Their courtyards, bastions, storerooms and accommodation reveal how commercial and military functions were combined within enclosed compounds. Their architecture records repeated occupation and adaptation by different European powers.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: The forts served trade in gold and later the Atlantic traffic in enslaved Africans. Their survival is evidence of those coercive systems and the international networks surrounding them. They are not simply monuments to construction skill or neutral symbols of overseas exchange.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: At Christiansborg, archaeologists working with descendant communities found house foundations, local and imported ceramics, beads and smoking pipes. Three stones with charcoal suggested a cooking area, but that identification is interpretive. These discoveries bring nearby households into a history often told only through the castle.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Pottery studied from the 2016 Christiansborg garden excavations includes soot-marked vessels consistent with cooking. Stepped rims may have supported lids. The report had not yet obtained chronometric dates, so its broad post-seventeenth-century context does not justify assigning each sherd to a particular colonial year.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Incised bowls known as weika are compared with vessels used to grind condiments, while other forms served food or carried liquids. These functional comparisons help reconstruct household work, but vessel shapes could have overlapping uses. A surviving fragment does not identify the exact meal once prepared in it.

passages.title: Buildings and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Regional pottery traditions include hand coiling, apprenticeship and open firing. Engmann uses those traditions as comparisons, not direct observation of the excavated pots’ manufacture. Clay suitable for pottery is scarce at Osu, and the origins of most recovered vessels remain uncertain.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: Fishing supported an extensive division of labour. Men generally worked at sea, while women processed catches and organised trade into inland markets. Women also advocated more productive nets. Decisions about equipment therefore affected fishers, processors and traders differently, rather than benefiting a single undifferentiated community.

passages.title: Fishing, innovation and coastal livelihoods
passages.text: African entrepreneurs developed and adapted large ali drift nets and yevudor beach seines. Accounts disagree over their first introduction. From 1898 to 1923, disputes concerned juvenile fish, declining catches, prices and the larger rewards claimed by equipment owners. More productive technology also raised questions about conservation and access to earnings.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: Tetteh Quarshie, a blacksmith from Osu, returned from Fernando Po with cocoa in 1879 and cultivated it at Akwapim Mampong. Farmers obtained pods from his farm and spread cultivation. Earlier Dutch and missionary introductions mean that his contribution is better understood as successful propagation than the first arrival of cocoa.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: From 1886, the Aburi Botanical Garden also supplied cocoa planting material. Expansion depended on farmers establishing and tending trees as well as these distribution networks. The crop’s spread was a process of agricultural adoption involving many cultivators, not the work of one planter alone.

passages.title: Cocoa farming and scientific work
passages.text: The Central Cocoa Research Station opened at Akim Tafo in 1938 to investigate pests and diseases affecting farms. Its successor, the West African Cocoa Research Institute, expanded the programme in 1944 to include soils and cultivation practices. Scientific investigation developed around practical problems in a major agricultural livelihood.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: Achimota opened in 1927 and developed school, teacher-training and higher-education branches. Its curriculum brought science and vocational work together with art, music and African dance. The institution provides a concrete example of education combining technical preparation and cultural expression, without implying that such opportunities were available to every child.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The University of Ghana preserves a catalogue record for Gold Coast Leader issues from April to July 1907, published at Cape Coast. Its description identifies local and international political and social reporting. This archival record documents a local newspaper culture; it does not establish the views of every resident.

passages.title: Education, print and political change
passages.text: The Ghana Independence Act ended British governmental responsibility for the new country from 6 March 1957. It also restricted future British legislation for Ghana to measures requested and consented to by Ghana. The legal change concerned sovereignty, not the disappearance of the communities previously governed as colonial subjects.

The colonial constitutional order gave way to independent Ghana on 6 March 1957. The Gold Coast name and British responsibility ended; the population, settlements and working traditions continued into a new political history. The map’s earlier record endpoints are coverage boundaries, not separate dates of national independence.

sectionTitles: A republic and a transformed river
Cloth and carpentry that carry stories

passages.text: Independent Ghana became a republic in 1960. Its modern history includes interrupted parliamentary government, new infrastructure, inventive crafts and public-health projects.

passages.title: A republic and a transformed river
passages.text: The map begins in 1960, when Ghana became a republic, three years after independence from Britain. Independence and the establishment of a republic were separate milestones in the country’s political history.

passages.title: A republic and a transformed river
passages.text: Ten women entered the National Assembly in 1960 through a temporary measure intended to bring women into parliamentary life. Representation is part of everyday history too: who can speak in the chamber affects whose concerns reach government.

passages.title: A republic and a transformed river
passages.text: Article 1 of the 1992 constitution begins: “The Sovereignty of Ghana resides in the people of Ghana”. This is an attested English writing sample. In plainer English, governing authority belongs to the people; it is a constitutional principle, not a claim that political life always matches it.

passages.title: A republic and a transformed river
passages.text: The Akosombo hydroelectric project was constructed from 1961 to 1965. Its dam turned the Volta’s moving water into electricity through turbines and generators. The project created a huge engineered landscape, connecting river management with factories, homes and national development.

passages.title: A republic and a transformed river
passages.text: The new reservoir also displaced communities. InOctober 1964,2,063 residents of Worobong moved to Amate, together with settlers from other villages. Historian Stephan Miescher follows these households as well as the dam: producing electricity could mean losing one’s old home and fields.

passages.title: Cloth and carpentry that carry stories
passages.text: Kente makers weave narrow strips on horizontal looms and join them into cloth. Silk, cotton and rayon offer different possibilities. Patterns receive names drawn from sayings and social situations, so a carefully chosen cloth can communicate more than a favorite color.

passages.title: Cloth and carpentry that carry stories
passages.text: Kente skills travel through families, apprenticeships and schools. A community’s chief weaver can settle disputes, maintain production standards and connect makers with trading networks. Learning to weave therefore involves people and institutions as well as nimble fingers.

passages.title: Cloth and carpentry that carry stories
passages.text: Paa Joe’s red-pepper coffin, made around 1992, uses painted wooden planks to honor work such as growing or selling peppers. Ga workshops around Teshi and Nungua developed these striking forms. The museum stresses that specialty coffins are exceptions; most funerals use simpler rectangular ones.

passages.title: Cloth and carpentry that carry stories
passages.text: Samuel Narh Nartey made a Nokia-phone-shaped coffin in 2007 for an exhibition. Its painted screen says “Hello”. He had trained for eleven years with Paa Joe. This museum commission shows skilled carpentry responding to new technology, rather than evidence that every phone owner wanted the same funeral.

passages.title: School facilities and children’s health
passages.text: A 2021 UNICEF report describes new changing rooms and urinals for schoolgirls in northern Ghana. Privacy, cleanliness and somewhere to manage menstruation made attending lessons more comfortable. A school’s essential equipment includes facilities that rarely appear in the class photograph.

passages.title: School facilities and children’s health
passages.text: Completed in 2020, the programme built 101 urinals with changing rooms across four districts, reaching more than 10,000 schoolgirls. These local improvements made attending school more comfortable. Plumbing and private space can make an educational difference alongside books and teachers.

passages.title: School facilities and children’s health
passages.text: At Ghana’s malaria-vaccine pilot launch on 30 April 2019, six-month-old Susana and Abigail received the first vaccinations in the programme. Ghana joined Kenya and Malawi in testing routine delivery. Parents, nurses and researchers all contributed to learning how a new health tool could work outside a laboratory.
Ghana continues as an independent state. Coups ended particular governments, while constitutional rule resumed in 1993. Political changes did not end its communities or their creative work.

passages.text: Goguryeo was the largest and most martial of Korea's Three Kingdoms, holding the north of the peninsula and much of Manchuria from its mountain fortresses. Its painted tombs are the fullest picture of life in early Korea, and its art reached Japan through Baekje and its own monks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Tomb murals show hunts, processions, wrestlers, dancers, the sun crow and the moon toad, and the four directional animals, painted with a sense of movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze crown ornaments, earrings and belt fittings show skilled metalwork.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist sculpture and temple building grew after the religion arrived in 372; the gilt-bronze Buddha of 539 from Yeonga is the oldest dated Korean Buddhist image.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mountain fortresses of fitted stone, built to the ridgelines, guarded the valleys and river crossings.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron lamellar armor for horse and rider equipped heavy cavalry, as the tomb paintings show.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Sundo arrived from Former Qin with images and sutras, and the court adopted Buddhism; a Confucian academy, the Taehak, was founded the same year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native shamanic and ancestral rites continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Complex of Koguryo Tombs in North Korea and the capitals and tombs of the kingdom in China were both listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, the tenth-century dynasty that took its name from Goguryeo.

After decades of war with Silla and Tang China, Goguryeo fell when Pyongyang was taken in 668. Tang set up a protectorate over the north; Silla held the peninsula south of the Taedong river and pushed the Tang armies out by 676.

passages.text: The Göktürk Khaganate was the first empire to bear the name Türk. Founded by Bumin in 552, it stretched from Manchuria to the Black Sea, split into eastern and western halves in 583, submitted to Tang in 630 and 657, and rose again as the Second Khaganate in 682. Its stone inscriptions are the oldest Turkic writing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The stelae of Kül Tegin (732) and Bilge Qaghan (735) in the Orkhon valley carry the oldest long texts in the Old Turkic script, the first Turkic writing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Tengri, the sky, gave the khagan his mandate; shamans and the sacred Ötüken forest stood at the center of belief.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Taspar Qaghan patronized Buddhism and had sutras translated into Turkic, though Tengri worship remained the rule.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The khaganate held the Silk Road from China to Persia, with Sogdian merchants as its traders and scribes.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Sogdian Maniakh, an envoy of the khagan, reached Constantinople to open a silk route around Sasanian Persia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Türk first appears in history with this empire.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Orkhon inscriptions remain the chief source for early Turkic language and history.
An alliance of Uyghur, Basmyl and Karluk tribes overthrew the khaganate; the Uyghur Khaganate rose in its place in 744.

sectionTitles: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
Learning and a small writing sample

passages.text: The Golden Horde grew from the western conquests of the Mongol Empire and became a major power connecting the Eurasian steppe, Rus principalities and trading cities. Its history includes skilled metalwork, multilingual books, mobile households and ambitious urban building. The later Great Horde appears under the map’s 1492 label. The dated examples below distinguish fourteenth-century daily life from the politics of the late fifteenth century.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Batu’s forces conquered the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas in 1236-1240. His dynasty descended from Jochi. The map’s first appearance in 1279 therefore comes decades after its rise.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Berke was Muslim, and all khans from Öz Beg onward followed Islam. An alliance with Egypt’s Mamluk rulers in 1262-1263 also shows how diplomacy reached far beyond the steppe.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Bolgar preserves a mosque, minaret, mausoleums, baths and palace remains. These buildings make urban life visible alongside the better-known horse-riding armies. Its history also joins nomadic communities to settled craft and trading centers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: At Kitsivka 1 in present-day Ukraine, archaeologists found pottery, metal vessels, tools and clothing fittings from the Golden Horde period. The settlement stood near a river crossing. Such finds reveal everyday work and connections, rather than just the names of rulers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A steel helmet decorated with silver may bear Jani Beg’s name. The Metropolitan Museum treats that reading as a possibility, not a certainty. The object still shows skilled metalworking and the use of inscriptions on prestigious equipment.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A silver half-dirham of Tokhtamysh in Oxford is only 18 millimeters across. Its mint name, royal titles and religious words fit on that small surface. Coins could carry both money value and a ruler’s public message.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Ibn Battuta described felt-covered homes carried on wagons, with horses, oxen or camels pulling them. Moving house could mean taking the house along. His account describes travelers and a royal camp, not every household.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: He recorded millet porridge with mare’s milk, meat and pasta cooked with milk. These are a visitor’s observations, not a menu shared by everyone across an enormous territory.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Elite wives and princesses could control property and exercise authority. Court households also depended on servants and enslaved people. A queen’s influence tells us little about the freedoms of the women serving her.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Black Sea markets traded grain, furs, wax and honey, alongside goods arriving from farther east. They also sold enslaved people. Commercial connections created wealth, but could bring captivity and family separation.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: The fourteenth-century Codex Cumanicus contains vocabulary in Latin, Persian and Cuman, a Turkic language. Preserved in Venice, it shows people assembling tools for communication across languages. A word list is a practical achievement: conversations do not translate themselves.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: Bolgar’s nomination dossier describes madrasahs, institutions for education, among its fourteenth-century urban developments. These references show organized learning, but do not tell us that every child attended school or had the same opportunities.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: An Arabic sample from Tokhtamysh’s late-fourteenth-century coin reads “السلطان الاعظم” (al-sultan al-aʿzam), meaning “the supreme sultan.” It is a royal title, not evidence that all residents spoke Arabic at home. This inscription belongs to the earlier Golden Horde, before the Great Horde’s final decades.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: An archaeological study published in 2002 counted 25 excavated Golden Horde bathhouses: 14 communal and 11 private. That was the evidence known to its author then. Baths were substantial urban buildings, with washing also important in Muslim religious life.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Bolgar’s fourteenth-century development included water supply and drainage, according to its heritage dossier. These systems required planning and maintenance. The evidence cited here does not establish what sort of toilet every household used; bathhouses and drains are not proof of a flush toilet in every home.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Medieval writers mention a hospital, or bimaristan, at Urgench. A modern study uses those reports to investigate care in the Golden Horde. Details reconstructed by comparison with other hospitals remain proposals, and the evidence does not establish a hospital in every town.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: A study of medieval accounts describes hot and mineral springs used as treatments, as well as bathing. This tells us what people tried when ill. It does not show that those treatments worked by modern medical standards.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Civil war followed Berdibeg’s death in 1359. Tokhtamysh later reunited much of the Jochid realm, but conflict with Timur weakened his position. The larger Golden Horde eventually divided into several states.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: By the 1430s, the Great Horde claimed to be the senior continuation of the old realm. Other khanates pursued their own authority.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Ahmed Khan withdrew from the Ugra confrontation in 1480. This weakened his claim over Muscovy, but the Great Horde continued afterward.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: In 1501-1502, harsh winter conditions, shortages and desertions undermined Shaikh Ahmed. Politics depended on feeding people and animals as well as winning alliances.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Crimea’s Mengli Giray defeated Shaikh Ahmed in 1502. Shaikh Ahmed survived. The often-repeated story that Sarai was destroyed that year is disputed.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Successor khanates inherited political and literary traditions of the Golden Horde. Its legacy reached across Crimea, Central Asia and Siberia. A political breakup did not make languages, skills or communities disappear.

The Great Horde lost power to the Crimean khan in 1502. This was a political defeat within a wider succession of states, not the disappearance of the Golden Horde’s peoples. Jochid political and literary traditions continued in successor khanates.

passages.text: Goryeo, founded by Wang Geon in 918, ruled a united Korea from 936 and gave the country its name. Its Buddhist court produced jade-green celadon, the Tripitaka Koreana and the first books printed from metal type.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: A ritual text, the Sangjeong Gogeum Yemun, was printed from metal movable type by the record of the time, more than two centuries before Gutenberg; the Jikji of 1377 is the oldest surviving book printed that way.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Tripitaka Koreana, the Buddhist canon in Chinese script, was carved on more than 81,000 wooden blocks between 1236 and 1251 as a prayer for deliverance from the Mongols.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Celadon with a jade-green glaze and inlaid black and white designs reached its height in the twelfth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist paintings on silk, gilt-bronze sculpture and sutras written in gold and silver on indigo paper.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Tripitaka blocks have been kept at Haeinsa temple since 1398 and can still be printed from after nearly 800 years.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was the state faith, with temples, festivals and monks who held rank at court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Chinese classics and composition began under King Gwangjong, with separate examinations for monks.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Korea comes from Goryeo, carried west by merchants and travelers.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Haeinsa's depositories for the Tripitaka Koreana were listed by UNESCO; the celadons are national treasures.
General Yi Seong-gye, who had turned his army back from a campaign against Ming in 1388, deposed the last Goryeo king and took the throne in 1392 as the founder of Joseon.

sectionTitles: At home: light, toilets and toys
Read a small piece of the palace

passages.text: This record concerns the Nasrid emirate centered on Granada, not every earlier state that occupied the city. From the thirteenth century until 1492, its rulers developed the Alhambra while households, craftspeople, farmers and scholars sustained a much larger society. The first atlas polygon is 1279; Nasrid rule in Granada began earlier.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: The Alhambra was a fortified city as well as a palace complex. Sultans shared this setting with officials, servants and elite soldiers. Its spectacular royal rooms therefore belonged to a working settlement with many occupations, not an empty architectural showpiece.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: Muhammad I’s Acequia Real brought water to the hilltop complex. Channels supported life and cultivation as well as fountains. Keeping a beautiful garden alive required controlling a practical water supply; the view was also an engineering achievement.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: The Generalife was an agricultural estate as well as a royal retreat. Its cultivation makes a useful distinction: some green spaces produced food rather than existing only for decoration. The continued garden history after 1492 should not all be projected backward into Nasrid times.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: Granada’s Madrasa Yusufiyya, founded in 1349, taught Islamic law and religious scholarship alongside Arabic and subjects such as astronomy, calculation and geometry. These studies helped prepare people for religious and administrative roles. It was advanced education, not a school attended by all children.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: The madrasa had resident students, teachers from al-Andalus and elsewhere, and income from endowed property. This shows how learning needed housing and long-term finance as well as books. The institution’s social role changed after the conquest.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: Muhammad V’s Maristán served poor Muslim patients. Its surviving foundation inscription dates construction to 1365 to 1367. An inscription and building history provide firmer evidence for this institution than a general claim that all medieval healthcare was either excellent or absent.

passages.title: Water, knowledge and public care
passages.text: The hospital reused an earlier structure and added an upper floor and pool. Its later conversion into a mint around 1499 to 1502 changed the interior. Present remains therefore contain several lives of the building, not a perfectly preserved fourteenth-century ward.

passages.title: At home: light, toilets and toys
passages.text: The Alhambra Museum’s household collection includes iron keys, portable lamps and braziers. Such objects helped people lock doors, continue activities after sunset and warm rooms. Their different finishes show that practical equipment could also express wealth.

passages.title: At home: light, toilets and toys
passages.text: Surviving hygiene objects include small washing basins and chamber pots used near sleeping spaces. These are evidence for bodily routines that palace photographs rarely show. The collection does not justify claiming that every home in the whole emirate had an identical water supply or toilet.

passages.title: At home: light, toilets and toys
passages.text: The museum notes that surviving Nasrid houses do not always reveal a fixed kitchen room. Cooking equipment could be moved to a courtyard or porch. Spindlewhorls, thimbles and needles also point to textile work within homes.

passages.title: At home: light, toilets and toys
passages.text: Clay whistles and miniature dishes survive from both the Nasrid and later Christian Alhambra. They reveal play as part of domestic life, but a particular toy needs its own dating before it can be called Nasrid. Children’s noise, apparently, has a long material history.

passages.title: At home: light, toilets and toys
passages.text: Some whistles were modeled as animals or people, and some used water to make their sound. The museum distinguishes these types. A small, inexpensive clay toy can tell us something a jeweled royal sword cannot: what someone might have played with.

passages.title: Read a small piece of the palace
passages.text: A Nasrid shield tile in the Alhambra Museum bears the Arabic motto “ولا غالب إلا الله”: “There is no victor but God.” The same dynasty’s motto recurs in palace decoration. This is Arabic language written in Arabic script, a statement of royal faith and legitimacy.

passages.title: Read a small piece of the palace
passages.text: The Alhambra’s inscriptions use both angular Kufic and more rounded cursive styles. Some name rulers, while others offer blessings or quote scripture. Writing itself became part of the architecture; different letterforms do not necessarily mean different languages.

The Catholic Monarchs, Isabella of Castile and Ferdinand of Aragon, took Granada in 1492, ending Nasrid sovereignty. The Alhambra became a royal residence under the conquerors, and Morisco craftspeople helped repair it. Political conquest did not instantly erase its people or skills, although their institutions and circumstances changed profoundly.

sectionTitles: Learning by doing, and living above the laboratory
Water and toilets beyond the map’s cutoff

passages.text: The Grand Duchy of Hesse was the state governed from Darmstadt, distinct from Electoral Hesse around Kassel. Created in 1806, it included separated northern and southern territories, with Rheinhessen added in 1816. This map shows only 1815 to 1878, not the state’s full lifetime: the monarchy continued until 1918. Its outline is a broad guide to changing territories, not a precise border for every displayed year.

passages.title: One state, several different provinces
passages.text: Hesse-Darmstadt became a grand duchy in 1806 and joined Napoleon’s Confederation of the Rhine. Its ruler’s new title accompanied a reshaping of the German political map. After Napoleon’s defeat, the state survived, unlike several other creations of his era.

passages.title: One state, several different provinces
passages.text: Rheinhessen became a province in 1816, with Mainz as its administrative center. It retained the Napoleonic civil law inherited from French rule, unlike the grand duchy’s other two provinces. Moving within the same state could therefore mean dealing with a different legal system.

passages.title: One state, several different provinces
passages.text: The constitution introduced in 1820 limited absolute government, but the grand duke still appointed his own ministers. Representative chambers participated under specified conditions, and noble privileges remained. A constitution changed the rules of government without turning this monarchy into a modern democracy.

passages.title: A dangerous sheet of paper
passages.text: Writing sample: the July 1834 pamphlet The Hessian Courier declared, “Friede den Hütten! Krieg den Pallästen!” It means, “Peace to the cottages! War on the palaces!” This transcription preserves the printed spelling Pallästen. Written by Georg Büchner and revised by Friedrich Ludwig Weidig, the pamphlet attacked inequality and the burdens imposed on ordinary people.

passages.title: A dangerous sheet of paper
passages.text: The pamphlet began with instructions to hide it from the police and share it only with trusted friends. Those precautions reveal the danger of circulating opposition writing. Its description of peasants supporting wealthy rulers was a political argument designed to provoke readers, rather than a detached account of every family’s life.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and living above the laboratory
passages.text: In 1824, Justus Liebig received a former military guardhouse in Giessen for his chemistry laboratory. The ground floor contained a main laboratory and smaller rooms for weighing, supplies, washing and writing. He later lived upstairs with his family and initially used a private room to teach twelve students. Home and workplace were very close neighbors.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and living above the laboratory
passages.text: Liebig improved the analysis of organic substances using equipment including a five-bulb device containing a potassium hydroxide solution. It absorbed carbon dioxide produced during combustion, helping chemists work out what a substance contained. Those linked glass bulbs were measuring tools, not elaborate laboratory decoration.

passages.title: Needles, nursing and new opportunities
passages.text: Adam Opel began making sewing machines in his parents’ house in Rüsselsheim in 1862, then moved production into an unused cowshed. By 1868, a new factory used a steam engine and employed forty people. This industrial story began with stitching clothes, decades before the company made cars.

passages.title: Needles, nursing and new opportunities
passages.text: Sophie Opel took responsibility for the company’s bookkeeping after her marriage to Adam in 1868, alongside household responsibilities. Her work connects a famous manufacturer’s history with the often less visible business of keeping accounts. A workshop needed numbers that added up as well as machines that worked.

passages.title: Needles, nursing and new opportunities
passages.text: Founded in 1867, the Alice nursing association paid for nurses’ training lasting four to five months. It aimed to improve care without requiring a particular religious affiliation. Training and organized support helped establish nursing as skilled work women could undertake, rather than simply assuming that kindness alone was enough.

passages.title: Needles, nursing and new opportunities
passages.text: Women campaigning in Darmstadt sought better schooling and access to paid employment. At a meeting in 1872, delegates demanded opportunities in postal, railway and telegraph services, along with more secular nursing education and kindergartens. These were demands for change, not a list of jobs already open equally to everyone.

passages.title: Water and toilets beyond the map’s cutoff
passages.text: Darmstadt’s growing population faced inadequate and polluted water supplies. Planning for a central system began in 1871; the waterworks opened in December 1880, after this map record ends but still within the grand duchy. Steam engines lifted groundwater and pumped it toward a reservoir on the Mathildenhöhe.

passages.title: Water and toilets beyond the map’s cutoff
passages.text: Toilet waste had often collected in pits and was taken away for fertilizer. New sewers did not instantly give everybody a flushing toilet: in 1884, 937 buildings were connected to Darmstadt’s sewer network, but only 187 had the new water closets. Plumbing progress arrived one building at a time.

The grand duke was deposed in 1918 and Hesse-Darmstadt became the republican Volksstaat Hessen. A new constitution followed in December 1919. The state’s institutions and communities continued through the change of government; 1878 is only this imported map record’s cutoff.

sectionTitles: Power and the people recorded on bark
Building with local traditions and foreign expertise
Fine work, written authority and religious life

passages.text: Moscow grew from a regional principality into the centre of an expanding state. Its rulers negotiated with and collected tribute for the Mongol khans before later asserting greater independence. Buildings and household records reveal the skilled labour and everyday administration behind that political growth.

passages.title: Power and the people recorded on bark
passages.text: Ivan I obtained the title Grand Prince of Vladimir from his Mongol overlords and collected tribute on their behalf. Moscow’s rise involved cooperation within a larger political system, not a continuous story of resistance from the beginning.

passages.title: Power and the people recorded on bark
passages.text: Ivan III conquered Novgorod in 1478 and Tver in 1485. These events expanded Moscow’s authority over other communities. Describing expansion as simply gathering land can hide the loss of those communities’ political independence.

passages.title: Power and the people recorded on bark
passages.text: Excavation in the Kremlin in 2007 recovered a 52-line document written in ink on birch bark. Dating to the late 1300s or early 1400s, it inventories Turabiy’s property. Managing a wealthy household required detailed records, not just a strong memory.

passages.title: Power and the people recorded on bark
passages.text: The inventory names dependents, silver issued for service and cooking vessels, including an iron vessel for brewing. These entries illuminate labour and provisioning in one estate. They are not a census of all Moscow households.

passages.title: Power and the people recorded on bark
passages.text: The document distinguishes riding horses from animals used for field work and carefully records their colours. A transfer of 26 horses involved witnesses. Describing property precisely helped people manage responsibilities and remember transactions.

passages.title: Building with local traditions and foreign expertise
passages.text: Aristotele Fioravanti arrived from Italy in 1475 to build Moscow’s Assumption Cathedral. He studied the cathedral at Vladimir and adapted that model. Architectural achievement could involve combining an admired local precedent with a visitor’s engineering knowledge.

passages.title: Building with local traditions and foreign expertise
passages.text: The new cathedral was consecrated in August 1479. Its construction changed masonry methods and internal space. The building’s survival gives evidence for planning, materials and skilled coordination; later decoration should not all be attributed to the original builders.

passages.title: Building with local traditions and foreign expertise
passages.text: The Kremlin’s surviving fortifications largely belong to rebuilding from the late 1400s into the early 1500s. Churches, gates and walls formed an interconnected centre of government and worship. Today’s complex includes additions from much later periods.

passages.title: Fine work, written authority and religious life
passages.text: An embroidered church textile from Maria Yaroslavna’s workshop combines silk, silver and gold threads with Italian damask. Dated to the late 1400s, it reveals demanding needlework and imported material within a princely religious commission.

passages.title: Fine work, written authority and religious life
passages.text: A Moscow silver coin made in the 1480s by the moneyer Aleksandro came from a hoard found in the Kremlin in 1930. Its small size does not make it simple: minting required controlled metalworking and dies that conveyed authority.

passages.title: Fine work, written authority and religious life
passages.text: Ioannes Vasilii dei gratia magnus dux means “Ivan Vasilievich, by the grace of God, grand duke.” This Latin wording appears on a building inscription for the Spasskaya Tower from 1491. It is a formal title, not everyday Russian speech.

passages.title: Fine work, written authority and religious life
passages.text: Vasily III founded Novodevichy Convent in the 1520s; its early stone cathedral dates to 1524 to 1525. A religious community was also part of Moscow’s wider built landscape. Most of the elaborate ensemble visible today belongs to later development.

Moscow’s state continued beyond the atlas’s 1530 endpoint. Ivan IV formally took the title of tsar in 1547, marking a change in royal status rather than a conquest or disappearance of the population. The later tsardom inherited the political centre and many institutions of the grand principality.

sectionTitles: Building and moving through a river landscape
Food, farming and differences within society

passages.text: Great Moravia was a ninth-century political formation ruled by the Mojmirid dynasty. Mikulcice preserves evidence of its centres, including bridges, churches, workshops and food remains. Slavic literary work accompanied religious and diplomatic change. Its political collapse in the early tenth century did not erase the population or every settlement; the map's 900-1000 interval is not its historical lifetime.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: Mikulcice occupied raised ground within the Morava floodplain. Its ninth-century defences combined timber and earth with a stone-facing wall. Waterways shaped both access and protection, making engineering part of everyday movement through the settlement.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: Archaeologists found wooden bridge remains in former river channels around Mikulcice. These crossings connected the fortified core with surrounding occupied areas, giving physical evidence of routes that no longer follow today's river course.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: The Czech archaeological atlas records a Great Moravian dugout canoe lifted at Mikulcice in 1967. The surviving vessel complements the bridge evidence for movement on and across water; 1967 dates its recovery, not its construction.

passages.title: Building and moving through a river landscape
passages.text: The acropolis contained a basilica and a building interpreted as a palace, while residential quarters extended into the outer bailey and beyond. Churchyards and burials help reconstruct institutions, but the entire population did not live inside the elite core.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: Mikulcice's plant remains include millet, wheat, rye, barley and oats. Millet dominates seed counts, but the archaeobotanical study shows that rankings change when weight and food value are considered. Many small seeds do not automatically mean most calories.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: Grape pips survived at Mikulcice as charred, mineralised and waterlogged remains. Their shapes raise questions about wild grapes and older cultivated varieties. Finding pips establishes grape use more securely than a particular vineyard, wine recipe or grape variety.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: A study of adults buried by Mikulcice's Church VI compared tooth and bone chemistry from the same people. The researchers interpreted the differences as more millet and less animal protein in childhood than adulthood, recovering changes within individual lives.

passages.title: Food, farming and differences within society
passages.text: The same study linked inferred social position with dietary differences, including greater animal-protein consumption among the elite. These findings concern the sampled cemetery population, rather than proving a uniform diet across all of Great Moravia.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: Great Moravian pottery includes both specialist workshop products and simpler domestic manufacture. The archaeological institute stresses that techniques changed at different speeds and served different customers, rather than replacing all older practices at once.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: A ninth-century silver chain earring from Mikulcice illustrates fine metalworking. Other elite jewellery used filigree and granulation alongside simpler ornaments. Finished objects show technical skill, but do not by themselves establish whether knowledge travelled with visiting artisans or returning apprentices.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: The institute also illustrates a ninth-century antler playing piece from Mikulcice decorated with a bowman. This small object adds leisure and imagery to a record often dominated by churches, weapons and prestigious graves.

passages.title: Craft, play and learning
passages.text: Constantine, later called Cyril, developed Glagolitic letters for Slavic religious writing. With Methodius, he helped build a literary and teaching tradition tied to Moravia's church diplomacy. Their mission entered a region where Christian institutions already existed.

The Mojmirid political structure collapsed in the early tenth century under Magyar pressure and internal strain. This ended a state, not its entire society. Reduced occupation at Mikulcice and the later reuse of Moravian identity make total depopulation an unsuitable description; the exact sequence remains debated.

passages.text: Great Zimbabwe was a stone-built center created by ancestors of the Shona. Its surviving walls preserve part of a larger settlement of homes, courtyards and monumental enclosures.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders fitted local granite slabs together without mortar. Successive courses stepped inward, giving the curving walls a stabilizing inward slope.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Eight surviving soapstone bird sculptures combine human and bird features. Their precise meaning remains uncertain; an association with royal authority is one interpretation.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Stone walls stood beside homes made from daga, a building material of earth, with thatched roofs. Painted surfaces and enclosed courtyards formed parts of the lived settlement.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavations recovered imported glass beads, ceramics from China and Persia, and coins from Kilwa. These objects place the inland settlement within long-distance exchange networks; they do not, by themselves, identify every trader or route.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Six soapstone birds came from the Hill Complex's Eastern Enclosure. Their setting supports interpretations involving ritual or royal authority, but their original arrangement and precise meaning remain uncertain.

Great Zimbabwe did not simply empty in 1450. A study combining radiocarbon dates, stratigraphy and imported objects places occupation at least into the sixteenth century and probably the seventeenth, after its main building peak in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The chronology does not identify a single conquest or establish one cause for the loss of political prominence. The site remains a place of spiritual practice for contemporary communities; the decline of a capital did not mean the disappearance of its people.

sectionTitles: A growing capital and the things beneath it

passages.text: This entry is modern Greece, whose independence was recognized in 1830, rather than the ancient Greek city-states. The imported map label begins in 1878. The country later passed through monarchies, republics, war and dictatorship before the restoration of democracy in 1974 and the constitution of 1975.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: Athens rebuilt the Panathenaic Stadium for the first modern Olympic Games in 1896. The setting drew on an ancient stadium, but the new international event required modern reconstruction and organization. A famous old place became the stage for a new sporting institution.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: After the upheavals of 1922, refugees arriving in Drama found temporary shelter in churches, mosques and houses. The Benaki Museum’s exhibition includes the Santirvan mosque’s use for housing. Objects carried by displaced families preserve memories of homes and communities left behind.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: Athens needed much more water as its population grew, especially after the arrival of refugees in the 1920s. The Marathon dam and a new tunnel and distribution network expanded the city’s supply. Everyday washing, cooking and drinking depended on engineering far beyond the kitchen tap.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: The Marathon dam was built between 1926 and 1929. Stone houses made for workers survive at the site, and the water museum preserves tools and film of construction. A large public work also meant a temporary community of people building, living and working together.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: Building the Athens metro required extensive archaeological excavation. The metro company records tens of thousands of finds from the work. A transport project therefore also became a major investigation of the city’s earlier streets, buildings and buried objects.

passages.title: A growing capital and the things beneath it
passages.text: Metro excavations uncovered wells, conduits and reservoirs beneath Athens, including deeply buried water structures. These remains show how earlier residents collected and moved water. Modern passengers can travel through a city whose underground layers preserve older answers to the same basic needs.

passages.title: Work, food, language and health
passages.text: On Chios, mastic growers make small cuts in trees so resin can collect and harden into drops. Preparing the ground, tending trees, gathering resin and cleaning it form a seasonal cycle. A tiny piece of mastic represents many separate tasks rather than simply picking something from a branch.

passages.title: Work, food, language and health
passages.text: UNESCO’s account describes mastic work as a family and community activity, with knowledge passed through practice and conversation. Cleaning the resin can bring people together to exchange stories. The social life around the work is part of the tradition alongside the finished product.

passages.title: Work, food, language and health
passages.text: In 1976, Greece established demotic Greek, the language form closer to everyday speech, in education. Administration followed in 1977. The change affected the language children encountered in school after a long debate over the relationship between spoken Greek and more formal written forms.

passages.title: Work, food, language and health
passages.text: Greece created its national health system, ESY, in 1983. The reform aimed to organize public healthcare on a common basis. Public and private services continued alongside one another, and later reviews identified uneven access and financing problems. Building a health system required more than passing its founding law.

passages.title: Work, food, language and health
passages.text: A chef in Koroni describes using seasonal ingredients and giving leftovers another purpose: baked vegetables can go into a pie, while fish bones become stock. This is one restaurant’s account of contemporary practice. Yesterday’s ingredients can get a second act instead of a trip to the bin.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Modern Greek, constitution article 1: “Όλες οι εξουσίες πηγάζουν από το Λαό”. Translation: “All powers derive from the people.” This excerpt uses the demotic wording introduced in 1986, preserved in Parliament’s consolidated constitutional text. It should not be mistaken for the exact language of the original 1975 printing.

Modern Greece continues as a republic. The 1974 referendum confirmed the rejection of monarchy after the military dictatorship collapsed. The state and its communities continued through the change of government. Its constitutional order was established in 1975 and subsequently revised.

passages.text: The Greek city-states formed a varied political and cultural world. These examples focus on Athens and Classical sculpture; Athenian institutions should not be assumed to describe every Greek community.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Athenian potters controlled the air admitted to a kiln in successive firing stages to produce contrasting black and red surfaces.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red-figure vase painting developed around 530 BCE. Brush-drawn details gave painters greater freedom to show anatomy, fabric and movement.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Polykleitos developed a system of bodily proportions. Many renowned Greek bronze compositions are known through later marble copies and written descriptions.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The marble Parthenon belonged to the building program associated with Perikles and the worship of Athena on the Athenian Acropolis.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: In Classical Athens, adult male citizens participated in the assembly. This was a particular civic institution, not political participation for every resident.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Different vessel shapes served storage, water carrying, drinking and ritual. Pottery images complement written evidence about Athenian life.

sectionTitles: A living landscape with a long history

passages.text: This record represents modern Greenland, whose 1960 map start comes after its 1953 incorporation into the Danish kingdom. Greenland later gained Home Rule and then expanded self-government. Inuit communities, language and knowledge remain central to a society with both towns and smaller settlements.

passages.title: A living landscape with a long history
passages.text: The Aasivissuit to Nipisat landscape preserves thousands of years of hunting and settlement. Large communal winter houses and inland caribou hunting features record organized work and shared living. The remains belong to several successive cultures, extending far earlier than this modern map record.

passages.title: A living landscape with a long history
passages.text: Caribou hunting used hides and drive systems, while coastal waters supplied fish and marine animals. Routes connected sea, fjords and interior across the seasons. Some hunting journeys still follow this broad pattern, linking present families with knowledge preserved in the landscape.

passages.title: A living landscape with a long history
passages.text: The national museum displays kayaks, open skin boats called umiaq, and dogsleds. Their forms were adapted to Arctic travel and hunting conditions. These were specialized technologies refined through experience, as carefully suited to their tasks as a modern vehicle.

passages.title: A living landscape with a long history
passages.text: One museum umiaq was still working in West Greenland until 1966. That date makes a useful surprise: skin boats belong to recent family memories as well as ancient history. The museum records continuing kayak and sled use especially in the north.

passages.title: Homes, schooling and medicine
passages.text: From the 1950s, housing schemes promoted larger new dwellings; later investment concentrated in open-water towns. Concrete apartment buildings accommodated newcomers, but housing shortages persisted. Decisions about where services were funded also encouraged families to leave smaller settlements.

passages.title: Homes, schooling and medicine
passages.text: Education reforms increasingly emphasized Danish. Between 1961 and 1976, more than 1,500 pupils went to Denmark after sixth grade, living with foster families. Such schooling offered qualifications but also separated children from familiar language, relatives and home surroundings.

passages.title: Homes, schooling and medicine
passages.text: Queen Ingrid’s Sanatorium opened in Nuuk in 1954 with 211 beds for tuberculosis patients. By 1962, the improved situation allowed it also to serve as a general hospital. This was a major change in access to treatment, although tuberculosis was not permanently eliminated.

passages.title: Homes, schooling and medicine
passages.text: Between 1955 and 1971, the specially built tuberculosis ship Misigssût travelled the coast to inhabited places. A visiting medical ship helped reach communities separated by sea and enormous distances. Public health needed a transport plan as much as a building.

passages.title: Music, language and governing together
passages.text: In drum dancing, a performer moves a qilaat drum and strikes its frame with a stick. Songs can concern hunting, affection, longing or humour. These living performances share stories of ordinary life at celebrations and gatherings, rather than treating heritage as silent museum objects.

passages.title: Music, language and governing together
passages.text: Historically, song duels could channel quarrels into performances that teased or mocked an opponent. Audience laughter helped decide the contest. The Greenlandic heritage inventory describes this as a way to reduce conflict, an argument with rhythm and an audience.

passages.title: Music, language and governing together
passages.text: Section 20 of the 2009 law reads in Kalaallisut: “Kalaallit oqaasii tassaapput Kalaallit Nunaanni pisortatigoortumik oqaatsit.” Translation: “Greenlandic is the official language in Greenland.” This is an attested modern legal sentence, written with Latin letters, rather than a reconstructed ancient phrase.

passages.title: Music, language and governing together
passages.text: The 2008 referendum supported expanded self-government, which began in June 2009. Greenland’s elected Inatsisartut and its government, Naalakkersuisut, make decisions in transferred fields. This history concerns Greenlanders seeking greater authority over their own lives and institutions.

Greenland continues as a self-governing part of the Danish realm. The 2009 framework recognizes a right to self-determination and provides a process for possible independence. This is an ongoing society, not a civilization that ended in 1960.

Plantation work and lives preserved in records

passages.text: Grenada’s history encompasses the main island, Carriacou and Petite Martinique. The present nation became independent in 1974 after French and British colonial rule. This account follows the islands through different political periods, from earlier communities to a society whose public life includes distinctive maritime and performance traditions.

passages.title: Early settlements and what pottery reveals
passages.text: The National Museum distinguishes early signs of human activity from evidence for permanent villages. Cut conch shells found near the airport have been displaced from their original contexts, while pottery-making settlements are better established from around 200 CE. A stray or redeposited object cannot by itself provide a complete settlement history.

passages.title: Early settlements and what pottery reveals
passages.text: A 2008 study examined sherds from Carriacou sites including Grand Bay and Sabazan, using mineral identification in thin sections and chemical analysis. Differences in clay and added material help investigate manufacture and exchange. The researchers found strong indications of nonlocal materials, while describing the source assignments as preliminary.

passages.title: Early settlements and what pottery reveals
passages.text: The same study discusses an inhaling bowl recovered at Grand Bay in deposits dated approximately 1000 to 1300 CE, alongside two museum examples lacking secure find contexts. Older luminescence dates led researchers to propose that such bowls might have travelled as heirlooms. That proposal does not turn the deposit into an earlier settlement.

passages.title: Early settlements and what pottery reveals
passages.text: The museum cautions against treating the colonial term Carib as one unchanging ethnic identity. French sources used different names for communities, and archaeological styles do not map neatly onto those labels. The islands’ earlier inhabitants had histories of movement and interaction that cannot be reduced to a simple story of one people replacing another.

passages.title: Plantation work and lives preserved in records
passages.text: French-period cultivation included indigo, cocoa, coffee, cotton and sugar. Under British rule, expanding sugar production combined smaller holdings into larger estates and intensified demand for enslaved labour. The landscape of export crops was built through coercion, not simply through the introduction of useful plants or agricultural equipment.

passages.title: Plantation work and lives preserved in records
passages.text: At emancipation, compensation went to owners, while the formerly enslaved received none. The museum connects this settlement with the persistence of estate wage labour after freedom. Ending legal ownership of people changed their status profoundly, but did not by itself give families land, savings or equal bargaining power.

passages.title: Plantation work and lives preserved in records
passages.text: An 1817 register records Malvina Wells, then a child, enslaved on Grand Bay estate in Carriacou. Scottish censuses later place her in Edinburgh, working as a lady’s maid in 1851 and managing her own household in 1861. Linking these records reveals a particular life across the Atlantic, beyond anonymous plantation totals.

passages.title: Plantation work and lives preserved in records
passages.text: Wells’s 1873 testament remembered relatives and a person in Grenada who regularly sent her newspapers. The bequests show continuing connections with her homeland. The records do not establish all her motives or the exact circumstances of her freedom, so neither gratitude toward former enslavers nor complete personal independence should be assumed.

passages.title: Documents, government and political change
passages.text: The 1763 treaty names Grenada and the Grenadines in the clause transferring them to Britain. Its language concerns the rights claimed by monarchs. Reading it as a diplomatic agreement keeps the imperial transfer separate from questions about the wishes or rights of the people who lived and worked on the islands.

passages.title: Documents, government and political change
passages.text: Saint-Aubin’s 1779 drawing depicts Governor Macartney surrendering his sword to the comte d’Estaing. Ink and wash present the French capture as a triumph. The work is evidence for how victory was represented, alongside the event itself; it does not offer an impartial view of the island’s inhabitants or their experience of war.

passages.title: Documents, government and political change
passages.text: Internal self-government, independence and revolutionary rule were distinct transitions. The 1983 invasion followed Bishop’s killing; elections followed in 1984.

passages.title: Skills, celebrations and continuing achievements
passages.text: Boatbuilders on Carriacou and Petite Martinique select trees partly for their natural bends, matching the timber to structural needs. Elders’ guidance, oral instruction and practical participation transmit the craft. This is accumulated knowledge of materials and shape, learned through building rather than through a single attributed invention.

passages.title: Skills, celebrations and continuing achievements
passages.text: Launching a boat is also a community event. Blessings, naming, food preparation and designated godparents involve people beyond the shipwrights. UNESCO’s account describes women increasingly contributing technical assistance as well. The finished vessel therefore carries a history of cooperation, teaching and celebration alongside its practical maritime use.

passages.title: Skills, celebrations and continuing achievements
passages.text: In Shakespeare Mas’, performers compete through remembered passages, rhetorical boasts and dramatic presentation. Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar is part of a wider repertoire that also includes historical and biblical material. Costume-making, memorization and delivery work together, while village teams gather support and celebrate their performers.

passages.title: Skills, celebrations and continuing achievements
passages.text: The tradition now includes women and girls, and transmission takes place through schools and organized activities as well as observation of experienced performers. UNESCO presents the possible connection with colonial classrooms as an interpretation. The 2024 inscription recognizes the continuing skill and social importance of the practice.

Colonial rule ended with independence in 1974; Grenada continues as a nation. The revolutionary government ended in the crisis of 1983, followed by elections and constitutional restoration. The separate map intervals are segments of coverage, not three different peoples or repeated national extinctions.
