passages.text: Hanover was a German electorate whose ruler also became king of Great Britain in 1714. The territories remained separate states. Hanover became a kingdom in 1814 and was annexed by Prussia in 1866, so the imported map’s later endpoint does not represent continued Hanoverian independence.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Herrenhausen’s great fountain required a waterworks, not just an impressive stone basin. Engineers used the River Leine to drive machinery that forced water toward the garden. By 1720 the jet reached roughly thirty-five metres: royal spectacle depended on practical engineering.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: The garden’s water system also needed extensive digging. Soldiers worked on the canal surrounding the Great Garden, while the machinery building stood on piles. Behind the elegant view were earthworks, structural supports and a great deal of labor.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: The Herrenhausen orangery was built in 1723 as winter shelter for plants grown in pots. Gardening therefore included moving and protecting living collections season by season. An orangery was a serious piece of plant-care infrastructure, not simply a decorative room with a citrus name.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Göttingen’s university opened in 1737 and became an important center of research and teaching. Its history later included mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss. The institution gives this small German kingdom a place in the history of science beyond the royal family.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: In May 1833 Gauss and Wilhelm Weber successfully tested an electromagnetic telegraph in Göttingen. A wire more than a kilometre long linked the physics collection with the observatory, crossing the town’s roofs and towers. Electricity could now carry signals between working scientists.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Their apparatus was an early working telegraph, not the internet in miniature. Its importance lay in turning electrical effects into a usable signaling experiment over a real distance. Later systems developed the idea further; several inventors contributed to telegraphy.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: Göttingen’s maternity institution offered lodging, food and care to women who were often unmarried. Directors’ diaries from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries preserve their experiences. This is unusually direct evidence for pregnancy and birth among people largely absent from royal portraits.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The arrangement came with obligations: patients performed light work such as spinning or weaving and became subjects for clinical instruction. Assistance and unequal power existed together. Describing the institution simply as free healthcare would hide the demands placed on women and their babies.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The 1824 boundary treaty with the Netherlands dealt with markers, ditches and drainage as well as lines on a map. One surviving archival map records the arrangements around the Twist area. Borders could alter the management of shared land and water used by rural communities.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: In 1837 King Ernst August rejected Hanover’s 1833 constitution. Seven Göttingen professors protested, including Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, better known for collecting stories. Their stand cost all seven their jobs; three were also ordered out of the kingdom.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The protest was about an oath and the limits of royal authority, not just a disagreement between a king and some famous authors. University teaching existed inside a political system that could dismiss its scholars. The episode made academic independence a very practical problem.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: German, Hanover’s constitution of 26 September 1833, section 3: “Die Regierungsform des Königreiches ist die erblich-monarchische.” Translation: “The kingdom’s form of government is hereditary monarchy.” The same constitution prescribed limits and obligations; four years later its revocation provoked the Göttingen professors’ protest.

Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866, ending its independent kingdom. Its territory became a Prussian province, while towns, universities and local communities continued. The map’s coverage extending to 1878 must not be read as a surviving sovereign Hanoverian state.

sectionTitles: Through the gate and into the market

passages.text: The Hausa states were a group of kingdoms and cities, not one empire with a single ruler. Kano offers unusually rich surviving walls, palace buildings, markets and manuscripts. This card uses named Kano evidence without treating it as a description of every Hausa household or town.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kano’s earthen defenses developed in stages. Nigeria’s heritage nomination describes earlier foundations, medieval building and a further extension in the 1500s. Surviving earthworks are evidence of repeated urban investment, not a wall built all at once.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kano’s gates controlled passage through its walls. The nomination links gateways, palace and market as parts of the historical city.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kurmi market was arranged in lanes specializing in different goods, including leatherwork, textiles, metalwork and spices. A shopper could head toward the right craft instead of searching one enormous jumble. The nomination also records the market’s continuing activity.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Rumfa, who ruled Kano from 1463 to 1499, is credited with the palace. The complex separates administration, family space and service areas. Its present layout records a living institution with a long building history, not a frozen fifteenth-century family photograph.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: In the 1490s, the scholar Muhammad al-Maghili visited Kano and Katsina. He wrote advice for Kano’s ruler Muhammad Rumfa. Political power involved arguments about justice and obligations as well as armies and walls.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: A manuscript of one of those works survives in Morocco’s national library. Its preservation there shows that the written connections of Hausa courts reached beyond today’s national borders. A surviving copy is not necessarily the author’s own handwriting.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: “تاج الدين فيما يجب على الملوك” is an Arabic title catalogued by Kano Archives: “The crown of religion concerning what is required of kings.” It belongs to the advice-to-rulers tradition associated with al-Maghili and Rumfa. The archive’s copy is not precisely dated here.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: Language and script are different things. Kano’s archive preserves Arabic histories alongside the Hausa Song of Bagauda in Ajami, meaning Hausa written with adapted Arabic letters. A page in Arabic-looking script is not automatically in the Arabic language.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: The archive’s digitization account describes locating manuscripts with community librarians and copyists, then photographing them on site. Preservation depends on families and local scholars as well as large institutions.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: Hausa identity developed through language, social relationships, migration and intermarriage. The scholarly summary on Hausaness specifically includes people of Fulani, Arab, Tuareg and Nupe backgrounds. A colored political area cannot contain all the ways people identified themselves.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: The political change beginning in 1804 created Sokoto’s emirates in much of Hausaland. It did not empty markets or make Hausa speech vanish. The atlas’s 1815 boundary marks a mapping transition, rather than the date every Hausa kingdom ended.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: Kano’s continuing market and preserved manuscripts show continuity. Altered buildings and recopied texts still require careful dating.

The Sokoto revolution beginning in 1804 changed rulership across much of Hausaland. Hausa communities and language continued through emirate and later colonial rule. There is no single extinction date for a people or uniform fall date for all these states.

passages.text: The Heian period was the high age of the Japanese court. With the Fujiwara regents running politics from Heian-kyo, the aristocracy turned to poetry, calligraphy and romance, and its women wrote the first great works of Japanese prose.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sei Shonagon finished The Pillow Book, her lists and observations of court life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The kana syllabaries took shape, so that Japanese could be written without Chinese.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Phoenix Hall of Byodoin at Uji was built for the Fujiwara, with its Amida by the sculptor Jocho.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Saicho founded Tendai on Mount Hiei and Kukai brought Shingon from China, the esoteric schools of the court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Genshin's Essentials of Rebirth spread devotion to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The sensibility of mono no aware, the pathos of passing things, ran through court writing.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Aristocratic life turned on poetry contests, music, calligraphy, incense and love affairs conducted by letter.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court women, writing in kana, produced the diaries and tales that define the age.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tale of Genji remains at the center of Japanese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The kana syllabaries are still the core of Japanese writing.
The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in the Genpei War, ending at Dan-no-ura in 1185; Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled from Kamakura and was named shogun in 1192.

sectionTitles: Public words and a short political life

passages.text: The Helvetic Republic was the centralized Swiss state established in 1798 under French influence and replaced in 1803. The atlas’s 1800 to 1815 interval extends into a different constitutional era. Its outline is a snapshot of changing borders, rather than a picture of today’s Switzerland or a republic that lasted until 1815.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: Representatives adopted the first Helvetic constitution at Aarau on 12 April 1798. A printed brochure survives in the Federal Archives. The new system created national ministries and reduced cantons to parts of a central administration, a sharp change from their earlier sovereignty.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: A map printed in August 1798 warned that its canton boundaries were provisional. Its maker advertised movable-type map printing that could quickly show revisions. There had been 22 cantons in April and 18 only weeks later: mapmakers had unusually fast-moving homework.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: Construction workers at Mümliswil found 173 silver coins in 1987, mostly French and Bernese. The latest was a Helvetic 40-batzen coin dated 1798. This gives the earliest possible burial date; the mixture shows that a new republic did not make older money vanish overnight.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: The republic tried to organize money around a franc divided into ten batzen and one hundred rappen. Its early coins used an armed Swiss figure with a liberty flag. A coin combined a practical unit for payments with a miniature statement about the new state.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer’s 1799 survey asked teachers what they taught, which books they used, and how long the school day lasted. It also asked whether children attended in summer or winter. A questionnaire preserves the practical questions behind an ambitious education reform.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Other questions asked about teachers’ families and children, second jobs, pay in grain or wood, and whether the school building was falling apart. Education depended on household livelihoods and buildings as well as lessons. The paperwork gets surprisingly close to ordinary family life.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Stapfer proposed lessons in French, drawing and singing alongside reading, writing and arithmetic, with improved teacher pay. His full bill failed in Parliament. Some educational councils nevertheless used the circulated plan as a guide, so rejected legislation could still influence classrooms.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Pestalozzi accepted work with children orphaned by the fighting at Stans. That institution closed in 1799 after about six months when its rooms were requisitioned. In 1800 he taught at Burgdorf and developed a boarding school, teacher training and an orphanage there.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Poor relief remained largely a local responsibility, and many communities lacked enough resources. The republic supported some needy people and charitable societies. Cantonal health commissions also struggled without effective common rules for medical practice: new offices could have much less power than their titles suggested.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: At Beromünster’s oath ceremony on 22 August 1798, a procession, musicians and girls singing patriotic songs accompanied the constitutional oath taken by 1,525 men. The official account describes two boys representing the French and Helvetic republics exchanging an embrace. Children helped stage an adult political message.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: A wooden liberty-tree board from Bauma in 1798 proclaimed “Alle haben gleiche Rechte”: “Everyone has equal rights.” The German words survive in a specific public inscription. They express the revolution’s ideal; the ceremony’s male oath-takers and the period’s conflicts remind us that its application was contested.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: The constitution promised press freedom, and publications reported parliamentary debates. Critics used the same opening. In November 1798 the government introduced censorship against opposition newspapers. Readers could encounter both the promise of public debate and attempts to restrict it within the republic’s first year.

Civil war in 1802 exposed the central government’s weakness. Napoleon’s Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803 ended the Helvetic Republic and restored a more federal structure, while retaining changes such as the status of former subject territories as cantons. Switzerland’s communities continued through this constitutional transformation.

passages.text: Otomí communities have a long history across central Mexico, with several languages and regional names, including Hñähñu. They did not form one unchanged kingdom. The broad 1492 to 1500 map label and the smaller 1530 to 1650 “Otomies” outline describe different areas and periods; this narrative also follows colonial communities around Guanajuato and Querétaro. Neither outline marks the full territory of today’s Otomí peoples.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango overlooks the Acambay valley from the San Miguel plateau. Builders levelled difficult ground and made broad terraces for temples and residential platforms. INAH identifies it as an Otomian settlement: a specific archaeological example, rather than the capital of every Otomí community.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango’s pottery helps trace connections. Excavators provisionally distinguished an earlier phase with incense burners, braziers and burial vessels resembling material at Tula, and a later phase with comparisons to Teotenango and Calixtlahuaca. Similar objects point toward relationships; they do not by themselves identify a conquering army.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The sixteenth-century Huamantla Codex was painted on bark paper. It recounts a group’s migration from Chiapan toward Tlaxcala, encounters and battles, and later Spanish arrival and a church. Images preserve an Otomí account of place and history within the colonial period.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Conservators studying the Huamantla Codex identified cochineal red in sampled paint. Looking through a microscope at tiny pigment traces helps explain how artists made the manuscript, alongside historical readings of its pictures. Material analysis supplies evidence that a modern photograph alone cannot provide.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Otomí communities made different political choices during Spanish invasion. At Tecoac in 1519, Otomí defenders guarded a Tlaxcalan frontier and fought Cortés’s force. Elsewhere some communities allied with Spaniards against Mexica power. One ethnic label cannot stand for a single decision made by everyone.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The later map’s northern outline belongs in the history of a mixed colonial frontier. Crespo and Cervantes examine Otomí-speaking settlement in Guanajuato and Querétaro, including the Sierra Gorda foothills. Some Otomí leaders participated in conquest and settlement, creating communities within a changing colonial political landscape.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: INPI emphasizes that households differ between regions: some are nuclear families, while others include extended relatives. Planting and harvest bring family members into shared work. Godparent relationships also create valued ties beyond a household, connecting families through religious and social responsibilities.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Mezquital valley, agave supported more than one craft. Its fibres supplied textiles, while its sap could be fermented into pulque. Fournier connects these activities with pottery for holding and processing sap, showing how a plant crop, containers and household work belonged to the same economy.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Working with scattered maguey plants also shaped where people lived. Fournier argues that their continuing care helped support permanent but dispersed settlements in the Mezquital. This is an interpretation of an economic landscape: a house did not need to stand in a dense city to belong to an organized farming community.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Tolimán area of Querétaro, Otomí-Chichimeca families maintain chapels devoted to ancestors. UNESCO describes annual journeys to sacred hills and Bernal rock, with ceremonies asking for water in a dry landscape. These are living local traditions with their own community setting.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Tolimán celebrations also involve chimales, large temporary structures made from reeds and leafy coverings. Their construction brings people together around an offering. A structure can be important even when its makers intend it to stand only for a celebration rather than for centuries.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: “Ki hats'i” means “Good morning”. INALI prints it as a common greeting in Hñähñu of the Valle del Mezquital and credits Nicandro González Peña for the recorded voice. This is a modern, regionally identified language sample; other Otomí varieties can use different forms.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: Otomí writing standards were developed with community representatives, teachers, activists, the Academy of Hñähñu Language and Culture, researchers and INALI. The participants came from several states. Agreeing how to write sounds can help people share teaching materials while recognizing regional diversity.

Spanish colonial rule changed political relationships, settlement and landholding, without bringing all Otomí communities to one common ending. Languages, families and local institutions continue. The map cutoffs of 1500 and 1650 are coverage dates, not the disappearance of a people.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing confederacy of nations. The Onondaga Nation's own accounts describe government, food, ceremonies and wampum as living practices connecting community responsibilities with historical memory.

passages.title: Government
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the Hoyane who represent their clans in council. They can remove a leader who fails to represent the clan, after warnings.

passages.title: Technology and memory
passages.text: Wampum makers cut, round, sand and drill shell beads. Woven strings and belts support the remembrance of agreements and their histories.

passages.title: Diplomacy
passages.text: Wampum strings can carry invitations to council meetings. They also identify leadership titles and give weight to a speaker's words.

passages.title: Food and daily life
passages.text: Corn, beans and squash are the Three Sisters. Onondaga food traditions also include fishing, hunting, gathering and sharing food within the community.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Thanksgiving Address opens gatherings by acknowledging people, the natural world and their interdependence. Speakers express it in their own words.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Clan Mothers help sustain ceremonies and teach younger generations. These are present-day responsibilities, not customs of a vanished society.

sectionTitles: Water had to arrive at the right speed
Buildings large enough to bring people together
A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
What can be read, and what continues

passages.text: Hohokam is an archaeological label for related material traditions of ancestral Sonoran Desert communities, not the known name of a single ancient nation. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is misleading: the large settlement pattern described here had changed by about 1450. This card explains the earlier canal-building communities and their continuing descendants, rather than placing an unchanged state in that late outline.

passages.title: Water had to arrive at the right speed
passages.text: Farmers built canals to bring river water to villages and fields. At S’edav Va’aki beside the Salt River, local bedrock helped direct water toward canal entrances. Choosing an intake location was an engineering decision tied to the landscape, before the long labour of digging even began.

passages.title: Water had to arrive at the right speed
passages.text: A canal that slopes too steeply sends water racing against its banks; one too level lets silt settle and obstruct the flow. The builders had to find a workable gradient and keep maintaining it. Making water travel gently across a dry landscape was a lasting technical achievement.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Excavated pithouses leave postholes and hard, smooth floors, sometimes with caliche plaster. At Pueblo Grande, archaeologists also found pits where builders prepared caliche. Burned pieces of wall daub can preserve impressions of grass and wood, allowing vanished walls to leave surprisingly detailed clues.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Groups of houses faced shared courtyards. Archaeologists interpret these clusters as settings for cooperation among related households, including food preparation, weaving and child care. The layout is observable; the precise family relationships are an interpretation. A courtyard could be a workplace and a place to keep children nearby.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Manos and metates, handstones and larger grinding surfaces, reveal food preparation near homes. Plant residues can sometimes identify what was ground. Other finds, such as prepared clay, help locate pottery work. Cooking equipment and craft materials let researchers reconstruct activities on a household scale.

passages.title: Fields and gathering grounds
passages.text: Cultivated foods included maize, beans and squash, while cotton supplied fibre. People also gathered cactus foods, mesquite pods and agave, and took fish and other animals. Irrigation did not make the surrounding desert irrelevant: families combined several sources of food and useful materials.

passages.title: Fields and gathering grounds
passages.text: Pueblo Grande’s residents accumulated rubbish in mounds near their homes. Some surfaces appear to have been burned and covered with fresh soil, perhaps to control smells and pests. Ancient rubbish management also created a useful archive: yesterday’s discarded fragments can become today’s evidence for everyday life.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: Oval depressions surrounded by earth banks are commonly called ballcourts. At S’edav Va’aki, the museum dates their wider importance to about 750 to 1200 and notes associations with exchange. Their exact activities remain uncertain; we cannot confidently supply teams, rules or a score for an ancient match.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: The Great House at Casa Grande was built in the fourteenth century. Builders mixed local calcium-rich caliche with water and piled it into thick walls. Horizontal joins still mark successive courses left to dry before more material was added. The building preserves the rhythm of its construction.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: The Great House also required wooden supports. The National Park Service describes timbers brought from forests as far as sixty miles away, with smaller saguaro ribs placed across supporting beams. A monument made from local earth still depended on planning, transport and materials from beyond the immediate settlement.

passages.title: A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
passages.text: At Snaketown, excavators found a shell ornament with a horned-lizard design still protected by a resistant coating. It had not yet passed through the etching stage. This unfinished object helps explain how makers shielded parts of a surface while an acid removed the exposed shell around the design.

passages.title: A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
passages.text: Shell specialist Chris Lange identifies fermented saguaro juice as a plausible weak acid for this process. Most dated etched-shell examples belong to about 950 to 1150. The objects show chemical craft knowledge, while the exact liquid used on an individual piece remains a proposed reconstruction.

passages.title: What can be read, and what continues
passages.text: Casa Grande’s builders left no securely readable written language in the evidence presented by the National Park Service. Its written visitor history begins with Eusebio Kino in 1694, centuries later. There is no translated ancient sentence to show here; descendant communities’ oral histories and the archaeological record remain distinct sources of knowledge.

Large settlements and canal networks changed during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; this is not evidence that their people vanished. S’edav Va’aki’s museum describes movement into smaller villages after 1400 and identifies continuing Akimel O’odham descendants. The 1500 map endpoint supplies neither a conqueror nor a single cause for these changes.

sectionTitles: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom

passages.text: Holstein was a duchy south of the Eider, joined under the Danish king after a territorial settlement in 1773. Farms, the port towns of Kiel and Altona, a university and a new canal connected its inhabitants to a wider world. The imported record covers 1783 to 1878, but Holstein did not remain a separate duchy throughout that span: Prussia formally incorporated it in 1867 after the wars of 1864 and 1866.

passages.title: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom
passages.text: A ceremony at Kiel Castle on 16 November 1773 made a major territorial settlement tangible. The representative of the Gottorf side handed over a key, a piece of turf and a green twig to the Danish king’s representative. These objects stood for the territory being transferred. A diplomatic agreement could arrive with a small piece of lawn.

passages.title: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom
passages.text: Salons in Kiel and Altona became places to read, discuss ideas, drink tea or coffee and smoke. Their participants questioned old privileges and debated how society should work. This educated circle was only a small minority of the population, but its conversations helped spread the ideas behind agricultural reform.

passages.title: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom
passages.text: Writing sample: a December 1804 ordinance proclaimed, “Die Leibeigenschaft ist in Unsern Herzogtümern Schleswig und Holstein, von dem 1sten Januar 1805 an, gänzlich und auf immer abgeschafft,” meaning “Serfdom in our duchies Schleswig and Holstein is completely and forever abolished from 1 January 1805.” This German text follows the historical society’s transcription of the ordinance.

passages.title: A duchy, its people and a promise of freedom
passages.text: Personal freedom did not automatically provide land or a secure income. Former serfs could become wage laborers or face expensive rents, while landlords shed older obligations to support dependents. The reform changed legal status decisively, but many households still had to struggle for food, work and a place to live.

passages.title: Ships, horses and railway bridges
passages.text: The canal built from 1777 to 1784 joined Kiel’s Baltic inlet to the Eider river route toward the North Sea. Six locks helped ships negotiate changing water levels. Warehouses at Holtenau, Rendsburg and Tönning stored and transferred cargo. Holtenau’s surviving warehouse was built while the canal itself was still under construction.

passages.title: Ships, horses and railway bridges
passages.text: At Landwehr, the new canal cut across an existing road, so builders provided a Dutch-style drawbridge. A horse station stood nearby. Horses walking on the towpath pulled ships through the canal: part of a vessel’s journey could depend on legs moving along the bank rather than sails moving above the water.

passages.title: Ships, horses and railway bridges
passages.text: The Altona to Kiel railway crossed difficult ground, including marshes and hills. Its construction required 333 bridges and culverts, the passages carrying water beneath the track. Regular trains began running on 9 September 1844, before the official opening ceremony on 18 September. Grand celebrations and the working timetable were separate events.

passages.title: Studying medicine and fetching water
passages.text: Kiel’s university had been founded in 1665, long before this map record begins. Professors and students enjoyed special privileges, including their own legal jurisdiction and exemption from certain taxes. These arrangements lasted into the nineteenth century and ended under Prussian rule in 1867. Being a university member could change which authorities dealt with you.

passages.title: Studying medicine and fetching water
passages.text: In 1802 the university took over Georg Heinrich Weber’s private clinic. The resulting academic hospital linked treatment with teaching and research at patients’ bedsides. Medical students could learn from actual illness as well as lectures. The institution helped connect university study with the urgent practical needs of people who were sick.

passages.title: Studying medicine and fetching water
passages.text: Kiel’s older water pipes included hollowed tree trunks joined together. An 1821 bequest helped replace wooden pipes in Holstenstraße with iron ones. Most residents collected water in containers from public outlets; wealthier households could pay for private connections. Carrying the day’s water was a regular household task, not a turn of a kitchen tap.

passages.title: Studying medicine and fetching water
passages.text: Wells were not automatically a clean alternative. Kiel’s archive history describes pollution from nearby latrines and leaking waste. In a crowded town, the places where people disposed of waste and obtained drinking water could sit dangerously close together. Water supply and toilets were parts of the same public-health problem.

passages.title: Studying medicine and fetching water
passages.text: In 1862 the king transferred the Schreventeich pond to Kiel, and new waterworks followed in 1863. They supplied untreated, unfiltered surface water. Piped delivery was convenient, but the technology did not yet guarantee clean drinking water. Some residents continued to prefer water from street pumps.

passages.title: Life under a new government
passages.text: After annexation, Prussian officials celebrated at Kiel Castle on 24 January 1867 with bells and salutes. Many local people had instead hoped for their own duke, Friedrich VIII. The new three-year military-service requirement also mattered to families; the state archive exhibition records young men emigrating to escape it.

Following the wars of 1864 and 1866, a patent of 12 January 1867 incorporated Schleswig-Holstein into Prussia. New provincial and district institutions replaced the earlier administration. The map’s continuation to 1878 therefore includes years under Prussian rule, rather than eleven additional years of a separate Holstein duchy.

sectionTitles: What kind of empire was this?
Families, toys and work at home
Food, care and the toilet question
Wars, agreements and the final crown

passages.text: The Holy Roman Empire was a changing network of kingdoms, principalities, church lands and self-governing cities in central Europe. Otto I’s coronation in 962 is its conventional starting point, but it was never a single modern nation with one language or one fixed border. The emperor was chosen by electors and shared power with other rulers. From cathedrals and law books to dolls, houses and latrines, surviving objects show many different lives within it.

passages.title: What kind of empire was this?
passages.text: Otto I’s coronation in 962 is the usual beginning of this medieval imperial line. Its rulers drew on older Roman and Frankish ideas, but the empire was not ancient Rome reborn or the later German nation-state. Its territories and institutions changed repeatedly over more than eight centuries.

passages.title: What kind of empire was this?
passages.text: Emperors had to work with powerful princes, bishops, abbots and cities. The realm contained multiple languages and peoples; over time, Catholics and Protestants also shared its political space uneasily. Imagine a very long meeting with many people who each brought their own rulebook. That image is an analogy, not a literal imperial procedure.

passages.title: What kind of empire was this?
passages.text: Jewish people also lived within the empire, although laws tied their security to rulers’ protection and could leave them vulnerable. Surviving Jewish communal sites in Speyer, Worms and Mainz show schools, synagogues, cemeteries and ritual baths. These communities were makers of their own history, not merely subjects of emperors.

passages.title: Buildings and rules of power
passages.text: Bishop Bernward of Hildesheim, a tutor and adviser at the Ottonian court, commissioned great bronze church doors with scenes from the Bible. Surviving metalwork reveals technical skill and artistic choices by workshops, even when individual craftspeople are unnamed.

passages.title: Buildings and rules of power
passages.text: Conrad II founded Speyer Cathedral in 1030. Henry IV later had it rebuilt with ambitious stone vaulting, and several emperors and kings were buried there. UNESCO also records later damage and restoration, so every stone visible today need not be eleventh-century work.

passages.title: Buildings and rules of power
passages.text: Charles IV’s Golden Bull of 1356 set out how a select group of prince-electors would choose the Roman king. Frankfurt’s city archive preserves a copy issued in 1366, not the only copy or a document handwritten by Charles himself. Its golden seal gave the law its familiar name.

passages.title: Buildings and rules of power
passages.text: The Golden Bull begins one section in Latin: “Omne regnum in se ipsum divisum desolabitur,” meaning “Every kingdom divided against itself will be laid waste.” This is a short sample of the law’s written language in the Latin alphabet, taken from a scholarly transcription of the 1356 text. Latin was an official written language, not everyone’s home language.

passages.title: Buildings and rules of power
passages.text: The 1495 Imperial Diet began reforms that included new court and regional structures. By 1663 the Imperial Diet had become a continuing congress of envoys. An emperor still mattered, but decisions and laws moved through institutions rather than arriving as one ruler’s personal command.

passages.title: Learning, language and invention
passages.text: The ShUM Jewish communities of Speyer, Worms and Mainz maintained religious study and shared rules. At Speyer, archaeology preserves traces of a yeshiva, a school for Jewish learning, beside a women’s prayer area and an underground ritual bath. The surviving walls reveal a particular community’s institutions, not a universal imperial school system.

passages.title: Learning, language and invention
passages.text: Gutenberg’s Mainz workshop printed a 42-line Latin Bible in the mid-fifteenth century using movable metal type. A contemporary model book and a notarial record help document this work. Printing accelerated the spread of books from Mainz across Europe; it did not instantly teach everyone to read.

passages.title: Learning, language and invention
passages.text: Printed pages helped Martin Luther’s ideas travel in the sixteenth century. Religion then divided rulers and communities; the Peace of Augsburg in 1555 did not settle every dispute. Reading, arguing and distributing texts could have very large political consequences.

passages.title: Families, toys and work at home
passages.text: Nuremberg workshops made small clay “Kruseler” figures, dressed in the elaborate ruffled headdress fashionable around 1400. Their repeated mould-made forms are evidence of toy production, not proof that every child could afford one. A little doll could carry the latest fashion in a very small package.

passages.title: Families, toys and work at home
passages.text: Albrecht Dürer’s Nuremberg house was both a home and a workplace from 1509. Its household included his wife Agnes, his mother, pupils and apprentices. An artist’s family could include several generations and trainees under one roof, although this prominent city house was not a model for every family.

passages.title: Families, toys and work at home
passages.text: A preserved room in Nuremberg’s Fembo House dates to about 1600. The decorated hall served celebrations and guests; everyday living quarters were on another floor, with servants’ rooms above. Even inside one rich household, a visitor’s splendid view was different from where most daily work happened.

passages.title: Families, toys and work at home
passages.text: The Germanisches Nationalmuseum’s Stromer dollhouse, made in Nuremberg in 1639, has 15 rooms and more than 1,000 miniature things. The museum says such houses taught growing boys and girls about household and business management rather than serving as ordinary playthings. It represents an ideal wealthy home, not a measured copy of a real one.

passages.title: Food, care and the toilet question
passages.text: In a reconstructed seventeenth- or eighteenth-century Nuremberg merchant kitchen, museum historians show workers making butter, cheese, soap and candles, while smoking, pickling and salting food for storage. This is a rich urban household’s work, not the menu of every village or century of the empire.

passages.title: Food, care and the toilet question
passages.text: A surviving medieval toilet opening between houses on Nuremberg’s Obere Schmiedgasse shows people could use a shared space without private stalls. The city’s tourism account calls it a Köttelgang. Toilets have history too, and this local survivor should not be mistaken for an empire-wide plumbing plan.

passages.title: Food, care and the toilet question
passages.text: Nuremberg’s Hospital of the Holy Spirit was founded between 1332 and 1339 by the wealthy Konrad Gross to care for older and needy people. This is evidence for organized support in one imperial city. Its name and foundation alone do not tell us whether a particular medical treatment succeeded.

passages.title: Food, care and the toilet question
passages.text: A printed herbal called the Hortus Sanitatis recommended St John’s wort for wounds and other complaints. It shows how some late medieval readers described remedies; it is not a modern test of safety or effectiveness. Medical knowledge, religious hope and household care could sit beside one another.

passages.title: Wars, agreements and the final crown
passages.text: The Thirty Years’ War, from 1618 to 1648, spread through imperial lands and drew in foreign powers with their own aims. The 1648 Peace of Westphalia brought a new political settlement. Neither “everyone fought for exactly one religion” nor “peace repaired every ruined life at once” describes what the museum records.

passages.title: Wars, agreements and the final crown
passages.text: Francis II gave up the Holy Roman imperial crown on 6 August 1806, after powerful member rulers allied with Napoleon and the structure was breaking apart. He had already taken the title Emperor of Austria. There was no single battlefield on which the people of the empire disappeared; its former territories followed different political paths.

The Holy Roman Empire ended as a political institution when Francis II abdicated its crown on 6 August 1806 amid withdrawal by member rulers and pressure from Napoleonic France. No one new state inherited the entire empire. Communities and cultures continued in many successor states. The map’s imported 1000 to 1783 interval is a coarse geometry span, not the historical founding or end date.

passages.text: Honduras became a separate state after withdrawing from the Central American federation in 1838. The modern republic includes diverse Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities with histories extending across national boundaries. Universities, surviving houses and oral traditions offer evidence beyond presidential politics.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: Honduras’s first state constitution in 1825 helped organize departments and other administrative divisions. The state separated from the federation in 1838. These dates concern political institutions, not the origin of all people living in the territory.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: Patriotic discussion meetings decreed in 1826 were intended for studying and debating laws with local and departmental authorities. Public education could involve civic conversation as well as school lessons. The decree shows an initiative, not proof that everyone participated.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: Women began entering the university in the 1920s, and the university exhibit records women graduating in pharmacy, medicine, law and engineering in subsequent decades. Access to professional education changed gradually and through struggle; it had not always been available on equal terms.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: The university’s historical collection includes microscopes, an ophthalmoscope set, a medical bag, a dental chair and extraction forceps. These are tangible witnesses to training and clinical work. They reveal tools used to examine and treat bodies, not just names of famous doctors.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: Construction of the Suyapa university campus began in 1965. Photographs document classrooms and laboratories, and the institutional account describes expanded regional centers and distance education. Extending higher education required facilities and ways to reach students beyond one central building.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and public life
passages.text: “La persona humana es el fin supremo de la sociedad y del Estado” means “The human person is the supreme purpose of society and the State.” This Spanish sentence opens Article 59 of the 1982 Constitution in the consulted consolidated text. It expresses a legal commitment.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: Villa Roy was designed by Augusto Bressanni and built with the work of master builder Samuel Salgado. Construction photographs document its foundations and rising walls in 1936. Such records show architecture being made, rather than only the polished mansion after completion.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: Julio Lozano Díaz and Laura Vijil made Villa Roy their home in 1940. Laura’s later bequest made it available for a national museum. This is the history of a wealthy household and a reused building, not a typical home for every Honduran family.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: Garifuna communities live in Honduras and neighboring countries after forced displacement from Saint Vincent in the eighteenth century. Their Arawakan language and cultural practices cross modern borders. A nation’s outline cannot contain the whole history of a people.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: Garifuna úragas are stories associated with wakes or large gatherings. Songs preserve knowledge about fishing, cassava cultivation and canoe-making. Learning can occur through listening and performance, alongside more formal kinds of instruction.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: Garifuna songs also include satire, with drums and dances that spectators can join. Elders sustain ceremonies and oral traditions. Participation connects generations, while migration and discrimination can make transmission harder; the traditions remain living practices.

passages.title: Homes, stories and continuity
passages.text: The Inter-American Commission documented the 28 June 2009 coup and serious human-rights violations that followed. Its investigators visited Honduras that August. This distinguishes a documented interruption of constitutional government from the ending of Honduras itself.

Honduras continues as a state despite changes and interruptions in government, including the 2009 coup. Its 1838 separation from the federation and the map’s 1878 coverage start mark different things. Neither date defines the lifespan of the country’s Indigenous or Garifuna communities.

sectionTitles: Political upheaval and a living voice

passages.text: Ho-Chunk homelands center on what is now Wisconsin and surrounding parts of the upper Midwest. The imported map is a broad regional outline, not a kingdom’s surveyed frontier, and its 1492 to 1500 interval is only map coverage. Today the Ho-Chunk Nation in Wisconsin and the Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska are distinct governments with a shared people’s history.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Ho-Chunk oral tradition describes an enduring relationship with the homeland. The Nation’s own account names Wisconsin, Minnesota, Iowa, Missouri and Illinois among its traditional lands. This community account gives a larger setting than the outline on this map and connects present generations with places important to their ancestors.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Gardens supplied corn, beans and other foods that could be dried for winter. The Milwaukee Public Museum describes storage in fiber bags and underground pits. A good harvest had to be followed by good storage: growing dinner was only the first half of keeping it available in January.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Dugout canoes helped people travel up the Fox and Wisconsin rivers on hunting journeys. The museum account describes leaving the canoes in a protected place when travelers continued overland. Boats, walking routes and knowledge of seasonal resources worked together across a landscape much larger than a single village.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Clans linked relatives and carried responsibilities. In the museum’s account, Ho-Chunk clan relatives helped provide children’s names; Thunderbird people had peacekeeping duties and Bear people had policing responsibilities. A family connection could therefore also tell someone what work they owed the wider community.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Black ash basket making could involve an entire family. The Museum of Wisconsin Art describes men preparing wood strips and carving handles, while women commonly dyed and wove the strips. Techniques and preferred colors passed between generations. Making the container began in the forest, well before anyone started weaving.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: Roadside basket stands connected Ho-Chunk households with travelers through Wisconsin. Museum researchers found sales records listing prices for different basket types. These were artworks and useful goods, but also family income that helped people remain together while outside policies repeatedly disrupted their lives.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: One surviving basket has a named maker: Alvina Foss, also known as Alvina Miner or Alvina Yellowthunder. The Smithsonian dates her Wisconsin Ho-Chunk basket to 1990 to 2000 and lists ash splints, wood and synthetic dyes. Its record preserves an individual artist within a much longer family tradition.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: The Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska’s language and culture program reported growing a garden with corn, beans, squash and a fourth companion, sunflower. Its 2021 account describes students and volunteers helping, with harvests shared at community gatherings and funerals. Gardening could feed people and create opportunities to work beside one another.

passages.title: Families, food and skilled work
passages.text: In fiscal 2025, the Ho-Chunk Nation’s agriculture department reported a produce-box pilot with 29 participants. Radishes from its fields also entered the Tribal Elder Food Box Program. These are recent examples of tribal farming linking growers, households and elders through an organized food supply.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: Jean Nicolet met Ho-Chunk people in 1634 during French efforts to build western trade relationships. The precise meeting place is disputed, and the written account was produced years later. The encounter belonged to a world of Indigenous alliances and choices that Europeans were trying to enter.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: Nineteenth-century United States policies repeatedly forced Ho-Chunk families westward through Iowa, Minnesota and South Dakota. Many returned to Wisconsin; others established a lasting home in Nebraska, where a reservation was created in 1865. The two present governments reflect this history of forced movement and persistence.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: Wisconsin families combined their own gardens with seasonal paid work picking crops such as strawberries, cherries and cranberries. They returned home between jobs to tend their food plots. The museum describes an economy built from several kinds of work, rather than a single job that stayed the same all year.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: HoChunk Renaissance in Nebraska rebuilt its teaching approach in 2003 around teams: a fluent speaker, an apprentice and a support worker. Classes reached settings from daycare to college. The apprentice could learn while helping teach, creating a path toward another generation of language teachers.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: The Ho-Chunk Nation’s official website greets visitors with “Hocąk Wazijacira Hižąkiišąną Hįįnį Karagiwiną”, translated there as “The Ho-Chunk Nation greets each and every one of you”. This is the Nation’s own modern written welcome, with its spelling preserved here.

passages.title: Political upheaval and a living voice
passages.text: The Wisconsin Ho-Chunk Nation describes separate executive, legislative and judicial branches, along with its General Council. Its courts include a Traditional Court as well as other judicial institutions. Modern self-government can therefore hold elected administration and community traditions within the same political system.

The map ends in 1500, but Ho-Chunk history continues through removal, return and institution building. The Ho-Chunk Nation and Winnebago Tribe of Nebraska remain separate sovereign governments. Families, artists, growers and language teachers continue to shape their communities.

passages.text: Hopewell names an archaeological tradition and far-reaching networks among Native American communities, especially famous for Ohio’s earthworks. It was not one tribe or empire. The Ohio florescence discussed here dates mainly to about 1 to 400 CE, roughly a thousand years before this imported map’s mistaken 1492 to 1500 interval. The outline must not be read as a Hopewell state existing in Columbus’s time.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and useful rubbish
passages.text: Away from the ceremonial centers, households lived in small, scattered settlements. Builders set wooden posts upright and filled the spaces with bark or mud-and-grass daub. Monumental gathering places and ordinary homes occupied different parts of the landscape.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and useful rubbish
passages.text: Excavated rubbish preserves seeds and nuts that reveal starchy and oily foods. Families stored harvests in pottery vessels. A discarded seed can tell an archaeologist more about dinner than the finest ceremonial ornament.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and useful rubbish
passages.text: Gardeners grew sunflower, squash, goosefoot, marshelder, maygrass and little barley. These crops belonged to a locally developed farming tradition long before corn and beans became important here. Some domesticated forms later disappeared, leaving archaeologists to study plants absent from today’s grocery shelves.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and useful rubbish
passages.text: Hunting, fishing and gathering remained central to food supplies alongside cultivation. Fields lay near family homes; researchers think people shifted cultivation when soils became exhausted. Raising food involved knowing both a planted plot and the surrounding woods and waterways.

passages.title: Engineering and patient observation
passages.text: Excavation at Hopeton found that builders stripped away topsoil before adding two or three layers of selected earth. Different wall sections used deliberate construction sequences. These were engineered monuments, assembled through many carefully organized loads of soil.

passages.title: Engineering and patient observation
passages.text: Burned logs in a Hopeton construction trench produced a radiocarbon date around 300 CE. Near a gateway, another excavation found a deep pit containing broken pottery and mica, interpreted as evidence of making ceremonial objects. Soil layers help connect particular activities to particular places.

passages.title: Engineering and patient observation
passages.text: At Seip and four comparable complexes, nineteenth-century surveyors recorded squares with sides approximately 1,080 feet long. The repeated dimensions suggest a shared unit of measure. Planning an enormous square meant getting the corners right long before satellite navigation existed.

passages.title: Engineering and patient observation
passages.text: Newark’s Octagon and its connected circle incorporate lunar alignments, including a moonrise along their connecting passage in the roughly 18.6-year cycle. Recognizing that pattern required observations extending well beyond a single season. The sky formed part of the monuments’ design.

passages.title: Beautiful materials and surviving messages
passages.text: At Seip, cloth survived between copper breastplates because copper salts helped preserve it. The park describes woven milkweed fibers dyed with curved and circular patterns. A material that normally decays can survive when the objects beside it create unusual preservation conditions.

passages.title: Beautiful materials and surviving messages
passages.text: Hopewell Mound Group yielded a mica hand, a copper bear paw and large ceremonial blades made from Yellowstone obsidian. Skilled makers transformed materials arriving through distant connections into striking shapes. Their presence documents networks; it does not make every owner a traveler to Yellowstone.

passages.title: Beautiful materials and surviving messages
passages.text: Lightning-whelk shells reached Ohio from coastal regions. Makers hollowed them into cups and used their inner columns for beads and pendants. Finds in ceremonial settings suggest special uses for these containers. One large shell could supply several quite different objects.

passages.title: Beautiful materials and surviving messages
passages.text: Writing: no readable Hopewell sentence can be supplied from the surviving evidence. The National Park Service reports no written records left by these communities. Their geometric monuments and symbolic objects communicate important ideas, but neither is a deciphered transcript of the language people spoke.

By about 400 CE, Ohio communities were using the major ceremonial centers less and depositing fewer distant materials there. The reasons remain debated. People and their descendants continued in the region as practices changed; an archaeological tradition’s transformation is not a population’s disappearance. The map’s 1500 endpoint is unrelated to this transition.

passages.text: Hopewell names a network of Indigenous communities and ceremonial traditions, rather than one kingdom. Ohio’s remarkable earthworks flourished especially around 1 to 400 CE. Families lived in small settlements, grew native seed crops and joined gatherings that required extraordinary planning. The broad map outline represents cultural connections, not a surveyed imperial border.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: Households in southern Ohio lived in small clusters of homes, with upright wooden posts and walls covered in bark or daub, a mixture including mud and grass. The enormous ceremonial enclosures were gathering places; everyday homes were scattered around the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: Gardens supplied sunflower, squash, goosefoot, marshelder, maygrass and little barley. These native crops belong to the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Corn and beans were not the foundation of the Ohio Hopewell menu: those crops became important in the region later.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: Hunting, fishing and gathering remained crucial alongside cultivation. Fields near family homes required clearing, planting and tending; the NPS suggests that growers shifted plots when soil became exhausted. Building a monument still depended on someone organizing supper.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: Flint bladelets were small, sharp tools for cutting, scraping and carving. They helped people process meat and skins and work other materials. Their modest size makes them easy to overlook beside giant mounds, but repeated household jobs depended on such portable equipment.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: At Seip, fragments of patterned cloth survived between copper breastplates because copper corrosion helped preserve the fibers. The NPS identifies milkweed fibers and dyed designs. Such rare scraps recover a little of the clothing and textile skill that usually decay underground.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and skilled hands
passages.text: Copper workers hammered, folded, drilled and rolled metal with stone and bone tools. Ceremonial ornaments included earspools, headdresses and small rattling pieces called tinklers. A polished ornament could bring both reflected firelight and a little sound to a gathering.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: Seip combined circles with a square whose sides measured about 329 meters. Similar dimensions at several neighboring complexes suggest shared measuring practices. Moving soil was only part of the achievement: builders had to agree where an enormous shape should go.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: Some Hopewell earthworks align with cycles of the Sun and Moon. Repeated observation across generations would have helped builders recognize those patterns. These carefully arranged landscapes joined engineering with ceremonial attention to the sky.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: Mica splits into thin, shining sheets. At Mound City, people shaped it into forms including a bird’s talon and a human hand. Large sheets came from distant sources such as the Blue Ridge Mountains, linking a fragile object to long journeys and relationships.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: Mound City’s Mound 13 contained a clay basin lined with mica sheets, with cremated remains and offerings above. The excavated arrangement shows a deliberate funerary setting. It also explains why a material valued for its gleam appears in a place of remembrance.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: Much copper in the Scioto earthworks came from the Lake Superior region. A copper falcon from Mound City survives in the park collection. Such objects connect distant mineral sources with local makers and ceremonies; the metal’s journey need not have been a single person’s trip.

passages.title: Earth, light and long connections
passages.text: No contemporary written passage survives here to quote and translate. “Hopewell” comes from a later landowner’s surname, not a known ancient self-name. Artifacts and landscapes preserve rich communication, but a carved bird or geometric enclosure cannot be read as an alphabetic sentence.

Around 400 CE, major earthwork ceremonies and the use of distant materials declined in Ohio. The reasons remain debated; descendants continued to occupy the region and cultivate food. This was a change in social practices, not the disappearance of the people, and the map’s 600 endpoint is not a conquest date.

passages.text: Hopi communities have longstanding homelands, farming traditions and distinct villages in northeastern Arizona. The living Hopi Tribe is a sovereign nation. This imported outline stretches much too far southwest, toward Baja California, to represent a reliable Hopi political boundary. Its 1500 to 1530 dates are map coverage, not the people’s beginning or ending; later observations below are dated as such.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: In a 2020 account, Hopi farmer Michael Kotutwa Johnson describes planting corn six to eighteen inches deep to reach moisture, with each clump three paces from the next. His dryland fields rely on rainfall rather than irrigation. Wide spacing and deep planting answer the particular challenges of his land.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: Johnson learned farming from his grandfather. He describes women selecting seed for the next planting and distributing the harvest, while men tend the fields. Seed saving joins practical judgment to family responsibility; next year’s field begins with decisions made over this year’s corn.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: Johnson describes December as a time to remain indoors and tell stories reinforcing Hopi traditions. Learning takes place through listening as well as working outdoors. His account connects the agricultural year with a season when children and adults share knowledge through words.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: Hopi legal scholar Pat Sekaquaptewa describes traditional clans organized through the mother’s line, with daughters and their families remaining in maternal homes. Female and male clan leaders held different responsibilities. Kinship was therefore part of housing and community organization, not simply a list of relatives.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: A 1995 account describes piki as extremely thin bread cooked from cornmeal, water and prepared plant ash. Skilled makers spread batter across a heated stone and lift it in delicate sheets. Bread can be so thin that its manufacture resembles handling paper, with considerably more heat.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: The same account describes piki stones passed from mothers to daughters and granddaughters. Preparing a stone involves shaping sandstone, polishing it and carefully conditioning its surface. A family kitchen object can carry both years of wear and generations of learned technique.

passages.title: Food, families and learning
passages.text: Children visiting a piki maker could receive a fresh roll, and the authors note that small children sometimes returned several times. The smell of cooking was clearly excellent advertising. Piki also figured in weddings, naming ceremonies and shared work meals in this account.

passages.title: Villages, artists and institutions
passages.text: Awatovi’s remains preserve the meeting of village and mission histories. Spaniards arrived in 1540, and a mission followed in 1629. Residents participated in the 1680 Pueblo Revolt; later religious and political divisions helped lead to the settlement’s destruction around 1700. The fate of one village was not the end of Hopi communities.

passages.title: Villages, artists and institutions
passages.text: A Smithsonian bowl collected in 1896 records artistic invention by Nampeyo, the Hopi-Tewa potter from Hano. She adapted a bird image from excavated Old Cunopavi pottery, adding a face and headdress in her own composition. Archaeological designs became resources for new artwork, rather than remaining only museum specimens.

passages.title: Villages, artists and institutions
passages.text: The Hopi Tribal Council established in 1936 represents the nation in dealings with other governments. Village representatives may be elected locally or appointed by a village leader. The structure reflects both cooperation between villages and the continuing importance of village-level authority.

passages.title: Living language and care
passages.text: Writing sample: “askwali” means “thank you” when spoken by a woman, as explained in a 2019 Northern Arizona University report about Hopi patients teaching visiting dental students. This is an attested modern Latin-script form of Hopi, not an inscription from the 1500s.

passages.title: Living language and care
passages.text: At the Hopi Health Care Center in Polacca, the same 2019 report describes dental students working in pairs, checking patients’ histories and gums before cleaning teeth. The partnership also took screenings and protective sealants into schools. Modern care involves local patients helping educate future clinicians.

passages.title: Living language and care
passages.text: The tribal education department explicitly aims to bring Hopi language and culture into schooling while using modern technology. Education therefore includes both maintaining inherited knowledge and preparing students to use contemporary tools. Language belongs in a living classroom as well as in an archive.

Hopi people continue as communities and as a sovereign tribal nation. Colonial missions, conflict and later federal policies changed political life, while villages, farming, language and institutions endured. The map’s 1530 cutoff marks neither conquest nor disappearance; the later examples here document continued creativity and self-government.

passages.text: Huanca, also written Wanka, refers to peoples of Peru’s central highlands. Research in the Mantaro region includes related but distinct Xauxa communities. The imported outline extends far north of this heartland and should not be read as an exact Huanca kingdom; 1492 to 1500 is only map coverage.

passages.title: Homes and working hands
passages.text: Tunanmarca preserves thousands of circular stone structures. A Ministry of Culture conservation report counted at least 4,280 across two residential sectors. The settlement belongs to the wider Huanca to Xauxa regional story; that count measures structures, not an exact number of families or inhabitants.

passages.title: Homes and working hands
passages.text: Mantaro researchers identified household compounds with one to six buildings around a central patio. The courtyard connected rooms and daily activities. Differences in masonry, compound size and objects help examine unequal household resources within these communities.

passages.title: Homes and working hands
passages.text: Local pottery continued to be made after Inca incorporation, even as imperial-style vessels entered households. Archaeologists interpret Wanka wares as the work of independent, part-time specialists. A new ruler did not immediately replace every familiar bowl in the kitchen.

passages.title: Homes and working hands
passages.text: Spindle whorls became more frequent in the excavated Inca-period material. These small weights helped spin wool into yarn, so they offer evidence of textile work. The change suggests intensified production, although an object count cannot tell us exactly how many hours each person worked.

passages.title: Food stores and imperial demands
passages.text: Rows of round and rectangular storehouses stood on Mantaro hillsides. Their placement encouraged airflow that helped keep stored foods cool, including tubers. Preserving a harvest required thought about the building and its setting, not just filling a room with potatoes.

passages.title: Food stores and imperial demands
passages.text: Local people supplied labor and goods to the Inca storage system. Accountants used knotted cords to record supplies, while leaders supervised the stores. These visible buildings advertised imperial resources, but who could obtain the food depended on political arrangements.

passages.title: Food stores and imperial demands
passages.text: In the Xauxa area, many earlier hilltop settlements were abandoned or reduced during Inca rule. People moved toward lower land better suited to maize farming. The change connected where families lived with the empire’s demands for agricultural production.

passages.title: Food stores and imperial demands
passages.text: Spanish visitors described festivities at Hatun Xauxa in 1533. Historian Manuel Perales argues that these gatherings need to be understood through Andean ceremonial competition and authority. They were more than a simple welcome party organized solely for arriving Europeans.

passages.title: Words, performance and continuity
passages.text: Accounts often reduce the conquest to a single Huanca alliance with the Spanish against the Incas. Perales challenges that picture of a uniform regional response. Different leaders and communities had their own interests, and later accounts shaped how those choices were remembered.

passages.title: Words, performance and continuity
passages.text: A short written example from modern Junín Quechua is “allawqa”, meaning “right”, as a direction. D’Altroy’s published glossary cites Cerrón-Palomino’s 1976 dictionary for this spelling. It is a documented later language sample, rather than a proposed preconquest inscription.

passages.title: Words, performance and continuity
passages.text: At Mito, the Huaconada brings masked dancers into the town during January’s first three days. Younger performers follow prescribed movements around elders, who have more freedom to improvise. Costumes and masks may pass from fathers to sons in this evolving regional tradition.

passages.title: Words, performance and continuity
passages.text: A recent Mito school project used local dance heritage to encourage children’s writing. Pupils joined workshops in mask carving, drawing, painting, sewing and weaving. Learning from community makers helped turn familiar cultural practices into subjects the children could describe and explain.

Inca expansion ended the independence of regional polities, and Spanish conquest brought another political transformation in the sixteenth century. Huanca identity and Quechua Wanka did not end with the map’s 1500 boundary. Contemporary language resources and community practices belong to a continuing, changing history.

passages.text: The Wari Empire grew from the Ayacucho highlands into a powerful network across much of Peru during the Middle Horizon, roughly 600 to 1000 CE. Its colonies, textiles and ceremonies linked diverse communities. “Huari” is another spelling. The imported 1279 endpoint extends well beyond the empire’s main period and must not be treated as its known fall date.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: Excavations at the Wari capital reveal white and red walls, sometimes with murals. The impressive stone-built city overlay earlier earthen buildings. These surviving surfaces help restore color to ruins that now look mainly like bare stone.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: Some sectors of the capital were organized around D-shaped temples. Their curved-and-straight plans provided recognizable ritual spaces within the city. Religious architecture was one way communities experienced imperial traditions close to where they lived.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: A surviving tunic dated 650 to 1000 CE consists of two woven panels joined while leaving a head opening. Cotton and camelid hair brought fibers from different environments into one garment. Its elaborate, labor-intensive quality makes it an elite example, rather than everyone’s daily outfit.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: Wari weavers created densely patterned textiles in small working sections; joins called lazy lines remain visible. Some pieces required more than one weaver. Cochineal insects supplied brilliant reds, turning tiny creatures into a major source of wardrobe drama.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: A Churunga Valley cache contained feathered panels rolled into ceramic jars. Blue and yellow macaw feathers came from rainforest birds far east of their desert burial place. Braided cords suggest attachment to a structure, but the panels’ exact use is unresolved.

passages.title: Cities, crafts and clothing
passages.text: Chemical analysis of potsherds shows that many Wari-style vessels were made from local clays in different regions. A shared decorative style could travel through ideas and skilled makers, without every cup being shipped from the capital.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: The pottery study sampled households, tombs and administrative centers. Some communities blended Wari imagery with local practice, while colonists elsewhere maintained their own production. Imperial life involved local choices, visible in the clay recipes of ordinary and ceremonial objects.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: At Cerro Baúl, brewery vessels retained traces of pepper-berry chicha, an alcoholic drink. The pottery was made with nearby clay. Researchers argue that locally available materials and drought-tolerant berries helped maintain production even when supply conditions changed.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: Brewing required practiced labor and timing. Experiments with Peruvian brewers helped researchers interpret the ancient work, while the excavated festival setting links drink-making to political hospitality. Invitations and shared meals could help renew relationships among leaders and their communities.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: An elite residential complex at Cerro Baúl had an entry courtyard with stone-faced benches and a recessed roofed structure. Excavators interpret it as a palace with space for official encounters. Seating and access could help organize who met whom and where.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: When Cerro Baúl was evacuated, some buildings were cleared while important spaces were ceremonially burned and serving vessels broken. The excavators interpret a planned closure involving a final round of feasting. Burnt architecture therefore does not automatically mean an enemy attack.

passages.title: Food, hospitality and information
passages.text: A loop-and-branch khipu from El Castillo at Huarmey preserves cords, attachments and colored wrappings as a recording device. Wari khipus remain largely undeciphered. This authentic object can be described, but no secure original-language sentence and translation can yet be extracted from it.

Wari imperial institutions fragmented around the end of the first millennium and early second millennium CE; local sequences differ. Damage and abandonment at the capital, and planned closure at Cerro Baúl, do not reveal one universal cause. Communities and artistic knowledge continued, later influencing Inca traditions. The map’s 1279 endpoint is not a supported empire-wide conquest date.
