passages.text: Teenek people speak a Mayan language and live especially in San Luis Potosí and Veracruz. Their history belongs to the diverse Huasteca region, whose inhabitants included several peoples. The 1492 to 1500 outline is a partial historical map label, not a single unified kingdom or the boundary of all living Teenek communities.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: At Las Flores, in present-day Tampico, one surviving mound measures about 36 metres across and 6 metres high. Excavators identified 26 successive floors inside it. Builders repeatedly enlarged and resurfaced a structure that now looks like one hill: archaeology can read its layers almost like pages.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: Las Flores builders protected earthen structures with lime coatings and crushed shell. INAH describes a thick shell layer treated with liquid lime and polished to help keep water out of the earth beneath. Coastal materials offered a practical answer to the problem of rain soaking a building.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: Tamohi stood beside the Tampaón River and occupied roughly 210 hectares. Its surroundings supported maize, beans, squash and chilli, as well as cotton. Food crops and useful fibres belonged to the same regional economy, while the river connected settlements and supplied a route through the landscape.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: Inside Tamohi’s painted altar, excavators found built benches and a central form with coloured decoration. The surviving figures have been interpreted as priests or gods. Visiting a ruined platform today can hide an important part of its original appearance: its surfaces once carried vivid painted scenes.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: The sandstone sculpture called the Huastec Adolescent is 145 centimetres tall and came from Tamohi. The museum notes carved teeth, pierced ears and nose, and a hand with a hole that may once have held a banner. Details of dress and display survive even when the original accessories do not.

passages.title: River towns, builders and artists
passages.text: A smaller figure appears on the Adolescent’s back, and designs cover his body. Scholars have proposed different divine identities, including a maize deity and Quetzalcoatl carrying the Sun. The scene should not be treated as a photograph of ordinary childcare; its meaning remains debated.

passages.title: Water, homes and shared meals
passages.text: At Tamtoc, channels and water-storage features were built around springs. Archaeologist Estela Martínez Mora connects these works with rituals concerning life and death. An offering near a spring included the sculpture now called the Scarred Woman. Water was both a daily resource and part of a sacred landscape.

passages.title: Water, homes and shared meals
passages.text: A Tamtoc residential complex excavated in 2015 had generous space and elaborate finishes. Martínez Mora suggests that it housed specialists who worked stone and shell during the town’s earlier urban period. A carefully finished house can reveal something about skilled work and social standing, alongside its rooms and walls.

passages.title: Water, homes and shared meals
passages.text: INPI describes Teenek families connected through mutual help. These networks include extended relatives, friends and ritual kin. Neighbours and family ties help organize work, while communal faena brings people together for tasks of shared interest.

passages.title: Water, homes and shared meals
passages.text: A modern gathering may include zacahuil: maize dough with meat and chilli, wrapped in banana or papatla leaves and baked. INPI records it at celebrations and market days. This is food made for sharing, rather than a tiny snack to slip into your pocket.

passages.title: Conquest, writing and continuing life
passages.text: Mexica rulers conquered parts of the Huasteca before Spanish invasion. During the sixteenth century, Spanish violence, encomiendas and cattle estates disrupted Indigenous communities. Land pressure continued after the initial fighting. These changes did not erase the people whose descendants still live in the region.

passages.title: Conquest, writing and continuing life
passages.text: “Nenek” means “Hello”. INALI prints this greeting in its western Tének phrase guide and credits Luis Flores Martínez and Esiquio Martínez Cruz for the text and recordings. It is a documented modern language sample from San Luis Potosí, written in Latin letters.

passages.title: Conquest, writing and continuing life
passages.text: In 2016, INALI presented a Tének edition of The Little Prince at the National Museum of Anthropology’s book fair. Language promoter Telésforo del Ángel Domínguez, from San Francisco in Chontla, Veracruz, spoke about reading literature in one’s own language. Contemporary publishing adds new books to a living language.

The map’s 1500 endpoint does not mark the disappearance of Teenek people. Communities in San Luis Potosí and Veracruz continue to speak their language, and modern publishing creates new reading opportunities. Ancient towns changed or were abandoned, while the history of their wider region continued.

sectionTitles: Art and institutions across political change

passages.text: The medieval Kingdom of Hungary connected monasteries, towns, farms and royal courts across a territory larger than modern Hungary. Surviving textiles, vessels, tiles and books reveal imported skills alongside local production. Ottoman expansion and rival claims to the crown divided political authority in the sixteenth century, while communities and institutions continued under different governments.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996, before the kingdom conventionally dated from 1000. Its churches were rebuilt repeatedly. The church begun in 1224 contains earlier remains, making the complex evidence of successive communities rather than one untouched medieval building.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Pannonhalma's red-marble Porta Speciosa leads into a cloister built in 1486. Later alterations changed doors and windows. Traces of an earlier cloister and refectory entrance show how prayer, movement and communal meals shaped the monastery's built environment.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A centaur-shaped bronze hand-washing vessel in the Hungarian National Museum was made at Hildesheim in the 1220s. Its arrival in Hungary may reflect court connections. The object demonstrates imported metalworking and elite washing practices, not a Hungarian invention of the form.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: The gilded-silver vessel from Beszterec, dated to the later eleventh century, carries a Greek inscription and animal ornament. Its partly reconstructed supports matter when reading its present appearance. Byzantine manufacture and religious use connected the kingdom with another artistic world.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Stephen and Gisela donated the textile now called the Coronation Mantle to the Szekesfehervar basilica in 1031. It began as a priestly vestment and later entered coronation ritual. A surviving object could acquire new political meaning long after its first use.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A STEPHANO REGE ET GISLA REGINA means ‘by King Stephen and Queen Gisela.’ These Latin words are embroidered in the dedication on the vestment donated in 1031 and later converted into Hungary’s coronation mantle. This is an earlier surviving inscription, not a new text made during the late-medieval map interval.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Late-fifteenth-century tiles from the Bothar workshop at Besztercebanya, now Banska Bystrica, include glazed images of saints. Unfinished and spoiled pieces survived as well. They reveal production behind the decorated stoves that changed domestic heating, rather than only finished luxury objects.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: A leather spectacle frame dated before 1470 was found behind an altar panel at Liptoszentandras, now Liptovsky Ondrej. It is direct evidence of an aid to sight. Its hiding place does not identify its wearer or establish how many people owned spectacles.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Fifteenth-century printed missals left blank spaces for initials and pictures to be painted by hand. Printing therefore worked alongside skilled manual decoration. The finished pages preserve cooperation between old and new methods of making books.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Matthias's Corvina library commissioned decorated manuscripts at Buda as well as obtaining Italian books. Study of the codex containing Pietro Ranzano's history of Hungary reassigned its production from Naples to Buda, showing why an Italian-looking style does not prove an Italian workshop.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: The library's surviving bindings and illumination help reconstruct an organised late-fifteenth-century workshop. High-ranking church patrons also ordered its books. These manuscripts record collaborative specialist labour and patronage, as well as the writings preserved on their pages.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The Nyirbator choir stalls name their Bathory patrons and the year 1511; another panel carries the maker's mark F. Marone. Inlaid cupboards display books and kitchen utensils. The furniture brings images of familiar possessions into an elaborate setting for worship.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The division of Hungary left several settings for skilled work. The museum documents mining and guild production in Royal Hungary, while Hutterite communities moving there and later to Transylvania practised tin-glazed pottery. Political boundaries did not halt the movement of craftspeople.

The defeat of 1526 and Ottoman occupation of Buda in 1541 unfolded in stages. Rival kingship, Ottoman conquest and the emergence of Transylvania divided the medieval kingdom. Habsburg rulers retained the Hungarian crown in Royal Hungary. Neither the earlier Hungary record’s 1492 endpoint nor the late-phase record’s 1530 endpoint marks the disappearance of Hungarian society.

sectionTitles: Homes and learning between the wars
Lives under dictatorship and through change

passages.text: This modern record spans regency, wartime persecution, communist rule and the 1989 to 1990 transition. Household objects and scientific work reveal experiences beyond government.

passages.title: Homes and learning between the wars
passages.text: The National Museum displays an Art Deco reading corner to evoke an interwar metropolitan apartment. Such interiors illustrate a particular educated urban milieu. They should not be mistaken for the housing available to every rural or working family.

passages.title: Homes and learning between the wars
passages.text: A 1928 honorary citizenship certificate for education minister Kunó Klebelsberg was set into an inlaid wooden cabinet. Pictures on the certificate celebrate his projects. Education could become a subject for ceremonial craftsmanship as well as classroom work.

passages.title: Homes and learning between the wars
passages.text: At Szeged, Albert Szent-Györgyi’s research connected ascorbic acid with vitamin C and identified paprika as a rich source. An ordinary food could supply material for careful laboratory experiments; the achievement depended on research, not a magical ingredient.

passages.title: Homes and learning between the wars
passages.text: Szent-Györgyi also studied biological oxidation: chemical processes through which living systems handle energy. His 1937 Nobel recognition placed work conducted in Hungary within an international scientific network, rather than making science the property of one nation.

passages.title: Lives under dictatorship and through change
passages.text: In 1944 Hungarian gendarmes, guided by German SS officials, deported hundreds of thousands of Jews. Most sent to Auschwitz were murdered. State history must include the families and communities targeted by persecution, not only public buildings and inventions.

passages.title: Lives under dictatorship and through change
passages.text: The museum preserves a hand from the Stalin statue toppled on 23 October 1956. A broken piece of bronze becomes evidence of political protest. It cannot on its own explain every participant’s hopes or the subsequent repression.

passages.title: Lives under dictatorship and through change
passages.text: A typewriter and family photograph help tell lawyer Miklós Hoffmann’s story. The photograph, dated around 1953, shows his daughter holding a goose during the family’s forced relocation. Ordinary possessions can carry the history of state coercion.

passages.title: Lives under dictatorship and through change
passages.text: A museum interior evokes a 1960s housing-estate home. It places furniture and domestic space beside the account of communist government. A reconstructed room illustrates a living arrangement; it is not a complete measure of everyone’s comfort or freedom.

passages.title: Lives under dictatorship and through change
passages.text: A piece of border wire represents the opening of Hungary’s Austrian frontier to East Germans in 1989. The political transition led to free elections in 1990. A modest fragment of infrastructure recalls a change with consequences beyond Hungary.

passages.title: Words, music and continuing institutions
passages.text: Magyarország független, demokratikus jogállam means “Hungary is an independent democratic state governed by the rule of law.” This Hungarian sentence is Article B(1) of the 2011 Fundamental Law. It states a constitutional principle, rather than proving how consistently that principle is fulfilled.

passages.title: Words, music and continuing institutions
passages.text: In the Táncház, or dance-house, teaching method, participants watch experienced dancers and learn by joining in to live music. Individual creativity remains part of learning. You do not have to begin as the best dancer in the room.

passages.title: Words, music and continuing institutions
passages.text: Dance-house events may also teach singing and handicrafts and explain ethnographic context. This documented safeguarding approach connects research with social participation. It is one way Hungarians pass on traditions, not a custom practiced identically by every household.

Hungary continues as a state. Communist rule ended, elections followed in 1990, and European Union accession came in 2004. These institutional transitions did not end its diverse communities and cultural practices.

sectionTitles: Family, guests and entertainment at court
A recorded greeting, and the missing Hunnic text

passages.text: The Hunnic Empire brought together people with different languages and ways of life in fifth-century Europe. Attila’s court received ambassadors, displayed fine craftsmanship and entertained guests with music. Beyond the court, archaeological research reveals communities adapting between farming and herding. Metal vessels, decorated weapons and scientific studies of ancient remains help recover lives missing from the written accounts. The imported map covers 400 to 500, but Hunnic power changed dramatically within that century; it was not one unchanging state lasting until 500.

passages.title: A powerful and diverse society
passages.text: Attila’s forces campaigned in Gaul in 451 and northern Italy in 452. Demands for tribute and territory made his regime a major pressure on Roman government.

passages.title: A powerful and diverse society
passages.text: A 2025 study found genetic links between some people of the European Hun period and earlier Xiongnu elites in Asia. It also found considerable diversity. This supports particular connections across Eurasia, not a claim that everyone called a Hun had one ancestry or one identity.

passages.title: A powerful and diverse society
passages.text: Priscus needed interpreters during his visit to Attila’s court in 449. He described people using Hunnic, Gothic and Latin, with Greek also spoken by some. Political power depended on people able to carry a message across languages.

passages.title: Food, farming and changing homes
passages.text: Scientists studied bones and teeth from five fifth-century cemeteries around the Roman frontier in Pannonia. Their chemical signatures showed varied diets and movement. These were mixed regional communities, not a sample that identifies every buried person as a Hun.

passages.title: Food, farming and changing homes
passages.text: Some individuals changed diet during their lifetimes, moving between patterns associated with farming and herding. The findings challenge a tidy division between settled Roman farmers and permanently wandering newcomers. A person’s way of making a living could change.

passages.title: Food, farming and changing homes
passages.text: Millet mattered in these diets. It tolerates dry conditions and grows quickly, making it useful to people balancing crops and animals. Ancient dinner leaves clues even when nobody saved the menu.

passages.title: Food, farming and changing homes
passages.text: Tree rings indicate severe dry summers during the 430s-450s. Researchers propose that drought strained farming and herding and contributed to conflict. Weather was one pressure among several, not an explanation for every raid.

passages.title: Family, guests and entertainment at court
passages.text: Priscus described Attila’s residence as carefully built from wood, with an ornamental enclosure. It was a substantial elite home, not simply a tent carried from one battlefield to another.

passages.title: Family, guests and entertainment at court
passages.text: In Kreka’s household, servants embroidered linen while she received the visitor’s gifts. Woolen mats covered the floor. This glimpse reveals skilled textile work and household hierarchy around one royal woman.

passages.title: Family, guests and entertainment at court
passages.text: At a banquet, guests received fine metal dishes while Attila used wooden tableware. Court ceremony even determined prestigious seating. The boss’s plain cup did not make the dinner informal.

passages.title: Family, guests and entertainment at court
passages.text: After dinner, performers sang about Attila’s victories by torchlight. Their songs made political memory part of an evening’s entertainment. We have the visitor’s description, not the lyrics or music.

passages.title: Craftsmanship and discoveries
passages.text: The Jakuszowice burial in southern Poland contained gold fittings for a symbolic bow, an iron sword and decorated horse equipment. The museum associates this early-fifth-century elite grave with Hunnic connections. A ceremonial bow signaled status; it was not an ordinary hunting bow left ready to shoot.

passages.title: Craftsmanship and discoveries
passages.text: Nearby settlement finds included Roman coins, glass beads and gaming pieces. The settlement belonged to the Przeworsk cultural tradition. These objects show connections around the elite burial, without turning every local resident into a Hun.

passages.title: Craftsmanship and discoveries
passages.text: Hunnic-type cauldrons often have raised decoration and distinctive knobs on their handles. Metalworkers cast sections and joined them; some surviving vessels have repairs. The conventional name describes an archaeological type, not a certificate naming the maker’s people.

passages.title: Craftsmanship and discoveries
passages.text: A cauldron fragment found near Ocsa in 2014 combined familiar raised bands with an unusual triangular pattern. Reporting it to a museum allowed researchers to study it. Even a broken piece can change the history of a craft.

passages.title: Craftsmanship and discoveries
passages.text: The Tortel cauldron was found damaged near a mound. Scholars debate the rituals surrounding such vessels, and many old discoveries lack secure excavation records. We cannot confidently label every cauldron as either a household cooking pot or a religious offering.

passages.title: Bathing and what remains unknown
passages.text: Priscus saw a bathhouse belonging to Onegesius, an important court figure. Stone had been brought from Pannonia to build it. This documents elite bathing, not a bathroom in every home.

passages.title: Bathing and what remains unknown
passages.text: The sources used here do not establish a typical household toilet, a general medical system or universal schooling. Court descriptions and grave goods leave large gaps. We can admire the practical knowledge behind textiles and metalwork without inventing a school timetable or a doctor’s handbook.

passages.title: A recorded greeting, and the missing Hunnic text
passages.text: Priscus records a man greeting him with “khaire,” meaning “hello,” in Greek. This small language sample comes from a conversation at the Hunnic court, preserved by a Greek writer. It is not a Hunnic greeting or an inscription made by Attila.

passages.title: A recorded greeting, and the missing Hunnic text
passages.text: No securely preserved Hunnic sentence is available to reproduce here. Linguistic arguments rely heavily on personal names recorded by outsiders. That evidence is too limited to supply a confident Hunnic phrasebook, and proposed language relationships remain debated.

Attila died in 453. Rivalry among his sons and defeat at Nedao around 454 broke Hunnic supremacy. Groups associated with the Huns continued afterward; by the 470s they were no longer a comparable power. The map’s 500 endpoint is not an extinction date.

sectionTitles: Craft, memory and the language returning to classrooms

passages.text: The Wendat, called Huron in many European records, built connected farming villages and a powerful confederacy in the Great Lakes region. Their descendants continue today. This map’s enormous outline across the Great Lakes and Quebec is not a reliable border of one Wendat state in 1500 to 1530. The history below distinguishes ancestral villages, the seventeenth-century confederacy and later communities.

passages.title: Living together and preparing food
passages.text: The Nation Wendat describes a longhouse as home to several families linked through one clan, making it a neighborhood within the village. Villages, sometimes enclosed by palisades, belonged to a larger network. Cooperation began at home, with relatives sharing space before leaders met across communities.

passages.title: Living together and preparing food
passages.text: Maize formed a major part of the Huron-Wendat diet, alongside other cultivated and gathered foods. Productive fields could yield surplus for exchange or for a disappointing harvest. Stored food was therefore both a household resource and a means of maintaining relationships beyond the village.

passages.title: Living together and preparing food
passages.text: Corn soup, often called sagamité, could be enriched with fish, meat or squash. Dried kernels were pounded into flour, and corn bread could be baked under hot ashes. The same crop entered several kinds of meal rather than arriving at every dinner in precisely the same form.

passages.title: Living together and preparing food
passages.text: Fishing involved nets, weirs and sometimes wooden spears fitted with barbed bone points. Whitefish, trout, sturgeon, pike and catfish appear in the historical account. Drying and smoking preserved much of the catch for later, turning a successful fishing trip into meals beyond that day.

passages.title: Living together and preparing food
passages.text: Historical descriptions of Wendat infant care include cradleboards padded with soft bulrush down and babies wrapped in furs. The plant supplied a light, warm cushioning material. Families used the properties of the surrounding landscape in caring for their youngest members as well as in feeding everyone else.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and changing alliances
passages.text: Some ancestral Wendat settlements contained shallow, keyhole-shaped pits interpreted as sweat lodges, inside or beside longhouses. Archaeologists suggest ritual, healing and social uses. This partly underground form largely disappears after about 1450, so it belongs to an earlier architectural history rather than every later village.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and changing alliances
passages.text: At the Mantle settlement, pottery resembling Oneida and Onondaga styles suggests that residents may have come from more than one community. Two European copper beads and an iron object also reveal distant connections. Objects can expose a village’s wider relationships even without a written list of its inhabitants.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and changing alliances
passages.text: French Jesuits and lay workers began building Sainte-Marie in 1639 as a mission headquarters in Wendat country. Its church, workshops and residences served the missionary project and people visiting it. The mission was a particular colonial community, whose aims and buildings should not stand in for all Wendat life.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and changing alliances
passages.text: The Wyandotte Nation explains that its later community joined survivors of the Tionontati, Attignawantan and Wenro following war in 1649 and 1650. These groups had distinct earlier identities. Their coming together helps explain why modern Wyandotte history is connected to the Wendat without simply being another name for the old confederacy.

passages.title: Craft, memory and the language returning to classrooms
passages.text: A tray from Quebec, dated to about 1860 and catalogued as Huron by the Metropolitan Museum, combines birchbark with moosehair. Those materials bring woodland resources into a carefully made decorative object. Its survival also places Wendat artistry centuries after the upheavals of the seventeenth century.

passages.title: Craft, memory and the language returning to classrooms
passages.text: Archivist François Vincent Kiowarini gathered dictionaries, phonetic transcriptions, petitions, maps and correspondence. His papers are preserved in the Wendat community archives. Keeping such documents gives later generations material to study their language and history through work done by community members themselves.

passages.title: Craft, memory and the language returning to classrooms
passages.text: At the modern Wahta’ school in Wendake, language teaching begins in kindergarten, and cultural activities include ash-basket making and beadwork. Children encounter that heritage alongside a wider school curriculum. Learning a language is not confined to deciphering an old page; it also happens between teachers and children today.

passages.title: Craft, memory and the language returning to classrooms
passages.text: Written language sample: Kwatatiah! The Nation Wendat’s language page glosses it in French as “Parlons!”, meaning “Let’s speak!” in English. This is a present-day community spelling used in language revitalization. It is offered as a modern written witness, not a recovered sentence from the year 1500.

Disease, warfare and famine shattered the old Wendat confederacy’s settlement network around 1649 and 1650. Survivors moved, joined other communities or rebuilt in new places, including near Quebec. Wendat people and related later nations endured. The map’s 1530 endpoint is neither this political upheaval nor the disappearance of a people.

sectionTitles: War, power and the costs of expansion
Remembering relatives and making new things

passages.text: Ibadan grew from an 1829 military settlement into a powerful Yoruba city-state led by warrior chiefs. The imported 1878 to 1914 interval continues beyond the start of British rule in 1893.

passages.title: War, power and the costs of expansion
passages.text: Ibadan’s nineteenth-century rulers were a military oligarchy: powerful chiefs, rather than an oba with an inherited royal position. The city attracted ambitious newcomers, but warfare also brought captives, destruction and insecurity to the surrounding country.

passages.title: War, power and the costs of expansion
passages.text: The early population included people from Ife, Oyo and Ijebu, living in different districts. Oyo leaders eventually prevailed. Ibadan’s army defeated forces from Ilorin at Osogbo around 1840, helping check their further advance and increasing the new city’s regional strength.

passages.title: War, power and the costs of expansion
passages.text: During the later wars, raiders threatened the farms that fed Ibadan. Samuel Johnson describes forts placed along vulnerable routes and hunters watching for attackers while cultivators worked. An army needed food, and protecting a farmer could matter as much as guarding a town gate.

passages.title: War, power and the costs of expansion
passages.text: The Kiriji settlement of 1886 did not instantly bring peace everywhere. Johnson describes further appeals, messengers and negotiations over the continuing Ibadan-Ilorin conflict. Ending a long war required agreements to be carried out in scattered camps, not simply a document signed in one place.

passages.title: Courtyards and family decisions
passages.text: A later architectural study describes the older compound model: rooms facing one or more courtyards, with covered verandas used for household work and cooking. These spaces put cooking, conversation and visiting close together. The researcher’s fieldwork was in the late 1960s, documenting a changing inheritance.

passages.title: Courtyards and family decisions
passages.text: In that compound model, the household head received visitors opposite the entrance, while guests, clients and more distant relatives often occupied rooms nearer the gate. The layout expressed social relationships. The study also emphasizes that only a few examples of this older form then survived.

passages.title: Courtyards and family decisions
passages.text: Anna Hinderer’s mission school began with a handful of children in 1853. Attendance depended on family choices: parents withdrew Adelotan and Abudu while she was away in 1854. School history therefore includes negotiations within households, not just the decisions of missionaries.

passages.title: Courtyards and family decisions
passages.text: Hinderer’s account describes stories, singing and a playgroup for the first pupils. When offered lessons while living at home, children wanted to continue coming. This is a particular mission classroom, remembered through its teacher’s letters, rather than a picture of every child’s education.

passages.title: Remembering relatives and making new things
passages.text: Nineteenth-century records describe relatives buried within household buildings and mourners gathering for music and meals. Such practices kept ancestors connected with family space. The arrival of church graveyards raised a serious question for converts: where would they belong after death?

passages.title: Remembering relatives and making new things
passages.text: Church burial created work for carpenters making coffins. Adeboye names James Okuseinde, Jacob Oja and F. L. Akiele among the early Christian craftsmen. Changes in religion could therefore reshape a workshop’s orders as well as the ceremonies held around a grave.

passages.title: Writing a city’s own history
passages.text: A small Yoruba writing sample is “Iwe Itan Ibadan”, meaning “History of Ibadan”, the title of Isaac Babalola Akinyele’s 1911 book as cited by historians. It grew from a public lecture requested by a local society. Residents were organizing, discussing and publishing their own past.

passages.title: Writing a city’s own history
passages.text: Ibadan’s later intellectual life included the university founded in 1948. Its first students began in buildings previously used as a military hospital; the chiefs and people provided land for a permanent site. A city associated with military power became an important place for medicine, science and learning.
British rule ended Ibadan’s independence in 1893. The map’s 1914 endpoint is a colonial cutoff. Families and institutions endured, and the city became a major educational center within Nigeria.

sectionTitles: Books, learning and a later written sample

passages.text: The map’s “Ibadites” label covers part of the central Maghreb in 1200 to 1279. It represents a religious and regional grouping, not the lifetime of one empire. The M’Zab oasis towns provide a concrete focus, while clearly dated later examples show communities adapting through colonial rule and beyond.

passages.title: Towns built around community life
passages.text: M’Zab’s fortified towns gather houses around a mosque whose minaret also served as a lookout. The mosque complex could hold grain and defensive supplies. Worship, shared reserves and protection therefore belonged to the same town center.

passages.title: Towns built around community life
passages.text: The compact houses form rings around that center. UNESCO describes a repeated basic house form that protects family privacy while fitting closely beside neighboring homes. The architecture makes room for both a household’s own space and life in a dense community.

passages.title: Towns built around community life
passages.text: In the water system described by architect Said Madani in 2022, paths between gardens become channels during floods. Openings admit water according to factors such as plot size, distance and palm trees. A walkway could have a second job when the water arrived.

passages.title: Water, gardens and practical engineering
passages.text: During field visits from 2006 to 2018, Boualem Remini studied Ghardaia’s floodwater capture. The muddy water carried fine particles useful to garden soils. Some also soaked underground or entered recharge wells, helping replenish a shallow water reserve after the flood had passed.

passages.title: Water, gardens and practical engineering
passages.text: Ghardaia’s underground galleries have air shafts, and their entrances can be shut when irrigation is complete or flooding threatens the palm grove. Remini describes earlier sliding stone closures and modern steel ones. Maintaining these moving parts mattered as much as digging the channels in the first place.

passages.title: Water, gardens and practical engineering
passages.text: Madani describes water controllers using mirrors or fire signals to communicate between diversion points. Their work combines knowledge of the weather with coordination on the ground. Good water sharing depends on people sending the right message, not just on a clever canal.

passages.title: Toilets and everyday adaptation
passages.text: A study based on 2019 interviews records both family dry toilets and shared facilities in Beni Isguen’s palm grove. These saved scarce water and collected material that residents used as fertilizer. The study documents a remembered and surviving practice, rather than an excavated toilet from 1200.

passages.title: Toilets and everyday adaptation
passages.text: The same researchers found that deep groundwater extraction and running water encouraged flush toilets during the twentieth century. Wastewater then created new problems where adequate sewerage was missing. Comfort at home and care for an oasis had to be worked out together.

passages.title: Toilets and everyday adaptation
passages.text: During the colonial period, Ibadi scholars traveled and exchanged ideas between M’Zab, Algiers, Tunis and Cairo. Jomier’s research traces reform debates from the 1920s to the 1950s. An oasis could be geographically remote while its readers remained connected to large cities.

passages.title: Books, learning and a later written sample
passages.text: Ibadi book collections can be as small as a few volumes in a family home or as large as an organized private library. Historian Paul Love’s work on North African collections records both surviving family libraries and books dispersed abroad. Preserving learning has often been household work.

passages.title: Books, learning and a later written sample
passages.text: A later Arabic example from the wider North African Ibadi tradition begins “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God”. Love transcribes it from folio 1b of Naples manuscript ARA 50, copied in 1762. The book came from Libya, so this is not evidence for a particular M’Zab classroom in 1200.

passages.title: Books, learning and a later written sample
passages.text: That manuscript leaves space for diagonal commentary around its main text. It also repeats the last word of one page at the beginning of the next, a device for keeping the sequence straight. Readers and copyists gave the book practical tools for study and navigation.

The label’s 1279 endpoint is a map cutoff, not the disappearance of Ibadi communities. France occupied M’Zab in 1882; Algeria became independent in 1962. These political changes transformed local life while the community continued.

sectionTitles: Learning, work and shared public life
Heat beneath the ground, and people above it

passages.text: The Iceland label begins in 1900, while the island was under the Danish crown. Home rule expanded in 1904, Iceland became a sovereign kingdom sharing Denmark’s monarch in 1918, and the republic was founded in 1944. Modern Iceland’s history combines fishing, public institutions and inventive uses of geothermal heat.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: The University of Iceland opened in 1911 by bringing together schools of theology, medicine and law, with an additional philosophy faculty. Its first academic year enrolled forty-five students, including one woman. An institution that would later grow much larger began with a very small student body.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: For its first twenty-nine years, the university occupied space in Parliament House. It moved into its own main building in 1940. Early students and professors therefore learned and taught in a building whose other job was running the country’s parliamentary business.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: At Siglufjörður, the Róaldsbrakki herring station dates from 1907. Its surviving rooms include accommodation for young women who came for seasonal processing work. The museum preserves the close relationship between earning a living, temporary housing and the summer fishing industry.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: On 24 October 1975, many Icelandic women stopped both paid work and household work for a day. Meetings and singing accompanied the protest. The Women’s History Archives preserves the event as a demonstration of how much ordinary society depended on women’s labor.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: Heated outdoor swimming pools are gathering places in Iceland, even in a cold climate. UNESCO’s account describes hot tubs as settings for informal debate and conversation. A discussion about the day’s news can happen while everyone is sitting comfortably in warm water.

passages.title: Learning, work and shared public life
passages.text: Swimming skills and pool customs pass between generations through family visits, lessons and school activities. The 2025 UNESCO decision notes the requirement for swimming lessons for children aged six to sixteen. Learning to swim is part of growing up within this public culture.

passages.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it
passages.text: Women in Reykjavík carried washing along the route called Laugavegur to the hot springs, using their natural heat for laundry. The work could involve a three-kilometer journey and heavy loads. Hot water was useful long before it arrived conveniently through a pipe at home.

passages.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it
passages.text: In 1930, a pipeline supplied geothermal water to public buildings near Reykjavík’s laundry springs. Later household district heating reduced the need to tend coal fires. Historian Odinn Melsted also shows that access spread unevenly and that easier heating did not make all the other housework disappear.

passages.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it
passages.text: When Eldfell erupted beside Heimaey’s town in January 1973, nearly all its residents were evacuated within six hours. A prepared civil-defense plan and the fishing fleet in port helped people reach the mainland. Boats normally used for earning a living became essential rescue transport.

passages.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it
passages.text: Crews sprayed seawater on the advancing lava during the Heimaey eruption. Cooling helped slow or divert some flows and reduce damage. The US Geological Survey stresses the special circumstances: a slow-moving flow, nearby seawater and good access for pumps and equipment.

passages.title: Heat beneath the ground, and people above it
passages.text: The 1944 republic ceremony at Þingvellir needed buses, repaired roads, tents and a stage for performances. Visitors endured wind and rain, and the proclamation was carried by radio. Creating a national celebration involved transport and shelter as well as speeches and flags.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Icelandic, article 1 of the 1944 constitution: “Ísland er lýðveldi með þingbundinni stjórn.” Translation: “Iceland is a republic with a parliamentary government.” This excerpt follows Alþingi’s official 2024 consolidated edition of the law that took effect on 17 June 1944.

Iceland continues as a republic. The 1944 change ended the shared monarchy with Denmark; it followed sovereignty in 1918 and earlier home rule. The map’s 1900 starting point therefore precedes both the sovereign kingdom and the republic.

passages.text: The Icelandic Commonwealth was a society of farms, chieftains and assemblies, without a resident king. Its Alþingi began in 930. The atlas shows only 1000-1200 of this longer history. Laws, farm buildings and books reveal both practical work and a strong tradition of preserving words.

passages.title: Law was something people heard
passages.text: The law speaker recited the laws over a three-year cycle and repeated the procedural rules each summer. Remembering and speaking clearly were important public skills. This was not the same as every household having a printed legal handbook.

passages.title: Law was something people heard
passages.text: Þingvellir's assembly heard announcements and legal business as well as speeches. Its present landscape should not be mistaken for a precisely preserved seating plan: even the exact site of the medieval Law Rock remains debated.

passages.title: Law was something people heard
passages.text: The assembly was also a gathering place for traders, workers and people looking for news or opportunities. It brought together more than official decision-makers. Political meetings could become important occasions in a dispersed rural society's social calendar.

passages.title: Law was something people heard
passages.text: Visitors built temporary booths with turf and stone walls, wooden frames and coverings. Most visible booth remains are from later centuries, built over older positions. An archaeological footprint may record several assemblies rather than one untouched Commonwealth camp.

passages.title: Farm rooms and changing landscapes
passages.text: The 1939 excavation at Stöng exposed a farmhouse with a hall and attached rooms, alongside evidence for a byre and smithy. Domestic life, livestock care and skilled repair occupied related spaces. The modern reconstructed farm is an interpretation based on excavation.

passages.title: Farm rooms and changing landscapes
passages.text: One attached room contained sunken vats and is commonly interpreted as a pantry; another with long trenches has been interpreted as a latrine. Those functional labels are archaeological interpretations, not signs left on medieval doors.

passages.title: Farm rooms and changing landscapes
passages.text: Stöng is often linked to Hekla's 1104 eruption, but environmental research shows continued activity in the wider valley for two centuries afterward. Volcanic ash can date layers; it does not justify saying that an entire region became empty on one day.

passages.title: Farm rooms and changing landscapes
passages.text: The environmental study examined nine soil profiles containing 92 volcanic-ash layers. Combining those layers with evidence of land use allows researchers to test older stories about sudden abandonment. Discoveries can revise a familiar heritage narrative.

passages.title: Books about rules and ideas
passages.text: The Alþingi decided in 1117 to have laws written down, and recording took place the following winter. The surviving Grágás tradition includes later copies and fragments. Beginning to write a law is not the same event as producing every surviving manuscript.

passages.title: Books about rules and ideas
passages.text: A mid 1200s Grágás fragment includes inheritance, support of dependents, property and Christian-law provisions. It later survived as reused book-cover material. Family obligations and practical disputes could be preserved on a sheet rescued from a very different job.

passages.title: Books about rules and ideas
passages.text: Manuscript AM 677 4to, made around 1200, contains Christian works translated from Latin into Icelandic. Its language and abbreviations help scholars study how early written Icelandic worked. Literature included translated teaching as well as the sagas now especially famous.

passages.title: Books about rules and ideas
passages.text: Hinn góði maður means “The good person.” It begins a passage quoted from AM 677 4to by the Árni Magnússon Institute in modernized spelling. This short Icelandic sample uses Latin letters; it should not be confused with a facsimile reproducing every medieval abbreviation.

Agreements in 1262-1264 brought Iceland under the Norwegian king and ended the Commonwealth's independent political arrangement. Farms, assemblies and Icelandic writing continued. The atlas's 1200 endpoint precedes this change and is not the date the Commonwealth fell.

sectionTitles: A town larger than its Roman past
Bath time, game time and writing

passages.text: The Idrisids were a dynasty of the western Maghreb, established when Idris I gained support at Walila, the former Roman city of Volubilis, in 788 to 789. Their state depended on local Amazigh communities and alliances. The map’s label “caliphate” and interval 800 to 1000 simplify a changing network of rulers, towns and territories.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: Walila did not begin with Idris I. Archaeologists distinguish earlier settlement from the enlarged town of the late eighth and ninth centuries. This matters because a Roman column reused in a medieval wall does not make the household living behind it Roman.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: In the Idrisid-period quarter outside Walila’s walls, new houses had several rooms, and older buildings were enlarged or divided. Some courtyards contained wells. One house had an entrance that turned before reaching the interior, interrupting a direct view in from the street.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: A furnace, ash pits and worked animal bones reveal craft activity in that quarter. Researchers interpret some of the bones as anvils used while making the serrated edges of sickles. The interpretation connects excavated workshop debris to agricultural tools, rather than to a royal treasure.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: Simple houses excavated inside the walls had beaten-earth floors and small grain silos suitable for household storage. The much larger stores in a separate elite complex suggest different scales of food management. Archaeology lets us compare homes without pretending that every family lived alike.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: A courtyard complex outside the walls had a kitchen, storage areas and an elaborate reception room. Its identification as a residence of Idris I or Idris II is a scholarly proposal, not a name written on the doorway.

passages.title: A town larger than its Roman past
passages.text: Fez grew from two early settlements on opposite sides of a river, associated with Andalusian and Kairouanese quarters. The early city developed between 789 and 808; the two parts were enclosed together under later Almoravid rulers. Today’s medina therefore contains several historical layers.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: Walila’s bathhouse, built in the late eighth or ninth century, included a cold pool and heated rooms. It places bathing within the material record of the early Islamic town. The building eventually ceased to function as a bath, so later finds require careful dating.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: Someone cut a small board into a step beside the bath’s cold pool: three rows of at least thirteen holes, about 34 by 10 centimetres overall. Waiting for a bath could apparently include a game. The holes survive; the players and their exact rules do not.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: Researchers compare the board with tab or sig games but do not claim a certain identification. Two bone dice from other buildings at Walila give additional evidence of play. They were not excavated with the bathhouse board, so we should not invent a complete boxed game.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: A silver coin of Idris II in the Jordan Ahli Bank catalogue carries علي, “Ali,” in Arabic. This is a short name, shown here in ordinary modern type from the catalogue transcription. Its presence invoked the dynasty’s descent from Ali; it is not evidence that every inhabitant could read.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: Coins were political messages as well as money. Idrisid silver named rulers and religious claims, giving contemporary evidence that can be compared with stories written centuries later. Their inscriptions also help identify mints and political connections.

passages.title: Bath time, game time and writing
passages.text: Burnt and collapsed deposits in Walila’s outer quarter contain locally made pots and coins of Muhammad ibn Idris, who ruled from 828 to 836. These finds date a change in occupation. The fire alone cannot identify an attacker or explain the ending of the entire dynasty.

During the tenth century, Idrisid rulers repeatedly faced Fatimid and Cordoban Umayyad intervention, with changing allegiances and periods of exile. Al-Hasan’s final attempt to return ended in defeat and death in 985. The dynasty’s political defeat did not remove the people, towns or religious memory associated with it.

passages.text: Awfāt, usually called Ifat, was a Muslim sultanate on the Ethiopian highland escarpment. Excavations distinguish its capital and royal cemetery from other towns, including Nora.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: Nora’s houses used stone and earth mortar, with niches in their walls. Pottery lay on earthen floors. Streets and open spaces connected the buildings.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: Unglazed pottery, imported beads and cowries survived at Nora. Iron rods may relate to currency described in medieval texts, but that identification remains a hypothesis.

passages.title: Homes, streets and possessions
passages.text: The 2008 excavations examined houses and two of Nora’s five mosques. The resulting volume studies pottery, glass, metal and animal remains together. A town’s history comes from ordinary discarded material as well as its largest buildings.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: Nora had a Great Mosque and four smaller neighbourhood mosques. Their distribution places religious buildings among residential areas. The large congregational building was only one part of the town’s religious landscape.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: The Great Mosque changed over time. Earlier stone columns were made from single pieces; a later phase used assembled column elements. Rebuilding altered how the roof was supported.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: In the small mosque labelled M2, one central column supported the prayer room. A courtyard lay to the south, while the prayer niche marked its northern side.

passages.title: Building and using mosques
passages.text: A worked stone object near M2 was interpreted as a basin for ritual washing. The interpretation connects an object with preparation for prayer, although its precise use is not directly recorded.

passages.title: Inscriptions and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Walasma tomb inscriptions preserve names, religious invocations and dates in the 1360s and 1370s. They provide evidence for the dynasty independent of later narrative histories.

passages.title: Inscriptions and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Nora’s occupation is dated broadly from the late thirteenth century to the first third of the sixteenth. That range describes a settlement, not a single ruler’s reign or an exact date when all its inhabitants left.

Awfāt probably lost its capital status after 1376. Later warfare brought Christian royal control over Ifat, while the Walasma dynasty continued elsewhere. Disagreements about rulers’ dates and continuing towns make a single universal “fall” date misleading.

sectionTitles: Riverside households in the wider region
A bird on wheels and changing towns
Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings

passages.text: Illyrian is an ancient label with changing meanings, applied to different peoples of the western Balkans. It does not describe one kingdom throughout this map’s 1500 to 400 BCE interval. The huge outline also includes northern Pannonian communities whose identity cannot simply be assumed Illyrian. Regional examples below include clearly marked later Hellenistic towns.

passages.title: Riverside households in the wider region
passages.text: At Donja Dolina on the Sava, Iron Age builders raised timber houses on strong oak piles. Platforms supported rooms, sometimes with porches, and walkways connected neighboring buildings. These northern communities offer a regional example of adapting a home to wet ground, not a standard house for every people called Illyrian.

passages.title: Riverside households in the wider region
passages.text: Donja Dolina’s archaeological finds include fishhooks, floats and net weights. Alongside fishing, residents grew cereals and legumes and kept domestic animals. Rivers, fields and herds supplied different parts of household food: dinner depended on several kinds of work.

passages.title: Riverside households in the wider region
passages.text: Pottery, metal tools and ornaments show craft production at Donja Dolina, whose position on the Sava supported exchange. The municipal archaeological history describes its early Iron Age growth into an important trading center. A riverside settlement connected people who lived well beyond walking distance.

passages.title: A bird on wheels and changing towns
passages.text: A burial mound at Glasinac yielded a remarkable small wagon in 1880. The Natural History Museum in Vienna dates it around 800 BCE. Its makers assembled bronze components around iron axles, putting considerable technical skill into an object much smaller than a real cart.

passages.title: A bird on wheels and changing towns
passages.text: The wagon carries a bird-shaped vessel with another bird forming its lid. Scholars interpret it as a ritual object, but its original story is not preserved. The object gives us a memorable image of religious imagination without supplying a readable explanation of the ceremony.

passages.title: A bird on wheels and changing towns
passages.text: At Dimal in present-day Albania, occupation began in the Iron Age, but the city flourished especially from the fourth to first centuries BCE. Its early urban core occupied a strongly fortified hilltop. This later city belongs to a different phase from most of the atlas’s earlier interval.

passages.title: A bird on wheels and changing towns
passages.text: Dimal expanded after Roman annexation in 205 BCE, adding a larger circuit of walls and public buildings. Conquest therefore did not produce the same immediate outcome everywhere. At this particular settlement, urban construction continued under the new political arrangement.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: Dimal’s excavators identified transport jars of types used for Italian wine, including Lamboglia 2 and Brindisi forms of the later second and early first centuries BCE. These containers suggest supplies arriving mainly from southern Italy. Pottery fragments can preserve the route of a drink long after the liquid has gone.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: Writing sample: locally produced Hellenistic roof tiles bear “ΔΙΜΑΛΛΙΤΑΝ,” meaning “of the people of Dimal.” Third-century BCE examples helped identify the ancient city. The wording is Greek, an attested public language in the region; it is not a deciphered sentence in an Illyrian language.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: At Rhizon, now Risan in Montenegro, researchers uncovered monumental buildings of the third century BCE. The complex had limestone floors, later replaced in one room with carefully selected pebbles. Excavators interpret the exceptional architecture as a palace, possibly associated with local kings; the ownership is an interpretation.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: The Rhizon buildings had broad entrances closed by wooden doors. Excavators recovered fragments of large door-knockers, and one doorway had molded decoration and half-columns. Even a doorway could announce that a visitor was entering an unusually grand building.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: At Bushati in Albania, a fourth-century BCE building stood at the end of a ceremonial approach and monumental stair. The excavators interpret it as a hall for communal religious or civic meals. It provides evidence for organized gatherings, although the report cannot give us the guests’ actual conversations or menu.

passages.title: Wine jars, public lettering and gatherings
passages.text: King Genthios issued bronze coins using types already familiar at Shkodra and Lissos. He allied with the Macedonian king Perseus and was defeated by Rome at Shkodra in 168 BCE. The numismatic study connects his minting with military expenses, showing how war could affect the money people encountered.

Roman expansion ended particular kingdoms and changed regional institutions over time. Genthios’s defeat in 168 BCE was one major event, not the disappearance of all western Balkan peoples. Dimal continued and later suffered destruction near the end of the first century BCE. The map’s 400 BCE endpoint is not a general cultural ending.

sectionTitles: A kingdom within a wider history

passages.text: Imbangala communities included the Kasanje kingdom, an important inland partner of Angola’s Atlantic trading towns. By the nineteenth century, independent merchants and local authorities shared power once concentrated at its royal market. This imported 1815 to 1878 outline lies east of the best-documented Kasanje center; the examples below explain related Imbangala history, not verified boundaries of one unified state.

passages.title: A kingdom within a wider history
passages.text: Kasanje had a much longer history than this map interval. Historian Joseph Miller places its development roughly between 1620 and 1912. The label Imbangala also has wider associations, so neither 1815 nor 1878 should be mistaken for the birth or disappearance of the people.

passages.title: A kingdom within a wider history
passages.text: As Kasanje’s central market lost its monopoly, clan leaders and other powerful people built followings through trade and distributions of goods. Authority could rest with several local patrons, rather than flow neatly down from a single king.

passages.title: A kingdom within a wider history
passages.text: Kasanje’s prosperity was entangled with enslavement. Captives were sent toward Luanda and across the Atlantic, while imported goods returned inland. Explaining the trade means remembering people separated from their homes, not merely adding up profitable cargoes.

passages.title: Trade, work and family networks
passages.text: Brazilian sugar-cane spirit, called jeribita, circulated as merchandise and diplomatic gifts. Enslaved Africans and their descendants produced it overseas; some captives sold through Kasanje therefore helped make the very commodity exchanged for other captives. The circuit was brutally unequal.

passages.title: Trade, work and family networks
passages.text: Portuguese officials sometimes portrayed Kasanje’s kings as drunken and unreliable to justify hostile policies. Curto found a revealing disagreement: Governor Miguel António de Mello blamed Portuguese-associated slave traders for disturbances. Colonial records themselves did not tell one consistent story.

passages.title: Trade, work and family networks
passages.text: Imbangala caravans later sought wax and rubber across a widening region. Younger entrepreneurs could build clients and wealth outside the authority of matrilineal family groups. A successful journey could change someone’s standing at home as well as fill a trading store.

passages.title: Trade, work and family networks
passages.text: Earlier evidence reveals practical trade beneath the headline cargoes. A critical edition of a 1755 to 1756 journey identifies hoe trading toward the upper Kwango as valuable information. Iron tools connected markets to the ordinary work of turning soil and growing food.

passages.title: A visit to Cassange in 1854
passages.text: Livingstone described traders’ houses built with wooden framework and mud, scattered across Cassange’s plateau. Manioc and maize grew nearby. This was a mixed commercial settlement: its buildings show one connected place, rather than a standard house for every Imbangala family.

passages.title: A visit to Cassange in 1854
passages.text: Behind those houses were kitchen gardens with potatoes, peas, cabbages, onions and tomatoes. The meal supplies make an inland trading town feel less abstract: someone still had to tend vegetables while merchants negotiated their deals.

passages.title: A visit to Cassange in 1854
passages.text: Ivory could be exchanged for bundles of cloth, beads, guns and powder. Livingstone compared inland and coastal prices. Carrying a valuable tusk was therefore also carrying purchasing power, although reaching the next market took labor and negotiation.

passages.title: A visit to Cassange in 1854
passages.text: A writing sample is “Illustrissimo Senhor”, meaning “Most illustrious sir.” Livingstone printed this Portuguese salutation from an Ambaca guide’s letters during his 1854 journey from Cassange. The guide even used gunpowder to make ink. This is trade-network correspondence, not an Imbangala-language quotation.

passages.title: Remembering rulers
passages.text: Kasanje’s king lists survived in multiple oral versions that historians compared with written records. Remembering a sequence of rulers was skilled historical work. Differences between versions can help researchers ask how political institutions preserved and reshaped memories.

The map ends in 1878, but Imbangala history does not. Kasanje experienced Portuguese occupation in the 1850s and renewed regional factional power in the 1860s. Miller follows the kingdom’s history to 1912. Its political structures changed over decades; local communities and historical memories continued.

sectionTitles: Opening the gate was a serious job
Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
A letter at the end of a reign

passages.text: Merina royal centres developed in Madagascar’s highlands, a landscape of palaces, ancestral places and cultivated land. This card follows that particular political tradition, rather than treating every Malagasy community as Merina.

passages.title: Opening the gate was a serious job
passages.text: Ambohimanga had fourteen gateways belonging to different phases of its defences. ICOMOS describes doors weighing as much as twelve tonnes and carefully controlled access. These entrances displayed royal status as well as regulating movement. Forgetting something outside could be inconvenient on a scale far beyond having to find your house key.

passages.title: Opening the gate was a serious job
passages.text: Inside the royal enclosure were two basins cut into rock, connected with the annual royal bathing ceremony. The surrounding spaces included royal burial places and an area for public pronouncements. Water here had ritual significance. These surviving basins are evidence for a particular court ceremony, not a picture of how every highland household washed.

passages.title: Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
passages.text: At Marorangotra, beside today’s Lake Mantasoa, researchers investigated heaps of slag, the waste left by making iron. They also found fragments of stone air pipes used in furnaces. The wider region was producing iron in the late nineteenth century, but the report does not establish when every deposit began. These are traces of skilled local production, not proof that ironworking arrived with European factories.

passages.title: Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
passages.text: A small excavation at Marorangotra also recovered pieces of a large cooking pot with a black graphite coating, alongside animal bones including zebu cattle. Such finds put ordinary equipment beside industrial waste. They do not reveal a complete workers’ menu: the bones are not automatically one meal, and the report leaves the deposits’ precise dates unresolved.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: In early nineteenth-century Antananarivo, school writing supplies could be scarce. One account describes smooth wooden boards rubbed with grease and dusted with ash. Pupils wrote with a wooden point, then wiped the marks away with a rag or finger. Reusable schoolwork did not require a battery, although keeping that board off your best clothes sounds sensible.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: Students helped produce Malagasy translations rather than simply copying their foreign teachers. They carried word lists home on slates and consulted relatives about suitable expressions. Families thus contributed knowledge to work that later appeared in books. The teacher might know the English word, while a child and their household knew better how to say it in Malagasy.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: The resulting work depended on people whose contributions were easily overlooked. An enslaved interpreter named Joseph helped missionary David Jones learn Malagasy. Larson’s research brings interpreters and pupils back into a history often told mainly through European missionaries’ names. Learning a language was a shared achievement, carried out within profoundly unequal relationships.

passages.title: A pattern beside the loom
passages.text: A Merina silk cloth in the British Museum, dated approximately 1875 to 1900, consists of two panels sewn together. Coloured stripes and floating threads create elaborate patterns. It belongs to a tradition of costly cloth associated with aristocratic dress and burial. Its arrival in the museum in 1969 is a collection date, not the date somebody wove it.

passages.title: A pattern beside the loom
passages.text: The museum describes nineteenth-century Merina weavers keeping designs on paper beside their looms. Extra thread controls helped them build bands of geometric decoration. That combination of a written plan and careful handwork makes the complexity easier to appreciate. The catalogue does not identify a secret meaning for every pattern, so a handsome zigzag need not become a mysterious code.

passages.title: Learning to care for patients
passages.text: The Antananarivo mission hospital opened in July 1865 as part of Andrew Davidson’s medical work. Malagasy students learned medicine, nursing and midwifery, and medical material was published in Malagasy. Two trainees, Andrianaly and Rajaonah, later studied in Edinburgh. Their careers show local learners becoming practitioners, rather than patients being the only Malagasy people in the story.

passages.title: Who did the work?
passages.text: The kingdom’s workshops made goods including glass and cannon, with Malagasy apprentices mastering new manufacturing techniques. But workers did not all choose their jobs. Fanompoana required unpaid labour for the state, and military conquest also enslaved people. Campbell’s history describes workers and soldiers fleeing harsh conditions. Achievements in production belong beside the experiences of the people required to produce them.

passages.title: A letter at the end of a reign
passages.text: The British Library catalogues copies of a letter dated 27 February 1897 in which General Gallieni ordered Queen Ranavalona III’s exile. The surviving catalogue gives a precise documentary trace of a political turning point. These are photocopies preserved in an archive, not an excavated object, and the catalogue description is different from reading the original letter itself.

French conquest in 1895 and annexation in 1896 ended the kingdom’s independence. Ranavalona III was forced into exile in February 1897, ending the monarchy. Merina communities continued under colonial rule. Neither the map’s change of label in 1878 nor its endpoint in 1914 dates this political ending.

sectionTitles: Art and institutions across political change

passages.text: The medieval Kingdom of Hungary connected monasteries, towns, farms and royal courts across a territory larger than modern Hungary. Surviving textiles, vessels, tiles and books reveal imported skills alongside local production. Ottoman expansion and rival claims to the crown divided political authority in the sixteenth century, while communities and institutions continued under different governments.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996, before the kingdom conventionally dated from 1000. Its churches were rebuilt repeatedly. The church begun in 1224 contains earlier remains, making the complex evidence of successive communities rather than one untouched medieval building.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Pannonhalma's red-marble Porta Speciosa leads into a cloister built in 1486. Later alterations changed doors and windows. Traces of an earlier cloister and refectory entrance show how prayer, movement and communal meals shaped the monastery's built environment.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A centaur-shaped bronze hand-washing vessel in the Hungarian National Museum was made at Hildesheim in the 1220s. Its arrival in Hungary may reflect court connections. The object demonstrates imported metalworking and elite washing practices, not a Hungarian invention of the form.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: The gilded-silver vessel from Beszterec, dated to the later eleventh century, carries a Greek inscription and animal ornament. Its partly reconstructed supports matter when reading its present appearance. Byzantine manufacture and religious use connected the kingdom with another artistic world.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Stephen and Gisela donated the textile now called the Coronation Mantle to the Szekesfehervar basilica in 1031. It began as a priestly vestment and later entered coronation ritual. A surviving object could acquire new political meaning long after its first use.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A STEPHANO REGE ET GISLA REGINA means ‘by King Stephen and Queen Gisela.’ These Latin words are embroidered in the dedication on the vestment donated in 1031 and later converted into Hungary’s coronation mantle. This is an earlier surviving inscription, not a new text made during the late-medieval map interval.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Late-fifteenth-century tiles from the Bothar workshop at Besztercebanya, now Banska Bystrica, include glazed images of saints. Unfinished and spoiled pieces survived as well. They reveal production behind the decorated stoves that changed domestic heating, rather than only finished luxury objects.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: A leather spectacle frame dated before 1470 was found behind an altar panel at Liptoszentandras, now Liptovsky Ondrej. It is direct evidence of an aid to sight. Its hiding place does not identify its wearer or establish how many people owned spectacles.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Fifteenth-century printed missals left blank spaces for initials and pictures to be painted by hand. Printing therefore worked alongside skilled manual decoration. The finished pages preserve cooperation between old and new methods of making books.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Matthias's Corvina library commissioned decorated manuscripts at Buda as well as obtaining Italian books. Study of the codex containing Pietro Ranzano's history of Hungary reassigned its production from Naples to Buda, showing why an Italian-looking style does not prove an Italian workshop.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: The library's surviving bindings and illumination help reconstruct an organised late-fifteenth-century workshop. High-ranking church patrons also ordered its books. These manuscripts record collaborative specialist labour and patronage, as well as the writings preserved on their pages.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The Nyirbator choir stalls name their Bathory patrons and the year 1511; another panel carries the maker's mark F. Marone. Inlaid cupboards display books and kitchen utensils. The furniture brings images of familiar possessions into an elaborate setting for worship.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The division of Hungary left several settings for skilled work. The museum documents mining and guild production in Royal Hungary, while Hutterite communities moving there and later to Transylvania practised tin-glazed pottery. Political boundaries did not halt the movement of craftspeople.

The defeat of 1526 and Ottoman occupation of Buda in 1541 unfolded in stages. Rival kingship, Ottoman conquest and the emergence of Transylvania divided the medieval kingdom. Habsburg rulers retained the Hungarian crown in Royal Hungary. Neither the earlier Hungary record’s 1492 endpoint nor the late-phase record’s 1530 endpoint marks the disappearance of Hungarian society.

passages.text: Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Road builders used bridges, stairs, paving and drainage suited to different terrain. The network linked centers of production, government and worship.

passages.title: Food and farming
passages.text: Communities built and maintained terraces that created level planting areas while resisting erosion. Water conduits also protected roads from damaging runoff.

passages.title: Water engineering
passages.text: Stone channels and storage facilities managed rainfall and snowmelt for resources shared among families.

passages.title: Storage
passages.text: Colcas were storehouses whose siting and construction kept supplies cool and dry. Their contents included potatoes, maize, quinoa, clothing and tools.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The road system moved goods including textiles, feathers, food and shell. It incorporated earlier routes and knowledge from Andean communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Andean languages and traditions continued under Spanish rule. Weavers combined established textile techniques and designs with new imagery.
Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532 and had him killed in 1533. Spanish conquest dismantled imperial government, while Andean peoples continued and adapted their traditions.
