passages.text: Inuit history spans many regional communities across the Arctic. Archaeologists use Thule for the material culture of their ancestors, whose eastward migrations helped shape life in Arctic Canada. This map’s 1492 to 1500 window is a short snapshot, not the lifespan of Inuit peoples.

passages.title: Homes and getting around
passages.text: In the Auyuittuq region, early Thule winter houses used stone, sod and whale bones. A low entrance led into a partly sunken interior. Whale ribs could support a roof covered with skins and sod: a large animal supplied building material as well as food.

passages.title: Homes and getting around
passages.text: Inside these houses, a rear platform provided sleeping space, with storage beneath. Side platforms held oil lamps and supported cooking and drying clothing. Keeping clothes dry was household work with consequences far beyond looking tidy.

passages.title: Homes and getting around
passages.text: Skin boats and sleds connected camps. Parks Canada describes kayaks, larger umiaqs and dog transport among the Thule technologies used around Auyuittuq. Different seasons changed which routes were open and which animals people sought.

passages.title: Homes and getting around
passages.text: Western communities developed their own solutions. Around the Beaufort Sea, driftwood provided logs for houses with raised living floors, lowered entrances and sod coverings. A useful building material could arrive on the coast without a nearby forest.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: Around the thirteenth century, Beaufort Sea communities developed net fishing and communal beluga hunts using kayaks. Such a hunt depended on several people coordinating their movements. The western history has its own pattern, rather than simply repeating Baffin Island’s story.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: Making fitted skin clothing required small, precise tools. The Memorial University account describes piercing holes with a bone awl, then sewing with a fine bone needle. A needle was much smaller than a harpoon, but both mattered to living in the Arctic.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: Thule finds include combs, needle cases and clothing fragments preserved in frozen deposits. These modest objects reveal grooming and repairs alongside hunting equipment. Archaeology can recover the work of maintaining a household, not only spectacular weapons.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: A published collection from Cape Walker includes a wooden doll and a miniature scraper or ulu made of baleen. These actual small objects bring children and play into the archaeological picture. Their exact games are harder to recover than the toys themselves.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: Parks Canada holds snow goggles dating to the mid-nineteenth century. Narrow eye slits reduced glare from snow and the risk of snow blindness. The specimen is later than this map snapshot, but records an ingenious protection that did not need glass lenses.

passages.title: Food, clothing and young learners
passages.text: At Many Caches in the western Arctic, carefully fitted limestone slabs form vaulted storage places. Research combines archaeology with Inuvialuit knowledge of hunting. Two dated caribou bones establish later use; they do not date every cache or prove the entire site began at once.

passages.title: Words that continue
passages.text: The modern Tusaalanga lesson writes “ᖁᔭᓐᓇᒦᒃ”, transliterated “Qujannamiik”, for “Thank you”. This is an attested Inuktut teaching sample. Other dialects use different expressions, so it should not be treated as the only Inuit way to give thanks.

passages.title: Words that continue
passages.text: The writing systems came much later than 1492. ITK’s history records nineteenth-century missionary publications in syllabics and later Inuit-led standardization. In 2019 it adopted a shared Roman-alphabet orthography while communities continued using syllabics and other regional systems.

There was no Inuit collapse in 1500. Inuit communities and languages continue, with their own organizations pursuing rights and self-determination. Colonial disruption and changing settlement patterns belong to the subsequent history; they do not turn a living people into an extinct civilization.

sectionTitles: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller

passages.text: This atlas record concerns the eighteenth-century Kingdom of Ireland, not medieval Gaelic kingdoms or today's Irish state. Its parliament and social institutions existed within a monarchy shared with Britain. The map continues the label to 1815, although the separate Irish parliament ended when the union took effect in 1801.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: The Irish Volunteers, formed in 1778, pressed for changes to restrictions on Irish commerce. In 1782 British ministers accepted major legislative changes. These developments concerned political and commercial power, not equal voting rights for every resident.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: The 1800 union legislation was debated and approved before it came into force on 1 January 1801. Keeping the law's passage and implementation separate helps explain why sources give both years.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: Marsh's Library opened under an Act of 1707 to give readers a place to study. Its first librarian, Élie Bouhéreau, was a Huguenot refugee from France. A Dublin institution preserved books and expertise carried across borders.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: By the mid 1760s, more than 1000 books had disappeared from Marsh's. Readers were then supervised at a table or locked into reading cages. The librarian's solution to book theft was considerably more dramatic than a reminder email.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Bartholomew Mosse founded Dublin's lying-in hospital in 1745 to provide maternity care and training. It moved to the present Rotunda site in 1757. These buildings document an organized response to childbirth needs, not proof that every mother could obtain safe care.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Plays, performances of Handel's music and lotteries raised money for the new maternity hospital. Entertainment and philanthropy were connected: an evening out could help pay for wards and equipment.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Lisburn's weavers brought cloth to the market house before a separate brown-linen market was built around 1750. Making cloth and finding buyers were linked stages of work. A successful textile industry still depended on many individual households and workers.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: The Royal Dublin Society, founded in 1731, offered premiums for tree planting from 1742. Awards were one way to encourage agricultural and economic experiments. They show what an institution promoted, not that every landowner followed its advice.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: The Society established its drawing school in 1750, teaching figure, landscape and ornamental work; architectural drawing followed in the 1760s. Art education could support useful design and building skills as well as pictures for display.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: In the early 1800s, Lisburn's market-house assembly room hosted dinners, dances, concerts and speakers. This example belongs after the 1801 union, within the atlas's later years. Changes in parliamentary government did not stop local social life.

passages.title: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller
passages.text: Jonathan Swift published the book usually called Gulliver's Travels in 1726. Its invented voyages let him criticize human behaviour and institutions. It is an achievement of imaginative writing, not evidence that tiny islanders or giant people actually existed.

passages.title: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller
passages.text: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World is part of the book's original English title. Here remote means far away. This short written sample comes from a specific 1726 work; it does not imply that English was everyone's home language in Ireland.

The separate Irish parliament ended under the union that took effect on 1 January 1801. Irish communities and institutions continued within the United Kingdom. The map's 1815 endpoint is a later coverage boundary, not the date Ireland lost its people or the year the parliamentary union began.

sectionTitles: A state, a name and public decisions
Electricity and the work of a home
Getting to school and playing together

passages.text: This is the modern Irish state, not a Kingdom of Ireland. Its constitutional development began before the first 1938 map snapshot: the Irish Free State dates to 1922, followed by the 1937 Constitution. Electricity, schooling, water supplies and community sport show how public changes reached ordinary households.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: The 1922 Constitution Committee left records of its work on the Irish Free State's institutions. Constitutions are written through discussion and choices, not simply discovered ready-made. This founding phase predates the atlas's 1938 beginning.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: The Republic of Ireland Act came into operation on 18 April 1949. The enactment and its commencement are different dates. This is a constitutional milestone in an already existing state, not the sudden appearance of Irish people or culture.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: Éire is ainm don Stát means “The name of the State is Éire.” It comes from Article 4 of the Constitution in the official online Irish text, which uses modern standardized spelling. Irish language and Latin script should not be confused with each other.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The Rural Electrification Scheme began in 1946; its first pole was erected at Kilsallaghan, County Dublin, on 5 November. Bringing power to scattered homes required surveying, poles, wires and crews. A switch on the wall was the visible end of a much larger job.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The 1957 ESB film More Power to the Farmer shows hand washing, butter churning and carrying water in buckets. Its demonstrations promoted electrical alternatives. This was a persuasive company film, so its scenes are evidence of an argument for change, not a neutral picture of every farm.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The film also shows customers asking about charges and deciding whether to sign up. A new machine could promise less work while still raising questions about cost. Household modernization depended on decisions as well as technology.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The 1961 census counted 301,774 farm dwellings; 237,904 obtained water from a well, fountain, pump or other source rather than a piped supply. These figures concern farm dwellings specifically. They show why fetching water remained a major practical issue.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: In that same farm-dwelling table, only 30,943 had use of a fixed bath and 31,500 a hot-water tap. A house with electrical light did not automatically have a modern bathroom. Different improvements reached families at different times.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: A 1967 Department of Education circular set out free post-primary education. Removing tuition costs changed the possibilities facing families, although educational access involves more than the price of lessons.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: The 1967-68 public accounts record free school transport from 1 April 1967. For a pupil living far from school, a practical way to get there mattered alongside classroom policy. A bus route could be part of an educational achievement.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: Hurling and camogie connect playing skills with clubs, families and local communities. UNESCO's 2018 description emphasizes learning through practice and coaching. It records a living tradition, not one frozen version played identically in every century.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: The same tradition depends on volunteers who coach, organize teams and help clubs operate. Social life includes the work surrounding a match, as well as the players on the field. The final score is only part of what a community makes together.

Ireland continues as a sovereign state. Constitutional milestones in 1922, 1937 and 1949 describe changes in its institutions, while membership of the European Communities began in 1973. Its people, languages, public institutions and everyday traditions continue to develop.

passages.text: Irlanda is this atlas's label for early medieval Ireland, here shown in 800-1000. It includes Gaelic kingdoms and monastic communities in a landscape increasingly connected with Scandinavian settlements. It is not the eighteenth-century Kingdom of Ireland or the modern Irish state. Books and excavated objects reveal overlapping cultural worlds.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: The eighth-century Ardagh Chalice combined silver with elaborate decorative work in other materials. Its many separately made elements had to be fitted together. An impressive church vessel was also the result of a highly organized craft process.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: Gold filigree, glass and enamel decorate the chalice. The names of apostles appear around its bowl. Ornament and writing worked together in a Christian ceremonial object, rather than serving as a guide to the drinking cups in ordinary homes.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: The chalice came to light in 1868 when a boy digging potatoes in Ardagh ringfort disturbed a flagstone. A smaller cup and four brooches were also found. A spectacular accidental discovery does not preserve every detail that a modern excavation would record.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: The Book of Kells was made around 800, but scholars cannot securely divide its production between Iona and Kells. The monasteries were connected. Its modern home in Dublin does not establish exactly where each medieval page was written.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: The book contains 340 parchment leaves made from calfskin. Specialists distinguish four major scribes and several artists. Writing, preparing pages and designing ornament were skilled tasks; “made by monks” leaves much of the actual work unexplained.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: Scientific study revised an attractive old story: the blue pigment probably did not come from expensive lapis lazuli. Indigo or woad provided blue. Testing the material can change the story told about an object's trade connections.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: Dublin excavations recovered more than 2,000 combs, including a small group identified as Scandinavian. Such personal objects reveal grooming and skilled manufacture; they are not merely decorations beside swords in a Viking display.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: Researchers examine the combs’ materials, manufacturing techniques and wear. Wear can help indicate how much an object was used before being discarded. A personal grooming tool carries evidence of both its maker’s skill and its owner’s repeated actions.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: The National Museum's Viking Ireland gallery uses excavated evidence to model a Dublin house. A reconstruction helps visitors imagine built space, but its finished appearance includes interpretation where wooden buildings no longer survive intact.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: The same exhibition brings together evidence for craftworking and trade. A town required people who made and repaired ordinary things as well as merchants. This urban example should not be projected unchanged onto every farm or monastery in Ireland.

passages.title: A writer and his cat
passages.text: Messe ocus Pangur Bán means “I and white Pangur.” These Old Irish words begin a ninth-century poem preserved in a manuscript on the European continent. They are evidence of Irish-language learning abroad, not an inscription excavated in an Irish house.

passages.title: A writer and his cat
passages.text: The poem compares a scholar's search for understanding with his cat's hunting. Its memorable pairing makes quiet study feel human. It describes one literary household, not proof that every Irish monastery kept a named cat.

The atlas changes this label at 1000, but Irish kingdoms, monasteries and Scandinavian-linked towns continued. The National Museum challenges the familiar tale that Clontarf in 1014 simply drove all Vikings out. Political change and cultural contact continued; neither date marks the disappearance of Ireland's people.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing alliance of Native nations whose heartlands include present-day New York. “Iroquois” is the imported map label. Its early outline extends far into New England and should not be mistaken for a precise boundary of the confederacy.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: Onondaga’s account of the Great Peace tells how the Peacemaker and Hiawatha helped bring formerly warring nations together. The longhouse became a political image: different nations could share responsibilities while retaining their own places within the alliance.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: At Onondaga, clan membership passes through mothers. People of the same clan in another Haudenosaunee nation are also treated as relatives. That connection could make a journey feel less like arriving among strangers and more like visiting extended family.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the spokesmen who represent their clans in council. They also have authority to remove a leader after warnings if he fails his responsibilities. Leadership is a relationship with the community, not simply a powerful man’s personal possession.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: The same account describes Clan Mothers naming babies and teaching younger and older people. Political responsibility, family life and education are closely connected. A child’s name belongs within a continuing community, with names available for later generations.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: A traditional Onondaga longhouse held related families of a clan. A newly married husband moved into his wife’s family longhouse. Aunts and grandparents helped raise children, so home life extended beyond the parents and children of one small household.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: At the Mohawk village of Garoga, archaeologists found thirteen longhouses within a palisade. Radiocarbon evidence places this settlement around 1550 to 1582. The remains give a particular village and period behind the general image of a Haudenosaunee longhouse.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: Garoga also yielded thousands of pottery fragments and 43 lumps of unfired clay, probably prepared for making vessels. Pots with carefully shaped collars and incised patterns served cooking and storage. An unfinished lump can reveal the workshop behind a finished bowl.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: Onondaga’s account of lacrosse describes handmade hickory sticks and teams formed by clans or by younger and older men. The game has ceremonial importance as well as athletic skill. Its meaning reaches beyond the score at the end.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: Wampum beads require cutting, rounding, smoothing and drilling shell. Speakers use the woven strings and belts to remember agreements and histories. The Onondaga Nation describes them as living records whose meaning is carried through knowledgeable people and repeated telling.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: An invitation to council could combine wampum with a notched wooden stick. Removing a notch each day counted down to the meeting. It was a calendar reminder with no battery to charge, carried together with the reason everyone needed to gather.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: A modern written Onondaga sample is “Oñgwehoñwe’”, translated by the Nation as “the Real People”. Its language page connects the term with songs and identity. This is today’s Latin-script presentation; wampum itself is not an alphabet spelling out these words.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: The 1779 American campaign burned villages and food supplies, causing displacement and hardship. Onondaga families later rebuilt in smaller houses while maintaining kinship and government. Their history continues beyond warfare and beyond the map’s 1783 endpoint.

War and dispossession greatly reduced Haudenosaunee lands, but the confederacy and its nations did not end in 1783. Member communities continue their governments, languages and ceremonies; Onondaga maintains its council and longhouse on part of its ancestral territory.

passages.text: Italy united as a kingdom in 1861 and made Rome part of the state in 1870. Many people still worked rural land or emigrated, and many could not read. Fascist rule from 1922 brought dictatorship, colonial war, antisemitic laws and World War II. Resistance and a 1946 popular referendum opened the republic, whose constitution protected rights and public health. Schooling, migration and appliances transformed family life, though homes and regions changed at different speeds. Italy continues; the imported map begins in 1878, after unification.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: The first Italian parliament met in 1861, and Rome was taken in 1870. The map’s 1878 beginning comes later than both events. “Italy” on a map does not mean every village immediately shared the same speech, schooling or comforts.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: In 1871 about 68.8% of people counted by Italian statistics could not read. That meant a posted law or newspaper was not useful to many families without someone to read it aloud. Education grew over generations rather than appearing overnight at unification.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Many Italians left poor rural areas for work abroad between unification and the postwar period. A departure could separate a family for years; later, migration from the south to northern factories reshaped households inside Italy too.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Fascists came to power in 1922, then dismantled political freedoms. Mussolini’s government invaded Ethiopia in 1935. The colonial war was part of the dictatorship’s history, not an achievement for the people attacked.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: In 1938 the Fascist state imposed antisemitic laws: Jewish teachers and pupils were driven from public schools, jobs were lost, and mixed marriages were banned. After German occupation began in 1943, Jews in Italy faced deportation and murder.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Italian partisans and other anti-fascists resisted the regime and Nazi occupation. In 1946 voters chose a republic after dictatorship and war. A government change did not erase bereavement or rebuild a home by itself.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: At unification most people could not read; by 1951, 90% of people aged six and older had at most primary school completion, according to ISTAT. Night and adult classes later helped people missed by childhood schooling. A child’s opportunities varied by place, class and gender.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: From 1960 to 1968 the broadcaster RAI taught basic literacy on television in “Non è mai troppo tardi,” or “It is never too late.” That is both a show title and a good family-life fact: a grandparent could become a student while sitting by the TV.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: After World War II, factories drew people from farms and southern regions to northern cities. By 1966 about 60% of families had a television and refrigerator, but only 32% had a washing machine. New appliances changed chores without making laundry vanish.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: The 1951 census asked separately whether a dwelling had piped drinking water, a latrine, a bath, electricity, gas and heat. Those were not automatic parts of a “home.” Later decades saw a marked rise in internal toilets and bathing facilities, with uneven regional progress.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: A bathroom statistic can hide a family’s daily puzzle: an inside toilet, running water and a warm shower are three different comforts. ISTAT tracks them separately, so one old house could have one but not the others.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: In 1946 women voted in the republic referendum and 21 women entered the constituent assembly. A mother or grandmother could now shape national law with a ballot, though work and family expectations still differed.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: The constitution, effective in 1948, says “La Repubblica tutela la salute come fondamentale diritto dell’individuo,” or “The Republic protects health as a fundamental right of the individual.” This is a short sample of written Italian from Article 32.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: In 1978 Italy created its public National Health Service, designed for universal access rather than care tied only to a particular job. It turned the constitution’s health principle into a wider system, though services still required funding and local organization.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: The 1978 mental-health reform shifted care away from the old asylum system and toward community-based approaches. Someone with a mental illness was a person to care for, not a life to hide away. Implementation and local conditions mattered.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italy was one of six countries that signed the 1957 Treaty of Rome establishing the European Economic Community. Trade and cooperation became part of the republic’s story, alongside the much smaller stories of homes and schools.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italian is the language of the constitutional line shown here, but some communities also maintain historical minority languages. The Italian state reports school and local efforts to keep those languages in use. One written sample cannot represent every voice.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italy continues as a republic. The 1861 kingdom, Fascist dictatorship and 1946 republican vote mark major state changes, but families, regional communities and languages carried their histories through them. The imported polygon does not certify each border or lived identity.

Italy continues as a republic chosen in 1946. The kingdom formed in 1861, while its people and regional communities have longer histories; Fascist rule and war did not end them. The map’s 1878 starting border is later than unification and is not a certificate of every border or language.

sectionTitles: An elephant helps with the weaving
Two dates on a piece of mail

passages.text: This 1878 to 1914 map entry concerns coastal trading settlements and the expansion of French rule in what became Côte d’Ivoire. The colony was formally created on 10 March 1893, after the map’s opening date. Its people belonged to different communities with their own histories; a colonial name and outline cannot turn them into one timeless culture.

passages.title: A port with many neighbours
passages.text: Grand-Bassam became the first colonial capital and an important port and trading centre. Its built landscape included a N’zima fishing village alongside districts assigned to administration, commerce and different populations. The town was both a place of everyday work and a physical expression of unequal colonial power.

passages.title: A port with many neighbours
passages.text: Galleries, verandas and gardens helped adapt buildings to the tropical setting. African, European and Middle Eastern residents brought different experiences to the town. UNESCO describes both coexistence and conflict: the surviving streets should not be mistaken for a postcard of everyone living on equal terms.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: Baule and neighbouring Guro weavers were known for indigo-and-white cotton cloth. On a narrow-band loom, heddle pulleys helped lift and separate threads so a shuttle could pass between them. This small moving part made repeated work easier, while the weaver supplied the skill and rhythm.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: One surviving Baule pulley has an elephant’s head. The museum dates it broadly from the nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century, so it cannot be assigned to a single map year. Carvers decorated tools used in public view: even a working loom could have a little elephant looking down.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: A Baule comb from central Côte d’Ivoire carries a rooster above its teeth. Made from ivory and metal and dated to the nineteenth or twentieth century, it shows the care given to personal objects. Its owner is unknown; we should not invent a hairstyle, wedding or family story for it.

passages.title: Markets before the colonial boundary
passages.text: Gold-working traditions long preceded French rule. An older Akan brass weight, dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century and attributed to Ghana or Côte d’Ivoire, belongs to a regional system for weighing gold. Such objects were cast by replacing a wax model with molten metal inside a mould.

passages.title: Markets before the colonial boundary
passages.text: The decree creating the colony did not itself establish peaceful control over every settlement. Historian Christophe Wondji’s study of Bingerville describes opposition from local Ebrié residents and an uprising in 1903. Building a new administrative centre meant taking decisions over places where people already lived.

passages.title: When disease interrupted the port
passages.text: A 1911 medical report described repeated yellow-fever outbreaks on the Ivory Coast between 1899 and 1905. It reported that steamers avoided the port for four months in 1903. Illness affected travel, commerce and livelihoods as well as the patients themselves; a harbour could be busy one season and isolated the next.

passages.title: When disease interrupted the port
passages.text: The report described a change toward drainage and mosquito-control measures, replacing earlier practices that included burning houses. This is evidence of changing public-health ideas at the time. It is not a complete account of every household’s sanitation, and it cannot tell us which toilets an ordinary family used.

passages.title: Two dates on a piece of mail
passages.text: A postcard caption describes loading mahogany onto the steamer Colonia at Grand-Bassam in September 1905. A message on its reverse is dated August 1906. These different dates distinguish the event represented from the later use of the card, an easy detail to miss when reading an old picture.

passages.title: Two dates on a piece of mail
passages.text: Another card carries “Embarquement des billes d’acajou”, meaning “Shipment of mahogany timber”. Its postmark reads 23 September 1907. This short French sample survives through the Smithsonian’s catalogue transcription. It records colonial printed language, not a greeting in one of the region’s African languages.

passages.title: Whose idea of a capital?
passages.text: Wondji’s research shows that colonial planners argued over the relationship between an administrative capital and a commercial port. Merchants and officials wanted towns to serve the collection and export of products. That helps explain the competition among Grand-Bassam, Bingerville and Abidjan, beyond simply comparing their buildings.

The 1914 map endpoint did not end French colonial rule. Côte d’Ivoire became independent on 7 August 1960. Grand-Bassam’s communities and crafts also continued beyond the colonial capital’s decline; political administration and the lives of a town do not share one ending date.

passages.text: This record follows independent Côte d’Ivoire, also called Ivory Coast in English, from 1960. Independence ended French sovereignty; it did not begin the histories of the many communities living within the new state.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: On 7 August 1960, the country gained independence from France. That same day, an American recognition letter went to Félix Houphouët-Boigny and the US consulate in Abidjan became an embassy: diplomatic paperwork provides a dated trail of the new republic entering international relations.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: Here is a short writing sample from Article 1 of the November 1960 constitution: “Union, Discipline, Travail.” In English, this French motto means “Unity, Discipline, Work.” The document also named French as the official language; this state text does not represent all the languages spoken at home.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: Peacekeeping was part of a difficult political recovery. The UN created UNOCI in 2004 to help implement a peace agreement. After the disputed 2010 presidential election, violence escalated when Laurent Gbagbo refused to leave office following the UN-certified victory of Alassane Ouattara; Ouattara was inaugurated in May 2011.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Attiéké begins as cassava rather than wheat. Producers grind the tubers, mix them with fermented cassava, turn the mixture into small grains and steam it. The cooled food can be packed in baskets lined with cassava leaves: a whole sequence of skilled work sits behind a seemingly simple plate.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: UNESCO’s account describes women preparing, preserving and selling attiéké, while men contribute to cultivation, harvesting, transport and grinding. Knowledge passes through watching, doing and spoken instruction within families. Learning to make dinner can also mean learning a business.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Attiéké connects ordinary meals with public occasions. It appears at home, in restaurants, at weddings and other gatherings. Its affordability helps explain its wide use, while production and sales provide income, especially for women.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Among Guro communities around Bouaflé and Zuénoula, a Zaouli performance joins several arts: a carved mask, woven costume, music, singing and fast-moving dance. The dancer is the most visible participant, but sculptors, textile workers and musicians help make the performance possible.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Zaouli is learned through people as well as objects. Experienced performers teach younger participants during lessons and performances, while festivals and dance competitions bring communities together. UNESCO’s account identifies seven mask types, each associated with a legend: a mask carries a story as well as a face.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: In UNICEF’s account of a 2018 Gonzagueville pilot, Adja, a mother of three, earned money collecting discarded plastic. Unpredictable prices sometimes left her storing sacks at home. Recycling therefore involved family income and working conditions, as well as getting rubbish out of streets.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: That pilot classroom used interlocking recycled-plastic bricks developed by the Colombian enterprise Conceptos Plasticos. The imported bricks were assembled in five days with a hammer, rather like an enormous construction toy. The report expected forty kindergarten pupils when term began; wider local production was still a future plan.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: In 2024, UNICEF reported replacing worn-out hand-powered pumps in nineteen Bounkani villages, improving drinking-water access for roughly 7,600 people. A functioning pump is an unglamorous achievement with a very practical audience: everyone carrying the next bucket.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: School hygiene needs maintenance as much as construction. The same 2024 report describes training 148 school principals and supervisors in Bouna and Ferkessedougou. Activities covered handwashing, wastewater, rubbish and toilet upkeep. A toilet is only useful if someone keeps it usable.

The republic did not end with its civil conflicts. UNOCI closed on 30 June 2017 after completing its mandate, while state institutions and community life continued. The mission’s departure marks a change in international support, not the disappearance of Côte d’Ivoire.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
Home life, including the toilet question

passages.text: Jamaica’s history is full of skilled makers and memorable voices. A carved wooden spirit figure, a kitchen recovered from the sea and locally made clay pots offer different windows into the past. Maroon traditions, Miss Lou’s performances and reggae show people creating, preserving and sharing knowledge across generations.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: A Taíno wooden figure known as the Birdman was reported found in a Jamaican cave in 1792. Its beak and wings combine bird and human features, with surviving shell inlay. Scientific study places its wood around 1000 to 1150 CE. Carved from hard guaiacum, it preserves extraordinary woodworking skill, although its precise original ritual setting is unknown.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: In Port Royal’s submerged Building 4, archaeologists found iron cooking pots, copper pails, a wooden bucket, pewter spoons and ceramic bowls on a brick kitchen floor. These objects survived the city’s 1692 earthquake. Together they reveal equipment for preparing and serving food; they do not identify the cooks or tell us exactly what was on the menu.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: Excavations at New Street in Port Royal recovered fragments of locally made cooking and storage vessels from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. DAACS researchers compare clay, firing traces and shaping marks to distinguish different ways of making pottery. Enslaved Jamaicans produced and traded these wares: the objects record craft and exchange within a system that denied their makers freedom.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: A small handmade clay whistle also came from the New Street excavations. Researchers think it was probably made in eighteenth-century Jamaica by an enslaved person. Its maker and user remain unidentified. We can recognise an object designed to make sound without deciding that it was definitely a child’s toy or inventing the tune someone played.

passages.title: Home life, including the toilet question
passages.text: Late seventeenth-century Port Royal inventories describe parlors used for both entertaining and sleeping. Some beds could fold away during the day. A room might have to be ready for visitors after being somebody’s bedroom. These lists record possessions after property owners died, so they show particular households rather than how every Jamaican lived.

passages.title: Home life, including the toilet question
passages.text: One Port Royal parlor inventory includes a “close stoole chaire”: a toilet chair of a type that held a chamber pot beneath the seat. Furniture could have a surprisingly practical second job. The inventory records the chair, but says nothing about who emptied its pot. That missing task matters when imagining the household’s daily work.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: At Moore Town in eastern Jamaica, Maroon heritage includes the abeng, a horn blown through an opening in its side and used for communication over distance. Descendants of communities that escaped enslavement preserve this knowledge alongside their own institutions and communally held land. Passing on a tradition can mean learning how to listen as well as how to make a sound.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: Moore Town’s Kromanti ceremonies bring together singing, dancing and distinctive drumming to invoke ancestral spirits. They draw on African traditions reshaped within the Maroon community. These are religious practices with meaning for participants, not simply a stage performance. UNESCO also records missionary opposition and migration as pressures on their transmission.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: As a girl in early nineteenth-century Kingston, Mary Seacole learned to care for patients by watching her mother at work. Her mother ran a lodging house where army officers and their families also received care. Seacole later helped with patients herself. In this household, learning a caring profession began through observation and participation, before her better-known work overseas.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: Louise Bennett-Coverley, known as Miss Lou, welcomed children into stories, folk songs, dance and poetry through her television programme Ring Ding. She championed Jamaican Creole as a language worthy of performance and literature. Children could hear familiar speech celebrated in public and participate in cultural life themselves. Their voices belonged in the show.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: Reggae grew from Jamaican musical creativity, especially in Western Kingston, drawing on earlier local styles and sounds circulating around the Caribbean and beyond. Its songs could address injustice and resistance as well as love and spiritual life. Listening to music can therefore open a conversation about society, not just provide a beat for dancing.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: In a 2017 letter, Edna Manley College described courses exploring reggae’s history and development, alongside a folk collection assembled by Olive Lewin. The college’s arts schools had come together in 1976. Learning about music could involve both performing it and studying how earlier generations made it: instruments and archives both had a place.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962, with Alexander Bustamante as its first prime minister. Responsibility shifted from British colonial control to Jamaica’s elected government. The change concerned who governed the country; its people’s languages, family knowledge and cultural creativity had histories reaching far beyond that constitutional date.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1962. Jamaica continues as an independent country, while communities sustain and reshape their own cultural traditions. Political independence is a change in sovereignty, not the beginning or ending of the island’s people.

passages.text: The Jin dynasty briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but internal weakness and uprisings by the peoples of the north led to the loss of the north in 316. The Eastern Jin survived in the south as a center of Chinese culture.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion, the most admired piece of Chinese calligraphy, at a spring gathering of poets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting begins to emerge as an independent art form; Gu Kaizhi paints the Admonitions scroll.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Huiyuan founds a Buddhist community on Mount Lu; translation projects and monasteries multiply.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Faxian sets out for India to collect Buddhist texts, and returns by sea fifteen years later.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, of the Wei to Jin transition, exemplify literati withdrawal and philosophical debate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Eastern Jin preserved Chinese high culture in the south while the north underwent ethnic mixing.
The last Eastern Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, a powerful general who founded the Liu Song dynasty.

passages.text: Joseon ruled Korea for more than five centuries under a Neo-Confucian order. King Sejong's court gave the country its alphabet, Hangul, and a run of scientific instruments; the dynasty survived Japanese and Manchu invasions and lasted, as the Korean Empire after 1897, until Japan annexed it in 1910.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: King Sejong created Hangul, published in 1446 as the Hunminjeongeum, so that ordinary people could read and write.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The cheugugi rain gauge, a standard cylinder read against a ruler, was set up across the provinces, nearly two centuries before the first European rain gauge of 1639.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Jang Yeong-sil's self-striking water clock, the Jagyeongnu, and armillary spheres and sundials for the royal observatory.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Chiljeongsan calendar reform computed the motions of the sun, moon and planets for Seoul's own meridian.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Heo Jun's Donguibogam, a medical encyclopedia, was published.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: White porcelain, plain or painted in cobalt blue, became the ware of the scholar's table.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, a daily record of every reign from 1392 to 1863, among the longest continuous histories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became state orthodoxy; Buddhism lost its land and court standing.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations on the Confucian classics selected officials, and the yangban scholar class ran the state.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Admiral Yi Sun-sin's turtle ships and cannon fleets cut the Japanese supply lines during the invasions of 1592 to 1598.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Gunpowder weapons, from hwacha rocket carts to ship-borne cannon, were made at state arsenals.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Hangul is the writing system of both Koreas today.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucian family and social values shaped Korean life for centuries.
Joseon was proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897 under the same royal house. Japan made it a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910.

passages.text: The K’iche’ built a powerful highland Maya political center at Q’umarkaj, also called Utatlán, in present-day Guatemala. Temples and elite residences stood beside neighborhoods whose excavated homes reveal another side of the capital. The map’s 1492 to 1500 window is a coverage slice, not the kingdom’s lifetime, and its outline is approximate. Spanish conquest in 1524 ended the capital’s independence; K’iche’ communities remain living communities.

passages.title: A capital beyond its temples
passages.text: Q’umarkaj occupied a naturally defended headland surrounded by ravines roughly 80 to 100 meters deep. Building a city here meant fitting houses and paths onto a plateau with very real edges.

passages.title: A capital beyond its temples
passages.text: Babcock’s survey distinguished grand temples and palaces, another elite residential zone, and commoner housing. A ditch separated elite and non-elite areas. Differences in architecture made social rank visible in the city itself.

passages.title: A capital beyond its temples
passages.text: Several excavated non-elite households arranged buildings around a patio on leveled talpetate, a hardened volcanic deposit. Their layouts differed from raised elite platforms decorated with painted plaster.

passages.title: A capital beyond its temples
passages.text: The central complex included the temples of Tohil and Awilix and a ballcourt. These places help explain why the ruined capital remains meaningful as a ceremonial landscape to K’iche’ spiritual practitioners.

passages.title: Homes, heat and skilled hands
passages.text: A western residential platform had a basin-shaped clay fire pit, soot-darkened pots, obsidian blades and animal bones; a rubbish deposit lay outside. Archaeologists read this untidy combination as evidence of domestic life. Ancient housekeeping leaves excellent clues.

passages.title: Homes, heat and skilled hands
passages.text: Construction traces included adobe, river stone and daub bearing cane impressions. A neighboring platform was added later. Macario suggests that the changing entrances and crowded space could reflect a growing family expanding its home.

passages.title: Homes, heat and skilled hands
passages.text: Stone-tool debris and blade cores at nearby El Resguardo suggest specialized obsidian working. The researchers identified the volcanic glass used there and at Q’umarkaj with the San Martín Jilotepeque source, about 40 kilometers away.

passages.title: Homes, heat and skilled hands
passages.text: Some other excavated commoner houses lacked fixed hearths. Babcock suggests ceramic braziers may have provided cooking heat or warmth. A single recipe for how every family cooked would miss this variation between households.

passages.title: Words and knowledge that travel
passages.text: The Popol Vuh brings together K’iche’ creation accounts, origins and spiritual history. The surviving Newberry manuscript has K’iche’ in Latin letters beside a Spanish translation. Its early-eighteenth-century copying date must be distinguished from the older traditions it preserves.

passages.title: Words and knowledge that travel
passages.text: A short K’iche’ sample is “WARAL xchiqatz'ib'aj wi”, translated by Allen Christenson as “HERE we shall write”. It appears at the beginning of his scholarly transcription of the Popol Vuh. This is a colonial literary text represented in modern scholarly spelling, not an invented ancient inscription.

passages.title: Words and knowledge that travel
passages.text: Maize knowledge is still shared in kitchens and classrooms. At a 2025 Santa Cruz del Quiché workshop, 30 students and six teachers learned to prepare tamalitos de siete camisas, locally called Ub’en. This documents a living regional tradition without assigning today’s recipe an ancient date.

passages.title: Words and knowledge that travel
passages.text: In Nahualá in January 2026, a workshop helped 25 children practice K’iche’ names for domestic animals through games and learning activities. Language continuity includes the everyday words children use around home, as well as famous sacred books.

passages.title: Words and knowledge that travel
passages.text: In 2026, bound facsimiles of the Popol Vuh reached libraries in Quetzaltenango, Guatemala City, San Marcos and Santa Cruz del Quiché. Schoolchildren can consult reproductions while the fragile manuscript is protected. A copy can carry a very old story to a new reader.

Spanish forces conquered Q’umarkaj in 1524. That political ending does not mark the disappearance of the K’iche’ people: their language, community authorities and sacred practices continue. The imported map endpoint of 1500 precedes the conquest.

sectionTitles: A visit in 1864, after the conquest

passages.text: Kaarta was a Bamana kingdom in western Mali, governed by the Massassi dynasty and often competing with Ségou. Family alliances, farming and warfare helped build its power. The imported map begins in 1783, long after its origins, and shows an unusually broad outline; neither its borders nor its 1878 endpoint precisely describe the independent kingdom.

passages.title: A kingdom and its neighbors
passages.text: A foundation tradition remembers Massa as a successful farmer who married daughters to men willing to join his household and support him. This is a story about how followers and alliances were assembled, rather than a securely dated census of one enormous family.

passages.title: A kingdom and its neighbors
passages.text: Kaarta’s ruling clan kept close control over provincial governors and military commanders. Members and allies shared allegiance to its guardian spirit. Politics involved religious obligations and kinship as well as armed force; a ruler needed organized supporters, not merely a grand title.

passages.title: A kingdom and its neighbors
passages.text: The royal economy drew on tribute, trade tolls and warfare. Captives could be forced into armies or sold, while women were taken into ruling households. Remembering these people matters: royal expansion could mean the destruction of someone else’s home and freedom.

passages.title: Meals, water and skilled hands
passages.text: At Moonia, in territory controlled by Kaarta, Gray’s party received couscous, milk and honey. Their host also supplied fresh water and lodging. A traveler’s special welcome does not describe every family’s dinner, but it gives us an actual meal rather than an invented royal menu.

passages.title: Meals, water and skilled hands
passages.text: At Kirrijou, a Khasso town under Kaartan power, Gray recorded grain, rice, groundnuts, onions, livestock and dairy foods. He also complained about shallow wells beside stagnant water. Abundant farmland and reliable drinking water were separate problems for households to solve.

passages.title: Meals, water and skilled hands
passages.text: Near Asamangatary, Gray described women making earthenware on a plain also known for rice and onions. Pots required skilled hands as much as fields did. His account places this district at the beginning of what he called Kaarta proper.

passages.title: A visit in 1864, after the conquest
passages.text: At Kouroundingkoto in February 1864, Mage heard weaving looms working outdoors. Nearby plains had cotton fields, and women and children gathered around the visitors. This glimpse connects growing a fiber, making cloth and village social life in the same small landscape.

passages.title: A visit in 1864, after the conquest
passages.text: A local religious teacher gave Mage a young goat. It accompanied the expedition and repeatedly stole couscous from village women, to the delight of the traveling party. Apparently a nineteenth-century goat could also mistake everybody else’s dinner for its own invitation.

passages.title: A visit in 1864, after the conquest
passages.text: After Dindanco, Mage met traders bringing slabs of rock salt from Nioro. He described blocks roughly 60 centimeters long and 40 centimeters wide. Salt reached households through several stages of exchange: much more work than shaking a little onto dinner.

passages.title: Messages, language and political change
passages.text: Park reported that Kaarta’s ruler issued an Arabic proclamation on a thin wooden board during the 1796 war with Ségou. Elders then explained it aloud. Written messages and spoken explanation worked together; Park did not preserve the original Arabic wording.

passages.title: Messages, language and political change
passages.text: A modern Bambara sample is “I ni sogoma!”: “Good morning!” Stephanie Tolk records it in a 2021 account of her Peace Corps service in Mali from 1998 to 2000. This is an attested modern greeting, not a transcription of Kaarta’s lost proclamation.

passages.title: Messages, language and political change
passages.text: Umar Tal entered Nioro on 11 April 1855. His forces imposed a new Islamic political order, but conquest did not immediately end resistance. Kaarta remained important to later Umarian states, connecting western recruiting areas with territories farther east.

The independent Massassi kingdom fell to Umar Tal in 1855. The name Kaarta continued for the region and its Umarian successor administration; an imported map extending to 1878 must not suggest that the old dynasty still ruled throughout that interval.

sectionTitles: A royal pantry and the union’s last years

passages.text: The Kalmar Union linked the crowns of Denmark, Norway and Sweden from 1397, with long interruptions in common rule. Its usual endpoint is Sweden’s separation in 1523, not the atlas’s 1530 boundary. The map also colors all Greenland: that vast shape must not be read as uniform settlement or effective royal control.

passages.title: Three crowns and difficult politics
passages.text: Margaret built power through Denmark and Norway before Swedish nobles sought her help against King Albert. Her young relative Erik became the shared king in 1397. A ruler could be crowned while someone else still made the most important decisions.

passages.title: Three crowns and difficult politics
passages.text: The surviving union letter was written on paper, with corrections and only some expected seals. Historians debate its formal status. It proposed a common ruler and cooperation abroad while each kingdom retained its own laws: joining crowns did not erase legal differences.

passages.title: Three crowns and difficult politics
passages.text: Opposition to the union also divided people within Sweden. Powerful families supported different sides, and Engelbrekt’s revolt began in 1434. The story was more complicated than three whole populations always agreeing or disagreeing with one another.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: Kalmar had roughly 2,000 inhabitants around 1400, a substantial Swedish town then. Ships carried out iron, butter, cheese and skins and brought back salt, cloth, wine and spices. A harbour connected local kitchens and workshops to distant producers.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: The town’s merchants met and celebrated in two houses belonging to the Guild of St Christopher. North of town, a hospice cared for sick and elderly people. Commerce, social gatherings and organized care all occupied identifiable places around the medieval streets.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: Kalmar’s church school stood beside St Nicholas’s church. Its schoolmaster in 1430 was Niclis Thoreri, or Nils Thoresson. Boys preparing for trades and commerce learned reading and writing; some future clergy continued to Linköping and even Paris.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: Dominican friars helped people draw up purchases and wills as well as preaching. The local hospice charged elderly residents according to their means. These institutions supplied practical services alongside religion: paperwork and care were part of their daily work.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: Excavators in Kalmar’s old harbour in the 1930s recovered many medieval gloves and shoes. Oxygen-poor mud protected leather that normally decays. Lost and discarded belongings can reveal everyday clothing more directly than an impressive royal portrait.

passages.title: Ports, schoolbooks and ordinary possessions
passages.text: In Bergen, Hanseatic merchants traded northern Norwegian stockfish under privileges granted by the crown. Bryggen’s narrow plots joined homes, offices and storage. Its present wooden buildings largely follow rebuilding after 1702, but preserve a layout with medieval roots.

passages.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years
passages.text: King Hans sailed toward a political meeting at Kalmar in 1495, hoping to gain the Swedish crown. His flagship Gribshunden sank off Ronneby. Excavators recovered pepper, cloves, ginger and saffron: the ship carried ingredients suited to an unusually wealthy table.

passages.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years
passages.text: The wreck’s saffron remained red-orange and released its smell when researchers put it in water. The peppercorns had lost their aroma. Five centuries underwater had treated the contents of this royal spice cupboard very differently.

passages.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years
passages.text: A wooden barrel on Gribshunden held remains of a sturgeon about two meters long. DNA helped identify the Atlantic species. Researchers connect this prestigious food with the king’s intended display of wealth; it is evidence for an elite voyage, rather than everybody’s dinner.

passages.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years
passages.text: A preserved copy of Stockholm’s council letter of 28 March 1521 names “Góstaff Ericsson oc hans parti”: “Gustav Eriksson and his party.” The old Swedish spelling belongs to a warning about the rebel later known as Gustav Vasa, not to a modern invented medieval phrase.

passages.title: A royal pantry and the union’s last years
passages.text: Christian II’s coronation celebrations in 1520 were followed by executions of bishops, nobles and townspeople in Stockholm. The violence failed to secure lasting control. Gustav Vasa gathered support and was elected Sweden’s king in 1523, ending the three-crown union.

Sweden’s break in 1523 ended the Kalmar Union as a three-kingdom political arrangement. Denmark and Norway remained joined for centuries afterward. Communities, ports, languages and trade continued across the changed political boundaries.

passages.text: The Kamakura period brought Japan's first warrior government. The shogunate at Kamakura ruled beside the old court in Kyoto, the samurai became the ruling class, and new Buddhist schools, Zen among them, reached both warriors and common people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Eisai brought Rinzai Zen from Song China, and Dogen founded Soto Zen in 1227; meditation and discipline appealed to the warriors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Honen's Pure Land school, then Shinran's True Pure Land and Nichiren's Lotus school of 1253, offered salvation to ordinary people.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Warrior ideals of loyalty and service took shape, later codified as bushido.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Unkei and the Kei school carved lifelike portraits of monks and guardian figures with inlaid crystal eyes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Kamakura, a bronze Amida more than 11 meters high, was cast.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Emaki handscrolls told war tales and temple legends; ink painting arrived with the Zen monks.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Samurai held land as vassals of the shogun and lived by the sword and the bow.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The court in Kyoto kept its ceremonies and titles while Kamakura held the armies and the law.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Mongol invasion fleets were repelled in 1274 and 1281, the second wrecked by a typhoon later called the kamikaze.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Shoguns governed Japan for nearly 700 years, until 1868.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zen shaped Japanese gardens, tea, ink painting and the martial arts.
Forces loyal to Emperor Go-Daigo took Kamakura in 1333. Ashikaga Takauji turned on the emperor and set up a new shogunate in Kyoto in 1336, the start of the Muromachi period.

Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
War and the end of German rule

passages.text: Kamerun was a German colonial territory imposed on diverse African societies from 1884. The map shows its enlarged outline near the First World War; its 1914 to 1920 display interval does not mean German rule lasted until 1920.

passages.title: Land, work and communication
passages.text: The coastal agreement of 12 July 1884 preserved cultivated land and town sites for their existing owners and successors, and promised respect for local customs. Those clauses matter: people accepting an agreement had expectations about homes and authority that German colonial expansion would violate.

passages.title: Land, work and communication
passages.text: Rubber and cocoa connected Kamerun to European factories, but the work could be brutal. Concession companies used forced labor, while military expeditions destroyed villages and seized land for plantations. A chocolate bar or rubber comb had a much longer human story than its shop label revealed.

passages.title: Land, work and communication
passages.text: A British cable connected the colony to the international telegraph network in 1893. A separate German connection through Togo followed in 1913. A coastal message could now cross an ocean without waiting for a ship to deliver the words.

passages.title: A schoolboy becomes a defender of homes
passages.text: Rudolf Duala Manga Bell learned German at a government school and, beginning in 1891, spent five years studying in Germany. He succeeded his father as a Duala leader in 1908. His education later helped him address the colonial authorities and reach readers and politicians overseas.

passages.title: A schoolboy becomes a defender of homes
passages.text: From 1911 the authorities forced land seizures and relocation in Duala. Their plan separated African and European residential areas with a strip one kilometer wide. For families, colonial racism meant losing familiar homes and neighborhoods, not simply seeing a different flag above an office.

passages.title: A schoolboy becomes a defender of homes
passages.text: Manga Bell used petitions and allies in the German press and parliament. In March 1914, a petition helped persuade the Reichstag to withhold funds for the expropriations while examining complaints. The authorities then prosecuted him in an unfair trial and executed him on 8 August 1914.

passages.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
passages.text: At Foumban, King Ibrahim Njoya and his scribes developed the Bamum script beginning around 1896. Its early signs included animals, body parts, foods and household objects. They repeatedly revised the system; in 1910 it was reduced to about seventy signs. This was an African intellectual achievement within the colonial era.

passages.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
passages.text: Surviving works from the script’s 1906 to 1908 phase include letters between Njoya and his mother and an agricultural calendar. Writing served family conversations and the farming year as well as royal affairs. Even a king could receive a letter from his mother.

passages.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
passages.text: Learners recited the Bamum signs in a fixed sequence, with pairs that often rhymed or shared an opening consonant. That gave memory a pattern to hold onto. In 2006, researcher Charles Riley also found the healer Zakari Nkepu teaching with a brush-written chart at his workplace.

passages.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
passages.text: Here are the first four signs of the modern Bamum recitation sequence: ꚠ ꚡ ꚢ ꚣ, read “a, ka, u, ku.” They are syllables, like the beginning of an alphabet recital, rather than a sentence. These are standardized digital forms of the signs.

passages.title: Writing, family letters and learning in Bamum
passages.text: A small language sample is “Ŋga nsapŋam,” the Latin-transcribed title of a Bamum proverb collection attributed to Njoya and published in 1987. Riley identifies the volume as “Collection of Bamum Proverbs.” This is a modern printed witness to that literary tradition; the displayed letters transcribe Bamum rather than reproduce its distinctive script.

passages.title: War and the end of German rule
passages.text: The First World War campaign depended on African soldiers on both sides. Cameroonian recruits knew forest and mountain routes, built defenses and supplied local fighting skills. The fighting was not simply a contest between a few European officers: local knowledge helped determine where armies could move and survive.

passages.title: War and the end of German rule
passages.text: Recruitment and advancing troops drove civilians from their villages. Early in 1915, thousands of refugees gathered around Allied posts at Edea and Kribi; other people hid in the bush or ended up in plantation camps. The collapse of German control brought partition, not immediate independence for these communities.

German control ended in the 1914 to 1916 campaign, with resistance at Mora lasting into February 1916. British and French administrations divided the territory; Germany renounced its colonial rights in 1919, and League mandates followed in 1922. The imported 1920 endpoint marks neither independence nor the disappearance of Cameroon’s peoples.

passages.text: The Kañari, also written Cañari, are a living Indigenous people whose historical core lies in southern Ecuador, especially Cañar and Azuay. The imported outline extends far into northern Peru and should not be read as a verified single Kañari kingdom. Its 1492 to 1500 dates mark map coverage; this card centres on the Ecuadorian homeland and distinguishes earlier communities, Inca rule and later life.

passages.title: A landscape with several histories
passages.text: At Ingapirca, archaeologists found stone foundations of earlier oval houses, drainage channels and paved streets beneath the Inca buildings. These remains show that people already lived and organized space here before the imperial monument was erected.

passages.title: A landscape with several histories
passages.text: The famous oval stone platform surrounds a sacred rock and supports a small temple divided into two rooms. This finely worked architecture belongs to the Inca rebuilding of an older Cañari centre. A visit to Ingapirca crosses several chapters of history within a few steps.

passages.title: A landscape with several histories
passages.text: Pilaloma preserves evidence of an earlier collective burial marked by a standing stone. Fresco identifies it as pre-Inca. Later ceremonial buildings incorporated this older sacred place, making the site a record of both continuity and changes in authority.

passages.title: A landscape with several histories
passages.text: Broken large vessels at La Condamine and La Vaguada provide evidence of preparing, fermenting and storing chicha for ceremonial meals. These are traces of the later complex’s busy food preparation, not just its impressive stonework. Feeding a gathering required vessels as well as temples.

passages.title: A landscape with several histories
passages.text: Ingapirca forms part of the Qhapaq Ñan road network. Its position tied a local sacred place to wider imperial movement and administration. The INPC describes roughly four hectares of monumental remains, with an earlier Cañari settlement beneath the Inca complex.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: In present-day Ingapirca parish, older weavers continue using looms to make items such as ponchos, shawls, belts and woven cloth. The local government also records embroidery and sewing. Clothing involves skills passed between generations, as well as choices about what to wear.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: The parish describes rural practices of reciprocal work, including cambia manos and minka, alongside exchanges of produce. Families strengthen community ties by working together and helping one another. These are documented living practices, rather than a claim that every ancient household worked identically.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: During the living Mama Danza tradition, performers commonly arrange themselves in two lines with two leaders, often in front of a church. The INPC associates it with Corpus Christi and describes a mixture of Andean and Catholic influences. Community celebrations have histories of their own, including change.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: A modern Kichwa sample is “Alli puncha”, meaning “Good morning”. It appears beside Spanish Buenos días on page 37 of Luz Alvacora Chima’s 2020 learning guide for seventh-grade pupils at Sisid, near Ingapirca. This is contemporary educational writing, not a sentence recovered from an ancient Cañari inscription.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: The Sisid guide turns greetings into an activity: children label pictures, translate expressions and practise greeting each other. A separate municipal workshop in Cañar brought 45 learners together through online and classroom lessons with bilingual educator Andrés Quinde. Language learning happens through use as well as memorization.

passages.title: Work, celebrations and learning
passages.text: Ancient Cañari and modern Kichwa are different languages. Glottolog describes Cañari as an extinct language known mainly from place names. No securely attested ancient written sentence was identified in the checked evidence, so the modern Kichwa greeting is clearly labelled rather than presented as preconquest speech.

passages.title: Conquests, memory and continued life
passages.text: Inca conquest involved moving people far from their original communities. The INPC’s historical study discusses Cañari transfers toward Cusco and warns that the number displaced or killed is not known. Imperial rebuilding therefore came with profound changes to families and settlements, not simply a new architectural style.

passages.title: Conquests, memory and continued life
passages.text: Under Spanish rule, encomienda, forced labour demands and resettlement altered access to land and resources. Some Indigenous chiefs remained intermediaries, but in an unequal colonial system. The historical study names Diego de Sandoval in 1538 and Gonzalo Pizarro in 1540 among early encomenderos in Cañari territory.

passages.title: Conquests, memory and continued life
passages.text: Today’s Kañari identity is not confined to the ruins. CONAIE identifies Kañari among Ecuador’s living highland Kichwa peoples, with their own organization and self-definition. Ingapirca’s museum likewise connects archaeological remains with contemporary clothing, food and sound traditions.

Independent Cañari institutions were transformed by Inca conquest and then Spanish colonial rule. Those political losses did not end the people. Kañari communities continue in Ecuador, and the imported endpoint of 1500 is a map cutoff rather than an extinction date.

passages.text: Kanem, east of Lake Chad, was the earlier heartland of Sayfawa power. Its beginnings remain uncertain; excavated settlements illuminate elite buildings and working materials.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: At Tié Kalaté S2, discarded bricks lie in a depression where clay was extracted and fired. Nearby residences stood on dunes.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: Tié’s substantial enclosure is a candidate for Njimi, the royal capital. The identification remains argued rather than confirmed by a naming inscription.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: A study of excavated iron nails distinguishes four main forms used in twelfth- to fourteenth-century Kanem. These ordinary fasteners preserve metalworking choices that monumental buildings alone cannot show. Their precise use must be established from archaeological context.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: At Tié, glass dominates the recovered beads, alongside smaller numbers made from ostrich eggshell, metal and stone. Bone pendants and cowries also served as ornaments. This assemblage describes personal adornment at the excavated site, not everyone’s dress.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Many glass beads are tiny cylinders or rounded forms. Makers cut drawn glass and often reheated it to soften sharp edges. Red-brown and yellow shades were common in the recovered collection.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Chemical analysis links a few beads with the glass industry around Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria. Much of the remaining glass has affinities farther east. The results support African exchange connections, while the exact routes and intermediaries remain uncertain.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: The Arabic Diwan preserves a royal succession record. Historians compare its chronology with other texts and archaeological dates.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Saharan exchange included enslaved people, horses and cloth. The court’s connections rested partly on coercion as well as commerce.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Cairo was an important meeting point for pilgrims from Kanem and later Borno travelling toward Mecca. Dewière’s study treats pilgrimage as religious practice that also carried people, goods and ideas between African regions.
In the late fourteenth century, the Sayfawa court left Kanem for Borno under pressure from Bulala rivals. Kanem continued under other rulers while the dynasty rebuilt its power west of the lake.
