passages.text: Borno developed west of Lake Chad as a centre of Sayfawa government and scholarship. Its history includes scholarly communities, farming settlements and changing dynasties, as well as royal capitals.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: At Garumele, a settlement associated with Borno’s history, excavators found abundant fish remains together with sheep, goat and cattle bones. Oral traditions connect it with royalty, but its precise occupation dates and capital status remain debated.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: The range and quantity of fish at Garumele suggest specialist fishing. Researchers propose that some fish arrived already processed, while herders supplied livestock. These are interpretations of bone distributions, not proof of a known market organisation or preservation recipe.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Borno depended on agriculture. Many people combined farming with seasonal crafts or trade. Kyari Mohammed stresses the importance of regional commerce alongside Saharan routes, challenging a picture of an economy sustained only by distant caravans.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Some scholarly villages combined study with farming and enjoyed royal exemptions. Students advanced from Quran memorisation to Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu translation and interpretation. Education rested on organised communities as well as individual teachers.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: The Konduga Quran survives as loose leaves kept in a leather folder and satchel. Italian watermarks identify imported paper. Different hands added Arabic commentary and Old Kanembu glosses around the main text, preserving several readers’ work.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: A later copy of the Konduga manuscript’s final page preserved its annotations as well as its Quranic text. The copy used a different page layout. This unusual duplication protected a record of teaching, not only the main scriptural passage.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Owners patched the Konduga Quran with paper strips and stitches after moisture damaged its lower margins. Repeated repairs show care across generations. A surviving manuscript can record maintenance and reuse alongside the original scribe’s achievement.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Extensive written annotations became less common during nineteenth-century upheaval, but handwritten Qurans and oral translation continued. Bondarev proposes links with political and educational changes; he does not establish one decree that ended the practice.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Rabih’s administration demanded produce and other revenues through local authorities under military supervision. Mohammed’s research describes confiscation and punishment as tools of rule. These burdens make the occupation a history of households and livelihoods as well as battles.

Rabih conquered Borno in 1893. French forces and African allies defeated him in 1900; colonial partition followed. Royal institutions and regional communities continued under altered authority, while the independent state’s political order ended through successive conquests rather than a single timeless “fall.”

sectionTitles: Skilled work, from baskets to steel

passages.text: The Kanien’kehá:ka, or Mohawk, are a continuing nation within the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Their communities have distinct local histories. This imported outline broadly follows the Mohawk Valley and St. Lawrence region; it does not mark one fixed border or imply that the nation ended in 1500.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: Mohawk clan identity traditionally passes from mother to child. The nation’s three clans are Bear, Wolf and Turtle, although Akwesasne also includes people from other Haudenosaunee clans. These relationships link families to responsibilities that extend beyond a single household.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: At Otsungo, a Mohawk archaeological site not disturbed by plowing, a magnetometer detected buried hearths arranged in rows. Their pattern helped researchers identify longhouses even where wooden walls had vanished. The places people warmed themselves and cooked can outlast the house itself.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: The New York State Museum explains longhouse construction using sturdy posts, bent rafters and sheets of bark. Bark lashings tightened as they dried. Building depended on choosing the right trees and harvesting materials at suitable seasons: the forest supplied both walls and fasteners.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: The museum’s Mohawk Valley village reconstruction places corn, beans and squash fields near fortified homes. Archaeological interpretation joins buildings with the land needed to feed their occupants. A village was more than the houses inside its palisade; its food-growing landscape mattered too.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Akwesasne cornwashing baskets have a zigzag weave that helps remove the outer hulls from boiled corn during rinsing. Other baskets use an open weave to sift cornmeal, leaving large pieces for further grinding. A kitchen tool’s pattern can be beautiful and useful at the same time.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Black ash supplies strong, thin splints for basketry, but the trees face environmental threats. Akwesasne’s environmental task force collects seeds, records where they grew, dries them and stores them for planting. Protecting a craft can begin with caring for a tree decades before it becomes a basket.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: For more than a century, many Kahnawà:ke men worked as ironworkers, often in the United States. The community’s account links this work to language change, as English became increasingly useful. Journeys for work connected life in Kahnawà:ke with distant construction sites.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Kahnawà:ke also maintains its own hospital, schools, social services, police service and media. These institutions are part of contemporary Mohawk life. A history card that stops at longhouses would miss children going to school, patients receiving care and a community managing everyday needs.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: The 1784 Haldimand agreement provided land along the Grand River for Mohawk and other Six Nations people after losses during their British alliance in the American Revolution. Its provision extended six miles on each side of the river. This history belongs to particular relocated communities, not to every Mohawk family.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: Akwesasne now crosses the Canada to United States border and the boundaries of Ontario, Quebec and New York. It has related but distinct traditional and elected governing bodies. The border divides jurisdictions, while family ties and community identity continue across it.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: The Akwesasne Child Care Program greets families with “She:kon/Hello!” Its exact written Mohawk greeting means “Hello!” This is a contemporary language sample from a working community service, not an invented phrase assigned to the map’s 1492 date.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: Kahnawà:ke’s language and cultural center began its adult immersion programme in 2002. The two-year course combines instruction with practical exercises and activities outside class. Adults study so that Mohawk can take a fuller place in conversations, families and community life.

War, displacement and colonial policies changed Mohawk communities without ending the nation. Kahnawà:ke, Akwesasne and other communities continue their own political and cultural work. The 1500 map endpoint is a display interval, not an event in which Mohawk people disappeared.

passages.text: The Kansa, Kanza or Kaw are a distinct Dhegiha-speaking people whose river villages and hunting grounds made them influential across Kansas. Their descendants continue as the Kaw Nation. The imported Kansas-region outlines and their 1492 or 1530 start dates are approximate map coverage, not proof of fixed borders or settlements that early; the Nation’s history describes migration toward the Plains over several centuries.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: By the middle of the eighteenth century, Kanza influence extended across much of northern and eastern present-day Kansas, with hunting grounds farther west. The state’s name preserves theirs. River valleys supported settlements and movement, while relations with neighboring peoples shaped access to resources and trade.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: In the early nineteenth century, households at Fool Chief’s Village lived in bark-covered houses with a central fire and sleeping bunks around the walls. Four to eight large posts supported a lodge, and a roof opening let smoke escape. A blanket or hide served as the door.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The yearly schedule combined farming and travel. Families planted in spring, went on a summer bison hunt, returned for the autumn harvest and hunted again in winter. A village could look quiet because its residents were away doing another essential part of their work.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Bison hides also connected Kanza households to distant markets. The historical society describes readily available manufactured trade goods in their villages. Hunting supplied both household needs and things to exchange, so changes in demand could reach far beyond the place where a hide was prepared.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The flood of 1844 devastated gardens on the Kansas River bottomlands, where Kanza women raised corn, beans, melons and other vegetables. Water swept away crops, houses and fences; another flood followed in 1845. Food security depended on weather and river behavior as well as diplomacy.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Kaw Mission opened classes in 1851 in a two-story stone building at Council Grove. About thirty Kanza boys lived in four upstairs dormitory rooms and studied reading, writing, spelling and arithmetic. Missionaries also sought to teach Christianity and reshape family life; this was far more than a new school building.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Families were selective about that mission: the historical society reports that only orphaned or dependent boys attended, and girls did not. The school closed in 1854 because of its costs. Kanza children’s education cannot be reduced to this short-lived institution or its missionaries’ ambitions.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1825 treaty cut Kanza-controlled land to a narrow reservation west of the future city of Topeka. The Nation describes roughly twenty million acres reduced to about two million. Promised annual payments did not undo the loss of hunting territory or prevent further demands for land.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1846 treaty required another major cession and a move toward Council Grove. Its promises included education, farming support and money for a replacement mill. Federal delays in defining the new reservation left people struggling through relocation, while treaty language offered protections that did not last.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 1873, the United States forced the Kanza from Kansas to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. Congressional action in 1872 had authorized the disposal of their remaining Kansas lands. Distinguishing those two years matters: a law could order removal before families were actually compelled to leave.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Oklahoma did not bring a permanent end to displacement. Kaw Reservoir later covered land associated with Washunga. The tribal council house, residents and cemetery had to be relocated. Places holding government business, homes and family memory were all affected by the reservoir project.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Under Chairwoman Wanda Stone and the Executive Council, the Nation entered federal self-governance arrangements with the Indian Health Service in 1995 and the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1996. These arrangements gave tribal administrators more control over adapting funded services to community needs.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: A small modern writing sample is “Nompéaⁿhi.”, translated in the Kaw Nation’s family language workbook as “I’m hungry.” The raised n marks part of the spelling. It is a useful household sentence from a teaching publication, not a reconstructed inscription from the map’s earliest year.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The same workbook teaches that a fuller sentence can say whether someone is sitting, standing or moving. Learners practice matching these words to the person they mean. Kanza grammar can keep track of posture while an English speaker is still deciding whether to say “fine” or “tired”.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 2025, language students made a film about the forced removal, acting in Kaá’nze with guidance from elders including Little Carol Clark, Lynn Williams and Lavina Spotted Bear. Kaw filmmaker Dylan Bellmard directed it. Children were learning language while helping tell a difficult part of their own history.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The Nation also offers language lessons built around family camping. At its museum, an exhibition combines audio stories with photographs, treaty reproductions and a clan book. These are practical ways to connect speaking, listening and looking at evidence across generations.

The imported map cutoffs do not mark the end of the Kanza people. Forced removal, allotment and reservoir construction transformed their homelands, but the Kaw Nation continues as a self-governing community with elected institutions, language teaching and services for its citizens.

sectionTitles: A kingdom rooted in a valley

passages.text: Kazembe was an eastern Lunda kingdom centred on the lower Luapula valley, in today’s Zambia and Democratic Republic of the Congo. Tribute, trade, fishing and cultivation supported it. The imported polygon is displaced south and east of that heartland.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: Kazembe’s heartland was the lower Luapula valley. Its influence extended beyond that core through flexible institutions and symbols of authority. This helps explain why the kingdom should not be imagined simply as a modern country with a uniformly administered border.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: The town council’s historical tradition recalls royal emblems including a knife, staff, belt, beads and a cutting of a mutaba tree. The living tree belongs beside portable regalia in that account: planting could connect a new royal seat with an older political inheritance.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: Lake Mweru and the Mofwe Lagoon supplied fisheries, while access to Katanga’s copper linked the valley to wider exchange. The council’s account places food resources alongside minerals in the kingdom’s prosperity. Fish mattered long before anyone made a modern economic chart.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: Livingstone recorded that a new ruler established his court in a new place. In November 1867 he described a reed enclosure with the queen’s house behind the chief’s, and cassava and cotton growing inside. A court included productive plants as well as royal rooms.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: At a royal appearance he noted decorated headgear and imported cloth, including material from Manchester. Those details connect a Luapula court to distant workshops. Imported fabric was incorporated into local displays of authority rather than simply replacing them.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: December entries list gifts of dried fish, beer and baskets of cassava. These particular exchanges show food moving through hospitality and royal relationships. They give us a more concrete picture than a general statement that people “lived by agriculture”.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: On New Year’s Day 1868 Livingstone described broad iron hoes and recorded buying them with cloth. A tool could cultivate soil and also be a valuable exchange object. Cloth, metal and food connected work in the field with a much wider trading world.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: Historian David Gordon traces how shrines and natural features became associated with ancestors and conquests. Remembering history through the landscape supported both Lunda migrant identities and Shila identities rooted in the valley. Different communities could remember the same political expansion differently.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: The Umutomboko ceremony’s modern public form developed under changing political conditions. University of Zambia research identifies government support in 1971 as an important step in popularizing it. A living tradition can grow and reorganize while drawing on older royal practices.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: The town council describes a ceremony presided over by Mwata Kazembe and attended by people from Zambia and the neighboring Congo. Such gatherings make the continued royal institution visible across a border that now divides parts of its historical social world.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: In a Lunda tale recorded by Robert Cancel, the trickster Kalulu asks his in-laws for farmland and plants an enormous garden. The story brings marriage, cultivation and cleverness together. It is a modern recorded performance, not a literal report of events at the old court.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: A short written trace from an outsider’s record is the Portuguese title “O Muata Cazembe”, meaning “The Mwata Kazembe”. Gamito’s expedition account survives in later editions. This title records the royal office in a visitor’s language; it is not claimed as indigenous court writing.

After defeat in 1899, Mwata Kazembe negotiated a settlement under colonial rule. The royal institution survived in altered form, rather than the people or their traditions vanishing. The map’s 1878 cutoff is earlier than that change.

passages.text: Cantia is a Latin name used by Bede for Kent. This card serves both imported labels, but the map’s Cantia outline spreads far beyond the south-eastern kingdom and must not be treated as its verified territory. The Cantia interval of 600 to 800 and Kent interval of 800 to 1000 are map coverage, not the lives of two separate kingdoms. The named sites below are in historical Kent; several institutions continued after royal independence ended.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: An Old English sample from Aethelberht’s laws reads “Gif feaxfang geweorð ·L· sceatta to bote.” In Christopher Monk’s translation, grabbing someone by the hair calls for compensation of fifty sceattas. The wording survives in a twelfth-century copy of a much earlier code. Hair-pulling even had its own entry in the legal price list.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.

passages.text: This entry covers Kenya under British colonial rule, especially the 1920s and 1930s. The colony and the coastal protectorate had different legal arrangements. Railways, towns and schools changed opportunities, but racial restrictions on land, movement and political power made those changes deeply unequal.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The railway reached Nairobi in 1899 and the lakeside terminus later named Kisumu in 1901. Transport infrastructure helped towns grow along the line. These dates describe the network inherited by people living in the 1920s, not new construction in the selected year.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: Indian workers and African labourers helped construct the railway, and some Indian workers also opened small shops. Rail history therefore includes migration, commerce and difficult labour, alongside engineering plans drawn by British officials.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The Smithsonian preserves a thin tin kipande case made in the 1920s, with loops for a neck chain. It once held folded employment papers dated 1925. An object small enough to wear could carry a government’s authority into a worker’s daily movements.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The papers in a kipande recorded an African owner’s name and work history and rules restricting movement. This specimen was collected much later, in 1986. Its museum arrival is not the date when the colonial identification system was used.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Colonial authorities restricted African ownership of urban land. Some employers provided only bachelor rooms for workers, making it difficult for families to settle together. Housing policy shaped who could live in a town, not merely how buildings looked.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Asian residents also faced restrictions on property ownership and representation, while some Nairobi neighbourhoods were demolished under public-health justifications. Historians describe African and Asian resistance to these policies; residents were not passive recipients of town planning.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Alliance School opened near Nairobi in 1926 under Protestant missions. By 1928 it offered a four-year secondary course and the Cambridge School Certificate. Schooling could become a route toward professional work, although access remained highly limited and unequal.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Earlier, Maseno pupils had demanded more than gardening, carpentry and hygiene instruction. A 1910 strike helped secure teaching in English, mathematics and geography. This background shows pupils themselves pressing to change what colonial-era education allowed them to learn.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: During the 1930s, Kikuyu independent schools drew on donated land, elected committees and community fundraising. Families helped create institutions when existing education did not meet their aspirations. Choosing a school could also express a position in religious and political debates.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: “Muigwithania”, meaning “The Reconciler”, is the Kikuyu title of the newspaper associated with the Kikuyu Central Association and Jomo Kenyatta. Surviving 1928 and 1929 issues preserve the language in the Latin alphabet. This sample follows the catalogue’s spelling.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: The same newspaper collection includes English translations and correspondence between colonial officials. Those documents preserve African arguments against colonial rule, but they also show how the state watched the press. An archive can record both a voice and the surveillance directed at it.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: Regional money changed from rupees through an intermediate florin to shillings and cents. The currency transition linked everyday purchases to decisions made by the East African Currency Board. Older and newer names for money could coexist while people adjusted.

British rule ended when Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963; it became a republic the following year. The 1938 map endpoint does not mark independence. Colonial institutions changed, while the people who had lived, worked and organized under them continued building their country.

sectionTitles: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample

passages.text: Kenya became independent in 1963 and a republic in 1964; the map’s 1960 start still falls within colonial rule. Its later history includes new public institutions, environmental organizing and mobile communication, alongside persistent inequalities. Daily experience differs between communities, towns and rural households.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: Kenya’s first independent government operated within the Commonwealth with a governor-general representing the monarch. In 1964 it became a republic. These were distinct constitutional steps, rather than a single moment when every inherited institution changed at once.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: The 2010 constitution reintroduced the Senate alongside the National Assembly. This restored a national institution that had disappeared earlier in independent Kenya’s history.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: The first national banknotes carried “Banki Kuu ya Kenya”, meaning “Central Bank of Kenya”, alongside the English name. This short Swahili sample is attested on the initial notes issued in 1966; official writing could appear in more than one language on a familiar everyday object.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: Those notes combined Jomo Kenyatta’s portrait with scenes of economic activity. Currency served as a means of payment and a portable statement about the new state. The paper in a pocket could carry both a price and a national story.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in 1977 after rural women reported drying streams, insecure food supplies and longer walks for firewood. Planting trees addressed everyday work and resources as well as the appearance of a landscape.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: The movement connected environmental work with community education and public participation. Maathai received the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize for work linking sustainable development, democracy and peace. The achievement involved organized groups of women, not just one celebrated individual planting alone.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: M-PESA launched in Kenya in 2007. Safaricom’s retrospective describes trial users sending money to one another when the original pilot had focused on loan repayments. Users helped reveal a different purpose for the technology: getting money to another person without carrying it there.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: The system connected phone accounts with ordinary cash: people could deposit money, send balances and redeem them. The innovation depended on a practical network around the phone, not only a clever screen menu.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2025 account of St. Marks Makutano school in Kitui describes cleaner toilets, running water, private spaces for girls and accessible cubicles. A school building is more usable when its toilets support privacy and different physical needs as well as classroom attendance.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: The same school’s health club tended a garden and made soap to help pay for cleaning supplies. Pupils took part in looking after facilities and explaining hygiene. Toilets may not win a school talent show, but keeping them usable takes organization and skill.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: Among coastal Mijikenda communities, Kaya forest traditions connect naming, marriage, reconciliation and remembrance with particular places. Councils of elders act as custodians. These are living community practices with local histories, not ceremonies shared identically by every Kenyan.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: Traditional rules governing Kaya resources have contributed to conserving biodiversity. UNESCO also records pressure from land demand and urbanization. Protecting a forest can therefore involve knowledge, relationships and community authority as well as preventing trees from being cut down.

Kenya continues as an independent republic. Colonial rule ended in 1963, while later constitutional reforms changed its institutions. Its communities, languages and social movements remain part of an ongoing history, with achievements and unresolved inequalities rather than a single ending.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.

sectionTitles: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
Learning and a small writing sample

passages.text: The Golden Horde grew from the western conquests of the Mongol Empire and became a major power connecting the Eurasian steppe, Rus principalities and trading cities. Its history includes skilled metalwork, multilingual books, mobile households and ambitious urban building. The later Great Horde appears under the map’s 1492 label. The dated examples below distinguish fourteenth-century daily life from the politics of the late fifteenth century.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Batu’s forces conquered the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas in 1236-1240. His dynasty descended from Jochi. The map’s first appearance in 1279 therefore comes decades after its rise.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Berke was Muslim, and all khans from Öz Beg onward followed Islam. An alliance with Egypt’s Mamluk rulers in 1262-1263 also shows how diplomacy reached far beyond the steppe.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Bolgar preserves a mosque, minaret, mausoleums, baths and palace remains. These buildings make urban life visible alongside the better-known horse-riding armies. Its history also joins nomadic communities to settled craft and trading centers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: At Kitsivka 1 in present-day Ukraine, archaeologists found pottery, metal vessels, tools and clothing fittings from the Golden Horde period. The settlement stood near a river crossing. Such finds reveal everyday work and connections, rather than just the names of rulers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A steel helmet decorated with silver may bear Jani Beg’s name. The Metropolitan Museum treats that reading as a possibility, not a certainty. The object still shows skilled metalworking and the use of inscriptions on prestigious equipment.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A silver half-dirham of Tokhtamysh in Oxford is only 18 millimeters across. Its mint name, royal titles and religious words fit on that small surface. Coins could carry both money value and a ruler’s public message.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Ibn Battuta described felt-covered homes carried on wagons, with horses, oxen or camels pulling them. Moving house could mean taking the house along. His account describes travelers and a royal camp, not every household.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: He recorded millet porridge with mare’s milk, meat and pasta cooked with milk. These are a visitor’s observations, not a menu shared by everyone across an enormous territory.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Elite wives and princesses could control property and exercise authority. Court households also depended on servants and enslaved people. A queen’s influence tells us little about the freedoms of the women serving her.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Black Sea markets traded grain, furs, wax and honey, alongside goods arriving from farther east. They also sold enslaved people. Commercial connections created wealth, but could bring captivity and family separation.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: The fourteenth-century Codex Cumanicus contains vocabulary in Latin, Persian and Cuman, a Turkic language. Preserved in Venice, it shows people assembling tools for communication across languages. A word list is a practical achievement: conversations do not translate themselves.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: Bolgar’s nomination dossier describes madrasahs, institutions for education, among its fourteenth-century urban developments. These references show organized learning, but do not tell us that every child attended school or had the same opportunities.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: An Arabic sample from Tokhtamysh’s late-fourteenth-century coin reads “السلطان الاعظم” (al-sultan al-aʿzam), meaning “the supreme sultan.” It is a royal title, not evidence that all residents spoke Arabic at home. This inscription belongs to the earlier Golden Horde, before the Great Horde’s final decades.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: An archaeological study published in 2002 counted 25 excavated Golden Horde bathhouses: 14 communal and 11 private. That was the evidence known to its author then. Baths were substantial urban buildings, with washing also important in Muslim religious life.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Bolgar’s fourteenth-century development included water supply and drainage, according to its heritage dossier. These systems required planning and maintenance. The evidence cited here does not establish what sort of toilet every household used; bathhouses and drains are not proof of a flush toilet in every home.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Medieval writers mention a hospital, or bimaristan, at Urgench. A modern study uses those reports to investigate care in the Golden Horde. Details reconstructed by comparison with other hospitals remain proposals, and the evidence does not establish a hospital in every town.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: A study of medieval accounts describes hot and mineral springs used as treatments, as well as bathing. This tells us what people tried when ill. It does not show that those treatments worked by modern medical standards.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Civil war followed Berdibeg’s death in 1359. Tokhtamysh later reunited much of the Jochid realm, but conflict with Timur weakened his position. The larger Golden Horde eventually divided into several states.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: By the 1430s, the Great Horde claimed to be the senior continuation of the old realm. Other khanates pursued their own authority.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Ahmed Khan withdrew from the Ugra confrontation in 1480. This weakened his claim over Muscovy, but the Great Horde continued afterward.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: In 1501-1502, harsh winter conditions, shortages and desertions undermined Shaikh Ahmed. Politics depended on feeding people and animals as well as winning alliances.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Crimea’s Mengli Giray defeated Shaikh Ahmed in 1502. Shaikh Ahmed survived. The often-repeated story that Sarai was destroyed that year is disputed.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Successor khanates inherited political and literary traditions of the Golden Horde. Its legacy reached across Crimea, Central Asia and Siberia. A political breakup did not make languages, skills or communities disappear.

The Great Horde lost power to the Crimean khan in 1502. This was a political defeat within a wider succession of states, not the disappearance of the Golden Horde’s peoples. Jochid political and literary traditions continued in successor khanates.

passages.text: The Khazar confederation linked the Black Sea, Caucasus and lower Volga from the mid-600s to the late 900s. Turkic rulers governed a population with many languages, livelihoods and religions. Its influence depended on trade and diplomacy as well as armies.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Writing around 960, King Joseph described leaving his winter city in spring for vineyards, fields and seasonal work. This is a ruler's account of his own world, but it reminds us that Khazar life included cultivation as well as herding.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Joseph described Jews, Christians and Muslims sharing an urban settlement. His account also mentions enslaved people. Religious variety and commercial connections did not make this an equal society.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Hasdai's letter reports ships carrying fish, skins and other merchandise from Khazaria to Byzantium. River and sea connections helped link northern resources with larger markets.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Joseph credited the earlier ruler Obadiah with supporting synagogues, schools and visiting Jewish scholars. This is evidence of how the court presented its religious learning, not proof that all children attended school.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: The British Museum displays iron stirrups and a bridle-bit from near Bielowodsk in the Perm region, dated to the 800s-900s. The possible grave context is uncertain; the objects are associated with the Khazars and their contacts.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Silver sheet decorates the bridle-bit with vines and flowers. The museum connects these motifs with Byzantine and Slavic art. Even horse equipment could carry designs across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Sarkel on the lower Don was built with fired brick and had towers, a moat and several internal sectors. These are excavated architectural features, more informative than merely calling the fortress powerful.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: At nearby Semikarakorsk, builders combined mud-brick defenses with fired-brick structures in the citadel. The different materials show local construction choices; fired brick was already used there before the Byzantine mission associated with Sarkel.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Workshops adjoined walls at Semikarakorsk and the Tsimliansk Right-bank fortress. These places supported work and administration as well as soldiers. Archaeologist Valery Flyorov warns that the biggest wall circuit need not have been the most defensible.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The Schechter letter credits a woman named Serah with encouraging a ruler's turn toward Judaism. It is a religious story preserved in a later copy, not a contemporary diary; nevertheless, its author gives a woman an active role in the court's remembered history.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The same letter describes a marriage between Joseph and an Alan king's daughter after conflict between their fathers. Its narrative presents marriage as a way of making political peace, rather than a model for all households.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: A small Hebrew sample is בארץ קזריא, meaning “in the land of Khazaria.” It appears in the Schechter letter, recto left, line 7. The surviving Cambridge manuscript is a later copy of a text about tenth-century Khazaria, not the ruler's original handwriting.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The famous Kyivan letter should not simply be called Khazar handwriting. A 2026 re-examination finds a mainly Slavic setting and treats a Khazar connection as possible rather than established. Different Hebrew documents need their own histories.

Rus and Turkic attacks broke Khazar power during the 960s. The traditional date 965 and Ibn Hawqal's account dated 968-969 cannot be neatly combined into one certain fall day. Refugees returned and communities continued; the map's 1100 endpoint is not an imperial lifetime.

sectionTitles: Named people, family memories and written words

passages.text: “Khoisan” is an umbrella label for diverse Khoe and San peoples, not one kingdom or one established language family. The map’s vast outline and 4000 BCE to 1530 CE interval cannot define a single people’s territory or lifespan. The examples below identify particular communities and distinguish archaeological evidence from later recorded lives.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: Linguists distinguish Kx’a, Tuu and Khoe-Kwadi among the language families grouped under the southern African Khoisan label. Shared click sounds do not make them one language. Khoe-Kwadi itself includes communities with different histories of herding and gathering; a language name is not a job description.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: A small toe bone from Spoegrivier Cave in Namaqualand helps date a major change. Researchers tested ancient proteins to distinguish sheep from similar wild animals, confirming a domestic sheep about two thousand years old. Herding arrived in a region where people already had deep knowledge of wild foods and animals.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: An ostrich egg could become a water container. A Peabody Museum object collected in 1958 is catalogued as a possible San water carrier, perforated at one end. The Origins Centre describes plugged eggshell containers used to save scarce water: a remarkably practical use for something that began as an egg.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: Food gathering also called for tools. The Origins Centre explains how San and Khoe women used pointed digging sticks to reach roots and bulbs, sometimes adding a stone weight with a hole through it. Its displayed example is dated 1970, documenting a later practice rather than fixing the invention’s date.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: The same museum shows the engineering of a composite hunting arrow: connected sections and an attached tip that could separate after striking. Hunters also made adhesives to fasten components. These were carefully designed tools, requiring knowledge of materials, animal behavior and tracking.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Among Nama pastoralists in the Richtersveld, a house can travel with its owners. Domed homes use woven rush mats that can be taken apart when families move between grazing places. UNESCO’s account describes a living tradition: moving house can mean bringing the actual house along.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Richtersveld grazing is organized across communally managed land and seasonal stockposts. Pastoralists also gather useful and medicinal plants and preserve stories connected to places. Knowledge of when to move animals and where to find plants is part of caring for both a household and a landscape.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Tsodilo in Botswana preserves more than 4,500 rock paintings. Its hills and waterholes remain sacred to San and Hambukushu communities. The paintings span different periods and are not all securely dated; the site is a record of many visitors and inhabitants, not an illustrated diary of one timeless population.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: The |Xam storyteller ||kabbo helped teach Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd his language after being released from a Cape Town convict station. Their recordings from the 1870s and 1880s eventually supplied the 1911 book Specimens of Bushman folklore. Remembering the speakers’ names restores people to an archive often known mainly by its collectors.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: A later childhood remembered in the archive belongs to |uma, who arrived in Cape Town in 1880 after abduction and separation from his family. He recalled his mother building their grass sleeping hut and gathering fruit and kernels. His affection for the fruit of the |kui tree preserves one child’s taste of home.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: |uma, Da, Tamme and !nanni made hundreds of drawings and watercolors showing remembered plants, animals, foods and routes. At Mowbray they also built grass huts for play, including one for other children in the household. Their pictures preserve detailed environmental knowledge alongside the ordinary wish to play and remember home.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: A modern written example of |Xam appears in South Africa’s coat of arms, introduced in 2000: “!ke e: /xarra //ke,” officially translated as “diverse people unite.” The special marks represent speech sounds. This is a modern commemorative use of the language, not a prehistoric inscription.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: In 2017, South African San representatives set out their own research ethics code. It asks researchers to explain projects clearly, respect privacy, acknowledge knowledge and share benefits fairly. Communities were defining how outsiders should work with them, including protections for children and family life.

The map stops in 1530, but these peoples’ histories do not. Later records document displacement and violence as well as family knowledge and creativity. Living Nama traditions and the San research code show communities maintaining culture and asserting rights in the present.

sectionTitles: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us

passages.text: Kyivan Rus was a changing network of rulers, towns and rural communities centered on Kyiv. Its builders made monumental churches, its craftspeople worked precious metals, and some residents sent wonderfully ordinary messages on birch bark. Its cultural inheritance reaches across present-day Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. These two map intervals cover different political phases: especially after the early twelfth century, a broad Rus label includes increasingly independent regional powers.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Princes governed networks of towns and dependent villages rather than neat modern provinces. Harvard’s cultural mapping project stresses that both internal and external boundaries changed. A colored outline is therefore a rough guide to a complicated political world.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Households depended on grain, livestock, fishing and hunting. Forests supplied materials and fuel.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: The Ruskaia Pravda collected rules about injury, property, debts and witnesses during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Surviving manuscripts are later copies, and scholars disagree about the dates of individual versions. This was a developing legal tradition, not one untouched book handed down from a single ruler.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Legal compensation differed with social rank. Enslaved people and people bound by debt lived alongside free householders and powerful elites. The beautiful objects in museums cannot tell us that everyone shared the same wealth or freedom.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Inheritance rules distinguished commoners, nobles and widows. Family relationships shaped who could receive property; wills could be spoken before relatives. Sorting out who got the family possessions was already serious business. These rules describe legal expectations, not every family’s actual behavior.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Saint Sophia in Kyiv preserves eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes, including the Virgin Orans with raised arms. Byzantine masters and local builders contributed to the cathedral under Yaroslav. The art makes religious teaching visible through images as well as words.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: The cathedral’s surrounding complex includes much later baroque buildings. A visitor can therefore see several historical periods at once. The eleventh-century mosaics and the later additions should not all be assigned to Yaroslav’s lifetime.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: A finger ring attributed to Kyiv and dated 1000-1200 combines silver, gilded silver and dark niello decoration. The Metropolitan Museum interprets its crosses as signs of Christian faith. This small object connects skilled metalwork with the beliefs of a particular wearer, whose name is unknown.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Gold and enamel jewelry now in the Metropolitan Museum came from Kyiv hoards discovered in 1842 and 1906. The 1842 find lay in the old apse of the Church of the Tithes. These objects reveal elaborate ornament, but their later sale and dispersal complicate efforts to reconstruct the original groups.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Pekarska’s research followed old reports and collections to reconnect scattered treasures. Some pieces had disappeared or been melted down. Knowing where an object was found can matter as much as knowing how brightly it shines.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Birchbark document 591 from Novgorod’s Nutny excavation is an alphabet dated approximately 1025-1050. Its opening letters are “а б в г д е ж”. Someone was practicing the building blocks of writing. The surviving exercise does not identify the learner’s age or prove that every child attended school.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Evidence for women’s schooling is fragmentary. An encyclopedia account associates Anna Vsevolodivna with a girls’ school at Saint Andrew’s convent in late-eleventh-century Kyiv. It is evidence of a particular institution, not universal access to education.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Manuscripts, inscriptions and birchbark documents preserve different parts of literate life. Monastic copying helped transmit books, while private letters preserve business and personal concerns. Many surviving manuscripts cannot be dated to a single year.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: In letter 246, dated roughly 1025-1050 with a possible later shift, Zhirovit complains to Stoyan that a debt has gone unpaid for nine years. The whole letter survived in Novgorod’s Nerevsky excavation. Chasing an overdue payment clearly predates email.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Letter 752, from Novgorod around 1100, complains about an unanswered invitation and asks for a reply. Its broken passages admit more than one reading, and its precise date is debated. Even with those gaps, the disappointment sounds familiar: messages had feelings attached long before phones did.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: A later Novgorod letter, number 227, addresses the writer’s mother and discusses payments and property. It dates to about 1160-1180, after Novgorod had gained political autonomy. It illustrates family dealings in the wider Rus cultural world, not continuing government from Kyiv.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Here is a short Old East Slavic sample in Cyrillic from that actual birchbark letter: “водае семоу :в: гривьне”, meaning “give this person two grivnas.” The letter в between marks represents the number two. The words come from document 227, not a modern phrase translated backward into medieval spelling.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Archaeologists have found eleventh-century wooden bathhouses in Novgorod. A specialist history also records late-eleventh-century masonry baths in Kyiv and Pereyaslavl, following Byzantine traditions. Warm washing places required fuel, water and labor as well as a building.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Bathhouses tell us about washing, but the sources used here do not establish the toilet arrangements of a typical Rus home. A bath is not automatically a bathroom with a flushing toilet. Household sanitation deserves its own evidence.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Orthodox tradition remembers Agapitus of Kyiv’s Cave Monastery as a healer using vegetables and prayer in the eleventh century. The church’s retelling is a saint’s life, with miraculous events. It shows how healing and holiness were linked in religious memory; it does not demonstrate that a remedy cured a particular illness.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Stories about the Cave Monastery also require careful dating. The first Kyivan Cave Patericon collection arose between 1215 and 1230, drawing on earlier traditions; surviving versions are later still. A story about an eleventh-century monk is not necessarily an eyewitness record written in his lifetime.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After Mstyslav’s death in 1132, regional rulers increasingly pursued their own interests. Kyiv remained important, but shared dynastic ancestry did not mean constant political unity.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Novgorod’s revolt in 1136 increased its autonomy. Its assembly and elected officials mattered, although wealthy families exercised great influence. Calling it a republic does not mean everyone had equal political power.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Kyiv was sacked in 1169 during conflict among Rus princes. Fragmentation involved destructive warfare as well as shifting political loyalties.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After these map intervals, the 1240 siege devastated Kyiv and the Church of the Tithes was destroyed. Surviving art, manuscripts and later traditions nevertheless show cultural continuities. Political defeat and destruction did not erase the people or everything they knew.

Rus political unity weakened gradually as regional principalities grew more independent. The map cutoffs at 1100 and 1200 are coverage boundaries, not extinction dates. Kyiv suffered Mongol conquest in 1240, while communities and cultural traditions continued across the region.

sectionTitles: Arts, education and the royal court

passages.text: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.

passages.text: Cassander, also spelled Kassander, took control of Macedonia after Alexander the Great’s empire fragmented. He was master of Macedon from 316 BCE and adopted the royal title around 305 BCE. The imported map record runs from 300 to 200 BCE, but he died in 297 BCE: most of that displayed interval belongs to later rulers, not his kingdom.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: Cassander married Alexander’s half-sister Thessalonike and rebuilt Thebes, but his consolidation of power was also violent. He had the young Alexander IV killed around 310 BCE, removing Alexander the Great’s son from the struggle for the throne.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: He established two major cities in strategic coastal positions: Cassandreia took his own name, while Thessaloniki took his wife’s. A city’s name could advertise a royal family almost as effectively as a coin.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: Thessaloniki’s foundation in 316/5 BCE brought together inhabitants from 26 surrounding townships. Building a new royal city meant moving people as well as laying out streets. The city’s later importance grew from this deliberate concentration of population around the Thermaic Gulf.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: Pella expanded northward in Cassander’s time. Its Hellenistic plan arranged buildings in regular blocks between straight streets, with a broad route through the centre. Planning a capital meant organising movement between the harbour, market and palace.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: The Hellenistic city had clay water pipes and large masonry drains with openings for cleaning. Water had to arrive, and wastewater had to leave. Those maintenance openings are a reminder that ancient plumbing needed somebody willing to do the unpleasant jobs.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: Pella’s houses commonly centred on courtyards, sometimes surrounded by colonnades. Rich households decorated dining rooms with mosaics; smaller houses might have just one broad porch. Surviving grand residences should not be mistaken for everybody’s address.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: The House of Dionysus has pebble mosaics dated 325 to 300 BCE, including Dionysus riding a panther and a lion hunt. These floors belong to the generation of Cassander’s rise. Dinner guests had dramatic scenes beneath their feet.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: At the palace, a swimming pool, dressing room and adjoining bath were built near the end of the fourth century BCE. Excavated pottery and coins help establish the date. The researchers identify this bathing suite as royal: the king’s swimming arrangements were not a public pool for the whole city.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: A small terracotta figure of sleeping Eros came from a child’s burial in Pella’s eastern cemetery and is dated 325 to 300 BCE. This quiet object brings a child into a history so often dominated by adult rulers and battles. Its burial context is known; the child’s personal story is not.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: A bronze coin dated about 305 to 297 BCE carries the Greek words ΚΑΣΣΑΝΔΡΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ, “of King Cassander”. This is the museum’s transcription of the ancient inscription, not a phrase invented for the card. Even a small coin could announce who claimed to rule.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: The same coin shows Heracles wearing a lion skin on one side and a young rider on the other. Cassander placed his own name beside familiar heroic and equestrian imagery. Royal messages travelled on objects people could hold in one hand.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: A recorded inscription from Cassandreia confirms land for Perdikkas, son of Koinos, including property previously allotted to his father and grandfather. The grant made ownership hereditary and allowed descendants to exchange or sell it. Family advantage could be written into royal decisions.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: That grant also exempted Perdikkas and his descendants from taxes on imports and exports connected with the property. It is a glimpse of unequal economic privilege: one favoured household received written advantages that should not be assumed for every farmer.

Cassander died in 297 BCE. Quarrels among his heirs soon destabilised Macedonia, which continued under other rulers. His personal kingdom therefore ended long before the imported map’s 200 BCE endpoint, while his new cities outlasted the dynasty.

sectionTitles: A king’s name and another king’s face

passages.text: Lysimachus built one of the kingdoms that emerged after Alexander the Great’s death. His power began in Thrace and later extended into western Anatolia and Macedonia. The imported map shows mainly Thrace from 300 to 200 BCE. That outline misses much of his later kingdom, and its dates continue long after his death in 281 BCE.

passages.title: Power around the straits
passages.text: After the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, Lysimachus gained extensive lands in Asia Minor. He later shared and then took control of Macedonia. His kingdom changed substantially within one lifetime, so a single Thracian outline cannot represent its maximum reach.

passages.title: Power around the straits
passages.text: Lysimacheia, founded in 309 BCE, bore the king’s name and stood in a strategic position near the Hellespont. After his death, other rulers repeatedly competed for it. A new city could outlast its founder while remaining caught between larger powers.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Across the water in Anatolia, Lysimachus refounded Ephesos around 300 BCE. The project gathered people from nearby smaller settlements into a planned city. The Austrian Archaeological Institute describes the resettlement as forced: a king’s impressive urban project could mean an unwanted move for a household.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Ephesos’s Hellenistic plan included a regular street grid and a fortification circuit about nine kilometres long along the hills. Those surviving walls help identify this early city beneath later building phases. Many famous monuments visible at Ephesos today were rebuilt or added under Rome.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Strabo, writing centuries later, tells an unsettling story about the move: Lysimachus allegedly blocked drains during heavy rain to flood the old settlement and make residents leave. This is an ancient author’s account, not an event established by excavated plumbing. It shows how coercive the king’s reputation could be.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: A marble land grant from Cassandreia, dated 285/4 BCE, lists wooded estates and a vineyard given to Limnaios, son of Harpalos. It identifies neighbours as well as areas. Royal property was described through usable resources and local boundaries, not just lines on a grand map.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: The same grant allowed Limnaios and his descendants to keep, sell, exchange or give away the estates. This is unusually direct evidence for inherited family wealth under Lysimachus. Such royal favour tells us about a privileged household rather than all rural families.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: An Athenian decree credits the poet Philippides with persuading Lysimachus to send 10,000 Attic medimnoi of wheat, distributed to Athenians in 299/8 BCE. A poet at court could do practical diplomatic work. In this case his useful words helped bring grain.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: After the battle of Ipsus, Philippides also secured the release of Athenian prisoners. Those who wanted to leave received clothing and travel money from him; others chose further military service. The decree counts more than 300 people helped. It preserves individual choices within a much larger war.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: Athens later rewarded Philippides with a bronze statue in the theatre, public dining privileges and a front-row seat at civic competitions. These honours reveal a social world in which poetry, festivals, generosity and royal connections could reinforce one another.

passages.title: A king’s name and another king’s face
passages.text: An Otago Museum silver coin minted at Colophon about 299 to 296 BCE reads ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩ[Σ] ΛΥΣΙΜΑΧΟΥ, “of King Lysimachus”. The brackets mark a restored letter in the catalogue’s transcription. This small Greek inscription comes from the Anatolian side of his kingdom, beyond most of the imported outline.

passages.title: A king’s name and another king’s face
passages.text: Lysimachus also issued coins showing Alexander with the ram’s horn of the god Amun, while Athena appeared on the reverse. The face was Alexander’s, although the money named Lysimachus. The British Museum explains this as a claim to inherit the conqueror’s prestige.

Lysimachus was killed fighting Seleucus at Corupedium in 281 BCE. His Asian lands passed to the Seleucids, while Macedonia entered another struggle for power. His kingdom did not survive intact until the map’s 200 BCE endpoint, although its cities and communities continued.
