sectionTitles: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
A king’s image and a written name

passages.text: Syphax ruled the Masaesyles in western and central North Africa during the late third century BCE. His reign ended in 203 BCE, before this record’s imported 200 to 100 BCE map interval. The outline cannot establish his kingdom’s dates or precise borders.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Siga in the west and Cirta farther east were royal centers. Syphax’s expanding kingdom brought different communities under one ruler, but its southern boundary remains uncertain.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Livy describes Syphax asking a Roman envoy to remain as an infantry instructor. Training meant organizing recruits and teaching them to keep formation: an army needed practice as well as horses and weapons.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: In Appian’s account, Syphax hosted the rival commanders Scipio and Hasdrubal at a banquet, where they shared a dining couch. That is one way to make awkward dinner guests sit together. The story reflects the king’s importance to both powers.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Syphax married Sophonisba, daughter of the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal, as their alliance strengthened. Royal family relationships and territorial competition were intertwined with the war.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: Excavations beside the Tafna at Siga found successive buildings and thick layers of broken pottery. The excavator placed this occupation broadly across the Hellenistic centuries, beginning before Syphax. His capital had an existing urban past.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: The Siga deposits included Campanian pottery and several amphora forms. These durable fragments give archaeologists evidence of containers and connections that survive when the people who handled them left no personal diary.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: Builders at Siga strengthened walls with dressed stone. Vuillemot suggested that one room had a sloping earthen roof waterproofed with lime, but could not decide whether these large rooms were homes or storerooms. Archaeology sometimes leaves the room labels blank.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: The nearby Beni Rhénane royal mausoleum illustrates regional building skill, although its date and royal owner are disputed. Craftspeople used stone from a nearby quarry and mortar incorporating local volcanic material and gypsum from the surrounding district.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: At Beni Rhénane, underground chambers followed the monument’s curved and straight sides. Stone barriers closed entrances. These remains reveal specialized stoneworking and careful planning in the region’s royal funerary tradition.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: A surviving copper coin cataloged as Syphax’s measures 25 millimeters across and weighs 7.38 grams. The small object carries a bearded royal portrait on one side and a galloping rider on the other.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: The rider’s cloak streams behind him and he holds a scepter; the king’s portrait wears a diadem. Those carefully chosen details turn a small piece of money into a portable statement of royal authority.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: The coin’s Punic writing includes “SPQ”, the consonants of the name Syphax in scholarly transliteration. The longer legend adds a royal title. This is a written sample from his coinage, shown in Latin letters rather than a reconstruction of the original engraved shapes.

Syphax lost his kingdom in 203 BCE and died in captivity in Italy. His son Vermina retained a reduced kingdom for a time, while Massinissa gained the eastern conquests. Numidian communities continued under new rulers.

sectionTitles: Political limits and a written voice

passages.text: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies formally united Naples and Sicily in 1816. This map label starts earlier, so the card also explains achievements under the preceding Bourbon crowns and the separate Napoleonic government on the mainland. The unified kingdom combined major scientific and industrial projects with political repression and repeated revolutions.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: At San Leucio near Caserta, silk machinery was installed in the 1780s with help from foreign specialists. The royal industrial settlement predates the formal 1816 kingdom. It linked imported expertise with the daily work of spinning and weaving luxurious cloth.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: The settlement’s 1789 code required education and regulated work and pay. It also abolished dowries within the community and prescribed uniform clothing. These were rules for a particular royal colony, not evidence that every woman and child across southern Italy enjoyed the same conditions.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: San Leucio’s rules included mutual assistance for elderly people and those unable to work. The planned expansion into Ferdinandopoli, however, was never completed as intended. Reforming a small community on paper and transforming an entire society were very different scales of ambition.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: The silk works depended on a branch of the Carolino aqueduct. After driving production, water returned to the Peschiera basin. The same royal landscape joined useful machinery and ornamental water: a beautiful fountain view could be connected to a working industrial system.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: Maria Carolina’s rooms at Caserta preserve a bidet, dressing table and bathtub among the furnishings studied by the museum. These objects make royal washing arrangements tangible. They are evidence for an elite interior, not a census of ordinary families’ plumbing.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: Palermo’s larger botanical garden was established from 1789 and inaugurated in 1795. Bernardino da Ucria arranged its collections using Linnaeus’s classification. Plants were being organized as teaching material, while the garden’s buildings provided spaces for study and cultivation.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: On 1 January 1801, Giuseppe Piazzi observed the object now called Ceres from Palermo. Further observations showed its movement, and Gauss later helped calculate its orbit. Now classified as a dwarf planet, Ceres connects Sicilian observation with an international mathematical effort.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: Naples’s Capodimonte observatory began under Joachim Murat in 1812 and was completed under Ferdinand I in 1819. The project crossed a change of regime. Its history is a useful reminder that an institution’s achievements cannot always be assigned neatly to one dynasty.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: The Naples to Portici railway opened on 3 October 1839. Its roughly 7.4-kilometre inaugural journey took about eleven minutes. It was a short route, but a real change in transport; the engineering drew on British locomotive designs and the work of Armand Bayard.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: In 1840 the crown began acquiring land for the Pietrarsa works. The surviving factory halls housed specialized stages of production and now contain railway collections. A steam railway required a continuing workforce and repair capacity, not just a ceremonial first ride.

passages.title: Political limits and a written voice
passages.text: Revolutions in 1820 and 1848 forced concessions before royal power reasserted itself. Sicilian demands for independence also conflicted with control from Naples. These struggles explain why scientific projects and royal factories could coexist with fierce opposition to the monarchy.

passages.title: Political limits and a written voice
passages.text: Italian, Giuseppe Piazzi’s words reproduced by INAF from his historical record: “non vi essendo Cielo più bello del Partenopeo”. Translation: “there being no sky more beautiful than Naples’s.” The phrase belongs to his discussion of Naples and its observatory. The exhibition does not date this individual quotation, so an exact year would be misleading.

Garibaldi’s campaign and Piedmontese intervention brought annexation in 1860. The Bourbon court’s last major stand at Gaeta ended on 13 February 1861, and the territory entered the new Kingdom of Italy. Resistance and social conflict continued afterward; this was the end of a state, not of southern Italian communities.

sectionTitles: Land loss, community art and language

passages.text: The Kiowa became a major southern Plains power through migration, horse-centered life and alliances. Earlier traditions place them much farther north. Both imported outlines, dated 1492 and 1530, show southern territory associated with later history; neither proves that early southern boundary. Kiowa people and their tribal government continue today.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Kiowa origin traditions place ancestors near the Missouri and Yellowstone headwaters. Later histories describe movement toward the Black Hills before the southern Plains. The remote sequence is uncertain, so tracing migration requires more care than coloring one large area and treating it as a timeless homeland.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Around 1790, Kiowa and Comanche leaders turned former hostility into an enduring alliance. Kansas Historical Society recounts Guikate spending a year with the Comanche before returning with a favorable report. The relationship strengthened their influence over hunting grounds, trade and military affairs across the southern Plains.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: In the horse-centered Plains period, bison hunting, gathered foods and portable homes helped Kiowa families move across large distances. Horses supported hunting and warfare, while hides supplied shelter. This way of life belongs to a changing historical period; horses should not be inserted into a scene dated 1492.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Tipi designs could belong to particular people and families. A Smithsonian model made by Tsakai between 1897 and 1904 preserves his father Bellowing Elk’s Black Star design, with white circles representing stars. It is a small model documenting an older design, not the family’s full-size home.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: A Kiowa cradleboard from about 1895 combines carved wood, hide, cloth, beadwork, ribbon and metal tacks. Museum cataloguers identify it as a baby carrier. Such an object brings childcare into the historical picture: families invested skilled work and decoration in something made for a very small passenger.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: A pictorial calendar records the spectacular meteor shower of 1833. In the entry reproduced by James Mooney, stars appear above a small child representing calendar keeper Set-t’an in his first winter. The drawing helps recall a named event and its story; it is not an alphabetic sentence.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: At Medicine Lodge Creek in 1867, Kiowa, Comanche and Plains Apache representatives negotiated with United States commissioners. The resulting agreements involved a reservation in present-day Oklahoma and the surrender of extensive lands. A treaty was supposed to establish obligations between governments; it did not make the signers’ peoples disappear.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: On September 28, 1874, United States troops attacked camps in Palo Duro Canyon occupied by Kiowa, Comanche and Cheyenne families. Soldiers burned homes and winter supplies and killed most captured horses. Destroying transport and stored food made it much harder for survivors to remain outside the reservation.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Lone Wolf challenged the federal government’s division and sale of reservation land. The Supreme Court ruled against him and the tribes in 1903. The National Archives preserves the case alongside the treaty record: legal documents reveal both Native efforts to defend agreements and the government’s power to override them.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Kiowa photographer Horace Poolaw recorded relatives and neighbors at weddings, parades, ball games and everyday outings from the 1920s onward. One surviving photograph shows his children Robert and Linda dressed up for their father’s camera around 1947. His pictures preserve community life from a family member’s viewpoint.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: In a Kiowa handgame described by anthropologist William Meadows, one team hides marked pieces while another guesses their location. Drumming and singing add distraction. Wooden sticks keep score; in the Kiowa version he describes, the team with fewer sticks wins. A calm face can be part of the strategy.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Hàyá èm bánmà?”, meaning “Where are you going?” The Kiowa Tribe’s language page prints the phrase with a pronunciation guide and linked lesson. The accents are part of the teaching spelling, and the sample is contemporary rather than an inscription from the map’s early dates.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Language preservation also means preparing new teachers. The department advertised a credentialed teacher-training program for 2025 to 2026 and explicitly recognizes different Kiowa orthographies. Its work links speakers, learners and community organizations so that written resources can lead back to people speaking together.

The imported map cutoffs precede much Kiowa southern Plains history. Military defeat and allotment transformed landholding and daily life, but Kiowa communities continued. Language teaching and community art remain part of that ongoing history.

passages.text: Kong became a major Dyula commercial and political center in what is now northern Côte d’Ivoire, connected with communities far into present-day Burkina Faso. Its rulers and allied warrior houses did not govern every place within a tidy border. The imported 1783 to 1914 interval is a map window, extending beyond the destruction of the old capital.

passages.title: Power and households
passages.text: Seku Wattara’s seizure of power early in the eighteenth century made Kong a force beyond its immediate surroundings. Its armies reached toward the Niger and fought Asante. Yet Launay emphasizes that nearby chiefdoms could trace connections to Kong without being directly governed by it.

passages.title: Power and households
passages.text: Watara warrior houses joined relatives with many dependants who farmed, traded or fought. Historian Mahir Şaul describes them as enduring social and economic units. Their power also rested on enslavement: captives could become household labourers or be sold through long-distance networks.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: Binger counted about 150 indigo dye pits in two parts of Kong. Their walls were waterproofed with material made from heated earth. Weaving spaces filled openings between houses: cloth production shaped the streets, and dyeing gave some corners a distinctly noticeable smell.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: Among requests recorded by Binger were help against Guinea worm and a way to drill through granite to obtain well water. These were practical concerns about health and water supply, voiced by the residents he met, rather than luxuries requested for a royal palace.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: The religious leader Sitafa supervised roughly twenty Arabic schools, according to Binger, and also taught adults and elders. Learning did not stop at childhood. The visitor describes senior townspeople attending discussions of religious books several times a week.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: An Arabic safe-conduct given to Binger in March 1888 begins “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God”. This is a normalized transcription of the surviving manuscript facsimile. Arabic served written diplomacy here; the sample is not written Jula.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: Kong’s small mosque has radiocarbon evidence reaching the seventeenth or eighteenth century. Oral tradition specifically credits Imam Barro with bringing plans from Djenné in 1729. The two kinds of evidence offer different levels of precision and should be read together.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: The region’s earthen mosques use rounded earth bricks and protective plaster. Timber poles projecting from walls help support the buildings and provide footholds for maintenance. The apparent sticks poking out are useful equipment: repairing a wall begins with somewhere to stand.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: Compared with Djenné’s architecture, these southern mosques often have stouter, tapering buttresses. ICOMOS connects the differences with wetter conditions and local building traditions. Builders adapted a shared architectural language to the weather and skills of their own communities.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: In fieldwork conducted in Burkina Faso in 2012, Coleman Donaldson documented Jula written in adapted Arabic script, including medicinal notebooks and texts composed for his research. This later evidence shows a living literacy associated with the former Kong region; it is not a surviving royal archive.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Donaldson prints “Kpón ká jùlakán”, translated “Kong’s Jula”. This is his modern Latin transcription of a name speakers used for a prestigious language form. His participants had not grown up in Kong, showing how the town’s linguistic reputation could travel beyond its streets.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Kong’s great mosque was destroyed during Samory’s campaign in 1897 and rebuilt by its community. Its continued maintenance is part of a living religious landscape. UNESCO’s 2021 inscription recognizes both the buildings and the knowledge needed to keep earthen architecture standing.

The destruction of Kong in 1897 broke the old capital’s position; the imported 1914 endpoint is not its conquest date. Colonial rule reshaped the region, while Kong’s residents rebuilt, worshipped and maintained their architectural traditions. The town and its communities did not disappear with the earlier political order.

sectionTitles: Children behind and in front of the camera
Making textbooks usable by more learners

passages.text: This modern record begins in 2020, although Kosovo declared independence in 2008. Recognition remains divided, and Serbia disputes that independence. The map’s separate outline represents one dataset’s treatment of this contested status. Within Kosovo, communities maintain crafts, educate children and make new cultural work alongside unresolved political questions.

passages.title: Silver threads and skilled hands
passages.text: Prizren is a major centre for filigree, the delicate craft of making silver jewellery and ornaments. A 2020 UNDP project documented local artisans and worked to preserve their skills. This is an inherited regional craft that continues in contemporary workshops.

passages.title: Silver threads and skilled hands
passages.text: Thirty young people and women from different communities received training through the project. Five continued in a six-month internship to develop their skills further. Learning such work takes repeated practice with experienced craftspeople, rather than simply memorising a decorative pattern.

passages.title: Silver threads and skilled hands
passages.text: A documentary about the project presented artisans and their work to a wider audience. Versions were offered in English, Albanian, Serbian and Turkish. Recording the craft helped preserve knowledge while making the workshops visible beyond the people who could visit them.

passages.title: Children behind and in front of the camera
passages.text: DokuFest’s 2023 children’s programme offered fifty-four films and seven workshops for ages six to twelve. Topics included children’s rights and climate change. A film festival could therefore also become a place for younger residents to learn, make things and discuss their world.

passages.title: Children behind and in front of the camera
passages.text: In 2023, DokuKids Summer School brought pupils and teachers together to make films and examine misleading online information. Workshops addressed digital literacy and responsible behaviour online. Children practised storytelling while asking whether the stories on their screens could be trusted.

passages.title: Children behind and in front of the camera
passages.text: The same educational programme introduced teachers to a digital library containing more than 150 films with worksheets. Educators from twelve partner schools explored using documentary films in class. Moving images could become evidence to discuss, rather than simply entertainment at the end of a lesson.

passages.title: Making textbooks usable by more learners
passages.text: In June 2026, more than forty educators, publishers, officials and disability representatives met in Istog to work on accessible digital textbooks. Their task was to learn how to produce learning materials that children with different needs could use.

passages.title: Making textbooks usable by more learners
passages.text: The proposed textbooks include functions such as reading text aloud, describing images, sign language and easier navigation. These features address different barriers. A picture that matters to a lesson needs an explanation for a pupil who cannot see it.

passages.title: Making textbooks usable by more learners
passages.text: The initiative planned a trial in ten schools after the training. That scale matters: the report documents preparation and a pilot, not proof that every child already had accessible materials. Teachers, publishers and disability organisations were involved in shaping the work together.

passages.title: Written languages and political decisions
passages.text: The cover of the September 2020 constitutional edition begins “Republika e Kosovës”, Albanian for “Republic of Kosovo”. The same letterhead also gives the name in Serbian and English. This is an attested modern printed example, not a reconstructed phrase from an earlier period.

passages.title: Written languages and political decisions
passages.text: Article 5 identifies Albanian and Serbian as official languages, with provisions for Turkish, Bosnian and Roma languages at municipal level or as specified by law. The constitutional text records a multilingual public framework for communities whose everyday speech is not all the same.

passages.title: Written languages and political decisions
passages.text: In 2010 the International Court of Justice concluded that the 2008 declaration did not violate international law. The Court carefully limited its answer: it was not deciding whether Kosovo had achieved statehood or requiring other states to recognise it.
Kosovo’s institutions and communities continue, while its status remains internationally contested and relations with Serbia remain a subject of negotiation.

passages.text: The Kuba kingdom brought together several principalities in Central Africa. Royal and aristocratic patronage encouraged inventive textiles, carved vessels and images through which rank and historical memory became visible.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Kuba makers wove raffia palm fibers into cloth. Women joined, dyed and embellished panels with embroidery and applique.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cutting embroidered raffia threads created a dense pile surface. Some panels were displayed as prestige objects and used as currency rather than worn.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Multiple cloth panels formed wrappers whose gathered edges moved with the wearer. Dress combined bodily movement with elaborate surface design.

passages.title: Historical memory
passages.text: Ndop sculptures memorialized rulers through idealized seated figures and identifying symbols. A strategy board identifies Shyaam aMbul aNgoong.

passages.title: Knowledge
passages.text: Kuba chronologies preserve references to a solar eclipse and Halley's comet, giving historians points for comparison with independently dated celestial events.

passages.text: Gunaikurnai people maintain Country, kinship and cultural knowledge across Gippsland. Stoneworking traces at the Knob and exceptionally preserved wood at Cloggs Cave connect material evidence with knowledge held by communities. Their history includes colonial displacement, the survival of family connections and continuing care for land and waters.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: Gunaikurnai brings together the recorded names Gunnai and Kurnai in a form agreed by the community. Different spellings in older records often reflect how outsiders transcribed speech; they should not automatically be treated as different peoples.

passages.title: People, names and Country
passages.text: The Gunaikurnai Land and Waters Aboriginal Corporation recognizes five major clans across Gippsland. Clan connections place responsibilities in particular landscapes, while families share wider relationships. A single outline on a map cannot capture all those connections.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: At the Knob on Brayakaulung Country, deep grooves in sandstone beneath the bluff record repeated sharpening of stone axe heads. Stone scatters, camps and scarred trees also survive, making this a landscape of skilled work as well as a gathering place.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Research published in 2024 described small fireplaces at Cloggs Cave near Buchan containing trimmed Casuarina sticks and fatty residues. Dating places these features about 11,000 to 12,000 years ago. The preserved wood provides unusually direct evidence of how people prepared and used plant materials.

passages.title: Material evidence and discovery
passages.text: Working with Gunaikurnai Elders, the Cloggs Cave researchers compared those finds with nineteenth-century descriptions of ritual specialists using treated sticks. They interpret a long transmission of ritual knowledge. The excavated objects and residues are observations; the connection across millennia is the study's argued interpretation.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Dooyeedang, the Avon River, linked high country with the Gippsland Lakes. Gunaikurnai accounts describe travel along it and foods including eels and fish. Moving through this river landscape connected meals and material resources with visits, exchange and relationships.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: The Knob hosted meetings where clans feasted, exchanged goods, shared news and held ceremonies. Such gatherings joined practical provisioning with social and cultural obligations; the place mattered for much more than a single activity.

passages.title: Food, travel and shared work
passages.text: Cultural fire is guided by knowledge of the season, the place and the purpose of a burn. Gunaikurnai accounts connect fire with land health, ceremony and communication. Renewing this practice draws on Elders' knowledge rather than treating every fire as an identical operation.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: During the mission era, people continued to meet at the Knob, sometimes secretly, to maintain family ties despite enforced separation. In 2010 the same place hosted the native title determination ceremony, linking legal recognition with a much older community history.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: Established in 2007, GLaWAC provides a community institution for representing Gunaikurnai people and caring for Country. Its public cultural protocols recognize that knowledge belongs to people and families and that perspectives within the community can differ.

passages.title: Displacement, recognition and learning
passages.text: The Cultural Hub at Forestec supports community programs and cultural learning. Stories and songlines connect knowledge with ancestors and places; teaching involves relationships and responsibilities as well as information that can be written down.

Gunaikurnai communities continue. Colonial displacement and mission control disrupted families and access to Country, but neither ended the people or their knowledge. Native title recognition, cultural learning and care for Country are later chapters of that continuing history.

passages.text: Kush was an African kingdom of the Middle Nile whose centers included Napata and Meroe. Its rulers and craftspeople developed distinctive monuments while exchanging ideas with neighboring societies. The royal city, religious settlements and industrial remains show a civilization extending well beyond its famous pyramids.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron-working remains and ceramic production areas at Meroe document skilled manufacture. They establish local production, not a claim that Kush invented iron smelting.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Reservoirs helped support settlements away from the Nile. Their remains are evidence for both engineering and the environmental conditions in which people lived.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Steep-sided pyramids, decorated funerary chapels and painted burial chambers gave Kushite royal commemoration a distinctive appearance.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Architecture at Meroe, Naqa and Musawwarat combined Kushite forms with elements associated with Egypt, Greece and Rome.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Gebel Barkal was a sacred landscape. Temples at its foot connected royal authority with the worship of Amun.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Meroitic political order ended in late antiquity, but burial traditions continued afterward. A kingdom's disappearance should not be read as the disappearance of its people.

passages.text: The Kushans, a Yuezhi clan from Bactria, built an empire from the Oxus to the Ganges in the first three centuries CE. They struck gold coins, stood at the crossing of the Silk Road, and under Kanishka became the great patrons of Buddhism and the art of Gandhara.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gandharan sculptors, drawing on Greek and Roman models, made some of the first images of the Buddha in human form, at the same time as the workshops of Mathura.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stupas and monasteries rose at Taxila, Peshawar and Hadda; Chinese pilgrims reported Kanishka's stupa at Peshawar as the tallest building they had seen.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire held the passes between the Silk Road, the Indus ports and the Ganges plain, and traded with Rome by sea and with Han China by land.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold coins on the Roman weight standard, showing Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist gods, circulated from Central Asia to the Ganges.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Kanishka's reign, beginning about 127 CE, is remembered in Buddhist tradition for a council in Kashmir that fixed the canon of the Sarvastivada school.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Hindu and Buddhist deities all appear on Kushan coins, and Bactrian, written in Greek letters, was the language of the state.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Gandharan Buddhist art traveled along the Silk Road to Central Asia and China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Kushan patronage helped carry Buddhism to Central Asia and on to China.
The Sasanians took Bactria and the west in the third century and set up Kushano-Sasanian governors; the last Kushan kings ruled in the Punjab in the shadow of the Guptas until about 375.

passages.text: The imported labels “Kushites” in 700 to 800 and “Cushites” in 900 to 1000 cover the Somali Horn. They are broad regional labels, not the Nile kingdom of Kush or a documented united empire. Cushitic is a family of related languages that includes Somali. This card follows regional communities through archaeology, with earlier and later examples clearly dated; it does not assign every ancient object to a modern people.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: At Xiis on the Gulf of Aden, excavators found imported pottery and glass in stone burial mounds. Goods came through connections reaching Roman territories, southern Arabia and Mesopotamia. The early centuries CE therefore reveal coastal people participating in far-reaching exchange, even without a large local city or imperial government.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: One Xiis child, estimated to have been about eight or nine years old, was buried with beads, an iron anklet and a glass flagon dated to the third century CE. The vessel probably came from Roman Syria or Cyprus. A small grave can preserve both personal care and a remarkably long journey.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: In the later medieval settlements surveyed around Borama, many houses used flat stones bound with mud. Typical examples had two or three rooms within about 20 to 40 square metres. At Fardowsa, two much larger six-room houses suggest that some households had considerably more space.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: The same survey found grinding stones and digging-stick weights near farming land. These are clues to daily work: preparing ground and turning grain into food. Some settlements had few imported luxuries, so their history cannot be told only through merchants and distant ships.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: Mosques were important gathering places in these later towns. At Abasa and Hasadinle, pillars helped support the roof. Their builders worked with the same stone-and-mud techniques used in houses, linking public religious spaces to skills also useful around the home.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A StateHorn account of historically documented pastoral life explains why movement mattered: rain could make a grazing area usable for a season, while dry months depleted wells. Along the Guban plain, shallow wells reached water beneath sandy ground. Knowing when and where to travel was a practical skill, not aimless wandering.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: At Siyaara near Berbera, archaeologists found thousands of local and imported pottery fragments dated from the tenth to sixteenth centuries. Seasonal fairs connected arriving ships with caravans and mobile herding communities. A place could become an important meeting ground without being a busy town every month of the year.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A milk pot collected in southern Somalia in 1934 to 1935 combines wood, woven plant fibre and a lid with a central knob. It is a much later example of household craftsmanship from within this broad region. The ordinary job of carrying and protecting milk required careful work with several materials.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: An Issa head-rest catalogued to about 1910 to 1912 is carved from wood, with a conical base and ornament. It stands just 14.5 centimetres high. This later Somali object offers a different answer to the bedtime equipment question: a pillow need not be a bag of feathers.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Here is a modern Somali writing sample: “𐒍𐒖𐒇 𐒈𐒝𐒑𐒛𐒐𐒘”, far Soomaali, meaning “Somali writing”. These are Osmanya letters, from a script devised in 1920 to 1922. The sample is printed in the Unicode Standard; it is not medieval writing from either map interval.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Getting Osmanya onto computers involved cooperation across generations. Michael Everson described how Osman Abdihalim Osman Yusuf Keenadiid and his family supplied a photocopied book that helped the encoding project. Their collaboration produced a revised proposal in 2001: preserving writing can involve family books as well as software.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: In 2015 to 2016, ten young adults from London’s Somali community worked with the British Museum’s Somali collections. They explored objects, contributed knowledge and developed new ways to tell their stories. Descendant communities are participants in explaining this heritage, not merely people described by old collection labels.

Neither 800 nor 1000 marks the disappearance of the Horn’s peoples. Later regional trade and settlement changed, including disruption around the end of the Adal sultanate in the sixteenth century. That was a transformation of particular political and commercial networks, not an ending for Cushitic-speaking communities.

passages.text: Kwakwaka’wakw refers to peoples who speak Kwak’wala, including distinct nations with their own names, territories and histories on northern Vancouver Island and the adjacent mainland. The map’s broad outline and dates from 1492 to 1650 do not describe one empire or the lifespan of these living communities. Examples below identify particular families and nations where the evidence allows.

passages.title: Families, witnesses and remarkable craftsmanship
passages.text: A potlatch marks major changes such as marriages, naming and the passing of chiefly rights. Guests serve as witnesses to the histories and privileges being publicly affirmed. Gifts acknowledge that responsibility. The gathering carries political and family obligations as well as the pleasure of sharing food and company.

passages.title: Families, witnesses and remarkable craftsmanship
passages.text: Gift lists change across generations. U’mista’s teaching resource compares nineteenth-century bentwood boxes, hides and canoes with later blankets and household goods. Modern examples include laundry baskets, towels and coffee. Even a very practical present can belong to a ceremony with deep historical meaning.

passages.title: Families, witnesses and remarkable craftsmanship
passages.text: Coppers are worked copper sheets shaped somewhat like shields and associated with exceptional wealth and power. U’mista explains that prestige includes the ability to distribute possessions at a potlatch. A valuable object therefore carried significance through its history and public relationships, not simply through the metal’s weight.

passages.title: Families, witnesses and remarkable craftsmanship
passages.text: A transformation mask in the American Museum of Natural History tells part of the G̱wawa̱’enux̱w story of Siwidi. A dancer appears as a sculpin, then a sea raven, before the mask opens to reveal a human face. Carving and movable parts help turn an ancestral story into unforgettable theatre.

passages.title: Families, witnesses and remarkable craftsmanship
passages.text: A carved feast dish in the same exhibition served oily foods including fish. Its opening for dispensing oil evokes a whale’s blowhole, while its design recalls Siwidi and undersea beings. A serving vessel could be both a useful piece of dining equipment and a carefully shaped carrier of family history.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: The provincial museum’s 1953 report describes Mungo Martin’s house with cedar boards, substantial timber framing and carved posts bearing hereditary family crests. Its design followed an older house at Fort Rupert, at a smaller scale. The building expressed particular family rights as well as the carpenter’s knowledge of wood.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: Kingcome’s tidal flats supported cultivated root gardens. Research coauthored by Clan Chief Adam Dick documents family plots and boundaries, some marked by wooden stakes and others remembered in relation to mountain peaks. These were worked and known places, although colonial officials often dismissed Indigenous cultivation when taking land.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: Adam Dick returned to the Kingcome root grounds with younger people in organized harvests in 1999, 2005 and 2008. His own family had taken him there as a child despite settler appropriation. Teaching where and how to gather linked practical food knowledge with continuing claims to an ancestral place.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: In the 1870s, a fish saltery helped draw ’Namgis people from their village on the Nimpkish River to Alert Bay. A mission, school, sawmill and colonial administration followed. U’mista’s history shows how jobs, institutions and pressure from newcomers reshaped where families lived.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: The ’Namgis salmon-enhancement project began in 1978. The fisheries agency’s 2015 account describes different incubators and rearing systems for chum, sockeye, coho and Chinook. Managing fish involved detailed knowledge of their life stages, with goals including food, ceremonial use and rebuilding salmon populations.

passages.title: Homes, gardens and working waters
passages.text: Contemporary housing has its own continuing work. At Fort Rupert, the Kwakiutl Housing Department coordinates repairs, renovation and new construction, and participates in emergency planning. This is one named community’s present-day housing system within the wider Kwakwaka’wakw world.

passages.title: Suppression, return and living words
passages.text: Canada outlawed potlatching in 1884. After Dan Cranmer’s 1921 gathering at Village Island, prosecutions in 1922 forced families to surrender ceremonial possessions or face imprisonment. The ban was removed in 1951, but recovering objects scattered through museums and private collections required decades more work.

passages.title: Suppression, return and living words
passages.text: Cultural centres at Cape Mudge and Alert Bay opened in 1979 and 1980 to receive returning treasures. Returns have taken different forms: U’mista’s 2020 newsletter describes a sun mask arriving on long-term loan in July 2019. The care and study of these objects continues in communities whose families remember their loss.

passages.title: Suppression, return and living words
passages.text: Art also moves into new materials. A Burke Museum exhibition records Charlie James and his granddaughter Ellen Neel painting crest figures in watercolor in 1927. It also includes Doug Cranmer’s 1992 River Monster silkscreen. Named artists and family teaching connect these works with a history of continuing invention.

passages.title: Suppression, return and living words
passages.text: Artist Cheryl Wadhams describes beginning formal Kwak’wala study in 2016 after promising her aunt she would learn. Among her first phrases was “dagans dlu t'sigwanu,” which she translates as “Socks & eggs.” It is an attested modern sample with a pleasingly everyday combination: getting dressed and breakfast in one small phrase.

passages.title: Suppression, return and living words
passages.text: Wadhams identifies connections to ’Namgis, Ma’amtagila and Mamalilikulla through her family. She recalls learning carving and design from her uncles, and describes traditional names, dances and positions held by herself, her husband and sons. Her account makes cultural learning a continuing family responsibility across generations.

The map’s 1650 endpoint does not end Kwakwaka’wakw history. Distinct nations and families continue their communities, ceremonies, language learning and care for returning treasures after generations of colonial suppression.

passages.text: Kyivan Rus was a changing network of rulers, towns and rural communities centered on Kyiv. Its builders made monumental churches, its craftspeople worked precious metals, and some residents sent wonderfully ordinary messages on birch bark. Its cultural inheritance reaches across present-day Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. These two map intervals cover different political phases: especially after the early twelfth century, a broad Rus label includes increasingly independent regional powers.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Princes governed networks of towns and dependent villages rather than neat modern provinces. Harvard’s cultural mapping project stresses that both internal and external boundaries changed. A colored outline is therefore a rough guide to a complicated political world.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Households depended on grain, livestock, fishing and hunting. Forests supplied materials and fuel.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: The Ruskaia Pravda collected rules about injury, property, debts and witnesses during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Surviving manuscripts are later copies, and scholars disagree about the dates of individual versions. This was a developing legal tradition, not one untouched book handed down from a single ruler.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Legal compensation differed with social rank. Enslaved people and people bound by debt lived alongside free householders and powerful elites. The beautiful objects in museums cannot tell us that everyone shared the same wealth or freedom.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Inheritance rules distinguished commoners, nobles and widows. Family relationships shaped who could receive property; wills could be spoken before relatives. Sorting out who got the family possessions was already serious business. These rules describe legal expectations, not every family’s actual behavior.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Saint Sophia in Kyiv preserves eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes, including the Virgin Orans with raised arms. Byzantine masters and local builders contributed to the cathedral under Yaroslav. The art makes religious teaching visible through images as well as words.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: The cathedral’s surrounding complex includes much later baroque buildings. A visitor can therefore see several historical periods at once. The eleventh-century mosaics and the later additions should not all be assigned to Yaroslav’s lifetime.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: A finger ring attributed to Kyiv and dated 1000-1200 combines silver, gilded silver and dark niello decoration. The Metropolitan Museum interprets its crosses as signs of Christian faith. This small object connects skilled metalwork with the beliefs of a particular wearer, whose name is unknown.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Gold and enamel jewelry now in the Metropolitan Museum came from Kyiv hoards discovered in 1842 and 1906. The 1842 find lay in the old apse of the Church of the Tithes. These objects reveal elaborate ornament, but their later sale and dispersal complicate efforts to reconstruct the original groups.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Pekarska’s research followed old reports and collections to reconnect scattered treasures. Some pieces had disappeared or been melted down. Knowing where an object was found can matter as much as knowing how brightly it shines.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Birchbark document 591 from Novgorod’s Nutny excavation is an alphabet dated approximately 1025-1050. Its opening letters are “а б в г д е ж”. Someone was practicing the building blocks of writing. The surviving exercise does not identify the learner’s age or prove that every child attended school.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Evidence for women’s schooling is fragmentary. An encyclopedia account associates Anna Vsevolodivna with a girls’ school at Saint Andrew’s convent in late-eleventh-century Kyiv. It is evidence of a particular institution, not universal access to education.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Manuscripts, inscriptions and birchbark documents preserve different parts of literate life. Monastic copying helped transmit books, while private letters preserve business and personal concerns. Many surviving manuscripts cannot be dated to a single year.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: In letter 246, dated roughly 1025-1050 with a possible later shift, Zhirovit complains to Stoyan that a debt has gone unpaid for nine years. The whole letter survived in Novgorod’s Nerevsky excavation. Chasing an overdue payment clearly predates email.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Letter 752, from Novgorod around 1100, complains about an unanswered invitation and asks for a reply. Its broken passages admit more than one reading, and its precise date is debated. Even with those gaps, the disappointment sounds familiar: messages had feelings attached long before phones did.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: A later Novgorod letter, number 227, addresses the writer’s mother and discusses payments and property. It dates to about 1160-1180, after Novgorod had gained political autonomy. It illustrates family dealings in the wider Rus cultural world, not continuing government from Kyiv.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Here is a short Old East Slavic sample in Cyrillic from that actual birchbark letter: “водае семоу :в: гривьне”, meaning “give this person two grivnas.” The letter в between marks represents the number two. The words come from document 227, not a modern phrase translated backward into medieval spelling.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Archaeologists have found eleventh-century wooden bathhouses in Novgorod. A specialist history also records late-eleventh-century masonry baths in Kyiv and Pereyaslavl, following Byzantine traditions. Warm washing places required fuel, water and labor as well as a building.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Bathhouses tell us about washing, but the sources used here do not establish the toilet arrangements of a typical Rus home. A bath is not automatically a bathroom with a flushing toilet. Household sanitation deserves its own evidence.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Orthodox tradition remembers Agapitus of Kyiv’s Cave Monastery as a healer using vegetables and prayer in the eleventh century. The church’s retelling is a saint’s life, with miraculous events. It shows how healing and holiness were linked in religious memory; it does not demonstrate that a remedy cured a particular illness.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Stories about the Cave Monastery also require careful dating. The first Kyivan Cave Patericon collection arose between 1215 and 1230, drawing on earlier traditions; surviving versions are later still. A story about an eleventh-century monk is not necessarily an eyewitness record written in his lifetime.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After Mstyslav’s death in 1132, regional rulers increasingly pursued their own interests. Kyiv remained important, but shared dynastic ancestry did not mean constant political unity.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Novgorod’s revolt in 1136 increased its autonomy. Its assembly and elected officials mattered, although wealthy families exercised great influence. Calling it a republic does not mean everyone had equal political power.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Kyiv was sacked in 1169 during conflict among Rus princes. Fragmentation involved destructive warfare as well as shifting political loyalties.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After these map intervals, the 1240 siege devastated Kyiv and the Church of the Tithes was destroyed. Surviving art, manuscripts and later traditions nevertheless show cultural continuities. Political defeat and destruction did not erase the people or everything they knew.

Rus political unity weakened gradually as regional principalities grew more independent. The map cutoffs at 1100 and 1200 are coverage boundaries, not extinction dates. Kyiv suffered Mongol conquest in 1240, while communities and cultural traditions continued across the region.

sectionTitles: A busy town with very different homes
A mirror, a shield and extraordinary craft

passages.text: La Tène names a widespread Iron Age archaeological culture and artistic tradition, conventionally about 450 to 50 BCE. It included many peoples, not one empire. This record’s 700 to 500 BCE interval is too early, and its small northern French outline cannot represent the wider culture.

passages.title: Farms, grain and everyday work
passages.text: At La Salmondière in Brittany, a farming estate developed from around 250 BCE. Curving enclosures surrounded small buildings supported by posts or foundation trenches. This local example puts cultivated land and household work beside the more familiar story of Iron Age warriors.

passages.title: Farms, grain and everyday work
passages.text: The same excavation identified a granary carried on four posts from the late Gaulish period. Postholes can reveal the shape of a wooden building long after its walls vanish. A few dark marks in the soil may be what remains of a household’s food store.

passages.title: Farms, grain and everyday work
passages.text: At Bibracte, hand mills ground wheat into flour for everyday meals. Producing flour was a task before cooking could even begin. Bread did not start as a tidy bag from a shop; somebody had to work the stone mill first.

passages.title: A busy town with very different homes
passages.text: Metalworkers lined the main street near Bibracte’s Rebout gate. One excavated bronze workshop specialised in fibulae, the fasteners used to hold clothing together. A small dress fitting could connect a household’s daily needs with the work of a skilled specialist.

passages.title: A busy town with very different homes
passages.text: Mount Beuvray has many springs. At the Saint-Pierre spring, excavation revealed a basin dating to the first century BCE, now evoked by a modern reconstruction. Water collection belonged to the town’s practical landscape; the feature should not be confused with a modern tap.

passages.title: A busy town with very different homes
passages.text: A rich resident’s enormous house at Bibracte, built near the town’s abandonment, had mosaics, wall paintings, baths, wastewater drainage and underfloor heating. These Roman-style comforts belong to a late, wealthy household. They do not prove that every earlier family had its own bathroom.

passages.title: A mirror, a shield and extraordinary craft
passages.text: The Desborough mirror from Britain, dated broadly from 50 BCE to 50 CE, used polished bronze for its reflective face. Its back carries intricate engraved curves and textured patterns. This later regional example shows that La Tène art could accompany personal grooming as well as warfare.

passages.title: A mirror, a shield and extraordinary craft
passages.text: The mirror was assembled from a cast handle, a bronze plate and a binding strip around the edge. Its maker may have planned the decoration with compasses. Both faces required skill: one had to reflect an image, while the other was an artwork in its own right.

passages.title: A mirror, a shield and extraordinary craft
passages.text: The Battersea shield facing combines shaped bronze sheets, concealed rivets and 27 red glass studs. Its makers raised the flowing decoration from the metal. Only the decorative metal front survives, not the original wooden shield behind it; the surviving object is beautiful but incomplete.

passages.title: Words that survive
passages.text: A gold coin attributed to 52 BCE bears “VERCINGETOR[IX]”, the name Vercingetorix in Latin letters. The brackets mark letters restored by the catalogue editor. This is an actual name on money, not a newly invented Gaulish sentence or a translation of what the pictured person was saying.

passages.title: Words that survive
passages.text: Gaulish inscriptions survive from the final years of the third century BCE onward, with later examples continuing under Roman rule. They provide direct evidence of language alongside Greek and Roman accounts. A surviving inscription proves someone wrote it; it does not establish that every child attended a writing school.

passages.title: Public memory and changing communities
passages.text: At the Swiss site of La Tène, weapons and other remains have inspired different explanations. The Laténium’s recent display presents a reconstructed monument celebrating warrior values in the third century BCE. This is an interpretation of a difficult site, not a surviving eyewitness description of a single ceremony.

passages.title: Public memory and changing communities
passages.text: Bibracte belonged to a wider growth of fortified towns in the late second century BCE. Workshops, homes and public spaces reveal places where people met and organised work. Within roughly a century of Bibracte’s foundation, Roman expansion had changed the political setting and the town was abandoned.

There was no single La Tène kingdom to fall. Conquest and changing settlement patterns reshaped different regions at different times. Bibracte’s abandonment is one local example, while the later British mirror shows that artistic traditions did not stop everywhere at one fixed continental date. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is much too early.

sectionTitles: Learning about electricity, then arguing over the bill
Water for drinking, and waste to keep out
A city that read and wrote back

passages.text: This Lagos record’s 1878 to 1914 window covers a port city already under British colonial rule, following annexation in 1861. It is not the founding date of Lagos or a period of independent kingship. Yoruba residents, Atlantic returnees, merchants, artisans and journalists helped shape the city as colonial government expanded around them.

passages.title: People and a changing port
passages.text: Forest products replaced enslaved people as the leading exports, but slavery’s history remained visible in the population. Returnees and descendants of people taken across the Atlantic arrived from places including Brazil and Sierra Leone. Their skills, religious institutions and connections helped make Lagos a major commercial centre.

passages.title: Houses worth looking up at
passages.text: Older Yoruba houses commonly arranged rooms around a courtyard. The Afro-Brazilian sobrado offered another plan: several storeys, decorated stucco walls, elaborate windows and a central hallway linking rooms. Wealthy clients adopted this style, giving returning craftspeople a busy market for their building skills.

passages.title: Houses worth looking up at
passages.text: Andrew Thomas’s Ebun House, built around 1913, was so impressive that a nickname described people losing their caps while craning their necks to admire it. That joke comes from the historical account, not our imagination. The mansion made its owner’s success visible from the street.

passages.title: Houses worth looking up at
passages.text: The Shitta Bey Mosque opened in 1894. Its design adapted forms familiar from Brazilian churches for Muslim worship, and Catholic craftspeople helped construct it. Architecture records cooperation across religious lines as well as a prosperous Muslim community’s ambitions and connections.

passages.title: Learning about electricity, then arguing over the bill
passages.text: Electricity entered Lagos classrooms before it entered ordinary street lamps. The CMS Grammar School taught scientific subjects, and an 1865 public lecture explained electricity and telegraphy with experiments. Learning about a new technology did not have to wait for a power station to arrive.

passages.title: Learning about electricity, then arguing over the bill
passages.text: Residents wanted electric light but disputed a proposed house tax to finance it. African representatives, newspaper writers and protesters helped defeat that funding plan in 1895. Their objection was about who should pay; it was not simply rejection of the technology.

passages.title: Learning about electricity, then arguing over the bill
passages.text: Electric street lights were operating by February 1898 after trial runs. African residents also obtained lighting in homes and religious buildings, although cost affected access. The system changed city evenings through both public lamps and private decisions about whether a household could afford a connection.

passages.title: Water for drinking, and waste to keep out
passages.text: Nineteenth-century households relied on springs and wells, despite living beside a lagoon and the sea. Some wells were contaminated by sewage from nearby cesspools. Getting water was only half the problem; keeping human waste away from it mattered just as much.

passages.title: Water for drinking, and waste to keep out
passages.text: In 1882, the colonial surgeon proposed covering wells, fitting pumps instead of lowering buckets on strings, and paving the ground around them. These were concrete ways to reduce contamination. Officials disputed the expense, so a sensible recommendation did not automatically become a working improvement.

passages.title: Water for drinking, and waste to keep out
passages.text: Just after this map window, the Iju waterworks were formally commissioned on 1 July 1915. The scheme included public fountains and fire hydrants. A water network could supply a drink and help firefighters, but access expanded unevenly rather than reaching every resident at once.

passages.title: A city that read and wrote back
passages.text: The Lagos Times of the early 1880s usually had four pages, about half occupied by advertisements and notices. Editorials, readers’ letters and local news filled the rest. Its pages mixed public arguments with the everyday business of selling things and announcing events.

passages.title: A city that read and wrote back
passages.text: “Iwe Irohin Eko” means “The Newspaper of Lagos.” Andrew Thomas began this Yoruba-English paper in 1888, charging twopence a copy. This Latin-script title follows the unaccented transcription in historian Nozomi Sawada’s study. It shows Yoruba readers demanding a place in the city’s print culture.

The 1914 endpoint marks incorporation into the larger colonial state of Nigeria, not the disappearance of Lagos. Nigeria became independent in 1960. The city’s families, businesses, languages and institutions continued through those political changes, while its colonial history remained part of a much longer urban story.

passages.text: Later Liang was the first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel who deposed the last Tang emperor, it controlled only part of northern China and faced constant military threats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kaifeng developed as the capital, though smaller and less cosmopolitan than Tang Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Five Dynasties period saw the rise of military strongmen who dominated politics.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Printing technology continued to develop during this unstable period.
Li Cunxu of Later Tang conquered Later Liang and captured its capital Kaifeng in 923.

passages.text: Latvia declared independence in 1918. Its interwar republic redistributed farmland and built universities, factories and public markets. Parliamentary democracy ended in the 1934 coup. Occupation in 1940 destroyed practical independence, although the Latvian state continued to exist in international law.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: The 1922 constitution gave voting rights to qualifying Latvian citizens of both sexes over 21. The first Saeima election drew more than 800,000 voters. Voting was a new way to shape the country, although the 1934 coup later closed parliament.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Land reform between 1920 and 1937 broke up large holdings. Land entered a State Land Fund and was redistributed to other residents as private property. For families receiving land, the republic’s decisions changed who controlled the fields and the future of a farm.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: The University of Latvia began in 1919 with nine faculties, including medicine, engineering, chemistry, agriculture and architecture. Veterinary medicine joined in 1920. Training people to design buildings, treat patients and care for farm animals belonged to the same effort to build a new state.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: In 1920, Riga’s new medical faculty received a former Orthodox seminary building. It became the Anatomikum, later housing anatomy, physiology, hygiene, microbiology and other departments. Students also learned in city hospitals, including the children’s hospital. Medical education needed laboratories and real clinical practice.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Riga’s radio service officially opened on 1 November 1925 with a transmission of Puccini’s opera Madame Butterfly. Experimental broadcasts had begun in October. A performance in the opera house could now reach listeners through a radio receiver, giving live music a new route into people’s homes.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: VEF in Riga began industrial production of Walter Zapp’s Minox camera in 1938, following his Tallinn prototype. Tallinn’s Photography Museum preserves an early Riga-made example with serial number 118 and its leather case. Making a tiny camera reliably was a factory achievement as well as an inventor’s idea.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Riga’s Freedom Monument was unveiled on 18 November 1935. Residents’ donations financed Kārlis Zāle’s monument to independence and those who had died fighting for it. Granite and copper turned a public fundraising effort into a lasting landmark.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Riga’s new Central Market opened in 1930 under roof structures reused from German Zeppelin hangars. Engineers used only their upper sections and built lower brick and concrete supports. Keeping the enormous original height would have made indoor temperatures difficult to manage. Even a market roof had to think about the groceries.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: The market combined electric lighting and central heating with an extensive basement network. Passages below the pavilions helped move and store goods away from the bustle above. Shopping depended on a less visible working world beneath the stalls.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Ķemeri’s state-funded hotel opened in 1936 with hydrotherapy rooms on its ground floor, allowing the resort to offer treatments throughout the year. Museum postcards show mud being collected and baths being prepared. These were historical treatment practices; the hotel’s architecture and equipment reveal the investment behind them.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Ķemeri also hosted major chess tournaments in 1937 and 1939 to attract visitors. A health resort could sell peaceful surroundings, social life and the excitement of a match. The spectators’ hearts may have raced even when the players remained firmly seated.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latvian, article 1 of the constitution adopted in 1922: “Latvija ir neatkarīga demokrātiska republika.” Translation: “Latvia is an independent democratic republic.” The sample follows the official 1993 republication of the earlier constitutional text.

The USSR occupied and illegally annexed Latvia in 1940. Nazi occupation followed, then Soviet rule returned during the war. Latvia retained legal state continuity and restored full independence in 1991. The map’s 1945 endpoint is not the date independence was first lost.

passages.text: Latvia restored full independence in 1991 after decades of occupation. The renewed parliamentary republic joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014. Its recent history includes new public institutions, converted scientific equipment and communities keeping local traditions alive.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: On 18 January 2014, thousands of people formed a human chain to pass books from Latvia’s old National Library building to its new home. The ceremonial move made readers part of the opening celebrations. A book could cross the city with a remarkable number of helping hands.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: The library’s People’s Bookshelf invited readers to donate a book with a personal note on its title page. Donated volumes were displayed in a glass wall rising through several floors. The collection preserves people’s attachments to books as well as the books themselves.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: At Irbene, former Soviet military intelligence antennas gained a scientific future after Russian troops withdrew in 1994. Researchers established a radio astronomy centre using dishes 32 and 16 metres across. Equipment once associated with secrecy became part of international efforts to study the universe.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: Irbene’s later telescope upgrades included extremely cold radio receivers to help measure faint signals. A research paper reports one part operating at 14 kelvin, close to absolute zero. From October 2015 the upgraded 32-metre telescope took part in joint international observing sessions.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: MikroTik was registered in Latvia in 1996 and develops networking products including routers, switches and wireless systems. These devices help move information between computers. Latvia’s modern technical work therefore includes the ordinary-looking boxes that let other people’s computers talk to each other.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Riga’s Daugavgrīva wastewater plant began operating in 1991. Sewage passes through mechanical cleaning before biological treatment using activated sludge, and a laboratory checks the treated water. Flushing a toilet starts a journey that needs pipes, pumps and a great deal of organized work.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Daugavgrīva’s equipment was upgraded in 1999, including aeration, screens and grit traps. Further biological treatment improvements followed in 2014. A functioning modern city depends on repeated investment in this hidden infrastructure, even when its residents rarely think about what happens after the flush.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: The Suiti community in western Latvia combines Catholic religious traditions with older local customs and modern life. Its cultural identity includes distinctive dress, food, celebrations and women’s drone singing, in which a sustained vocal sound accompanies the melody.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: The Suiti Cultural Heritage Foundation, established in 2013, organizes informal learning for ages ranging from preschool children to seniors. Its work connects handicrafts, music, local speech and seasonal celebrations. Keeping a tradition alive involves opportunities to practise it together, rather than only storing it in an archive.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Latvia’s Song and Dance Celebration grows from rehearsals in local groups and community centres. Most participants are amateurs, guided by conductors and instructors. The large festival is the visible result of many smaller evenings spent practising with neighbours, friends and fellow singers.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: In 1998 Latvia added a fundamental-rights chapter to its constitution. It includes protection for minority communities’ languages and cultural identities. These rights matter in schools, cultural associations and family life in a country whose residents have several linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latvian, article 112 of the constitution’s modern rights chapter: “Ikvienam ir tiesības uz izglītību.” Translation: “Everyone has the right to education.” The quotation follows the Saeima’s Latvian consolidated text. This chapter was added in 1998, long after the original 1922 constitution.

Latvia continues as an independent republic. Its 1991 restoration renewed the state established in 1918; the map’s 1994 label marks later coverage. Membership in the European Union is a subsequent chapter in that continuing history.

passages.text: León was a medieval Iberian monarchy with cities, monasteries and institutions of learning. Royal women shaped its buildings and books. Although the atlas keeps León separate until 1279, its crown was permanently united with Castile under Ferdinand III in 1230.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: In 1188, Alfonso IX’s royal assembly included representatives of towns alongside nobles and church leaders. UNESCO recognizes the Decreta as an exceptionally early documentary witness to European parliamentary practice. This was medieval representation, not voting rights for every adult.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: The Decreta emphasized procedures for accusations, witnesses and legal disputes. Instead of settling every quarrel through private force, the king promised routes through recognized courts. Rules tell us what authorities wanted people to do, not that every dispute was handled fairly.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Sealed summons were part of the documented legal system. A seal helped turn a written order into an identifiable act of authority. The surviving Decreta tradition includes later copies as well as original documents, so not every manuscript was physically written in 1188.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Alfonso IX founded Salamanca’s schools in 1218. This was an institution for advanced study, not a compulsory school for every Leonese child. It continued after the union with Castile, showing how a political boundary can change while a school survives.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: The 1047 Beatus manuscript commissioned by Ferdinand and Sancha has 98 vivid miniatures. Its pictures illustrate a commentary on Revelation, including fantastic creatures. It is a later copy of a much earlier work, not the lost original written by Beatus.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Making that book required 317 parchment leaves, two columns of writing and coordinated illumination. The library cautiously associates its production with Facundus and perhaps San Isidoro. Those qualifications matter: a beautiful manuscript does not automatically reveal a securely identified workshop.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: Ferdinand and Sancha built a palace beside San Isidoro in the mid-eleventh century. Two rooms survive. In the twelfth century, Infanta Sancha Raimúndez adapted the former royal gallery as her own chamber and oratory, a concrete example of a royal woman shaping domestic and devotional space.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The same room later became a scriptorium used by the canons. Its visible sixteenth-century wall paintings belong to another phase. A room’s latest decoration should not be used to reconstruct what a twelfth-century resident saw.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The ivory crucifix donated by Ferdinand and Sancha in 1063 had a cavity behind Christ intended for a relic of the True Cross. It could be carried or mounted for display. Its carving connects skilled material work with public religious practice.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: On the crucifix, Latin names and titles read “FREDINANDVS REX / SANCIA REGINA”: “Ferdinand the king / Sancha the queen.” The inscription identifies a royal couple. It gives Sancha an explicit written presence in the gift rather than leaving the queen invisible.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The royal burial chapel’s fresco of the announcement to the shepherds depicts pastoral life in a biblical scene. It is useful evidence for how medieval artists pictured herding, but it is not a photograph of a particular Leonese farm.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: San Isidoro’s defensive tower reused part of León’s Roman wall and later became a bell tower. In one structure, we can see military fabric being adapted for a religious community. Reuse carried older urban materials into the routines of medieval life.

Ferdinand III united León and Castile permanently in 1230. León’s separate royal succession ended, but its institutions, settlements and regional identity continued within the larger crown. The atlas’s 1279 endpoint is later than this political union and must not be interpreted as a separate conquest.
