sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

sectionTitles: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
Political voice, peace and school life

passages.text: Liberia declared independence in 1847, before this map record begins. Its history joins indigenous African communities with settlers from the United States and their descendants. Republican promises coexisted with unequal access to power; later coups and civil wars were followed by peacebuilding in which women’s organizations played an important role.

passages.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
passages.text: The American Colonization Society helped establish settlements for free and formerly enslaved Black Americans on the West African coast. It was a private organization. The independent republic proclaimed in 1847 developed special U.S. connections, but was not simply a U.S. state overseas.

passages.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
passages.text: “a Free, Sovereign and Independent State” appears in the 1847 constitution’s preamble. This original English sample states the founders’ claim to govern their own republic. In plain language, they were declaring that another country should not rule them.

passages.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
passages.text: The constitution divided government into legislative, executive and judicial branches and protected publication and political discussion. Its written promises provide a way to ask how later governments treated rights in practice.

passages.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
passages.text: David McClellan’s 1850 map includes water-depth soundings near the coast and sketches of mountains. It also marks indigenous communities and new settlements. A map could help a ship approach land while recording the ambitions and interests of its makers.

passages.title: Statehood, maps and a writing sample
passages.text: Customs duties on traded goods supplied much of the early government’s revenue. Indigenous traders and British merchants disputed the colonization society’s authority to collect them. Arguments over ordinary cargo and taxes helped push the settlers towards independence.

passages.title: Hospitality made visible
passages.text: A Dan feasting spoon at the Metropolitan Museum has a handle carved as human legs and feet. Dated broadly from the nineteenth to mid-twentieth century, it belongs to an artistic tradition associated with Dan communities in Liberia and neighbouring Côte d’Ivoire.

passages.title: Hospitality made visible
passages.text: Such ceremonial ladles honoured women known for generous hospitality. A titleholder organized important meals and fed travellers; successful farming helped make that generosity possible. This was a spoon with social responsibilities far beyond stirring one person’s lunch.

passages.title: Political voice, peace and school life
passages.text: Indigenous people were brought into an indirect relationship with central government through local officials in 1904, and voting rights expanded in 1946. These changes show why independence in 1847 did not immediately give everyone an equal political voice.

passages.title: Political voice, peace and school life
passages.text: Leymah Gbowee helped bring Christian and Muslim women together in a nonviolent peace movement. Women demonstrated publicly and travelled to the 2003 talks in Accra to press negotiators towards agreement. Organizing across religious lines became a practical political achievement.

passages.title: Political voice, peace and school life
passages.text: Gbowee and Ellen Johnson Sirleaf shared the 2011 Nobel Peace Prize with Yemen’s Tawakkul Karman. The award recognized efforts for women’s safety and participation in peacebuilding. Women were shaping decisions about the country’s future, alongside caring for families affected by war.

passages.title: Political voice, peace and school life
passages.text: At D. Tweh Memorial School in New Kru Town, pupils joined handwashing activities in October 2025. One student described reminding people to wash after using the toilet. The everyday work of protecting classmates included speaking up as well as turning on a tap.

passages.title: Political voice, peace and school life
passages.text: In Zwedru, students marked the same handwashing day with drama, music and football. A lesson about soap could arrive through a performance or a game. UNICEF’s account records these specific activities as part of a wider effort to improve hygiene.

Liberia’s first republic ended in the 1980 coup, but Liberia itself continued. The 2003 peace agreement and later reconstruction brought further change; the UN peacekeeping mandate ended in March 2018. Its communities continue building institutions and everyday lives after the wars.

passages.text: The Libya entry begins in 1938 under Italian colonial rule. Independence came in 1951, followed by monarchy, the 1969 military takeover and the upheaval of 2011. Its people’s histories also run through oasis houses, schools, manuscripts and the difficult work of supplying water in a desert country.

passages.title: Statehood, power and its costs
passages.text: Italy had combined Cyrenaica, Tripolitania and Fezzan as the colony of Libya in 1934. The map’s 1938 starting point therefore lies within colonial rule, not at the birth of an independent Libyan state.

passages.title: Statehood, power and its costs
passages.text: The colonial settlement project followed violent repression. Historian Ali Abdullatif Ahmida describes forced marches and concentration camps in eastern Libya between 1929 and 1934, where hunger and disease killed many civilians. Families and communities carried memories that official colonial accounts tried to suppress.

passages.title: Statehood, power and its costs
passages.text: The 1951 constitution initially joined three provinces in a federal hereditary monarchy. Its first article says “ليبيا دولة حرة مستقلة ذات سيادة”: “Libya is a free, independent, sovereign state”. This Arabic sentence is a small original-language sample from the country’s independence-era document.

passages.title: Statehood, power and its costs
passages.text: Significant oil discoveries in 1959 greatly increased public wealth. The benefits were unevenly shared, contributing to resentment before the 1969 coup. An expanding national income is not the same thing as every family becoming equally prosperous.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: At Ghadamès, older houses stack functions vertically: stores below, family rooms above, and terraces at the top. Covered alleys pass beneath overhanging rooms. The town’s builders made shade and dense construction part of everyday desert living.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: Rooftop terraces historically offered women privacy and routes between houses, while covered spaces below served other public activities. UNESCO also notes that people now return to use the old houses and spaces without residing there permanently; the old town is not a snapshot of all modern Libyan housing.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: Ghadamès grew around the Ain al-Faras spring and surrounding palm groves. Local water management is recorded in manuscripts, linking written records with the practical task of sharing an essential resource.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: Mud bricks, palm wood and stone foundations are part of Ghadamès’s construction traditions. Repairing these buildings requires the continuing knowledge of local craftspeople; protecting heritage is also work with real materials.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: The Great Man-Made River carries ancient groundwater through buried pipes from the Sahara towards coastal cities such as Tripoli and Benghazi. Built in the 1980s and 1990s, it makes a distant underground water reserve part of daily urban life.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: NASA’s account explains why this is called fossil water: it accumulated under wetter past climate conditions. The Kufrah district now has no permanent rivers or lakes. Large pipes carry water stored underground long ago across a landscape that looks very different today.

passages.title: Homes, water and education
passages.text: Articles 28 to 30 of the 1951 constitution treated education as a right and made early schooling compulsory for boys and girls and free in state schools. These are documented legal commitments, not proof that every child immediately had a nearby classroom.

passages.title: Repairing lives and preserving knowledge
passages.text: After Storm Daniel’s devastating floods in September 2023, recovery work included reopening schools, restoring primary health care and maintaining water and sanitation networks. A country’s history includes these repairs to ordinary life as well as changes of rulers.

passages.title: Repairing lives and preserving knowledge
passages.text: Part of Benghazi University’s manuscript collection was recovered in 2017 after looting. University staff worked to classify and digitally record the documents with UNESCO support. Religious, literary and scientific works could then become accessible again rather than disappearing with the damage.

passages.title: Repairing lives and preserving knowledge
passages.text: UNSMIL’s December 2023 statement recorded the frustration of Libyans who had registered for elections planned for December 2021 but never held. This is a dated example of the unresolved transition after 2011, not a claim that political history stopped there.

Libya continues beyond the fall of the monarchy and Qadhafi’s government. Conflict and competing political projects have affected its institutions, while communities continue rebuilding schools, homes, water systems and cultural collections.

sectionTitles: A pocket-sized machine with a big job
What people made for other countries

passages.text: Liechtenstein is a small Alpine principality with a much longer history than this map record suggests. The principality dates from 1719 and became sovereign in 1806. Its mapped interval of 1994 to 2020 is a dataset window, not the country’s lifespan. Modern Liechtenstein combines a hereditary prince, elected institutions and internationally connected industries.

passages.title: A pocket-sized machine with a big job
passages.text: An earlier industrial success helped shape the modern country: the Curta mechanical calculator. Curt Herzstark brought his invention to Liechtenstein after surviving imprisonment in Buchenwald. The princely family founded the Contina company in 1946, and its Mauren factory was completed in 1948.

passages.title: A pocket-sized machine with a big job
passages.text: The smaller Curta was only 53 millimetres across and 85 millimetres high, yet could display an eleven-digit answer. The larger model extended that to fifteen digits. These were precision mechanical instruments small enough to carry, decades before pocket electronic calculators became ordinary.

passages.title: A pocket-sized machine with a big job
passages.text: Curtas came in protective tins. An advertising leaflet from about 1949 or 1950 pictured the calculator beside chess pieces to explain its size. Museum exhibits preserve prototypes, photographs and brochures, allowing us to follow an invention into factory production and customers’ hands.

passages.title: What people made for other countries
passages.text: After 1945, industrial production increasingly concentrated on specialised technology. Examples included Hilti fastening equipment, Hoval heating and air systems, and vacuum technology at Balzers. A small country could manufacture components and tools for projects far beyond its own borders.

passages.title: What people made for other countries
passages.text: Other industries served very different daily needs: precision mechanical parts, dental products, convenience food and electronic connectors. These examples help explain why modern Liechtenstein’s economy cannot be understood only through castles and banks. Workshops and factories were also central to its transformation.

passages.title: Education and family life
passages.text: In its 2018 United Nations review, Liechtenstein described vocational training and academic study as alternative routes for young people. Its dual education system connected education with preparation for skilled employment. Learning a trade was an established part of the country’s educational landscape.

passages.title: Education and family life
passages.text: A family-law change taking effect in January 2015 made joint custody the usual arrangement after separation or divorce. The same United Nations review discussed this change as a response to evolving family life and children’s rights.

passages.title: Education and family life
passages.text: An independent human-rights institution began operating in 2017. It incorporated the Ombuds Office for Children and Young People, which had existed since 2009. An ombuds office gives people a place to raise concerns about rights and treatment by institutions.

passages.title: Who could vote and serve?
passages.text: Women obtained the national vote in 1984, after proposals had failed in 1971 and 1973. The first woman entered parliament in 1986. These changes were therefore quite recent when the map’s modern record begins in 1994.

passages.title: Who could vote and serve?
passages.text: Voters approved enlarging parliament to twenty-five members in 1988. The upper and lower parts of the country elected fifteen and ten respectively. The parliament’s own history explains this arrangement as protection for the smaller Lower Country district.

passages.title: A short sample of German
passages.text: Article 2 of the 1921 constitution says state authority is anchored “im Fürsten und im Volke”, meaning “in the Prince and in the people”. This is the German wording in the consolidated constitutional text. The phrase captures the combination of monarchy and popular government.

passages.title: A short sample of German
passages.text: Article 6 identifies German as the state and official language. The constitution itself is consequently also an example of formal written German used in public life. Its legal vocabulary differs from the informal language that families use at home.
Liechtenstein continued beyond the map’s 2020 endpoint. Its long-established sovereignty and European economic links did not end when this imported record stopped.

passages.text: Tlingit homelands include coastal and inland communities connected through clans, trade and language. This broad imported coastal outline is not a single kingdom or a precise boundary. The examples here identify particular communities, especially the Kiks.ádi at Sitka and Huna Tlingit at Glacier Bay.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skill
passages.text: At Glacier Bay, clan histories connect particular places to ancestors, songs, crests and responsibilities. Gathering foods such as salmon, halibut, berries and gull eggs also maintains relationships with the homeland. A place that a visitor calls wilderness can be a deeply familiar family landscape.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skill
passages.text: Sitka Kiks.ádi families moved from winter villages to salmon-stream camps in summer. Some camp houses used bark or boards brought from winter houses; structures could serve as both dwellings and smokehouses. Seasonal moving could involve taking parts of the house along.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skill
passages.text: Elder Herbert Hope supplied a map of remembered fishing structures in 1993. Archaeologists later found a salmon gaff, woodworking tools and hand-forged nails near a depression. These finds supported the identification of a smokehouse location remembered through family knowledge.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skill
passages.text: Food storage was part of preparing for difficult seasons. At the Sitka site, archaeologists investigated depressions interpreted as possible food caches; a tree growing into one showed that the pit was already there around 1830. The interpretation combines the ground’s shape, artifacts and tree growth.

passages.title: Engineering and resistance
passages.text: Traditional wooden halibut hooks used a carefully shaped frame and barb. Sealaska Heritage explains that their proportions targeted medium-sized halibut while tending to spare very small and very large fish. The design depended on knowing how a halibut sucks food into its mouth.

passages.title: Engineering and resistance
passages.text: Tlingit artist Héendei Donald Gregory taught hook-making in a 21-part video series released in 2021. Lessons include preparing, naming and baiting hooks. A useful fishing tool can carry artistic and spiritual knowledge as well as instructions for getting dinner onto the line.

passages.title: Engineering and resistance
passages.text: Before the 1804 Russian attack, defenders built Shís’gi Noow beside shallow tidelands. The shallows kept heavily armed ships farther from the walls. Choosing the ground was part of the defense: geography could reduce an enemy’s advantage in cannon.

passages.title: Engineering and resistance
passages.text: The defenders repelled the first Russian landing, but the loss of reserve gunpowder made continued defense difficult. The Kiks.ádi withdrew on the Survival March. Families abandoned houses and possessions to preserve their community and continue resistance from another position.

passages.title: Engineering and resistance
passages.text: Withdrawal did not mean immediate submission. The Kiks.ádi blocked trade bound for Russian Sitka and dealt with American traders instead. In the early 1820s they rebuilt homes beside the Russian settlement, creating an uneasy neighborhood of trade, negotiation and competing claims.

passages.title: Language and a living homeland
passages.text: The 2009 Dictionary of Tlingit records “Gunalchéesh!” with the translation “Thank you!” This is an attested modern written sample, with its spelling and accent marks preserved. It should not be mistaken for an inscription left at the 1804 fort.

passages.title: Language and a living homeland
passages.text: The dictionary credits fluent speakers Anita Lafferty, John Marks, June Pegues and Helen Sarabia as its main language consultants. Preserving a language means listening carefully to knowledgeable people, including their examples, humor and differences in regional speech.

passages.title: Language and a living homeland
passages.text: The Huna Ancestors’ House at Bartlett Cove opened on 25 August 2016 after years of collaboration between the Hoonah Indian Association and the National Park Service. Carved screens and posts accompany a place for community gatherings, teaching and renewed connections with Glacier Bay.

The Russian settlement at Sitka and the 1867 transfer of Alaska did not end Tlingit people or their clan relationships. The modern Huna Tribal House is one example of continued cultural authority and community teaching. The map’s 1500 endpoint has no meaning as a national collapse.

sectionTitles: A wooden town that left detailed traces
Food, games and the evidence they leave
Rulers spoke to a wider world

passages.text: This record concerns medieval Lithuania, including the grand-ducal centres of Kernavė and Vilnius. It belongs to a world of timber towns, defended hills, workshops and diplomatic letters. Its 1400 map endpoint does not mark the end of the Grand Duchy or of Lithuanian communities.

passages.title: A wooden town that left detailed traces
passages.text: Wet deposits at Kernavė preserved wooden buildings, fences and objects of leather, bark and bone. Much of this material would decay in drier ground. Preservation gives an unusually close view of the thirteenth- and fourteenth-century town.

passages.title: A wooden town that left detailed traces
passages.text: Excavated yards combined a dwelling with workshops and other working buildings. Jewellers, smiths and bone workers occupied these spaces over generations. Home and workplace could share a fence line, so skilled production belonged inside neighbourhood life.

passages.title: A wooden town that left detailed traces
passages.text: Split-plank floors and clay ovens survived in Kernavė’s homes and workshops. Ovens provided heat and cooked food. A medieval household needed building skills and fuel before anyone could enjoy a warm room or meal.

passages.title: A wooden town that left detailed traces
passages.text: Conifer logs and plank roofs formed buildings assembled without nails; expensive forged iron details were rare. The modern open-air houses are research-based reconstructions, not medieval structures that somehow escaped seven centuries of weather.

passages.title: Food, games and the evidence they leave
passages.text: Researchers study animal bones from Kernavė to investigate livestock, meals and the relationships people had with dogs and horses. Remains from a princely residence can be compared with town deposits. An elite table should not automatically become everybody’s menu.

passages.title: Food, games and the evidence they leave
passages.text: An antler pawn only 1.85 centimetres tall came from a peat layer at Vilnius Lower Castle in 1988. The layer dates to the late 1300s or 1400s, crossing this map’s endpoint. Lathe turning helped produce its compact, regular shape.

passages.title: Food, games and the evidence they leave
passages.text: A taller antler object from the same excavation is interpreted as a possible king or queen. Its identification remains qualified. Even a tiny game piece requires careful comparison before archaeologists can confidently name it.

passages.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world
passages.text: Gediminas’s letter of 25 January 1323 invited merchants, farmers, craftspeople and clergy to come to Lithuania. The list shows what a ruler hoped newcomers would contribute. An invitation is evidence of policy, not a count of who actually arrived.

passages.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world
passages.text: In civitate nostra regia dicta Vilna means “In our royal city called Vilnius.” This Latin phrase is quoted from the 1323 letter by Lithuania’s National Library. It shows diplomatic writing about Vilnius, not the everyday language of every household.

passages.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world
passages.text: Kernavė’s five hill forts belonged to a larger settlement landscape, including homes, workshops and burial places. Viewing only the defensive hills would miss the people who supplied the settlement with food, goods and skilled work.

passages.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world
passages.text: In 1386 to 1387, Jogaila promoted Lithuania’s conversion, a bishopric at Vilnius and cathedral construction. These institutional changes did not instantly make everyone’s beliefs identical. A ruler’s religious programme and ordinary practice need separate evidence.

passages.title: Rulers spoke to a wider world
passages.text: During the 1390 attack on Kernavė, the nomination’s historical account says retreating defenders burned the castle. The old valley town was not rebuilt in the same form. Destruction changed this settlement; it did not extinguish Lithuania.

The Grand Duchy continued after 1400. The Union of Lublin in 1569 created a shared commonwealth with Poland, while Lithuanian institutions and communities continued within that arrangement. Kernavė’s local destruction and the atlas’s changing labels must not be mistaken for a national extinction.

sectionTitles: Independence and who had a voice
Building a capital and connecting homes
Families, music and lives across borders

passages.text: This record covers Lithuania’s interwar state and the wartime years included by the atlas. Independence was proclaimed in 1918, before the first 1920 snapshot. New institutions, modern buildings and broadcasting developed, but democracy was overthrown in 1926 and independence was lost to Soviet occupation in 1940.

passages.title: Independence and who had a voice
passages.text: The Council of Lithuania signed the independence act on 16 February 1918 in a rented Vilnius apartment. The building also housed a well-known pastry shop. A moment of national politics occurred amid ordinary commercial and residential life.

passages.title: Independence and who had a voice
passages.text: Atstatanti nepriklausomą means “restoring an independent…” These Lithuanian words come from the 1918 declaration, as quoted by the National Museum. The short excerpt belongs to a political document and uses Latin letters with Lithuanian diacritics.

passages.title: Independence and who had a voice
passages.text: The following day, women protested in Kaunas because none had been included in the Council that declared independence. The episode shows disagreement about whose participation counted, even during a celebrated founding moment.

passages.title: Independence and who had a voice
passages.text: Armed officers interrupted parliament during the December 1926 coup. Antanas Smetona became president, and the Third Seimas was dissolved in April 1927. Interwar statehood must therefore be distinguished from uninterrupted democratic rule.

passages.title: Building a capital and connecting homes
passages.text: Kaunas served as provisional capital from 1919 to 1939. Public buildings and homes expanded within an inherited street plan. Modernization involved adapting an existing town, rather than clearing a blank space and beginning again.

passages.title: Building a capital and connecting homes
passages.text: The New Town developed as an administrative centre, while Green Hill followed a garden-suburb plan from 1923. Their different streets and building patterns preserve contrasting ideas about where people should work, live and spend time outdoors.

passages.title: Building a capital and connecting homes
passages.text: Lithuanian radio began broadcasting from Kaunas on 12 June 1926. Hearing information and performances at home introduced a new daily rhythm. Access still depended on having or sharing a receiver; a national broadcast was not proof that every family listened.

passages.title: Building a capital and connecting homes
passages.text: The museum preserves a Philips Deutschland 456A radio made in 1936 to 1937. A receiver was both equipment and furniture. Its case and controls help make early broadcasting a household experience, rather than just a date in a communications timeline.

passages.title: Families, music and lives across borders
passages.text: The Hofmekler family moved from Vilnius to Kaunas in 1920. Several family members played different instruments, and Michelis helped organize early radio concerts. Their work documents a Jewish contribution to the city’s musical life through named people and surviving records.

passages.title: Families, music and lives across borders
passages.text: The National Museum estimates that about 104,000 people left Lithuania between 1918 and 1940, many heading to South America. An independent state could still have families separated by work and migration. Departure did not necessarily end their connections.

passages.title: Families, music and lives across borders
passages.text: Migrants also sent money and parcels home. The museum records substantial support from Lithuanian Americans during the first independence decade. Family networks crossed oceans and contributed to the resources available within the new state.

passages.title: Families, music and lives across borders
passages.text: The signatories’ museum preserves objects such as Aleksandras Stulginskis’s watch, carried through public service and later deportation. Personal possessions can connect official history with a life’s changes, but a famous person’s object is not a typical household sample.

passages.title: Families, music and lives across borders
passages.text: Soviet occupation in 1940 ended independent government. Nazi occupation followed in 1941, bringing the Holocaust to Lithuania; renewed Soviet rule followed in 1944. These were violent changes affecting real communities, not a peaceful sequence of map colours.

The Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in June 1940 and annexed it that summer. Nazi occupation and the Holocaust followed, then renewed Soviet rule. The atlas extends this label to 1945, but the independent interwar government had already ended. Lithuania’s people continued through persecution, resistance, exile and later restoration.

sectionTitles: Objects in a pocket and tools in a laboratory
Skills passed around a family and community

passages.text: This record represents restored independent Lithuania, not a state founded in 1994. Independence was re-established in March 1990, and a constitution followed in 1992. Scientific work, changing currency and living musical and craft traditions show different ways this society continued to develop.

passages.title: Restoring institutions
passages.text: On 11 March 1990, the Supreme Council adopted the act re-establishing the Lithuanian state. Soviet political and economic pressure followed. A declaration began a difficult process; it did not mean outside authorities immediately accepted the decision.

passages.title: Restoring institutions
passages.text: Soviet forces attacked broadcasting facilities in Vilnius in January 1991, killing civilian defenders. Remembering these events explains why broadcasting buildings became places of national memory. Public communication and the defence of institutions were closely connected.

passages.title: Restoring institutions
passages.text: Lietuvos valstybė yra nepriklausoma demokratinė respublika means “The State of Lithuania is an independent democratic republic.” This is Article 1 of the constitution approved in 1992, quoted from the official Lithuanian text. It is a written constitutional principle.

passages.title: Objects in a pocket and tools in a laboratory
passages.text: Lithuania adopted the euro on 1 January 2015, replacing the litas. Everyday prices, wages and cash payments moved to a different unit. Currency change is a practical household experience as well as a central-bank decision.

passages.title: Objects in a pocket and tools in a laboratory
passages.text: Lithuanian euro designs feature Vytis, the mounted figure from the national coat of arms, on their national side. Sculptor Antanas Žukauskas prepared the designs. A small circulating object can combine a shared European currency with a specifically Lithuanian symbol.

passages.title: Objects in a pocket and tools in a laboratory
passages.text: Vilnius University describes how the SYLOS laser system grew from experiments combining available components into a complex research instrument. Success required funding, testing and cooperation between scientists and companies. The story involves patient development rather than one sudden flash of inspiration.

passages.title: Objects in a pocket and tools in a laboratory
passages.text: The system helps researchers investigate matter and molecular processes. The university also trains new laser specialists. Claims about possible future medical uses should remain possibilities; a powerful laboratory tool is not automatically an available treatment.

passages.title: Skills passed around a family and community
passages.text: Sutartinės are multipart songs associated especially with northeastern Lithuania. Singers may enter at different times, interlocking their musical phrases. What sounds simple on paper requires careful listening to other people, not just remembering one’s own tune.

passages.title: Skills passed around a family and community
passages.text: The lyrics address subjects including work, weddings, family and historical events. UNESCO’s 2010 account describes women’s vocal traditions and instrumental versions often played by men. These are documented practices, not fixed rules for every Lithuanian musician.

passages.title: Skills passed around a family and community
passages.text: Sodai ornaments are assembled from prepared grain stalks into hanging geometric forms. Making one begins with the material: growing grain, choosing straw and treating it. A delicate decoration carries agricultural and craft knowledge inside its shape.

passages.title: Skills passed around a family and community
passages.text: Sodai may hang above a cradle or family table, expressing wishes for happiness and harmony. Makers teach within families and through workshops open to different ages. UNESCO’s 2023 description records a living practice, not proof that every home has one.

passages.title: Skills passed around a family and community
passages.text: After independence was restored, diaspora groups sent medicines, medical supplies and books to Lithuania. The National Museum’s migration account follows these networks. Family and community connections abroad could become practical support during institutional and economic change.

Lithuania continues as an independent state. Restoration in 1990, the constitution of 1992, European Union membership in 2004 and euro adoption in 2015 are distinct milestones. None should be replaced by the atlas’s 1994 starting snapshot or treated as an end to Lithuanian society.

passages.text: The Liu Song was the first of the Southern Dynasties, ruling from Jiankang. Despite political instability, this period saw significant cultural and intellectual achievements in the south.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi proposes the Daming calendar, the first in China to allow for the precession of the equinoxes.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi (429 to 500) bounds pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927, a precision not bettered anywhere for about nine centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The poet Xie Lingyun (385 to 433) develops landscape poetry as a major genre.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Southern culture developed distinctive characteristics that influenced later periods.
The last Liu Song emperor was deposed by Xiao Daocheng, who founded the Southern Qi dynasty.

passages.text: “Lombard duchies” is the map’s collective label for southern territories between 800 and 1000. Benevento, Salerno and Capua developed distinct political histories; this was not one unchanging country. Local evidence comes from courts, garrisons and monasteries, including the autonomous imperial abbey of San Vincenzo al Volturno on the frontier. The outline simplifies a much more complicated distribution of power.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: In 849, civil conflict ended in a division between Benevento and Salerno. The change created rival centers rather than replacing every local institution at once. Princes, bishops and abbots all held influence. The map’s neat colored area compresses a landscape of competing authorities and changing alliances.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: Capua’s cathedral history begins with a foundation attributed to Landulf in 856 and a dedication in 861. A church provided a place for worship and a public expression of authority in a growing political center. The cathedral was repeatedly rebuilt afterward, so today’s building is not an untouched ninth-century time capsule.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: San Vincenzo al Volturno stood between Lombard Benevento and Frankish territory. Charlemagne placed it under his protection in 787, and it remained an autonomous imperial institution after the division of 849. Its excavations illuminate life in this border region, without making the monastery an ordinary possession of a Lombard prince.

passages.title: Meals, washing and useful rubbish
passages.text: At San Vincenzo, a collective washing area called a lavatorium stood near the dining spaces. Monks washed hands and faces before meals. The site also preserves ninth-century kitchens and a large refectory. The lavatorium was a washroom, not a toilet: medieval building labels need translating as carefully as medieval words.

passages.title: Meals, washing and useful rubbish
passages.text: The abbey’s refectory measured about 31 by 11 meters. Archaeologists identified a main entrance for the monks on the west and access from the kitchens on the east. Feeding a community required planned routes for people and food. Even without a surviving menu, doorways reveal something about how dinner was organized.

passages.title: Meals, washing and useful rubbish
passages.text: Food waste from the ninth-century kitchen passed through a sloping drain toward the Volturno River. Fish bones recovered from its deposits included freshwater and marine species, such as tench and sea bass. The bones connect meals to different fishing environments. For an archaeologist, yesterday’s discarded dinner can become a particularly informative discovery.

passages.title: Meals, washing and useful rubbish
passages.text: Soldiers at Salerno’s Arechi Castle also needed dependable pots. Finds associated with garrisons from the late ninth to early eleventh centuries include ordinary cooking and storage vessels, generally made locally in repeated forms. This evidence extends a little beyond the map’s 1000 endpoint. Much of castle life involved keeping people fed, not standing dramatically on battlements.

passages.title: Crafts and stories
passages.text: Researchers analyzed 136 glass samples from ninth-century San Vincenzo and its workshops. Much of the glass had been made by remelting older Roman material, including mosaic cubes and window glass. Craftspeople turned old glass into colored decoration, vessels and windows. Recycling here involved heat, judgment and control of color, rather than simply putting fragments into a bin.

passages.title: Crafts and stories
passages.text: Excavations along the Volturno uncovered evidence of metalworking, including a furnace for casting bells dated to the eighth or ninth century. Making a bell required specialists to prepare a mold and handle molten metal. The discovery adds heavy workshop labor to the quieter image of a monastery devoted only to books and prayer.

passages.title: Crafts and stories
passages.text: The crypt associated with Abbot Epiphanius, who governed from 824 to 842, preserves painted Christian scenes, including the Annunciation and Nativity. These images helped create a setting for devotion and storytelling. The abbot himself appears in the decoration, linking a named person to a surviving ninth-century religious space.

passages.title: Crafts and stories
passages.text: A later written account, the Chronicon Vulturnense, was compiled around 1130 and tells the abbey’s earlier history. Its distance from the events matters: it preserves institutional memory, rather than reporting every ninth-century episode as an eyewitness diary. Archaeologists can compare such writing with the buildings, furnaces and food remains found underground.

passages.title: Spoken words reach parchment
passages.text: A judgment made at Capua in March 960 preserves a short vernacular phrase: “Sao ko kelle terre”, meaning “I know that those lands…” The document’s main language is Latin, but witness testimony was recorded in an early regional Italian form. This is a modern transcription of the surviving wording, not a reconstruction of the Germanic Lombard language.

passages.title: Spoken words reach parchment
passages.text: The case concerned land claimed by Rodelgrimo of Aquino and the abbey of Montecassino. Before Judge Arechi, witnesses supported the abbey’s possession of the property for thirty years. A practical argument over fields helped preserve some of the earliest famous Italian vernacular writing. Nobody had to invent a literary masterpiece to leave historians an important sentence.

passages.title: Spoken words reach parchment
passages.text: An attack in October 881 burned and badly damaged San Vincenzo. Surviving monks took refuge with the Lombard princes of Capua; rebuilding came later. This was a serious rupture for one community, rather than the end of all southern Lombard life. Monasteries and cities could have sharply different experiences in the same generation.

Southern Lombard rule continued beyond 1000. Salerno fell to Robert Guiscard in 1077, while Benevento’s final Lombard prince died that year and the city passed into papal government. The map label’s endpoint does not mark a shared collapse.

sectionTitles: New uses for old buildings and knowledge

passages.text: The map calls these territories “Lombard principalities,” but its 600 to 800 outline combines northern lands associated with the kingdom at Pavia and the southern duchies. They were not one continuous collection of equal, independent principalities. The narrative follows Lombard Italy and its local communities, with named examples beyond the map’s incomplete outline. Frankish conquest changed the northern monarchy in 774, while southern Lombard rule continued.

passages.title: Kings, dukes and public words
passages.text: Lombard forces entered Italy in 568 and gradually established a kingdom centered on Pavia. Dukes governed important territories, and the southern centers of Spoleto and Benevento could act with considerable independence. Byzantine rulers still held other parts of the peninsula. Travel between Lombard regions therefore did not mean traveling through one uninterrupted country.

passages.title: Kings, dukes and public words
passages.text: King Rothari issued a written collection of laws in 643. It used Latin but preserved some Lombard words. Compensation for injuries depended on the victim’s social position, so the same harm did not bring the same payment for everybody. Writing rules down made royal authority visible, while also recording the inequalities of the society.

passages.title: Kings, dukes and public words
passages.text: A tiny Latin sample appears on the bronze plaque associated with King Agilulf, now in Florence’s Bargello: “VICTURIA”, meaning “victory.” The early seventh-century object shows the ruler with armed attendants and winged Victory figures. Its lettering is evidence of Latin being used to proclaim Lombard kingship, not a sentence in the spoken Lombard language.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: A study of the sixth- to eighth-century cemetery at Collegno, near Turin, combined graves, ancient DNA and chemical measurements of human remains. Researchers reconstructed several related family groups and found that newcomers joined the community. The local elite developed from people with varied backgrounds. A grave’s ornaments alone cannot tell us someone’s entire identity.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: At Collegno, chemical evidence suggests meals containing plant foods and animal protein, with some people eating more millet than others. Close relatives sometimes had similar dietary patterns. The researchers found no significant dietary difference between the biological sexes in their sample. These are traces of one community’s eating, rather than a menu followed throughout Lombard Italy.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: Cividale, a major Lombard center in Friuli, supplies useful comparisons even where the imported outline misses it. Combs from local burials were made from animal bone and could have one or two rows of teeth. Carved bone hairpins helped hold up hair or secure a veil. Grooming left sturdy little traces after the hairstyles themselves disappeared.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: Bone also became entertainment equipment. Cividale finds include six-sided dice and playing counters, while pieces interpreted as parts of a game board survive too. The museum cautiously compares some possible games with draughts. We know people had the pieces; we do not have the full rulebook or the arguments about who cheated.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: Animal bones placed in some Cividale graves are interpreted as funeral food offerings, including pork, birds, sheep or goats, and shellfish. Such deposits reveal how mourners equipped the dead. They should not be treated as a shopping list showing what every family ate on an ordinary Tuesday.

passages.title: Families, food and small possessions
passages.text: At Cividale’s Gallo cemetery, women’s brooches and a weaving sword from grave 9 connect dress and textile tools with public status. The museum interprets the weaving sword as a mark of rank. A tool associated with making cloth could carry meaning beyond the workshop, much as an elaborate belt could do for a warrior.

passages.title: New uses for old buildings and knowledge
passages.text: At Torba, an old defensive tower became part of a women’s religious community in the eighth century. Nuns adapted rooms for burial and prayer. The surviving painted figures belong to a building used and altered over centuries. Reusing a fortress as a monastery changed the work done there without requiring every wall to be rebuilt.

passages.title: New uses for old buildings and knowledge
passages.text: In Benevento, Duke Arechis II founded Santa Sofia around 760 and placed a convent beside it under his sister Gariperga. Surviving fresco fragments tell Christian stories, including the Annunciation and Visitation. The complex joins a ruler’s family, women’s religious leadership and painters’ skill in one place that visitors can still study.

passages.title: New uses for old buildings and knowledge
passages.text: Education also connected distant courts. Paul the Deacon taught Adelperga, the daughter of King Desiderius, and followed her to Benevento when she married Arechis II. His work as a teacher and historian helped turn remembered events into written history. This is evidence for elite learning, not proof that every child could attend a school.

passages.title: New uses for old buildings and knowledge
passages.text: Charlemagne took Pavia in 774 and ended the rule of King Desiderius. Southern Benevento followed a different path and continued as a Lombard political center. The change in the northern crown did not erase the people, laws, buildings or skills described here. The map’s shared label should not give them all one identical ending.

The northern monarchy passed to Charlemagne in 774. Benevento’s Lombard rulers survived in the south, so this broad map category has no single disappearance date. Its 800 endpoint is a change in the imported map labels.

passages.text: Lombardy is a regional label here, not one continuous independent kingdom. The atlas assigns it changing patches around Mantua and other Lombard districts between 1650 and 1815. This card therefore presents dated examples from the region and names their local settings, rather than pretending that all belonged to the same ruler.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: Mantua’s last Gonzaga ruler departed in 1707, and Austrian government followed in 1708. Later administrative reforms tied Mantua more closely to Milan. These changes matter because a label reading “Lombardy” can conceal quite different local histories and arrangements of power.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: Bergamo’s great Venetian walls belong to a system of sixteenth- and seventeenth-century defences designed for the age of gunpowder. Projecting bastions changed the shape of a fortified city. They are evidence of military engineering and Venetian government, not proof of an independent Lombard kingdom.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: A 1721 land record identifies a Sulbiate parcel owned by Giovanni Cottica as cultivated land with vines. This is a rare chance to look below the level of princes at a specific piece of working countryside. The later silk mill on the site should not be projected backward into 1721.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: Mulberry growing and silkworm raising connected Lombard agriculture with textile production during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. The Sulbiate site’s history records that wider setting before its later industrial use. A silk economy needed leaves and living caterpillars as well as skilled workers and machinery.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: In 1715 a musician connected with the Polish court visited Stradivari’s Cremona workshop in connection with a commission for twelve violins. Fine instruments could move through international court networks. The workshop’s reputation was built from carefully made objects, not from a factory producing identical modern instruments.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: Surviving Cremonese workshop materials include moulds, drawings, clamps, gouges, planes, files and calipers. A form marked G is associated with the 1715 Cremonese violin. These objects show planning and measurement behind the finished instrument: music began with plenty of quiet, patient woodworking.

passages.title: Towns, fields and workshops
passages.text: The Cremonese violin’s label reads “Antonius Stradivarius Cremonensis faciebat anno 1715”: “Antonio Stradivari of Cremona made [it] in the year 1715.” This is the catalogue’s transcription of the actual Latin label, not a newly invented motto. Latin could advertise a maker inside a musical instrument.

passages.title: Books, performances and experiments
passages.text: Mantua’s Teresiana library opened to the public on 30 March 1780. A public library widened access beyond a private household’s shelves, although access to books still depended on literacy and circumstances. Its opening is a specific institutional achievement, not evidence that every child received schooling.

passages.title: Books, performances and experiments
passages.text: Mantua’s eighteenth-century scientific theatre hosted learned and civic gatherings as well as selected performances. Its 1767 contract excluded activities including gambling and acrobatics. “Scientific theatre” did not mean an auditorium full of laboratory benches: debate, ceremony and entertainment could share an architectural setting.

passages.title: Books, performances and experiments
passages.text: Bartolomeo Stefani’s L’arte di ben cucinare was printed at Mantua in 1662 and survives in a facsimile catalogued by the Warburg Institute. Its banquet material records elaborate culinary practice. A printed cookery book tells us about skilled cooking and display, not what every farming family ate each evening.

passages.title: Books, performances and experiments
passages.text: Volta’s battery, announced in 1800, stacked different metals with wet cardboard between them. Zinc, copper and salty moisture produced an electric current by chemical action. The key achievement was a continuing source of electricity, opening experiments that a brief spark alone could not sustain.

passages.title: Books, performances and experiments
passages.text: The 1815 imperial patent created the Kingdom of Lombardy-Venetia within the Austrian monarchy. The word “kingdom” on a document did not erase the region’s different towns, institutions or previous rulers. It marks a new governing arrangement after the upheavals of the French period.

The map’s 1815 endpoint coincides with the creation of Austrian Lombardy-Venetia, not the death of a single long-lived state called Lombardy. Regional communities and crafts continued under changed government. The imported polygons remain too inconsistent to assign one precise political identity throughout this entry.

passages.text: Colonial Louisiana connected Gulf settlements with the Mississippi valley through French claims, trade and settlement. Indigenous peoples, Africans and Europeans shaped its life under deeply unequal conditions. This map shows a limited Gulf-area slice; neither its outline nor its 1715 to 1783 dates represents the entire colonial territory or history.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: Excavations at Old Mobile, capital of French Louisiana from 1702 to 1711, have uncovered the sites of eight buildings and thousands of objects. These remains preserve an early phase before the map’s start, showing a colony made of particular settlements rather than continuous occupation across its vast claims.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: At Port Dauphin, the port serving French Mobile from 1702 to about 1725, archaeologists uncovered houses and a barrel well. A container made for storing goods could become part of a water-supply structure. Ordinary construction details help explain how a settlement functioned.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: Indigenous people taught settlers ways to prepare maize and supplied powdered sassafras, or filé, to thicken stews. Corn could be boiled, roasted or ground; treating kernels with lye produced hominy. Local knowledge helped newcomers turn unfamiliar ingredients into everyday meals.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: In 1718, colonial administrators sought rice from West Africa together with enslaved people knowledgeable about its cultivation. African expertise helped shape Louisiana’s food history, but it arrived through a system that forced people to labor far from their homes.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: New Orleans was founded in 1718 beside a bend of the Mississippi. Engineers laid out a regular street grid despite the surrounding swamps and risk of flooding. The plan survives in the French Quarter, a lasting trace of an ambitious and difficult urban project.

passages.title: Households, water and food
passages.text: After fires in 1788 and 1794, Creole townhouses became common in rebuilt New Orleans. Their courtyards contained service spaces, and toilets were typically separate privies at the rear. A handsome street-facing house could still require a trip outdoors for the bathroom.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: Twelve Ursuline nuns arrived in 1727 to establish a convent, care for the sick and educate girls. After the Natchez attack of 1729, they cared for widows and orphans of French soldiers. Their institution brought schooling and hospital work together.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: The Ursulines also enslaved African and Indigenous people who cooked, cleaned and worked in the hospital. White pupils received a broad education, while enslaved residents received religious instruction only. Care and learning existed within, and helped sustain, the colony’s unequal social order.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: French Louisiana repeatedly lacked enough coins. Scarcity of reliable small money complicated wages and purchases even when merchants had goods to sell. The Historic New Orleans Collection traces these problems through surviving monetary objects and administrative history.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: Banque Royale notes issued in France in 1719 to 1720 helped fuel speculative excitement about Louisiana. The museum preserves a hundred-livre note dated August 1719 and a fifty-livre note from September 1720. Promises printed on paper were tied to investors’ distant hopes for colonial wealth.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: “Les enfants qui naîtront de mariages entre esclaves seront esclaves” means “Children born from marriages between enslaved people will be enslaved.” This French sentence opens Article 9 of Louisiana’s 1724 Code Noir, in a published transcription. The law deliberately made enslavement hereditary.

passages.title: Education, money and written power
passages.text: France’s 1803 sale transferred its Louisiana claim to the United States after decades of Spanish administration. The transaction changed imperial control; it did not mean that Indigenous nations had freely sold their homelands. Colonial boundaries and the rights of people living within them were different matters.

French rule gave way through the 1762 to 1763 partition and Spanish administration; the western territory and New Orleans passed to the United States through the 1803 purchase and subsequent transfers. Communities continued under new governments. The imported 1783 endpoint is not a single end date for colonial Louisiana.

sectionTitles: Living with a river that spreads out
Things people made and words they wrote

passages.text: The Lozi kingdom brought together different peoples around the upper Zambezi floodplain in what is now western Zambia. Rulers, councils and skilled communities organized a landscape shaped by seasonal water. The map’s 1783 to 1914 interval is coverage, not the kingdom’s complete lifetime.

passages.title: Rulers, councils and political change
passages.text: Government had northern and southern centers: Namuso, eventually based at Lealui, and Lwambi, eventually based at Nalolo. The southern authority was subordinate, but this arrangement helped govern a long floodplain from more than one capital.

passages.title: Rulers, councils and political change
passages.text: People could take disputes to a local kuta, or court, and appeal to higher courts at a chief’s capital. Political life involved procedures and arguments over rights, as well as the commands of a king.

passages.title: Rulers, councils and political change
passages.text: Kololo conquerors introduced Sotho political and military practices and their language into the region. Their commerce included enslaved people and ivory, exchanged for imported cloth, beads and firearms. Their rule ended in 1864, but the linguistic influence lasted after their soldiers lost power.

passages.title: Rulers, councils and political change
passages.text: Lewanika strengthened kingship and expanded Lozi influence before colonial control became effective. His career involved rebuilding a state after succession struggles, not simply deciding how to respond to Europeans.

passages.title: Living with a river that spreads out
passages.text: Families built homes on raised mounds, adding soil to keep their living space above regular floods. Zambia’s 2009 heritage account describes continuing maintenance: even an island made by people needs occasional topping up.

passages.title: Living with a river that spreads out
passages.text: Canals served boats, drained waterlogged ground and connected settlements. The Mwayowamo canal, built between 1887 and 1889, linked Lealui and Limulunga and supplied water to Lealui. Moving water was a major public achievement.

passages.title: Living with a river that spreads out
passages.text: Fishing weirs called malelo held water as the flood receded. Opening a small gap directed escaping fish into a waiting basket. Dinner could depend on a carefully placed hole in a wall.

passages.title: Living with a river that spreads out
passages.text: Seasonal moves to higher ground became the celebrated Kuomboka journey. The king traveled from Lealui toward Limulunga with music and boats; other floodplain residents also relocated. The reverse journey had its own name, Kufuluhela.

passages.title: Things people made and words they wrote
passages.text: A Lozi basket dated about 1900 to 1920 is woven from makenge root fiber and pigment. At 62 centimeters long, it is a substantial container, with carefully balanced animal figures decorating its lid and sides.

passages.title: Things people made and words they wrote
passages.text: Lozi women made tightly coiled baskets to hold valuable goods. Under Lewanika, demand from missionaries and other outside customers expanded production and encouraged animal designs alongside older geometric patterns. Craftspeople responded creatively to a changing market.

passages.title: Things people made and words they wrote
passages.text: A wooden lidded dish attributed by the Smithsonian to King Lewanika carries two antelopes on its lid. Dated to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, it gives the ruler another role to consider: maker of beautifully carved objects.

passages.title: Things people made and words they wrote
passages.text: A short written Lozi expression is “minya mupu na ngombe”, translated as “the owner of land and cattle”. Nyambe Sumbwa’s 2000 study prints this description of the Litunga in Latin script. It expresses an idea about kingship, not an ancient inscription.

Treaties beginning in 1890 reduced royal independence under British colonial administration. The map’s 1914 endpoint is not the disappearance of the Lozi people or monarchy. Customary institutions continued, and the region became part of independent Zambia in 1964.

passages.text: Luba political life joined sacred kingship with council authority. Artworks could carry political knowledge, embody ancestral relationships, or serve highly practical purposes within elite daily life.

passages.title: Knowledge and memory
passages.text: Lukasa boards use carved forms or attached beads and shells to organize histories, genealogies and significant places. Their interpretation depends on trained specialists.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The mbudye association includes women and men who interpret political principles and can restrain or reinforce chiefly authority.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Female figures on royal seats, staffs and other court objects relate to ancestral kings and the sacred character of rule.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Carved headrests protected elaborate hairstyles while their owners slept. A nineteenth-century example repeats the hairstyle in the sculpture itself.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A headrest can create a strong sculptural composition with slender limbs and open spaces while still supporting the sleeper's head.

sectionTitles: A small state in a changing Germany
Homes hidden behind the grand streets
Older people, kitchens and household comforts

passages.text: Lübeck remained a small trading republic long after the medieval Hanse’s greatest days. This card follows the eighteenth- and nineteenth-century city, through French occupation, constitutional reform and German unification. The imported 1715 to 1878 dates are only map coverage. Its 1715 outline is grossly overbroad and must not be read as territory actually ruled by Lübeck.

passages.title: A small state in a changing Germany
passages.text: War reached the streets on 6 November 1806, when French troops fought Prussian forces led by Blücher at Lübeck. The French entered and plundered the city. Occupation continued until 1813, so the free-city label on a long timeline should not suggest uninterrupted independence.

passages.title: A small state in a changing Germany
passages.text: In 1820, Hamburg, Bremen, Frankfurt and Lübeck chose Lübeck as the home of their shared appeals court. These four surviving free cities cooperated on justice while keeping separate governments. A small state could supply an important institution to its neighbors.

passages.title: A small state in a changing Germany
passages.text: The upheavals of 1848 brought an elected parliament and opened civic citizenship to Jews. Civic citizens could participate, but citizenship and simply living in the city were different categories. The reform therefore widened political participation without giving every resident a vote.

passages.title: Homes hidden behind the grand streets
passages.text: Behind imposing merchants’ houses lay narrow alleys lined with tiny rented homes. These housing patterns had medieval roots and remained part of the later city. Porters, day laborers and craftspeople lived in one- or two-storey huts, often with only one room. A handsome street front could conceal a very crowded neighborhood.

passages.title: Homes hidden behind the grand streets
passages.text: Some alleys provided charitable housing. The von Höveln complex had been intended for poor or elderly people since 1483, but its surviving small houses date from a complete rebuilding in 1792. Giving an old foundation new buildings was one way the eighteenth-century city continued to care for selected residents.

passages.title: Homes hidden behind the grand streets
passages.text: Writing sample: a 1797 property record lists “Im Grünen Gang 4 Wohnsäale”, meaning “Four living quarters in the Green Alley.” This German wording is preserved in a modern archive transcription. Such plain inventories help historians recover rented living spaces that seldom appear in grand portraits or ceremonial histories.

passages.title: Older people, kitchens and household comforts
passages.text: The medieval Holy Spirit Hospital continued to house older and needy residents. In the early nineteenth century, wooden compartments were inserted into its great hall, giving residents small individual spaces. These were known locally as Kabäuschen. The institution had 170 places, and the last occupants did not leave these old compartments until 1970.

passages.title: Older people, kitchens and household comforts
passages.text: Care inside the hospital depended partly on property far outside its walls. Its foundation owned villages, farmland and estates, including holdings on the island of Poel. Income and accumulated assets helped pay for upkeep and expansion. The money behind a bed in town might begin with land in the countryside.

passages.title: Older people, kitchens and household comforts
passages.text: The Behnhaus, remodeled around 1800 and occupied by the Behn family from 1823, shows a wealthy household’s arrangements. An office and reception room faced the street, while a kitchen behind the main hall sent food upstairs by a small lift. Dinner could change floors without using the staircase.

passages.title: Older people, kitchens and household comforts
passages.text: Three connected salons occupied the first floor, with guest rooms and servants’ chambers higher up. Today’s green patterned wallpaper in the reception room is a reconstruction based on a surviving historical fragment. Conservators also uncovered layers of paint on the woodwork: even a wall can keep a household diary.

passages.title: Water, railways and something sweet
passages.text: The Wakenitz waterworks began operating in 1867. Steam engines lifted river water, sand filters cleaned it, and pumps sent it into a water tower. The combined machinery and filtration made water supply a city-scale engineering task. It required much more than finding a river and hoping for the best.

passages.title: Water, railways and something sweet
passages.text: Railways changed Lübeck’s links with other ports. The line through Büchen was completed in 1851 after opposition from Denmark, which controlled surrounding territory. A direct railway to Hamburg opened in 1865. Routes and neighboring governments mattered to merchants as much as the goods sitting in their warehouses.

passages.title: Water, railways and something sweet
passages.text: Johann Georg Niederegger took over a confectionery business in 1806 and moved into his own premises on Breite Straße in 1822. The firm’s records connect Lübeck’s famous sweet-making tradition with a particular shop and family business. Marzipan history has room for actual shopkeepers as well as tempting legends.

Lübeck continued as a German constituent state beyond the map’s 1878 cutoff. Its statehood ended in 1937 under the Greater Hamburg legislation, when it was incorporated into Prussian Schleswig-Holstein. The city itself continued.

passages.text: Lunda rulers adapted aspects of Luba kingship while maintaining their own political independence. Trade routes and relationships with neighboring courts supported the movement of materials, artistic forms and political ideas.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: By 1650, Mwaant Yaav Naweej had connected his capital with Atlantic trade. This commerce included enslaved people as well as forest products.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Lunda outposts participated in copper exchange, while settlements near Lake Mweru linked the interior with eastern commercial routes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rulers commissioned artists from client peoples, including Chokwe carvers, to make prestigious court objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Accounts of Chibinda Ilunga describe a founding culture hero. They are traditions of legitimacy, not a dated eyewitness biography.

passages.title: Music and memory
passages.text: In related Chokwe court art, a chief holds a lamellophone associated with historical recitation and praise. The object shows how music and political knowledge could meet.
