passages.text: Lusatian culture is an archaeological label for related communities of the Late Bronze Age and Early Iron Age across parts of central Europe. It does not identify one kingdom or a securely named ancient people. The map’s 700 to 500 BCE window shows only part of this longer history.

passages.title: A wooden neighbourhood
passages.text: Biskupin’s island settlement contained 106 houses arranged in thirteen rows, separated by timber-covered streets. A street also ran around the perimeter. The layout shows substantial planning and cooperation: building a whole neighbourhood required more than one enthusiastic person with an axe.

passages.title: A wooden neighbourhood
passages.text: Its rampart used timber boxes filled with earth, sand and stones. Slanting stakes on the lake side helped break waves and ice. Water provided protection but also threatened the buildings, so the settlement’s engineering had to deal with both people and the lake.

passages.title: A wooden neighbourhood
passages.text: A bridge provided access through a gate. The familiar tower seen at the museum today is hypothetical; the ancient wall’s original height is unknown. Reconstructing a settlement helps us imagine living there, but some parts necessarily go beyond what survived underground.

passages.title: What plants can tell us
passages.text: A study of six Bronze Age sites in the Carpathian foothills, including Janowice and Tworkowa, identified seeds, fruits and wood. Common millet was the most widespread cultivated cereal in these Lusatian assemblages. Small surviving seeds can reveal an important food crop without preserving the finished meal.

passages.title: What plants can tell us
passages.text: The same research examined weeds and discarded firewood. Weeds help identify cultivated and disturbed ground; wood reflects the trees available around settlements. Such scraps connect meals and fuel gathering with the landscape beyond the houses, rather than showing village life as a collection of isolated pots.

passages.title: What plants can tell us
passages.text: Reading Museum’s account of Lusatian farming includes cattle and pigs among the principal domestic animals. Their bones help distinguish livestock keeping from hunting. Meat came through the work of raising animals, and the balance of foods should not be assumed identical at every settlement.

passages.title: Children and very small pots
passages.text: An excavation near Muskau recorded a child’s urn with twenty-six beads lying in a row, probably once threaded as jewellery. Such a find preserves something personally meaningful alongside the burial. It cannot tell us the child’s name, but it keeps an individual life in view.

passages.title: Children and very small pots
passages.text: A miniature clay scoop from a burial at Bielsko is less than two centimetres high. The National Museum in Lublin discusses two possibilities: a toy, or a small symbolic version of an everyday vessel. It would fit a pretend kitchen beautifully, but that does not prove how it was used.

passages.title: Children and very small pots
passages.text: Small clay discs from Lusatian sites have also prompted debate. Suggested uses include toys, spindle whorls, pottery-finishing tools and ritual objects. This is a useful archaeological puzzle: the same shape can serve different purposes, and finding a round object does not automatically solve the mystery.

passages.title: Learning from the surviving traces
passages.text: The first estimates of Biskupin’s age changed as research improved. Tree-ring analysis eventually identified a great concentration of timber cut in winter 738/737 BCE. A wooden beam can act like a calendar, provided its sequence of growth rings can be matched to a dated reference.

passages.title: Learning from the surviving traces
passages.text: Early researchers brought different specialists into Biskupin’s investigation, including people studying animals, plants, landforms and building design. This matters because a pot, a fish bone and a wooden post answer different questions. Understanding daily life depends on putting those clues together.

passages.title: Learning from the surviving traces
passages.text: The cited finds do not provide a securely identified written sentence in a Lusatian language. We should not turn marks on pottery into a made-up alphabet or assign a modern nationality to their makers. Craftsmanship and careful construction survive here much more clearly than spoken words.

Lusatian traditions changed unevenly as new regional patterns appeared. Around Bełchatów, some finds combine traits called Lusatian, Pomeranian and Cloche-Grave, making a clean replacement difficult to describe. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is not a known extinction or the fall of a single state.

passages.text: Luxembourg’s name covers a duchy ruled within larger dynastic empires and, from 1815, a grand duchy. Partition in 1839, the fortress settlement of 1867 and the end of its personal union with the Netherlands in 1890 changed its territory and institutions. The earliest map polygons should not be read as the borders of today’s independent country.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: A Boch teapot made at Septfontaines between 1767 and 1786 survives in the national museum’s collections. Its earthenware body carries blue decoration inspired by Chinese designs. It is a precise household object, showing how local manufacture participated in international fashions.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: The 1843 school law made German and French part of primary education. This helps explain why language history cannot be reduced to one language per country. A child might meet different languages at home, in lessons and in official writing.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: Luxembourg’s iron industry depended on minette, local iron ore. Exploiting those deposits reshaped southern places such as Esch, Schifflange and Dudelange. Mines, furnaces and workers’ settlements made industrial geography quite different from the view of a country made only of castles.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: The railway connection to Thionville opened in 1859, linking Luxembourg more closely to surrounding markets. Railways served heavy industry as well as travelers. Their arrival also became a literary event: a steam locomotive could inspire a poem, not just a timetable.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: In 1911 several major iron and steel enterprises combined to form ARBED. The merger illustrates the scale of the industry that had developed from local ores and cross-border transport. It was an industrial organization, not the beginning of metalworking in Luxembourg.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: Nineteenth-century families also left Luxembourg for France and the Americas. Genealogists must follow these journeys and the effects of shifting borders in the archives. Family history can be international even when the village where a story began is very small.

passages.title: Homes, language and work
passages.text: The compulsory sickness-insurance law of 31 July 1901 covered workers against illness. It drew on a German insurance model under government supervision. This was an important step toward organized social protection; it should not be described as universal modern healthcare arriving all at once.

passages.title: Public life and independence
passages.text: The 1867 international settlement required the fortress to be dismantled and the Prussian garrison to leave. Walls that had dominated the capital gave way to new possibilities for urban growth. A diplomatic agreement thus changed the space available to people walking around the city.

passages.title: Public life and independence
passages.text: German troops occupied Luxembourg in August 1914, with its railways and steel making it strategically important. National institutions remained, but occupation constrained the country. This was not the same political situation as normal peacetime independence.

passages.title: Public life and independence
passages.text: Women received voting rights in 1919 and participated in the referendum on monarchy and economic alignment. Voters favored keeping the monarchy and preferred economic union with France; the eventual agreement instead linked Luxembourg with Belgium in 1921. Votes and diplomatic outcomes did not line up perfectly.

passages.title: Public life and independence
passages.text: At local fairs, musicians perform the Hämmelsmarsch while collecting contributions. The melody’s beginnings are uncertain, but Michel Lentz supplied nineteenth-century lyrics. It is a social tradition with identifiable later evidence, not something we can confidently project into every earlier century.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Luxembourgish, Michel Lentz’s railway poem De Feierwon (1859): “De Feierwon dén as berêt”. Translation: “The fire wagon is ready.” Here the fire wagon is the steam train. The government’s literary booklet reproduces this historic spelling; it is not a phrase reconstructed from modern Luxembourgish.

Luxembourg continues as a grand duchy. Its connection to the Dutch crown ended in 1890, while German occupation in both world wars interrupted sovereignty without permanently ending the state. The surviving country is smaller than the historic duchy because of earlier territorial partitions.

sectionTitles: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
Carving, memory and a documented removal

passages.text: Māori communities maintained distinct iwi and hapū histories through trade, technological change and colonisation. This card follows named examples of food production, fishing, carving and language education. The imported map endpoints do not mark an end to Māori society.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: A study of seven ancestors from Tamahere site S14/487, dated about 1700 to 1780, found diets predominantly based on plants. Archaeological context supports cultivated root crops as important foods. Isotopes do not identify each meal, and this small sample cannot describe all Māori diets.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: The teeth of two children in the Tamahere study preserve a changing dietary signal consistent with weaning onto plant foods within their first two to three years. This is a finding about those children, not a universal rule for childhood across iwi.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Te Papa’s pā kahawai lure OL000106/10, dated broadly to 1750 to 1850, combines a shaped and polished pāua-shell shank with a shell barb and tightly bound muka fibre. Fine notches decorate the shell. It preserves several stages of skilled manufacture in one small fishing implement.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Kākahu provided warmth and protection, while particular cloaks also expressed status and relationships. Their continued use as esteemed gifts and at funerals connects material workmanship with honour, care and ancestral memory. Everyday use and ceremonial importance should not be treated as interchangeable.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In the early 1840s, carvers led by Raharuhi Rukupo created Te Hau ki Tūranga at Orakaiapu pā, Manutuke. The whare whakairo belongs to Ngāti Kaipōhō of Rongowhakaata. Its carved ancestors and memorial purpose joined artistic work to hapū history and relationships.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In 1867 Crown troops dismantled Te Hau ki Tūranga and removed it despite objections. Rukupo recorded that he had refused requests to give it up. This documented removal is part of the building’s history alongside its artistry.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: The Rongowhakaata settlement deed signed in 2011 acknowledges the wrongful taking of Te Hau ki Tūranga and records the Crown’s apology. The account recognises the harm caused by separating the taonga from its community.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Treaty signed in 1840 survives in texts with different meanings. The Māori text speaks of kāwanatanga in Article 1 and guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga in Article 2; the English text uses sovereignty. Treating these as identical obscures the historical disagreement.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863 enabled land confiscation from communities labelled rebellious. Confiscation also took land from Māori who had remained neutral or supported the government. The effects differed by region, with severe losses in Waikato and Taranaki.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki connects seasonal knowledge with remembrance and sharing the harvest. Communities observe it in different ways and at different times. Its significance joins practical attention to the year with relationships among the living and the dead.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Pukeatua kōhanga reo opened in Wainuiomata in April 1982. The movement places children in Māori-language immersion environments and gives whānau responsibility for running centres. Education here includes language, relationships and cultural knowledge transmitted through daily life.

Māori have no cultural fall date. Colonial war and confiscation transformed landholding and political authority, while communities persisted. Te Tiriti remains central to the history of their relationship with the Crown. Kōhanga reo exemplifies continuing whānau-led work to pass language and knowledge to future generations.

sectionTitles: Baths, exercise and hopes for health

passages.text: This map label fits Antigonid Macedonia and the network of Greek allies led by its kings around 200 BCE. The late-third-century Hellenic alliance was a coalition, not one uniformly governed country. The imported outline also sweeps across islands and places whose relationships with Macedon varied. Its 200 to 100 BCE interval extends beyond the monarchy’s defeat in 168 BCE.

passages.title: Kings and partners
passages.text: Antigonus Doson’s alliance, formed around 224/223 BCE, grew from cooperation with the Achaean League against Sparta. Historian Graham Shipley describes it as a means of exercising power through other political communities. Its members retained identities and institutions of their own; a single map colour cannot display all those relationships.

passages.title: Kings and partners
passages.text: A treaty fragment from Dion records Philip V and the people of Lysimacheia promising not to ally with enemies of the other party. Oaths invoked gods, including Zeus and the gods of Samothrace. The broken inscription preserves a real negotiated relationship behind the map’s broad label.

passages.title: Kings and partners
passages.text: Polybius explains how several ranks of long pikes projected ahead of a Macedonian phalanx. He also stresses its need for suitable ground and the danger of losing formation. This was coordinated work by many soldiers, whose effectiveness depended on terrain and teamwork rather than weapon length alone.

passages.title: Markets and records
passages.text: Pella’s Agora combined buying, selling, production and administration around a large central court. Excavators found workshops alongside shops and official premises. The capital’s marketplace was a working neighbourhood as well as a space where people met.

passages.title: Markets and records
passages.text: Sawn animal bones help identify butcheries in Pella’s Agora. Other rooms contained narrow jars for perfumes and aromatic oils. Excavated rubbish and containers let archaeologists distinguish businesses whose signs and shopkeepers’ voices have disappeared.

passages.title: Markets and records
passages.text: Clay sealings from papyrus documents were found in Pella’s city archive. The fragile writing materials have not all survived, but the seals preserve traces of organised paperwork. Running a kingdom required records as well as royal speeches.

passages.title: Markets and records
passages.text: A silver drachma of Philip V in the Walters Art Museum, catalogued to 220 to 179 BCE, carries ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΦΙΛΙΠΠΟΥ, “of King Philip”. This is an attested ancient Greek coin legend, given in modern transcription. The tiny inscription put royal authority into everyday circulation.

passages.title: Baths, exercise and hopes for health
passages.text: Pella had a public bath in use from the last quarter of the fourth century to the end of the second century BCE. A channel for heating beneath the floor was added toward the end of that span. The warm-floor improvement belongs to the later building history, not automatically to Philip V’s reign.

passages.title: Baths, exercise and hopes for health
passages.text: Researchers interpret one room in the palace palaestra as a training space with suspended leather bags filled with sand. They were something like punching bags. The complex served the royal household and its young attendants, so this evidence describes courtly training rather than a school available to every child.

passages.title: Baths, exercise and hopes for health
passages.text: A votive inscription from the first half of the second century BCE identifies a Pella sanctuary with Darron, a deity associated with prayers for sick people. This is evidence of seeking divine help in illness. It does not establish that the sanctuary’s rituals could cure disease.

passages.title: Baths, exercise and hopes for health
passages.text: The sanctuary complex included courtyards, a horseshoe-shaped fountain and a cistern. Excavators also recovered figurines and a small altar in a room used for offerings. Water, gathering places and gifts all formed part of the setting in which worshippers sought help.

passages.title: Religion and learning in public
passages.text: At Dion, a marble dedication names Philip V as a donor to Zeus Olympios. It was later reused in a house. The king’s name dates the inscription only to his reign, 221 to 179 BCE; its exact occasion is unknown. The fragment shows royal participation in an important Macedonian sanctuary.

passages.title: Religion and learning in public
passages.text: An earlier Hellenistic tomb at Pella, dated to the early third century BCE, shows figures interpreted as philosophers and a central man with a celestial sphere. The sphere has prompted an identification as an astronomer. This older monument records an interest in intellectual identity before the map’s selected period.

Rome defeated King Perseus at Pydna in 168 BCE and ended the Antigonid monarchy. Macedonia was reorganised, and a Roman province followed in 148 BCE. Cities, workshops and religious life continued after the royal government disappeared. The map’s 100 BCE endpoint should not be mistaken for the end of an independent Macedonian kingdom.

sectionTitles: The details that help a child learn
A name changes, a state continues

passages.text: North Macedonia is the modern state that became independent from Yugoslavia in 1991. Its imported map begins in 1994 and should not be confused with the ancient Macedonian kingdom or the wider geographical region. Its communities combine inherited crafts and performances with modern schools, museums and institutions.

passages.title: A dance learned together
passages.text: Kopachkata is a social dance from Dramche in the Pijanec region. Dancers form a semicircle and hold one another’s belts, with crossed arms. The shared formation requires people to coordinate their movement, rather than each dancer choosing an independent route across the floor.

passages.title: A dance learned together
passages.text: The dance moves from walking into small quick steps and more energetic movements. In its digging figure, the left foot repeatedly strikes the ground while the dancer balances on the right. The name and footwork make sense together when the dancers disturb the dust.

passages.title: A dance learned together
passages.text: Experienced dancers guide beginners, who can watch the steps and gradually take more demanding positions. Weddings and public or religious celebrations provide occasions to perform. The practice passes on movement, music and a way of taking part in community gatherings.

passages.title: A museum built from solidarity
passages.text: Skopje’s Museum of Contemporary Art grew from international solidarity after the 1963 earthquake, before the present republic became independent. An artists’ association called for donated works to help the city rebuild its cultural life. The collection preserves that response across later political changes.

passages.title: A museum built from solidarity
passages.text: The museum opened its new building in 1970, providing a permanent home for the collection. Earlier exhibitions had occupied rented space downtown. Building a museum required rooms, conservation and organisation alongside the generosity of artists who sent their work.

passages.title: A museum built from solidarity
passages.text: Its early programme included the graphic work of Picasso and exhibitions of Pop Art alongside Macedonian and other Yugoslav artists. Local artists encountered different ways of making images through these displays. The institution became a meeting point for national and international art.

passages.title: The details that help a child learn
passages.text: In a 2024 UNICEF interview, Hristina described how visual displays and assistive technology helped her autistic daughter learn in a mainstream school. The example shows how the arrangement and equipment of a classroom can matter as much as the lessons written on a timetable.

passages.title: The details that help a child learn
passages.text: Educational assistants receive guidance from resource centres, including teaching materials, exercises and advice from mentors. These centres developed from former special schools after changes in education policy. Their role is to help children participate in regular school communities.

passages.title: The details that help a child learn
passages.text: Hristina also described cooperation between teachers and parents, and regular review of her daughter’s support. She stressed that suitable education should be a right rather than a matter of luck. This is one family’s account of progress and continuing needs.

passages.title: Macedonian writing in a pocket
passages.text: An official banknote specification records the Macedonian words “десет денари”, meaning “ten denars”. They are printed in Cyrillic on the ten-denar note. This small sample comes from a documented modern object used for payment, rather than an invented greeting.

passages.title: Macedonian writing in a pocket
passages.text: The same banknote design uses an ancient marble torso as its main image and tiny repeated letters among its security details. Modern printing turns a cultural object into an image many people can handle. The ancient sculpture and the modern currency belong to different historical periods.

passages.title: A name changes, a state continues
passages.text: The agreement with Greece resolved the country’s international name dispute, with the relevant procedures completed in February 2019. North Macedonia joined NATO in March 2020. These were diplomatic changes in a continuing state, not the creation of a new population.
The republic continues under the name North Macedonia. The 2019 name change altered its official designation, while its communities, institutions and independent statehood continued.

sectionTitles: A basket with a carefully dressed outside
A new cloth that learned from old cloths
When medicine had a transport problem
School equipment includes toilets and game pieces
A family outing can be a performance lesson
A poet in the struggle for independence

passages.text: Madagascar’s history includes coastal food crops, highland weaving and many local traditions. These examples belong to particular places and communities, rather than one timeless island-wide culture.

passages.title: Tiny grains, long journeys
passages.text: Charred rice from early deposits at Mahilaka gives a glimpse of food at a northwestern port established around the tenth century. A 2016 study found rice dominating the sampled food-crop remains. The grains connect meals with wider Indian Ocean movements of crops; they do not identify the ancestry of each person who ate them.

passages.title: Tiny grains, long journeys
passages.text: Researchers recovered these fragile plant traces by processing soil in water and catching material in fine sieves. Under microscopes, they compared seeds with reference specimens. A grain too small to notice while digging can become evidence for what people grew or ate. Burnt dinner occasionally has a very long research career.

passages.title: A basket with a carefully dressed outside
passages.text: A Madagascar basket and lid made around 1900 have two woven layers sewn together. The outer layer is finer, with purple, blue and green patterns; the British Museum tentatively identifies the material as palm leaf. Its construction shows makers combining plaiting, sewing and colour. The collection record does not tell us what its owner kept inside, so snacks remain a tempting guess, not an archaeological discovery.

passages.title: A new cloth that learned from old cloths
passages.text: Martin Rakotoarimanana’s 1998 silk mantle, now at the Metropolitan Museum, renews a Merina textile tradition. Weavers studied historic cloths preserved in the British Museum, then made new works rather than exact copies. This is a case of learning from objects: a museum collection can help skilled makers recover techniques and develop their own designs.

passages.title: A new cloth that learned from old cloths
passages.text: The patterned tradition uses extra loom controls to raise selected threads and create bands of decoration. Some motifs draw on local trees and flowers. Producing such cloth takes planning as well as patient handwork: the design has to become an arrangement of threads. The museum associates these costly historical textiles with Merina elites, not everyone’s everyday wardrobe.

passages.title: When medicine had a transport problem
passages.text: The Institut Pasteur de Madagascar’s history describes a practical obstacle in the 1890s: vaccines sent from Paris could lose activity during the long journey. A local vaccine institute was established in 1898, and its first smallpox vaccine doses were produced in November 1899. Making medicine close to where it was needed was part of the challenge, alongside knowing how to make it.

passages.title: When medicine had a transport problem
passages.text: Producing rabies vaccine took longer because of technical difficulties. The institute records its rabies service opening on 6 January 1901. The two dates show why establishing a laboratory and getting each service working are different milestones. This account concerns one institution’s development, rather than the beginning of all medical knowledge or care in Madagascar.

passages.title: Learning beneath the jacarandas
passages.text: A 2022 university magazine traces higher education through earlier medical, law, science and humanities schools to the University of Madagascar in 1961. Its editorial also describes students relaxing beneath flowering jacarandas on the Ambohitsaina campus. Institutions have formal dates, but student life includes much more ordinary moments: a patch of shade between lessons belongs in the story too.

passages.title: School equipment includes toilets and game pieces
passages.text: At Iabomary in southeastern Madagascar, a 2021 UNICEF report describes new school latrines, handwashing facilities and ceramic classroom water filters. Eight-year-old Eliane said that washing her hands also kept her books cleaner. Teachers learned to include hygiene in the school day. A better place to learn needs practical facilities as well as desks and lessons.

passages.title: School equipment includes toilets and game pieces
passages.text: A 2024 UNICEF report follows pupils in southern Madagascar playing iKa’lio in two teams. The board game helps girls and boys discuss periods, school toilets and support from adults. A girls’ club and a parent-teacher committee continue the conversations. Learning about growing up can involve moving game pieces and asking questions, rather than trying to work everything out alone.

passages.title: A family outing can be a performance lesson
passages.text: Hiragasy combines song, dance and speech in public performances from Madagascar’s central highlands. UNESCO describes a usual structure with drumming, greetings, stories, dancing and songs, often involving two troupes. The words explore civic and moral questions as well as entertaining listeners. A gathering can be a show and a conversation about how people live together.

passages.title: A family outing can be a performance lesson
passages.text: Children can learn hiragasy by travelling with their parents and joining performances. Family participation passes on timing, stories and ways of speaking to an audience. It is a form of education through doing and listening. For some children, following the family on tour also means learning how to help put on the show.

passages.title: A poet in the struggle for independence
passages.text: Jacques Rabemananjara was among the Malagasy deputies imprisoned after the events of 1947. His long poem Antsa expressed attachment to his island and hopes for freedom. In a 2016 commemorative speech, France’s president acknowledged the violent repression and honoured its victims. Literature and later public remembrance are part of this history alongside official changes of government.

French colonial rule ended with Madagascar’s independence on 26 June 1960. The island’s communities continued through that change and later political transformations. The older map intervals ending in 1914 and 1938 are breaks in this map’s coverage, not dates when Madagascar’s people disappeared.

In a 2016 commemorative speech, France’s president acknowledged the violent repression and honoured its victims. Literature and later public remembrance are part of this history alongside official changes of government.

French colonial rule ended with Madagascar’s independence on 26 June 1960. The island’s communities continued through that change and later political transformations. The older map intervals ending in 1914 and 1938 are breaks in this map’s coverage, not dates when Madagascar’s people disappeared.

passages.text: Madagascar’s history includes coastal food crops, highland weaving and many local traditions. These examples belong to particular places and communities, rather than one timeless island-wide culture.

passages.title: Tiny grains, long journeys
passages.text: Charred rice from early deposits at Mahilaka gives a glimpse of food at a northwestern port established around the tenth century. A 2016 study found rice dominating the sampled food-crop remains. The grains connect meals with wider Indian Ocean movements of crops; they do not identify the ancestry of each person who ate them.

passages.title: Tiny grains, long journeys
passages.text: Researchers recovered these fragile plant traces by processing soil in water and catching material in fine sieves. Under microscopes, they compared seeds with reference specimens. A grain too small to notice while digging can become evidence for what people grew or ate. Burnt dinner occasionally has a very long research career.

passages.title: A basket with a carefully dressed outside
passages.text: A Madagascar basket and lid made around 1900 have two woven layers sewn together. The outer layer is finer, with purple, blue and green patterns; the British Museum tentatively identifies the material as palm leaf. Its construction shows makers combining plaiting, sewing and colour. The collection record does not tell us what its owner kept inside, so snacks remain a tempting guess, not an archaeological discovery.

passages.title: A new cloth that learned from old cloths
passages.text: Martin Rakotoarimanana’s 1998 silk mantle, now at the Metropolitan Museum, renews a Merina textile tradition. Weavers studied historic cloths preserved in the British Museum, then made new works rather than exact copies. This is a case of learning from objects: a museum collection can help skilled makers recover techniques and develop their own designs.

passages.title: A new cloth that learned from old cloths
passages.text: The patterned tradition uses extra loom controls to raise selected threads and create bands of decoration. Some motifs draw on local trees and flowers. Producing such cloth takes planning as well as patient handwork: the design has to become an arrangement of threads. The museum associates these costly historical textiles with Merina elites, not everyone’s everyday wardrobe.

passages.title: When medicine had a transport problem
passages.text: The Institut Pasteur de Madagascar’s history describes a practical obstacle in the 1890s: vaccines sent from Paris could lose activity during the long journey. A local vaccine institute was established in 1898, and its first smallpox vaccine doses were produced in November 1899. Making medicine close to where it was needed was part of the challenge, alongside knowing how to make it.

passages.title: When medicine had a transport problem
passages.text: Producing rabies vaccine took longer because of technical difficulties. The institute records its rabies service opening on 6 January 1901. The two dates show why establishing a laboratory and getting each service working are different milestones. This account concerns one institution’s development, rather than the beginning of all medical knowledge or care in Madagascar.

passages.title: Learning beneath the jacarandas
passages.text: A 2022 university magazine traces higher education through earlier medical, law, science and humanities schools to the University of Madagascar in 1961. Its editorial also describes students relaxing beneath flowering jacarandas on the Ambohitsaina campus. Institutions have formal dates, but student life includes much more ordinary moments: a patch of shade between lessons belongs in the story too.

passages.title: School equipment includes toilets and game pieces
passages.text: At Iabomary in southeastern Madagascar, a 2021 UNICEF report describes new school latrines, handwashing facilities and ceramic classroom water filters. Eight-year-old Eliane said that washing her hands also kept her books cleaner. Teachers learned to include hygiene in the school day. A better place to learn needs practical facilities as well as desks and lessons.

passages.title: School equipment includes toilets and game pieces
passages.text: A 2024 UNICEF report follows pupils in southern Madagascar playing iKa’lio in two teams. The board game helps girls and boys discuss periods, school toilets and support from adults. A girls’ club and a parent-teacher committee continue the conversations. Learning about growing up can involve moving game pieces and asking questions, rather than trying to work everything out alone.

passages.title: A family outing can be a performance lesson
passages.text: Hiragasy combines song, dance and speech in public performances from Madagascar’s central highlands. UNESCO describes a usual structure with drumming, greetings, stories, dancing and songs, often involving two troupes. The words explore civic and moral questions as well as entertaining listeners. A gathering can be a show and a conversation about how people live together.

passages.title: A family outing can be a performance lesson
passages.text: Children can learn hiragasy by travelling with their parents and joining performances. Family participation passes on timing, stories and ways of speaking to an audience. It is a form of education through doing and listening. For some children, following the family on tour also means learning how to help put on the show.

passages.text: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.
The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.

sectionTitles: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today

passages.text: Makkura is the map’s name for Makuria. Its capital, Dongola, grew around a fortified centre beside the Nile. Houses, churches and workshops reveal a city of builders and makers as well as rulers.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: House A at Old Dongola had a bathroom with heated water and painted walls, plus a toilet upstairs. These excavated features show that some residents devoted considerable effort to comfort and sanitation. An upstairs toilet belongs in the history of medieval engineering too. This particular house does not tell us that every family enjoyed the same facilities.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: A study of four Dongola house compounds, spanning the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, examined chemical traces in floors. Comparisons with reference samples helped locate activities, especially food preparation, where few visible objects remained. A swept floor can still hold clues. The researchers found that similar-looking homes could be used in different ways as residents’ needs changed.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: From the fourteenth century onward, many Dongola dwellings grouped small residential buildings around a shared courtyard. Rooms included benches and storage spaces for vessels and equipment. Archaeologists examine how shared and separate working areas shaped household relationships. A floor plan can suggest how people met and worked together, but it cannot establish every resident’s family tree.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A rubbish deposit beside Dongola’s monastery church contained pottery fragments used for writing exercises. Examples include a Coptic alphabet and archangels’ names written in an unpractised hand. Other pieces carry Greek grammar exercises. Broken pottery could serve as a writing surface. These finds show learning, although they do not reveal every pupil’s age or how many children attended lessons.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A monastery room yielded two groups of dishes bearing the names of religious leaders Lazaros and Stephanos. Each group included roughly ten pots. Writing could identify belongings as well as record prayers. These names connect ordinary tableware with particular people, though the finds do not prove whether each leader ate alone or shared meals with others.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: Some Dongola inscriptions switch between Greek and Old Nubian. Other texts present psalms in both languages, sometimes alternating the language from verse to verse. This makes multilingual religious life visible on the walls. The texts preserve written choices, but they do not tell us that every resident spoke both languages fluently.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: A land-sale document from Qasr Ibrim names a woman, Kapopi, selling property inherited from her mother to Neuesi, an official’s daughter, and Anenikoli. A 2019 reanalysis dates it to November 1, 1191, while noting an older discussion using 1190. This northern Nubian record preserves a woman acting in a property transaction, without proving that every woman had identical rights or wealth.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: Old Nubian land sales often described a plot by naming neighbouring owners and the land upstream and downstream along the Nile. The 2019 study argues that descriptions normally proceed from south to north. Finding your field depended on relationships between people and places: the neighbours were part of the address. Some readings and exact locations remain uncertain.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: A pot beneath the pavement of the church on Kom D at Dongola contained a necklace of about one hundred beads. Materials included coloured glass, faience, shell, bone and stone. Researchers interpreted it as a seventh-century foundation deposit. The necklace shows materials brought together in an unusual setting; its placement does not tell us who previously wore it, or whether anyone did.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: Dongola ornaments included marine shells altered for suspension. Some cowrie shells had their upper surfaces removed or pierced; larger cone shells had their tips cut off. One pierced shell still had a leather thong. These objects connect inland adornment with marine materials and skilled preparation, while the route taken by each shell remains unknown.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: Dongola’s Mosque Building preserves an Arabic foundation inscription dated 1317. Architectural study shows the earlier monumental hall being adapted for worship, including a prayer niche and new plaster over painted walls. Its earlier role as a royal audience hall is an interpretation of its plan and decoration. One building’s conversion did not mean that every resident changed religion that year.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: In a discovery announced in 2023, archaeologists investigating a later house found an opening into a small painted chamber below its floor. One scene shows a Nubian ruler with Christ and Archangel Michael. Preliminary reading of a difficult inscription mentions a King David and protection for a city. The identification and historical occasion were still being investigated: a dramatic painting is not a photograph of a known event.

Makuria fragmented during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The court left Dongola in the 1360s, but the city continued under a smaller kingdom and later within the Funj sphere. Changes of government and religion unfolded over time. The map’s 1492 endpoint does not establish a single conquest or the disappearance of Nubian communities.

passages.text: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

sectionTitles: A cooking pot with its own feet
A game with room for the pieces
Family gatherings with words worth practising
Many family histories, more than one kind of evidence

passages.text: Malagasy history brings together varied communities and long-distance connections. Research into ancestry finds both African and Asian contributions, with regional differences. No single family custom, craft or royal dynasty represents everybody on the island.

passages.title: A cooking pot with its own feet
passages.text: Northern Madagascar’s stone-vessel industry flourished during the centuries around 800 to 1500. Tripod pots from Vohémar have three feet that could hold the bowl over a fire. Soot and burnt residues show heating, while finds in settlements support everyday use alongside burial uses. The residues have not established exactly what every pot contained.

passages.title: A cooking pot with its own feet
passages.text: Broken stone pots were sometimes repaired instead of discarded. At Vohémar, two surviving examples were held together with iron bands and mortar. Other fragments have drilled holes for joining pieces with metal clamps. Repairs show the value placed on keeping a vessel useful. A cracked pot could get another chance, though a repaired pot was not necessarily watertight.

passages.title: Books made from local materials
passages.text: The Bibliothèque nationale de France describes manuscripts from southeastern Madagascar written in Arabic characters to record Malagasy. Several are on locally made Antaimoro paper. Writing systems can travel and be adapted to a different language: using Arabic letters does not mean that the words on every page are Arabic. These manuscripts preserve a regional tradition of keeping knowledge in writing.

passages.title: Books made from local materials
passages.text: One volume, catalogued as Malayo-polynésien 285, combines Antaimoro paper with a binding of zebu hide. The record identifies both the writing surface and the cover. A book is also a made object, requiring materials and practical skills as well as words. This particular binding does not tell us how every Malagasy book was produced.

passages.title: Wooden houses and family patterns
passages.text: Zafimaniry builders in Madagascar’s southeastern highlands use wooden joints in which a shaped end fits into a matching opening. UNESCO describes houses and tombs assembled without metal nails or hinges. Different tree species suit different jobs. Good building depends on knowing the material as well as making the pieces fit; this tradition has a great deal of knowledge tucked into its joints.

passages.title: Wooden houses and family patterns
passages.text: Carving appears on Zafimaniry walls, window frames, stools, chests and tools. Some patterns have named meanings: UNESCO describes a spider’s-web motif associated with family ties and a honeycomb with community life. The decoration can therefore carry ideas about relationships as well as display skill. These meanings belong to this tradition, rather than being a dictionary for every pattern across Madagascar.

passages.title: A game with room for the pieces
passages.text: A fanorona board in Islington’s educational handling collection is made from light wood, with black lines and little side drawers for the playing pieces. Two players move along the board’s lines and try to capture their opponent’s pieces. This collected example uses plastic pieces, so it illustrates a continuing game rather than an ancient excavated set. Even a strategy game benefits from somewhere to put everything away.

passages.title: A game with room for the pieces
passages.text: The same collection tells a story about Prince Andriantompokoindrindra, who was so absorbed in fanorona that he failed to return to his father and lost the chance to become king. It is presented here as a traditional story, not a verified explanation of a royal succession. It certainly gives the familiar request to stop playing a game unusually high stakes.

passages.title: Family gatherings with words worth practising
passages.text: Kabary is an art of public speaking using proverbs, carefully arranged phrases and wordplay. It commonly involves two speakers addressing a gathering, and some performances last hours. Skill lies in choosing and arranging words for the occasion. A speech can be something people come together to enjoy, rather than merely an announcement before the interesting part.

passages.title: Family gatherings with words worth practising
passages.text: Kabary also belongs at family gatherings where several generations take part. UNESCO describes growing participation by women and younger people in an art formerly associated especially with older elite men. A tradition can continue while the people who perform it change. Listening, joining in and learning how to speak are part of its social life.

passages.title: Many family histories, more than one kind of evidence
passages.text: A 2017 genetic study sampled 2,704 people in 257 Malagasy villages. Its results supported ancestry connected with both eastern Africa and Southeast Asia, with differences across the island. Such research can help investigate population history, but it does not identify the family who owned an excavated pot or decide somebody’s cultural identity. Archaeology, languages and community histories ask related questions using different evidence.

Malagasy peoples continue today, with local traditions, shared connections and changing ways of life. Living practices such as kabary show participation across generations. The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not an extinction date, nor the end of Malagasy culture.

sectionTitles: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
A university begins in a former school
Pupils who asked for better toilets

passages.text: Malawi’s regional history includes rock paintings, shared meals and skills learned through practice. Evidence comes from archaeological sites and from living communities whose traditions differ across the country.

passages.title: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
passages.text: At Chongoni, red rock paintings include circles, radiating lines and other geometric patterns made with red oxide pigment. Researchers associate this earlier tradition with hunter-gatherers. Suggested links with rainmaking are interpretations, rather than translations of a known written code. A circle on a rock does not come with its original caption.

passages.title: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
passages.text: Later Chongoni paintings used white clay for animal-like and other figures. Many are linked with Chewa women’s ceremonies, and painting continued into the twentieth century. Excavations also recovered hunted-animal bones around two thousand years old. Researchers warn that these finds are difficult to connect with particular paintings: dating a meal’s remains does not automatically date the art nearby.

passages.title: Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
passages.text: Nsima is a thick porridge made with maize flour, and its name also refers to a wider culinary tradition. UNESCO’s account follows the work from growing and storing maize through pounding, preparing accompaniments and serving. The finished bowl is only the last stage of a much longer chain of skills.

passages.title: Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
passages.text: Sharing nsima provides an occasion for families to spend time together. Children learn food skills from adults through practice, while recipes, schoolbooks and festivals offer other ways to pass on the tradition. Learning dinner can involve both a book and watching someone who already knows what to do.

passages.title: The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
passages.text: In Tchopa, a Lhomwe performance from southern Malawi, dancers move in a circle and cross one another’s paths to drums of three sizes. Some carry packs containing farming tools, animal skins, puppets or old kitchen utensils. The equipment links performance with work and everyday objects. Getting ready for this dance can involve more than finding your shoes.

passages.title: The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
passages.text: Tchopa knowledge passes through rehearsals and performances, with children increasingly joining older practitioners. The group also has roles for costume makers, drum makers and musicians. UNESCO describes members helping one another during bereavement or illness and sharing farm labour when someone is overburdened. The relationships continue after the dancing stops.

passages.title: Care as a community gathering
passages.text: Vimbuza is a healing tradition associated with Tumbuka communities in northern Malawi. UNESCO describes people staying in a healer’s village house, with singing, drumming and dance forming part of their care. Women and children gather around the person receiving the ritual. This account records cultural understandings of illness and spiritual help, and shows care involving a wider community. It does not establish that the ritual cures an illness.

passages.title: A university begins in a former school
passages.text: The University of Malawi began teaching on 29 September 1965 with ninety students in Blantyre, using a former secondary-school campus. Its institutional establishment had come in 1964. The small first intake helps make a large institution’s beginning easier to picture: a university can start with a group of learners before it develops several campuses and colleges.

passages.title: A university begins in a former school
passages.text: The university’s history records Kamuzu College of Nursing joining as a constituent college in September 1979, followed by a College of Medicine in Blantyre in 1991. These institutions made training nurses and doctors part of the university’s work. The dates describe that institutional history, rather than when Malawians first practised healing or cared for sick relatives.

passages.title: Pupils who asked for better toilets
passages.text: A 2024 UNICEF report describes the water, sanitation and hygiene club at Mbande Primary School in Karonga. Its student chairperson, Gladson Kaunda, said members met on Mondays and pressed the school committee for more toilets and spaces for adolescent girls. They received supplies including buckets and soap. Pupils were helping shape their school environment as well as learning in it.

passages.title: Pupils who asked for better toilets
passages.text: At Mkazomba Primary School in Lilongwe, a 2024 UNICEF report describes a solar-powered water system with storage tanks, taps and handwashing facilities. Pupils had previously walked to a village well to fetch water. Water nearer their classrooms also helped with cleaning toilets, and local community members received maintenance training. Keeping a school running involves pipes and practical skills as well as lessons.

British rule ended when Nyasaland became independent Malawi on 6 July 1964. The country became a republic in 1966 and continued through the change from Banda’s rule to multiparty government in 1994. The map’s earlier start date does not make Malawi independent in 1920, and changes of government did not end its communities.

sectionTitles: A modern country and its written voices
People who keep buildings and books alive

passages.text: The modern Republic of Mali emerged from decolonization in 1960. It is a separate state from the medieval Mali Empire, although its communities preserve and reinterpret much older histories.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: This map record represents the modern republic. In 1960, the former French Sudan separated from the short-lived federation with Senegal and became the Republic of Mali. It was not the medieval empire surviving unchanged.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: Mali’s recent political history includes a 2012 rebellion and coup, followed by military takeovers in 2020 and 2021. These changes disrupted government without ending the country. Families’ experiences of conflict, displacement and rebuilding belong beside the stories of presidents and soldiers.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: A 2016 Bamanankan writing sample is the published title “taamacogo yɛlɛma : mun na hadamaden bɛ jͻ ka taama”, paired with “The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright”. Malian writer Ismaila Samba Traoré translated Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s story. The Latin-based spelling preserves sounds beyond ordinary English letters.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: Djenné’s Great Mosque receives new earthen plaster before the rains. In 2025, communal work took place on 25 May and 12 June. The current building dates to 1907, while the town’s Islamic architectural history is much older.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: The plaster called banco mixes earth and water with natural additives, including rice bran, baobab powder and shea butter. The Barey-Ton association of masons organizes the work. A magnificent building needs recipes and regular maintenance, as well as an architect’s original idea.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: Men, women, children and visitors join the annual event, which also passes knowledge to younger generations. Conservation becomes a public occasion. Keeping a landmark standing can mean getting together and getting muddy.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: During the 2012 occupation of Timbuktu, residents and the heritage organization SAVAMA-DCI rescued most of the city’s ancient manuscripts. Many moved to Bamako. These were family and institutional collections, protected through local effort at considerable risk.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: A 2015 conference identified suitable storage boxes and digitization as urgent needs for the rescued manuscripts. Saving a book from destruction is only the beginning: paper also needs careful handling, suitable storage and people who can help future readers use it.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: At Markala, Bambara, Bozo, Marka and Somono communities hold festivities with masks, puppets, drums and dancing. Animal figures express social virtues. The celebrations follow harvest rites and lead into a period of fishing, connecting performance with the working year.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Markala’s festivities also create opportunities to discuss quarrels between families and communities. Older people teach young initiates ritual skills. A puppet performance can therefore be entertainment, education and a setting for repairing relationships.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Senufo balafons have wooden keys above gourd resonators. In the form described by UNESCO, delicate membranes made from spider egg-sac material cover holes in the gourds and change the sound. Ingenious musical engineering does not always involve electricity.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Children begin learning on smaller balafons before moving to full-sized instruments with a teacher. Music accompanies work, celebrations and funerals. These Senufo traditions cross borders into neighboring countries, illustrating why a cultural map never fits perfectly inside a political one.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: In 2019, Fatoumata Barry taught displaced families in Sévaré through puzzles and playful demonstrations. Ada Diagayété helped compare washing with and without soap. Their stadium shelter had gained sixteen latrines, six showers and six taps: teaching and practical facilities worked together.

Mali continues as a country despite prolonged conflict and political upheaval. Its communities maintain social life, education and heritage through these disruptions; a coup is not the disappearance of a people.

passages.text: Mali connected West African gold-producing regions with a wider commercial and intellectual world. Mansa Musa became internationally famous through his pilgrimage, while architecture and oral performance preserved different forms of cultural memory.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo during his pilgrimage in 1324 to 1325. His distribution of gold made a strong impression on contemporaries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque traces its initial construction to Musa's return from pilgrimage. Later rebuilding means the surviving fabric represents multiple periods.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mosque architecture and scholarship connected Timbuktu to Islamic networks while local building practices remained central.

sectionTitles: Family, learning and a roof with a history

passages.text: This late Mali entry concerns smaller Manding powers in the Upper Niger region. Kangaba’s rulers claimed Mali’s inheritance and defended access to goldfields. It should not be read as Mansa Musa’s much earlier empire surviving with unchanged institutions.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Historian Jan Jansen argues that refuges and fortified places formed coordinated groups along Kangaba’s northern frontier. His reconstruction uses geography, buildings and genealogies together, and is an interpretation of a poorly documented political landscape.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: The Niger and western escarpment limited cavalry movements. Defenders adapted their forces to this terrain: a river, a cliff and a flat corridor posed very different problems for a mounted army.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Gold and the trade in enslaved people helped sustain the ruling elite. The wealth behind political survival therefore also depended on coercion and on people whose lives were disrupted by warfare.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Kangaba’s later importance does not prove it was the medieval empire’s capital. Historians have questioned how that identification entered colonial accounts. A community can inherit an important political tradition without every remembered location being securely established.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Kangaba’s circular Kamablon, which UNESCO’s nomination dates to 1653, shelters objects important to the community and serves as a meeting place. Its thatched roof is renewed every seven years in a ceremony that continues today.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: In the documented modern ceremony, young people about twenty or twenty-one remove the old roof and build its replacement under elders’ supervision. Practical construction skills and explanations of the building’s meaning are learned together: roofing is also a history lesson.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Keita clan members and Diabate griots organize the ceremony, while griots from Kela recount Manden history. Gathering also provides opportunities to strengthen relationships and settle disagreements. This is a living practice, not proof that every detail was identical in 1653.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Stories about marriages between Muslim scholars and warrior families helped explain political legitimacy in the wider western Sudan. Jansen’s study examines how a child’s success in such stories connected ancestry to the right to rule.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Those accounts sometimes emphasize descent through women and sometimes through men. They reveal arguments about inheritance and authority among elites; they cannot tell us the marriage arrangements of every family in Kangaba.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: The Manden Charter survives as an oral heritage associated with the region. Its living presentations discuss peace, education, food security and respect for people. Recognizing its cultural importance is different from claiming that an original medieval written constitution survives.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: UNESCO describes the Charter’s teaching as passing between generations through local gatherings and ceremonies. Speech, performance and memory are therefore historical evidence too, though scholars must ask when particular versions were recorded and how they changed.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: A contemporary regional written tradition appears in al-Saʿdi’s seventeenth-century Arabic chronicle, whose title is “تاريخ السودان”: “History of the Sudan”. Here Sudan means the broad West African region. This is an external regional comparison, not a surviving Kangaba court text; the spelling is attested in its published Arabic edition.
The map stops in 1783, but Kangaba’s authority continued. Nineteenth-century warfare and new alliances reshaped the region; its peoples and traditions did not vanish with an imperial label.

sectionTitles: Crafts that carry names and meanings

passages.text: The Mamluk sultanate centred on Cairo and governed Egypt and much of Syria. Rulers drawn from military households supported institutions and specialised crafts. Surviving buildings and objects illuminate urban services, skilled labour, trade and the public display of authority.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Military recruits entered the ruling system through enslavement, education and training, followed by manumission and service. Advancement was not solely hereditary. This path to elite office depended on coercive recruitment and should not be confused with freedom from social hierarchy.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Trade in silks and spices helped finance patronage. Textiles and carpets also circulated internationally. Skilled production connected merchants and workshops with wealthy buyers well beyond the sultanate.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qalawun’s complex on Cairo’s al-Mu’izz Street joined a school, mosque, tomb and hospital. The arrangement brought teaching and care into an architectural foundation that also preserved the ruler’s memory. The building’s functions were broader than royal burial alone.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Shaykhu’s sabil, established in 1354, supplied water to passers-by. Its rock-cut rooms have openings to cisterns below, and jars were used in distribution. The surviving structure shows how storage and service worked together in a city street.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qayitbay’s fifteenth-century complex combined a madrasa, a public water facility and a kuttab for Qur’anic teaching to poor Muslims. A courtyard and surrounding halls organised the school. Education, water supply and commemoration shared one foundation.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Wooden furnishings at Qayitbay’s madrasa include a pulpit and a Qur’an reciter’s chair inlaid with ivory. Their construction demonstrates skilled joinery and ornament in objects used for teaching and worship, alongside the stonework of the building.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A glass lamp made for Amir Qawsun around 1329 to 1335 combines a blown body and applied foot with enamel and gilding. Its inscription identifies the patron. The museum regards a mosque or tomb-hospice as its probable destination, rather than a proven findspot.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fourteenth-century tray stand bears a cup emblem and an inscription naming Husain, son of Qawsun. Brass was worked and inlaid with contrasting metals. Stands of this kind held trays of fruit and other food, connecting elite dining with symbols of court office.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: The Five Medallion Carpet, dated around 1500, uses wool for its foundation threads and knotted surface. Repeated geometric forms organise the long design. Its attribution to Egypt, probably Cairo, remains an attribution, not a documented excavation location.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fifteenth-century engraved brass box names Muhammad al-Hamawi, the timekeeper at Damascus’s Umayyad Mosque. His office supervised prayer times and announcements concerning Ramadan. The box probably held food; it documents a specialist’s role without itself being a timekeeping instrument.

Ottoman conquest ended the Egyptian sultanate in 1517. Tuman Bey was captured and executed in Cairo after resisting the invasion. Mamluk elites retained influence under Ottoman rule, so the loss of the sultanate did not immediately eliminate its military households or social power.

passages.text: Mandan communities built farming villages along the Missouri River and became important partners in Plains exchange. The imported outline lies near their historic village country in present-day North Dakota, but its dates describe map coverage. Mandan people remain a distinct people within today’s Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Double Ditch, north of present-day Bismarck, preserves a Mandan village occupied for roughly three centuries, from around 1490 to 1785. Its name is misleadingly modest: researchers have identified four successive defensive ditches. The settlement’s changing boundaries record a community repeatedly rebuilding its surroundings.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Geophysical instruments revealed buried hearths, storage pits and two previously unrecognized fortifications at Double Ditch. Archaeologists then checked the signals through excavation. The combination uncovered parts of village life that a walk across the grassy surface could easily miss.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Mandan farmers raised corn, beans, squash, sunflowers and tobacco. Stored harvests supported village life and exchange with other Plains communities, while hunting supplied bison and other animals. A farming village could therefore be a trading destination as well as a place to grow dinner.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Community-authored teaching materials describe women owning and building earthlodges, with men helping move heavy logs. Wood, branches, grass and earth formed substantial homes. Mandan builders used clay in their coverings, and strong roofs could become places to sit and watch village activity.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Relatives often placed their lodges near one another. Children could play close to family while adults visited and worked. The same teaching account describes cottonwood collected after spring ice had knocked trees down, then left to dry: housebuilding began well before the house appeared.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Harvest preservation required practical defenses against hungry animals. Raised drying platforms helped keep food away from dogs. Women dried crops for later use, turning a short growing season into meals that could last through much colder weather.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Underground food caches were lined with grasses and sticks, reached by a ladder and carefully covered. Some were inside lodges, others outside. Concealing the lid protected an important family store: the pantry could be beneath your feet.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: In the game called tchung-kee, Mandan and Hidatsa players rolled a small stone ring and threw long poles, trying to send a pole through the moving opening. The challenge joined timing, aim and competition. A little ring could demand a surprisingly large amount of skill.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: The American Fur Company built Fort Clark beside a Mandan village in 1830 to 1831. In 1832, the steamboat Yellow Stone delivered goods and carried beaver pelts and bison robes back toward St. Louis. Village trade now connected households to a much longer commercial river route.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: In 1837, the steamboat St. Peters arrived carrying people infected with smallpox. A devastating epidemic swept through the Mandan village at Fort Clark. Survivors left to join Hidatsa communities near the Knife River. These were catastrophic human losses, followed by survival and rebuilding rather than the end of Mandan people.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: Commissioned in 1905, Sitting Rabbit’s remarkable map stretched along a canvas more than 23 feet long. It recorded Missouri River places and older villages through Mandan knowledge and pictorial detail. The river’s bends were adapted to the long format, creating a historical landscape that could be unrolled.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: The Garrison Dam project displaced families from fertile Missouri bottomlands in the twentieth century. MHA Nation’s history describes lost farms and communities and relocation onto less productive uplands. A change in the river’s level could therefore alter food production, neighboring relationships and the places where family memories lived.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: A modern Mandan writing sample is “Ráátinitak shí’sh.” The MHA Nation website translates it as “It is good that you all arrived”. The site prints distinct Hidatsa and Arikara welcomes beside it, making clear that the three affiliated peoples have different languages.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: A Mandan alphabet coloring book published in 2016 invites children to trace letters and words and use a color key. Its exercises make literacy something a child can practice with a pencil.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: MHA Nation’s language programs maintain separate work for Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara. Mentor-and-apprentice learning connects experienced speakers with learners who can become future teachers. Modern classes and children’s resources belong to the continuing history of these communities.

The imported endpoint of 1783 is not an ending for the Mandan people. Epidemics, relocation and later flooding of river-bottom lands transformed community life. Mandan identity and language work continue within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.
