sectionTitles: Many communities and an early urban world
Households, skilled hands and material clues
Music, teaching and a modern written sample

passages.text: “Mandes” is a broad map label for diverse Mande-speaking peoples, not one kingdom. Its enormous 900 to 1000 polygon should not be read as a precise language frontier. Regional archaeology and clearly dated later examples reveal distinct communities, occupations and artistic traditions; they do not give every enclosed settlement one identity.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: Mande is a language family with dozens of members, divided into major Western and South-Eastern branches. Sharing linguistic relationships does not make their speakers one dynasty, religion or occupation. The map’s short label covers a far more varied human story.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: At Jenné-jeno in Mali, excavators traced a city that had grown to roughly thirty-three hectares by about 600 to 800 CE. Its substantial mud-brick enclosure and neighboring settlement mounds show urban life before the Mali Empire. This is regional evidence, not a census of its residents’ languages.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: The 1977 excavations at Jenné-jeno recovered evidence of African rice, fish and cattle. These linked floodplain farming, fishing and herding in an economy that supported permanent settlement. A city’s history can begin with reliable meals as well as famous rulers.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: Sandstone grinding equipment and volcanic stone ornaments found in the delta had to come from beyond the local floodplain. The excavators also identified distant copper and gold connections during the first millennium CE. Everyday food preparation and personal decoration both depended on exchange.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: Later excavations at Jenné-jeno found relatively little variation between sampled areas in quantities of imported copper, stone and other goods. That complicates an easy picture of one fabulously rich quarter. The researchers caution that vanished materials, including textiles, could once have displayed differences that no longer survive.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: At nearby Djenné, a different, later excavation uncovered a well lined with stacked pots whose bottoms were open. Lower occupation deposits were provisionally dated to the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries. Ceramic vessels could serve underground engineering as well as kitchens.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: A photograph taken in Sissingué in 1992 records potter Fatoumata Kouyaté beginning a vessel with a cylinder of clay. She presses and hollows it by hand, then draws the sides upward. This named craftswoman’s method makes the shaping process visible, before firing turns soft clay into a useful container.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: A Malinke hunter’s shirt in the Carlos Museum, made in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, carries leather packets, shells, claws and horns on cloth. Its attachments expressed accumulated knowledge and protective beliefs. The garment could become a changing record of its wearer’s experience.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: At Nyagassola in Guinea, the Dökala family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a balafon associated with Manding epic traditions. Its twenty wooden slats have calabashes beneath them. UNESCO’s account describes a living musical responsibility passed within a family, not simply an old object in storage.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: The Balatigui, the instrument’s guardian, also teaches balafon to children from about seven years old. UNESCO identified the departure of young people from the village as a threat to transmission. An instrument’s future depends on someone learning how to play it.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: A 2004 N’Ko encoding proposal prints “ߕߐ߮”, transliterated tô and translated “name”. It explains that related Manding varieties can share this spelling while pronouncing it differently. This is an attested modern written example; N’Ko was devised in 1949, long after the map’s medieval interval.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: N’Ko records vowels and tone with letters and added marks. Its decorative sign “߷”, called gbakurunen, represents the three stones that hold a cooking pot over a fire and marks major text divisions. A familiar household arrangement thus has a place on the written page.

The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not the fall of the Mande-speaking peoples. Different communities subsequently joined or formed states, changed livelihoods and developed new forms of writing and art. Their shared language relationships never gave them one founding date or a single ending.

passages.text: Manteño-Huancavilca is a broad archaeological label for coastal Ecuadorian societies, including communities of Manabí and the Santa Elena region. It should not flatten their distinct identities into one uniform empire. The map’s 1492 to 1500 slice and approximate coastal outline are coverage choices, not their beginning and ending. The Guancavilca identity maintained in Sacachún is more specific than this combined label.

passages.title: Coastal power and connections
passages.text: Manteño sailors used rafts fitted with sails for river and ocean travel. Spondylus shells were valuable exchange goods. These connections linked coastal production with wider trade, making seafaring skill an important part of regional influence.

passages.title: Coastal power and connections
passages.text: The rafts could be steered with guaras, boards lowered or raised through the raft as adjustable keels. Marcos emphasizes this as a technical achievement: the sailors could choose a course rather than simply drift wherever the current carried them.

passages.title: Coastal power and connections
passages.text: Power was not always held by men. Research on sixteenth-century coastal settlements identifies a woman ruling Achira and several subordinate lordships. The authors suggest that this center occupied an important position in regional trade, but emphasize that further documentation is needed.

passages.title: Coastal power and connections
passages.text: U-shaped stone seats were associated with political and religious elites. Craftspeople carved them from single blocks of rock. Their striking form made a seat itself an emblem of authority: this was furniture with a public message.

passages.title: Food, water and household work
passages.text: At Hojas-Jaboncillo, the surviving landscape includes houses, temples, wells, water channels and storage structures. Managing water mattered alongside monumental building. The paths through the site pass evidence of everyday supply systems as well as ceremonial places.

passages.title: Food, water and household work
passages.text: A 2015 study of two domestic rubbish deposits at Loma del Secal identified bowls, cooking pots, griddles, ladles and spindle whorls. Broken household equipment gives archaeologists a much fuller picture than a collection of spectacular ornaments alone.

passages.title: Food, water and household work
passages.text: At the La Y complex, investigators recorded eight circular depressions thought to be underground storage structures. Their proposed function is useful evidence for food management, though a depression in the ground does not come with its original contents conveniently labeled.

passages.title: Food, water and household work
passages.text: Marcos interprets modified hillsides as productive landscapes with systems for collecting and distributing moisture from cloud forest. He links underground storage to surplus maize. This is the researcher’s reconstruction of how farming and political organization worked together.

passages.title: Food, water and household work
passages.text: Salango’s long coastal history can also be studied underwater. A survey recovered three diving weights, two net weights and an anchor. These finds illuminate marine harvesting, but the study’s multi-period setting does not assign every object specifically to Manteño times.

passages.title: Images, language and living memory
passages.text: A clay figure in Madrid’s Museo de América wears a large headdress, ear ornaments, necklace and wristbands while seated on a stool. Although traditionally labeled a censer, the museum rejects that simple functional identification. Its elaborate appearance suggests elite ritual imagery; its original archaeological setting is poorly documented.

passages.title: Images, language and living memory
passages.text: No securely translated preconquest sentence can be supplied from the evidence checked for this card. Gómez Rendón investigates old place-names and personal names to recover traces of coastal languages. Those linguistic clues and decorative images should not be turned into an invented alphabet or a made-up greeting.

passages.title: Images, language and living memory
passages.text: Sacachún’s residents campaigned to bring home San Biritute, a stone human figure about 2.35 meters tall. Removed in 1952, it returned on 16 July 2011. Local associations with rain and fertility make its return a story of community memory, not merely the movement of a museum object.

passages.title: Images, language and living memory
passages.text: At Hojas-Jaboncillo, the Catarama library includes a play and learning space for children. Community workshops also reproduce Manteño designs in screen printing. Archaeological knowledge can become something young people use and make, as well as something they see behind glass.

Spanish conquest and colonial resettlement transformed coastal political life during the sixteenth century; Charapotó’s destruction in 1534 is one documented example. There was no single extinction date for all communities covered by this label. Guancavilca community identities and heritage claims continue, and the map endpoint of 1500 is earlier than these colonial changes.

sectionTitles: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
Growing food in a cooler environment

passages.text: East Polynesian voyagers established communities in Aotearoa around the thirteenth-century transition to the fourteenth. This early-period card follows settlement, food production and watercraft through named archaeological sites. Māori histories encompass distinct communities and traditions; this map label does not identify a single kingdom.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: At Wairau Bar, unfinished adzes and stone-working waste record the shaping of argillite brought from the Nelson and D’Urville Island region. The concentration suggests organised production, potentially supplying other communities, rather than only occasional tool repair.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Wairau Bar fishing equipment adapts Polynesian designs to local materials, including moa bone and stone where tropical pearl shell was unavailable. Middens also contain fish, shellfish, birds, dogs and marine mammals. Early livelihoods drew on several resources.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Isotope analysis distinguishes childhood environments recorded in tooth enamel from later diets recorded in bone. Wairau Bar ancestors show differences in food and likely mobility; those signals do not identify a precise birthplace for every person or a uniform diet for the settlement.

passages.title: What the Wairau Bar settlement preserves
passages.text: Ornaments and equipment accompanied some Wairau Bar burials, including drilled moa eggs, worked teeth and adzes. These objects document distinctive treatment of the dead. They cannot, by themselves, establish a complete hierarchy of occupations or rank among the living.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: At Triangle Flat in Golden Bay/Mohua, planting pits dated to 1290 to 1385 contained microscopic starch interpreted as kūmara-like, alongside evidence attributed to taro and yam. The finding places horticultural experimentation within the early settlement period.

passages.title: Growing food in a cooler environment
passages.text: Triangle Flat lies within the customary jurisdiction of Manawhenua ki Mohua. Its garden evidence challenges the assumption that early southern settlers relied almost entirely on hunting and gathering after abandoning tropical crops. That conclusion concerns this investigated landscape, not every settlement.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A surviving canoe hull from Anaweka on the South Island’s northwest coast was shaped from native mataī wood. Internal ribs and a longitudinal stringer were carved into the hull, while lashing holes joined components. These features reveal construction knowledge beyond simply hollowing a log.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: Additional holes beside damaged lashings show repairs to the Anaweka hull. Caulking helps date its final use to approximately 1400; older wood dates do not establish when the canoe was built. Researchers reconstruct the wider vessel from a surviving component.

passages.title: The Anaweka canoe
passages.text: A turtle carved in relief on the Anaweka hull resembles motifs in other Polynesian traditions. The researchers interpret it as evidence of cultural connections. It does not establish a uniquely identifiable departure island or the biography of the people aboard.

passages.title: Communities across generations
passages.text: Local groups maintained their own authority and relationships through genealogy, mana and tapu. Exchange carried valued materials such as pounamu, obsidian and harakeke among communities. Shared practices coexisted with regional histories and changing social ties.

The map’s 1530 endpoint is a change in coverage, not the disappearance of Māori. Colonial confiscations later dispossessed many communities, while iwi, hapū and whānau continued. The kōhanga reo movement, beginning in 1982, is one example of community-led language transmission across generations.

sectionTitles: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
Carving, memory and a documented removal

passages.text: Māori communities maintained distinct iwi and hapū histories through trade, technological change and colonisation. This card follows named examples of food production, fishing, carving and language education. The imported map endpoints do not mark an end to Māori society.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: A study of seven ancestors from Tamahere site S14/487, dated about 1700 to 1780, found diets predominantly based on plants. Archaeological context supports cultivated root crops as important foods. Isotopes do not identify each meal, and this small sample cannot describe all Māori diets.

passages.title: Food and childhood at Tamahere
passages.text: The teeth of two children in the Tamahere study preserve a changing dietary signal consistent with weaning onto plant foods within their first two to three years. This is a finding about those children, not a universal rule for childhood across iwi.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Te Papa’s pā kahawai lure OL000106/10, dated broadly to 1750 to 1850, combines a shaped and polished pāua-shell shank with a shell barb and tightly bound muka fibre. Fine notches decorate the shell. It preserves several stages of skilled manufacture in one small fishing implement.

passages.title: Fishing and the meaning of clothing
passages.text: Kākahu provided warmth and protection, while particular cloaks also expressed status and relationships. Their continued use as esteemed gifts and at funerals connects material workmanship with honour, care and ancestral memory. Everyday use and ceremonial importance should not be treated as interchangeable.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In the early 1840s, carvers led by Raharuhi Rukupo created Te Hau ki Tūranga at Orakaiapu pā, Manutuke. The whare whakairo belongs to Ngāti Kaipōhō of Rongowhakaata. Its carved ancestors and memorial purpose joined artistic work to hapū history and relationships.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: In 1867 Crown troops dismantled Te Hau ki Tūranga and removed it despite objections. Rukupo recorded that he had refused requests to give it up. This documented removal is part of the building’s history alongside its artistry.

passages.title: Carving, memory and a documented removal
passages.text: The Rongowhakaata settlement deed signed in 2011 acknowledges the wrongful taking of Te Hau ki Tūranga and records the Crown’s apology. The account recognises the harm caused by separating the taonga from its community.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Treaty signed in 1840 survives in texts with different meanings. The Māori text speaks of kāwanatanga in Article 1 and guarantees tino rangatiratanga over lands, villages and taonga in Article 2; the English text uses sovereignty. Treating these as identical obscures the historical disagreement.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The New Zealand Settlements Act of 1863 enabled land confiscation from communities labelled rebellious. Confiscation also took land from Māori who had remained neutral or supported the government. The effects differed by region, with severe losses in Waikato and Taranaki.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki connects seasonal knowledge with remembrance and sharing the harvest. Communities observe it in different ways and at different times. Its significance joins practical attention to the year with relationships among the living and the dead.

passages.title: Authority, land and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Pukeatua kōhanga reo opened in Wainuiomata in April 1982. The movement places children in Māori-language immersion environments and gives whānau responsibility for running centres. Education here includes language, relationships and cultural knowledge transmitted through daily life.

Māori have no cultural fall date. Colonial war and confiscation transformed landholding and political authority, while communities persisted. Te Tiriti remains central to the history of their relationship with the Crown. Kōhanga reo exemplifies continuing whānau-led work to pass language and knowledge to future generations.

sectionTitles: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
Gardening and the work of clothing

passages.text: This record follows Māori communities in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Gardens, crafts and ancestral taonga reveal knowledge rooted in particular places. Iwi and hapū had distinct histories and authority, not a single state.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Ōtuataua Stonefields at Ihumātao preserve rows, heaps and mounds associated with cultivation on volcanic ground. The specialised system may have developed by the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Adding sand and gravel and arranging stone helped growers manage soil and growing conditions.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Shell middens at Ōtuataua, including deposits dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century, show that coastal foods accompanied gardening. Habitation areas and storage features place food production within a lived landscape rather than an isolated agricultural installation.

passages.title: Ōtuataua: a worked and inhabited landscape
passages.text: Today’s stonefields contain features from different periods. Māori gardens, house sites, cooking shelters and terraces share the landscape with nineteenth-century European drystone walls. A visible wall is therefore not automatically evidence of a pre-contact Māori garden boundary.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: In the middle Waikato Basin, modified soils and borrow pits record intensive horticulture from the sixteenth century. Gardeners moved gravel into cultivation areas. Storage pits and planting features add evidence of sustained labour in managing root crops.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Whatu forms cloth by twining horizontal threads around vertical ones with the fingers. Muka fibre extracted from harakeke supplied material for cloaks. Raranga uses plaiting, commonly for mats and baskets. These related crafts solve different structural problems.

passages.title: Gardening and the work of clothing
passages.text: Rain capes combine a worked foundation with overlapping plant strips that shed water. Scraped sections allowed the strips to be attached as the garment grew. The construction joined knowledge of fibre preparation, fastening and weather protection; no exact invention date is established here.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Te Papa presents weaving’s whakapapa through Hine-te-iwaiwa, guardian of weaving, childbirth and lunar cycles. In this tradition, women transmit the skills and knowledge. Craft is understood through relationships among people, ancestors and the natural world as well as through technique.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: Uenuku, an ancestral carving held at Te Awamutu Museum, represents an atua of Tainui. Tainui tradition associates the spirit of Uenuku with the voyaging waka. The museum gives a broad traditional dating range; this card does not convert it into a precise manufacture year.

passages.title: Knowledge, ancestry and the seasons
passages.text: For many iwi, Matariki’s return to the winter dawn sky marks a new year. Remembrance, harvest thanksgiving and sharing food connect observation of the heavens with community life. Timing and observance vary among iwi; there was no single uniform national calendar.

Māori communities continue beyond this map interval. Ōtuataua retains local ancestral connections. Later colonial confiscation caused dispossession, while iwi and hapū persisted. Kōhanga reo supports continuing cultural transmission.

passages.text: Mapuche communities have a long history across parts of present-day Chile and Argentina. The map shows only a brief interval during nineteenth-century invasions of their territories. Local communities and leaders formed changing alliances; they were not one uniform kingdom.

passages.title: A home built together
passages.text: The ruka is a place for household life, work and community gatherings. Its hearth connects cooking with conversation, and activities such as weaving and basketry can share the same interior. The museum stresses that home design must make room for these living practices.

passages.title: A home built together
passages.text: Historical accounts describe different family arrangements rather than one standard household. Some nineteenth-century polygamous families had several hearths within a ruka. Hearths can therefore tell a social story as well as a story about keeping warm and preparing food.

passages.title: A home built together
passages.text: Pascual Coña recalled house-building as a community undertaking. A respected neighbour organized workers, who gathered timber and vines to bind the frame. Building a home called for cooperation and practical knowledge of local materials.

passages.title: A home built together
passages.text: Food was part of that work. Coña’s account describes drinks, mote and meat prepared for the people building the house, followed by eating and conversation around the hearth. The housewarming began with the people who had actually helped raise the house.

passages.title: Games, boats and learning
passages.text: Palin brings communities together through play, food and discussion. It can carry political, spiritual and social purposes as well as competition. Families and visitors help make the event, so the important activity extends well beyond the players holding sticks.

passages.title: Games, boats and learning
passages.text: A traditional pali ball could be shaped from a rounded growth on a tree, then scraped into a sphere. Other versions used wool and coverings. Makers adapted materials while preserving a game in which players drive the ball toward the opposite end.

passages.title: Games, boats and learning
passages.text: A single-log canoe was recovered from Lake Lanalhue in 1995. The museum displays the hollowed trunk but does not give a secure construction date in this account. Its surviving wood is direct evidence of skilled water transport in the region.

passages.title: Games, boats and learning
passages.text: Community research connects these canoes with exchange, kinship and friendship between settlements. A water route could carry goods and knowledge together. Recalling the boats also helps explain how the coastal territory was connected before many journeys moved onto roads.

passages.title: Remembered lives and continuing words
passages.text: Pascual Coña narrated his life to a missionary in the 1920s, looking back at the nineteenth century. The resulting text preserves a Mapuche voice through the work of a transcriber. It is invaluable, but readers should remember how the spoken account became a book.

passages.title: Remembered lives and continuing words
passages.text: Chile’s national library preserves a photograph of a girl and young woman beside a loom, dated around 1860. It records people and weaving equipment close to this map’s period. Like many early photographs, its posed arrangement is part of the evidence.

passages.title: Remembered lives and continuing words
passages.text: In Marjorie Huaiqui Hernández’s modern story, a child says “Wanglen pigen iñche”, meaning “My name is Wanglen”. The printed Mapudungun appears on page 87 of Palabras de tierra y sol. This is an actual contemporary literary sample, not invented dialogue for an ancient person.

passages.title: Remembered lives and continuing words
passages.text: Chilean troops suppressed the major 1881 to 1882 uprising and completed their planned occupation campaign in 1883. New land arrangements impoverished many communities and restricted their autonomy. The map’s 1880 cutoff falls before this decisive stage of conquest.

Mapuche political autonomy and landholding suffered greatly under nineteenth-century military conquest and settlement. The people did not disappear: communities, Mapudungun, cultural work and new political strategies continued. The imported 1880 endpoint is neither their beginning nor their end.

passages.text: The Maratha state founded by Shivaji in the Western Ghats broke Mughal power in the eighteenth century and, as a confederacy of chiefs under the Peshwa at Pune, ruled or taxed most of India by the 1750s. Its horsemen, hill forts and revenue administration made it the last great Indian power before the British.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Light cavalry that lived off the country and struck and withdrew defeated slower Mughal armies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Shivaji's chain of hill forts, Raigad, Pratapgad and Sinhagad among them, controlled the passes of the Western Ghats.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A navy under Kanhoji Angre held the Konkan coast against the Portuguese, the Siddis and the East India Company.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in a Vedic ceremony asserting independent Hindu kingship.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Ashtapradhan, a council of eight ministers, ran war, revenue, foreign affairs and religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Marathi, with Sanskrit terms replacing Persian ones in Shivaji's chancery, became the language of state.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Revenue came as chauth and sardeshmukhi, a quarter and a tenth of the yield, collected directly from the land.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Maratha wars drained the Mughals; after the defeat at Panipat in 1761 the confederacy recovered and held Delhi's emperor as a client.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Marathi identity and the memory of Shivaji remain central in Maharashtra.
The East India Company beat the confederacy in three wars; the Peshwa surrendered in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War and his lands were annexed.

sectionTitles: Discoveries beneath the shore and town

passages.text: Martinique’s history spans a plantation colony and a continuing Caribbean society within France. Writers and musicians developed distinctive cultural forms. Its separate map intervals do not represent an unchanged government.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: At Anse Trabaud in Sainte-Anne, excavators recovered wood, seeds and probable calabash fragments from deeply buried coastal deposits. These fragile materials add evidence that ordinary pottery assemblages cannot supply. The report describes exceptionally good preservation, while treating several botanical identifications as preliminary.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: Manchineel stones in one sediment sample suggest a coastal environment where the poisonous tree grew. They are not evidence that people ate its fruit. Together with the sequence of sand and organic deposits, plant remains help reconstruct the changing surroundings in which the village’s inhabitants lived.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: Saint-Pierre’s port area preserved stacks of imported porcelain and earthenware sealed by the 1902 disaster. Researchers identified heat-marked impressions of straw used as packing. Plates that had been stored for sale therefore reveal both overseas supply and the practical work of transporting fragile goods.

passages.title: Discoveries beneath the shore and town
passages.text: The same ceramics research distinguishes imported tableware from locally made water vessels and industrial pottery. Sugar moulds, molasses pots and roof tiles served different tasks from cups and plates. Marks and clay types help investigate workshops, although several proposed manufacturing places remain tentative.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Plantation slavery survived the changes of imperial control around 1800. When France recovered Martinique in 1802, the incoming administration maintained an existing system of coercion. The island’s chronology therefore differs from that of colonies where the 1794 abolition had actually taken effect.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: The events of May 1848 involved enslaved workers at Le Prêcheur, Morne-Rouge and Saint-Pierre. Their mobilization and the ensuing violence forced an early local proclamation of abolition. The distinction between the uprising on 22 May and the decree on 23 May makes the participants’ agency visible.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Freedom left difficult questions about land and work unresolved. Compensation was eventually arranged for those claiming losses from emancipation, while formerly enslaved people received none. Abolition ended legal enslavement but did not itself create equal access to property.

passages.title: Work, records and freedom
passages.text: Copies of parish and civil registers were collected to safeguard legal rights and administration. These records let researchers follow particular households through births, marriages and deaths.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Tropiques began in 1941 through collaboration among teachers and writers including Aimé and Suzanne Césaire and René Ménil. Its essays and poetry treated Caribbean experience as a subject of intellectual creation. Literary scholar Olga Hel-Bongo explains how apparently cultural subjects could carry criticism of colonial authority.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Suzanne Césaire helped bring manuscripts to the censorship authorities. The journal’s contributors used indirection as well as open argument; censorship interrupted publication in 1943. Their achievement involved editing, securing print and reaching readers under pressure, alongside the writing itself.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: The community association AM4 describes the tibwa as two dry hardwood sticks that maintain a repeating rhythm, struck against a drum’s rear or sometimes bamboo. The bèlè drum uses a wooden barrel body and an animal-skin head; the player sits astride it and works with hands and heel.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: Singing moves between a lead voice and a responding chorus. Instrument combinations vary by region and kind of music, so one ensemble cannot represent every Martinican practice. The tradition depends on shared timing, remembered verses and skilled interaction as much as on the construction of instruments.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: In 1946, Césaire presented a parliamentary report supporting departmental status. The record of his interventions also includes food supply, protections for agricultural workers and bringing unused land into cultivation. These questions connect constitutional change with the daily concerns of households and labourers.

passages.title: Writing, music and public knowledge
passages.text: The 1902 catastrophe gave the Pelean eruptive type its name and helped scientists understand violent volcanic processes. The forests and volcanoes of northern Martinique entered UNESCO’s World Heritage List in 2023 for their geological and ecological importance. Recognition preserves both scientific evidence and places inseparable from local memory.
Colonial administration gave way to departmental status in 1946. Territorial institutions changed again in 2015, within France. Martinican society continues across these changes.

passages.text: Ancient Mauretania occupied parts of today’s Morocco and Algeria, far north of modern Mauritania. Its towns combined local traditions with Punic and Mediterranean connections. The map ends in 1 BCE, during a kingdom that continued under Juba II and his successors into the first century CE.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: At Volubilis, archaeologists uncovered part of an early wall built from unfired bricks on a stone base. Much of the earlier city lies beneath later buildings, so the surviving Roman streets cannot simply be treated as a complete picture of the Mauretanian town.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: Punic and Neo-Punic inscriptions from Volubilis attest connections with the Carthaginian world. One inscription names magistrates called suffetes, suggesting that local government borrowed an institutional model without making the city merely a copy of Carthage.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: Imported Campanian pottery, transport amphorae and coins from places such as Cadiz show that Volubilis participated in wider exchange. A pot’s place of manufacture helps trace a journey; it does not by itself identify the language or ancestry of its owner.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: At Lixus, excavated houses dated to the third or second centuries BCE had two storeys and lacked the central atrium or peristyle familiar from many Roman textbook houses. North African city dwellers had architectural traditions of their own.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: Lixus stood on a hill above the Loukkos river, several kilometres from the Atlantic. Its position connected a settlement and its surrounding farmland with river and sea routes, rather than separating city life from the coast.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: The sanctuary at Lixus contained several temples built and rebuilt over different periods. Ancient stories associated the place with Hercules and the Garden of the Hesperides, but archaeologists do not treat a mythical origin as an excavation date.

passages.title: City life before Roman annexation
passages.text: A study of 26 amphora samples from recent Lixus excavations identified several clay fabrics compatible with southern Spain rather than local production. These late Mauretanian and Roman containers show that even a fish-processing centre could import some of its packaging.

passages.title: Royal images and learning
passages.text: A silver coin in the British Museum pairs Juba II’s portrait with Cleopatra Selene’s. The queen appears as a named royal figure in her own right, making a small object evidence for the public presentation of a ruling couple.

passages.title: Royal images and learning
passages.text: Juba II wrote in Greek on geography and other subjects. His works drew on earlier authors and research across a wider Mediterranean world; scholarly activity helped give his court cultural distinction as well as political connections.

passages.title: Royal images and learning
passages.text: A later coin from 11 or 12 CE bears the Latin sample “REX IVBA”, meaning “King Juba”. The use of V for the vowel written u in modern texts is ordinary Latin inscriptional spelling. This surviving coin comes just after the map entry’s 1 BCE endpoint.

passages.title: Royal images and learning
passages.text: On that coin Juba wears a lion skin, while a cornucopia and trident appear on the other side. The museum interprets these as claims about heroic ancestry, prosperity and maritime power: a tiny coin could carry a large royal message.

passages.title: Royal images and learning
passages.text: Roman annexation changed political authority, but Volubilis retained local inhabitants and some earlier institutions. New monuments were added to an existing city. A change of rulers did not mean that its residents woke up without their previous history.

The killing of King Ptolemy in 40 CE ended the dynasty, and Roman annexation followed. The map’s 1 BCE endpoint is therefore not the kingdom’s fall. Towns, farming communities and local traditions continued within a changed provincial order.

sectionTitles: A modern republic with older places

passages.text: Mauritania became independent from France on 28 November 1960. This modern republic must be distinguished from ancient Mauretania farther north. Its desert towns and teaching traditions are much older than the state, while the 1960 atlas outline represents modern territorial coverage rather than the birth of those communities.

passages.title: A modern republic with older places
passages.text: Independence in 1960 followed French rule. The diplomatic record identifies 28 November as the decisive date and names Moktar Ould Daddah as prime minister at recognition. The republic joined an international system of states, but its residents’ connections across desert, river and coast long predated that event.

passages.title: A modern republic with older places
passages.text: The older towns of Ouadane, Chinguetti, Tichitt and Oualata served trans-Saharan caravan routes. Their surviving fabric developed over medieval centuries, not after independence. Courtyard houses cluster along twisting lanes near mosques with square minarets, preserving the physical arrangement of communities built around travel, trade and religious learning.

passages.title: A modern republic with older places
passages.text: The ksour also contained warehouses for protecting goods. Dense building patterns, blank outer walls and internal courtyards show how household space and storage fitted a desert setting. UNESCO identifies sand movement and changing construction methods as conservation problems: keeping an old town alive requires care for ordinary houses as well as celebrated monuments.

passages.title: Classrooms, language and the coast
passages.text: A mahadra classroom can be a tent with mats, carpets and cushions on the ground. In the tradition described by UNESCO in 2023, listening and memorizing connect students with teachers and with one another. Religion, language and literature share the learning space; a permanent school building is not the only setting for serious study.

passages.title: Classrooms, language and the coast
passages.text: Mahadra learning also includes reading animal tracks, recognizing medicinal plants and using stars to find direction. Poetry and storytelling pass through the same community networks. These descriptions record kinds of knowledge people teach, rather than establishing the effectiveness of every historical remedy.

passages.title: Classrooms, language and the coast
passages.text: The official Arabic constitution prints the motto “شرف،إخاء، عدل”: “Honor, Fraternity, Justice.” This sample is from article 9 of the 1991 constitution as revised, in the Constitutional Council’s online text. Article 6 recognizes Arabic, Pulaar, Soninke and Wolof as national languages, showing that one Arabic quotation cannot represent every Mauritanian voice.

passages.title: Classrooms, language and the coast
passages.text: At Banc d’Arguin, Imraguen fishers work on foot with nets and from sailing boats called lanches. The park authority describes lateen sails and a prohibition on motorboats within the protected fishery. Knowing the shallow water, wind and fish movements matters as much as owning a boat.

passages.title: Classrooms, language and the coast
passages.text: Fishing households’ work continues after a catch comes ashore. The park’s 2010 to 2014 management plan records support for women processing and marketing poutargue, a preserved fish-roe product, and transport for village cooperatives. Food preparation, preservation and selling were part of the economy, not a footnote to the fishermen’s work.

passages.title: Water, rights and continuity
passages.text: UNICEF’s energy case study describes manually drilled boreholes combined with solar pumps, storage reservoirs and small distribution networks. Five drilling stations with solar pumping were supported in 2020 and 2021, alongside training for local operators. A pump needs someone who can maintain it after the installation team has left.

passages.title: Water, rights and continuity
passages.text: A photograph in the same report shows a woman cleaning a solar panel serving a cooperative’s market garden. The caption explains that pumped water supports crops, income and fruit and vegetables for children. In this setting, cleaning a panel is part of the work that helps dinner grow.

passages.title: Water, rights and continuity
passages.text: Legal reform did not immediately end inherited forms of exploitation. In 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child welcomed stronger anti-slavery law but reported continuing caste-based slavery affecting children. It called for investigations, freedom, family support and access to school. The concern was people’s lived freedom, beyond words in legislation.

passages.title: Water, rights and continuity
passages.text: The 2019 transfer from one elected president to another was a political milestone identified by the UN Peacebuilding Commission. It did not mean that the state began again or that all social problems were solved. Mauritania’s history continues through institutions, local learning and the daily work of its diverse communities.
Mauritania remains a continuing republic whose independence dates to 1960. Changes of leadership are distinct from the survival of its communities and from the much older desert towns they preserve.

passages.text: Maya history encompasses distinct societies and city-states. Tikal, Calakmul, Palenque and Copan supported royal courts with specialized artists; their political histories should be explored individually rather than compressed into one Maya empire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Some court artists signed their work. The sculptor Chakalte' left his name on a relief showing Shield Jaguar IV receiving tribute.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Stoneworkers carved and polished limestone vessels with tools and abrasives. Shell, bone, jade and fired clay offered other media for intricate objects.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Blue-green jade evoked water, new growth and primordial beings. It became material for offerings, ornaments and royal regalia.

passages.title: Writing and history
passages.text: Tikal's carved and painted inscriptions preserve dynastic history and relationships with other cities. They document particular courts, not a single pan-Maya government.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Tikal combined monumental precincts with residential districts and reservoirs known today as aguadas. Its surrounding settlements also supported agricultural production.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: After several Classic-period kingdoms declined, northern centers such as Chichen Itza continued commissioning major artworks. Political collapse in one region did not end Maya history everywhere.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Tikal's Corriental reservoir, researchers identified zeolite and coarse quartz in dated sediment layers. They interpret these minerals as evidence of a water filter; its proposed stone supports and woven matting are a reconstruction, not a surviving intact installation.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Water-jar fragments occur throughout Corriental's excavated sediment sequence, linking the reservoir to everyday water collection. The filter evidence comes from this particular reservoir, not from every Maya city.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Copan, exposed layers of the Acropolis preserve earlier plaza floors and covered water outlets beneath later construction. These buried surfaces reveal repeated rebuilding of the city rather than a monument created in a single episode.

Maya societies did not share one fall date or one conqueror. UNESCO places Copan's abandonment in the early tenth century, while northern centers continued major artistic production after many Classic courts declined; a local city's decline cannot stand for the end of all Maya societies. Maya communities continue today, with living languages and cultural traditions.

sectionTitles: Rulers, traders and a hilltop court
Meals, fields and getting a caravan ready

passages.text: Mbailundu, also called Bailundo, was an Umbundu-speaking kingdom in Angola’s central highlands, enriched by caravan commerce. Its rulers negotiated with foreign traders and missionaries before Portuguese conquest. The imported outline sits far north of Bailundo itself; it cannot be read as a reliable kingdom boundary.

passages.title: Rulers, traders and a hilltop court
passages.text: Ekuikui II sought schooling as well as diplomatic leverage. His 1884 letter requested someone to teach his children reading and writing; other letters asked for pens, envelopes and ink. The king was actively choosing foreign connections, rather than simply waiting for visitors.

passages.title: Rulers, traders and a hilltop court
passages.text: The royal court on Halavala’s rocky height overlooked the Portuguese fort built in 1895. Colonial officers complained that their fort was badly exposed beneath it. A flag and a fort did not automatically give newcomers control of the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Rulers, traders and a hilltop court
passages.text: The conflict of 1902 to 1904 involved different local groups, European and Creole commercial interests, and Portuguese colonial forces. Their goals were not identical. Research based on contemporary reports shows how the war opened the way for a stronger colonial occupation.

passages.title: Meals, fields and getting a caravan ready
passages.text: An early twentieth-century Umbundu chronicle remembers women fetching river water, cooking funge, and carrying seeds, hoes and baskets to the fields. Feeding households and growing the next harvest made for a crowded morning.

passages.title: Meals, fields and getting a caravan ready
passages.text: The same chronicle describes men preparing woodland beehives for honey and saleable wax. Bees did the collecting; people supplied the housing and harvested the results. This is one remembered occupation, not a rule for every man.

passages.title: Meals, fields and getting a caravan ready
passages.text: Caravan preparations could begin the year before departure. Travelers grew tobacco and saved salt and beads to buy food along the route. A journey needed a portable pantry budget long before anyone shouldered the first load.

passages.title: Meals, fields and getting a caravan ready
passages.text: A 27-centimeter wooden female figure from Bailundo was catalogued in Hambly’s 1934 expedition report as a diviner’s aid for choosing a caravan route. The carving records travelers’ spiritual concerns about uncertain journeys; its purpose was recorded belief, not demonstrated navigation technology.

passages.title: Law, learning and written words
passages.text: The chronicle’s court heard complaints about theft, injury and unpaid debts. People received an appointed hearing day; elders gathered before the ruler entered. Law was a public event with witnesses and carefully staged authority.

passages.title: Law, learning and written words
passages.text: “Efetikilo ko Bailundo” means “The Beginnings of Bailundo.” It heads an Umbundu chronicle recorded between 1903 and the 1930s, preserved in Harvard’s missionary archives. This is an attested text in Latin letters, with uncertain individual authorship.

passages.title: Law, learning and written words
passages.text: Protestant missions from 1881 and Catholic missions from 1896 contributed to Bailundo’s schools and vocational instruction. Education developed through competing religious institutions, not a single school system.

passages.title: Law, learning and written words
passages.text: Later, in the 1930s, the colonial town had electricity and piped water. These dated improvements belong to a changed urban settlement, decades after the independent kingdom’s heyday.

passages.title: Memory after conquest
passages.text: A large statue of Ekuikui II was erected in Bailundo in 2010. Melnysyn contrasts its national resistance symbolism with the king’s complicated alliances, including support against rival kingdoms. A monument tells us about later remembrance as well as the ruler it portrays.

Portuguese warfare destroyed Bailundo’s political autonomy around the turn of the twentieth century; a colonial district followed in 1904. The map’s 1914 endpoint marks neither that conquest nor the disappearance of the community.

sectionTitles: Families, small farms and useful gardens
Low German stories traveled beyond state borders

passages.text: Mecklenburg-Schwerin was a northern German duchy formed by the partition of 1701 and raised to a grand duchy in 1815. Its world included powerful landowners, farming villages, Baltic ports and elaborate court residences. This imported record covers 1783 to 1878, but its earlier outline extends into neighboring Mecklenburg-Strelitz and must not be treated as an exact border. The grand duchy itself continued until the monarchy ended in 1918.

passages.title: Who had a say?
passages.text: The old constitution gave power to the ruler, landed estates and represented towns. People living on the duke’s own domains had no representation in the estate assembly, while tenants on noble estates were represented through their landlords. Having a home in the country did not mean having an equal voice in its government.

passages.title: Who had a say?
passages.text: A constitution introduced on 10 October 1849 promised equality, personal freedom and freedom of belief and conscience. It also separated the courts from the other branches of government. Opponents challenged the change, and an arbitration decision in September 1850 restored the older estate constitution. Political reform could move backward as well as forward.

passages.title: Families, small farms and useful gardens
passages.text: Mueß, now preserved in Schwerin’s open-air museum, contained households with very different access to land. In 1857 its eleven Büdner, or smallholders, grew rye, oats and potatoes. These were practical crops for food and farming, rather than a display garden arranged for visitors. The museum’s village history anchors the crop list to that particular year.

passages.title: Families, small farms and useful gardens
passages.text: The museum describes smallholder plots of roughly three to nine hectares, about seven to twenty-two acres. Such holdings could be too small to support a family on their own, so household members also needed wages or craft income. A family’s working day might combine its own plot with work for somebody else.

passages.title: Families, small farms and useful gardens
passages.text: In the village history’s account of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, a farm commonly passed to the eldest son or to the husband of the eldest daughter. Younger children often became servants on other farms. Inheritance rules could therefore determine where siblings lived and how they earned their food after leaving home.

passages.title: Families, small farms and useful gardens
passages.text: One old climbing bean has a family history. The museum records the Kröger family near Hagenow growing their yellow-podded variety since 1850 and passing its seeds between generations. In 1997 the family offered it to the museum. Saving seed preserved an edible inheritance that could fit in a small packet.

passages.title: Families, small farms and useful gardens
passages.text: An 1888 description by teacher E. Gang, later than this map record but still within the grand duchy, inspired the museum’s reconstructed teacher’s garden. Its model combines vegetables, a tree nursery, a bee shed and mulberry hedges. Teachers were expected to help demonstrate useful cultivation. The present garden is a reconstruction from written plans, not an unchanged nineteenth-century plot.

passages.title: Paper palaces and sea air
passages.text: Ludwigslust’s workshops produced decorations from papier-mâché that could resemble marble, porcelain or gilded sculpture. Workers pressed paper into molds made of materials such as wood, plaster or clay, then finished and painted the results. Courtly splendor depended on skilled hands and clever surfaces. Something looking tremendously heavy might have paper inside.

passages.title: Paper palaces and sea air
passages.text: In 1773, before this map record starts, the duke ordered old official papers to be reused by the workshops. Handwritten notes and columns of numbers still survive on the backs of some objects. Production continued into the early nineteenth century. An old tax record could have a second career helping a palace look expensive.

passages.title: Paper palaces and sea air
passages.text: The court returned to Schwerin in 1837, and the palace was rebuilt into its present elaborate form by 1857. Architects including Georg Adolf Demmler and Friedrich August Stüler drew on models such as Chambord in France. Its towers evoke older castles, but much of the residence is a nineteenth-century creation.

passages.title: Paper palaces and sea air
passages.text: Heiligendamm’s first bathhouse opened on 21 September 1793 after the duke’s physician promoted bathing in seawater. He even supplied rules warning against bathing immediately after a strong emotional upset. Aristocratic and wealthy visitors helped the resort grow. The beach became a setting for treatment, fashionable company and carefully organized leisure.

passages.title: Low German stories traveled beyond state borders
passages.text: Writing sample: “Läuschen un Rimels” is Low German in Latin letters, meaning roughly “Tall tales and rhymes.” The University of Greifswald catalogs this exact title on Fritz Reuter’s seventh edition, published by Hinstorff in Wismar in 1864. The phrase gives a small taste of a regional literary language used for humorous stories and verses.

passages.title: Low German stories traveled beyond state borders
passages.text: Reuter came from Stavenhagen, but his first edition appeared while he lived outside Mecklenburg-Schwerin, in Treptow in Prussian Pomerania. Friends helped pay for the 1853 publication, and Fritz and his wife Luise packed and mailed the books. The first 1,200 copies sold out. A successful literary career began with teamwork and parcels, as well as writing.

Grand Duke Friedrich Franz IV abdicated on 14 November 1918. Mecklenburg-Schwerin became a republic, adopting a new constitution in 1920. The monarchy’s end came forty years after this imported record stops, so 1878 is a map cutoff rather than the state’s collapse.

sectionTitles: A worked landscape and changing alliances

passages.text: Menominee communities have deep roots around Green Bay and the Menominee River. The map uses Menomini for one record and Menominee for another; these are spellings of the same people. Its broad upper Great Lakes outlines and early dates are approximate coverage, not precise borders or a founding year. Today’s Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin governs from Keshena.

passages.title: A worked landscape and changing alliances
passages.text: A study published in 2025 documented extensive ancestral Menominee farming at Sixty Islands on the Menominee River. Drone laser mapping revealed clustered ridges beneath forest cover. The garden beds, roughly four to twelve inches high, supported crops including maize, beans and squash in a region with a challenging growing season.

passages.title: A worked landscape and changing alliances
passages.text: Excavations in 2023 sampled three agricultural ridges at different distances from the river. Radiocarbon evidence indicates repeated rebuilding across approximately six centuries, from around 1000 to 1600. These were landscapes maintained through generations of work, not just convenient patches of naturally fertile ground.

passages.title: A worked landscape and changing alliances
passages.text: French fur trading from the later seventeenth century encouraged smaller, mobile bands and winter trapping camps. Families exchanged furs for knives, cloth, firearms and metal cookware. Leaders increasingly needed diplomatic skills to manage relationships with traders and neighboring peoples.

passages.title: A worked landscape and changing alliances
passages.text: After an 1848 treaty proposed removal to Minnesota, Oshkosh and other leaders resisted. Menominee people remained in Wisconsin; a temporary Wolf River reservation was followed by the permanent reservation established in 1854. Staying close to their homeland was a major political achievement.

passages.title: Food, homes and responsibilities
passages.text: The museum’s account describes summer villages with rectangular bark cabins and peaked roofs, while winter camps used bark-and-mat wigwams. Households moved with seasonal work and food supplies. A family’s home life therefore involved several familiar places rather than one building occupied throughout the year.

passages.title: Food, homes and responsibilities
passages.text: Wild rice was important enough to give the Menominee their widely used name. The museum describes Great Lakes households cooking it with vegetables, meat or maple sugar, and sometimes parching it as a treat. Birchbark containers helped store a harvest that had to last beyond its short gathering season.

passages.title: Food, homes and responsibilities
passages.text: The College of Menominee Nation explains clan responsibilities through its Clans Story. Bear is associated with civil administration, Crane with construction, and Moose with camp security and oversight of wild-rice harvests. In this account, belonging carried duties toward the wider community, including how an important food resource was shared.

passages.title: Food, homes and responsibilities
passages.text: The 2021 Harvest of the Moon curriculum connected foods with Menominee language, seasonal knowledge, recipes and artwork by Daniel Grignon. Twenty-five sets went to school Language and Culture teachers that May. Coloring pages and food lessons offered children several ways to explore the same subject with their hands, eyes and words.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: Congress passed the Menominee Termination Act in 1954, and implementation followed in 1961. It removed federal recognition and services without making Menominee people disappear. The tribal timeline describes the closure of Keshena’s hospital soon afterward, showing how a change in government policy reached directly into everyday access to care.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: Community resistance included a 1964 petition and the later DRUMS campaign for restoration. On December 22, 1973, the Restoration Act became law. Rebuilding government and services required further work after that victory; the act marked a decisive reversal of termination rather than an instant repair of its damage.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: Menominee forestry combines timber production with responsibility for the forest’s future. In his conference paper, Menominee Tribal Enterprises leader Adrian Miller describes balancing income with ecological, spiritual and cultural obligations. Managing a sawmill and caring for a homeland belong within the same set of decisions.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: Community leaders created the College of Menominee Nation’s Sustainable Development Institute in 1993. Its work brought together education, governance, commerce and natural-resource management. Research and training grew from questions the community already faced: how to make a living while keeping the land healthy for those who follow.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: Lemley and Teller’s language research followed relationships between elders, adult teachers and younger learners. Some children encountered Menominee through grandparents at home; others needed school programs for that opportunity. Their interviews show why storytelling and everyday conversation matter alongside formal lessons.

passages.title: Restoration, forests and learning
passages.text: An attested example in the same study is “Maec waewaenen,” translated as “Thank you very much.” The phrase appears in a participant’s response during the research. It is a recorded modern Menominee expression, preserved here in the spelling used by Lemley and Menominee educator John Teller.

The map’s cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of the Menominee. The nation survived land loss and federal termination, regained recognition in 1973, and continues its government, family life, education and stewardship in Wisconsin.

passages.text: Mercia was a kingdom in central England. Large earthworks and the Staffordshire Hoard offer different views of its region: organized construction and highly skilled early medieval metalwork.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Offa's Dyke used a bank and ditch to mark a frontier. English Heritage dates its construction probably to the 780s.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Staffordshire Hoard fragments include intricate gold and garnet decoration. Their designs have connections across several European regions.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Many hoard fragments belonged to an elaborate helmet. Modern reconstruction relies on study of the surviving pieces rather than discovery of an intact helmet.

passages.title: Evidence and daily life
passages.text: The hoard reveals elite craftsmanship and equipment. Its burial location alone cannot identify every maker or make it a representative sample of ordinary Mercian households.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Scholars from Mercia contributed to the translations supported by Alfred of Wessex. Learned activity crossed the boundaries between neighboring kingdoms.

sectionTitles: Opening the gate was a serious job
Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
A letter at the end of a reign

passages.text: Merina royal centres developed in Madagascar’s highlands, a landscape of palaces, ancestral places and cultivated land. This card follows that particular political tradition, rather than treating every Malagasy community as Merina.

passages.title: Opening the gate was a serious job
passages.text: Ambohimanga had fourteen gateways belonging to different phases of its defences. ICOMOS describes doors weighing as much as twelve tonnes and carefully controlled access. These entrances displayed royal status as well as regulating movement. Forgetting something outside could be inconvenient on a scale far beyond having to find your house key.

passages.title: Opening the gate was a serious job
passages.text: Inside the royal enclosure were two basins cut into rock, connected with the annual royal bathing ceremony. The surrounding spaces included royal burial places and an area for public pronouncements. Water here had ritual significance. These surviving basins are evidence for a particular court ceremony, not a picture of how every highland household washed.

passages.title: Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
passages.text: At Marorangotra, beside today’s Lake Mantasoa, researchers investigated heaps of slag, the waste left by making iron. They also found fragments of stone air pipes used in furnaces. The wider region was producing iron in the late nineteenth century, but the report does not establish when every deposit began. These are traces of skilled local production, not proof that ironworking arrived with European factories.

passages.title: Ironworking leaves a very durable mess
passages.text: A small excavation at Marorangotra also recovered pieces of a large cooking pot with a black graphite coating, alongside animal bones including zebu cattle. Such finds put ordinary equipment beside industrial waste. They do not reveal a complete workers’ menu: the bones are not automatically one meal, and the report leaves the deposits’ precise dates unresolved.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: In early nineteenth-century Antananarivo, school writing supplies could be scarce. One account describes smooth wooden boards rubbed with grease and dusted with ash. Pupils wrote with a wooden point, then wiped the marks away with a rag or finger. Reusable schoolwork did not require a battery, although keeping that board off your best clothes sounds sensible.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: Students helped produce Malagasy translations rather than simply copying their foreign teachers. They carried word lists home on slates and consulted relatives about suitable expressions. Families thus contributed knowledge to work that later appeared in books. The teacher might know the English word, while a child and their household knew better how to say it in Malagasy.

passages.title: Schoolwork on an ash-covered board
passages.text: The resulting work depended on people whose contributions were easily overlooked. An enslaved interpreter named Joseph helped missionary David Jones learn Malagasy. Larson’s research brings interpreters and pupils back into a history often told mainly through European missionaries’ names. Learning a language was a shared achievement, carried out within profoundly unequal relationships.

passages.title: A pattern beside the loom
passages.text: A Merina silk cloth in the British Museum, dated approximately 1875 to 1900, consists of two panels sewn together. Coloured stripes and floating threads create elaborate patterns. It belongs to a tradition of costly cloth associated with aristocratic dress and burial. Its arrival in the museum in 1969 is a collection date, not the date somebody wove it.

passages.title: A pattern beside the loom
passages.text: The museum describes nineteenth-century Merina weavers keeping designs on paper beside their looms. Extra thread controls helped them build bands of geometric decoration. That combination of a written plan and careful handwork makes the complexity easier to appreciate. The catalogue does not identify a secret meaning for every pattern, so a handsome zigzag need not become a mysterious code.

passages.title: Learning to care for patients
passages.text: The Antananarivo mission hospital opened in July 1865 as part of Andrew Davidson’s medical work. Malagasy students learned medicine, nursing and midwifery, and medical material was published in Malagasy. Two trainees, Andrianaly and Rajaonah, later studied in Edinburgh. Their careers show local learners becoming practitioners, rather than patients being the only Malagasy people in the story.

passages.title: Who did the work?
passages.text: The kingdom’s workshops made goods including glass and cannon, with Malagasy apprentices mastering new manufacturing techniques. But workers did not all choose their jobs. Fanompoana required unpaid labour for the state, and military conquest also enslaved people. Campbell’s history describes workers and soldiers fleeing harsh conditions. Achievements in production belong beside the experiences of the people required to produce them.

passages.title: A letter at the end of a reign
passages.text: The British Library catalogues copies of a letter dated 27 February 1897 in which General Gallieni ordered Queen Ranavalona III’s exile. The surviving catalogue gives a precise documentary trace of a political turning point. These are photocopies preserved in an archive, not an excavated object, and the catalogue description is different from reading the original letter itself.

French conquest in 1895 and annexation in 1896 ended the kingdom’s independence. Ranavalona III was forced into exile in February 1897, ending the monarchy. Merina communities continued under colonial rule. Neither the map’s change of label in 1878 nor its endpoint in 1914 dates this political ending.

passages.text: The Marinids made Fez a royal capital and sponsored an urban culture of learning, worship, commerce and craftsmanship. Their new town stood beside the older medina, creating a capital with complementary royal and civic spaces.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Fez Jedid was founded in 1276 beside Fez el-Bali. It included the palace, fortifications, military headquarters and residential districts.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Madrasas and mosques are among the principal monuments associated with the city's Marinid flourishing in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries.

passages.title: Daily life and trade
passages.text: Fondouks, houses and fountains belonged to the capital's urban fabric alongside royal and religious buildings.

passages.title: Arts and legacy
passages.text: Fez's architecture brought local skills into conversation with influences from Andalusia and other African and eastern centers. Its craft traditions continued beyond any one dynasty.

passages.text: Meroë was a royal centre of Kush in the Middle Nile region of present-day Sudan. This entry focuses on its later history: towns, temples, farms and workshops as well as royal pyramids. The map’s span from 500 BCE to 500 CE is broader than the conventionally defined Meroitic political period.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: The heritage landscape links the royal city of Meroë with Naqa and Musawwarat es-Sufra. Temples, palaces and steep-sided pyramids show several kinds of royal and religious activity, rather than one gigantic cemetery standing alone in a desert.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: Reservoirs known as hafirs collected seasonal water in the inland landscape. Their surviving earthworks make water management visible: people needed ways to store water beyond the immediate banks of the Nile.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: Excavators at nearby Hamadab mapped a town with a temple, public square, administrative building, public well and workshops. These facilities put worship, government, water collection and manufacture into the same urban neighbourhood.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: Hamadab households contained kitchens, cooking pots, storage containers and hearths. Such ordinary finds help archaeologists ask how meals were prepared and supplies stored, questions that a royal tomb alone cannot answer.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: A trench through Hamadab’s main road exposed about four metres of occupation deposits. Streets and houses were repeatedly used and altered; archaeologists read those layers to reconstruct a town’s changing life.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: Pottery kilns and large ceramic assemblages at Hamadab document local craft production. Nowotnick’s study compares vessels from workshops and late Meroitic houses, connecting the making of containers with the people who used them.

passages.title: Towns, buildings and skilled work
passages.text: Meroë’s ironworking left slag, furnace fragments, charcoal and ore. Modern smelting experiments test how furnaces could have operated, while the excavated debris supplies the evidence. An experimental success is a model of ancient work, not proof that every workshop followed one recipe.

passages.title: Food, family and written words
passages.text: Plant remains attest winter wheat and barley alongside summer crops including sorghum and beans. This double-cropping system linked different foods to different seasons and to irrigation, rather than relying on a single harvest calendar.

passages.title: Food, family and written words
passages.text: Wiritelito’s funerary stele from Karanog, dated to the later third century CE, names her mother, father and other relatives. Her father is identified as a scribe. A memorial can preserve a family network as well as one person’s name.

passages.title: Food, family and written words
passages.text: The same stele asks that Wiritelito receive abundant water, bread and good meals after death. These are funerary wishes, not a literal shopping list, but they reveal how everyday sustenance entered ideas about the afterlife.

passages.title: Food, family and written words
passages.text: A short Meroitic sample is “𐦳𐦣𐦫”, read qor, “the ruler”. It follows Talakhidamani’s name in line 2 of an inscription found in Meroë’s Amun temple in 2012, dated around the late third or early fourth century CE. This is a standardized typed rendering of the published reading, not a tracing of the worn stone.

passages.title: Food, family and written words
passages.text: Knowing the signs does not mean understanding every sentence. Royal Meroitic texts can be badly eroded and use vocabulary that remains uncertain. Scholars distinguish readable names and titles from proposed translations of longer passages.

passages.title: What changed
passages.text: A 2023 study tested tooth enamel from people and animals at thirteen cemeteries. Its isotope results suggest increasingly dry conditions and changing food production around the kingdom’s end. The authors present environmental stress as one possible contributor alongside political and economic pressures.

Meroitic royal power broke down in the fourth century CE. The roles of internal change, neighbouring peoples and Aksumite campaigns remain debated; a single destruction story is too simple. Successor communities and later Nubian kingdoms continued in the region.
