passages.text: Meskwaki is the people’s own name; Fox is the French-derived label used on this map. The imported outlines place an earlier record in southern Michigan and a later one in Wisconsin, offering broad phases rather than precise migration boundaries. Meskwaki history includes movement into Iowa and a continuing nation there. Alliance with the Sauk did not make the two peoples identical.

passages.title: Conflict, diplomacy and land
passages.text: Competition and conflict around the fur trade drew the Meskwaki into prolonged wars with New France in the early eighteenth century. The University of Iowa’s archaeological teaching history describes movement away from Wisconsin and eventually into Iowa. Communities adapted through migration and alliances rather than remaining inside a fixed map outline.

passages.title: Conflict, diplomacy and land
passages.text: Meskwaki and Sauk communities allied in 1735 after French attacks. United States officials later grouped them as Sac and Fox, but they remained distinct peoples. Combined treaty names can obscure that distinction.

passages.title: Conflict, diplomacy and land
passages.text: At site 11ML6 near Arrowsmith, Illinois, archaeologists documented defensive ditches, semi-subterranean structures and evidence of gunfire. Lenville Stelle argues that this is the Meskwaki fort besieged in 1730. The evidence supports an early eighteenth-century conflict site, although attaching a precise historical event remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Conflict, diplomacy and land
passages.text: Ten gunflints from that investigation included locally made Burlington chert examples and French-made pieces. A gunflint helped a firearm produce its spark. Imported equipment could be traded and reused, so finding French manufacture does not by itself reveal the nationality of the person who fired the gun.

passages.title: Conflict, diplomacy and land
passages.text: On July 13, 1857, Meskwaki purchasers acquired the first 80 acres of their Iowa settlement after removal to Kansas. Buying land created a durable base for returning families. The settlement’s history centers on this community initiative, rather than on a reservation simply assigned by the federal government.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: The nation’s history of the harvest celebration describes corn being cooked, dried, packed in sacks and stored in deep pits within summer homes. Dancing, feasting and games accompanied the harvest before families departed for winter hunting. Spring brought the work of repairing wickiups and planting again.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: An Iowa State University exhibition records a cradleboard used by John Young Bear for his baby, Co-Ques-Se-We. Curved wooden boards, leather ties and a wooden hoop with yarn formed a carefully made family object. Naming its users helps restore an individual child and parent to a museum collection.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: A ribbon-appliqué skirt by Meskwaki artist Frank Pushetonequa combines hand stitching with commercial cloth and cut ribbons in red, purple, green and yellow. The museum traces its purchase from the artist in 1982 or 1983. Fine handwork and purchased materials belonged together in this continuing artistic practice.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: The modern annual powwow developed through changing forms of community gathering. Field Days between 1902 and 1912 included games and social activities, and a committee organized the first annual powwow in 1913. The organizers’ history connects that event with earlier harvest celebrations while showing that its format evolved.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: In 2022, Red Earth Gardens described weekly produce distributions through its Diabetes Share Program. Cooking demonstrations on the last Wednesday of the month welcomed community members beyond program participants. A garden’s work extended from growing vegetables to helping neighbors share food and ideas in the kitchen.

passages.title: Families, food and celebration
passages.text: A 2025 report follows students out of the classroom during their Meskwaki language period to harvest Tama Flint corn at East Farm. Adults guided them through picking, husking and shelling the colorful ears. Language learning could therefore involve a real crop and experienced community teachers alongside spoken words.

passages.title: Education, language and returning knowledge
passages.text: The industrial day school opened in 1896 divided time between morning lessons and afternoon agriculture or carpentry. Two years later, a boarding school opened at Toledo without tribal leaders’ support. These arrangements made schooling a struggle over who would direct children’s lives, as well as what subjects they would study.

passages.title: Education, language and returning knowledge
passages.text: At his 2021 graduation, Namabyewa, Romeo Buffalo, said “Kemiskawisibeni etatagi asemietiwaki.” The tribal newsletter gives the meaning as “We are strong when we help each other.” It labels the English a translation of the meaning, not a word-for-word rendering. This is an attested modern Meskwaki speech preserved in writing.

passages.title: Education, language and returning knowledge
passages.text: Red Earth Gardens began in 2013 as part of the nation’s food-sovereignty work. Its teaching and youth opportunities connect agricultural skills with the ability of the community to shape its own food supply. Growing food also creates places where younger people can learn through shared work.

passages.title: Education, language and returning knowledge
passages.text: In April 2026, Historic Preservation Director Johnathan Buffalo reported the return of more than 200 objects from the Missouri State Museum’s Mary Alicia Owen collection. Meskwaki representatives had begun pursuing their return in 1993. The homecoming made a long museum negotiation part of present-day cultural life.
The imported map cutoffs do not end Meskwaki history. The Meskwaki Nation in Iowa continues its government and community on land first purchased in 1857.

passages.text: Mexico became independent in 1821, after centuries of Indigenous histories and Spanish colonial rule. The republic, restored after a brief second empire, entered an era of rail construction and the long presidency of Porfirio Díaz. Revolution began in 1910, and a 1917 constitution reshaped land, work and education claims. Children’s schools, tortilla-making kitchens and access to doctors or toilets tell a less uniform story than the border. Mexico continues with many Indigenous languages and communities; the imported map begins only in 1878.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: After a long war, Mexico achieved independence in 1821. The 1824 constitution made it a representative federal republic. The 1878 date in this map is only the first imported border view, not the country’s birthday.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Mexico later endured foreign intervention and a second empire. The republic was restored in 1867. Its governments changed, while Indigenous peoples and local communities continued their own lives through these state transitions.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: During the long Díaz era, railways connected mines, farms and cities, often with foreign capital. Trains could move goods faster, but a new line did not make land, wages or political influence equal for everyone.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Revolution broke out in 1910 as several movements fought over power and land. It was not one army or one neatly finished day. The 1917 constitution was a major result, including claims about education, land and labor.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Women organized against Díaz, wrote, carried supplies, nursed wounded people and sometimes fought. Carmen Serdán also helped organize military nurses. The word “soldadera” hides many different jobs, risks and political choices.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: The revolution’s constitution made workers’ claims part of the national legal framework, alongside land and education. A right written in 1917 still had to be fought for at a particular farm, mine or factory.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Article 27 placed land and water questions at the center of the new constitutional order. In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas expropriated the oil industry after a conflict between workers and companies, invoking national resource rights.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A 1925 plan for rural schools asked teachers to connect lessons with daily village life and avoid rigid classroom routines. A child might learn through local work and community problems, though schools differed widely and did not reach every child.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: The original 1917 constitution opened Article 3 with “La enseñanza es libre” or “Teaching is free.” That is a brief sample of written Spanish from the period; the education article has been amended since, and many Mexican children also speak Indigenous languages.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A tortilla begins before the frying pan: maize is simmered with food-grade limewater, rested, milled into dough and cooked. This ancient nixtamal process makes everyday food more nourishing. In Náhuatl, a tortilla is called “tlaxcalli.”

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A warm tortilla can also be an edible wrapper for beans, vegetables or meat. Families and regions prepare maize in many ways, including tamales and atole; the tortilla is a continuing tradition, not proof that every household eats the same dinner.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: Toilet history is less glamorous but just as revealing. Mexico’s census tracks toilets, piped water and drainage separately, because a flush toilet, a latrine and a sewer connection are different things. Whether your home had one depended on place and resources.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: Mexico’s many Indigenous languages remain living home and community languages. A 2020 census count used by INPI found over seven million speakers. Spanish on a constitution page cannot stand in for what every grandparent, child or neighbor speaks.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: Mexico founded the IMSS in 1943 to combine health care and social protection for covered workers and their families. A workplace card could help when someone got sick, but many people outside formal employment needed different routes to care.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: From the 1970s, IMSS programs extended some services to poorer communities without ordinary payroll coverage. That later expansion is a clue that earlier worker insurance had not reached everyone.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: The 2000 presidential election brought a party change after decades of dominance by one party. The electoral institute describes this as an alternation built on earlier reforms; it did not mean all problems were solved in one vote.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: Mexico continues as a federal republic. Its 1821 independence, 1867 restoration, 1917 constitution and 2000 electoral change mark different transformations of a continuing country; none is the first day of its Indigenous peoples.

Mexico continues as a federal republic. Independence came in 1821, the republic was restored in 1867, and the 1917 constitution still frames state history. Indigenous peoples and languages continue across all those dates; the imported 1878 border snapshot does not verify their territories or every historic boundary.

sectionTitles: River villages, skilled work and recreation

passages.text: The Miami, or Myaamia, are a Great Lakes people whose farming villages and river connections supported wide regional influence. The broad Myaamia and narrower Miami outlines are approximations. A separate Oklahoma outline dated 1492 is anachronistic: Miami settlement there followed nineteenth-century removals. Miami communities continue in Oklahoma, Indiana and beyond.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami villages stood near rivers that connected settlements through canoe travel. The Indiana community’s history places their homeland across parts of present-day Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan. Hunting, fishing and cultivation worked together in a landscape where water routes could link relatives and trading partners.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami white flour corn drew an early eighteenth-century observer’s attention for its fine husks and pale flour. Historian Cameron Shriver follows this crop through later sources, including twentieth-century Miami farmers. Corn was both a lasting food tradition and an agricultural achievement maintained through enormous political change.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In a 2023 account, weaver Jared Nally describes harvesting inner bark from trees such as basswood and gathering other plant fibers later in the year. Separating usable fibers and rolling or spinning thread could take as long as weaving itself. A finished textile contains a great deal of work that is easy not to see.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: The winter game snowsnake sends a length of wood sliding through snow. Players try to make it travel farther and straighter than an opponent’s throw. Myaamia community programs have been reviving the game: snow becomes a playing surface, and the snake is reassuringly wooden.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Lacrosse remains an opportunity to meet relatives and neighbors as well as compete. A 2022 community account describes an annual Myaamia game with Seneca-Cayuga participants, including youth camps. It also distinguishes older games from newer adaptations that introduce Myaamia language into familiar card games.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In 2024, Myaamia sugar camps operated in Ohio, Indiana and Oklahoma. Sap was boiled down into syrup or sugar; a typical maple yield required about 40 gallons of sap for one gallon of syrup. Oklahoma participants also tapped black walnut because local sugar maples were scarce. Breakfast sweetness required buckets of effort.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Miami leader Little Turtle helped lead a Native coalition that defeated United States forces in 1790 and 1791. Before the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, he urged peace. These changing decisions belonged to a wider struggle over homelands involving several allied peoples, rather than one isolated Miami army.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 required extensive land cessions. Further treaties narrowed Miami control over their homeland, and an 1840 agreement called for removal beyond the Mississippi. Treaty dates mark government decisions; the forced journey itself came later.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: On October 11, 1846, five canal boats carrying Miami people reached Cincinnati. There they were forced aboard the steamboat Colorado to continue west along the Ohio River. A university archival exhibit places this transfer within the removal journey, revealing how ordinary transport networks became instruments of forced displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Other Miami families secured permission to stay in Indiana. Their descendants form the Miami Nation of Indiana, with continuing government, cultural programs and relationships to western Miami relatives. Its own history distinguishes that community’s existence from its lack of federal recognition as a sovereign tribal nation today.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The western Miami faced another move after an 1867 treaty, with migration from Kansas into present-day Oklahoma in the late 1860s and 1870s. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma established its government there. That sequence explains why an Oklahoma polygon cannot accurately represent Miami territory in 1492.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: Language revitalization draws on documents spanning the late 1600s through the 1960s. A Myaamia Center report explains how researchers analyze old records, compare forms and develop resources for present-day use. The work connects archival scholarship with families learning words together; it is a gradual effort across generations.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.

passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.

passages.text: These entries follow Milan through Spanish and Austrian government, with the last Sforza years at the beginning of the earlier map interval. They are phases of a changing territorial state, not two unrelated civilizations. Its surviving hospital, theatre, libraries and printed books show care, work and argument alongside imperial rule.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: Milan’s great hospital, the Ca’ Granda, had been founded in 1456, before these map intervals. Its foundation ceremony included small vessels of oil, wine, milk, honey and water and a lead book. These were symbolic deposits, not a recipe for treating patients.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: The Ca’ Granda’s buildings grew over roughly three centuries, helped by citizens’ gifts and bequests. The recurring Festa del Perdono raised support. Hospital care depended on lasting institutions and donors, not simply on a duke paying for one impressive building and walking away.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: The hospital placed latrines in corridors beside the wards. Channels supplied with rainwater helped carry waste away. Convenient toilets were part of the architectural plan centuries before modern hospital plumbing; surviving remains have also been altered, so today’s building is not an untouched fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: Wastewater from the hospital passed under the Naviglio canal and toward agricultural land used for irrigation and fertilizing. That is evidence of engineered drainage and reuse, not proof of modern sewage treatment or protection from infection. The unglamorous pipes deserve a place beside the grand courtyards.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: A courtyard originally associated with baths was used for servants and nurses by the early seventeenth century. Such changing uses remind us that a hospital needed workers and service spaces as well as beds. The elegant architecture was also somebody’s workplace.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: A new assessment of Milanese taxable wealth was completed in 1560. Officials sought to distribute costs, but urban and rural interests and existing privileges complicated the process. A government’s demand for money reached farms and households, even when its records speak in the language of institutions.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: The Sforza Castle became a barracks during foreign rule. Its changing function is a reminder that a former prince’s residence could become a military workplace. Spanish, Austrian and French rulers reused the same formidable building rather than rebuilding Milan from scratch after every conquest.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: Brera’s art collection began in 1776 in connection with the academy, giving students examples to study. Its formal museum opened in 1809, after this Austrian phase. Many later additions came from suppressed religious houses: a museum’s collection can preserve the effects of political upheaval.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: After the Jesuit establishment passed to the state in 1773, Brera gathered learning institutions in one complex, including an observatory, botanical garden and library. The Braidense library opened to the public in 1786. Books, plants and the sky became neighboring subjects of investigation.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: La Scala opened in 1778 with Salieri’s Europa riconosciuta, replacing a theatre destroyed by fire. Maria Theresa authorized the new building, designed by Giuseppe Piermarini. Its name preserves the church formerly on the site; the audience was entering a newly constructed theatre, not an ancient Roman one.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: La Scala’s boxes had owners whose names can be traced in archival records beginning in 1778. An evening at the theatre was also a social occasion shaped by property and status. The records illuminate the people who held boxes, not a representative sample of every Milanese family.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: The Italian title “Dei delitti e delle pene” means “On Crimes and Punishments.” A surviving 1764 edition preserves these words from Cesare Beccaria’s famous argument about criminal justice. The Milanese author published in Livorno; a book could travel across political borders faster than a government changed its laws.

French conquest in 1796 ended this phase of Austrian government and brought new political arrangements. Milan remained inhabited and important. Neither the 1715 endpoint of the first map entry nor the 1800 endpoint of the later one is a reliable single date for the city’s “fall.”

passages.text: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.

passages.text: This combined map label covers separate powers in western Tanzania: Mirambo’s Urambo, neighbouring Unyanyembe, and Nyungu-ya-Mawe’s state in Ukimbu. Their alliances and rivalries changed. The outline is not evidence that Mirambo ruled all three, or that his state survived until the imported endpoint of 1914.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Unyanyembe’s royal centre at Itetemia stood beside the growing commercial town of Tabora. Its links to long-distance trade made it influential in its own right. It was a competitor of Mirambo’s Urambo, not simply a district in his empire.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Nyungu-ya-Mawe appointed military governors, called vatwale, to supervise provinces in Ukimbu and channel resources toward his centre. He and Mirambo were once allies, but control of caravan routes strained their relationship by 1880. One map colour hides considerable political disagreement.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Mirambo often kept chiefs who submitted to him, while replacing others with local headmen after conquest. Communities supplied fighters and provisions. His military success therefore depended on village labour as well as battlefield leadership, and imposed heavy demands on conquered people.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Mid-nineteenth-century observers described Nyamwezi women growing and processing grain, making meals and brewing grain beer. Some women travelled with caravans, sometimes with babies. Their work helped keep both households and long journeys going; experiences differed sharply between free and enslaved women.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Local specialists exchanged baskets, pottery, stools, bark boxes, mortars and pestles between villages. Smiths and medical practitioners also supplied skills that a household might seek from outside. Everyday equipment had makers, repairers and trading routes of its own.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Many Nyamwezi caravan porters were skilled wage workers. They could stop a march to demand better terms. Cloth and beads served as pay and bought provisions along the road: your wages could arrive as fabric rather than coins.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: A caravan guide needed languages as well as a good sense of direction. The kirangozi located paths, food and water and negotiated payments to chiefs. Getting everyone safely to the next meal was part of the job description.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Contact with coastal traders also carried ideas about healing into inland communities. Pallaver traces the gradual borrowing of practices without assuming that everyone immediately converted to Islam. Towns such as Tabora were meeting places for knowledge as well as merchandise.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Farmers in Unyanyembe adjusted crop choices to rainfall. Millet and sorghum tolerated drought better than rice and maize; stored harvests helped bridge bad seasons. A well-stocked granary could matter as much as a well-stocked armoury.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Warfare encouraged people to gather inside large stockaded settlements. Abandoned land returned to bush, creating conditions favourable to tsetse flies and threatening cattle. Defensive walls solved one danger while changing the landscape around them.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Drought and warfare fed each other in Mirambo’s final years. Raids seized food and people for agricultural labour, while fighting destroyed fields. Famine weakened his system before tributaries rebelled after his death in December 1884.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Written Swahili survives in a list apparently naming people captured by Mirambo: “hao kila mtu kwa watu wake”, translated as “each is there for his men.” Shown here is the editor’s Roman transcription of Arabic-script Swahili. The document’s precise date and origin are unknown; it is not Mirambo’s autograph.

Mirambo’s state fragmented after his death in 1884. Unyanyembe fell under German conquest from 1893; Nyungu’s political system in Ukimbu was dismantled in 1895. These were separate endings, not a shared collapse in 1914. Nyamwezi and Kimbu communities continued under changing rule.

passages.text: Mixtec rulers governed several competing kingdoms in southern Mexico, linked by marriages, warfare and trade. The imported “empire” outline is misplaced west of much of the Mixtec heartland; it should not be read as their territorial boundary.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw joined Tilantongo, Teozacoalco and Tututepec under his rule. His story was exceptional within a landscape of competing kingdoms. A powerful ruler could unite several courts without creating one permanent empire for every Mixtec community.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: The Tonindeye Codex unfolds like a concertina. Its 47 painted deerskin leaves carry a prepared pale surface and vivid pigments. Fully extended, the book is more than eleven metres long: this family history would not fit across an ordinary kitchen table.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: One codex scene shows Lady Five Flint giving birth to an heir, with the child still connected by the umbilical cord. Births and marriages mattered because claims to land and rule depended on relationships between families.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: A short reading supplied by the museum is “Iya Nacuaa”, meaning “Lord 8 Deer”. This is a scholarly Latin-script rendering of the ruler’s name represented in the pictorial manuscript, dated 1200 to 1521; its painted signs are not alphabetic letters.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: Calendar names linked a person to a day in a 260-day cycle. Animal signs and other images helped identify those days. In 2021, Mixtec researchers used the surviving books together with Indigenous knowledge to reinterpret their communities’ histories.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: Excavations at Yucundaa uncovered a palace with patios and rooms reserved for rulers and nobles. Architecture suggests that these spaces combined residence, ritual and formal meetings. For the court, home and workplace could be parts of the same complex.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: At that palace, investigators compare doorways, room plans, renovations and refuse from an associated rubbish deposit. Even royal rubbish has something to say: discarded material helps test ideas suggested by impressive walls and painted histories.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: Cotton moved between different environments. A historical study describes the inland kingdom of Teozacoalco obtaining it from the coast near Tututepec. A cloth’s story could therefore begin in warm coastal fields and continue in workshops far inland.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: A Mixtec gold necklace in the Met has beads shaped like jaguar teeth. Its delicate loops were modeled in wax and cast in metal, a technique called false filigree. What looks like tiny bent wires could begin as a carefully shaped wax model.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: The museum compares this necklace with objects excavated in Monte Albán’s Tomb 7. That tomb contained mixed remains of men, women and children, suggesting reuse or secondary burial. Its riches cannot securely identify one famous king as the principal occupant.

passages.title: Colonial upheaval and continuing communities
passages.text: Spanish conquest in Oaxaca involved rival local alliances as well as armed expeditions. Some Zapotec rulers sought help against Tututepec; other communities resisted. These choices had local purposes, even as Spanish rule brought new forms of domination.

passages.title: Colonial upheaval and continuing communities
passages.text: Ancient DNA from ten people buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa identified Salmonella Paratyphi C. Researchers propose it as a strong candidate behind the local 1545 epidemic. Teeth preserved evidence that could help investigate a catastrophe centuries after the people died.

Spanish rule and colonial tribute transformed Mixtec kingdoms during the sixteenth century; the imported 1530 cutoff is not one empire’s fall. Mixtec peoples, languages and historical traditions continue, and Indigenous scholars actively interpret the surviving books.

passages.text: Mixtec history connects distinct kingdoms and communities in Oaxaca. Painted books record ruling families whose interests sometimes conflicted. Archaeology adds the work of farmers, householders and craftspeople to histories often centred on dynasties.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: At Nicayuhu, archaeologists excavated Postclassic houses beside terraced fields. Stone foundations and repeatedly renewed floors show long use. Rooms around patios included hearths; sloping floors and heated annexes were interpreted cautiously as possible steam baths.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Nicayuhu households used ordinary pottery and stone tools. Obsidian blades were scarce and sometimes reshaped to prolong their working life. The excavated assemblages reveal maintenance and economical reuse alongside the better-known luxury arts.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Lama-bordo terraces trap soil carried by seasonal runoff behind barriers. Nicayuhu’s excavated layers suggest gradual construction and repair. Pérez Rodríguez argues that households could create these productive fields without a royal administration directing every stage.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Pérez Rodríguez’s later interviews document farmers’ detailed knowledge of soils, weather, plants and pests. Households still built, maintained and farmed lama-bordos. Comparison with excavated terraces helps explain this durable farming practice without assuming that ancient labour arrangements were identical to modern ones.

passages.title: Books and historical knowledge
passages.text: Codex Bodley is a long painted deerskin strip folded into pages. A white preparation layer supported the images, while red bands organised the reading. Its format made relationships among people, places and events visible across successive panels.

passages.title: Books and historical knowledge
passages.text: Bodley includes genealogies of families that sometimes opposed each other. Pohl treats its selection and arrangement of stories as a historical problem, not a neutral list of kings. Its painting date remains unresolved after 1500 and may be early colonial.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: A gold necklace at The Met combines jaguar-tooth-shaped beads with small bells. Artisans modelled delicate loops in wax before casting them in metal. This “false filigree” technique produced intricate links without attaching separate wires afterward.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: The necklace’s bells lacked clappers but could strike one another as the wearer moved. Jaguar imagery associated the ornament with power. The Met compares it with an excavated Tomb 7 necklace; the museum’s object is not itself recorded as that tomb find.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: Mixtec painters decorated ceramic vessels with animals, deities and geometric designs in several colours. Tripod vessels and cups with shaped supports show that the pot’s structure contributed to its effect as much as its painted surface.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: Rattles, scrapers, conch instruments and drums occur in burial assemblages described by the Museo Chileno. Their presence suggests music’s ceremonial importance. These finds preserve instrument types, although they cannot recover a performance’s full sound or meaning.

passages.title: Communities across political change
passages.text: Spanish rule brought compulsory labour demands and introduced crops and livestock. Cochineal dye and cotton textiles became important colonial products. These changes affected what households made and owed, without replacing every older crop, skill or community relationship.

passages.title: Communities across political change
passages.text: INPI’s contemporary account describes migrants maintaining ties with their places of origin and taking part in communal responsibilities. This is evidence of continuing, changing Mixtec communities. It should not be used as a timeless description of every preconquest household.

Mexica expansion and then Spanish colonial conquest altered the kingdoms’ authority. Encomienda and other colonial demands reshaped work and landholding. Mixtec communities and cultural knowledge continued through these changes; there was no single event that ended the people’s history.

passages.text: Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Potters used molds to produce standardized vessel shapes while varying their painted and sculpted decoration.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Many vessels combine red and cream slip painting with modeled figures. Complex scenes could cover the surface of a stirrup-spout bottle.

passages.title: Portraiture
passages.text: Portrait bottles may depict recognizable individuals. Scholars debate how their social identities related to the vessels' eventual placement in burials.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Fine decorated pottery also occurs in residential compounds. Wear, repairs and excavated household contexts show that many vessels served the living before burial.

passages.title: Food and gatherings
passages.text: Decorated vessels participated in household rituals and feasts, including the sharing of food and corn beer.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Images include crops, animals, healers and supernatural beings. They are a visual source, but an image alone cannot tell us every detail of the activity it depicts.

passages.text: The Duchy of Modena and Reggio was an Este-ruled state in northern Italy, with Modena as its capital after the loss of Ferrara in 1598. This imported 1650 to 1815 record is only a rough guide: its outline extends too far north toward Mantua, and the continuous date range hides the interruption of ducal rule from 1796 to 1814. The restored duchy survived well beyond 1815, ending in 1859.

passages.title: A capital rebuilt around a court
passages.text: In 1598, before this map interval, the Este rulers lost Ferrara to the papacy and moved their capital to Modena. They retained Modena, Reggio and Garfagnana. The new capital inherited court collections, administrative traditions and a dynasty whose ambitions were larger than one city.

passages.title: A capital rebuilt around a court
passages.text: The restoration of 1814 did not simply switch an old government back on. Francesco IV issued a plan of government on 28 August, organizing centralized institutions under the ruler’s personal control. Records from these ministries survive, showing how a small duchy managed finance, education, diplomacy and internal affairs.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Modena had an inland port. Francesco I’s Darsena began operating around the middle of the seventeenth century, and in 1667 sloping loading areas were added so carts could reach the water’s edge. Heavy goods could travel by boat before continuing their journey on wheels.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Canals powered mills and machinery used for spinning and making paper. Washwomen cleaned clothes in spring-fed channels and spread them on meadows outside the walls. Water was a workplace as well as a route for travelers: the same city needed laundry, flour, cloth and transport.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Wells supplied drinking water to homes, courtyards and public fountains. The city’s coat of arms even shows two crossed drilling tools, honoring the skill of reaching groundwater. A detailed city plan drawn by Giovanni Battista Boccabadati in 1684 records canals and underground drains, helping us reconstruct this watery landscape.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: Bernardino Ramazzini taught medicine in Modena from 1682 and published his study of workers’ illnesses in 1700. He treated occupation as a serious clue when investigating disease. The health of people who earned their living with their hands belonged in medical scholarship too.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: Writing sample: the Latin title of Ramazzini’s 1700 Modena book is “De morbis artificum diatriba,” meaning “A discussion of the diseases of workers.” The University of Iowa preserves and catalogs this edition, printed by Antonio Capponi. Latin let scholarly readers in different countries share a medical argument.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: In the expanded version of his treatise, published after he moved to Padua, Ramazzini connected stoneworkers’ dust with breathing problems and described irritation suffered by laundry workers. He considered both harmful substances and awkward bodily movements. These observations concern several occupations and places, not a survey proving that every Modenese worker had the same illness.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: University teaching was renewed in Modena in 1682 with subjects including philosophy, medicine, law and theology. Municipal resources and donations helped support it. In 1772, ducal reform placed the university under direct state control and funding, connecting advanced education more closely to government needs.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: Part of the new hospital opened on 30 November 1758. The duke commissioned medals to place in its foundations, turning the building itself into a message for the future. The surviving complex reminds us that eighteenth-century urban improvement included places intended for treating illness.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: The Albergo dei Poveri, built between 1764 and 1771, combined support for destitute people with work. In 1788 it became the Albergo delle Arti. These names describe an institution that joined charity, training and labor; they should not be mistaken for an ordinary hotel where guests booked a holiday.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: In 1758, the duke set aside part of his court garden for medicinal plants. A public botany chair followed, and the garden came under university administration in 1772. Beds of useful plants surrounded a central pool that supplied irrigation and held aquatic species. This garden was a living classroom.

The duke left Modena in June 1859, and provisional governments replaced the Austria-Este administration. The state archive preserves the assembly’s decrees ending the dynasty and seeking union with Sardinia. The duchy’s end belonged to Italian unification, not to the imported map cutoff of 1815.

sectionTitles: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
Making pots, painting animals and learning skills

passages.text: Mogollon is an archaeological name for varied farming communities of the American Southwest and adjoining northern Mexico, not one empire. This map’s outline is displaced far south into Mexico and does not reliably show that culture area. Its 800 to 1000 interval also covers only part of a much longer history. The named regional examples below extend beyond those dates.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: In the Tularosa Basin, the people archaeologists call Jornada Mogollon first built circular houses partly dug into the ground, framed with wooden beams. Later houses included square adobe buildings. These changing plans show families solving the problem of shelter in different ways over time.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: At Lake Lucero and the Huntington site, villages stood near places where rainwater flowed down from the San Andres Mountains. The surrounding landscape also supplied salt and gypsum. Archaeologists suggest some gypsum was processed into wall plaster, turning a local mineral into part of a home.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Farming in the Tularosa Basin supplemented hunting and gathering. Deer, rabbits and birds remained important quarry, while pottery and bow-and-arrow technology appear in the archaeological record. A village’s food supply depended on several activities rather than a single dependable harvest.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Gila’s Cave 1 has small storage rooms, a fire pit and a larger area interpreted as a once-enclosed living space. Places for supplies, cooking and family activity fitted within the natural shelter. The open ruin visitors see is missing walls and coverings that once shaped daily movement.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Of 32 plant species identified in the Gila dwellings, 24 were wild. Grapes, berries, acorns and piñon nuts joined cultivated corn, beans and squash. That plant list records a much wider pantry than the label farmer might suggest.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: The south-facing Gila caves offered shelter and useful seasonal temperature regulation, above a canyon with a year-round stream. Protected maize cobs survived for centuries inside. A dry, sheltered corner can preserve evidence of an ordinary meal far longer than an exposed field can.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Yucca sandals found at Gila show plant fibers becoming footwear. The park also describes yucca as a possible shampoo ingredient. Those are different kinds of evidence: excavated sandals are actual objects, while the washing use comes from knowledge of what the plant can do.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Original wooden roof beams remain in Gila’s Cave 3. Matching their tree-ring patterns helps archaeologists date the timber and place much of the room building in the 1280s. A tree’s cut date supplies a strong clue, though reused or stored wood need not mark construction day exactly.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Heavy soot on cave ceilings and artifacts from earlier cultural groups indicate temporary sheltering long before the masonry rooms were built. The cave therefore holds several histories at once. An older hunting tool found there need not have belonged to the later house builders.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: One Mimbres bowl in the Metropolitan Museum depicts two rounded rabbits and dates broadly from the mid-ninth to twelfth century. Rabbits were both familiar food animals and popular painted subjects. The vessel lets us see an artist’s choices without pretending the picture captions itself.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: Western New Mexico University’s museum includes miniature vessels and pots identified as children’s work among its Southwest collections. These objects widen the story beyond accomplished adult makers. Small hands and learners also belong in the history of a craft, even when their names are lost.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: Writing: no readable Mogollon-language sentence is supplied. The Gila park identifies its builders through archaeology and notes that they left oral history rather than a written language. Painted animals, geometric decoration and rock images are not a deciphered transcript that can be given an invented translation.

Mogollon settlements and material traditions changed along different regional paths, with many mountain communities relocating before about 1450. Their people did not simply vanish. Researchers connect their descendants with several later Southwestern communities, although the exact relationships remain debated. The map’s 1000 endpoint marks neither a conquest nor the end of this longer history.

sectionTitles: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
Money with a name and an animal

passages.text: The map’s medieval Moldova means the principality usually called Moldavia in English. It was not the modern Republic of Moldova. The imported outline is misleading: it omits Suceava and much of the principality’s historical western territory. Suceava’s fortress and town were major centres of princely government, craft production and household life during the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Archaeologists at Suceava identified fifteenth-century houses built from wood covered with clay. Some stood on stone foundations, and some had cellars. Ordinary construction materials can leave clues even when the wooden building itself has disappeared.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Tile stoves were a recurring feature of the fifteenth-century town’s houses. Some tiles were simple, while others carried elaborate Gothic decoration. A source of indoor warmth could also be a large decorative feature, rather like furniture that happened to heat the room.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Workshops stood among homes rather than in a completely separate industrial district. Excavations identified jewellery-making, bronze-working and bone-working near residences. Richer houses and modest dwellings also occurred alongside one another, complicating a simple picture of separate rich and poor neighbourhoods.

passages.title: Money with a name and an animal
passages.text: Under Stephen the Great, who ruled from 1457 to 1504, the Suceava mint produced silver groși and half-groși. Coins excavated at Orheiul Vechi include his issues. Their designs combine the ruler’s name, a shield and an aurochs head with other heraldic symbols.

passages.title: Money with a name and an animal
passages.text: A typeI coin legend reads “MONETA MOLDAVIE”, Latin for “money of Moldavia”. The museum transcribes it beside the aurochs-head design. Scholars disagree about the exact issuing dates, but the proposed typeI ranges fall within Stephen’s early reign, between 1457 and 1476.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: A charter dated 17 March 1492 confirmed villages held by Şteful and his sister Marina after they lost the document inherited from their grandfather. Even a medieval family could face the dreaded missing-paperwork problem. Here, a replacement record protected a brother’s and sister’s property claim.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: Other surviving documents record gifts by the treasurer Iuga to Putna Monastery in 1476. Such records connect named officials, religious institutions and property. Donations were also transactions that people wanted written down and remembered.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: A 2022 exhibition assembled forty-one documents issued by Stephen’s chancery between 1458 and 1503, plus Iuga’s three records. Most were issued at Suceava, with others at Vaslui, Iași or Bădeuți. Their dates and places let historians follow a government operating through several princely residences.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Suceava’s late-fourteenth-century fortress remained a principal residence of Moldavian rulers for almost two hundred years. Surviving carved stonework records building methods and decoration, including Gothic themes prominent in the fifteenth century. Government required rooms and skilled builders as well as rulers.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Late-fourteenth- and early-fifteenth-century Moldavian churches could be decorated with ceramic discs, cross-shaped floral pieces and bricks, some glazed. These elements formed coloured bands around windows and beneath roofs. Fired clay contributed to the appearance of important public buildings as well as domestic heating.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Siret’s Holy Trinity Church preserves this kind of ceramic architectural decoration. Archaeological fragments also come from Suceava, Cetatea Albă, old monasteries and other settlements. Comparing intact buildings with excavated pieces helps researchers reconstruct decorative traditions that no longer survive everywhere.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: The oldest surviving bells assigned to the medieval Moldavian state date from Stephen the Great’s reign. Bells can preserve inscriptions, decorations and coats of arms as well as producing sound. They are material records of the people and institutions that commissioned them.
Moldavia did not disappear in 1492. Much later, the 1859 election of Alexandru Ioan Cuza in both Moldavia and Wallachia began their union, leading toward the modern Romanian state.

sectionTitles: A woven wall could tell a family story
Writing and living with political change

passages.text: The Republic of Moldova declared independence in 1991 and adopted its constitution in 1994. This is the modern state, not the medieval principality of Moldavia. The outline includes territory beyond the central government’s effective control in Transnistria, so it must not be read as a map of uniform political control.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Wall carpets in Moldova and neighbouring Romania traditionally helped insulate and decorate houses. Patterns could identify a weaver’s community. Their makers combined practical household use with complex colour and design, turning a warm wall covering into something worth displaying.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Carpets also formed part of brides’ dowries and accompanied important family ceremonies. In funeral customs they could symbolise passage to the afterlife. These are documented cultural meanings attached to textiles, rather than properties of the wool itself.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Weavers work on vertical or horizontal looms, building the design through repeated thread work. Skills have passed through families and also through classes, workshops and museums. The craft links patient hand movements with memories of particular people and places.

passages.title: Welcoming spring with two colours
passages.text: Mărțișor customs celebrate the beginning of spring with red-and-white threads that people make, give and wear. The shared regional tradition includes untying the thread when a flowering tree, swallow or stork signals spring’s arrival. Weather watching becomes part of a personal ornament.

passages.title: Welcoming spring with two colours
passages.text: Older women, teachers, craftspeople and museum workshops teach thread-making skills. UNESCO records the practice in Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia. People attach protective meanings to the colours and objects, while children learn a small craft that can be given to someone else.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: A school assessment conducted in 2023 and 2024 covered 968 institutions in Moldova. At that time, pupils in 88 schools had access only to outdoor toilets. This is a concrete reminder that school life includes warmth, privacy and a place to wash hands as well as textbooks.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: At Baimaclia’s Mihai Eminescu Gymnasium, staff described the difficulty of children going outside to use toilets in cold weather. Hard water affected pipes and fixtures, and there was no central sewerage connection. Improving a bathroom could therefore involve both plumbing and wider village infrastructure.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: A 2026 workshop taught school staff how to inspect and maintain sanitation facilities, spot faults and keep supplies available. A new tap is useful only while water comes out of it. The programme treated everyday cleaning and repairs as part of protecting children’s learning environment.

passages.title: Schooldays during a pandemic
passages.text: In August 2020, national ministries and international partners produced Romanian-language handbooks for pupils returning to education during COVID-19. The guides addressed the journey to school, classrooms, libraries, canteens and toilets. They also included advice about emotional well-being.

passages.title: Schooldays during a pandemic
passages.text: A My Schedule section helped students record opening times, lesson starts, canteen access and digital learning tools. Separate materials served primary, secondary and vocational education. These surviving guides show how an international emergency rearranged the ordinary timetable of a child’s day.

passages.title: Writing and living with political change
passages.text: The 1991 independence declaration describes Moldova as “SUVERAN, INDEPENDENT ŞI DEMOCRATIC”, meaning “sovereign, independent and democratic”. This Romanian wording appears in the Constitutional Court’s 2022 printed edition, page 11. It is a documented modern text using Latin letters, not a medieval inscription.

passages.title: Writing and living with political change
passages.text: Armed conflict in 1992 divided control around the Dniester, also called the Nistru. Later negotiations included practical confidence-building between the sides. The OSCE’s 2014 account emphasised solutions that could improve daily contacts while the larger political dispute remained unresolved.
The modern republic continues; the unresolved Transnistrian conflict complicates effective control within its internationally recognised borders.

sectionTitles: Early power had to be negotiated
Household objects from the later period

passages.text: These records trace two stages of Montenegro’s earlier political history: the eighteenth-century world of Cetinje’s bishops and the later internationally recognised state. The imported outlines appear too broad for their earlier dates, especially before the Balkan Wars; they should not be treated as precise historical borders. The nineteenth-century household objects, school and book described below belong to that later development, not automatically to the 1715 snapshot.

passages.title: Early power had to be negotiated
passages.text: Danilo Petrović was chosen as metropolitan of Cetinje in 1697. Religious and political leadership overlapped, while local leaders remained powerful. Decisions depended on assemblies, alliances and negotiation as well as the bishop’s personal authority.

passages.title: Early power had to be negotiated
passages.text: In 1713, a court of sixteen leading men was created to settle serious disputes between clans and communities. It lacked reliable means to enforce every judgment. Creating a court and making its decisions effective were separate tasks.

passages.title: A later state takes shape
passages.text: Montenegro also had governors, or guvernadurs, alongside the bishops. The museum’s statehood display traces this office from 1717 to its abolition in 1830. Competing institutions help explain why the earlier country cannot be pictured as a modern administration run by one ruler.

passages.title: A later state takes shape
passages.text: A billiard table brought from Austria in 1840 stands in Njegoš’s former residence. The building became known as Biljarda. Government, literature and an indoor game met in the same setting; even a prince-bishop could enjoy trying to make a difficult shot.

passages.title: A later state takes shape
passages.text: Cetinje’s secular school opened in 1834, initially serving boys from wealthier families. The museum exhibits photographs of the monastery setting and the later school at Dobrsko Selo. Schooling expanded through particular institutions, with access much narrower than universal education.

passages.title: A later state takes shape
passages.text: The Cetinje printing house produced teaching books, official proclamations and the journal Grlica in 1835. Preserved examples show how print supported both learning and government. The press connected the work of setting individual letters with public communication across the country.

passages.title: Household objects from the later period
passages.text: The nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century ethnographic collection includes elliptical wooden barrels called burilos for carrying and storing water. Wooden strips were held together with metal hoops. Before a tap could be assumed, a household needed suitable containers and somebody to bring the water home.

passages.title: Household objects from the later period
passages.text: A household display brings together a cradle, children’s toys, a wooden dough tray and iron equipment for a hearth. A cooking pot could hang from chains above the fire. These objects place childcare and food preparation in the same busy domestic space.

passages.title: Household objects from the later period
passages.text: For a family patron saint’s celebration, special bread could be marked with a carved wooden seal. One displayed type bears abbreviated Greek Christian lettering. The loaf joined cooking with religious observance, while the seal allowed the same design to be pressed into fresh dough.

passages.title: A hospital and its specialists
passages.text: Danilo I hospital opened at Cetinje in 1873. Petar Miljanić later directed it from 1884 to 1897 and practised both surgery and eye medicine. The hospital’s documented staff and building show the growth of organised medical services in the later principality.

passages.title: A nineteenth-century book in Cyrillic
passages.text: The title “Горскій віенацЪ” means “The Mountain Wreath”. These are the historical Cyrillic forms transcribed in the Matica Srpska Library’s catalogue of Njegoš’s 1847 edition. The book is catalogued as Serbian; its older spelling differs from the modern form of the title.

passages.title: A nineteenth-century book in Cyrillic
passages.text: That edition was printed by the Mechitarist press in Vienna, with a portrait and 116 numbered pages. A Montenegrin ruler’s work therefore depended on printing beyond his own state. The surviving book connects local literary creation with an international network of production.

In 1918 an assembly deposed King Nikola and voted to merge Montenegro with Serbia, leading into the new Yugoslav kingdom. The decision was contested, and diplomatic recognition lingered: the United States withdrew recognition in 1920. Neither imported endpoint marks the disappearance of Montenegrin communities.

passages.text: This record begins while Montenegro was still joined with Serbia. A referendum in 2006 led to a separate independent republic. The modern outline therefore crosses a major change in sovereignty; it should not imply that Montenegro was already independent in 1994. Its families, coastal associations and northern farming communities continued through that change.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: The Boka Navy of Kotor preserves seafaring traditions through a voluntary cultural association. Membership is open to men, women and children. Its modern work commemorates maritime life and brings generations together, rather than functioning as a present-day combat navy.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: At formal celebrations, members wear colourful traditional uniforms, carry historic weapons and perform the kolo circle dance. The coordinated steps make a public ceremony out of inherited movement and dress. Historic objects become part of a performance in the town’s shared spaces.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: The association transmits knowledge of maritime history, customs and traditional skills. Younger participants learn through involvement with older members. Its heritage includes people remembering and practising together, alongside the uniforms and objects that can be displayed in a museum.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: The Preschool for All campaign began in March 2015 in five northern municipalities with particularly low attendance. UNICEF and the education ministry worked with local preschools and communities. Some places had available classroom capacity but needed stronger connections with families.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: Arts and educational events invited parents and young children to experience preschool activities. Partners included drama, music and ballet institutions, as well as teacher educators. Learning through songs, movement and play could help families picture what a preschool day offered.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: The campaign expanded to six more northern municipalities in 2016. Its posters show children painting, shaping clay, reading picture books and playing. These surviving campaign materials document the everyday activities used to explain early learning to the public.

passages.title: Cheese is also a livelihood
passages.text: At the 2017 Days of Pljevlja Cheese, producers presented cheeses and cream for judging, tasting and sale. Around a hundred producers submitted 172 samples. The event connected household and farm production with customers beyond an individual village.

passages.title: Cheese is also a livelihood
passages.text: Pljevlja cheese received national protection of its origin in 2017. The event included producers from the wider cross-border Drina-Tara region as well as Montenegro. A named local food could support both a sense of place and practical cooperation between farming communities.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: Article 1 of the constitution begins “Crna Gora je nezavisna i suverena država”, meaning “Montenegro is an independent and sovereign state”. This attested Montenegrin sentence uses Latin letters. The constitution was adopted in October 2007, after the independence referendum.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: The constitution gives Cyrillic and Latin scripts equal status and identifies several languages in official use. A country’s written life can therefore use more than one alphabet. These provisions concern public institutions, alongside the languages used within individual households.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: The 2007 constitution also describes the state as ecological and committed to social justice. Such language sets out constitutional goals. It records how lawmakers defined the republic, rather than proving that every environmental or social problem had been solved.

passages.title: A close and consequential vote
passages.text: In the May 2006 referendum, 55.5 percent of valid votes supported independence. The result led to the June declaration. The vote also shows that citizens held different views about their state’s future, even as the new republic’s institutions took shape.
The union with Serbia ended for Montenegro in 2006, and the independent republic continued. This was a change in sovereignty, not an ending of the country’s communities or cultural life.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community

passages.text: Montserrat’s history includes Indigenous beadmaking, plantation labour, community schooling and music. Volcanic eruptions forced major changes after 1995, but the island’s society continued. This card connects discoveries and everyday life across the two map records for the same island.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At precolonial Trants, stone and shell beads survive alongside evidence of unfinished production. David Watters’s research identified manufacturing stages showing that island craftspeople worked imported raw materials. Other beads may have arrived already finished. A necklace can therefore reveal both skilled local work and connections across the sea; it does not by itself identify the wearer’s rank.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At Little Bay’s eighteenth-century cattle mill, archaeologists exposed a masonry channel in 2006. It carried pressed cane juice through the mill wall toward the boiling house, where the juice became sugar. This surviving connection helps reconstruct the sequence of plantation work. The archive also reports missing field records, so later sediment and pottery cannot simply be treated as the mill’s original floor.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: In Area 2 of Little Bay’s workers’ village, a ditch cut around a house platform appears to have diverted rainwater from the home. Stone alignments also suggested steps and supports. These modest traces illuminate household care under slavery. Erosion and later land use damaged the site, making a complete reconstruction of each home impossible.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: The workers’ village also yielded fragments of handmade earthenware associated with cooking, eating and storing water. Some vessel identifications remain tentative because the pieces are small. Imported ceramics and bottle glass occur too. A broken pot is useful evidence, but it cannot tell us every ingredient in the family’s supper.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: After apprenticeship ended, emancipated Montserratians founded primary schools for their children. Brown University’s project chronology records seventeen schools in 1840, compared with one in 1838. Archaeologists excavated a schoolhouse on Potato Hill, where toys were among the finds. Education became part of building life after slavery.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: In July 2012, seven Montserrat Secondary School pupils aged thirteen to sixteen joined a three-week archaeology programme. They excavated, washed and labelled finds, and then led public tours. Lessons included reading old documents critically. Here, learning history meant doing some of the investigating and explaining it to the adults.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: Goat water belongs in a dinner bowl: despite the name, it is a meat stew. The tourism authority describes it as a communal dish at weddings, christenings, parties and funerals, and a favourite Friday lunch. Cooking over a wood fire contributes flavour. The shared meal brings people together at very different moments in family life.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: AIR Montserrat opened in 1979 and brought recording technology and musicians to the island. Its studio history lists work by local artist Arrow as well as Dire Straits, the Police and other visiting performers. Hurricane Hugo damaged the building and equipment in 1989, ending this studio’s operation years before the volcano crisis.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: The eruption that began on 18 July 1995 changed where people could live and work. Plymouth was evacuated repeatedly before the final evacuation in April 1996. Pyroclastic currents, fast-moving mixtures of volcanic material and gas, reached the town in 1997. Losing a capital and homes was a human disaster, not a disappearance of Montserratian people or identity.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: Even the scientists had to move. The observatory began in temporary premises in Plymouth, relocated as evacuation zones expanded, and eventually operated from Mongo Hill, where staff could not actually see the volcano. A purpose-built facility followed in 2003. Monitoring depended on instruments and teamwork as well as watching the mountain.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: Volcano monitoring combines several kinds of clues. Instruments record earthquakes, ground movement and gas emissions; solar-powered remote stations can send measurements back to the observatory. These observations help scientists assess changing conditions. Montserrat’s scientific achievement includes sustained measurement and communication, rather than a machine that predicts an eruption with certainty.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: At the National Museum in Little Bay, visitors can learn about precolonial life and more recent history, and try playable musical instruments. Preserving culture can involve making a sound yourself as well as looking at an old object. The museum represents continuing community work in the island’s north.

Montserrat continues as a British Overseas Territory. Plymouth’s evacuation and destruction changed where people lived, while cultural and scientific institutions continued elsewhere. The constitution introduced in 2011 did not grant independence. The map’s endpoints are not the end of Montserratian society.
