sectionTitles: A capital for rulers and students

passages.text: This entry covers Morocco from 1300 to 1492, chiefly the later Marinid era and the transition to Wattasid rule. Fez was a centre of government, learning and skilled production. The regional label spans political change rather than one uninterrupted dynasty.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: The Marinids built Fez Jdid in 1276, before this entry’s first map year. It provided a new royal and military quarter beside the older city. A medieval capital could grow by adding a government town rather than by demolishing its existing neighbourhoods.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Marinid expansion reached Tunis in 1347, but the Black Death in 1348 and subsequent rebellions helped undermine this wider ambition. The dynasty’s cultural monuments outlasted its ability to hold a large North African empire together.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Buinaniya Madrasa in Fez was built in the 1350s. Its plan includes two facing classrooms and a prayer hall. A school building brought teaching, worship and the movement of students into one carefully arranged space.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Water crossed the madrasa’s southern side in a channel from the Wadi Lamtiyyin; two small bridges gave access to the prayer hall. A courtyard basin and an associated ablution building remind us that water supply and washing were practical parts of institutional life.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: A hydraulic clock stood opposite Buinaniya. Water, architecture and the scheduling of communal life were connected here. The madrasa’s surviving fabric also includes later repairs, so a present-day view cannot be treated as an untouched photograph of the 1350s.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: A Quran volume now in the Bavarian State Library was associated with the Marinid ruler Abu Yaqub Yusuf, who reigned from 1286 to 1307. It is the last part of a twelve-volume set, written on parchment in Maghribi script: a substantial book project rather than a pocket paperback.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A fourteenth-century door from a ruined Fez house survives in the Batha Museum. Its wood and wrought iron preserve a large main door with a smaller gate inside. Domestic craftsmanship deserves attention alongside the palace and mosque.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: That door has two knockers of different sizes. The museum explains that the higher, larger one allowed a visitor riding a mule to knock without dismounting. Medieval convenience: the doorbell was adapted to the transport!

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A ceiling fragment from the al-Misbahiya madrasa, built in 1346 to 1347, combines carved cedar pieces into stars and other geometric shapes. Traces of red, white, green and blue show that this wooden surface was once much more colourful than plain brown timber.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A tile panel from Buinaniya was made by removing parts of the glazed surface so that script stood out against the exposed background. The Batha fragment was recovered during modern restoration. It records both medieval craft and the later work of conserving it.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A silver half dirham struck at Azammur under Abd al-Haqq II names its ruler and mint. It weighs about 0.65 grams. Such a small object can locate an otherwise poorly documented mint within the political history of the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: The coin’s reverse includes امير المسلمين, “commander of the Muslims.” This Arabic title is shown in modern type from the published transcription. The coin belongs to Abd al-Haqq II’s reign, 1420 to 1465, rather than to every period labelled Morocco.

The Marinid dynasty ended when Abd al-Haqq II was killed during the Fez rebellion of 1465. The Wattasids subsequently established their own government, securing Fez in 1472. Fez’s households, schools and workshops continued across the political transition, which falls inside this map entry’s dates.

sectionTitles: Cities and the people who sustained them
Light, food and words at home

passages.text: This map window spans the later Saadian era, the rise of Alaouite rule in the seventeenth century, and the protectorates established in 1912. Its 1650 to 1938 dates are mapping limits, not Morocco’s lifetime.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Moulay Ismail, who reigned from 1672 to 1727, made Meknes his capital. The palace city and older medina were distinct ensembles divided by walls. Their different spaces preserve a ruler’s administrative ambitions alongside an existing urban community.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Meknes’s surviving heritage includes hammams, merchant inns, private houses and large granaries as well as palaces. These buildings span several periods. They make washing, storage, commerce and shelter visible beside royal display; they should not all be assigned to one sultan.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: The royal state also relied on coercion. Historian Chouki El Hamel studied registers used under Moulay Ismail to justify enslaving Black Moroccans, including people who had been free. The policy provoked opposition among Muslim scholars; official paperwork could manufacture a claim to ownership rather than prove a just right.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Sultan Sidi Mohamed ben Abdallah, ruling from 1757 to 1790, developed Essaouira as a royal Atlantic port. Its planned fortifications drew on European military design within a Moroccan urban setting. Goods could pass between inland African routes, the coast and European shipping.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Essaouira’s population included Muslim, Jewish and Christian communities and people of different backgrounds. Its port was a meeting place as well as a defensive project. The surviving town preserves the settings of exchange without implying that every resident experienced identical opportunities.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: A treaty concluded in 1786 formalised relations with the United States. In 1821, Sultan Moulay Suleiman gave the Americans a building in Tangier for their diplomatic mission. The surviving institutional history shows diplomacy expressed through both written agreements and a very tangible house.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: A nineteenth-century batta jug in the Batha Museum held lamp oil. It has a rounded body, narrow neck and pouring lip, and stands only 14 centimetres high. Before an electric light switch, keeping a lamp supplied required small, purpose-made containers like this.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Fez and Meknes potters made these jugs for different markets. Green examples went particularly to southern oasis regions, while urban buyers could obtain more elaborate multicoloured decoration. One familiar vessel shape could be adapted to several customers.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: A shallow Fez dish from the first half of the nineteenth century is 40 centimetres across. Dishes of this type served bastila, a filled pie, but this especially symbolic example may have been primarily decorative. A beautiful plate is not proof of the exact meal once eaten from it.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Its blue decoration was painted with cobalt oxide and its yellow with an iron-based pigment. A mosque-like arch frames a word arranged as a mirror image. The dish shows potters combining material knowledge, architectural references and writing on a domestic form.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: The dish’s Arabic word is الملك, al-mulk, “sovereignty” or “power,” interpreted by the museum as divine power. It is printed here in ordinary letters; the original is highly stylised, mirrored Kufic. This is an attested object inscription, not a phrase invented for the card.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Later in this entry’s period, the French Protectorate developed a planned capital at Rabat, especially from 1912 to 1930, alongside older urban layers. Its government buildings and neighbourhoods record colonial intervention as well as architectural exchange.
The 1912 protectorates limited Moroccan sovereignty without abolishing the monarchy. Independence returned in 1956. The map’s break at 1938 is not a conquest date or the disappearance of Morocco.

sectionTitles: Institutions, writing and a changing capital

passages.text: Modern Morocco regained independence in 1956, before this map entry begins. Its Arabic- and Amazigh-speaking society includes varied urban and rural communities. The examples below describe specific institutions and practices, not every household.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: The 2011 constitution describes Morocco as a constitutional monarchy. A constitutional text tells us how institutions are formally defined; it should not be mistaken for proof that every declared right or principle is fully realised in everyday life.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: A short Arabic writing sample appears in Article 4: الله، الوطن، الملك, “God, Homeland, King.” These are the words of the state motto in a specific published document, presented here in normal Arabic type.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Article 5 recognises Amazigh alongside Arabic as an official language. That provision matters for a country whose heritage cannot be reduced to one language. A written constitution records a legal commitment, while the practical history of language use is more varied.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Rabat’s protected urban landscape includes an early twentieth-century planned capital alongside much older quarters and monuments. Its buildings make different periods visible in the same city. Modern residents use and conserve a place inherited from both precolonial and colonial histories.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Some imported modern outlines include Western Sahara. Its sovereignty is disputed, and the United Nations lists it as a Non-Self-Governing Territory. A map polygon is not evidence that this dispute is settled.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Couscous preparation is shared heritage across Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and Tunisia. UNESCO’s 2020 record describes forming and steaming cereal grains and combining them with ingredients that vary with season and place. There is no single recipe that represents every household.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Learning to make couscous often happens through watching and helping within families and communities. The meal brings people together, while the equipment connects cooks with potters and makers of wooden utensils. A bowl of food has quite a workforce behind it.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: In southwest Morocco, producing argan oil involves harvesting and drying fruit, removing pulp, cracking the hard shells, sorting kernels, grinding and kneading. UNESCO documents a chain of skilled tasks rather than one magical squeeze of a tree.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Argan knowledge has often passed between women, including mothers and daughters, through practice. Artisans make the hand mills and other equipment. Precise handling during processing is part of the skill, not simply a list of ingredients.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Argan oil also appears in social life: UNESCO records its use as a wedding gift and in special dishes. These are documented practices of particular communities. They should not be projected automatically onto every Moroccan wedding or earlier century.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Gnawa music and ritual carry memories of communities shaped by slavery and its aftermath. UNESCO’s record describes stringed instruments and metal castanets in urban traditions, with different instrumental combinations elsewhere. Music preserves histories that a political timeline can easily overlook.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Gnawa gatherings may include extended ritual performance, and practitioners transmit their knowledge through associations and festivals as well as community life. Healing is part of participants’ religious understanding; describing that belief is different from recommending a medical treatment.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Noor I, near Ouarzazate, began operating in February 2016 with 160 megawatts of solar generating capacity. The project brief distinguishes this completed plant from later phases then being developed. It is a concrete example of Morocco building modern energy infrastructure, alongside its better-known historic monuments.

Morocco continues as a state and a living society. Independence in 1956 and constitutional change in 2011 mark transformations rather than a final fall. An open-ended map entry does not predict an unchanging future.

passages.text: Mossi political history includes several kingdoms in present-day Burkina Faso. Their populations developed through conquest, migration and incorporation of existing communities. Ouagadougou was influential, but it was not an ancient capital governing every Mossi kingdom.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Duperray’s research describes kingdoms formed through encounters between incoming ruling lineages and established populations. Political incorporation did not erase differences of origin. This helps explain why a single map label covers multiple communities and centres of authority.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Yarse communities included Muslim merchants. Oral traditions link many lineages with Mande origins, while others became Yarse through local relationships. Duperray’s interviews reveal changing identities rather than a merchant population with one uniform ancestry.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: The protectorate treaty of January 1897 helped France claim a wider territory. Beucher argues that officials enlarged the apparent authority of Ouagadougou’s ruler, the Moogo Naaba, to justify colonial control. The resulting hierarchy cannot simply be projected backward.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A Smithsonian Mossi vessel, made in the middle or late twentieth century, carries impressed patterns below and incised zigzags above. The museum describes pottery used for water, grain, cooking and brewing beer, placing decorated ceramics within ordinary household work.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The Smithsonian’s technique account describes shaping clay over a mould, then adding coils to build the upper vessel. Drying, decoration and firing followed. Millet stalks, wood and manure supplied fuel. Both men and women participated in these pottery traditions.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A late twentieth-century Mossi shawl in the British Museum consists of thirteen narrow cotton strips sewn together. Handspun thread, indigo dye and additional patterned weft at the ends show several kinds of work within one textile.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The museum suggests this cloth may be a diisa prestige shawl, given by a mother to a son on marriage and later used as a burial shroud. That social interpretation is qualified; it is not a securely documented biography of this particular textile.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The High Museum’s karan-wemba figure represents an honoured older woman. Its ridged coiffure and geometric bodily marks connect sculpture with appearance and social status. Patt relates the work to Yatenga traditions while stressing differences among Mossi artistic communities.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: Radiocarbon analysis placed the High Museum figure’s wood around the sixteenth century. Wood age does not establish when an artist carved it. Patt considers the possibility of a much later sculpture made from old timber, so an exact early creation date remains unproven.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The PLU collection account describes carving masks from green wood with an adze and knife, then smoothing them with rough leaves. A mask’s performance required further work: fibre fittings, clothing and rattles connected the carved object with a moving, sounding costume.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The same account places cooking, grinding and grain storage within household compounds. These workspaces connect the material arts with food preparation and farming. They describe recorded Mossi settings, not a single house plan shared by every kingdom or historical century.

French forces occupied Ouagadougou in September 1896, followed by the 1897 protectorate. Other kingdoms had their own encounters with colonial rule. Royal authority was constrained and reshaped; this political change did not mark the disappearance of Mossi people or their artistic traditions.

sectionTitles: What a ship’s jars can tell us
A fort that had to save the rain
Grandparents and children in the orchestra

passages.text: Mozambique’s Indian Ocean coast connected local communities with distant trading worlds. Its history also lives in musical skills shared across generations and in the cloths through which women remember their lives. These stories follow particular places and communities within a diverse country.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: The wreck identified as Nossa Senhora da Consolação, lost near Mozambique Island in 1608, yielded containers known as olive jars. A 2023 study compares their thick walls and rounded shapes with other shipwreck finds. Such jars could carry oil, wine or foodstuffs, and their forms helped them fit within a curved hull. The name does not prove that every recovered jar still contained olives.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: Two pots from the same collection were identified with the local Lumbo pottery tradition. They raised a puzzle: was that tradition used later than some land excavations suggested, or did hurried recovery mix material from different wrecks? Mahumane and Simbine leave both possibilities open. A pot can be an exciting discovery partly because it creates a better question, not because it instantly settles one.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: São Sebastião Fortress collected rain from its roofs into cisterns. UNESCO’s history explains how stored water helped people withstand a Dutch siege in 1607 and also supplied visiting ships. Its construction had drawn on stonemasons from Goa, local residents and enslaved labourers. The surviving building preserves engineering achievements within a history of unequal power and coerced work.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: A 2009 restoration report describes repairing channels, pipes and cisterns, then sending water to a new cistern outside the fort for island residents. A roof could work as part of a water supply as well as keep rain off a room. Looking after an old building could therefore help maintain something people needed every day.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: Junior architect Mohammad Cassimo told the restoration team that he had grown up on the island and wanted to help restore it. He joined surveys and daily supervision of the work. His account links learning a profession with caring for a place remembered from childhood.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: Mozambique Island includes stone-and-lime buildings in the north and a southern neighbourhood called macuti, after its palm-leaf roofs. UNESCO describes different building traditions shaped by African, Swahili, Arab and European connections. The island is a lived-in town as well as a heritage site, with homes forming an important part of what survives.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: A 2014 conservation report explains that macuti roofing was becoming harder to obtain and some residents preferred metal roofs. It also records efforts to repair houses and discuss conservation in schools. Keeping an architectural tradition alive involves residents’ costs and choices, as well as the appearance of a roof. A home has to be somewhere people can actually live.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The same report includes a photograph of a public toilet built in 2012 and describes residents and the municipality cleaning living areas. It also records work on water supplies and damaged cisterns. Toilets belong in the history of a town just as much as palaces do: people need practical services while living among historic buildings.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The island’s old hospital dates to 1877. In 2015, the health ministry began conservation work that included cleaning, surveying the structure and investigating drainage and cisterns. This record shows how caring for a healthcare building also meant caring for the systems behind its walls. It does not establish which treatments every patient received there.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: Chopi timbila ensembles in southern Inhambane bring together wooden xylophones of different sizes. Calabashes beneath the wooden bars act as resonators, with beeswax helping seal them. UNESCO’s account describes children playing alongside their grandfathers. Learning means listening and practising within an ensemble, where a young player can hear an experienced musician right beside them.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: These performances are also a way to comment on community life. New pieces accompany weddings and other gatherings; the m’zeno song can use humour and sarcasm to address current events. A musician’s hands may play different rhythms at the same time. The music can ask both the audience and the player to pay close attention.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: A capulana bought in Maputo’s Elephant market in September 2003 has printed circles showing Mozambique’s provinces, surrounded by spears and shields. The British Museum records it as cotton and says cloths of this type are worn by women. The catalogue tentatively places its manufacture in India. Something bought for wearing can also reveal the movement of designs and goods across borders.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: In 2019 and 2020, the WITH Coastal Style project worked with women in Katembe’s fishing communities across Maputo Bay. Researchers collected stories connected with capulanas, including cloths preserved and passed between generations. The project brought these memories into museum and community exhibitions. Keeping a piece of cloth can help a family keep a story, too.

passages.title: Masks, voices and growing up
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2023 account of Makonde mapiko describes masked dancers representing people or animals, with drums and a choir. Performances accompany rites of passage and also other occasions. Singers may challenge the masked dancers with provocative songs. Learning the dance helps pass on community values while young people navigate growing up; it is one particular tradition within Mozambique’s many communities.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: A UN report from 1966 preserved testimony about the effects of colonial labour systems. Speakers described workers compelled into jobs or crop production and men leaving to seek wages abroad, separating families. The record shows why accounts of ports and plantations must also ask who did the work and what choices they had. It records testimony and arguments presented to the committee, rather than a census of every household.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: The island’s Slave Memory Garden commemorates slavery along the Indian Ocean coast. A 2015 government report records restoration work there and describes the memorial as a joint Mozambique and Réunion initiative. The garden makes remembrance part of the present-day town, asking visitors to consider the people whose forced journeys also shaped its maritime history.

Portuguese colonial sovereignty ended when Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975. The country continued through civil war, the 1992 peace agreement and the 1994 multiparty elections. Those political transitions did not erase its communities or the local histories carried in buildings, objects and living practices.

passages.text: Muisca communities lived in Colombia’s eastern highlands, farming, weaving, trading and making extraordinary metal offerings. They belonged to several interacting chiefdoms rather than one centrally ruled empire. The map’s eight-year window is only a snapshot of a much longer history.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: At the Spanish arrival in 1537, at least four large regional chiefdoms centred on Bogotá, Tunja, Duitama and Sogamoso. Each included smaller communities and local leaders. Their relationships were political and religious, but they were not all subjects of a single king.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Maize was a staple alongside potatoes, beans, squashes and other crops. The Gold Museum’s educational account describes soups, tamales and arepas. A familiar-looking maize meal could connect modern visitors with ingredients cultivated in these highlands centuries ago.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Households worked their own plots and also supplied labour for leaders’ fields. The museum links this tribute to ceremonies and large gatherings. Food production supported both family meals and the occasions that brought communities together.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón could be exchanged for cloth, pottery and produce. Cotton arrived from warmer environments. Traders connected communities with different resources, so a highland household did not have to grow or make everything it used.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: In 1969 a farmer found the famous gold raft inside a ceramic container in a cave near Pasca. It did not come out of Lake Guatavita. Recording where an object was actually found matters, even when a more famous place dominates the story.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: The raft is interpreted as a ceremonial offering representing a leader and attendants. The museum relates it to accounts of chiefly installation and gifts placed in sacred water. It is a miniature ritual scene, rather than proof of a lost city made of gold.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: Its makers cast the raft in one piece using a lost-wax mould. The museum considers 1200 to 1500 a likely period, while emphasizing that an exact manufacture date cannot be established. A tiny object can preserve a remarkably complicated piece of metalworking.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: A different offering from Fusagasugá shows an arched-back feline with whiskers and protruding eyes. Only a few centimetres long, the flat metal animal nevertheless looks ready to spring. The museum dates this lost-wax casting broadly to 600 to 1600.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: Microscope-based research examined thirteen groups of Muisca offerings and distinguished the work of multiple makers. Details of wax modelling and casting let researchers investigate artists and apprentices, rather than treating every small gold figure as anonymous treasure.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: A short Muisca sample in a seventeenth-century baptism sermon is “mue zemosqua”: “I bathe you”. Saravia’s edition prints this wording from an anonymous manuscript now in Colombia’s National Library. Its Latin-script religious text records language under colonial evangelization, not preconquest alphabetic writing.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: The sermon describes a priest pouring water during baptism. The surviving manuscript connects the study of language with a concrete encounter between children, families and missionaries. Its religious purpose also shaped which words its compiler chose to preserve.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: A colonial-period burial from Pisba preserved a woven cap, a headband and a two-colour cotton bag alongside other belongings. Such finds show that practices and craft knowledge continued after Spanish conquest, even as communities experienced deep political and religious pressure.

Spanish conquest beginning in 1537 broke apart the larger Muisca chiefdoms and imposed encomienda tribute. Local leadership and communities continued within those unequal colonial arrangements. The imported 1500 endpoint predates this upheaval and is not a historical collapse.

passages.text: Muscogee histories connect southeastern ancestral places, a changing network of towns and continuing nations. Ocmulgee's surviving clay architecture, town councils and later government buildings show different forms of collective life. The later Creek Confederacy and the present Muscogee Nation must not be projected unchanged onto the map's fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Ocmulgee is an ancestral homeland of the Muscogee Nation. Its long occupation is evidence of successive communities at a place; it does not establish that the later Creek Confederacy existed throughout all those earlier centuries.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The Earth Lodge preserves an original clay floor dating approximately to the early eleventh century. The enclosing walls and roof visitors see were reconstructed in the 1930s. Separating those elements helps distinguish surviving archaeology from a modern interpretation of the building.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Seats, a central hearth and a raised bird effigy were formed into the floor. Their arrangement supports interpretation as a special gathering place. Differences in seating do not by themselves establish a complete social hierarchy, an interpretation the park's bulletin explicitly questions.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The round lodge used internal roof supports, while nearby houses were usually smaller and rectangular. Different building forms reveal deliberate choices about public and domestic space. The exact meanings of the bird's imagery remain uncertain.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Historic towns placed council houses beside ceremonial plazas, with grounds for ball play and chunkey nearby. A meko worked with advisers. These spaces joined public decisions, gatherings and recreation within a town.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Maternal clans organized belonging, while people also maintained ties to particular towns. The confederacy included speakers of different languages. A shared political network did not erase those local relationships and differences.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: During the eighteenth century, deerskin commerce displaced the earlier trade in enslaved people. Relations with colonial traders affected town alliances and livelihoods. Exchange offered opportunities while also drawing communities into violent external demands.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Before removal, Muscogee households included farmers and cattle owners, and some people enslaved others. This varied economy matters: forced migration uprooted established livelihoods and also carried the coercion of slavery into the new western setting.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: From 1878 to Oklahoma statehood in 1907, the Council House at Okmulgee housed the Principal Chief, Supreme Court, education offices and National Council chambers. Its rooms show government as everyday administrative work as well as public ceremony.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The Nation was forced to leave the building at statehood and regained it in 2010. Restoration completed in 2018 recovered its historic room layout for interpretation. Regaining a building was an act of stewardship by an existing Nation, not the creation of a new people.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The constitution's election certificate records ratification on 6 October 1979. Its separate executive, legislative and judicial articles set out national institutions, while article II protects the organization of tribal towns. The document records both change and continuing local traditions.

passages.title: Removal and survival
passages.text: In 1836 and 1837, United States authorities forced large numbers of Muscogee people toward Indian Territory by land and water. Detention, inadequate supplies and dangerous travel caused profound suffering. Communities rebuilt afterward while maintaining ties to southeastern homelands.

Coerced land cessions and removal transformed Muscogee political geography in the nineteenth century. Later allotment and statehood imposed further losses, but the Muscogee Nation and its communities continue. The map's 1492 to 1500 interval is not a supported lifespan for the people or the later confederacy.

passages.text: Mutapa was a Shona state of the northern Zimbabwe plateau and adjacent Zambezi lowlands, with connections extending into present-day Mozambique. It existed before the map’s 1492 start and continued after its 1650 endpoint. Older European maps often exaggerated the reach of its rulers.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Baranda, near Mount Fura and the gold-bearing Mukaradzi valley, is usually identified with the trading place Massapa. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century remains include local pottery, imported ceramics and glass, revealing a substantial African settlement within an international trading world.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Soot on Baranda pots points to cooking, while burnishing tools support local manufacture of its polished graphite-coated pottery. Traders needed meals as well as merchandise; kitchens were part of this commercial settlement’s working life.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: The published Baranda assemblage includes 9,006 sherds of locally made pottery. Most vessels served daily needs, but the researchers argue that some pottery also circulated in exchange. A broken cooking pot can therefore help tell both a household and a trading story.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Chemical analysis of Baranda’s glass beads identifies a south Asian origin for most of those studied. The beads were small, but their journeys connected inland African communities with production and exchange across the Indian Ocean.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Researchers combined bead shapes, excavated layers, X-ray fluorescence and Raman spectroscopy. These methods check the glass itself rather than assigning a date from colour alone; attractive objects can also be surprisingly informative scientific samples.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Baranda’s ironworking remains include furnace material, slag and air-pipe fragments. Study of these residues distinguishes smelting ore from later work on the metal, making skilled production visible even when a complete furnace no longer survives.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Comparing Baranda with the much earlier Swart Village suggested changes in ironworking practice. The authors explicitly challenge the idea that African metal production stayed unchanged for two thousand years; local technologies had histories of experimentation and adaptation.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: A Portuguese account quoted in the historical synthesis describes a royal compound with separate dwellings for the ruler, queen and attendants, surrounded by a wooden enclosure. This is evidence about a court household, not the floor plan of every family’s home.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: The same description places clay-covered wooden buildings beneath thatched roofs. Political importance did not require every palace to be built like Great Zimbabwe’s surviving stone walls; different building materials could house an important court.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: Diogo de Alcaçova’s early report drew on people at Sofala and focused on gold, rival rulers and possible alliances. Historian Ana Cristina Roque shows why these reports must be read as interested Portuguese accounts, not neutral surveys of the entire interior.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: The 1506 letter contains the Portuguese words “o nome de rey he Menamotapam”: “the title of the king is Menamotapam”. The spelling comes from the published original text. It records a foreign writer’s rendering of the royal title, not a Shona sentence written by the Mutapa court.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: Historians compare oral genealogies with contemporary documents because neither gives a perfectly straightforward succession list. David Beach’s study revised earlier reconstructions, illustrating how questioning a source can make the history more accurate rather than less valuable.

Mutapa power contracted and shifted through succession conflicts, Portuguese encroachment and the rise of Rozvi power. Smaller dynastic centres survived long after 1650. Colonial expansion eventually removed their independent power, while communities and some royal lineages continued.

sectionTitles: River villages, skilled work and recreation

passages.text: The Miami, or Myaamia, are a Great Lakes people whose farming villages and river connections supported wide regional influence. The broad Myaamia and narrower Miami outlines are approximations. A separate Oklahoma outline dated 1492 is anachronistic: Miami settlement there followed nineteenth-century removals. Miami communities continue in Oklahoma, Indiana and beyond.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami villages stood near rivers that connected settlements through canoe travel. The Indiana community’s history places their homeland across parts of present-day Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan. Hunting, fishing and cultivation worked together in a landscape where water routes could link relatives and trading partners.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami white flour corn drew an early eighteenth-century observer’s attention for its fine husks and pale flour. Historian Cameron Shriver follows this crop through later sources, including twentieth-century Miami farmers. Corn was both a lasting food tradition and an agricultural achievement maintained through enormous political change.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In a 2023 account, weaver Jared Nally describes harvesting inner bark from trees such as basswood and gathering other plant fibers later in the year. Separating usable fibers and rolling or spinning thread could take as long as weaving itself. A finished textile contains a great deal of work that is easy not to see.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: The winter game snowsnake sends a length of wood sliding through snow. Players try to make it travel farther and straighter than an opponent’s throw. Myaamia community programs have been reviving the game: snow becomes a playing surface, and the snake is reassuringly wooden.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Lacrosse remains an opportunity to meet relatives and neighbors as well as compete. A 2022 community account describes an annual Myaamia game with Seneca-Cayuga participants, including youth camps. It also distinguishes older games from newer adaptations that introduce Myaamia language into familiar card games.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In 2024, Myaamia sugar camps operated in Ohio, Indiana and Oklahoma. Sap was boiled down into syrup or sugar; a typical maple yield required about 40 gallons of sap for one gallon of syrup. Oklahoma participants also tapped black walnut because local sugar maples were scarce. Breakfast sweetness required buckets of effort.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Miami leader Little Turtle helped lead a Native coalition that defeated United States forces in 1790 and 1791. Before the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, he urged peace. These changing decisions belonged to a wider struggle over homelands involving several allied peoples, rather than one isolated Miami army.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 required extensive land cessions. Further treaties narrowed Miami control over their homeland, and an 1840 agreement called for removal beyond the Mississippi. Treaty dates mark government decisions; the forced journey itself came later.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: On October 11, 1846, five canal boats carrying Miami people reached Cincinnati. There they were forced aboard the steamboat Colorado to continue west along the Ohio River. A university archival exhibit places this transfer within the removal journey, revealing how ordinary transport networks became instruments of forced displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Other Miami families secured permission to stay in Indiana. Their descendants form the Miami Nation of Indiana, with continuing government, cultural programs and relationships to western Miami relatives. Its own history distinguishes that community’s existence from its lack of federal recognition as a sovereign tribal nation today.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The western Miami faced another move after an 1867 treaty, with migration from Kansas into present-day Oklahoma in the late 1860s and 1870s. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma established its government there. That sequence explains why an Oklahoma polygon cannot accurately represent Miami territory in 1492.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: Language revitalization draws on documents spanning the late 1600s through the 1960s. A Myaamia Center report explains how researchers analyze old records, compare forms and develop resources for present-day use. The work connects archival scholarship with families learning words together; it is a gradual effort across generations.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.

sectionTitles: Clothes, hair and a special drink
A seat, a family and a sound

passages.text: This map groups northern European Bronze Age communities under a very broad label. Its outline reaches far beyond Scandinavia into eastern Europe, so it cannot stand for one kingdom or shared way of life. The examples here focus on well-documented Danish and Scandinavian communities; Denmark’s Bronze Age is conventionally dated about 1700 to 500 BCE.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: At Bjerre Site 7 in northwestern Denmark, a ninth-century BCE longhouse was at least fifteen metres long. Fire pits, grains and food crusts show that much cooking happened at its eastern end. Thin-walled serving vessels concentrated farther west, suggesting different tasks in different parts of the house.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: Nearly 1,800 pieces of raw amber were recovered at Bjerre. Some lay in storage pots or compact clusters. Researchers suggest the household collected and stored amber for exchange, possibly obtaining metal in return. A farm could therefore be connected to distant places while producing much of its own food.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: Bjerre also produced evidence of flint tool making and small-scale metalworking, including crucible and mould fragments. Bronze Age does not mean people stopped using stone. Householders selected materials for particular jobs, and flint remained useful for cutting, scraping and other everyday work.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: A young woman buried at Egtved in 1370 BCE wore a short tunic and a skirt made from cords, with a spiral-decorated bronze belt plate. Her teeth suggest she was about sixteen to eighteen. Preserved clothing lets us see a real outfit rather than imagine everyone in generic animal skins.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: Her belongings included a horn comb, a small bark box with a bronze awl, and traces of a hair net. Such objects connect dress with work and grooming. The burial is unusually rich evidence, so it should not be treated as the standard wardrobe of every household.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: A bark bucket from the same grave retained residue from a fermented drink, probably beer sweetened with honey. Analysis also identified berry-related evidence, wheat and bog myrtle. Pollen can preserve clues to ingredients, although it does not supply an exact recipe or prove what everyone drank daily.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: At Guldhøj, a man buried in the later fifteenth century BCE had a folding chair placed at his feet. It was made from ash wood with dark pitch inlaid into carved decoration. The seat had been otter skin, of which only a fragment survives. Portable furniture has a very long history.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: Three oak-coffin burials at Borum Eshøj held an older woman, an older man and a younger man. Wood for at least two coffins was felled in 1351 BCE. They may have been related, but the attractive idea of a small family remains an interpretation rather than an established family tree.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: Curved bronze trumpets called lurs had a mouthpiece at one end and a decorated plate at the other. Modern players can produce a range of natural notes on surviving examples. We can hear the instruments, but we do not know the actual tunes people played at Bronze Age gatherings.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: The Trundholm Sun Chariot, made around 1400 BCE, places a horse and a decorated sun disc on wheels. The museum interprets it as the sun’s journey with a divine horse. It is a striking model of movement and belief, not an ordinary cart shrunk for archaeological convenience.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: A ship appears on a ceremonial sword from Rørby, with crew members drawn as short lines. Related ship images were carved into rock in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The repeated motif links objects and landscapes across the sea without telling us the names of the people aboard.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: These ships, spirals and sun images offer a visual language, but the cited examples are not a deciphered alphabet. This card cannot provide an attested sentence spoken or written by their makers. Their pictures survive more clearly than their words.

Around 500 BCE, Danish communities increasingly worked iron from local deposits, marking the conventional beginning of the Iron Age. This was a change in technology and society, not the fall of one northern empire. The vast imported outline cannot give every community the same ending.

sectionTitles: Water for a city and a school

passages.text: This record begins while Namibia was still under South African rule. Independence came on 21 March 1990 after a long liberation struggle and international negotiations. Modern Namibia includes many languages and communities, with distinctive achievements in water engineering and living traditions of music, craft and shared celebration.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: Hosea Kutako’s appeals against South African rule reached the United Nations through Reverend Michael Scott from 1946. Decades of petitions, political organizing and international debate followed. Independence required Namibians’ sustained efforts, not merely a new name printed on a map.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: In 1959, resistance to forced removal from Windhoek’s Old Location ended in deadly violence. Apartheid planners moved Black residents toward Katutura. Museum documentation records doors marked with letters assigning different African groups to separate areas, making racial classification visible in the built environment.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: Preparing the 1989 election meant reaching rural voters as well as towns. UNTAG reports that mobile teams covered some 2,200 rural registration points. Elections and the constituent assembly then helped turn a negotiated settlement into institutions for an independent country.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: Windhoek began adding highly treated reclaimed wastewater to its drinking-water supply in 1968. In a dry region, engineers found a way to use water again. The achievement depends on treatment and checking water quality; simply reusing dirty water would be a completely different matter.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: The newer Goreangab reclamation plant, operating from 2002, uses multiple treatment barriers before its water is blended with other supplies. This is an important sanitation story: wastewater becomes a resource through carefully managed engineering, not through wishing very hard at a tap.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: At Onakatumbe Combined School in 2017, handwashing stations stood near classrooms and toilets. Children practiced washing before snacks and after toilet visits. Learning to use soap became part of the school day alongside reading and mathematics.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: A broken borehole at King Kauluma Combined School in late 2017 disrupted meals and closed flush toilets. UNICEF’s 2018 account describes pupils bringing small bottles from home until a tanker supplied the school. Water infrastructure mattered to eating, learning and using the loo at once.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: For northern Namibia’s Oshituthi shomagongo festival, men carve wooden cups and tools from cattle horns while women prepare baskets and clay pots. Fruit gathering and juice processing involve younger people too. A celebration begins long before anyone arrives to sing or dance.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: As women prepare the fermented marula drink, they also share songs, poems, family concerns and craft knowledge. Young people learn by watching and joining the work. The gathering links food preparation to conversation and education, rather than separating those parts of life.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: Nama and Damara ancestral music accompanies occasions such as weddings and celebrations welcoming rain. A UNESCO-supported documentation project in 2018 and 2019 worked with community knowledge. Musical skill survives through people teaching and performing it, as well as through recordings.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: A written Oshindonga example appears in a 2013 community consent letter: “Omukanda gwepitikilo”, translated there as “Certificate of Consent”. The document authorized a heritage nomination on behalf of northern traditional authorities. Communities were writing their own decision into the preservation process.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: The republic’s constitution supplies an English sample: “This Constitution shall be the Supreme Law of Namibia.” In plain language, the constitution is the highest legal authority. The sentence comes from Article 1, linking the written founding document to the new state established in 1990.

Namibia continues as an independent republic. The 1945 start of this map record belongs to the period of South African rule; it is not Namibia’s independence date. The decisive constitutional transformation occurred in 1990, while families and cultural communities span both periods.

sectionTitles: A palace well and a busy city
A written voice and its stories

passages.text: The Naples entry samples the southern mainland kingdom during Spanish viceregal rule. It is more than the city of Naples, and it should not be silently merged with Sicily. Spanish government lasted from 1503 to 1707, beyond the map’s 1530 to 1700 interval. Palace archaeology, banking records and music schools offer unusually concrete windows into life in its capital.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: The Royal Palace begun in 1600 was designed by Domenico Fontana as a residence for the Spanish viceroys. A royal building did not mean the Spanish king personally lived there year-round: the viceroy governed on his behalf.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: Excavations in 1999 to 2000 recovered around 5,000 objects and ceramic fragments from a well at the older palace. The well probably first supplied water and later received rubbish. Broken things can be wonderfully informative: an archaeologist’s useful evidence may once have been somebody else’s unwanted mess.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: The palace-well finds include pottery from Naples and other Italian production centers, as well as Spanish wares from places such as Manises and Valencia. They reveal connections through objects used or discarded at this particular site. A palace deposit is not a random sample of every Neapolitan kitchen.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: A blue-and-white Chinese porcelain bowl from the late sixteenth century appeared among the well’s finds. It shows that an object could reach Naples through long-distance exchange. One bowl does not establish who transported it, who ate from it or whether a Chinese community lived beside the palace.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: Naples’ water administration left records of expenditure on the Carmignano aqueduct in 1629 and later water concessions. These documents show that moving and allocating water required money and rules. They cannot, by themselves, tell us what kind of toilet or wash space an individual family possessed.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The Monte della Pietà began in 1539 to make interest-free loans against pledged possessions for people in need. It later accepted deposits and received royal recognition as a bank in 1584. Charity and finance developed together rather than occupying entirely separate worlds.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: Household belongings could become temporary security for a loan. The Pietà accepted linen, wool and silk as well as precious objects. The bank archive distinguishes limited interest-free lending from other loans that charged interest: “charitable bank” did not mean that every transaction was free.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The Annunziata bank, established in 1587, helped support an orphanage, hospital and girls’ school. Another bank founded in 1589 was connected with the Incurabili hospital. Financial records therefore preserve practical links between savings, credit and the care of vulnerable people.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The early Neapolitan conservatories cared for poor or abandoned children. Music formed part of their religious activities in the sixteenth century. The name later became strongly associated with professional musical training, but these institutions began with a wider charitable purpose.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: During the seventeenth century, conservatory musicians increasingly performed for paying patrons, and musical training attracted outside pupils. Performance could support an institution as well as teach a trade. This does not mean all Neapolitan children learned music or that every child in care became a celebrated composer.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: Giambattista Basile’s Lo cunto de li cunti appeared after his death in installments from 1634 to 1636. Written in Neapolitan, its fifty tales reshaped storytelling traditions into elaborate literature. Stories can preserve language and imaginative worlds without being literal reports of daily events.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: The title “Lo Cunto de li Cunti” means “The Tale of Tales.” This short Neapolitan sample uses Latin letters and is attested in the original title transcribed in a later scholarly edition. Its repeated word cunto makes the title sound like an invitation to settle in for another story.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: Basile’s collection also includes verse interludes voiced by figures such as cooks, servants and household officials. Their presence brings work and social hierarchy into the literary performance. These are crafted voices, however, not interviews with real palace employees or a census of ordinary family life.

Spanish viceregal rule ended in 1707, rather than at the atlas’s 1700 cutoff. The Kingdom of Naples and its population continued under subsequent rulers. This entry’s ending therefore describes a change of government, not the destruction of Naples or the disappearance of its culture.

passages.text: The Nara period gave Japan its first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo, laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. The court ran the country under the ritsuryo codes, made Buddhism a state religion and compiled its first histories and poetry.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Manyoshu, an anthology of 4,516 poems by emperors, courtiers and frontier guards, was compiled; its latest dated poem is from 759.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Kojiki, and in 720 the Nihon Shoki, recorded the myths and early history of the imperial line.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze figure about 15 meters high, was dedicated in a ceremony attended by monks from India and China.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Shomu ordered a state temple and nunnery in every province.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ritsuryo codes, the Taiho of 701 and the Yoro of 718, organized government, taxes and land on Tang models.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning was taught at the state academy to train officials.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese characters were used for all government records, and census and tax registers were kept on paper.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Trunk roads with post stations linked the capital to the provinces.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Manyoshu remains the foundation of Japanese poetry.
Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, in 794, the start of the Heian period.

sectionTitles: A homeland visible in material evidence

passages.text: The Narragansett are a continuing Native nation of the Rhode Island region, with coastal settlements, inland resources and important relationships with neighboring peoples. Their leaders were major participants in seventeenth-century New England politics. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is a broad ancestral-area sketch, not a modern reservation boundary or the lifetime of the nation.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: Salt Pond, archaeological site RI 110 at the head of Point Judith Pond, preserves a large coastal village dated by the state’s account to about 1100 to 1300 CE. Archaeologists found traces of houses, other structures, cooking places and food storage. These are clues to a working community, not simply isolated valuable objects.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: Plant specialists found maize in five archaeological features at Salt Pond. Their 2008 study combines these remains with associated dating evidence to establish cultivation before European settlement. Charred food that survived underground can answer questions that a written visitor’s description never addressed.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: A Narragansett basket dated to around 1675 survives in the Rhode Island Historical Society’s collection as 1842.2.1. Basswood splints and corn husk are combined with red wool. A later note describes a hurried gift, but the museum calls most of that story myth. The basket itself preserves evidence of careful weaving.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: In 2013, Rhode Island’s transportation department purchased approximately 52 acres containing the Salt Pond site after a dispute over proposed housing. The Narragansett Tribal Historic Preservation Office participated in its protection. Archaeological knowledge here depended on decisions about roads, development and the survival of a culturally important place.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: Lorén Spears describes winter villages sheltered by inland woods and located near fresh water. Summer brought movement toward bays and salt ponds. Seasonal living joined access to food, building materials and protected places, rather than keeping every household in one location year-round.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: Fishing weirs guided fish into places where people could catch them. Women dried or smoked catches for later meals, while older children helped tend gardens. Seaweed and fish fertilized crops. Family food supplies depended on coordinated work on land and water.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: In 1636, Canonicus and Miantanomi permitted Roger Williams to settle at Providence. Spears explains the agreement as permission to use land under Narragansett authority. Colonists’ treatment of such agreements as outright purchases helped turn diplomatic arrangements into disputes over sovereignty.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: The December 1675 Great Swamp attack killed Narragansett civilians as well as fighters during the regional war. Colonists subsequently enslaved survivors, including people sent to the Caribbean. Remaining Narragansett joined with Niantic relatives and allies, rebuilding community amid devastating losses.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: The Narragansett Dawn, edited by Princess Redwing and Ernest Hazard in 1935 and 1936, carried language lessons, cultural and political discussion, and news of births and deaths. Copies preserved by the University of Rhode Island show a community describing itself in print, including the everyday milestones that larger histories can overlook.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: An attested modern written greeting is “Asco wequassinummis, neetompooag!” Lorén Spears translates it as “Hello my friends” at the start of her 2017 Tomaquag Museum account. This is a named Narragansett writer’s published language sample, rather than a phrase reconstructed for the map’s fifteenth-century setting.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: Spears’s 2017 account of Nikommo describes a gathering with a feast, social activities and gifts for people in need. Clothing, toys and handmade items could circulate through the giveaway. The occasion connected celebration with looking after other households: sharing was part of the event itself.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: A 2018 Tomaquag Museum article shows Skyla Jennings, identified as Narragansett, learning basket making in an arts-and-wellness class. Another photograph shows Lorén Spears teaching corn-husk doll making. These named examples document learning through hands and materials alongside classroom education in a modern community.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: An 1882 auction broadside documents the sale of reservation land during Rhode Island’s attempt to dissolve Narragansett political status. Treating Native people as isolated individuals could make collectively held land easier to sell. The document is evidence of a state policy, not proof that the nation consented to disappear.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: Narragansett people continued monthly meetings and their annual August gathering after the state’s attempted detribalization. They retained recognized leaders and raised money for land claims. These ordinary acts of meeting, contributing and choosing representatives helped sustain institutions when outsiders claimed the community had ended.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: A land-claim settlement in 1978 restored approximately 1,800 acres, and federal acknowledgment followed in 1983. The tribal history also records a longhouse built in the early 1940s as a meeting place. A continuing nation needed spaces for practical government as well as ceremonies.

Narragansett sovereignty and landholding suffered severe losses through colonial war and later state policies, but the people and their institutions continued. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only an imported coverage cutoff; federal acknowledgment in 1983 recognized an enduring community.

sectionTitles: A spa town, a train and traveling water
A crowd demanded a different government

passages.text: The Duchy of Nassau was a small German state between the Rhine, Main, Lahn and Dill, existing from 1806 to 1866. Its rulers joined older territories into a new administration, while schools, spas and the mineral-water trade changed local life. This imported record runs from 1815 to 1878, but its later years are misleading: Nassau had lost independence to Prussia in 1866.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: Nassau-Usingen and Nassau-Weilburg joined to form the duchy in 1806. Their agreement of 5 September called for bringing their troops together under common administration. Even a small new state had practical problems to solve: soldiers and officials who had served different rulers now needed to work together.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: The government reorganized Nassau into twenty-eight administrative districts in 1816, each headed by an appointed official. Earlier reforms had abolished serfdom in 1808 and compulsory labor obligations in 1812. These changes altered what rulers and landlords could demand from inhabitants, while leaving strong authority in the state’s hands.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: Writing sample: the 1814 constitutional edict declares, “Wir haben keine Abgaben von Unsern Unterthanen erhoben, außer für Bedürfnisse des Staats,” meaning “We have levied no taxes on our subjects except for the needs of the state.” This German passage survives in an 1817 printed collection. It is the rulers’ account of their conduct, rather than proof that subjects agreed with every tax.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: The school reform of 1817 required boys and girls to attend elementary school from six to fourteen, without distinctions of social rank or religion. It aimed to bring children into shared schools and applied throughout the year. The curriculum included language, numbers, measuring, religion and singing: more than memorizing a few prayers.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: Teacher preparation mattered too. The reform drew on reports commissioned from all twenty-eight districts in 1809 and on the educational methods of Pestalozzi. Officials also regulated classrooms, furniture, teaching materials, salaries and inspection. A new school policy required desks and trained adults as well as a grand announcement.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: An agricultural institute opened in Idstein in 1818 and later moved to Hof Geisberg near Wiesbaden. There, winter teaching allowed young farmers to study while remaining available for farm work during the growing season. The school also offered advice and helped develop new fruit-tree varieties. Education had to fit around crops that would not wait.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: Nassau organized a network of doctors employed as public officials, aiming to make medical care available to poorer inhabitants as well as wealthy patients. Municipalities paid two thirds of their salaries. The reform connected local tax money with an everyday need: someone trained to help when a household faced illness.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: An orphan fund established under the 1816 poor-relief edict supported the care and education of children who had lost their parents. A widows’ and orphans’ fund followed in 1820. These institutions show how family crises became a concern of public administration, although they were not the same as today’s universal welfare arrangements.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: Wiesbaden gained a Kursaal in 1810 as a place for social gatherings. Licensed gambling found a permanent home there that May. The spa town offered visitors sociability and entertainment alongside treatment; not every activity promising excitement was likely to improve a visitor’s wallet.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: A palace built between 1813 and 1820 for the hereditary prince took on a different role: it housed the museum, state library and government offices. Rooms intended for a royal household became places for collections, books and administrative work. Its later use preserves a small story of how public institutions grew.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: The first scheduled train left Wiesbaden for Kastel on 10 March 1840; the connection to Frankfurt opened on 13 April. Railways added a new way to reach the spa town and neighboring commercial centers. Trips that once depended on roads, horses or boats could now include a railway timetable.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: Niederselters shipped mineral water in pottery jugs across Europe. A jug recovered from a wreck in the Bay of Gdańsk was dated around 1820. Its stamp carries Selters and HN, short for Herzogtum Nassau, or Duchy of Nassau. A container lost with a ship became evidence of long-distance trade.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: The municipal account reports one to two million jugs filled annually between 1806 and 1830. Apothecaries, doctors, merchants and innkeepers sold the water, which customers valued as a supposed remedy. Filling and transporting all those vessels joined a local spring to potters, traders and consumers far beyond Nassau.

passages.title: A crowd demanded a different government
passages.text: In March 1848, reformers circulated nine demands through leaflets and word of mouth. On 4 March, Duke Adolph accepted them before a large crowd in Wiesbaden. Promises included press freedom and freedom of association and religion. News could travel on paper, but conversation helped carry it across the countryside.

Nassau sided with Austria in the war of 1866. After Austria’s defeat, Prussia annexed the duchy, ending its independence. The territory’s inhabitants and local communities continued under a different government; the map’s continuation to 1878 must not be read as another twelve years of ducal rule.

passages.text: Natal was a British colony on southern Africa’s Indian Ocean coast, with African communities, settler farms and towns, and Indian workers and traders. Plantation labour, schools and printing presses all shaped its history. It was distinct from the neighboring Zulu kingdom.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: The colony’s dates begin before this map record. Britain annexed Natal in 1843 and initially administered it from the Cape; Natal became a separate colony in 1856. The imported 1878 starting point is a surviving map snapshot, not the founding year.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Natal was a British colony while the Zulu kingdom remained a separate African state. Britain’s 1878 ultimatum demanded changes that would destroy Zulu independence, and invasion followed in 1879. Their proximity on a map must not erase the distinction between colony and kingdom.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: The Truro arrived in November 1860 with Indian indentured workers. Their contracts supplied labour to colonial employers, especially plantations. Later Indian traders also came independently, so “Indian migrant” did not describe one occupation or one route into Natal.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Historian Jo Beall documents women plucking tender tea leaves on Natal estates. Men and children also worked in estate production, with tasks divided by age and gender. Tea in a cup concealed a demanding sequence of picking, carrying and processing.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Women’s work continued after paid estate tasks. Household duties and small garden plots helped feed children and adults. Beall’s research places this less visible labour beside employers’ records, showing why a wage or contract alone cannot describe a family’s working day.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: In 1861 Bauboo Naidoo opened a shop in Durban’s Field Street selling condiments and foods missing from workers’ rations. The tiny detail matters: migration carried tastes and cooking knowledge, and people sought familiar ingredients rather than simply accepting an employer’s menu.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: John and Nokutela Dube founded Ohlange in 1901 after gaining experience in the United States. The school connected education with African institution-building. Remembering both founders keeps Nokutela’s contribution visible beside the much more frequently named John Dube.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: A short isiZulu writing sample is “Ilanga lase Natal”, meaning “The Natal Sun”. The newspaper began under John Dube at Ohlange in 1903. A newspaper title could announce a public voice in a reader’s own language before they had read a single article.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: The surviving Ilanga collection allows readers to study an African newspaper as a sequence of issues, rather than only a famous editor’s biography. Its establishment at Ohlange links a school to the work of printing and distributing information.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: At Phoenix, a printing press became part of a communal settlement. Gandhi bought the land in 1904 and moved the press for Indian Opinion there from Durban. Producing a newspaper involved physical work as well as ideas: the entire press had to change address.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: Phoenix residents cultivated food gardens and experimented with communal self-sufficiency. The settlement also provided meals, accommodation and education for families of people involved in nonviolent protest campaigns. Political activity depended on ordinary tasks such as feeding children and keeping a place to sleep.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: Recruitment of Indian indentured labour for Natal ended in 1911 after decades of mistreatment and controversy. The workers and their descendants did not disappear when recruitment stopped; Indian South African communities continued building families, businesses, associations and public lives.

Natal joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910 and became a province. Its communities continued through this change of government. The map record extends to 1914, but that endpoint is not the colony’s constitutional ending.
