passages.text: Natchez communities farmed the lower Mississippi landscape and gathered at ceremonial mound centres. By the late seventeenth century, their settlement districts retained substantial autonomy. The Great Sun’s prominence did not make every local chief his obedient provincial governor.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Natchez farmers grew maize, beans and squash while also hunting, fishing and gathering wild foods. Many families lived on dispersed farms and travelled to mound centres for gatherings, rather than residing permanently beside the ceremonial buildings.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Grand Village excavations recovered charred maize, hickory nuts and black walnut shells. Common beans came from a context associated with French trench excavation. The remains support a varied food history, but mixed deposits cannot identify every meal’s date or maker.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: A clay pipe from Grand Village has incised chevrons around its bowl and a zigzag beneath it. Other pipe fragments retain interior charring. These small finds preserve both deliberate surface decoration and traces of use.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Neitzel interpreted a carefully modelled clay fragment as an imitation of a European brass bell. Its incisions and suspension hole suggest a maker adapting an introduced form in another material. The surviving fragment does not prove how the complete object sounded.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: Emerald Mound carries secondary mounds on a vast raised platform. Unlike centres arranged around a ground-level plaza, its ceremonial space occupied the platform’s summit. The surviving structure shows how earthmoving could create an entire elevated setting for public activity.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: The monument required repeated movement and placement of soil. The National Park Service illustrates a possible basket-carrying process, but exact crew sizes and working schedules remain unknown. Its scale demonstrates collective achievement without supplying a documented construction diary.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: Barnett describes matrilineal moieties, or paired social divisions, providing marriage partners and reciprocal services. Their competition included stickball. Such relationships linked kinship, obligations and recreation; European comparisons with their own class systems could obscure how they worked.

passages.title: Exchange and historical evidence
passages.text: In the early eighteenth century, Natchez people sought firearms, metal cooking pots and woollen cloth from French settlers. Havard’s research also describes settlers depending on Native hunting and healing knowledge. These relationships involved mutual exchange before open warfare devastated them.

passages.title: Exchange and historical evidence
passages.text: Natchez is generally classified as a language isolate: no close linguistic relatives are established. The Sam Noble Museum’s catalogue names Nancy Raven, Sam Watt and Peggy Leaf among the people whose knowledge contributed to Mary Haas’s field notebooks.

passages.title: Displacement and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Refuge among Creek and Cherokee communities did not end displacement. Many Natchez descendants later experienced forced removal to present-day Oklahoma. These nineteenth-century events followed the earlier French war and should not be compressed into one migration.

passages.title: Displacement and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Natchez Nation compiled an English-to-Natchez wordlist, documented by UBC researchers in 2023. It drew on speakers and other resources and invited contributions for new terms. Language work makes continuity visible beyond accounts that end with the eighteenth-century war.

French military retaliation in the 1730s forced Natchez people from their homeland; some captives were enslaved in the Caribbean. Survivors joined other Native communities, and descendants continued their history through later removals. The destruction of those settlements was not the extinction of the people.

sectionTitles: Family introductions, learning and a living language

passages.text: The Navajo, or Diné, are a living Indigenous people whose homeland spans the American Southwest. Navajo Nation sources call it Diné Bikéyah. This shared card covers the map’s Navajo, Navaho and Diné Bikéyah labels. Their different outlines and 1492 to 1650 date windows are imported coverage, not reliable borders or the beginning and ending of a single state.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: In northwestern New Mexico, Navajo builders made small masonry pueblitos during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Many stood on boulders or outcrops with wide views. They provided shelter and cooking space as well as refuge during conflict, so a defensible position also had to work as a home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Pueblito remains include roofs, hooded fireplaces, nearby hogan foundations and small openings used to check a doorway. A family could cook, keep out weather and watch an entrance in the same compact building. These practical architectural details survive alongside the story of warfare.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Diné weavers adopted wool from introduced churra sheep and incorporated it into their textile traditions. The upright loom let makers build a cloth through the patient crossing of threads. Behind a finished blanket stood an entire chain of work, beginning with keeping the animals alive.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: At Hubbell Trading Post, established in Ganado in 1878, Navajo customers exchanged blankets, wool, sheep and pelts for goods such as flour, coffee, tools and cloth. The post also supplied news and jobs. A shopping trip could therefore carry both household supplies and neighborhood information home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: The predominantly red geometric style called Ganado Red became associated with the trading post. Hubbell promoted particular designs for outside buyers, while Navajo weavers supplied the artistry and labor. Rugs linked skilled household production to a market whose tastes could influence what makers were asked to weave.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: A 2016 Hubbell workshop offered hands-on dyeing, spinning and weaving, together with learning about Churro sheep. The program had begun in 2000 to share fiber skills and animal husbandry. Before anyone could weave a beautiful design, the wool still had to become usable yarn.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: In 1864, United States forces drove Navajo people from their homeland to Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico. In a 2018 anniversary message, Navajo leadership remembered four years of imprisonment and suffering there. The Long Walk was forced displacement, not a voluntary migration to find better farmland.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The treaty concluded at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868 allowed a return home. Its text also promised the purchase of 15,000 sheep and goats and support for the journey. Reading the document makes rebuilding tangible: families needed animals, food and transport as well as permission to leave.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first modern Navajo council was created in 1923, and reforms in 1989 reorganized national government through separated branches. These are changes in the institutions of a continuing people. They should not be mistaken for the invention of Navajo community life or its first traditions of leadership.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first group of 29 Navajo Marine recruits arrived for training in May 1942. They helped develop a military code with an initial vocabulary of 211 terms and a system for spelling English letters. The achievement combined language expertise, memorization and radio training; it was more than ordinary conversation overheard on a battlefield.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Navajo scholar Shelly C. Lowe explains that her clan comes through her mother and passes to her children. Introducing clan relationships and home community helps people place one another within a network of relatives. An introduction can be a miniature family map rather than just a name.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Remembering school in Ganado, Lowe describes designing rugs on craft paper, beadwork and other cultural arts in class. She also heard Navajo from school cooks and aides as well as relatives. Language and skills traveled through ordinary encounters, from the classroom to the people preparing lunch.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Written language sample: yá’át’ééh, translated by Lowe as “It is good,” is a Navajo greeting printed in her 2022 interview. This is an attested modern spelling of a living language. It is not presented as an inscription surviving from the map’s sixteenth-century window.

The Diné endured forced removal and returned after the 1868 treaty. Their nation, families and language continue, with government institutions changing over time. None of the imported map endpoints should be read as the extinction of the Navajo people.

sectionTitles: A court with gardens and practical government
Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet

passages.text: The kingdom of Pamplona, later called Navarre, linked communities on both sides of the Pyrenees. Royal government, pilgrimage routes and towns left a rich written record. Its atlas interval 1000 to 1530 spans both independent monarchy and the conquest beginning in 1512; the single outline cannot represent every later division between Upper and Lower Navarre.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Charles III and Queen Eleanor transformed Olite’s palace during his 1387 to 1425 reign. Its irregular towers, rooms and gardens grew into a complex royal residence. This was exceptional courtly luxury, not a model of the typical Navarrese family home.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: The municipality names Martín Périz of Estella as a master of masonry and Lope “el Barbicano,” a Muslim craftsman from Tudela, for carpentry. Named workers make the palace more than an anonymous royal achievement; different skills and communities helped create it.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Water from the Cidacos was raised with a bucket mechanism to the reservoir tower and distributed through lead pipes to gardens and fountains. The royal greenery depended on engineering and maintenance, not a naturally self-watering castle.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Olite’s court kept a menagerie including lions, a camel and an ostrich, as well as birds and hunting animals. These creatures advertised wealth and connections. Their presence does not tell us how comfortably the animals lived.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: The Fuero General was compiled in the thirteenth century in Navarro-Aragonese. No author is securely identified, and it gained authority gradually through judicial use. A legal tradition could develop through repeated copying and practice rather than one dramatic founding decree.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Codex A1, a fourteenth-century copy of the Fuero, uses black and red ink and includes Philip III’s 1330 amendment. This particular book makes change visible: law was revised, not simply frozen forever in a medieval manuscript.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: At Roncesvalles, the bishop of Pamplona organized a brotherhood of clergy and laypeople to care for pilgrims in 1127. The institution expanded during the 1130s. Hospitality at a mountain crossing meant dealing with travelers’ practical needs, not only maintaining a church.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Kings, nobles, bishops and grateful pilgrims gave the Roncesvalles institution land and income. Those endowments supported assistance. A hospital needed continuing resources; an impressive founding story alone could not feed the next group of tired travelers.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Surviving charters for Puente la Reina and Sangüesa from 1122, and San Saturnino in Pamplona from 1129, show how towns along the pilgrimage world were organized through written privileges. The archive also preserves an Irache charter concerning a pilgrims’ hospital.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Two officials, Martín de San Martín and Machín de Zalba, exchanged short letters on the same sheet, probably in 1416. The first asks about a tax reduction and then about dinner plans. Medieval office correspondence could switch from money to supper surprisingly quickly.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Zalba replied that he could not attend dinner because he had guests at home, then answered the tax question in Basque. The pair switched between Navarrese Romance and Basque. This proves these particular officials could use both, not that every inhabitant had the same language skills.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: San Martín’s Basque farewell reads “jaunatiçula egun hon”: “May God give you a good day.” The spelling is preserved in the archive’s transcription of the probably 1416 letter. Basque was written here in Latin letters, within a document otherwise using Romance.

Ferdinand’s invasion in 1512 began a prolonged conquest, not an instant disappearance of Navarre. Upper Navarre joined the Castilian crown in 1515 while retaining important institutions. Lower Navarre followed a separate path and was incorporated into the French monarchy in 1620. Communities and regional identities continued on both sides of the mountains.

sectionTitles: Making a living in a dry landscape

passages.text: Nasca, also spelled Nazca, describes related communities of Peru’s dry southern coast, famous for painted pottery and enormous ground drawings. Their history grew from Paracas traditions and continued into the eighth century CE. The imported 100 BCE to 600 CE span covers only part of this changing cultural tradition, not the lifespan of a single unified kingdom.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: At Marcaya, households of both high and low status possessed colorful painted ceramics. Fine-looking pottery was therefore not reserved for the very richest. Excavating homes helps reveal who actually used the objects that later ended up in museum cases.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Certain vessel shapes at Marcaya were restricted to higher-status homes. Vaughn interprets these households as intermediaries between the village and gatherings at Cahuachi. Sharing a broad pottery tradition could coexist with differences in influence and special serving equipment.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: An isotope study in the Las Trancas Valley found greater meat consumption among higher-status people, while access to maize was less sharply divided. Food choices can leave chemical traces in human remains, helping researchers study inequality beyond impressive buildings and rich graves.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Puquios collect groundwater through underground galleries for fields and household use. A major archaeological survey proposed their origins during middle or later Nasca times, rather than the earliest phase. Their construction dates remain a research question, so they should not all be assigned one birthday.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Nasca potters applied colored slips before firing, making decoration more durable than earlier post-fired paint. This allowed rich colors and intricate designs to become part of the pot’s surface. Even a beautiful bowl still had to survive its trip through the fire.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: A bottle dated 1 to 400 CE shows hummingbirds feeding from flowers painted at the bases of its two spouts. Artists worked the vessel’s shape into the scene. Nasca pottery depicts many plants and animals, including more than twenty kinds of birds.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Pigments, brushes and polishing tools found at Cahuachi preserve traces of ceramic production. Elaborate bottles accompanied feasts, processions and offerings there. The artists’ skill helped make public gatherings visually memorable as well as socially important.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: A Nasca vessel depicts a procession of finely dressed people playing panpipes, accompanied by dogs and carrying parrots. The scene offers a lively glimpse of performance and valued birds. It records an artistic representation, rather than the exact sound of a surviving song.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Geoglyph makers removed dark weathered stones to expose a lighter surface underneath. They created animal figures, spirals, rectangles and very long straight lines. The desert itself became the drawing surface, using straightforward techniques on an extraordinary scale.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: The Nasca to Palpa drawings accumulated over many generations, including a Paracas phase before classic Nasca. Some broad tracks could accommodate groups of people. Archaeologists connect the landscape with ritual activity, while the precise purpose of every figure remains unresolved.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Plant evidence from the lower Ica Valley suggests that clearing huarango woodland for fields made irrigation and soils more vulnerable to major floods. The trees had supplied food, fuel and protection for the valley floor. This is a local environmental history, not a complete explanation for every Nasca community.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: No securely readable Nasca inscription supplies an original-language sentence and translation. Painted beings and geoglyphs communicated ideas visually, but recognizing a hummingbird is different from reading words. Their spoken language cannot simply be recovered by treating each picture as an alphabet letter.

The decline of Cahuachi’s regional ceremonial influence brought reorganization rather than the disappearance of all Nasca people. Excavations at Late Nasca Cocahuischo reveal communities maintaining and changing their traditions. Wari influence later helped reshape the region. The map’s 600 CE cutoff is earlier than the end of the usual Late Nasca chronology, around 750 CE.

sectionTitles: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
A prince’s letters and a changed world

passages.text: The Ndebele kingdom developed in what is now Zimbabwe under Mzilikazi and his successor Lobengula. It incorporated people of different origins into a powerful regional state. This record concerns northern Ndebele history, rather than every community elsewhere bearing the Ndebele name.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: Mzilikazi left Zululand in 1822 and built a new state through migration, warfare and incorporation of other communities. By about 1840 it was established in the Zimbabwe region. The kingdom’s population was therefore more varied than a single royal genealogy suggests.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: Lobengula founded Old Bulawayo in 1870, then left it in 1881 for a new capital near the present city. The old settlement was burned. The move means that an account simply saying “Bulawayo” needs a date before it can be placed accurately.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: The Old Bulawayo heritage site includes the Indaba tree, associated with public affairs, and the location of a Jesuit mission. These features put discussion and religious encounters beside royal residences in the landscape of a capital.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: A museum reconstruction made in 1998 included eight beehive-shaped houses, the king’s residence, a wagon shed, palisade and cattle enclosure. These were modern reconstructions of a historical settlement; a destructive fire in 2010 became another chapter in the site’s history.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Research on Old Bulawayo pottery draws on comparison with Ndebele potters and household practice. Vessel shapes can suggest different jobs, but the comparison must be tested against excavated remains. A broken pot is useful evidence precisely because researchers ask how it was actually used.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: The comparative research describes imbiza vessels used in cooking porridge and preparing beer. Other vessels are associated with serving beer and ceremonies. A family’s pottery collection could therefore connect everyday food preparation with larger gatherings and ritual obligations.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Soot can help investigators recognize cooking pots, but it can also hide decoration. Archaeologists must look past a vessel’s dirty surface to understand both use and design. The washing-up that nobody finished can become a clue centuries later.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Aberdeen’s museum preserves a wooden straining spoon catalogued as Matabele. It is only 22.7 centimetres long, a kitchen-sized object rather than royal regalia. Its exact manufacture date is unrecorded, so it offers material context without being assigned to a particular year of Lobengula’s reign.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: After conquest, Lobengula’s son Njube was educated at Zonnebloem in Cape Town. Colonial authorities resisted his return because of his political significance. Schooling in this case also separated a young man from home and placed limits on his freedom to travel.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: Njube’s 1898 letters ask for money for books and mention debt from tram travel. These details show a student managing very ordinary expenses while living through extraordinary political upheaval. A royal family’s history can include a troublesome transport bill.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: His 14 October 1898 English letter includes: “Will you please let me go Home fore Holiday”. In modern spelling, he asks permission to go home for a holiday. This is his attested written voice, including “fore”; it is not offered as an isiNdebele-language sample.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: The British South Africa Company’s 1893 campaign was a war of conquest. Historian Paul Gundani examines how supporters used religious and moral arguments to justify it. Reading those arguments critically helps distinguish claims made by invaders from the consequences for the people they defeated.

The kingdom lost its independence in the British South Africa Company’s conquest of 1893. Ndebele people and language continued beyond that defeat. The imported map interval extending to 1914 should not be read as another twenty-one years of independent royal government.

sectionTitles: Conquest and lives beyond the court

passages.text: Ndongo was a kingdom in the Kimbundu-speaking region of present-day Angola. Its ruler, the Ngola, held authority through relationships with local polities. Its political history cannot be reduced to a fixed territory ruled uniformly from one capital.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: The Kwanza corridor connected farming, pastoralism, iron production and salt supplies with trading settlements. Angola’s heritage account places this exchange before Portuguese conquest. Food and working materials circulated alongside the later expansion of captive trading.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: Kabasa, also written Cabaça, was both a royal centre and an important market. Other fairs operated under royal officers. Markets supplied neighbouring communities and linked more distant places, making their regulation a practical part of government.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: River navigation linked parts of the interior with coastal exchange. The Kwanza had both navigable stretches and obstacles; overland paths and scattered markets also mattered. The trading landscape was a network of different routes, not one uninterrupted river highway.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Local sobas governed smaller polities that entered the king’s orbit through conquest or agreement. Thornton describes expansion as incorporation of these units. Their own rulers remained important, helping explain why alliances could shift during wars with the Portuguese.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Jesuit accounts from the 1580s recorded hundreds of local political units. Thornton treats the unusually precise reported count as possible evidence of fiscal knowledge gained at court. It is testimony about administration, not a modern census independently confirmed for every settlement.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Kijiko were unfree people who could hold revenue-collecting roles. Capturing them disrupted Ndongo’s administration. Fonseca stresses that Portuguese translations as “slaves” can conceal these particular functions.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: At Kindonga, Njinga’s supporters stored food and weapons on Kwanza islands. Their knowledge of branching channels helped them avoid pursuing forces. Geography, provisioning and local experience worked together in resistance.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: A lunga, a double metal bell, marked authority in a military camp. Fonseca describes a demand that Njinga surrender hers when seeking an ally’s protection, linking a tangible object with a political negotiation.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Njinga offered refuge to people escaping enslavement and recruited African soldiers trained in Portuguese service. This brought people with different experiences into her following. Protection and military organisation helped rebuild power after displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Resistance to Portuguese conquest did not mean opposition to all enslavement. From Matamba, Njinga exchanged captives for Dutch support and firearms. Her alliances could protect followers while harming those captured as enemies.

passages.title: Conquest and lives beyond the court
passages.text: After Pungo Andongo fell in 1671, members of the royal family were deported to Brazil and later Portugal. Lara follows these exiles through Atlantic records. The kingdom’s defeat continued in the displacement of identifiable people, beyond the battlefield itself.

Portuguese forces captured Pungo Andongo in 1671 after a siege, killing its ruler and ending that royal centre’s resistance. Njinga had died in Matamba in 1663. These separate events should not be collapsed into one ruler’s defeat or the disappearance of Mbundu communities.

sectionTitles: The map label crosses a revolution
Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question

passages.text: This “Netherlands” map label covers roughly 1715 to 1800, not a single unchanged state. The Dutch Republic governed the northern provinces until 1795. William IV became stadtholder in 1747, a war with Britain strained the republic after 1780, and Dutch Patriots aided by France established the Batavian Republic in 1795. Portraits, decorated homes, guild manuals and school scenes show some lives, while poor sanitation and smallpox show common risks. Dutch overseas companies and plantations brought goods and profits through conquest and enslaved labor. The 1800 endpoint belongs to this imported map record; the Netherlands did not vanish then.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: For most of this map’s 1715 to 1800 span, the northern Netherlands was a republic of provinces, not a modern unified kingdom. The States General handled shared matters while provincial power remained important.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: In 1747 William IV became stadtholder across the republic’s provinces. It was still called a republic, but the Orange family’s office grew more dynastic. Families could disagree strongly about whether that was good government.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: The war with Britain from 1780 to 1784 battered the Dutch navy, trade and finances. Patriots blamed the old leadership and pushed for more political voice; some were forced into exile before returning with French support.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: In January 1795 the old republic gave way to the Batavian Republic. A national assembly met in 1796; a constitution followed in 1798. This is the era’s main political break, not the map’s round-number endpoint in 1800.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: A 1798 draft constitution said “Alle menschen zijn, als menschen, aan elkander gelijk,” or “All people, as people, are equal to one another.” It is original Dutch writing, though its promised equality did not include women or enslaved people.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: The Rijksmuseum’s eighteenth-century rooms show how wealthy families invested in decorated houses and portraits. A canal-house parlor could be dazzling, but it should not be mistaken for every Dutch child’s home.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: An eighteenth-century schoolroom print shows a teacher checking a girl’s work while a boy writes, and the teacher holds a paddle. It shows that children could learn, and that classroom discipline might be less charming than the picture.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: An Amsterdam silversmith printed a detailed how-to book in 1721 and sold it through his guild. Learning a craft could involve reading instructions as well as watching and practicing, though such access varied by trade and family.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: Museum collections show musicians, shopkeepers and families as well as grand merchants. Portraits record a particular person’s resources and choices; they are clues to social life, not a fair survey of a whole population.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: The VOC brought pepper, tea, coffee, textiles and porcelain from Asia, backed by soldiers and authority to wage war. A cup of tea in a Dutch home could connect to a much harsher story abroad.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Dutch plantations in Suriname produced sugar and other crops through the forced labor of enslaved Africans. People who escaped slavery formed Maroon communities and fought and negotiated for freedom. Profits in Europe hid those lives.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: War and company debts brought the VOC close to collapse; its charter ended on 1 January 1800. The people and territories under Dutch rule did not gain freedom simply because the company’s paperwork ended.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Crowded Dutch towns struggled with waste and unsafe water. Some Amsterdam canal houses had cesspits; poorer households might use a bucket or tub as a toilet. Emptying it was a daily chore, and waste could end up in a canal.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Smallpox was a grave threat to Amsterdam children in the eighteenth century. Cowpox vaccination arrived in Amsterdam around 1800, at the edge of this map span, and uptake differed by class. Medicine offered hope but not an instant rescue for everyone.

The old Dutch Republic ended in 1795 and the Batavian Republic carried political reform into the next century. The imported Netherlands record stops at 1800, but the land, people and new state continued. Dutch colonial rule and enslavement continued beyond that map endpoint as well.

passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Dutch engineers and designers experimented with ways to manage water and domestic space. This chapter pairs a steam pumping station with an adaptable family home.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda pumping station opened at Lemmer in 1920 to help prevent flooding in low-lying Friesland, using steam power to move water.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda installation integrated a boiler house, chimney, fuel storage, drainage canal and sluices. Water management required an entire connected system.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Truus Schroder-Schrader commissioned the house designed by Gerrit Rietveld in Utrecht in 1924. Its design expressed ideas associated with De Stijl.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Schroder House used a flexible internal arrangement so rooms could change with their functions. Furniture and interior space were treated as parts of one design.

passages.text: Aotearoa New Zealand's history includes Māori settlement and innovation, colonization, campaigns for rights and the development of a modern state. Archaeological remains, carved buildings, petitions and homes reveal both achievement and unequal power. Constitutional independence developed through several steps; no single change of title explains the whole story.

passages.title: Early settlement seen through archaeology
passages.text: Research places Polynesian settlement of Aotearoa around 1300 CE. At Wairau Bar, evidence extends beyond burials to structures, cooking and stone-tool production. A large stone-lined oven and animal remains help reconstruct village activities during an early phase of Māori history.

passages.title: Early settlement seen through archaeology
passages.text: The 2009 Wairau Bar research followed an invitation from Rangitāne mana whenua alongside the return and reburial of ancestral remains. Geophysical survey and excavation examined the wider settlement. The history of research therefore includes community authority and relationships, as well as what was found.

passages.title: Carving, architecture and colonial loss
passages.text: Raharuhi Rukupō began Te Hau-ki-Tūranga at Manutūkē in 1842 as a memorial to his elder brother. Expert carvers worked on its posts and structure. Rukupō learned inherited techniques and later adopted steel tools, showing innovation within an established artistic tradition.

passages.title: Carving, architecture and colonial loss
passages.text: The government had Te Hau-ki-Tūranga dismantled and removed in 1867 during the confiscation of Tūranga lands. Payments went to people later found not to be its owners. Its subsequent museum display must therefore be understood alongside the coercive circumstances of removal.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: Te Tiriti o Waitangi and its English counterpart were signed in 1840, but their terms concerning authority differ. The Māori text uses kāwanatanga and guarantees tino rangatiratanga; the English text speaks of sovereignty. Those differences matter when interpreting what rangatira and the Crown understood they had agreed.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: The surviving 1893 women's suffrage petition consists of sheets gathered across the country and pasted into a roll by Kate Sheppard. Its physical form records collective organizing through meetings, travel and persuasion, not only the actions of a single prominent campaigner.

passages.title: Documents, authority and the vote
passages.text: The Electoral Act signed on 19 September 1893 gave women the parliamentary vote. Earlier petition campaigns had failed in the Legislative Council. The successful reform followed repeated organizing and political struggle rather than a sudden, unopposed concession.

passages.title: Technology, food and work
passages.text: The sailing ship Dunedin carried a successful frozen-meat shipment to Britain in 1882 using a coal-powered freezing plant. Meat from Totara Estate moved by rail to Port Chalmers before freezing aboard. The achievement depended on an organized chain of workers, transport and temperature control.

passages.title: Technology, food and work
passages.text: Refrigerated shipping needed marketing and insurance arrangements as well as machinery. Its growth supported meat and dairy exports and reshaped farming. This was an application and organization of refrigeration technology, not evidence that refrigeration itself was invented in New Zealand.

passages.title: Homes and ordinary lives
passages.text: The house at 12 Fife Lane in Miramar opened in 1937 as the first of the Labour government's new state houses. Photographs of the opening made it a public symbol, but for David and Mary McGregor it was also a family home entered by crowds of visitors.

passages.title: Homes and ordinary lives
passages.text: David McGregor worked as a tram driver. The family initially paid rent and later bought the house under a changed policy. Following one household links a national housing program with wages, tenure and the practical wish for a secure place to live.

passages.title: Scientific work across borders
passages.text: Born and educated in New Zealand, Ernest Rutherford developed the nuclear model of the atom in 1911 while working in Manchester. Scattering experiments involving Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden helped establish a small central nucleus. His achievement belongs to an international research setting, not an isolated national invention.

passages.title: Changing constitutional relationships
passages.text: New Zealand adopted the Statute of Westminster on 25 November 1947. The Constitution Act 1986 later removed the remaining provision for British legislation. These milestones show a gradual change in the state's relationship with Britain, rather than an independence date inferred from a map boundary.

New Zealand continues as a state. Its relationship with Britain changed through dominion status, the 1947 statute adoption and later constitutional reform. Māori communities and authority have their own continuing histories, including the unresolved consequences of colonial land loss and differing understandings of Te Tiriti.

sectionTitles: River travel, food and adaptable homes
Teaching, writing and bringing fish back

passages.text: The Nimiipuu, commonly called Nez Perce, built influential networks of villages, fishing places and travel routes across the interior Pacific Northwest. Their homeland includes parts of present-day Idaho, Oregon and Washington. The two imported outlines are rough regional footprints, and their 1492 and 1500 starting dates do not mark the people’s beginning. Nimiipuu communities continue today.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: Leaders did not all have the same job. The Tribe’s history describes separate expertise in fishing, hunting, warfare and religion, with councils guiding decisions. Knowledge and skill mattered when communities chose leaders. Political life grew from the work people needed to do together.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: River benches provided level places for villages. People caught salmon through much of the warmer season and dried fish for winter. Canoes made by burning and chipping logs connected settlements and trading partners. A river could serve as pantry, road and meeting place at once.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: Horses reached Nez Perce communities in the early eighteenth century and expanded travel for hunting, including journeys for bison. This added new possibilities to an older river-based economy. The canoe did not suddenly become useless when someone acquired a horse.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: Camas gathering rewarded patience: leaving small bulbs underground helped provide another harvest. At Weippe Prairie in September 1805, visiting expedition members saw families digging, cleaning and preparing bulbs. Earthen kilns cooked the food, which could then become bread and other meals.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: Expedition member Patrick Gass thought camas bread tasted rather like pumpkin bread. The guests kept accepting so much food that Nez Perce leaders eventually asked them to pay for more. Hospitality had limits, even for travelers with a very large appetite.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: Tule stems contain spongy, air-filled tissue. Woven into mats, they insulated homes, swelled in wet weather to keep rain out, and shrank in dry weather to allow ventilation. Lightweight mats could be rolled up for moving camp: the walls could travel with the household.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: The same mat-making skills furnished sleeping surfaces, room dividers and places to dry food. Sedges supplied cordage with little preparation beyond drying. Such plant technologies turned riverbank materials into a whole household toolkit, including ways to organize space and preserve the harvest.

passages.title: River travel, food and adaptable homes
passages.text: A cradleboard in the park museum, dated about 1900, combines a wooden support, soft buckskin and a velveteen hood. Its label describes grandmothers, mothers, aunts and older sisters carrying children. This object makes family care visible alongside the better-known stories of chiefs and battles.

passages.title: Treaties, war and enduring relationships
passages.text: Gold discovered inside the reservation in 1860 brought newcomers onto protected land. The 1863 treaty proposed a drastic reduction of the reservation. Bands whose homes lay outside the new boundary refused to sign. The United States nevertheless ratified the document, creating a dangerous gap between its demands and those communities’ consent.

passages.title: Treaties, war and enduring relationships
passages.text: In 1877, several non-treaty bands fled the United States Army with families and horses. Their journey lasted 126 days and covered more than 1,170 miles. The attack at Big Hole killed children and other civilians as well as warriors. The final siege at Bear Paw ended in October.

passages.title: Treaties, war and enduring relationships
passages.text: Some families escaped into Canada; others were sent through Kansas into Indian Territory. In 1885, survivors were finally allowed back to the Northwest, but Joseph’s band was placed on the Colville Reservation rather than returned to Wallowa. Exile separated relatives long after the fighting ended.

passages.title: Teaching, writing and bringing fish back
passages.text: Ida Blackeagle learned cornhusk weaving at twelve and later taught at Lapwai High School. In 1966, she and Viola Morris became park cultural demonstrators. Their teaching carried craft knowledge between generations. Cornhusks themselves had become an important substitute when nineteenth-century restrictions limited access to older basket materials.

passages.title: Teaching, writing and bringing fish back
passages.text: The Tribe’s language page prints “’íin ’eekíce poxpok’láana” with the translation “I see a ball”. This modern teaching sentence uses a spelling system approved by an advisory board of Elders. The page explains that ordinary Nimipuutimt sentences use lowercase letters, so the small initial letter is intentional.

passages.title: Teaching, writing and bringing fish back
passages.text: In 1994, the Tribe obtained coho salmon eggs that otherwise faced disposal and began a restoration effort. Tribal fisheries staff raised and released young fish to rebuild a vanished run. A tribal commission account explains how biological work depended on treaty rights, negotiations and funding as well as hatchery tanks.

The imported map cutoffs do not end Nimiipuu history. The 1877 war and exile transformed lives, but communities continue in Idaho, Washington, Oregon, Canada and elsewhere, connected by family relationships and cultural work.

sectionTitles: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers

passages.text: Ngarrindjeri communities connect the lower Murray, lakes, Coorong and Sea Country through law, kinship, food and cultural responsibility. Fishing technology, feather flowers and David Unaipon's papers reveal skill and invention in different settings. Their history continues through dispossession, environmental disruption, community teaching and public advocacy.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: The community's Sea Country Plan describes Tendi as a council that makes and interprets Ngarrindjeri law. Ngartji relationships with particular animals and plants bring obligations to care for them and their habitats.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: Fish, shellfish, waterbirds and plants supported settled life and gatherings. Nets made from bulrush fibers, bone or shell hooks, stone traps and woven weirs show different ways of working with water and animal behavior.

passages.title: Water, food and institutions
passages.text: Bark canoes, reed rafts and floating platforms supported work on the water. Food storage and smoke-drying fish helped supply gatherings and exchange with neighboring communities. These practices joined making, preservation and social relationships.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: A bouquet made at Point McLeay in the 1920s, now in the National Museum of Australia, uses feathers from pelicans and other Coorong birds. Makers drew dye from crepe paper soaked in water, then colored the feathers. The object records skilled adaptation of available materials.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: The Point McLeay mission began in 1859 on land too small for the families moved there. Ngarrindjeri people developed fishing, boat making, wool washing, weaving and other enterprises. Feather flowers provided income while also carrying ecological and artistic knowledge.

passages.title: Feather flowers, work and environmental knowledge
passages.text: Changes to river flows and wetlands affect materials as well as food. The museum account describes freshwater sedges used in weaving becoming scarcer. Maintaining a craft therefore also depends on the health and accessibility of the places that supply it.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: Patent 15624, dated 3 September 1909, records David Unaipon's improved mechanical motion device. Applied to sheep shearing, it converted rotary movement into straight-line motion. The patent and accompanying diagrams provide a specific record of an inventor working on an industrial problem.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: In an April 1914 letter to Herbert Basedow, Unaipon asked for financial help to develop his machine. A following memorandum offered conditional government assistance. These papers reveal the difficulty of obtaining support; a patent alone does not demonstrate profitable manufacture.

passages.title: David Unaipon: invention and the surviving papers
passages.text: Unaipon also collected and wrote stories. Material from his manuscript appeared under William Ramsay Smith's name in 1930. Work with Unaipon's descendants later restored his authorship in the 2001 publication of Legendary Tales of the Australian Aborigines.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: Elder Ellen Trevorrow teaches weaving and cultural storytelling at Camp Coorong. Her work connects the making of baskets and sculpture with learning across generations. Participants learn through shared activity and conversation as well as looking at finished objects.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: Camp Coorong activities also include walks with Elders to learn about animals, food plants and Country. Such teaching connects practical knowledge with the responsibility to understand and care for the places where it is used.

passages.title: Teaching and cultural continuity
passages.text: The Sea Country Plan describes colonial land loss and mission pressure on language and belief. Its response is continuing Ngarrindjeri participation in decisions about land and waters, with cultural responsibilities informing future management.

Ngarrindjeri people and cultural life continue. Dispossession and changes to rivers and wetlands damaged livelihoods and access to Country, but Raukkan, Camp Coorong and living artistic practices show continuing community history. There is no single fall year or successor state that describes that experience.

sectionTitles: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital
Learning, women’s leadership and written words

passages.text: The Bangwato state was an influential Tswana polity in what is now Botswana. Under Khama III, diplomacy helped defend it against takeover by Cecil Rhodes’s company, while British protectorate rule constrained its independence. This map shows only part of a longer history of changing capitals and continuing communities.

passages.title: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital
passages.text: In 1895, Khama III travelled to Britain with Sebele I and Bathoen I to oppose Rhodes’s expansion. Meetings and public campaigning helped keep their territories out of his company’s hands. The achievement preserved room for local rule, although the British protectorate remained a colonial arrangement.

passages.title: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital
passages.text: Khama linked political authority closely to his Christian church. His correspondence shows that religious affiliation could affect permission to settle in his territory, and temperance rules were enforced through both church and chiefly power. His resistance to outside domination coexisted with restrictions on his own subjects.

passages.title: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital
passages.text: Water helped decide where the capital stood. In 1900, a traveller reported women drawing water from deep wells in the Lotsane riverbed and paying grain for each pot. The move to Serowe in 1902 followed years of shortages, negotiations and population movements.

passages.title: Diplomacy, authority and a moving capital
passages.text: Drought and failed harvests were followed by rinderpest in 1896, killing most cattle. That was a household disaster as well as an economic one: livestock, crops and available water all came under pressure together.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shoes
passages.text: Daily work linked the homestead, arable fields and cattle post. Women generally maintained homes and did much farming, while men and boys worked with cattle. Photographs taken around 1895 at Palapye show women thatching roofs and pounding maize: a busy household required far more than a roof overhead.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shoes
passages.text: Three surviving tools make those activities tangible: a food-storage basket, an iron hoe for cultivation and weeding, and a multipurpose knife used at cattle posts. Museum researchers connect them to different working places rather than treating them as anonymous ornaments.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shoes
passages.text: A wooden spoon collected in the 1890s is almost a metre long. It served communal cooking in large pots. This was serious stirring equipment: slipping it into a lunchbox would have been an ambitious plan.

passages.title: Homes, meals and shoes
passages.text: One pair of 1890s sandals was made from the soft forehead skin of a cow. The collection also records clothing made from both leather and woven fabric. Skilled leatherworkers adapted familiar materials while tastes and available goods changed.

passages.title: Learning, women’s leadership and written words
passages.text: Church schools opened new opportunities, but education remained unequal. Museum researchers note that girls often attended while boys worked at cattle posts, yet lessons channelled girls toward domestic subjects. School could widen a child’s possibilities and reinforce expectations about their future work at the same time.

passages.title: Learning, women’s leadership and written words
passages.text: Semane Setlhoko Khama was a teacher before becoming Khama’s wife in 1900. She supported women teachers and girls’ schooling, and later, under Tshekedi’s regency, promoted midwifery and medicine. Her work places education and children’s health alongside diplomacy in the story of political leadership.

passages.title: Learning, women’s leadership and written words
passages.text: “a re tshwarisane” means “let us work hard hand in hand” in the published translation of Khama’s Setswana letter dated 12 February 1923. He was discussing support for teachers. This attested phrase comes from correspondence after the map’s endpoint, showing that local writing and government continued.

passages.title: Learning, women’s leadership and written words
passages.text: In 2026, artefacts taken overseas during Khama’s reign returned to the Khama III Memorial Museum in Serowe. Their unveiling brought household objects, clothing and community memories back together. History here is also something living communities preserve and interpret for themselves.

The imported record ends in 1914, but Khama III lived and ruled until 1923. The Bangwato community, its leadership and its cultural institutions continued through later political changes. The museum in Serowe now preserves objects and memories from this longer history.

passages.text: Nicaragua became separate from the Central American federation in 1838. Its history includes poetry, community performance, monetary change and ambitious education projects, alongside dictatorship, revolution and repression. The map’s 1878 beginning is a coverage date, not the country’s founding.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: Nicaragua issued decimal one-centavo coins in 1878. Before national issues became established, foreign and Central American coins circulated at legal equivalents. Buying and selling could require understanding how different pieces of money related to a common unit.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: A 1912 law adopted the córdoba, with the first new notes and coins entering circulation in 1913. Currency reform changed the objects used in everyday transactions. A banknote is a historical document that many people handled without ever visiting an archive.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: El Güegüense is performed during Diriamba’s San Sebastián festivities, combining theatre, music and dance. The text is probably rooted in the early eighteenth century, while performance continues in modern Nicaragua. The older origin and present practice should not be collapsed into one date.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: Its central character appears cooperative with colonial officials while using clever language to evade their demands. The satire makes authority look less impressive. Historical resistance can appear in jokes and verbal maneuvering as well as in open confrontation.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: Wooden masks, costumes and hats identify characters, while violins, guitars and drums accompany dancers. The performance is carried by craftspeople, musicians and actors together. Preserving the words alone would preserve only part of the tradition.

passages.title: Money, performance and written language
passages.text: “Juventud, divino tesoro, ¡ya te vas para no volver!” means “Youth, divine treasure, already you leave, never to return!” These Spanish lines open Rubén Darío’s Canción de otoño en primavera in the 1905 collection Cantos de vida y esperanza. They are attested poetry, not an invented national saying.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: During the 1980 literacy campaign, young volunteers lived in rural areas while teaching reading and writing. UNESCO’s archival description records roughly 60,000 participants and a five-month campaign. The experience brought urban learners and rural households into sustained contact.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: The campaign archive preserves letters, diaries, interviews, cassette tapes and exercise books in Spanish, Creole English, Miskito and Sumu. These materials record both teaching and personal experience. A notebook or recording can reveal a national project from closer to the classroom.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: A Mayangna project in BOSAWAS documented local names and knowledge of fish and turtles through interviews and community assemblies. These animals matter as food sources as well as subjects of classification. Knowledge included behavior, habitat, harvesting and stories.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: By 2016, collaborators had produced Mayangna and Spanish teacher manuals, workbooks, posters and fish cards for young pupils. Teachers were encouraged to involve community knowledge holders. Children could study local nature through their own language and relatives’ expertise.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: The Somoza regime collapsed in 1979, and the 1990 election brought victory for the opposition coalition led by Violeta Barrios de Chamorro. These changes altered government while Nicaragua and its communities continued. Neither event is a national extinction date.

passages.title: Learning and political change
passages.text: In 2018, an Inter-American Commission investigation documented severe violations connected with repression of protests, affecting students, journalists and human-rights defenders. This is a dated finding about state violence, which belongs alongside cultural achievements in an account of the country.

Nicaragua continues as a state. The end of Somoza rule in 1979, the 1990 electoral transition and later repression changed political life without ending the country or its Indigenous and Afro-descendant communities. The imported map interval is not a claim that Nicaragua began in 1878.

sectionTitles: Music and the art of getting along
A schoolbook that talks about toilets

passages.text: Niger became independent from France in 1960. Its modern history joins changing governments with farmers’ environmental innovations, multilingual communities and everyday efforts to improve health and education.

passages.title: A country and changing governments
passages.text: Niger became independent on 3 August 1960. It is a separate country from Nigeria, its southern neighbor. The names can look confusingly similar on a small screen, but their colonial and national histories are different.

passages.title: A country and changing governments
passages.text: Hamani Diori’s single-party government was overthrown in 1974 after devastating drought and accusations of corruption. In 1991, unions, students and political groups pressed for change through a national conference. Its debates prepared a transition toward multiparty government.

passages.title: A country and changing governments
passages.text: A military takeover in July 2023 again interrupted constitutional government. The UN country team reported that the crisis and sanctions affected development work. Political upheaval reaches beyond offices into the planning of services that families use.

passages.title: Farmers as experimenters and teachers
passages.text: Farmer Ali Malam improved his land by protecting promising shoots growing from old stumps and roots, then pruning away others. This farmer-managed regeneration let existing root systems support trees again. Sometimes a future tree is already waiting underground.

passages.title: Farmers as experimenters and teachers
passages.text: Sakina Mati used similar methods and earned money from branches, pods, bark and fruit. She formed a women’s group to discuss restoring trees. The 2018 account follows local people as innovators and teachers, with practical knowledge passed from one farm to another.

passages.title: Farmers as experimenters and teachers
passages.text: Mati and Malam shared their experiences on Radio Zumunci. At a temporary phone station in Bakabé, people queued to ask questions; the programme ran half an hour overtime. A good farming idea can travel by radio as well as by road.

passages.title: Music and the art of getting along
passages.text: Tuareg women make and play the imzad, a bowed instrument with one string. Half a dried gourd forms its body, covered with skin and fitted with a wooden bridge. The player rests it on her knees: a small instrument can carry a powerful musical voice.

passages.title: Music and the art of getting along
passages.text: Imzad performances bring music and poetry together at gatherings. Knowledge is learned through listening and watching experienced performers. The tradition belongs to communities across Niger, Mali and Algeria, whose cultural connections cross modern borders.

passages.title: Music and the art of getting along
passages.text: In recognized joking relationships, people from linked communities exchange playful teasing while accepting duties to help one another and settle disputes peacefully. The jokes depend on a relationship and shared rules; they are not a license to insult anyone at random.

passages.title: Music and the art of getting along
passages.text: UNESCO describes these exchanges at markets, water points, fields, offices, weddings and family gatherings. Humor can open a conversation across differences of age or status. Here, learning how to joke is also learning how to live with other people.

passages.title: A schoolbook that talks about toilets
passages.text: A 2009 government pupil booklet bears the French title “J’apprends l’hygiène avec Amina et Amadou”: “I learn hygiene with Amina and Amadou”. This is a short attested writing sample from an everyday educational object, rather than a royal inscription.

passages.title: A schoolbook that talks about toilets
passages.text: The booklet’s fictional children discuss water, food and keeping toilets usable. One story gives their school separate latrine blocks and a cleaning rota for girls and boys. These scenes show what the project wanted pupils to learn, not proof that every school already had those facilities.

passages.title: A schoolbook that talks about toilets
passages.text: In another illustrated episode, Moussa slips on wastewater and drops his exercise book. The lesson links a messy street with household drainage. It is an unusually memorable school warning: bad sanitation can spoil your homework before the teacher even sees it.

Niger continues as a country despite changes of government and serious pressures on livelihoods and services. Its farmers, families and cultural communities continue adapting rather than disappearing at a political turning point.

sectionTitles: A new colonial border, older peoples
Markets, reading, school and the family purse

passages.text: British administrators combined northern and southern protectorates into colonial Nigeria in 1914, joining many older societies without their consent. A tiny property-qualified electorate got a limited vote in 1922. Farmers and traders supplied cocoa, palm produce, groundnuts and cotton; women’s market networks also organized major protests. Yoruba newspapers, carving and woven cloth reveal creative life beyond colonial offices. Schools and health programmes grew unevenly. Nigeria became independent in 1960, not at the imported map’s 1938 endpoint.

passages.title: A new colonial border, older peoples
passages.text: In 1914 British rule joined the northern and southern protectorates. The new territory contained communities with much older histories, including kingdoms, emirates and towns. Amalgamation made a colonial administration; it did not invent the people.

passages.title: A new colonial border, older peoples
passages.text: The 1922 constitution offered just four elected legislative seats, three for Lagos and one for Calabar, with an income requirement that shut out most people. A small ballot box was not national self-government.

passages.title: A new colonial border, older peoples
passages.text: Colonial marketing boards bought and graded cocoa, palm produce, groundnuts and cotton. Which crop mattered to a household varied widely by region, while export prices were set in a larger imperial market.

passages.title: A new colonial border, older peoples
passages.text: Political changes in the 1950s gave regions more autonomy. On 1 October 1960 Nigeria became independent; in 1963 it adopted a republic. Neither date means all regional arguments or colonial inequalities vanished.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: In southeastern Ngwa communities women cultivated and processed palm produce, sold kernels and helped pay household bills. When tax assessment threatened their autonomy in 1929, women organized what is remembered as the Women’s War, rather than waiting for colonial officials to speak for them.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: In Abeokuta, the Women’s Union led by Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti challenged taxes and colonial-era authority in the 1940s. Food prices, trade and political rights belonged to the same household conversation.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: Lagos readers could find politics, sports, medicine advertisements, proverbs and serialized stories in Yoruba newspapers. Akede Eko was a weekly from 1928. A newspaper was both news and something to talk about with neighbors.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: “Itan Igbesi-Aiye Emi” means “The story of my life.” These original Yoruba words open the title of I. B. Thomas’s Segilola story, serialized in Akede Eko from 1929 to 1930. They show a written language and a playful, sometimes controversial popular fiction, not a colonial decree.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: The Yoruba sculptor Olowe of Ise carved extraordinary palace doors in the early twentieth century, showing a royal visit by British officials. A 1920s indigo aso oke wrap shows narrow handwoven cotton strips, silk and careful stitching. These are specific artworks, not a single national dress.

passages.title: Markets, reading, school and the family purse
passages.text: Western Nigeria began free primary schooling in 1955; Eastern Nigeria and Lagos expanded programmes in 1957. Children’s opportunities varied by region, fees, gender and available teachers, so a new school promise did not mean an identical classroom everywhere.

passages.title: Clinics, films and toilets
passages.text: Lagos health officials made mobile films in the 1930s about malaria, baby health and even building latrines. The films show that sanitation mattered, but they do not prove every household had a safe toilet. Audiences could laugh at or challenge a film as well as learn from it.

passages.title: Clinics, films and toilets
passages.text: A family’s access to a clinic, clean water or a latrine depended on town, income and colonial priorities. The government’s own health-film campaign treated these as problems needing work, not services already solved.

passages.title: Clinics, films and toilets
passages.text: Commercial oil was found at Oloibiri in 1956, just before independence. It would transform government revenue but eventually raise difficult questions about the land and water of Niger Delta communities.

On 1 October 1960 the colonial territory became an independent federal state. The republic followed in 1963. People, languages and local institutions continued across independence, while debates about federal power, resources, schooling and colonial legacies remained. The imported 1938 map endpoint is not the date Britain left.

sectionTitles: An independent country with many voices
School, screens and the family table

passages.text: Nigeria became independent from Britain in 1960 and a federal republic in 1963. Its many language communities built a shared state amid regional conflict. Coups and the Biafran war from 1967 to 1970 devastated families; elected civilian rule returned in 1999 after further military periods. Today Nollywood films, schools and community life show creative energy, while Nigerian health teams helped contain Ebola and wild polio. Oil revenues coexist with severe pollution in parts of the Niger Delta, and many households still need safe water and toilets. The republic and its people continue.

passages.title: An independent country with many voices
passages.text: Independence on 1 October 1960 created a self-governing federation. In 1963 a republican constitution replaced the British monarch as head of state. Nigeria’s state changed twice within three years; its communities were much older.

passages.title: An independent country with many voices
passages.text: After coups in 1966, the Eastern Region attempted to secede as Biafra in 1967. The war lasted to 1970 and hunger struck civilians. One child later remembered a refugee camp, donated food, medicines and a school uniform for life after the war.

passages.title: An independent country with many voices
passages.text: Nigeria had an elected civilian government from 1979 to 1983, then further military rule. Civilian presidential government returned in 1999; the new constitution says political authority belongs to the people.

passages.title: An independent country with many voices
passages.text: The country’s languages include Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba, English and hundreds of others. A child can hear one language at home, another at school and a third in a film or market. Language policy aims to support this diversity, although practice varies.

passages.title: An independent country with many voices
passages.text: The 1999 constitution begins “We, the people of the Federal Republic of Nigeria.” This short original English sample is from a governing document. Its words promise popular authority; citizens still debate how fully institutions deliver that promise.

passages.title: School, screens and the family table
passages.text: Regional free-primary-school efforts began before independence; the federal Universal Basic Education programme followed in 1999. Whether a child can attend regularly still depends on teachers, distance, safety and family resources.

passages.title: School, screens and the family table
passages.text: Nollywood grew into a huge film industry, with an estimated 2,500 films a year around 2021. Families may watch a story on a phone or television, then argue about its characters as enthusiastically as any film critic. This is an example of popular culture, not what every household watches.

passages.title: School, screens and the family table
passages.text: The Nigerian language policy names several widely used languages and calls for translation and public use beyond English. That matters when a parent tries to understand a school notice, health message or ballot information.

passages.title: School, screens and the family table
passages.text: Oil became a major industry after the 1956 Oloibiri discovery. In Ogoniland, a 2011 UN assessment found long-term oil pollution of land and drinking water. A government revenue statistic cannot tell a family whether the nearest well is safe.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: In 2014 Nigerian health workers traced contacts, informed communities through local radio and contained an imported Ebola outbreak. WHO declared that outbreak over in October. It took a team, not a miracle.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: Vaccination and surveillance helped Nigeria and the African region gain wild-polio-free certification in 2020. This does not mean every form of polio or every childhood health problem vanished; health workers keep checking and vaccinating.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: A 2021 national water-and-sanitation survey estimated about 48 million Nigerians still practiced open defecation. A toilet needs safe design, water or maintenance, privacy and a way to wash hands; the answer varies greatly by community.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: In parts of the Niger Delta, oil pollution threatens water used for drinking and farming. In some other places, sanitation access is the more immediate challenge. Either way, clean water is part of health, family work and dignity.

Nigeria continues as a federal republic. Independence, a new constitution, military interruptions and the return to civilian rule changed its institutions; none ended its older communities or languages. Families continue to build livelihoods, schools, art and healthier neighborhoods while arguing over the country’s future.

passages.text: Blackfoot peoples have homelands on the northern Plains across today’s Canada to United States border. The confederacy includes distinct nations with related languages and histories. Its two imported outlines are broad approximations, not fixed borders or proof of one centrally ruled empire.

passages.title: Nations and a hunting landscape
passages.text: The present Blackfoot Confederacy brings together Siksika, Kainai, northern Piikani and Aamskapi Pikuni, the Blackfeet Nation in Montana. Related identity does not erase their separate governments. The international border cuts across relationships with a homeland older than either modern country.

passages.title: Nations and a hunting landscape
passages.text: At Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Alberta, stone cairns mark lanes that channelled bison toward a cliff. Layers of bones below and camps nearby preserve repeated communal hunts over millennia. Success depended on coordinated people, local geography and knowledge of the animals’ movements.

passages.title: Nations and a hunting landscape
passages.text: The camps below the jump were places for cutting up animals and preparing food, hides and other materials. The archaeological landscape therefore records far more than the dramatic moment at the cliff: processing a large hunt meant a great deal of shared work afterward.

passages.title: A home that could travel
passages.text: Blackfoot Crossing’s Siksika account describes women as owners and caretakers of tipis. The central fire, bedding, containers and utensils had their places within the shelter. A portable home still required planning, maintenance and rules about how space was used.

passages.title: A home that could travel
passages.text: Buffalo-hide covers and wooden poles could travel with a family. Poles were arranged into a travois to carry possessions, first pulled by dogs and later by horses. Larger animals could carry larger loads, helping change the scale of a household’s travelling equipment.

passages.title: A home that could travel
passages.text: Stones once used to hold tipi covers down can survive as rings after the shelters themselves are gone. The park’s account distinguishes those rings from later use of pegs. A circle of ordinary stones may be the trace of a room where people once slept and talked.

passages.title: A home that could travel
passages.text: The Siksika account describes cooking in a rawhide-lined pit by adding heated stones to water. Heat moved from the fire into the container through the stones. The cooking vessel did not have to sit directly over a flame to make soup.

passages.title: A home that could travel
passages.text: A short modern written sample is “Niitsitapi”, translated by Blackfoot Crossing as “the Real People”. This spelling comes from a Siksika cultural source using Latin letters. It identifies a living people; the painted designs on tipis are not simply an alphabet spelling the word.

passages.title: Agreements, schools and endurance
passages.text: Treaty 7 was negotiated at Blackfoot Crossing in 1877. The Canadian Museum of History explains that First Nations approached treaties as agreements for peace and mutual support, while Canada sought land for settlement. Oral understandings and the written document did not neatly coincide.

passages.title: Agreements, schools and endurance
passages.text: A silver medal now in the Canadian Museum of History was presented to a Blackfoot delegate during those negotiations. Its clasped-hands image and 1877 inscription provide a surviving object from diplomacy whose promises remain important to the nations involved.

passages.title: Agreements, schools and endurance
passages.text: The surviving Old Sun school building on Siksika lands served a residential-school system that separated children from family life. University of Calgary documentation records survivors’ loneliness, including children who could see home from school yet could not freely return to their families.

passages.title: Agreements, schools and endurance
passages.text: Old Sun became an adult-learning facility in 1971 and an independent community college in 1978. The Siksika-led college now includes Siksika Knowledge courses as well as accredited programmes. Transforming the building’s purpose has made education a means of community direction and renewal.

The Blackfoot nations continue on both sides of the border. Loss of bison, colonial control and schooling policies caused profound harm, but no 1783 “fall” ended the people. Their own governments, cultural institutions and relationships with the land carry the history forward.
