passages.text: The Orange Free State was a white-ruled republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Bloemfontein became its administrative centre, while the struggle over land drew Basotho and other African communities into conflict with the settler state. Its imported map interval also covers later British rule.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: Britain recognized the new republic at the Bloemfontein Convention in 1854 without consulting African chiefdoms. The agreement did not settle the frontier with Moshoeshoe’s Basotho kingdom. Political recognition on paper therefore left fundamental disputes over who possessed the land.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: The Free State’s expansion cost Basotho communities much fertile land. Conflict concerned fields, grazing and livestock, not an empty strip between two colored shapes. Basotho farming and political life continued beyond the republic’s borders and within the wider region.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: The First Raadsaal began in 1849 as a school and also served as a church. In 1854 it became the republic’s assembly hall and offices. A building could host lessons, worship and government in succession: the rooms did not insist on just one career.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: When the assembly moved to larger premises in 1856, the old building returned to schooling until 1877. Today it is restored as a museum. Its changing uses provide evidence for the institutions of a growing town without making its present display an untouched classroom.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Before a piped supply, Bloemfontein households and businesses relied on streams, fountains, wells, dams and boreholes. Water had to be carried in buckets. A drink, a wash and cooking a meal all began with somebody moving a heavy load.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Water shortages became critical in 1894. The Modder River scheme, approved in 1896, brought water to town in 1899 through pumping facilities and pipes around Naval Hill. This changed urban infrastructure, though the account does not show every home receiving equal service.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Freshford House, completed in 1897, preserves the setting of an affluent Bloemfontein household. Red brick walls, bay windows, a carved wooden veranda and cast-iron details show the materials and decorative choices of this home. Its comfort should not stand in for the lives of the town’s poorer residents.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Bloemfontein’s Wagon Museum holds ox wagons, transport wagons, a stagecoach, mule wagons and smaller carts. These different vehicles remind us that carrying freight and carrying passengers presented different problems. The collection also discusses transport used by Black people in the early twentieth century.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Earlier ox wagons could slow down with metal skidpans chained beneath their rear wheels. The wheels stopped turning while the shoes dragged along the ground. It was an effective answer to a very serious downhill question: how do you persuade a loaded wagon to stop?

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: A Dutch phrase from the 1893 pass law is “verblijf brief”, meaning “residential pass”. The law required Black location residents over sixteen, women as well as men, to carry one. This small writing sample came from paperwork that could determine whether somebody was arrested.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: Contemporary newspapers reported police raids in Waaihoek, including arrests of residents without passes. One resident complained about officers entering houses and dragging out older women. These accounts restore African households to a city history too easily told only through presidents and public buildings.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: The National Museum was founded in 1877 and opened in 1878. Its first honorary curator, Hugh Exton, sought public donations, and collections grew until the old Raadsaal needed extensions. Collecting natural and human history became another form of organized learning in the republic.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: During the South African War, British scorched-earth operations destroyed farms, and camps imprisoned Boer families and Black civilians. Poor food, water and sanitation caused terrible suffering. The Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902 ended the war, after Britain had already proclaimed annexation in 1900.

The independent republic was defeated in the war ending in 1902. Its territory became the Orange River Colony, which joined the Union of South Africa in 1910. The peoples and settlements continued; the map record’s 1914 endpoint does not extend republican independence to that date.

passages.text: Oromo communities transformed the Horn of Africa through migration, farming, herding, commerce and varied forms of government. This broad map label is not one empire: Gadaa institutions and later Gibe kingdoms represent different political histories. The imported southern outline cannot show the full distribution of Oromo people.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Historian Mohammed Hassen places Oromo expansion within the wider sixteenth-century wars that weakened neighboring Christian and Muslim states. Migration involved settlement and new alliances as well as fighting; it was not a single army following one permanent ruler.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Gibe rulers benefited from customs duties and gifts carried along organized caravan routes. Products moved north through Gojjam and east through Shawa; commerce connected the kingdoms with much larger networks.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: The Gibe kingdoms also became important centers of Islamic study. Their combination of agriculture, commerce and scholarship reminds us that Oromo history includes towns and classrooms as well as cattle and migration.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Cooperation across political boundaries could restore trade. Ishikawa’s study of the Gondar period finds that migrant communities south of Lake Tana worked with Oromo groups south of the Blue Nile, helping revive long-distance exchange.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: In UNESCO’s account of living Gadaa institutions, five classes take turns in authority, with leadership changing every eight years. A governing class includes a chairperson, officials and an assembly. Power comes with a timetable, not an automatic lifetime appointment.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: Participation is structured by gender and family. Men enter classes to which their fathers belong; women are consulted on decisions protecting women’s rights. Calling this a democratic tradition should not hide these particular rules of membership.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: Oral historians teach law, history, calendars, ritual and conduct. Meetings may gather under a sycamore tree, while children learn at home and school. A tree can shade a serious political classroom without needing a blackboard.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: Borana communities, one part of the Oromo world, manage ancient tula wells in southern Ethiopia. Research published in 2011 traced a system operating for more than five centuries. Its survival depends on customary rules, repairs and surrounding grazing land, not just a hole in the ground.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: A 1994 research synthesis describes chains of workers passing buckets up deep well shafts, then onward to livestock troughs. Other people regulate the queue, clear manure and repair clay troughs. Getting cattle a drink can require an entire shift of water engineers.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: In the same research, Borana women rotated market duty: one carried dairy products to sell for her friends. Sharing the journey saved other households a long walk and left time for their own demanding work.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: In the same late twentieth-century research, a gorfa milk container was woven from asparagus-root fibers, smoked inside, then used for souring and churning milk. A golondi was carved from wood and carried by herders. Clever containers served different jobs, just as a lunchbox differs from a mixing bowl.

passages.title: A little written Oromo
passages.text: “Umurii” means “Age,” and “Mallattoo” means “signature.” These Oromo words appear beside English translations on the community consent form submitted for UNESCO recognition of Gadaa. They show contemporary Oromo in Latin letters; they are not presented as a text from the map’s early centuries.
The map stops at 1815, but Oromo history continues. Gadaa remained a living institution recognized by UNESCO in 2016; later kingdoms and communities followed different political paths.

passages.text: The Osage, or Wahzhazhe, are a living people whose villages and power shaped the Missouri and central Plains region. The imported outline stretches far beyond documented core settlement areas; it should not be read as one Osage empire’s precise boundary. The map’s 1492 to 1783 interval is coverage, not the nation’s lifetime.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Osage histories connect the people with the Ohio and Mississippi valleys before later settlements in Missouri. Andrea Hunter’s tribal historical-preservation study brings oral accounts, language and archaeology together. It also challenges older attempts to identify Osage ancestors simply by matching pottery styles with northern archaeological cultures.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: At Osage Village in western Missouri, excavations revealed rectangular houses around 30 to 50 feet long and 15 to 20 feet wide, with east-facing doorways. The remains turn a place mentioned in eighteenth-century accounts into a settlement whose rooms and entrances can be studied.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Families at that Missouri village grew corn, beans and squash. They also gathered fruit, fished nearby rivers and oxbow lakes, and hunted. Their food supply came from several environments, so village life involved both cultivated gardens and journeys beyond them.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Osage teaching materials describe bent-frame lodges made with poles planted in the ground and tied together. Flexible young wood curved into walls, while mats, bark or hides covered the frame. Builders could remove coverings before a hunt and leave the framework standing for their return.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Inside a lodge, low benches along the walls served for sitting and sleeping. Woven mats, hides, storage bags and bowls filled the household space; smoke escaped through roof openings above the fires. Several families might share one building, making room for relatives as well as belongings.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Village layout could express social relationships. Osage educational material describes an east-west central road, with Sky and Earth divisions placed on opposite sides and clan households grouped together. A clan is a network of related families; the plan made those connections visible in the arrangement of homes.

passages.title: Homelands, houses and regional influence
passages.text: Fur commerce made the Osage important partners for French traders. Missouri State Parks describes their major role in the trade along the Missouri River. This commercial power rested on access to hunting grounds and settlements, not on Europeans arriving in an empty landscape.

passages.title: Dispossession and protecting a future
passages.text: Nineteenth-century cessions and forced movement displaced Osage communities from older homelands. After losing their Kansas lands, the Osage purchased land from the Cherokee Nation in 1872 in what became Oklahoma. The archival agency guide records the purchase and federal trust arrangement, an important part of the nation’s land history.

passages.title: Dispossession and protecting a future
passages.text: Under the 1906 allotment arrangement, the Osage mineral estate remained communally owned while royalties were divided into inherited shares called headrights. This distinction between land at the surface and resources beneath it shaped the oil era. It also made control over inheritance intensely consequential for families.

passages.title: Dispossession and protecting a future
passages.text: During the 1920s, outsiders murdered Osage people in schemes to obtain oil wealth and inherited headrights. These were attacks on families as well as property. Remembering the victims and the circumstances matters, while the nation’s history extends far beyond the crimes committed against it.

passages.title: Dispossession and protecting a future
passages.text: In 2009, the Osage Nation purchased the summit property at Sugarloaf Mound in St. Louis to protect a sacred ancestral place. Its preservation office describes fencing, monitoring and landscaping intended to stabilize the mound. Caring for an old earthwork became a practical responsibility in the present.

passages.title: Writing, learning and community life
passages.text: “𐓓𐒰͘𐓏𐒰𐓁𐒻𐓍𐒷” is printed beside “Tree of Gifts” in a 2021 Osage Nation announcement. Children’s wishes were represented by ornaments for sponsors to fulfil. This short sample comes from a modern community program, showing Osage writing used in the work of caring for children.

passages.title: Writing, learning and community life
passages.text: The present Osage alphabet is a modern language project. A 2014 encoding proposal describes work led by Mogri Lookout with teachers, linguists, artists and community members. Designing letters and making them usable on computers helped support the language; the alphabet should not be projected backward onto ancient objects.

passages.title: Writing, learning and community life
passages.text: After food-supply disruption in 2020, the Osage Nation invested in Harvest Land’s greenhouse, aquaponics facilities and orchard. Its program account describes produce for community meals and educational work with children. This was a modern effort to strengthen local food production using both plants and technical infrastructure.

passages.title: Writing, learning and community life
passages.text: The constitution ratified in 2006 organized legislative, executive and judicial branches and affirmed equal votes for Osage citizens. Its preamble links present government to earlier clan history and obligations toward children, elders and future generations. Political continuity includes making new institutions as circumstances change.

The Osage did not disappear at the map’s 1783 endpoint. Cessions, forced relocation, allotment and violence transformed their circumstances. The Osage Nation continues through its citizens and government, with a constitution that explicitly connects current responsibilities to past and future generations.

passages.text: The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy used Ravenna as a royal center. Its surviving buildings and personal ornaments show both distinctive traditions and close engagement with the Roman world.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Theodoric's mausoleum used large blocks of Istrian stone arranged around a central space.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo began as Theodoric's palace chapel. Its mosaics combined Roman traditions with eastern Mediterranean influence.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arian Baptistery preserves imagery expressing the court's Christian faith. The Archbishop's Chapel represents a different Christian community in the same city.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: In wider Ostrogothic dress, pairs of shoulder brooches secured women's long garments. Decorated belts, necklaces and other jewelry completed the ensemble.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A surviving brooch attributed to wider Ostrogothic material culture was cast in silver, with silver covering its copper-alloy pin. It combined practical fastening and ornament; the record does not establish manufacture in Italy.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Ravenna passed from Ostrogothic to Byzantine rule. Buildings surviving together today belong to different patrons and periods; San Vitale's Justinianic decoration should not be credited to Theodoric.

sectionTitles: Family work, food and sacred places

passages.text: Otomí communities have a long history across central Mexico, with several languages and regional names, including Hñähñu. They did not form one unchanged kingdom. The broad 1492 to 1500 map label and the smaller 1530 to 1650 “Otomies” outline describe different areas and periods; this narrative also follows colonial communities around Guanajuato and Querétaro. Neither outline marks the full territory of today’s Otomí peoples.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango overlooks the Acambay valley from the San Miguel plateau. Builders levelled difficult ground and made broad terraces for temples and residential platforms. INAH identifies it as an Otomian settlement: a specific archaeological example, rather than the capital of every Otomí community.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango’s pottery helps trace connections. Excavators provisionally distinguished an earlier phase with incense burners, braziers and burial vessels resembling material at Tula, and a later phase with comparisons to Teotenango and Calixtlahuaca. Similar objects point toward relationships; they do not by themselves identify a conquering army.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The sixteenth-century Huamantla Codex was painted on bark paper. It recounts a group’s migration from Chiapan toward Tlaxcala, encounters and battles, and later Spanish arrival and a church. Images preserve an Otomí account of place and history within the colonial period.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Conservators studying the Huamantla Codex identified cochineal red in sampled paint. Looking through a microscope at tiny pigment traces helps explain how artists made the manuscript, alongside historical readings of its pictures. Material analysis supplies evidence that a modern photograph alone cannot provide.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Otomí communities made different political choices during Spanish invasion. At Tecoac in 1519, Otomí defenders guarded a Tlaxcalan frontier and fought Cortés’s force. Elsewhere some communities allied with Spaniards against Mexica power. One ethnic label cannot stand for a single decision made by everyone.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The later map’s northern outline belongs in the history of a mixed colonial frontier. Crespo and Cervantes examine Otomí-speaking settlement in Guanajuato and Querétaro, including the Sierra Gorda foothills. Some Otomí leaders participated in conquest and settlement, creating communities within a changing colonial political landscape.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: INPI emphasizes that households differ between regions: some are nuclear families, while others include extended relatives. Planting and harvest bring family members into shared work. Godparent relationships also create valued ties beyond a household, connecting families through religious and social responsibilities.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Mezquital valley, agave supported more than one craft. Its fibres supplied textiles, while its sap could be fermented into pulque. Fournier connects these activities with pottery for holding and processing sap, showing how a plant crop, containers and household work belonged to the same economy.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Working with scattered maguey plants also shaped where people lived. Fournier argues that their continuing care helped support permanent but dispersed settlements in the Mezquital. This is an interpretation of an economic landscape: a house did not need to stand in a dense city to belong to an organized farming community.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Tolimán area of Querétaro, Otomí-Chichimeca families maintain chapels devoted to ancestors. UNESCO describes annual journeys to sacred hills and Bernal rock, with ceremonies asking for water in a dry landscape. These are living local traditions with their own community setting.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Tolimán celebrations also involve chimales, large temporary structures made from reeds and leafy coverings. Their construction brings people together around an offering. A structure can be important even when its makers intend it to stand only for a celebration rather than for centuries.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: “Ki hats'i” means “Good morning”. INALI prints it as a common greeting in Hñähñu of the Valle del Mezquital and credits Nicandro González Peña for the recorded voice. This is a modern, regionally identified language sample; other Otomí varieties can use different forms.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: Otomí writing standards were developed with community representatives, teachers, activists, the Academy of Hñähñu Language and Culture, researchers and INALI. The participants came from several states. Agreeing how to write sounds can help people share teaching materials while recognizing regional diversity.

Spanish colonial rule changed political relationships, settlement and landholding, without bringing all Otomí communities to one common ending. Languages, families and local institutions continue. The map cutoffs of 1500 and 1650 are coverage dates, not the disappearance of a people.

sectionTitles: Trade, making things and family knowledge

passages.text: Odawa communities were major traders and diplomats around the Great Lakes, connected through kinship and waterways. They were not one centralized empire. The broad lake-region outline is only a rough map of homelands; the separately labeled Oklahoma outline represents a much later homeland after nineteenth-century removal, despite its imported 1492 date.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: At the straits joining Lakes Michigan and Huron, Odawa communities occupied an important meeting place. Historian Michael McDonnell emphasizes their far-reaching trade and family connections. European traders and officers needed to negotiate within these networks; possessing a fort did not automatically make them masters of the surrounding country.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: Birchbark canoes were essential transport around the straits. Mackinac State Historic Parks explains why: they were light, maneuverable and repairable, suited to rivers and sheltered lake routes. European fur traders adopted this Indigenous technology too. Waterways connected communities without requiring a road through every stretch of forest.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: A museum pair of Odawa moccasins, dated about 1825 to 1835, combines hide with cloth, silk and glass beads. Its maker placed cut silk shapes beneath outlines of white beads, using different bead sizes on the cuffs and upper surfaces. Everyday footwear could carry careful design and skilled handwork.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: The moccasins were bought at Crown Point, Indiana, a fur-trade depot. The Smithsonian connects them with Odawa traders traveling from western Michigan across the Great Lakes and as far as the Manitoba prairies. A pair of shoes can be evidence of travel and exchange as well as clothing.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: In a 2019 tribal newsletter, Cheyenne Kiogima described making an aankinaagan, a birchbark infant carrier, while expecting a baby. Renee “Wasson” Dillard taught her. Her father supplied bark gathered about twenty years earlier, so the baby’s carrier also held a material connection to its grandfather.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: Kiogima arranged two bark sheets with their grain running in different directions and sewed with prepared roots. Making the carrier took a day, apart from harvesting the materials. Her older daughter watched, and Kiogima hoped she would remember the work and eventually pass it on to another generation.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: Lizzie Lavore Wolfe taught Ottawa language and customs to her grandson Clarence King. A history she wrote in a 1916 letter was found in a trunk after her death, then typed and preserved by relatives and another tribal member. Family teaching and a saved piece of paper both helped knowledge travel forward.

passages.title: Trade, making things and family knowledge
passages.text: One family memory gives Clarence King’s language teaching a playful twist: his dog Biscuit responded to Ottawa commands. A relative remembered trying English without success, then watching Biscuit become lively when King spoke. Apparently the human visitor, rather than the dog, needed another language lesson.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: Odawa leader Pontiac, also known as Obwandiyag, helped organize resistance to British power around Detroit in 1763. After a surprise attack failed, his forces besieged the fort but did not capture it. Allied actions elsewhere formed a wider conflict; the coalition was loosely organized, not Pontiac’s single state.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: At Greenville in 1795, Ottawa leaders negotiated alongside other Native nations after defeat at Fallen Timbers. The Ottawa Tribe’s historical account points to clan symbols on signatures, including an otter associated with Ottawa leaders. A drawn mark could express political identity without being an alphabetic sentence.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: Removal from Ohio in the 1830s happened in separate journeys, including travel overland and by boat. The Ottawa Tribe’s account emphasizes the difficulty of rebuilding afterward: illness, exposure and hunger followed displacement. These journeys concern ancestors of the Oklahoma community, rather than every Odawa family.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: Kansas did not provide lasting security. Land fraud and broken federal obligations led Ottawa leaders to negotiate a purchase from the Shawnee in Indian Territory. The 1867 treaty confirmed that arrangement, and families moved south. This is the nineteenth-century history behind the Oklahoma map footprint, not an event in 1492.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: The United States terminated federal recognition of the Ottawa Tribe of Oklahoma in 1959, then restored it in 1978. Those government decisions changed legal relations and services; they did not turn the people’s existence off and on. Tribal families continued through both periods.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: Michigan has distinct Odawa governments with their own histories. The Little Traverse Bay Bands and Little River Band both had federal recognition reaffirmed in 1994. Little River identifies its roots in Grand River Ottawa bands along several western Michigan rivers. These communities are not branches of the Oklahoma government.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: A modern Odawa-dialect greeting is “Aanii! Aaniish naa?”, given as “Hi! How are you?” on Laurentian University’s Indigenous Student Affairs language page. The university labels the dialect explicitly and provides learning resources. This written example represents a documented teaching form, rather than a reconstructed medieval inscription.

passages.title: Power, removal and continuing communities
passages.text: The Oklahoma tribe’s Adawe Cultural Center offers language learning and directs families to recordings, dictionaries, games and related community resources. It also links Little Traverse materials. Shared learning can cross the boundaries between governments while preserving the identities of the people using it.

Odawa history continues beyond the imported map cutoff. Different communities remain in the Great Lakes region and in Oklahoma, maintaining their own governments and family connections. Removal and changes in federal recognition are major chapters in that history, not the disappearance of the people.

sectionTitles: Trade, homes and things for a wedding
Baths, care and where waste went

passages.text: The Ottoman state grew from one of several small principalities in northwestern Anatolia into a vast empire in the Balkans, western Asia and North Africa. It was ruled by a sultan but never contained only one people, language or religion. Its frontiers, institutions and local lives changed over six centuries. Buildings, court records, pottery, clothing, public baths, a coin and even an 1893 toilet report let us see more than palaces and battles.

passages.title: An empire of many places
passages.text: Around 1300, the Osmanli were one among several Anatolian principalities. The familiar founding date 1299 is a convention for a gradual political beginning, not a signed birth certificate for an empire. Early rulers expanded into former Byzantine lands in Anatolia and the Balkans.

passages.title: An empire of many places
passages.text: Bursa’s early Ottoman rulers built charitable and commercial complexes funded through endowments called waqfs. Their buildings included markets, inns, schools and baths; the nearby village of Cumalıkızık helped support the system. This is evidence for a linked city and rural landscape, not a plan copied into every province.

passages.title: An empire of many places
passages.text: The empire eventually governed parts of the Balkans, Anatolia, the Arab lands and North Africa. Muslim, Christian and Jewish communities spoke different languages and kept local practices; power from Istanbul often concentrated in major cities. A single colour on a map hides these differences and the changing degree of control.

passages.title: Capitals and skilled makers
passages.text: In 1453 Ottoman forces took Constantinople, ending the eastern Roman government there. Mehmed II rebuilt the city as his capital, commissioning palaces and a mosque complex with educational, social and commercial functions. The Byzantine people and buildings did not all disappear; Hagia Sophia was an earlier Christian church converted to an Ottoman mosque.

passages.title: Capitals and skilled makers
passages.text: Sinan designed the Süleymaniye Mosque complex in Istanbul between 1550 and 1557. UNESCO lists a school, medical school, hospice, bath and market spaces alongside worship. A building complex could be a small neighbourhood of services as well as a landmark on the skyline.

passages.title: Capitals and skilled makers
passages.text: At Edirne, Sinan’s Selimiye complex, built for Selim II, brought a great domed mosque together with schools, a library and a covered market. Its Iznik tiles show many specialized hands behind an imperial commission. The patron’s name survives; the makers’ collective work deserves attention too.

passages.title: Capitals and skilled makers
passages.text: A cobalt-blue dish made at Iznik around 1580 to 1585 has patterned petals that draw on designs circulating across Asia. The dish proves a kiln and painter could transform borrowed motifs into something new; it does not tell us every household ate from such pottery.

passages.title: Capitals and skilled makers
passages.text: The stone bridge at Mostar in Bosnia was built in 1566 in an Ottoman frontier town. What visitors cross today is a careful reconstruction: the original was destroyed in 1993 and the span rebuilt in 2004. The town’s bazaar and homes also speak to life around the bridge, not just imperial engineering.

passages.title: Trade, homes and things for a wedding
passages.text: Cairo traded Yemeni coffee and Indian cloth and spices; Aleppo and Bursa sold silk; Damascus supplied caravans heading toward Mecca and Medina. These routes moved goods through different climates and languages. A market stall could connect distant places without making those places culturally the same.

passages.title: Trade, homes and things for a wedding
passages.text: Safranbolu, a caravan town in Anatolia, preserves houses with built-in shelves, benches and fireplaces. Halls called sofa connected rooms that could serve different purposes. Its market and residential quarters differed by community and local custom, a reminder that an “Ottoman home” had no single design.

passages.title: Trade, homes and things for a wedding
passages.text: A nineteenth-century Ottoman bride might wear a red robe called an entari or a later bindallı gown, embroidered with metal-wrapped thread. The Met shows how dress varied by place, faith and wealth; professional embroiderers often made the elaborate work. No single wedding outfit dressed every bride in this very large empire.

passages.title: Trade, homes and things for a wedding
passages.text: A sixteenth-century Iznik-style tankard in the British Museum carries an Ottoman Turkish saying around its body. The catalogue translates it roughly as “The house of the world is an inn.” A drinking vessel became a little reminder that life is temporary; we do not know its original owner or every occasion it was used.

passages.title: News, family and learning
passages.text: From the mid-sixteenth century, Istanbul coffeehouses offered many adult men a place to hear news, tell stories, play games and find work contacts. They were not every person’s living room: access and customs varied. For an adult visitor, the latest news might arrive with a cup of coffee and several opinions.

passages.title: News, family and learning
passages.text: More than 1,800 early-seventeenth-century Kayseri court cases studied by historian Ronald Jennings include women as parties. Such records can reveal property, family and business disputes and women’s legal activity. Court users were not a random sample of all women, so these cases should not become a rule for every Ottoman household.

passages.title: News, family and learning
passages.text: Some late Ottoman boys left villages for state middle schools in provincial towns, receiving uniforms and living in dormitories. A Cambridge history uses this journey to explain new paths into government service. It describes a selective route to education, not a school day shared by every child or a diary of one named boy.

passages.title: News, family and learning
passages.text: The state also took some Christian boys from their families through the devşirme levy, converted them to Islam and trained them for military or palace service. Some rose to high office, but advancement does not erase the coercion of child removal and slavery. This practice changed over time and was especially important in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

passages.title: Baths, care and where waste went
passages.text: A public hammam was a place to wash and meet others. Surviving Ottoman bath wrappers and embroidered towels show craft alongside the practical business of drying off; bath scrapers helped clean skin. A steamy social visit sounds pleasant, but it is evidence for particular urban bath cultures, not everyone’s weekly routine.

passages.title: Baths, care and where waste went
passages.text: Bayezid II’s Edirne complex, completed in 1488, included a hospital, medical school, pharmacy area, guest spaces and a soup kitchen. Its rooms show organized care and teaching, and sources describe dietary ideas then used in treatment. A surviving hospital building cannot prove that every patient was cured.

passages.title: Baths, care and where waste went
passages.text: An 1893 inspection of the Ottoman government offices in Istanbul found staff toilets with broken pipes, too little cleaning water and accumulated waste. Engineers proposed new pipes and siphons; an 1890 plan shows a linked row of toilet cubicles. The plans reveal a sanitation problem and a proposed fix, not proof that every home suddenly gained plumbing.

passages.title: Writing on a coin
passages.text: A gold coin minted in Constantinople in 1909 under Mehmed V has an Arabic-script inscription. Its reverse includes “ضرب في قسطنطینیّة ۱۳٢٧”, translated by the British Museum as “Struck in Constantinople 1327.” The number is an Islamic-calendar year, corresponding to 1909 CE. The museum identifies this inscription as Arabic, while Ottoman Turkish was another written language of the empire.

passages.title: Writing on a coin
passages.text: A coin’s words could name a ruler, a mint and a date, yet they do not prove the person holding it could read them. The British Museum’s older Iznik tankard carries Ottoman Turkish writing, while this later coin carries Arabic. Those two objects alone show more than one written language in the empire.

passages.title: Reform, violence and an ending
passages.text: The Tanzimat reform era began in 1839 with efforts to reorganize law, administration and schools, including claims of legal equality for Ottoman citizens. A constitution and parliament followed in 1876, but war and political repression interrupted that experiment. Reform was real, uneven and contested.

passages.title: Reform, violence and an ending
passages.text: During World War I, leaders of the Ottoman government ordered the deportation and mass murder of Armenians. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum identifies the 1915 to 1916 campaign as genocide. Armenian men, women and children suffered; survivors and descendants continued Armenian life. This history must not be softened into a vague story about imperial decline.

passages.title: Reform, violence and an ending
passages.text: On 1 November 1922, the Turkish Grand National Assembly abolished the Ottoman sultanate. The caliphate remained a separate title until 1924. The political institution ended after war, territorial loss and competing governments; no single modern country simply replaced every former Ottoman province.

The Ottoman sultanate was abolished by the Turkish Grand National Assembly on 1 November 1922, after World War I, territorial losses and struggle over government. A separate caliphate continued until 1924. Former Ottoman lands followed different paths, and their peoples and traditions did not vanish. The imported 1920 to 1930 polygon is a coarse map interval that extends beyond the sultanate’s historical end; no one successor polity is substituted for this three-continent empire.

sectionTitles: Objects in ordinary and spiritual life

passages.text: Ovimbundu names communities of Angola’s central highlands, not one kingdom. Earlier political loyalties centered on places such as Bailundo, Bié and Huambo. A broader shared identity developed through commerce, colonial pressures and missionary institutions. This map’s 1878 to 1914 block compresses that varied history.

passages.title: Kingdoms, caravans and fields
passages.text: Bié was a major inland trading hub with routes toward both Luanda and Benguela. Visiting traders established households with women, children, helpers and enslaved people. The caravan network moved through settled communities; it was not simply a line of travelers crossing empty land.

passages.title: Kingdoms, caravans and fields
passages.text: After the loss of political autonomy, farming did not simply stop prospering. Neto traces increased maize and bean production and local commerce, helped by the railway after 1910. Some households adapted successfully even while colonial authorities reduced the power of local rulers.

passages.title: Kingdoms, caravans and fields
passages.text: That adaptation came under unequal conditions. Missionaries reported taxes and forced labor imposed on peasants; later European settlement, labor demands and pressure on land deepened hardship. Economic growth in one decade should not hide who carried its burdens.

passages.title: Homes, sanitation and play
passages.text: During his 1929 to 1930 fieldwork, Hambly described families helping build houses: men assembled walls while women and children supplied wet clay. Children enjoyed trampling it with their feet. Building day could include an excellent excuse for getting muddy.

passages.title: Homes, sanitation and play
passages.text: Hambly also saw pits containing maize husks and sweet-potato refuse, and reported use of the bush for toileting. These are specific early twentieth-century observations, not evidence that all highland villages shared one sanitation system.

passages.title: Homes, sanitation and play
passages.text: Hambly’s accounts from his 1929 to 1930 fieldwork include spinning tops, counting games and children pretending to lead caravans. Boys lashed small loads between forked sticks and marched singing. Even make-believe travelers knew that properly packed luggage mattered.

passages.title: Objects in ordinary and spiritual life
passages.text: The Museu Nacional catalogue records wooden spoons, a flour sieve, baskets and a comb in Celenia Pires’s collection, donated in 1936. Such objects turn attention from kings to cooking, carrying, sorting food and personal care: indispensable skills that rarely headline political histories.

passages.title: Objects in ordinary and spiritual life
passages.text: A small perforated gourd rattle collected at Dondi accompanied a diviner’s songs, according to notes dated 1932. Its seeds made the sound. The object helps document the music surrounding spiritual consultation, without establishing that the divination worked.

passages.title: Objects in ordinary and spiritual life
passages.text: A carved woman collected at Benguela shows a married woman’s hairstyle and fibre plaits described as a fertility charm. Museum curators suggest possible use by a diviner. The wood, cloth and metal embody careful craft; the precise use remains uncertain.

passages.title: Learning, printing and health education
passages.text: At Dondi, the Currie Institute opened for boys in 1914; the Means School followed for girls in 1916. Mission stations sent selected pupils onward. Girls gained educational opportunities, but training also reflected restrictive expectations about their future family roles.

passages.title: Learning, printing and health education
passages.text: “Viovusenge” means “things of the bush.” It is the Umbundu title of Mabel Stokey’s book printed at Camundongo in 1916. This attested Latin-letter sample comes just after the map interval; its Portuguese title translation appears in the same volume.

passages.title: Learning, printing and health education
passages.text: A 1926 schoolbook on tropical hygiene was printed in Portuguese and Umbundu. Madaleno Chipa translated its Umbundu text. Health education therefore involved local language expertise and printing work, alongside the mission’s religious project.

Portuguese domination curtailed the autonomy of highland polities, but the Ovimbundu did not disappear in 1914. Farming, trade and community life continued through colonial restructuring. The end of this imported map block is not the end of a people.

sectionTitles: An actual city, built room by room
Family memory and a little written Yoruba

passages.text: Oyo was a powerful Yoruba kingdom and empire whose cavalry, markets and tributary relationships connected northern Yorubaland with routes toward the Atlantic. Its history includes both the older capital, Oyo-Ile, and a smaller kingdom rebuilt farther south after the imperial collapse. The map’s broad coverage should not be read as one unchanged empire lasting to 1914.

passages.title: An actual city, built room by room
passages.text: Brian Hallam’s survey of Oyo-Ile records a palace made of many courtyards surrounded by rooms. Compounds belonging to leading chiefs stood nearby. A palace was a whole neighborhood of activities, rather than one throne room.

passages.title: An actual city, built room by room
passages.text: South of that palace was a large water reservoir; to its east lay the Akesan market. The survey describes traders’ booths shaded by trees. Water storage, shopping and royal administration occupied neighboring parts of the city.

passages.title: An actual city, built room by room
passages.text: At nearby Kosso, surviving walls reached about six metres. Builders laid thick courses of earth and let each dry before adding the next. Archaeologists suggest some high holes held scaffolding, but the holes’ precise uses still need research.

passages.title: Cooking, craft and everyday company
passages.text: Cooking and serving bowls excavated at Ede-Ile carry potters’ marks. Ogundiran and Saunders studied them across occupations from the early 1600s to the 1820s to investigate how makers and vessels connected households within the empire. An ordinary bowl can preserve a maker’s social world.

passages.title: Cooking, craft and everyday company
passages.text: Charcoal from Bara’s Oyo-period contexts, dated roughly 1570 to 1835, includes several woodland tree groups, including Terminalia and Senegalia. Families had to obtain suitable fuel before a meal could even begin. These fragments record that work, although they cannot tell us the complete dinner menu.

passages.title: Cooking, craft and everyday company
passages.text: The Bara study found different proportions of wood in different deposits. Access, season and the tasks being performed may explain the variation. The researchers treat these as possibilities, not proof that every household followed one firewood rule.

passages.title: Cooking, craft and everyday company
passages.text: Ede-Ile began as an Oyo frontier camp and developed into a town connecting inland routes with the coast. Its clay tobacco pipes document an Atlantic-introduced habit becoming part of local social life during the 1600s to 1800s.

passages.title: Cooking, craft and everyday company
passages.text: Those pipes resemble examples from Oyo-Ile, but resemblance does not settle where they were made. Ajibade’s chemical study is a step toward identifying production and exchange. Similar-looking pipes need not have come from the same workshop.

passages.title: Family memory and a little written Yoruba
passages.text: A later Oyo-Yoruba memorial figure at the Met, dated broadly to the nineteenth or twentieth century, combines carved wood with camwood powder, beads and blueing. Its surface bears evidence of handling, so use and care matter alongside carving skill.

passages.title: Family memory and a little written Yoruba
passages.text: In the tradition described by the museum, a mother bathed, dressed, adorned and ritually fed a figure made after a twin’s death. It remained a relationship with a loved person. These are memorial objects, not evidence that every Yoruba family held identical beliefs.

passages.title: Family memory and a little written Yoruba
passages.text: “Bu omi fun mi ki nmo” means “Give me some water to drink” in Samuel Crowther’s 1852 Yoruba vocabulary. This is Yoruba in the book’s Roman-letter spelling, a later printed witness to the language, not writing copied from an imperial palace wall.

passages.title: Family memory and a little written Yoruba
passages.text: A small sentence can reveal an ordinary concern across centuries: somebody is thirsty. Crowther’s dictionary also supplies practical examples about corn for a horse and yam for a child under the same verb. Language learning did not have to begin with royal proclamations.

passages.title: What changed, and what survived
passages.text: Oyo’s collapse was a sequence. Afonja’s rebellion, the Muslim movement at Ilorin and earlier civil wars all mattered. Robin Law dates the old capital’s abandonment to about 1836; rebuilding at modern Oyo preserved kingship without restoring the former empire.

The old empire broke apart in the early 1800s and Oyo-Ile was abandoned around 1836. A smaller kingdom was rebuilt farther south. Yoruba people, language and institutions continued; the collapse of imperial power was not their disappearance.

passages.text: The kingdom of Pagan, on the Irrawaddy, united the Burmese lands under Anawrahta in the 1050s and made Theravada Buddhism the faith of the country. Its kings and people covered the plain of Bagan with thousands of temples in two hundred years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: More than 2,000 temples and stupas still stand at Bagan out of some 10,000 built between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ananda temple, finished about 1105 under Kyansittha, with its four standing Buddhas and gilded spire.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Burmese writing, adapted from the Mon script, appears on the Myazedi inscription of 1113 beside Pyu, Mon and Pali.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Anawrahta adopted Theravada Buddhism under the Mon monk Shin Arahan and in 1057 took Thaton, bringing its monks and scriptures to Pagan.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Contacts with Sri Lanka in the twelfth century renewed the monastic ordination and the Pali canon.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Weirs and canals in the Kyaukse district fed the rice that paid for the temples.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bagan was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism remains the religion of most of Myanmar.

Mongol armies invaded in 1277 and 1287, and King Narathihapate fled and was murdered by his own son. His successors ruled as Mongol vassals until the three brothers of Myinsaing deposed the last of them in 1297.

sectionTitles: A province with a distinct legal inheritance

passages.text: This Palatinate record represents Bavaria’s province west of the Rhine, acquired in 1816 and administered from Speyer. It was called the Rheinkreis before receiving the name Pfalz in 1838. It combined territories with different earlier histories and was not the medieval Electoral Palatinate. The imported span starts a year early, in 1815, and stops in 1878 without a historical collapse. Its western outline is also overbroad: it includes Saarbrücken, which belonged to Prussia after 1815.

passages.title: A province with a distinct legal inheritance
passages.text: Bavarian rule did not sweep away the province’s French legal inheritance. The Code civil and local self-government arrangements remained, giving the Palatinate a different legal setting from Bavaria east of the Rhine. Government changed hands, but people did not simply wake up with every rule governing property and civil life replaced.

passages.title: A province with a distinct legal inheritance
passages.text: In 1849 revolutionaries formed a provisional government in the Palatinate while campaigning for the constitution drafted by the Frankfurt parliament. Their break with Bavaria was intended to help establish a constitutional German nation. It was a brief revolutionary challenge within a wider German movement, rather than the foundation of a lasting independent Palatine kingdom.

passages.title: Crowds, flags and public voices
passages.text: At the Hambach Festival on 27 May 1832, merchants, craftspeople, winegrowers, small farmers and laborers joined students and other participants. Women were explicitly invited to the political gathering. The procession climbed toward the castle with music and flags, turning a public celebration into a demand for freedom and national unity.

passages.title: Crowds, flags and public voices
passages.text: Writing sample: the surviving festival flag bears “Deutschlands Wiedergeburt,” meaning “Germany’s rebirth.” Johann Philipp Abresch carried it up the hill on 27 May 1832, and it was raised beside a Polish flag. The German words, in Latin letters, made a political hope visible to a crowd; this was writing meant to be seen at a distance.

passages.title: Crowds, flags and public voices
passages.text: The authorities responded with repression, including bans on political associations and meetings. Organizers Johann August Wirth and Philipp Jakob Siebenpfeiffer were acquitted in the main trial but later imprisoned for insulting officials and eventually went into exile. Public speech could have consequences far beyond the day of a festival.

passages.title: Land, schoolrooms and traveling livelihoods
passages.text: Farm inheritance often divided property among heirs in the Palatinate. This differed from the custom of keeping a holding together under one heir in much of Old Bavaria. Sharing land between children could also leave the next generation with smaller plots. Family arrangements therefore helped shape the countryside as well as individual households.

passages.title: Land, schoolrooms and traveling livelihoods
passages.text: Most children attended elementary schools, commonly organized by religious confession. The province also had some shared schools and Jewish schools. Many new school buildings included accommodation for teachers. A teacher’s workplace and home could occupy the same building, bringing lessons and household life close together.

passages.title: Land, schoolrooms and traveling livelihoods
passages.text: A Pirmasens mayor’s report counted 150 women and girls carrying shoes for sale in 1830. Selling journeys could last weeks, including six to eight weeks for travel into Switzerland. Shoemaking supported work far beyond the workshop: somebody had to carry the finished pairs to buyers and spend long periods away from home.

passages.title: Land, schoolrooms and traveling livelihoods
passages.text: Pirmasens shoemakers sometimes used Brotbücher, literally bread books. A master recorded what a worker was owed, and the worker could use that entry to obtain shop credit until the shoes sold. The arrangement became especially restrictive when the master also owned the shop and required workers to buy there. Shoes, wages and groceries could become tied together.

passages.title: Land, schoolrooms and traveling livelihoods
passages.text: In the nineteenth-century Palatine uplands, some families earned money through traveling musicians. Performers left villages such as Mackenbach and Jettenbach for months or even years, while children learned instruments for a possible future in the trade. Earnings from music could help pay for homes, fields and education. Practice could become preparation for a family livelihood.

passages.title: Coal, colors and workers’ households
passages.text: The Ludwigsbahn railway reached completion in August 1849, connecting the Rhine with the Bexbach coal district. Coal transport was its central purpose, but the railway company also published a guide in 1854 to promote the region’s scenery and historic places. The same tracks could carry industrial fuel and visitors looking for an outing.

passages.title: Coal, colors and workers’ households
passages.text: BASF was founded in Mannheim in 1865, but its factory went up across the Rhine in Ludwigshafen after an attempted land purchase on the Mannheim side failed. The business aimed to produce dyes and the chemicals needed to make them. A company named for Baden became a major industrial presence in the Bavarian Palatinate.

passages.title: Coal, colors and workers’ households
passages.text: BASF hired a company physician in 1866, one year after its foundation. Workers’ health had become part of the factory’s own organization. The much larger clinic and advanced equipment described in later company histories belong to around 1900; the 1866 appointment was an earlier step, not a fully developed modern hospital.

passages.title: Coal, colors and workers’ households
passages.text: Construction of BASF’s Hemshof housing settlement began in 1872, with more than 400 apartments. In 1875 the company also established sickness benefits paid from its own funds. These were particular arrangements for its workforce, not services automatically available to everyone in the province. A job could be connected to housing and support during illness as well as wages.

The province did not end in 1878. It remained linked to Bavaria through later upheavals, including occupation and territorial changes after the First World War. Nazi rule weakened that administrative connection. After the Second World War, the main Palatinate territory became part of the new state of Rhineland-Palatinate in 1946. Regional communities and identity continued.

passages.text: These imported Paleo-Inuit outlines cover Newfoundland. This card follows regional Dorset communities and earlier Groswater traditions, rather than a kingdom. They should not be confused with the later Thule ancestors of living Inuit.

passages.title: A community beside the sea
passages.text: At Phillip’s Garden, large quantities of harp-seal bones show the importance of seasonal hunting. The exposed coast put people near migrating animals. Returning to a productive place could tie the year’s food supply to familiar homes and neighbours.

passages.title: A community beside the sea
passages.text: Dorset soapstone lamps burned animal oil for heat and light. This made household fuel less dependent on finding firewood. Cooking vessels and lamps belonged to a wider stone-working tradition, with local choices shaped by available materials.

passages.title: A community beside the sea
passages.text: Excavations changed the apparent size of Phillip’s Garden houses. Features first interpreted as walls proved to be internal platforms. Once those spaces were included, some houses had much larger footprints than their visible central hollows suggested.

passages.title: A community beside the sea
passages.text: These houses could have raised sleeping areas, storage pits and entrances facing the sea. Substantial construction and repeated use have led researchers to suggest that several families sometimes lived and hunted together. That interpretation is particularly associated with this site.

passages.title: A community beside the sea
passages.text: Not every hollow marks a house occupied at the same moment. Researchers combine mapping, excavation and radiocarbon dates to reconstruct settlement. Phillip’s Garden accumulated through centuries of returning, rebuilding and changing activities, rather than one enormous village census.

passages.title: Making things and learning skills
passages.text: At Fleur de Lys, unfinished vessel shapes and removal scars remain in the rock. They preserve stages of making soapstone containers, while spoil heaps and discarded tools reveal the labour around them. A quarry wall can be a record of work.

passages.title: Making things and learning skills
passages.text: To begin a vessel, workers prepared the rock face, separated a rough shape, extracted it and finished it. Soapstone was relatively easy to carve, but a pot still required planning and careful blows: one bad crack could spoil considerable effort.

passages.title: Making things and learning skills
passages.text: Small, roughly made pots provide a possible glimpse of children. John Erwin argues that low extraction scars and unfinished-looking miniatures may represent young learners copying adults. This is a reasoned archaeological interpretation, not proof that every miniature was a toy.

passages.title: Making things and learning skills
passages.text: The Phillip’s Garden tool inventory includes scrapers, needles and awls used in working skins, as well as tools for making other equipment. Preparing and repairing clothing was part of the same skilled material world as manufacturing hunting gear.

passages.title: Small evidence, large questions
passages.text: Beetle remains help reconstruct changes around Phillip’s Garden. Species with different habitat needs reveal shifts in vegetation; researchers concluded that people harvested trees and altered their surroundings more than previously appreciated. Tiny insects supplied evidence the larger artifacts could not.

passages.title: Small evidence, large questions
passages.text: Limestone conditions at Port au Choix helped preserve organic remains unusually well. This is why bones and other fragile evidence survive alongside stone. Archaeological detail depends partly on what the soil protects, so equally busy communities can leave very different records.

passages.title: Small evidence, large questions
passages.text: Carved animals and human figures are known from the wider Dorset world, including Labrador. They are important visual evidence, but no securely deciphered Dorset text supplies a translated sentence. Their makers’ spoken words should not be replaced with invented modern Inuit dialogue.

Dorset occupation ended in Newfoundland around 800 CE, beyond both map endpoints. Causes remain uncertain: proposed hunting failures are not a demonstrated explanation. Other Arctic regions followed different chronologies, so this cannot date every Paleo-Inuit tradition’s ending.

passages.text: Panama became independent from Colombia in 1903. The canal opened in 1914, the beginning of this map record, and transformed international shipping. Its history also belongs to workers and their families, Afro-descendant performers, farmers and craftspeople; the canal came under Panamanian control in 1999.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: Independence on 3 November 1903 came with support from US warships. A treaty soon granted the United States extensive rights in a strip across the isthmus. Panama’s national independence and foreign control of the canal therefore began together, creating a lasting political tension.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: The construction administration divided workers into gold and silver payrolls. Race and citizenship shaped placement, with consequences reaching far beyond wages: housing, schools, libraries, toilets and drinking fountains were segregated. Families encountered the hierarchy in ordinary daily routines.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: Employee complaints survive in US archives. Some Black US citizens entitled to gold-roll privileges carried special metal checks or marked commissary books to prove eligibility, yet still met discrimination. The records let workers challenge the official story in their own voices.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: Sanitation teams fitted screens to windows and doors and fumigated houses in Panama City and Colón. Waterworks also reduced dependence on household water containers where mosquitoes could breed. Sewers and paved streets formed part of the effort to make the construction zone healthier.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: Building Gatun Lake required relocating settlements in the future reservoir. Meanwhile, stronger railways hauled excavated earth and delivered supplies, including refrigerated food. The great engineering project changed both the landscape and where people could live.

passages.title: A canal built by people
passages.text: In the original canal, locks lift ships to Gatun Lake, about 85 feet above sea level, and lower them again. Water flows into chambers by gravity. Think of a staircase whose steps fill with water, with an entire ship standing on each step.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: Making a Panamanian pinta’o hat begins well before weaving: growers supply several plants, and artisans prepare fibers and use mud in coloring processes. Braids and patterned strips become the finished hat. A single object connects cultivation, patient handwork and design.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: Families pass hat-making skills between generations, while cooperatives and a hat museum in La Pintada help organize and share knowledge. The museum displays hats from different periods. Everyday clothing can preserve a history that is comfortable enough to wear.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: Congo festivities among Afro-descendant communities remember liberation from colonial enslavement. Songs and dancing also portray daily life. Performers dance barefoot as an expression of connection with the earth; celebration carries historical memory through bodies, music and gathering.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: A queen and court preside over Congo ritual performances, whose season runs from January into Ash Wednesday. Dramatic encounters with devils form part of the story. Families, schools and weekend workshops help children learn roles, music and meaning.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: “El español es el idioma oficial de la República” means “Spanish is the official language of the Republic.” This is Article 7 of Panama’s constitution, quoted from its official 2004 consolidated publication. The short sentence is an actual legal text in written Spanish.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: A National Guard coup in 1968 began a period of military dominance. In December 1989, US forces intervened and removed Manuel Noriega’s regime. These changes reshaped government; they did not end Panama’s existence as a country.

passages.title: Craft, celebration and political change
passages.text: At noon on 31 December 1999, Panama assumed control of the canal. The transfer changed who administered this strategic waterway, rather than creating a new country. Its anniversary is remembered as a major milestone in national sovereignty.

Panama continues as a state. The 1914 map start corresponds to canal-era coverage, while independence dates to 1903. Transfer of the canal in 1999 marked a major change in sovereignty and administration within the continuing republic.

sectionTitles: Early Rome and the evidence it left
Books, family care and city water

passages.text: The Papal States were territories governed by the pope as a temporal ruler, alongside his religious role. Their changing extent and interrupted history differ from the continuing institution of the Holy See. The atlas separates an early entry around 800 from a later one, but neither coverage boundary is a reliable foundation or fall date.

passages.title: Early Rome and the evidence it left
passages.text: Charlemagne was crowned emperor in Rome on Christmas Day in 800. A famous Vatican painting depicts the ceremony, but it was made in the Renaissance and gives historical figures the faces of later rulers. It is evidence for how later popes remembered the event, not an eyewitness image from 800.

passages.title: Early Rome and the evidence it left
passages.text: Pope Paschal I rebuilt Santa Prassede in the ninth century. Reused granite columns and richly colored mosaics survive in a church that later generations repeatedly altered. Reusing older stone connected new construction to Rome’s material past; it does not make every part of the present building ancient.

passages.title: Early Rome and the evidence it left
passages.text: The San Zeno chapel at Santa Prassede was associated with Paschal’s mother, Theodora. Its mosaics bring a named family relationship into a monumental religious setting. This was exceptional papal patronage, not evidence that ordinary mothers received comparable chapels.

passages.title: Early Rome and the evidence it left
passages.text: The San Zeno mosaics are dated to Paschal I’s pontificate, 817 to 824, using inscriptions and written evidence. The heritage catalogue also identifies nineteenth-century restoration in papal portraits. A beautiful surviving image may contain medieval work and much later repair: dating the building is only the first step.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: In 1475 Sixtus IV gave the Vatican Library a formal foundation and financial support, with Bartolomeo Platina as librarian. A library needed staff, rooms and money as well as manuscripts. This was a learned institution attached to papal government, not universal public education.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: The Vatican Library kept rules for reading and records of books lent outside. Registers covering 1475 to 1547 survive. Even in a famous manuscript collection, somebody had to know who had borrowed what: the missing-library-book problem is considerably older than a school backpack.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: Melozzo da Forlì painted Sixtus IV with Platina and members of the pope’s family in the old library. The museum identifies papal nephews among the figures. This is a commissioned image of patronage and connections, not a neutral group photograph of everyone who worked there.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: Santo Spirito’s foundling wheel allowed an infant to be placed inside and turned toward the hospital. A bell alerted the nuns, who arranged care with wet nurses. The institution dates the wheel’s presence cautiously, probably to the fifteenth century; the mechanism cannot supply the missing stories of every family.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: The wheel’s opening limited the size of a child who could be passed through it. Older children could still be received through the hospital entrance. That practical detail matters: the device was one route into care, not a complete description of whom the hospital accepted.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: The Acqua Felice works of the 1580s brought water to Rome’s hills, partly reusing an ancient aqueduct. The monumental Fountain of Moses advertised the achievement. Supplying elevated neighborhoods required engineering as well as a handsome fountain; this evidence does not mean every household had indoor running water.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: A short inscription on the fountain reads “COEPIT PONT. AN. I ABSOLVIT III MDLXXXVII”: “He began in the first year of his pontificate; completed [it] in the third, 1587.” The Latin abbreviation and Roman numerals recorded construction in the pope’s regnal years. This is an attested inscription, transcribed by Rome’s heritage page.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: The fountain’s Moses attracted criticism because he holds the tablets of the Law beside water coming from the rock, although the biblical episodes occur in a different order. Monumental art could get a very public editorial review. The criticism concerns the story being represented, not whether the waterworks functioned.

passages.title: Books, family care and city water
passages.text: In 1555 Paul IV imposed the Roman ghetto and severe restrictions on Jewish residents, including forced residence and property sales. Families also faced identifying marks and limits on work. Papal patronage of beautiful churches and books coexisted with policies that constrained another community’s daily life.

Italian forces captured Rome in 1870 and annexed the remaining papal territory. The Holy See continued as a religious and diplomatic institution. Vatican City was created by the 1929 Lateran settlement; it should not be substituted for the much larger historical Papal States or dated to the atlas’s 1878 endpoint.

passages.text: This map label covers eastern New Guinea and nearby islands long before a single state united them. Papua New Guinea became independent in 1975. Communities had their own languages, farming systems and exchange networks; later colonial administrations, warfare and nation-building changed their political relationships.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: Kuk’s buried cultivation mounds and drainage ditches preserve a much older history beneath today’s farmland. UNESCO dates clear agricultural change to roughly 7,000 to 6,400 years ago. These are ancient predecessors of the modern country, whose name should not be projected back onto a prehistoric state.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: At Kuk, farmers propagated crops including bananas, taro and yams and later dug drainage channels with wooden tools. Managing wet ground helped make planting possible. The surviving landscape records repeated changes in practice rather than one invention that stayed exactly the same forever.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: Motu-speaking communities carried pottery by large sailing canoes to Gulf communities in the hiri exchange, returning with sago and canoe hulls. The voyages connected households making cooking pots with households producing food. A useful kitchen vessel could travel far beyond its maker’s village.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: An 1885 observation described hiri canoes carrying, on average, more than fifteen hundred pots each. Women’s pottery production and men’s canoe preparation required extensive coordination. Before the dramatic departure came a great deal of clay-working, building and packing.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: Powerhouse preserves a finely looped bilum bag catalogued to 1960 to 2001. In his 2022 interpretation, Papua New Guinean scholar Michael Mel points to its fine continuous string, strengthened handles and carefully finished opening as signs of exceptional skill.

passages.title: Land, food and skilled hands
passages.text: Mel explains how bark fibers were cured, teased into strands and rolled on the maker’s thigh to form string. He interprets the bag as a first-child carrier whose open loops allowed air through. Its exact regional attribution differs between the old catalog and his assessment.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: Tok Pisin developed through contact among people speaking different languages, including workers brought together on Pacific plantations. Its history extends beyond New Guinea into wider labor networks. People created a shared means of communication under difficult and unequal conditions.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: “Nau gavmen i tok” means “Now the Government is talking.” This Tok Pisin opening comes from an Australian Second World War leaflet reproduced and translated by linguist Peter Mühlhäusler. It is wartime persuasive writing in Latin letters, not an ancient traditional saying.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: Germany annexed the northeast in 1884, while Britain established control in the southeast and formally annexed it in 1888. Australia assumed administration of Papua in 1906. These were imposed colonial jurisdictions across already inhabited lands, not empty spaces waiting for names.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: Australian archives preserve correspondence on constitutional change alongside photographs of independence celebrations. The records trace the shift from an appointed legislative council to an elected House of Assembly in 1964. Written files and photographs document different parts of the same transition.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: Michael Somare’s ministry, formed after the 1972 election, pursued self-government and independence. Self-government began on 1 December 1973, followed by independence on 16 September 1975. The present state’s beginning therefore lies centuries after the map’s imported 1715 starting point.

passages.title: Languages, government and independence
passages.text: The constitution’s preamble honors inherited customs and connects individual dignity with community interdependence. It also favors consensus in resolving problems and places power in the people through elected representatives. The founding text brought several principles of national life together in writing.

Colonial administration ended with independence in 1975, and Papua New Guinea continues as a state. Its many communities did not begin with independence. The imported 1715 date is geographical coverage, not the founding of a unified Papua New Guinean polity.
