passages.text: Paracas communities lived along Peru’s southern coast and made extraordinary textiles and painted pottery. This was a varied cultural world, not a single documented empire. The imported 400 to 100 BCE map interval captures a late slice of a much longer tradition. Dry coastal cemeteries preserve evidence of clothing, skilled work and the importance of ancestors.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: A bowl dated 350 to 200 BCE alternates human and feline heads with falcons around its interior. Facial details let researchers distinguish the creatures: pointed ears help identify cats, while the birds have beaks, wings and tails. A dinner-sized vessel could hold an intricate visual world.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: Paracas potters mixed pigments with a binding material and applied paint after firing. The result could be brilliantly colorful but fragile. Curators suggest that such carefully painted vessels were intended for special uses; they were not necessarily the pots used for daily cooking.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: One textile border was woven from camelid hair, then covered so completely with embroidery that the base cloth disappeared beneath the stitches. Red, green, blue and yellow figures fill the surface. Producing it required two different skills: making the fabric and building the image on top.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: Repeated figures on the same border use a cycle of four colors in changing combinations. The pattern is carefully organized, not a row of identical copies. Looking for each color’s next appearance is a small puzzle left by a highly accomplished textile maker.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: Burial bundles could contain mantles, turbans, tunics, loincloths and skirts, along with food and other offerings. This preserves a much wider wardrobe than a single famous cloak suggests. The surviving assemblages combine clothing with ceremonial care for the dead.

passages.title: Clothing, color and skilled hands
passages.text: Cloths with stitched sample figures survive from Paracas Cavernas and early Nasca contexts. Peters interprets them as models to copy. Such objects give a concrete glimpse of how complex visual knowledge could be retained and passed between textile workers.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: In the Chincha Valley, investigations around Huaca Soto found evidence of people living and farming between large platform mounds. Communities also fished the sea. Monumental centers belonged within a productive landscape of fields, homes and coastal resources.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: At Cerro del Gentil, a deposit associated with closing a ceremonial court contained maize, beans, cassava, guava and other plants. Cotton and reeds were there too, useful for cloth, rope and baskets. Archaeologists reconstruct both food preparation and craft materials from these remains.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: The same court deposit contained remains from twenty kinds of shellfish, mainly marine species. The site lies about seventeen kilometers from the beach, so seafood had to travel inland. A feast could bring together foods and people from different parts of the valley.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: Paracas Cavernas is known for trepanation, an operation that opened the skull by carefully scraping bone. Peters records four examples in the later Necropolis cemetery as well. These remains document practiced medical intervention, although they do not preserve the patients’ own accounts of treatment.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: A painted cotton panel probably served as a face for a funerary bundle. Its central figure has a bird on the torso and snake-like forms around the head. Such an object helped give the wrapped ancestor a visible presence during mortuary practices.

passages.title: Meals, health and remembering people
passages.text: No securely readable Paracas sentence survives to reproduce with a translation. Embroidered figures, colors and arrangements formed a rich visual language, but their precise meanings remain partly uncertain. We can show and describe authentic images without turning them into invented written words.

Paracas traditions changed through interaction with Topará and the developing Nasca world. The famous Necropolis at Wari Kayán includes Topará-associated ceramics and material spanning roughly 150 BCE to 200 CE, so “Paracas” museum labels do not always describe one uniform phase. The map’s 100 BCE endpoint is a coverage boundary, not the sudden extinction of these communities.

passages.text: Paraguay became independent in 1811, before the map’s 1815 beginning. Wars and dictatorship profoundly affected its people, while household crafts, Guaraní language traditions and shared drinks remained part of social life.

passages.title: A house, its objects and public memory
passages.text: The Casa de la Independencia in Asunción was built in 1772 and hosted meetings connected with the 1811 independence movement. Its rooms surround a courtyard. A domestic building became a political meeting place before it became a museum in 1965.

passages.title: A house, its objects and public memory
passages.text: The museum identifies a desk-chest as belonging to Fernando de la Mora. Furniture joins weapons and official documents in the collection. Political history also passed through rooms where people sat, stored papers and worked.

passages.title: A house, its objects and public memory
passages.text: An eighteenth-century bed appears in the museum’s bedroom display. It brings private routines into a story often told through public ceremonies. A curated interior helps visitors imagine domestic space, but should not be mistaken for an untouched room occupied continuously since independence.

passages.title: A house, its objects and public memory
passages.text: The Archives of Terror preserve official records of policing and persecution under Alfredo Stroessner. Found in 1992, they supplied evidence for investigating human-rights abuses. Records created to control people can later be used to expose that control.

passages.title: A house, its objects and public memory
passages.text: The archive also documents cooperation between South American dictatorships through Operation Condor. Paraguay’s history of repression therefore crosses national borders. Preserving the records helps account for people harmed by state institutions rather than allowing their experiences to disappear.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: The objects of tereré include a jug or thermos, a vessel holding yerba mate and a metal or cane drinking straw called a bombilla. The cold drink makes a familiar set of tools part of everyday sociability.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: Pohã ñana herbal knowledge passes through families alongside tereré practices. People associate herbs with healing in this tradition. That cultural association is evidence about beliefs and learning, not proof that every preparation safely treats illness.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: Preparing and drinking tereré provides time for conversation and friendship. UNESCO’s account emphasizes a practice shared by diverse participants. A drink can organize a social occasion as effectively as an invitation announcing a formal meeting.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: Piribebuy’s Poncho Para’í de 60 Listas has a body, bands and an edging made through different craft processes. Weavers specialize and cooperate to assemble the garment. The result depends on teamwork as well as individual skill.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: The craft uses cotton threads and handmade equipment, including wooden tools and seats. Materials and tools are part of the knowledge, not merely background supplies. A finished poncho conceals many small decisions about how to make it.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: Poncho techniques have passed from mothers to daughters through demonstration and practice. A safeguarding school adds another route for transmission. The 2023 UNESCO listing records a tradition requiring support, not a craft whose continuation can be taken for granted.

passages.title: Sharing drinks and making clothes
passages.text: “El Paraguay es un país pluricultural y bilingüe” means “Paraguay is a multicultural and bilingual country.” It is Article 140 of the 1992 constitution. The article names Spanish and Guaraní as official languages and also recognizes other Indigenous and minority languages as cultural heritage.

Paraguay survived the nineteenth-century war and continues as a state. Stroessner’s dictatorship ended in 1989, and a new constitution followed in 1992. These political transitions did not erase its communities or make Guaraní cultural life a thing of the past.

passages.text: The Pawnee are a continuing nation of four bands with deep roots in the central Plains. Their linked Oklahoma outline is incorrectly placed in 1492; migration there occurred in 1874 to 1875. This narrative follows both the Plains homelands and the later Oklahoma community.

passages.title: An inhabited archaeological landscape
passages.text: The Pawnee Nation identifies four bands: Čawî’, Kitkahaki, Pitahawirata and Skidi. Their histories and communities belong within a shared nation without making every village identical. This diversity matters when interpreting an object or practice from one particular settlement.

passages.title: An inhabited archaeological landscape
passages.text: The Pawnee Indian Museum in Kansas protects an excavated earth-lodge floor inside its building. Visitors encounter the actual footprint of a home, rather than only a reconstruction. Its location in the Republican River valley connects it with the Kitkahahki band’s settlement history.

passages.title: An inhabited archaeological landscape
passages.text: In the village described by the Kansas museum, dome-shaped earth lodges could shelter large extended-family groups. Substantial posts supported the roof, a central hearth supplied heat, and entrances faced east. Maintaining a home meant caring for its wood-and-earth structure as well as its residents.

passages.title: An inhabited archaeological landscape
passages.text: Excavated Pawnee villages in Nebraska date from the 1600s through the 1870s. Their remains show changes from square houses to round lodges. Collections include decorated pots from Butler County and a bowl from Colfax County, evidence of skilled local container-making before metal vessels became widespread.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: Families planted corn, beans, squash and pumpkins, then stored harvests in pits for later use. The farming village and the hunting camp were parts of the same yearly routine. A full storage pit helped bridge the gap between harvest time and the next growing season.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: During seasonal bison hunts, people took portable shelters and supplies westward, using dogs and later horses to pull travois. Archaeologists have also excavated hunting camps with butchered bison bones. The remains connect the travel described in historical accounts with work performed at particular camps.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: Deb Echo-Hawk began the Pawnee Seed Preservation Project in 1998. Families supplied ancestral seeds for renewal, and a partnership later brought planting back to Nebraska. Saving a seed variety requires growing it successfully again; a packet stored forever cannot produce the next generation.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: The first Nebraska planting in 2004 failed after seeds went into cold ground too early. A later planting succeeded. The project now links gardeners with Pawnee researchers who measure how varieties perform, combining inherited knowledge, careful observation and patient trial and error.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: The July 2015 tribal newspaper is headed “CHATICKS SI CHATICKS”, with the English gloss “Men of Men”. This is an attested modern written Pawnee name in the Nation’s own publication. Its printed spelling is preserved here rather than replaced by a reconstructed ancient phrase.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: That issue describes the Veterans Homecoming as a gathering begun in 1946 to welcome people home from the Second World War. Families returned for dancing, food, games and remembrance. The 2015 programme included contests for young children as well as older dancers.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: Removal to Indian Territory in 1874 to 1875 followed sustained pressure on Pawnee lands and lives. Allotment in 1893 then broke up communal landholding and opened much of the reservation to outsiders. These events explain why the Oklahoma outline belongs to a later chapter than the map suggests.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: Former Pawnee Industrial School buildings now house tribal offices and educational uses. The school closed in 1958 and its land returned to the Nation in 1968. Places once tied to outside control have become resources for Pawnee administration and learning.

The Pawnee Nation continues through its four bands, government and community institutions. Removal ended settlement in particular Plains villages and allotment reduced landholdings; neither event made the people disappear. The Nation’s constitution records ongoing political organization well beyond the map’s 1783 endpoint.

passages.text: The Duchy of Parma and Piacenza was a northern Italian state ruled by several dynasties. The map’s 1650 to 1815 interval hides French administration beginning in 1802 and formal imperial incorporation in 1808. A restored duchy continued after Napoleon, well beyond 1815. The outline is approximate, rather than a precise border across these political changes.

passages.title: Dynasties and disrupted borders
passages.text: French rule developed in stages. After Duke Ferdinando died in 1802, an administrator governed in Napoleon’s name. Conscription and the Napoleonic civil code followed in 1805, and the Taro department was formally created in 1808. Such changes affected military service, laws and the language of official documents.

passages.title: Dynasties and disrupted borders
passages.text: After Napoleon’s fall, restoring government required rebuilding the duchy’s finances and administration. Minister Filippo Magawly directed that work from 1814. Maria Luigia, formerly empress of the French, reached Parma on 20 April 1816 to govern the duchy assigned to her. Her arrival falls just beyond the imported map interval.

passages.title: Schools, books and the problem of finding a book
passages.text: The 1768 educational constitutions reorganized instruction from primary schooling to the university. Parma’s reforming government supported institutions including a botanical garden, an antiquities museum and a public library. These projects helped train professionals and collect knowledge, although a law about education does not tell us that every child could attend.

passages.title: Schools, books and the problem of finding a book
passages.text: Parma’s first chemistry chair was established within medicine in 1767. The following year, the former Jesuit complex of San Rocco became the ducal university’s home after the Jesuits were expelled. Scientific education was growing, but changes to teaching institutions could also involve forceful political and religious conflict.

passages.title: Schools, books and the problem of finding a book
passages.text: The Palatina Library began as a public-benefit project in 1761 and was officially inaugurated in 1769. Librarian Paolo Maria Paciaudi assembled thousands of books through purchases and scholarly contacts. Building a library meant finding the books first, not merely building beautiful shelves.

passages.title: Schools, books and the problem of finding a book
passages.text: Paciaudi recorded books on movable catalogue slips instead of only in a bound register. The slips included an author, title, publication details, comments and the book’s location. A new acquisition could get a new slip without requiring a librarian to rewrite a whole book of entries.

passages.title: Letters were made by hand
passages.text: Giambattista Bodoni arrived in 1768 to establish and direct the royal printing shop. He supervised the making of presses and tools, with both the workshop and his lodgings inside the Pilotta complex. Producing elegant pages depended on practical labor, from preparing equipment to arranging and printing the type.

passages.title: Letters were made by hand
passages.text: Writing sample: a 1769 festival book begins its Italian title “Descrizione delle feste celebrate in Parma l’anno MDCCLXIX.” This means, “Description of the festivities celebrated in Parma in the year 1769.” The museum transcribes the title of Bodoni’s book for Duke Ferdinando’s wedding to Maria Amalia. The Roman numerals spell out the year.

passages.title: Letters were made by hand
passages.text: Bodoni’s widow, Margherita Dall’Aglio, continued running the printing shop after his death. In 1818 she published his great typographic manual in two volumes. It displayed letterforms and decorative designs accumulated over his career. This achievement belongs to the restored duchy, after the map’s cutoff, and depended on her continuing the work.

passages.title: Food, a walk and care for children
passages.text: Before this map interval, an official document of 1612 specified places whose cheese could be sold as Parmigiano. It named dairying areas around Parma, including Fontevivo and Noceto. Protecting a food’s geographical reputation was already serious business, although this early rule was not the same system as today’s protected designation.

passages.title: Food, a walk and care for children
passages.text: Parma’s new promenade and coffee pavilion opened on 24 June 1766. The regional heritage catalogue connects that evening with the local custom of walking outdoors in the Saint John festivities to encounter the dew. A stroll could combine fresh air, company and a fashionable new place to pause.

passages.title: Food, a walk and care for children
passages.text: During the eighteenth century, Parma’s old hospital was divided into the Misericordia section for care of the sick and injured and the Esposti section for foundlings. Assistance to children without parental care therefore formed part of this large institution’s responsibilities, alongside treating illness.

passages.title: Food, a walk and care for children
passages.text: The Farnese Theatre was a place for exceptional court celebrations rather than an everyday evening out. Its elaborate productions were so costly that it was used only nine times, from its opening in 1628 to the last dynastic event in 1732. Even dukes could build a stage that was expensive to keep busy.

Ducal rule collapsed in 1859. Duchess Luisa Maria left Parma in June, Austrian troops withdrew from Piacenza, and provisional authorities pursued union with Sardinia. The territories entered the process of Italian unification. The imported ending in 1815 instead falls near the beginning of the restored duchy.

passages.text: The Parthian Empire, ruled by the Arsacid dynasty from 247 BCE to 224 CE, held Iran and Mesopotamia between Rome and the steppe for nearly five centuries. Its armored lancers and horse archers, its great noble houses and its grip on the Silk Road made it Rome's only equal in the East.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Parthian shot: horse archers turned in the saddle to shoot behind them at full gallop.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Carrhae in 53 BCE, horse archers and cataphracts, riders and horses in scale armor, destroyed a Roman army under Crassus.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The empire sat astride the Silk Road; Chinese silk reached Rome through Parthian middlemen who kept the two ends apart.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Envoys from Han China reached the Parthian court in the 110s BCE, and in 97 CE the Han envoy Gan Ying got as far as the Persian Gulf.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zoroastrian, Greek, Babylonian and Jewish communities kept their own cults, and the kings styled themselves friends of the Greeks on their coins.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Arsacids claimed descent from the Achaemenid king Artaxerxes II.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Sasanians inherited Parthian cavalry, provinces and great noble houses.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Parthian, a Middle Iranian language written in its own script, was still used in the Sasanian royal inscriptions.
Ardashir I of Persis defeated and killed the last Arsacid king, Artabanus IV, at Hormozdgan in 224 and founded the Sasanian dynasty.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: Families planted corn, beans, squash and pumpkins, then stored harvests in pits for later use. The farming village and the hunting camp were parts of the same yearly routine. A full storage pit helped bridge the gap between harvest time and the next growing season.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: During seasonal bison hunts, people took portable shelters and supplies westward, using dogs and later horses to pull travois. Archaeologists have also excavated hunting camps with butchered bison bones. The remains connect the travel described in historical accounts with work performed at particular camps.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: Deb Echo-Hawk began the Pawnee Seed Preservation Project in 1998. Families supplied ancestral seeds for renewal, and a partnership later brought planting back to Nebraska. Saving a seed variety requires growing it successfully again; a packet stored forever cannot produce the next generation.

passages.title: Food for a changing year
passages.text: The first Nebraska planting in 2004 failed after seeds went into cold ground too early. A later planting succeeded. The project now links gardeners with Pawnee researchers who measure how varieties perform, combining inherited knowledge, careful observation and patient trial and error.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: The July 2015 tribal newspaper is headed “CHATICKS SI CHATICKS”, with the English gloss “Men of Men”. This is an attested modern written Pawnee name in the Nation’s own publication. Its printed spelling is preserved here rather than replaced by a reconstructed ancient phrase.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: That issue describes the Veterans Homecoming as a gathering begun in 1946 to welcome people home from the Second World War. Families returned for dancing, food, games and remembrance. The 2015 programme included contests for young children as well as older dancers.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: Removal to Indian Territory in 1874 to 1875 followed sustained pressure on Pawnee lands and lives. Allotment in 1893 then broke up communal landholding and opened much of the reservation to outsiders. These events explain why the Oklahoma outline belongs to a later chapter than the map suggests.

passages.title: Printed words and continuing community
passages.text: Former Pawnee Industrial School buildings now house tribal offices and educational uses. The school closed in 1958 and its land returned to the Nation in 1968. Places once tied to outside control have become resources for Pawnee administration and learning.

The Pawnee Nation continues through its four bands, government and community institutions. Removal ended settlement in particular Plains villages and allotment reduced landholdings; neither event made the people disappear. The Nation’s constitution records ongoing political organization well beyond the map’s 1783 endpoint.

passages.text: Peru proclaimed independence in 1821, decades before this map record begins. The republic encompasses coastal, Andean and Amazonian communities whose histories extend far beyond the state. Its story includes railways and libraries, living textile and pottery knowledge, and the difficult work of confronting political violence.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Awajún potters in northern Peru use grinding and polishing stones, wooden tools and brushes made with human hair. They collect materials, shape, fire, decorate and finish their vessels. Designs draw on plants, animals, mountains and stars, turning careful observation into useful objects.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Awajún pots serve for cooking, drinking and sharing food as well as ceremonies. Elder women known as Dukúg pass knowledge to other women in their families. Growing the plants used in production is part of the work, so the craft reaches from garden to hearth.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: On Taquile in Lake Titicaca, men and women make textiles as an everyday activity. Garments may be knitted or woven on four-stake ground looms. A knitted chullo keeps ears covered; a wide calendar belt depicts agricultural and ritual cycles.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Taquile’s crafts school helps younger people learn textile skills. Makers have also introduced contemporary images while retaining established techniques. Tourism supplies income, but greater demand can change materials and meaning, a handmade tradition has to negotiate a changing market.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: The National Library opened in September 1822 with more than eleven thousand volumes, including books from former Jesuit collections and private gifts. San Martín donated about six hundred. The early republic invested in a place where knowledge could be collected and consulted.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: After wartime looting in 1881, Ricardo Palma sought donated books through letters to writers abroad. A devastating fire followed in 1943. Jorge Basadre’s rebuilding effort included professional staff training and a National School of Librarians in 1944: recovering a library required people as well as shelves.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: The 1821 founding decree described the library as devoted “a la ilustración universal”, “to universal enlightenment.” The National Library reproduces this Spanish phrase from San Martín’s decree of 28 August. It captures an early republican ambition to support independence through learning.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: A railway between Lima and Callao opened in 1851, linking the capital and its port. Railway building later reached other regions: the first locomotive entered Cusco in September 1908. Travel and shipping were being reorganized, but connection arrived at different times in different places.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: The Lima mint produced eight-real coins under both royal and republican authority in 1821 to 1822. Their different shields make political change visible in objects used for payment. A person examining two coins can see a revolution in the designs without reading a whole proclamation.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: Peru participated in the Peru to Bolivian Confederation from 1836 until its dissolution in 1839. That short-lived arrangement belongs between independence and the later republic. National political structures changed even while towns, farms and trading relationships carried on.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented killings, disappearances and other abuses during the 1980 to 2000 conflict, committed by insurgent organizations and state agents. Rural and Indigenous-language communities suffered disproportionately. Its investigation made those unequal experiences central to the national account.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: Families of disappeared people organized to seek information and justice, often with women sustaining the effort through years of uncertainty. The commission recognized their persistence. Public memory was built through the work of relatives and communities, not only through official hearings.

Peru continues as a republic. Changes of government, the nineteenth-century confederation and the internal armed conflict altered its institutions without ending the country or its diverse peoples. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage date, not the beginning of Peruvian society.

passages.text: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Their history survives in carved stones, workshops, food remains and outside accounts. The evidence reveals connected regional societies, not a single unchanged state. Political authority and language changed as Alba emerged, without a securely established single date when all Picts disappeared.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Written references to Picts begin in the late third century. This first surviving name is not a secure founding date for a people or kingdom.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Fortriu, a powerful kingdom by the seventh century, is now located around the Moray Firth. Its full extent and relationship with smaller regions remain debated.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Rhynie's fifth- and sixth-century settlement had successive ditches and a larger timber palisade. The Craw Stane stood near an entrance. These excavated relationships connect symbol stones with an inhabited, repeatedly remodelled place.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: An iron axe-shaped pin from Rhynie resembles the axe on the Rhynie Man stone. Clay moulds for comparable pins establish local manufacture, linking a carved image to the work of metalworkers.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Rhynie's ditch deposits contained imported amphora fragments, continental glass, crucibles and metalworking tools. The vessels demonstrate exchange connections, while production debris shows that the settlement also made valuable objects.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Around 700, Portmahomack's workers carved stone, worked metal and glass, and processed hides interpreted as parchment production. Combined with its burial pattern and infrastructure, this supports identification as a monastery.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Cattle bones dominate Portmahomack's animal remains. The researchers connect cattle with food, possible dairying and hides for parchment. Supporting a religious community required husbandry and skilled processing as well as prayer.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: After the monastic phase, a Portmahomack workshop became a kiln barn with an upper floor and flue. Its alteration, together with grain remains, makes a change in everyday work visible in the buildings.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Charred barley and evidence for oats and wheat at Lairg document cultivation from about 450 onward. Such environmental traces reveal food production even where early medieval houses are difficult to identify.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: The Hilton of Cadboll cross-slab, erected around 800, places a woman prominently in a hunting scene. The original was later cut and reused as a grave marker; the stone at the site today is a replica.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Bede reports that King Naiton asked Ceolfrid for guidance on Easter and builders for a stone church. His account shows royal interest in religious calculation and imported expertise, although it presents these exchanges through Bede's Christian viewpoint.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Burning and broken sculpture mark Portmahomack's destruction around 800. A Viking raid is a proposed explanation, not an identified attacker. Workers subsequently cleared debris and resumed metal and glass production.

Pictish power centres shifted during the later ninth century, and Alba extended uneven authority into the Highlands in the tenth. This was a prolonged political and cultural transformation. The evidence does not support one conquest date or the disappearance of an entire population.

sectionTitles: Learning, patronage and the wider state

passages.text: Medieval Poland developed from Piast centres into a kingdom with towns, religious communities, mining enterprises and a university. Its political geography changed through fragmentation and renewed royal authority. Bridges, excavated buildings, municipal layouts and written records offer different views of everyday work and learning. The union with Lithuania in 1569 transformed the state while the Polish Crown continued within the Commonwealth.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Remains of two tenth-century wooden bridges lie in Lake Lednica beside the island stronghold. They connected its palace and chapel complex with routes towards Poznan and Gniezno. The timbers document organised construction and access across water, beyond the history of individual rulers.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: Excavators uncovered two depressions in the Lednica chapel in 1988 and 1989. The museum interprets them as baptismal basins. They support discussion of early Christian practice, but identifying them with Mieszko's own baptism remains an interpretation rather than a witnessed event.

passages.title: Discovering the early centres
passages.text: At Giecz, foundations of an unfinished palace and chapel belong to the late tenth century; a stone stronghold church dates to the early eleventh. Unfinished work is evidence too: a surviving plan does not mean the planned building was completed or used.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Krakow's charter of 1257 helped shape a merchants' town whose market, streets and public buildings remain legible. Wawel formed a distinct royal and episcopal centre. The city's accumulated buildings reflect repeated construction, not a single medieval building campaign.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Kazimierz, chartered in 1335, began as a separate town beside Krakow. Catholic and Jewish communities shaped its later streets, religious buildings and customs. Its medieval origin should not be used to assign every surviving synagogue or house to the founding year.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: Wieliczka produced salt from brine before deep mining expanded in the thirteenth century. An exploratory shaft found in the Saltworks Castle courtyard preserves evidence of that transition. The casing shown to visitors has been reconstructed, so the presentation includes both remains and modern interpretation.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: By the late thirteenth century, the Cracow Saltworks joined mines and salt-processing facilities at Wieliczka and Bochnia. Administration and sales connected underground labour to royal income and distant markets. The enterprise needed coordination above ground as well as extraction below it.

passages.title: Urban communities and salt workers
passages.text: The mines preserve galleries, tools and spaces later adapted for chapels or storage. UNESCO cautions that much surviving technical evidence is from the eighteenth century onward. Medieval methods are partly known from documents and reconstructions; the whole visitor route is not a medieval workplace.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Casimir III founded the University of Krakow in 1364. Teaching faltered after his death, and a renewed charter followed in 1400 through the patronage of Jadwiga and Wladyslaw Jagiello. Institutional continuity required renewed resources and organisation rather than one founding act alone.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Endowed university chairs supported subjects including astronomy, mathematics, grammar and rhetoric. The Corpus Academicum project identifies patrons such as Jan Stobner and Katarzyna Mezykowa. Teaching depended on people financing particular posts, not only on royal sponsorship.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: Fifteenth-century Krakow attracted scholars in law and mathematical astronomy. Nicolaus Copernicus began his studies there in 1491. His attendance belongs to the history of this teaching community; it should not imply that all his later astronomical work was completed at the university.

passages.title: Learning, patronage and the wider state
passages.text: The 1569 Act of the Union of Lublin records a new constitutional relationship between the Kingdom of Poland and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania. A surviving legal act makes the transition more specific than describing Poland as simply falling to a neighbouring country.

The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth in 1569. Polish institutions and communities continued within that arrangement. The imported map interval ending in 1400 is neither the kingdom's extinction nor the date of this constitutional transformation.

sectionTitles: A shared state with unequal freedoms
Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
A short sample of written language

passages.text: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth joined two states in 1569 and became a major European power. Its inhabitants built palaces and synagogues, observed the heavens, traded, farmed and debated how government should work. Nobles enjoyed political privileges that most residents did not share. These cards cover the seventeenth-century state and its later, diminished territory, with dated examples of both impressive achievements and ordinary household needs.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: The Union of Lublin was concluded on 1 July 1569. A shared parliament linked the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania, while Lithuanian and local assemblies continued. The Commonwealth was a negotiated political union, not simply a new name for one modern nation.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Noblemen elected the monarch after the last Jagiellon king died in 1572. Political rights centered on the nobility, or szlachta. Peasants working under serfdom did not enjoy those same freedoms.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Large estates relied on agricultural labor, including compulsory service from peasants. Grain production connected rural livelihoods with trade. Wars and epidemics could destroy crops, workshops and households, not just change the names on a map.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Greek Catholics, Protestants and Jews lived within the Commonwealth’s changing boundaries. Their rights were unequal and changed over time. The existence of several faiths did not guarantee freedom from discrimination.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: Jan III Sobieski acquired the Wilanów estate in 1677. Its palace grew from a modest residence into a richly decorated building with separate royal apartments, gardens and a working estate. Surviving decoration presents a ruler interested in art and learning as well as military glory.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: The wooden synagogue at Gwoździec, in present-day Ukraine, was built around the middle of the seventeenth century. Paintings and biblical texts covered its interior. Separate spaces accommodated men and women; a later annex also served as a school and a warmer place for winter worship.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: Its painted interior was renovated in 1729. The spectacular ceiling seen in POLIN Museum today is a modern reconstruction, made in 2011-2012 using traditional tools and materials. It helps explain lost craftsmanship, but it is not the original timber roof.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: In Gdańsk, Johannes Hevelius published detailed lunar observations in Selenographia in 1647. He drew phases and surface features and proposed names for them. Careful description and illustration were important achievements even when later astronomers chose different names.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: His 1673 book Machina coelestis illustrated instruments and a rooftop observatory, with Elisabeth Hevelius among those shown working. After her husband’s death, Elisabeth completed the publication of his star research in 1690. Astronomy here was also a family collaboration.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: Maria Kazimiera, later queen, adopted a French fashion for receiving visitors while reclining in bed. Letters and diaries record the custom in 1662, before her marriage to Sobieski, and later at court. A formal visit did not always require the hostess to get up. This was elite fashion, not a description of every home.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: A letter from 1696 even connects royal family life with the problem of persuading adults to hold a grandchild. The museum’s study uses these personal messages alongside diaries: intimate family concerns can survive in the same archive as affairs of state.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: POLIN’s account of eighteenth-century Jewish towns brings markets, taverns, homes and synagogues together. Household life and commerce were closely connected, with women playing important roles in the home. One community’s routines cannot stand in for every town or religious group.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: The Commission of National Education began work in 1773 after the suppression of the Jesuit order disrupted schooling. Reformers reorganized schools, planned teacher training and expanded lessons in Polish and the sciences, including physics and geometry. New curricula did not mean equal schooling for every child.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: The Society for Elementary Books, founded in 1775, prepared textbooks and syllabuses. Some of those books remained in use during the nineteenth century. Educational reform meant practical work on what teachers and pupils would actually read.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Around the middle of the seventeenth century, Adam Kazanowski’s Warsaw palace had a two-room bath with tubs and a controlled supply of steam. The furnace stood outside the bathing rooms, possibly below them. That last detail is an interpretation, not a securely observed floor plan.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Bathhouses could combine washing with socializing and services such as shaving, cupping or tooth extraction. The museum study describes varied buildings and customers. These historical treatments tell us what was offered, not whether it was safe or effective.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century noble household inventories list basins, pitchers, combs and shaving equipment. Richer households could display silver fittings. Researchers must also allow for increasingly detailed inventories: more entries on paper do not automatically mean a sudden invention of cleanliness.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Eighteenth-century inventories also mention copper chamber pots kept under beds; the wealthiest could own silver ones. A fancy material did not give the pot a fancy job. These were possessions of particular households, not proof that everyone had the same toilet arrangements.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: In early-modern Gdańsk, latrines commonly stood at the back of town plots. Excavations preserve timber linings of pits, while the buildings above them are often missing. Archaeologists therefore combine remains with pictures and written descriptions when reconstructing the whole structure.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Those pits also collected discarded objects and organic waste. Studying their contents can reveal food and living conditions. Yesterday’s rubbish can become tomorrow’s historical evidence, although an object in a cesspit does not by itself explain why it ended up there.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Gdańsk’s pharmacies were supervised by a city physician and civic officials. In 1665, Johann Ernst Scheffler and Johan Fabritius produced the Dispensatorium Gedanense, an official list of medicines. This records efforts to organize pharmacy practice; a medicine’s inclusion does not prove that it worked.

passages.title: A short sample of written language
passages.text: On the façade of Wilanów Palace, the Latin inscription “REFULSIT SOL IN CLYPEIS” means “the sun shone on the shields.” It belongs to the imagery of Sobieski’s late-seventeenth-century residence and adapts a biblical phrase. This is a real architectural inscription, not a phrase invented for this card.

passages.title: A short sample of written language
passages.text: The shields also recalled the Sobieski family’s emblem. The museum’s art-historical study interprets the decoration as a statement about royal authority. Latin served this learned public message; it was not the everyday language of all the Commonwealth’s residents.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Russia, Prussia and Austria took territory in the first partition of 1772. The Commonwealth survived with reduced territory. Its later appearance under the map label “Poland” refers to this remaining state, not a new country founded in 1783.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: The Constitution of 3 May 1791 separated branches of government and abolished the liberum veto, which had allowed a deputy to obstruct parliamentary proceedings. Its text survives in manuscripts and contemporary printed editions. Constitutional design is a documented achievement, even though its implementation was cut short.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Article IV placed peasants under the protection of law and government, but also preserved obligations arising from agreements with landowners. It did not abolish serfdom. The distinction matters: a promise of protection was not the same as equal freedom.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Russia and Prussia carried out the second partition in 1793. The uprising led by Tadeusz Kościuszko in 1794 was defeated. Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the remaining territory in 1795, ending the Commonwealth’s independent institutions.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Partition changed people’s rulers rather than making communities disappear. Jewish residents, for example, came under Austrian, Prussian or Russian government, with new laws shaping daily life. The histories of the Commonwealth’s inhabitants continued beyond the state’s ending.

The third partition in 1795 divided the Commonwealth’s remaining territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria. Independent government ended; its diverse communities continued under new rulers. The imported endpoint of 1800 for the later map record has therefore been corrected to 1795.

sectionTitles: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
Health, homes and a sample of Polish

passages.text: The imported “Poland” map record begins around 1920 and has no fixed end, but it covers several distinct regimes. An independent republic formed in 1918, was attacked and partitioned by Germany and the Soviet Union in 1939, and emerged from the war with changed borders under communist rule. Solidarity and the 1989 elections helped restore democratic government. Life ranged from Yiddish-speaking towns and rural workers’ homes to shipyard families and modern cities. Polish mathematicians’ Enigma work was a major wartime contribution. The country continues; a single map label cannot show its changing borders or its Jewish and other minority histories.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: Poland regained independence in 1918 after more than a century of partition. Its borders were fought over from 1919 to 1921, so the map’s approximate 1920 start is not the moment Polish history began.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: The 1921 March Constitution set out a parliamentary republic. Political conflict did not disappear, and “Poland” in this map is not a single unchanging government.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: In 1932 mathematician Marian Rejewski and Polish Cipher Bureau colleagues found ways into Germany’s Enigma machine. It took mathematics, teamwork and a great deal of pencil work. No magic decoder ring was involved.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: In July 1939 Polish intelligence shared its Enigma methods with British and French codebreakers. Their head start became part of a much larger Allied decoding effort.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: Germany attacked from the west on 1 September 1939; Soviet forces entered from the east on 17 September. The two powers divided Poland, while a Polish government-in-exile and resistance continued the fight.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: German occupiers created ghettos and killing centers and murdered most Polish Jews. Nazi violence also targeted many non-Jewish Polish civilians. The Holocaust must not be turned into a story of ordinary wartime inconvenience.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: After the war Poland’s borders shifted west, and communist authorities ruled the country. The 1980 Solidarity movement grew from shipyard strikes into an independent union and broad opposition. Negotiations and the partly free 1989 election opened the path to democracy.

passages.title: Borders, governments and a clever cipher
passages.text: Poland adopted its current constitution in 1997, joined NATO in 1999 and entered the European Union in 2004. These are milestones of the current republic, not endpoints for the country.

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: Before 1939 Polish Jewish neighborhoods held shops, schools, synagogues and homes where Yiddish could be heard; Friday evenings brought the Sabbath for observant families. Jewish life was varied, not one costume or one custom.

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: A Jewish child in interwar Poland might attend a Polish state school, a Hebrew-language school, a Yiddish-language school or a religious school. Families debated what language and future an education should serve.

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: POLIN’s interwar exhibit includes a cinema and café: children and adults also watched films, read and met friends. Remembering these ordinary pleasures helps show what wartime persecution destroyed.

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: A World War II museum reconstructs one Warsaw professional family’s flat in 1939, 1943 and 1945. Its wartime rooms show substitute food, mended clothes, a displaced lodger and hidden school materials. This is one city family’s story, not every Polish home.

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: During the 1980 Gdańsk Shipyard strike, families brought workers food, medicine and money at the gate. Union politics was also a family logistics problem: how do you keep people fed while they remain at work on strike?

passages.title: Children, families and neighbors
passages.text: Communist authorities launched an antisemitic campaign in 1968 that drove many Jewish citizens to leave Poland. Jewish communities endured and, after 1989, rebuilt public cultural life.

passages.title: Health, homes and a sample of Polish
passages.text: A Warsaw Jewish nursing school founded in the interwar years taught anatomy, hygiene and bacteriology. Nurses later cared for children under Nazi occupation, when medicine and safety were desperately scarce.

passages.title: Health, homes and a sample of Polish
passages.text: A 1930 worker-housing agreement required enough roofed outdoor privies near homes and told residents to keep them clean. A rule on paper does not prove every household had a decent toilet. It does show how practical sanitation was part of labor conditions.

passages.title: Health, homes and a sample of Polish
passages.text: The 1997 constitution begins Article 1: “Rzeczpospolita Polska jest dobrem wspólnym wszystkich obywateli.” In English: “The Republic of Poland is the common good of all its citizens.” This is an original Polish-language line, not a reconstructed ancient phrase.

Poland continues. The interwar republic was invaded and partitioned in 1939; communist rule followed the war, and democratic government was restored after 1989. Its people, borders and institutions changed, while Polish Jewish and other minority histories remain part of this story. The imported “poland-1920” label has an open end and cannot validate any one historical border.

passages.text: This chapter follows Renaissance planning and learning in Poland-Lithuania. Zamosc offers a local view of how architectural ideas, commerce and education could meet in one deliberately planned town.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Union of Lublin joined the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania in the Commonwealth under one monarch in 1569.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the late sixteenth century, Bernardo Morando designed Zamosc using Italian Renaissance ideas of an ideal city, adapted to Central European architectural traditions.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zamosc was conceived as a trading centre on a route connecting western and northern Europe with the Black Sea. Arcaded merchants' houses enclosed its main market square.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Founder Jan Zamoyski established the Zamosc Academy. The planned town combined education with residential, commercial and civic functions.

sectionTitles: A shared state with unequal freedoms
Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
A short sample of written language

passages.text: The Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth joined two states in 1569 and became a major European power. Its inhabitants built palaces and synagogues, observed the heavens, traded, farmed and debated how government should work. Nobles enjoyed political privileges that most residents did not share. These cards cover the seventeenth-century state and its later, diminished territory, with dated examples of both impressive achievements and ordinary household needs.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: The Union of Lublin was concluded on 1 July 1569. A shared parliament linked the Polish Crown and Grand Duchy of Lithuania, while Lithuanian and local assemblies continued. The Commonwealth was a negotiated political union, not simply a new name for one modern nation.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Noblemen elected the monarch after the last Jagiellon king died in 1572. Political rights centered on the nobility, or szlachta. Peasants working under serfdom did not enjoy those same freedoms.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Large estates relied on agricultural labor, including compulsory service from peasants. Grain production connected rural livelihoods with trade. Wars and epidemics could destroy crops, workshops and households, not just change the names on a map.

passages.title: A shared state with unequal freedoms
passages.text: Catholics, Orthodox Christians, Greek Catholics, Protestants and Jews lived within the Commonwealth’s changing boundaries. Their rights were unequal and changed over time. The existence of several faiths did not guarantee freedom from discrimination.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: Jan III Sobieski acquired the Wilanów estate in 1677. Its palace grew from a modest residence into a richly decorated building with separate royal apartments, gardens and a working estate. Surviving decoration presents a ruler interested in art and learning as well as military glory.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: The wooden synagogue at Gwoździec, in present-day Ukraine, was built around the middle of the seventeenth century. Paintings and biblical texts covered its interior. Separate spaces accommodated men and women; a later annex also served as a school and a warmer place for winter worship.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: Its painted interior was renovated in 1729. The spectacular ceiling seen in POLIN Museum today is a modern reconstruction, made in 2011-2012 using traditional tools and materials. It helps explain lost craftsmanship, but it is not the original timber roof.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: In Gdańsk, Johannes Hevelius published detailed lunar observations in Selenographia in 1647. He drew phases and surface features and proposed names for them. Careful description and illustration were important achievements even when later astronomers chose different names.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and observing the heavens
passages.text: His 1673 book Machina coelestis illustrated instruments and a rooftop observatory, with Elisabeth Hevelius among those shown working. After her husband’s death, Elisabeth completed the publication of his star research in 1690. Astronomy here was also a family collaboration.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: Maria Kazimiera, later queen, adopted a French fashion for receiving visitors while reclining in bed. Letters and diaries record the custom in 1662, before her marriage to Sobieski, and later at court. A formal visit did not always require the hostess to get up. This was elite fashion, not a description of every home.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: A letter from 1696 even connects royal family life with the problem of persuading adults to hold a grandchild. The museum’s study uses these personal messages alongside diaries: intimate family concerns can survive in the same archive as affairs of state.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: POLIN’s account of eighteenth-century Jewish towns brings markets, taverns, homes and synagogues together. Household life and commerce were closely connected, with women playing important roles in the home. One community’s routines cannot stand in for every town or religious group.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: The Commission of National Education began work in 1773 after the suppression of the Jesuit order disrupted schooling. Reformers reorganized schools, planned teacher training and expanded lessons in Polish and the sciences, including physics and geometry. New curricula did not mean equal schooling for every child.

passages.title: Family, visitors and learning
passages.text: The Society for Elementary Books, founded in 1775, prepared textbooks and syllabuses. Some of those books remained in use during the nineteenth century. Educational reform meant practical work on what teachers and pupils would actually read.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Around the middle of the seventeenth century, Adam Kazanowski’s Warsaw palace had a two-room bath with tubs and a controlled supply of steam. The furnace stood outside the bathing rooms, possibly below them. That last detail is an interpretation, not a securely observed floor plan.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Bathhouses could combine washing with socializing and services such as shaving, cupping or tooth extraction. The museum study describes varied buildings and customers. These historical treatments tell us what was offered, not whether it was safe or effective.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Seventeenth- and eighteenth-century noble household inventories list basins, pitchers, combs and shaving equipment. Richer households could display silver fittings. Researchers must also allow for increasingly detailed inventories: more entries on paper do not automatically mean a sudden invention of cleanliness.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Eighteenth-century inventories also mention copper chamber pots kept under beds; the wealthiest could own silver ones. A fancy material did not give the pot a fancy job. These were possessions of particular households, not proof that everyone had the same toilet arrangements.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: In early-modern Gdańsk, latrines commonly stood at the back of town plots. Excavations preserve timber linings of pits, while the buildings above them are often missing. Archaeologists therefore combine remains with pictures and written descriptions when reconstructing the whole structure.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Those pits also collected discarded objects and organic waste. Studying their contents can reveal food and living conditions. Yesterday’s rubbish can become tomorrow’s historical evidence, although an object in a cesspit does not by itself explain why it ended up there.

passages.title: Washing, toilets and healthcare
passages.text: Gdańsk’s pharmacies were supervised by a city physician and civic officials. In 1665, Johann Ernst Scheffler and Johan Fabritius produced the Dispensatorium Gedanense, an official list of medicines. This records efforts to organize pharmacy practice; a medicine’s inclusion does not prove that it worked.

passages.title: A short sample of written language
passages.text: On the façade of Wilanów Palace, the Latin inscription “REFULSIT SOL IN CLYPEIS” means “the sun shone on the shields.” It belongs to the imagery of Sobieski’s late-seventeenth-century residence and adapts a biblical phrase. This is a real architectural inscription, not a phrase invented for this card.

passages.title: A short sample of written language
passages.text: The shields also recalled the Sobieski family’s emblem. The museum’s art-historical study interprets the decoration as a statement about royal authority. Latin served this learned public message; it was not the everyday language of all the Commonwealth’s residents.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Russia, Prussia and Austria took territory in the first partition of 1772. The Commonwealth survived with reduced territory. Its later appearance under the map label “Poland” refers to this remaining state, not a new country founded in 1783.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: The Constitution of 3 May 1791 separated branches of government and abolished the liberum veto, which had allowed a deputy to obstruct parliamentary proceedings. Its text survives in manuscripts and contemporary printed editions. Constitutional design is a documented achievement, even though its implementation was cut short.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Article IV placed peasants under the protection of law and government, but also preserved obligations arising from agreements with landowners. It did not abolish serfdom. The distinction matters: a promise of protection was not the same as equal freedom.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Russia and Prussia carried out the second partition in 1793. The uprising led by Tadeusz Kościuszko in 1794 was defeated. Russia, Prussia and Austria divided the remaining territory in 1795, ending the Commonwealth’s independent institutions.

passages.title: Reform, partitions and what continued
passages.text: Partition changed people’s rulers rather than making communities disappear. Jewish residents, for example, came under Austrian, Prussian or Russian government, with new laws shaping daily life. The histories of the Commonwealth’s inhabitants continued beyond the state’s ending.

The third partition in 1795 divided the Commonwealth’s remaining territory among Russia, Prussia and Austria. Independent government ended; its diverse communities continued under new rulers. The imported endpoint of 1800 for the later map record has therefore been corrected to 1795.

passages.text: Pomeranian culture developed during the Early Iron Age in northern Poland and spread into other regions. Its face-decorated burial urns are especially recognizable. These were communities sharing practices, not one known kingdom. The map’s narrow northern outline misses much of their wider distribution, and its 200 CE endpoint extends too late.

passages.title: Fields, tools and workshops
passages.text: Pomeranian communities lived in small open settlements with houses supported by wooden posts. Farming included wheat, barley and rye, alongside livestock keeping. The museum synthesis describes flexible use of lighter soils, reminding us that everyday life involved fields and animals as well as elaborate graves.

passages.title: Fields, tools and workshops
passages.text: A wooden ard from Lisie Jamy survives in Gdańsk’s collection. Dated broadly to the Early Iron Age, it shows the sort of soil-working equipment used in this regional world. Wood usually decays, so such a tool supplies evidence that metal objects alone would miss.

passages.title: Fields, tools and workshops
passages.text: A hoard from Rekowo contains bronze axes and ankle ornaments, catalogued as Pomeranian and dated broadly between 700 and 400 BCE. Tools and dress ornaments required skilled metalworking. The hoard groups useful and decorative objects together, without preserving its owner’s reason for depositing them.

passages.title: Pots with faces
passages.text: A face urn from Gościcino is dated about 550 to 400 BCE. Its human features belong to a vessel made to hold cremated remains. These striking pots put a face into the archaeological record, but that does not make them reliable portraits of particular individuals.

passages.title: Pots with faces
passages.text: Researchers once tried sorting face urns into male and female examples by deciding which faces were prettier. Gdańsk’s museum explains that anthropological study undermined that approach. Archaeology improves when an appealing assumption is tested against the actual remains.

passages.title: Pots with faces
passages.text: Face urns could show people, animals and horse teams. Their origins are debated: proposed connections include Etruscan vessels in Italy and earlier eye-decorated urns farther north. Similarity provides a question to investigate; it does not by itself establish one migration or a shared identity.

passages.title: Remembering relatives
passages.text: Some graves were chambers built from stone slabs, with gaps filled by rubble and clay and a large stone above. They could hold several urns or more than a dozen. Constructing and revisiting such a burial place required practical work as well as mourning.

passages.title: Remembering relatives
passages.text: The Poznań exhibition describes cist graves receiving additional burials over generations. This gives a picture of repeated family remembrance rather than every funeral creating a completely separate monument. Archaeologists still need evidence from the remains before reconstructing particular biological relationships.

passages.title: Remembering relatives
passages.text: Urns sometimes carry hunting scenes or pictures of pins, shields and spears. Such designs preserve recognizable equipment and activities. The drawing is evidence of what people chose to depict, rather than a complete inventory of what each household owned.

passages.title: Adornment, images and missing words
passages.text: Bird images occur only occasionally on Pomeranian pottery and other objects in the Poznań exhibition. Their relative scarcity is worth recording, but it does not tell us how often people watched birds, told stories about them or heard them around their settlements.

passages.title: Adornment, images and missing words
passages.text: The Chojnice exhibition brings together bronze jewellery, tools and grooming implements alongside urns. These objects connect the funerary evidence with dressing and caring for the body. An ancient person’s possessions could include practical personal equipment as well as conspicuous ornaments.

passages.title: Adornment, images and missing words
passages.text: The images on these urns are not securely deciphered sentences. No writing sample in the makers’ own language is established by the sources used here. A picture of jewellery can tell us something about appearance while leaving the wearer’s name and spoken words unknown.

By the later third century BCE, archaeological patterns associated with Przeworsk and Oksywie replaced Pomeranian traditions in different areas. This is not a recorded conquest of one state. People and practices changed, while the map’s extension to 200 CE misleadingly prolongs the label.

passages.text: This chapter follows Portuguese architecture and learning from the sixteenth to eighteenth centuries, through Lisbon's Belem complex and Coimbra's colleges, laboratories and printing facilities.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Belem, the Hieronymites monastery combined richly carved Manueline decoration with spaces for worship, meals, study and communal life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Belem tower incorporated ribbed cupolas inspired by Islamic architecture. Its design records artistic exchange across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Coimbra University has occupied the Royal Palace of Alcacova since 1537 and expanded through a network of colleges.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: In the eighteenth century, Coimbra added chemistry and other laboratories, a botanical garden and a university press. These facilities linked teaching, experimentation and the circulation of books.

sectionTitles: What a ship’s jars can tell us
A fort that had to save the rain
Grandparents and children in the orchestra

passages.text: Mozambique’s Indian Ocean coast connected local communities with distant trading worlds. Its history also lives in musical skills shared across generations and in the cloths through which women remember their lives. These stories follow particular places and communities within a diverse country.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: The wreck identified as Nossa Senhora da Consolação, lost near Mozambique Island in 1608, yielded containers known as olive jars. A 2023 study compares their thick walls and rounded shapes with other shipwreck finds. Such jars could carry oil, wine or foodstuffs, and their forms helped them fit within a curved hull. The name does not prove that every recovered jar still contained olives.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: Two pots from the same collection were identified with the local Lumbo pottery tradition. They raised a puzzle: was that tradition used later than some land excavations suggested, or did hurried recovery mix material from different wrecks? Mahumane and Simbine leave both possibilities open. A pot can be an exciting discovery partly because it creates a better question, not because it instantly settles one.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: São Sebastião Fortress collected rain from its roofs into cisterns. UNESCO’s history explains how stored water helped people withstand a Dutch siege in 1607 and also supplied visiting ships. Its construction had drawn on stonemasons from Goa, local residents and enslaved labourers. The surviving building preserves engineering achievements within a history of unequal power and coerced work.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: A 2009 restoration report describes repairing channels, pipes and cisterns, then sending water to a new cistern outside the fort for island residents. A roof could work as part of a water supply as well as keep rain off a room. Looking after an old building could therefore help maintain something people needed every day.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: Junior architect Mohammad Cassimo told the restoration team that he had grown up on the island and wanted to help restore it. He joined surveys and daily supervision of the work. His account links learning a profession with caring for a place remembered from childhood.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: Mozambique Island includes stone-and-lime buildings in the north and a southern neighbourhood called macuti, after its palm-leaf roofs. UNESCO describes different building traditions shaped by African, Swahili, Arab and European connections. The island is a lived-in town as well as a heritage site, with homes forming an important part of what survives.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: A 2014 conservation report explains that macuti roofing was becoming harder to obtain and some residents preferred metal roofs. It also records efforts to repair houses and discuss conservation in schools. Keeping an architectural tradition alive involves residents’ costs and choices, as well as the appearance of a roof. A home has to be somewhere people can actually live.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The same report includes a photograph of a public toilet built in 2012 and describes residents and the municipality cleaning living areas. It also records work on water supplies and damaged cisterns. Toilets belong in the history of a town just as much as palaces do: people need practical services while living among historic buildings.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The island’s old hospital dates to 1877. In 2015, the health ministry began conservation work that included cleaning, surveying the structure and investigating drainage and cisterns. This record shows how caring for a healthcare building also meant caring for the systems behind its walls. It does not establish which treatments every patient received there.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: Chopi timbila ensembles in southern Inhambane bring together wooden xylophones of different sizes. Calabashes beneath the wooden bars act as resonators, with beeswax helping seal them. UNESCO’s account describes children playing alongside their grandfathers. Learning means listening and practising within an ensemble, where a young player can hear an experienced musician right beside them.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: These performances are also a way to comment on community life. New pieces accompany weddings and other gatherings; the m’zeno song can use humour and sarcasm to address current events. A musician’s hands may play different rhythms at the same time. The music can ask both the audience and the player to pay close attention.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: A capulana bought in Maputo’s Elephant market in September 2003 has printed circles showing Mozambique’s provinces, surrounded by spears and shields. The British Museum records it as cotton and says cloths of this type are worn by women. The catalogue tentatively places its manufacture in India. Something bought for wearing can also reveal the movement of designs and goods across borders.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: In 2019 and 2020, the WITH Coastal Style project worked with women in Katembe’s fishing communities across Maputo Bay. Researchers collected stories connected with capulanas, including cloths preserved and passed between generations. The project brought these memories into museum and community exhibitions. Keeping a piece of cloth can help a family keep a story, too.

passages.title: Masks, voices and growing up
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2023 account of Makonde mapiko describes masked dancers representing people or animals, with drums and a choir. Performances accompany rites of passage and also other occasions. Singers may challenge the masked dancers with provocative songs. Learning the dance helps pass on community values while young people navigate growing up; it is one particular tradition within Mozambique’s many communities.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: A UN report from 1966 preserved testimony about the effects of colonial labour systems. Speakers described workers compelled into jobs or crop production and men leaving to seek wages abroad, separating families. The record shows why accounts of ports and plantations must also ask who did the work and what choices they had. It records testimony and arguments presented to the committee, rather than a census of every household.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: The island’s Slave Memory Garden commemorates slavery along the Indian Ocean coast. A 2015 government report records restoration work there and describes the memorial as a joint Mozambique and Réunion initiative. The garden makes remembrance part of the present-day town, asking visitors to consider the people whose forced journeys also shaped its maritime history.

Portuguese colonial sovereignty ended when Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975. The country continued through civil war, the 1992 peace agreement and the 1994 multiparty elections. Those political transitions did not erase its communities or the local histories carried in buildings, objects and living practices.
