The surviving building preserves engineering achievements within a history of unequal power and coerced work.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: A 2009 restoration report describes repairing channels, pipes and cisterns, then sending water to a new cistern outside the fort for island residents. A roof could work as part of a water supply as well as keep rain off a room. Looking after an old building could therefore help maintain something people needed every day.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: Junior architect Mohammad Cassimo told the restoration team that he had grown up on the island and wanted to help restore it. He joined surveys and daily supervision of the work. His account links learning a profession with caring for a place remembered from childhood.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: Mozambique Island includes stone-and-lime buildings in the north and a southern neighbourhood called macuti, after its palm-leaf roofs. UNESCO describes different building traditions shaped by African, Swahili, Arab and European connections. The island is a lived-in town as well as a heritage site, with homes forming an important part of what survives.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: A 2014 conservation report explains that macuti roofing was becoming harder to obtain and some residents preferred metal roofs. It also records efforts to repair houses and discuss conservation in schools. Keeping an architectural tradition alive involves residents’ costs and choices, as well as the appearance of a roof. A home has to be somewhere people can actually live.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The same report includes a photograph of a public toilet built in 2012 and describes residents and the municipality cleaning living areas. It also records work on water supplies and damaged cisterns. Toilets belong in the history of a town just as much as palaces do: people need practical services while living among historic buildings.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The island’s old hospital dates to 1877. In 2015, the health ministry began conservation work that included cleaning, surveying the structure and investigating drainage and cisterns. This record shows how caring for a healthcare building also meant caring for the systems behind its walls. It does not establish which treatments every patient received there.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: Chopi timbila ensembles in southern Inhambane bring together wooden xylophones of different sizes. Calabashes beneath the wooden bars act as resonators, with beeswax helping seal them. UNESCO’s account describes children playing alongside their grandfathers. Learning means listening and practising within an ensemble, where a young player can hear an experienced musician right beside them.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: These performances are also a way to comment on community life. New pieces accompany weddings and other gatherings; the m’zeno song can use humour and sarcasm to address current events. A musician’s hands may play different rhythms at the same time. The music can ask both the audience and the player to pay close attention.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: A capulana bought in Maputo’s Elephant market in September 2003 has printed circles showing Mozambique’s provinces, surrounded by spears and shields. The British Museum records it as cotton and says cloths of this type are worn by women. The catalogue tentatively places its manufacture in India. Something bought for wearing can also reveal the movement of designs and goods across borders.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: In 2019 and 2020, the WITH Coastal Style project worked with women in Katembe’s fishing communities across Maputo Bay. Researchers collected stories connected with capulanas, including cloths preserved and passed between generations. The project brought these memories into museum and community exhibitions. Keeping a piece of cloth can help a family keep a story, too.

passages.title: Masks, voices and growing up
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2023 account of Makonde mapiko describes masked dancers representing people or animals, with drums and a choir. Performances accompany rites of passage and also other occasions. Singers may challenge the masked dancers with provocative songs. Learning the dance helps pass on community values while young people navigate growing up; it is one particular tradition within Mozambique’s many communities.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: A UN report from 1966 preserved testimony about the effects of colonial labour systems. Speakers described workers compelled into jobs or crop production and men leaving to seek wages abroad, separating families. The record shows why accounts of ports and plantations must also ask who did the work and what choices they had. It records testimony and arguments presented to the committee, rather than a census of every household.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: The island’s Slave Memory Garden commemorates slavery along the Indian Ocean coast. A 2015 government report records restoration work there and describes the memorial as a joint Mozambique and Réunion initiative. The garden makes remembrance part of the present-day town, asking visitors to consider the people whose forced journeys also shaped its maritime history.

Portuguese colonial sovereignty ended when Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975. The country continued through civil war, the 1992 peace agreement and the 1994 multiparty elections. Those political transitions did not erase its communities or the local histories carried in buildings, objects and living practices.

sectionTitles: Removal, different nations and living language

passages.text: Potawatomi communities helped shape the Great Lakes through farming, fishing, trade and alliances. The imported Michigan outline and broader Bodéwadmi homeland outline are rough historical associations, not fixed borders of one centralized state. Today distinct Potawatomi nations continue across the United States and Canada, with different histories of staying, moving and rebuilding.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: Potawatomi people are associated with the keeping of fire in the Three Fires relationship with Ojibwe and Odawa communities. These were closely connected but distinct peoples. Their histories describe movements around the Great Lakes, so a single map outline cannot capture every community or every generation.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: French trade made Potawatomi communities important regional partners during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Fur exchange connected villages to European goods and diplomacy, while marriages also linked families across those encounters. Trade brought opportunities alongside conflicts over land and political influence.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: A wigwam’s framework used bent saplings covered with birchbark, hides or cattail mats. Potawatomi travelers could also use lighter bark-and-pole shelters. The Cultural Heritage Center explains that housing choices depended on movement and available materials: the best home to stay in was not always the easiest one to pack.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: Seasonal work linked families to particular places. Spring maple sap drew people to sugar camps; late summer and autumn brought wild-rice harvesting and preparations for winter. Moon names could vary between Potawatomi groups, reflecting local surroundings rather than one universal printed calendar.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: Wild-rice harvesting can be a two-person canoe job. One person steers while the other bends stalks over the boat and taps them with wooden sticks. Some seeds land inside the canoe; others fall back into the water, helping seed the next crop.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: Food traditions also live in particular families. In a 2019 interview, Kaya DeerInWater recalled offering wild-rice porridge to his two young sons: one rejected it, while the other eagerly asked for more. Even a culturally important first food can meet a very small, very firm opinion.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: A modern Cultural Heritage Center display depicts spearfishing from a birchbark canoe. Its tools and reconstructed scene explain how Great Lakes waterways supplied food as well as routes for travel. The display is a museum interpretation of earlier life, allowing visitors to examine equipment at close range.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: A Prairie Band Potawatomi cradleboard made between 1880 and 1900 survives in the National Museum of the American Indian. Its carved wood, hide ties and glass beadwork combine practical baby transport with careful making. It was collected from Ci-pa-do-wa in Kansas in 1910, after its period of manufacture.

passages.title: Great Lakes life and knowledge
passages.text: The moccasin game combines concealment, guessing, music and score sticks. In the Cultural Heritage Center’s account, musicians can distract the guessing player while teams compete to collect sticks. Games offered social time and demanding concentration, even when the equipment looked simple.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: In 1838, soldiers forced a group of Potawatomi from northern Indiana toward a Kansas reserve. More than forty people died on the journey remembered as the Trail of Death. The march belongs to a wider history of repeated removals, not the experience of every Potawatomi community in exactly the same way.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: Leopold Pokagon and his community negotiated a right to remain in Michigan, then fought efforts to dislodge them. Land purchased near present-day Dowagiac helped preserve that foothold. The Pokagon Band’s history explains how its present community descends from those who remained, rather than from the Oklahoma removal route.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: The Citizen Potawatomi path developed separately. An 1861 treaty tied individual land allotments to United States citizenship, and families later selected a new reserve in Indian Territory. The first families arrived there in 1872. Other Potawatomi nations retained different communities, governments and homelands.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: The modern written sentence “Bodéwadmi ndaw.” means “I am Potawatomi.” Language director Justin Neely prints the phrase in a 2016 teaching column. His explanation also discusses related names and varying translations of the people’s name; the sample follows this particular community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: In 2022, the Citizen Potawatomi language department reported preparing thousands of words and recordings for an object-recognition learning tool. A learner could photograph something such as a chair or door and hear its Potawatomi name. Children’s books supported learning away from the screen as well.

passages.title: Removal, different nations and living language
passages.text: Citizen Potawatomi Nation joined the new Bodéwadmi Confederation of Tribal Nations in July 2026. The organization, formed the previous year, links distinct nations and rotates administrative leadership with the gathering host. Cooperation crosses today’s national border without making all participating communities a single tribal government.

The map cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of Potawatomi people. Removal, land loss and separate rebuilding produced different community paths. Potawatomi nations continue to govern, teach their languages and cooperate while retaining their own identities.

passages.text: Poverty Point was a great Indigenous earthwork and exchange center in northeastern Louisiana, especially around 1700 to 1100 BCE. Hunter-fisher-gatherers organized its remarkable construction. Whether it housed a large permanent population or hosted repeated gatherings remains debated. The imported outline is misplaced west of the actual site and should not be read as a reliable cultural boundary.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: The builders chose Macon Ridge, elevated above nearby lowlands beside Bayou Macon. That setting offered access to waterways while reducing exposure to ordinary flooding. The landscape was part of the engineering plan before anyone carried the first basket of soil.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: Six curved earthen ridges surround a large plaza, with the outer arc extending more than a kilometer across. Builders combined mounds, open spaces and passageways into a coordinated design. These were planned public works made by people who relied largely on wild foods.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: Materials travelled extraordinary distances: research identifies Arkansas quartz crystal, soapstone from the Atlanta area and copper from the Great Lakes. The collection makes Poverty Point visible as a meeting point in extensive networks of movement and relationships.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: A 2025 interpretation proposes seasonal or temporary gatherings for trading, worship and cooperative building. Researchers point to the lack of securely identified long-term houses and burials. Other presentations describe a residential center, so the size and permanence of its population remain active questions.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: Stone tools include projectile points and tiny flint implements for cutting, scraping and engraving. Clarence Webb studied how local gravel could supply small tool cores. Even where prized stone came from far away, makers looked for useful materials close at hand.

passages.title: A landscape made by cooperation
passages.text: Archaeologists recovered polished bone awls and needles, beads and pendants. These small finds bring sewing, piercing and personal adornment into a story often dominated by mountains of earth. Perishable clothing itself has not survived well enough to reconstruct a complete wardrobe.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: Cooks heated molded clay objects in earth ovens, then used the stored heat to cook food. In a region without abundant local stone, clay offered a practical substitute for hot rocks. The “cooking equipment” drawer would have looked surprisingly lumpy.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: Broken soapstone bowls were sometimes repaired, reused or transformed into beads and pendants. Imported stone was worth keeping after a vessel broke. One object could have a second career, moving from holding food to being worn.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: Charred remains include hickory nuts, pecans, acorns and walnuts, alongside evidence for wild fruits and seeds. Nut shells survive especially well when burned, so their abundance in excavations partly reflects preservation as well as what people ate.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: Food remains vary between Poverty Point-related sites. River and coastal communities had different local resources, and excavation methods also affect what researchers recover. There was no single identical meal eaten throughout this wide network.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: Red jasper owl ornaments and clay human figurines show careful observation and miniature craftsmanship. Their precise meanings are uncertain. A palm-sized owl can preserve an artist’s choices even when the story told about that owl is lost.

passages.title: Dinner, objects and what survives
passages.text: The builders left no contemporary written record from which to quote a sentence. Their own name for this place is unknown; “Poverty Point” came from a nineteenth-century plantation. The surviving earthworks and objects must therefore carry much of the historical evidence.

The main occupation is commonly dated to an end around 1100 BCE, although the reasons for leaving remain uncertain. A later Indigenous group built another mound around 700 CE. Changes at this particular gathering place do not establish that its builders’ descendants vanished. The imported 1000 BCE endpoint is approximate coverage.

sectionTitles: A network of towns and families
Treaty terms, continuing craft and recorded language

passages.text: Powhatan names a people and town as well as the later paramount chief and wider network of Algonquian-speaking communities in Tidewater Virginia. This record’s tiny Richmond-area outline and 1492 to 1500 dates cannot depict the much larger chiefdom known in 1607. The card follows that wider history, with named local examples rather than treating every community as identical.

passages.title: A network of towns and families
passages.text: When the English established Jamestown in 1607, Wahunsunacock, usually called Powhatan by the newcomers, exercised authority over more than 30 tribal groups. Their own chiefs remained important. His network had expanded from six inherited groups through marriage alliances and coercion, combining negotiation with force.

passages.title: A network of towns and families
passages.text: Leadership in much of the Indigenous Chesapeake followed descent through the mother’s family. A chief’s brothers and sisters could therefore come before his own children in succession, and women could be chiefs. European ideas about a prince simply inheriting his father’s throne do not fit this pattern.

passages.title: A network of towns and families
passages.text: At Werowocomoco, archaeologists found post stains, hearths and pits that survived below later plowing. Houses used frames of saplings covered with woven mats. A dark mark in the soil can reveal where a wooden wall once stood even after the wood itself has disappeared.

passages.title: A network of towns and families
passages.text: Much of Werowocomoco’s pottery contained crushed shell mixed into the clay. Makers left fabric impressions or stamped lines on the surfaces. Those fragments help researchers identify the settlement’s sequence, while also preserving tiny traces of the textures that craftspeople worked with.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: Chesapeake households drew food from fields, forests and water: crops, shellfish, game and fish all mattered. Seasonal movement included winter hunting camps away from town. Late winter could bring the hardest stretch, when stored supplies ran low and finding game became difficult.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: Dugout canoes carried people for fishing, trade, warfare and governing a river-connected territory. Jamestown Settlement’s guide describes vessels reaching 40 feet long. Burning and scraping wood hollowed the trunk, a demanding job that turned a tree into a useful route across the water.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: Powhatan households generally cooked outdoors, according to the museum’s account. Pots, smoking racks and fires made cooking areas busy workspaces. Getting dinner ready also depended on fishing, farming, hunting and gathering, so the meal represented work done far beyond the person tending the pot.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: Pamunkey artist Ethan Brown depicts a child on a raised platform watching a cornfield and frightening away hungry animals. He presents the scene as an interpretation of ancestral life. For that child, protecting the harvest meant being a very active scarecrow, with considerably more responsibility than a straw one.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: Mussel shells served as shaving tools, according to the park’s account of Powhatan daily life. Women also made mats, baskets, pots and cordage and learned to recognize edible plants through changing seasons. Household expertise involved knowing materials and landscapes as well as having steady hands.

passages.title: Food, transport and everyday jobs
passages.text: During the winter of 1608 to 1609, English demands for corn met harvests already reduced by severe drought. Food shortages helped turn exchange into threats and violence. The farming families were managing their own supplies and hunger; the colonists were not asking from an endlessly full pantry.

passages.title: Treaty terms, continuing craft and recorded language
passages.text: The treaty of October 5, 1646 required Necotowance to acknowledge the English Crown’s authority and allowed the governor to confirm successors. It also demanded 20 beaver skins each year. These provisions made the unequal political relationship concrete through authority over leaders and a recurring payment.

passages.title: Treaty terms, continuing craft and recorded language
passages.text: A pottery school opened on the Pamunkey reservation in 1932 to help women earn money during the Great Depression. Brown includes it in his family and community history. The tradition changed its economic setting while skilled makers continued turning local clay into objects people could use and sell.

passages.title: Treaty terms, continuing craft and recorded language
passages.text: Written language sample: suckahanna, “water.” The park’s trail brochure identifies this Virginia Algonquian word in records made by John Smith and William Strachey. It is a colonial observer’s written rendering of a spoken language, not a surviving Powhatan-authored inscription or a newly invented translation.

War and the 1646 treaty greatly reduced the chiefdom’s political independence. That transformation did not erase its constituent peoples. Pamunkey and other descendant communities continued, preserving and adapting traditions despite lost land and colonial pressure. The imported 1500 endpoint belongs to the map record, not to their survival.

sectionTitles: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom

passages.text: Roman Mstyslavych united Galicia and Volhynia in 1199, creating a powerful state in southwestern Rus. His successors negotiated between local nobles, neighbouring kingdoms and Mongol overlords. Its towns supported crafts and ambitious builders. The imported outline’s southern extent is uncertain and should not be treated as a precise historical border.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Danylo accepted a crown from Pope Innocent IV in 1253 while seeking military help against the Mongols. A crown could advertise royal standing, but it could not supply an army by itself. The hoped-for western assistance did not arrive in the form Danylo needed.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Danylo had already visited Batu Khan’s court and acknowledged his supremacy in 1246. Later Mongol pressure forced the dismantling of fortifications. The kingdom’s survival therefore involved uncomfortable compromises as well as victories; paying homage and surrendering defences limited what its rulers could do.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Trade connected the principality with other Rus lands, Poland, Hungary, Bohemia, Lithuania and the Byzantine world. Merchants crossed political and linguistic frontiers that a coloured map can make look much more solid than they were in everyday commercial life.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: At Danylo’s residence in Kholm, now Chełm in Poland, excavators have recovered walls and architectural fragments made with green local stone. The chronicle also describes white and green building materials. The remains give archaeologists a way to test a written description against an actual building site.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: The green stone was relatively easy to carve into mouldings and intricate reliefs. Its beauty came with a practical drawback: wet, freezing conditions could damage it. Medieval builders had to juggle appearance, workability and durability, much as builders still do when choosing materials.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: Researchers studying white building pieces from the residence identified a material they interpret as an artificial, marble-like stone. Their analysis suggests chalk and silica from horsetail plants, hardened under hot, wet conditions. This proposed recipe makes the building site look surprisingly experimental, with plants contributing more than garden decoration.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: The Galician-Volhynian Chronicle combines narratives centred on Danylo with a later Volhynian section. Its authors favoured strong princes and criticized rebellious nobles. They were skilled storytellers with political loyalties, so their descriptions are valuable evidence that historians compare with archaeology and other texts.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: Volodymyr Vasylkovych, a later thirteenth-century ruler in Volhynia, supported churches, literature and ecclesiastical art and assembled a substantial library. The chronicle praised his learning. Books required expensive materials and skilled labour, making a princely library both a personal interest and an important act of patronage.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: Zvenyhorod was already an important town before the union of 1199. Its wet ground preserved wooden building remains, wooden dishes and leather footwear that often decay elsewhere. These earlier finds let us picture kitchens, feet and household work, instead of seeing the region only through its rulers.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: Archaeologists identified craft and household areas along the Bilka River and recovered many ornaments, including glass jewellery. Together, the workshop landscape and personal possessions reveal a town where skilled production and dressing up were parts of life long before the united principality was founded.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: A birchbark letter from around 1120 to 1140 records Goven’s widow demanding sixty kunas connected with a boat. She threatens to bring a prince’s official if the debtor refuses. The message preserves a woman pursuing a household claim, with the distinctly unromantic problem of collecting money owed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The same earlier Zvenyhorod letter opens “ѿ говѣновое : ко нѣжьньцю”, meaning “From Goven’s widow to Nezhenets”. This is the catalogue’s historical Cyrillic transcription with editorial word divisions; “widow” is supplied from the interpretation. It illustrates local writing before the kingdom’s foundation, rather than a thirteenth-century royal document.

The death of Yurii II Boleslav in 1340 ended the united state’s dynastic phase and brought prolonged competition between Polish and Lithuanian rulers. Its territories were divided through subsequent struggles. The map’s 1279 cutoff is a coverage limit, not the kingdom’s historical ending.

sectionTitles: A river city and its workshops
Useful objects and places of learning

passages.text: Kyiv’s regional principality remained important after the wider Rus world divided among competing dynasties. Its river trade, craft neighbourhoods and religious buildings connected it to distant places. The Mongol attack of 1240 devastated the city, but political and urban life continued in changing forms.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Kyiv stood where north-south and east-west trade routes met. Competing dynasties fought for its prestigious throne. This regional principality covered only part of the wider Rus world that had earlier acknowledged Kyiv’s leadership.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Podil, the lower riverside district, contained a harbour, customs house and large marketplace. Potters, pitch makers and tanners worked in different quarters. Merchants arriving by water entered a busy working landscape below the upper town, where goods had to be unloaded, assessed and exchanged.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Archaeologists have identified glass-working complexes in twelfth- and early thirteenth-century Podil. Workshops belonged to household properties, with small furnaces inside wooden buildings. Their locations near waterways made practical sense where hot work and timber walls created a serious fire risk.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Some glass workers reheated ready-made glass rather than making every ingredient from scratch. Crucibles, lumps of glass, damaged products and furnace deposits help identify the process. A broken bead can therefore be valuable evidence: a modern excavator may be delighted by what a medieval craftsperson threw away.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Podil’s workshops produced beads, bracelets and rings in different colour ranges. One workshop’s products emphasized blue, pale blue and green; another used yellow, green, pale blue and violet. These were ornaments made in batches for a market, bringing colour into the archaeological record without revealing each buyer’s wealth.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: A study of the middle Dnipro region shows that bone and antler tools remained useful in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Craftspeople used them for work involving leather, fur and textiles. Pointed pieces had several functions, so calling every sharp bone an awl would oversimplify the evidence.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: The same regional study examines bone skates used for moving over snow and ice. Wear on some examples suggests that they instead served as tools. Archaeologists compare working surfaces carefully: an object shaped like a skate does not automatically prove that its owner spent the afternoon skating.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Saint Sophia’s eleventh-century interior still preserves mosaics and frescoes made with Byzantine and local participation. The Virgin Orans raises her hands in prayer, while other compositions show Christ and the apostles. These older images remained part of the religious environment inherited by the later principality.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: The Kyiv-Pechersk monastery began in the eleventh century and developed around caves overlooking the Dnipro. It became a major religious and cultural centre. Its familiar skyline includes much later rebuilding, so the large Baroque complex visible today is not a photograph of what thirteenth-century Kyiv looked like.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Saint Sophia’s walls preserve notes made by clergy as well as visitors. Researcher Viacheslav Korniienko describes names accompanied by tally marks that counted services performed for particular people. The cathedral thus holds traces of practical record-keeping alongside its grand religious paintings.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Korniienko also identifies writing exercises and drawings that he interprets as pupils’ caricatures of teachers. Wax tablets were available for writing, yet some marks ended up on the cathedral walls. Students finding an unofficial extra surface for their work may sound rather familiar.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: “Господи, помози” means “Lord, help”. These words begin a common medieval prayer formula scratched into Saint Sophia’s walls, quoted by the reserve’s researcher. They are shown in his normalized Cyrillic transcription of the historical Church Slavonic wording, rather than copied from one individual graffito’s letter shapes.

Kyiv’s political status changed repeatedly after 1240. Under Lithuanian rule the principality was abolished, later restored, and finally replaced by Kyiv voivodeship in 1471. The city survived these changes. Its imported map endpoint of 1279 is not the date when Kyiv ceased to exist.

passages.text: Polotsk was a Rus principality centred on the Western Dvina in what is now northern Belarus. River connections supported Baltic trade, while rival branches of its ruling family shared and contested power. Its surviving art and excavated household objects reveal both ambitious religious patronage and busy urban communities.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Connections along the Western Dvina and Neman linked the Polotsk lands with Baltic trading centres. Important towns included Minsk, Vitebsk and Drutsk. Political authority was divided among princely relatives, so the region’s economy cannot be reduced to a single ruler sitting in one capital.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Saint Sophia Cathedral was built in the eleventh century, before the map’s displayed phase. Parts of its foundations, apses, masonry and wall paintings survive beneath and within later rebuilding. The cathedral visible today therefore contains several historical buildings’ worth of change, rather than an untouched medieval exterior.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Euphrosyne of Polotsk founded a women’s religious community and became an important patron of sacred art. The twelfth-century Saviour church and the cross commissioned in 1161 connect a named woman with major artistic work. Her influence is visible in expensive objects and architecture, not only in later stories about her.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: The Saviour church’s medieval builders used thin bricks, lime mortar and specially shaped bricks for curved details. A staircase runs within the western wall, leading to an upper gallery with small chapels. Such compact planning made a relatively small building contain several distinct spaces for worship.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: The church preserves extensive twelfth-century wall painting beneath much later decoration. Modern conservators separated later painted layers and transferred them to new supports while revealing the older frescoes. Restoring this building meant saving more than one period of art, rather like carefully keeping every layer of a very fragile cake.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Polotsk excavations produced large wooden pestles and parts of barrels used in household work. A thirteenth-century barrel base even retained a cucumber seed. It is a tiny piece of later evidence, but a useful reminder that food storage depended on containers somebody had to make and maintain.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Archaeologists found livestock buildings and manure in towns of the Polotsk lands. Thirteenth-century deposits at Polotsk were particularly rich in it. Animals belonged inside the urban economy, bringing food and useful materials along with a smell that no reconstruction painting can quite deliver.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Wooden spades from Polotsk were cut from single pieces of timber and lacked iron edges. Their shape suited softer ground. These plain tools put gardening and digging beside the finer crafts usually displayed in museums: much of daily work involved ordinary materials and repeated effort.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Twelfth- and thirteenth-century chess pieces were found in Polotsk and neighbouring towns. Many were abstract forms carved or turned from bone, rather than tiny realistic kings and horses. A surviving piece preserves the possibility of an evening’s game, although it cannot tell us who won.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: Lazar Bogsha’s cross of 1161 had a wooden core covered with gold and gilded silver plates, with settings for gemstones and relics. The precious surface depended on a carefully assembled structure beneath it. Surviving photographs document an object that combined carpentry, metalwork and religious devotion.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: Its enamel images were made directly on the cross’s own plates, an important detail in Alekseev’s study. They were designed for this commission rather than simply attached as ready-made decorations. Saints and plant-like ornaments turned a small surface into an exceptionally intricate composition.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: One word in the cross’s inscription is “злото”, meaning “gold”. This is the historical word in Alekseev’s Cyrillic transcription, with our literal English translation. The longer inscription recorded the gift and its value and warned against removing it: the beautiful object also carried its own instructions.

Polotsk was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1307 and retained a measure of autonomy afterward. Its political institutions changed while the city continued. The imported map ends this record in 1200, well before that transition.

sectionTitles: Documents and buildings that travelled through time

passages.text: Vladimir-Suzdal became a leading power in northeastern Rus, supported by fertile agricultural districts and connections to Volga trade. Its princes sponsored distinctive white-stone churches, while townspeople made tools, ornaments and household goods. Political power later fragmented and came increasingly under Mongol and Muscovite control.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: The fertile Suzdal Opolye supplied an agricultural base, while the Volga connected the region with eastern trade. Rulers benefited from both food production and movement along rivers. Their power rested on working landscapes and transport routes as well as soldiers and impressive stone buildings.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: Archaeology shows that Suzdal continued growing after the princely centre shifted to Vladimir in 1157. Some nearby rural settlements lay only a few hundred metres from its developed areas. Fields, gardens and town streets formed a close patchwork, with no neat modern boundary between urban and rural life.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: By the later thirteenth century, the territory directly controlled by the grand prince had shrunk as separate principalities multiplied. Mongol khans awarded the right to hold the senior title. A grand-sounding title therefore did not always mean that its holder directly governed every town coloured into the older region.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Suzdal’s excavated combs include many from twelfth- and early thirteenth-century layers. Double-sided examples often had closely spaced teeth on one edge and wider teeth on the other. Hair care had its own equipment, and an ordinary morning could begin with a familiar battle against tangles.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Most identifiable comb material in Baranov’s study was dense deer antler, with animal bone used less often. Some combs were cut from one piece; others were assembled from separate parts. Making a useful comb required selecting suitable material and cutting a row of small, regular teeth.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Workshop evidence links Suzdal’s bone and antler workers with combs, small crosses and knife handles. Unfinished and defective pieces help identify production rather than just ownership. A broken object can be especially useful to an archaeologist when it reveals what a craftsperson was trying to make.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: A lead seal found in Suzdal carries a princely sign attributed to Yuri Dolgoruky. Such seals were attached to documents, which could disappear while the metal survived. The find helps connect the town’s archaeological remains with the ruler whose administration made it an important centre before Vladimir’s rise.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: Another seal belonged to Gregory, a notary, and dates to an earlier phase around Vladimir Monomakh’s time. Its Greek text contains errors that researchers use to discuss where its stamp was made. A tiny object preserves contact with Byzantine documentary habits, although Gregory’s exact employer remains uncertain.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: The region’s buildings were faced with carefully worked blocks of white limestone. Their stone carving made walls into places to look closely, not simply surfaces that held up roofs. Saint Demetrios in Vladimir is among the best-known surviving examples of this decorated architecture.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: Vladimir’s Assumption Cathedral preserves a medieval building with important later painting, including work associated with Andrei Rublev in 1408. Its different layers should be read separately: a twelfth-century structure can carry art made long after the powerful pre-Mongol principality had changed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: An inscription on the cathedral at Pereslavl-Zalessky records Prince Andrei’s assassination in 1174 and names people blamed for it. Researchers used detailed photographs and three-dimensional modelling to improve the reading. They propose that it was carved in 1175 or 1176, making it a near-contemporary response to political violence.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The inscription includes “Овому вѣчная память”, meaning “Eternal remembrance to him”. This follows the scholarly edition’s simplified historical Cyrillic transcription, with our English rendering based on its Russian translation. The words commemorate the dead prince; they are part of a political and religious message carved into a church wall.

Vladimir’s grand-princely authority gradually passed into the hands of Moscow’s rulers. In 1389 Dmitry Donskoy transmitted it to his son as an inheritance. This was a long political transformation; the map’s 1279 endpoint is only a coverage boundary.

sectionTitles: Money and the work of exchange
A later letter brings us closer to a person

passages.text: Wallachia occupied a position between the Danube and Carpathian trading routes. Princes, merchants, farmers, craftspeople and religious communities supported its economy. Coins and monastery buildings reveal early-fifteenth-century activity, while a later letter preserves the concerns of a named person communicating across the mountains.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: In Mircea the Elder’s time, Wallachian ducats and smaller bani circulated alongside coins of earlier rulers. A change of prince did not require every older coin to vanish. Surviving money shows a layered everyday economy.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: Foreign currency entered Wallachia while local issues travelled abroad. Coin finds make exchange visible, although a coin’s presence alone cannot identify its owner. Trade connected the principality with wider Danubian and Central European routes.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: The ruler needed money for troops as well as commerce. The museum links increased minting with both demands. A coin could help purchase goods or finance military power; its meaning depended on how it was used.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: A study of 66 early coins of Mircea held in Budapest uses X-ray analysis to investigate their metal composition. Researchers combine measurements with hoard histories. Where an old collection’s findspot is uncertain, the study identifies that limitation.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Wallachia’s routes carried cloth, tools, weapons, spices and other goods between different markets. Merchants required local transport and provisioning. Imported objects therefore depended on many workers who never travelled the full distance themselves.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Brașov supplied agricultural tools and manufactured goods to neighbouring regions and received their products. Its borderland position made it a meeting place for traders. Cross-mountain exchange could matter to a household’s tools as much as to a prince’s revenue.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Cozia Monastery stands beside the Olt. Its late-1380s foundation and 1388 charter precede this atlas segment but explain a major institution already present in 1400. Buildings and documents can establish different parts of the same history.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Cozia’s early interior painting is dated to 1390 to 1391. Producing such an interior required organized craft work as well as patronage. The surviving church should be read in layers, because later repairs changed parts of its appearance.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Carved window surrounds and rosettes at Cozia belong to its early decoration. The church record also dates painting renewal and a fountain to 1517. Attractive details seen together today need not all have been made at the same time.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: In 1521 Neacșu of Câmpulung warned Johannes Benkner of Brașov about Ottoman preparations. This is later than the map’s 1492 endpoint. A named letter writer lets us see information moving through personal contacts, not only royal proclamations.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: Ипак дау щире (Ipak dau știre) means “And again, I give notice.” This Cyrillic-script sample reproduces the opening formula of Neacșu’s 1521 letter in a modern transcription. A Slavonic linking phrase introduces Romanian words; the message illustrates the difference between a language and the letters used to write it.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: Neacșu asks the recipient to keep his words private and refers to reports from other people, including a relative. The letter exposes a chain of information and uncertainty: its warnings tell us what the writer had heard, not everything that actually happened.

Wallachia did not disappear at the atlas’s 1492 endpoint. Its later political history continued for centuries. In 1859 Wallachia and Moldavia elected the same ruler, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, creating the union from which the modern Romanian state developed. This later institutional union is distinct from the medieval interval shown here.

passages.text: This chapter follows the designed landscapes and museum ambitions associated with Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It focuses on architects, craftspeople and the institutions that organized their work.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederick II commissioned Sanssouci between 1745 and 1747. The palace later hosted the French writer Voltaire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Potsdam's parks combined architecture with landscape gardening. Builders, painters, sculptors and gardeners contributed to the ensemble.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: During the nineteenth century, Peter Joseph Lenne planned changes to the Havel landscape around Potsdam. Designed parkland linked water, buildings and views.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Museum Island project in Berlin began in the nineteenth century. It treated museum architecture and the display of art and archaeology as a connected public undertaking.

sectionTitles: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
A language survives in later pages

passages.text: Medieval Prussians were Western Baltic communities, distinct from the later German kingdom. Regional groups had different histories. Trading settlements, burials and later writings illuminate particular places and periods.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: At Truso, near modern Elbląg, excavators found rows of timber houses and working areas. Most evidence dates before or around 1000. The port connected Scandinavian and Baltic networks; it should not stand for every Prussian village.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Some Truso houses had three rooms, with hearths and loom remains indicating different activities. Households needed space for work and storage as well as sleep. The archaeological plans reveal arrangements that written accounts rarely describe.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: The port preserved remains of clinker-built boats, whose overlapping planks were joined with iron rivets. Surviving details suggest vessels around nine to eleven metres long. Boatbuilding knowledge supported the movement of goods and people.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Truso’s combs and weights can be compared with finds from other Baltic ports. Matching types help investigate connections and chronology, but a familiar object design does not identify an individual owner’s birthplace or language.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: The settlement’s drainage ditch removed excess water and divided areas of activity. The nearby stream was also regulated. Keeping a working waterfront usable required routine control of water, as well as boats and successful trading.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Truso smiths used imported iron bars and local bog iron to make tools and weapons. Weaving traces occur in many buildings. Manufacturing belonged inside the settlement’s daily work; trade was not simply waiting for a foreign ship to unload.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: An illustrated mid-eleventh-century grave assemblage from Irzekapinis in Sambia includes weapons, horse equipment, pottery and parts of weighing equipment. Their association records one burial’s treatment. It does not tell us what every person owned during life.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: Regional groups included Sambians, Natangians and Bartians. Local leadership and assemblies varied; one atlas colour simplifies communities that did not share a centralized national government.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: Missionaries Adalbert and Bruno died in 997 and 1009 during missions in the region or its borderlands. Christian accounts preserve these events through the particular viewpoints of missionary writers.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: Kayle rekyse is an Old Prussian greeting, translated “Hello, mister!” in the study of the Basel Epigram. It appears on folio 63ra of manuscript F.V.2 beside a text dated 1369. This attested sample is later than the atlas’s 1000 to 1200 interval.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: The epigram’s handwriting and several readings are debated. Comparing letter shapes and paper watermarks helps scholars test interpretations. Its playful greeting belongs to a particular manuscript setting, not a reconstructed conversation invented for medieval Prussians.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: Longer Old Prussian texts survive in sixteenth-century Christian catechisms; the Elbing vocabulary records words with German equivalents. These later documents preserve language knowledge while also reflecting the religious and educational purposes of their compilers.

The Teutonic Order conquered the Prussian lands during the thirteenth century, after the atlas segment ends. War, displacement and unequal rule transformed communities, but people and their language survived for generations. Later language loss and assimilation were processes, not a disappearance of everyone in one conquest year.

passages.text: Pskov was a northwestern Rus city with its own civic institutions, law and coinage. Its builders developed a distinctive church architecture beside the Velikaya River. Moscow ended its republican government in 1510, although local crafts, buildings and urban life continued.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Pskov’s builders combined compact, roughly cubic church bodies with domes, porches and open belfries. Their use of local building materials and restrained decoration gave the city a recognizable architectural character. The school reached particular prominence in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Churches stood within gardens, walls and fences rather than appearing as isolated monuments. UNESCO recognizes ten surviving religious monuments representing this architectural tradition. The whole group spans several centuries, so its oldest and newest buildings should not all be imagined standing together in republican Pskov.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: The veche, or civic assembly, was an important institution of Pskov’s republic. Its bell could call people together and became a powerful symbol of local government. In January 1510, Vasily III ordered the bell removed and the assembly and elected posadnik offices abolished.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Pskov began issuing its own coins in 1425, including the denga and a smaller denomination called the chetverettsa. Different principalities still used their own monetary systems. A merchant therefore needed to recognize more than a coin’s shine before agreeing that a payment was sufficient.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Some Pskov coins show Prince Dovmont holding a sword, while others carry a leopard on the reverse. The museum dates the leopard design from 1460. These images made civic identity portable: a little piece of Pskov could travel in somebody’s money pouch.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: The Judicial Charter survives in manuscript copies made after the republic’s ending. Its text combines several layers of law, and scholars debate its compilation dates. Modern editors divide it into 120 articles covering courts, property, inheritance and offences, a remarkably detailed window into the disputes people expected to face.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: The charter allowed a master craftsman to sue for unpaid wages. It also recognized certain property claims by dependent workers and herdsmen. Making something useful and actually getting paid could be separate problems, familiar enough to need written rules.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: Women could inherit property and make wills. If a husband died without a will, his widow could use his property while she remained unmarried. These rules tell us how lawmakers organized household security; they do not establish that every widow could easily enforce her rights.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: The charter required children to support their parents or risk losing their inheritance. Family care thus appeared in property law as well as personal obligation. It is a practical reminder that medieval households had to plan for ageing relatives, just as they had to plan for children.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: An earlier birchbark letter from Kiurik and Gerasim asks Onfim to send squirrel skins because customers want them. It also complains that a man named Ksinofont has damaged their business. The catalogue places the letter around 1260 to 1280: medieval commerce came with impatient messages and troublesome partners.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: Another letter asks Vatsiuta to load cloth promptly onto a boat and present it as his own. The sender promises to settle the transport charge. This late thirteenth- or early fourteenth-century message makes river transport tangible, down to the awkward question of who would pay for the journey.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Pskov letter 6 begins “ѿ кюрика и ѿ герасима”, meaning “From Kiurik and from Gerasim”. These are historical Cyrillic forms in the scholarly transcription, with word divisions added by editors. The greeting introduces an ordinary commercial letter, rather than a royal proclamation or a church service.

Vasily III of Moscow ended Pskov’s republican institutions in 1510 and replaced their authority with his governors. Pskov remained an inhabited and productive city. The map’s 1530 endpoint is an imported coverage boundary, not the republic’s ending date.

passages.text: The Ptolemies governed Egypt from Alexandria as Macedonian monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Their kingdom brought Greek-speaking rulers into a society with enduring Egyptian languages, temples and crafts. Surviving decrees and estate papers reveal both royal institutions and everyday work.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone preserves a priestly decree honoring Ptolemy V in 196 BCE. Soldiers found it reused in a fort at el-Rashid in 1799, so its discovery location is not the original setting of the decree.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian and Greek versions address different readers of the same royal decree. This is evidence of multilingual administration and priestly authority, not three different spoken languages.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Villagers digging for fertilizer uncovered the Zenon archive near ancient Philadelphia in 1914 to 1915. The documents illuminate a third-century BCE estate, but their exact original findspot was not recorded.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A lease copied in a lawsuit prepared by Zenon required tenants to grow wheat and barley and deliver grain rent at Philadelphia. Clauses about seed advances and outstanding debts reveal how agricultural work depended on both produce and credit.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: The same document allowed recovery from debtors, their guarantors and their property. Read beside its crop instructions, it shows the unequal bargaining power behind estate production, rather than an idyllic picture of farming.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A papyrus dated 7 May 254 BCE records a stolen donkey. This small dispute survives because estate papers were kept, giving a glimpse of transport animals and ordinary losses outside royal histories.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: Eratosthenes worked at the Alexandrian library in the third century BCE. He compared summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria with an estimated distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: His original measurement treatise is lost; the method survives in later authors. Uncertainty about the length of the stadium makes a single modern claim for his percentage accuracy misleading.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: The sieve associated with Eratosthenes identifies prime numbers by removing multiples. It is a concrete example of mathematical reasoning connected with Alexandria's scholarly world.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Temple workshops made faience vessels and colorful glass inlays. Egyptian and Greek forms coexisted, and royal portraits could combine Greek hair with Egyptian poses.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Egyptian temples remained centers of scholarship and worship, supported by rulers who also promoted their own royal cults.

passages.title: Trade and correspondence
passages.text: Zenon's files include letters about shipments of wheat and wine as well as official and personal business. Their survival connects agricultural production with transport and administration, rather than treating trade as an abstract royal achievement.
Roman takeover in 30 BCE ended the dynasty after Cleopatra VII's defeat. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continued beyond the change of rulers.

passages.text: Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: At Chaco, builders planned multistory Great Houses whose construction could span generations. Their masonry and shared layouts mark a regional architectural tradition.

passages.title: Science and landscape
passages.text: Many Chaco structures were oriented toward solar, lunar or cardinal directions. Their placement linked buildings to a meaningful surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mesa Verde preserves farming terraces, check dams, reservoirs and ditches as well as houses. These remains document the engineering of everyday subsistence.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads connected Chaco Great Houses across the region. Some major buildings may have hosted periodic ceremonies and exchange rather than dense permanent populations.

passages.title: Living architecture
passages.text: At Taos, families maintain adobe homes by renewing earthen plaster. Taos describes that work as an ongoing connection between ancestors and the present.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Changes in ancestral settlements did not end Pueblo life. Mesa Verde remains a living connection to present-day Pueblo peoples, and Taos continues as a sovereign community.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

passages.text: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.

passages.text: Qin began as a frontier state of the Zhou in the Wei River valley in 770 BCE and grew, by reform and conquest, into the power that unified China in 221 BCE. The empire created a centralized bureaucratic state that replaced feudal fragmentation. Though the dynasty lasted only fifteen years, its institutional innovations became the foundation of all subsequent Chinese empires.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin reward farming and soldiering, punish by fixed law and break the power of the old nobility, the Legalist programme the empire would follow.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Legalism becomes state orthodoxy, emphasizing strict laws, harsh punishments and absolute state power.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Books of rival philosophies are ordered burned, and by tradition scholars are executed the next year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The First Emperor seeks immortality through alchemy and travels to sacred mountains.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of weights, measures, axle widths and written script across the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Construction of the Great Wall begins, connecting earlier defensive walls along the northern frontier.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Terracotta Army, some 8,000 life-size soldiers, is completed to guard the First Emperor's tomb; work had begun on his accession in 246 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, crossbow mechanisms and standardized coinage show unified artistic standards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The small seal script standardized for official use, later replaced by clerical script.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The empire divided into thirty-six commanderies governed by appointed officials rather than hereditary lords.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Corvée labor conscripted for massive public works: roads, the Lingqu canal linking the Yangzi and Pearl river systems, and the Epang palace.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Harsh legal code applied uniformly across the empire.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Standardized bronze coins in round shape with square hole become the empire's currency.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial highways facilitate military movement and commercial exchange.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name China probably derives from Qin, by way of Sanskrit and Persian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Centralized bureaucratic administration replaced feudalism in all subsequent dynasties.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Standardized writing enabled cultural unity across linguistic diversity.
After the First Emperor's death, popular rebellions and civil war led to the dynasty's collapse in 206 BCE; Liu Bang, the victor of the wars that followed, founded the Han.

sectionTitles: Letters and people beyond a ruler

passages.text: Rabih Fadlallah built a military state through conquest and enslavement, eventually occupying Borno in 1893. This map’s eastern polygon lies far from his later capital, Dikwa: it cannot show the full extent of his changing power.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Rabih had served the slave-trading forces associated with Zubayr and his son Sulayman. After their defeat, he and followers moved west; commanders elected him amir in 1879. His mobile force preceded the later state centred on Dikwa.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Raiding devastated communities in southern Chad and northern Central Africa. Captured people could be forced into Rabih’s army, so military growth also meant families separated and people deprived of freedom. Resistance to French conquest does not erase these harms.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Military commanders supervised local rulers and collected resources through enlarged territorial holdings. Rabih retained some experienced Borno officials, but their room to act depended on submission to his authority.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Before the invasion, weekly markets connected farmers and townspeople through grain, milk products, fish, meat and building materials. War and neighbouring states’ blockades damaged those networks. The loss was felt in ordinary shopping and meals, not just in royal income.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Food shortages worsened by 1898. Areas such as Gujba, which escaped some destruction, became important sources of grain. An army could capture a capital quickly; rebuilding the farming that fed it was much harder.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Travelling toward Dikwa after Rabih’s defeat in 1900, Émile Gentil first mistook newly planted fields for empty plains. He then noticed channels designed to hold rainwater. The apparent emptiness was a visitor’s misunderstanding of farming.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Gentil’s June 1900 journey also records local people bringing fresh milk and butter. Millet fields and livestock supported settlements along his route. These are observations from just after the war, rather than a menu for every household.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Dikwa’s palace builders bundled smaller timbers into supporting pillars where large wood was scarce. Gentil described thick walls, several courtyards and plastered surfaces: practical engineering on a grand scale.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: In the market Gentil saw local cotton alongside imported fabrics, sugar, coffee, tea and metal goods. His account describes a busy city after conquest; it does not cancel the evidence of severe wartime disruption elsewhere.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: A letter of 28 November 1894 from al-Sanusi al-Bakr proposed trade on behalf of Rabih and the ruler of Wadai. It discussed animals, textiles and guns, but also trading enslaved people. Diplomatic paperwork exposes coercion behind the word commerce.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: Writing sample: “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God,” appears in that 1894 Arabic letter’s opening. This is a normalized transcription from the published edition. The author was al-Sanusi, writing about Rabih’s trade interests; these are not words from a verified Rabih autograph.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: Rabih’s death did not make his followers disappear. His son Fadlallah led a surviving force, and families moved with the defeated army. Their later negotiations and flight belong to the story too, beyond a map’s single ending date.

Rabih died in the battle near Kousseri on 22 April 1900. Fadlallah and other survivors continued resisting and negotiating into 1901. Colonial partition followed; the peoples and communities affected by these wars continued their own histories.
