sectionTitles: A small republic with powerful neighbors
Memorials, a message and the end

passages.text: The Free City of Kraków was a small republic created in 1815 under the protection and supervision of Austria, Prussia and Russia. It included surrounding countryside as well as the city. Austria annexed it in 1846; the atlas’s 1878 endpoint belongs to map coverage, not continuing republican independence.

passages.title: A small republic with powerful neighbors
passages.text: The state included Kraków, seventeen rural communes and three privately owned small towns: Chrzanów, Trzebinia and Nowa Góra. Its story therefore includes villagers and small-town residents, rather than only the people living around Kraków’s famous market square.

passages.title: A small republic with powerful neighbors
passages.text: A Governing Senate and an Assembly of Representatives handled legislation and administration. University and cathedral representatives also participated in the political structure. The protecting powers could intervene above these institutions, and eventually controlled Senate appointments: the word “free” did not mean unrestricted sovereignty.

passages.title: A small republic with powerful neighbors
passages.text: Different legal inheritances coexisted, including the Napoleonic Code, Austrian rules and the republic’s own legislation. Officials and residents had to work through this layered legal landscape. A border or government changing did not automatically replace every rule governing property and disputes.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: Between 1822 and 1830, former fortifications became much of the public garden now called Planty. A stretch around the Barbican and St Florian’s Gate survived. Space once meant to keep people out became a place where residents could walk around their city.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: After 1826, work extended around Wawel Hill, with vineyards and peach orchards on its southern slopes. Later Austrian military rebuilding destroyed them. The republic’s landscape included productive gardens as well as monuments: there were peaches below the royal hill.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: Czernichów’s school history records that residents paid contributions toward a new school building in 1839, ordered by the republic’s Senate. This connects a national decision with money raised locally. It was a village classroom project, distinct from the agricultural school founded there much later.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: The 1817 regulations reorganized Kraków’s Jewish communal administration. Committees oversaw welfare, charity and the hospital. These arrangements show a community providing care while negotiating a state that increasingly directed its internal institutions.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: A Jewish school with a Polish curriculum moved into Kazimierz’s town hall in 1835. Families faced pressures about language, schooling and residence: officials made some privileges conditional on clothing, education and wealth. The republic’s liberal reputation must be read alongside these discriminatory conditions.

passages.title: Gardens, classrooms and care
passages.text: At the university, Walenty Litwiński taught criminal law and procedure using European legal scholarship. He was elected rector repeatedly between 1814 and 1821 and also played a political role. The city’s university was part of its civic life as well as a place for lectures.

passages.title: Memorials, a message and the end
passages.text: Kościuszko’s commemorative mound was built between 1820 and 1823 by paid local workers and volunteers, including visitors. Soil from places associated with his battles became part of it. Building a memorial was a shared physical undertaking: people helped make the hill, not just admire it.

passages.title: Memorials, a message and the end
passages.text: In 1838 the Senate ordered a medal honoring Florian Straszewski’s work improving the city. Its Polish inscription ends “Senat i lud Krakowa”: “The Senate and people of Kraków.” This short writing sample belongs to a dated commemorative object, linking public gratitude to the new gardens.

passages.title: Memorials, a message and the end
passages.text: A deposit placed in St Mary’s church-tower finial in 1843 included a city plan, newspaper, coins and a Straszewski medal, recorded when the finial was opened in 1912. A church roof could double as an archive deliberately left for future readers.

passages.title: Memorials, a message and the end
passages.text: Foreign troops occupied Kraków in 1831 and again from 1836, when forces of the three protecting powers entered. Austrian troops stayed until 1841. After the failed uprising of 1846, Austria incorporated the city and district into its monarchy, ending the republic’s separate political institutions.

Austria annexed the Free City after the uprising of 1846. The republic ended, while Kraków’s residents, university, religious communities and public gardens continued within a different state. The imported outline remaining until 1878 does not preserve its former constitutional status.

passages.text: Seven Valais districts developed a republic from older institutions shared with the bishop of Sion. Their decisive assertion of sovereignty began in 1613. This atlas’s 1530 to 1800 span includes that earlier arrangement and extends beyond the republic’s end in 1798.

passages.title: Seven districts, unequal freedoms
passages.text: Communes elected local officials and sent instructed representatives to district councils. Delegates could not simply invent new policies: unexpected questions needed consultation at home. Political participation nevertheless became increasingly concentrated among influential families.

passages.title: Seven districts, unequal freedoms
passages.text: The seven districts governed Monthey and Saint-Maurice as subject territories. Governors served rotating two-year terms and accounted to the common diet. The republic therefore combined self-government for its ruling districts with unequal status for other valley communities.

passages.title: Water, bread and learning
passages.text: Mountain farming depended on channels called bisses, or Suonen in the German-speaking upper valley. Irrigation helped meadows grow hay for livestock through winter. Members of water associations contributed labor according to their landholdings: getting water to a field was also a collective obligation.

passages.title: Water, bread and learning
passages.text: The Grand Bisse de Vex was already an inherited piece of infrastructure: a surviving act dates its creation to 1453. A 1476 agreement regulated water sharing and maintenance duties across communities. Its twelve-kilometer course carried water through several jurisdictions; the water needed agreements as well as a downhill route.

passages.title: Water, bread and learning
passages.text: Rye bread had a long place in Valais food, with written evidence reaching back to 1209. Rye tolerated difficult mountain conditions, and the bread’s keeping qualities made it valuable in valley households. Today’s protected commercial designation is much newer than this food tradition.

passages.title: Water, bread and learning
passages.text: A recipe preserved in the Stockalper cookbook mixes chopped liver with eggs, cream, ginger, pepper, nutmeg and raisins before baking. The combination may surprise a modern sandwich-maker. It records an elaborate kitchen preparation, rather than a menu that every farming family could afford.

passages.title: Water, bread and learning
passages.text: Brig’s Jesuit college occupied a new building in 1673 and included boarding accommodation. Its 1686 agreement provided for a full secondary course, logic and moral theology. Enrollment fluctuated between roughly eighty and 150 pupils before 1738: this was a particular boys’ institution, not universal schooling.

passages.title: An Alpine commercial hub
passages.text: Gaspard Stockalper gained the Valais salt monopoly in 1647, improved the Simplon route and built a canal between Vouvry and Collombey in 1651 to 1659. Transport, mining, lending and military business were connected parts of his fortune. Control over routes and essential supplies could translate into political power.

passages.title: An Alpine commercial hub
passages.text: Stockalper’s palace at Brig, begun after 1649, placed an arcaded courtyard beside three massive stone towers with onion-shaped roofs. Its size advertised the wealth of a merchant and officeholder in a small Alpine town. The surviving building makes his ambition unusually easy to see.

passages.title: An Alpine commercial hub
passages.text: Writing sample: the cookbook dated 1581 in the Stockalper archive includes the early German instruction “Nembt ein leber”: “Take a liver.” This is wording from a preserved recipe, quoted in a modern scholarly-based transcription. Its spelling offers a tiny glimpse of written German used in a practical household text.

passages.title: An Alpine commercial hub
passages.text: Stockalper became the republic’s leading magistrate in 1670, but powerful opponents in four districts moved against him in 1677 to 1678. He lost his public offices and part of his property. His story illustrates how quickly commercial dominance could become a political liability.

passages.title: An Alpine commercial hub
passages.text: In 1798 the old subject relationship broke down. Lower Valais gained freedom, and a short-lived ten-district republic replaced the seven-district order before incorporation into the Helvetic Republic under French pressure.

The seven-district republic ended in the upheaval of 1798, when Valais entered the Helvetic Republic. Later governments included another republic and a French department before Valais became a Swiss canton in 1815. These were new political arrangements; the atlas’s 1800 endpoint is a map convention.

passages.text: For four centuries one government ruled every shore of the Mediterranean, from the Atlantic to the Euphrates and from Hadrian's Wall to the first cataract of the Nile. Rome invented little that was wholly new and perfected almost everything it borrowed: Greek architecture became concrete vaults, Etruscan drains became aqueducts, and a city-state's customs became a body of law that most of Europe still lives under. Its language, Latin, is the parent of Spanish, Portuguese, French, Italian and Romanian.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Roman concrete, opus caementicium, mixed with volcanic ash so that it set even under water. The harbour moles built with it at Caesarea and Portus still stand.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: Vitruvius completes De architectura, ten books on building, water, machines and city planning that guided Renaissance architects fifteen centuries later.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Colosseum opens: about 50,000 seats, a retractable awning, and eighty entrances so the whole crowd could leave in minutes.

passages.title: Inventions and building
passages.text: The Pantheon's concrete dome, 43.3 meters across, is completed under Hadrian. It is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Pliny the Elder publishes the Natural History, thirty-seven books that try to gather everything then known about the natural world.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Ptolemy, working in Alexandria, writes the Almagest, the geocentric model of the heavens that stood for 1,400 years, and a Geography that placed the known world on a grid of coordinates.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Galen arrives in Rome. His dissections of animals describe the nerves, the heart and the pulse, and his anatomy is taught in Europe until the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Aqueducts: eleven serve the city of Rome by 226 CE, feeding public fountains, baths and a sewer system, the Cloaca Maxima, that still drains the Forum.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Roads: about 80,000 km of paved highway across the empire by the second century, cambered for drainage, with milestones and way stations a day's ride apart.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The codex, pages bound at the spine, begins to replace the scroll; by the fourth century it is the normal form of the book.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The mills at Barbegal near Arles: sixteen water wheels in two descending rows, grinding grain for a whole town.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Virgil dies leaving the Aeneid unfinished. Augustus orders it published against the poet's wishes, and it becomes Rome's national epic.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ovid completes the Metamorphoses, the retelling of Greek and Roman myth that fed European painting and poetry for two thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Trajan's Column: a 30-meter spiral of carved relief telling the story of the Dacian wars in 155 scenes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Portrait sculpture that shows the sitter warts and all, mosaic floors from Britain to Syria, and the wall paintings of Pompeii, sealed by Vesuvius in 79 CE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Roman law: the praetors' edicts and the jurists' commentaries, later gathered under Justinian, are the root of the civil law systems of continental Europe and Latin America.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Seneca, Stoic philosopher and tutor to Nero, is ordered to kill himself, leaving the Letters to Lucilius. Stoicism was the working philosophy of the Roman elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Constantine's Edict of Milan grants freedom of worship. Christianity, persecuted a decade earlier, becomes the religion of the emperors.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Edict of Thessalonica makes Nicene Christianity the state religion.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Public baths in every town, with hot and cold rooms, exercise yards and libraries. Entry cost a quadrans, the smallest coin.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: A market the size of the Mediterranean: Spanish olive oil, Egyptian grain, Gaulish wine and Indian pepper moved in amphorae. Monte Testaccio in Rome is a hill made of an estimated 53 million broken oil jars.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Insulae, apartment blocks of five or more storeys, housed most of Rome's roughly one million people, the largest city in the world until the nineteenth century.

On the death of Theodosius I in 395 the empire was divided between his sons Arcadius and Honorius and never reunited. The Western half fell in 476; the Eastern half, which we call Byzantine, lasted until 1453.

sectionTitles: A road built for armies, then everyone else
A bedroom full of almost-real things
Party cups with a name on them
School was not the same for every child
A tiny piece of real Latin

passages.text: Rome’s republic emerged around 509 BCE, although its earliest story comes mostly from much later writers. By the third century BCE it governed peninsular Italy, and then expanded around the Mediterranean. Citizens argued over offices and power while conquered peoples and enslaved workers experienced that expansion very differently. The map interleaves “Rome” (500 to 100 BCE) and “Roman Republic” (400 to 1 BCE). These are coverage labels, not separate states or precise lifespans.

passages.title: A road built for armies, then everyone else
passages.text: The Via Appia began in 312 BCE under Appius Claudius Caecus and first linked Rome to Capua. Its straight route served military expansion. As the network grew, it also connected towns, farmland and trade. The present heritage route includes centuries of later construction, so its full length did not spring up in one Republican building season.

passages.title: A road built for armies, then everyone else
passages.text: UNESCO describes milestones, fountains and stopping places along the Via Appia. A traveler could use the road without paying a toll. That does not mean every journey was pleasant: reaching the next water stop still took real work from people and animals.

passages.title: Water had somewhere to go
passages.text: The Cloaca Maxima carried drainage from Rome’s Forum area toward the Tiber. The river could also flood that low ground. This large drain was infrastructure for a city built around wet valleys, not evidence that every household had a flushing toilet.

passages.title: A bedroom full of almost-real things
passages.text: A villa bedroom painted around 50 to 40 BCE at Boscoreale showed imaginary courtyards, fountains and a glass bowl of fruit. The fruit looked inviting, but it was part of a wall painting. This was an elite home; its vivid walls tell us about one household’s taste, not the décor of every Roman bedroom.

passages.title: A very specific ancient snack
passages.text: Cato’s second-century BCE farm book gives a recipe for savillum: cheese, flour, honey and an egg baked in a dish, then finished with more honey and poppy seeds. That is a recipe someone wrote down, not proof that every Roman child ate the same dessert. It sounds sticky enough to require a good napkin.

passages.title: A very specific ancient snack
passages.text: The same book describes a dish it calls “Punic porridge,” made with soaked groats, fresh cheese, honey and egg. The name is Cato’s label; it does not prove exactly how people in Carthage prepared their breakfast.

passages.title: Party cups with a name on them
passages.text: A mid-first-century BCE set of silver dining vessels, said to have come from Tivoli, includes cups, a pitcher, a ladle and spoons. Inscriptions on two cups and a ladle record their weight and name Sattia, daughter of Lucius, as owner. Those objects give a woman’s name from a luxury dining set; they do not describe a typical household’s cupboard.

passages.title: Party cups with a name on them
passages.text: The Metropolitan Museum suggests this silver may have been hidden during late Republican civil unrest. That is possible, but nobody left a note explaining why it was buried. The surviving cups tell us much more securely about dining equipment than about the owner’s last day.

passages.title: School was not the same for every child
passages.text: In the late Republic, some families taught young children at home; affluent households could hire a tutor. Other children might attend a teacher for letters, writing and arithmetic. Access depended on family resources, and many children did not receive the same schooling.

passages.title: School was not the same for every child
passages.text: A well-off child might be accompanied by an enslaved pedagogue who kept track of lessons and sometimes helped teach. That is a reminder that skill and knowledge existed among people denied freedom. A wealthy pupil could get help with homework from someone who had far fewer choices.

passages.title: An appeal for healing
passages.text: A Roman terracotta model of a breast, dated broadly to the third through first centuries BCE, was dedicated at a healing shrine. A person could offer a body-part model when seeking help from a god. The object does not tell us who made the offering, what illness they faced, or whether they recovered.

passages.title: A tiny piece of real Latin
passages.text: A gold coin minted in Rome in 46 BCE carries C·CAESAR COS·TER in the Roman alphabet. The abbreviated Latin means “Gaius Caesar, consul for the third time.” The letters advertise a politician’s office on a portable object. This is one surviving inscription, not a sign that everyone could read or afford a gold coin.

The Republic did not end in a single assassination. Caesar was killed in 44 BCE; civil conflict continued, and Octavian received the title Augustus in 27 BCE after consolidating power. The political system changed into an imperial regime, while Roman people and much of their built and cultural world continued. The map labels end around 100 BCE (Rome) and 1 BCE (Roman Republic), on either side of that political transition.

sectionTitles: Schoolwork and the objects around it
Making a home and welcoming spring

passages.text: The Romanian state grew from the 1859 union of Wallachia and Moldavia and later passed through monarchy, dictatorship and republican government. This map record begins in 1878. Schools, postal buildings, family crafts and surviving documents reveal how institutions and everyday life changed across its long modern history.

passages.title: Schoolwork and the objects around it
passages.text: Casa Școalelor was established in 1896 to support primary-school construction and manage education funds. Money came from state support and donations. Expanding education required buildings and reliable funding, not simply announcing that children should learn.

passages.title: Schoolwork and the objects around it
passages.text: A school-prize medal dated 1927 to 1930 shows an open book, inkwell and writing quill. Its Romanian inscription PREMIUL I means “First prize.” This small object preserves both a written-language sample and the public celebration of a pupil’s achievement.

passages.title: Schoolwork and the objects around it
passages.text: Designs dated 1947 in the museum’s collection show pupils in a classroom and girls at a loom. They were prepared for educational fundraising stamps. These are images of the education promoted by their makers, not photographs of every Romanian classroom.

passages.title: Messages, buildings and public services
passages.text: Romania’s first postage-due stamps appeared in 1881 in six denominations. Postal staff used this kind of stamp to collect missing postage. Even an unpaid letter could leave a small paper trace of how a public service worked.

passages.title: Messages, buildings and public services
passages.text: Bucharest’s Postal Palace was constructed in 1894 to 1899 and inaugurated in 1901. Alexandru Săvulescu designed its monumental facade. The building later became the National History Museum, giving a communications building another public purpose.

passages.title: Messages, buildings and public services
passages.text: Allegorical sculptures on the Postal Palace represented subjects including railways, electricity and mechanics. Such decoration advertised modern services and technical ambition. Some statues were damaged in the 1940 earthquake and others removed because they were unsafe.

passages.title: Making a home and welcoming spring
passages.text: Traditional wall carpets could help insulate homes before becoming chiefly decorative furnishings. Techniques, sizes and patterns differed by region and use. A woven object can therefore be practical household equipment as well as a work of art.

passages.title: Making a home and welcoming spring
passages.text: Contemporary carpet makers continue to teach and adapt the craft, documented through village research and exhibitions. Shared heritage with the Republic of Moldova does not mean every carpet or household follows one pattern.

passages.title: Making a home and welcoming spring
passages.text: For Mărțișor, people make and exchange red-and-white threads around the beginning of March. Local customs may connect removing them with a blossom, swallow or stork. The gift marks a seasonal relationship between people, rather than providing real protection from illness.

passages.title: Making a home and welcoming spring
passages.text: Older women, teachers, craftspeople and museum workshops help younger people learn the thread-making tradition. The documented custom crosses national borders and generations. Making a small gift together can be a form of social learning.

passages.title: Difficult history and continuing society
passages.text: Under Ion Antonescu, Romanian authorities participated in the persecution and murder of Jews during the Second World War. This history concerns specific institutions, perpetrators and victims. The violence must remain part of the story alongside cultural accomplishments.

passages.title: Difficult history and continuing society
passages.text: After King Michael’s forced abdication in 1947, the royal palace was nationalized. It later housed art collections and was badly damaged during the events of December 1989. A single building preserves evidence of successive regimes and the vulnerability of cultural objects.

Romania continues as a republic. The monarchy’s end in 1947 and the 1989 upheaval were major changes of government, not the disappearance of its people. The 1991 Constitution established a new legal framework; communities, languages and cultural practices continued through these political transformations.

sectionTitles: A changing kingdom in an older landscape

passages.text: Rozvi power grew in the late seventeenth century and became influential across the Zimbabwe plateau. Its rulers took over older political and settlement landscapes. The map’s 1650 start is earlier than that rise, and its 1815 endpoint precedes the major nineteenth-century breakup.

passages.title: A changing kingdom in an older landscape
passages.text: Archaeology shows that the foundations at Danamombe, Naletale and Zinjanja predate Rozvi rule. Their later political importance should not make all the earlier builders disappear from the story. A new dynasty could inhabit and reinterpret an existing place.

passages.title: A changing kingdom in an older landscape
passages.text: Changamire Dombo’s campaigns challenged Portuguese positions in the late 1600s. Later Rozvi authority also depended on relationships with local rulers, rather than one ruler personally administering every settlement inside a solid map colour.

passages.title: A changing kingdom in an older landscape
passages.text: The economy rested heavily on cattle and crops, including millet and sorghum. Gold and ivory also entered exchange networks. A kingdom remembered for warfare still needed people tending herds and bringing in harvests.

passages.title: A changing kingdom in an older landscape
passages.text: Trade through Zumbo continued despite conflict with Portuguese interests. African traders carried goods between the interior and border markets, so excluding particular foreign merchants did not necessarily end long-distance exchange.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: Naletale’s walls use carefully placed granite without mortar. Herringbone, chevrons, checks and contrasting stone create different patterns. The walls display planning and workmanship as well as separating and supporting parts of a settlement.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: Nearby Nsalansala has decoration on the inside of its stone enclosure. This detail changes how we imagine the buildings: some carefully arranged patterns were intended for people within the space, not only for someone approaching from outside.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: Ancient mines and finds such as metal bangles, needles and spearheads reveal another side of the Naletale landscape. Mineral extraction, metalworking and exchange accompanied the construction of its elaborate stone centres.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: At Danamombe, excavators found a spindle whorl, a tool associated with spinning thread, alongside pottery and other household material. Such finds bring textile work into a history often illustrated mainly with walls and weapons.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: Another Danamombe excavation recovered a mbira key. It is a small surviving part of a musical instrument, a reminder that sound and performance belonged to these settlements even though most of the music itself cannot be excavated.

passages.title: Beautiful walls and ordinary activities
passages.text: Layered house floors, ash, charcoal, grinding equipment and animal remains help reconstruct repeated occupation. These materials do not all date to one reign, so a particular object cannot automatically be assigned to a named Rozvi king.

passages.title: Memory, language and surviving people
passages.text: Rozvi oral narratives connect named hills, buildings and other places with ancestors and royal power. The authors of a recent study argue that these narratives should be tested alongside excavation evidence, while recognizing that places can carry several competing memories.

passages.title: Memory, language and surviving people
passages.text: A modern recorded Shona form is “varozvi”, glossed as “destroyers” in the archaeological study. It helps explain the historical name, but this printed transcription is not a surviving inscription from Dombo’s reign. No securely checked contemporary indigenous written sentence is reproduced here.

In the nineteenth century, internal disputes and incoming armies broke apart central Rozvi power. Some leaders continued resistance, while others and their communities entered new political relationships. Rozvi identities and traditions survived the state’s fragmentation.

sectionTitles: An uncomfortable building and useful rubbish
Writing and the transfer to Canada

passages.text: Rupert’s Land was the Hudson’s Bay Company’s claimed trading territory in the Hudson Bay watershed, established by an English charter in 1670. Indigenous nations lived and governed there. The map’s 1783 to 1815 slice is shorter than the company jurisdiction’s history. Its imported outline extends beyond that watershed and remains unverified.

passages.title: Trading across a huge watershed
passages.text: A “made beaver” was a unit of value based on one prime beaver skin. Traders could reckon an exchange in beavers without handing over a tidy stack of coins. The fur trade had its own accounting vocabulary.

passages.title: Trading across a huge watershed
passages.text: York boats moved freight inland using a square sail and oars. The largest reached about 40 feet long and could carry more than seventy-five packs averaging forty kilograms each. Eight oarsmen supplied the engine when wind would not cooperate.

passages.title: Trading across a huge watershed
passages.text: Thanadelthur, a Dene interpreter, helped bring Dene and Cree negotiators to a peace agreement in 1715 to 1716. She spoke several languages and completed the expedition’s final leg herself after illness and hunger stopped others. Trade routes were also diplomatic achievements.

passages.title: Families, learning and unequal opportunities
passages.text: Many European traders and Indigenous women formed lasting marriages recognized through local custom. Some couples later held Christian ceremonies, with several children baptized together. The records reveal families spanning cultures, rather than a trading world populated only by solitary men.

passages.title: Families, learning and unequal opportunities
passages.text: Indigenous women hunted, trapped, fished and prepared food. Their work helped sustain trade communities. In the nineteenth century, increasingly racist colonial social rules could exclude these women from circles that had previously accepted their families.

passages.title: Families, learning and unequal opportunities
passages.text: Small company schools opened at Moose Factory, Eastmain, York and Churchill in 1794. Some locally born sons also entered apprenticeships. After the 1821 merger, however, company hierarchies increasingly blocked their promotion: education did not guarantee equal treatment.

passages.title: An uncomfortable building and useful rubbish
passages.text: At York Factory, archaeologists found an older star-shaped fort beneath the later warehouse. Built in 1788 to 1795, the “Octagon” combined accommodation and storage around a courtyard. Its remains survived beneath the depot constructed during the 1830s.

passages.title: An uncomfortable building and useful rubbish
passages.text: The Octagon’s heavy foundations proved poorly suited to ground that froze and heaved. Brick, stone and rigid walls cracked under that movement. A building design that behaved well in Britain had encountered a very different landlord: permafrost.

passages.title: An uncomfortable building and useful rubbish
passages.text: Excavators recovered a thick ring of household rubbish around the fort, probably tossed from windows. They also found cellars, chimney remains and a possible oven from the 1810 cookroom. Yesterday’s untidy habits became tomorrow’s archaeological evidence.

passages.title: Writing and the transfer to Canada
passages.text: A short Latin sample is the company motto “Pro pelle cutem”: “skin for skin.” Historian E. E. Rich identifies prints of the arms and motto dating to 1679. Its deeper joke or intended message remains debated; the wording itself is securely attested.

passages.title: Writing and the transfer to Canada
passages.text: When Canada sought control, the Red River Métis resisted and established a provisional government. Negotiations helped produce the Manitoba Act of 1870. The Métis community participated as a negotiating partner in creating Manitoba, rather than simply receiving a new ruler.

passages.title: Writing and the transfer to Canada
passages.text: The Manitoba Act promised 1.4 million acres for Métis children. Canada did not implement that commitment diligently; a 2013 Supreme Court decision recognized the failure. The territorial transfer therefore left a major legacy of unresolved land rights.

The company jurisdiction was incorporated into Canada in 1870, following the 1869 surrender agreement. The map endpoint of 1815 is not its ending. Indigenous and Métis peoples continued their own communities and struggles over land and government.

sectionTitles: A space station and borders that matter

passages.text: The Russian Federation took shape as the Soviet Union broke apart in 1991 and continued the Soviet UN seat. A 1993 constitution laid out a federal state, but families faced inflation, lost earnings and strain on services during the transition. Wars in Chechnya harmed civilians. Russian engineers also helped launch the first module of the International Space Station. School languages, kitchens and bathrooms vary across this vast country. Russia continues; the imported map starts in 1994, and later Russian claims over Ukrainian land are not validated by its polygons.

passages.title: After the Soviet Union
passages.text: In December 1991 Russia told the UN that it would continue the Soviet Union’s seat, including its Security Council seat. This was a change in state structure, not the beginning of the peoples living across its lands. The map’s 1994 start is later still.

passages.title: After the Soviet Union
passages.text: A new constitution was adopted in December 1993. It described a federation and individual rights. The constitutional text was later amended, including in 2020, so a card should not pretend every line stayed frozen since 1993.

passages.title: After the Soviet Union
passages.text: Moving from Soviet planning toward markets brought rapid inflation, lower real earnings and rising poverty in the 1990s. A family could discover that money saved for school shoes bought less the next week. World Bank researchers also warned that poverty measurements from this transition were imperfect.

passages.title: After the Soviet Union
passages.text: Russia’s 1998 debt and currency crisis shook jobs and savings; economic growth returned in the following years. Recovery was a real change, but national averages cannot describe every household.

passages.title: After the Soviet Union
passages.text: The wars in Chechnya in the 1990s and around 2000 caused major civilian suffering. Human Rights Watch interviewed witnesses to attacks, killings and displacement. A border label saying “Russia” does not tell a Chechen child what safety meant at home.

passages.title: Homes, school and health
passages.text: Some Russian cities had communal apartments where each family occupied a room and neighbors shared the kitchen, bathroom and toilet. If another family was making dinner, privacy and cooking time became a social negotiation. This was one housing type, not every Russian home.

passages.title: Homes, school and health
passages.text: Rosstat’s census separates individual houses, separate apartments and communal apartments and asks about rooms and amenities. Its toilet questions distinguish an indoor flush toilet from other arrangements. “Has a bathroom” is not a useful answer unless one asks whose door it is behind.

passages.title: Homes, school and health
passages.text: The constitution protects children and families and promises health care through public institutions. During the 1990s transition, however, World Bank research found that health and education systems were under severe strain. A right on paper and an easy appointment at a clinic were different things.

passages.title: Homes, school and health
passages.text: Article 43 of the Russian constitution says “Каждый имеет право на образование,” meaning “Everyone has the right to education.” This short Cyrillic sample comes from a Russian legal text; the constitution also recognizes native-language use, and schools serve communities with many other languages.

passages.title: Homes, school and health
passages.text: Russia spans communities with different languages and school needs. UNESCO documents programs for Indigenous and minority languages, including regional efforts. A child learning in Siberia or Kalmykia need not have the same home language as a child in Moscow.

passages.title: A space station and borders that matter
passages.text: Russian engineers built and launched Zarya in 1998, the first International Space Station module. It was funded by the United States, built in Moscow and launched on a Russian rocket. “Zarya” means “sunrise”: a good name for a spacecraft that spent sixteen days alone before its new neighbor arrived.

passages.title: A space station and borders that matter
passages.text: The station was a collaboration involving Russia, the United States, Japan, Canada and European countries. A machine over Earth shows that scientific achievements can have many passports and many teams.

passages.title: A space station and borders that matter
passages.text: In 2014 the UN General Assembly reaffirmed Ukraine’s sovereignty and called on states not to recognize Russia’s change of Crimea’s status. A map polygon or government claim cannot by itself make a disputed annexation internationally accepted.

passages.title: A space station and borders that matter
passages.text: Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The UN General Assembly demanded that Russia stop the invasion and withdraw. This is part of the Russian state’s recent history and of Ukrainian families’ lives; the cartographic display must not quietly treat occupied Ukrainian land as recognized Russian territory.

passages.title: A space station and borders that matter
passages.text: Russia continues as a state, while former Soviet republics are separate countries and many peoples within Russia have distinct languages and histories. The 1994 imported border start is a dataset limit, not a founding date or proof of later territorial claims.

The Russian Federation continues after emerging from the Soviet breakup in 1991. The imported 1994 map start is later than that transition. The UN General Assembly did not recognize Russia’s 2014 change to Crimea’s status and demanded withdrawal after the 2022 invasion of Ukraine; map polygons cannot settle those territorial questions.

sectionTitles: Power over a vast and varied world
Homes, family and a visit with berries
School, medicine and the necessary room

passages.text: The Russian Empire was a huge Romanov-ruled state, formally named an empire after Peter I took the title of emperor in 1721. It included many peoples, languages and faiths across Europe and Asia. Palaces and maps tell only part of its history: peasants, Indigenous communities, craftspeople, railway workers, schoolchildren and families lived different lives within its shifting borders. The monarchy ended in March 1917; the later map interval does not prolong its rule.

passages.title: Power over a vast and varied world
passages.text: Peter I took the title of emperor in 1721 after the Northern War. The state and its rulers had earlier histories; 1721 marks the formal imperial title, not the moment every part of the later empire appeared.

passages.title: Power over a vast and varied world
passages.text: Under Catherine II, the empire annexed Crimea in 1783 and took part in the partitions of Poland. These were conquests and coerced transfers of power over people who already lived there, not empty spaces appearing on a map. The empire also ruled many other peoples and regions in different ways.

passages.title: Power over a vast and varied world
passages.text: Russian colonizers in Siberia and Alaska relied at times on Indigenous knowledge, including Aleut place names, kayaks and navigation methods. Indigenous people were historical actors with their own communities; a Russian map label must not make their expertise disappear.

passages.title: Power over a vast and varied world
passages.text: An 1827 atlas mapped towns, forts, roads, factories and provincial borders, and tabulated distances in versts. For officials it was a tool for governing and travel. For us it also shows what the state wanted to count; the map is not proof that every drawn boundary was accepted locally.

passages.title: Capitals, craft and discovery
passages.text: Saint Petersburg was founded in 1703 and became a capital in 1712, before the formal imperial title. Builders and craftspeople from different places worked there. Its planned avenues and canals were a capital-city project, not the look of every town in the empire.

passages.title: Capitals, craft and discovery
passages.text: Imperial workshops at Peterhof and Yekaterinburg shaped hardstone into court objects. The Peterhof workshop began in 1721 and the Yekaterinburg workshop in 1726. Those polished pieces required skilled quarrying, cutting and finishing, even when a ruler received the credit.

passages.title: Capitals, craft and discovery
passages.text: The imperial porcelain manufactory founded in 1744 made elaborate ceramics for court patrons. A decorated cup tells us about artists and wealthy buyers, but not what a poor household used for breakfast.

passages.title: Capitals, craft and discovery
passages.text: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev published an early periodic table in a journal of the Russian Chemical Society. A surviving copy is held by the Science Museum. Organizing elements by recurring properties helped chemists predict and investigate substances, rather than merely memorize a list.

passages.title: Capitals, craft and discovery
passages.text: Construction of the Trans-Siberian Railway began in 1891 to connect and supply distant imperial territories. Conditions were dangerous: accidents, disease and exposure affected workers, and prisoners were used to finish sections. Train travel has a cost that the postcard view misses.

passages.title: Homes, family and a visit with berries
passages.text: Serf emancipation in 1861 freed roughly 23 million people from legal bondage to landowners, but many families received inadequate land and owed long redemption payments. Freedom on paper did not make a difficult harvest or a debt disappear.

passages.title: Homes, family and a visit with berries
passages.text: A photographer around 1909 pictured three young women offering berries beside a wooden izba, or rural house, near the Sheksna River. The fruit and house make a vivid family-life glimpse; the posed image cannot stand for every village or tell us what the women did after the camera left.

passages.title: Homes, family and a visit with berries
passages.text: An early nineteenth-century silk and gold veil at the Met probably belonged to a wealthy peasant wedding outfit. Another surviving headdress shows skilled textile work. The museum says “probably” about the veil: we can admire it without pretending to know the bride or every family's wedding customs.

passages.title: Homes, family and a visit with berries
passages.text: In many late imperial villages, older people spent their last years at home with help from relatives and neighbors. Village communes had a duty to aid them, but a study finds support was uneven. Grandparents did not all enjoy the same safety net.

passages.title: School, medicine and the necessary room
passages.text: After 1864, local zemstva in much of European Russia handled work such as schools, roads and health services. Their reach varied across the empire, and a school being planned did not mean every child could attend.

passages.title: School, medicine and the necessary room
passages.text: The government required doctors for several kinds of schools beginning in 1872. A 1907 report counted 1,559 registered school physicians, including 86 women, covering 1,702 institutions. Researchers stress that rules were often ahead of staff and resources, so this was no universal school checkup.

passages.title: School, medicine and the necessary room
passages.text: Zemstvo medical services expanded after 1864, but a study of remote Olonets province describes long distances, little money and difficulty attracting doctors. A sick child in a northern village might be far from professional help even while officials described a growing health service.

passages.title: School, medicine and the necessary room
passages.text: In Saint Petersburg, many eighteenth-century homes used courtyard wooden privies above cesspits; waste had to be removed. The city opened a public lavatory near Mikhailovsky Manege in 1871. A palace bath and an urban privy were very different experiences, and neither describes sanitation across the empire.

passages.title: Words on a map
passages.text: A map made in 1796 to 1800 bears the Cyrillic title “Генеральная карта Российской Империи на сорок одну губернию разделенной”. The Library of Congress translates it as a general map of the Russian Empire divided into forty-one provinces. It is a small, sourced sample of written Russian, in the catalog's transcription of this specific map.

passages.title: Words on a map
passages.text: That map title names an empire and its provinces from an official cartographer's perspective. The people under the empire also wrote and spoke many other languages. A Russian inscription shows one written language of government; it is no claim that everyone could read or used Russian at home.

passages.title: Revolution and an ending
passages.text: The 1905 revolution brought strikes, unrest and pressure on Nicholas II to allow an elected Duma. The concession did not make imperial government fully democratic, and conflict over power continued.

passages.title: Revolution and an ending
passages.text: World War I brought fighting, shortages and political crisis. Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March 1917 by the Gregorian calendar; Russians using the Julian calendar called the uprising the February Revolution. The formal imperial monarchy ended then, before this map's last imported 1920 interval.

passages.title: Revolution and an ending
passages.text: After the abdication came a Provisional Government, further revolution and violent civil conflict. Different communities sought autonomy or independence; the Soviet Union was formed in 1922. No single country immediately inherited every imperial subject or border.

Nicholas II abdicated on 15 March 1917 in the Gregorian calendar amid world war and revolution, ending the Russian imperial monarchy. A Provisional Government, competing movements and civil war followed; the Soviet Union was formed in 1922. Peoples, families and languages across former imperial lands continued, often on different political paths. The imported 1914 to 1920 map interval is a coarse snapshot and extends beyond the monarchy's actual end.

sectionTitles: Stories and words on a page

passages.text: Rwanda’s nineteenth-century kingdom joined royal authority to farming, cattle keeping, craft production and elaborate oral traditions. Power changed through expansion and conflict, and households owed unequal obligations to rulers and chiefs. The kingdom later operated under colonial rule; it did not simply vanish at the map’s 1914 endpoint.

passages.title: Power and the working week
passages.text: Historians reconstruct the kingdom from oral accounts alongside later written records. Jan Vansina’s work challenges the image of a timeless, unchanged monarchy: the state expanded, absorbed older communities and experienced struggles among rulers and powerful families. Its past contains political change, not one eternal social arrangement.

passages.title: Power and the working week
passages.text: In a 1907 diary, Jan Czekanowski recorded a five-day cycle in Marangara: two days of work for a chief, two for oneself and one of rest. Other entries differ. This is evidence for locally varying labour demands, not a universal five-day calendar for every Rwandan household.

passages.title: Power and the working week
passages.text: Obligations could include crops, beer, pots, mats, metalwork, building houses or transporting goods. These demands tied workers and households to chiefs. Government relied on things and labour people supplied, rather than only coins paid as taxes.

passages.title: Power and the working week
passages.text: In 1912 the challenger Ndungutse gained support in the north partly by promising to abolish compulsory labour. German troops and forces loyal to King Musinga suppressed the revolt. Complaints about work obligations could therefore become a struggle over who had the right to rule.

passages.title: Households, fields and surviving objects
passages.text: Claudine Vidal’s study describes farming families in central, southern and western Rwanda growing beans, sorghum, sweet potatoes and bananas with metal hoes. They manured fields and used fallow periods. Keeping a household fed required knowledge of soils and seasons as well as hard work.

passages.title: Households, fields and surviving objects
passages.text: The same account describes light wooden homes covered with branches and reeds, enclosed by hedges and tied bamboo. Parents and unmarried children lived in dispersed household compounds. Looking across the hills would reveal homes among fields, rather than everybody packed into a single village.

passages.title: Households, fields and surviving objects
passages.text: Families also remembered devastating famines by name. Too much rain or prolonged drought could threaten people and cattle together. These oral recollections supplied a way to date remembered events, connecting a family’s timeline to the seasons when food had failed.

passages.title: Households, fields and surviving objects
passages.text: The traditional palace at Nyanza is a museum reconstruction made with traditional materials. It helps explain royal architecture, but it is not an untouched nineteenth-century house. The nearby modern palace belongs to the twentieth-century reign of Mutara III Rudahigwa, a later phase of the monarchy.

passages.title: Households, fields and surviving objects
passages.text: A coiled basket acquired from Rwanda in 1921 held a calabash of beer served to a chief, according to its collection record. Millet stalks and papyrus leaf form its structure, with soot used for dark coloring. This slightly later object preserves precise evidence of materials and skilled household craft.

passages.title: Stories and words on a page
passages.text: Before widespread writing, senior family members and storytellers passed on tales orally. Eugène Hurel collected stories between 1908 and 1919. His publications preserved Rwandan voices through a missionary’s recording and translation, which later scholars have carefully re-examined.

passages.title: Stories and words on a page
passages.text: A young character in the tale Rusarurubirizi says “Ngiiye kuu náama.” The translation is “I’m going to the toilet.” This Kinyarwanda sample uses the 2023 editors’ spelling and tone marks for a tale published in 1922, not an ancient manuscript. Even folktale heroes sometimes need a bathroom excuse.

passages.title: Stories and words on a page
passages.text: Hurel published a Kinyarwanda language manual in 1911, and early dictionaries followed. These books belonged to the growth of writing and mission education in the colonial period. Kinyarwanda’s rich spoken literature existed before it was represented in these printed grammars.

The map’s 1914 cutoff is not the monarchy’s fall. Royal government continued under colonial rule before being replaced by a republic in 1961, amid political upheaval and anti-Tutsi violence. Rwandan families, language and cultural knowledge continued across these changes.

sectionTitles: From colonial rule to a republic
Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution

passages.text: This record spans Belgian administration and independent Rwanda, which became sovereign in 1962. The 1994 genocide against the Tutsi devastated families and institutions. Rwanda’s continuing story also includes craft communities, education, public-health work and practical innovations in delivering medical supplies.

passages.title: From colonial rule to a republic
passages.text: The modern map begins in 1945, before independence. A United Nations resolution ended the Belgian-administered trusteeship on 1 July 1962 and recognized Rwanda and Burundi as separate sovereign states. The two neighboring countries must not be treated as one continuing polity.

passages.title: From colonial rule to a republic
passages.text: The monarchy was replaced in 1961 amid anti-Tutsi violence, displacement and exile. The National Electoral Commission’s history records intimidation during that year’s campaigns and referendum. The transition to a republic was therefore a painful struggle, rather than a change of title agreed by everyone.

passages.title: From colonial rule to a republic
passages.text: In 1994, extremists organized genocide against the Tutsi; moderate Hutu were also killed. The international tribunal’s record documents responsibility for these crimes. Families suffered enormous losses, and remembering victims is an essential part of understanding the country’s later history.

passages.title: Objects, family work and learning
passages.text: A grass-plaited anklet collected at Ruhondo in the Ruhengeri district around 1947 is preserved in the British Museum. The register says women wore such anklets in sets. A small woven object records clothing, manual skill and personal adornment near the beginning of this map interval.

passages.title: Objects, family work and learning
passages.text: At Rwesero, a palace completed in 1958 was never occupied by the king, who died in 1959 before its inauguration. Courts and other government offices later used it, followed by a museum. A building made for royalty found a succession of public purposes.

passages.title: Objects, family work and learning
passages.text: Women working with the artisan organization Azizi Life describe weaving together as a chance to discuss farming, raising children and family problems. Cooperative work provides companionship as well as goods to sell. This is a documented modern experience, not a claim that every Rwandan household lives alike.

passages.title: Objects, family work and learning
passages.text: In 2018, pupils from Dove Montessori school visited Azizi Life’s Kigali studio and watched an artisan named Alex create an imigongo design before making their own paintings. Learning a craft could involve meeting a working artist and trying the technique, rather than only reading about it.

passages.title: Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution
passages.text: In Bugesera, community health worker Theoneste Nezehose helped farmer Esther Urimubenshi’s family learn about mosquito nets and reducing mosquito breeding sites. WHO’s 2023 account links this local support to Rwanda’s wider malaria programme. Prevention entered family life through a person who knew the community.

passages.title: Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution
passages.text: Nezehose also described receiving supplies and training from Mayange Health Centre, seven kilometres away, and sending weekly reports. Community care connected diagnosis, treatment and referral to a larger health service. A village health worker was part of a working network, rather than a substitute for one.

passages.title: Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution
passages.text: At an early-childhood centre described by UNICEF, small children feared large open toilet holes. New pans used a weighted flap that closed the pit after use, with handwashing taps nearby. Good design considered a toddler’s size: a toilet should not feel like a giant scary hole.

passages.title: Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution
passages.text: Rwanda launched medical drone deliveries from Muhanga in October 2016 with Zipline. The initial project aimed to get blood products to health facilities faster and reduce waste from their short shelf life. Its practical challenge was getting the right medical supply to a patient in time.

passages.title: Healthcare, toilets and a written constitution
passages.text: The 2023 constitutional text begins “Twebwe, Abanyarwanda”, with the official English translation “We, the People of Rwanda”. This Kinyarwanda sample appears beside English and French versions in the gazette. Parallel columns make the same constitutional opening readable in several languages.

Rwanda continues as an independent state. Independence in 1962 ended Belgian administration, while the genocide of 1994 profoundly changed families and institutions without ending Rwandan society. Its contemporary history includes remembrance, rebuilding and continuing work in homes, schools and health services.

sectionTitles: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan

passages.text: Ryazan’s principality continued after its old capital’s destruction in 1237, with Pereyaslavl Ryazansky becoming its later centre. Moscow absorbed it in 1521. Archaeology reveals crafts, homes and children’s games. The imported map outline is grossly overbroad and should not be read as a reliable historical boundary.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: At excavation 47 in Old Ryazan, archaeologists uncovered two neighbouring properties with houses, workshops and outbuildings. Collapsed clay ovens mark where households heated rooms and cooked. The remains place paid craftwork close to domestic life: going to work might mean crossing the yard rather than travelling across town.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: One property contained bronze dies for shaping silver ornaments, along with parts of scales, small weights, tweezers and spilled metal. Together these finds identify jewellery production more securely than a single lost earring would. One die carried a centaur with sword and shield, a tiny warrior ready for repeated impressions.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: An excavated pit beneath a dwelling is identified by the researchers as a cellar used for ice storage. Underground storage helped households manage food before electric refrigerators. Its survival adds a practical detail to the same neighbourhood where attractive ornaments were being made.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: A bone chess piece from the southern property dates to the late twelfth or first half of the thirteenth century. Its abstract shape belongs to an eastern style of set; two projections may represent an elephant’s tusks. The museum interprets this costly game as evidence of a prosperous household.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: The craft neighbourhood also yielded pendants made from Byzantine copper coins and fragments of green-glazed clay toys. The toys resemble southern Rus pottery of the early thirteenth century. Adults’ ornaments and children’s playthings both preserve connections beyond the city, without telling us who personally carried them there.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: Gold ornaments uncovered by people working near the old city’s cathedral in 1822 helped draw scholarly attention to Old Ryazan. Another hoard was excavated inside a house oven in 1950. People chose different hiding places for valuables; the objects survived because their owners did not recover them.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: A hoard discovered near Isady, about four kilometres east of Old Ryazan, included neck rings, bracelets and silver money ingots. Because it was found outside the city, its setting matters. The excavation team discusses settlements and a possible route to a river landing, rather than assuming every treasure came from the capital’s houses.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The museum’s food summary covers medieval and later deposits from Pereyaslavl, including rye, oats, buckwheat, millet and fish bones. These finds reveal ingredients used across several periods. They cannot all be securely assigned to the independent principality before 1521.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The Vvedensky excavation revealed successive wooden street surfaces, with boards resting on three long pine supports. The museum describes them in its medieval-town account without assigning every layer an exact date. Walking here could sound like footsteps on a wooden floor.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The museum reports bird-shaped whistles, rattles and about thirty pine-bark boats among the Vvedensky finds. It imagines children sailing them on the nearby Lybid. Exact layers are unspecified: these are evidence of the town’s past play, not a precisely dated toy collection.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: A thirteenth- or fourteenth-century drawing scratched into birch bark shows a horse and people. It was found during pipe work near the later Vvedensky excavation. Museum researchers interpret its style as a child’s drawing, while identifying some figures only tentatively. A small scrap preserves someone’s view of ordinary movement and company.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: A fifteenth-century birch-bark fragment from Pereyaslavl contains the Cyrillic word “невѣриѧ”, literally “unbelief”. This Church Slavonic sample comes from a religious prophecy associated with Easter-date calculations. The scholarly catalogue dates the fragment about 1450 to 1500; it is not a complete message, and the word is shown in the editor’s historical transcription.

Moscow incorporated the Ryazan principality in 1521. Its towns and inhabitants continued under new rulers. Old Ryazan’s destruction in 1237 preceded the principality’s final political ending by centuries.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: One property contained bronze dies for shaping silver ornaments, along with parts of scales, small weights, tweezers and spilled metal. Together these finds identify jewellery production more securely than a single lost earring would. One die carried a centaur with sword and shield, a tiny warrior ready for repeated impressions.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: An excavated pit beneath a dwelling is identified by the researchers as a cellar used for ice storage. Underground storage helped households manage food before electric refrigerators. Its survival adds a practical detail to the same neighbourhood where attractive ornaments were being made.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: A bone chess piece from the southern property dates to the late twelfth or first half of the thirteenth century. Its abstract shape belongs to an eastern style of set; two projections may represent an elephant’s tusks. The museum interprets this costly game as evidence of a prosperous household.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work in Old Ryazan
passages.text: The craft neighbourhood also yielded pendants made from Byzantine copper coins and fragments of green-glazed clay toys. The toys resemble southern Rus pottery of the early thirteenth century. Adults’ ornaments and children’s playthings both preserve connections beyond the city, without telling us who personally carried them there.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: Gold ornaments uncovered by people working near the old city’s cathedral in 1822 helped draw scholarly attention to Old Ryazan. Another hoard was excavated inside a house oven in 1950. People chose different hiding places for valuables; the objects survived because their owners did not recover them.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: A hoard discovered near Isady, about four kilometres east of Old Ryazan, included neck rings, bracelets and silver money ingots. Because it was found outside the city, its setting matters. The excavation team discusses settlements and a possible route to a river landing, rather than assuming every treasure came from the capital’s houses.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The museum’s food summary covers medieval and later deposits from Pereyaslavl, including rye, oats, buckwheat, millet and fish bones. These finds reveal ingredients used across several periods. They cannot all be securely assigned to the independent principality before 1521.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The Vvedensky excavation revealed successive wooden street surfaces, with boards resting on three long pine supports. The museum describes them in its medieval-town account without assigning every layer an exact date. Walking here could sound like footsteps on a wooden floor.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: The museum reports bird-shaped whistles, rattles and about thirty pine-bark boats among the Vvedensky finds. It imagines children sailing them on the nearby Lybid. Exact layers are unspecified: these are evidence of the town’s past play, not a precisely dated toy collection.

passages.title: Treasures, meals and play
passages.text: A thirteenth- or fourteenth-century drawing scratched into birch bark shows a horse and people. It was found during pipe work near the later Vvedensky excavation. Museum researchers interpret its style as a child’s drawing, while identifying some figures only tentatively. A small scrap preserves someone’s view of ordinary movement and company.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: A fifteenth-century birch-bark fragment from Pereyaslavl contains the Cyrillic word “невѣриѧ”, literally “unbelief”. This Church Slavonic sample comes from a religious prophecy associated with Easter-date calculations. The scholarly catalogue dates the fragment about 1450 to 1500; it is not a complete message, and the word is shown in the editor’s historical transcription.

Moscow incorporated the Ryazan principality in 1521. Its towns and inhabitants continued under new rulers. Old Ryazan’s destruction in 1237 preceded the principality’s final political ending by centuries.

sectionTitles: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom

passages.text: The Sámi are a continuing Indigenous people with several languages and regional cultures across northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. The map’s broad northern outline and 1500 BCE to 800 CE interval do not establish a single ancient kingdom or a fixed ethnic boundary. Early evidence needs careful interpretation; the later examples below show how Sámi households, skills and languages continued to develop.

passages.title: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom
passages.text: At Levänluhta in western Finland, people buried their dead in what was probably a small pond between about 300 and 800 CE. Most of the recovered individuals were women and children. The unusual cemetery raises questions about who was buried there; it does not by itself identify their language.

passages.title: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom
passages.text: Researchers connect Levänluhta with Sámi history through earlier genetic work and place names. Food-isotope results show varied diets drawing on land, the sea and fresh water. This is evidence from one Iron Age community south of much of today’s Sámi homeland, not a universal Sámi menu.

passages.title: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom
passages.text: The Levänluhta study found that the largest dietary group continued using marine foods after the sixth-century cold period, with a greater marine contribution in some seventh-century burials. Several food sources may have helped people endure environmental shocks. We know the pattern from their remains, not from a surviving shopping list.

passages.title: Early evidence, without inventing an ancient kingdom
passages.text: Reindeer herding developed gradually and differently across regions. Early Sámi economies combined hunting and fishing with smaller numbers of tame animals, including animals used for transport or as decoys. A familiar modern image of large reindeer herds should not be projected unchanged back into the Bronze Age.

passages.title: Medieval homes and practical skills
passages.text: At Brodtkorbneset beside the Pasvik River, seven stone hearths stand in a row; nearby Steintjørna has eight. Radiocarbon evidence places the main occupation between the late eleventh and late thirteenth centuries. Archaeologists interpret the hearths as the centres of neighboring households, probably sheltered by tents.

passages.title: Medieval homes and practical skills
passages.text: Food remains at these Pasvik sites include reindeer, whitefish, pike and a little sheep. The animal bones help reconstruct meals and economic choices. Identifying reindeer bones does not automatically tell researchers whether each animal had been hunted or herded.

passages.title: Medieval homes and practical skills
passages.text: Brodtkorbneset also produced an iron fishhook, a knife, a hide scraper and a fragmentary comb. Pieces of flint were used with fire-making tools to produce sparks. A place remembered mainly for stone hearths also held work on food, clothing, personal grooming and the daily job of getting a fire started.

passages.title: Medieval homes and practical skills
passages.text: In historically documented Kola Sámi siidas, groups separated during spring, summer and autumn to fish, hunt and tend reindeer, then reunited at a winter village. Kinship and shared access to resources linked these households. The year’s social calendar followed useful places as well as changing seasons.

passages.title: Medieval homes and practical skills
passages.text: Siida’s Skolt Sámi Heritage House displays a smoke sauna, a storehouse and a root-sewn boat alongside homes. Some buildings reconstruct earlier practices using written and oral evidence. The boat is a reminder that useful building materials included roots as well as timber.

passages.title: Objects, children and living languages
passages.text: A collection returned to the Sámi Museum Siida in 2024 included a cheese mould from Enontekiö dated 1797 and crossbow stocks reaching back to 1730. Alongside textiles and sledges, such objects preserve practical knowledge. Studying them can help craftspeople recover techniques and pass skills between generations.

passages.title: Objects, children and living languages
passages.text: In modern Sámi language nests, young children encounter a Sámi language through everyday play and conversation. Adults use that language from the beginning, even when a child initially understands little; children may choose which language they speak. Learning happens while doing things together, not only during a vocabulary lesson.

passages.title: Objects, children and living languages
passages.text: Writing sample: “Enâmeh láá mii párnááh” means “These lands are our children.” Siida chose this Inari Sámi title from a poem by Matti Morottaja for its renewed exhibition. It is modern, attested community writing, giving an idea about land and responsibility a memorable voice.

passages.title: Objects, children and living languages
passages.text: A second small sample comes from Northern Sámi: “Movt manná?” means “How are you?” UiT’s university phrase guide prints the expression with its English translation. Northern Sámi and Inari Sámi are distinct languages, so their written forms should not be treated as interchangeable.

Sámi people and languages continue beyond the map’s 800 endpoint. Representative institutions, museums and language programs support cultural life today. This record does not describe a people who vanished when an ancient political state fell.

passages.text: Sabini is the Latin name behind the English “Sabines”, communities of ancient central Italy. This shared card focuses on evidence from Cures and Eretum in the Tiber valley. The map splits the name between 500 to 323 BCE and 323 to 300 BCE; its broad, changing outlines are not verified Sabine borders. Earlier finds below provide context, and neither cutoff marks the disappearance of these communities.

passages.title: A house with a loom and an oven
passages.text: At Cures, archaeologists reconstructed an eighth-century BCE hut with two rooms. A rectangular room held a loom and other domestic activities; a rounded room contained an oven and cooking and serving pots. Making clothes and preparing meals shared a very compact address.

passages.title: A house with a loom and an oven
passages.text: The settlement also had water cisterns, grain stores and a clay-settling tank connected to a pottery kiln. Water storage and food reserves were practical necessities. The evidence describes those installations; it does not identify a toilet system or tell us how every household disposed of waste.

passages.title: A house with a loom and an oven
passages.text: Local pottery stood alongside imported Etruscan vessels. Bronze ornaments, pins and beads of glass paste and amber also survive. These objects show craft skills and connections with neighbouring communities; they do not mean everyone could afford the same wardrobe or tableware.

passages.title: A kitchen accident becomes evidence
passages.text: Archaeologist Alessandro Guidi describes a Cures hut apparently abandoned after a fire, probably beginning in the oven room. Burned deposits preserved dozens of complete or reconstructible pots. A terrible day for its occupants left an unusually useful record of what had been inside.

passages.title: A kitchen accident becomes evidence
passages.text: Several fine vessels occurred in pairs or sets of four or six. Guidi connects their decoration, fabric and repeated forms with shared meals or banquets. That is an interpretation of this particular collection, not proof that every Sabine dinner came with matching crockery.

passages.title: Who got the spectacular tomb?
passages.text: An early sixth-century BCE burial at Eretum contained a carriage decorated with bronze, elaborate horse equipment and expensive vessels. Spits and fire supports suggest the ritual importance of banqueting. A rich funeral displays what a powerful group wanted remembered, not an average family’s grocery list.

passages.title: Who got the spectacular tomb?
passages.text: After the middle of that century, monumental family tombs reveal another way of displaying authority. Some male burials included a lituus, a curved staff associated with an augur’s religious office. Political influence and religious responsibilities could belong to the same powerful families.

passages.title: Who got the spectacular tomb?
passages.text: A later sixth-century tomb contained a terracotta throne and evidence of sacrificed horses. The CNR report interprets its occupant as a king. The objects support an argument about exceptional rank; they do not supply a complete list of rulers or the borders of their power.

passages.title: A small sample of surviving writing
passages.text: “toútaíh” is a scholarly transliteration of a word on the Cures stone inscription. Linguist Raoul Zamponi glosses its noun as “people, community” and identifies the form as locative singular. It belongs to the South Picene inscription corpus; this is a real ancient word, presented in modern Latin-letter transcription.

passages.title: A small sample of surviving writing
passages.text: The stone has two lines running from right to left. Its line break is a distinctive feature within the group discussed by the museum. We can study a writer’s choices even when much of the message remains difficult to interpret; surviving inscriptions cannot tell us how many children learned to write.

passages.title: Family memory and modern detective work
passages.text: Colle del Forno’s underground chamber tombs had wall recesses and access corridors. Older and newer burials occupied the same tombs, showing repeated use over generations. Those spaces preserve evidence of continued burial traditions, though they cannot give us a complete family tree.

passages.title: Family memory and modern detective work
passages.text: Tomb 11 was robbed in 1970. At least 145 objects were sold to a Copenhagen museum the following year and returned to Italy in 2016. Recovering them helped bring a scattered archaeological story back together. Knowing where an object came from matters as much as admiring its shine.

Roman expansion brought the region under Roman power; the Fara in Sabina museum identifies the campaign of Manius Curius Dentatus in 290 BCE as the turning point. This falls after both imported map cutoffs. A change of rulers did not make the inhabitants vanish, and the archaeological record should not be compressed into the ending of one uniform Sabine state.
