passages.text: The Safavids, who took Tabriz in 1501, made Twelver Shia Islam the religion of Iran and gave the country the shape and identity it has kept since. Shah Abbas I's Isfahan, the carpets, the painted manuscripts and the long wars with the Ottomans mark their two centuries.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Shah Abbas I made Isfahan his capital and laid out the Naqsh-e Jahan square with the Shah Mosque, the Sheikh Lotfollah mosque and the Ali Qapu palace.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Ardabil carpet of 1539 to 1540 and the court workshops set the standard for Persian carpets, which reached European palaces by the thousands.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Reza Abbasi and the Isfahan painters, and the Shahnameh made for Shah Tahmasp with its 258 miniatures.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ismail I proclaimed Twelver Shia Islam the state religion at Tabriz and brought Shia scholars from Lebanon and Iraq to teach it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A clerical hierarchy, the shrines of Mashhad and Qom and the mourning rites of Muharram took root.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Armenian Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians lived as protected communities, with periods of pressure.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Shah Abbas moved Armenian merchants from Julfa to New Julfa in Isfahan; their network carried Iranian silk to Venice, Amsterdam and India.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Isfahan grew into one of the largest cities of the seventeenth century, with its bazaar, bridges and gardens.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Twelver Shia Islam remains Iran's state religion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Naqsh-e Jahan square was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Carpets and miniature painting remain the arts Iran is known for.
Afghan rebels took Isfahan in 1722 after a siege. Nader, an Afshar Turkmen general, drove them out, ruled through puppet Safavid shahs, and took the crown himself as Nader Shah in 1736.

passages.text: Saint Kitts and Nevis became an independent federation in 1983. Its history also lives in household objects, classroom craftwork and Christmas street theatre.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: At Coconut Walk on Nevis, the 1998 excavations recovered a polished shell pendant shaped like a tooth, with a tiny suspension hole drilled from both sides. Most pottery in the assemblage was assigned broadly to about 500 or 600 to 1500 CE. The finds reveal skilled work before European colonization.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: At colonial Jamestown, excavators found handmade cooking jars with soot, a handled cooking bowl and a coalpot or brazier. These Afro-Caribbean vessels show food preparation alongside imported European pottery. The clay was thought local, but the report explicitly left that identification awaiting scientific examination.

passages.title: Archaeology: ornaments, supper and toilets
passages.text: Toilets leave history behind, too. Jamestown deposits dated around 1850 to 1880 included decorated chamber pots and washing basins. These are tangible evidence of household hygiene; the pots alone cannot tell us exactly where each family kept them or how waste was disposed of.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: Brimstone Hill’s impressive walls depended on the skill and forced labour of enslaved Africans. Builders used locally quarried basalt blocks around a rubble core, with limestone around openings and corners. Construction developed from 1690 over the following century. Britain’s military abandoned the fortress in 1853; that was the end of its garrison role, not the end of island society.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: After apprenticeship ended in 1838, plantation workers still faced a difficult bargain: employment could be tied to a home and a plot for growing food on estate land. Losing a job could mean eviction. Some workers moved into Basseterre, where overcrowding and inadequate sanitation became major concerns. Work, family housing and public health were closely connected.

passages.title: Building, homes and work
passages.text: The St. Kitts sugar factory stopped operating on 23 July 2005. This closed a major chapter of plantation-linked industrial work, rather than ending the country’s history. The date is a useful reminder that an economic institution can disappear while the communities shaped by it continue.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: Ismay Burt began as a pupil teacher and later trained in Antigua. After receiving a craft-training grant in 1946, she shared skills with teachers at Warner Park: hats, bags, fans and baskets made from screw pine. Learning could turn leaves into useful objects and an income. Her home also became a meeting place for people entering teaching.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: May Stevens became matron of Cunningham Hospital in 1949, the first person born in the St. Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla presidency to hold that post. Student nurses also worked as staff, making regular training difficult. Stevens supported further study, including evening English and mathematics classes in 1960. Better healthcare involved teaching and organization as well as treatment.

passages.title: Learning, nursing and community life
passages.text: Burt’s teaching extended into neighbourhood celebrations. She trained the Newtown Junior Choir, organized a Christmas programme and helped provide gifts for less privileged children. After retiring, she continued craft teaching and hosted a Golden Age Club. One person’s biography shows how school, music and care across generations could overlap.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: Christmas Sports are street performances, so the name does not mean a football tournament. Masquerade dancers wear ribbons, mirrors and bells, accompanied by bamboo fife and drums. Moko Jumbie performers dance on stilts above the crowd. The National Archives describes changing costumes and participation, reminding us that living traditions keep adapting.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: The Mummies are actors, rather than wrapped archaeological remains. Their name comes from mummers, and the play brings together figures such as saints, a captain and a doctor in staged confrontations. Fife and drum accompany the troupe. The National Archives notes that their costumes changed to resemble those of the masquerade.

passages.title: Street theatre and living traditions
passages.text: Kindergartens and primary schools helped pass on masquerade dance, especially around Christmas. Groups also performed at private parties and tourism events beyond the holiday. A cultural-department registration programme began in 1995. Preservation here includes children learning steps and performers earning fees, alongside the older street celebrations.

British sovereignty ended with independence in 1983. The federation joined St. Kitts and Nevis, while Anguilla followed a separate political path. Nevis received its own island administration under the new constitution. Communities, crafts and performance traditions continued through these institutional changes; the imported map’s 2020 endpoint is not a date when the country ceased to exist.

sectionTitles: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom

passages.text: Saint Lucia’s island history reaches far beyond the independent state established in 1979. Archaeological sites preserve evidence of earlier craft and coastal life. French and British colonization brought plantation slavery, while struggles over freedom and self-government changed political institutions. Kwéyòl celebrations, scholarship and literature are continuing parts of this history.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Morne Lezard, a 2002 survey recovered small chert flakes, blade tools and hammerstones in test pits above the Balenbouche River. These remains, alongside previously collected ground-stone axes, identify an area of stoneworking. Their concentration helps researchers study where tools were made, without identifying the makers from pottery labels alone.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Saltibus Point, the team excavated shell tools, griddle fragments and bones of turtles and fish. A fragment of a spindle whorl and a shaped shell inlay added evidence of craft. The refuse deposit brings food preparation and manufacture into view together; some shell fragments initially described as scoops may instead be natural breakage.

passages.title: Work, slavery and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: A government order of 1832 regulated the time enslaved plantation workers could spend cultivating allotted food plots. sectionTitles: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
Land, forced migration and continuing communities

passages.text: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines became independent in 1979. This geographic history includes the earlier Kalinago and Garifuna presence, colonial rule and struggles over land and labour. Indigenous village remains, farming practices and community knowledge reveal lives beyond changes of government.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: At Argyle, archaeologists recovered the plans of eleven houses. Two larger elongated structures were interpreted as men’s houses through comparison with Raymond Breton’s historical descriptions. The excavated outlines provide evidence of building arrangements; their proposed social functions depend on interpretation as well as the physical remains.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: The village also yielded pottery, beads, axe heads and European wares. Ceramic connections extend toward South America and the Greater Antilles. Reconstruction involved local experts and Kalinago and Garifuna participants in choices about wood, binding and roofing, bringing archaeological evidence into discussion with living building knowledge.

passages.title: Discoveries, buildings and a surviving object
passages.text: A carved coconut-shell ladle in the West India Committee collection bears Chatoyer’s name and the date 1773 on a silver rim. Its exact provenance is unknown, and its handle may be a later addition. Association with a diplomatic gift is plausible, not proven by the inscription alone.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The 1763 treaty speaks in the language of possession by crowns. Saint Vincent’s Indigenous inhabitants were not parties to that agreement. The treaty therefore documents an imperial claim, while later negotiations and wars show that control on the ground remained contested.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The Garifuna Heritage Foundation connects the forced exile of 1797 with communities in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. Its account also stresses enduring ties with people on Saint Vincent. Deportation was a catastrophic loss of homeland and autonomy, followed by cultural survival across new places.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: UNESCO’s recognition concerns Garifuna language, dance and music in Central America. Oral narratives, songs and participatory performances transmit knowledge associated with cassava cultivation, fishing and canoe building. Their 2008 inscription followed a 2001 proclamation; neither date marks the beginning of the culture.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Research on women estate workers links their withdrawal from plantation labour after apprenticeship to abusive working conditions. Growing and selling provision crops offered an alternative. This helps explain emancipation through choices about work and household survival, alongside the legal dates that changed labourers’ status.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Arrowroot cultivation and starch processing have supported families in northern and northeastern Saint Vincent, particularly Indigenous communities. A 2019 design brief describes the crop’s dense roots and leafy cover as useful on loose volcanic soils, while noting that unusually heavy rain could still erode fields. Agricultural knowledge here involves both production and care for sloping land.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: The same brief describes an existing factory where grinding had to pause while starch settled under gravity. Its proposed replacement aimed to connect processing more effectively with pulverizing and packing. The document reveals how growers’ livelihoods depended on factory maintenance and processing capacity; the proposal alone does not prove the new plant was operating.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Craftworkers use bamboo, banana fibre, palm leaves and grasses for baskets, mats, hats and other objects. Wood carving, clothing, steel pans and goatskin drums also appear among documented local industries. These practices combine knowledge of materials with the needs of households, performers and markets.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: During the 2020 to 2021 eruption, the UWI Seismic Research Centre, Montserrat Volcano Observatory and local monitoring staff combined earthquake records, gas measurements, cameras and ground movement data. Expanding the instrument network made changes in activity easier to observe. Scientists interpreted several kinds of evidence together rather than relying on a single warning signal.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: On 8 April 2021, increased activity prompted a red alert and evacuation before explosions began the next day. The researchers emphasize preparedness, communication and uncertainty in forecasting. The achievement was a coordinated response involving scientists, authorities and residents, with decisions made before the eventual course of the eruption was known.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: After the eruption, northern residents used photography and community walks to document changes in their surroundings. Participants also helped identify locations for rain gauges and monitored rainfall with scientific support. Their photographs were exhibited in Kingstown and Sandy Bay in 2022, making local experience part of the record of recovery.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: Adult suffrage and self-government developed through several institutional changes. The 1951 voting reform was followed by ministers in 1956 and associated statehood in 1969. These dates distinguish broader political participation from full independence, which required another constitutional settlement.

Colonial rule ended with independence in 1979, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines continues as a nation. The earlier defeat and deportation of Garifuna communities did not end their culture or ties with the island. Separate map intervals do not represent repeated national extinctions.

passages.text: A carved coconut-shell ladle in the West India Committee collection bears Chatoyer’s name and the date 1773 on a silver rim. Its exact provenance is unknown, and its handle may be a later addition. Association with a diplomatic gift is plausible, not proven by the inscription alone.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The 1763 treaty speaks in the language of possession by crowns. Saint Vincent’s Indigenous inhabitants were not parties to that agreement. The treaty therefore documents an imperial claim, while later negotiations and wars show that control on the ground remained contested.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: The Garifuna Heritage Foundation connects the forced exile of 1797 with communities in Honduras, Belize, Guatemala and Nicaragua. Its account also stresses enduring ties with people on Saint Vincent. Deportation was a catastrophic loss of homeland and autonomy, followed by cultural survival across new places.

passages.title: Land, forced migration and continuing communities
passages.text: UNESCO’s recognition concerns Garifuna language, dance and music in Central America. Oral narratives, songs and participatory performances transmit knowledge associated with cassava cultivation, fishing and canoe building. Their 2008 inscription followed a 2001 proclamation; neither date marks the beginning of the culture.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Research on women estate workers links their withdrawal from plantation labour after apprenticeship to abusive working conditions. Growing and selling provision crops offered an alternative. This helps explain emancipation through choices about work and household survival, alongside the legal dates that changed labourers’ status.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Arrowroot cultivation and starch processing have supported families in northern and northeastern Saint Vincent, particularly Indigenous communities. A 2019 design brief describes the crop’s dense roots and leafy cover as useful on loose volcanic soils, while noting that unusually heavy rain could still erode fields. Agricultural knowledge here involves both production and care for sloping land.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: The same brief describes an existing factory where grinding had to pause while starch settled under gravity. Its proposed replacement aimed to connect processing more effectively with pulverizing and packing. The document reveals how growers’ livelihoods depended on factory maintenance and processing capacity; the proposal alone does not prove the new plant was operating.

passages.title: Farming, household work and craft
passages.text: Craftworkers use bamboo, banana fibre, palm leaves and grasses for baskets, mats, hats and other objects. Wood carving, clothing, steel pans and goatskin drums also appear among documented local industries. These practices combine knowledge of materials with the needs of households, performers and markets.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: During the 2020 to 2021 eruption, the UWI Seismic Research Centre, Montserrat Volcano Observatory and local monitoring staff combined earthquake records, gas measurements, cameras and ground movement data. Expanding the instrument network made changes in activity easier to observe. Scientists interpreted several kinds of evidence together rather than relying on a single warning signal.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: On 8 April 2021, increased activity prompted a red alert and evacuation before explosions began the next day. The researchers emphasize preparedness, communication and uncertainty in forecasting. The achievement was a coordinated response involving scientists, authorities and residents, with decisions made before the eventual course of the eruption was known.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: After the eruption, northern residents used photography and community walks to document changes in their surroundings. Participants also helped identify locations for rain gauges and monitored rainfall with scientific support. Their photographs were exhibited in Kingstown and Sandy Bay in 2022, making local experience part of the record of recovery.

passages.title: Scientific work and public participation
passages.text: Adult suffrage and self-government developed through several institutional changes. The 1951 voting reform was followed by ministers in 1956 and associated statehood in 1969. These dates distinguish broader political participation from full independence, which required another constitutional settlement.

Colonial rule ended with independence in 1979, and Saint Vincent and the Grenadines continues as a nation. The earlier defeat and deportation of Garifuna communities did not end their culture or ties with the island. Separate map intervals do not represent repeated national extinctions.

passages.text: The Samanids, a Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara from 819 to 999, presided over the revival of Persian as a written language after two centuries of Arabic. Their court fed the poets and scholars of the Islamic Golden Age in Central Asia.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Avicenna was born near Bukhara; his Canon of Medicine remained a standard medical text in Europe and the Islamic world into the seventeenth century.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Al-Biruni was born in Khwarazm and began his work in astronomy and mathematics as the Samanid age ended.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rudaki, called the father of Persian poetry, wrote at the court of Nasr II.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Ferdowsi began the Shahnameh, the Persian epic, under Samanid rule; he finished it in 1010.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bowls and plates from Nishapur and Samarkand carry black Kufic proverbs on white slip.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Persian became a language of court and literature beside Arabic; the vizier Bal'ami's Persian version of Tabari's history was made for the amir.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The dynasty was Sunni and patronized Hanafi scholars, and Bukhara became a center of Islamic learning.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Bukhara and Samarkand were the Silk Road's markets between China and the Islamic west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Samanid silver dirhams were carried north along the Volga in such numbers that hoards of them turn up across Russia and Scandinavia.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Persian literary revival shaped the Ghaznavid, Seljuk and later courts.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The mausoleum of the Samanids in Bukhara, a cube of patterned brick, is among the oldest surviving Islamic monuments in Central Asia.
The Karakhanids took Bukhara in 999 while the Ghaznavids, once Samanid slave-governors, took Khurasan south of the Oxus.

passages.text: The Sámi are an Indigenous people whose homeland, Sápmi, crosses northern Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia’s Kola Peninsula. They speak several related languages and have pursued varied livelihoods, including fishing, hunting, handicrafts and reindeer husbandry. No single occupation or modern national border defines the whole people.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Fishing in seas, lakes and rivers supported many Sámi communities, while organized hunting required knowledge of animal routes and behavior. Surviving pit systems record collective work in hunting landscapes. Reindeer herding became highly visible, but treating every Sámi family as a herd-owning household obscures this wider economic history.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: A seasonal herding camp needed pasture, fresh water, fuel, building materials and suitable dry ground. Cold springs or ground suitable for storage helped keep milk. Choosing a location therefore involved practical knowledge of several resources at once, rather than simply following animals without a planned pattern of return.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Reindeer milking was labor-intensive and could involve the whole family. Herders moved among different milking grounds during summer; mountain routes also used snow patches where animals found relief from insects and heat. These are descriptions of particular herding systems, not evidence that the same schedule applied to coastal fishers or every Sámi region.

passages.title: Food, movement and household knowledge
passages.text: Sámi languages are related but distinct. In Finland, Northern Sámi, Inari Sámi and Skolt Sámi each have their own communities and histories. Language is part of work and the transmission of skills, as well as schooling and literature. Calling all of these languages a single uniform tongue would hide that diversity.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Duodji joins making, use and cultural knowledge. Materials include birch bark, roots, hide, sinew and reindeer antler. Portable containers, knives and clothing were shaped for particular tasks and for movement where required. Craftsmanship also continues as art and a livelihood; a museum object is one moment in an evolving practice.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: The náhppi, a vessel for milking reindeer, illustrates how a household object’s form addressed a practical problem: limiting spillage. Containers could be carved from birch burls or root growths. Such work required understanding the material as well as the task. This is a documented object type, not a claim about an excavated specimen’s date.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Tirro Farm at Siida represents nineteenth-century Sámi life in permanent houses. Its place among movable tents, shelters and storage buildings makes an important distinction visible: Sámi architecture included several forms, suited to different livelihoods. The museum setting is a curated presentation, rather than an untouched nineteenth-century village.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Siida also preserves Mirhamintupa, a courthouse moved from the Inari-Kittilä border. Names and inscriptions left by people awaiting sentences survive on its walls. The building offers a different kind of evidence from hunting tools: a physical trace of encounters with judicial authority, preserved in a structure relocated for interpretation.

passages.title: Craft, buildings and historical evidence
passages.text: Medieval sagas and chronicles describe Sámi people through their authors’ interests. Ottarr’s account, for example, connects northern resources with tribute. Such texts can reveal trade and relations of power, but they should not be read as a complete census, a neutral ethnography or proof that every named northern group was identical.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Border closures divided grazing systems that had crossed what became national frontiers. Some herders moved from Kautokeino to Karesuando after 1852 and continued using Finnish winter pasture as Swedish subjects, until the later closure blocked that route too. State lines changed practical access to land without making Sámi relationships stop at those lines.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: The Swedish school system distinguished children by their families’ livelihoods and offered mobile herders’ children inferior conditions. Sámi delegates challenged both the physical accommodation and the limited educational expectations in 1918. Their demands show parents and organizers seeking the knowledge children needed for a changing society, while resisting policies imposed upon them.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Elsa Laula Renberg helped bring together the cross-border Sámi congress held in Trondheim on 6 February 1917. Organizing across state boundaries became an enduring part of Sámi public life. The event is commemorated by Sámi National Day, linking contemporary civic expression with an earlier achievement in collective representation.

passages.title: Restrictions, organizing and continuing institutions
passages.text: Finland’s Sámi Parliament works on language, culture and Indigenous status, while the Skolt Sámi also have a separate decision-making body. Norway and Sweden have their own Sámi parliaments. These institutions should be understood in their particular settings; they are not a single sovereign state governing all of Sápmi.

The Sámi continue as a people across several states, maintaining languages, livelihoods, cultural institutions and political representation. Borders and state policies restricted land use and shaped community life, but there was no single event in which a unified Sámi kingdom fell. The imported map intervals describe coverage, not the people’s lifetime.

Norway and Sweden have their own Sámi parliaments. These institutions should be understood in their particular settings; they are not a single sovereign state governing all of Sápmi.

The Sámi continue as a people across several states, maintaining languages, livelihoods, cultural institutions and political representation. Borders and state policies restricted land use and shaped community life, but there was no single event in which a unified Sámi kingdom fell. The imported map intervals describe coverage, not the people’s lifetime.

sectionTitles: A home with colour, food and work
What can bones tell us about dinner?
Public life with unusually good seats
Written language: a signature made with a shoe
Rome won wars, but people kept living

passages.text: The Samnites were Oscan-speaking communities of central and southern Italy, including Samnium. Their history includes fortified settlements, skilled builders and long struggles with Rome. The map’s approximate 500 to 323 BCE coverage is only part of that story; several objects below come from later Samnite communities.

passages.title: A home with colour, food and work
passages.text: At Monte Vairano, stone walls enclosed a hilltop settlement with gates and homes. Beside the southern gate, archaeologists excavated a house with red plaster above a black base and a floor made from lime and crushed terracotta. Ancient interiors could be colourful even when their ruins look grey.

passages.title: A home with colour, food and work
passages.text: Coins beneath that house’s floor date the floor to between 214 and 150 BCE. This is later than the map’s Samnite window. A coin lost or buried during building can help date a room, rather like finding a dated newspaper under an old floorboard.

passages.title: A home with colour, food and work
passages.text: The house contained cups, plates, cooking pans, lamps and loom weights. A storage vessel still held farro, a kind of wheat, and legumes. These finds bring cooking, storing food and making cloth into the same household story, although they cannot identify every person who performed those jobs.

passages.title: A home with colour, food and work
passages.text: Excavators also found a deep circular cistern at the settlement, with walls made using broken roof tiles. Water storage was a practical engineering concern. This evidence does not tell us that each home had a private bathroom or a flush toilet; a cistern alone cannot answer the toilet question.

passages.title: What can bones tell us about dinner?
passages.text: Researchers studied carbon and nitrogen in human remains from Opi Val Fondillo, a community of the sixth and fifth centuries BCE. Their results suggest a diet largely based on land-grown foods, with relatively limited animal protein for many sampled people. These are long-term dietary clues, not a recovered weekly menu.

passages.title: What can bones tell us about dinner?
passages.text: Some people had different nitrogen results, including differences between male and female samples. The researchers discuss food access alongside health and physiological explanations. It would be too confident to turn those measurements into a rule that every Samnite family always served identical portions, or always favoured one person at dinner.

passages.title: Public life with unusually good seats
passages.text: Pietrabbondante was a major sanctuary of the Pentri Samnites. Its temple-theatre complex, built around the late second and early first centuries BCE, served religious and political purposes. Public worship, meetings and decisions about a community’s affairs could happen in connected spaces. This impressive later complex postdates the imported map window.

passages.title: Public life with unusually good seats
passages.text: The theatre preserves stone seats with shaped backs and armrests carved as winged lions’ paws. Someone thought seriously about sitting comfortably, even without cushions surviving to prove it. A nearby public residence accommodated important priests and magistrates visiting for religious and political gatherings.

passages.title: Written language: a signature made with a shoe
passages.text: A roof tile from Pietrabbondante, dated around 100 BCE, carries four shoeprints and two short messages, one in Oscan and one in Latin. Linguist Katherine McDonald interprets them as the work of two enslaved women, or possibly freedwomen, who handled wet clay tiles. The writing preserves a tiny moment in working life.

passages.title: Written language: a signature made with a shoe
passages.text: A short Oscan sample is “segnatted. plavtad”, meaning “signed with a footprint”. This is a Roman-letter transliteration of an inscription originally written in the Central Oscan alphabet. Forget a fancy signature: this worker left a shoeprint. The tile is later than the map’s displayed Samnite period.

passages.title: Written language: a signature made with a shoe
passages.text: The paired inscriptions show that these particular workers could write sentences. They do not tell us how they learned, whether they attended a school, or how common literacy was among other women. McDonald also notes uncertainty about whether Detfri, one word in the inscription, is a personal name or a designation.

passages.title: Written language: a signature made with a shoe
passages.text: Oscan was a language, not just one alphabet. Writers used different alphabets derived from Etruscan, Greek or Latin traditions in different regions and periods. Surviving texts appear on pottery, stone and metal, including dedications and legal or religious documents. A language could travel between materials as well as scripts.

passages.title: Rome won wars, but people kept living
passages.text: In 290 BCE, after further Roman campaigns, the remaining Samnite opponents sought peace. A recent study describes their likely subordination within Rome’s alliance system, while stressing gaps in the ancient accounts. Losing military independence did not prevent later generations from building the houses and sanctuary described here.

passages.title: Rome won wars, but people kept living
passages.text: Samnites later participated in the Social War against Rome, which began in 91 BCE. Roman citizenship expanded during the conflict, although some Samnite and Lucanian resistance continued. Political rights and alliances changed through a violent process; there was no single day on which an entire people simply vanished.

Roman expansion gradually changed Samnite political independence, alliances and citizenship. Peace in 290 BCE was followed by further conflicts, including the Social War centuries later. The map stops at 323 BCE because of its imported coverage, not because Samnite communities ended in that year.

passages.text: Samoa has a long history of Pacific voyaging, skilled craft and family-based social institutions. This card follows the western islands through colonial government and independence, with clearly identified earlier background. Samoan people and culture also extend to American Samoa and overseas communities; the modern state is not the whole Samoan world.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: Pottery fragments recovered during construction of the Mulifanua ferry berth on Upolu in 1973 included the tooth-stamped decoration associated with Lapita. Their context links the islands to a much older Pacific settlement history, long before the modern state.

passages.title: Discoveries and the deeper past
passages.text: A 2001 radiocarbon study placed occupation of the Mulifanua site around 930 to 800 BCE. These are calibrated estimates for a particular archaeological site, not an exact founding date for Samoa or a date assigned from a later genealogy.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: A Samoan tattooing implement in Te Papa combines a bone comb, turtle-shell plate and wooden handle. A mallet drives the toothed edge, while combs of different widths make broad areas or fine lines. The object makes the precision of the tattooist's craft visible.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Ie Samoa fine mats are woven from narrow pandanus strips and finished with feathers and fringe. Preparing and weaving such fine material takes sustained skill and labor; the mats are valued for workmanship and the histories they acquire through exchange.

passages.title: Craft knowledge and achievement
passages.text: Fine mats circulate at weddings, funerals and other gatherings, reaffirming relationships between families. Village committees and master weavers teach the practice, making production a form of shared knowledge as well as individual artistry.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: The aiga, or extended family, connects daily life with service, respect and reciprocal care. Family members exchange food, money and practical support, including across national borders. These obligations are lived and debated differently by different generations.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Matai titles, genealogies, language and ceremonial responsibilities are parts of fa'asamoa. Together they organize belonging and public relationships; the term does not describe an identical way of life for every Samoan household.

passages.title: Daily life and social obligations
passages.text: Christian teaching introduced by John Williams in 1830 became part of a changing religious landscape. Samoan forms of church life developed in close relationship with fa'asamoa, rather than simply replacing every earlier social institution.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The arrival of the influenza-infected Talune in 1918 led to a devastating epidemic under New Zealand administration. The disaster affected families and food production, making colonial governance part of everyday experience as well as constitutional history.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: The Mau pursued self-government through organized, nonviolent resistance. In December 1929, colonial police killed peaceful demonstrators, including Tupua Tamasese Lealofi III. The movement's history records Samoan political action, not merely a transfer between foreign rulers.

passages.title: Colonial rule and political agency
passages.text: In 1936 New Zealand recognized the Mau as a legitimate political organization and repealed the Samoan Offenders Ordinance. Independence still required a longer struggle and arrived on 1 January 1962.

passages.title: Language and continuity
passages.text: Samoan language nests and school programs in New Zealand connect language learning with shared leadership and cultural knowledge. These institutions show how communities maintain and reshape connections to Samoa across generations of migration.

Colonial administration of Western Samoa ended with independence on 1 January 1962. Samoan communities, chiefly institutions and cultural practices continue in the independent state, American Samoa and the diaspora. A last map observation is not the end of the people or their history.

sectionTitles: Building a public identity in stone
A small state among large events

passages.text: This map shows one nineteenth-century interval in San Marino’s much longer history as a small republic on Mount Titano. Its 1815 and 1878 endpoints do not mark a founding or collapse. Public institutions and households occupied the same compact hilltop setting, while new associations and postal services connected residents with a changing world.

passages.title: Sharing the risk of illness
passages.text: In 1876, the Società Unione added mutual assistance for artisans and workers to its activities. Members faced the danger that illness or interrupted work could remove their income. Regular contributions created a shared fund to help when an individual household met trouble.

passages.title: Sharing the risk of illness
passages.text: The society’s manifesto, dated 30 June 1876, appealed to workers’ dignity and solidarity. It argued that assistance could come from their own savings together, instead of dependence on someone else’s generosity. This document gives an unusually direct glimpse of organised social support.

passages.title: Sharing the risk of illness
passages.text: The association continued after this map interval. In 1890 it established a grain store intended to supply families at controlled prices, with instalment payments and favourable interest. Access to everyday food became another practical purpose of collective help.

passages.title: Letters with the republic’s name
passages.text: A postal agreement in 1865 allowed Italian stamps to be used in San Marino. The republic added its own name to the dated cancellation mark and used blue ink. Official postal history notes that Italian rules disallowed that ink because it corroded cancellation handstamps.

passages.title: Letters with the republic’s name
passages.text: The date stamp bore the Italian words “REPUBBLICA DI SAN MARINO”, meaning “Republic of San Marino”. The philatelic administration transcribes this wording in its account of the 1865 arrangements. A small mark on an envelope carried the state’s identity into ordinary correspondence.

passages.title: Letters with the republic’s name
passages.text: On 1 August 1877, San Marino issued its own postage stamps, printed in Turin in five values from two to forty centesimi. The 1877 agreement with Italy required each side to use its own stamps. Selling stamps also provided income for the republic.

passages.title: Building a public identity in stone
passages.text: The white Carrara-marble Statue of Liberty was donated in 1876 by Countess Otilia Heyroth Wagener. Sculptor Stefano Galletti represented liberty as a woman wearing a crown of three towers. The miniature towers refer to the fortified city around the square.

passages.title: Building a public identity in stone
passages.text: The present Public Palace came later, between 1884 and 1894. Local stoneworkers were employed on its construction, while selected artisans supplied ironwork, furnishings and decoration. Its medieval-looking architecture is therefore also a record of nineteenth-century design and skilled employment.

passages.title: Building a public identity in stone
passages.text: UNESCO notes that the historic centre was extensively restored and reconstructed from the late nineteenth century into the twentieth. Some of its apparent medieval unity reflects those later choices. Meanwhile, the centre remained inhabited and continued to house the republic’s public institutions.

passages.title: A small state among large events
passages.text: The two Captains Regent share the highest office of state, changing every six months. Their paired office has medieval roots. This recurring transfer of responsibilities was already a long-established institution during the nineteenth-century period shown on the map.

passages.title: A small state among large events
passages.text: In 1849 Giuseppe Garibaldi arrived with about two thousand followers seeking refuge from Austrian and Roman forces. San Marino’s authorities negotiated time for them to leave. The episode placed a very small republic in the middle of Italy’s struggle over its political future.

passages.title: A small state among large events
passages.text: Abraham Lincoln wrote warmly to San Marino’s Captains Regent in 1861, acknowledging the historical standing of their small state. The exchange illustrates how the republic cultivated recognition and friendship far beyond its immediate Italian neighbours.
San Marino continued as a republic after 1878. The map’s endpoint is a coverage limit; later buildings and mutual-aid projects belong to the continuing community.

sectionTitles: Power, work and the wider world
Neighbours, fields and women in the records

passages.text: Medieval Sardinia was an island of competing kingdoms, farming villages, monasteries and trading towns. Its four giudicati were ruled by sovereigns called judges. The map’s single island-wide colour hides these separate governments and later Pisan, Genoese and Aragonese influence; “Kingdom of Sardinia” is not a suitable description of one continuous island-wide state from 1000 onward.

passages.title: Power, work and the wider world
passages.text: By the middle of the eleventh century, Cagliari, Arborea, Torres and Gallura were separate kingdoms. Their judges governed territories divided into districts called curatorie. A “judge” here could be a ruler, not simply the person who settled an argument in court.

passages.title: Power, work and the wider world
passages.text: Rulers donated land and churches to religious communities connected with places as far away as Montecassino and Marseille. Monasteries helped link Sardinia to wider European religious and cultural networks, while Pisa and Genoa pursued commerce and political influence.

passages.title: Power, work and the wider world
passages.text: Iglesias grew into an important thirteenth-century town beside valuable silver deposits. Mining helped make it a target: Aragonese forces and their Arborean allies besieged the Pisan town in 1323, and it surrendered on 14 January 1324 after seven months.

passages.title: Power, work and the wider world
passages.text: Reports sent to the Aragonese king in 1308 describe Iglesias enclosed by high battlemented walls and twenty towers. Outside stood a wooden palisade and a ditch, obstacles intended to keep soldiers and siege machines away from the stone defenses.

passages.title: Neighbours, fields and women in the records
passages.text: At Geridu, near modern Sorso, excavations expose a rural community’s fourteenth-century surroundings: water, vineyards, vegetable plots, orchards and pasture. Its small buildings clustered around open spaces used for daily activities. Home life spilled outside the front door.

passages.title: Neighbours, fields and women in the records
passages.text: Archaeologists have uncovered more than fifteen homes near Geridu’s church, cemetery and a larger privileged building. Written records mention the village in 1112. Its population declined from the mid-fourteenth century, and it was abandoned by 1427; the excavated village is a particular community, not a model for every Sardinian home.

passages.title: Neighbours, fields and women in the records
passages.text: The condaghi, monastery record books, preserve purchases, disputes and people who otherwise might disappear from history. At the women’s monastery of San Pietro di Silki, abbesses administered property. These books particularly record cases the institution won or settled, so the monastery’s voice is louder than its opponents’ voices.

passages.title: Neighbours, fields and women in the records
passages.text: The same records reveal sharp limits to freedom. Abbesses could participate in exchanges of unfree people, and some exchanges were annulled because the ruler’s permission was missing. A woman holding authority in a monastery did not mean that all women, or all families, controlled their own lives.

passages.title: Paint, laws and written Sardinian
passages.text: Saccargia’s church belonged to the Camaldolese monks by 1112. Its contrasting light and dark stonework makes the building striking from outside; Romanesque paintings survive in its apse inside. Skilled builders and painters made religious spaces into some of the island’s most lasting medieval achievements.

passages.title: Paint, laws and written Sardinian
passages.text: In the late fourteenth century, Eleonora of Arborea promulgated the Carta de Logu. It combined civil and criminal rules with rural legislation developed under her father, Mariano IV. The law used an Arborean form of Sardinian and remained influential long after her kingdom disappeared.

passages.title: Paint, laws and written Sardinian
passages.text: A tiny sample of its written language is “Nos Elianora”, meaning “We, Eleonora”. These are words from the prologue, shown here in a modern transcription of the historic Sardinian text. The ruler explains that her subjects should know the rules by which they are expected to live.

passages.title: Paint, laws and written Sardinian
passages.text: Article 86 addressed dishonest measures and weighing scales. An official who found a false measure could trigger a fine payable within fifteen days, with corporal punishment for failure to pay. Shopping already had a familiar problem: was the seller really giving you the promised amount?

passages.title: Paint, laws and written Sardinian
passages.text: Article 87 prohibited taking goshawks or falcons from their nests. The district official had to bring an offender before the ruler. These birds mattered to elite hunting, so this protection should not be mistaken for a modern wildlife conservation programme.

Arborea’s defeat at Sanluri in 1409 and the sale of its remaining dynastic rights in 1420 marked decisive steps in Aragonese consolidation. Sardinia’s people, villages and laws continued under new rulers. The map’s 1492 cutoff is a coverage boundary, not the disappearance of the island or its society.

sectionTitles: Government, defence and getting an education
Books and a small sample of Sardinian
Families, illness and evidence from teeth

passages.text: This Sardinia record covers the island kingdom under the Spanish crown during 1530 to 1700. Sardinians lived with local institutions, maritime dangers, religious learning and recurring epidemics. The island-shaped outline is reasonable as a regional frame; its dates are a map window within a much longer history.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Sardinia’s parliament had three estates, or stamenti: clergy, nobles and representatives of the seven royal towns. It negotiated taxes and proposed legislation for royal approval. This gave organized groups a bargaining role, but was not an assembly elected by every adult on the island.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: In Cagliari, the estates could meet in different buildings: church representatives at the archbishop’s residence or cathedral sacristy, nobles at the church of the Speranza, and town representatives at the municipality. Delegates carried messages between them and the viceroy. Government involved plenty of walking as well as talking.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Philip II established the Royal Administration of the Towers in 1587 to organize coastal defenses, soldiers and supplies. Guards watched for hostile ships. For coastal communities threatened by raids, keeping watch over the sea was a serious, organized job.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: A tower’s entrance could stand about four to six metres above the ground. Guards reached it by a wooden or rope ladder and then pulled the ladder inside. Reaching the rooftop lookout could require another ladder through a hatch or stairs built into the thick walls.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Early-sixteenth-century Cagliari and Sassari supported public grammar schools. Language could be political: in 1567, Philip II required the Jesuits at Sassari’s college to use Castilian in teaching and even in preaching in the city. Local elites wanted their sons to master it alongside their humanistic studies.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Cagliari’s university received papal authorization in 1607 and a royal foundation privilege in 1620; arrangements for teaching were still being implemented in 1626. The proposed funding split costs between church and city. Establishing a university meant finding rooms and money as well as signing an impressive parchment.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: The papal authorization envisaged subjects including medicine, law, philosophy and Latin, Greek and Hebrew. In the royal arrangements, Cagliari’s council would select the rector for a three-year term, while the archbishop could confer degrees. These documents reveal how civic and church authorities shared responsibility for higher learning.

passages.title: Books and a small sample of Sardinian
passages.text: Nicolò Canelles established a printing shop in Cagliari in 1566. Copies preserved in the University Library document this early local printing enterprise. Books could now be produced on the island through a durable workshop, adding a new craft to its cultural life.

passages.title: Books and a small sample of Sardinian
passages.text: Gerolamo Araolla’s collection of 1597 mixed Sardinian, Italian and Spanish poetry. Its original printed heading includes “RIMAS DIVERSAS SPIRITUALES”, meaning “Various spiritual poems”. This is a transcription of an attested title, recorded by the modern editor from the surviving Cagliari copy, not a newly composed example of Sardinian.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: During Alghero’s plague outbreak of 1582 to 1583, the physician Quinto Tiberio Angelerio organized restrictions later published as fifty-seven instructions. One rule allowed only one member of a household to go shopping, with permission. Another required people outside to carry a six-foot cane to keep their distance.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: The rules also told physicians to visit patients regardless of wealth: richer people would pay, while the city would cover poor patients. Pharmacies had to maintain supplies. These prescriptions show an effort to organize public help during a crisis, although the surviving rules cannot prove that every patient received it.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: Some prescriptions came from mistaken explanations of disease: bells and artillery were supposed to purify the air. The same programme used isolation and heated objects and textiles. Angelerio worked before the bacterium and flea transmission were understood; his booklet combined observation with the medical ideas of his time.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: Teeth offer a different window into life. Researchers examined 160 people from Alghero’s plague cemetery, including 79 children or adolescents. Cavities, tartar and tooth loss suggested substantial carbohydrate consumption and poor oral hygiene. This is an inference from one burial population, not a menu for every Sardinian family.

The map ends in 1700, but Spanish rule did not instantly end then. Sardinia passed to Austrian control in 1708, was retaken by Spain in 1717, and came under the House of Savoy in 1720. Its institutions and communities continued through these changes of dynasty.

sectionTitles: A capital powered by water and work

passages.text: The House of Savoy governed a changing collection of Alpine and Italian territories, with Turin becoming its capital in 1563. Its rulers acquired the Sardinian crown in 1720. The three map labels belong to successive phases of this dynastic state, although “Sardinia-Piedmont” is premature for the map’s 1650 starting date.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: When Marguerite of France formally entered Turin on 7 February 1563, municipal officials arranged a canopy and prepared the streets. City accounts record the work and expense behind the ceremony. A royal welcome required ordinary people to build, organize and pay, not simply wave at a procession.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Turin’s municipal mills used water from the Dora to grind grain. In 1679 the city expanded their capacity as population and demand grew. Bread depended on machinery, water management and decisions about shared infrastructure as well as on farmers’ harvests.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Silk production connected mulberry growing and silkworm keeping with skilled processing. In the 1660s Turin supported a water-powered silk mill associated with Galleani. The technology improved production, but luxurious cloth still depended on the labor of people far removed from the court wearing it.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: A silk works commissioned at Venaria in 1670 included machinery and a professional training school. Visitors could see the work from the street. Industrial skill was something to teach and display: this royal neighborhood offered a glimpse of manufacturing as well as grand architecture.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Before mechanization, silk thread was largely processed by hand, with women providing much of that labor. The machines produced a finer, stronger and more consistent thread. The change affected working routines as well as the appearance and value of the finished material.

passages.title: Schools, land and care

sectionTitles: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
Later villages and a real written message

passages.text: Sarmates is this map’s name for Sarmatian peoples, a varied Iranian-speaking world associated with the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The imported outline for 100 to 1 BCE is an approximate regional label, not the frontier of a single state. Earlier Lower Volga evidence and later communities in Hungary and Roman Britain are identified separately below; neither the people nor their history stopped at the map’s endpoint.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Dating Sarmatian arrivals in the Lower Don is an archaeological puzzle. A stamped Rhodian amphora, black-glazed drinking cups and molded bowls helped Glebov and Dedyulkin place some early complexes in the middle decades of the second century BCE. Imported containers can act as time clues when a grave has no written date.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Lower Don graves of the second and first centuries BCE contain large metal mirrors with raised rims and projecting handles, as well as smaller flat disks without handles. Many retained traces of cases; one had a stand. Looking at your reflection could involve a carefully protected portable object rather than a bathroom wall.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Only about a fifth of the mirrors in that study survived whole. Some were cut, bent or broken, and the author interprets much of this damage as part of funerary rituals. A broken mirror in a grave therefore need not mean its owner was simply careless with their belongings.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: An earlier Lower Volga study examined fifty-eight children and adolescents from burials dated 400 to 100 BCE. Researchers recorded dental tartar, including deposits on baby teeth, and one case of tooth decay in a teenager. Such small traces let children enter a history often dominated by warriors and wealthy adults.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: At Sadovy Kurgan near Novocherkassk, excavated in 1962, a burial lay in a rectangular pit beneath wooden planks and reeds. Scholarly discussion places the assemblage broadly in the first century BCE. Although robbers had entered the grave, equipment deposited around it still preserved traces of the funeral gathering.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: Two bronze cauldrons at Sadovy were blackened with soot. The excavator connected them with cooking for the funeral feast. Eight silver bowls had been stacked upside down and covered with a larger silver vessel. Even a lavish ceremony involved the practical business of cooking and gathering the dishes together.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: Sadovy’s large decorative roundels were made from hammered silver covered in gold leaf. Griffins and feline animals filled their surfaces. Thin precious layers could create a brilliant effect without making every part solid gold. Their construction records the work of specialists in shaping, covering and joining metal.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: A later gold collar from Khokhlach, another burial mound near Novocherkassk, belongs to the first century CE. It had three joined rings, turquoise settings and pairs of facing lions. The Metropolitan Museum’s example is a nineteenth-century electrotype copy; the ancient original is in the Hermitage. The distinction matters when following an object’s story.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: Centuries later and west of this map’s outline, Sarmatian communities farmed on the Great Hungarian Plain. At Rákóczifalva-Bagi-földek, fourth- and fifth-century CE plant remains emphasize cereals, while animal remains are dominated by cattle. These villagers combined crops and livestock in a landscape of fields, grassland, floodplain woods and river.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: At the same Hungarian site, researchers identified twelve grape pips from four pits. They suggest contacts with Roman food traditions and possibly food exchange with Roman provinces. A few seeds can raise interesting questions about meals, but they do not establish that every household owned a vineyard.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: Writing sample: “DEO SAN” opens a stone inscription from Ribchester in Britain dated 31 August 241 CE. Expanded as “Deo sancto,” it means “To the holy god.” The dedication concerns Apollo Maponus and a Sarmatian cavalry unit. This later Roman military text is Latin, not an example of the Sarmatians’ own language.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: The same inscription names Aelius Antoninus, a Roman officer from Melitene near the Euphrates. His dedication links an officer from the eastern empire, a unit carrying a Sarmatian name and a fort in Britain. The surviving stone is part of a monument’s pedestal, with a relief of Apollo beside the text.

There was no single Sarmatian state to fall in 1 BCE. Communities continued through the Roman centuries. Later Hunnic expansion broke up Alanic political alliances within this wider world, while different groups moved, joined new coalitions or continued in regions such as the Caucasus. Political labels and communities changed along different paths.

sectionTitles: A farm was a cluster of buildings
A later voice in Old Saxon

passages.text: The continental Saxons were communities in northern Germany whose leaders and settlements formed a loose political network. This card follows their early medieval world and conquest by the Franks. The imported 500 outline stretches implausibly far into Jutland; it is not a reliable kingdom boundary, and this record is distinct from the kingdoms of Anglo-Saxon England.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: At Warendorf, seventh- and eighth-century farmsteads included a large living hall, barns, stores and smaller buildings. Archaeologists reconstructed these layouts from excavated traces. A household’s work spread across a whole yard, with places for animals, equipment, supplies and making things.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: Successive buildings occupied the same ground several times. Timber posts could decay or buildings could burn, so a farm needed repair and replacement. Those overlapping post-holes help archaeologists recover the settlement’s history, rather than treating every mark as a building that stood at once.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: Warendorf stood beside a crossing of the Ems. Its sunken buildings are interpreted mainly as spinning and weaving workshops, with other possible uses. The evidence connects household craft with a settlement positioned on a route for people and goods.

passages.title: A burned loom leaves clues
passages.text: At nearby Milte, an early medieval workshop contained charred timber and clay loom weights. Fire had destroyed the wooden loom, but left enough evidence to recognise textile work. The excavation report does not yet give the loom a narrow date within the early medieval period.

passages.title: A burned loom leaves clues
passages.text: Excavators recovered seven complete weights and fragments of twelve more. Fragile examples were lifted inside blocks of soil so conservators could expose them carefully. These objects once kept threads under tension, part of the patient work needed to turn yarn into cloth.

passages.title: The kitchen’s pottery collection
passages.text: Warendorf’s everyday ceramics included bowls, rounded vessels and early globular pots. Some had holes below the rim for suspension; others had broad handles. A pot’s shape could preserve clues to handling and use even when only broken pieces survived.

passages.title: The kitchen’s pottery collection
passages.text: Most pottery was relatively coarse, but some vessels had fine clay and carefully smoothed surfaces. Pottery imported from the Rhineland also reached the settlement. A rural household’s material world could include objects made beyond its own region.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: Saxon society was unequal. Nobles enjoyed privileges, while other people were free, partly dependent or unfree. The absence of one permanent king did not mean that everybody had the same rights or control over their own work.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: War with Charlemagne’s Franks began in 772 and continued in repeated campaigns until 804. Incorporation changed political rule and strengthened Christian institutions. Families experienced these decades through conflict and disruption, while subsequent generations lived under the new order.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: Some Saxon aristocratic families made marriage connections with Frankish elites and sent children into monasteries. Such institutions created paths into religious life and learning for privileged households. That evidence does not establish universal schooling for Saxon children.

passages.title: A later voice in Old Saxon
passages.text: The Heliand preserves the words “gesidos mine”, meaning “my companions”. They appear in a speech by Jesus in section 56. This is a scholarly transcription in Latin letters of attested Old Saxon, from a poem that retells Gospel stories in alliterative verse.

passages.title: A later voice in Old Saxon
passages.text: The poem was composed in the first half of the ninth century, after the independent period shown on the map. A major manuscript was copied around or shortly after 850. Its survival shows how Saxon language and poetic traditions continued within a Christian literary setting.
Frankish conquest was completed through campaigns ending in 804, just beyond the map’s endpoint. Saxon communities continued within the Carolingian realm.

sectionTitles: A music lesson from the nineteenth century

passages.text: Saxony became a kingdom in 1806, after the beginning of this map record, and lost substantial territory in 1815. Its nineteenth-century story includes constitutional conflict, technical education, manufacturing, railways and music. The kingdom’s institutions and population continued beyond the map’s 1878 endpoint until the monarchy ended in 1918.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: After unrest in 1830, Saxony adopted a constitution in 1831. The elderly King Anton shared government with his nephew Friedrich August during this transition. Reform grew out of political pressure and negotiation rather than a smooth royal decision to modernize everything at once.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: The constitution provided a route to challenge administrative decisions through law. That mattered because government affected property and livelihoods. It was a step toward legal restraints on administration, not a guarantee that everyone enjoyed the political rights available in a modern democracy.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: Chemnitz’s Royal Technical School opened in 1836 in response to demand for technically trained workers. Local manufacturing needed people who could understand materials and machinery. Education was increasingly connected to the practical problems of workshops and industry.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: The school’s early library collected books on machinery, chemistry and textiles alongside geography, surveying and road building. Technical education crossed subject boundaries. A future engineer might need a map and a chemistry book as much as a drawing of a machine.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: At Dresden, Carl Gustav Carus directed the royal midwives’ school from 1814 and taught obstetrics. Training people who assisted births was a concrete form of medical education. It concerned the care of mothers and babies, although the existence of a school does not measure access for every family.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: Museum researchers date Carl Julius Borcherdt’s first Chemnitz steam engine to 1836 using nineteenth-century accounts. They question an older 1829 claim. Industrial history depends on checking records, not repeating an impressive “first” until it becomes accepted by habit.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: The Göltzsch valley railway bridge was built between 1846 and 1851. Weak ground forced engineers to rethink its central supports and use larger openings. A design that looks orderly today preserves a response to awkward conditions discovered during construction.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: The viaduct used roughly 26 million bricks, with local clay helping make that choice practical. Granite was used where stresses required it. Its great size depended on repeated small components and careful material choices, not simply on making everything out of the strongest-looking stone.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: Construction employed an average of about 770 workers. The 1851 opening connected the finished structure to a wider railway route. Behind the celebrated engineering were years of quarrying, brickmaking, transport and work at height, tasks hidden when a train crosses in a few moments.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: Felix Mendelssohn helped establish Leipzig’s conservatory, which opened in 1843. Organized musical training became one of the city’s enduring institutions. Music was both an art heard in performance and a craft learned through sustained instruction.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: Robert Schumann’s published advice urged young musicians to train their ears, listen attentively and avoid reducing practice to mechanical finger exercises. These are instructions aimed at learners, not a description of every Saxon child’s upbringing. Access to an instrument and lessons was uneven.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: One rule says “Spiele immer, als hörte dir ein Meister zu.” It means “Always play as though a master were listening to you.” The German appears in the 1850 first printing of Schumann’s advice. An imaginary expert could apparently help with practice even before recorded lessons existed.

The Saxon monarchy ended in 1918, when the king relinquished the throne during the revolution. Saxony continued under republican institutions. Neither the 1815 loss of territory nor this map record’s 1878 endpoint meant that its people, industry or cultural life disappeared.

sectionTitles: What a town ate and threw away

passages.text: The later kingdom of Scotland joined regions with different languages, traditions and political histories. Its surviving record includes trading towns, universities, churches and royal documents. The atlas interval 1000-1715 is map coverage: political union with England occurred in 1707, and Scotland's communities continued afterward.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Waterlogged deposits in medieval Perth preserved plant remains from floors, rubbish pits and latrines. Many come from the 1100s-1200s. Things discarded in a damp backyard can be better evidence for dinner than a royal chronicle.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Perth's plant remains include oats and barley, with less wheat, alongside berries, apples and hazelnuts. Figs, grapes and walnuts point to imported foods. Their presence shows access, not that every household enjoyed the same menu.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Moss was gathered for several purposes, including bedding and toilet hygiene. Archaeologists must use context to distinguish those activities. Medieval shopping lists could include useful plants that a modern supermarket would put nowhere near the food aisle.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Perth's narrow property plots accommodated households and urban trades, including work on animal skins. The town's river crossing and overseas connections linked local labour to distant customers. This urban evidence cannot stand for all Scottish homes.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: The Lewis hoard contains 93 gaming objects, including pieces from at least four chess sets. Most were carved from walrus ivory, probably in Norway around 1200; some used whale teeth. Their thrones, clothing and faces preserve a carver's close attention to detail.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: Lewis belonged to the Norwegian kingdom when the chess pieces were probably buried. The Isles passed to Scotland in 1266. Including them here shows the changing regional history, not that a Scottish royal workshop necessarily made them.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: No one securely knows who buried the pieces or why. A merchant's stock and a local powerful owner's possessions are possibilities. The discovery accounts also conflict. Treasure can produce excellent questions without supplying a complete adventure story.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: Teaching began at St Andrews in 1410, and papal documents formally established its university in 1413. Organized higher learning was an achievement, but admission to such study was far narrower than access to a modern school.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: St Andrews Castle preserves a mine and countermine associated with its 1546-47 siege. Attackers dug toward the defenses while defenders dug to intercept them. The surviving tunnels make military engineering visible beneath a former bishop's residence.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The Protestant Reformation of 1560 changed church institutions and worship. St Andrews Castle's history includes religious conflict before that turning point. Religious change was lived through buildings, communities and authority, not simply one ruler choosing a new label.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The 1320 Declaration of Arbroath appealed to the pope on behalf of the kingdom's political community. It argued for independence under Robert Bruce. A forceful diplomatic letter states its authors' case; it is not a survey of every inhabitant's opinions.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The letter's Latin includes propter libertatem solummodo, “for freedom alone.” This follows the National Records of Scotland's scholarly text of the 1320 letter. The archive distinguishes that edition from an exact transcription of its surviving document; Latin was an international language of diplomacy.

On 1 May 1707 Scotland and England became the kingdom of Great Britain with a shared parliament. Scotland retained important legal institutions, and its people, languages and regional identities continued. The atlas's 1715 boundary is not the date of this union and should not be presented as Scotland's disappearance.
