sectionTitles: A small book with several lives

passages.text: Here Scots means early Gaelic-speaking western communities associated with Dál Riata and its successors, rather than all modern Scottish people or speakers of the later Scots language. Dunadd and island monasteries reveal craft, food, learning and sea connections.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Excavations at Dunadd found moulds and debris from a seventh-century workshop making fine metalwork. Brooch production involved planning, heating and finishing. This earlier evidence shows the skills behind the ornaments worn by powerful households.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Some Dunadd brooch designs adapted Anglo-Saxon forms. Imported pottery and glass also reached this Argyll hillfort. Objects crossed political and language boundaries; a foreign-looking ornament does not by itself identify its wearer's birthplace.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: The early excavations recovered 54 stone querns used to grind grain. Feeding a gathering required repeated physical work before anyone sat down to a feast. A royal meeting also needed someone to make the flour.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Dál Riata contained several kindreds with their own territories. Scholars have suggested that Dunadd offered a meeting place between them. The footprint carved near its summit is interpreted as an inauguration feature, not a surviving royal footprint pressed into wet rock.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: Iona was connected to Ireland and mainland Scotland by boat. Its island position could help communication rather than simply isolate its community. The standing thirteenth-century abbey is much later than Columba's sixth-century foundation.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: Adomnán's Life of Columba, written before 704, mentions fishing nets, deer traps and salt stores. This earlier monastic account gives specific glimpses of obtaining and preserving food; it is also a saint's biography with a religious purpose.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: The same account mentions harvest labour, book satchels and ink horns. Monastic learning depended on farming and supplies as well as prayer. A beautifully written page had a working community behind it.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: At Inchmarnock, excavators recovered slates carrying trial letters, designs and scraps of text. Some are interpreted as pupils' work. Reusable stone offered a surface for practice before committing writing to costly parchment.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: The Inchmarnock collection includes Latin and Gaelic writing, with ogham examples dated broadly to the seventh-ninth centuries. Other slates are much later. Finding several scripts together does not make every inscription contemporary.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: The Book of Deer is a small parchment Gospel book, about 16 by 11 centimetres. Cambridge's catalogue dates its main production to the late 800s or early 900s and cautiously suggests Scotland. Its compact size contrasts with the labour of preparing skin, copying and painting.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: The book contains a service for visiting the sick alongside Gospel texts. This is evidence of religious care, not proof of an effective medical treatment. Gaelic notes about Deer's property were added in the 1100s, well after the main book.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: In principio, “In the beginning,” appears at the opening of John on folio 42r of the Book of Deer. It is Latin written in an Insular manuscript, not a sample of everyday Gaelic speech. The short phrase introduces a sacred text.

Dál Riata’s political world changed, but Gaelic-speaking communities continued through later kingdoms and island societies. The map changes labels at 1000; that is not an extinction date or proof of an unbroken independent western state.

sectionTitles: More than life in the saddle
A ruler’s name and a changing political world

passages.text: Scythian communities north of the Black Sea included powerful rulers, horse riders, farmers and craftspeople. This map isolates 400 to 323 BCE, within a much longer history. Its sweeping outline reaches far beyond Pontic Scythia and omits important southern areas; it should not be read as the border of one empire. The examples below distinguish fourth-century objects from earlier settlements and later changes.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: Bilsk in today’s Ukraine was a substantial settlement complex in the wider Scythian-era world. Fortifications linked several settlements, and excavators found pottery ovens, metalworking installations, granaries and different kinds of houses. Its earlier history gives horse-centered stories some useful neighbors: potters, metalworkers and people keeping grain dry.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: Millet, wheat and barley were cultivated around Bilsk, alongside animal husbandry. Granaries made harvested food something that could be stored rather than eaten immediately. Farming and herding belonged together here; a family’s food supply depended on more than whatever could fit in a saddlebag.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: A study of Ukrainian sites dating broadly between 700 and 200 BCE used chemical signatures in teeth to investigate movement. All fifteen sampled Medvin teeth, and twenty-one of twenty-five from Mamai Gora, fell within the researchers’ estimated local strontium ranges. Many sampled people therefore appear to have spent childhood locally.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: The same study found differences in diet between communities. Millet contributed more strongly at Bilsk and Medvin than at Mamai Gora. One Mamai Gora man had different strontium signatures in teeth formed at different ages, suggesting movement during childhood. Staying near home was common in the sample, but it was not everyone’s story.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: At Bilsk’s Tsaryna Mohyla sector, pottery from the late seventh to early fifth centuries BCE preserves an earlier kitchen history. Handmade cooking pots often carried raised clay bands; bowls, ladles and large storage vessels could have polished surfaces. Later layers brought more jugs, mugs and small vessels. Even cupboard fashions changed.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: A gold griffin ornament at the Metropolitan Museum, dated to the fifth century BCE, is only 2.7 centimeters high. A small loop on its back allowed attachment to clothing. Its bird head, wings and feline body made a miniature fantastic animal wearable. Its reported northern Black Sea origin is less certain than its surviving construction.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: On 21 June 1971, Borys Mozolevskyi discovered the famous gold pectoral at Tovsta Mohyla, near present-day Pokrov in Ukraine. It lay in the passage leading to the central grave. This fourth-century BCE neck ornament weighs 1,149 grams and measures 30.6 centimeters across: spectacular craftsmanship with considerable weight behind it.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: The pectoral’s makers formed four hollow gold rods to look like twisted ropes. They cast tiny figures using the lost-wax process and soldered them into the composition. The museum counts forty-eight figures. Hollow construction and careful joining helped turn metalworking knowledge into an intricate object rather than a solid lump.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: Look closely at the pectoral’s upper register and everyday animal care appears among the gold. A boy milks a sheep; a foal nurses beside its mother. These are crafted scenes, not a census of children’s chores, but they bring feeding and tending animals into an object made for an exceptionally wealthy setting.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: Writing sample: “ΑΤΑΙΑΣ” is the Greek-letter name “Ataias,” usually called Ateas in English. It appears on silver coins catalogued for this fourth-century BCE Scythian ruler. This is a real ancient written name in Greek lettering, not a surviving sentence in the Scythian language.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: One of Ateas’s silver coins pairs the head of Heracles in a lion skin with a mounted archer shooting while his horse gallops. The combination brought a Greek heroic image and steppe-style horsemanship onto the same small object. Coins could advertise a ruler while circulating through exchange.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: Ateas died fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE. His activities are particularly associated with the western steppe, and scholars question whether he ruled all Scythia. A king’s defeat therefore cannot stand in for the disappearance of every community covered by a much larger map label.

The map stops in 323 BCE, not at a demonstrated collective collapse. Major steppe changes followed in the early third century BCE; their causes remain debated. Later Scythian communities developed in Crimea and the lower Dnieper, with different settlements and political arrangements.

sectionTitles: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
Sites, sources and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Samori Ture built a state through conquest, trade and Islamic authority in the later 1800s. Often called the Wassoulou or Samorian empire, it shifted eastward under French military pressure. “First” and “Second Samori Empire” describe different territorial phases of the same ruler’s state. Its independent history ended with his capture in 1898, not with the 1900 to 1914 interval currently attached to those two map labels.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: Samori’s armies depended on supply networks. Earlier muskets came chiefly through Freetown, while horses came from the northwestern Sudan. These routes connected inland politics with coastal commerce.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: In 1891 to 1892, negotiations with Freetown traders brought breechloading and repeating firearms. Legassick also records a local firearms industry established by this period. Adaptation meant acquiring weapons and developing skilled work to support them.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: After French advances restricted western supplies, Samori sought weapons through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast and horses through Mossi country. Existing African trade routes became crucial to the state’s survival.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: The Buré goldfields mattered to Samori’s economy. When French forces occupied Buré in 1885, his armies drove them back. Control of a resource region could be as consequential as control of a capital.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Samori sought an agreement with the British authorities in Sierra Leone and also negotiated treaties with France. His strategy combined fighting and bargaining; African rulers were participants in diplomacy, not merely spectators to European decisions.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Trade also carried a terrible cost: Samori captured and sold people to help finance guns and horses. Resistance to French conquest did not mean freedom for everyone living under his own expanding power.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Yves Person’s chronology records a decision in 1892 to move east with a substantial part of the population. A moving state meant uprooted households as well as marching soldiers. The chronology establishes the displacement without telling us every family’s experience.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: The same chronology records scorched-earth tactics in 1891. Destroying resources could obstruct an advancing army while making civilian life more precarious. Military success and the welfare of local people cannot be treated as the same thing.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Sordi’s fortified settlement in northern Côte d’Ivoire became part of the struggle between Kénédougou, Samori’s forces and French expansion. Historian M’Brah identifies occupation by Samori’s sofa troops from 1896 to 1898. A single site reveals overlapping rulers and local experiences.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: M’Brah traces Diawala’s growth to people dispersed from Sordi and to exiles returning after Kénédougou’s defeat in 1898. Related families reunited and organized a new settlement. Political defeat changed where people lived; it did not erase their family connections.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Accounts of Samori need careful comparison. Legassick’s article explicitly warns that some French visitors’ descriptions were imaginative or unreliable. Historians use local traditions and archival evidence together instead of treating an officer’s vivid story as automatic fact.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: This dossier has not verified a short original-script passage from a securely identified Samorian document. Arabic scholarship belonged to the wider region, but substituting an unrelated manuscript would give a false impression. Household sanitation and specific medical routines also remain unestablished by the sources used here.

passages.title: Capture and continuing communities
passages.text: French forces captured Samori on 29 September 1898. He was exiled to Gabon and died in 1900. His death date is therefore not the date a “first” or “second” empire began; those map labels need chronological correction.

Samori’s capture by French forces in 1898 ended his independent state. Exile and his death in 1900 followed. The region’s communities continued under colonial rule; the changing imperial labels describe political power, not the appearance or disappearance of a people.

passages.text: Segu was a powerful Bamana kingdom along the Niger in present-day Mali. Its armies, farmers, boat operators and artists made the river towns a major regional centre. Royal wealth also depended on warfare and the enslavement of captives.

passages.title: Rulers and the river
passages.text: Biton Kulibali built his power through the tonjonw, an association that became a standing army. Raids supplied captives, some forced into military service and others sold to obtain horses, weapons and luxury goods.

passages.title: Rulers and the river
passages.text: Mungo Park reached Segu in July 1796 and described four walled towns on both banks of the Niger. He saw flat-roofed clay houses, some two storeys high and whitewashed, alongside mosques. The capital was a cluster of settlements connected by water.

passages.title: Rulers and the river
passages.text: Park recorded a fare of ten cowrie shells for a river crossing. The ferries were worked by enslaved people for the king. Some boats joined two hollowed trunks end to end and could carry horses as well as passengers: this was a serious transport service.

passages.title: Work, meals and hospitality
passages.text: When Park was stranded outside the town, a woman returning from field work offered shelter. Her household supplied a mat, a lamp and fish cooked over embers. This encounter in a traveller’s diary preserves a family’s generosity across a language barrier.

passages.title: Work, meals and hospitality
passages.text: After the meal, the women in that household spun cotton and sang through part of the night. Park’s account catches work and social life happening together. Cloth did not begin in a shop: somebody first had to turn fibre into thread.

passages.title: Work, meals and hospitality
passages.text: The Met’s account of Bamana village life describes extended families cultivating fields, with outlying plots demanding seasonal labour at planting and harvest. Farming supported the social world celebrated in sculpture, even though kings and battles occupy more space in written histories.

passages.title: Work, meals and hospitality
passages.text: Bamana society also included specialist craft groups and enslaved people. A beautiful carved object belonged to a society with unequal ranks and demanding labour. Appreciating the maker’s skill should include remembering the different circumstances of the people who produced food, cloth and tools.

passages.title: Animals, families and words
passages.text: A surviving Ci Wara headdress combines features associated with an antelope and other burrowing animals. In performance, paired dancers wore carved headdresses and raffia while women sang encouragement. The spectacle celebrated agricultural skill: farming could have its own cheering section.

passages.title: Animals, families and words
passages.text: The story of Ci Wara tells of a partly human, partly animal being who taught cultivation. This is a sacred origin story, not an archaeological account of agriculture’s invention. The museum’s nineteenth to early twentieth century carving shows how that story took visible form.

passages.title: Animals, families and words
passages.text: A Bamana mother-and-child figure at the University of Michigan dates to the late nineteenth or early twentieth century. Its subject foregrounds motherhood and the continuation of a community across generations. It belongs to the cultural world that continued after the kingdom’s conquest.

passages.title: Animals, families and words
passages.text: A later Bamana power object, or boli, in the Met contains wood, cloth and accumulated organic materials. Offerings changed its surface over time. Its lumpy outline records repeated acts of care and ritual, rather than a sculptor aiming for a neatly polished finish.

passages.title: Animals, families and words
passages.text: Try a short greeting in modern written Bambara: “I ni sɔgɔma”, meaning “Good morning”. The Peace Corps lesson prints this in today’s Latin alphabet. It introduces the continuing language; it is not presented as the spelling on an eighteenth-century royal document.

Umar Tal conquered Segu in 1861. The Bamana kingdom lost its independence, while its people, farming traditions and artistic practices continued under changing governments. The map record’s 1815 cutoff precedes this conquest.

passages.text: The Great Seljuk Empire, founded when Tughril took Nishapur in 1037, brought Oghuz Turkic rule to Iran, Iraq and Anatolia under a Persian administration. Its sultans protected the Abbasid caliphs, built madrasas and mosques, and opened Anatolia to the Turks.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The vizier Nizam al-Mulk and his rival Taj al-Mulk added the two great brick domes to the Friday Mosque of Isfahan in 1086 and 1088.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Persian poetry, calligraphy and lustre ceramics flourished under Seljuk patronage; Omar Khayyam wrote the quatrains later gathered as the Rubaiyat.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk founded the Nizamiyya of Baghdad, first of a network of madrasas teaching Shafi'i law and theology.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Alp Arslan's victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkic settlement.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Nizam al-Mulk's Book of Government set out the Persian art of kingship for the sultans.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Jalali calendar, computed by Omar Khayyam and colleagues for Malik Shah, fixed the year to the spring equinox with an error of about one day in 3,770 years, less than the Gregorian calendar's.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Khayyam's treatise on algebra classified cubic equations and solved them with conic sections.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Turkic settlement of Anatolia that followed Manzikert led to the Sultanate of Rum and, in time, the Ottomans.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The madrasa became the standard school of Sunni learning.

After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire split among his heirs and their atabegs. The last sultan of Iraq, Tughril III, was killed in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish, who took Iran; the Seljuks of Rum in Anatolia lasted until 1308.

Clothing as invention and historical evidence
Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
Brighton: cattle, schooling and recorded everyday life
Immokalee: work, homes and women’s organizing
Tampa: family, archives and the costs of growth

passages.text: Seminole history in Florida grew from several southeastern Indigenous communities, migration and resistance to colonial expansion. It includes related but distinct peoples and governments. This account follows that wider history and the modern Seminole Tribe of Florida, with separate sections about its reservation communities.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: A chickee’s cypress-log frame and palmetto thatch offered shelter that could be assembled with locally available materials. The Tribe’s account connects its widespread use with movement under military pressure. Building skills continue in commercial work, using newer equipment alongside knowledge of timber and thatching.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Corn-based sofk and a pot kept warm at the hearth formed part of household food routines. The Tribe’s food account also emphasizes change: contemporary families buy ordinary groceries and prepare traditional dishes on special occasions. A historical food practice should not be treated as every family’s unchanging daily menu.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Early twentieth-century camps traded hides, feathers, fruit and nuts for equipment and goods such as sewing machines and kettles. Everglades drainage and declining markets changed those livelihoods. Agricultural labor, cattle work and tourism became increasingly important ways to earn money.

passages.title: Homes, food and making a living
passages.text: Black Seminole communities included people who had escaped enslavement and established towns in Florida. They maintained alliances with Indigenous Seminoles and fought alongside them. Removal to Indian Territory exposed Black Seminoles to kidnapping and renewed enslavement, showing that a shared military struggle did not remove the distinct dangers they faced.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Hand-sewn appliqué and machine-made patchwork are different techniques. Earlier clothing used traded cotton and applied decoration; sewing machines reached Seminole camps in the late nineteenth century. Around 1920, women developed colored geometric bands sewn into garments, turning an adopted machine into a means of distinctive artistic invention.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Surviving garments, photographs and paintings allow historians to compare changing skirts, capes, shirts and jackets. Patchwork also became a source of income in tourist markets and a skill transmitted within families. Its modern development does not make it less meaningful as Seminole cultural expression.

passages.title: Clothing as invention and historical evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologists survey areas before development, record finds and map sites so important places can be protected. Their work combines field investigation with stewardship of the cultural landscape. An object’s presence on a modern reservation, by itself, does not establish that its maker used a modern tribal name.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: Big Cypress citrus development began with studies of agricultural suitability and soil. Clearing for a new grove started in 1987, and the first trees were planted in 1989. The project initially emphasized local employment; low industry returns later shifted attention toward efficient production. Economic development required changing plans as conditions changed.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: The building reopened as To-Pee-Kee-Ke Yak-Ne in 2019 had been built by the Bureau of Indian Affairs in the 1950s. Elders recalled Council meetings, children’s activities, Head Start and shelter during Hurricane Donna. Its successive uses preserve a history of government, education, recreation and emergency refuge in one place.

passages.title: Big Cypress: agriculture and a building’s many lives
passages.text: The renewed center included exhibits about reservations and cattle raising, together with the museum’s oral-history office. People could share memories where community life already happened. The building is therefore both historical evidence and an active place for creating an archive in the community’s own voices.

sectionTitles: Art, public memory and language teaching

passages.text: The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma grew through the rebuilding of communities after forced removal from Florida in the nineteenth century. Its history joins farming, band government, religious life, education and artistic work. It is a continuing nation with institutions distinct from the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

passages.title: Farming, kinship and public responsibility
passages.text: Historical bands maintained communal fields worked by their members. Their harvest helped feed visitors, support orphans and people in need, and meet communal expenses. Farming was therefore connected with public responsibility as well as individual households’ subsistence.

passages.title: Farming, kinship and public responsibility
passages.text: Band membership normally followed the mother, while changing bands required the agreement of both communities. Chiefs, assistants and counselors dealt with rules and disputes. Bands could be known by a chief’s name, so a changed name in a record does not necessarily mean a wholly new population.

passages.title: Farming, kinship and public responsibility
passages.text: Two Freedmen bands were recognized in 1866. Their place in the band structure records the long relationship between Seminoles and people of African descent. Their history is part of the Nation’s institutions and community life, rather than an incidental episode in a story only about warfare.

passages.title: Farming, kinship and public responsibility
passages.text: Religious life includes Christian churches as well as ceremonial traditions. Mvskoke-language hymns continued in Oklahoma congregations, and some Christians also participated in traditional ceremonies. These practices show people combining commitments rather than all following one uniform path of religious change.

passages.title: Schools, buildings and documentary discoveries
passages.text: Emahaka Academy’s four-story brick building, established in 1894 near Wewoka, had running water, steam heat and fireplaces. Its curriculum ranged from arithmetic to foreign languages. These details show substantial institutional investment in education, while admission rules and boarding arrangements also placed children within a closely regulated environment.

passages.title: Schools, buildings and documentary discoveries
passages.text: At Mekasukey Academy, students raised livestock and vegetables and produced dairy foods. The school had electricity and indoor plumbing, but teachers prohibited children from speaking their Native language during the term. Material provision and educational opportunity thus existed alongside practices that suppressed language and identity.

passages.title: Schools, buildings and documentary discoveries
passages.text: The Oklahoma Historical Society’s catalogue lists Mekusukey school rosters, admission applications, progress reports, medical records and correspondence from 1910 to 1929. These records can connect institutional history with individual children’s lives. The catalogue establishes what survives; it does not tell us what every student experienced.

passages.title: Schools, buildings and documentary discoveries
passages.text: Mekasukey closed in 1930 and its main building later burned. School closure ended an institution, not the Seminole Nation. Documentary records and the commemorated site preserve different kinds of evidence, which must be distinguished from a complete surviving campus.

passages.title: Art, public memory and language teaching
passages.text: Enoch Kelly Haney, a Seminole artist who also served as a legislator and tribal chief, created The Guardian. The bronze figure was cast in sections, and Haney drew on members of his own family for its facial features. A monumental public artwork thus carries both individual craftsmanship and family connections.

passages.title: Art, public memory and language teaching
passages.text: The Guardian stands on the Oklahoma Capitol dome, while a smaller replica is displayed inside. The two settings offer different encounters with the same composition: a distant civic landmark and a figure that visitors can examine more closely. This is a documented modern work, not an archaeological representation of ancient Seminole clothing.

passages.title: Art, public memory and language teaching
passages.text: At Wewoka, the Margaret Jane Norman Gallery preserves paintings, sketches and sculpture by Haney and other artists. Workshops and storytelling make the museum a place for learning as well as display. Its collection represents several artists and tribal backgrounds; it should not be treated as uniformly Seminole in authorship.

passages.title: Art, public memory and language teaching
passages.text: The Nation’s Adult Immersion Program pairs beginning Mvskoke learners with fluent speakers. Sustained daily practice and preparation to teach others make language transmission a deliberate educational undertaking. The program describes what it aims to achieve; those aims do not by themselves measure every participant’s proficiency.

passages.title: Losses, rebuilding and continuing government
passages.text: Civil War divisions sent Union supporters toward Kansas while other Seminoles joined the Confederacy. The 1866 settlement imposed severe changes to territory and required emancipation and citizenship for former slaves. Wewoka developed as a new capital after the war, making political rebuilding part of the history of place.

passages.title: Losses, rebuilding and continuing government
passages.text: Allotment divided collective territory into individual holdings. Sales and fraud then stripped many Seminole people of land. The discovery of oil brought wealth to some owners who retained property, but it did not reverse the broader pattern of dispossession.

passages.title: Losses, rebuilding and continuing government
passages.text: The General Council draws representatives from the Nation’s bands and legislates for citizens, enterprises and tribal property. The museum’s account also describes departments for housing, education, language, environmental work and family services. Government continues through these practical responsibilities, as well as through its constitutional framework.

The Seminole Nation of Oklahoma continues. Removal, war, allotment and federal interference transformed landholding and government, but did not end the people’s history. Later constitutional organization, public services and language programs form part of that continuity. The imported 1492 to 1500 interval is not a historical date for an Oklahoma Seminole nation.

passages.text: These historical Senegal labels cover changing regional and colonial footprints. The 1530 outline stretches far south beyond modern Senegal and does not establish a unified state or a French colony at that date. Later snapshots narrow to coastal Senegal; the 1900 record represents colonial territory. This phased narrative follows documented communities and institutions, while the modern republic has its own card.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: A French chartered company established itself at Saint-Louis in 1659. Traders used the Senegal River to seek gum arabic, hides, gold and enslaved people. The island settlement depended on waterways and surrounding communities; its commercial importance should not be mistaken for French control of the whole region.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Historian Alain Sinou emphasizes African and mixed-ancestry merchants in the settlement’s development. Saint-Louis had neither farmland nor a freshwater source sufficient for its needs, so its survival depended on mainland supplies and negotiated relationships. The river was a route to dinner and drinking water as well as to commercial cargo.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Some signares, women of property in Saint-Louis and Gorée, controlled substantial houses and commercial wealth. Scholarship also records their ownership of enslaved domestic workers. Their influence challenges a history that notices only European men, while the labour supporting affluent households must remain visible too.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Surviving Saint-Louis houses reveal practical design choices. Shops occupied large ground-floor rooms, while upper rooms had high wooden ceilings and many openings. Balconies and broad verandas created shaded space. The city’s heritage description helps explain how trade, household life and the search for cooler air could share one building.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Roger Pasquier’s study of food supply from 1840 to 1870 describes millet used for couscous and sanglé, alongside wheat flour for bread and rice eaten across communities. Rice became especially useful when millet was scarce. Feeding a town meant organizing trade and transport, not simply growing food inside its boundaries.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Enslaved families also acted to change their lives. Research on liberation registers from 1857 to 1903 identifies adults and children who fled together to demand freedom. Ninety percent of the family units identified in that study were headed by women. Family attachment could become a reason to take enormous risks together.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: “Grammaire de la langue woloffe” means “Grammar of the Wolof Language.” This French title appears on P.-David Boilat’s 1858 book, published by the Imprimerie Impériale. The title is an attested sample of writing from the period; its historical spelling of “woloffe” is retained rather than silently modernized.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: European print was only one route into writing. Boston University’s Ajami research documents African languages written in adapted Arabic scripts and the preservation of Wolof manuscripts. These traditions remind us to look beyond French-language books when asking who studied, composed texts or passed knowledge between generations.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: A teacher-training college was created at Saint-Louis by an order of 24 November 1903. The institution later known as William Ponty trained educators for French West Africa. Its much later student papers, beginning in 1933, preserved studies of community life: that documentary legacy continued beyond this map record’s 1914 endpoint.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: The Faidherbe Bridge’s spans arrived from France in separate pieces in 1897. The bridge joined a city already organized around quays and river crossings. UNESCO dates its inauguration to 19 October: engineering altered movement around Saint-Louis while the older street pattern remained recognizable.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: The Dakar to Saint-Louis railway was completed in 1885. Research traces how it drew merchants, migrant workers, formerly enslaved people and farmers into the peanut-growing region. Rails carried crops toward markets, but their social effects depended on the people who moved, worked and traded along them.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: Peanut production involved much more than harvesting a field. Cropper’s study describes women sowing, weeding and shelling, while migrant farm workers also grew crops or sold charcoal on their own account. Peanuts supplied food and livestock feed, and their byproducts could become fuel. Almost every part of the crop acquired a job.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: Saint-Louis remained a major colonial centre, but its role changed when Dakar became the capital of French West Africa in 1902. Senegal’s own colonial capital stayed at Saint-Louis much longer. One city losing a particular administrative title did not mean its households, crafts or trade disappeared.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: Blaise Diagne won election as Senegal’s deputy on 10 May 1914. His campaign called for a lycée, teacher-training and medical schools in Dakar, and defended freedom of religious conscience. The demands show education and health as political questions, not simply gifts that colonial officials decided to distribute.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: A bubonic-plague epidemic struck Dakar in 1914. Colonial officials blamed African residents, expelled people from the centre and burned homes. Historian Tobias Warner connects these measures to the creation of the segregated Médina neighbourhood. An epidemic became a struggle over who could live where, and on what terms.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: Residents resisted through a general strike, political action and street protest. Their response makes the history of sanitation more than a story of official orders: people argued about what protection should mean and about the destruction of their homes. Médina later became an important place of cultural creativity.

passages.text: These historical Senegal labels cover changing regional and colonial footprints. The 1530 outline stretches far south beyond modern Senegal and does not establish a unified state or a French colony at that date. Later snapshots narrow to coastal Senegal; the 1900 record represents colonial territory. This phased narrative follows documented communities and institutions, while the modern republic has its own card.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: A French chartered company established itself at Saint-Louis in 1659. Traders used the Senegal River to seek gum arabic, hides, gold and enslaved people. The island settlement depended on waterways and surrounding communities; its commercial importance should not be mistaken for French control of the whole region.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Historian Alain Sinou emphasizes African and mixed-ancestry merchants in the settlement’s development. Saint-Louis had neither farmland nor a freshwater source sufficient for its needs, so its survival depended on mainland supplies and negotiated relationships. The river was a route to dinner and drinking water as well as to commercial cargo.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Some signares, women of property in Saint-Louis and Gorée, controlled substantial houses and commercial wealth. Scholarship also records their ownership of enslaved domestic workers. Their influence challenges a history that notices only European men, while the labour supporting affluent households must remain visible too.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Surviving Saint-Louis houses reveal practical design choices. Shops occupied large ground-floor rooms, while upper rooms had high wooden ceilings and many openings. Balconies and broad verandas created shaded space. The city’s heritage description helps explain how trade, household life and the search for cooler air could share one building.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Roger Pasquier’s study of food supply from 1840 to 1870 describes millet used for couscous and sanglé, alongside wheat flour for bread and rice eaten across communities. Rice became especially useful when millet was scarce. Feeding a town meant organizing trade and transport, not simply growing food inside its boundaries.

passages.title: Trading towns and household work
passages.text: Enslaved families also acted to change their lives. Research on liberation registers from 1857 to 1903 identifies adults and children who fled together to demand freedom. Ninety percent of the family units identified in that study were headed by women. Family attachment could become a reason to take enormous risks together.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: “Grammaire de la langue woloffe” means “Grammar of the Wolof Language.” This French title appears on P.-David Boilat’s 1858 book, published by the Imprimerie Impériale. The title is an attested sample of writing from the period; its historical spelling of “woloffe” is retained rather than silently modernized.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: European print was only one route into writing. Boston University’s Ajami research documents African languages written in adapted Arabic scripts and the preservation of Wolof manuscripts. These traditions remind us to look beyond French-language books when asking who studied, composed texts or passed knowledge between generations.

passages.title: Writing and learning
passages.text: A teacher-training college was created at Saint-Louis by an order of 24 November 1903. The institution later known as William Ponty trained educators for French West Africa. Its much later student papers, beginning in 1933, preserved studies of community life: that documentary legacy continued beyond this map record’s 1914 endpoint.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: The Faidherbe Bridge’s spans arrived from France in separate pieces in 1897. The bridge joined a city already organized around quays and river crossings. UNESCO dates its inauguration to 19 October: engineering altered movement around Saint-Louis while the older street pattern remained recognizable.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: The Dakar to Saint-Louis railway was completed in 1885. Research traces how it drew merchants, migrant workers, formerly enslaved people and farmers into the peanut-growing region. Rails carried crops toward markets, but their social effects depended on the people who moved, worked and traded along them.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: Peanut production involved much more than harvesting a field. Cropper’s study describes women sowing, weeding and shelling, while migrant farm workers also grew crops or sold charcoal on their own account. Peanuts supplied food and livestock feed, and their byproducts could become fuel. Almost every part of the crop acquired a job.

passages.title: Bridges, crops and changing capitals
passages.text: Saint-Louis remained a major colonial centre, but its role changed when Dakar became the capital of French West Africa in 1902. Senegal’s own colonial capital stayed at Saint-Louis much longer. One city losing a particular administrative title did not mean its households, crafts or trade disappeared.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: Blaise Diagne won election as Senegal’s deputy on 10 May 1914. His campaign called for a lycée, teacher-training and medical schools in Dakar, and defended freedom of religious conscience. The demands show education and health as political questions, not simply gifts that colonial officials decided to distribute.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: A bubonic-plague epidemic struck Dakar in 1914. Colonial officials blamed African residents, expelled people from the centre and burned homes. Historian Tobias Warner connects these measures to the creation of the segregated Médina neighbourhood. An epidemic became a struggle over who could live where, and on what terms.

passages.title: Politics and an epidemic in 1914
passages.text: Residents resisted through a general strike, political action and street protest. Their response makes the history of sanitation more than a story of official orders: people argued about what protection should mean and about the destruction of their homes. Médina later became an important place of cultural creativity.

The imported endpoints of 1878 and 1914 mark map coverage, not the extinction of Senegalese communities or the end of French rule. Colonial rule continued into the twentieth century; Senegal’s independence and the dissolution of the Mali Federation came in 1960.

sectionTitles: A meal, a canvas and a classroom

passages.text: Senegal emerged as a separate republic in 1960 after the brief Mali Federation. Its history includes influential arts institutions, public-health research and the work of sustaining democratic government.

passages.title: Independence and public life
passages.text: Senegal and the former French Sudan briefly formed the Mali Federation, independent from France in June 1960. Senegal withdrew on 20 August. Today’s Senegal and Republic of Mali therefore share part of their independence story, but are separate countries.

passages.title: Independence and public life
passages.text: The UN’s 2024 regional report records both pre-election tensions and a democratic transfer of power in Senegal. Elections are historical events involving voters, courts, candidates and public argument, not simply a new portrait in a government office.

passages.title: Independence and public life
passages.text: An attested French writing sample is Senegal’s motto: “Un Peuple - Un But - Une Foi”. It means “One People, One Goal, One Faith”. The presidency explains it as an aspiration to shared national life, unity and purpose.

passages.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom
passages.text: Ceebu jën developed in Saint-Louis fishing communities. Fish, broken rice and seasonal vegetables form its familiar foundation, but recipes vary. A shopping basket might include carrots, cabbage, cassava or okra: a national dish still leaves room for local cooks.

passages.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom
passages.text: UNESCO’s account describes cooking techniques passed from mothers to daughters and meals often eaten by hand at home. Restaurants commonly provide spoons or forks. Kitchen knowledge is learned through watching, practicing and eating together, rather than only by reading a recipe.

passages.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom
passages.text: The meal also has manners: the bowl is steadied with the left hand, and rice should not be dropped. The quality of fish and vegetables can express the importance of an occasion or affection for a guest. Hospitality can be deliciously specific.

passages.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom
passages.text: Artist Iba Ndiaye returned to Dakar at Senghor’s invitation around independence to establish a national fine-arts school. Born in Saint-Louis, he had studied in France. Education and international exchange helped shape modern Senegalese painting alongside older artistic traditions.

passages.title: A meal, a canvas and a classroom
passages.text: Ndiaye’s Tabaski III, painted in 1970, represents the Islamic Feast of Sacrifice in a West African setting. The oil painting is on plywood and measures 1.5 by 2.5 meters. That is a substantial surface on which to bring local experience into an international art conversation.

passages.title: Skills that protect health
passages.text: At Kaffrine in 2022, UNICEF described girls missing school because of menstrual stigma, inadequate toilets and lack of supplies. Private, functional facilities mattered alongside information. Staying in a classroom can depend on what is available down the corridor.

passages.title: Skills that protect health
passages.text: Nogaye and Ndela joined a group of forty-seven young women and men learning to sew reusable menstrual pads. Their ten-day training combined sewing with business skills. Ndela reported 20,900 pads produced for distribution to schools, connecting paid local work with pupils’ needs.

passages.title: Skills that protect health
passages.text: The Institut Pasteur de Dakar manufactures yellow-fever vaccine and conducts disease research. Its work links technicians, laboratory equipment and production facilities with public health across Africa. Senegal’s scientific achievements include making essential materials, not only publishing discoveries.

passages.title: Skills that protect health
passages.text: The institute also tests drinking water and food, while its surveillance network helps detect unusual illness. Scientific work reaches into ordinary meals and clinic visits: a laboratory can investigate things far too small to see in a glass of water.
Senegal continues as a republic. The peaceful transfer following the tense 2024 election is one chapter in an ongoing political history, not an ending for its people or institutions.

sectionTitles: Mining towns and the tools of authority
Books, textiles and a riverside capital

passages.text: This card concerns medieval Serbian principalities, the Nemanjic kingdom and empire, and later successor lordships. Their borders and institutions changed over time. Quarry settlements, burnt food, fish bones, illuminated books and a seal-maker's tool reveal work and learning beyond royal campaigns. Evidence from a monastery or court describes that setting, not every household.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Near Studenica, marble quarries and remains of a workers' settlement connect the Church of the Virgin with the people who extracted and shaped its stone. The monastery's finely finished surfaces depended on a wider landscape of skilled and demanding labour.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Studenica's Church of the Virgin combines a domed interior with an exterior drawing on Romanesque architecture. Its design became a model for other monasteries. Builders adapted forms circulating across the Adriatic and Byzantine worlds rather than working within a sealed national tradition.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Paintings made in the Church of the Virgin in 1208 and 1209 organise religious figures through expressive gestures and carefully conceived space. Their surviving setting lets historians study images as part of a building used for worship, rather than as detached museum pictures.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Charred remains from twelfth- and thirteenth-century buildings at Ras include bread wheat, rye, barley, oats and millet. Wheat was most abundant in the studied samples. Weeds mixed with grain, including corncockle, preserve traces of crop handling as well as the crops themselves.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: The Ras study also identified a round piece of burnt bread, cereal remains in a pot and fragments of peach stones. These finds bring prepared food and fruit into view. They document particular deposits, not a complete menu or the quantities eaten by every resident.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Waste deposits at Studenica from the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries contained catfish, carp and pike alongside migratory sturgeon. The researchers connect the sturgeon with the distant Danube. Feeding a monastery could involve both nearby fishing and longer supply routes.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Studenica's fish bones preserve information about body parts, size and cutting. The authors suggest that some large fish arrived whole, perhaps dried or salted. Preservation methods are an interpretation of the remains; the bones do not supply a surviving recipe.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: Excavation at Drenje in Rudnik revealed secular buildings and three churches, two Orthodox and one Catholic, in a settlement flourishing during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. These remains suggest a varied religious landscape. Identifying the area specifically as the medieval market remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: A seal-die from a pit at Rudnik bears Prince Lazar's name and a helmet with horned ornament. Dated to his rule there between 1373 and 1389, it is a tool for producing official impressions. No matching impression was known to the study's authors.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The late twelfth-century Miroslav Gospel combines writing on parchment with gilding and painted decoration. Its illuminations draw on Italian and Byzantine artistic traditions. The manuscript shows bookmaking as a collaboration of textual, material and visual skills shaped by connections beyond one court.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The Miroslav Gospel arranges readings for liturgical use rather than simply presenting an unbroken narrative. Its language and spelling also preserve evidence of a regional scribal tradition. A book could guide repeated communal worship while carrying the choices of the people who copied it.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: An embroidered priestly stole, or epitrachelion, from the Church of Saints Peter and Paul near Novi Pazar preserves another demanding craft. The National Museum dates its style to the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. This ceremonial garment cannot stand for ordinary clothing.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: Smederevo's new court was built at the meeting of the Danube and Jezava in 1428 to 1430. Its builders faced shortages of local stone, bringing material from farther away and reusing older masonry. The fortress records transport and salvage as well as defensive planning.

Ottoman conquest of Smederevo in 1459 ended the remaining Serbian despotate. The medieval empire had fragmented much earlier; 1389 was not the date when all Serbian political institutions vanished. Settlement at Smederevo and religious communities such as Studenica continued under changed conditions. The imported map endpoint of 1300 is not a historical fall date.

sectionTitles: Political participation and care during war

passages.text: This record follows Serbia after international recognition of its independence in 1878, through its kingdom and the First World War. Banks, water systems, museums and universities developed alongside parliamentary conflict and devastating war. It ends around the transition into a larger South Slav state, not the end of Serbian communities.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Before Belgrade’s water-supply system opened in 1892, Knez Mihailova Street depended on courtyard wells and the Delijska Fountain. Fetching water was part of household work. The new system changed a practical daily task, not merely the city’s appearance.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Electric street lighting arrived in Belgrade in 1891, with an early lantern at the corner of Kralja Petra and Knez Mihailova. Lighting a street extended useful public space after dark, although one lamp does not prove every household had electricity.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: After recognition of independence, Serbia minted gold twenty-dinar coins in 1879. In 1884 its new national bank issued hundred-dinar notes payable in gold. Paper money depended on confidence in an institution as well as the paper’s printed design.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: The bank began operations in July 1884, following legislation passed the previous year. It supplied credit and handled currency issuance. Establishing an institution required rules and staff, not simply printing an impressive-looking note.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Привилегована Народна банка Краљевине Србије means “Privileged National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbia.” This Serbian Cyrillic title is attested in the bank’s catalogue of a book published in Belgrade in 1909, covering its first twenty-five years.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: Milutin Milanković joined the University of Belgrade in 1909 and shared an office with Mihailo Petrović. One taught applied mathematics and the other theoretical mathematics. A scientific community grew through colleagues teaching and exchanging ideas.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: In 1912 Mladen Berić defended the university’s first doctoral dissertation in mathematical sciences before a commission including Petrović and Milanković. Advanced education required teachers able to train a new generation, not just individuals making discoveries alone.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: Petrović constructed a hydro-integrator in 1900, a calculating instrument using water, and received a bronze medal at the Paris exhibition. Mathematical work could take the form of a physical device as well as equations on a blackboard.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: The National Museum had been founded in 1844 to collect and preserve antiquities, before this map interval. Its continued work made objects available for study. A museum collection is assembled through choices, rather than being a complete sample of everyone’s past.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: The constitutions of 1888 and 1903 shaped parliamentary life and the role of parties. The Assembly’s history records changes in the balance between monarchs, governments and representatives. Rules about participation had consequences for how power could be challenged.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: Assembly meetings took place in several buildings and cities, including a school in Niš. During wartime, public institutions had to adapt their location and routines. Parliamentary history therefore includes ordinary rooms temporarily used for extraordinary decisions.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: Nurse Ljubica Luković cared for wounded people from Serbian and opposing armies. A Red Cross notice records that she worked at Valjevo during the 1915 typhus epidemic and died after becoming infected. Her story shows the human labour behind wartime healthcare.

Serbia entered the new South Slav kingdom in 1918. Its independent kingdom was incorporated into a larger state, while communities and institutions continued in a changed framework. The atlas extends this label to 1920; that endpoint should not turn the 1918 transition into two additional years of unchanged sovereignty.

sectionTitles: Conflict and the limits of a map

passages.text: This record begins while Serbia was part of a federation with Montenegro. The state union changed in 2003 and ended in 2006, after which Serbia continued separately. Modern Serbian life includes family celebrations, skilled pottery, education and public institutions, alongside the consequences of conflict and contested political boundaries.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia entered the United Nations in November 2000. Its official name changed to Serbia and Montenegro in 2003. These dates explain why a map labelled Serbia in the 1990s needs a federal context.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: Montenegro declared independence in June 2006. Serbia continued the former union’s United Nations membership, while Montenegro joined separately. A change in international representation is one documented way to follow the institutional transition.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: Serbia’s new constitution was approved by referendum in October 2006 and proclaimed in November. It defines state institutions and legal rights. A constitution is evidence of stated rules; it is not proof that every rule is fulfilled in practice.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Some Orthodox families celebrate Slava in honour of a patron saint, gathering relatives, friends and neighbours. UNESCO’s 2014 record describes a decorated cake, wine and a candle. This is a specific religious family tradition, not a universal Serbian custom.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Knowledge of Slava is passed through families, with women playing a major teaching role in the documented practice. Preparing food and welcoming guests help transmit social knowledge as well as religious meaning.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Zlakusa potters mix clay with calcite and shape vessels on a wheel turned by hand. Making a pot takes several stages over seven to ten days, including drying and firing. The cooking vessel has already required patience before dinner begins.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: The craft produces pots and pans suited to cooking and serving, with shapes adapted to modern kitchens. Learners work alongside experienced makers; school classes and public demonstrations also help. Tradition here includes practical adaptation.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: Народна банка Србије means “National Bank of Serbia.” The name appears in Serbian Cyrillic and Latin letters on the 2003 hundred-dinar note. Its official design specification supplies a precise witness for this short sample of modern written Serbian.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: The note’s Nikola Tesla imagery includes an electromagnetic engine. Its specification also describes features visible under infrared and ultraviolet light. Scientific commemoration and anti-counterfeiting technology share the same everyday object.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: The floods of 2014 damaged schools and disrupted healthcare. Some schools became temporary shelters and others ended the year early. UNICEF’s account shows why protecting children’s routines includes safe buildings, clean surroundings and functioning public services.

passages.title: Conflict and the limits of a map
passages.text: Fighting in Kosovo in 1998 to 1999 displaced civilians and destroyed homes; NATO began air strikes against Yugoslavia in March 1999. The United Nations documented humanitarian consequences. A political map cannot convey the experiences of families forced to move.

passages.title: Conflict and the limits of a map
passages.text: Kosovo declared independence in 2008. The International Court of Justice concluded in 2010 that the declaration did not violate international law. That narrow finding was not a ruling requiring every state to recognize Kosovo, and does not by itself validate this atlas’s borders.

Serbia continues as a state after the 2006 end of its union with Montenegro. Its present-day institutions and communities did not begin from nothing at the atlas’s 1994 starting snapshot. Kosovo’s separate declaration and international legal debate require explicit treatment rather than a claim that one map colour resolves them.

passages.text: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades to record the king's divinations. The earliest inscriptions date from the reign of Wu Ding.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Horse-drawn chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from the steppe, and are used for hunting, display and war.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak. The Houmuwu ding from Anyang, the heaviest bronze vessel known from the ancient world, weighs 832 kg.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A ten-day week and the sixty-day cycle of ten stems and twelve branches, still used in the Chinese calendar, organized Shang time; oracle bones are dated by the cycle.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs; the undisturbed tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding, held 755 jades and 468 bronzes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming, with rice and wheat as lesser crops, supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Silk production, evident from the impressions of silk wrappings preserved on bronze vessels.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, given by the king as rewards and buried with the dead as wealth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange

sectionTitles: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge

passages.text: Shawnee communities have deep ties to the Ohio Valley and histories of movement across eastern North America. Today distinct Shawnee nations continue. This map’s 1530 to 1783 outline is a regional snapshot, not the complete territory of every Shawnee community or the lifetime of the people.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Lower Shawneetown stood near the meeting of the Ohio and Scioto rivers and became a major diplomatic and trading centre in the mid-eighteenth century. Shawnee hosts negotiated with other Native peoples and European representatives. Its river location connected local households to political decisions across a much wider region.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: At the Bentley part of Lower Shawneetown, pebble-lined post settings outlined a building at least 30 feet wide and 50 feet long. Nearby rubbish included Native pottery alongside imported knives, scissors and mouth harps. People used new goods while continuing local manufacturing traditions: old and new could share a kitchen.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: The Eastern Shawnee history describes summer villages of bark-covered houses, with a larger council house for gatherings. In autumn, extended families moved into smaller hunting camps. This seasonal pattern linked farming, stored food and hunting rather than fitting everyone into a single permanent village.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Agriculture helped organize the ceremonial year. The Eastern Shawnee account describes a spring bread dance around planting, a green corn dance as crops ripened, and an autumn bread dance around harvest. The food calendar was also a calendar for coming together.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: In 1808, the brothers Tenskwatawa and Tecumseh established Prophetstown near the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers. Tenskwatawa’s religious renewal movement and Tecumseh’s diplomacy drew people from several nations. The settlement became a centre for a confederation opposing further loss of Native land.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Shawnee leaders did not all choose the same strategy. Black Hoof favoured peaceful adaptation, while Tecumseh sought a wider alliance to resist US expansion. American troops burned Prophetstown after the 1811 battle; Tecumseh continued seeking allies until he died at the Thames in 1813.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: The 1831 removal agreement for Wapakoneta and Hog Creek Shawnees transferred their remaining Ohio reserve lands to the United States. The treaty promised a more secure western home. Reading its provisions alongside removal history shows what officials pledged, rather than proving that every family freely welcomed the journey.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: The Shawnee Indian Mission Manual Labor School opened at Fairway, Kansas, in 1839. Shawnee children lived there, and three substantial brick buildings survive. The Shawnee Tribe has worked to recover the children’s history and assess the site, bringing family and community questions into its interpretation.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 preservation statement, Chief Ben Barnes described children sleeping in the mission’s attic after work in its fields. The buildings hold evidence of a demanding residential-school routine. Investigating them is also about understanding what children experienced, beyond the institution’s name and architecture.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: A modern pottery project brought Shawnee citizens and scholars together with Wyandotte potter Richard Zane Smith. A replica Fort Ancient vessel was used to cook corn and venison. Making and using a pot can test practical questions about food preparation while researchers investigate its relationship to Shawnee ancestral traditions.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: The Shawnee Sun began publication in 1835 using a printing system developed by missionary Jotham Meeker. A surviving November 1841 sheet is held by the University of Missouri-Kansas City. It is evidence of nineteenth-century Shawnee-language printing within a missionary setting, not an ancient alphabet or universal literacy.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: “Hato Caakiwiyeefa” means “Hello everyone”. Roy Baldridge used the greeting in the Shawnee Tribe’s Fall 2024 message from its chiefs, where the English meaning is printed alongside it. This is an attested modern Shawnee sample in Latin letters, from a community publication addressed to its readers.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: When language classes moved online during the pandemic, the Shawnee Tribe could reach learners living far apart. Its immersion program worked with first-language speaker George Blanchard and emphasized listening and speaking in small classes. Digital lessons supported a goal that was very personal: using Shawnee in everyday conversation.

The destruction of towns, the collapse of Tecumseh’s wartime alliance and forced removal caused profound losses. They did not end Shawnee life. The Eastern Shawnee Tribe, Absentee Shawnee Tribe and Shawnee Tribe are distinct contemporary nations; the map’s 1783 cutoff is only a coverage boundary.

sectionTitles: Which Shewa are we looking at?
Beads, families and words that survive

passages.text: This imported Shoa record covers 1279 to 1492, but its outline lies far northeast of the Shewa sites discussed here. Medieval Shewa included different Muslim, Christian and Indigenous communities. The card presents regional evidence; it does not claim that one independent kingdom ruled this entire area throughout the map interval.

passages.title: Which Shewa are we looking at?
passages.text: An Arabic chronological record describes the fall of the Makhzumi dynasty to the Walasma in 1285. Researchers still cannot securely locate the places named in those annals. The better-documented town of Nora belongs to later Ifat history, providing regional context rather than an identified old Shewa capital.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: At Nora, builders used local volcanic stone: mostly rhyolite, with some cut ignimbrite blocks. They levelled house interiors and laid clay floors, moulding ovens into the clay itself. The kitchen was partly built into the floor, rather than assembled entirely from movable appliances.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Nora’s small rectangular rooms had walls roughly 40 to 50 centimetres thick. Their dimensions could support short beams beneath flat earth-covered roofs, the excavators suggest. Narrow doors, windows and wall niches made these substantial houses more than empty stone boxes.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Grinding equipment occurs throughout Nora’s archaeological levels and surrounding landscape. It points to the repeated work of processing crops. Nearby terraces and reservoirs are intriguing, but the 2024 excavation report says their medieval date remains unproved: an old-looking waterwork still needs dating.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Animal bones from Nora include cattle, sheep and goats. Butchers left cuts on some bones, and broken long bones preserve traces of food preparation. Researchers examined material from houses and a rubbish heap: yesterday’s discarded scraps can become tomorrow’s evidence about dinner.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Some cattle lived long enough to develop heavily worn teeth. The animal specialist suggests they may have supplied milk or traction before slaughter. A cow could therefore contribute much more than meat, although the bones alone cannot tell us which household milked it or what it pulled.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: Beside a small Nora mosque stood a large basalt stone. Archaeologist Stéphane Pradines interprets it as a footrest used during washing before prayer, comparing similar arrangements elsewhere. This is a specific proposed use for a surviving object, not proof of a fully excavated public bathhouse.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: The same mosque’s prayer room measured about 19 square metres and had a central column supporting its roof. It served worship on a much more intimate scale than a vast cathedral. Its courtyard and carefully arranged entrances show how a small building could organize communal activity.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: In the Christian kingdom, royal camps could contain separate areas for the ruler’s household, soldiers, officials and livestock, sometimes divided by palisades. Researchers have explored a possible fifteenth-century royal camp in Menz, northeastern Shewa. A travelling court required space for both political business and animals.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: Shay communities lived in this wider region from about the ninth to fourteenth centuries. At Meshala Maryam, a burial mound contained human remains, pottery, beads and metal ornaments. Repeated use suggests a family tomb. Their distinct burial traditions should not automatically be labelled Christian or Muslim because of nearby states.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: A 2023 study analysed 34 glass beads from two Shay burial sites. Their chemistry connects the glass with several manufacturing traditions, including the Middle East, Egypt and the Indian Ocean world. Tiny ornaments reveal wide trading connections, even when the route taken by a particular bead remains unknown.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: “هذا قبر” means “This is the tomb.” These Arabic words open the published transcription of tomb T9 at Awfat, dated April to May 1364. The inscription commemorates a religious scholar associated with the Walasma. It is a later Ifat writing sample in regional context, not a Makhzumi royal document.

The old Muslim Shewa dynasty ended in 1285, but this imported record extends to 1492 without a securely identified corresponding fall. Regional communities continued under changing powers. Nora’s excavated urban history itself reaches into the early sixteenth century, so 1492 should not erase its inhabitants.
