passages.text: Shoshoni is an older spelling of Shoshone. This broad map entry covers communities across the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains, rather than a single kingdom. Its outline combines regional homelands, while the dates mark imported map coverage. The examples below identify particular communities so that one family’s history does not become everybody’s story.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Some regional bands were identified by foods strongly associated with their home areas, such as salmon or pine nuts. These names reflected local knowledge and relationships. The Northwestern Band’s history describes many smaller family groups, a useful reminder that this enormous map shape never had one royal capital.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the Bear River and Cache Valley region, winter camps used dense willows and brush for protection from wind and snow. The Northwestern Band also describes nearby hot springs, fish and game. Choosing a campsite meant knowing a whole neighborhood of useful places, not simply finding an empty patch of ground.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In August 1805, expedition observers described Lemhi Shoshone fishing barriers made from poles and willows. Basket traps caught fish moving in both directions. Narrow basket ends could be untied to remove the catch: river engineering with a built-in opening for dinner.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Cameahwait explained the landscape to Meriwether Lewis by drawing rivers on the ground and making small mounds to represent mountains. His account warned of difficult routes. In this 1805 meeting, the visitor’s notebook depended on a local expert’s knowledge of the country.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Lewis also recorded Shoshone women making and repairing his party’s moccasins. He described hide robes that served as daytime clothing and nighttime covers. Those August 1805 observations preserve a glimpse of the skilled work that kept travelers shod and warm.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Yellowstone archaeologists associate a pottery tradition called Intermountain Ware with Shoshone presence roughly seven centuries ago. Fragments of cooking vessels can preserve traces of everyday activities long after their owners’ camps have disappeared. This is a regional archaeological clue within a much longer history of people using Yellowstone.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Eastern Shoshone leader Washakie worked through a period of expanding settlement and military pressure. The tribe’s history connects treaties in 1863 and 1868 with the eventual Wind River reservation. Washakie favored a place familiar as a wintering area, tying political negotiations to lived knowledge of the landscape.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: On January 29, 1863, United States troops attacked Northwestern Shoshone families at Bear River. The massacre devastated this community. Its later history includes the return of land: the Northwestern Band purchased a substantial part of the massacre site in 2018, strengthening its role in caring for the place.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Mae Timbimboo Parry began writing down elders’ histories while she was still in high school. Her grandfather had survived Bear River as a child. She later challenged accounts calling the massacre a battle, helping bring community testimony into the public history of the event.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: For Timbisha Shoshone families in Death Valley, houses built in the 1930s came without indoor plumbing or electricity, and residents shared a water tap. Their seasonal travel out of the heat later became an excuse for officials to destroy empty houses. A home could be occupied seasonally and still be somebody’s home.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Timbisha women including Pauline Esteves and Barbara Durham helped lead the struggle for a secure homeland. Federal recognition in 1983 and the Timbisha Shoshone Homeland Act in 2000 were major steps. This southern community has its own history, rather than serving as a stand-in for every Shoshone nation.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: A recorded Duck Valley expression is “Hakanni e?”, translated “How are you?” in the University of Utah’s Shoshoni dictionary. Its entry credits Crum, Crum and Dayley’s 2002 work. This is an attested modern spelling of a spoken expression, offered with its regional attribution.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: The Shoshoni Talking Dictionary grew through collaboration with communities and young learners. Its history describes work with Ely Shoshone beginning in 2008 and later recordings involving youth and elders. A digital dictionary can carry pronunciation as well as print, preserving differences between speakers and communities.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: At Fort Hall, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ language and culture program describes archives supporting family history, land claims and language learning. Shoshone and Bannock instruction are identified separately. Family records can therefore help both a child asking about relatives and a nation documenting its rights.

The map’s 1783 cutoff is not an ending for Shoshone peoples. Distinct communities and governments continue, including Eastern Shoshone, Northwestern Shoshone and Timbisha Shoshone. Their histories include losses of land and lives, but also continuing language work, leadership and claims to home.

passages.text: Shu Han claimed legitimacy as the true successor to the Han dynasty, ruling Sichuan under Liu Bei and his famous chancellor Zhuge Liang. Though the smallest of the Three Kingdoms, it became the most romanticized in later literature.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The repeating crossbow, known since the Warring States, was improved under Zhuge Liang by tradition, along with the wooden ox, a wheelbarrow-like cart for carrying supplies over mountain roads.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Sichuan's irrigation, built around the Dujiangyan works of the third century BCE, was kept up and extended to feed the state.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian legitimacy theory justified resistance to Cao Wei.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Loyalty and righteousness became central virtues in Shu Han ideology.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhuge Liang became the archetype of the brilliant but tragic loyal minister in Chinese culture.
Cao Wei general Deng Ai led a surprise attack through mountain passes and captured Chengdu, forcing Liu Shan to surrender.

passages.text: This late-medieval label begins under the Angevin monarchy, but the Sicilian Vespers of 1282 separated the island’s political future from the mainland kingdom centered on Naples. Aragonese rulers governed the island, while rival kings retained overlapping claims and names. Some imported map shapes combine both territories after their political separation; this card does not treat that shape as one uncontested state.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: The uprising of 1282 helped bring Peter of Aragon to the Sicilian throne and began a long struggle with the Angevins. Calling every southern territory “Sicily” hides this division. The island and the mainland could share a royal title while fighting over who had the right to use it.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: The 1302 peace allowed Frederick of Aragon to retain the island under the title king of Trinacria. The arrangement did not remove every rival claim, and another settlement followed in 1372. Medieval sovereignty often involved layered titles and obligations rather than a neat modern border.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: A privilege of 1283 allowed Messina to choose consuls who handled Sicilians’ civil disputes outside the kingdom. Merchants needed representatives and procedures far from home. Maritime connections involved contracts and arguments as well as ships arriving with attractive goods.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: Messina received extensive privileges for its silk industry in 1292, and its trade helped sustain an annual fair established in 1416. Silk connected specialized craft labor with long-distance exchange; the fair also gave buyers and sellers a recurring place in the calendar.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: Excavated pottery from Mazara del Vallo and Castronovo shows that fourteenth- and fifteenth-century households encountered imported Iberian ceramics alongside regional wares. A decorated bowl can therefore help trace a trading network, although it cannot tell us the nationality of everyone who ate from it.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: The same pottery study includes locally circulated brown-and-green decorated vessels and cooking pots. Kitchenware deserves attention alongside expensive imports: distribution inside Sicily connected craft workshops with everyday buyers. Broken pots can reveal ordinary commerce that royal chronicles barely mention.

passages.title: An island in Mediterranean networks
passages.text: Sugar manufacture needed specially shaped ceramic vessels to crystallize sugar and collect the liquid draining away. Scientific study of medieval and early-modern Sicilian pots identifies different production centers and choices of clay and design. Producing a sweet ingredient also required potters who understood heat and strength.

passages.title: Care, learning and painted stories
passages.text: Palermo reorganized charitable care in 1442 by bringing smaller hospitals, including San Bartolomeo, into the Ospedale Grande. The archival history makes this an institutional change we can date. It does not establish that everyone had access to modern-style hospital treatment.

passages.title: Care, learning and painted stories
passages.text: The great Triumph of Death fresco, painted around 1440 to 1450, once stood in the courtyard of Palermo’s hospital in Palazzo Sclafani. Its anonymous artist presented death among people of different social ranks. The painting offers evidence of ideas about mortality, not a photographic record of a particular epidemic.

passages.title: Care, learning and painted stories
passages.text: The Steri palace’s wooden ceiling, painted in 1377 to 1380, turned the room above its visitors into a world of stories. One scene shows Tristan and Isolde playing chess, alongside biblical and other legendary material. A noble household could display its reading culture overhead.

passages.title: Care, learning and painted stories
passages.text: Catania received royal permission for a university in 1434, a papal bull in 1444, and began teaching in 1445. Subjects included theology, law, philosophy and medicine; the first recorded degree was awarded in civil law in 1449. Creating a university required several steps, not one ceremonial announcement.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latin, the title of Pietro Geremia’s inaugural address at Catania on 18 October 1445: “De laude scientiarum.” Translation: “In praise of the branches of knowledge.” This attested scholarly title illustrates the Latin of university learning; it is not a claim that Sicilian families spoke Latin at the dinner table.

The island kingdom continued under changing dynastic arrangements and became part of the Spanish monarchy. The map’s 1492 cutoff does not mark its destruction. Its political history must also remain distinct from that of the mainland kingdom of Naples, despite their competing uses of the name Sicily.

sectionTitles: Food, trade and the working city

passages.text: The island kingdom of Sicily was governed for much of this interval within the Spanish monarchy, usually through a viceroy. Eighteenth-century wars brought Savoyard and Austrian rule before the Bourbons gained the island. Its parliament, ports, grain supply and cities had their own histories; Sicily was not simply another name for Naples.

passages.title: Food, trade and the working city
passages.text: Messina’s sixteenth-century silk industry had a specialized consulate, granted in 1520, while the harbor served trade and major fleet expeditions. Silk merchants and textile workers lived in a port whose commercial opportunities could be entangled with military demands.

passages.title: Food, trade and the working city
passages.text: Sicily exported grain while its own towns needed reliable bread supplies. Urban provisioning bodies organized wheat and flour distribution, baking contracts and regulated prices. A grain-producing island could still face arguments over who received the harvest and what a loaf should cost.

passages.title: Food, trade and the working city
passages.text: The western and central producing regions supplied other parts of Sicily as well as foreign buyers. Export permits issued through the Maestro Portulano could themselves be traded. The journey from field to loaf therefore passed through officials and markets, not only millstones and ovens.

passages.title: Food, trade and the working city
passages.text: Palermo bought the great Pretoria fountain in 1573 after it had been made for a Florentine garden. Moving a monumental artwork gave the city a new civic centerpiece. What now seems inseparable from one town can have a history that began in another.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: During the plague of 1575 to 1576, physician Giovanni Filippo Ingrassia helped organize isolation and health facilities in Palermo. Isolation was not his invention: historians identify earlier use. His importance lay in how medical advice and civic administration were brought together during a crisis.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: Research on that epidemic also examines the coercive side of public-health measures: movement and behavior were controlled by authorities. The authors interpret this partly as social control. That is a historical argument, not proof that disease prevention was merely a pretext or that patients had modern rights.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: The earthquake of 1693 devastated southeastern towns. Rebuilding was not identical everywhere: Catania largely used its old site, while Noto was created on a new one. Surviving street plans therefore record decisions made after a disaster, as well as architects’ tastes.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: At Ragusa and Palazzolo Acreide new urban centers developed beside older ones; Caltagirone was repaired. Together the towns preserve a remarkable concentration of late Baroque buildings. The achievement was collective reconstruction by communities, builders and patrons, not the work of one ruler with one plan.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: Prisoners in Palermo’s Inquisition jail left drawings and words on the walls. These surviving graffiti preserve voices from confinement that official case files cannot fully replace. Their later rescue and conservation matter: the marks survived because people chose not to erase them.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: Palermo’s first teaching garden for medicinal plants was planted in 1780 on a former powder-magazine site near Porta Carini. It belonged to the new academy’s teaching program. The larger botanical garden visited today came later, so the two sites should not be confused.

passages.title: Health, disaster and learning
passages.text: A reform at Catania in 1779 expanded teaching, including a chair of experimental physics. The university’s history contrasts this with the earlier dominance of Aristotelian natural philosophy. Learning about nature increasingly involved dedicated experimental instruction, not simply reading inherited authorities.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Italian, the opening of Ingrassia’s printed book title (Palermo, 1576): “Informatione del pestifero, et contagioso morbo”. Translation: “Account of the pestilential and contagious disease.” The full title identifies the Palermo and Sicilian epidemic of 1575 to 1576. This is an attested book title, with its older spelling retained.
The map’s 1783 endpoint is not a Sicilian collapse. The Bourbon island kingdom continued through the Napoleonic era and was formally joined with Naples in the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816.

sectionTitles: An independent country and children’s lives

passages.text: These two map records follow Sierra Leone through British colonial government and independence on 27 April 1961. The later label begins in 1960, one year too early to represent an independent state. Earlier coastal outlines also must not be read as control of the entire later country: Britain declared the inland protectorate only in 1896.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Britain made Sierra Leone a colony in 1808, but its later national territory was not one uniform colony from that date. The hinterland became a protectorate in 1896. Keeping those categories separate helps explain why an early map outline can exaggerate the reach of a colonial administration.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Bunce Island preserves the walls of a slave-trading complex used from the late 1600s to 1807. Its merchants’ quarters, gunpowder store, cookhouse and captive holding yard made a connected system. These ruins show how buildings helped organize the imprisonment and forced transport of people across the Atlantic.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Rice-growing expertise traveled under terrible circumstances. Captives from this West African rice-growing region were sought by plantation owners in South Carolina and Georgia. Their agricultural knowledge was valuable, although the people who possessed it were denied freedom and the rewards of their work.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Fourah Bay College began in 1827. Its later waterfront building opened in 1848 on a site previously connected with slave trading; the heritage survey records that its roof used timber from condemned slave ships. The material of a coercive trade was literally reused in a place of learning.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: A Mende country cloth made before 1899, now catalogued in Brighton, has sixteen blue strips sewn into a large textile. Makers spun cotton into thread, dyed it and wove narrow lengths on a tripod loom before joining them edge to edge. A big cloth did not require a giant loom.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: Country cloth could communicate wealth and prestige as well as keep a body covered. The same catalogue records the Brighton example as 1.55 metres wide and 3.7 metres long. Its seams preserve the practical decisions of spinners, dyers, weavers and stitchers, even though the maker’s name is unrecorded.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: A short written Krio sample is “fes di it kam”, translated “Bring the food here.” It appears as example 27 in Malcolm Awadajin Finney’s 2013 linguistic survey. This is a modern scholarly transcription in a Latin-based script, not a colonial inscription; the sequence of verbs is a normal grammatical construction.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: Krio has a history of educational exclusion as well as creativity. Finney describes pupils once being punished for speaking it at school, followed by its later inclusion in education and extensive use in radio, television and political speech. A language can flourish in public life after institutions have tried to silence it.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: Independence came on 27 April 1961, not at the atlas’s 1960 label change. The diplomatic record marks that day explicitly. A new international status changed who governed the country; it did not replace its communities, local languages or accumulated knowledge with a completely new population.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: After a devastating civil war, disarmament helped make elections possible in May 2002. The United Nations account emphasizes Sierra Leoneans’ own determination to secure peace, alongside international support. Rebuilding involved restoring local administration and helping former fighters return to civilian work, not simply announcing that shooting had stopped.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: At Services Secondary School in Freetown, UNICEF reported in February 2023 that girls met weekly with trained peer mentors to discuss menstruation. Kits included reusable pads, underwear, soap and instructions; teachers and boys also joined the effort to reduce stigma. Ordinary supplies and accurate information can determine whether a pupil feels able to attend lessons.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: A 2022 account from Jui gives a family example: Abdul Sesay used his school peer-mentor training to reassure his sister Daniella when her first period made her afraid to attend school. He encouraged her to speak with their grandmother and explained how to obtain pads. Education could travel home in a brother’s schoolbag.
Colonial rule ended in 1961. The war’s end and elections in 2002 opened another period of rebuilding; neither change meant the disappearance of Sierra Leone’s people or languages.

passages.text: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southeast around Gyeongju, and by 676 had brought most of the peninsula under one rule. Its bone-rank aristocracy, gold crowns, Hwarang youth bands and Buddhist temples made a distinctive civilization that lasted nearly a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler uprights, hung with jade and gold spangles, from the royal mound tombs of Gyeongju.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha facing the sea, were begun; UNESCO listed both in 1995.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cheomseongdae, a stone tower built in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632 to 647), is among the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The bone-rank system fixed a person's rank, office and even the size of their house by birth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Hwarang, bands of aristocratic youths, trained in arms, song and Buddhist and Confucian teaching, and led Silla's armies.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism became the state religion after the martyrdom of Ichadon, and temples rose across the kingdom.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Gyeongju grew into a planned capital of palaces, temples, markets and tiled houses, with the Anapji pleasure pond laid out in 674.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court culture prized refinement, poetry in the hyangga form and Buddhist devotion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Gyeongju Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Unified Silla's administration, Buddhism and script laid the foundations of later Korean culture.
The last king, Gyeongsun, surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule counted from its traditional founding in 57 BCE.

sectionTitles: Art, school and skills passed between generations

passages.text: The modern Slovak Republic became independent on 1 January 1993 when Czechoslovakia divided peacefully. This is the republic that continues today, not the separate Slovak state of the Second World War. The map starts its modern label in 1994, after the actual founding.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: Slovakia’s first satellite, skCUBE, launched on 23 June 2017. The Slovak Organisation for Space Activities worked with universities and companies, and more than sixty volunteers contributed. A small spacecraft could bring together students, engineers and radio enthusiasts.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: skCUBE suffered a problem shortly after launch, but ground stations in Slovakia continued receiving its transmissions. It operated for 569 days without a restart before stopping in January 2019. Engineering history includes learning from a mission that did not work exactly as planned.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: The Danube dam dispute inherited by Slovakia began with a 1977 treaty between Hungary and Czechoslovakia. The project combined electricity generation, navigation and river engineering. Changing a river shared with a neighbor raised questions about water flows and the environment as well as machinery.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: In April 1997, judges of the International Court of Justice visited the dam sites. It was the Court’s first site visit in its fifty-year history. Sometimes deciding an international legal case means putting down the paperwork and going to look at the river.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The Danubiana museum opened in September 2000 on a peninsula at the Čunovo reservoir, south of Bratislava. Dutch collector Gerard Meulensteen and Slovak gallery founder Vincent Polakovič helped create it. A waterside setting became a meeting place for Slovak and international contemporary art.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Danubiana’s collections include paintings by international artists, contemporary Slovak work and outdoor sculpture. Its history records a move into a nonprofit public institution with majority state participation in 2012. Caring for modern art involves collections, buildings and long-term public support.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Puppetry in Slovakia includes families who carve figures, make costumes, write stories and perform them. Children can meet the craft through workshops and performances, while experienced puppeteers teach newcomers. One small wooden character may require several different people’s skills.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The fujara is an unusually long wooden pipe with just three finger holes, associated with shepherds in central Slovakia. Makers often decorate their instruments individually. The older pastoral tradition continues through musicians and craftspeople, giving this very tall instrument a life beyond the sheep pasture.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Traveling tinkers once repaired damaged kitchen vessels using wire and tin. Today, the Považské Museum at Budatín presents both older work and contemporary wire designs. A practical skill for keeping a pot useful became a craft that could also make decorative objects.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The education ministry describes ten years of compulsory school attendance, lasting through the school year in which a pupil reaches sixteen. This is the modern educational system. Children’s learning has its own timetable, quite separate from the much older history of the region.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: On 1 January 2009, Slovakia replaced the koruna with the euro. For the first sixteen days, people could pay using either currency. Shops and families had to learn new prices, with one euro officially equal to 30.1260 koruna.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Slovak, article 1 of the constitution: “Slovenská republika je zvrchovaný, demokratický a právny štát.” Translation: “The Slovak Republic is a sovereign, democratic state governed by law.” This wording is taken from Parliament’s official 2019 consolidated edition of the constitution originally adopted in 1992.

The Slovak Republic continues as an independent state. Its modern beginning was the agreed division of Czechoslovakia in 1993, rather than a conquest or the disappearance of the communities that had lived together in the federation.

sectionTitles: Spacecraft and the things a town needs

passages.text: Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991, following the independence plebiscite of December 1990. It adopted a new constitution that December and joined the European Union in 2004. Its continuing republic combines modern research and public services with older local crafts and communal traditions.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Photographs of Ljubljana during the 1991 war show shopping for supplies, air-raid warnings and parents appealing for their sons’ safety. The City Museum preserves these alongside official events. Independence was experienced in households and streets as well as in government buildings.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Slovenian beekeeping often places wooden apiaries close to family homes. Beekeepers work with the native Carniolan bee and pass practical knowledge between generations. Looking after the hives can be part of a household’s yearly routine, involving observation, patience and respect for the bees.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Painted panels on beehives carry religious images and scenes from everyday life. The paintings form a recognizable part of Slovenian beekeeping culture. A row of hives can double as a miniature outdoor picture gallery, with a very busy workforce living behind it.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Bobbin lacemakers twist and cross threads wound around wooden bobbins. A paper pattern is attached to a cylindrical pillow, supported in a basket or wooden base. The finished lace can become clothing decoration or household textiles. Those apparently tangled threads have a carefully organized plan.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Lacemaking knowledge moves through families and neighborhood groups, often from older women to younger learners. Gathering to work also creates time for conversation and friendship. UNESCO’s account describes a social activity as well as the skill needed to produce a fine pattern.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: The Škofja Loka Passion Play brings a large community into the streets to perform a religious drama in older local language. UNESCO’s nomination described about nine hundred performers and four hundred helpers. Costumes, scenery, music and rehearsals make it a shared undertaking well beyond the acting.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Slovenia’s NEMO-HD satellite launched in September 2020. The sixty-five-kilogram spacecraft was designed for Earth observation using video and several bands of light. Ground stations and image-processing systems were part of the project, because pictures from orbit still need people and computers back on Earth.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: The same launch carried TRISAT, a five-kilogram satellite developed by the University of Maribor and SkyLabs. Its mission was designed to test miniature space electronics and an optical sensor. Small satellites can provide a demanding test bench for very small components.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Ljubljana’s Reuse Centre opened in 2013 to repair and repurpose objects, while providing employment opportunities. One example in the city’s environmental report is a shoe cupboard made from an old gaming machine. An object could retire from one job and start another.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Ljubljana’s regional waste centre combines mechanical sorting and biological treatment with facilities for treating liquid that drains from landfill. The mid-2010s project deals with several different problems hidden inside the ordinary act of throwing something away.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Slovenia’s basic school lasts nine years and usually begins at age six. The government also describes after-school programs for the first five years, including study, play and other activities. For working families, the school day can involve more than classroom lessons.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: In 2016, Slovenia added a right to drinking water to its constitution. The provision treats water resources as a public good and gives household drinking-water supply priority. This records a public commitment about how an everyday necessity should be managed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Slovenian, article 1 of the 1991 constitution: “Slovenija je demokratična republika.” Translation: “Slovenia is a democratic republic.” The wording is preserved here in the official legal database’s consolidated text, rather than a photograph of the first printed edition.
Slovenia continues as an independent republic. Its historical starting point is independence in 1991; the map’s first modern Slovenia snapshot in 1994 should not be read as its founding year.

sectionTitles: Lessons that traveled to the students
A written greeting and a political ending

passages.text: The Sokoto Caliphate grew from the Islamic reform movement and warfare begun by Usman dan Fodio in 1804. The atlas labels its earlier Nigerian phase “Fulani Empire” and its later phase “Sokoto Caliphate”; these are connected parts of one political history, not two unrelated civilizations. Scholarship, textile production and an economy relying heavily on enslaved labor all shaped its society.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Nana Asma’u, 1793 to 1864, wrote, taught and managed a large household. Mack and Boyd describe her work in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamachek. She belonged to a family of scholars, but her teaching reached beyond that family.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Asma’u trained traveling women teachers called jajis. They took verse lessons to women in other communities, including learners taught at home. A lesson could travel with its teacher instead of requiring everyone to reach one school building.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Recitation and memorization helped lessons spread to relatives and neighbors. Written poetry and oral teaching worked together; listening to a poem could make someone a participant even without owning a manuscript.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: The surviving Admonition poem is in Hausa Ajami, with vowel marks helping readers sound out the text. Boston University dates its composition between 1855 and 1857. The reproduced copy is an undated printed witness, not a sheet known to be in Asma’u’s hand.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: Asma’u’s elegies remember women’s practical care. Zaharatu assisted at births; Aisha helped orphans and widows. Such named work shows that community history included caregiving, not only the careers of male rulers.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: Admonition treats obtaining food and seeking education as legitimate reasons for women to leave home. It also asks wives to follow lawful marital obligations. This was a religious argument made within her society, not a claim that its rules matched modern equality.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: The poem tells believers to observe ritual washing, while allowing dry ablution during illness. The editors explain that earth or sand could be used when water was unavailable or a person was sick. This concerns religious practice; it does not establish a citywide plumbing system.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: It also encourages charity and extra help for people in need. Alongside prayer and study, generosity belonged in the moral life Asma’u was teaching. Her verses are evidence of ideals being urged, not proof everyone always lived up to them.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: Plantations around Sokoto, Kano, Zaria and other towns supplied food and raw materials. Salau lists millet, sorghum, cotton and indigo among the goods tied to this economy. Everyday eating and dressing depended on large amounts of agricultural work.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: That work often came from enslaved people. Salau distinguishes supervised labor gangs, work alongside owners and arrangements requiring payments to owners. Different arrangements did not remove the fundamental denial of freedom.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: Muhammad Bello promoted agricultural settlement as part of consolidating the state. Lovejoy connects these policies with textile production in southern Kano and northern Zaria: fields, spinning, weaving, dyeing and trade belonged to an interconnected economy.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: No single plantation export crop dominated the whole caliphate. Food markets and textile making were both important. This helps explain why a history of the state must include workshops and farms, not just armies.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم” means “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.” This Arabic invocation opens the scanned printed witness of Admonition, before its Hausa Ajami verses. Here it is shown without vowel marks. The surviving printed copy is not known to be in Asma’u’s own hand.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: British forces took Kano and Sokoto in 1903 amid the wider European partition of the caliphate’s territories. Loss of independent government did not end Muslim scholarship or the communities whose lives had made the state.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: Asma’u’s educational work remained influential long after her lifetime. SOAS’s account of her writings and Jean Boyd’s scholarship documents a continuing legacy of women teaching women, rather than a tradition that simply stopped when the state was conquered.

Colonial conquest ended the independent Sokoto Caliphate in 1903. Its territories were divided under European rule, while Muslim communities and traditions of scholarship continued. The later 1914 map endpoint is not the end date of independent Sokoto.

passages.text: Solomon Islands includes communities with distinct languages, artistic practices and island histories. Canoe ornaments, feather currency, shellwork and recordings reveal how people made useful objects, exchanged goods and performed together. Independence in 1978 began a new political chapter within much older and continuing cultural histories.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: A late nineteenth- or early twentieth-century nguzunguzu at the Metropolitan Museum combines blackened wood with nautilus-shell inlay. The collection tentatively attributes it to New Georgia. Its carved face and hands show the close relationship between boat decoration, bodily ornament and spiritual protection.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: Such figures were lashed near the base of a canoe's prow rather than carved as a permanent part of the hull. They could be removed, exchanged or transferred between boats. Canoes supported fishing and transport as well as warfare, so their making joined practical skill with ceremonial importance.

passages.title: Canoes, carving and skilled materials
passages.text: The names and interpretations of canoe figures vary between western island communities. Modern artists continue to use their forms as cultural and national symbols. A museum example can illuminate one tradition without representing every community in the country.

passages.title: Feather currency and exchange
passages.text: Te Papa holds a twentieth-century tevau collected on Peleni in the Santa Cruz Islands in 1969. Specialists attached small red feathers to overlapping platelets and decorated the coil with shell and fiber. Leaves and oilcloth protected this particular example during storage and travel.

passages.title: Feather currency and exchange
passages.text: Tevau could be exchanged for goods and services, including canoes, crops and pigs, and given in marriage ceremonies. Their value reflected color, condition and skilled labor; fading feathers could reduce it. This was a regional system of valuables, not a single currency used uniformly across all the islands.

passages.title: Shellwork and everyday connections
passages.text: In her fieldwork account of Baegu communities on Malaita, Kay Ross described ornaments made from small red, white and black shell discs. Plant fiber joined discs into planned geometric arrangements for belts and armbands. Fine finishing could make both sides presentable.

passages.title: Shellwork and everyday connections
passages.text: Ross also described coastal and inland communities exchanging fish and taro. Shell valuables circulated at weddings and feasts, where relatives helped assemble gifts. Her account records particular communities and a particular period, rather than a timeless rule for all Solomon Islanders.

passages.title: Music preserved in recordings
passages.text: Hugo Zemp's recordings of Fataleka and Baegu music, released in 1973, document bamboo panpipes, clapping sticks, singing and dance. Performances place instruments within funeral and other ceremonial settings, allowing listeners to hear coordination between people as well as individual sounds.

passages.title: Music preserved in recordings
passages.text: The album identifies Afunakwa as the singer of the lullaby Rorogwela. Other tracks feature women and girls singing or performers playing bamboo instruments. Named performers and recorded contexts help keep an account of music connected to people rather than an anonymous national style.

passages.title: Political change and continuing communities
passages.text: Internal self-government began on 2 January 1976, followed by constitutional negotiations in London in 1977. Debate included regional finances and the place of the Western Solomons in the new country. Independence emerged through negotiation and disagreement, not a universally shared timetable.

passages.title: Political change and continuing communities
passages.text: The Independence Order names 7 July 1978 as the appointed day. That document provides a precise date for the political transition, while art objects and recordings document cultural work that both preceded independence and continued afterward.

British protectorate rule ended with independence on 7 July 1978. Solomon Islands continues as a country whose communities have varied histories, languages and traditions. The political transition did not end regional identities, exchange relationships or creative practice.

Milk, health and voices worth preserving

passages.text: The Somali Republic formed in 1960 by joining territories formerly administered by Britain and Italy. Its later history includes military government, civil war and renewed federal institutions.

passages.title: Union, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: On 1 July 1960, the former British Somaliland and the former Italian-administered territory united as the Somali Republic. A constitution followed in 1961. The imported outline represents that territorial framework; it does not establish who controlled every place in every later year.

passages.title: Union, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in October 1969. His overthrow in 1991 was followed by civil war and repeated attempts to rebuild national government. These were changes in political authority, with devastating consequences for families and institutions.

passages.title: Union, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: The 2012 constitutional framework provided for a federal parliament with two chambers. The Upper House did not begin functioning until 2016, when states selected senators. Designing an institution on paper and making it work were separate stages.

passages.title: Union, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: Somaliland’s sovereignty remains disputed. Israel recognized it in December 2025, while Somalia objected and the African Union reaffirmed Somalia’s unity. The UN Security Council had reaffirmed Somalia’s sovereignty earlier that month. A single color on this map cannot resolve those competing positions.

passages.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio
passages.text: In October 1972, the government adopted a modified Latin alphabet for Somali. Language specialists worked on textbooks, grammar and a dictionary. This was an important standardization of written Somali, rather than the invention of the Somali language.

passages.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio
passages.text: A literacy campaign began in towns in 1973 and later spread to rural areas. Teachers, students, civil servants and members of the armed services taught after their regular work. Classrooms could depend on a whole community’s spare hours, not just a school timetable.

passages.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio
passages.text: A published Somali writing sample is “Kacaanka Jira: Ama Muxuu Aadamuhu U Socdaa Isagoo Adhax Taagan”, paired with “The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright”. Khaloudy Mohamed Sa’eed and Abdillahi Raage translated Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s story for Jalada in 2016. It shows the language in modern literary use.

passages.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio
passages.text: The SOMDEL education programme, launched in 2001, combined radio lessons, printed materials and local tutorials. Lessons covered reading, arithmetic, health and livelihoods. Teachers could replay recordings where radio reception was poor: the classroom’s teacher could arrive on a cassette.

passages.title: Learning to write and learning over the radio
passages.text: Halimo, a tailor in Hargeisa, began SOMDEL classes in 2004. She reported that literacy helped her measure cloth, keep accounts and record customers’ debts, while helping her children with homework. School skills could matter at the sewing table as well as in an examination.

passages.title: Milk, health and voices worth preserving
passages.text: A study published in 2010 describes women’s networks carrying camel milk from mobile herders to Puntland’s towns. Men generally milked the camels in the studied households; women then decided how to allocate milk between children, other household needs and sale.

passages.title: Milk, health and voices worth preserving
passages.text: Collectors followed herds as they moved and traded milk for cash or household goods. Transporters carried it toward urban markets and brought supplies back. This was a carefully organized supply chain, even without a supermarket warehouse or refrigerated delivery van.

passages.title: Milk, health and voices worth preserving
passages.text: At Godod School in Mudug, a 2024 report describes a lesson on menstruation and reusable pads. Student Nafiso explained that buying pads could strain her family’s budget. Water, toilets, clear information and private facilities all helped students manage ordinary bodily needs while staying in class.

passages.title: Milk, health and voices worth preserving
passages.text: Radio Mogadishu’s archive holds roughly 45,000 audio tapes recording politics, language and cultural life. A 2026 preservation project addressed aging tapes and damage. A nation’s history can survive in recorded voices as well as stone monuments, but both need care.
Somalia continues as a state, with federal institutions and unresolved territorial disputes. War and changes of government did not end Somali communities, language or cultural life.

passages.text: The Song dynasty oversaw an economic and technological revolution in China, though military weakness led to the loss of northern China in 1127. Printing, gunpowder, the compass and paper money transformed society, while Neo-Confucianism shaped intellectual life.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Bi Sheng invents movable type printing, though woodblock remained more common.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first gunpowder formulas for military use appear in the Wujing Zongyao military manual.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Shen Kuo describes the magnetic compass for navigation in his Dream Pool Essays.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Paper money, the jiaozi, issued by the government to facilitate commerce, the first state paper currency.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Early-ripening Champa rice from Vietnam is distributed to farmers, allowing two harvests a year in the south.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting reaches its peak with masters like Fan Kuan and Guo Xi.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Porcelain production perfects celadon and qingbai wares.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhu Xi (1130 to 1200) synthesizes Neo-Confucianism; his commentaries on the Four Books, completed about 1190, became the examination curriculum for six centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Maritime trade with Southeast Asia, India and the Middle East expands dramatically.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Porcelain exported throughout Asia and eventually to the Middle East and Africa.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Song technological innovations transformed the world when transmitted to Europe.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Neo-Confucianism became the dominant ideology in East Asia until the nineteenth century.
The Mongol conquest was completed when the last Song emperor drowned at the fall of the final Song stronghold at Yamen in 1279; Kublai Khan ruled China as the Yuan dynasty.

passages.text: Songhai's wealth linked Gao and the Niger region to trans-Saharan commerce. Its surviving monuments make construction, religious practice and shared maintenance visible alongside the better-known history of its rulers.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At Gao, the Tomb of Askia combines an earthen pyramidal tower with mosque buildings, a cemetery and an assembly space.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Projecting wooden supports form permanent scaffolding. Renewing rain-eroded plaster is part of the building's continuing life.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: During the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, Timbuktu was a center of Islamic learning and manuscript exchange.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Timbuktu's market brought together manuscripts, salt, gold, cattle and grain. Scholarship existed within a busy commercial city.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The mosques of Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia preserve an earthen architectural tradition shaped by successive restorations.

passages.text: The Republic of South Africa began in 1961 under apartheid, after a referendum that excluded Black people. Pass laws, segregated schools and forced removals shaped daily life, while students, workers, families and artists resisted. A Cape Town hospital team performed the first human-to-human heart transplant in 1967, even as medical access remained unequal. The first national nonracial vote in 1994 brought constitutional democracy, and the 1996 Bill of Rights promised equality, schooling, health care and dignity. Today the country’s many languages and communities thrive amid serious inequalities, including in water and toilets; its history continues.

passages.title: From apartheid republic to democracy
passages.text: On 31 May 1961 the Union became a republic after a referendum restricted by race. The imported map begins this record around 1945, but that year did not create the republic. Apartheid had begun under the Union in 1948 and carried on.

passages.title: From apartheid republic to democracy
passages.text: Pass books controlled Black South Africans’ movement; residential and public spaces were separated by racial law. Families navigated restrictions on where they could live, work, visit and study. Resistance never disappeared.

passages.title: From apartheid republic to democracy
passages.text: In 1976 students in Soweto rose against apartheid education. Their protest is a reminder that children were political actors, not merely people waiting for adults to change the law.

passages.title: From apartheid republic to democracy
passages.text: In April 1994 all adult South Africans could vote in a national election regardless of race. Nelson Mandela became the first president of the new democratic government in May. This was a hard-won change in who could shape the country.

passages.title: From apartheid republic to democracy
passages.text: The 1996 constitution protects equality and dignity and sets out rights to education, health care, water, housing and children’s protection. A written right is a promise and a tool for change, though it does not instantly deliver a clinic or tap to every home.

passages.title: Languages, school and family life
passages.text: South Africa has many home languages. In the 2022 census isiZulu was reported most often at home by 24.4% of people aged at least one, isiXhosa by 16.3% and Afrikaans by 10.6%. A map label cannot tell you what language a family speaks at dinner.

passages.title: Languages, school and family life
passages.text: “Nkosi Sikelel’ iAfrika” means “God Bless Africa.” This short original isiXhosa hymn line was written in 1897, sung at anti-apartheid meetings and became part of the combined national anthem in 1997. A few words carry different histories in different voices.

passages.title: Languages, school and family life
passages.text: The National School Nutrition Programme gives eligible children a nutritious meal at school. Its guidance includes protein, fruit or vegetables and starch; some schools grow gardens. For a pupil, learning can begin with lunch as well as a lesson.

passages.title: Languages, school and family life
passages.text: Apartheid-era forced removals and migrant labour left long family and housing inequalities. The Bill of Rights protects family-linked needs such as housing and children’s care, but families continue to do the daily work of keeping children fed and safe.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: At Cape Town’s Groote Schuur Hospital in December 1967, a team carried out the first human-to-human heart transplant. Christiaan Barnard led it, but donor Denise Darvall’s family, recipient Louis Washkansky, nurses, technicians and many specialists were essential. A medical first is a team and family story.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: South Africa’s HIV epidemic took many lives. After campaigns for treatment and policy change, public antiretroviral therapy began in 2004. Medicines helped people live longer, while access and prevention remained ongoing work.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: The 2022 census found 70.8% of households used a flush toilet nationally. In Limpopo, 57.9% used a pit toilet with or without a ventilation pipe. That is why a question about “the South African toilet” has no single answer: province, income and service access matter.

passages.title: Medicine and the toilet question
passages.text: Under apartheid, public toilets and other amenities were separated by racial law. The democratic constitution rejects that hierarchy, but today’s census shows that unequal sanitation did not vanish with the signs.

The Republic of South Africa continues. The 1994 election and 1996 constitution ended white-minority constitutional rule and established democracy; they did not erase the effects of dispossession and apartheid overnight. Its people, languages, schools, arts and public-health work keep changing the country.

sectionTitles: A colony built on contested land

passages.text: South Australia was founded as a British settler colony in 1836 and gained its elected parliament in 1857. The map shows a late colonial slice, when farming, mining and new infrastructure transformed daily life while Aboriginal peoples faced dispossession.

passages.title: A colony built on contested land
passages.text: South Australia recruited free settlers rather than receiving transported convicts to construct its public works. Farms grew wheat and grapes, pastoralists raised livestock, and copper mines attracted workers. These opportunities for newcomers accompanied the loss of Aboriginal land and deaths from introduced disease.

passages.title: A colony built on contested land
passages.text: The 1836 Letters Patent included a protection for Aboriginal people’s occupation and enjoyment of their lands. Reading that promise beside the history of dispossession reveals a central contradiction of the colonial project: words on official parchment did not ensure protection in practice.

passages.title: A colony built on contested land
passages.text: At Burra, miners and their families dug homes into creek banks because conventional housing was scarce and costly. Some dwellings had several rooms. Flooding in 1851 devastated this improvised neighbourhood; most dugout homes were abandoned by about 1860.

passages.title: A colony built on contested land
passages.text: Burra’s copper industry imported Cornish steam engines, hauled inland on purpose-built bullock wagons. Smelting also drew workers from Germany and mule drivers from Chile. A mining town in South Australia was connected to people and machinery on several continents.

passages.title: Public health and everyday learning
passages.text: In 1877, Adelaide had thousands of cesspits beneath the city, while raw sewage also reached the River Torrens. Toilets created a city-sized problem long before every household could simply flush and forget. New drainage was an important public-health investment.

passages.title: Public health and everyday learning
passages.text: The underground sewerage system was completed in 1881. Waste went to a sewage farm near Islington, where land treatment was part of the disposal system. By 1885 it handled almost two million gallons daily: an impressive amount of unglamorous engineering.

passages.title: Public health and everyday learning
passages.text: The Education Act of 1875 made school attendance compulsory on a part-time basis. That qualification matters: the new rule was a step towards public schooling, rather than today’s full school timetable arriving everywhere overnight.

passages.title: Messages and votes
passages.text: Completed in 1872, the Overland Telegraph linked Adelaide and Darwin. Connection to the submarine cable then shortened communication with Europe from months to hours. Messages travelled electrically, but maintaining the long line still required workers, supplies and difficult journeys.

passages.title: Messages and votes
passages.text: The line used about 36,000 poles and eleven repeater stations to refresh the signal. Its route drew upon Aboriginal travel routes and water knowledge. Those stations also became starting points for further settler expansion into the interior.

passages.title: Messages and votes
passages.text: Charles Todd’s 1872 announcement includes the English words “a line of communications two thousand miles long.” In everyday modern terms, he meant a messaging connection about 3,200 kilometres long. The museum reproduces this contemporary wording: an engineer announcing that the wires finally joined.

passages.title: Messages and votes
passages.text: The 1894 women’s suffrage petition carried more than 11,600 names. Its sheets were glued together, rolled up and tied with a gold ribbon. Organizing votes for women involved thousands of conversations and signatures, not just one dramatic parliamentary speech.

passages.title: Messages and votes
passages.text: Parliament passed the suffrage bill in December 1894; royal assent followed in February 1895. Women, including Aboriginal women, gained eligibility both to vote and to stand for parliament. The achievement came after repeated failed attempts and persistent campaigning.

On 1 January 1901, South Australia became a state of the Commonwealth of Australia. Federation divided powers between state and federal governments; it did not end the community or erase its parliament. The map’s 1900 endpoint marks the approach to that transition.

sectionTitles: A new country with older histories
Saving records and making history public
School, water and skilled local work

passages.text: South Sudan became independent from Sudan on 9 July 2011 after a referendum. This map’s modern-country layer begins only in 2020, so its first displayed year is not the country’s founding date. Older communities and histories also extend across the border separating the two modern states.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: The 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement set the path toward a vote on southern Sudan’s future. In January 2011, voters overwhelmingly chose separation, and independence followed that July. South Sudan and Sudan therefore became distinct countries, while families and historical connections continued across the new international boundary.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: Fighting broke out in December 2013, only two years after independence. The United Nations strengthened its mission’s civilian-protection role. A revitalized peace agreement was signed in September 2018, but signing a document was one step in a difficult process of making communities safe.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: Here is Juba Arabic in the scholarly spelling recorded by linguists: “ána kan déru áynu akú tái”, translated “I wanted to see my brother.” The Latin letters and accents reproduce an attested modern transcription. This small family sentence offers a language sample without pretending it is an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Saving records and making history public
passages.text: War left many administrative records damaged, scattered or stored in sacks in damp rooms. Archivists and their partners worked to clean, sort, box and digitize surviving papers from the colonial period through the 1980s. Sometimes preserving history starts with the distinctly unglamorous job of rescuing a pile of paper.

passages.title: Saving records and making history public
passages.text: In November 2017, the Tarikh Tana radio series brought archival documents into public conversation. South Sudanese panelists discussed a different document each week on Eye Radio, alongside exhibitions. History could be heard on a radio as well as read in an archive, reaching people beyond a reading room.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: A 2021 education case study describes repairs to girls’ latrines and installation of handwashing facilities at two schools in Torit County. These changes helped pupils manage everyday needs, including menstruation. Returning to class after COVID-19 closures involved usable toilets and privacy as well as reopening school gates.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: The same programme supported mothers’ groups and girls’ clubs. Older female pupils trained to encourage others to return to school and to speak up about education. Learning was supported by relationships across generations: classmates and mothers could help address concerns that a textbook alone could not solve.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: Yei’s upgraded water system opened in May 2023 with five boreholes, 59 water kiosks and about 33 kilometres of pipe. Solar power ran the system, and chlorination helped keep the water safe. Water services need pumps, treatment and maintenance together; sunshine alone cannot make a dirty cup clean.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: At Boma Hospital, solar equipment installed in late 2022 supplied lights and reliable power for vaccine storage. In a May 2023 report, staff described easier night-time deliveries and better temperature control. Electricity changed very practical tasks: seeing a patient clearly and keeping essential medicines appropriately cool.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: In a 2025 account from Mangaten, 21-year-old Veronica interpreted for a women’s support group while studying international relations in Juba. The programme combined emotional support with skills such as making soap and weaving baskets for sale. Her story shows education, care and earning a living meeting in one person’s working week.

passages.title: A sporting first
passages.text: At the Paris 2024 Olympic tournament, South Sudan’s men won their first Olympic basketball game, defeating Puerto Rico 90 to 79 in Lille. Nuni Omot scored the country’s first Olympic basketball points. A young state could now add an international sporting achievement to the stories told about it.

passages.title: A sporting first
passages.text: The win required more than one star. Carlik Jones recorded 19 points, seven rebounds and six assists, while four teammates also scored at least ten points. South Sudan collected 55 rebounds against Puerto Rico’s 37. A missed shot was often the beginning of another chance, not the end of the play.

South Sudan continues as an independent country. In April 2025, UN officials warned that renewed military confrontation threatened the peace process. That dated warning shows why the 2018 agreement should not be presented as a complete end to violence, even as citizens continue schooling, research, work and cultural life.

passages.text: Architecture and painting show different sides of Spain's sixteenth- and seventeenth-century culture: a royal monastery organized around worship and learning, and pictures shaped by observation and international exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Philip II founded El Escorial in 1563. Juan Bautista de Toledo designed the complex, and Juan de Herrera completed the work after Toledo's death.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: El Escorial combined a monastery, church, palace, school, seminary and royal library around courtyards. Religious life, royal authority and study occupied one complex.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Early in his seventeenth-century career, Velazquez painted kitchen scenes known as bodegones and studied figures directly from life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Velazquez became painter to Philip IV in 1623. Later at Madrid, Venetian paintings and contact with Rubens helped shape his art.

passages.text: Srivijaya, a Malay kingdom based at Palembang on Sumatra from the seventh century, controlled the Strait of Malacca and the trade between India and China. Its rulers were patrons of Buddhism, and Old Malay, the language of its inscriptions, became the lingua franca of the archipelago.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The kingdom taxed ships passing the strait and made its ports the entrepot of the sea route between India and China.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Camphor, resins, gold, tin and spices went out; Chinese and Indian goods came in.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Missions to the Tang and Song courts kept the China trade open, and Arab writers knew the maharaja of Zabaj as lord of the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Chinese monk Yijing stopped at Srivijaya in 671 and found more than a thousand monks; he advised pilgrims to study Sanskrit there before going on to India.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Kedukan Bukit inscription of 683, in Old Malay, is the oldest dated text in the language.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mahayana Buddhism had royal patronage; the scholar Atisha studied at Srivijaya for twelve years before carrying its teaching to Tibet.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the trading language of the region and is the root of modern Malay and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The pattern of a port kingdom ruling the strait passed to Malacca.
The Cholas sacked the ports in 1025, Malayu at Jambi took the lead, and Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit pressed on Sumatra; Majapahit's attack on Palembang in 1377 ended the old kingdom.

passages.text: This long map record spans Anglo-Egyptian colonial rule, Sudan’s independence in 1956 and later upheavals. It also contains a border error: South Sudan became a separate country in 2011, although the imported shape continues to include it. Sudan’s history includes irrigation, medical education, literature and community organization as well as conflict.

passages.title: Water, farming and medical learning
passages.text: The Sennar Dam was completed in 1925 on the Blue Nile, helping supply the Gezira irrigation scheme between the Blue and White Niles. Canals carried water into agricultural land, connecting a major engineering project with the timing and work of farming.

passages.title: Water, farming and medical learning
passages.text: Gezira’s organization divided responsibilities between government, the managing company and tenant farmers. Cotton linked the scheme with commercial markets, while sorghum and forage crops also appeared in crop rotations. Behind the canals were negotiations about labour, management and returns.

passages.title: Water, farming and medical learning
passages.text: Khartoum’s Kitchener School of Medicine opened on 29 February 1924 and used Khartoum Hospital for teaching. Its first course lasted four years, with a small intake. Students learned in a working medical institution as well as in classrooms.

passages.title: Water, farming and medical learning
passages.text: Ali Bedri was among the 1928 graduates and later held senior hospital posts and became minister of health. Sudanese graduates developed medical services and public institutions. The school eventually became part of the University of Khartoum.

passages.title: Water, farming and medical learning
passages.text: The Midwifery Training School opened in Omdurman in 1921. Its history brings childbirth and women’s professional knowledge into the picture of colonial medicine, alongside hospitals and male doctors. Training involved negotiation with existing practitioners and local social life.

passages.title: Women’s education and an Arabic title
passages.text: Ahfad’s educational roots reach back to Babiker Badri’s girls’ school at Rufa’a in 1907. Later intermediate and secondary schools preceded the women’s college of 1966. This was a sustained Sudanese educational initiative across several generations.

passages.title: Women’s education and an Arabic title
passages.text: Ahfad’s Rural Extension Program began in 1973 and became required in 1978. Students worked with rural communities through field learning, research and service. Learning could mean listening to a community’s priorities far from a lecture hall.

passages.title: Women’s education and an Arabic title
passages.text: “موسم الهجرة الى الشمال” is the Arabic title of Tayeb Salih’s novel, known in English as “Season of Migration to the North”. This sample follows the spelling in a library catalogue for a 1997 edition; the novel was first published in 1966.

passages.title: Women’s education and an Arabic title
passages.text: Salih’s novel follows a young man returning to a Sudanese village after studying abroad. Its movement between places helped make questions of colonialism, home and identity part of an internationally read Sudanese literary achievement.

passages.title: Political change and keeping daily life going
passages.text: South Sudan became independent on 9 July 2011 after a referendum. This was a major change in the territory of Sudan. The two countries have separate histories after that date, even when an imported map polygon fails to separate them.

passages.title: Political change and keeping daily life going
passages.text: A transition towards civilian rule began in 2019, but a military coup in October 2021 interrupted it. Fighting between rival armed forces erupted in April 2023. These changes deeply affected civilians’ ability to stay at home, work and attend school.

passages.title: Political change and keeping daily life going
passages.text: UNDP’s 2025 account describes women-led community kitchens serving people displaced by war alongside host communities. Organizing ingredients, cooking and sharing meals became part of local emergency action. Neighbours helped sustain daily life under extremely difficult conditions.

passages.title: Political change and keeping daily life going
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2025 reporting describes health facilities and mobile teams continuing emergency care in conflict-affected areas. Keeping services operating depended on people, supplies and routes that could still be reached. The report records relief work within an ongoing crisis.

Sudan continues as a country; its peoples have not vanished amid war or political rupture. South Sudan separated in 2011. The civilian transition and conflict beginning in 2023 belong to an unresolved recent history, while community organizations continue working to sustain lives.

passages.text: The Sui dynasty reunited China after three centuries of division, creating institutions that the Tang would inherit and perfect. Its ambitious building projects and military campaigns exhausted the state, leading to its rapid collapse.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Grand Canal's main sections are dug between 605 and 610, connecting the Yellow River and Yangzi River systems for grain transport.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of coinage, weights and measures across the reunified empire.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism receives imperial patronage; Emperor Wen styled himself a Buddhist universal monarch.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Civil service examinations begin, recruiting officials by Confucian learning; the jinshi degree dates from about 605.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Grand Canal remained China's main north-south transport artery for over a thousand years.
Emperor Yang's disastrous Korean campaigns and excessive building projects led to widespread rebellion; he was assassinated by his own guards in 618.

passages.text: Sukhothai, which broke from Khmer rule about 1238, is remembered as the first Thai kingdom. Its inscription of Ram Khamhaeng describes a father-king, its sculptors made the walking Buddha, and its script became the Thai alphabet.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Ram Khamhaeng inscription, dated 1283, says the king devised the Thai script from Khmer models; some scholars date the stone itself to the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The walking Buddha, a figure in motion cast in bronze, is Sukhothai's own creation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Lotus-bud chedis at Wat Mahathat and Sri Lankan-style bell stupas; glazed Sawankhalok stoneware was exported across the region.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism of the Sri Lankan school, brought by monks from Nakhon Si Thammarat, became the state religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The inscription describes a king who hears any subject's grievance when they ring the bell at the palace gate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Town of Sukhothai and Associated Historic Towns were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Thai alphabet descends from the Sukhothai script.
Ayutthaya reduced Sukhothai to a vassal in 1378 and, when its royal line ended in 1438, made it a province.
