sectionTitles: Fields, trees and a child’s memories

passages.text: Damagaram grew around Zinder in present-day Niger, connecting farming districts with Saharan caravan routes. Its sultans developed a powerful nineteenth-century state. The 1878 to 1900 map window spans its conquest; the outline is displaced northeast of the capital.

passages.title: A capital built and maintained
passages.text: Zinder is near 9° east and 13.8° north, outside this imported polygon. The mismatch matters: the capital’s palace, old Birni quarter and farming hinterland should not be relocated to fit the map. This card describes the documented sultanate while leaving that border problem visible.

passages.title: A capital built and maintained
passages.text: Birni’s earthen walls were built in the mid-1850s with seven named gates. They enclosed a capital whose streets and markets connected local life to wider trade. Surviving wall traces and the pattern of gates provide physical evidence of the fortified town.

passages.title: A capital built and maintained
passages.text: The palace combines thick earthen walls, roof terraces and three large courtyards, with many rooms on two levels. Spaces separate reception and private life. The building was a place where visitors met authority and a household where the sultan’s family lived.

passages.title: A capital built and maintained
passages.text: Conservation researchers named palace masons Zakari Mallam Sanda, Abdou Ali and Issoufou Mallam Mom. They described the hard work of renewing mud plaster, sometimes spoiled by rain soon afterward. An earthen palace is not a finished object left alone: skilled people repeatedly keep it standing.

passages.title: Fields, trees and a child’s memories
passages.text: Caravan revenues, internal taxes and the capture and sale of enslaved people supported the state. Tanimoune appointed representatives in localities as his power expanded. This linked distant villages to the court, but it also meant demands on farmers and coercion against subject communities.

passages.title: Fields, trees and a child’s memories
passages.text: Damagaram protected useful trees and distributed gao seeds. Farmers valued gao trees for improving fields and for leaves and pods that fed sheep and goats when other grazing was scarce. The landscape was partly cultivated above the crops as well as beneath them.

passages.title: Fields, trees and a child’s memories
passages.text: Tree protection was enforced harshly under the sultans, including severe punishments. The surviving agricultural achievement should not hide that coercion. The researchers found that later farmers continued regenerating these useful parklands after the political system and its penalties changed.

passages.title: Fields, trees and a child’s memories
passages.text: Dorugu, a boy from the region, recalled his father farming and playing drums. When he begged to help, his father initially thought him too small, then had a blacksmith make him a hoe. It is a rare individual childhood memory behind the larger story of fields and rulers.

passages.title: Fields, trees and a child’s memories
passages.text: In the same account, the family went early to the farm while his mother prepared food and brought it to them. Dorugu remembered being so absorbed in working that his father had to remind him to eat. This is one family’s remembered routine, not a rule for every household.

passages.title: Words, history and continued life
passages.text: “Muka zakka ga Zinder” means “We arrived at Zinder.” It comes from Dorugu’s dictated Hausa account printed in 1862, in Schön’s Roman-letter transcription. The arrival followed his capture in a slave raid: these simple words preserve the voice of someone affected by the region’s violence.

passages.title: Words, history and continued life
passages.text: Arabic manuscripts preserve another perspective. Historian Seyni Moumouni’s 2022 edition translates a local chronicle covering nineteenth-century Zinder and its fall to the French. Such texts let historians compare local accounts with colonial reports rather than relying only on the conquerors’ version.

passages.title: Words, history and continued life
passages.text: After conquest, the palace remained a centre of customary authority and ceremonies. Niger’s 2006 heritage submission described the sultan as its guardian, responsible for living there and maintaining it. Continued palace life should be distinguished from the independent state that had ended.

French conquest ended Damagaram’s independence in 1899. A sultan remained under the new colonial order, while trade, taxes and land management changed. Its people, farming practices and palace traditions continued.

passages.text: This label refers to Tippu Tip’s commercial and military power in eastern Congo, centred on Kasongo. Ivory trading, slavery and caravan routes linked it to Zanzibar. The imported 1878 to 1914 outline overstates its duration: colonial conquest broke this power in the 1890s, well before the map endpoint.

passages.title: How power was built
passages.text: Tippu Tip said that kinship with Kasongo’s ruler helped him gain authority in Utetera. His account traced this connection through an enslaved grandmother and presented his acceptance as voluntary. Historians treat that story critically: it is also an ambitious ruler’s explanation of why he deserved to rule.

passages.title: How power was built
passages.text: The trading domain depended on alliances, armed followers and links with Zanzibar. Tippu Tip also accepted a position within Leopold II’s Congo Free State. Rivals could cooperate when it suited them; the later war should not hide the earlier bargains between European officials and slave-trading leaders.

passages.title: How power was built
passages.text: Enslavement separated relatives and placed people under others’ control. Women’s family connections sometimes influenced their position in a captor’s household, but that did not make their capture voluntary. A history focused only on successful merchants misses the people whose coerced labour sustained their wealth.

passages.title: Homes, meals and making things
passages.text: Excavations in 2018 and 2019 confirmed Old Kasongo, called Tongoni, and large platforms supporting merchants’ residences. A house attributed to Tippu Tip measured about 10.9 by 6.6 metres. Archaeologists suggest that the raised platforms could also help defend the settlement.

passages.title: Homes, meals and making things
passages.text: Carved doors, lintels and windows decorated merchants’ houses, connecting inland architecture with the Swahili coast. After conquest, some fittings were reused in colonial buildings before entering museums. A surviving door can therefore tell several stories: skilled workmanship, domestic life and the dismantling of a town.

passages.title: Homes, meals and making things
passages.text: A CT scan of one carved lintel identified its wood, with some certainty, as African crabwood found in eastern Congo. The researchers suggested that coastal craftspeople may have worked with local timber. The design travelled a long way; the tree may have grown much closer to home.

passages.title: Homes, meals and making things
passages.text: After the 1893 capture, military doctor Sidney Hinde described stores of rice, maize and coffee and gardens containing oranges, guavas, mangoes and other fruit. His account shows a substantial food-producing settlement, although his admiration for prosperous estates tells us little about the workers who supplied them.

passages.title: Homes, meals and making things
passages.text: Hinde also reported carved beds with silk mosquito curtains and mattresses that soldiers seized. These were furnishings in wealthy households, not a picture of everyone’s bedroom. They reveal both long-distance access to luxury textiles and the way conquest turned someone’s belongings into another person’s loot.

passages.title: Learning, letters and living memory
passages.text: Kasongo had Quran schools where children learned to read and write. Kalenda Njike, a son of the leader Ngongo Lutete, was among their pupils. A later photograph from 1904 shows children using wooden writing boards, evidence that this educational tradition continued after the merchants’ military defeat.

passages.title: Learning, letters and living memory
passages.text: Writing sample: “nataka mashauri kwako” means “I want your advice.” Sayf bin Rashid wrote this Swahili phrase from Kasongo to the official Tobback on 13 May 1891. His letter used Roman letters, with an Arabic signature; here a word split across two manuscript lines is joined.

passages.title: Learning, letters and living memory
passages.text: Cloth could settle a food bill. A surviving receipt dated 25 January 1892 records 410 lengths of cloth owed for rice supplied to the Stanley Falls official Tobback. Such paperwork gives a concrete glimpse of the wider trading network: textiles were payment as well as clothing.

passages.title: Learning, letters and living memory
passages.text: During research meetings in Kasongo in 2021 and 2022, residents asked for protection of the old settlement and a community museum. Family memories helped explain objects kept abroad. They wanted future generations to learn this difficult history in Kasongo itself, close to the places their ancestors knew.

Kasongo fell to Congo Free State forces in 1893, and the wider campaign ended in colonial victory in 1894. This destroyed the trading rulers’ political dominance, not the communities of Maniema or their Swahili and Islamic traditions.

sectionTitles: A house around a patch of sky
What was here before the fort?
Someone drew boats on the wall
Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves

passages.text: Zanzibar’s history includes Swahili communities, Omani royal government and connections with India, Arabia and Europe. Stone Town’s streets and buildings preserve that mixture. Palace life, shopkeeping and plantation labour offer very different views of the same society.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: Stone Town’s historic houses often used coral limestone, mangrove timber and lime mortar. Many larger houses arranged long, narrow rooms around an open courtyard. The building’s shape helped organise domestic space around that opening. A handsome carved entrance belonged to a practical building, not merely a decorative front.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: The town also included simpler single-storey Swahili houses and Indian bazaar buildings centred on a duka, or shop. Those differences matter: a palace cannot stand in for everybody’s home. Shop spaces are reminders that urban life involved buying, selling and making a living as well as royal ceremonies.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: Excavations in the Old Fort’s western courtyard in 2017 and 2018 traced occupation back to an eleventh-century Swahili settlement beside the beach. Imported ceramics helped researchers investigate long connections with the Gulf. A broken pot can reveal a trading relationship, although it cannot by itself tell us the language or birthplace of its owner.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: The same site later held a Portuguese trading establishment and an Augustinian mission. Omani builders reused the church within a square fort; nineteenth-century expansion produced two courtyards. A place can preserve several political histories in its walls. The present fort therefore does not represent one untouched building from a single moment.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Researchers recorded ship drawings scratched into dry plaster at the Old Fort, especially inside its southwestern tower and along its ramparts. Hulls, masts and rigging appear in the marks. Building history and vessel types suggest a mid- to late-nineteenth-century date. The drawings are material traces of somebody looking closely at ships.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Who held the sharp point? The researchers suggest members of the fort’s garrison, who had access to these spaces and could see shipping nearby. Their makers remain unidentified.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: At Mtoni palace, researchers excavated a water channel in 2008. Their architectural study connects the palace’s water supply with a nineteenth-century aqueduct from the Chem Chem spring. This is practical evidence behind a grand residence: bringing water to the household required planned structures, not just a good view of the sea.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: Mtoni’s bathing complex included cold-water bathhouses and a separate heated bath. The latter had cold, warm and hot rooms with a boiler. These were facilities of a royal household, not evidence that everyone in Zanzibar had such a bathroom. Even within the palace, different bathing arrangements served different residents.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: The cold-water bathhouses also had latrines that were emptied through hatches at the rear. Channels ran beneath the bathing complex, while raised back rooms accommodated washing and toilet use. Royal architecture needed arrangements for waste as well as impressive reception rooms. Somebody still had to do the emptying.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Princess Salme, later known as Emily Ruete, remembered lessons in the royal household on an open veranda. Children used bamboo pens, homemade ink and cleaned camel shoulder blades as writing surfaces. Enslaved people prepared the bones. This was her recollection of an elite nineteenth-century childhood, not a description of every Zanzibar school.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Before lessons, Salme recalled children wrestling and climbing a balustrade. A lookout coughed when the teacher approached, and everybody hurried to sit down. The account comes from memory, but the scene is wonderfully recognisable: an unusually well-coordinated effort to look as though absolutely nothing had been happening.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: In her household, girls were taught reading while boys also learned writing. Salme secretly copied characters onto a bone, then learned more with help from an enslaved writing teacher. Her story records both a girl pursuing an excluded skill and knowledge held by a person whose own freedom was denied.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: At the nineteenth-century plantation site of Mgoli on Pemba, a 2004 excavation uncovered a partly dismantled baraza, a bench outside a stone house. Beside it lay a packed-rubble floor interpreted as a place for drying cloves. A working floor at Bweni and local residents’ knowledge supported that interpretation.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: Freshly picked cloves had to dry before export, and enslaved workers supplied the plantation labour. Croucher suggests that a bench beside the drying area could let owners watch that work while also serving as a social space. The bench and floor were excavated; this explanation of surveillance is an interpretation of their position.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: Merchant Tharia Topan commissioned the building later called the Old Dispensary; its foundation stone was laid in 1887. After his death, his wife Janbai oversaw the project, but the completed building still needed money for equipment and staff. A fine building alone did not make a working clinic. It began operating under new ownership in 1900.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: The early dispensary treated patients in three ground-floor rooms used for consultations, treatment and pharmacy services. Apartments occupied the upper floors. After later closure and restoration, the building returned to healthcare use as the Aga Khan Health Centre. Its history joins medical work, housing and the challenge of adapting an old building to a new purpose.

The sultanate ended in the revolution of 12 January 1964, which replaced the monarchy with a republic. Zanzibar united with Tanganyika on 26 April that year. Its communities continued, and Zanzibar later developed its own House of Representatives within Tanzania. The map’s endpoint in 1914 is not this political ending.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
Food tools with stories to tell
Homes, clothes and travelling by river

passages.text: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: The Surinaams Museum preserves a mahogany four-poster bed made in 1829 by the furniture maker Podekowitz on Paramaribo’s Wagenwegstraat. It belongs to a collection rich in furniture associated with the colonial elite. This was substantial, carefully made furniture, rather than a picture of how everyone slept. A single grand bed cannot represent all the country’s bedrooms.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Needlework samplers in the same museum record how young European women practised embroidery and mending in the late nineteenth century. Surviving stitches make learning visible: someone had to repeat a movement, control the thread and improve. The collection also preserves early-twentieth-century baby clothes. These are particular surviving objects, rather than evidence that every family dressed or taught its children alike.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Gerrit Schouten’s 1817 miniature scene shows a riverboat with six enslaved rowers, a steersman and a covered passenger compartment. The shelter has windows with shutters propped open by sticks. The model records both ingenuity and inequality: passengers could travel out of the sun and rain while others did the rowing. It is an artist’s carefully constructed view, not a photograph of a named journey.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Afáka Atumisi developed a writing system for Ndyuka. Its signs represent syllables. A 2012 study explains that the sign for tu, meaning two, uses two strokes, while fo, meaning four, uses four. A little counting can help a reading lesson. The system is a distinctive achievement in making spoken language visible, though some signs can represent more than one sound.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Immigration registers for indentured workers arriving from British India between 1873 and 1916 can record parents, siblings and other relatives. Officials later added marriages, children and sometimes grandchildren born in Suriname. These documents help descendants reconnect family stories across oceans. Some registers were lost or badly damaged, and spelling varies, so an unsuccessful name search does not show that a person never existed.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In September 2024, nineteen volunteers aged 12 to 70 joined a supervised archaeology project at Jodensavanne. Four young participants came from neighbouring Redi Doti, an Indigenous village. The work included excavation, maintenance and conservation; a caption records young volunteers sifting earth for artifacts. Learning about the past can involve patient observation and teamwork as well as books.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Jodensavanne’s heritage is cared for through cooperation with Redi Doti. UNESCO describes the Indigenous village and the Jodensavanne Foundation sharing responsibility for preservation and agreeing together on changes to the management plan. This recognises living communities as participants in caring for history. A historic site is also part of someone’s present-day neighbourhood.

Suriname gained internal autonomy in 1954 and became an independent republic in 1975. These changes ended colonial government, not the histories of its communities. Crafts, languages and family knowledge continue through living people, with traditions changing as they are shared.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
Food tools with stories to tell
Homes, clothes and travelling by river

passages.text: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

sectionTitles: A very old search for colour
Leaves, fibres and a patient colour test
A village built to explain a village

passages.text: Eswatini’s history reaches from Stone Age pigment mining to the classrooms of Waterford Kamhlaba. Archaeological materials, school records and the accounts of working craftspeople offer different windows into learning, creativity and everyday life.

passages.title: A very old search for colour
passages.text: At Lion Cavern in the Ngwenya mountains, people mined ochre, mineral material used for pigment, long before the modern kingdom existed. A 2024 study refined the dating of intensive mining to about 48,000 years ago. Researchers used a method that measures signals stored in sediment grains. The date concerns this archaeological mining evidence, not the age of every painted surface in Eswatini.

passages.title: A very old search for colour
passages.text: Ochre pieces from Sibebe carry grooves made by grinding or scoring. The same study compared the chemical make-up of archaeological pieces with mineral sources, connecting many finds to Ngwenya. Such matches help trace movement through a landscape. They do not tell us whether each piece travelled with its user, passed between neighbours, or changed hands several times.

passages.title: Leaves, fibres and a patient colour test
passages.text: Tintsaba describes how its weavers prepare sisal leaves for baskets and other objects. The useful fibres are hidden inside the fleshy leaf. Scraping removes that flesh; drying turns the remaining strands into weaving material. Younger leaves provide a pale fibre that takes colour well. A finished basket therefore contains a great deal of skilled work before the first coil is made.

passages.title: Leaves, fibres and a patient colour test
passages.text: The maker’s dyeing account includes tea for earthy shades as well as other dye powders. Workers test a few fibres before committing a whole bundle to a colour, then rinse and dry the strands in shade to avoid fading. A little test can save a lot of weaving material. This is a described workshop practice, not evidence that every basket uses only natural dyes.

passages.title: School could involve a mountain
passages.text: Waterford Kamhlaba opened near Mbabane on 3 February 1963 with sixteen boys. Its own history explains that founder Michael Stern wanted pupils of different backgrounds to learn together in opposition to apartheid. Parents helped build the school: architect Pancho Guedes contributed designs without a fee. This particular school’s beginnings tell a story of educational choices and practical cooperation, not of identical schooling across the country.

passages.title: School could involve a mountain
passages.text: Waterford’s account of outdoor learning remembers geology trips, visits to rock art, hikes in the Komati Gorge and camping during the 1960s to 1980s. The landscape became part of the lesson. Outdoor education grew more formally in the 1990s, with activities including climbing, kayaking and hiking. A school day did not always mean staying at a desk, although these were organised trips, not permission to wander off.

passages.title: A bottle’s second career
passages.text: Ngwenya Glass says its handmade glassware uses recycled glass, much of it collected soft-drink bottles. Its workshop makes drinking glasses and jugs alongside animal sculptures. The maker dates the business’s revival to 1987. An empty bottle can therefore become material for something carefully shaped and used again. The recycling claim comes from the producer’s account, rather than an independent audit of its entire environmental impact.

passages.title: A bottle’s second career
passages.text: The same account describes schools joining clean-up and bottle-collection work, with the company providing support such as building materials and sponsorship for football teams. This links a workshop’s raw materials with school life beyond its own doors. It is an example of a particular programme, not a claim that children everywhere in Eswatini collected glass for their schooling.

passages.title: Money with corners
passages.text: Eswatini introduced its own currency on 6 September 1974, six years after independence. The first banknotes were for one, two, five and ten emalangeni; a twenty followed in 1978. The Central Bank’s history separates these dates clearly. Having a new country and having a new set of notes were different events, even though both were marked on the same day of the year.

passages.title: Money with corners
passages.text: The first 1974 coins were not all little circles. The two-cent piece was square with rounded corners, while the one-cent and fifty-cent coins had twelve sides. Other small coins had scalloped edges. The Central Bank records these shapes alongside their values. A handful of change could have doubled as a tiny geometry lesson, though its owner probably had shopping in mind.

passages.title: A village built to explain a village
passages.text: Mantenga Cultural Village is a reconstruction of a mid-nineteenth-century Swazi village. The tourism authority describes guides explaining how huts are made, what different buildings are for, and the role of a traditional healer. Visitors can see demonstrations of food preparation, grass plaiting and beadwork. This is a place for interpreting history, rather than a collection of houses all surviving untouched since the 1850s.

passages.title: A village built to explain a village
passages.text: Mantenga also presents sibhaca performances with high kicks, drumming and singing. These public shows bring movement and sound into the visit alongside architecture and craft. A scheduled performance at a cultural attraction is a particular setting for an art form; it does not tell us that every historical family gathered for the same show at the same hour.

British sovereignty ended with independence on 6 September 1968. The kingdom continued, and adopted the name Eswatini in 2018. The end of the older Swaziland map interval is not the extinction of a people or the collapse of the modern country.

passages.text: Early-modern Sweden supported both industrial communities and elaborate court art. Falun's copper landscape and Drottningholm's theatre reveal very different kinds of skilled work.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the seventeenth century, Falun copper production helped make Sweden a major European metal producer. Mining shaped the surrounding economy and settlement landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Falun's seventeenth-century planned town and mining settlements preserve evidence of workers' housing as well as production facilities. Industrial history includes the communities around the mine.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Drottningholm's eighteenth-century theatre used machinery that could change scenery while the curtain stayed up. Stage sets and working mechanisms survive.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Drottningholm's Chinese Pavilion reflects eighteenth-century European engagement with Asian design. Nearby Canton Village included manufacturing buildings and court living quarters.

passages.text: This modern Swedish record begins with the atlas’s 1914 snapshot, long after the kingdom itself began. The twentieth century brought broader political participation and changes in housing, family policy and medicine. Surviving appliances, photographs, laws and institutional records make these developments tangible.

passages.title: Making political participation broader
passages.text: The 1921 election was the first parliamentary election with equal suffrage for women and men. Five women took seats in 1922. The dates separate winning an election from beginning parliamentary work; neither means representation became equal overnight.

passages.title: Making political participation broader
passages.text: Sweden replaced its two parliamentary chambers with one in 1971. Changing an institution’s structure is different from founding a new country. The elected assembly continued to make laws and supervise government.

passages.title: Making political participation broader
passages.text: All offentlig makt i Sverige utgår från folket means “All public power in Sweden proceeds from the people.” It opens Chapter 1 of the Instrument of Government. This sample follows the official consolidated Swedish text of the law adopted in 1974.

passages.title: Kitchen measurements and washing days
passages.text: The Home Research Institute was established in 1944 by women’s and homemakers’ organizations, with state funding. Researchers timed tasks and measured kitchens. The distance from cupboard to sink became something to investigate scientifically, not merely endure.

passages.title: Kitchen measurements and washing days
passages.text: The institute brought together household teachers, chemists, nutrition researchers, sociologists, architects and engineers. Domestic work became a subject for specialist study. Recognizing its complexity challenged the idea that running a household required no expertise.

passages.title: Kitchen measurements and washing days
passages.text: Modern housing projects promoted hot water, bathrooms and shared laundry rooms. The laundry was intended to reduce demanding domestic labour, especially women’s work. These were reform goals; the museum’s account does not prove identical facilities in every Swedish home.

passages.title: Caring for babies and hearts
passages.text: Parental insurance introduced in 1974 allowed both mothers and fathers to take paid time away from employment to care for a newborn. The initial allowance was 180 days per child. Family care became a responsibility recognized through public policy.

passages.title: Caring for babies and hearts
passages.text: In that first year, mothers took 99.5 percent of parental-benefit days. Giving both parents an entitlement did not immediately produce equal participation. The historical figures show a gap between a policy’s possibilities and everyday choices.

passages.title: Caring for babies and hearts
passages.text: In October 1958, surgeon Åke Senning implanted a pacemaker developed by Rune Elmqvist in Arne Larsson. The museum preserves an early model from 1958 to 1960. This achievement concerned an implantable device; earlier external pacemakers already existed.

passages.title: Caring for babies and hearts
passages.text: The first implanted device worked only for hours before replacement. Transistors helped make the equipment small enough, and later improvements increased reliability. A successful medical technology can emerge through repeated correction rather than a flawless first attempt.

passages.title: Continuing connections
passages.text: Sweden entered the European Union on 1 January 1995, alongside Austria and Finland. Membership changed its international institutional relationships. It did not end Swedish statehood, language or local communities.

passages.title: Continuing connections
passages.text: The constitution describes government through elected representatives and local self-government. It also identifies protection for cultural and linguistic minorities. These written principles reveal public commitments; assessing their implementation requires evidence beyond the wording of the law.

Sweden continues as a state. Democratic reforms, the 1971 parliamentary reorganization and European membership in 1995 changed its institutions without representing national extinction. The atlas’s 1914 starting point is a coverage choice, not the kingdom’s founding date.

passages.text: Sweden and Norway shared a king from 1814 until 1905, but they were not simply one country. Norway kept its constitution, parliament and much domestic self-government, while disputes over the monarch and foreign affairs sharpened over time. A child in this era might help on a farm, learn to read, hear folktales, fear smallpox, or trek to a cold outdoor privy. Those experiences differed by class, place and language; Sami children in Norway faced forced assimilation in school. Norway declared the union dissolved in 1905 and Sweden accepted independence after negotiations. The imported map interval, about 1815 to 1914, outlasts the real union.

passages.title: A union with two governments
passages.text: In 1814 Norway left its old union with Denmark, adopted a constitution and fought a short war with Sweden. The settlement joined Norway and Sweden under one king, but Norway kept its own parliament and much control over home affairs.

passages.title: A union with two governments
passages.text: The Norwegian constitution said “Kongeriget Norge er et frit, selvstændigt, udeleligt og uafhændeligt Rige.” That means Norway was a free, independent, indivisible and inalienable realm. Its next words placed it in union with Sweden under one king.

passages.title: A union with two governments
passages.text: Norway’s parliament gained leverage in a long struggle with the king. In 1884 the monarch had to appoint a Norwegian government backed by the parliamentary majority, a breakthrough for parliamentarianism.

passages.title: A union with two governments
passages.text: Norwegian shipping and trade made separate consuls abroad a major issue. When King Oscar II refused a Norwegian consular law, Norway’s parliament declared the union dissolved on 7 June 1905. Sweden recognized independence after a referendum and negotiations.

passages.title: A union with two governments
passages.text: Women could not vote in the 1905 referendum, yet Norwegian women organized 244,765 signatures for separation. It was impressive political action by people the ballot box had excluded.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: On a Swedish farm in the 1890s, children might fetch wood and water, mind younger siblings, pick berries or help with animals. Parents and children all worked; family labor mattered even when school attendance was expected.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: Sweden’s 1842 school ordinance expanded basic schooling. By late century a child was expected to spend years in school, but farm work could interrupt lessons. A desk and a milk pail could compete for the same afternoon.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: An 1826 diary by Swedish parsonage daughter Sofi Rönnqvist mentions reading aloud, coffee visits, dances, illness and caring for her father. It is a rare peek at one family’s social life, not a portrait of every household.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: In Norway, Asbjørnsen and Moe collected folktales as people argued over national identity. A story told by a fire could end up in a book and become part of a wider debate about what was “Norwegian.”

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: A Norwegian women’s reading association founded in 1874 shared books, lectures and reading circles. Access to education and universities was unequal; friends making a library together was a way to open a door.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: The two kingdoms also included Sami homelands. Norwegian authorities increasingly pressed Sami pupils to use Norwegian in school, especially later in the century. A classroom could therefore threaten a child’s home language.

passages.title: Children, work and stories
passages.text: Late nineteenth-century Norwegian towns grew around factories and processing of fish and timber, while many Swedish people emigrated because of hardship and scarce land. The union era was no single rural picture.

passages.title: Health, washing and the toilet question
passages.text: Sweden began smallpox vaccination in the early nineteenth century. That was a real tool against a dangerous infection, though families still faced other illnesses and unequal access to care.

passages.title: Health, washing and the toilet question
passages.text: Heating water to wash bodies and laundry took time and fuel. In Norway the 1860 health law and public baths were part of a hygiene campaign; private bathrooms remained mainly for wealthier homes late in the century.

passages.title: Health, washing and the toilet question
passages.text: In parts of rural Norway even an outhouse was uncommon in the mid-nineteenth century. Many people simply went outdoors. A grand royal palace tells you very little about a farm child’s bathroom break.

passages.title: Health, washing and the toilet question
passages.text: Stockholm households mostly used courtyard dry privies, and waste could contaminate wells. Water-flush toilets reached only a small number of wealthy homes by 1895. Keeping drinking water away from waste mattered more than fancy porcelain.

The Swedish-Norwegian union ended in 1905. Norway became an independent kingdom after its parliament’s declaration, referendum and negotiations with Sweden. Both kingdoms and their peoples continued; the imported map label extends to 1914 even though the shared monarchy did not.

sectionTitles: Work, learning and the old cantons

passages.text: Switzerland grew from a confederation of cantons into a modern federal state through war, negotiation and constitutional change. The old alliance was not yet the Switzerland established in 1848. These two map labels share a connected history, with the French-backed Helvetic Republic and later settlements clearly separated.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: A family’s home could also be a textile workshop. Merchants supplied raw material, sometimes lent looms, and paid for finished cloth according to quantity and quality. Children joined adults in production; working at home did not automatically mean choosing your own hours.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: In eighteenth-century Appenzell, some weaving took place in low, humid cellars with narrow windows. Damp air helped the threads, even if it was hardly a luxury office. Embroidery required a different workspace with better light: the craft shaped the house.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: Basel’s university was disrupted by the Reformation in 1529 and reopened under municipal oversight in 1532. Teaching did not simply disappear in between: Oswald Bär performed a public anatomical dissection in 1531. Religious and political upheaval could alter the classroom itself.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: Education had costs that not every family could meet. Basel created scholarships for poor boys in 1533 using former ecclesiastical resources, and an Erasmus foundation supported needy students from 1538. These targeted arrangements were not universal access to university.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: Erasmus’s New Testament appeared from Johann Froben’s Basel press in 1516 with Greek text and a new Latin version. Comparing manuscripts, editing type and organizing printing made this a collaborative scholarly achievement, not a book created by a lone author overnight.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: The Greek manuscripts behind Basel scholarship had traveled. Material associated with John of Ragusa linked the city’s libraries to Byzantium. A printed page could therefore carry the results of journeys, copying and argument across several generations.

passages.title: Work, learning and the old cantons
passages.text: In 1799, during the Helvetic Republic, education minister Philipp Albert Stapfer sent schools a questionnaire of roughly sixty questions. More than 2,400 replies survive, mostly from teachers, describing lessons, personnel, local conditions and money. They preserve differences between real classrooms rather than one imaginary “Swiss school.”

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: The federal Factory Act of 1877 prohibited factory employment below age fourteen and limited the working day. Its scope matters: protection for factory children did not instantly abolish children’s work in farms or home industries. A law was an important change, not a magic off-switch.

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: A historical account of the Gubel institution at Neuägeri describes girls working and studying around demanding textile shifts. Reports of tired pupils make the conflict between production and learning visible. This is a specific institution, not evidence that every Swiss child lived the same way.

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: Industrial schedules helped create a market for foods that were quick to prepare. The museum’s account follows firms such as Maggi and includes a 1910 image of food production. Soup could become a factory product long before the microwave appeared.

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: Chocolate makers refined texture as well as flavor. Daniel Peter developed milk chocolate in the 1870s, while Rodolphe Lindt’s conching process of 1879 helped make it smoother. These were particular technical improvements, not proof that Switzerland invented every kind of chocolate.

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: A surviving nineteenth-century bidet at Jegenstorf Castle looks like mahogany furniture, with a removable ceramic basin and a cover. It belonged in a world of bedroom washing equipment. Fancy woodwork could conceal a very practical job; one castle object does not describe every household’s bathroom.

passages.title: Industrial life and expanding rights
passages.text: Swiss women gained the federal vote in 1971. Cantonal voting rights followed different paths: the Federal Court required Appenzell Innerrhoden to admit women in 1990, and women first participated in its cantonal assembly in 1991. “When women could vote” therefore needs a level of government.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: German, constitution of 1848, article 4: “Alle Schweizer sind vor dem Gesetze gleich.” Translation: “All Swiss are equal before the law.” Parliament’s historical discussion reproduces the sentence and explains its limits: women were still excluded from political equality. A promise on paper and its reach in practice are different questions.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latin, the title used for Erasmus’s 1516 edition: “Novum Instrumentum.” In this biblical context it means “New Testament.” The short title illustrates the Latin language of learned publishing in Basel; it does not mean that ordinary conversation throughout the cantons was in Latin.

The Old Confederation ended as a political order in 1798. Switzerland continued through new constitutional forms and became a federal state in 1848; the modern country continues. The map’s split between its two labels should not be mistaken for the disappearance and replacement of its people.

sectionTitles: Seafaring and the journeys of objects

passages.text: Taíno describes diverse late precolonial Caribbean societies, especially in the Greater Antilles, rather than every population that previously lived on the islands. Their communities combined farming, ceremonial gatherings and connections maintained through travel across the sea.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: Starch analysis of clay griddles reveals different foods at neighbouring sites. El Flaco in the Dominican Republic yielded evidence especially of maize; La Luperona of zamia; and Palmetto Junction in the Turks and Caicos Islands of manioc. These are findings from sampled tools, not complete menus.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: A clay griddle’s shape does not prove that it cooked only cassava bread. Microscopic residues reveal a wider range of plant preparation. Some surfaces may also have served for processing without heating, so researchers compare plant traces, damage and archaeological context.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: The Smithsonian describes bohío houses made with local materials such as palms and vines. Its conuco examples show family gardens as working spaces whose crops changed after plants arrived from other continents.

passages.title: Food and household materials
passages.text: Dried calabash gourds became bowls, spoons, containers and maracas. One plant supplied household utensils and musical instruments, joining practical work with performance.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Ceremonial plazas hosted batey, a team game played with a rubber ball. These substantial communal spaces also supported ritual gatherings. Their central position shows that organised recreation and public life mattered alongside subsistence work.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Areytos brought together storytelling, song, dance and drumming. Their forms varied with occasions such as celebrations, deaths or conflict. They carried collective knowledge through performance rather than following one uniform programme on every island.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: A British Museum duho, or ritual seat, was carved from dense guayacan wood as a crouching human figure. Geometric patterns mark its back. The object combines furniture, bodily imagery and close attention to a difficult, durable material.

passages.title: Games, performance and skilled carving
passages.text: Gold inlays accent the duho’s eyes, mouth and shoulders. The museum interprets these features through chiefs’ and ritual specialists’ relationships with ancestor spirits. Its radiocarbon range, 1292 to 1399, concerns the wood; it cannot identify an exact day or year of carving.

passages.title: Seafaring and the journeys of objects
passages.text: Canoes carried people and goods between islands. Colonial accounts describe arrivals from other islands for exchange, while decorated vessels could also express status. Maritime knowledge made water a route of social connection as well as a demanding physical environment.

passages.title: Seafaring and the journeys of objects
passages.text: Another duho, from Eleuthera in the Bahamas, has an inscription recording that James Thompson found it while enslaved around 1820. He was free when he sold it to a missionary in 1835. Its later collection history adds another colonial story to the older object.

passages.title: Knowledge carried forward
passages.text: The Smithsonian guide pictures Leonarda “Doña Esmeralda” Morales-Acevedo stripping maguey fibre for hammock thread in Puerto Rico. This named maker’s work documents living craft knowledge, while contemporary Taíno cultural movements challenge accounts that declare all Caribbean Native people extinct.

Spanish colonization killed, displaced and enslaved Native people and undermined their political and religious institutions. Survivors carried knowledge into changing Caribbean communities. Contemporary Taíno identities and cultural renewal make an extinction ending inaccurate, even while the scale of colonial destruction must remain clear.

sectionTitles: Writing and a name that traveled

passages.text: Takrur was an influential kingdom and commercial center in the Senegal River valley, especially prominent in the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Its name later traveled far beyond its original homeland. The map’s 1000 to 1279 span selects part of that medieval history; it should not be confused with the separate eighteenth-century label “Tekrur”.

passages.title: A trading kingdom
passages.text: War Jabi’s adoption of Islam in the eleventh century mattered politically as well as religiously. Arabic writers connect his reign with Islamic law. A ruler’s conversion tells us about court policy; the region’s religious life developed over a longer and more varied history.

passages.title: A trading kingdom
passages.text: Al-Idrisi’s twelfth-century account describes merchants arriving with wool, copper and other goods, and leaving with gold and enslaved people. Trade brought wealth and far-reaching contacts, but also depended on coercion and the forced movement of people.

passages.title: A trading kingdom
passages.text: A later Arabic description by al-Qazwini presents Takrur as a large, unwalled town containing Muslims and followers of other religions. This is a reminder that medieval authors did not always give the same picture: towns and communities changed, and reports had different sources.

passages.title: Crafts visible in the ground
passages.text: Sincu Bara is a major archaeological site in the wider Senegal valley, covering roughly 67 hectares. It helps reveal the society from which medieval states emerged. Its precise relationship to named capitals remains uncertain, so its finds are regional evidence rather than a labeled royal household.

passages.title: Crafts visible in the ground
passages.text: Copper-alloy finds from Sincu Bara include rings, decorated disks and bells. Scientific analysis distinguishes brass, leaded brass and copper. A glittering ornament was the result of skilled material choices, not simply a lump of metal beaten into whatever shape happened to appear.

passages.title: Crafts visible in the ground
passages.text: New excavations in 1991 and 1992 changed the site’s story. Researchers placed the arrival of copper-based metals around 800 to 900 CE, later than earlier estimates. Separating disturbed layers helped reveal change that had previously been mistaken for centuries of sameness.

passages.title: Crafts visible in the ground
passages.text: Iron smelting was another substantial regional skill. David Killick studied furnace residues and radiocarbon dates from several Senegal valley sites, spanning many centuries. These remains preserve the work of people controlling fire, ore and airflow, essential skills behind useful metal objects.

passages.title: What went into a meal
passages.text: Charred seeds from seven Senegal valley sites show pearl millet as the most common identified crop in nearly every examined assemblage. The strongest occupation evidence largely predates 1000 CE. These small remains reveal the agricultural foundations supporting the later medieval communities.

passages.title: What went into a meal
passages.text: People also used wild plants. Jujube fruit was abundant in some excavated communities and scarce in others, alongside varied grasses and tree fruits. Even within one river valley, dinner did not follow a single standard menu: local resources and choices mattered.

passages.title: Writing and a name that traveled
passages.text: Here is the name in Arabic: “تكرور”, or “Takrur”. This spelling is printed as the headword of the 2011 scholarly encyclopedia entry. Arabic authors discussed the kingdom in medieval geographical works; this is a modern printed witness to the name, not a newly discovered medieval inscription.

passages.title: Writing and a name that traveled
passages.text: Historian Umar al-Naqar traced how the name broadened among pilgrims and migrants in the Middle East. It could refer to West African Muslims who came from far outside the original kingdom. The reputation of a place sometimes travels farther than the armies of its rulers.

passages.title: Writing and a name that traveled
passages.text: This wider meaning caused confusion even in medieval times. Al-Naqar discusses an account in which Mali’s Mansa Musa objected to being called ruler of Takrur, since Takrur was only part of his much larger realm. Names on maps need context as well as spelling.

Takrur lost its earlier predominance as Mali expanded during the thirteenth century. The imported 1279 endpoint is not a securely established single destruction date. Its communities continued, and the name retained a much broader life in Muslim geography and identity.

passages.text: The Tang dynasty is considered China's golden age, marked by cosmopolitan culture, Buddhist flourishing, poetic achievement and international trade. Chang'an became one of the world's largest cities, connected by the Silk Road to Central Asia, India and Persia.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The Diamond Sutra, the world's oldest dated printed book, produced using woodblock printing.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The first written warning of gunpowder's power appears in a Daoist alchemical text, describing a mixture of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal that burst into flame.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The great poets Li Bai, Du Fu and Wang Wei create masterpieces of Chinese verse.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Buddhist cave temples at Dunhuang filled with murals and sculptures.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: True porcelain, the white Xing wares of Hebei, is made, though it remained rare and precious.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Xuanzang travels to India, returning in 645 with Buddhist texts that he translates.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Christianity arrives in Chang'an with the missionary Alopen; the Xi'an Stele of 781 records its reception.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an reaches a population of about one million, with foreign merchants, monks and diplomats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Tea drinking becomes widespread; Lu Yu writes the Classic of Tea.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Silk Road trade connects China to Central Asia, Persia and the Mediterranean.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Tang poetry became the standard for later Chinese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Overseas Chinese still call a Chinatown a Tangrenjie, the street of the Tang people.
The An Lushan Rebellion of 755 fatally weakened the dynasty; regional military governors gained power, and the last Tang emperor was deposed by Zhu Wen in 907.

passages.text: The map’s 1920 to 1938 record is labelled with Tanzania’s later name. At that time the mainland territory was Tanganyika, administered by Britain under a League of Nations mandate. Tanzania’s union with Zanzibar came only in 1964. This card follows Tanganyika’s interwar farmers, readers, workers and colonial institutions.

passages.title: Crops, work and learning
passages.text: On Kilimanjaro, African smallholders grew coffee alongside European settlers. Colonial encouragement of local growers provoked settler opposition. Coffee history therefore includes a contest over who could farm and sell, as well as the plants themselves.

passages.title: Crops, work and learning
passages.text: The Kilimanjaro Native Planters Association brought growers into organized politics. Cooperative legislation in 1932 and coffee controls in 1937 shaped how crops reached markets. An association and its paperwork could matter to a farming household as much as a harvest.

passages.title: Crops, work and learning
passages.text: Sisal production expanded rapidly in Tanganyika and Kenya during the 1920s and 1930s. The Depression brought low prices and unstable markets, creating conflict between producers and merchants. More output did not automatically mean a more secure income.

passages.title: Crops, work and learning
passages.text: Economic historian Sascha Klocke identifies restricted educational opportunities for Africans as a major barrier to advancement in paid employment. The supply of trained workers helped determine who obtained skilled jobs and higher wages.

passages.title: Crops, work and learning
passages.text: Klocke’s study also separates racial discrimination from shortages of trained personnel. These interacted: importing skilled workers could widen income differences while inadequate African education helped preserve the shortage. Colonial wage inequality cannot be explained by one pay rule alone.

passages.title: A newspaper on the table
passages.text: “Mambo Leo” means “Affairs of Today”. This attested Swahili title belonged to a monthly launched by the Education Department in January 1923. It is a small original-language sample of the printed material circulating during this map period.

passages.title: A newspaper on the table
passages.text: Mambo Leo printed entertaining stories, arranged pen friendships and carried notices looking for missing people. A newspaper could help someone find a correspondent or reconnect with a person, alongside passing on official news.

passages.title: A newspaper on the table
passages.text: The paper’s early topics included agriculture, education, veterinary matters and football. Its staff selected news according to government policy, including support for Swahili in primary schools. Useful reading and colonial persuasion occupied the same printed pages.

passages.title: River households and health policy
passages.text: In Ulanga, river communities used canoes for transport and combined fishing with other work. The Kilombero floodplain offered fertile land, but seasonal floods interrupted routes and separated places. Water was both a resource and a practical constraint.

passages.title: River households and health policy
passages.text: Food production varied with local conditions: rice grew in lowlands and uplands, while farmers also cultivated maize and sorghum with hoes. Pogoro near the floodplain grew more rice than highland Pogoro. A community name alone does not tell us what was for dinner.

passages.title: River households and health policy
passages.text: During the 1930s, colonial officials debated moving scattered communities into concentrated settlements as a response to sleeping sickness. In Ulanga, proposals preceded the outbreak recorded in 1939. Medical goals became entangled with power over where families could live.

passages.title: River households and health policy
passages.text: Tanganyika’s 1961 constitution marked a later political transformation beyond the map’s interwar interval. Independence changed sovereignty; the people who had farmed, read newspapers and worked under colonial rule did not disappear when the legal framework changed.

British rule ended with Tanganyika’s independence on 9 December 1961. Tanganyika joined Zanzibar on 26 April 1964 to form the union later named Tanzania. This imported interwar record should not be read as evidence that the United Republic already existed in the 1920s.

sectionTitles: Institutions and an original Swahili title
Privacy at school and stories across borders

passages.text: This record begins before Tanzania existed as a union. Tanganyika became independent in 1961; its 1964 union with Zanzibar created a state with both union and Zanzibar institutions. Later history includes socialist development projects, difficult rural reforms, international railway building and continuing community efforts in education.

passages.title: Institutions and an original Swahili title
passages.text: The 1964 union brought Tanganyika and Zanzibar together, while retaining a separate Zanzibar government alongside the union government. The country’s political structure therefore cannot be understood simply as the mainland absorbing an island with no institutions of its own.

passages.title: Institutions and an original Swahili title
passages.text: “Azimio la Arusha” means “Arusha Declaration”. The words appear in the title of TANU’s Swahili pamphlet of 1967, preserved in Indiana University’s collection. The short title introduces a document that shaped political debate about the country’s future.

passages.title: Institutions and an original Swahili title
passages.text: The declaration outlined socialist policies associated with Julius Nyerere, including nationalization and restrictions on leaders’ private economic interests. Scholarship also traces debate among trade unionists and others: political ideas developed through argument as well as presidential speeches.

passages.title: Institutions and an original Swahili title
passages.text: Later villagization included forcing rural people to move into planned villages. Promises of improved services did not remove the disruption of relocation or make every household willing to participate. Development history includes the choices governments denied people as well as the facilities they hoped to build.

passages.title: Rails and adult classrooms
passages.text: The TAZARA railway linked Dar es Salaam with Kapiri Mposhi in Zambia. Tanzania, Zambia and China signed the construction agreement in 1967; full operations began on 14 July 1976. It provided a route to the coast outside the southern transport corridor controlled by white minority regimes.

passages.title: Rails and adult classrooms
passages.text: The difficult Mlimba to Makambako section required bridges, tunnels and extensive earthworks. Chinese, Tanzanian and Zambian workers built the line together. A railway achievement includes surveying, construction and maintenance skills, rather than merely the moment a locomotive arrives.

passages.title: Rails and adult classrooms
passages.text: Tanzania’s community-based adult education programme began in 1993. UNESCO describes learners meeting in primary schools after children went home, using Kiswahili and discussing practical topics such as farming, health and household finances. A classroom could have a second working day.

passages.title: Rails and adult classrooms
passages.text: One group of women learned tailoring from a local craftsperson and used a group loan to buy a sewing machine for making school uniforms. Bookkeeping accompanied sewing skills. Reading and arithmetic helped connect lessons with running a small shared enterprise.

passages.title: Privacy at school and stories across borders
passages.text: At Bahati School in Dar es Salaam, UNICEF’s 2017 report describes separate toilet blocks, handwashing stations, safe drinking water and an accessible toilet. The facilities made drinking, washing and taking a private break possible within the school day.

passages.title: Privacy at school and stories across borders
passages.text: Students at Bahati took turns checking cleanliness, and a health teacher met girls to discuss puberty and hygiene. The menstrual hygiene room held clean pads. Privacy and an adult who will answer questions are practical parts of making a school usable.

passages.title: Privacy at school and stories across borders
passages.text: Abdulrazak Gurnah, who grew up in Zanzibar, received the 2021 Nobel Prize in Literature. His novels explore colonialism and the experience of refugees across cultures. A literary achievement can carry a place’s difficult histories to readers far beyond its borders.

passages.title: Privacy at school and stories across borders
passages.text: Gurnah left Zanzibar amid persecution in the 1960s and later settled in England. His life connects East Africa with a wider diaspora. His novels follow individuals crossing cultures and carrying memories of places they have left.

Tanzania continues as the union formed in 1964. Independence, union and later reforms changed political institutions without ending the histories of mainland and island communities. The map’s 1960 start predates both Tanganyika’s independence and the union.

passages.text: Teke communities connected the Congo River’s great markets with forest and savanna producers. The kingdom centred on Mbé and its Makoko formed part of this wider, diverse Teke world. This imported 1878 to 1914 outline covers a period of French colonial intervention, rather than the kingdom’s complete lifespan.

passages.title: Power, place and negotiation
passages.text: The river was a commercial meeting place, not an empty route waiting for Europeans. Teke intermediaries linked communities across forest, marsh and plateau, trading both raw materials and finished goods. Their knowledge of suppliers, customers and routes was an important source of influence.

passages.title: Power, place and negotiation
passages.text: In 1882 an American diplomat described the French treaty language as difficult to interpret. He also reported Stanley’s claim that a local chief understood his agreement as a land lease. The documents therefore record competing colonial claims as well as African decisions; signing did not create a shared understanding of sovereignty.

passages.title: Power, place and negotiation
passages.text: Mbé was a capital that moved. According to the royal domain’s heritage record, the capital shifted after a king died, and abandoned royal settlements became sacred forests. Remembering a ruler could therefore mean protecting a living landscape rather than preserving one permanent palace.

passages.title: Power, place and negotiation
passages.text: The Ngantsibi, or queen, was a guardian of authority during a vacancy in the kingship, rather than simply the king’s wife. Her residence at Ngabé and places of initiation formed part of the royal landscape. Political authority had important female custodians.

passages.title: Food, travel and skilled hands
passages.text: Brazza’s 1880 notes describe a royal meal of pounded cassava leaves enriched with pounded kernels, served on plates. He contrasted it with plain leaves eaten in a famine elsewhere. The same staple could become a different meal depending on ingredients, resources and circumstances.

passages.title: Food, travel and skilled hands
passages.text: The same visitor watched maize beer being made from grain that was first sprouted and dried, then pounded. Large stores of dried cassava and sprouted maize also appear in his account. Feeding a community involved planning and processing, well before anyone sat down to eat.

passages.title: Food, travel and skilled hands
passages.text: On the Congo in September 1880, river travellers declined to cross when wind against the current raised dangerous waves. Experienced paddlers understood when to wait. A canoe journey could have a timetable, but the river still got a vote.

passages.title: Food, travel and skilled hands
passages.text: A surviving early twentieth-century Teke raffia cloth is a small square with yellow and black stripes and fringed edges. Woven cloth could carry value as well as pattern: buyers and sellers negotiated its worth through width and quality. A careful weaver was making more than something attractive to wear.

passages.title: Ancestors, performance and writing
passages.text: A nineteenth-century ancestor figure preserves a sculptor’s precise slit eyes, patterned cheeks and projecting beard. Its body contains bonga, substances believed to activate ancestral power. Small figures could be sold in markets, while larger works were commissioned for communities: artistic skill supported both households and public life.

passages.title: Ancestors, performance and writing
passages.text: French observer Edouard Ponel recorded chiefs using such figures during important discussions in the 1880s. Palm wine and kola became offerings intended to bring ancestors into the conversation. The sculpture was an active participant in decision-making as its users understood it, rather than merely a room decoration.

passages.title: Ancestors, performance and writing
passages.text: One Kidumu mask, probably made in the early twentieth century and collected in 1929, divides its design into upper and lower zones. Its performer cartwheeled, connecting the worlds of living people and ancestors through movement. This was one Teke performance tradition, not a uniform custom across every community.

passages.title: Ancestors, performance and writing
passages.text: Writing sample: “Au nom de la France” means “In the name of France.” These French words open the act of 3 October 1880 reproduced in the official gazette. They show the language of the colonial claim. They are neither Teke-language writing nor words composed by the Makoko himself.

French colonial rule reduced the kingdom’s political independence; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. Teke communities and royal traditions continued. The Mbé heritage account records enduring investiture and funeral rites, family genealogies and sacred forests that preserve the memory of earlier rulers.

sectionTitles: What this name can and cannot tell us
A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey

passages.text: This imported “Tekrur” record covers 1715 to 1783 in southeastern Senegal and its vicinity. A matching independent kingdom with those exact dates has not been securely identified. The examples below concern named regional societies, especially Bundu and neighboring Futa Toro; they explain the setting without silently substituting either state for the uncertain map label.

passages.title: What this name can and cannot tell us
passages.text: “Tekrur” was not always a narrow political label. Umar al-Naqar traced its use for West African Muslim people far beyond the original medieval kingdom. Similar spelling alone does not prove that two map records describe the same state.

passages.title: What this name can and cannot tell us
passages.text: Bundu, a separately documented state in eastern Senegal, emerged around the end of the seventeenth century. Michael Gomez compares differing traditions about its founder Malik Sy. Those accounts show why the history of a named kingdom needs more than a borrowed label on a map.

passages.title: What this name can and cannot tell us
passages.text: In Bundu, Maka Jiba’s eighteenth-century government expanded cultivation and sought trade with French establishments on the Senegal and English traders on the Gambia. Access to land and commercial routes helped build power. This is Bundu’s history, offered as regional context.

passages.title: What this name can and cannot tell us
passages.text: Neighboring Futa Toro underwent an Islamic revolution culminating in 1776. Teachers, students and religious reformers moved between communities, carrying political arguments with them. Bundu’s rulers responded to those pressures while protecting their own authority and interests.

passages.title: A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey
passages.text: Ayuba Sulayman Diallo, an imam’s son from Bundu, was enslaved in 1731 and taken to America. He regained freedom, traveled to London and returned to Africa in 1734. His surviving writings make an individual West African voice unusually visible in this period.

passages.title: A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey
passages.text: Diallo’s experience also exposes slavery’s tangled history. Before his own capture, he had participated in selling enslaved people. His suffering and remarkable return should be remembered alongside that involvement, rather than turning a complex person into a simple adventure hero.

passages.title: A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey
passages.text: Thomas Bluett’s 1734 account says Diallo learned Arabic and the Qur’an with his father alongside a ruler’s son. Teaching joined family life, scholarship and political connections. This is a report about a particular educated household, not a claim that every child received the same training.

passages.title: A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey
passages.text: Bluett also records a naming celebration held when a baby was seven days old. A name was written on a smooth board, food was shared with guests and poorer neighbors, and the name was written again on paper. Writing could enter family life from its very beginning.

passages.title: A family, a scholar and an Atlantic journey
passages.text: Diallo’s archive includes letters, Qur’an copies and examples made while discussing Arabic with acquaintances in Britain. These documents show scholarship being used across great distances. Literacy was part of his life before captivity, not a skill first handed to him in Europe.

passages.title: Nearby river communities in 1795
passages.text: On the Falemé, Park described fishers guiding a strong current through stone barriers into long cane baskets. Smaller fish were caught with cotton nets. This was practical engineering: the river’s own force helped keep fish from swimming back out.

passages.title: Nearby river communities in 1795
passages.text: At Koorkarany, Park was shown Arabic manuscripts, and a teacher explained passages in Mandingo. The visitor in turn displayed an Arabic grammar. The encounter reveals readers discussing books across languages, rather than a landscape without written learning.

passages.title: Nearby river communities in 1795
passages.text: A regional language sample is “ali bæ si”, translated “sit all down” in Park’s 1799 book. He records it at a wrestling gathering in Koojar in 1795. This is his historical Latin transcription of Mandingo, not a manuscript or proof of the uncertain Tekrur record’s official language.

The imported 1783 cutoff cannot securely be matched to the fall of a particular Tekrur state. Bundu and other regional societies had separate later histories. This record therefore retains an explicit identity limit rather than inventing a conquest or equating it with medieval Takrur.
