passages.text: Teotihuacan was a major urban center in central Mexico. Its public monuments, apartment compounds and specialized arts connected a large city with other Mesoamerican communities through exchange and influence.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The urban layout incorporated the San Juan River, whose course was altered to cross the Avenue of the Dead.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Builders used talud-tablero profiles, combining sloping and upright wall sections, in civil and religious architecture.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Apartment compounds grouped connected rooms around open courtyards. They provided durable shared housing for much of the city's population.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murals decorated many buildings, especially residential compounds. Artists also made mold-pressed ceramics and geometric stone faces.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imported craft goods included worked obsidian and Thin Orange pottery. Stackable bowls made long-distance transport more practical.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The Met's updated account places burning in the monumental core around 550 CE and marked population decline after 600. The people responsible are unidentified.

sectionTitles: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom

passages.text: The Teutonic Order combined a religious community, military organization and Baltic territorial rule. Its conquests imposed Christian rule on Baltic peoples, while its castles contained kitchens, offices, music rooms and ingenious heating. This map joins Prussian and Livonian territories whose political histories differed; many everyday details come from Malbork.

passages.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom
passages.text: Malbork’s Gdanisko tower served as the castle’s main medieval toilet. Its arches let water flow underneath and carry waste away. The journey to the bathroom was part of a carefully planned system, complete with a substantial tower.

passages.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom
passages.text: The same tower could serve as a final defensive refuge. At first, part of its wooden connecting passage could be raised; later builders replaced the passage with a permanent masonry corridor. A toilet that doubled as a last defensive refuge gives “occupied” an unusually serious meaning.

passages.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom
passages.text: Furnaces heated fieldstones, which stored warmth and released it through channels into the rooms above. This helped heat large spaces while conserving scarce local firewood. The castle’s comfort depended on masonry, airflow and somebody keeping the fire going.

passages.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom
passages.text: Ceramic or metal covers over the floor openings regulated the heat entering the room. Adjusting a cover was the medieval version of changing the heating setting. Many surviving furnaces were rebuilt in the nineteenth century, so today’s visible equipment includes later restoration.

passages.title: Warm rooms and a very unusual bathroom
passages.text: Archaeological work at the castle’s research centre uncovered another heat-storage furnace, described by the museum as one of the earliest surviving examples there. The museum report does not give it a precise date. Discoveries beneath later buildings can add a new chapter to the history of keeping warm.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: Meals for the Great Refectory came from a neighboring kitchen with a large hearth beneath a powerful chimney hood. A small cook’s room and a store stood nearby. Impressive dining halls needed practical workspaces, ingredients and cooks behind the scenes.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: Painted draperies decorate the cook’s chamber today, but the museum dates them to the early twentieth century. They belong to the castle’s restoration story. Looking closely at a historic room means distinguishing medieval fabric from the choices of later decorators.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: In the convent’s common room, knights spent some free time listening to music from a gallery along the north wall. The setting provided a shared place to relax. Even a community famous for armor and fortifications had occasions when the important equipment was musical.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: The infirmary cared for aged and weakened knights. It had its own dining room, chapel and bath, bringing meals, worship and washing close to residents who needed support. These arrangements describe care within the castle’s religious community.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: A sickroom adjoined the infirmary dining hall, with a toilet in a nearby annex. The museum also identifies later alterations, including stained glass installed in 1918. The rooms combine traces of medieval care with centuries of reuse.

passages.title: Dinner, music and care
passages.text: The Order’s financial officer had a suite containing living space, a treasury and a servant’s room. Surviving mill equipment is displayed near the convent kitchen. Money, grain and household labor supported the castle as surely as its walls did.

passages.title: Books, buildings and regional endings
passages.text: Malbork was built on an exceptional scale in Gothic brick. Its later conservators developed careful recording and restoration methods; those records helped reconstruction after severe damage in the Second World War. What survives reflects both medieval builders and people who studied their work centuries later.

passages.title: Books, buildings and regional endings
passages.text: A short Latin writing sample is “Chronicon Prussiae”, meaning “Chronicle of Prussia”. This is the title of the 1679 printed edition of Peter of Dusburg’s medieval chronicle preserved by the Bavarian State Library. The witness is a later printed book, not the author’s original manuscript.

passages.title: Books, buildings and regional endings
passages.text: Livonia had several centres of power; the Order’s local branch was the strongest, rather than the only authority. In 1561 its last master, Gotthard Kettler, became Duke of Courland and Semigallia after an agreement with the Polish-Lithuanian ruler. This northern story continued after Prussia’s separate transformation.

In 1525 Albert adopted Lutheranism, made the Order’s Prussian lands a secular duchy and paid homage to the Polish king. The Livonian branch followed a different path to its 1561 settlement. The religious Order continued elsewhere. The imported 1530 cutoff is therefore neither the end of every branch nor the disappearance of Baltic communities.

sectionTitles: A kitchen discovery that changed its job

passages.text: Thrace was a region of different peoples, towns and kingdoms, rather than one state lasting throughout the map’s 1500 to 500 BCE interval. Its imported outline extends too far west to serve as a reliable political boundary. Bronze Age treasures belong to the earlier story; the homes, inscriptions and famous tombs below are explicitly later evidence.

passages.title: Metalworkers and a buried treasure
passages.text: The Valchitran treasure includes gold vessels, lids and a striking three-part container. The surviving group weighs more than twelve kilograms. Broadly assigned to the Late Bronze Age, it gives this earlier period a tangible achievement: highly skilled workers could shape and join precious metal into elaborate forms.

passages.title: Metalworkers and a buried treasure
passages.text: Two brothers discovered the treasure while working in a vineyard in 1924. Thirteen objects eventually entered the museum collection, after damage and disturbance. Scholars have proposed drinking and ritual uses for the vessels; their exact original arrangement and ceremony remain uncertain.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: At Adzhiyska Vodenitsa, usually identified as Pistiros, houses had mud-brick walls, timber elements and tiled roofs. A planned settlement developed during the fifth century BCE. These buildings belonged to a Greek trading community in inland Thrace, illustrating the region’s mixture of communities.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: One excavated house contained large storage jars and many drinking cups. Its excavators suggest that it may have served as a tavern. That is a plausible interpretation of the equipment, rather than an ancient sign saying that drinks were for sale.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: A coin hoard lay beneath the floor of that house. Three sheep knucklebones were placed on top of its container; such bones were used for games. Money and gaming pieces ended up together in a hiding place that its owner never successfully emptied.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: Molds and production waste show local work in bronze, silver and gold. Imported wine containers and fine pottery connect the settlement with Aegean markets. Its workshops and shops operated within long-distance networks rather than relying only on products made next door.

passages.title: A kitchen discovery that changed its job
passages.text: Some unusual clay objects from the settlement were long described as nozzles for metalworking bellows. A 2026 study instead identifies them as movable cooking supports, comparing their shapes with examples from Greek settlements elsewhere. An apparent workshop tool can turn out to belong beside dinner.

passages.title: A kitchen discovery that changed its job
passages.text: Several of these supports came from residential areas with sunken houses dated to the first half of the fourth century BCE; others came from sealed household rubbish deposits. Their contexts strengthen the kitchen interpretation. They help identify cooking practices without telling us precisely what was in each pot.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: Writing sample: a Greek charter found near Vetren contains “τοῖς ἐμπορίταις,” meaning “to the merchants,” in line 8. The text dates after 359 BCE. This is the inscription’s wording in a modern scholarly transcription with accents, and an example of Greek used in the region, not a translated Thracian sentence.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: The charter protected traders and described their dealings with Thracian rulers and communities. It preserved privileges associated with the earlier king Kotys. Because the stone was reused as building material, scholars debate the precise location of its Pistiros; the trading rights are clearer than the stone’s original address.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: The tomb at Kazanlak, built near the end of the fourth century BCE, has a narrow corridor and a circular burial chamber decorated with paintings. Funeral scenes preserve clothing, gestures and ceremonial display. They show how an elite burial was imagined, rather than an ordinary family’s dining room.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: At Sveshtari, a third-century BCE Getic tomb has ten carved female figures whose bodies merge with plant forms. Some original ochre, brown, blue, red and lilac coloring survives. Ancient stone interiors could be brightly painted; today’s pale museum sculptures can give a misleading impression.

Thrace did not end at the map’s 500 BCE cutoff. Later kingdoms, cities and communities continued through repeated changes of rule. Rome organized Thrace as a province around 46 CE, while local traditions survived within the imperial world.

sectionTitles: Building a city high in the Andes

passages.text: Tiwanaku was a major highland city near Lake Titicaca and the center of far-reaching religious and political connections during the first millennium CE. Its communities also settled lower valleys. “Tiahuanaco” is an older spelling. The broad imported outline is not proof of uniform imperial control, and its 1279 endpoint substantially outlasts the city’s main occupation.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: At roughly 3,850 meters above sea level, Tiwanaku stood in a demanding highland environment. Most buildings were made of earth, while major ceremonial structures used stone. The spectacular monuments are only the visible fraction of a much larger lived-in settlement.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Akapana had seven terraced levels and an internal drainage system. Managing rainwater mattered even in monumental ceremonial architecture. Carefully built channels helped water leave the structure instead of simply soaking through it.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Pumapunku masons shaped andesite blocks with precise recesses and finished details before assembly. Small holes helped workers grip and position some blocks. Their achievement becomes more impressive when studied as skilled human work, with identifiable building techniques.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Modern researchers have made small three-dimensional models of the scattered Pumapunku stones to test how they fit. Reassembly is difficult because many pieces were removed or broken after abandonment. A convincing model must work with the surviving blocks, rather than an imagined perfect temple.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Residential compounds grouped smaller buildings around open patios. Stone foundations helped protect adobe walls from rising moisture. Excavated cooking and storage pottery, bone tools and food remains recover the ordinary work that kept households going beside the famous monuments.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Some Tiwanaku homes incorporated burials beneath living areas. The placement brought certain dead relatives or ancestors into the spaces used by later residents. Archaeologists therefore study domestic buildings as places of family memory as well as cooking and sleeping.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Food remains vary among neighborhoods. Quinoa was widespread, with tubers and maize also present. Maize was not confined to the grandest residences: its differing distribution suggests that household connections and access mattered alongside social rank.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: At Cerro San Antonio in Peru’s Locumba Valley, plant remains show that Tiwanaku settlers retained familiar highland foods, including quinoa and related plants, in a lower-altitude setting. Moving house did not mean forgetting what tasted like home.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Raised fields around Lake Titicaca placed crops on elevated beds separated by channels. Erickson’s research emphasizes that such systems could be built and maintained in manageable local units. Their scale does not by itself prove that a ruler commanded every farming household.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Keros were flaring cups used for chicha, a fermented corn drink, at ceremonies and everyday gatherings. They could be made from wood, clay or precious metal. Sharing drinks helped sustain relationships; the container could also advertise its owner’s standing.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: One wooden kero, dated 500 to 1000 CE, carries four winged staff-holding figures carved around its surface. Two have feline faces and two have bird-of-prey heads. The cup turns in the hand like a small gallery of powerful beings.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: No securely readable Tiwanaku sentence survives for an original-language sample and translation. Carved figures on monuments and vessels carried meaning, but they are not a deciphered written text. Even applying the later name Viracocha to Tiwanaku’s central staff-bearing figure remains uncertain.

A 2023 radiocarbon study places rapid urban collapse around 1010 to 1050 CE, before the later drought often blamed for it. This finding concerns Tiwanaku itself: traditions continued in other communities, and visitors returned afterward. Its urban institutions changed dramatically, but its people did not vanish. The imported 1279 map endpoint is not a supported collapse date.

passages.text: The Tibetan Empire rose under Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century and for two hundred years matched Tang China and the Arab caliphate for control of the Silk Road, from the Tarim Basin to the Himalaya. It gave Tibet its script, its first monasteries and its Buddhism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Songtsen Gampo married Princess Wencheng of Tang, who brought a Buddha image and texts to Lhasa; a Nepalese princess, Bhrikuti, is remembered as his other Buddhist queen.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Tibetan script was created, by tradition by Thonmi Sambhota, from an Indian script of the Gupta type.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Samye, the first Tibetan Buddhist monastery, was completed under Trisong Detsen, and Buddhism spread beside the native Bon rites.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Jokhang temple was built in Lhasa and became Tibet's holiest shrine.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tibetan armies fielded armored cavalry and took fortified towns with methods learned from China and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tibet held the Tarim oases and, from 786 to 848, Dunhuang, taxing the Silk Road between China, India and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A Tibetan army occupied the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A peace treaty with Tang was carved in Tibetan and Chinese on a pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tibetan script is in use today across Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalaya.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Buddhism became the core of Tibetan identity and culture.
The emperor Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and the empire broke into rival kingdoms, the Era of Fragmentation, that lasted until the eleventh century.

passages.text: This record begins in 1920 with the French-administered eastern part of former German Togoland, rather than the full earlier German colony. The French mandate was formalized in 1922, followed by UN trusteeship. Independent Togo dates from 27 April 1960.

passages.title: Borders, government and words
passages.text: Togo became independent on 27 April 1960, after a period as a UN Trust Territory under French administration. Sylvanus Olympio was prime minister at independence. The colonial division is important: today’s country did not simply inherit the whole territory once labelled German Togoland.

passages.title: Borders, government and words
passages.text: Gnassingbé Eyadema governed for 38 years before his death in 2005. His son Faure was first installed by the military, stepped down under pressure, and then won an election marred by severe irregularities and violence. This succession changed the president without ending the ruling family’s political influence.

passages.title: Borders, government and words
passages.text: The 2024 constitution supplies a short French writing sample in Article 2: “Travail - Liberté - Patrie”, meaning “Work, Liberty, Homeland”. These are the words of the national motto, reproduced in a dated legal text. Togo’s many spoken languages and cultural traditions extend well beyond this official French formula.

passages.title: Homes and fabrics with stories
passages.text: Koutammakou stretches across northeastern Togo and northwestern Benin. Batammariba builders make earthen tower-houses known as sikien, with takienta as the singular. The buildings belong to a living cultural landscape of farming, family relationships and ritual places, not merely to an abandoned archaeological site.

passages.title: Homes and fabrics with stories
passages.text: The houses organize practical work vertically: animals have space on the ground floor, while granaries stand on the terrace. UNESCO describes households maintaining traditional buildings alongside newer rectangular homes. A family can adapt its housing while preserving architectural knowledge and places used in religious life.

passages.title: Homes and fabrics with stories
passages.text: Togolese businesswomen known as Nana Benz helped connect local cloth buyers with European manufacturers. Their influence reached beyond selling finished fabric: exclusive patterns and commercial relationships gave particular traders considerable authority. Clothing therefore tells a story about women’s enterprise as well as the people wearing it.

passages.title: Homes and fabrics with stories
passages.text: One print was named Santana after the influential trader Madame Santa Anna Nelly, who held exclusive rights to it. Another bird design was called Air Afrique in Togo and had different names elsewhere. The same patterned fabric could carry several stories as it moved between markets and communities.

passages.title: Health achievements and useful toilets
passages.text: In 2022, WHO validated Togo’s elimination of trachoma as a public-health problem. Earlier milestones covered Guinea worm, lymphatic filariasis and sleeping sickness. These were major achievements by health workers and communities; they did not mean that every infection everywhere had vanished or that surveillance could stop.

passages.title: Health achievements and useful toilets
passages.text: The trachoma programme linked medical work with facial cleanliness, safe water and better sanitation. The disease can damage eyes after repeated infections, so prevention reaches into everyday washing and household routines. Health progress here involved ordinary water and hygiene services as well as specialized treatment.

passages.title: Health achievements and useful toilets
passages.text: A WHO and UNICEF report found that the share of Togo’s schools with basic sanitation rose from 44 percent in 2016 to 65 percent in 2019. School-led hygiene work and construction programmes contributed. Even after that improvement, many classrooms still lacked the supporting facilities children needed.

passages.title: Health achievements and useful toilets
passages.text: The same report describes separate toilets for girls and boys, including facilities that help adolescent girls manage menstruation. Privacy and working wash facilities can determine whether a pupil can comfortably stay at school. A toilet door that closes properly deserves more credit than it usually gets.

passages.title: Health achievements and useful toilets
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2021 report recorded 14 family and five school latrines using biogas technology. Biodigesters could turn waste into cooking fuel, with treated residues used as fertilizer. This small programme linked sanitation with less firewood use: the toilet was being asked to do a second job.

Togo continues as a state. International IDEA records Faure Gnassingbé moving into the powerful new office of President of the Council of Ministers in May 2025 under a changed constitutional system. Changes of office should not be confused with the disappearance of the country or its communities.

passages.text: Tula in central Mexico was a major city of craftspeople, traders and monumental builders. Its political reach remains debated: connections through objects and stories do not by themselves establish the borders of a Toltec empire.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: An excavated obsidian workshop combined residential compounds, refuse dumps and probable outdoor working spaces. Microscopic fragments in soil helped identify places where stone was worked. Production took place within a lived environment, not only inside monumental buildings.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: The workshop received large, roughly prepared obsidian cores from more than one source. Craftspeople reduced them into cores for narrow blades, blades themselves and further blade products. The discarded pieces preserve stages of this skilled manufacturing sequence.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: Tohil plumbate vessels at Tula connect the city with pottery production in Chiapas and Guatemala. Tracing where ceramics were made reveals routes of exchange; finding a foreign vessel does not show that its makers were governed from Tula.

passages.title: Making tools and moving goods
passages.text: Potters used multiple brushes together to paint repeated lines, and moulds helped produce vessels efficiently. Excavated moulds turn a proposed manufacturing technique into a directly documented practice.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: At rural Tepetitlán, hearths and cooking vessels identify areas where meals were prepared and eaten. A patio also contained an altar and other activity remains, suggesting that ordinary work and shared ritual occupied connected domestic spaces.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: Tepetitlán yielded many cooking pots but few fragments of the usual griddle type. The researcher offered alternative explanations, including use of other vessels. Archaeology cannot turn this small sample into certainty that residents did, or did not, make tortillas.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: Carbonised maize stems and roots at Tepetitlán provide evidence for cultivation and burning harvested fields. Other remains include amaranth and wild plants such as prickly pear and mesquite. Their survival helps reconstruct resources without supplying a complete household diet.

passages.title: Cooking, gathering and shared space
passages.text: The plant study also identified materials used as fuel, including thorny shrubs, yucca and prickly pear. Keeping a hearth burning required knowledge of the surrounding dry landscape, alongside the work of raising crops.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Human-shaped columns on Pyramid B once supported a temple roof. Carved equipment includes spearthrowers and butterfly-shaped breastplates, while surviving pigment shows that the figures were coloured. Structure and representation worked together.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: A clay warrior wearing a jaguar helmet was fired and inlaid with mother-of-pearl. Pohl connects its shell material with the Gulf of California. The object combines modelling, firing and inlay with access to distant materials.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Reclining sculptures known as chacmools turn their heads sideways and support a receptacle on the abdomen. Tula’s architectural friezes also feature jaguars, coyotes, eagles and feathered serpents, placing powerful imagery within public ceremonial settings.

passages.title: Stone, colour and public architecture
passages.text: Housing varied in scale, construction and location. The museum describes groups of rooms arranged around shared patios, where domestic and ritual activities could take place. The city’s inhabitants did not all live in one standard kind of house.

The Tollan city was abandoned and monumental buildings burned, but these were not necessarily one event. The 2021 study leaves the destroyers unidentified. Later visitors and settlers reused the ruins, so political collapse did not erase the place or its significance.

passages.text: Tonga's modern kingdom combines a continuing monarchy and parliamentary institutions with vigorous traditions of textile work, poetry, language and community exchange. Surviving barkcloth can record particular events and reveal how makers worked. Political changes in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries reshaped government without ending Tongan cultural life.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: A 1940s ngatu hingoa at Te Papa depicts a Spitfire seen from below. It commemorates Tongan support for the Allied war effort. Its makers are unnamed in the surviving collection history, so the detailed design should not be assigned to an invented individual artist.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: Conservation examination of that cloth identified two layers of beaten mulberry bark, joined unevenly. The proposed starch adhesive and plant dyes remain qualified identifications. Damage, joins and repairs allow the cloth to be studied as a made object as well as an image.

passages.title: Objects that remember events
passages.text: Another large ngatu was made for Elizabeth II's visit in 1953 and later placed beneath Queen Salote's coffin on her return to Tonga in 1965. Its changing ceremonial use gives one textile a history spanning celebration and mourning.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: In a koka'anga work party, women join sheets of beaten inner bark in overlapping layers. They rub dye over cloth laid above kupesi pattern boards, bringing the designs through the surface, then add details by hand. The technique combines repeated patterns with individual decisions.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: Lines and numbers at the cloth's border mark langanga, units used to measure its growing length. Te Papa explains that the unit varies with the equipment and the maker. The markings record practical production knowledge, rather than a universal fixed metric.

passages.title: Making, measuring and exchanging cloth
passages.text: Ngatu circulate as gifts at weddings, funerals and other gatherings. Exchanges with makers of pandanus mats connect communities with different plant resources. Cloth therefore participates in relationships as well as furnishing and dress.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: The first parliament opened on 16 September 1875 to discuss the new constitution. Its members included ministers, nobles and elected representatives. This opening date records an institutional event; it is not the day Tongan people or their islands began to have a history.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: Charles St Julian sent George Tupou I a copy of Hawaii's 1852 constitution. Tonga's parliamentary history identifies it as an influence on the new constitutional text. This is a documented Pacific connection in political ideas, not evidence that the two systems were identical.

passages.title: Ideas and political institutions
passages.text: The original parliament could debate taxation and public spending and make laws, while questions such as succession to the throne remained outside its authority. These distinctions show how representation developed within a monarchy.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Queen Salote contributed poetry and songs to Tongan cultural life. Her work used the Tongan language creatively, making the history of monarchy also a history of composition and performance.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Tongan migrants in New Zealand first held language-specific church gatherings in private homes and later established larger congregations. Since the 1980s, community preschools have helped children learn Tongan. These institutions support language through regular shared activity.

passages.title: Language, creativity and community life
passages.text: Czarina Wilson's Tonga-flag face mask, made in May 2020, entered Te Papa's collection. It records a designer applying her skills to a new public-health need. Contemporary objects like this keep the cultural story open beyond historical monuments and royal occasions.

The British protectorate ended in 1970, and Tonga joined the Commonwealth that year. The kingdom continues. Its constitution, community institutions, language and artistic practices have changed across generations rather than ending at the map's last recorded snapshot.

passages.text: Totonac histories belong to the varied coastal and mountain landscapes of Veracruz and Puebla. Cities and communities shared some practices with neighbours while retaining local differences. Cempoala provides a documented example of urban life, rather than a model for every Totonac settlement.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: Cempoala’s production areas lay both within and beyond its dispersed urban settlement. Cultivation and residence were interwoven, so the city should not be imagined as a compact block of buildings surrounded by all of its fields.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: INAH describes walls protecting Cempoala against floods, channels bringing river water into the city and drains carrying wastewater toward cultivation. Managing water involved supply, protection and disposal together.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: Cempoala’s temples included square and circular foundations. The circular building associated with Ehecatl contrasts with the square-based Quetzalcoatl temple, showing variation within one ceremonial centre.

passages.title: Water, cultivation and city design
passages.text: At Yohualichan, INAH interprets architectural niches as references to caves in the surrounding region. Niches also appear at other sites, including El Tajín. Shared forms reveal connections, but alone cannot demonstrate that all such places belonged to one political state.

passages.title: Food and textile skills
passages.text: INPI’s account of later Totonac cuisine describes maize, beans and many edible greens, along with foods such as bocoles and handmade tortillas. This is evidence of a living regional cuisine; its complete modern ingredient list should not be projected into preconquest kitchens.

passages.title: Food and textile skills
passages.text: Backstrap weaving produces garments and household cloths. INPI describes Papantla makers using cotton or acrylic thread for a raised, soft-textured finish called confitillo. The presence of newer fibres shows a craft tradition adapting its materials.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: In the Voladores ceremony, four performers descend on ropes from a tall pole while the caporal plays a flute and small drum above them. The coordinated movement, music and height make the ceremony a demanding collective performance.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: UNESCO describes the ceremony as expressing relationships with nature and spiritual powers, including the sun and winds. It is especially associated with Totonac communities but also practised by other peoples. One community’s version should not stand for every performance.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: The Centre for Indigenous Arts organises learning through houses devoted to pottery, textiles, music, cuisine and other arts. Elders teach values alongside technique. Totonac language is a medium of instruction, making cultural transmission part of everyday educational practice.

passages.title: Performance and shared knowledge
passages.text: The centre’s safeguarding work includes recovering techniques and restoring plants and trees needed for artistic practice. This links the future of crafts with their material environments, as well as with the teachers and apprentices who keep knowledge in use.

Alliance against the Mexica did not preserve independence from Spain. Colonial rule imposed labour and religious demands and later reorganised local authorities. Totonac communities continued, adapting institutions and maintaining languages and creative traditions; no single city’s decline ends their history.

sectionTitles: Family, food and care in living traditions
Learning, ceremony and a written greeting

passages.text: Totonac communities have lived across the coastal plains of Veracruz and the northern mountains of Puebla. Their history includes powerful centers such as Cempoala and enduring local identities, rather than one unchanging empire. The imported 1492 to 1500 window is a map snapshot; its outline shows only part of a wider region. Totonac people and languages continue today.

passages.title: Cities, power and water
passages.text: Cempoala gathered tribute from surrounding communities before Spanish arrival. INAH describes it as the head of roughly fifty towns with several ethnic affiliations. Totonac political influence therefore involved a diverse regional population, not a city inhabited by only one people.

passages.title: Cities, power and water
passages.text: In 1519, Cempoala’s leadership allied with Hernán Cortés against Mexica power. The choice arose within an existing struggle over tribute and domination. It was a political decision by Indigenous leaders whose communities had their own interests.

passages.title: Cities, power and water
passages.text: Water from the Actopan River was carried toward Cempoala by gravity. Drainage served houses and major buildings, while raised platforms helped adapt construction to low ground. The city’s planners had to think about where water would go after it arrived.

passages.title: Cities, power and water
passages.text: INAH describes ducts carrying wastewater from homes and buildings toward cultivated areas. This is unusually concrete evidence about urban sanitation and farming. It does not identify a particular toilet design, so the card cannot furnish every ancient bathroom.

passages.title: Cities, power and water
passages.text: The Building of the Little Faces preserves sculptural and painted decoration; El Pimiento has tiers ornamented with stone skulls. Their arrangement around open plazas shows how architecture shaped shared ceremonial space, alongside the less conspicuous infrastructure that supported households.

passages.title: Family, food and care in living traditions
passages.text: INPI’s ethnographic account describes compadrazgo, ritual co-parenthood, as a network connecting personal and working relationships. Bonds formed around baptisms, marriages and funerals can extend mutual obligations beyond the immediate household. This is documented community life after Christianity’s arrival, not a universal preconquest rule.

passages.title: Family, food and care in living traditions
passages.text: The same account describes midwives caring for mothers during pregnancy and birth, with traditional knowledge including plants and temazcal steam baths. These are reported healing practices and beliefs; the evidence does not establish that every treatment was effective or used by every family.

passages.title: Family, food and care in living traditions
passages.text: A cultural inventory follows maize through a very practical sequence: kernels are prepared as nixtamal, ground on a metate or in a mill, and cooked as tortillas on a comal. Atoles and fermented maize drinks broaden the menu. A single crop can keep a kitchen remarkably busy.

passages.title: Family, food and care in living traditions
passages.text: In 2026, Papantla cook Micaela Simbrón Rodríguez of Mujeres de Humo shared Totonac cooking through pulacles, bocoles and molotes. Her work gives this heritage a named contemporary teacher, rather than leaving traditional food as an anonymous list of dishes.

passages.title: Learning, ceremony and a written greeting
passages.text: The Totonac Centre for Indigenous Arts includes house-schools for pottery, textiles, healing, music and cooking. At the House of Elders, students learn the values surrounding creative work. Instruction in Totonac connects practical skill with language and community knowledge.

passages.title: Learning, ceremony and a written greeting
passages.text: The center also links cultural teaching to replanting trees and other plants needed for artistic practice. Materials have to grow somewhere before a maker can use them. Protecting a craft can therefore include caring for the landscape that supplies it.

passages.title: Learning, ceremony and a written greeting
passages.text: In the Voladores ceremony, four flyers descend on ropes while a fifth participant, the caporal, plays flute and drum from above. UNESCO describes it as a ritual expressing relations with nature and the spiritual world. Several peoples practice versions of it; it is especially associated with Totonac communities.

passages.title: Learning, ceremony and a written greeting
passages.text: A modern written greeting in the central-northern Totonac variety Tutunakuj is “Tun Kuil’”, meaning “Good morning”. INALI publishes it with text and voice by Elías García Aparicio and the Spanish translation “Buenos días”. The Latin-letter spelling belongs to this documented variety, not to an invented ancient inscription.

Totonac alliance with the Spaniards was followed by colonial religious and labor demands and the reorganization of local authorities. The end of earlier political arrangements did not end the people. Totonac communities, languages and institutions remain active; 1500 is merely the imported map endpoint.

passages.text: Tuareg communities speak related Amazigh languages and have lived across the central Sahara and its southern margins. These three map labels are broad cultural snapshots, not one empire. Their outlines are unreliable: one reaches the Nile region and another the Atlantic. The dated examples below distinguish medieval trading places from later Tuareg towns and living traditions.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: At medieval Tadmekka in northeastern Mali, stone compounds, mosques, caravan lodgings and livestock enclosures crowded a town of roughly 125 acres. Arabic gravestones and Tifinagh inscriptions survive nearby. This mixed trading centre offers a concrete setting for Saharan exchange during the map’s medieval centuries.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Excavators at Tadmekka found a tiny piece of Chinese porcelain and silk whose embroidery was probably added locally. Goods moved through chains of markets across enormous distances. Ordinary pottery mattered too: jars and bowls served cooking, storage and the transport of food.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Agadez grew in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, after the dates shown by these map labels. As Tuareg groups settled, the boundaries of their camps helped shape the town’s eleven irregular neighbourhoods. A street plan can preserve the memory of a campsite.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Agadez builders worked with earthen bricks for houses, religious buildings and the sultan’s palace. The mosque’s minaret rises about 27 metres. Maintaining such buildings requires continuing craft knowledge; UNESCO’s 2013 assessment describes neighbourhood authorities participating in their care.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: A twentieth-century wooden tent pole from Niger shows that portable homes could contain carefully made decoration. Its upper part has seven projecting flanges, with geometric patterns cut into the wood. The Smithsonian preserves it as an example of Tuareg household craftsmanship.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: In the Peabody Museum’s Tuareg collection, women’s leather travelling bags held personal possessions, while decorated locks protected large bags. Another object is a hollow ring filled with seeds: moving a hand makes it rattle. Jewellery could supply its own tiny soundtrack.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: Tuareg societies included powerful nobles, herders, specialist artisans and enslaved people whose labour sustained households. Their experiences differed sharply. The fine objects in museum collections also reflect that inequality: wealth and freedom were not shared equally.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2013 account describes women making the imzad from half a dried gourd, stretched skin and a wooden bridge. One string and an arched bow produce its music. The player rests the instrument on her knees while accompanying poetry and songs.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: Imzad skills pass through watching, listening and practice. Performances bring together women musicians, men singing or reciting poems, and other participants calling out. Music is also played for sick people as part of local healing beliefs, offering comfort and a shared social occasion.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: At Ghat in the mid nineteenth century, traveller James Richardson described children reciting Qur’anic lessons after dark. He also reported that the governor’s daughters learned to read. The account even mentions sand being used as a surface for writing practice.

passages.title: A written language sample
passages.text: “Wăr tatəw ăssukăr.” means “Don’t forget the sugar.” This is the editors’ normalized Latin reading of a Tuareg phrase recorded in Arabic script at Ghat in 1850, in a manuscript associated with Muhammad Sharif. It preserves a later local voice, not medieval wording.

passages.title: A written language sample
passages.text: The phrasebook also contains a delicious translation accident. An Arabic instruction to shut a tent door was read as a statement putting sugar at its entrance. Similar-looking words caused the mix-up; the editors trace it to the Arabic teaching text used in 1850.

The map’s 1300 endpoint is not an ending for Tuareg peoples. Colonial conquest, drought, migration and new national borders transformed their lives. Communities continued, including town residents, musicians, craftspeople and pastoral families.

sectionTitles: Print and the end of the republic

passages.text: The Transvaal record crosses several governments: British annexation, the restored South African Republic, war, and a British colony. Gold mining transformed the region, drawing workers and investors into a society in which white political rights coexisted with coercive controls over African residents.

passages.title: Gold and political power
passages.text: The map begins in 1878, just after Britain annexed the South African Republic in 1877. Republican government returned in 1881 after war. These changes matter: “Transvaal” names a region whose government and relationship with Britain changed during the same map interval.

passages.title: Gold and political power
passages.text: Gold discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886 brought prospectors, industrialists and work-seekers from far beyond the region. Mines and the growing city of Johannesburg transformed the landscape. Their wealth depended on labour as well as geology, and left lasting environmental damage.

passages.title: Gold and political power
passages.text: Industrial development included much more than extracting gold. Sammy Marks and partners built a distillery at Eerste Fabrieken, followed by glass and jam or preserve factories. Bottles and preserved food linked manufacturing to things people used in everyday households.

passages.title: Gold and political power
passages.text: Mine dust could cause silicosis, a serious lung disease. Elaine Katz’s research on the mines from 1886 to 1910 shows how owners promoted the unsupported idea that short contracts protected African workers. A worker returning home could still carry the consequences of dangerous work.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: The Pioneer Museum preserves an 1848 farmhouse at Hartebeestpoort with clay walls, a thatched roof and earthen floors. Its present furnishings interpret nineteenth-century rural life. Local building materials produced a very different home from the later grand houses of mining wealth.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: That museum surrounds the house with a traditional herb and vegetable garden, orchard, vineyard and wagon house. These are interpreted surroundings, not an untouched 1848 garden. They help visitors think of a farm home as a workplace that grew food and maintained transport.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: At Zwartkoppies, the Marks family’s later house grew to forty rooms. Sammy and Bertha had first lived in a simple thatched clay house while the new home was built. Their move makes the contrast between modest shelter and concentrated industrial wealth unusually tangible.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: The Sammy Marks Museum reports that almost all its displayed household contents belonged to the family, including silver, porcelain and furniture. Unlike a room assembled from unrelated period pieces, this collection can reveal one affluent household’s choices. It remains one family’s life, not everybody’s.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: Paul and Gezina Kruger’s Pretoria home was built in 1884 and is now furnished to reflect their residence. The museum also preserves the president’s railway coach. House and carriage show how political office connected a domestic household to official travel.

passages.title: Homes and unequal freedom
passages.text: Beside Kruger’s house, the site remembered as gaMohle was associated with enforcing pass laws from 1896. The standing commissioner’s building dates from 1932. Its earlier history exposes the restrictions imposed on African movement alongside the republic’s claims to freedom from Britain.

passages.title: Print and the end of the republic
passages.text: “De Volksstem” is a short Dutch writing sample from the title of a Pretoria newspaper first issued in 1873. It means “The People’s Voice”. The University of Pretoria preserves historical documentation of the paper; the familiar-looking Latin letters carried Dutch, rather than automatically Afrikaans.

passages.title: Print and the end of the republic
passages.text: The war of 1899 to 1902 extended far beyond armies. African people worked as scouts, drivers, blacksmiths and builders, and British forces confined both Boer families and Black civilians in camps. Food shortages, poor sanitation and disease made civilian life perilous.

The Treaty of Vereeniging on 31 May 1902 ended the republic’s independence. The Transvaal subsequently became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910. Farmers, miners, towns and African communities continued through these political transformations; the imported 1914 endpoint is not a separate fall.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
Learning by doing, and political change

passages.text: Trinidad and Tobago have distinct island histories, brought together in one country. Their everyday creativity includes stone tools, skilfully tuned steel, cooking traditions and community teaching. Each example below identifies its place and period.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, a settlement dating to around 5000 BCE, archaeologists found stone pestles, grinders, an axe and cutting flakes. Layers of discarded shells also survive. The tools and refuse reveal practical work and food gathering. A midden, archaeologists’ name for accumulated rubbish, can preserve an excellent record of everyday life, though it is nobody’s idea of a tidy kitchen.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At wreck site TRB-5 in Tobago’s Rockley Bay, a 2014 excavation recovered bricks still joined with mortar, copper sheet and wood fragments. Researchers interpreted these as possible remains of a ship’s galley, or kitchen. The finds date broadly to the seventeenth century; association with the 1677 battle is supported, but the vessel’s exact identity remained uncertain in the report.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: The same test trench yielded four forks and five spoons. These small objects bring eating aboard ship into view alongside the cannon. They show that studying a wreck can recover traces of meals as well as battles. The report does not identify the diners, their food on a particular day, or whether everyone aboard had similar utensils.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: NALIS’s account of Indian heritage in Trinidad names a belna, a rolling pin; a chauki, a board for working dough; and a sil and lorha, stones used for grinding. Such equipment accompanied cooking knowledge reshaped in Caribbean homes. Familiar foods involve practiced movements and specialised tools. The kitchen has its own vocabulary, and learning a word can also mean learning a skill.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Chinese shopkeepers became part of village life in Trinidad. NALIS describes a credit arrangement called trusting: customers could take groceries and pay later, while the shopkeeper recorded purchases and repayments in a copy book. A small notebook connected household needs with a local business. This is a documented practice, rather than a claim that every shop offered identical terms.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Trinidad’s immigration registers can record a person’s village in India, relatives, ship and assigned estate. These documents help descendants piece together family histories across oceans. Archivist Helena Leonce also describes missing records and arrivals through other Caribbean colonies. A gap in one register is a research problem, not evidence that a family has no history.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: At Christmas, parang musicians visit homes with instruments such as the cuatro, guitar and maracas, while hosts offer food and drink. NALIS recalls nighttime visits that sometimes woke relatives and friends. It gives the idea of an alarm clock a much more musical interpretation. The account describes a particular festive tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Steelpan developed through experimentation in Trinidad during the 1930s and 1940s. Makers shaped metal containers and tuned parts of the playing surface to different pitches. Earlier tamboo-bamboo groups made percussion music with cut bamboo tubes. The new instrument grew through many people’s work; accounts disagree about assigning its invention to a single person.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: A steelband’s engine room is its percussion section, which helps keep the music moving together. NALIS lists bottle and spoon, maracas and assorted iron among its instruments. Here the engine runs on rhythm. The phrase is a useful reminder that a musical ensemble depends on timing and coordination as well as the performers carrying the tune.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: In January 2023, Trinidad’s Santa Rosa First Peoples Community helped present the Caribbean Ties exhibition. Community members added baskets, hammocks, ceremonial clothing, photographs and foods including cassava. An ajoupa, a tapia hut, housed the exhibition. People shared their own knowledge and heritage in a community setting, showing that Indigenous history includes living voices as well as excavated objects.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Tobago’s Moriah Ole Time Wedding, documented in July 2017, recreated an older wedding celebration at the village’s Moravian church. A procession then carried the celebration through Moriah with participants and onlookers. It was a heritage performance, using humour and participation to share memories of social life. The staged ceremony should not be mistaken for a record of one historical couple’s marriage.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: In a 2015 project concluding at Speyside Secondary School in Tobago, students built solar ovens from boxes, reflective material, insulation and clear plastic wrap. They tested the ovens with bread dough. The winning design baked its loaf all the way through. The exercise turned energy science into something visible and practical, with a result rather easier to inspect than an invisible sunbeam.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: Independence and becoming a republic happened in different years. In 1962, Trinidad and Tobago became independent while retaining the monarch as head of state. In 1976, a president replaced that role. The distinction helps explain how a country can govern itself while still sharing a monarch with other countries.

British colonial rule ended at independence in 1962; republican status followed in 1976. Trinidad and Tobago continues as a country. Its communities keep creating and sharing traditions, including First Peoples’ knowledge, music and food.

sectionTitles: A port connected to several worlds

passages.text: Tripolitania was the western Libyan region centered on Tripoli. During much of this map interval, the Karamanli family ruled with considerable autonomy while acknowledging Ottoman authority. Direct Ottoman administration returned in 1835. The coastal outline is not the full territory claimed by Tripoli’s governors, and neighboring Cyrenaica has a separate history.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: By the late seventeenth century, Tripoli already brought together Arabic-speaking townspeople, Ottoman soldiers and their families, Jewish merchants and craftspeople, and European consular communities. Enslaved people brought from south of the Sahara and captured at sea were also part of this unequal urban society.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: Yusuf Karamanli’s demands for increased payments helped trigger war with the United States in 1801. The 1805 treaty included a ransom for prisoners but ended American tribute to Tripoli. Maritime diplomacy concerned real sailors’ freedom as well as state revenues.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: After 1835, Ottoman governors operated through provincial and district officials, with local leaders advising at lower levels. Control remained uneven, especially away from towns. A neatly organized administrative chart was easier to produce than obedience across a large region.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: The eighteenth-century Ahmad Pasha Karamanli mosque formed a complex with a school and cemetery. Its entrances opened toward nearby markets. Religious learning, commerce and family remembrance occupied neighboring spaces in the working city.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: An inscription at the Ahmad Pasha mosque praises its patron for providing flowing water at a public fountain. Flowering tile panels surround the lettering. The monument advertised useful urban provision as well as a ruler’s piety and prestige.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم” means “In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.” This Arabic opening appears on the Ahmad Pasha mosque’s eighteenth-century foundation inscription. The sample is a normalized transcription, without the original calligraphic layout and vowel marks.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: In the early nineteenth century, naval captain Mustafa Gurgi commissioned another richly decorated mosque complex. Researchers used its 1844 waqf deed, an endowment document, to study the building’s setting. Architecture leaves both stonework and a paper trail.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: In a letter dated 9 September 1783, Miss Tully describes roof rainwater draining into cisterns beneath courtyards. Flat roofs also served for drying fruit. The house could help collect tomorrow’s water and prepare the pantry.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: Tully describes affluent women turning courtyards into reception rooms for celebrations: mats and carpets covered the floor, cushions supplied seats, and an awning provided shade. Outdoor space became a room for a special occasion.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: At bathhouses, Tully observed wealthy women attended by enslaved women who washed their hair with orange-flower water and arranged elaborate braids. The luxurious routine depended on other women’s coerced labor.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: A travelers’ inn funded by the ruler’s wife offered rooms, storage, a courtyard well and space for pack animals. Tully reports simple sleeping mats and gates locked overnight. Hospitality required practical arrangements for people and cargo.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: During plague in May 1785, Tully’s consular circle prepared household quarantine. New servants had to bathe and remain isolated for two weeks. This records one privileged community’s precautions amid a frightening epidemic.

Karamanli rule ended in 1835, before the imported 1878 endpoint. Ottoman government continued until Italy’s invasion in 1911 and the 1912 settlement. Colonial conquest met prolonged local resistance; Tripolitania’s communities and regional identity continued.

passages.text: Tsimshian communities belong to the Skeena River and northern British Columbia coast, with a later community at Metlakatla, Alaska. Related Gitxsan and Nisg̱a’a peoples remain distinct neighbors. This map outlines part of a diverse homeland; its 1492 to 1500 interval is coverage, not a people’s lifetime.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: On Pike Island, three former village sites and two petroglyph sites lie along the protected waters of Metlakatla Pass. Trails connect settlement remains; carved images survive on shoreline boulders. The largest village area, used both before and after European contact, measures about 211 by 70 metres.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: Around the wider pass, archaeological remains include house depressions, canoe landing places and shell middens. Parks Canada identifies a particularly dense sequence of winter villages from about 500 to 1770. These traces connect homes, boats and meals across a worked coastal landscape.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: Kitselas Canyon guarded a route between the coast and the interior. Its surviving evidence includes five village sites, carved poles, caches and house depressions. In the nineteenth century, the fortified village of Gitlaxdzok and another permanent village occupied positions from which residents could influence trade through the Skeena corridor.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: The Nine Tribes of Lax Kw’alaams built power through alliances, strategic marriages and military action. Their trade connections followed routes carrying valuable eulachon oil into the interior. Community history emphasizes these relationships and decisions, rather than explaining political power simply as a result of plentiful fish.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: In 1834, the Hudson’s Bay Company built Fort Simpson at Lax Kw’alaams on a site controlled by the Gispaxlo’ots leader Legex. He required payments for trading there. Tsimshian people also supplied wood and labor; their seasonal activities shaped how the fort could operate.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: Tsimshian clan membership comes through the mother. The four clans are associated with Killer Whale, Wolf, Eagle and Raven. Crests can identify a clan or an extended family and carry histories and inherited rights; they are much more than decorative animal pictures.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: At Metlakatla potlatches, guests witness proceedings such as naming and succession. Hosts feed them and provide gifts in thanks. Dance, masks and family histories help make those rights publicly known, so a feast also performs serious political and legal work.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: Gitga’at families travel to Kiel camp on Princess Royal Island for spring harvesting. Their Nation’s 2024 account describes collecting red laver seaweed in May and preserving food for later months. Harvesting joins practical work with time together and opportunities for younger relatives to learn.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: The same account describes slicing halibut thin for drying after returning to Hartley Bay, then smoking heads and backbones for soup. It also recalls exchanging harvested seaweed at Kitamaat for eulachon grease. A fishing trip could supply several kinds of meal and goods for trade.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: A 2023 Gitga’at food guide describes dayks, a dessert of berries with whipped grease, snow or water and sugar. The recipe illustrates the community’s living food traditions, including later ingredients. Snow can enter the dessert bowl, but this modern description is not evidence for sugar in a precontact kitchen.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: William Duncan’s mission at Metlakatla, British Columbia, began in 1862. In 1887, he and part of the Tsimshian community moved to Alaska; others remained in British Columbia. Metlakatla Pass and Pike Island retain their connection to the Canadian Metlakatla First Nation, so the move did not empty an entire homeland.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: The Alaska community’s 1944 constitution records the establishment of its Annette Islands reserve in 1891. It provided for a twelve-member council, elected officials and community management of land. These institutions belong to a particular Tsimshian community, not to a government ruling all Tsimshian peoples.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: Public health had its own place in that constitution. A three-member committee was to help preserve birth and death records, cooperate with health officials, maintain sanitary conditions and enforce quarantine rules. Community government included the everyday work of keeping households and public spaces healthy.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: A modern Sm’algya̱x language exhibit prints “‘Niit, nda wila waan”, translated “Hello, how are you doing?” The museum credits the Ts’msyen language authority, Sarah Booth and the Haayk Foundation for its language material. This is an attested contemporary spelling, not a claimed fifteenth-century inscription.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: At Gitxaała’s Lach Klan School, education from early childhood through Grade 12 includes language, culture and learning on the land alongside provincial requirements. Its published programs also include breakfast, snacks and fruit and vegetables. Teaching and feeding children are part of the same daily community work.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: Canadian Metlakatla’s heritage staff combine elder interviews, community mapping and archival research, storing knowledge in digital maps for land and marine decisions. They also monitor archaeological resources such as canoe runs, fish traps and culturally modified trees. New tools help communities care for inherited places.

The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an ending. Colonial missions, settlement and restrictions changed Tsimshian lives, while distinct First Nations in British Columbia and the Metlakatla Indian Community in Alaska continued. Their governments, cultural teaching and stewardship remain active; no single successor state replaces them.

passages.text: The Moscow-centred Russian state became a tsardom when Ivan IV was crowned in 1547. It endured a severe succession crisis, then continued under the Romanovs. Expansion, printing and skilled crafts accompanied deep social inequality. Peter I adopted the imperial title in 1721, marking its transition into the Russian Empire.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: Ivan IV’s coronation took place in the Kremlin’s Dormition Cathedral on 16 January 1547. Religious ritual and royal regalia presented his authority as sacred. The ceremony matters because the map’s imported label begins earlier, when Moscow’s ruler still held the grand-princely title.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: Saint Basil’s Cathedral was built in Moscow from 1555 to 1561 to commemorate victory over the Kazan Khanate. Its clustered churches turned a military conquest into a major architectural commission. The complex changed afterwards; the church dedicated to Basil the Blessed was added in 1588.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: The early seventeenth-century Time of Troubles brought famine, political breakdown, rival claimants and foreign intervention. In 1613 an assembly chose the young Mikhail Romanov as tsar. Establishing a dynasty did not instantly repair ruined farms and towns, but it restored a continuing line of rulers.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: The law code adopted in 1649 tied privately owned peasants and their descendants to their landlords’ estates. It also removed time limits on pursuing fugitives. For these families, moving away to seek a better life could bring forced return; the state’s growing strength did not mean growing freedom for everyone.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: During the seventeenth century, Russian expeditions crossed Siberia and reached the Pacific. Fur tribute, called yasak, helped drive this expansion. Historian Denis Shaw emphasizes coercion and violent conflict as well as journeys and geographical knowledge: these were inhabited lands whose peoples faced new demands from an expanding state.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Ivan Fedorov and Petr Mstislavets completed the Apostle in 1564, Moscow’s first precisely dated printed book. It contained biblical Acts and Epistles and took about eleven months to produce. The edition carried features useful for church reading as well as reading at home or in a monastic cell.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Printing red and black on the same page required careful work. For the Apostle, the letters intended to print in red were raised above the rest, printed, then removed before the black text was added. A misaligned sheet could spoil the effect; attractive pages depended on workshop skill.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Moscow’s Kislovskaya quarter housed suppliers of sour cabbage, soaked apples, pickled cucumbers and kvass for the court. Preserving food made winter supplies possible. Archaeologists found cellar pits in the neighbourhood, connecting the written history of its food workers with the spaces in which they worked.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Seventeenth-century layers in that quarter yielded green-glazed stove tiles, a miniature ceramic jug and an enamelled copper-alloy cross. These finds bring colour into an otherwise earth-brown excavation. They also help distinguish the tsardom’s neighbourhood from the larger eighteenth- and nineteenth-century estates built over it.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Kolomenskoye’s water tower, built in the 1670s, raised water from a source beneath it to a large barrel above. Water then travelled through wooden pipes to palace buildings. Researchers describe pumps or a bucket mechanism: even a royal water supply needed somebody’s machinery to do the lifting.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: In 1654 the Apothecary Chancery organized a school to train medical practitioners. Thirty musketeers and musketeers’ sons were assigned to foreign medical teachers, with interpreters helping lessons along. Graduates served with army regiments or the chancery. This was a small specialist programme, far from healthcare for every household.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Karion Istomin’s 1696 primer taught letters, syllables, numbers and religious texts. Only twenty copies were printed for an edition intended for Tsarevich Alexei. A surviving proof copy bears editorial corrections, while red letters in a poem spell out the author’s name. Even a royal schoolbook needed proofreading.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The primer addresses “к юношам учитися хотящим”, literally “to young people wishing to learn”. This is its historical Church Slavonic wording in the library’s normalized Cyrillic transcription, rather than a reproduction of the printed letter shapes. The greeting makes a seventeenth-century textbook sound pleasantly welcoming.

Peter I accepted the title emperor in 1721 after the Treaty of Nystad ended the Northern War with Sweden. The tsardom became the Russian Empire through a change of political title and institutions, not the disappearance of its population. The imported 1530 to 1783 map range spans both earlier and later phases.

sectionTitles: Monuments and the evidence for power
Changing institutions and a living legacy

passages.text: The Tu'i Tonga chiefly line was associated with monumental centers on Tongatapu and far-reaching Pacific relationships. Excavated stone tools, royal tombs and collected household objects reveal different aspects of this history. Sacred chiefly rank, practical government and overseas exchange changed over time; they should not be compressed into a single unchanging empire.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: At Heketa in eastern Tongatapu, fieldwork recorded house and seat platforms, a tiered tomb and the Ha'amonga trilithon. Their arrangement joined domestic, ceremonial and chiefly spaces. Clark and Reepmeyer interpret this complex as part of a new political order taking shape in the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: Ha'amonga is built from two upright coral-limestone slabs supporting a third slab across the top. Tonga's heritage submission links it to Tu'itatui through oral tradition. The monument demonstrates large-stone construction; a proposed astronomical purpose is less securely established.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: The langi at Lapaha are raised burial platforms faced with carefully fitted stone. Moving, shaping and placing those blocks required coordinated labor. The structures preserve evidence of chiefly funerary practice, while continued care connects them with living communities.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: A 2014 study compared the chemistry of stone tools from Tongan chiefly centers with Pacific stone sources. Many pieces came from Samoa or Fiji, and one adze was traced to the Society Islands. The findings show material moving over long sea routes.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: In that study, 29 of 44 analyzed adzes and flakes from the state-period sample were nonlocal. The authors interpret the concentration of imports at chiefly centers as evidence of intensified exchange and political connections. Imported stone alone does not establish conquest of its source island.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A wooden kali in the Cook-Forster collection has a narrow head support carried on curved legs. Eighteenth-century observers described Tongans using these objects while sleeping. This household object shows careful woodworking directed toward an ordinary bodily need.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A food hook in the Pitt Rivers Museum retains an original wooden disk painted with bird figures. The hook attached to it is a later replacement. Reading that repair history matters: the whole object on display cannot be treated as untouched evidence from the collecting voyage.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Te Papa's account of eighteenth-century Tonga describes ngatu barkcloth used for bedding and clothing as well as other everyday purposes. Making useful cloth from inner bark connected plant cultivation, beating, joining and decoration with household life.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Clark and Reepmeyer connect Heketa's ceremonial spaces with kava drinking and presentation of first fruits to chiefs. In their interpretation, cultivated food and formal gatherings helped express the sacred standing of the Tu'i Tonga.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: The Tu'i Ha'atakalaua and Tu'i Kanokupolu lines exercised governing authority as the Tu'i Tonga retained sacred rank. Their relationships developed through succession, marriage and conflict. A list of Tu'i Tonga titleholders is therefore not a complete list of rulers exercising the same powers.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: Laufilitonga, the last Tu'i Tonga titleholder, died in 1865. George Tupou I's constitutional government followed in 1875, but the earlier transfer of power was a process rather than a single foreign conquest.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: At Lapaha, community leaders and researchers have worked together to repair stone structures and train residents in conservation. The tombs remain places of cultural responsibility, with archaeological research contributing to their protection.

The Tu'i Tonga title ended with Laufilitonga's death in 1865, after governing power had already shifted among chiefly lines. Tonga developed a constitutional monarchy under George Tupou I in 1875. Tongan communities and their heritage continued; neither date marks their disappearance.
