passages.text: Venezuela’s modern state separated from Gran Colombia in 1830, before this map interval. Oil, university architecture and living food traditions show different aspects of its history; political transitions and migration have reshaped communities without ending them.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: The 1830 Congress of Valencia adopted a constitution separating Venezuela from Gran Colombia. That event concerns the modern state’s political form. It was not the beginning of the region’s Indigenous peoples, settlement or cultural life.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: Marcos Pérez Jiménez was overthrown on 23 January 1958. Diplomatic records describe the political opening that followed and the country’s dependence on oil revenues. A change of regime could alter public life while leaving major economic challenges in place.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: Carlos Raúl Villanueva’s university campus in Caracas brought buildings, artworks and landscaped spaces into one design during 1940 to 1960. Reinforced concrete enabled distinctive modern forms. Education received a carefully designed setting rather than simply a collection of classrooms.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: The Aula Magna incorporates Alexander Calder’s Cloud forms, and the campus also includes an Olympic Stadium and Covered Plaza. Art belongs to places where people gather and move. Its setting matters as much as the individual object.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: Patios and latticed windows adapt the campus to a tropical environment. These architectural choices join modern construction with older ways of managing light and air. A building’s cleverness can lie in what it lets through as well as what it keeps out.

passages.title: Institutions, buildings and work
passages.text: John Vachon’s 1944 photographs of Standard Oil operations survive at the Library of Congress. The catalog describes drilling, a refinery and workers’ children learning carpentry. This group records particular industrial settings, not a complete picture of every worker’s family life.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: Cassava bread is part of Venezuelan food traditions shared with several Caribbean and Central American countries. The round breads differ in thickness, texture and flavor. One familiar food can connect communities without requiring everyone’s version to taste the same.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: Knowledge of making cassava bread passes within households and communities, as well as through culinary teaching. The practice connects daily meals with Indigenous and African heritage. These are skilled food traditions, not evidence that a single recipe has remained unchanged everywhere.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: In the Blessed Palm tradition, mountain journeys include storytelling and tending trails as well as gathering leaves for Holy Week. Religious observance, social memory and environmental work meet in the same activity.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: Palmeros changed from cutting palms completely to pruning them, alongside new educational work involving young people. The safeguarding program shows that maintaining a tradition can require changing how it is practiced. Conservation can include learning a better way to gather.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: “El idioma oficial es el castellano” means “The official language is Spanish.” This is Article 9 of the 1999 constitution in its 2009 gazette version. The same article also recognizes Indigenous languages for Indigenous peoples. Spanish writing therefore does not imply a monolingual country.

passages.title: Food, learning and language
passages.text: UNHCR recorded more than 7.9 million Venezuelan refugees and migrants worldwide at the end of 2024, most within Latin America and the Caribbean. Many faced barriers to housing, services and work. This dated figure records displacement; it does not mean Venezuelan communities ceased to exist.

Venezuela continues as a state, while its communities also live across a large diaspora. The 1830 separation, 1958 regime change and 1999 constitution mark political transformations. Neither those changes nor the map’s 1878 start represent the disappearance of its peoples.

passages.text: Venice joined lagoon engineering to a far-reaching artistic culture. This chapter follows the city and its painters during the Renaissance; it does not yet cover the republic's entire history.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: During the republic, canals connected settlements consolidated from lagoon islands. Hydraulic and architectural work continually reshaped the relationship between the city and its surrounding water.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: In sixteenth-century Venice, Titian, Veronese and Tintoretto developed influential approaches to painting. Their work later shaped artists including Rubens and Velazquez.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: After moving from Verona in the 1550s, Veronese found both civic and church commissions in Venice. Artistic employment crossed religious and governmental settings.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The lagoon included fishing settlements and artisan communities such as Murano. Venice's palaces were part of a larger landscape of work and settlement.

passages.text: New Spain was a Spanish viceroyalty ruled from Mexico City from 1535 until independence in 1821. Its territory at different times stretched beyond present-day Mexico to parts of Central America, the Caribbean, North America and the Philippines. This vast colonial map contained many Indigenous nations, Africans, Europeans and mixed communities, not one uniform people. Coerced labor and epidemics caused great harm, while Indigenous officials defended land, Nahua students produced bilingual history, and craftspeople carried ideas across the Pacific. The imported border ends around 1715, well before the political end in 1821.

passages.title: A very large, unequal colony
passages.text: Spain created a viceroyalty in 1535, with its capital in Mexico City. At its greatest reach its jurisdiction included places far beyond modern Mexico. This imported polygon runs only from about 1530 to 1715 and cannot show every later border.

passages.title: A very large, unequal colony
passages.text: Conquest, disease and forced labor devastated many Indigenous communities. Their children and descendants remained, however, keeping languages, farming and legal claims alive under colonial rule.

passages.title: A very large, unequal colony
passages.text: A 1571 codex records Nahuatl officials complaining about mistreatment and underpayment by a Spanish administrator. It is a good reminder that Indigenous people argued in court and made records; they were not silent figures in somebody else’s history.

passages.title: A very large, unequal colony
passages.text: New Spain included Indigenous, Spanish, African and mixed communities with very unequal power. Later casta paintings tried to sort families into ranked categories; the pictures were an artist’s and patron’s scheme, not a complete portrait of how every family lived.

passages.title: Language, school and invention
passages.text: Nahua students helped make the Florentine Codex, writing Nahuatl in Latin letters beside Spanish translation and their own images. It preserved knowledge of food, plants and social life even while colonial authorities pursued conversion.

passages.title: Language, school and invention
passages.text: At Tepotzotlán, a Jesuit college taught some Indigenous boys and later elite students. Another school trained missionaries in Native languages. A child’s chance to study depended strongly on identity, place, family and gender.

passages.title: Language, school and invention
passages.text: The Royal Academy of San Carlos, founded in 1783, taught drawing and art. New Spanish artists also made portraits, city views and paintings for churches, using European, Indigenous and Asian-influenced traditions.

passages.title: Language, school and invention
passages.text: The Manila galleon brought Chinese silk and porcelain to Acapulco and carried American silver across the Pacific. A decorated dish in a New Spanish home could therefore tell a story that crossed oceans.

passages.title: Food, baths and medicine
passages.text: An eighteenth-century kitchen could contain turkey, pork, chile, cheeses and fruit preserves. Chocolate was popular across social groups. The mix of ingredients is much more interesting than a claim that everybody ate one “colonial meal.”

passages.title: Food, baths and medicine
passages.text: At the Tepotzotlán college, a botica stored medicines while the infirmary garden grew medicinal plants. Jesuits studied Indigenous healing knowledge as well as treating the sick. That was one institution; most families’ care varied widely.

passages.title: Food, baths and medicine
passages.text: Mexico City’s viceroy issued a 1793 rule for public baths and temazcales, including separate facilities and signs for men and women. The rule says poorer residents especially used the steam baths. So yes, a colonial government spent ink on bathhouse signs.

passages.title: Food, baths and medicine
passages.text: A small sample of official written Spanish is “baño y temazcal para mujeres,” meaning “bath and steam bath for women.” The 1793 ordinance required such lettering on a permanent sign; it shows how a written rule met an everyday door.

passages.title: Food, baths and medicine
passages.text: The colonial museum’s kitchen, refectory, pharmacy and convent rooms help imagine one institutional household. A mining family, Indigenous village or port neighborhood could look very different, so no single museum room stands for all New Spain.

passages.title: Change, not disappearance
passages.text: Independence fighting began in 1810 and lasted through different leaders and factions until 1821. The end of Spanish viceregal rule was a long and violent political transition, not the end of the people living there.

passages.title: Change, not disappearance
passages.text: Independent Mexico inherited most of New Spain in 1821, but not the Caribbean or the Philippines. Later borders changed again. The card’s 1715 map endpoint is especially easy to mistake for a fall date, so the historical ending is stated separately.

The Spanish viceroyalty ended as Mexico gained independence in 1821. Mexico inherited most, but not all, of its territory; the Caribbean and Philippines had different futures. Indigenous and other communities continued despite colonial harm. The imported 1715 map endpoint marks a data snapshot, not the end of New Spain.

sectionTitles: Water, silver and the cost of wealth
An Indigenous author and a writing sample

passages.text: The Viceroyalty of Peru was a Spanish colonial government centered on Lima, made its capital in 1542. Its cities, mines and Indigenous communities were connected through commerce, craft and coercive labor. This card explains the wider history around the map’s 1650 to 1715 interval, including Indigenous criticism of colonial rule and the government’s eventual defeat.

passages.title: Water, silver and the cost of wealth
passages.text: Potosí’s silver industry used artificial lakes and aqueducts to supply water-powered mills. Crushing and processing ore, then making coins, required a chain of specialized places and workers. A mountain of silver was also an enormous water-management problem.

passages.title: Water, silver and the cost of wealth
passages.text: Indigenous workers compelled to serve through the mita helped sustain Potosí’s wealth. Their neighborhoods lay apart from Spanish residents across an artificial river. The surviving city plan records an unequal social order as well as impressive engineering.

passages.title: Water, silver and the cost of wealth
passages.text: Mercury from Huancavelica helped process silver. The colonial draft-labor system sent workers into dangerous mining conditions and disrupted the communities supplying them. The heritage nomination for Santa Bárbara describes both this industrial connection and its human cost.

passages.title: Water, silver and the cost of wealth
passages.text: Lima’s builders combined local and European skills, adapting materials and techniques to earthquakes. Churches, hospitals, schools and houses were practical structures as well as statements of power. Their survival reflects repeated rebuilding, not a city preserved untouched since its founding.

passages.title: Cups, crafts and distant connections
passages.text: Andean kero cups were often made in pairs for the ceremonial sharing of chicha, a fermented corn drink. Exchanging a drink could express a relationship between people. The paired vessels give historians evidence about social practice as well as carving skill.

passages.title: Cups, crafts and distant connections
passages.text: A Quechua kero from seventeenth- or eighteenth-century Peru shows women, flowers and large parrots. Its feline handles changed how the decorated surface could be arranged. Traces of colored resin remind us that a worn museum object could once have looked much brighter.

passages.title: Cups, crafts and distant connections
passages.text: Some colonial Andean textiles incorporated Chinese animals and peonies inspired by imported silks. Materials and designs crossed oceans before local makers adapted them. A tapestry can therefore preserve evidence of connections far beyond the town where it was woven.

passages.title: Cups, crafts and distant connections
passages.text: A gold cup recovered from the Atocha shipwreck of 1622 was designed to hold a bezoar, a stone-like deposit from a camelid’s stomach. People believed it could counter poison. That belief explains the object; it does not establish that the treatment worked. An expensive cup could carry a very questionable health accessory.

passages.title: Cups, crafts and distant connections
passages.text: A highland lectern from around 1700 combined a wooden core with worked silver sheets showing angels and elaborate foliage. Such objects required coordination between different crafts. Their gleaming surfaces can hide the less glamorous structure that made them usable.

passages.title: Families, education and the hospital
passages.text: San Marcos university was founded in Lima in 1551. Higher education became one of the colonial capital’s enduring institutions. A university’s existence, however, tells us about an institution; it does not mean that all children in the viceroyalty could attend school.

passages.title: Families, education and the hospital
passages.text: San Andrés hospital’s admission books from 1711 to 1714 recorded patients’ origins, marital status and family descent. October 1713 entries included a free child and adult classified using a colonial mixed-ancestry category. These were exceptions to the hospital’s usual identification with Spanish patients.

passages.title: Families, education and the hospital
passages.text: Later in the colonial period, theatre rent helped support San Andrés hospital. The theatre reopened in 1761 and was leased for income. Entertainment and care were linked through a very concrete financial arrangement: a performance venue could help pay hospital expenses.

passages.title: Families, education and the hospital
passages.text: An anatomical teaching space opened at San Andrés in 1792. Medical students learned there, connecting the hospital with professional education. This later development belongs to the viceroyalty’s history after the map’s selected interval.

passages.title: Families, education and the hospital
passages.text: In 1792, digging a deep bone-storage pit at the hospital reached groundwater. An official worried about nearby household wells, and advisers recommended partly filling the excavation with rubble, lime and brick. The record preserves a sanitation concern and proposed response, not proof that contamination or illness occurred.

passages.title: An Indigenous author and a writing sample
passages.text: Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala wrote and illustrated a long critique of Spanish colonial government. His manuscript combines Spanish with substantial Quechua passages and proposes reforms. It preserves a particular Indigenous author’s arguments, rather than a single view shared by every Andean community.

passages.title: An Indigenous author and a writing sample
passages.text: The title includes the Spanish words “buen gobierno”, meaning “good government”. This short sample follows the Royal Danish Library’s catalog transcription of his manuscript title, using ordinary Latin letters. The phrase captures his demand for a better way to govern; his criticism was itself part of colonial history.

Independence was proclaimed in Lima in 1821, but the royal government continued in the southern highlands. Sucre’s victory at Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 brought the decisive royal capitulation. The map’s 1715 endpoint precedes these events by more than a century; it is not the viceroyalty’s historical end.

sectionTitles: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power

passages.text: Created in 1776 with Buenos Aires as capital, this Spanish colonial administration linked Atlantic ports with interior provinces and the silver economy of Upper Peru. Its territory crossed several present-day countries. The map’s 1800 to 1815 interval is a late coverage slice; revolution broke its authority apart at different times in different places.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: The port of Buenos Aires shipped precious metals arriving from Potosí, alongside cattle products. Interior mining and Atlantic commerce were linked across long distances. Spanish commercial restrictions also encouraged smuggling, so official rules never tell the whole story of what crossed the docks.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: Colonial society ranked people unequally, distributing privileges through a racial and social hierarchy. Indigenous communities faced tribute and compulsory labor within the inherited colonial system. The administration’s increased revenue and control carried heavy human costs.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: The viceroy’s Buenos Aires headquarters was a fortified complex with a ditch and drawbridge. Inside were the residence, treasury offices, stores and armory. By the late eighteenth century, administration and military defense shared the same enclosure.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: Creation of new courts, treasury bodies and the commercial consulate multiplied paperwork. Officials needed laws that had previously been sent to Lima or other jurisdictions. Building a new administration required copying and organizing documents as well as appointing powerful men.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: Museum collections preserve an eighteenth-century bedhead used by Viceroy Sobremonte in Córdoba and a finely inlaid desk associated with Bishop Azamor. Such objects reveal elite furnishings and skilled woodworking. They represent particular wealthy households, rather than everyone’s bedroom.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: Water sellers carried river water in large containers on two-wheeled ox carts. Obtaining household water depended on workers, animals and streets long before a citywide piped supply. Turning a tap was not yet a Buenos Aires household routine.

passages.title: Government, trade and everyday objects
passages.text: Street vendors brought firewood, milk, pastries and brooms through the city. Some brooms and dusters used bird feathers. These small trades connected household chores with the street economy: buying something for dinner or sweeping could begin at the front door.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: The Buenos Aires Protomedicato, established in 1779 and inaugurated in 1780, supervised healing professions. Its branches included oversight of surgeons, apothecaries, veterinarians and barbers who practiced medical procedures. Deciding who could treat a patient was a matter of government as well as individual skill.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: A medical school was established under the Protomedicato in 1799 and began courses around 1801. The university’s historical account notes disagreement over the precise opening year. This institution helped train doctors and surgeons locally before the later University of Buenos Aires existed.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: The Niños Expósitos press began in 1780 and printed material serving the Spanish Crown’s government. Its surviving output also extends into the independent era. The same printing technology that circulated royal authority could later carry the words of a different political order.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: Francisco Cabello y Mesa founded the Telégrafo Mercantil in Buenos Aires in April 1801. Its subjects included commerce, agriculture, politics, economics and history. A reader could encounter practical economic information and discussion of the wider region on the same printed pages.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: British attacks in 1806 and 1807 encouraged the organization of urban militias. Their political importance outlasted the fighting. In May 1810, Buenos Aires replaced Viceroy Cisneros with a governing junta, but this did not produce immediate agreement across all the former viceroyalty’s regions.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: “Cada pueblo nombrará uno, o mas comisionados al efecto” means “Each town will appoint one or more commissioners for that purpose.” Viceroy Elío’s October 1811 Montevideo edict addressed property claims during a military withdrawal. Its Spanish wording survives in a contemporary newspaper transcription.

passages.title: Medicine, print and the breakup of royal power
passages.text: Revolutionary forces entered Montevideo on 23 June 1814, ending Spanish rule in that city. Governments aligned first with Buenos Aires and then with Artigas followed. This was part of a contested regional breakup, rather than a single peaceful transfer to one successor country.

The viceroyalty fractured through revolution and war. Buenos Aires displaced its viceroy in 1810, Elío still issued orders from Montevideo in 1811, and that city’s Spanish government fell in 1814. The map’s 1815 endpoint should not imply uninterrupted royal rule until then; successor states emerged through further conflicts.

passages.text: Vijayanagara, founded on the Tungabhadra in 1336, ruled the south of India for three centuries and made its capital, today's Hampi, one of the largest cities in the world. It kept the temple culture of the Tamil and Kannada country alive and traded horses and spices with the Portuguese, the Arabs and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gopurams, towered gateways, and pillared halls carried Dravidian temple building to its most elaborate.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529) the Krishna temple was built at Hampi and the Vittala temple gained its stone chariot and musical pillars.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Krishnadevaraya kept eight Telugu poets at court and wrote the Amuktamalyada himself; Kannada, Tamil and Sanskrit letters flourished too.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Arab and Portuguese traders sold the warhorses the empire needed; Hampi's markets sold diamonds, spices and cloth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Portuguese Domingo Paes, who saw the city about 1520, called it as large as Rome and the best provided city in the world.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Estimates of the capital's people run to several hundred thousand, among the largest cities of the sixteenth century.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Canals from the Tungabhadra and large tanks watered the fields around the city.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Group of Monuments at Hampi was listed by UNESCO; more than 1,600 remains survive.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The empire's temple styles and its Nayaka successors kept Hindu kingship alive in the south.

The Deccan sultanates crushed the imperial army at Talikota in 1565 and sacked the capital. The Aravidu kings ruled a shrinking realm from Penukonda, Chandragiri and Vellore until Bijapur and Golconda took the last of it in 1646.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

passages.text: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.

sectionTitles: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis

passages.text: Visigothic royal power had an earlier centre at Toulouse and a later Iberian kingdom associated with Toledo. This card concentrates on the later kingdom, where excavated workshops and houses complement royal gifts, law and Latin scholarship. These different records show inventive adaptation of inherited traditions, but also inequalities and coercion within society.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Large houses in the early Visigothic city had circulation spaces leading to rooms, cooking areas and stables. Some were divided and enclosed during the seventh century. Changing walls and multiplying kitchens reveal households adapting existing buildings, rather than a town frozen in its founding plan.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: Beside Reccopolis's main street, shops opened toward customers while workshops, stores and living spaces extended behind them. A circular glass furnace and associated processing structures survive. These remains place skilled production inside the town, close to both commercial activity and the palace approach.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work at Reccopolis
passages.text: The eastern craft building contained moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metalworking waste. Together these objects identify making and weighing, not merely possession of finished jewellery. They show the tools and discarded material behind the ornaments that survive in museum collections.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Reccopolis received water through a masonry aqueduct with a channel lined in waterproof mortar containing crushed ceramic. Surveyed remains preserve Roman construction principles in a late sixth-century project. Parts of its route remain missing and are reconstructed through terrain analysis rather than direct excavation.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: Researchers argue that the aqueduct supplied more than the royal complex, proposing public distribution within the town. The volume of water and the hilltop setting support this interpretation. A complete network of household pipes and public fountains has not been excavated.

passages.title: Water engineering and its limits
passages.text: A tiled drain carried water from the courtyard of house 16000 toward the street. Other small drains and concave street surfaces suggest open channels for rain and overflow. This evidence should not be enlarged into a claim that the city possessed a complete underground sewer network.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: The Guarrazar treasure includes gold crowns and crosses decorated with stones, pearls and cut crystal. Letters hanging from Recceswinth's crown identify its royal donor. These were offerings for religious settings; the suspended crown should not be imagined as the king's everyday headwear.

passages.title: Goldwork, gifts and survival
passages.text: Guarrazar goldsmiths combined pierced or embossed sheets with settings and chains; some smaller crowns used open latticework. The treasure was concealed and later dispersed after its nineteenth-century discovery. Concealment shows an effort to protect valuable objects, but does not by itself establish one precise historical emergency.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: Isidore of Seville's Etymologies organised subjects from grammar and mathematics to farming, textiles and household equipment through explanations of words. This was a work of compilation and interpretation. Its account of a craft does not establish that Isidore invented it or personally observed every process.

passages.title: Organising and preserving knowledge
passages.text: A manuscript of the Etymologies held by the Real Academia Espanola dates to the twelfth century, centuries after Isidore wrote. Such copies demonstrate the work's continuing transmission. The age of a surviving manuscript must be kept separate from the age of the text it carries.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: A declaration addressed to Recceswinth in 654 required Jewish converts at Toledo to renounce Sabbath observance, religious festivals and dietary distinctions. Its coercive setting matters: the document records demands on a community, not free evidence that its members welcomed those demands.

passages.title: Law and unequal religious life
passages.text: Erwig's law of 681 threatened Jews who delayed baptism for themselves, their families or enslaved people with physical punishment, exile and confiscation. Royal religious uniformity came at others' expense. A prescribed penalty shows what authorities demanded, not proof that enforcement was identical everywhere.

The Umayyad conquest began in 711 and displaced Visigothic royal government over several years. It did not remove the peninsula's whole population or immediately empty its towns. Reccopolis continued into the Islamic period before declining much later, and Isidore's work continued to be copied. The map endpoint of 800 is not the kingdom's fall date.

sectionTitles: A small object for a familiar task
A tiny Latin message of power

passages.text: Visigothic history connects mobile Gothic groups with kingdoms centred first on Toulouse and later on Toledo. This imported 400 to 600 record changes from a Balkan snapshot to territory in Gaul and Iberia. Those outlines should not suggest one fixed homeland or a continuously occupied border; the people and their political institutions changed over time.

passages.title: Making a capital at Toulouse
passages.text: At Toulouse, excavators found an imposing complex beside the Roman city wall, interpreted as the probable royal palace. It included a vestibule, corridors and connected rooms, one with an apse. New rulers adapted a Roman city rather than building everything on an empty site.

passages.title: Making a capital at Toulouse
passages.text: Monumental buildings along the Garonne included churches and a rectangular structure with a surrounding gallery. Its purpose remains uncertain, possibly funerary. The arrangement suggests coordinated building projects, showing how rulers and religious institutions could change the appearance of a city.

passages.title: Making a capital at Toulouse
passages.text: Brooches, earrings and belt buckles preserve traces of personal dress in Toulouse and its countryside. Some burial grounds appear to have served both local inhabitants and newcomers. Shared places complicate any simple picture of two populations living completely separate lives.

passages.title: A small object for a familiar task
passages.text: Bone combs from rural estates in southwestern Gaul have a single row of teeth, rounded backs and decoration made of small circles. Comparable forms occur around the Black Sea. Such connections help archaeologists investigate movement and cultural contacts through an object used for everyday grooming.

passages.title: Homes, water and workshops
passages.text: At the site identified as Recópolis near Zorita de los Canes, excavated houses contained rectangular rooms arranged around courtyards. Rooms served living, cooking, storage and animal-keeping functions. This gives a much fuller picture of domestic space than a palace plan alone.

passages.title: Homes, water and workshops
passages.text: The houses used stone footings, plastered earth walls and tiled roofs, with floors of packed clay or lime mortar. Excavators recovered cooking pots, jugs, bowls and bottles, including some imported North African ceramics. Ordinary households participated in wider Mediterranean exchanges.

passages.title: Homes, water and workshops
passages.text: The settlement used both an aqueduct and cisterns. The aqueduct collected spring water outside the city, probably supplying its highest area. Having an aqueduct does not establish that every house had running water; different parts of the settlement used different arrangements.

passages.title: Homes, water and workshops
passages.text: Workshops made glass tableware, including cups and plates, while a metalworking area yielded moulds for earrings and rings, balance pans and metal waste. These finds reveal specialised crafts and the tools behind finished objects, from shaping a vessel to weighing valuable material.

passages.title: Roman traditions carried on
passages.text: At Mérida, some mosaics remained in use, were repaired or were newly made well into the sixth century. A change of ruler did not instantly erase older skills or tastes. The museum’s material shows how late Roman and Visigothic-period urban life overlapped.

passages.title: Roman traditions carried on
passages.text: Mérida’s surviving objects include pottery, church sculpture and many funerary inscriptions. These materials illuminate different activities: preparing food, decorating worship spaces and commemorating the dead. Much of this city’s evidence concerns its wider population, rather than identifying the ancestry of each maker.

passages.title: A tiny Latin message of power
passages.text: A gold coin of Reccared I, who ruled from 586 to 601, bears the Latin word “REX”, meaning “king”. The coin found at Begastri was minted at Toledo. Its lettering also names that mint as TOLETO, a compact declaration of authority on a small object.

passages.title: A tiny Latin message of power
passages.text: This tremissis weighs about 1.48 grams and measures 18 millimetres across. Its royal portrait appears on both faces. The coin provides evidence for gold-working, monetary standards and royal representation, though it does not tell us what every household could afford to buy.

The imported interval ends in 600, but the Toledo kingdom continued into the eighth century. Muslim-led conquest beginning in 711 overthrew its central monarchy. Communities and inherited traditions continued under new political arrangements.

sectionTitles: Later life under the Golden Horde

passages.text: Volga Bulgaria developed around the middle Volga and Kama rivers, far from Danube Bulgaria. Its towns connected northern forests with Islamic trading networks. Islam, adopted officially in 922, became central to its history. Many famous buildings and objects at Bolgar belong to the later Golden Horde period and are dated separately here.

passages.title: Markets and making a living
passages.text: Bolgar stood near the junction of the Volga and Kama river systems. Its archaeological layers preserve successive communities and cultural connections, rather than a single frozen moment of “Bulgar civilization.”

passages.title: Markets and making a living
passages.text: Medieval Bolgar became known for leatherwork as well as long-distance trade. Craft production was part of what made the town valuable; river traffic did not consist only of goods passing through from somewhere else.

passages.title: Markets and making a living
passages.text: The twelfth-century traveller Abu Hamid al-Gharnati described exchanging iron goods, including fishing harpoons, for northern furs. This is a particular visitor's account of trade, not proof that every transaction followed the same bargain.

passages.title: Markets and making a living
passages.text: Rulers collected duties from foreign ships and caravans. Trade therefore supported political institutions as well as individual merchants, though customs revenue tells us little by itself about the comfort of an ordinary household.

passages.title: Games and practical learning
passages.text: A rook in the Bolgar Museum-Reserve was carved from elk antler with a forked top. The museum dates it broadly to the 1100s-1300s, spanning independent Bulgaria and Golden Horde rule. It is tangible evidence of board gaming, without telling us who won.

passages.title: Games and practical learning
passages.text: That rook is only about four centimetres across. Its abstract shape belongs to the wider tradition of shatranj, a predecessor of modern chess. A familiar-looking game can have unfamiliar rules.

passages.title: Games and practical learning
passages.text: Arabic literacy connected the region with a wider world of scholarship, including medical writing. The National Library of Tatarstan highlights access to eastern physicians' works after Islam's adoption; that is evidence of learning, not a guarantee that historical remedies worked.

passages.title: Games and practical learning
passages.text: A decorated inkwell lid dated to the second half of the 1200s survives at Bolgar. Copper and silver decoration surrounds an Arabic wish for the owner's success and wellbeing. This was an expensive writing accessory in a city already under Mongol rule.

passages.title: Later life under the Golden Horde
passages.text: Fourteenth-century Bolgar had public bathhouses; excavators identified five. Their social role extended beyond washing. This evidence comes after the independent Bulgar state, showing how urban life continued under different rulers.

passages.title: Later life under the Golden Horde
passages.text: The Red Chamber bath had a changing room with stone seats, washing spaces and a service area with boilers and a furnace. Bathing required people to heat water and maintain the building, not merely an impressive dome.

passages.title: Later life under the Golden Horde
passages.text: Underfloor heating warmed the bath, and ceramic pipes carried water and drainage. That is evidence for engineered communal washing facilities; it does not establish that every house had plumbing or a private toilet.

passages.title: Later life under the Golden Horde
passages.text: A limestone gravestone dated 1317 commemorates the goldsmith Shahidullah. Its translated epitaph praises regard for scholars, widows and orphans. It preserves a family's public memory of a person and valued conduct, rather than an average biography of the whole city.

passages.title: Later life under the Golden Horde
passages.text: The gravestone uses Arabic script for a Turkic language identified by the museum as Tatar. The inkwell's blessing is Arabic. One script could serve different languages; neither object should be presented as an early, pre-conquest Bulgar text.

passages.title: A small writing sample
passages.text: محمد رسول الله means “Muhammad is the messenger of God.” These Arabic words appear on a silver coin catalogued as a probable Volga-Bulgar imitation of Samanid money naming Nasr II, who ruled in 914-943. The coin has no surviving mint or date, so its local attribution remains uncertain. This is religious Arabic, not a sentence in the Bulgar spoken language.

Mongol armies seized and burned Bolgar in 1236. Independent Volga Bulgarian government ended, but the city recovered as an important Golden Horde centre. Its inhabitants and traditions contributed to later regional societies, and Bolgar remains a place of pilgrimage for Tatar Muslims.

sectionTitles: A capital built for several kinds of life
Arabic writing and the limits of a sample

passages.text: Wadai, also written Ouaddai, was a sultanate in present-day eastern Chad. Abd al-Karim established its Muslim dynasty in the seventeenth century. The imported start in 1530 precedes that dynasty, and the map stops in 1900 before French conquest.

passages.title: A capital built for several kinds of life
passages.text: The surviving palace at Ouara, also called Wara, includes a two-storey royal residence, a watchtower and a large audience building. Its layout separated different activities within a substantial walled compound.

passages.title: A capital built for several kinds of life
passages.text: The heritage survey records separate quarters for royal wives and concubines. This is evidence about an unequal court household, not a model for every family in Wadai. Architecture can show social divisions as well as impressive building skills.

passages.title: A capital built for several kinds of life
passages.text: A fired-brick mosque stands outside the palace enclosure, measuring about twenty-five by twenty-seven metres. Religious activity had its own substantial building alongside the court, rather than existing only inside the ruler’s residence.

passages.title: A capital built for several kinds of life
passages.text: Wara’s rulers left it during the nineteenth century, with drought given as the reason in Chad’s heritage nomination. The later capital was Abéché. Water conditions could therefore affect where a royal court and its dependants lived.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: A more direct caravan route from Cyrenaica to Wadai opened around 1809 or 1810. It later connected Wadai with Benghazi across eastern Libya, showing that inland political power depended partly on long journeys through oasis country.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: From the 1860s, Sanusiya religious networks helped merchants communicate, resolve disputes and travel more securely. Shared institutional ties could connect traders of different backgrounds; cooperation was as necessary as pack animals for keeping a caravan route useful.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: The sultanate’s commerce included enslaved people. Its rulers’ wealth and regional influence must therefore be understood alongside the suffering of those captured, sold and transported, rather than presented simply as an attractive story of desert trade.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: Wara attracted scholars and students, including connections with the Funj lands farther east. Books on Islamic law and religious tradition entered its markets along with cloth and other goods, making learning part of the movement of people and merchandise.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: In the early nineteenth-century account attributed to al-Tunisi, women carried paired baskets to market and collected water and firewood. These observations show demanding everyday work, although one visitor’s generalizations should not be treated as rules for every household.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: The same account describes men spinning and weaving, and garments assembled from narrow strips of cloth. Clothing involved skilled work and joined pieces of fabric; it was not simply something purchased ready-made from a distant caravan.

passages.title: Trade, learning and everyday work
passages.text: Al-Tunisi’s account describes an ornament called amchinga, with silver crescents, coral and amber. Such details make personal adornment visible, while the writer’s comparisons between peoples reveal his own preferences and prejudices rather than objective rankings of cultures.

passages.title: Arabic writing and the limits of a sample
passages.text: The Arabic spelling “وداي” reads “Wadai”. This is the standard printed form in a modern scholarly reference, not a transcription of a particular old letter. The same reference reproduces a nineteenth-century Arabic letter sent by Bornu’s Sheikh Umar to Wadai’s ruler Muhammad Ali, evidence of diplomatic writing.

passages.title: Arabic writing and the limits of a sample
passages.text: Dijon’s manuscript catalogue records a 260-leaf Arabic book seized in Wadai during fighting in 1908. It cautiously identifies it as possibly a Quran. The record shows both a written religious culture and the colonial violence through which some books entered European collections.

French forces defeated Wadai in 1909, after this map entry ends. Colonial conquest replaced its independent government; it did not erase the region’s communities, languages, learning traditions or memories of the sultanate.

passages.text: Mapuche histories encompass autonomous communities, exchange and creative work across southern South America. Relations with neighbours changed over centuries. Colonial resistance and later dispossession belong to this history alongside farming, family knowledge and living artistic traditions.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The lof organised related families. In the historical model described by the National Library, a longko led a local group with limited authority. Wider alliances could form during war without creating a ruler with permanent jurisdiction over every community.

passages.title: Families, land and local authority
passages.text: The same account describes local leaders allocating fields to families and reassigning plots while depleted ground recovered. Reserve land provided another resource. Access depended on social relationships as well as cultivation, and arrangements changed under later restrictions.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Textile specialists Matilde Painemil and Cristina Manquepi contributed family histories and practical knowledge to the museum’s collection study. Their expertise connected the handling of old cloth with forms and meanings still understood by makers.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: The textiles discussed include makuñ mantles, headbands and chañuntuku, thick woven saddle coverings. These are distinct objects for dress and other uses, rather than interchangeable examples of a single decorative pattern.

passages.title: Weaving knowledge into daily life
passages.text: Painemil describes design as mental and creative work, sometimes connected with dreams. She also teaches classes and makes commissioned textiles. Her account presents weaving as a skilled livelihood and an ongoing artistic practice, not merely repetition of inherited designs.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Mapuche silverwork includes the linked breast ornament trapelakucha, earrings called chaway and fastening pins such as tüpu. Specialists Antonio Chihuaicura and Marco Pailamilla examined such pieces with the museum, bringing makers’ knowledge to the interpretation of their construction and use.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Following nineteenth-century dispossession, families sometimes exchanged silver objects for food. The museum links these losses to the formation of public and private collections. An ornament’s museum history can therefore record hardship as well as artistic skill.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: The same account describes craft knowledge surviving within families and being renewed through workshops, new pieces and replicas. Studying an old silver ornament and making a new one can both contribute to this continuing practice.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: Potter Celinda Huaiquil explains links between water, women’s knowledge and ceramic vessels. Duck-shaped ketru metawe can pour liquids, including muday in ceremonies. Her interpretation joins close observation of living creatures with the practical work of shaping clay.

passages.title: Silver, clay and sound
passages.text: José Cayuqueo makes ritual drums using laurel wood and goatskin. He and Hernán Marinao also describe wooden pifüllka instruments accompanying the drum and supporting a machi’s ceremony. These are named makers’ accounts of living musical practice.

passages.title: People tell their own histories
passages.text: Manuel Manquilef’s writing and Pascual Coña’s orally narrated life preserve Mapuche perspectives on historical change. Coña’s account was recorded by a missionary, so the circumstances of recording matter alongside the narrator’s knowledge.

Chilean and Argentine expansion dispossessed communities and restricted land and movement. Later migration brought many Mapuche people to cities. These transformations did not end Mapuche life: makers, teachers, families and organisations continue to sustain and reshape their cultures.

passages.text: The Kansa, Kanza or Kaw are a distinct Dhegiha-speaking people whose river villages and hunting grounds made them influential across Kansas. Their descendants continue as the Kaw Nation. The imported Kansas-region outlines and their 1492 or 1530 start dates are approximate map coverage, not proof of fixed borders or settlements that early; the Nation’s history describes migration toward the Plains over several centuries.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: By the middle of the eighteenth century, Kanza influence extended across much of northern and eastern present-day Kansas, with hunting grounds farther west. The state’s name preserves theirs. River valleys supported settlements and movement, while relations with neighboring peoples shaped access to resources and trade.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: In the early nineteenth century, households at Fool Chief’s Village lived in bark-covered houses with a central fire and sleeping bunks around the walls. Four to eight large posts supported a lodge, and a roof opening let smoke escape. A blanket or hide served as the door.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The yearly schedule combined farming and travel. Families planted in spring, went on a summer bison hunt, returned for the autumn harvest and hunted again in winter. A village could look quiet because its residents were away doing another essential part of their work.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Bison hides also connected Kanza households to distant markets. The historical society describes readily available manufactured trade goods in their villages. Hunting supplied both household needs and things to exchange, so changes in demand could reach far beyond the place where a hide was prepared.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The flood of 1844 devastated gardens on the Kansas River bottomlands, where Kanza women raised corn, beans, melons and other vegetables. Water swept away crops, houses and fences; another flood followed in 1845. Food security depended on weather and river behavior as well as diplomacy.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Kaw Mission opened classes in 1851 in a two-story stone building at Council Grove. About thirty Kanza boys lived in four upstairs dormitory rooms and studied reading, writing, spelling and arithmetic. Missionaries also sought to teach Christianity and reshape family life; this was far more than a new school building.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Families were selective about that mission: the historical society reports that only orphaned or dependent boys attended, and girls did not. The school closed in 1854 because of its costs. Kanza children’s education cannot be reduced to this short-lived institution or its missionaries’ ambitions.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1825 treaty cut Kanza-controlled land to a narrow reservation west of the future city of Topeka. The Nation describes roughly twenty million acres reduced to about two million. Promised annual payments did not undo the loss of hunting territory or prevent further demands for land.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1846 treaty required another major cession and a move toward Council Grove. Its promises included education, farming support and money for a replacement mill. Federal delays in defining the new reservation left people struggling through relocation, while treaty language offered protections that did not last.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 1873, the United States forced the Kanza from Kansas to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. Congressional action in 1872 had authorized the disposal of their remaining Kansas lands. Distinguishing those two years matters: a law could order removal before families were actually compelled to leave.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Oklahoma did not bring a permanent end to displacement. Kaw Reservoir later covered land associated with Washunga. The tribal council house, residents and cemetery had to be relocated. Places holding government business, homes and family memory were all affected by the reservoir project.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Under Chairwoman Wanda Stone and the Executive Council, the Nation entered federal self-governance arrangements with the Indian Health Service in 1995 and the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1996. These arrangements gave tribal administrators more control over adapting funded services to community needs.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: A small modern writing sample is “Nompéaⁿhi.”, translated in the Kaw Nation’s family language workbook as “I’m hungry.” The raised n marks part of the spelling. It is a useful household sentence from a teaching publication, not a reconstructed inscription from the map’s earliest year.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The same workbook teaches that a fuller sentence can say whether someone is sitting, standing or moving. Learners practice matching these words to the person they mean. Kanza grammar can keep track of posture while an English speaker is still deciding whether to say “fine” or “tired”.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 2025, language students made a film about the forced removal, acting in Kaá’nze with guidance from elders including Little Carol Clark, Lynn Williams and Lavina Spotted Bear. Kaw filmmaker Dylan Bellmard directed it. Children were learning language while helping tell a difficult part of their own history.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The Nation also offers language lessons built around family camping. At its museum, an exhibition combines audio stories with photographs, treaty reproductions and a clan book. These are practical ways to connect speaking, listening and looking at evidence across generations.

The imported map cutoffs do not mark the end of the Kanza people. Forced removal, allotment and reservoir construction transformed their homelands, but the Kaw Nation continues as a self-governing community with elected institutions, language teaching and services for its citizens.

sectionTitles: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
Sites, sources and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Samori Ture built a state through conquest, trade and Islamic authority in the later 1800s. Often called the Wassoulou or Samorian empire, it shifted eastward under French military pressure. “First” and “Second Samori Empire” describe different territorial phases of the same ruler’s state. Its independent history ended with his capture in 1898, not with the 1900 to 1914 interval currently attached to those two map labels.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: Samori’s armies depended on supply networks. Earlier muskets came chiefly through Freetown, while horses came from the northwestern Sudan. These routes connected inland politics with coastal commerce.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: In 1891 to 1892, negotiations with Freetown traders brought breechloading and repeating firearms. Legassick also records a local firearms industry established by this period. Adaptation meant acquiring weapons and developing skilled work to support them.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: After French advances restricted western supplies, Samori sought weapons through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast and horses through Mossi country. Existing African trade routes became crucial to the state’s survival.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: The Buré goldfields mattered to Samori’s economy. When French forces occupied Buré in 1885, his armies drove them back. Control of a resource region could be as consequential as control of a capital.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Samori sought an agreement with the British authorities in Sierra Leone and also negotiated treaties with France. His strategy combined fighting and bargaining; African rulers were participants in diplomacy, not merely spectators to European decisions.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Trade also carried a terrible cost: Samori captured and sold people to help finance guns and horses. Resistance to French conquest did not mean freedom for everyone living under his own expanding power.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Yves Person’s chronology records a decision in 1892 to move east with a substantial part of the population. A moving state meant uprooted households as well as marching soldiers. The chronology establishes the displacement without telling us every family’s experience.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: The same chronology records scorched-earth tactics in 1891. Destroying resources could obstruct an advancing army while making civilian life more precarious. Military success and the welfare of local people cannot be treated as the same thing.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Sordi’s fortified settlement in northern Côte d’Ivoire became part of the struggle between Kénédougou, Samori’s forces and French expansion. Historian M’Brah identifies occupation by Samori’s sofa troops from 1896 to 1898. A single site reveals overlapping rulers and local experiences.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: M’Brah traces Diawala’s growth to people dispersed from Sordi and to exiles returning after Kénédougou’s defeat in 1898. Related families reunited and organized a new settlement. Political defeat changed where people lived; it did not erase their family connections.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Accounts of Samori need careful comparison. Legassick’s article explicitly warns that some French visitors’ descriptions were imaginative or unreliable. Historians use local traditions and archival evidence together instead of treating an officer’s vivid story as automatic fact.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: This dossier has not verified a short original-script passage from a securely identified Samorian document. Arabic scholarship belonged to the wider region, but substituting an unrelated manuscript would give a false impression. Household sanitation and specific medical routines also remain unestablished by the sources used here.

passages.title: Capture and continuing communities
passages.text: French forces captured Samori on 29 September 1898. He was exiled to Gabon and died in 1900. His death date is therefore not the date a “first” or “second” empire began; those map labels need chronological correction.

Samori’s capture by French forces in 1898 ended his independent state. Exile and his death in 1900 followed. The region’s communities continued under colonial rule; the changing imperial labels describe political power, not the appearance or disappearance of a people.

sectionTitles: Learning, beautiful pages and small change

passages.text: The Wattasids governed from Fez in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, after serving as powerful officials under the Marinids. The map has two spellings for this dynasty. Neither its break at 1530 nor the later label’s continuation to 1650 marks the actual lifetime of Wattasid rule, which ended in 1554.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: Portugal captured Asilah in 1471, taking members of the Wattasid leader’s family prisoner. A subsequent agreement helped him turn towards Fez, which he entered in 1472. Coastal warfare and dynastic family fortunes were tightly connected.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: In 1515, a Portuguese expedition tried to establish a fortified base at Mamora. Wattasid opposition, including artillery served by Christian gunners, forced its withdrawal. The episode complicates any picture of armies divided into perfectly separate religious teams.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: Badis on the Mediterranean coast had a ruler from the Wattasid family who operated with considerable independence. A surviving commercial treaty with Venice, dated 1508, shows how coastal rulers could negotiate their own trading relationships.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: A treaty is a different kind of surviving object from a fortress: its clauses preserve negotiated arrangements between people who wanted goods and ships to move. The Badis agreement is evidence for one specific diplomatic connection, not proof that all Moroccan ports followed identical rules.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: The later writer Luis del Marmol described Andalusian refugees developing gardens, silkworm cultivation and sugar production at Medgara in the late fifteenth century. García-Arenal discusses this account alongside later wartime destruction. It is an attributed historical account, not an excavated inventory of every farm.

passages.title: Ports, rulers and changing fortunes
passages.text: Knowledge of court life could cross a change of dynasty. Dakhlia discusses al-Arifa bint Nedjju, a senior woman of the Wattasid royal household, among people who transmitted court customs to the Saadians. Political history included the expertise of palace women as well as male officeholders.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: Leo Africanus described students at Fez listening while a teacher explained a text and its difficult passages. Students also debated before the teacher. His account of the early sixteenth century survives through later editions and translations, so it should be read as a situated observer’s description.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: The same account says earlier college endowments had supported clothing and food, whereas students in his day were left with lodging and relied on other support. The detail makes education’s everyday cost visible: a classroom alone does not feed its students.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: A Quran manuscript in Morocco’s National Library, inventory 1304, is assigned stylistically to the fifteenth or sixteenth century. Its pages are green, with seven lines of silver writing and gold chapter headings. A book could be an extraordinary crafted object as well as a text.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: Coloured vowel signs and decorative verse markers helped organise that manuscript’s Arabic text. Only part of its original twelve-volume set survives. The missing volumes remind us that a museum object is often a fragment of a much larger historical possession.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: An undated silver quarter dirham attributed to Sultan Ahmad’s reign, 1526 to 1545, carries الحمد لله, “praise be to God,” in Arabic. The short sample follows a photographed specimen’s published transcription. Its exact minting year and excavation provenance are not known.

passages.title: Learning, beautiful pages and small change
passages.text: Later history: a Quran copied at Marrakech in 1599 for Muley Zaydan belongs to the Saadian dynasty, not the Wattasids. It is now in El Escorial. This is why a map label persisting into the 1600s cannot safely identify the ruler who commissioned a particular book.

Saadian expansion ended Wattasid rule in 1554 after a contested transition. The replacement of the dynasty did not end Fez, its inhabitants or its scholarly and craft traditions. The imported “Watassid Morocco” label continuing to 1650 includes decades of later history and should not be treated as a reliable dynastic boundary.

passages.text: Wadawurrung Country includes landscapes around Geelong, Ballarat and the surrounding coast and plains. Stone arrangements, fishing places, plant knowledge and living art illuminate a history much older than colonial settlement. Wadawurrung people continue to care for Country and sustain cultural life after dispossession and environmental disruption.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: Wurdi Youang is an egg-shaped arrangement of basalt stones near Little River. A published survey describes an east-west axis and prominent stones at the western end. Its construction date is unknown, so the surviving arrangement cannot support a precise founding date or an age-based world record.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: The 2012 study identified two sets of alignments toward solstice and equinox sunsets and tested whether they might arise by chance. The authors interpret deliberate astronomical orientation. That finding does not establish every purpose of the place or recover all the knowledge associated with it.

passages.title: Stone arrangements and careful interpretation
passages.text: A public cultural assessment records stone fish traps at Point Lillias in Corio Bay. Basalt lines in the tidal zone and oral history support their interpretation. One site also has later oyster-industry remains, so the report distinguishes Indigenous use from subsequent modification.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Murnong, or yam daisy, supplied edible tubers on the plains. Accounts assembled in the cultural assessment describe digging sticks used to harvest them, with tubers eaten raw or roasted. Grazing animals introduced during colonization damaged this food landscape.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: River red gum bark furnished material for bowls and shields. Golden wattle gum served as food and an adhesive for making implements. The same landscape could supply meals, containers and the means to repair or join tools.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The Wadawurrung Country Plan identifies reeds and grasses as resources for flour, weaving and string, alongside tubers, lilies, ochre and wood. Its priorities connect the health of plants with the continuation of practical and cultural knowledge.

passages.title: Food, materials and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Waterways, wetlands and Sea Country form connected responsibilities in the plan. Fish, eels, birds, camping places and cultural sites matter together, rather than being separated into food resources on one side and culture on the other.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The community's artists directory includes Tammy Gilson's weaving and Jenna Oldaker's painting, digital art and cultural education. These named practices show people carrying knowledge through both established materials and newer media.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The corporation was founded on 12 October 1998. Its initial appointment as a Registered Aboriginal Party came on 21 May 2009, with further Country included in 2013. These dates document recognition of an organization's role, not the creation of Wadawurrung identity.

passages.title: Creative practice and continuing authority
passages.text: The Country Plan links language, stories, ceremony and family participation with the protection of places and species. Development, extraction and environmental change therefore affect both ecosystems and the settings where cultural knowledge is practiced.

Wadawurrung people continue. Colonization brought dispossession and major changes to food landscapes, including damage from introduced grazing animals. Community institutions, artists and Country planning sustain cultural responsibilities; the final year shown for a map snapshot is not an extinction date.

sectionTitles: A royal island and remarkable sewing
People remembered in bone and stone

passages.text: Welsh is a broad people-and-region label, not the name of one united state in 800-1000. Kingdoms such as Brycheiniog and Gwynedd had their own courts and connections. Excavations reveal fine clothing, farming, trade and commemoration; these regional examples should not become universal Welsh customs.

passages.title: A royal island and remarkable sewing
passages.text: At Llan-gors Lake, excavations revealed an artificial island associated with the rulers of Brycheiniog. Brushwood and sandstone formed its body, reinforced by oak plank palisades. Creating a royal site required moving ordinary materials in large quantities.

passages.title: A royal island and remarkable sewing
passages.text: The site was built in the 890s and lasted only briefly before fire. A chronicle records a Mercian attack at the lake in 916, including captives. Connecting that written event with the archaeological burning is plausible, but remains an interpretation.

passages.title: A royal island and remarkable sewing
passages.text: A charred clothing fragment survived in waterlogged silts beside the island. Conservators separated its fragile layers to reveal birds, vines and lions. What first looked like a burnt lump became evidence of exceptionally skilled needlework.

passages.title: A royal island and remarkable sewing
passages.text: The base cloth had 23 linen threads per centimetre, decorated with silk and linen. A hem and belt loop suggest a garment, but its full shape and owner are unknown. Calling it definitely a queen’s dress would go further than the evidence.

passages.title: Work and exchange on Anglesey
passages.text: Llanbedrgoch produced coins and lead weights before major excavation began. Anglo-Saxon coins and Viking-associated weights show contact around the Irish Sea. They do not by themselves prove that everyone at the site came from overseas.

passages.title: Work and exchange on Anglesey
passages.text: Postholes and other traces revealed halls used around 890-970, with another large building dated broadly 855-1000. These were not stone castles. Archaeologists reconstruct timber structures from the features left in the ground.

passages.title: Work and exchange on Anglesey
passages.text: Iron leatherworking tools, bucket fittings and household objects came from a deposit of discarded material. The settlement’s life included making, repairing and carrying things as well as political power.

passages.title: Work and exchange on Anglesey
passages.text: The museum describes crop growing, livestock and crafts alongside contact with merchants. Farming and trade supported one another. Seaborne connections did not mean that dinner arrived entirely by ship.

passages.title: People remembered in bone and stone
passages.text: Five people were buried in the filled ditch at Llanbedrgoch during the late 900s. Their unusual treatment has prompted suggestions of violence or captivity. The circumstances are uncertain; Viking contacts do not identify the people responsible.

passages.title: People remembered in bone and stone
passages.text: Researchers made facial reconstructions from four of the skulls. Such models help visitors encounter individual people, but soft tissues and appearance involve estimates. Similar-looking faces are not a DNA-tested family tree.

passages.title: People remembered in bone and stone
passages.text: The tenth-century Conbelin Cross at Margam bears knotwork, Christian figures and a hunting scene. Its Pennant sandstone carving connected religious commemoration with skilled stonework. The person remembered in the inscription is not fully identifiable.

passages.title: People remembered in bone and stone
passages.text: CONBELIN P[O]SUIT HANC CRUCM means “Conbelin erected this cross.” Brackets show a letter restored by the editor. This is Latin in the Conbelin Cross inscription, not Old Welsh; the rest asks for commemoration of a person whose name is damaged.

Welsh people did not end in 1000. Regional states and later princedoms continued, facing changing alliances and English conquests in later centuries. Welsh language and identity also continued. The end of the atlas segment is a map boundary, not a people’s extinction or a single conquest date.
