passages.text: Wessex was a kingdom in southern England. Under Alfred, royal support for reading and translation linked learned texts with the skilled production of books and precious objects.

passages.title: Learning
passages.text: Alfred commissioned translations of religious works from Latin into Old English. Copies circulated within his kingdom.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Some books were accompanied by reading pointers called aestels. The Alfred Jewel may have formed the head of one, but its function remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The jewel combines gold, colored cloisonne enamel and rock crystal. A figure appears beneath the crystal, and an animal-like head forms the base.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: An inscription names Alfred as the person who ordered the object made. The museum dates it to his reign, 871 to 899.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The figure beneath the crystal may personify sight, fitting a possible reading aid. The museum presents this identification as uncertain.

passages.title: Ideas and institutions
passages.text: Alfred's law code drew on earlier West Saxon, Mercian and Kentish rules. His government also supported fortified market settlements, connecting defense with economic activity.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Wessex became the base from which Alfred's successors expanded royal power across England. This was a process of political consolidation, not the disappearance of West Saxon people.

passages.text: The western Frankish kingdom continued through struggles among royal families and regional powers. This entry’s 900 to 1000 coverage includes both late Carolingian kings and Hugh Capet’s accession in 987. Monastery documents, manuscripts and excavated villages reveal lives that cannot be reduced to a sequence of kings.

passages.title: Families, villages and food stores
passages.text: In 923 Queen Eadgifu took her young son Louis to England after his father lost power. He returned in 936 as King Louis IV. His childhood illustrates how royal family connections could provide refuge during political crises, and how a future king might grow up far from his kingdom.

passages.title: Families, villages and food stores
passages.text: At Saint-Gilles de Missignac near Aimargues, excavation revealed a village with a particularly active phase between the ninth and eleventh centuries. Houses, paths, courtyards, a church and a cemetery show a lived landscape. This southern village provides a local example, not a model of every western Frankish settlement.

passages.title: Families, villages and food stores
passages.text: Missignac’s excavated houses were often built of earth, with one or two rooms; archaeologists suggest upper spaces sometimes stored hay or grain. Some buildings used stone bases and tiles. These observations come from a settlement occupied over centuries, so the surviving plan should not be read as one frozen moment.

passages.title: Families, villages and food stores
passages.text: Archaeologists identified about 450 grain-storage pits across Missignac’s occupation. They did not all operate at once. A large archaeological total can represent generations of storage and replacement: it does not mean one extraordinarily hungry family had 450 pantries.

passages.title: Families, villages and food stores
passages.text: Finds at Missignac include weaving weights, sickles and milling stones, linking household life with cloth production, harvesting and grinding grain. Some abandoned storage pits later received rubbish. The objects preserve traces of work even where written records do not tell us who performed it.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: When William founded Cluny around 910, his gift included a rural estate with resources such as vineyards, meadows, woods, mills and ponds. A monastery required a working economic base. Prayer might organize its day, but food and maintenance still had to come from somewhere.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: Cluny’s foundation arranged for its community to choose later abbots after Berno, its first leader, and placed the house under papal protection. These provisions shaped who could control the institution. They describe this monastery’s legal arrangements rather than independence from every outside pressure.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: In 931 Abbot Odo received papal authorization to reform other monasteries that wished to adopt Cluny’s observance. The community’s influence could therefore extend through practices and institutional connections. The enormous later medieval church at Cluny should not be projected backward into this early foundation.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: Gerbert taught at Reims from the 970s after earlier study in Catalonia. His career linked learning in different regions, and he later became Pope Sylvester II in 999. Mathematics and teaching formed part of this story alongside church politics.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: Evidence for Gerbert’s mathematics includes a letter explaining place-value multiplication and Richer’s description of an abacus with twenty-seven columns. Moving a counter between columns changes its value. Modern classroom reconstructions can illustrate the principle, but their added colors or teaching tricks are not automatically medieval evidence.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: A surviving Romance oath begins “Pro Deo amur et pro christian poblo”: “For the love of God and for the Christian people.” It belongs to the Strasbourg alliance of 842, before this map interval. The wording offers a brief glimpse of written speech distinct from the Latin framing narrative.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: The Strasbourg oaths are preserved in Nithard’s history through a manuscript copied in the late tenth or early eleventh century, now BnF Latin 9768. It is not a signed document from the 842 ceremony. The dates of an event, its composition and a surviving copy can differ substantially.

passages.title: Learning, religion and readable words
passages.text: Carolingian coins of the eighth through tenth centuries were mostly silver. Their designs could include crosses, royal monograms, temple forms and mint names. Such small objects joined writing, authority and exchange; finding a coin does not establish that every household transaction used money.

Hugh Capet’s election in 987 ended the sequence of western Carolingian kings and began a new dynasty. The kingdom continued. Its people, villages and institutions did not vanish at that change or at the map’s 1000 endpoint.

passages.text: West Germany was the common Cold War name for the Federal Republic of Germany, founded in 1949 in the western occupation zones. Its Basic Law and elected parliament endured after 1990. In its early decades, families faced severe housing shortages; later growth brought new homes, refrigerators and washing machines to many. Workers recruited from abroad and their children became part of the country, while women pressed against unequal roles and students challenged schools and authority. West Germany as a separate map label ended with reunification in 1990, but the Federal Republic continued. The imported map covers only 1960 to 1994.

passages.title: Democracy and its limits
passages.text: The Federal Republic began in 1949. Voters chose Bundestag representatives in free elections, unlike the GDR’s controlled Volkskammer before 1990. West Berlin had a special status and did not hold the same Bundestag elections.

passages.title: Democracy and its limits
passages.text: The Basic Law begins “Die Würde des Menschen ist unantastbar,” or “Human dignity is inviolable.” That small written German sample helped set the republic’s legal direction after Nazi rule.

passages.title: Democracy and its limits
passages.text: Students protested in the 1960s over crowded universities, education reform and old ideas about authority. The debates showed that democratic life includes arguments in classrooms and streets, not just votes on election day.

passages.title: Democracy and its limits
passages.text: The GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. Thus “West Germany” ended as the name for one half of a divided country, but the Federal Republic’s Basic Law and elected institutions continued.

passages.title: Crowded rooms to consumer goods
passages.text: In 1949 the western republic had far more households than available dwellings. A 1950 survey found roughly three households for every two homes, and only about half had a cooking place to themselves. Privacy, kitchens and toilets mattered as much as the national flag.

passages.title: Crowded rooms to consumer goods
passages.text: The 1950 housing law supported affordable construction. More than five million homes were built with public help by 1960, although early subsidized flats were small and allocated according to need.

passages.title: Crowded rooms to consumer goods
passages.text: By 1965, refrigerators and washing machines had reached most households; supermarkets and television ads changed shopping. The “economic miracle” was built by workers and did not mean everyone could buy everything at once.

passages.title: Crowded rooms to consumer goods
passages.text: West Germany’s statutory health insurance continued an older system and expanded during the republic. The practical family question was whether a sick child could see a doctor without paying the whole bill at the door; insurance rules helped answer it.

passages.title: Work, school and changing families
passages.text: The 1950s celebrated a mother-at-home ideal, but more married women took paid work. Women often received less pay for the same work; legal equality and everyday equality moved at different speeds.

passages.title: Work, school and changing families
passages.text: From 1955 to 1973 the government recruited workers from Italy, Turkey, Spain and six other countries. Many lived in strict dormitories at first. After recruitment stopped, many stayed and brought families: the supposedly temporary “guest” had children, neighbors and a long future.

passages.title: Work, school and changing families
passages.text: West German education came under fire in the 1960s for unequal opportunities and overcrowded universities. Pupils did not all receive the same route to higher study; reformers argued over who school was really for.

passages.title: Work, school and changing families
passages.text: Industrial growth helped many households buy more, but employers’ profits rose faster than wages at points and workers fought over pay and hours. A new fridge did not settle arguments about who worked, earned and cooked.

passages.title: Work, school and changing families
passages.text: For families with relatives in East Germany, the 1961 Berlin Wall turned an ordinary visit into a political problem. The two state cards describe different daily lives, but many family stories crossed the divide.

West Germany as a Cold War half-country label ended when the GDR joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990. The Federal Republic itself continued with its Basic Law and elected parliament; millions of East and West residents and migrant families entered this new chapter together. The imported 1994 endpoint is not a second unification.

sectionTitles: Water, rights and a new federation

passages.text: Western Australia developed from the Swan River settlement established in 1829. This map record covers its late colonial decades, including responsible government in 1890 and the gold rushes that drew many newcomers onto Aboriginal lands.

passages.title: Building and describing the colony
passages.text: Convicts built Fremantle’s prison from limestone quarried at the site during the 1850s. Other convict gangs worked on colonial infrastructure. More than 9,700 men were transported to Western Australia before transportation ended in 1868; their labour left highly visible buildings.

passages.title: Building and describing the colony
passages.text: Convict James Roe described Fremantle in English: “Conspicuous above all rises the prison.” In plainer words, the prison stood out above everything else. Fremantle Prison reproduces his observation with his convict number, 6709, a view of the town from someone held there.

passages.title: Building and describing the colony
passages.text: Pearlshell already had deep significance in Aboriginal exchange and ceremony. Carved riji shells circulated across northwestern and central Australia during the nineteenth century, valued for connections with water, rain and life. Colonial pearling entered an existing world of shell knowledge.

passages.title: Building and describing the colony
passages.text: The pearling industry could be brutal: Aboriginal women were sometimes forced to dive. Later Asian workers also supplied skilled labour. The Western Australian Museum’s interpretation preserves this history alongside the attractive shells, so the industry’s beauty does not hide the people who suffered.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: Discoveries at Coolgardie in 1892 and Kalgoorlie in 1893 brought a rush of migrants. Some found work rather than fortunes, and new businesses followed. Aboriginal communities experienced disease, dispossession and restricted access to precious water as the fields expanded.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: Water was so scarce that prospectors used dryblowers to separate gold from soil rather than relying only on wet panning. The machine’s sifting action adapted prospecting to the dry environment. Gold hunting did not always involve the familiar image of a pan in a stream.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: Many new arrivals lived in canvas shelters over wooden frames, with floors of sand or canvas. Packing cases and used kerosene tins became furniture. Wealthier mine managers could afford brick houses, giving the same goldfield very different levels of domestic comfort.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: Heat, blowing dust, expensive fresh water and typhoid made family life difficult in the early goldfields towns. Tree cutting for mining, locomotives and water condensers worsened the dust. The practical challenge was getting through an ordinary day as well as finding gold.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: The Coolgardie safe offered food cooling without electricity. Water soaked cloth around a cupboard; evaporation carried heat away. A breezy position helped it work. This technology appeared in the 1890s and remained useful in rural households well into the next century.

passages.title: Goldfields households
passages.text: A food safe’s legs could stand in tins of water to discourage ants, while its covering kept flies and other animals away. Imagine a cupboard wearing wet clothes and standing in little moats: practical engineering for protecting dinner.

passages.title: Water, rights and a new federation
passages.text: Goldfields residents pressed for reliable fresh water in the 1890s. The resulting pipeline eventually stretched more than 600 kilometres from the Perth region. It opened in 1903, after federation: an important colonial project whose benefits arrived in the state period.

passages.title: Water, rights and a new federation
passages.text: Responsible government arrived in 1890, and legislation extended voting rights to women in 1899. Political equality remained incomplete: racial restrictions still excluded many Aboriginal people. The expanding settler electorate and the people displaced by settlement did not enjoy the same political power.

Western Australia joined the Commonwealth on 1 January 1901 and became a state. Its 1900 referendum supported federation after prolonged debate. The imported 1900 endpoint belongs to this constitutional transition, not the disappearance of Western Australia or its peoples.

sectionTitles: A capital glittering with tiny stones
A gold bracelet buried in a changing Britain
A noisy bath at a Gallic family estate
A ruler’s name on a measuring tool

passages.text: The western Roman court emerged as a distinct governing center after Theodosius I died in 395 CE. It ruled from Italy, with Ravenna becoming its capital in 402, while Roman power in Britain, Gaul, Spain and North Africa changed at different times. Mosaics, letters and buried objects show a world that did not vanish when an emperor lost his throne. The map’s Western Roman Empire polygon runs from 400 to 500 CE; those rounded dates are map coverage, not an exact lifetime.

passages.title: A capital glittering with tiny stones
passages.text: Ravenna became the western court’s capital in 402. Its fifth-century religious buildings preserved mosaics made from many small pieces. The monument traditionally called Galla Placidia’s mausoleum is small outside but richly decorated inside with a dark blue mosaic background. Court life could invest in art even as political control elsewhere was weakening.

passages.title: A capital glittering with tiny stones
passages.text: The Neonian Baptistery at Ravenna preserves marble, stucco and a multicolored mosaic dome. It shows how builders and artists joined older Roman methods with Christian imagery. The UNESCO group also contains sixth-century buildings, so those later monuments should not all be credited to the western emperors.

passages.title: A gold bracelet buried in a changing Britain
passages.text: A gold bracelet from the Hoxne treasure shows a hare pursued by a hound, other facing animals and leafy decoration. That is a tiny animal parade on a piece of jewelry, made for someone able to own gold. It tells us about a craftsperson’s skill and a wealthy owner’s taste, not what most Britons wore.

passages.title: A gold bracelet buried in a changing Britain
passages.text: The Hoxne treasure, found in Suffolk, was buried in the early fifth century as Britain passed out of Roman central control. It held thousands of coins as well as jewelry and silver. The reason this particular owner buried the treasure remains unknown; its discovery does not prove everyone in Britain fled at once.

passages.title: A noisy bath at a Gallic family estate
passages.text: Sidonius Apollinaris described the baths at his wife’s estate, Avitacum, in fifth-century Gaul. The hot room had water pipes and a heated floor; a cold room and a larger pool followed. This was the home of a wealthy family, not a claim that every western household had a private bath.

passages.title: A noisy bath at a Gallic family estate
passages.text: Water came into the pool through six lion-head spouts. Sidonius joked that the noise made people standing together seem to be sharing secrets because they had to shout to be heard. A Roman bath could be sociable and spectacular, though servants kept such a household running.

passages.title: A noisy bath at a Gallic family estate
passages.text: Sidonius also mentioned a storeroom beside a space where women in the household did weaving. The letter gives a glimpse of work next to leisure: an elegant bathing room and the labor that supplied and maintained the estate belonged to the same home.

passages.title: Lessons, letters and summer heat
passages.text: In another letter, Sidonius teased a teacher for wearing a heavy gown while students sat through a hot summer lesson. He invited the teacher to his cooler country house. The joke records a real social relationship, but it comes from an educated aristocrat’s letters, not a survey of every child’s school day.

passages.title: Lessons, letters and summer heat
passages.text: In fifth-century Gaul, classical grammar and rhetoric remained important among aristocratic families even as the political world changed. Researchers find that these literary networks narrowed. A teacher in Sidonius’s circle cannot stand for the schooling available to all children.

passages.title: A ruler’s name on a measuring tool
passages.text: A copper-alloy weight made in Honorius’s reign, between 395 and 423 CE, carries the Latin name and title D N HONORIVS AVG, split across its face. The abbreviations mean “Our lord Honorius Augustus.” This is an attested Latin sample in Roman letters on a tool for checking a gold solidus, not a sentence invented for this page. It does not tell us how many people could read it.

passages.title: Why losing Carthage mattered
passages.text: Vandal forces took Carthage in 439. North Africa contained some of the west’s richest tax lands, and losing their revenue made it harder for western rulers to pay and equip armies. The change reached far beyond a line on a map: a court needed food, money and people to keep governing.

passages.title: Why losing Carthage mattered
passages.text: In 451 the Roman commander Aetius fought Attila’s army with Visigothic, Frankish and other allies. The western army was not simply “Romans against everyone else.” Neighbors and former rivals could cooperate when a new threat arrived, even while political control over their territories was changing.

In 476 the general Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus and ruled Italy without replacing him with another western emperor. This is the usual date for the end of the western imperial court, not a date when Roman people disappeared. Julius Nepos, displaced from Italy in 475, lived until 480; eastern emperors continued in Constantinople. The Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy began after Odoacer’s rule, in 493. The map’s Western Empire feature extending toward 500 is a coarse snapshot, not evidence that the old court still ruled then.

passages.text: The Western Zhou established the political and philosophical foundations of Chinese civilization. Through a system of enfeoffment and the concept of the Mandate of Heaven, they created a model of legitimate rulership that endured for three millennia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven concept emerges, stating that Heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Duke of Zhou articulates the theory of dynastic succession and the ruler's moral responsibility.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor worship becomes formalized in ritual bronze vessels and temple ceremonies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The first smelted iron in China, blades set in bronze handles, appears at the very end of the period; iron remained rare beside bronze.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Improved bronze casting techniques for ritual vessels, bells and weapons; the yongzhong bell, hung at an angle and struck at two points, takes its form.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The songs of the Classic of Poetry (Shijing), court hymns and folk songs, date from this period; the anthology was assembled later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The core of the Book of Changes (Yijing), the hexagram and line statements, takes shape as a divination manual; the philosophical commentaries came centuries later.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze inscriptions become longer and more literary, recording royal deeds and land grants; the Mao Gong ding carries about 500 characters.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Regional lords governed territories from walled cities, owing military service and tribute to the Zhou king.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The well-field system supposedly divided agricultural land into nine plots, with the center plot worked for the lord.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Confucius later idealized the Western Zhou as a golden age of virtue and proper ritual.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mandate of Heaven justified political change throughout Chinese history until the empire ended in 1912.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhou ritual codes influenced East Asian court ceremonies for centuries.
Quanrong nomads allied with disaffected lords sacked the capital Haojing and killed King You, forcing the court to flee east.

sectionTitles: At home and through the seasons
Survival, gathering and a living language

passages.text: Wichita communities farmed, traded and defended settlements across the southern Plains. Wichita Proper, Waco, Taovaya, Tawakoni and Kichai histories feed into today’s Wichita and Affiliated Tribes. The map’s broad Kansas-to-Texas outline and 1492 start are imported coverage, not the borders or founding date of one kingdom. The living nation continues beyond the map’s 1783 cutoff.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: Trade linked Wichita ancestors with communities far beyond their fields. New Mexican pottery, turquoise and obsidian reached the Plains, while exchanges with Caddo communities brought valued bow wood and pottery. Horses, metal tools and guns later changed these networks, with Wichita traders also passing imported goods to Comanche partners.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: A 2020 drone study examined an ancestral Wichita settlement near Arkansas City, Kansas, which some researchers identify with the Etzanoa visited in 1601. Thermal and multispectral images revealed a large circular earthwork beneath an apparently ordinary field. The authors compare it with council circles at other Great Bend sites; its precise purpose remains debated.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: The same survey covered about 18 hectares and identified possible house basins as well as the circular feature. Heat differences and vegetation patterns helped researchers investigate buried structures without digging through the whole settlement. The study demonstrates how an archaeological landscape can survive beneath later land use.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: In 2017, Wichita State student Mitchell Young found a Spanish horseshoe nail 87 centimeters down in an old storage pit at the proposed Etzanoa site. Archaeologist Donald Blakeslee suggested that its unbent condition suited an object traded rather than lost from a horse. That interpretation connects a tiny find with a much larger encounter.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: In 1759, Taovaya and other Wichita defenders, with Comanche allies, resisted a Spanish expedition at the Twin Villages on the Red River. The Spanish force withdrew and left its two cannon behind. These communities could coordinate a formidable defense when an invading army threatened their settlements.

passages.title: Villages, diplomacy and discoveries
passages.text: The fortified northern village combined a timber stockade with earthworks and a moat. Fields nearby produced maize, beans, pumpkins and watermelons. A town could therefore be both a busy agricultural center and a carefully engineered defensive position; food production and military strength were closely connected.

passages.title: At home and through the seasons
passages.text: In the tribal history’s account of the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, women planted corn, beans and squash. Beans climbed the cornstalks. Pumpkin strips were dried, woven into mats and folded for storage: a pantry item that could be rolled up. Food also went into hide bags in underground caches.

passages.title: At home and through the seasons
passages.text: A grass house could accommodate ten to twelve relatives, including married daughters, their husbands and children. After returning from winter hunts, families repaired the houses. Women and boys climbed the cedar framework to attach bundles of bluestem grass, making spring repairs a family climbing project.

passages.title: At home and through the seasons
passages.text: The year moved between village gardens and winter bison hunts. On the hunt, related families camped in tipis, and women sliced and dried meat for later use. Portable shelters and preserved food allowed households to travel while remaining connected to their farming villages.

passages.title: At home and through the seasons
passages.text: The Wichita-Pawnee Visitation brings relatives and friends together through alternating hosts, meals, dances and gifts. The tribal account even includes cleaning the camp before departure. Hospitality involves both the memorable celebration and the practical work that makes a gathering possible.

passages.title: Survival, gathering and a living language
passages.text: At Camp Holmes in 1835, Wichita representatives helped bring Comanche allies into a treaty recognizing rights to their homelands. Recognition did not prevent later dispossession. In 1863 Confederate forces drove Wichita people north into Kansas; without farmland, families endured hunger and epidemics before survivors returned to Indian Territory in 1867.

passages.title: Survival, gathering and a living language
passages.text: Government boarding schools punished Wichita children for speaking their language. Around the turn of the twentieth century, allotment broke reservation land into individual parcels and opened the remaining land to settlers. Tawakoni Jim and others resisted this assault on shared lands and village life.

passages.title: Survival, gathering and a living language
passages.text: Community gathering places helped families rebuild connections after allotment. Research with Wichita collaborators documents ichaskhah, a Camp Creek gathering ground near Anadarko used from the 1930s into the early 1960s. Families camped there for visits, meals, handgames and dances, and the gatherings also supported political decisions.

passages.title: Survival, gathering and a living language
passages.text: A small example from the tribe’s language-class dictionary is “so:ti:cʔa,” translated as “Thank you.” This is an attested modern teaching form of Wichita. It gives today’s readers a usable glimpse of the language that families and language workers are sustaining.

The 1783 map cutoff is not the end of Wichita history. Despite war, removal, disease and allotment, Wichita and Affiliated Tribes continues as a living nation with government and community life centered near Anadarko, Oklahoma.

passages.text: Wampanoag peoples belong to southeastern Massachusetts and eastern Rhode Island, including the island of Noepe, or Martha’s Vineyard. Their communities had local leaders, coastal and inland resources, and lasting relationships with neighboring peoples. This imported mainland outline omits important island homelands. Its 1492 to 1500 dates describe map coverage, not the beginning or disappearance of the Wampanoag.

passages.title: Communities and material discoveries
passages.text: Early seventeenth-century Wampanoag towns had their own sachems and councils. Leadership could be held by women: Awashonks led at Sakonnet, and Weetamoo at Pocasset. Political life involved several communities and leaders rather than a single ruler issuing instructions to every household.

passages.title: Communities and material discoveries
passages.text: At Eel River Farm in Plymouth, archaeologists identified a seasonal coastal village and places where people manufactured quartz tools. Ten archaeological projects recovered 37,970 objects. The collection spans different periods, with most material predating European contact; the earliest finds do not make every house or workshop equally old.

passages.title: Communities and material discoveries
passages.text: A pottery fragment in Plimoth Patuxet’s collection, catalogued as 19PL522.1977, belongs to the museum’s broad Woodland-period range of about 3,000 to 1,000 years ago. Its educational account explains how crushed stone or sand strengthened local clay. Rounded cooking pots could rest among supporting stones beside a fire: a useful pot did not need a flat bottom.

passages.title: Homes, travel and growing up
passages.text: Aquinnah’s account describes a wetu framed with bent cedar saplings, tied with plant fibers and covered with bark or reed mats. A roof opening let smoke escape, while additional mats lined the inside. Building a comfortable home required knowing which plants could bend, tie, cover and insulate.

passages.title: Homes, travel and growing up
passages.text: A mishoon was a canoe hollowed from a single tree. Plimoth Patuxet’s modern reconstruction explains the older combination of controlled fire and scraping with stone, shell or bone tools. Such boats carried people for fishing, travel and exchange. The museum example demonstrates a technique; it is not an excavated ancient canoe.

passages.title: Homes, travel and growing up
passages.text: Plimoth Patuxet describes seventeenth-century Wampanoag children learning to swim in ponds and the sea, an important skill around canoes. They also made small clay pots and played a catching game with a ring attached by a string to a stick. Practice could be useful and fun at the same time.

passages.title: Homes, travel and growing up
passages.text: In Aquinnah’s present-day Cranberry Day account, children may miss school to join the harvest with elders on the second Tuesday of October. Stories, an open cooking fire and a shared meal accompany picking. This is a documented community gathering today, not a timetable inferred for every Wampanoag village in 1492.

passages.title: Encounters, choices and losses
passages.text: Epenow, taken from Noepe in 1611, used his captors’ hopes of finding gold to arrange a return voyage. In Aquinnah’s account, relatives attacked the ship while he jumped overboard and swam away. His escape makes clear that Wampanoag people were responding to kidnapping well before the Mayflower arrived.

passages.title: Encounters, choices and losses
passages.text: In the years immediately before Plymouth’s settlement, epidemics devastated Wampanoag communities. Tisquantum returned in 1619 to find that his family and most of Patuxet had died. The English settlement occupied this emptied village. An apparently available place concealed a terrible recent history.

passages.title: Encounters, choices and losses
passages.text: Ousamequin’s 1621 agreement with Plymouth was a political decision. In a recorded interview, Wampanoag historian Nanepashemet explained it as an effort to obtain useful allies and weapons while confronting Narragansett strength. This interpretation restores strategic calculation to a relationship often reduced to a friendly feast.

passages.title: Encounters, choices and losses
passages.text: Metacom’s War, often called King Philip’s War, brought catastrophic losses in 1675 and 1676. Metacom was killed, and surviving Wampanoag and other Native people faced enslavement, displacement and confinement. These events broke political power and separated families; they did not eliminate Wampanoag identity.

passages.title: Encounters, choices and losses
passages.text: Colonial control continued through everyday economic pressure. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, debt could lead to loss of land or indentured labor, while many Wampanoag men supported households through fishing and whaling. Survival involved adapting work as well as defending community ties.

passages.title: Writing and renewed learning
passages.text: The Museum of the Bible preserves a 1663 Bible printed in Cambridge in Wôpanâak, catalogued as BIB.003870. Its creation involved John Eliot and Native linguistic collaborators. The object documents seventeenth-century printing in the language within a missionary project, rather than proving that all Wampanoag people then read printed books.

passages.title: Writing and renewed learning
passages.text: A modern written sample is “Mukayuhsak Weekuw,” translated by the Mashpee Wampanoag Tribe as “The Children’s House.” Its August 2019 report uses this name for the language-immersion school and records 25 children aged two to seven during the completed 2018 to 2019 school year. Here, language learning included ordinary classroom life.

passages.title: Writing and renewed learning
passages.text: The Wôpanâak Language Reclamation Project began in 1993 with jessie little doe baird and participating Wampanoag communities. Work with linguists combined old deeds, wills, petitions and religious texts with evidence from related languages. Documents once produced in colonial conditions became resources for teaching children their community’s language again.

passages.title: Writing and renewed learning
passages.text: Aquinnah received federal recognition in 1987. Its tribal history also records a 1995 agreement with the town covering mutual police, fire and medical assistance. These are modern governmental arrangements serving a continuing community whose history extends far beyond the small interval displayed on this map.

The map stops at 1500, but Wampanoag history continues through colonial violence, land loss and continuing communities. Aquinnah’s recognized government and cooperative language reclamation are later chapters of that history, not a new people replacing an extinct one.

passages.text: Württemberg’s map record begins before it became a kingdom in 1806. Its nineteenth-century rulers and communities confronted famine, constitutional disputes and the demands of industry. Agricultural schools, charitable institutions and railways provide concrete evidence for efforts to change everyday life. The monarchy survived the map interval and ended in 1918.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: The disastrous harvest year 1816 followed the eruption of Mount Tambora in 1815. Food shortages helped motivate a new agricultural institution at Hohenheim. A distant volcanic eruption and local farming policy became connected through the urgent problem of getting enough to eat.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: The Hohenheim institute opened in 1818 with director Johann Nepomuk Hubert Schwerz, two other teachers and 16 pupils. Agriculture was taught alongside mathematics, physics, chemistry, mineralogy and botany. Improving farming meant combining practical work with several kinds of scientific knowledge.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: Hohenheim combined teaching with an experimental and model farm, and an affiliated orphanage. The institution linked education, demonstrations and welfare. Its early scale was modest: a famous modern university grew from a small group trying to address immediate problems.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: Queen Katharina supported a central charitable association in 1817 to organize help during hardship. This created a more coordinated institution for assistance. Royal patronage mattered, but the practical work depended on people collecting resources and delivering support.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: The Katharinenstift opened in 1818 as a school offering higher education for girls. It widened educational opportunities for its pupils, but its elite character should not be confused with universal access. A new school could be important without serving every child in the kingdom.

passages.title: Food, farms and learning
passages.text: The royal couple also supported a savings bank in 1818. An institution for depositing savings belonged to the same reforming environment as education and agricultural improvement. Everyday finance, as well as the great affairs of government, was becoming part of organized public policy.

passages.title: Care, transport and public space
passages.text: Stuttgart’s Katharinenhospital opened in 1828 after construction begun in 1820. It addressed overcrowded and outdated medical facilities. The surviving building history shows healthcare requiring money, space and organization, rather than depending only on individual doctors’ knowledge.

passages.title: Care, transport and public space
passages.text: Württemberg’s first railway service ran between Cannstatt and Untertürkheim in 1845. The first operating stretch was not yet a complete network reaching everywhere people wanted to go. Railways grew section by section, connecting existing settlements and activities.

passages.title: Care, transport and public space
passages.text: Connecting Cannstatt with Stuttgart required the Rosenstein tunnel, built in 1844 to 1846 beneath the palace’s central axis, and a bridge across the Neckar. The engineering route passed through a royal landscape. A palace could become a landmark above the railway as well as beside it.

passages.title: Care, transport and public space
passages.text: Cannstatt’s mineral waters attracted affluent visitors during the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Drinking halls and resort life made health-seeking a social activity. These visits tell us about historical beliefs and leisure; they do not establish that every claimed treatment worked.

passages.title: A negotiated constitution in German
passages.text: The 1819 constitution followed years of disagreement between the crown and representatives of the estates. The poet Ludwig Uhland was among the defenders of constitutional rights. Political writing, public debate and institutional negotiation were intertwined rather than separate hobbies.

passages.title: A negotiated constitution in German
passages.text: Section 6 states “Der Sitz der Regierung kann in keinem Falle außerhalb des Königreichs verlegt werden.” This means “The seat of government may under no circumstances be moved outside the kingdom.” The German rule is a precise reminder that where a government operated could itself be a constitutional issue.

Württemberg’s monarchy ended in 1918 and republican government followed. Membership in the German Empire from 1871 had already changed its political setting without immediately ending the kingdom. The map’s 1878 boundary is therefore neither its founding nor its fall.

passages.text: Wurundjeri people connect Birrarung and surrounding Country through language, family, leadership and skilled work. Greenstone quarrying, William Barak's drawings and community canoe building reveal different ways of making and sharing knowledge. Colonial dispossession changed access to land, but Wurundjeri identity and cultural responsibilities continue.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: At Wil-im-ee Moor-ring, Mount William, quarry pits, waste stone and working areas preserve the remains of greenstone tool production. Makers shaped rough hatchet heads at the quarry; recipients could then grind and finish them for their own needs.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: Hatchets supported canoe building, food gathering and the manufacture of wooden implements. Mount William greenstone travelled through exchange: visitors brought goods including possum-skin cloaks and spears. The quarry therefore connects household work with relationships between communities.

passages.title: Greenstone tools and exchange
passages.text: In the 1880s, William Barak described quarry access to Alfred Howitt. His account identifies Billibellary as a custodian approached through messengers. It adds evidence of authority and negotiated access to the physical traces of stoneworking.

passages.title: Art as a cultural record
passages.text: Barak's Untitled drawing of 1899, now in the National Gallery of Victoria, uses pencil and watercolor to show a ceremonial gathering. An inscription on its calico wrapping dates the gift to Annie Danks to January 1899, giving the work a documented personal history.

passages.title: Art as a cultural record
passages.text: The drawing includes possum-skin cloaks, feather headdresses, boomerangs used as clapsticks, fires and animals. These details communicate clothing, movement and performance through an artist's composition; the image is a cultural account, not a complete inventory of every Wurundjeri ceremony.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Simon Wonga and William Barak helped establish Coranderrk in 1863 for Wurundjeri and other displaced Kulin people. They sought space for a community amid colonial dispossession. The station provided a place to live, but its administration constrained people's control over their land.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Barak became Ngurungaeta after Wonga's death in 1874. His petitions to retain Coranderrk show leadership exercised through negotiation and written advocacy, alongside the cultural knowledge communicated in his pictures.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: In the 2012 Kooroong project, community members worked greenstone into axes and used them to remove bark from a river red gum at Plenty Gorge for a canoe. The project brought stoneworking, tree knowledge and boat construction together in a living practice.

passages.title: Leadership and everyday community life
passages.text: Wurundjeri accounts treat landforms and habitats as integral parts of cultural heritage. Care for Country includes relationships and continuing practices, as well as protecting individual sites or objects.

passages.title: Returns and continuing institutions
passages.text: Descendants established the Wurundjeri corporation in 1985. The return of part of Coranderrk, including its cemetery, in March 1998 restored a connection to a place with deep family significance, without undoing every earlier loss.

passages.title: Returns and continuing institutions
passages.text: Land titles for Wil-im-ee Moor-ring and the Sunbury Rings returned in 2012. In 2017, Elders addressed Victoria's Parliament as part of advocacy for Birrarung. These events show cultural authority expressed through landholding and public decision-making.

Wurundjeri people continue despite dispossession and reserve controls. Coranderrk belongs to that history, but does not define its beginning or end. Descendants sustain leadership, artistic knowledge and responsibilities to Birrarung and Country through family life and community institutions.

sectionTitles: Print, education and a later childhood

passages.text: Xhosa-speaking societies of South Africa’s Eastern Cape combined farming, cattle keeping, craftsmanship and rich oral and written traditions. Their rulers and communities faced repeated colonial wars and dispossession. The map’s broad label covers several political communities, whose alliances and experiences were not identical.

passages.title: War, belief and political choices
passages.text: After the famine associated with the 1856 to 1857 cattle-killing, thousands of Xhosa people were moved into the Cape Colony as laborers. Colonial occupation also removed land from Gcaleka ruler Sarhili. The disaster reshaped households as well as boundaries.

passages.title: War, belief and political choices
passages.text: Alliances divided communities. During the 1877 to 1878 war, Sandile led some Rharhabe into resistance while others remained aligned with the Cape government. Mfengu forces were major colonial allies. This was a struggle involving African political choices alongside imperial power.

passages.title: War, belief and political choices
passages.text: Peires links the 1856 to 1857 cattle-killing beliefs to the deadly cattle lungsickness epidemic that began in 1854, together with indigenous and Christian ideas of renewal. Understanding that setting helps explain people’s hopes without treating the prophecy as true or the victims as a joke.

passages.title: Objects for everyday living
passages.text: A museum study records Xhosa milk vessels made from soft woods, alongside evidence of earlier basket containers. The materials changed, but the practical problem remained the same: carrying and storing a food central to cattle-keeping households.

passages.title: Objects for everyday living
passages.text: A Xhosa necklace collected around 1877, South African Museum object SAM-10920, uses small pieces of fragrant tambuti wood. Jewelry could appeal to the nose as well as the eye. The surviving object makes a personal fashion choice tangible.

passages.title: Objects for everyday living
passages.text: The ugwali instrument combined a wooden or reed stave, a sinew string and a flattened feather quill. Early nineteenth-century writers recorded it among Xhosa musicians. A modest handful of materials could become an instrument with a distinctive sound.

passages.title: Objects for everyday living
passages.text: Xhosa pipe makers lined wooden bowls with sheet metal to protect the wood from burning. Museum examples even preserve printing on recycled tin. The object shows careful fitting, material knowledge and reuse.

passages.title: Objects for everyday living
passages.text: Craft workers drilled narrow channels through wooden pipe stems and closed unwanted drill exits with closely fitted wooden plugs. Later souvenir production adapted these skills to visitors’ tastes. The finished smooth surface could conceal several stages of painstaking work.

passages.title: Print, education and a later childhood
passages.text: “Indaba” means “News.” It was the title of a Xhosa-language monthly published at Lovedale from 1862 to 1865. Its title offers a small sample of written Xhosa from the map’s own nineteenth-century period.

passages.title: Print, education and a later childhood
passages.text: Despite missionary editorial restrictions, writers including John Muir Vimbe, William Kobe Ntsikana and Tiyo Soga contributed to Indaba. Soga’s translation of the first part of The Pilgrim’s Progress appeared in 1867. Xhosa authors used print to build a literary public.

passages.title: Print, education and a later childhood
passages.text: The literary story continued after 1878. As editor of Isigidimi in the 1880s, W. W. Gqoba published poetry that challenged missionary education. Schools and newspapers offered opportunities, but African writers also questioned the inequalities within them.

passages.title: Print, education and a later childhood
passages.text: For a later glimpse of a related Xhosa-speaking community, Nelson Mandela remembered his Thembu childhood at Qunu in the 1920s: children shaped clay oxen, wagons and birds, and slid down a sloping rock on flat stones. His memoir gives us a named childhood, not a universal custom.

Sandile died during the 1878 war, and colonial expansion continued afterward. Political defeat did not end Xhosa communities, language or literature; the imported endpoint marks a colonial conflict, not a people’s disappearance.

passages.text: The Xia is the first dynasty in Chinese tradition, associated by most Chinese scholars with the Erlitou archaeological culture of the middle Yellow River valley. Whether it was a historical state or a later political myth remains debated outside China, but the material culture of the period shows the first large-scale bronze production and palace architecture in the region.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Erlitou casts the earliest Chinese bronze ritual vessels, small jue wine cups, in sectioned clay moulds, the piece-mould method the Shang would carry to its height.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Flood control and irrigation works are attributed by tradition to the founder Yu the Great; the story is legend, but the Yellow River floodplain was being farmed and managed in this period.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Plain bronze jue and jade blades, sceptres and cong tubes from Erlitou set the forms that later dynasties elaborated and decorated.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Turquoise-inlaid bronze plaques with animal designs, and a dragon of some two thousand turquoise pieces laid on a body in an Erlitou tomb.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Ancestor offerings and divination with burnt animal bones appear in the archaeological record, anticipating Shang and Zhou religion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The legend of Yu controlling the floods established the model of the virtuous ruler who brings order from chaos.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming and pig husbandry supported growing populations in the Yellow River valley.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Rammed-earth foundations and walls enclosed the palace compound at Erlitou, a walled precinct of about eleven hectares.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: In the traditional histories the cycle of dynasties begins with the Xia: Tang of Shang overthrows its last king, and the Zhou later name the pattern the Mandate of Heaven.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name Xia later became synonymous with Chinese civilization itself, in the word Huaxia.
According to tradition, the tyrant Jie was defeated by Tang of Shang at the Battle of Mingtiao.

passages.text: The Xin dynasty was a brief interregnum when Wang Mang attempted radical reforms inspired by ancient Zhou ideals. His policies failed to address real economic problems and natural disasters, above all the Yellow River's change of course, and ended in widespread rebellion.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Mang claims the Mandate of Heaven has transferred to him based on omens and classical precedents.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Reforms modeled on the ancient Zhou well-field system and ritual codes.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Private land ownership abolished; all land declared the king's fields, to be redistributed in equal shares. The order was withdrawn within three years.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The trade in slaves banned, though the ban was widely ignored.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: State monopolies on salt, iron, coinage and liquor, and a bureau to lend to farmers and steady prices.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Wang Mang's failure discredited radical reform and strengthened conservative Confucianism.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: His reign became a cautionary tale about ignoring economic realities for ideological purity.
Rebel armies captured Chang'an in 23 CE and killed Wang Mang; a Han prince, Liu Xiu, restored the dynasty in 25 as Emperor Guangwu.

passages.text: The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire, united by Modu Chanyu in 209 BCE and ruling Mongolia and the lands to its west for three centuries. Their mounted archers, tribute treaties with Han China and left-and-right administration set the pattern for the Turkic and Mongol empires that followed.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Composite bows of horn and sinew, shot from the saddle, made every herdsman a warrior.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bronze and iron for weapons and harness; gold plaques of animals in combat for the elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The chanyu ruled under Heaven, Tengri, with shamans and seasonal gatherings to sacrifice to ancestors, heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Elite tombs at Noin-Ula held Chinese silks, lacquer and Bactrian textiles beside the dead.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The heqin treaties from 198 BCE brought Han princesses, silk, grain and wine to the chanyu as the price of peace.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Xiongnu taxed the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin and traded horses and furs to China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Xiongnu model of steppe empire was followed by the Turkic khaganates and the Mongols.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Their name may lie behind the Huns of European sources, though the link is unproven.

The confederation split into southern and northern halves in 54 BCE. Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89 CE, and by 93 the Xianbei had taken over the steppe; the Southern Xiongnu lived on as Han clients inside the Great Wall.

passages.text: Yakama communities belong to the Columbia Plateau of present-day Washington. The map’s Yakima and Yakama labels show differently sized regional outlines, not the boundaries of a single ancient state. The fourteen tribes and bands confederated under the 1855 treaty had distinct earlier identities. This card follows Yakama history into that later nation; its institutions should not be projected into the map’s 1492 or 1530 scenes.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Before Fort Simcoe became the first formal Yakama agency in 1859, the place was Mool-mool, a seasonal camp with bubbling spring water. Families stopped there while hunting, fishing, gathering roots and picking huckleberries. A later military and administrative location had an older life as a busy food-gathering crossroads.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Chief Kamiakin’s garden in the Upper Ahtanum Valley grew corn, peas, potatoes, squash, melons and wheat before the 1855 war. A ditch about a quarter-mile long brought water to it. Gardening was part of his community’s changing economy alongside seasonal fishing and gathering.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Signed on June 9, 1855, the treaty named fourteen tribes and bands as a confederated nation and ceded extensive lands to the United States. It set aside a reservation. Ratification followed in March 1859, nearly four years after the signing.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: War followed in 1855 amid settler encroachment and killings. Kamiakin helped lead resistance, and his forces initially drove back an American military expedition. Colonel George Wright’s 1858 campaign broke organized resistance. Kamiakin stayed away from the reservation and eventually lived at Rock Lake.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The treaty’s practical details reach right into family life. Article 3 reserved fishing at customary places and hunting and gathering on open, unclaimed land. Article 5 promised schools, a hospital, medicines and a physician. These were written government commitments, not proof that every promised service arrived.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The tribal council formally established in 1944 has fourteen members, recalling the treaty’s fourteen signers. The museum describes a General Council of adult members electing representatives by raised hands. The nation officially adopted the spelling Yakama in 1994; older records commonly say Yakima.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: The seasonal round was a moving food calendar. A historical reconstruction describes spring root digging, summer fishing and travel to cooler high ground, followed by mountain huckleberry gathering. Knowledge of when different foods were ready helped families use several landscapes across the year.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: Winter brought families back to sheltered valley camps with stored roots, berries, salmon and venison. People repaired homes, made tools and clothing, and visited one another. The pantry had been assembled over many months; winter preparation involved much more than one enormous shopping trip.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: In a 1995 cultural-resources memorandum, Florence Aguilar explained meals beginning with water, followed by salmon, deer or elk, roots and berries, and ending with water. Her account connects eating with gratitude and responsibility for the waters that sustain salmon.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: A Yakama basket in the National Museum of the American Indian combines cedar roots, beargrass, sedge and hide thong. Its maker used coiling and imbricated decoration, layering materials into a patterned surface. The museum received it in 1957, but does not know its maker or manufacture date.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: At the intertribal fishery of Celilo Falls, Yakama and other fishers worked from platforms above dangerous currents. Raymond Matheny’s 1952 notes describe long-handled nets and compulsory safety ropes. Some fishers worked in groups and divided the proceeds from the fish they sold.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: On March 10, 1957, water backed up behind The Dalles Dam and submerged Celilo Falls. The government paid compensation for flooded fishing sites, but did not buy away treaty fishing rights. Losing the falls damaged a place of work, trade, family memory and ceremony.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: A small written sample of modern Ichishkíin is “Shix̱ iwá wyáx̱ayx̱t”, translated “Life is Good”. It appears as a storybook title on the Yakama language program’s page, credited to the Northwest Indian Language Institute and recorded by the nation’s program. This is contemporary teaching material.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: Language lessons can accompany the busiest moments of parenting. The Yakama program offers resources for nursing, babyboards and diapering through meet-ups with Ttáwax̱t Birth Justice Center. Its handwashing poster and video bring language into hygiene routines too. Even changing a diaper can have vocabulary practice attached.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: The nation’s 2017 coho restoration plan reported fish returning to Wenatchee and Methow watersheds and reproducing naturally. It also reported that local broodstock had replaced reliance on transfers from the lower Columbia. Building self-sustaining populations remained a long-term project, with monitoring as well as hatchery work.

The imported map cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of Yakama people. The later nation continues through its government and treaty relationship, while language programs help families carry Ichishkíin into everyday life.

passages.text: Yakama communities belong to the Columbia Plateau of present-day Washington. The map’s Yakima and Yakama labels show differently sized regional outlines, not the boundaries of a single ancient state. The fourteen tribes and bands confederated under the 1855 treaty had distinct earlier identities. This card follows Yakama history into that later nation; its institutions should not be projected into the map’s 1492 or 1530 scenes.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Before Fort Simcoe became the first formal Yakama agency in 1859, the place was Mool-mool, a seasonal camp with bubbling spring water. Families stopped there while hunting, fishing, gathering roots and picking huckleberries. A later military and administrative location had an older life as a busy food-gathering crossroads.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Chief Kamiakin’s garden in the Upper Ahtanum Valley grew corn, peas, potatoes, squash, melons and wheat before the 1855 war. A ditch about a quarter-mile long brought water to it. Gardening was part of his community’s changing economy alongside seasonal fishing and gathering.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Signed on June 9, 1855, the treaty named fourteen tribes and bands as a confederated nation and ceded extensive lands to the United States. It set aside a reservation. Ratification followed in March 1859, nearly four years after the signing.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: War followed in 1855 amid settler encroachment and killings. Kamiakin helped lead resistance, and his forces initially drove back an American military expedition. Colonel George Wright’s 1858 campaign broke organized resistance. Kamiakin stayed away from the reservation and eventually lived at Rock Lake.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The treaty’s practical details reach right into family life. Article 3 reserved fishing at customary places and hunting and gathering on open, unclaimed land. Article 5 promised schools, a hospital, medicines and a physician. These were written government commitments, not proof that every promised service arrived.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The tribal council formally established in 1944 has fourteen members, recalling the treaty’s fourteen signers. The museum describes a General Council of adult members electing representatives by raised hands. The nation officially adopted the spelling Yakama in 1994; older records commonly say Yakima.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: The seasonal round was a moving food calendar. A historical reconstruction describes spring root digging, summer fishing and travel to cooler high ground, followed by mountain huckleberry gathering. Knowledge of when different foods were ready helped families use several landscapes across the year.

passages.text: The Yamato period covers the rise of a single Japanese state from the chiefdoms of the Kofun age. Great keyhole-shaped tombs mark the power of the early rulers; in the sixth and seventh centuries the court took Buddhism, writing and Chinese-style government from Korea and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun mounds for rulers; the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, is 486 meters long.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses, houses and dancers stood on the mounds.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, iron swords and gilt-bronze horse trappings came from Korea and China and were buried with the chiefs.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism arrived from Baekje, and the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over whether to accept it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution set out Buddhist and Confucian principles for officials.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native kami worship, later called Shinto, continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools and weapons improved through smiths and ore from the Korean kingdoms.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese writing was adopted for court records; the inscribed sword from Inariyama, dated to 471, is among the earliest texts written in Japan.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Taika Reform began to remodel the court and its land system on Tang lines.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The imperial line that emerged in this period continues to the present.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group was listed by UNESCO.
The court moved to a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710, the start of the Nara period.

sectionTitles: Children and the people around them
What science can tell us, and what remains a question

passages.text: Yamnaya names widespread communities of the late fourth and third millennia BCE, known especially from burial mounds and animal herding. They were not one kingdom. The imported map’s 3000 to 2000 BCE span and outline are a rough regional display, not the full chronology or distribution: important early evidence predates it, and related sites extend farther west.

passages.title: Milk remembered by teeth
passages.text: A 2021 study found dairy proteins in fifteen of sixteen Early Bronze Age samples of hardened dental plaque from the steppe. This material, called dental calculus, can trap traces of meals for thousands of years. An ancient tooth sometimes keeps a better food diary than its owner ever could.

passages.title: Milk remembered by teeth
passages.text: Some proteins identified milk from sheep, goats and cattle. They establish dairy consumption, but not a particular recipe. Fresh milk, fermented drinks and processed foods remain possibilities. The researchers emphasize that regular dairy use could coexist with the rarity of the genetic variant associated with digesting milk easily in adulthood.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: In southern Kalmykia, surveys found early third-millennium burial sites beside lowland rivers and on nearby higher ground. Differences in the seasons when graves were built helped researchers reconstruct movements between pastures. Their picture is of groups returning through a local landscape, rather than wandering without a route.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: The same Kalmykia research describes braided mats made from reeds, reed mace and wormwood, interpreted as insulation for portable homes. Plant fibers required gathering and skilled work even where stone buildings were scarce. A movable home still needed someone to make it comfortable.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: Small bone pins from Yamnaya graves in Kalmykia have hammer-shaped heads and finely cut decoration. Their survival shows attention to small crafted objects alongside large burial mounds. We can admire the engraving without pretending to know exactly what each pattern meant to its maker.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: Mykhailivka, on the lower Dnipro, preserves a different side of this world. Its middle and upper layers, attributed to the Yamnaya cultural community, contained workshops for metal, stone and bone objects, surrounded by substantial stone walls and deep ditches. Herding traditions could coexist with places where craftspeople repeatedly gathered and worked.

passages.title: Wooden wheels and journeys
passages.text: Real wooden vehicle parts survive in Yamnaya graves. A 2021 survey collected forty-three well-described examples containing wagons or their components, often wheels. Most vehicles were heavy and had four wheels. These finds document substantial woodworking and transport technology; they are not evidence that everyone owned a wagon.

passages.title: Wooden wheels and journeys
passages.text: People sometimes dismantled a wagon before placing it in a grave: wheels stood separately, while the body could form a bed or a cover. At Izobilnoe near the Urals, clay copies of wheels were arranged like those of a real vehicle. Practical transport also had a place in ceremonies for the dead.

passages.title: Children and the people around them
passages.text: At Boldyrevo-4 in the Southern Urals, archaeologists studied three children, each about six years old, buried in two graves beneath early mounds. The complex dates to around 3300 to 3100 BCE, before this map entry begins. A much larger mound for adults later covered the earlier children’s burials.

passages.title: Children and the people around them
passages.text: The Boldyrevo children’s graves contained pots similar in shape and decoration but made by different techniques. Their burial mats also used different organic materials. Researchers suggest related but distinct groups contributed these objects. Such differences let archaeologists investigate connections between communities without having a written family tree.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Ancient DNA has changed the scale of the story. A major 2015 study found substantial Yamnaya-related ancestry in sampled Corded Ware people from Germany, supporting large movements from the steppe into central Europe. Genetic connections reveal ancestry; they do not by themselves identify someone’s language, personal loyalties or membership in a kingdom.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Writing and language: no attested written sentence from Yamnaya communities is available to quote. Researchers investigate possible Indo-European language connections by comparing later languages alongside archaeology and biological evidence. A reconstructed ancient word can be useful scholarship, but it would not be an inscription that a Yamnaya person left for us.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Did Yamnaya people ride horses? Researchers disagree about how securely the evidence answers that question. A 2024 review warns that skeletal changes attributed to riding could also reflect wagon travel or other activities. A 2026 response argues for early riding using several kinds of evidence. The debate concerns how to recognize an activity that leaves no simple label.

Yamnaya traditions changed at different times across a very large area. In Kalmykia, distinctive Catacomb burial practices overlapped with late Yamnaya groups by the middle of the third millennium BCE. The map’s 2000 BCE endpoint does not mark the fall of a kingdom or the disappearance of its descendants.

passages.text: Msiri’s Yeke kingdom developed in nineteenth-century Katanga, with Bunkeya as a major political and trading centre. Nyamwezi migrants and local communities built connections around copper, ivory and other goods. Enslavement and armed coercion were also central to its power.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: Msiri’s power depended on routes linking inland producers with Atlantic and Indian Ocean commerce. European expeditions followed established routes used by African traders. They arrived in a connected political landscape, not a blank space waiting to be discovered.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: Sanga resistance disrupted caravans moving toward the Atlantic, and Msiri’s forces tried to restore control. Local opposition mattered alongside European pressure. A royal claim to a large territory did not mean that everyone within it accepted the ruler’s authority.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: The museum’s regional history describes migrants arriving in different caravans, marrying into surrounding communities and incorporating young people of varied origins. Yeke society took shape through these relationships. A common political identity did not require every family to have the same birthplace.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Copper production in the wider region long predated Msiri. The Bunkeya research project notes evidence reaching back to the fifth century. His kingdom drew on an established field of knowledge and resources; it did not invent the region’s metallurgy.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Nicolas Nikis describes later demonstrations by experienced Yeke smelters near Likasi. They used a two-stage process of smelting and refining in temporary structures, then collected molten copper in a crucible. These recorded demonstrations help recover practical expertise that political documents rarely explain.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Those smelters poured copper into open molds made from clay or termite-mound material, commonly producing rectangular ingots for further working. A useful mold could begin with carefully chosen local earth. The result was a transportable material that other craftspeople could reshape.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Oral traditions recorded among smelters credited Sanga specialists with teaching copperworking to Yeke newcomers. Learning a craft crossed community boundaries. The story identifies skilled local teachers instead of giving every technical achievement to a conquering ruler.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Research on nineteenth-century trade distinguishes copper used in wider exchange from ivory over which Msiri sought tighter control. Copper could also decorate prestigious equipment. The same material moved between practical trade, skilled production and displays of status.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: Maria de Fonseca, one of Msiri’s wives, belonged to a Portuguese trading family. Her image survives in an 1893 European travel publication discussed by historian Rachel Taylor. Such pictures are evidence of how observers represented women, and need interpretation alongside the women’s political and family connections.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: A short sample from a modern printed Yeke song collection is “Linumba”, translated there as “The Great House”. The title appears in the royal heritage site’s bilingual collection. It is continuing written cultural expression, not an inscription securely dated to Msiri’s reign.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: The Bunkeya Plurielle project combines archaeology, documents and oral accounts, working with local communities and artists. It also trains students from the University of Lubumbashi. These are research aims, and they promise ways to study households and crafts beyond the familiar story of Msiri’s death.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: After Msiri’s death, his successor Mukanda Bantu accommodated Congo Free State rule. The shift preserved a form of Yeke leadership but redirected it within a violent colonial order. Survival of a ruling family was not the same thing as continued independence.
Msiri was killed during the Stairs expedition on 20 December 1891. Congo Free State domination followed; Yeke communities continued. The map’s 1914 endpoint extends beyond the independent kingdom.

passages.text: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

passages.title: Worldview and institutions
passages.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.

passages.title: Food and seasons
passages.text: Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.

passages.title: Art and diplomacy
passages.text: Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

passages.title: Political history
passages.text: Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in 1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

passages.title: Digital knowledge
passages.text: The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in 2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.
