sectionTitles: Work, international connections and difficult histories

passages.text: Founded in 1918, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes became Yugoslavia in 1929. After wartime partition and conflict, a six-republic socialist federation emerged in 1945.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Rapid urban growth created a serious need for housing after the Second World War. Architects used prefabricated construction to build on a large scale. The resulting apartments were also experiments in arranging limited space for ordinary activities such as sleeping, eating and family gatherings.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Yugoslav apartment designs could include rooms with several uses, flexible layouts and balconies extending living space outdoors. Architects compared ideas through competitions and published plans. A modest flat still required careful thought about where people would cook, work, rest and spend time together.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: The 1963 earthquake devastated Skopje, in the Yugoslav republic of Macedonia. Its reconstruction brought together local and international planners, including Japanese architect Kenzo Tange. New buildings and city plans emerged through this collaboration, making rebuilding both an urgent practical task and an architectural experiment.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Davorin Savnik designed the ETA 80 telephone for Iskra in 1979. Its unusually flat, clean shape attracted attention in industrial design. The Museum of Architecture and Design preserves the model, a reminder that an object used for an ordinary phone call could also be carefully designed.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Niko Kralj’s folding Rex lounge chair dates to 1956. Cuts in its plywood help the wood curve into the seat and back, while the whole chair folds away. It solves two domestic problems at once: somewhere comfortable to sit and somewhere to put the chair afterward.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Branko Ćopić’s children’s story first appeared as Ježeva kuća in 1949, illustrated by Aljoša Josić. The museum catalogue records a print run of five thousand and an Italian translation in 1951. A story associated with generations of childhood reading could travel across languages quite quickly.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Youth work actions combined organized labor with group life. The Museum of Yugoslavia describes competitions between brigades in work, sport and cultural activities, as well as shared songs and greetings. Their surviving objects and memories connect construction projects with the experiences of young participants.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Workers’ self-management became a central idea in Yugoslav socialism. The constitutional law of 1953 assigned management rights to workers and producers. These legal arrangements aimed to give workplaces a role in running enterprises, within a system that still had Communist political leadership.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Belgrade hosted the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. Yugoslavia sought international relationships beyond membership in either of the Cold War’s rival military blocs. The meeting placed the country in a network with states across Africa, Asia and other regions.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Economic changes in the 1960s brought both opportunities and unemployment. More Yugoslav citizens went abroad for work. Migration connected household income and family decisions with foreign labor markets, even while relatives and homes remained in the federation.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: During the Second World War, the Ustaša regime operated the Jasenovac camp system in the Axis-aligned Independent State of Croatia. Serbs, Jews, Roma and political opponents were persecuted and killed there. This wartime regime must be distinguished from both the earlier Yugoslav kingdom and modern Croatia.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Serbian in Cyrillic, article 1 of the 1946 constitution: “Федеративна Народна Република Југославија је савезна народна држава републиканског облика”. Translation: “The Federal People’s Republic of Yugoslavia is a federal people’s state of republican form.” This excerpt follows the Archives of Yugoslavia’s edition of the historical text.

The six-republic federation dissolved in 1991 and 1992 amid war and displacement. Serbia and Montenegro formed a smaller Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992, with different territory and membership. Map coverage ends in 1994, later than the federation.

sectionTitles: Music and cities imagined in miniature

passages.text: This record follows Congo-Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from the late colonial period into independence. Zaire was its name from 1971 to 1997; it is a different state from neighboring Congo-Brazzaville.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: The successive names Congo-Leopoldville, Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zaire do not identify three vanished populations. The UN’s country-name record tracks changes in official terminology. Keeping the dates straight also prevents confusion with the separate Republic of the Congo across the river.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: The independence crisis brought the first UN peacekeeping operation in 1960. Later wars in 1996 to 1997 and 1998 to 2003 involved regional forces and armed groups. The UN’s 2025 history describes continuing violence and displacement, a serious part of modern life alongside cultural achievement.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: Article 1 of the constitution, in its 2011 edition, prints the motto “Justice - Paix - Travail”: “Justice - Peace - Work”. This is a short attested French writing sample. The same article recognizes Kikongo, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba as national languages, showing that official French is only part of the linguistic picture.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Congolese rumba belongs to communities in both Congo states and their diaspora. Musicians perform it at celebrations and in mourning, in homes, public spaces and religious settings. Its social life extends far beyond the concert stage or a famous recording.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Younger musicians learn through neighborhood clubs, schools and community organizations. Established performers train apprentices in playing and making instruments. A musical tradition survives through rehearsal, teaching and practical work as well as moments when an audience gets up to dance.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Kinshasa-based artist Bodys Isek Kingelez built dazzling architectural models from paper, packaging, plastic, cans and bottle caps. Everyday discarded materials became towers and public spaces. His creations ask viewers to imagine how cities might serve people better.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: In Kimbembele Ihunga, made in 1994, Kingelez reimagined his home village with a stadium, banks, restaurants and skyscrapers. Ville Fantome, from 1996, pictured a peaceful city that needed neither police nor doctors. These were artistic hopes, not claims that real communities had solved every problem.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: An IITA project launched in 2023 sought to strengthen cassava growing and processing in the DRC, including flour for breadmaking. The plan linked farmers, processors and bakeries. A familiar crop could become part of an effort to reduce dependence on imported wheat.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: The cassava project also addressed processing and access to buyers. Growing a crop is only one part of getting food onto a household table: roots must reach the right place in usable condition, and farmers need customers as well as harvests.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: At Chirhavanyi Primary School in Walungu, a new water supply and hygienic toilets arrived in 2021. Fourteen-year-old Asifiwe later described being able to wash her hands at school. An ordinary school break no longer needed to revolve around finding water.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: At nearby Izenge Health Centre, Chinama described previously leaving her sick daughter to fetch water far away. A water point close to the rooms changed that task. Infrastructure matters at the scale of one parent trying to care for one child, as well as in national statistics.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: Doctor Denis Mukwege shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize for work against sexual violence in war. At Panzi Hospital in Bukavu, his team cared for injured women and girls. Their achievement joined skilled medicine with advocacy for survivors’ dignity and protection.
The state continued after the end of Mobutu’s regime and the name Zaire in 1997. Subsequent wars and continuing armed violence did not erase Congolese communities, institutions or creative life.

sectionTitles: Woodworking in the very distant past
A game board with room for thought
Making dinner could be a group project
Learn the dance by joining in
Building a university, then training teachers

passages.text: Zambia’s regional history includes extraordinary traces of early woodworking and the ordinary skills of preparing and sharing food. Archaeological finds and local accounts reveal different kinds of knowledge, separated by immense stretches of time.

passages.title: Woodworking in the very distant past
passages.text: Excavations at Kalambo Falls in 2019 uncovered two logs joined through a deliberately shaped notch. Their waterlogged deposits were dated to roughly 476,000 years ago, with a margin of uncertainty. Researchers interpret them as parts of a wooden construction. A platform, walkway or foundation is possible; the find is not a complete house with a known floor plan.

passages.title: Woodworking in the very distant past
passages.text: The wet conditions at Kalambo helped wood survive where it would usually decay. The researchers also had to protect it after excavation. They used photographs and digital models to examine the shaping marks while keeping the pieces submerged. Studying an ancient wooden object could mean photographing it in a bath, rather than simply drying it and putting it on a shelf.

passages.title: A game board with room for thought
passages.text: A wooden cisolwa board in the British Museum has four rows of eight holes. The catalogue attributes it to Lala makers in Zambia and dates it approximately between 1957 and 1972. It is more than a metre wide. This game took up rather more space than a phone screen. The object preserves a material trace of play, even though its catalogue does not explain every move.

passages.title: Making dinner could be a group project
passages.text: Sociologist Mwizenge Tembo describes preparing maize meal with help from children, relatives and neighbours. After kernels were removed from the cobs, women and girls pounded the maize, sometimes accompanying the work with songs. His account draws on fieldwork in 1980, 1985 and 1993, especially around eastern Zambia. It makes the labour behind a meal visible, alongside the cooperation involved.

passages.title: Making dinner could be a group project
passages.text: Tembo explains how nshima, a thick porridge, is eaten with another dish that might contain vegetables, beans, meat or fish. Diners shape a small portion in one hand and dip it into the accompanying dish. Conversation and hospitality form part of his account too. The meal is a social occasion as well as a way to satisfy hunger.

passages.title: Recipes can have a calendar
passages.text: A 2016 Bioversity International project in the Barotse Floodplain brought people together in cooking groups. Its description records recipe sharing, cookbooks and seasonal food calendars, connecting available ingredients with family meals. The calendar helped make a practical question visible: what food is available at this time of year? This example concerns the participating communities, rather than one menu followed across Zambia.

passages.title: Learn the dance by joining in
passages.text: Kalela developed in colonial-era Luapula and was taken up by mine workers. UNESCO describes dancers moving in two or three lines, singing as they go forwards and backwards around central drums. Lead singers and dancers help guide the group. The performance depends on people coordinating movement, rhythm and voice, making it both skilled work and a shared occasion.

passages.title: Learn the dance by joining in
passages.text: Kalela skills are passed on through songs, poetry, watching and participation. Some groups also organise lessons with experienced drummers when they need new musicians. Performances belong to occasions ranging from weddings to public celebrations and funerals. There is more than one way to learn: sometimes a lesson has a teacher at the front, and sometimes it has a drumbeat in the middle.

passages.title: Building a university, then training teachers
passages.text: The University of Zambia began its first academic session at Lusaka’s Ridgeway Campus on 17 March 1966. That first day followed a commission, planning, legal establishment and recruitment of staff. The university’s own history separates the start of classes from the later July ceremonies. A school’s beginning can have several important dates, depending on whether we mean its paperwork, its buildings or its students.

passages.title: Building a university, then training teachers
passages.text: The School of Education opened in April 1966 with forty-two graduates studying for a postgraduate teaching certificate. By 1969 its programmes also included training for primary teachers and courses in library studies. Preparing people to teach, and people to organise books and information, helped extend the work of learning beyond the university’s own classrooms.

British rule ended on 24 October 1964, when Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia. The republic continued through later changes in its political system, including the return to multiparty elections in 1991. The earlier map intervals are not dates when Zambian communities disappeared.

sectionTitles: A house around a patch of sky
What was here before the fort?
Someone drew boats on the wall
Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves

passages.text: Zanzibar’s history includes Swahili communities, Omani royal government and connections with India, Arabia and Europe. Stone Town’s streets and buildings preserve that mixture. Palace life, shopkeeping and plantation labour offer very different views of the same society.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: Stone Town’s historic houses often used coral limestone, mangrove timber and lime mortar. Many larger houses arranged long, narrow rooms around an open courtyard. The building’s shape helped organise domestic space around that opening. A handsome carved entrance belonged to a practical building, not merely a decorative front.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: The town also included simpler single-storey Swahili houses and Indian bazaar buildings centred on a duka, or shop. Those differences matter: a palace cannot stand in for everybody’s home. Shop spaces are reminders that urban life involved buying, selling and making a living as well as royal ceremonies.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: Excavations in the Old Fort’s western courtyard in 2017 and 2018 traced occupation back to an eleventh-century Swahili settlement beside the beach. Imported ceramics helped researchers investigate long connections with the Gulf. A broken pot can reveal a trading relationship, although it cannot by itself tell us the language or birthplace of its owner.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: The same site later held a Portuguese trading establishment and an Augustinian mission. Omani builders reused the church within a square fort; nineteenth-century expansion produced two courtyards. A place can preserve several political histories in its walls. The present fort therefore does not represent one untouched building from a single moment.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Researchers recorded ship drawings scratched into dry plaster at the Old Fort, especially inside its southwestern tower and along its ramparts. Hulls, masts and rigging appear in the marks. Building history and vessel types suggest a mid- to late-nineteenth-century date. The drawings are material traces of somebody looking closely at ships.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Who held the sharp point? The researchers suggest members of the fort’s garrison, who had access to these spaces and could see shipping nearby. Their makers remain unidentified.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: At Mtoni palace, researchers excavated a water channel in 2008. Their architectural study connects the palace’s water supply with a nineteenth-century aqueduct from the Chem Chem spring. This is practical evidence behind a grand residence: bringing water to the household required planned structures, not just a good view of the sea.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: Mtoni’s bathing complex included cold-water bathhouses and a separate heated bath. The latter had cold, warm and hot rooms with a boiler. These were facilities of a royal household, not evidence that everyone in Zanzibar had such a bathroom. Even within the palace, different bathing arrangements served different residents.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: The cold-water bathhouses also had latrines that were emptied through hatches at the rear. Channels ran beneath the bathing complex, while raised back rooms accommodated washing and toilet use. Royal architecture needed arrangements for waste as well as impressive reception rooms. Somebody still had to do the emptying.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Princess Salme, later known as Emily Ruete, remembered lessons in the royal household on an open veranda. Children used bamboo pens, homemade ink and cleaned camel shoulder blades as writing surfaces. Enslaved people prepared the bones. This was her recollection of an elite nineteenth-century childhood, not a description of every Zanzibar school.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Before lessons, Salme recalled children wrestling and climbing a balustrade. A lookout coughed when the teacher approached, and everybody hurried to sit down. The account comes from memory, but the scene is wonderfully recognisable: an unusually well-coordinated effort to look as though absolutely nothing had been happening.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: In her household, girls were taught reading while boys also learned writing. Salme secretly copied characters onto a bone, then learned more with help from an enslaved writing teacher. Her story records both a girl pursuing an excluded skill and knowledge held by a person whose own freedom was denied.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: At the nineteenth-century plantation site of Mgoli on Pemba, a 2004 excavation uncovered a partly dismantled baraza, a bench outside a stone house. Beside it lay a packed-rubble floor interpreted as a place for drying cloves. A working floor at Bweni and local residents’ knowledge supported that interpretation.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: Freshly picked cloves had to dry before export, and enslaved workers supplied the plantation labour. Croucher suggests that a bench beside the drying area could let owners watch that work while also serving as a social space. The bench and floor were excavated; this explanation of surveillance is an interpretation of their position.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: Merchant Tharia Topan commissioned the building later called the Old Dispensary; its foundation stone was laid in 1887. After his death, his wife Janbai oversaw the project, but the completed building still needed money for equipment and staff. A fine building alone did not make a working clinic. It began operating under new ownership in 1900.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: The early dispensary treated patients in three ground-floor rooms used for consultations, treatment and pharmacy services. Apartments occupied the upper floors. After later closure and restoration, the building returned to healthcare use as the Aga Khan Health Centre. Its history joins medical work, housing and the challenge of adapting an old building to a new purpose.

The sultanate ended in the revolution of 12 January 1964, which replaced the monarchy with a republic. Zanzibar united with Tanganyika on 26 April that year. Its communities continued, and Zanzibar later developed its own House of Representatives within Tanzania. The map’s endpoint in 1914 is not this political ending.

passages.text: Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders reshaped hillsides with terraces, dams and conduits. Water management and the creation of level spaces were integrated into urban development.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Temples and platforms framed a long ceremonial esplanade. Open spaces were as important to the layout as the buildings themselves.

passages.title: Writing and arts
passages.text: Carved reliefs with hieroglyphic inscriptions survive alongside tombs and temples, giving evidence of visual art and record making.

passages.title: Public life
passages.text: The ceremonial center included a ball court. Its built spaces supported activities beyond the palaces and burial places of elites.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Monte Alban maintained relations with Teotihuacan. Those contacts connect Oaxaca's history to other contemporary Mesoamerican centers.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: UNESCO dates Monte Alban's long florescence from about 500 BCE to 850 CE, followed by decline. This is the trajectory of a city, not an extinction date for Zapotec peoples.

sectionTitles: Palaces and a city under the trees

passages.text: Late medieval Zapotec Oaxaca contained competing kingdoms and towns, including Mitla and Yagul. The map label “Zapotec Empire” should not imply that one ruler governed this entire outline. These communities inherited a much longer history of cities, trade and writing.

passages.title: Palaces and a city under the trees
passages.text: Yagul’s Palace of Six Patios included spaces interpreted as public and private, with central courts perhaps used by the ruler’s family. Doorways and room arrangements help archaeologists investigate who could enter and how household life overlapped with government.

passages.title: Palaces and a city under the trees
passages.text: Mitla’s great columned hall used six large stone columns to support wooden beams and a flat roof. INAH suggests a civic or administrative function. Those columns were practical engineering as well as an impressive sight for anyone entering the room.

passages.title: Palaces and a city under the trees
passages.text: The famous geometric patterns at Mitla were made in several ways. Some use many small fitted stones; others carve larger sections into single blocks. From a distance they can resemble patterned cloth, but a close view reveals the stoneworker’s planning and precision.

passages.title: Palaces and a city under the trees
passages.text: A 2025 lidar study mapped more than 1,100 buildings at Guiengola, a fifteenth-century Zapotec settlement. Laser measurements revealed a fortified city covering about 360 hectares, with roads, temples and ballcourts, rather than simply a soldiers’ fortress.

passages.title: Palaces and a city under the trees
passages.text: Guiengola had different neighbourhoods for elites and commoners. Comparing the space occupied by residences and ceremonial buildings gives researchers a way to investigate inequality. The families who cooked, repaired houses and supplied the city belonged in its history too.

passages.title: Household work across the centuries
passages.text: Earlier evidence from Lambityeco connects salt production directly with ordinary houses. At least nine of twenty-three production mounds examined in a research study also had evidence of commoner residences. Work could happen around the home rather than in one central factory.

passages.title: Household work across the centuries
passages.text: Those salt-working areas were scattered around Lambityeco. Their distribution suggests that producers were not all confined to a single workshop or neighbourhood. This is Classic-period background, several centuries earlier than the map’s 1279 starting snapshot.

passages.title: Household work across the centuries
passages.text: In a much later example, Zapotec textile artist Porfirio Gutiérrez works with natural dyes and knowledge learned through family practice. Cactus-dwelling cochineal insects produce a powerful red dye. A colour farm can be small enough to grow on cactus pads.

passages.title: Household work across the centuries
passages.text: Gutiérrez’s work links Teotitlán del Valle with a Zapotec community in California. His studio offers younger people a way to learn weaving, dyeing and care for plants. This is a modern continuation of knowledge, not a claim that every medieval loom worked identically.

passages.title: Writing, families and political change
passages.text: A tiny colonial Zapotec sample is “Niça”, meaning “water”. Juan de Córdova printed it on folio 9r of his 1578 grammar. The Ticha project preserves the wording: this is Latin-script Zapotec recorded after conquest, distinct from the region’s earlier hieroglyphic traditions.

passages.title: Writing, families and political change
passages.text: Ticha also preserves seventeenth- and eighteenth-century Zapotec wills and legal documents. These texts let readers encounter people arranging property and family affairs in their own language. They extend the written record beyond royal monuments and famous battles.

passages.title: Writing, families and political change
passages.text: Spanish authorities relocated Yagul’s population during the sixteenth century to help form Santa María de la Asunción Tlacolula. Moving a town changed where people lived; it did not mean that Zapotec communities or languages ceased to exist.

Spanish conquest and colonial administration reshaped different Zapotec kingdoms during the sixteenth century, through campaigns, alliances and resettlement. There was no single empire ending at the map’s 1492 cutoff. Zapotec communities continue in Oaxaca and beyond.

sectionTitles: Markets and the people who made cloth

passages.text: The Abdelwadids, also called Zayyanids, made Tlemcen the capital of a kingdom in the central Maghreb. Emerging from Zenata leadership as Almohad power weakened, they supported a city connected to trans-Saharan and Mediterranean trade.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: A marble tablet from Tlemcen’s bazaar carries an inscription dating it to 1328 and identifying it as a cubit measure. Its ruled line is divided into four parts. The object made a common unit of length physically available in a place of commerce.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The catalogue reports that this tablet was found set into the bazaar wall. It is evidence for a local measurement standard, not proof that the ruler invented the cubit or that every sale followed the rule without dispute.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: Textile production employed both men and women in Zayyanid Tlemcen. A study of the industry links its growth to available raw materials, trading connections and expertise arriving from al-Andalus. Making cloth connected household livelihoods with the city’s wider economy.

passages.title: Markets and the people who made cloth
passages.text: The same study describes demand from different social groups, including elite customers seeking refined fabrics. Quality and finish mattered to makers as well as access to materials. The surviving record does not justify treating every textile worker as prosperous.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: An inscription dates the Sidi Bel-Hasan mosque to 1296. Onyx columns support horseshoe arches dividing the prayer hall into three aisles, while cedar roof structures carried tile coverings. A relatively small building brought together stoneworking, carpentry and brick construction.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Traces of coloured paint survive on the mosque’s plaster decoration. Its prayer niche combines inscriptions and floral ornament with a muqarnas dome, formed from small projecting cells. Later alterations mean that the building’s present appearance is not wholly medieval.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: At the royal Mechouar, Abu Hammu Musa I completed a mosque in 1317 to 1318. The square minaret preserves panels of small columns and arches against tiled mosaics. Its decoration records skilled work within the court’s architectural setting.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: Tlemcen’s teaching took place in mosques and madrasas, with study of Islamic law, Qur’anic interpretation, hadith and Sufism. Rulers’ support helped attract teachers and students from other regions, connecting the city with a wider scholarly world.

passages.title: Architecture and learning
passages.text: The Mechouar began as Yaghmurasan’s royal seat in the thirteenth century and was enlarged by successors. Modern conservation has also shaped it: a project sheet records major work on tile and plaster decoration between 2008 and 2012. Present surfaces need to be read alongside that restoration history.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Two gold dinars in the Bibliothèque nationale de France, catalogued as Lavoix 986 and 987, name Tlemcen and two rulers. Mohamed Elhadri argues that they belong to sixteenth-century Zayyanids acknowledging the Ottoman sultan Süleyman, rather than an earlier Marinid and Nasrid alliance.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: Elhadri tests that attribution against the names, titles and mint formulas on the coins and the chronology of political alliances. The case shows why a familiar royal name alone may misdate an object, especially when local monetary forms survive changes of overlord.

passages.title: Coins and contested sovereignty
passages.text: In 1517, one Tlemcen faction invited Aruj from Algiers while another backed the Zayyanid ruler with Spanish help. Aruj was killed after fleeing in 1518. Local choices and rivalries were central to this struggle, alongside the ambitions of larger powers.

Ottoman expansion ended Zayyanid rule around the middle of the sixteenth century. Sources date the final transition differently; approximately 1554 is a conventional endpoint. The royal citadel passed into Ottoman use, while Tlemcen and its inhabitants continued beyond the dynasty.

passages.text: The Zenú are a living Indigenous people of Colombia’s Caribbean lowlands. Their ancestors built farming landscapes threaded with canals and made remarkable gold ornaments. This map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is a snapshot, centuries later than the greatest expansion of the ancient waterworks; it is not the lifetime of the people or a single unchanged kingdom.

passages.title: Water, power and remarkable objects
passages.text: The ancient system combined long drainage channels with raised planting beds. Around San Marcos, its traces still mark the ground. Diverting floodwater into lower wetlands helped keep homes and crops usable; the engineering involved a whole landscape, rather than one impressive building.

passages.title: Water, power and remarkable objects
passages.text: At some San Jorge settlements, earthen house platforms stood two to three metres high. Archaeologists identified villages with more than a hundred homes, separated by short channels and household garden areas. Raising the floor was a practical answer to an extremely wet neighbourhood.

passages.title: Water, power and remarkable objects
passages.text: Political and religious leadership included women. Early colonial accounts describe Finzenú’s important ceremonial centre as governed by a female chief with authority over nearby settlements. The museum connects this evidence with the prominence of female figures in the region’s pottery.

passages.title: Water, power and remarkable objects
passages.text: A gold bird staff head at the Metropolitan Museum, dated broadly to 1 to 1000 CE, has a patterned tail and spirals across its chest. Its cap fitted over a wooden staff, fastened through two holes. The wood has not survived the humid lowland environment.

passages.title: Water, power and remarkable objects
passages.text: The same bird’s delicate metal “threads” were cast, not woven together after casting. Goldworkers first modelled fine details in wax, then used the lost-wax process. The museum interprets such staff heads as emblems of rank and office; its animal designs could also convey social identity.

passages.title: Homes, meals and skills
passages.text: The Museo del Oro reconstructs ancient houses as rectangular, with pitched roofs and spaces for cooking and social life. Their raised islands were linked by canoe travel. Visiting a neighbour could involve paddling rather than taking a dry path.

passages.title: Homes, meals and skills
passages.text: Cleaning channels was necessary work. The museum’s account explains that receding floodwater left fish trapped in pools, so clearing mud and vegetation could also provide food. Sediment moved onto planting beds supplied nutrients for crops such as cassava, squash and sweet potatoes.

passages.title: Homes, meals and skills
passages.text: Zenú caña flecha weaving remains a skilled livelihood. Artisans bleach plant fibres or dye them black, then braid contrasting nature-inspired designs called pintas. Artesanías de Colombia estimates roughly ten days for an ordinary hat: a finished sombrero vueltiao contains a great deal of patient finger-work.

passages.title: Homes, meals and skills
passages.text: A 2025 craft manual shows how a sombrero vueltiao changes shape during sewing. The maker starts with a small polygonal centre, sews braid in a spiral, bends the work upward to make the crown, then bends it again for the brim. Flat braid becomes a three-dimensional hat.

passages.title: Words, change and continuity
passages.text: A small modern language witness is “huru”, meaning “home”. Colombia’s Ministry of Culture records the word from a Zenú community language coordinator while describing neighbours and children meeting at home to learn. This is an attributed modern written record, not an ancient inscription or a reconstructed sentence.

passages.title: Words, change and continuity
passages.text: The same ministry study reports elders passing language knowledge to learners and children, sometimes with notebooks and written dialogues. It explicitly discusses disagreement with older claims that the language had vanished. The account preserves community testimony; it does not establish how widely the language is spoken today.

passages.title: Words, change and continuity
passages.text: In 1534 Pedro de Heredia campaigned into Finzenú and pursued gold from Indigenous graves. Spanish colonial administration later required Indigenous labour and tribute through encomiendas. These were major changes in power and daily obligations, not the disappearance of the Zenú people.

The great floodplain system changed and contracted before Spanish conquest; its decline cannot be assigned to one securely established cause. Colonial rule then disrupted political autonomy. Zenú communities and craft traditions continue, so the imported map endpoint in 1500 is not an extinction date.

A carefully carved place to rest
A VIP with a very practical job
Classes before the campus was ready
Family knowledge belongs in the kitchen too

passages.text: Zimbabwe’s regional history includes the workshops and farms of Great Zimbabwe, carved household objects and living musical traditions. These examples span different periods and communities; the modern republic is not the same political institution as the medieval capital.

passages.title: Small finds behind the famous walls
passages.text: At Great Zimbabwe, archaeologists recovered ceramic discs used as weights when spinning cotton. These modest objects point to skilled textile work behind the much more conspicuous stone walls. A spindle weight is a clue to making thread, not a surviving wardrobe: it cannot tell us every garment people wore. The settlement’s occupation extended from about the eleventh into the seventeenth century.

passages.title: Small finds behind the famous walls
passages.text: Charred sorghum recovered at Great Zimbabwe provides evidence of a crop people used. Slag, ores and furnace tubes point to metalworking, while crucibles preserve another part of the craft process. These finds reveal farming and manufacturing alongside long-distance trade. A burned grain can help reconstruct a food history, although it cannot supply the cook’s complete recipe.

passages.title: A carefully carved place to rest
passages.text: A wooden headrest by a Shona artist, dated from the late nineteenth to mid-twentieth century, has a small upper platform, a figure-eight-shaped base and a support carved with circles and angular patterns. The Met’s catalogue discusses several possible meanings for the decoration and leaves the question open. This household object shows considerable carving skill; we cannot read its owner’s dreams from the patterns.

passages.title: Music from a spoon handle
passages.text: Mbira/Sansi makers attach metal keys to a wooden board, sometimes adding a calabash or wooden resonator. UNESCO’s joint account for Malawi and Zimbabwe records keys made from spoon handles, bicycle spokes or spring wire. Fingers and thumbs pluck the keys. A piece of metal that once belonged in a kitchen or on a bicycle can take on a musical job.

passages.title: Music from a spoon handle
passages.text: Families have passed on mbira-making and playing through apprenticeship, while some schools and formal teachers also teach these skills. Musical patterns repeat with small changes and interwoven melodies. Learning involves hearing and practising those relationships, whether a relative teaches at home or an instructor leads a lesson.

passages.title: One drummer, many moving parts
passages.text: Mbende Jerusarema is associated especially with Zezuru Shona communities in eastern Zimbabwe. UNESCO describes a master drummer, wooden clappers, handclapping, whistles and energetic movements by women and men. Some crouching and kicking movements imitate a burrowing mole. Coordinating all those parts is a group skill, even when a single master drummer leads the rhythm.

passages.title: A VIP with a very practical job
passages.text: Peter Morgan dates his original Blair toilet design to 1973. Here VIP means ventilated improved pit: the design combines a pit with a vent pipe and a screen for flies. The pipe helps control smells, while the screen traps flies. The initials may sound glamorous, but the engineering tackles an everyday problem: making a toilet more pleasant to use.

passages.title: A VIP with a very practical job
passages.text: Researchers studying 238 households with Blair VIP latrines in Mbire district during 2020 and 2021 found that some toilets lacked vent pipes or fly screens. Householders valued privacy and easy cleaning, but costs, flooding and incomplete construction could make facilities difficult to use. The study shows why inventing a useful toilet and keeping it working for a family are connected but different tasks.

passages.title: Classes before the campus was ready
passages.text: The University of Zimbabwe’s history records early classes for about sixty-eight students at a temporary address on Baker Avenue, now Nelson Mandela Avenue. It dates these classes to 1952, before the 1955 royal charter and the move to Mount Pleasant in 1957. A university could begin with students and lessons while its permanent home was still taking shape.

passages.title: Classes before the campus was ready
passages.text: The medical school opened in 1963 with an affiliation to the University of Birmingham. The institution later became the University of Rhodesia and was renamed the University of Zimbabwe after independence in 1980. Its history connects medical training with changing university partnerships and political institutions, without suggesting that every family had equal access to care.

passages.title: A banknote with fourteen zeros
passages.text: The Smithsonian holds a Zimbabwean banknote with a face value of 100 trillion dollars: 100,000,000,000,000. It bears the date 2008 and pictures balancing rocks on one side, with Victoria Falls and a buffalo on the other. The enormous number belongs to a period of hyperinflation, when prices rose rapidly. More zeros on a note did not mean families could buy more with it.

passages.title: Family knowledge belongs in the kitchen too
passages.text: In a 2019 FAO report from the Honde Valley, Loice Chideya invited her husband, Syndon Samukute, to a ten-day nutrition workshop. He then took up cooking for their children and demonstrated porridge made with ingredients including butternut squash and peanut butter. The story follows one family sharing skills and changing expectations about who prepares dinner.

passages.title: Family knowledge belongs in the kitchen too
passages.text: The same programme organised nutrition circles where participants exchanged food-preparation knowledge and discussed hygiene and family care. Learning continued through conversation with neighbours as well as through workshops. The report describes a practical social gathering: people compared what to grow, what to cook and how to share household responsibilities.

Zimbabwe’s independence on 18 April 1980 ended British sovereignty after the colonial period and the unrecognised Rhodesian declaration. The republic continues through later constitutional and political changes. The 1920 and 1960 map labels do not make it independent earlier, and the older Great Zimbabwe settlement belongs to a separate historical setting.

passages.text: The Zulu kingdom grew out of the political transformations of southern Africa around the turn of the nineteenth century. Shaka’s reign began in 1816. Its history includes farmers, herders, families and artists as well as soldiers. The later Zululand entry crosses the British conquest and colonial administration.

passages.title: Power and conquest
passages.text: Zulu state-building drew on cattle wealth, alliances and military organization. Shaka ruled from 1816 to 1828, but the regional changes had begun earlier. The map’s 1783 label should not turn his later kingdom into a fully formed eighteenth-century state.

passages.title: Power and conquest
passages.text: British officials wanted to bring Zululand into a larger colonial federation. King Cetshwayo rejected demands that would surrender his authority and dismantle his army. British forces invaded in January 1879.

passages.title: Power and conquest
passages.text: Zulu forces defeated the British at Isandlwana in January 1879, but a renewed invasion ended in defeat at Ulundi that July. Cetshwayo’s attempts to negotiate peace did not prevent the second British advance.

passages.title: Power and conquest
passages.text: Conquest did not bring a simple peace. British partition helped produce further struggles over authority and land; formal annexation came in 1887. Colonial administration was partly financed through a hut tax, bringing imperial rule directly into household budgets.

passages.title: Homesteads, work and skilled hands
passages.text: A characteristic Nguni homestead placed dwellings around a central cattle enclosure. The arrangement connected houses, family relationships and livestock in one working space. Architectural studies describe regional conventions, not an identical plan followed by every Zulu family.

passages.title: Homesteads, work and skilled hands
passages.text: SAHO describes a household economy in which women cultivated grain and managed much domestic work, while men herded cattle, built structures and made tools and weapons. These linked tasks sustained communities and armies alike.

passages.title: Homesteads, work and skilled hands
passages.text: One Zulu wooden headrest in the British Museum was made before 1865. Its four long legs support an oval resting surface, darkened with pokerwork. It is 19 centimetres high: a carefully carved personal furnishing, not a modern fluffy pillow.

passages.title: Homesteads, work and skilled hands
passages.text: A spectacular nineteenth-century vessel at the Met was carved from one block of wood, with a separate lid and a surrounding four-legged support. It belongs to a group associated with Zulu-speaking carvers near Natal, including the named artist Unobadula.

passages.title: Homesteads, work and skilled hands
passages.text: Those carvers worked for local elites and European customers; examples appeared at London’s 1862 International Exhibition. The Met vessel’s original use remains uncertain: little wear and no detected residue caution against confidently calling it an everyday beer pot.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: Locust damage in the 1890s and cattle diseases worsened the effects of colonial dispossession. More men sought wages on railways and mines. Families’ changing work patterns had political and environmental causes, not a sudden loss of agricultural knowledge.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: A written isiZulu sample is “Ilanga lase Natal”, translated “The Natal Sun”. John Dube founded this newspaper in 1903. Its Latin-letter title is a real historical example of written isiZulu, from the colonial period rather than Shaka’s court.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: Ilanga provided a space for African writers and political discussion. Its existence after conquest shows that Zulu-speaking people continued shaping public life through print as well as oral culture; losing an independent kingdom did not end their history.

The independent kingdom was defeated in 1879, followed by partition, conflict, annexation in 1887 and incorporation into Natal in 1897. Zulu people, language and cultural institutions continued beyond the map’s 1914 endpoint.

sectionTitles: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
Gardens that hold on to water

passages.text: The A:shiwi, or Zuni, are a living Pueblo people with ancestral settlements in western New Mexico. Hawikku was one of several major communities. The map’s 1530 to 1650 interval captures part of the colonial encounter; it does not define Zuni society’s lifetime.

passages.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
passages.text: At Hawikku, archaeologists identified six large building groups separated by passages and small plazas. Parts rose one to three stories. Such a pueblo required coordinated building and shared circulation space, while its households lived close enough to hear plenty of their neighbors’ daily activity.

passages.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
passages.text: Hawikku’s builders bound local sandstone with adobe mortar or red clay, then smoothed walls with plaster. Rooms and foundations survive alongside unexcavated areas, preserving this careful combination of stone masonry and earthen finishing.

passages.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
passages.text: A jar excavated in 1920 from Room 172 of Hawikku’s House Group F is dated 1630 to 1680 by the Smithsonian. It was built by coiling clay, then painted and glazed. Its recorded room context and probable A:shiwi attribution make it a specific witness to craft during the colonial period.

passages.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
passages.text: Coronado’s forces attacked and occupied Hawikku in 1540. A mission was established there in 1629, bringing new religious demands and tensions. The pueblo’s substantial buildings existed before these arrivals; Spanish hopes of finding cities of gold tell us about the invaders’ expectations, not Zuni priorities.

passages.title: Homes and objects from ancestral towns
passages.text: In 1680, A:shiwi communities joined the Pueblo Revolt against Spanish colonizers and the mission at Halona was burned. The Zuni Tribal Archives records its later reestablishment around 1700. Resistance and rebuilding changed the use of familiar places while Zuni communities continued.

passages.title: Gardens that hold on to water
passages.text: A photograph catalogued to about 1912 shows women planting Zuni waffle gardens. Small square depressions held water carried from the river in buckets. Their name describes the garden’s patterned surface; breakfast waffles were not growing in the soil.

passages.title: Gardens that hold on to water
passages.text: In its 2021 gardening program, the Zuni Youth Enrichment Project enrolled 100 families and distributed 88 rain barrels; 12 families requested gutter kits. Catching roof runoff brought another water source to home gardens. The practical goal was to keep useful rain from simply running away.

passages.title: Gardens that hold on to water
passages.text: The local utility partnered with the youth project on rain collection and water-bill rebates. Garden irrigation could then use stored rain while conserving the municipal supply for households. Water management linked children’s activities, family gardening and public infrastructure.

passages.title: Gardens that hold on to water
passages.text: The youth project’s food programs began with lessons in traditional waffle gardens led by local agriculture leaders. Its later activities include young interns teaching younger children and school classes preparing meals. Growing and cooking food become ways for different generations to learn together.

passages.title: Keeping knowledge in community hands
passages.text: For the Hawikku exhibition opened in 2002, Zuni representatives selected 221 objects from the Smithsonian collection. Displaying these ancestral materials in the community connects archaeological finds with descendants’ own accounts. It also invites discussion of the earlier excavations, which the museum explicitly describes as controversial.

passages.title: Keeping knowledge in community hands
passages.text: The museum’s map-art exhibition brings together 31 paintings by 16 Zuni artists. These works record migration histories, ancestral places, water, plants and other relationships. A map can express remembered connections and cultural meaning as well as distances and boundary lines.

passages.title: Keeping knowledge in community hands
passages.text: The tribal newsletter reported a 2022 film of the Zuni Turkey Maiden story, developed through a community oral-history project. Earlier recordings of elders from the 1960s helped inspire new performances. Film and online viewing carried a long tradition into a different medium, within community storytelling protocols.

passages.title: Keeping knowledge in community hands
passages.text: Writing sample: “Elahkwa” means “Thank you,” as printed with its translation on the A:shiwi A:wan Museum’s contact page. This is contemporary community writing in the Latin alphabet. It represents the living Zuni language, rather than a reconstructed inscription from Hawikku.

Zuni people did not disappear when particular ancestral pueblos were abandoned or when colonial rule changed. Their community preserves and interprets those places, teaches language and maintains its own governing institutions. The map’s 1650 cutoff is only a coverage limit; the Pueblo of Zuni continues today.
